en: Private Notes on the Words and Phrases of the Sublime Sutra (Myōkyō-mon-ku-shishi-ki),
Table of Contents, Volume One.
Preface Chapter, First.
Volume Two:
From "The Method of Explaining the Text" to the end of "Such Causes and Conditions.
Volume Three begins.
From the Explanation According to the Teachings (*yōkyō-shaku*) of the "Thus Ends" passage of the Sūtra,
Scroll Four;
from the "King’s City" section to the end, explaining the meaning of the rank (*i*) that all are *arhats*.
Fascicle Five:
Praising the Virtues of the Arhats; Fascicle Six: The Entirety of Maudgalyāyana.
From Kātyāyana down to the section on the categories of the assembly of Bodhisattvas,
Volume Seven;
from the vertical praise of the Bodhisattva’s virtues to the end of the general preface.
Volume Eight:
Introduction to the Separate Explanations; Volume Nine.
The Tenth Fascicle of the Commentary on the Introduction to the Chapter on Doubt;
the Second Chapter, the Chapter on Expedient Means, is fully explained. Title.
Fascicle Eleven: The Chapter on Expedient Means (Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta), from the beginning to the end of the "Requesting Clarification of Doubts" (Paripṛcchā-parivarta) in Fascicle Twelve.
The Thirteenth Fascicle: From the Chapter on Fully Expounding the Past Buddhas to the End of the General Inquiry on Opening the Vehicles for Humans and Gods;
An Exegesis of the Text from the "Chapter on Expedient Means."
Fascicle Fourteen:
Explanation of the Text for the Third Chapter, "Entering through Parables" (Incomplete).
End of the Table of Contents for the *Private Notes on the Words and Phrases of the Wondrous Sutra*.
Private Notes on the Words and Phrases of the Sublime Sūtra, Scroll One (This is merely a draft and has not yet been fully detailed).
Composed by the Stone Drum Śramaṇa, Śākyamuni Zhìyún.

This text consists roughly of three parts: first, the manifestation of the title; second, the transmission and intent of the narrative; and third, the formal analysis and explanation. Now, the explanation begins.
These three constitute the specific divisions of the conditioned; first, regarding the general title, it follows the conclusion at the end of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), which states:
"The *Xuanyi* has already been discussed above; now we shall explain the text below. Thus, from this point onward, it properly constitutes the second section:

the exegesis of the scriptural text. As for the title *Wenju* (Textual Phrases), its explanation also consists of three parts, the first of which is the statement of the fundamental tenet (*zongzhi*).
Next, the third section, "Clarifying the Fundamental Intent," is explained in three parts. First, regarding the statement by the compilers of the record:

having already presented the preface and the causes for the lecture, they now explain the meaning of the phrases and sentences of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. In contrast to the two characters "Profound Meaning" (*xuanyi*) used previously, the present title follows directly from its intended subject;
therefore, it is called "The Phrases and Sentences of the *Wonderful Sutra*. If one directly grasps this intent, how could there be any further discrepancy?
Nowadays, the various schools of the Śākya followers are in such disarray that their doctrines, principles, texts, and meanings are all in opposition to one another;

this appears to be because they do not grasp the underlying intent, which leads to such a state of affairs. Since the deviations of these schools are numerous, it is now necessary to provide a brief exposition to remedy the extreme contradictions of the ancients, thereby clarifying the original intent.
Within this, according to what has been seen and heard, there are four distinct positions. The first says: "Text" refers to—
"Texts" (*wenzi*) refers to all the words contained within this entire scripture. "Phrases" (*juzi*) refers to the chapters and sections;
that is, what is currently being explained as a commentary, which divides the textual passages of the scripture into sections so that one may recognize the beginning and end of each passage.

It is called "Texts and Phrases" (*Wenju*) because it serves as a glossary for the preceding *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). Furthermore, another interpretation states: "As explained above, although the 'expounding of names' (*xiao ming') appears similar..."

Having departed from the substance that corresponds to the name, the name and reality have already diverged; thus, when one attempts to harmonize with the intended meaning, it can no longer be attained.
One who wishes to avoid such divergence and harmonize with the intent must understand that the single character "wen" (text) does not differ in meaning from the preceding term "ju" (phrase).
When the entire body of the scripture is categorized and explained, all these words and chapters and sentences are called "ju"; it does not refer exclusively to the categories themselves.
Because Wenzheng (Wen Zheng) derived his name from the combination of these two characters, he spoke of "words and phrases" (*wenju*).

If this is the case, then there is no longer the error of the mutual discrepancy between name and reality that has occurred hitherto. Furthermore, another says: "The meaning as explained above is also not yet fully understood. Why?

If the single character 'dividing the text' (*fenwen*) were attributed to the Sūtra itself, there would be two faults: first, the essence [of the Sūtra] would be insufficient; second, there would be a contradiction."
Regarding the title *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), it specifically refers to the analytical exposition (*ke-shi*) of a single sutra;

since this entire work of ten fascicles consists of words and phrases that proceed directly from such analytical exposition, it is named after its essential substance, hence it is called *Wenju* (Textual Phrases). In this way, the two aforementioned errors are avoided.
Regarding the fourth point, there is yet another view: since each of the three preceding explanations possesses its own logic, which one is correct and which is incorrect? Thus [the question arises].
Since each partial view is not ultimately exhaustive and there is nothing that cannot be accommodated, it is appropriate to preserve them all. Now, these four explanations are presented:
first, names are established by directly classifying the subject and object; second, names are established by explaining the subject and object through their classification;
third, names are established by directly explaining the essence of the subject itself; and fourth, as there is no separate entity, the preceding three are collectively preserved. Thus it is said:
Since a single name may encompass these three meanings, it is appropriate to preserve them all.
Although the following section should provide a detailed analysis of each, among these four different interpretations, the first is generally accepted as correct.

Furthermore, while all four explanations characterize the preceding by means of the succeeding, the first and last are direct [definitions], whereas the middle two characterize the preceding by way of its incorrectness.

Regarding this clarification: first, if one looks back from before the division, then losing one's spouse would contradict the principle of division; second, if one looks forward from the time of division, it would not be established and would cause others to be ruined as well;
third, if one looks back from before the division, neither [of these] applies, and thus they are not the intended meaning.

How can division be considered analogous? If one follows the previous case, it remains non-applicable; it is not merely a matter of oneself. If this capacity for full realization were also to be so, what else could there be?
If one takes the scriptures as the standard, then what is the use of the first [category]? As for the second, its capacity for delusion and error is extreme.
The fourth and the "dark yawn" (āndhya) are entirely devoid of awakening and understanding; the third is likewise not in accord with them. How could these be considered correct?

Even if one wishes to claim they are universal, one does not know that they are collectively erroneous. How can a person who does not recognize right from wrong at all be permitted to deliberate upon this essential matter? Therefore, the Confucianists...
To distinguish between right and wrong while understanding the principles of meaning is what is called being a scholar (*śi*).

Now, since you do not distinguish or understand anything at all, how can you be considered one who studies this marvel? Among students, many belong to this class; therefore, you must especially examine and be cautious regarding them.

The various interpretations of the śramaṇas are thus all contrary to the fundamental tenets and fail to achieve a comprehensive synthesis. I now maintain that names are established based on their referents, and it is through names that they are manifested.
The current interpretations fail to examine the origins of this text; even if they do provide explanations, what purpose do they serve?

I maintain that this passage is most direct and easy to understand, yet all existing commentaries laboriously avoid the straightforward and instead follow circuitous detours, shifting from the simple to the complex.
Since the single meaning is not clarified and the three names are simultaneously undermined, I do not know how it has come to this state.

How lamentable, how lamentable! Regarding the clarification of the fundamental tenets at the conclusion, there are five sections: first, describing the different general principles for establishing the names of the various schools;

second, clarifying that the meaning of the preceding and following texts may be relied upon as authoritative; third, the formal explanation of the title; fourth, concluding with the essential points of the school;
and fifth, a general explanation of the benefits and harms. As for the first, the different principles for establishing the names of the various schools through interpretation: [End of segment]
There are two distinctions regarding the title *Dà yǒu*: first, naming it according to both the subject (the agent) and the object;

second, naming it directly according to the object alone. Within each of these two categories, there are further two sub-types. First, regarding the two [types] based on dividing the work into two sections:

this is as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* commentary, where the title of the commentary is called the *Xuánshù* (Profound Commentary), and the title of the commentary on the main text is called the *Wénshù* (Text Commentary) (as seen in various ancient editions, the titles are all thus). Furthermore, as in the case of the [commentary on the] *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*.

The *Guangmingyun* (Clouds of Radiance) explains this sutra in two parts: first, it explains the title; second, it explains the text. Both of these constitute the title by way of the union of the subject and the object.

As for combining these two to form the title, it is just as when explaining various minor sutras that are not divided into two separate sections, one simply combines the title and refers to them as "the commentary on such-and-such sutra," "the meaning-commentary on such-and-such sutra," or "the meaning-record on such-and-such sutra," as is fully detailed [in those works].

In the commentaries on the various minor sutras, this principle is applied at the outset to form a combined title; subsequently, one proceeds directly from the "purpose for which" [the work was written] to establish the title.

Regarding the first case, as in these commentaries and the *Great Sutra*, the titles are given directly as *The Profound Meaning of the Wondrous Sutra* (*Miaojing xuanyi*) and *The Textual Phrases of the Wondrous Sutra* (*Miaojing wenzhu*).
The two titles for the *Great Sutra* are likewise. Regarding the second case, as in the *Zhi guan*, the name is established directly from the "reason why" [the work was written].
Nevertheless, although these belong to the same school and are both titles established based on the substance [of the text], there is indeed a reason for this difference.
That is to say, since the Great Master Jingming (Vimalakīrti) composed the work himself for the sake of others as a sovereign, he did not preface it with a narrative account of its origins;

thus, the title was entrusted to him directly. In contrast, both this [text] and the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* include recorded narratives, as they were preceded by extensive accounts that narrated their origins.

The principles for explaining [this work] have already been clarified by the meaning of the title itself; there is no need to rely on prolixity, and thus we proceed directly from the subject matter of the title.

It is the same with *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation): because the introductory section, both general and specific, has already completed its exposition of the matters recorded in the commentary.
Yet, even this does not yet exhaust its profound subtlety. Why is this? "Miao" (Wondrous) is a term of praise (as in the current *Xuánwén*).
The term *mahā* (Great) and these three [titles] are all names of praise intended to manifest that these three all emerge from a single wondrous sutra and equally reveal its sublime meaning;
thus, they are collectively praised and named accordingly, and these three names are established for this reason.
In this way, the original intent is fully realized; I hope you will reflect upon this.
Next, regarding the textual meaning that may be relied upon, the *Sūtra* states: "If one forgets the chapters and verses, explain them so that they are mastered.

The *Commentary* (*Śāstra*) states: "The preceding [passage] has few *danda*-divisions; this is a brief text. This chapter and its verses are many; this is an extensive text. The *Glorious Commentary* (*Prabhāsa-ṭīkā*) by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha states:

"Because the phrases within it follow one another according to their thematic affinity and are gathered together in one place, it is called a 'chapter' (*varga*). The *Glorious Commentary* by Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
It is said that because Ānanda transmitted the various phrases and sentences of this sutra neither more nor less than they were, it is called "As It Was" (yathābhūta).
Based on these passages, we know with certainty that the two characters of the title, *wén* (phrase) and *jù* (sentence), both belong to the sutra itself and are part of what is explained;
they cannot be divided into the subject and the object, nor can they be regarded exclusively as the means by which one believes.

Furthermore, the initial title of the *Xuanyi xu* (Preface to the Profound Meaning) states "Private Notes on the Origins"; it also says, "I have written this down to transmit it," and that the *Xuanyu* consists of ten fascicles each;
it further says, "This is recounted from the core of my mind. Finally, it concludes by stating, "The Profound Meaning has already been discussed above;
now I shall explain the text below. Regarding the first note at the beginning of this text, it says: "Having heard the Master’s lecture once, I recorded the difficult points."

Furthermore, it says: "The detailed explanation of the title of the sutra has already been stated above. Moreover, as soon as this section concludes, the method for the detailed explanation of the text itself is presented:
beginning from 'Thus' (evam) and ending with 'retreats' (vyavalokya), every single phrase and sentence is interpreted by means of the four meanings.

Based on these various texts, the meaning is definitively established: it is known that this name was originally explained by the Master [Kui]ji in his *Shuji* (Commentary). This explains its significance.
Since the meaning has already been made manifest, there is no need for prolixity; therefore, I have directly adopted the underlying reason as the title.
This chapter contains two points: first, to clarify the scriptural passage explained by this vision; second, to clarify why it is named according to its capacity and cause.
Although this title appears ordinary on the surface, its profound purport is not so. Commentators have long been vying to provide merely conventional interpretations. If...

If one were to immediately determine the actual meaning, there would certainly be great alarm and doubt; therefore, for now, let us proceed with a preliminary overview, and later we shall definitively establish it through a detailed explanation.

First, regarding the term "words and phrases" (*vyañjana*): speaking in a preliminary sense, "words" (*vyañjana*) refers to the written characters, while "phrases" (*pada*) refers to the syntactic units.

Generally speaking, the substance of a scripture consists of five elements: sound, names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), words (*vyañjana*), and meaning (*artha*). Among these four capacities and their corresponding objects, sound is the real entity, while the others are not.

The three are provisional designations (*prajñapti*). "Phoneme" (*śabda*) refers to sound; "name" (*nāman*) is that which can invoke an object; "phrase" (*pada*) refers to the differentiation of distinctions;
and "syllable" (*vyañjana*) refers to the characters that serve as the basis for both names and phrases. These four constitute the provisional and real aspects of the "fishing net" (*sūtra*).
"Meaning" (*artha*) is the principle to be expounded; all things are thus. Having previously discussed the profound meaning of the Sūtra individually, now...
This general explanation of the *fàn* (trap) and *tí* (rope) of the sutra is provisionally named after the two categories—general and specific—of the objects being explained;

thus it is called "The Wondrous Sutra’s Words and Phrases. Although such an explanation has not yet reached the ultimate limit, it nonetheless immediately surpasses all previous commentaries and is utterly free from their former faults.
Students should try to reflect upon this. Since it does not yet fully accord with the fundamental purport, it must be correctly clarified. Why?
The reason why the various Śākyas were unable to approach [this work] was truly because they did not know the origin of the essence of these names and texts.
Furthermore, the Sūtra manifests only two matters, namely name (*nāman*) and phrasing (*vyañjana*); this commentary then explains these two.

Name governs the wondrous principle of the entire treatise and is discussed first; thus it is called the "Profound Meaning" (*xuan yi*). Phrasing binds the wondrous raft of the entire treatise; this present work is its explanation.
Therefore, it is called "words and phrases" (*vyañjana-pada*); thus these two names are set in opposition because their textual form and intended meaning are entirely equal.
To understand this meaning, one must first know what the initial name signifies. Now, "mysterious" (*xuan*) is a term that denotes both selection and excellence;

the object signified by this excellence is "that which is selected," which distinguishes it from mere words and phrases. When the meaning is revealed and transmitted, its own essence becomes manifest, refined and precise.
The term "mysterious" (*xuán*) refers to things that lie beyond words and images; thus it is "concise. Furthermore, because it signifies a profound and subtle meaning, it is "excellent.
Thus, the single character *xuán* contains two meanings, while the character "meaning" (*yì*) explains five layers.

Since subject and object, essence and function, are clarified together, they are termed "Mysterious Meaning" (*Xuányì*). Once one understands this Mysterious Meaning, if each and every phrase and sentence [of this text]...

The phrasing of this [text] is capable of being both concise and beautiful. As for "concise," it differs from those profound discourses (*xuántán*) that rely on dark characters and phrases to manifest beauty through their meaning;
as for "beautiful," it reveals the superior and wondrous efficacy of the means (*quán*).

Since "phrasing" (*wén*) refers to names based on forms and sounds upon material objects, and is not a designation for things external to the profound manifestations (*xuángxìng*), it is therefore both concise and a term of praise.
Because it embodies this meaning, it is indeed "beautiful" (*mei*). Thus, the Confucian definition of "literature" (*wen*) as "beauty" is precisely its correct significance.

This single character "literature" (*wen*) combines both subject and object; the single character "phrase" (*ju*) penetrates the five dharmas, such that both subject and object, essence and function, are manifested together.
Therefore, it is said: "Literature and phrases. As for how literature can manifest beauty: first, it can swiftly clarify the Way and its righteousness; second, it can guide...
To comprehend the fundamental nature of things, the meaning of the present text is likewise so.

The Sūtra says, "Delightfully expounding this sūtra"—this meaning reveals the wondrous Way all at once and fully articulates the intention of the Supreme Sage; therefore, it is said that "the former vows have been fulfilled.
These are the two meanings of manifesting excellence within the present text. All of these are contained within the Sūtra itself, as taught by the Great Master.
Regarding what has been explained and recorded, both the general and specific prefaces have already clearly elucidated their underlying causes and conditions.

Since the meaning of the commentary is sufficient to manifest the intent, there is no desire for prolixity; therefore, the title is taken directly from what was explained and recorded, hence it is called the *Myōkyō Monku* (The Words and Phrases of the Wondrous Sutra).
Furthermore, this title contains two layers of subject and object, yet there is still no desire for prolixity. Why is this interpretation [necessary]? Not only... [text ends]
The meaning of the textual passages is essential and superior to that of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), revealing itself as even more lofty and profound.

Not only can these two names be applied throughout the entire school, but all [passages] therein may be fully harmonized; how could it be merely that they differ from previous explanations and are free from the aforementioned errors?
What has been explained above is sufficient to eliminate doubt; yet, as habitual attachments accumulate over time, one will surely find it strange upon first hearing it. Furthermore...
One must entrust this matter to a clear explanation. For the principle of "wén" (text/pattern) involves both the particular and the universal.

If one says that "wén" is identical to "zì" (character), this refers to the particular; if one says that "wén" can manifest meaning (*yì*), this refers to the universal. What is now called "wén" follows precisely this universal sense:
that which, throughout an entire work, serves as the means (*quán*) to reveal and bring forth the Way and its principles is collectively termed "wén."

According to various treatises, four factors are primarily explained—namely, name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and so forth—as briefly clarified above. If one follows the sūtras, five factors are primarily explained:

namely, speech (*vākya*), syllable (*akṣara*), phrase (*pada*), verse (*gāthā*), and chapter (*varga*). This is as follows: based on principle there is speech; based on speech there are syllables; syllables accumulate to form phrases;
phrases accumulate to form verses; verses accumulate to form chapters; and chapters accumulate to form sections (*śāstra*). If the Buddha is present...
In the world, generally there is only sound; however, if transmitted after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa onto leaves and silk, it then extends to form (*rūpa*).

This is explained at length in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) within the commentary on the word "text" (*wen*). These instances all refer to "text," and here the term "text" precisely accords with this meaning of "text.
How is this clarified? First, by relying on the meaning: as explained above, both names are identical in their meaning. Second...

As for the term "text" (*wen*), according to the passage cited previously from the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), the *Shuwenxin* (Exposition of the Heart of the Text), and many other places, it universally refers to what is taught throughout an entire work as being the "text.
For this reason, we know that "text" applies to everything; how could one possibly restrict the explanation solely to written characters?
To do so would be a contradiction and a harm of the utmost degree. Thus, in the world there is the saying: "The 'text' of the three villages is called ritual (*li*)."
The *Lèdǎnjì* (Treatise on the Joy of the Classics) and other works shall be explained in their respective order. Furthermore, as the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* asks:
"How does one understand characters and the meaning of characters?"—the subsequent *Wénzì Pǐn* (Chapter on Characters and Syllables) answers and clarifies this meaning.

This is done by using the metaphors of the worldly "half" and "full" texts to illustrate the supramundane teachings of the "half" and "full. The worldly "half" refers to the *Siddham* alphabet and treatises on various characters.

This refers to the specific treatises (*pṛthag-śāstra*); "Full" (*pūrṇa*) refers to the Vyākaraṇa [grammar] treatises, which fully elucidate worldly instruction—this refers to the general treatises (*sāmānya-śāstra*).
Just as these worldly categories of "Half" and "Full," "General" and "Specific" serve as metaphors, the "Half" and "Full" of the supramundane are likewise both general and specific.
By this, it is clearly proven that the texts possess both general and specific aspects; now, one should follow the general sense and not be dogmatic.

Furthermore, it is not only in the West [India] that the distinctions between the general and specific categories of Confucian and Buddhist treatises are more clearly evident here in this land [China]. Why is this?

For instance, regarding the six scripts and eight styles, or even the twelve, when these are collectively discussed as all written characters, they are generally given the name *Shuowen* (Explanations of Characters);
thus, "writing" (*shu*) is the general term. This is the specific treatise. If one speaks of "earthly writings" (*diwen*), such as mountains and rivers...

The patterns of plants and trees; the patterns of celestial phenomena (the sun, moon, and stars); the patterns of human culture (rites, music, and classics); the patterns of form (the five colors); the patterns of sound (the five musical notes);

and the patterns of emotion (the five natures, namely benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and sincerity)—these six types of patterns are said to be able to manifest the reality of the Way across all phenomena and guide the expression of the human spirit.

Therefore, there is nothing that is not a pattern. This is the general theory of "pattern" (*wen*). From these various internal and external examples, one can truly know that "pattern" has distinct meanings.

The "Pervasion" (tong) is distinct; yet the title and text here are precisely the "Pervasion" that extols all functional capacities of the "trap" (quan), and the beauty manifested therein is likewise the principle of the various differences among all such functional capacities.
Thus, its relationship with the two characters "Profound Meaning" (xuanyi) as a title is clearly evident in its structural force.

Someone asked: "The single character 'yi' (principle) is said to penetrate through each of the five layers of the sentence; yet while the words must necessarily be universal, the names are essentially distinct.
How can they be made identical? Answer: "When one grasps the meaning, one forgets the words; why then seek further for their verbal completeness?

When the meaning is fully realized, the subtle principle is revealed; thus, a single word can encompass all texts. Since one perceives the phenomena and the Dharma, one does not speak of 'one' as being universally pervasive."
It is simply that they are distinct yet one; to treat them as entirely different would not suffice to exhaust their literary form, as it would completely contradict the meaning of the preceding text.
Moreover, the intent of this sutra is to show that by grasping one, all are known—how could it concern merely five?
It must certainly be without difference or variation. Since the meaning of the preceding text is so extensive, one ought to know its essential convergence. What is this profound [convergence]?
The *Yi* (Meaning) expounds the essential purport of the one sublime sutra as taught by the Great Master;
the *Wenju* (Words and Phrases) records the most exquisite interpretive devices (*quanshen*) for the one sublime sutra as explained by the Great Master.

The profound and ultimate principles are fully revealed in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), while the vast and ultimate interpretive devices are entirely manifested in the *Wenju*. Thus, it should be known that these two texts each fulfill their respective roles.

By using these two characters as the title, the essential subtlety of both the subject and object of the entire sutra is revealed together. Furthermore, "Profound Meaning" (Xuanyi) refers to the sutra;
its meaning is deep and far-reaching, and this depth and distance constitute "profound" (xuan). "Textual Phrases" (Wenju) refers to the sutra;

its words are skillful and marvelous, and these words—such as the aforementioned five factors beginning with "phrase" (ju)—are skillful and marvelous, which constitutes "text" (wen). This is the [meaning of] the sutra.
These two phrases encompass the entirety of the scripture’s text and meaning; the significance of these two phrases that comprise the two names leaves nothing further to be omitted.
Thus, one should know that the two names are themselves the scripture—this is the essential meaning of these two phrases.

Furthermore, "text" (*wen*) and "phrases" (*ju*) are the skillful means (*upāya*) of the scripture; the five dharmas beginning with "phrases" constitute the method of observation, while "text" is the immediate [expression].
Furthermore, it is precisely because of the "expedient" (upāya) that the square is made to become round; thus it is said that "skillfully penetrating the square" is itself the true secret.
It is precisely because of the "text" (vyañjana) that chapters, verses, and so forth all serve as the function of the "wondrous raft" (miāo quán).

Moreover, if one speaks in general terms, the expedient is able to manifest the reality (bhūtatathatā), while the words and phrases are able to manifest the wondrous principle; thus, the means and the end are identical. Furthermore, regarding the means...

Within [the term] "middle" (*madhya*) itself there is the capacity and the object; within the "textual passages" (*vyañjana*) themselves there is likewise the capacity and the object—there is nothing that is not thus.

Furthermore, the reality (*tattva*) revealed by the skillful means (*upāya*) is precisely that which possesses the five dharmas (*pañcadharma*); reality is precisely the profound [nature], and the five dharmas are precisely the meaning (*artha*).

This, moreover, is the profound meaning (*xuan-yi*). The two characters for "skillful means" exhaust the entire capacity of this treatise; that which is revealed by this capacity is the wondrousness of the entire treatise.

In principle, nothing is omitted; the two characters "present text" (*jin-wen*) encompass the subtle *means* (*upāya*) of the sutra without remainder, and the two characters "profound meaning" (*xuan-yi*) encompass the subtle *object* (*artha*) of the sutra completely.
Therefore, one should know that these two names refer solely to the meaning of the subtle and wondrous skillful means of this single treatise.

Furthermore, "Profound Meaning" (*xuan-yi*) refers to the wondrous Dharma of the sutra; "profound" (*xuan*) is precisely "wondrous" (*miao*), for which reason the character "profound" (*xuan*) is glossed as "deep and wondrous."

The meaning (*yi*) is the Dharma; thus, all five layers are called "Profound Meaning" (*xuanyi*), meaning that all five layers are the wondrous Dharma. Furthermore, as for the "Words and Phrases" (*wenju*) being the wondrous Dharma:
"words" (*wen*) means wondrous. The character "wondrous" (*miao*) is glossed as "excellent"; when a thing is the most excellent among all things, it is called "wondrous.

Therefore, in ancient translations, this "Wondrous Dharma" was also called the "Excellent Dharma. As for "words" (*wen*), they mean "beauty. Among all beautiful things in the world, there is none that surpasses [this].

Regarding "words" (*mon*), words are themselves the sublime; regarding "phrases" (*ku*), phrases are the Dharma, meaning the teachings. The sublime has no separate essence other than the beauty of the Dharma;
words have no separate Dharma other than their meaning. These three names—phrase, word, and so forth—are understood through various perspectives.
Based on these meanings, the intent of the established [terms] is simply to collectively manifest the two dharmas of the sublime principle and the sublime teaching.

This is the essence and function [of the text]. Someone asked: "If this is the case, both names involve the 'subject' (neng) and the 'object' (suo). I wish to hear the explanation of this. [The Master] replied:
"There are two objects and two subjects. The two objects pertain to the Sūtra; the two subjects are the *Xuan yi* (Profound Meaning).

That is to say, the five characters of the title at the beginning of the Sūtra—both collectively and individually—constitute the fivefold objects to be explained. The ten fascicles of the *Xuan yi* are precisely the explanation of the profound meaning of the Sūtra."
The "Meaning" (*yi*) refers to the twenty-eight chapters of the sutra, which are the textual passages to be explained; the ten volumes of the "Textual Passages" (*wenju*) explain their meaning.
Second, this is why it is so named: these constitute the four realities (*si shi*). If one recognizes these four things, how could there be any delusion?
Otherwise, one cannot help but be deluded. The preceding four sections have manifested these two names and possess this functional efficacy.
If one understands these essential points, there will be no meaning that does not penetrate and no text that is not comprehended.

Thus we know that when this school establishes these two names, they must be essential; how could anything further be added? How could a mere ordinary interpretation possibly comprehend these essential points?
Think on this, think on this!
Someone asked, "Is there any benefit in explaining it in this way? He replied, "I do not dare claim to seek benefit; rather, I wish only to avoid harm. For what reason?
The various previous explanations all deviate from the fundamental essence and contradict the textual meanings. They split the two names into fragments and fail to unify the four essentials.
How could these not be harmful? Now, being free from these four faults and possessing the four capabilities, it is not merely that there is no harm, but one actually perceives [the truth]."
What is meant by "profound benefit" if it is not this? Furthermore, how could it be merely that the profound meaning of the text and the practice of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* are revealed simultaneously?
When the ancients attained two or three [stages], they considered it a great joy; now, having attained one and seven, how could it be merely three?
Do not harbor any doubts. Xuanchang once said, "First rectify the names"; how true and essential these words are! How much more so in a case such as this—how could one simply remain indifferent?
I am fortunate that we have exchanged these teachings together to clarify their names and meanings; even if you consider them non-essential, how would they differ from the ways of the common folk?
What I have explained above may not yet be entirely perfect or fully satisfying to your lofty views, but I offer it merely as a means for my own self-exhortation and consolation.
Many in the world have raised doubts as to why the name of the author is not inscribed here below.
Some explain that his name has already been mentioned in the two preceding sections—the "Profound Meaning" (*xuan yi*) at the beginning and the "General Preface" (*tong xu*).

Furthermore, they argue that the formal style of this particular treatise is distinct from others, and since this is well known to the world, there is no need for further elaboration. I, however, say that this is not necessarily the case. What harm is there in inscribing it? It simply...

Since ancient times, many authors have not inscribed their own names upon their works; thus, although many writings of the ancients are found at Nanshan, the fact that they are unsigned leads to lamentation over the unknown authorship.
Such instances are very numerous among secular texts as well; therefore, I too have for the most part refrained from explicitly titling them here.
Some old manuscripts, however, do title them as "Spoken by the Disciple of the Master Zhizhe of Tiantai at Yedu."
The *Guanjing siji* (Private Record of the Empowerment): These titles were all added by later generations; it is the custom for various texts to be titled in this manner.

I fear that such titles may not have captured the essential point. In fact, according to the beginning of this text and the conclusion of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) of the *Dajing*, the title should properly read:
"Recorded by the Disciple, the Śramaṇa Guanding of Dànqiū. As for those who say "Zhāng'ān and others," this refers to the original location of the Venerable Master.
The name of this place is indeed the ancient Chang’an County of Taizhou (which is the present-day Linhai County). From this point on, it has not been appropriately designated;
for what reason? Furthermore, places such as Nanyue and Tiantai do not take their names from their original locations—why must this necessarily be so?
Moreover, it contradicts the Venerable One’s own words regarding the location, as will be explained later. When the predecessors heard this, they all considered it to be correct.
In studying this, one should fortunately be free from confusion or stagnation; furthermore, there is no need to change the title at the beginning.

Regarding the second section below, which explains the annotations: in ancient editions of this text, some were written in white characters, or they appeared beneath the general title and its phrases, yet most were annotated under the first chapter, the "Introduction" (*Nidāna-varga*), and were all explained together without distinction.

Regarding the reason for this, it is said that this is the "Danchu" (Cinnabar Hill) preface; however, as for the further clarification of the Great Master’s intent in explaining the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) as presented in the preceding "Separate Preface to the Profound Meaning" (*Xuan Yi*), it would have been more appropriate to annotate it beneath the general title of the *Wenju*.

Although most of these annotations are currently found beneath the subsequent sections of the text, there is no great harm in this—consider it so—but since this has already been explained extensively previously, I shall here provide only a brief annotation.

Although the general framework is common, the intent of the text lies in the particular; thus, while it was previously stated that there are ten sections each in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text), here we focus solely on the *Wénjù* (Textual Phrases).

This is precisely because we wish to manifest the particular by means of the general, yet still reveal the general itself, so as not to treat it as exclusively particular—since the Sublime is without fixed direction.
You shall see its meaning when the text is subsequently analyzed; although the wording in this commentary is brief...

There are still three distinctions: first, an exaltation of the Dharma transmitted; second, the time and place of the transmission; and third, the purpose of the transmission. Regarding the first, there are two parts:
the former is the preliminary, and the latter two are the main body. As for the main body, it is because this Dharma is subtle and wondrous, difficult to hear, yet fortunately heard;
how could one have heard it by one's own power? It was through the infinite great compassion, great vows, and spiritual power of the various sages, worthies, and Great Masters.
Through the power of skillful mastery in transmission, this teaching shall be passed down until the end of time, so that all who see or hear it may obtain such sublime benefit.

This constitutes the supreme offering among all offerings—a Dharma-offering. Furthermore, it is said that if one hears the Dharma with joy and praise, even uttering but a single word, one has already made an offering to all Buddhas of the three periods of time. This is the grand principle of the path to enlightenment and the essence of the myriad practices.
This is the essential outline; it is for this very reason that the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and others performed ascetic practices and widely propagated [this teaching].
Therefore, first offer the highest praise, and then clearly elucidate the records and transmissions. Contemplate this, contemplate this!
This is identical in intent to the general preface at the beginning of the preceding *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). That text first praises the Master by means of ten virtues;
this is to praise the person who can expound this Dharma, which is simultaneously to praise the Dharma itself.

Now, the initial six difficulties praise the Dharma, which is to praise the Dharma spoken by the aforementioned person, and is also to praise that person. This is because the person and the Dharma have never been separate from one another.
Because they differ, each is cited in turn to manifest their equality. Furthermore, the initial passage praises [the Dharma] by means of six difficulties;

this is precisely the text from the Sūtra that praises the Dharma, which possesses two meanings: first, praise, and second, inspired admiration. Praise refers to extolling the Dharma, while inspired admiration refers to being moved to a state of profound longing and veneration.
Now, the Sūtra’s text praising the Dharma contains the application of the principle (*dharmanaya*), the analogy (*upamāna*), and the synthesis (*anusandhi*).
This is the text from the *Dharmapada* cited here: "The appearance of the Buddhas in the world... even such a person is likewise rare.

It should not be derived from the latter two [categories], as that would result in a reversal of the logical sequence; reflect on this, reflect on it!

Although the phrasing is no different when explained directly through the scriptural Dharma, the intended meaning of the analogy and its application remains consistent with the six [types of] *tánhuá* (lotus flowers) and so forth.
One should know that although the current text and the scripture both praise the Dharma, there are points of agreement and points of difference. Why is this? Because the scripture is...
The Buddha’s praise of the Dharma he has taught refers to the sūtras spoken by the Buddha; this present praise is that of the disciples who transmit and recount them.
This is intended to exhort beings to generate the utmost respect, faith, and realization toward what the Buddha has taught.
Furthermore, this present [praise] reveals one’s own honoring of the Teacher’s words as the basis for transmission and recitation, and it likewise exhorts others to do the same.

In the Sūtra, the section on the "Traces" (迹門) was limited to four [periods] because the Teacher, in order to exhort the assembly of that time, spoke only of the beginning and end of the teaching regarding the traces.

However, in this present case, as those who receive the teaching in a different era and a different region recount it, two additional periods must be added to make six. There is a further reason for this, which may be inferred by comparing it with the Sūtra.
One can understand this for oneself; although the specific applications differ in this way, the underlying principles and the logic of their operation are universally applicable.
Therefore, we now borrow this principle. This single point must be thoroughly mastered—reflect upon it, reflect upon it!
Among these, there are three pairs and six items: the first two concern the Buddha, the next two concern the teacher, and the final two concern oneself.

Since this Dharma originally arose from the Buddha’s teaching, it concerns the Buddha; since it is transmitted in the final age, it concerns the teacher; and since one receives and upholds it, it concerns oneself.

Because the Buddha possesses both person and Dharma, there are two [items] concerning the teacher; because there is transmission, there are two [items] concerning oneself, consisting of receiving and expounding.

Therefore, there are also two types of utility. Utility must begin with the master; thus, at the beginning, there is the person. A person must have the Dharma; thus, there is the codification and transmission of the Dharma.

Because later generations and different regions differ, there is the transmission [of the teachings]. Because one receives personal instruction from oneself, there is the bestowal. Because one correctly receives what has been bestowed, there is the reception.
Having received it, one transmits and communicates it; thus, there is the exposition. The principle of exposition and transmission reaches its ultimate limit here and cannot go further.
Because of the excesses and deficiencies [in the faculties], there are these three pairs and six single [categories] and their sequence; the brief summary is thus.

The sequence of the four [subsequent] sutras can also be understood by analogy. Furthermore, since these six are collectively praised as the "Sublime Dharma," each one carries the significance of the word "is" (iti).
That is to say: "The Buddha is the one who appears in the world"—this is difficult. In the next two passages, this is self-evident; next, it is opened up.
Awakening is difficult; hearing the Master’s exposition is difficult; memorizing it even once is difficult—all these meanings must be fully present.

Within the text, depending on the length of the phrasing, some may be present while others may be absent, yet the illustrative examples of these meanings must all be complete. In this way, one merely follows the general and specific [distinctions] as established by the treatise;
one must not contrast them with other [texts] to clarify their commonality or exclusivity, for that would contradict the meaning of the word "here" (*hi*) used in the text.
Regarding the general and the specific within this context: if one looks at them in relation to the rest, both are specific;

furthermore, within this discussion, "general" and "specific" refer to the fact that the six [perfections] are the specific, while being collectively termed "difficult" constitutes the general. Moreover, it should be understood that there are three types of general and specific within this:

first, the specific-general, referring to the six and the difficulties; second, the general-specific, where the six remain general while the difficulties are specific; third, the specific-in-the-sublime, where the specific resides within the sublime.
Since both the general and the specific [aspects] are individually difficult to explain through the six [categories], one must contemplate them exhaustively in this manner.
First, regarding the praise of the Buddha, it refers to the wondrous person and the wondrous Dharma; it is also the wondrous form and the wondrous voice.

The essential points of its utility do not exceed the person and the Dharma, for the benefits derived from seeing and hearing do not go beyond form and voice. Therefore, herein [the text] correctly...
Regarding the praise of the Dharma by way of the person: it is because the Buddha is the wondrous person who has attained and taught it, that the excellence of the Dharma is further emphasized.
However, in explaining these six [categories], each one should be endowed with three meanings—the first being specific and the latter two being general.

If one does not recognize this meaning, even if one provides an explanation, it cannot be called essential. The initial phrase, "The Buddha appears," etc., refers precisely to the wondrous response to conditions.
Furthermore, the Buddha is the person of ultimate and wondrous enlightenment, the master of this sublime teaching. "World" (*loka*) refers to the mundane world of all birth and death.
To speak briefly from a specific perspective, the time and place of the three realms, five turbidities, and eight sufferings within the impure land of shared residence is called the world.
If one discusses it according to the principle of the identity of the fundamental and the derivative:
Thus, this single world is itself the threefold world-system (*traidhātuka*). By way of analogy, it refers to kingdoms, cities, and villages; by way of the dharma, it corresponds to all worlds.
There are two meanings for "emergence" (*niṣkramaṇa*): first, renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*); second, manifestation (*abhinirvṛtti*). As the text says:
"The burning gates were safely exited," and "The Tathāgata has already departed from the fire-house of the triple world," as in the *Avataṃsaka*.
There is a chapter titled "Detachment from the World" (*Lokātikrama-parivarta*); because these [teachings] are practiced and realized by oneself, they are called "transcendence.
The text says: "Appearing in the world like the rising of a great cloud. A verse states: "The Dharma King who destroys existence appears in the world.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* contains the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter (*Tathāgatotpatti-saṃbhava-parivarta*). These are all for the purpose of awakening others; because he manifests in the world for this reason, it is called "appearing in the world" (*lokāvatāra*).

That is to say, the Great Compassion of the Ultimate (Wuji) manifests traces in the three lands according to the response to conditions from the fundamental realm of tranquil light realized by itself, leading sentient beings to return together to that fundamental realm of tranquil light. Thus, the text says:

"The Tathāgata is the father of all the worlds," and so forth, down to "teaching and transforming them until they attain unsurpassed Bodhi. This is precisely its meaning; although it encompasses both [aspects].
The meaning is that it is now precisely appearing in the world. Although this one essential point is raised, it possesses two meanings:
because [the realization] is necessarily from oneself, others come to know it through oneself.

Since the wondrous substance of knowledge and vision has been perfected for a very long time, and yet it had never before been encountered, when they saw it from afar at the site of enlightenment (Śīla-maṇḍala), they were greatly terrified, thinking it was kings and such. Thus it is said.
He continued to conceal his supreme excellence and manifested a coarse and inferior form for over forty years before finally revealing it;

he first presented the immediate traces and only later the distant origin, as clearly elucidated in the *Śraddhā-bodha* (Faith and Understanding) and *Āyuṣ-pramāṇa* (Life Span) chapters. How could one not find faith difficult to attain?

As the text says: "The appearance of Buddhas in the world is remote, and encountering them is difficult"—this is verified here by the Great Matter (*mahā-kārya*). Thus, the cause of this great matter is established.

The appearance of a Buddha in the world requires wondrous conditions to bring about wondrous responses; for if the profound mechanism is not truly present, how could the supreme response be difficult to attain?
It is for this reason that it is said to be difficult. When it is said that "this Dharma is difficult to expound," "expounding" refers to sound, which is precisely this wondrousness.
While it pervades all things, its specific manifestation lies in what we now take as our primary object of veneration: the Sahā World.
The Buddha’s work through sound takes form as voice; since the wondrous form has appeared, the wondrous sound is proclaimed. Thus it is said that "the Buddha speaks.
Because it is difficult to believe in the truth when it is taught after a long time, he first used this [expedient] to guide them, yet they fainted and fell to the ground.
Consequently, he subsequently matured them through the four flavors of the Dharma; only then, being about to expound the teaching in full, did he first employ various [skillful means].

Only after being startled and alerted does one finally find joy; this joy is followed by various kinds of great convenience, only then leading to faith and understanding, as detailed in the two gates of the Trace and the Origin (*jiben*).
Since it is only through the power of the Correct [Dharma] that it is difficult to hear, is this not truly "difficult"?

The text says, "Even if [the Buddha] appears in the world," which refers precisely to this meaning. However, it is only through a wondrous vessel that one can receive the wondrous teaching and the wondrous [Dharma].
Since the vessels [of the recipients] are not easily brought to perfection, how could the wondrous teaching not be difficult to convey?

This is precisely why it is said that its exposition is difficult. Next, regarding the translators: they set aside the general to follow the specific, as their work does not concern the rest; thus it says "this.

As for the term "translators," because dialects differ, they translate the sounds of those foreign dialects so that they may accord with the language of this land. Thus it is said by the Confucian school.
Because he possessed the renown for transmitting and conveying the languages of the four quarters, the *Liji Wangzhi* (The Rites, System of Kings) commentary states:
"The official who transmits the languages of the East is called a *ji* (conveyor); this means he conveys and transmits internal and external speech.

The official who transmits the languages of the South is called a *xiang* (modeler); this means he models after and conveys internal and external speech. The official who transmits the languages of the West..."
He was called Di-di; "di" means knowledge, referring to one who understands and transmits the languages of the barbarians so that they may be known to the Central Kingdom.
The official who transmits the languages of the North is called Yi; "yi" means to set forth, meaning to explain the words of those outside and within so as to bring them into mutual understanding.
Although the distinctions in the classics are thus, in common worldly usage, he is simply called—

Therefore, we now simply follow the conventional usage and call it "translation" (*yi*). As previously stated, "translation" was rendered as "transmission" (*chen*) based on the explanation of the term by the translator Sengyou of Liang in his *Chusanzang jiji*.
This means transmitting and explaining the languages of two countries so that they may meet and correspond with one another.
If one speaks in terms of its meaning, it is also appropriate; for "translation" (*yi*) means "to change" (*yi*), signifying a mutual transformation.

This is because the words of two different regions must be made mutually intelligible. Now, the Supreme Person (the Tathāgata) is without fixed direction in his transformative activity, yet for the sake of transformation he must have a specific location.
Thus, he was in the Western Extremity, the distant land of the Five Indias within Jambudvīpa, in the midst of the Great Trichiliocosm.

The people there are originally of the lineage of Brahmā; they are practiced in both the language and the script of that heaven. It was in that land that the Buddha appeared and preached this wondrous [Dharma].
The scriptural texts state that all things depend upon those [originals]; if they were not translated, there would be no benefit here [in this land].
Now, to transmit those sublime words from there to these humble expressions is called "translation" (*chuan-yi*).

However, this land of Zhendan is separated from that India by a vast distance of more than one hundred thousand *li*—some say one hundred and eight thousand *li*. The mountains and rivers are layered with perilous obstacles, inhabited by both humans and beasts.
Among those who have traveled back and forth across these many difficulties, two or three out of ten have reached their destination; how much less so for one who is not such a person?

Unless the proper time arrives, the journey is not undertaken in vain. Thus, after the sublime sound [of the Dharma] ceased to flourish, although more than a thousand years passed and numerous schools of translation appeared, few were able to master its essence in its entirety.
It was only with the emergence of Master Kumārajīva that the teachings overflowed throughout the world. Judging by this, [the significance of his work is clear].

Is it not true that the difficulty of translation is difficult to believe? Formerly, when Master Mian Tianming translated from Sanskrit into Chinese, he identified five points where the original was lost and three types of things that could not be changed.
As for the five: first, the Sanskrit language is exhaustive and precise, yet it had to be rendered according to the conventions of the land of Qin;

second, the Sanskrit scriptures are fundamentally sublime, whereas the people of Qin prefer the elegant and flowery, so the transmission had to conform to the popular mind—though this was not impossible; third, the Sanskrit scriptures are detailed and comprehensive...
As for the fact that the exhortations and explanations are repeated with such earnestness—three or four times without wearying of the prolixity—and yet now only three are performed:
this is because the Sanskrit expositions on meaning are based precisely on the disordered arrangement of words;

upon reviewing the preceding discourse, the phrasing is no different, whether it be a thousand or a hundred repetitions, yet the fourth [repetition] does not persist. Since the matter is already fully accomplished, I shall now proceed to other matters, having already set forth the preceding words.

Subsequently, he spoke [of the five losses], which completely eliminate these five fundamental defects. Regarding the "three difficulties of change": Now, the *Prajñā* [sūtras] proceed from the mind of the Threefold Clarity;

what the Sage has expounded face-to-face must necessarily accord with the times. Yet, the customs of the age have their ups and downs, while the refined and ancient [language] is adapted to the present time—this is the first difficulty. Furthermore, the gap between the foolish and the wise is as vast as heaven and earth, such that even a sage cannot easily ascend [to them];
yet one now desires to use [the language of] a thousand years ago—[this is the second difficulty]. The text continues: "The text continues... (Note: The source fragment appears to be truncated).
First, the subtle words of the Sage were transmitted as a mandate to the kings of a hundred generations;

second, in the debased customs of later ages, not long after Ānanda produced the scriptures, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa commanded five hundred arhats possessing the six supernatural powers to examine and transcribe them one after another. Now that more than a thousand years have passed, people employ their own contemporary perspectives to edit and determine the texts.
If even those Arhats were so cautious and reverent, how can these people of the cycle of birth and death be so indifferent and complacent?
"Is this not the very courage of one who knows the Dharma? Thirdly, having traversed these five losses and three difficulties in translating from Sanskrit into Qin, how can one not be cautious?
Furthermore, following the eminent monk Yancong, he composed the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Discerning the Correct) to provide precepts for translation.
Having first described Master Dao’an’s 'five losses and three difficulties,' he stated that the scriptures..."

It is easy to find precedents among the names of the worthy sages; yet, though one constantly reflects upon their character and discernment, one ultimately feels ashamed when compared to those who possess both the "water" (wisdom) and the "mirror" (clarity).
What they possessed was eightfold: First, they received the Dharma with a sincere heart, vowing to benefit all people without begrudging the passage of time—this is the first requisite.

Second, as they were about to tread the field of enlightenment, they first made firm the feet of their precepts, remaining untainted by slander or suspicion—this is the second requisite. Third, they thoroughly understood the Tripitaka, their comprehension of its meanings being comprehensive and penetrating.

1. His two eyebrows hang down; he does not suffer from darkness or stagnation. 2. He extensively consults the ancient classics and supplements his scholarly compositions; his phrasing is neither vulgar nor clumsy. 3.
His demeanor is impartial and magnanimous, his capacity vast and harmonious; he does not favor dogmatic adherence. 4.

He is deeply immersed in the Way and its arts, indifferent to fame and profit; he does not desire to boastfully display himself. 5. He mastered the Sanskrit language and was thus proficient in correct translation. 6. [He did not] seek to be ostentatious.
Seventh, he has extensively read the *Cangjie* and *Erya*, and possesses a rough familiarity with seal script (*zhuànshū*). Eighth, he is not ignorant of these texts; thus, he is fully prepared.

Only when one is so prepared can they be considered a true recipient [of the teachings]. From what the two virtuous sages above have clarified, one further understands the difficulty of transmission and translation.
Will not later students then believe in this and apply themselves with vigor? Therefore, I have related these matters in full. However, this is merely what I have observed.
The general discourse has not yet been fully revealed here; as for this sutra, there must furthermore be its specific meaning.

Why is this? If it were not for the fact that in this final age of this land there exists this wondrous sutra, and the great compassion of the various sages adds the power of their vows to secretly provide protection, so that all matters are brought together through a wondrous operation, then in the end nothing could ever be achieved. Thus, it is truly not easy [to encounter]. Therefore...
It is truly difficult to transmit and translate [the teachings].

From the perspective of one who has attained awakening, this refers to the Master who personally instructed him in the wondrous Way—namely, the Great Master Tiantai—who was able to awaken to this wondrous Dharma himself.
At the beginning of the "Profound Preface" (*Xuanyi*), among the ten virtues by which he is praised, this is the very first.
Second, praising him by way of his own realized virtues: he said that he had never heard a lecture yet understood the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*) on his own;

being able both to understand and realize it, he was further able to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and attain *dhāraṇī*. These qualities together constitute his own spontaneous awakening to this wondrous Dharma.

The specific details of these matters and their characteristics are recorded in detail in the biographies and chronicles of the transmission of the Buddha-dharma to the East; how could they not exist?
The Buddha remained in the world for more than thirty years, maturing beings through countless skillful means.

Yet, when he was about to correctly expound the wondrous realm of the three mysteries—a realm that is difficult to conceive—even those present at the assembly who gazed up at such rare excellence heard it again and again and still failed to awaken, remaining in doubt and confusion.
How much less, then, in this degenerate age, could those of inferior capacity awaken on their own? This is why...

Is it not extremely difficult to know this? Were it not for having personally beheld the golden countenance and heard the wondrous voice at Vulture Peak in the past, how could one come to know this in this life? It is truly not easy; that is why it is so difficult.
Regarding the phrase "hearing the Master’s discourse on the difficult": although the transmitter of the tradition explains it as a general difficulty, it is distinct in its specific meaning.

It refers to the Venerable Danqiu’s admonition to "criticize and examine oneself. This means that hearing the discourse on this wondrous Dharma from a master who has already attained wondrous realization is difficult;

it implies that although the Great Master himself had already realized this Dharma wondrously and subsequently proclaimed it for others, one might—due to adverse conditions—fail to hear it repeatedly.
It is said that when the Master lectured on the *Nanxuan xu* (Preface to the Profound Mystery), he remarked: "Neither two nor three" refers precisely to this matter.

Furthermore, as you possess the perfect voice (*pariśuddha-svara*) capable of manifesting extraordinary powers to universally awaken all beings before proclaiming the wondrous teaching, yet there are many who do not hear it, the text says:

"Those who are not present at this assembly, you should proclaim the teaching for them. This indicates that even during the Buddha’s own lifetime, those who were rightfully entitled to hear it still failed to do so.
How much more so, then, for those in the final age! Thus we know that hearing this teaching is indeed difficult.
Furthermore, when the Dharma Master Jiāxiáng Jízàng was at the end of his life in Kuàijī, he led a multitude down to request the Great Master to lecture on this wondrous sutra.

The Master accepted the invitation, intending to do so during the summer retreat; however, due to unfavorable circumstances arising within the retreat, the opportunity was lost and he did not get to hear it. One can truly know from this that it is indeed difficult. Therefore...
The text states: "To hear this Dharma even throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas is difficult.
If these sublime Dharma, this sublime teacher, the time, the place, and the companions—all these favorable conditions—do not coincide, then one will never be able to hear it.
Because such a wondrous sutra as this is not easily encountered, it is therefore difficult."

"Difficult to record after hearing once" means that it is difficult to hear [the Master] preach this wondrous Dharma only once and then record and circulate it. What was previously called "difficult to hear" referred to hearing it only once;
here, it clarifies that recording and transmitting it immediately upon this single hearing is what constitutes the difficulty.
This explains the difficulty of internal understanding and external recording for the sake of transmitting it to others. If one follows the scriptural text, one is indeed capable [of doing so].

If the difficulty of listening is based on the meaning, then the difficulty of faith, understanding, and realization is as explained in the subsequent text. My current intention is precisely to question the difficulty of understanding;

to lament that one does not understand is to say that one cannot retain it, and that which is difficult to retain is precisely what is difficult to understand. To discuss this separately is the intent of Danqiu:

the point lies precisely in self-examination. Why is this? For instance, even regarding the two gates expounded by the Buddha’s own golden mouth which [the disciples] personally received at that time—yet...
The scriptures are vast; though one studies them again and again, up to three times, one still cannot fully comprehend them.

However, if one follows the intent of the present sutra-commentator (*jingjia*), this single character is established as possessing three meanings: *yi* (meaning), *so* (principle), and *li* (reason).

This is because the subsequent passage enumerates the names of these three meanings in their correct order. These three constitute both the general and the specific; the three themselves are the specific, and all are termed [the specific].

The term *xu* (序) signifies "introduction" (*tong*). Because it varies according to specific matters, there are three distinct types; all are intended to introduce and clarify the formal exposition (*zhengshuo*), and thus all three are equally "introductions.

Since they are all introductions, they are termed the "three introductions" (*san xu*). If one considers the conventional understanding of the term or the explanations provided in the subsequent commentary, these characters should be rendered as "gradual" (*jian*), "thread" (*xu*), or "narration" (*xu*).
This corresponds to the meaning of "sequence" (*cixu*) found at the beginning of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*.
The term "xu" (序) in its sense of "sequence" corresponds here to the character "xu" (緒); the term "xu" (序) in its sense of "introduction" corresponds here to the character "xu" (敘).

If, as in the *Guangming shu* (Commentary on the Light), the first instance of "xu" is rendered as "xu" (緒) and the second as "faqi" (發起)—which corresponds here to "xu" (序)—and the subsequent instance is rendered as "xushu" (敘述), which corresponds here to the meaning of "xu" (敘), such differences appear at first glance to have been altered by later generations.

If one understands the underlying principles, there is nothing that is not permissible. Why is this? According to worldly instructions and commentaries, the phonology and meaning of these three characters are identical;

they are interchangeable and both are valid. Therefore, using them interchangeably is of no consequence. Furthermore, although the names differ slightly in three places, their phonology and meaning are identical.
The reason they are not designated as "gradual" (*jiàn*) and so forth here is that, while this is indeed logically correct, it is primarily intended to manifest... [the true nature].
The meaning does not intend for the phonetic expression to be identical to the original characters; therefore, it is not so.

Nevertheless, one must invariably use this single term "sequence" (*xu*) as a thread to unify them, because they are based upon this. Thus, when reflecting upon them, first there is the general (*tong*), and next there are the two particulars (*bie*).
Because the two sequences are explained in combination, there are three. Why are there two [particulars]? Because there is one primary [general], there are two particulars.
Because form and sound are distinct, there are three [categories]; because they depend on what is appropriate for the occasion, sometimes they do not require two, and thus there may be only one;
therefore, while the textual expression may not be complete, the meaning must necessarily be present. Next, I shall explain these three meanings.

For each, I will first cite the relevant scriptural passages to present their methods, and subsequently clarify their meanings, which can be sought within the text. If you wish to examine them in detail...

Exhausting their full extent and enumerating them one by one, each possesses four aspects: namely, the subtle analysis (*vibhaṅga*), the meaning (*artha*), the connection (*saṃbandha*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*).

This is because both the text and its meaning constitute the body of the connection. Thus it is so. Now, regarding the initial explanation: first, as for the "five matters," they may be understood from the sutra;
here, although the general introduction (*nidāna*) may consist of six or seven items, in reality there are only five. These very five matters serve as [the basis].

Regarding the sequence of the title and the general application of the term *guàn* (crown): although it is now pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*), the world refers to placing a crown upon the head as "crowning" (*guàn*), which carries the meaning of placing or wearing it.
As for the meaning of the "crown-ornament" (*guānmǐn*), the *Erya* states that "head" (*shǒu*) means "beginning" (*shǐ*); "beginning" is synonymous with "initial" (*chū*).

Ānanda, viewing the Buddha’s distinct meanings, considers both [the title and the text] to be collectively termed "sūtra. Because it generally precedes the specific introduction (*biéxù*), it is placed before it.
It is said that the "Preface" (*xu*) is not the meaning of "first" (*shou*); how then can one use "first" to explain "preface"? Now, we say this is not so.

There are three types of prefaces, and since this [type] concerns sequential order, it ought to occupy the very beginning; thus it is called the "Preface to the First" (*cishou xu*). Furthermore, when viewed in relation to the main exposition (*zhengshuo*), it also occupies the position immediately following [the title], which is why it is called the "Preface to the First.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "Generally, that which is placed at the beginning of a written work is termed a 'preface' (*xu*). It is now as described here.
Because these [sūtras] occupy the initial position in the sequence of the Buddha’s scriptures, they are called "Order" (*krama*). The *Guangming shu* (Commentary on the Light) states:

"Because they reside at the beginning of this collection and crown the head of all teachings, they are called 'Order'. These explanations all maintain that the Buddha’s scriptures are arranged according to the sequence of their primary exposition, and thus occupy the first place;
this is precisely what was meant by the previous definition where "order" (*xu*) was explained as "beginning" (*chu*). If one says "crowning" (*guan*) is the same...

"Shou-shou" (each at the head) means that it should originally be called the "Initial Preface" (*chuxu*); yet, because it is placed after the main exposition (*zhengshuo*), it is termed the "Postscript" (*houxu*).
It is called the "Initial Preface" (*shouxu*) because it follows the final testament (*yizhu*), and it is called the "Subsequent Preface" (*cixu*) because it follows the end of the sutra.

If one says it is the "head of the sequence of the assembly," this refers merely to its position within the general order. Now, I maintain that "crown" (*guan*) carries the meaning of "head" (*shou*); this has not been previously considered.
After hearing this transmission, when later students first encountered the two commentaries by the Great Master, they once lectured on this meaning, claiming it was profoundly profound.
However, upon examining the Great Master’s two commentaries, they realized it was entirely incorrect.
That people today still cling to what the Master discarded as being correct is truly because they fail to comprehend the intent of the Great Master’s exegesis. Hereafter—
Many students are unable to see this deeply and thus take it for granted; now, I shall further assist them in clarifying it. Why is this? Because there are two types of sūtras:

those concerning the Buddha’s presence and those concerning the period after his parinirvāṇa. Regarding the sūtras from the time of his presence, this [sūtra] is second; regarding the sūtras from the period after his parinirvāṇa, it stands at the very beginning.
Since we are currently dealing with the sūtras from the period after his parinirvāṇa, its sequential position is at the very start; therefore, it is called "next" (second).
The first section begins with "By delusion" and everything below it constitutes the Sūtra. The meaning of the second section has already been explained as before.

Furthermore, regarding "the first and the initial": this refers to when the Sūtra was first compiled, the mind first established this matter so that it would serve as the sequential order for the subsequent formal collection;
therefore, it says "again thus. If they are identical, it is because they are both the gradual unfolding of a single Sūtra.
Furthermore, in entering the Buddha-dharma, faith is the primary beginning; these five matters are precisely intended to generate faith for those born in the final age.
This is according to the discourse on practice, as this [faith] occupies the very first position in the sequence. If one explains it in this way, what would be untenable?
Not only does this interpretation not harm the meaning here, but the two previous explanations by the Great Master become even clearer through it. Reflect upon this.
Following the contemplation, the explanation proceeds from the middle section regarding the six auspicious signs of the emission of light. There are two sets of six signs for each land;
the "light" is one sign common to both, serving as the final sign for this land and the first for the other lands.
While the remaining signs are distinct to each, the current mention of "emitting light" followed by "six" encompasses the entirety of these two sets of six.

The text of this auspicious preface concludes here. Regarding the term "initiation" (*qǐfā*), it refers to both the spiritual capacity (*jī*) and the teaching (*jiào*). These two characters have both general and specific meanings;

"end" (*duān*) signifies the root or the beginning. Among the five [auspicious signs], the first is the most primary cause for the correct [teaching], and thus it is called the "initial cause" (*yuánduān*).
The remaining four all take this as their root, and the various meanings of the formal exposition all derive from this.
Because it arises, the text is concise; because its auspicious signs manifest the ten subtleties (*daśa-sūkṣma*), it serves as the foundation.
Since the foundation inherently subsumes the branches, the assembly’s gathering is not mentioned, nor are their doubts, for these do not belong to the foundation itself and are addressed later.

Otherwise, the phrase "the ultimate source" would be difficult to maintain; thus the commentator says: "To clarify the source, the radiance is emitted and the auspicious signs are manifested. This opens [the discourse].

It summarizes the profound origins of manifold doubts and encompasses the pure essence of all categories; therefore, it is called a "Preface" (*xu*). This statement precisely accords with the meaning of the current text and serves as its exegesis.
According to secular usage, this corresponds to the meaning of "thread" (*xu*); thus, the *Chunqiu Shu* (Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals) explains the character for "preface":
"A preface is a thread; it means to lift up the essentials of the net, like drawing out a thread from silk. Therefore, it is so named.

The preface to that commentary is simply this much; as for the phrase "like silk" (*sī*), it means that when drawing out silk, one first lifts its *wén* (the root or base), which is called the "thread-end" (*sī-xù*).
This refers to the very beginning of the silk—the source from which the silk is taken—hence it is called a "thread-end.
The composition of the sutra and its written text are both similar to that [process], and therefore they are called "threads" (*xù*).
