they do not yet specifically address this single sutra. If one grasps the general principle without losing the specific details, one will not fail; otherwise, both will be lost. This sequence and arrangement thus universally encompasses everything.

The author and the commentator have fully exhausted the origins and developments of both its strengths and weaknesses; this is truly a universal standard for the world and an essential model for our own school.

Therefore, I have here provided a detailed account of these initial points, while not further discussing the remaining texts. I am constantly moved to long sighs by the fact that the essential depths of this literature cannot be discerned by commentators.
However, as I have not yet had the leisure to provide a complete exposition, I have merely set it forth briefly as before, perhaps following [the previous approach].

To have divided this sutra into sections immediately after the "Direct Discussion" (Qinlun) two days prior was an extreme error; it fails to grasp the overall purport of the work, which is why such a mistake occurred. Why is this so?
In the subsequent text, before the actual commentary begins, the author first clarifies the method for explaining the text.
Here, too, it is the same: before analyzing the content, he first clarifies the general framework of the structural divisions. This is sufficient as a basis and can serve as a reliable guide.
For example, why is it that upon merely seeing the words of the *Lotus Sūtra*, one immediately treats them as the correct section?
Or, as some say, this sentence merely concludes and rebukes the previous [section], which had the fault of being both abbreviated and extensive; it does not concern the entirety of what preceded.

Is it not the case that the entirety of what preceded was entirely absent in the Middle Ages and has not yet passed? What fault is there in this abbreviation? Therefore, one should not rely exclusively on later generations; however, within this [text]...
What is called "middle" here is merely the middle among things; it is the principle that is appropriately termed "middle," not a principle that is not the middle.
This meaning is the same as the meaning of the two types of "middle" found below: the middle as a numerical category and the middle as a name.

Regarding the commentary from this point onward, some say: "From here below, the division into 'the middle position' (*chùzhōng*) is clarified; this further has two parts: first, the various masters, and second, Tiantai. Now I say:
if it is already established that this is the section on the meaning of the "middle position," then it is already correctly identified;

why then is it presented twice? This completely deviates from the fundamental intent and contradicts one's own words. Now I say: from this point downward is precisely the formal structural analysis (*kēpàn*).

Since this sutra follows the preceding general explanation of the method, it is here that the correct judgment of this sutra begins. This section is divided into two parts: first, presenting alternative classifications; second, the current correct judgment.

Within the presentation of alternatives, there are two sub-sections: first, describing the divergent views; second, clarifying their inadequacy. In the description of the current correct judgment, the meaning of its being the "proper middle way" is revealed;

it would be as clear as pointing at one's own palm—what need is there for erroneous words? The initial presentation of alternatives is further divided into two: first, the description; second, [the refutation].

Regarding the formulation [of the *Abhidharmakośa*], there are seven categories when classified by person (*pudgala*) and five when classified by doctrine (*dharma*), as the first three schools share the same doctrinal tenets.
Consequently, the ancient and modern commentaries and classifications must indeed be numerous. Among those prevalent in the present day, these five schools are the most prominent;

since their prominence renders others unnecessary to discuss, I have specifically cited these five to demonstrate their differences. However, within this work, I shall merely recount them without engaging in critical analysis.
The subsequent passage does not merely conclude with an exhortation; since these [sections] differ and yet are not employed [as such], one must briefly understand their underlying reasons.
Now, following this, I shall briefly clarify them. Each [section] should consist of five parts: first, the person; second, the point where the text is formally divided;
third, that specific meaning; fourth, the present intention; and fifth, the distinct section that clarifies and establishes the differing meaning.
At the beginning of the dawn, the Dragon Master (Longshi) should be as described in his original biography, though I have not yet had the leisure to search for it.

This master’s analysis of the text consists of three sections: first, an analysis based on the three parts of the introduction; second, an analysis based on the two meanings of form and sound; and third, an analysis based on the two gates of cause and effect.

His purpose in making these three points is precisely to clarify that the text contains these three meanings. The final section concerns the underlying intent, wherein he initially employs the teachings of the Master Miti (Miaole).

Regarding the "intention" (*abhiprāya*), the next two [categories] are its own specific intention; the first three do not appear in the textual passage because they are identical to the latter ones in this school’s textual passage, and thus are not mentioned.

Next, within the section on the "rain of meanings," twenty-seven chapters are cited in total; however, the text is unified under only two types, as both their names and meanings are presented together.
At that time, the extant version of the sutra was still lacking the portion concerning *Dharmatā*, and therefore only two [types] were present.
Seventeenth: "Comprehensive" (*tong*) refers to the meaning of the essential summary; that is to say, when speaking of the essential summary, there are only these two meanings.

In the text, the initial section establishes the scope and indicates one meaning through the title of the chapter, while the subsequent section explains the reason for this, stating that the Tathāgata’s speech and teaching throughout his entire life consist of only these two kinds, as explained in this passage of the sutra.
The phrase "expedient means" (*upāya*) and so forth refers to verbal expression; that is, it refers to explicit teaching, which is the instruction of sound. How is it known that the text speaks thus?
It is explained by citing the principle that one reality is taught as three. "One reality" refers to the teaching of the actual truth, while "three" refers to the teaching of expedient means.
This means that the true principle is that there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), which is taught as three for the sake of sentient beings as an expedient.
Regarding the explanation of the Three Vehicles, the three cycles of teaching—brief and extensive—consist of nothing other than these two;
for this reason, it is known that the text of this initial section clarifies only these two. This is the underlying principle by which one knows it to be so.

Furthermore, because there are distinctions between the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination, there are the first ten chapters. Below, the subsequent meaning will be explained, and there is also textual evidence for this.

The reason why [the Buddha] can be known is that the body of the Tathāgata possesses these two aspects; the following scriptural passage clarifies these two. How is it explained that one knows this to be so?
It is interpreted by citing the passage beginning with "In truth, far... and so forth. "In truth, far" refers to the reality of the body;
"proclaiming near" refers to the expedient means of the body. Because he attained Buddhahood long ago in reality, it is called "real."

Because the distant [teaching] serves as a skillful means for beings, it proclaims the near; thus, the abbreviated and the extensive teachings spoken throughout the three periods of time are merely these two.
For this reason, one knows that the subsequent scriptural text clarifies only these two; therefore, the meaning is exactly as previously stated.

Furthermore, because there is a distinction between the three parts, the text begins and concludes accordingly. If this has been the case from the outset, yet people all claim it is not so—[this is incorrect].
Later, I happened to see a follower of that school compose a treatise establishing its doctrine; it did not at all contradict what I had previously encountered.
Thus, I know that this was brought about by the natural course of principle. Furthermore, observing that the various commentaries do not align with one another, they have also greatly erred.
I shall briefly conclude thus for now, as I have not yet had the leisure to provide a detailed account. If one follows the two texts described by Jiaxiang, they state: "First..."

Up to the "Peaceful Practices" chapter, the text proceeds from the emergence [of the Stupa] until the end of the sutra; for these two sections, there are respectively the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination, which differ from the arrangement of this current text.

Furthermore, according to the account of Master Yao by another school, it is said that prior to the "Dharma Teacher" chapter, the "expedient means" (*upāya*) and the "reality" (*bhūta-artha*) were explained;
from the section on Prabhūtaratna down to the "Supernatural Powers" chapter, the "expedient means of the body" and the "reality of the body" are manifested.
Thus, the first section is identical to the present [text] and differs from the Master Zang’s; the second section differs from the present [text] and also differs from Master Zang’s.
Since the present [text] now states that both are identical, one does not know why they differ in this way.

This is likely due to later generations altering the commentaries (*zhangshu*) after they were circulated, or perhaps due to the proliferation of erroneous oral traditions. Although there are slight differences, in the end, these two [versions] are fundamentally the same.

Each section consists of three parts; this is certain. Regarding the next two sections: the first two revealed the two meanings of the Buddha’s transformation [of beings], while these [current] two clarify that those two previous intentions are now realized as the single vehicle (ekayāna). Because they re-reveal the former meaning, these two are further elucidated.
Since they are directly the same as the two previous intentions, why is it that the text does not mention the "Introduction" at the beginning, yet later proceeds to the "Peaceful Abiding"?
Although this practice indeed follows the previous two intentions, it is here treated directly according to the primary teaching (zhengzong).

Therefore, the preceding section did not mention the introduction (xu), and furthermore, the portion from "the sudden emergence" [of the stupa] onwards need not necessarily encompass the entire sutra.

This is because the two aspects of the meaning established by the three chapters on "Holding the Stupa" and "Peaceful Abiding" belong to the former; thus they pertain to the causal gate (yinmen). Since they give rise to what follows, they pertain to the resultant gate (guomen). Thus, the former...

This discrepancy arises because the subsequent [sections] are based on the arising [of the teaching], while the preceding [sections] are based on its establishment; thus, there is this difference. If one follows Jiaxiang’s account regarding the placement of these texts, they are perfectly aligned.
This is because the four chapters are also the "entrance gate for the circulation" (liú-tōng yīn mén). Thus, Jiaxiang identifies three [aspects]:
the reason he takes the preceding [sections] as the cause for circulation is that the convergence of the three vehicles into one and the correct establishment of the One Vehicle constitute the cause.

Therefore, the subsequent section on the "Gate of the Result" (phala-mukha) precisely reveals that the Tathāgata’s distant result precedes the entry into the cause of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) and the attainment of the result of the One Vehicle;
thus, by excluding its remote conditions and grasping the literal meaning of the text, it extends from this chapter downward.
Next, regarding the statement that the two masters are the same: this refers to Dharma Master Yin of Zhongxing Temple during the Southern Qi dynasty, whose case is as stated in his own biography.

As for Dharma Master Yao, he is as previously mentioned. Regarding the similarity in the division of the text, according to Jiaxiang’s commentary, the initial exposition of Master Long’s division of the text contains only the first of the two preceding points;
it lacks the first three sections as well as the subsequent two gates on cause and effect within the second section.
There remains a slight difference: the first fourteen chapters clarify the "words" (vākya), while the latter fourteen chapters clarify the "body" (kāya).
Each of these two sections contains three parts. At that time, there was no chapter on "Dharmatrāta"; this must have been a statement by the Tripitaka Master based on his own interpretation.
He first recounted the account of the Master Nāga exactly as it stands, and then he recounted the account of the Master Yin, saying: "Master Yin opened [the text]..."

This sutra consists of four general sections: first, from the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta) through the end of the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta), it establishes the "Peaceful Practices" (Anrakugyō);

second, from the "Chapter on the Recitation of the Sutra" (Shōkyōshutsu-bon) down to the beginning of the "Chapter on Distinction" (Funbetsu-bon), including the verses spoken by Maitreya prior to that point, these two and a half chapters clarify the "Expedient Means of the Body" (Shin-fūben) by opening up the near to reveal the far; third, from this point onward until the end of the sutra.

Regarding this section on the dissemination (*parīndanā*), it is further stated that although the "Peaceful Practices" (*anurakṣaṇā*) are described as the causal portion (*hetu-bhāga*), the three chapters from "Beholding the Stūpa" (*stūpa-darśana*) onward also constitute the gradual unfolding of the core principles of the fruition (*phala*). Therefore, one must view them from both perspectives. Why?

Because through the beholding of the stūpa, Many Treasures (*Prabhūtaratna*) assists in ensuring the longevity of those who seek to propagate the sutra; thus, there arise the "Chapter on Upholding" (*dhāraṇī-paṭala*) and the "Peaceful Practices. Consequently, these are transmitted.
Because it pertains to the cause, it belongs to the section on causes. Next, there is the emergence of the Bodhisattva specifically as the basis for the lifespan;
since he emerges by seeking life from what preceded, the first three chapters also contain the sense of establishing the lifespan.
Therefore, one must discuss both aspects. Now, although this account of Master Yin (Vasubandhu) contains some minor differences and omissions, it nonetheless possesses [the full meaning].
Regarding the meaning of the three preceding sections: the middle two parts constitute the "Correct Teaching" (*samyag-deśanā*) within the first three segments of the *Longshi* (Dragon Master).
Thus, one should know that the textual divisions of those three segments are identical to the textual divisions of the current first three texts.
Master Yin’s division of the "Correct" into two corresponds precisely to the second category of the two types of meaning established by the Dragon Master. Next, we shall discuss cause and effect.
This is precisely the meaning of the two gates concerning cause and effect presented earlier; since they differ slightly but are largely the same, we know their intent is identical.

As for why Jiaxiang did not mention the three layers of the Dragon Master (Longshi), it may be because the texts he consulted differed, or because he did not see the original text and thus encountered variations in oral transmission.
Alternatively, while the general principles of the treatises are the same, they are not necessarily identical in every detail.
If Master Tong was already like this, how could it be otherwise for Master Yao? In the commentaries of recent times, this is nowhere clearly seen;
even Jiaxiang [Jizang] did not mention it. Now, having briefly examined the lineage of that school, I have recorded the meaning of that master as follows:
"Although Master Yao’s classification contains twenty-seven sections, they are condensed into two: the two [stages of] Expedient Means and the two [stages of] Reality."
Therefore, the Sūtra states: "The Dharma Master opens the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*) and reveals the mark of reality.

Prior to the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stūpa," it generally clarifies what is termed "skillful means" and so forth; from the "Jeweled Stūpa Chapter" down to the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers," it manifests the skillful means of the body and so forth.

Now, observing this judgment, it encompasses both the previous intentions: first, the division into three, and second, the division into two. Why is this? Since it says "directly until... [the text continues].

By the power of spiritual efficacy, it is known that what follows is the section on circulation (*pravartana*). Since the section on circulation has already been opened at the end, it naturally serves as the introduction to what precedes it;

thus, one knows that both [sections] are established as the main body (*śarīra*) of the teaching from which they are opened. Therefore, this single phrase contains the intent of both the "three" and the "one" in the two-fold judgment.
Furthermore, regarding the latter [section], if the meaning of cause and effect is further clarified through two gates, then the three sections will be fully complete. For this reason:
I recognize that the general principles of these three masters are identical. Since their general principles are the same, a brief explanation of their intentions has already been provided above.
Nevertheless, there are those who have studied their doctrines and claim that the previous discussion of the meaning of "body" (kāya) was uniquely attained by Master Yao;

they assert that he established it through ten broad categories, surpassing all others past and present. A rough outline of this is as given before, though I cannot describe his specific intentions in full detail.

Even so, as for the intention behind not employing [this method] now, what is it? If the names, textual locations, and meanings of the three initial sections were no different from the meaning of the first section here, there would certainly be no contradiction.
However, as for the judgment based on the "body of words" (*śarīra-vākya*), this does not yet exhaust its profound essentials. Why is this?
Because each of the two gates possesses the transformative activity of the three mysteries (*triguhyaka*), and each likewise possesses the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*tattva*).

If one directly interprets [the term] as "opening and revealing" (*kaixian*), both the provisional and the real aspects of the verbal body (*yan-shen*) lose their respective meanings; furthermore, the significance of "opening and revealing" is not manifested.
Although one may cite the passage on "opening and showing" (*kaishi*) to establish the name, one only obtains its substance while losing its function.

Even if one claims that the meaning is complete within the name, it ultimately cannot serve as an analogy. Since the meanings of "far" and "near" within the sutra have not been clarified at all, it is simply unacceptable to designate [the teaching] by such a name.

If one clarifies the revelation and manifestation (*kaikishin*) according to each of the two gates—the provisional traces (*jaku*) and the fundamental reality (*hon*)—then there is no aspect of the various three mysteries (*sanmitsu*) that is not fully encompassed.

For this reason, it is unnecessary to employ a sequential order. Regarding the gate of cause and effect (*inhōmon*): in both gates, whether from the perspective of the teacher or the disciple, cause and effect are both fully present within the scriptural texts;
since they cannot be cited in their entirety here, they cannot be judged one-sidedly. Now, regarding the revelation and demonstration according to these two gates:
Since this meaning was already extensively refuted in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) above, it is not employed here.

Next, as for Master Xuanchang—this master was a disciple of Chan Master Xuanzhi of the Later Wei dynasty, as recorded in his own biography—he also distinguishes three meanings based on cause and effect, because he maintains that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* itself explains the principle of cause and effect. That is to say:
This means that the first [section] is the cause of illumination, the next is the fruit of illumination, and the last is the protection and maintenance of the practice;

these constitute the persons and dharmas who precede the cause and fruit. The reason why the two sections on cause and fruit begin and end in this manner is likely because each possesses the significance of three parts;
thus, the text does not repeat itself, and the underlying meaning is necessarily so. The first three [sections] can be understood, while the subsequent text is likewise deficient in its realization.

For many reasons, the discourse proceeds directly from the *Dhāraṇī-parivarta* (Chapter on Upholding). This is because the *Stūpa-parivarta* (Chapter on the Stūpa) serves as a proof for the preceding section on the causes for the propagation [of the teaching].

Furthermore, in the *Dhāraṇī-parivarta*, the various bodhisattvas make vows and there is the passage on "Peace and Bliss" (*Anurakṣaṇā*). Consequently, Mañjuśrī requests the teaching of the methods for widespread proclamation;

thus, the bodhisattvas from other directions request the propagation, summoning those from the lower regions who emerge in a leap, thereby establishing the section on the fruits [of the practice]. For these reasons, it continues from the *Dhāraṇī-parivarta*.
Regarding the section on the fruits [of practice], there is a gradual analysis of the three ways of rejoicing in the Dharma Master;

since all clarify the section on the fruits of hearing and retaining [the teachings] and designate those who gain benefit as "merit," they are all indeed fruits. As for the section on Not Disparaging, it clarifies that the Buddha attained the Buddha’s spiritual power by propagating the sutra:

first, it clarifies the Buddha’s power and its wondrous, boundless application; subsequently, it clarifies that by upholding the sutra, one swiftly attains such fruits. Thus, [the structure is established].

These all belong to the category of the "Fruits" (*phala*). From the section on "Accumulation" (*saṃbhāra*) downward through the next seven chapters, the various great sages collectively propagate and uphold the persons and dharmas who practice the aforementioned causes and fruits; therefore, this constitutes the "Section on Upholding" (*parigraha-bhāga*). Such is their intent.
If one does not employ it now, the partiality regarding cause and fruit is already the same as before; moreover, to speak directly of cause and fruit alone is insufficient.
Furthermore, the distinction between the beginning and end of the text is not far removed from that of the three previous masters;
the protection and preservation [of the teaching] remains no different, and the names and meanings of its circulation are likewise inferior.

Why, then, not simply rely on the ancients' division of this single scripture into three major sections, further dividing the "Correct Exposition" (Saddharma-paryāya) into two gates? Such an approach would be superior to the current judgment; therefore, the present interpretation is truly inadequate.
This is acceptable.
Next, regarding the fact that one school does not mention specific names, it is likely because those individuals were still living at the time and thus could not be specifically identified.

This [explanation] is also broadly divided into three parts. First, concerning the "essence" (tǐ): the intended meaning is that this precisely opens up the provisional (kāpika) to reveal the real (bhūtārtha), clarifying the Dharma of the One Vehicle.
Because this is the principle underlying the name of this wondrous Dharma, it is called the "essence" (*tattva*), which refers to the essence itself. This passage precisely clarifies this point;
therefore, from its beginning to its end, the text is consistent with this. The merit of receiving and upholding [this teaching] is extensively elucidated by these various passages.

The emergence of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, the Bodhisattvas, and the fact that the World-Honored One Śākyamuni had long since attained [enlightenment], and so forth, all pertain to the propagation and maintenance of what preceded.
This is because it is brought about by the wondrous Dharma. To praise the original vows clarifies why the bodhisattvas propagate this wondrous Dharma in such a manner;
it is all to manifest that they possess original vows, for without them it would not be so. Thus, it is precisely to manifest their possession of them.
Furthermore, the first part is the formal exposition of the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, while the subsequent part cites its great merit to exhort sentient beings.

Holding fast to the sublime Dharma previously expounded and the excellent original vows [contained in] the concluding sections, one widely propagates the aforementioned sublime Dharma. Although that was his intention, it is not so in reality.
The "Exposition of the Essence" (*Myōtai*) is merely the "Correct Explanation" (*Shōsetsu*); its name is not as manifest as the title of the "Main Section" (*Shūshō*).

Consequently, the merit of its proper upholding is lost, and since the time has long passed, the excellence of the original vows cannot reach those who would propagate them; furthermore, it is entirely deficient.
Regarding the *yōchi* (causes and conditions), because it does not directly manifest the meaning of the three divisions, it is most improper and therefore not employed.
Next, another school describes [the divisions] as four sections; this too is omitted here as its intent is similar to the previous case.

This master establishes these four names, which fully accord with the various schools and are not far removed from them; there is nothing by which they may be altered, yet for the sake of temporary convenience, they are opened up.
If one takes four [sections] and expects them to correspond to one [chapter], it becomes excessive; if one expects them to correspond to two gates, they remain insufficient.
Since it is not entirely without flaw, this too is not adopted. Next, the explanation of the person at Guangzhai Temple is as clarified previously.

It is divided into three major sections, which follows the intention of Master Mitian. Furthermore, the locations of these three segments of text should also be the same as those in the subsequent current text. Therefore—

The abbreviated sections not presented here can be understood from the two introductory passages already explained above. Regarding the section on the causes and effects of the main body (*maula-bhāga*), one should follow the text from the "Expedient Means" chapter through to the end of the "Peaceful Conduct" chapter, where the initial emergence of Maitreya’s verses occurs, as previously noted and as recorded in the commentary of Master Yin by Jiaxiang.
As for the two sections of the dissemination (*prabheda*), although they lack a formal beginning or end, they may likewise be inferred accordingly.

One should proceed from the verses following Maitreya’s [section] through the end of the "Chapter on Not Despising" (Adhimātra-pūjā) for one's own practice, and from the "Supernatural Powers" (Rddhi) onwards for the transformation of others.

This can be known by dividing the preceding six sections into twenty-four parts; however, their specific names and locations are not mentioned here, as they are fully contained in that commentary (*śāstra*).
I once saw the unrevised version of Danqiu, which states therein: "The twenty-four sections are as follows..."
What was stated elsewhere must have been recorded in a separate manual by Danqiu, which has been fully transcribed;

I have merely noted it here as "and so forth" (yúnyún) to avoid excessive prolixity. Since neither this record nor its commentary exists today, it must have been lost long ago, and there is nothing left to describe.
Nevertheless, based on the subsequent passages in our own school’s texts and the usage found in the works of Jiaxiang [Jizang]:
According to the Master Yin’s judgment, their names and textual locations may also be inferred; I shall briefly describe them here.

Furthermore, as for the first two prefaces, each consisting of five sections, the text itself makes them manifest, so there is no need for further discussion. Second, regarding the four sections of the "Cause" (hetu) gate within the main body, the first is the initial brief exposition at the beginning of the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means), which moves [the audience's] attachments and gives rise to doubt. From the "Threefold Request" (*Triyācana*) onwards is the second section, which moves [their] attachments.
The third section, "Extensive Explanation of Severing Doubt and Generating Faith," consists of the five chapters from the chapter on the Dharma Master onwards;
this should be titled the fourth [section], "Encouragement to Uphold," because it contains the subsequent propagation.

Regarding the four aspects of the gateway of the fruit, the first is the initial arousal [of the aspiration], which is the present introduction to the Root Chapter (*mūla-parivarta*), consisting of the praise and the granting of permission.

The second section below is the brief exposition on dispelling doubt and requesting [the teaching]. The third section below is the articulation of doubt and the formal request. The fourth section below is the "Chapter on Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*).

Regarding the two types of circulation [of the Dharma] that follow, each consists of three parts. First, concerning the three aspects of one's own practice: the first half of the chapter is designated by Jiaxiang as the "Brief Exposition";

the two chapters on "Rejoicing" (*Anumodanā*) and the "Dharma Master" (*Dharmabhāṇaka*) are designated as the "Extensive Exposition"; and the single chapter on "Never-Disparaging" (*Sadāparibhūta*) serves as the "Realization."

The accomplishment of the first two [aspects] may also be understood as being like this [in the case of] his own practice; the three aspects of transforming others consist of: (1) the general clarification of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*);

(2) the specific clarification of exhortation, encouragement, and entrustment; and (3) the six chapters from "To Bhaiṣajyarāja" onwards, which clarify protection, maintenance, and circulation—these being the three aspects of transforming others.
One should understand that the beginning and end [of the sūtra] are likely to be thus; however, it cannot yet be definitively settled, so let us know this briefly for now.
If one seeks this further later on, these twenty-four sections can be understood in brief.

However, as many of them share the same intent as the present [work], their names and locations have been omitted from the text; where it says "note (etc. beneath the text, it means they are simply present there.
Regarding the titles, the textual locations, and the meanings of these twenty-four sections, none of these three types of content appear in the texts hereafter for future students.
Knowing that this intention exists, I have sought it out and, wishing to avoid excessive verbiage, have directly annotated [the text] as follows (etc.).
If one considers such a structural analysis from the perspective of the time, it was truly preeminent; thus, it is believed that when people said, "Regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*, Guangzhai is superior;
regarding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Kaishan is excellent," they were indeed right. However, if considered from my current perspective, these are merely divergent interpretations. What of it?

If one were to divide the "Threefold Greatness" (sanming) into the central principle, the cause, and the effect—each further subdivided into four—one would lose the three aspects of both the fundamental and the manifested, and the sublime purport of this single sutra would be entirely lost; therefore, this approach is not adopted here.
Since the time Master Kumārajīva translated and transmitted the teachings, although many divisions have been made, the several schools prior to him were the most crude and superficial.

Furthermore, because the School of Characteristics (Xiangzong) has long been practiced, I shall now briefly describe it in order to distinguish it from divergent interpretations; thus, the *Prolegomenon* states:
"Alternatively, by citing the divergent interpretations of various masters and verifying their lack of perfection," which refers precisely to this intent.
Next, the following provides a summary and earnest exhortation, which likewise summarizes the preceding section’s intent to merely recount [the views] without adjudicating their right or wrong.

Although the classifications of the aforementioned masters were not entirely in accord with the Sage’s intention, later students and beginners need not give rise to disputes or contention over them as to what is right or wrong.
This is because each [view] reflects the personal inclinations and preferences of those individuals.

Those who differ [in their views] all consider themselves to have attained what they ought to pursue; each gains benefit according to their own inclinations. Those who judge right and wrong, however, each lose the advantage of being suited to their own inclinations.
For this reason, one should not engage in contention by asserting "right" or "wrong. Since many among the younger generation act in this manner, this exhortation is given.

Regarding the term "human sentiment" (*qíng*): "sentiment" (*qíng*) refers to reality (*qíngshí*). Thus, in common usage, "sentiment" is glossed as "reality"; that is, each person clings to their own [view].
To hold this view as correct while rejecting others as contrary to human nature is to cling to a fixed calculation;

yet there is no such difference, for it is precisely the nature of the human heart (*qing*) that varies. Thus, the Confucian commentary explains that "nature" refers to the differing inclinations and preferences of the mind; this is its meaning.

Because they differ, there are various discrepancies and approximations. Although these may not fully accord with the intention of the Sage, each considers itself to have attained the truth—just like the spring orchid and the autumn chrysanthemum.

The chrysanthemums each suit the beauty of their own season and do not apologize for one another; this refers to the "exclusive longevity" (tánshòu), meaning that each is dedicated solely to its own excellence, which is considered to accord with principle.
It is not only the authors who are thus; those who receive and study [the teachings] are likewise so.

Each takes what they personally revere as superior and excellent, giving rise to joy, faith, and understanding, thereby producing the wholesome and extinguishing the unwholesome, or perhaps awakening to the Way.

One obtains four benefits [by upholding this teaching], whereas if one reviles it, the loss is extreme; this refers to the gains and losses regarding the four *siddhāntas* that accord with worldly sentiment (*anuvṛtti-siddhānta*). This is precisely the Buddha’s transformation that accords with worldly sentiment. Here, however, we are discussing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the former was intended to refute the heterodox and establish the orthodox; the latter is intended to clarify the ultimate and eliminate delusion. Thus, although the words differ, the intent is one. It is like the case of the three vehicles and the one vehicle: when the three are established, they refute the one; when the one is established, it subsumes the three. Below, by means of a single character, it is revealed what the original text was. Although he knew with certainty that the preceding character was a mistake, he could not yet discern what the original character was;
thus he harbored this doubt for many years, searching and investigating without ceasing. Suddenly, in the final year of the Dali era...
At Tiantai Foliang Temple, I encountered a senior practitioner who showed me a manuscript that had not yet been revised or annotated.

Upon examining this chapter, I saw that the character "前" (qián) was originally written as two characters; only then did I realize that the text had been abbreviated by taking the first part of one word and the second part of another, thereby merging three segments into one.
Consequently, my accumulated doubts were all at once dispelled, and through the discovery of this single character, I came to understand the previous two interpretations.

It will certainly result in ten kinds of obstructions and difficulties, which shall dissolve like melting ice. The *Analects* says, "A single word may cause one to lose the trustworthiness of mourning"—this refers precisely to this situation.
Someone might ask: "Since the former case involved two parties being unaware, how can it be the same here? Now, let us clarify the reasons; they do not exceed two types:
first, because later generations have altered the text; second, because the cursive forms of characters are so easily confused during transcription.
It was due to this error that such things occurred; for instance, it is said that whether a sutra is large or small, it must be divided into three sections.
Later generations, not understanding this, claimed that all [sutras] ought to follow this pattern and consequently changed the character "zhī" (之) to "qián" (前).

For example, when a great sutra says "yì wèi yún zǒu" (義未云走), although I am not clever, many scholars do not understand the meaning of the character "zǒu" (走). Among them, there are even those who change it to "sī" (厶).
Furthermore, if one recognizes that the character "厶" (si) is the character for "private" and consequently uses it as such, there are two errors:

failing to understand the meaning of the character "走" (zǒu) and failing to recognize the phonetic value of the character "厶. To make such an alteration without due consideration is exactly like this.

It is also like when, in a text, there is a term such as "qìlèi-xìn" (class-affinity letter), and someone who does not understand it takes "qì" (qi) to mean "to raise" and consequently changes it to "jǔlèi" (raising-class).
Furthermore, there are those like [the author of] the *Tanyan lun*, who, failing to understand the meaning of the character "弄" (nòng), altered it to "挊"; this has already been explained above.

Such instances among later generations where people lack discernment and arbitrarily alter characters within the scriptures are quite numerous. Examples of such indiscriminate usage of characters include what was clarified previously:
changing "礪" (lì) to "隨" (suí) in accordance with others, and changing "豫" (yù) to "預" (yǔ) in the *Dajing shu* (Commentary on the Mahāyāna Sūtra).
Regarding the use of the word "buddha" (佛) as a cause for the Way, the questions and answers serve to bring benefit. The preceding text is a continuation of this theme.

There are countless instances such as these—where characters like "lǔ" and "yú," or "jìn" and "shī" are confused in common parlance—all of which stem from the fact that various characters were transmitted through cursive or formal scripts with overlapping forms, leading to such errors in transcription until they reached this state. Now, concerning these two characters:
Because its cursive form is entirely indistinguishable from the preceding character "qian" (前), the two were changed to "qian" as a general convention;
although there are two distinct conditions for the former, the definitive reason lies solely in the latter.

Furthermore, the Great Master praised this single character as being like the snapping of a string that halts the music—when ten difficult points are at a critical juncture, how could one possibly deliberate over it as if it were merely the character "ting" (仃)?
"Alas! It has long been suspended and cut off from the past; now that we have fortunately encountered it, I pray you will continue it.

This is surely the intention of the Great Master Danqiu—to cause it to flourish when the time is right. How could anyone else possibly continue it? Some may say: 'The two [versions] do not correspond;
there is no prior prophecy. Or they may say: 'It is simply that one has not yet understood it. Since this is already a single scripture, why are there two layers of doctrinal analysis?"
Since two judgments have already been made, why must one necessarily follow the latter two and not the former three?
Although it is a single sūtra, it possesses two gates and cannot be treated in a one-sided manner; thus, both judgments are required.

Furthermore, these two gates constitute the great matter of all Buddhas and the essential core of this single sūtra; moreover, they are particularly convenient for interpretation and elucidation. Therefore, one must necessarily follow them.
The latter two and the former one are not so; therefore, they do not follow [the same principle]. Question:

If one were to establish a single direction (ekānta), what fault would there be such that you say it is "not permissible"? Answer: If one were to apply a single direction universally, the intermediate [teachings] would not be entirely correct explanations, thereby losing the intent of the two gates.

If one were to apply a single direction exclusively to the Trace Gate (jijimono), there would be no entrustment (fujukku); if applied to the Source Gate (honmon), there would be no certification of faith (shōshin).
Because one loses the meaning of the sutra, it is necessary that the single and the multiple correspond to one another rather than being treated unilaterally.
Question: Since the direct [teaching] is broadly divided into three, and these two gates are opened within the "Correct Exposition" (Shōsetsu), what fault is there in not doing so?

Answer: These two gates of the "Original" (Hon) and the "Traced" (Jaku) are the great causes for the Buddhas' entry and exit [into the world], and they are the basis for the arising and ceasing of the various teachings.

Since the profound source of its meaning is severed from all conceptual nets (*sūtra*) and its exposition transcends the multitude of external appearances, it opens two gates, each divided into three parts, to manifest its essence.
It entrusts the wondrous application of maintaining clarity (*vidyā-dhara*) in infinite ways; that previous masters missed the essential point was precisely because they deviated from this.
Now, by receiving this principle, it is not so [any longer]. Question: Since it must necessarily consist of two or three [parts], why is there no "entrustment" (*parindanā*) at the beginning?
Regarding the subsequent lack of a testimony of faith (*śraddhā-pratyaya*), the previous [section] has already been explained; why then should there be further confusion?

It is because two gates are to be revealed, and thus both sets of three [sections] are required. Since this is a single sūtra, there cannot be two separate events. If that is so, other sūtras are also single [in nature]; why then do they have two [sets]? [The answer is:
although other sūtras may have two layers of entrustment (*parindanā*), they ultimately never have two layers of initiation (*samutthāna*), nor do they possess such extensive [repetition].
The matter of the "Great Circulation" (Dà liútōng) applies directly to a single period; it is not because this [text] is so profound and transcendent that it cannot be categorized by analogy.
Even though other sutras may have multiple sets of three sections, they ultimately do not transcend these first three. All of these are merely matters within a single trace (yī jì).
Question: Since both the universal (tōng) and specific (bié) meanings must coexist and cannot be established in isolation, why is one chapter sometimes designated as the "Universal Preface" (Tōngxù)?
Furthermore, the five intermediate chapters may be considered the "Separate Introduction" (*prastāvanā*) or the "Main Exposition" (*samyag-deśanā*);

the half-chapter on the "Emergence from the Earth" may be considered the "Main Exposition" or the "General Circulation" (*parīndanā*); and the eleven and a half subsequent chapters may be considered the "General Circulation" or the "Specific Circulation.
Since each of these is but a single textual unit, by what logic can they be directed in two ways? This meaning is firmly established.
As for those who doubt, how could there be anyone capable of penetrating [this meaning]? Now that I have encountered one who inspires me, I shall venture to explain it.
However, the general outline is much like the previously clarified intent of "one scripture and two gates. Why is this so?

Furthermore, within the initial preface, the general preface is fundamentally both general and specific, while the specific preface is fundamentally specific. Although the explicit intent of the specific preface is distinct, its implicit meaning remains general because it is contained within the one.
The "separate" [preface] primarily distinguishes the manifest meaning by following the implicit meaning of the "general"; thus, both constitute the General Preface.
Since the two gates are divided such that the implicit meaning of the general follows the manifest meaning of the separate, both constitute the Separate Preface.

In this way, as the one sutra and its two gates are not mutually separated, so too these general and separate aspects follow one another without even a moment's interval; this extends even to the four propositions, which are beyond the reach of discursive thought.
Among these, the five intermediate grades, being situated within a single sutra, are explicitly categorized as belonging to the provisional (迹, *jì*) dissemination;
yet secretly they initiate the fundamental (本, *běn*). Furthermore, although they constitute the primary dissemination, they also incidentally benefit those in the present.

Because they follow the general, the secret, and the incidental, they are considered the "correct teaching. Although they are divided into two sections, they appear after the provisional section because they follow the particular, the explicit, and the correct.

Regarding the circulation [of the teaching], since they are not mutually separated, it is also as previously explained: the emergence of half a chapter is also due to a central point within a single sutra.

Furthermore, this serves to manifest the particular (viśeṣa) by means of the general (sāmānya), and because it distinguishes the particular through the general, it belongs to the "Correct Exposition" (bhūta-deśanā).

Since it is divided into two distinct parts, it initiates the "Root Section" (mūla-parivarta); because the general follows from the particular, it further functions as the prologue for the subsequent eleven chapters.

The first half of the sutra, having completed the formal exposition, provides a general exhortation to propagate and uphold [the teaching]; because the specific follows from the general, it is categorized as the "general circulation" (sāmānya-prasaraṇa).

Since the circulation is divided into two gates, the specific gate follows after the main gate; because it is contrasted with the preceding specific [gate], it is further termed the "specific circulation.
As these two gates of the sutra are not mutually separated, these two meanings also invariably accompany one another; the four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) can be understood accordingly.
Truly wondrous and boundless! Reflect upon it, reflect upon it! Regarding the question of the common and the specific, why is it that each of the two gates has its own common and specific aspects?
Why is it that the Trace Gate (Jikimon) has two texts while the Source Gate (Honmon) has only one? Answer:

Because the Trace Gate precedes [the Source Gate] and was not yet completed, it possesses two texts. As for the Source Gate, because it is taught with the intention of being subsequent, it has only one. This is the general principle.
If one were to investigate the reality of the matter at first glance, even the "Root Chapter" (Honmon) itself possesses two aspects. Why is this?

Since it is stated that those of the four levels of faith in the present age have "heard of the Buddha’s lifespan being long and far-reaching," this constitutes a distinct circulation (ryūtsū) of the Root [Chapter]. As for those from the five grades (gopon) downward, it is simply stated that they have "heard this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*," without mentioning the "lifespan.
From this, we know that these are exclusively cases of general circulation (tōryūtsū). Thus, it is known that [the Root Chapter] likewise [has these two aspects].

There are two meanings that are equally balanced: just as within the "Trace" [Teaching], although the Introductory Section is distinct, it must reside within the General [Section] because the Fundamental Section is placed after the extinction;
likewise, although the Introductory Section is general, it must reside within the Distinct [Section] because the Fundamental Section exists inherently there.
It is the same in the subsequent "Circulation" [Section]: although the five chapters below are distinct, they must invariably be general because there is a preceding distinct section.
Although the fourfold faith applies universally, it must specifically correspond to what precedes; while it corresponds specifically to what follows, it also applies universally.
Thus, these two sections share one common introduction and each has its own individual introduction; they share one common circulation and each has its own individual circulation.
All things are perfectly equal, with none being uneven. From this, one knows that this sutra is not merely a vessel for meaning, but that its essential purport is subtle and profound.

That this peerless one has now expounded its principles and numerical categories as something extraordinary—if it were not so, who could have unveiled these profound secrets or opened this weighty gate?
I have always felt deep joy and gratitude at having encountered such a treasure; yet, my strength being meager and inferior, I have been unable to fully develop and propagate it.
I hope that throughout the future, it may be praised and extolled, for the younger generation is formidable and should indeed be courageous and vigorous.
The preceding section has briefly analyzed the matter as an opportunity arose. Below, I shall further explain the analytical passage within the commentary (*śāstra*).

If one grasps the intent expressed above, there would likely be no need for further explanation; however, for those who have not yet done so, I shall provide a brief clarification. First, regarding the meaning of the initial question:

this inquiry is specifically formulated based on the two or three topical sections mentioned previously. As for the statement, "Is it according to what you have seen?"—it asks whether the answer conforms to what has been observed.
The revisions for this section pose questions such as: "How can one sutra have two parts—the Introductory, the Proper, and the Propagation?
Why does the Root Chapter lack such [parts]? Why does the Trace Chapter consist only of the single Propagation? These serve as questions for the subsequent answers and have been further refined;
though condensed into a single inquiry, they encompass three meanings, while the latter two serve as the basis for the answers.

Upon its commencement, one should proceed to explain and resolve the doubts. Although the question contains three points, it actually consists of two: [the first] concerns the introduction and the dissemination; the second, which follows, addresses the main teaching itself.
If there is no hindrance to the correct meaning, it will establish itself. This is precisely because the "one" and "two" are connected; thus it is said: "How can there be two?
In the response, first the explanation is given, followed by a concluding demonstration. Within the initial section, various sutras are cited in a general manner to illustrate and clarify the point.

Now, my initial intention was first to cite the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* to clarify that it possesses many introductory sections; subsequently, I cited the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* to clarify that it has many circulated versions.

The conclusion clarifies that these do not conflict with this [present work], so there is certainly no hindrance. My intention regarding the *Avataṃsaka* is to clarify that within that single sūtra there are many distinct introductions;
therefore, it says "assembling the multitude in various places," for the act of assembling the multitude involves the Buddha emitting light to summon those from the ten directions.
Since the auspicious signs were manifested to inspire the assembly when the Bodhisattva arrived, this constitutes the Specific Introduction (*nidāna*).
Generally speaking, at the beginning of each of the seven locations and nine assemblies of that sutra, there are four elements: time, place, principal teacher, and retinue.

This single phrase [“the Buddha was staying at... with a great assembly”] encompasses those four. Here, “the Buddha” is the principal teacher; “the assembly” is the retinue; and “[staying at... is the place.

Since an assembly must necessarily have a time, the four types of completeness (*catuḥ-saṃpad*) all arise at that specific occasion; therefore, they all belong to the "Specific Introduction" (*pratyeka-nidāna*).
As for the phrase "in various places," this refers to the seven locations (*sapta-sthāna*); by citing the locations, the assemblies are subsumed.

If this were the case, there would be nine specific introductions, as is clearly evident from the text of that sutra itself. Next, the *Āgama* is cited to demonstrate that a single sutra may possess multiple general introductions (*sāmānya-nidāna*). Thus it is said.
This is because it is a brief citation of the first among the five matters of the general preface (*sūtra-pūrva-vastu*).
Since those scriptures collect many sūtras of varying lengths into a single collection, they are collectively named *Āgama*. Within this, the minor sūtras each have their own individual titles;

however, because their paper count is small compared to the collective title, they resemble chapters (*pāda*). Thus, at the beginning of every text, the five matters are established, and it is said that "chapter by chapter" [they are so].
These two examples demonstrate that the present sutra has two distinct introductory sections (*nidāna*).

Next, citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, specifically the second fascicle, there is the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Āyusya-parivarta*), which corresponds to the twenty-seventh chapter of the aforementioned [text], the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Parindanā-parivarta*).

This refers to the subsequent entrustment, for entrustment is precisely the dissemination (*parivarta*). This example answers the previous question regarding the inclusion of the dissemination section.

The examples cited previously are all instances of mutual illustration, clearly demonstrating that each [sūtra] possesses multiple introductory sections (*nidāna*) and main bodies of text (*pravartana*).
This serves as a response to the previous question: "How can a single sūtra have two introductory sections and a main body?

Regarding the phrase "none of these contradict," this concludes the preceding citations and illustrations to clarify the present intent; it means that in each of these sūtras, there are individually many introductory sections and main bodies of text.
The general principle is not in conflict with this specific case; yet, since this single sutra contains two prefaces, how could there be any contradiction?

This is the question raised here, which is then resolved by this concluding critique. However, one must understand that there is an underlying intention of analogy (*upamāna*) for the full meaning of this passage to be exhausted.
Why is this so? Because even in those aforementioned sutras and others, each is still permitted to have multiple prefaces and main texts without contradiction.
Since these [previous] points are contradictory, why would this present sutra—being merely twofold—be able to create an obstacle or give rise to doubt?
Were it not so, the preceding meaning would remain unresolved, and the subsequent point could not be easily explained.
Next, the two doubts are explained: the first arises because of the preceding Āgama, and the second arises because of the preceding *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
First, fearing that the previously cited Āgama contains many general introductory sequences (*sāmānyanidāna*), a doubt arises, saying:

"If that is so, why does this present sūtra not likewise place the five matters at the beginning of its 'Root Chapter' (*mūlaparivarta*)? To address and explain this, it is said: "Because it is not the primary opening."

Furthermore, the sequence of the headings is as previously explained. Next, regarding the explanation of the causes: the number of doubts in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is identical to what was stated before.

As for those circulated separately, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* has two sections, whereas this present sutra has two in its "Original Gate" (*honmon*) but only one in its "Trace Gate" (*shakumon*).

Because it contains exhortations to uphold [the teaching] but lacks the formal entrustment (*parindanā*), it is called "separate. Although the previous two doubts have been resolved, many further obstacles still arise.
What is meant by this? It refers to the *Āgama*, which is neither a sequential [text] nor has the *Mahāvaipulya* been completed. If one explains it thus, the *Āgama* includes various other sūtras;

therefore, although it is not the primary sequential text, it is still permissible to establish the five matters therein. In the present case, since the root text is a single sūtra, it is not the primary sequential text and thus the five matters cannot be established.
As for the *Mahāvaipulya*, because it adapts directly to the requirements of the time, it remains so even though it is not yet complete.

However, since the preceding discussion addressed the entrustment (*parindanā*) of this sutra while simultaneously discussing the initiation of the "Original Gate," the entrustment had not yet been fully treated.

If that is so, then this is not a parallel case; how can it be cited as such? It is precisely for this reason that what was said previously—namely, that one must understand the "analogy by way of comparison" (*upamāna*)—is correct.

If one were to take it in a general sense, it could serve as a category of example; however, if discussed according to its actual substance, it is merely an analogy intended to clarify the meaning of that [other] sutra.
If even a single [text] can accommodate many, how much more so this [work], which cannot possibly lack both? Although the *Avataṃsaka* contains many [elements], it serves as the primary model;
for while that [work] consists of a single general introduction followed by many specific ones at the end of each assembly, it also includes praises of the Dharma and exhortations to uphold it.
Though these differ from the present case, they nonetheless share the same underlying meaning. Therefore, using the *Avataṃsaka* as a model is quite sufficient.

The following two cases are merely general analogies. That is to say, since even a single sutra referred to generically as "Āgama" may possess multiple common introductory sections (*nidāna*), how much more so should there not be two distinct introductions for the present work?

This is because both the *Mahāratnakūṭa*—consisting of over forty assemblies—and the new *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*—consisting of sixteen assemblies—are likewise compilations of many sutras, and their structural principles are identical.
Within the Āgamas, there are all such matters as these; this constitutes many general and specific instances that can be used as analogies.
Because they had not yet been translated during the time of the Imperial Court’s compilation, he broadly cited those Āgamas as analogies.
As for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, since its force of analogy still exists, how could it be otherwise? It cannot stand alone, and thus they are combined. Next, the conclusion and demonstration:

The meaning of "existence" therein and "non-existence" here is roughly as follows. One may also conclude and explain that the meaning of "if there is" and "if there is not" within this context is such;
therefore, it is said, "it is thus, it is thus. These words of "it is thus, it is thus" serve to conclude and indicate what has been explained previously, and do not refer to what follows.

From here below begins the fourth section: Explaining the Textual Methodology. This sutra is titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; its purport is profound and vast.
Although the structural analysis (*ko-p’an*) has exhausted its essentials, the interpretation must attain its proper method.

The title of this sutra is *Saddharma*, as can be roughly understood from the aforementioned structural analysis; however, to explain it in detail, nothing short of its subtle methodology will suffice. Therefore, it is explained next.
As for the methods: since they are so subtle that it is difficult to apply them while following the text without first gaining a comprehensive understanding, I shall first explain them in detail.
This sutra requires special attention; other cases may be understood by analogy. Therefore, this must be distinguished, whereas others are omitted for brevity.
Otherwise, how could the profound and subtle significance be revealed? Thus, one must clarify the methods and expound the means for revealing the profound significance. Since these are esoteric...

If one were to proceed directly through the text without first providing a preliminary analysis and explanation, there would be no way to comprehend it; therefore, it is necessary to first briefly clarify its characteristics.
Since this sutra specifically requires supplementation from other texts, we shall provide a detailed analysis here, while other texts may be understood by analogy;
thus, they are not discussed beforehand. This section consists of three parts: first, the enumeration of the numbers; second, the listing [of the items]; and third, the detailed explanation.

It is called the "Threefold Exegesis. First, regarding the term *tiē* (postscript/application): *tiē* refers to "application" (*pèitiē*), which means attaching and following along with the text to provide a word-by-word commentary.

Furthermore, *tiē* also means "detailed instruction" (*wěitiē*), which carries the sense of "probing and informing"; it refers to employing specific methods to comment on the text word by word so that the meaning of the passage becomes clear, smooth, and secure.
The phrase "as four" indicates the enumeration. Alternatively, it is said that these four are precisely the methods.

Regarding the enumeration of the dharmas: first they are presented as headings, and subsequently explained as the basis. Alternatively, it may be said that these headings indicate the capacity for those four enumerations, and the subsequent listing of names follows from this.
Or, one might say collectively that they indicate the two sets of dharma enumerations; both interpretations are logically consistent.

For now, we shall follow the second sense, meaning that the method for applying the text being clarified here consists of four parts. One should consider that the enumeration is established for the purpose of composition.

The reason for employing these four [categories] is that there are further sacred words (*āgama*) available as authoritative evidence to demonstrate their characteristics, enabling one to recognize them in advance.
Although the textual descriptions of their essential forms need not be exhaustive, their meaning is fully conveyed; thus, there are these four.

Next, regarding the enumeration of their names, each of these four individually corresponds to the fourfold exposition found in the commentaries on the text—namely, the listing of the names and numbers of those four dharmas.

...up to the point where the characteristics of those four dharmas are demonstrated; that is, because one first provides these four kinds of explanations for those four dharmas, it is designated as "four.
Next, following the four names previously listed, their meanings and characteristics are explained, which consist of four distinct parts.

Within the initial listing of the numbers: first, the numbers are correctly listed; second, the functions and differences are clarified. Regarding the first of these, the correct listing of the numbers: [The text continues with the specific enumeration and analysis of the four dharmas.]
One should say "listing the names" (*ming liè*); why then do you say "listing the numbers" (*shù liè*)? Other texts do not follow this precedent.
Furthermore, to claim that "number" is merely "name"—as in the expression "names and numbers"—is incorrect. Now, I maintain that the single word "now" (*jīn*) here seems to contain two meanings:
namely, indicating the number and listing the names. In full, it should read: "Now, by means of four dharmas, I shall annotate and explain the scriptural text. What are they?"
The "four" refers to the four [categories] such as causes and conditions; here they are briefly indicated by a single term, hence it is said thus.

Among these, the numbers one, two, three, and so forth are the numerals, while the rest are names. Alternatively, the enumeration may serve as the general heading, while the specific numbers one, two, and so forth constitute the listing of names.
From "Beginning with 'Thus'... onwards, this section discusses the differences in the momentum and numerical application of the *śāstra*, which corresponds to the two points previously distinguished.
Reflect on this now according to the latter meaning: the application and its presence or absence; the causes and conditions, which clarify the origins from which the teaching arises;
the distinctions among the teachings produced as categorized by doctrine; and the manifestation of the fundamental and the derivative (*honji-suijaku*).
There has been this for a long time. Contemplating the clarity of the mind reveals that regarding the three kinds of wondrous functions, there is no cause more essential or ultimate than this.
It is precisely for the practitioner of today to cultivate and thereby attain it.
Since the Way is entirely complete within the mind, one should seek it within oneself rather than focusing exclusively on external matters. The explanation of the method listed above is thus; below—
The application of clarity and the enumeration of momentum differ; the text contains three sentences. First, it clarifies that its substance necessarily possesses four aspects.

Second, it clarifies that one must first grasp the essential source. Third, it clarifies that value lies in the essential meaning rather than in voluminous writing, which can be sought out; the subsequent text further explains this in detail.
Herein, the initial listing serves as the sequence for citing evidence, while the second explanation establishes the primary discourse on the enumeration of momentum.

This serves as the basis for the subsequent demonstration of the characteristics, which will be seen by oneself later. Next, the reason for this clarifies the purpose for employing the four dharmas mentioned above to provide an explanation;
"reason" (so-yi) carries the sense of causal conditions (*pratyaya*) as well as the sense of underlying intent (*abhiprāya*).
Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying the reason for the number four, and second, clarifying the reason for the four names. Furthermore, there is first the number and then the names.
Furthermore, the reason for the first four [categories] is as follows; next, the reason for these four is due to what was previously stated regarding the intent behind enumerating them.
Since these are the four dharmas, it is necessary to clarify the reasons for both of these; this is precisely the explanation of their names and numbers.

Moreover, they arise from the preceding mention of "abiding in the middle. As for the initial question, it was because it was previously stated that [the method] is employed throughout from beginning to end.
Regarding the "four meanings that clarify the text," why is it that this [section] does not simply reduce the scope and exclusively use the four as the basis for explanation?
What is the reason for this? "Fēi" means "not so. This phrase "for this one reason" calls back to the three preceding points;

this [section] directly discusses their general enumeration without yet entering into their specific names. The answer consists of three sentences, which respond to the three preceding reasons. First, the response:

The second [section] answers the first [point] not extensively, while the third answers it concisely, specifically employing four intentions. That is to say, if one were to explain extensively, it would exceed the four limits;
if the words deviate from reason, they become prolix. Since the wise value principle, they do not favor such deviations and prolixity, as these cause the intellect to retreat.
Therefore, it is said that this causes the intellect to regress; for those of later generations who are studious, clear-headed, and intelligent, [this teaching] serves to inspire them.

Regarding such a person, Zhongni said, "The younger generation is to be feared"; thus, it is called wisdom (*jñāna*). The explanation is fundamentally intended to cause beings to reach the essential point.
If one’s application of the mind and practice are already manifold, yet one does not act accordingly, what is the purpose?
For this reason, it does not exceed four; if it were reduced by even one from these four, the meaning and intent of the sutra would not be able to be fully encompassed, clarified, and explained.

The commentary exists primarily to clarify the meaning of the sutra; since that meaning is not fully evident, what purpose would a commentary serve? For this reason, it is impossible to omit even one of these four.
These two points are essentially complementary chapters. Furthermore, there are two further meanings: namely, the distinction between persons and the distinction between dharmas.

In this text, for the sake of brevity, only the first point is revealed. When we reach the actual commentary below, the remaining two will be clarified. Failing to grasp this intention, one will find it difficult to harmonize the text.

First, there is the reason for the classification according to the teachings (*yōkyō*); next, the actual clarification of the classification according to the teachings; and finally, the conclusion. This is the first [section].

Regarding the term "universal" (*tong*): it universally encompasses the six sense objects throughout the ten directions, reconciling the provisional and the real, and all matters of response and transformation;

thus it is called "universal. Now, this treatise discusses the matters of response and transformation regarding the Buddha-vehicle within the teachings of sound in this land; therefore, it is "particular" (*bie*).

It cites the universal to give rise to the particular, and because it is through the particular that the truth is correctly revealed, it is "correct" (*zheng*). Without the teaching, there would be no capacity for such [realization].

This must be clarified because it is being distinguished and manifested; one should know that although these two phrases differ in their general and specific aspects, both clarify the relationship between response and stimulus (*ganying*).
Here, the former [phrase] merely cites the stimulus, while the latter merely cites the response; by citing each from one side, the equality of their meaning is revealed.

Furthermore, one must know that the former phrase has many general meanings, while the latter phrase has many specific distinctions; otherwise, they cannot be harmonized. This was previously explained.

Although this resonance (ganying) is as vast as empty space, it does not transcend the matters of the six sense objects, provisional and ultimate truths, and their convergence, as fully explained in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and other texts.
Regarding what is called "sound in this land," sound refers to verbal teaching;

because the capacities and inclinations (*mōki*) differ, this land takes this as its stimulus for resonance, and thus the Tathāgata provides the corresponding benefit through it. Nevertheless, it is not [the case that this is the only mode].

One does not attain the Way because of other dusts; it is only because they are few that one speaks of them as secondary, whereas the primary ones are numerous, and thus it is said so. It is the same with other lands.
"Amṛta" (sweet dew) is the medicine of immortality in the heavens, which is a metaphor for the Great Nirvana and its four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Gate" refers to verbal teaching; "opening" means revealing. This means that one teaches and benefits others through vocal instruction in accordance with their capacities.
This is for the purpose of revealing the gate of Great Nirvana to all sentient beings, enabling them to thereby penetrate and realize the secret treasury of the three virtues.
Furthermore, regarding such terms as "Buddha-activity," there are both general and specific meanings.

The general meaning refers to using these vocal sounds as the Buddha’s activity for the benefit of sentient beings. The specific meaning refers to using these vocal sounds to act as [a teacher] for all sentient beings.
The matter of attaining Buddhahood is likewise the meaning of the "Gate of Ambrosia" (*amṛta-dvāra*). As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "There is nirvāṇa and there is great nirvāṇa.

Since nirvāṇa has both small and great aspects, its gates are the same. Although these gates exist both generally and specifically, according to the intent of the provisional teachings, they are fundamentally intended for distinction.
To clarify the intent of this present sūtra, they should all be understood in their specific sense. Thus, the provisional and the real, the coarse and the subtle, are mutually dependent.

The essential meaning of "severance" (jue) is entirely contained within these few words; yet, this is not merely the provisional teaching (yiao jiao), nor does it accord with the initial textual exposition of the sequence of the Original and the Traced (benji). One should reflect upon this.

Next, in clarifying the reason for the sequence of the Original and the Traced, it is further necessary to explain them by means of the Original and the Traced, precisely because they occupy a middle position.
Furthermore, what is the meaning of this being considered the "middle way"? Within this sutra, the matters of the *honji* (original ground) and *suijaku* (traces) are extensively discussed.
Previous explanations based on the classification of teachings (*kyōhan*) were essential for their respective divisions, yet they did not address the relationship between the distant and the near.

If one does not further rely on the *honji-suijaku* perspective, the intent of the sutra remains incomplete; it is only through this interpretation that the true essentials can be fully harmonized. Therefore, this [interpretation] is truly essential.
To abide in the middle, one must next further explain this by referring back to the original source. The text also contains three points:
first, it clarifies the provisional teaching, which pertains to the immediate traces; second, it clarifies that one must further discuss the distant origin;

and third, if one does not discuss the origin but knows only the immediate benefits, one has not yet recognized the distant advantages, and thus the intent of the sutra remains uncomprehended. Finally, it concludes with the distant origin as the essential point, for it is necessary to abide in the middle.

One must rely on this [distinction] to explain the general meaning of these three greatnesses, which is also as previously stated. Although the first [section] cites both of the preceding two [greatnesses], it does so to present the causes and conditions for establishing the correct teaching;

that is, it specifically takes up the sequence of the causes and conditions for the establishment of the teaching. Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*) and "reality" (*tattva*): "expedient means" refers to the three [vehicles], while "reality" refers to the Perfect [Vehicle].

Within the three expedient vehicles, two are shallow and distinct, while one is deep; because the name "expedient means" applies universally to all three, it is necessary to further [distinguish them].

This is a distinct statement. What is meant here is that "expedient" (*upāya*) and "real" (*tattva*) refer to the distinctions between the four teachings and five periods in terms of the depth of their doctrines and the sequence of time—namely, the horizontal and vertical classifications.
Furthermore, because the expedient and real were previously divided into separate streams and fixed, they are considered "shallow";
whereas now, they are merged into a subtle and boundless synthesis, and are thus considered "deep. "Deep" refers to the wondrous, while "shallow" refers to the coarse. This is indeed the case.

This refers to what is called "the coarse and the subtle. Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "I shall now explain that which is the foremost, most difficult to believe and most difficult to understand"—this is precisely its meaning.

While the meaning of the provisional teachings (*kyō*) must indeed be understood in this way, although these various functions of the provisional teachings are revealed to demonstrate such differences and convergences, they are all merely matters of manifested traces (*jiseki*) and do not pertain to the fundamental reality (*honji*) or the long-term perspective.
