This first anticipates the inquiry by asking: "For what reason is it possible to be thus? Therefore, it says, "For what reason?
Next, the text directly cites the passage from the latter part of the *Honmon* (the "Original Gate") concerning the benefits across the three periods of time to explain the following section.

The Tathāgata raises these three matters to manifest that he possesses these three powers; thus, he is able to benefit sentient beings throughout the three periods of time. However, as for these three phrases...
Although these are sequentially applied to the three periods of time for practical use, each individual name and meaning is itself non-spatial and cannot be fixed or localized.
When the Tathāgata gave these names at that time, he intended precisely to manifest the nine periods within these three;
therefore, by citing them to explain the three periods, one explains the nine periods, and even every thought-moment. It is for this reason.

Because it is subtle and wondrous, and without fixed direction, it is called "spontaneous preaching. As explained in the subsequent text, one should know that this is a general discussion of the meaning of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

If one were to distinguish them individually—such as each world and each type—one would find that each possesses the meaning of the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold purposes), which alone exhausts their full significance.
This is as detailed in the section on "Function" in the *Xuanyiwen* and in the subsequent passage on "Entering."
This explains it.

The preceding section has finished explaining the causes and conditions; from the next phrase onward, the conclusion summarizes the resulting cause, meaning that by virtue of the aforementioned causes and conditions, the "Preface Section" (序分) arises. That is to say, it is due to the three periods of time and the two gates mentioned previously.

Taking the three capacities—those of the vehicle (*yāna*), the lineage (*gotra*), ripening (*paripāka*), and liberation (*vimukti*)—as the cause, and the Buddha’s response to these three capacities as the condition, through the conjunction of these causes and conditions, the introduction (*nidāna*) of the wondrous teaching arises.

If the preceding section is taken as the three causes and conditions, then this passage should conclude by stating: "Because of such factors as these, there is the sequence of the introduction and the main body."
This constitutes a general division; however, since this specific colophon has now been composed, the preceding section is not treated as a general division.

Nevertheless, it actually possesses the sense of being a general introduction, serving as the basis for the subsequent transmission following the main body of the text. Because the introduction occupies the very beginning, it is here treated separately according to its specific origin.
This refers to the circumstances under which the Buddha himself delivered the introduction at that time, rather than the introduction compiled after his passing by those who gathered the scriptures.

Because it is the cause that leads [to the main teaching], the statement regarding the sequence and division lies precisely in distinguishing the general introduction from the specific intent of compilation and circulation after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
thus, it does not concern the present. Therefore, the next part directly cites the specific introduction—reflect on this, reflect on this.
The following phrase clarifies the cause leading to the main exposition (bhāṣya), meaning that by means of the causes and conditions of the introductory section, one arrives at the main exposition.
Therefore, based on the preceding introduction, it is established that by initiating the hearing of the correct teaching, one obtains various benefits such as the seeds [of enlightenment];

taking this as the cause and the Buddha’s arising [of the teaching] as the condition, through the conjunction of these causes and conditions, there occurs the arising of the wondrous and correct teaching.
Within the text, the causes, conditions, and that which is produced can be fully investigated; the first assembly is as follows in the three types mentioned in the subsequent passage.
The "rare and extraordinary auspicious signs" refer to the six signs manifested in the two lower lands. "Yong-yong" (reverently gazing) means looking up with respect;

the text says "gazing up and awaiting with reverence," which means that upon witnessing these extraordinary signs, all develop a heart of reverence and yearning, desiring to hear the complete, perfect, and wondrous Way.
Taking this as the cause, the Buddha arises to cause them to open, show, awaken to, and enter it.
Entering into this is precisely for the purpose of planting seeds, ripening them, and liberating them; therefore, it is taught that there is a "Section on Correct Exposition.

The final line below clarifies the causes and conditions by which the "Section on Circulation" arises. Although the text here is somewhat brief, it nonetheless possesses the significance of being derived from the correct [teaching].
Although the initial portion clarifies the responsive conditions, [the subsequent section] serves as the basis for the arising of the Section on Circulation.

This refers to the fulfillment of the causes and conditions for the response [of the Buddha]. The phrase "not only" clarifies that the preceding two parts both concern benefiting sentient beings while the Buddha was still in the world;
furthermore, it shows that these two present sections will also respond to and benefit those with the karmic conditions after his parinirvāṇa.

Therefore, it is said "not only," so as to allow for universal application. The formal conclusion of the compilation (*saṃgīti*) lies precisely here; thus, one should know that the universal introduction (*sāmānyanidāna*) belongs to the compilation.
Because it collects and circulates the benefits for the final age, there is good reason why the ancients also called this the "Preface for Circulation.

Regarding the phrase "in the latter five hundred years," the various sūtras and śāstras differ; however, according to the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, the present time constitutes five hundred-year periods.
Thus it is said: in the first hundred years, liberation is firm; in the second hundred years, meditative concentration is firm.
In the third five-hundred-year period, the firmness of observing the precepts [prevails]; in the fourth five-hundred-year period, the firmness of extensive learning;
and in the fifth five-hundred-year period, the firmness of practicing generosity. What is now called the "final five" refers precisely to this last hundred-year period.

If one follows the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, it clarifies that there are five distinct periods of five hundred years each. The first through the fourth are the same as previously mentioned, with the exception of the fifth.
Regarding the statement that "the five hundred years of fierce contention shall endure," this refers to the final fifth period of five hundred years.

If one speaks of a single five-hundred-year period alone, it remains somewhat restricted to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (the *Zhengfa nianchu jing*). However, if it refers to the fifth of five hundred-year periods, it corresponds to the *mofa* (Dharma-ending age).
Such differences likely arise from the distinctions between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings; for the most part, this follows the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*.
This passage is intended to refer specifically to the present sutra; for at the end of the "Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter in the latter part of this scripture, there is mention of these "five hundred.

This refers to the period when the merit of the Dharma gradually thins, defilements gradually increase, and holy sages gradually diminish, and it is said thus because [the Buddha] exhorts [them] to circulate [the teaching] as a causal condition for benefits such as planting seeds [of merit].
The previous brief explanation of the three parts was thus; however, if one relies solely on this [explanation], although the text is concise, it does not fully accord with the underlying principle.
Why is this? Because, compared to what preceded it, the causes are extremely numerous while the three parts that arise from them are only one;
thus, the cause is vast and extensive, whereas the fruit is exceedingly subtle. Now, within this [section], we clarify...

Although this single phrase concerning the introduction, the main body, and the circulation contains the meanings of both types of introduction, main body, and circulation, it is because it fully elucidates the causes and conditions of the two gates and three divisions. Furthermore, how could it merely contain one, two, or three;
rather, this single phrase itself contains the meanings of the three types of two gates and three divisions, as it fully elucidates the causes and conditions of the three periods.
This is due to the conditions [of the teaching]. Furthermore, why should this single phrase alone not inherently contain the meanings of the immeasurable two gates and three divisions?
This is because it was previously explained that the three periods and nine periods of time are infinite and inexhaustible in every moment.
As the Sūtra says: "Since I attained the Way from immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable kalpas in the past, I have always been present..."
This is because this teaching of the Dharma transforms and edifies beings, remaining eternally present and indestructible until the end of the future;
it is only in this way that the cause and effect are properly encompassed by their respective characteristics. One may infer the fruit from the cause, as a single word summarizes all.
Therefore, the text speaks directly of the Prologue, the Main Body, and the Circulation alone—neither cumbersome nor lacking in completeness; it may truly be called perfect in every respect.
The previous summary was composed of two sections of three parts each, with the text slightly corrected for this purpose.
If that is so, why are there now four sections of three? The former was a major outline, and its text consisted merely of two gates, each with three parts;

whereas the present one provides a detailed analysis of its causes and conditions, as the Fundamental Gate fully possesses the three periods of time. What was previously called "taking the essential meaning" refers precisely to this.
In this way, the principles and the resulting benefits of this sūtra are so profound and vast that even the great void would not suffice as a metaphor;
how could they possibly be compared to the benefits resulting from other sūtras?
When explaining the principles of this sūtra in such a manner, how could it be the same as the interpretations of other masters? To say otherwise would be utterly inferior.

Observing how past and present commentators have explained these causes and conditions—some drawing upon the intent of various sūtras and śāstras, others following the literal phrasing and specific details of the current text—their words are merely prolix while their underlying meaning remains obscured.
It can truly be said that although they possess the traces [of the teaching], their minds regarding those traces are ultimately quite vulgar.
A person of clear wisdom will certainly know this for themselves without waiting for a full exposition; for now, I shall briefly indicate what has not yet been addressed.
How could one possibly detail them all? This is, in brief, the nature of the causes, conditions, and benefits of these three sections of this sutra.
Next, regarding the demonstration of the characteristics of the teaching: this refers to a brief exposition of the characteristics of interpreting this sutra according to its teachings.
Since the teachings possess both general and specific aspects, if their characteristics were not distinguished, the meaning of this sutra would not be revealed.
One must clarify that this sutra uses the teachings on the two types of "coarse" [causes]—the "perishing" and the "awaiting"—to reveal the Perfect and Wondrous teaching; this is its characteristic.

Although the previous demonstration of the characteristics of causes and conditions was already sufficient to know this wondrousness, the primary intent of the preceding section did not focus on the differentiation of the various teachings;
therefore, it is necessary to clarify this further, which is why the text provides an extensive analysis herein.
The provisional teachings are coarse and manifest, while this reality is subtle and wondrous; such is their characteristic. Within this, it is also demonstrated by means of three divisions.

However, this is done according to the general pattern of a single set of three divisions, without distinguishing between the provisional and the fundamental, or the first and second [sets]. Although there is a distinction between near and far within these two, they are both the Buddha-vehicle of the Perfect Teaching;
thus, they are treated generally. Furthermore, the preceding section on causes and conditions and the subsequent conclusion clarify that the three [vehicles] arise from [this reality].
The "causal" (hetu) [section] also merely speaks generally of one type of threefold division, yet its meaning encompasses multiple types as clarified previously;
here it is likewise. It merely speaks generally of "one and three," which refers to the second and third, and even to many sets of three.

Since the intended meaning can be understood by following the momentum of what preceded, it is sufficient to state it generally. Within this, each of the three divisions contains five phrases, all of which...
The first four [phrases] exclude what is not, while the last one reveals what is; that which is excluded consists of the five vehicles and the seven expedient means (*upāya*).
Since these are all provisional teachings bestowed in the past to guide and bring others to maturity, they are not the original intention.

Otherwise, it would imply a lack of seed-potential (*gotra*), whereas here we are precisely opening and breaking through [delusions]; therefore, none of them apply. Since these do not apply, it is the One Reality of Perfection (*ekayāna-saṃpūrṇa*).
This fuses and transcends the subtle and wondrous characteristics of the teachings. Each of these selections is not the Middle Way; rather, the four phrases all pertain to the first [category]:

first, the Human and Heavenly (Śrāvaka) vehicle; next, the three [subsequent] vehicles. These also follow the conventional order. Within the first, the Human and Heavenly vehicle, it is called "clearly ascending" because it contrasts with the three lower realms of turbid sinking;
this teaching is precisely the Way of the Distinction between Ming and Qing. Second, the Two Vehicles are the Path of the Lesser Vehicle.

The interpretation of principle is narrow; because it contrasts with the inferior [teachings] while encompassing the Great [Vehicle], it is called "small. Since phenomena and principle are mutually identical, it encompasses the three vehicles.

Because it shares the same practice as the *Pitaka* yet does not accord with it, it is "not the same. Because it is neither prior nor subsequent, it is termed "turbid. For what reason are these not provided with a preface? The meaning is as follows:
the correct explanation for this is clarified in the middle [section]. Herein, "upright," "straight," and so forth, accord with the principle.
Because the Way is free from the two extremes and from deviance or crookedness, it is called "straight and upright" (*ṛju*).

The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* states that one "practices the great straight path without hindrance," which is precisely the meaning of being straight and upright. Because it is straight and upright, one abandons expedient means (*upāya*).

Expedient means refers to the preceding [teachings] of the five periods and seven assemblies; because these are abandoned, there is no hindrance. This term "abandonment" carries the meanings of refuting, abolishing, opening up, merging, awaiting, and severing.
It is contained therein: the Unsurpassed Way is the true path practiced by all Buddhas.
Since this preface is composed for that very purpose, it is the Preface to the True Doctrine (*zhengzong*).
As the True Doctrine itself abandons expedient means to speak only of this reality, the preface is written solely for this and not for that; therefore, as stated previously, it does not...

The meaning lies in this: the skillful means that were previously abandoned were simply errors. In other sutras, there are expressions such as "following others," which may be combined with other elements or used alone, or may be employed in conjunction with others;
however, because this sutra speaks exclusively according to its own intention, it directly abandons the path of skillful means.
As for the Unsurpassed Way, in contrast to the preceding skillful means, it is the true and real Way, which is also the Buddha.

If one correlates "Perfect Way" (Yuán-dào) with the title of the scripture, it is precisely the "Sublime Way" (Miào-dào). Since [the Way] is already correct and simply constitutes relinquishment, to compose a preface would merely be to initiate and dismantle the preliminary expedient methods;
since those methods no longer exist, there is nothing further for which to compose a preface. Thus, it is said that "no [preface] is made," and so forth.
This clearly reveals that [the author] still maintains the intention to distinguish the right from the wrong. The following two examples are likewise so. This is the central point.

This is not like the previous [section], where right and wrong were clarified by way of the path; here, all is clarified by way of wisdom. Since the preceding [discussion of] humans and devas concerns worldly dharmas, this is stated accordingly.
Thus, the following three are all supramundane dharmas, each of which possesses a metaphorical dharma (*dṛṣṭānta-dharma*).

The glow of a firefly removing darkness and illuminating objects is the most inferior; it is a metaphor for the wisdom of analytical observation (*vicaya-jñāna*) that contemplates arising and ceasing and breaks down all phenomena.
Because it is the most clumsy method for eliminating delusions and revealing principle, it is used as a metaphor; subsequent examples should be understood by analogy with this.
This metaphor originates from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which states: "A Bodhisattva practicing Prajñā for a single day illuminates the world like the sun, surpassing the light of fireflies.

This refers precisely to the practice of the Tripiṭaka. Therefore, the metaphor of the lamp of wisdom is now employed to represent the Tripiṭaka, while the metaphor of the torch represents that which is common to both the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas.

To "penetrate and reach" means that all phenomena are immediately empty; this differs from the "storehouse" (ālayavijñāna) and the "analytical reduction" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), which is why it is called "the essence of phenomena.
The metaphors of the stars and the moon distinguish them: the stars represent the wisdom prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), while the moon represents the wisdom attained upon entering the stages.

Because it illuminates the provisional aspects of the path of the *śāsana*, it is likened to the moon. Now, although the two preceding teachings differ, both illuminate emptiness; thus they are equal in meaning to the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) of the Distinct Teaching (*bipartite teaching*), and correspond accordingly.

Regarding "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that all-knowledge is the wisdom of the two vehicles, while the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) properly corresponds to the ten practices (*daśapratipatti*).

Because it issues forth into the provisional (*niryūha*) and penetrates the differences among all phenomena—differing from what precedes and following what comes after—it properly corresponds to this stage.

Since the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*) cultivate the middle [wisdom] and have not yet realized it, they also encompass this location; therefore, one should specifically point to the knowledge of the paths within the ten practices. The word "thought" (*cintā*) is not used here.
As for the reference [to the sun], it does not explicitly state that this dharma is such. Why? Because it does not employ it to introduce what precedes;

since it has already served as an introduction by means of the "expedient means of relinquishment" (*prahāṇopāya*)—merely teaching the Unsurpassed Way—it would be redundant to speak further of these matters here. Therefore, it does not specifically point to it.

Within this context, the metaphor of the sun’s radiance represents the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-encompassing wisdom). Among things in the world that dispel darkness and illuminate objects, nothing surpasses the sun; thus, it is used as a metaphor.
There is nothing that surpasses the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) for eliminating delusions and revealing the principle; this is because this sutra speaks exclusively of this wisdom.

When the light of the sun appears, other lights become useless; likewise, when the knowledge of all modes is expounded, all other forms of knowledge are subsumed and cease to exist. Thus, it correctly teaches this [wisdom] while not teaching those other things.

Next, regarding the "words" (*akṣara*) in the section on circulation, these refer to the Teaching. To exclude what is not [the ultimate], it is as previously stated: the initial metaphors of the *śāla* leaf and so forth represent the teachings for humans and devas;
this is the passage from the "Chapter on the Infant’s Practice" (*Bālaputradharmaparyāya*) of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

The Sūtra clarifies that there are many kinds of infants, but Danqiu (Zhiyi) judges them collectively as nothing other than the partial and the perfect—that is, the gradual and the sudden—because the core tenets of that Sūtra consist of only these two.
Each of these is numerous, and I shall not describe them all in detail here; this "yellow leaf" refers specifically to the infant among humans and devas.
The term "infant" is used as a general metaphor for those of minor virtue, yet this refers to the very smallest of infants.
Although this single passage could be explained at some length, I have summarized it by extracting the essentials. As the Sūtra says: "Just as when that infant cries out..."
The parents then gave him only yellow leaves from a willow tree, saying, "This is your gold. Upon seeing this, the child immediately began to cry bitterly.
Or, they might give him wooden oxen, wooden horses, or wooden figures of men and women; when the infant sees these, he conceives of them as real and stops crying.
This is used as a metaphor for how the Tathāgata, in order to stop sentient beings from committing various grave evils, speaks to them [in this way].
In the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa), there are [the qualities of] permanence, bliss, self, and purity. When sentient beings hear of this, they take pleasure in being born in the heavens;

consequently, they cease to commit evil and instead perform various wholesome deeds. The Sūtra merely summarizes and combines the four virtues of the heavens. According to the commentary (*shu*), it correlates them as follows:

the willow tree represents false permanence; the yellow leaves represent false purity; the wooden ox and wooden horse represent false bliss; and the wooden man and wooden woman represent [false self].

Although this false self (mṛṣātman) offers these counter-arguments, it does not explain their underlying reasons. Now, it is said that [these beings] are called "false" because they are soft and difficult to destroy, therefore "permanent";
because their physical forms are bright and clear, therefore "pure"; because they ride on vehicles for sport, therefore "joyful";

and because they resemble humans, yet are not truly so—failing to understand this, they mistakenly claim them to be such; thus, all are termed "false. Furthermore, the sutra merely combines [the first four] with those in the heavens.

Regarding the phrase "virtue does not speak of the human realm," Danqiu’s commentary states: "The meaning here, when inferred, should include four examples within the human realm—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—which are omitted from the text for brevity.
This intention is precisely that because the Buddha fully expounds the vehicles of humans and devas to cease the three lower evil realms, these [four examples] must exist.

Now, taking the intent of the text, this serves as a general metaphor for the teachings of humans and devas; the "half-syllable" (ardhamātrā) is contrasted with the "full" (pūrṇa) to obtain [the complete meaning].

This name also appears in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, both instances serving as metaphors. Within the sūtra, only the "full letters" (*pūrṇākṣara*) that can fulfill [the meaning] are mentioned—namely, the *Vyākaraṇa*—while the "half-letters" (*ardhākṣara*) which serve as the metaphors themselves are not mentioned; it is unclear what these refer to.

Commentators of both ancient and modern times have followed the text wherever it exists and provided explanations for it, yet where the text lacks [such terms], they simply remained silent. However, since the sūtras consistently employ analogies, the full letters must indeed be present.
For example, regarding the "half-syllable" (*ardha-akṣara*): how could one speak only of the Dharma without mentioning its analogy? This is certainly not yet fully understood.
According to the *Wenzi pin* (Chapter on Syllables), the half-syllable refers to the *Siddham* script of the Western lands, or perhaps to the phonemes (*mātṛkā*).

The Sūtra itself states that because it is the root of all sūtras, records, and treatises, it is called the "Fundamental. In the secular world of the Western lands, it is used for the instruction of beginners.

One must first study these half-syllables (*ardha-akṣara*) and only thereafter practice the remaining full-syllables (*pūrṇa-akṣara*); thus the Sūtra says, "First teach the half-syllables, and only then teach the full-syllables.
The *Vyākaraṇa* treatise uses this as a metaphor for first teaching the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) and subsequently expounding the Full Teaching (*Pūrṇa-deśanā*).

Since this is identical to what is traditionally recorded regarding the secular laws of the West, we know that by means of those worldly [distinctions between] the two—the half and the full—[the distinction between the vehicles is established].

The Buddha’s teaching of the two vehicles—the provisional and the ultimate—that transcend the mundane world, is thus clarified. Although Master Lang of Hexi personally received the *Nirvāṇa Tripiṭaka* from the Buddha, his own commentaries remain incomplete;
I too lack the leisure for a full discussion at present. For now, one should understand it as follows:
the "half-syllables" (*ardha-akṣara*) serve as a metaphor for the ninefold teachings of the Hīnayāna, that is, the Tripiṭaka, because they do not fully expound the ultimate principle.

The name "Half-Sequence" (Ban-ci) is not found in the texts of the *Sūtras* or *Śāstras*, nor in the treatises on common and distinct characters; it is merely established by analogy with what precedes and follows, based on the principles and meanings of the Dharma.

This is because within the *Śāstras* there are the names "Common Teaching" (*sāmānya-dharma*) and "Distinct Teaching" (*viśeṣa-dharma*), and since "teaching" (*dharma*) refers to words and letters, these names are derived from the meanings they express.
It should be understood that both the provisional and the ultimate are fundamentally and correctly wondrous; as such, they have already transcended these [distinctions].

Since the Coarse [Teaching] lacks these qualities, what could possibly be circulated within it? In the Sūtras, the "full letters" (*pūrṇākṣara*) serve as a metaphor for the Vaipulya and the twelve divisions of the scriptures;
because this name still applies [to them], it is called the "perfectly full letters," which refers to the Great Parinirvāṇa and the perfectly wondrous twelve divisions.
These all constitute the primary teaching (*samyak-siddhānta*), which is absolute and beyond dependence. Among these, the first five phrases all refer to the "letters."

Why does it not say, "Because they are taken as texts according to the teachings they follow"? Since the latter [passages] are all worldly characters (*laukika-akṣara*), one could not initially claim them to be worldly characters.
These three sections point to the same single dharma; for what reason are they initially called "the Way" (*mārga*), next called "wisdom" (*jñāna*), and finally called "characters"?
This is likely because, when not yet differentiated, they collectively manifest a single consistency; yet, if they were to be distinguished...
This refers to the teaching on the object, the wisdom, and the doctrine—or alternatively, the teaching on principle and practice—which constitutes three of the four "ones" in the correct exposition.
The sequence is likewise as follows: the order in the sutras is thus, the profound meaning (*xuan-yi*) is also thus, and the underlying principle should also be so.
The essential intent here is to clarify, in general, the characteristics of the teachings concerning the various triads of dharmas, such as the three virtues; therefore, this is said.

Likewise, the general principle of the wondrous teaching does not transcend the two aspects of the relative and the absolute. Within this context, although the phrasing appears to be relative, its meaning simultaneously encompasses the absolute.
This means that these three categories—which exclude the provisional [teachings] such as the five and seven periods—are all identical to the real; the real is identical to the provisional.
They are neither provisional nor real, yet they are both provisional and real. In this way, these four propositions exhaustively encompass all phenomena.
Being neither right nor wrong, subtle and without fixed direction, and inconceivable—this is called the "Ultimate Wonder," which is the characteristic of this teaching.
Thus, the preceding conditions and causes, upon reaching this gate, together accomplish this Ultimate Wonder.
Next, to demonstrate the characteristics of the fundamental and the trace: this sutra fully elucidates this meaning;

now, to summarize it briefly, it means to analytically reveal the characteristics of the two periods—the fundamental and the trace—of this sutra, which are both wondrous and absolute across three divisions.
What are the characteristics of these two sets of three? There are six phrases in the text that reveal these characteristics, which, when grouped together, constitute three [sections]. First:

There are two lines that directly indicate the primary aspect (*hon-sō*). Following this, there are three subsequent lines that reveal the provisional aspect (*shaku-sō*), and finally, one line serves as a metaphor to clarify the preceding two aspects.
Within the first of these two primary aspects, the initial portion excludes the primary cause (*hon-in*), for what is proclaimed therein is not something separately grasped;
the subsequent single line directly indicates the primary fruit (*hon-ka*), for it is that which is expounded therein. This constitutes the reason for the beginning of the primary aspect.

Regarding the necessity of distinguishing the cause: since it has already been stated that what was first taught long ago is the "original" (hon), this term applies generally to both cause and effect.

However, in the present context, we are concerned with the effect and not the cause; to focus on the cause would entail errors, as clarified in the text. Therefore, it is necessary to distinguish [the meaning].

The intent here is precisely to distinguish [this Buddha] from other Buddhas, for it correctly receives the teachings on the original and manifested traces (*honjaku*) of Śākyamuni Buddha, and it correctly elucidates [the matter].

Since the Honored One himself has explained his own original and manifested traces (*honjaku*), how could one take as authoritative what was proclaimed by other Buddhas during the causal stage? If one were to take the words of other Buddhas, the fault would be as stated in the text;

therefore, we know that the intent is precisely to explain [the Buddha's own] meaning. Because the long practice of the path corresponds to the subsequent original fruit, it constitutes the original cause.
This is because all Buddhas of the three periods of time, when preaching the *Lotus Sūtra*, invariably employ two gates and three divisions.

It is said that the former Buddhas were also equal [to Śākyamuni]; thus, when the four phrases are first spoken at the beginning of the *Honmon* (Original Gate), they all state "all Buddhas," which refers precisely to this meaning.
Regarding the phrase "the Buddhas, viewed in relation to one another, are infinite": generally speaking, "original" (*hon*) is a term for the very beginning;

here, we are specifically discussing the exposition of this wondrous Dharma by Śākyamuni Buddha upon his initial attainment of enlightenment as being the "original. One must not point to distant causes as the original.
If one were to take what is proclaimed by others as being the words of other Buddhas, then there would have to be yet another Buddha before those other Buddhas.
Since it is stated that [the lineage] is beginningless, how could it have an end? This is not the intended meaning of our school;

therefore, such views must be excluded, for this is the primary treatise on the fundamental intent of the World-Honored One. To avoid prolixity, I shall not elaborate further on the interpretation of the meaning of the Buddha’s infinite intention.
The elucidations found in the *Mahādharmaparyāya-sūtra* have not yet been set forth; this phrase precisely serves to distinguish it from others.

Examine this carefully without doubt. Next, the primary exposition demonstrates that the wondrous threefold [nature] taught by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni constitutes the fundamental characteristic.

There is both a heading and an explanation, which may be understood as follows: when the wondrous cause is first fulfilled and the wondrous fruit is initially perfected, responding according to the conditions of sentient beings, it is termed [the response].

The superior, middling, and inferior words of the initial attainment of Buddhahood are precisely what is meant by the "virtue in the beginning, middle, and end" found in the sūtras; they are also called the "three words.
Thus, the words and the virtues share the same essence but differ in their functions. Since the "initial" refers to the fundamental meaning, it serves as its own explanation.
In this way, the meaning of the "fundamental" is self-evident and does not require further elaboration; therefore, it is said that "the intent can be understood."
The following three phrases clarify the three periods of the present and the future within the intermediate stage.

Although what is taught in all three periods clarifies both the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (saku), they are all designated as "traces" (saku). This is because subsequent events arise from the preceding original source (honzon);
therefore, they are all termed "traces. The term "intermediate" refers to the period after the initial realization of the single teaching of the ultimate reality and prior to the present day.
This is called the "intermediate period. As will be explained in detail below, this duration is extremely long;
even Maitreya, who is currently in the position of the Regent (Upapadya), does not yet equal it.

Therefore, it is stated generally that "since that time, I have always been here preaching the Dharma and transforming beings," as there were no occasions to emerge from this state other than during those two periods for the sake of converting others. For now, I shall briefly cite this point.

These two [examples] manifest the traces of the intermediate stage through the analogy of "furious exertion" (*visphūrjita*). In the sequence of the following text, they serve as direct metaphors for benefiting sentient beings in the present;

yet, here they are used as metaphors for the future because there are two meanings involved. The "shaking and brandishing" on the left and right represents the present, while the preceding [example] represents the future.
Since both of these explanations exist in the subsequent text, the former is for the present and this one is further for the future. If that is so...
The term "great power" (*mahāvega*) also possesses two meanings; how could it merely possess the two capacities of "exertion" (*vikrama*)? It should also possess the meaning of "transcendence.

Since this one [term] already possesses three [meanings], the other two follow by analogy; it is for this reason that the preceding citation was used to prove and explain the nine times (*navadhvika*).

The subsequent passage provides a detailed proof of its eternal and long-lasting nature, meaning that it reaches the limitlessness of the future. Question: Should it not simply be "correctly corresponding"?

Although each [text] has its own origin (*hon*) and manifestation (*saku*), each consists of three parts: the first parts are all termed the "origin" (Hon-san-bun), and the latter parts are all termed the "manifestation" (Jaku-san-bun).

The characteristics of origin and manifestation are thus clearly revealed; why then should the origin be omitted? Furthermore, the middle and lower sections are both termed "superior" (jō), the intermediate section is termed "middle" (chū), and from today onward they are all termed "inferior" (ge).
Thus, the origins are collectively termed the "introduction" (jo), and the intermediate sections are collectively termed the... [text ends].

If one asks whether it is correct that both "present" and "past" are designated by the term *liutong* (circulation), is this not so? Answer: Viewing it from a general perspective, it is indeed as you have argued;

however, there must be a profound underlying intent. Although we have not yet been able to ascertain it definitively, the reason why [the previous masters] did not previously speak of it with such sincerity was likely because they wished to take these three periods and three teachings—both the provisional and the real—and blend them together to establish them as a single reality.

This is because it reveals the subtle and wondrous principle that is without fixed direction. For example, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* possesses three parts, all of which are called the "Introduction";

the *Dharma* section has three parts, all of which are called the "Main Body"; and the *Sūtra of the Contemplation of Samantabhadra* also possesses three parts, all of which are called the "Circulation.
This is precisely because they collectively reveal this wondrous principle. Although these examples are not entirely identical, they are partially similar.

If one says this is not so, please wait for the insight of the wise. When it was asked why the fourfold distinctions of the provisional and the real (*honjaku*)—which were both clarified in the preceding section on causes and conditions—are not treated identically here, the answer is as follows: In the previous section, the sequence followed the structural divisions of the sutra’s text;

since the traces (*ke*) are used to reveal the source (*hon*), the traces were presented first and the source second. Furthermore, within the source itself, nothing is not subsumed under the three periods of time; therefore, the present day has been excluded [from the fourfold classification].

The preceding sections were all titled "Past"; here, in the main treatise, the relationship between the fundamental and the manifested is clarified by explaining how the fundamental descends to manifest.

Therefore, the fundamental is presented first, followed by the manifested. Furthermore, within the manifested itself, there are distinctions among three periods; thus, it is separated from the preceding "Past" to establish this intermediate stage, each for its own specific reason.
Consequently, there is no contradiction. Other differences exist and may be sought within the text; they cannot be described exhaustively here.

Next, the analogy of the "pair" reveals the characteristics of both the original (hon) and the trace (jaku), demonstrating why the respective determinations of the original and trace in the preceding [analogy] were established.
The "many branches and leaves" metaphor refers to the three layers of teaching mentioned above; the "single root" metaphor refers to the very first teaching mentioned above.

The inability to point directly at [the object] serves as a metaphor for the necessity of determining the original and trace individually, just as previously stated. This underlying intent is now made explicit through this combined analogy.
Regarding the passage "Because it emerges from this," the commentary states [as follows]. Question: It may be acceptable for [the four phrases] to be mutually dependent;

however, when one reaches the state of "absolute transcendence" (*juedai*) and discusses the inconceivable through these four phrases, how could it be appropriate to proceed in such a manner? Answer: We are currently discussing the characteristics (*xiang*) of the original and the trace (*benji*), not the nature (*xing*) of the original and the trace.

How can you suddenly raise this objection? Furthermore, we are currently discussing the original and the trace, not yet discussing the coarse and the subtle (*chumiao*); how can you suddenly [introduce this]?

The subtle meaning is difficult to fathom, and since the aspect of mutual dependence has not yet been discussed, how can one hastily raise the objection regarding absolute transcendence? This is certainly inappropriate.
Yet, such instances are numerous in the world—not merely one or two—and they all arise from a failure to reflect, leading instead to blind faith based on deluded sentiments.
Reflect upon this! The two meanings previously presented—the causal conditions and the provisional teachings—both apply within this gate.
The "present-day traces" (*jīng rì zhī jì shì*) mentioned previously refers precisely to the intent of this section when it was said that the teaching is explained by taking its underlying meaning.

The two sections encompass one another, and their meanings are fully exhausted; there is only a distinction between the general and the specific. Since the preceding "causes and conditions" (*yīn yuán*) constitutes the general framework for both the provisional and the real (*běn jí*) in this treatise, these four sections of the provisional and real both contain the principles of causes and conditions and the analysis according to the teachings (*yuē jiào*). Thus, it is so stated.
Such is the general outline of the provisional and ultimate aspects (*honji-suijaku*) of this sutra, as explained in detail in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) and the subsequent commentary.
Next, to demonstrate the aspect of contemplating the mind means to reveal that by observing one's own body and mind, one inherently possesses the aforementioned [realms].
The characteristics of the threefold merit within the sutras elucidated herein are as follows.

How does one observe that one’s own mind inherently possesses the meaning of the Prologue, the Main Body, and the Circulation of a sublime sutra? The text correctly reveals this meaning in two layers:
first, by taking the Three Studies as the three parts; second, by taking each of these three individually as three parts. Regarding the first of these, there is first the general [explanation].

To mark and distinguish them in sequence, the reason for designating these three as the three divisions of the mind is that while the three stages of understanding (*adhimukti*), practice (*caryā*), and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) constitute the essentials, among all practices this [stage] is the most essential; furthermore, it corresponds precisely to the meaning of the three divisions found in the sūtras, whereas the other three do not.
Therefore, one must rely on these three. Why? Because the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* regards [this stage] as the Great Nirvāṇa.

This sutra is the foremost of practices; it is considered the wondrous beginning of the practice of peace and bliss, the initial gateway to the secret treasury, and the path that leads to the sublime Way.
How could there be anything that does not proceed by means of this? Therefore, it is the essential core of practice.

That one can attain right concentration through the precepts, and that through right concentration one possesses the function of wisdom, is precisely the same as the meaning of the sequential transmission of this sutra. It is just like [observing] one's own mind.
Reasoned observation that can abandon the faults of the two karmas is not merely morality; it is the samādhi of a mind that is equanimous and tranquil.
It is the wisdom that clearly understands the nature and characteristics of all phenomena without obstruction.

Within the single mind of sublime contemplation, these three are distinguished as being like the three parts of a single sublime sūtra; as in the "Peaceful Practices" (Anrakugyō) below, non-attached right contemplation can abandon the ten [faults].
The precept is that which eliminates all afflictions; concentration is that which abides in mental tranquility and immobility like Mount Sumeru;

and wisdom is that which contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena while they exist through causes and conditions. All three practices are fully present within the mind of wondrous contemplation, and because they follow this same sequence, it constitutes the essential convergence.
Thus, the three meanings are synthesized and correspond respectively to the three divisions of the sutra.

First, similarity by way of cause and condition, as previously explained; second, similarity by way of essential outline, for the Tathāgata taught that the three divisions of the sūtra constitute the most essential outline, and now, in practicing contemplative cultivation, these same three are likewise the most essential outline;
third, similarity by way of function, for the Tathāgata’s teaching of the sūtra in its three divisions was able to bring about the karmic conditions of the two assemblies.

All have attained realization and entry into the wondrous Way; now, observing their mental activities, one sees that by means of these three, they will certainly transform all birth and death to enter the secret treasury.
These three sections are briefly explained because their meanings correspond to one another.
Below, the fulfillment of this is further revealed separately; previously, for the time being, these three were treated as three general divisions without specific correlation.

Now, to further address this specifically, we shall discuss it according to two meanings: first, regarding practice; second, regarding the Dharma-gate. Regarding practice, one should focus on self-cultivation;
regarding the Dharma-gate, one focuses on the application of transforming others. Thus, that which is practiced and that which is employed are both person and Dharma.

In the cultivation of the initial mind, one must first eliminate evil, then establish stability, and finally attain illuminating penetration. Therefore, the *Benye jing* (Sutra of Fundamental Karma) says: "Precepts eliminate..."
That form is not fixed and that there is no mind, yet through the wisdom of awakening one realizes that perceptions are empty—this is precisely its meaning.

To be of benefit to others, one must first observe, then enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and only thereafter eliminate evil and give rise to goodness for the sake of sentient beings; this is as it is said: "The Buddha shall eliminate and sever [these].
The text states that the traces come later because the application of the matter is clearly manifested therein. This is the sequence of these two or three stages.

Regarding the meaning of the three sections of the sutra, it can be understood now that the three sections of the "Contemplation of the Mind" (Guanxin) are precisely suited to the sequence of practice, just as was indicated at the beginning and explained above. As for whether these two [approaches] are superior or inferior:

although the three metaphors explained in the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*—such as the thief, the bonds, and the executioner—appear to have degrees of superiority and inferiority, they must necessarily depend upon one another.

This is because the preceding precedes and the succeeding succeeds; how much more so now, when these three are all the practice of the wondrous mind, which, though lacking sequential order, are explained here in sequence.
Furthermore, within each of the aforementioned three, they are each divided into three parts, for there is a specific significance that necessitates this further explanation.
This is also like what was previously discussed regarding the general and specific aspects of the three divisions of the Sūtra, wherein it was generally stated that each possesses [these qualities].

Regarding the three parts and three meanings within the *śīla* (precepts): the preliminary procedures (*pūrvakalpa*) constitute the introduction; the formal motion followed by the fourfold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) constitutes the main body;
and the conclusion of the ritual constitutes the dissemination. This can be understood as discussing the three [parts] based on the beginning and end of receiving the precepts.

As for "preliminary procedures," because the performance of the fourfold proclamation is itself the formal reception [of the precepts], all methods prior to the formal motion are considered preliminary procedures. Furthermore, [the rest of the text follows].
The preliminary practices (*pūrvāṅga*) may be taken as the introduction, the actual reception (*samādāna*) as the main body, and the subsequent maintenance as the dissemination;

this is a general explanation of the three parts based on the time of reception. Since this concerns the specific rules for those who have left the household life, it is not detailed here, as the members of the Saṃgha should know it themselves.
Next, regarding the determination of these three parts: the twenty-five preliminary practices constitute the introduction, while the actual sitting and cultivation of entry constitutes the main body.
Emerging from samādhi while walking, standing, or engaging with various circumstances is for the purpose of propagating the twenty-five expedient means, as explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*;
it cannot be fully understood here. Next, based on what is clarified in the subsequent sections of this sutra regarding the entry and emergence of virtuous persons, three texts are established.
Because it is convenient to follow the sequence of the sutra, it is said that one emerges from and dwells in samādhi; this is the true concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
This is because each of the hundreds of thousands [of dharmas] possesses these three; and because they are wondrous in all three respects, they are called "all-good.

Furthermore, although from the perspective of the sutra they are excellent fruits and functions, from the perspective of their meaning, they actually encompass the initial cultivation as well, due to their perfect and subtle nature. The reason for this can also be understood.

Next, among the three types of wisdom, according to the text, they correspond respectively to emptiness, provisionality, and the middle. Regarding the sequence of emptiness and provisionality as primary and middle as secondary:

This name was circulated based on the *Benye jing* (Scripture of Fundamental Karma), yet although that scripture does not explicitly state "immediate" (*ji*), its sequence is such that it would be inconvenient to align it with the Threefold Division of the teachings; therefore, "the Middle" (*zhong*) is taken as the primary meaning, while "immediate" is used merely for the sake of circulation. Nevertheless, even with this alignment, the meaning remains unsettled. Why is this? For when the three contemplations are explained, they are all described as "immediate emptiness," "immediate conventionality," and "immediate the Middle. It has not yet been stated that "the Middle" is itself "immediate. Furthermore, the *Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue* states: "The Middle Way is the ultimate principle; it is neither empty nor conventional, yet it is immediately both empty and conventional. This indicates that "the Middle" is the ultimate principle, while "immediacy" refers to the two gates of emptiness and conventionality. Therefore, one should understand that the term "immediate" applies to the two gates of emptiness and conventionality, whereas "the Middle" is the ultimate principle. Consequently, the meaning of "immediate" is established through the Threefold Contemplation. Thus, it is said: "The three gates are immediate; the Middle is the ultimate principle. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *Fahua xuanyi* states: "The three gates are immediate; the Middle is the ultimate principle. This means that the three gates are immediate, while the Middle is the ultimate principle. This is because the Middle Way is the ultimate principle, and the two gates of emptiness and conventionality are immediate. Therefore, the meaning of "immediate" is established through the Threefold Contemplation. Thus, it is said: "The three gates are immediate; the Middle is the ultimate principle. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *Fahua xuanyi* states: "The three gates are immediate; the Middle is the ultimate principle. This means that the three gates are immediate, while the Middle is the ultimate principle. This is because the Middle Way is the ultimate principle, and the two gates of emptiness and conventionality are immediate. Therefore, the meaning of "immediate" is established through the Threefold Contemplation. Thus, it is said: "The three gates are immediate; the Middle is the ultimate principle. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *Fahua xuanyi* states: "The three gates are immediate; the Middle is the ultimate principle. This means that the three gates are immediate, while the Middle is the ultimate principle. This is because the Middle Way is the ultimate principle, and the two gates of emptiness and conventionality are immediate. Therefore, the meaning of "immediate" is established through the Threefold Contemplation. Thus, it is said: "The three gates are immediate; the Middle is the ultimate principle. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *Fahua xuanyi* states: "The three gates are immediate; the Middle is the ultimate principle. This means that the three gates are immediate, while the Middle is the ultimate principle. To claim that hearing [the teaching] is itself emptiness, itself the Middle, and itself the Provisional is not only inconsistent with the meaning, but also contradicts the sequential order of contemplation set forth in the sutras.
Since the sequential contemplation cannot be established, the analytical meaning (prabheda-artha) certainly cannot be accomplished.

If you argue that because it is "inconceivable" (acintya), there is no meaning that is not attained—then since the Provisional is also inconceivable and wondrous, for what reason could it not be considered the correct teaching? As the Sutra says:
Illuminating both truths simultaneously, with each moment of mind extinguished in stillness, one naturally flows into the Middle Way; is this not itself the propagation [of the teaching]?

If the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* takes the first two contemplations as the introduction, attaining entry into the Middle Way as the main practice, and simultaneous illumination as the propagation, this interpretation is particularly subtle and excellent.
However, the meaning of the present text seems to take the three contemplations directly as the mind itself.

Regarding these three aspects being different from that [previous] interpretation, I now say: if one takes them directly as names corresponding to the sequence previously mentioned—namely, the provisional (*jia*) within emptiness (*kong*)—this is acceptable.
Alternatively, following the meaning, they may also be taken directly as in the commentary text;
since emptiness, the provisional, and the middle (*zhong*) are all wondrous and inconceivable, there is nothing that would be incorrect in either case.
Question: Regarding the three divisions of the precepts, these are the most minimal and coarse phenomena; yet this treatise discusses wondrous contemplation—why does it rely upon these? Answer:
How could that which is wondrous in its absolute transcendence (*atyantānapekṣa*) not be wondrous? Not a single form or a single fragrance fails to be the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*).

In agriculture, commerce, and industry, there is no contradiction with the true reality (*dharmatā*). How, then, could there be such [limited] precepts? As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies, the Bodhisattva cultivates morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
The three types of noble practice lead to entry into Great Nirvana: the cultivation of precepts fulfills the various sections of the *Vinaya*;

the cultivation of meditative concentration penetrates all mundane and supramundane realms; and the cultivation of wisdom gives rise to the wisdom of the Four Truths—such as the truth of non-arising—which simultaneously realizes Great Nirvana.
Since this present [text] employs that same intent, it is explained by means of those principles. Question: By what means is this grasped?
Is it distinct from the provisional teachings of the Lesser Vehicle? Answer: Because it is cultivated with the mind of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, its name is eternally and vastly different [from them].
People do not understand this meaning; some say that the sutra also clarifies the Lesser Vehicle, while others say it is a gradual teaching of the Mahāyāna.
Thus, those who are unaware of the provisional and the real may call it "Lesser" upon seeing it, or call it "Gradual" upon seeing it—this can be described as the vision of those with small wisdom.
How could those who are ignorant and do not realize this even in their daily lives be deemed worthy of discussing its ultimate subtlety?
What is clarified here is entirely the practice of the wondrous mind; it constitutes the cause for the secret treasury. Question:

Why is this not explained in terms of the Bodhisattva precepts? Answer: The Bodhisattva precepts apply universally to both the laity and the ordained. This [present explanation] accords with that principle as well as the text of the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra.
Furthermore, because this [text] separately clarifies the precepts of the renunciant bodhisattva, it is explained in terms of this;

moreover, since both sutras equally clarify the complete sequence of the three trainings for the renunciant bodhisattva, it is convenient for correlating them with the meaning of the three divisions, whereas other cases would not be so convenient, and thus one must follow the specific rather than the general.
Additionally, because this sutra reconciles the provisional and the ultimate, it is necessary to proceed from the subtle to the manifest.
It is not discussed separately; consider this again. Previously, in the first section, it was treated as a general whole, thus encompassing all coarse [precepts].

Now, by approaching it from a specific perspective, it universally subsumes all precepts—consider this, consider this. Question: Why is there a discussion of two layers within the meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while for the others there is only one?
Answer: Because this scriptural text itself contains this teaching; its names and meanings are broad and manifest, whereas the others are easily understood.

Since this is understood by way of illustration, I shall not elaborate further. Now, in discussing the contemplation of the mind (*cittānupaśyanā*), all rely upon external matters to reveal the central principle of the mind.

The Sūtra is divided into three parts—Introduction, Main Body, and Circulation—and the mind is likewise divided into three parts: Precepts, Concentration, and Wisdom. Thus, the internal and external are already aligned, and the phenomena and principles are fully exhausted.
Since the Sūtra is already divided into these three, there is no need to further open each of them into three or four; nor are the precepts, concentration, and wisdom themselves further subdivided.
If wisdom is further divided into three, upon what is this based? If there were nothing [to base it on], how could it be called "revealing principle by relying on phenomena" (*shili xianli*)?

If there is something to rely upon, then why do all commentators say it is merely "pointing toward that" (*qu'er er yi*) without any distinct standard? Now, I say these words are not yet fully understood;
they possess profound significance and are extremely close at hand, yet people have simply failed to see them for a long time. Why is this so? This...

When discussing the general, the specific, and their combination, they constitute four phases of the threefold contemplation; this refers precisely to the four phases of the threefold characteristics within the demonstration of the fundamental and the manifested.
The reason for this is that when discussing contemplative understanding, one must necessarily revise the previous three matters;

since the explanation of those three matters does not go beyond the fundamental and the manifested, it is essential to rely upon the fundamental and the manifested to encompass the preceding three, as previously stated.

To clarify why this is so, first the "Original" (hon) is clarified; next, the "Trace" (jaku) is shown as vast. Immediately following, it says: "Simply contemplate the height and breadth of one's own mind.
This refers to performing the contemplation of the Original and the Trace based upon one's own mind, which universally corresponds to the three preceding sections. Now, this case is likewise:

following the four previous sections on the Original and the Trace, it clarifies the contemplation of those four sections, which is precisely the contemplation of the Original and the Trace. Furthermore, regarding the preceding "Original":

Within the provisional traces (*jì*), the first set constitutes the "root" (*běn*), while the subsequent three sets clarify that the traces share a common basis in a single root and cannot be transmitted as distinct roots and traces.
Here, too, it is the same: the first set provides a general exposition of the three dharmas of precepts, concentration, and wisdom;

although each subsequently opens into three further categories, these are merely variations of the aforementioned three dharmas. Thus, the first three are established first to serve as the foundation for the latter three.
The reason why these latter three "traces" (ji) are established based on the preceding "root" (ben), and why one focuses on these three dharmas rather than others, is truly for a specific purpose;
namely, because the meanings of root and trace correspond to one another, one focuses on these three dharmas.
For this reason, it is clear that these four [sections] are modeled after the four previous instances of root and trace to elucidate the contemplation of root and trace. If...
If one can investigate these three aspects within one’s own mind, then all myriad practices will be present, the Buddha-wisdom may be opened, and the wondrous Way may be realized;
this is equal in merit to the three divisions of the sutra. Based on this sutra, the characteristics of the three aspects of contemplating the mind are roughly as follows;
they may be understood through the mind but cannot be fully expressed in words.
The four preceding sections constitute the first part, which briefly demonstrates the four characteristics of this sutra according to the three divisions;

this concludes that section. From here below is the second part, which provides a summary and exhortation. This consists of three sentences: first, it summarizes the brief exposition to indicate its extensive application;
next, it exhorts one to infer the extensive meaning from the brief; finally, it clarifies that the intent of the extensive explanation does not transcend the brief, provided one is skillful.

Regarding the "Brief Exposition," one should know for oneself that it is established at the beginning of the extensive [exposition]. Because it is restricted to the three divisions, it is a brief indication of the general structure.
The phrase "it should be applied below" means that, having proceeded toward the body of the brief exposition, one enters into the detailed textual explanation.

Just as the general structure of the three sections was briefly indicated above, one should understand that every chapter and sentence of this entire scripture likewise possesses these [three divisions].
Regarding the four meanings, if one were to explain them, they must all employ these four modes of interpretation to fully exhaust their intended significance.
As for the phrase "spoke and withdrew," the text at the end of the sutra says "departed" (*qu*); "departed" corresponds to "coming," and "withdrew" (*tui*) corresponds to "advancing.

There are many such names that can be understood through reflection; it simply means that the assembly withdrew and dispersed once the sutra was concluded. This sentence provides a general clarification.
The general structure and scope of this treatise should be understood in this manner. Although the principles and structural patterns are thus, one may only know their meaning through analogy;
it is not possible to record them all in writing, as that would be excessively prolix.
Therefore, for future students, one should be able to infer the detailed meaning from the preceding brief explanation. It is difficult to provide a definitive analysis of every textual detail.
"Difficult" refers to the fact that the subject matter is vast and extensive. How can one understand this vastness through a brief comparison?

Although the scriptural text is extensive, it does not go beyond the four points previously summarized; therefore, by diligently contemplating those four brief points, there will be nothing in the extensive text of the entire treatise that is not understood.
Thus it says, "The practitioner should skillfully contemplate them," and so forth. "Different terminology" refers to [the same point expressed] in a single...
This is because the categories and linguistic distinctions are extensive; however, the underlying meaning is the same, as it does not go beyond the four previously mentioned meanings.

Below, two matters are cited together as a metaphor for the aforementioned similarities and differences, which can be understood through this analogy. The character "轍" (zhé) refers to the tracks of a carriage.

Regarding the character "鹹" (xián), there has been a tradition since ancient times of writing it directly as "咸" (xián), signifying that all things converge in the sea, with a meaning identical to the "共" (gòng) used above; nowadays, both are written as this character "鹹."

The intent is to take the analogy of the ocean, where all waters share the same salty taste, as being identical to "converging on saltiness. These words serve as an illustration, and their meaning is universally applicable.

In the preceding enumeration, it was stated that one should always interpret the text by means of the four intentions; here, however, they are recorded briefly—sometimes as one, two, or three—as the priority lies in grasping the essential meaning.
If one cannot grasp the previous [explanation], the four characteristics shown in brief may be used to enter the text, even if they are not fully detailed.

Yet one can grasp its intended meaning; thus we know that those who enter the text without it being exhaustive yet are able to fully grasp the meaning do so entirely through the merit of the brief indication of the four characteristics.
It is therefore known that these four characteristics, presented in brief, constitute the model for briefly grasping the meaning of the entire treatise;
hence, what was previously called the "method for explaining the text" resides precisely here. This concludes the explanation of the preceding section.

That the essential meaning can be grasped even when not fully set forth in the headings is clear from the fact that the two meanings presented in the preceding chapters serve as the basis for the subsequent three chapters, which explain those two meanings. As previously clarified,
if one attains this understanding, one will not only grasp the meaning of this single sutra, but will come to understand all sutras without exception.
This is the general framework of its interpretation; thus, these four modes of explanation are briefly presented as a model for all subsequent exegesis.
Some may ask: "Do these four interpretations apply solely to the present sutra, or do they also extend to other teachings?
To answer this point, there are both common and specific applications, which shall be distinguished later.

Question: Regarding the two gates of the Trace and the Origin within the first portion, the summary further states that if one relies on the latter two or three [gates] to provide an exegesis, then for the single category of "causes and conditions," the exegesis of the textual meaning clearly requires a thorough understanding from beginning to end. As for the provisional and real aspects of the Trace Gate, they must be distinguished according to the teachings;
as for what is discussed in the Origin Gate regarding the distant and the near, it pertains exclusively to the Perfect and Real. Thus, with respect to...

The teaching should reside solely in the traces (*śeṣa*), while the fundamental [meaning] (*mūla*) is appropriate only for the distant; yet now, regarding the teaching, it still pervades the fundamental, and the distant and near also pervade the traces.
Thus, the explanation of the text (*śāstra-vyākhyāna*) and the topical outline (*pariccheda*) appear to conflict. How are they to be reconciled? Answer: There are both general and specific meanings.

The topical outline clarifies the specific beginning and end of the text, and thus follows the specific; the explanation of the meaning clarifies the general sense, and thus follows the general. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

Although the Prologue (Honmon) discusses the perfect and real, because the names and meanings of "original" and "traced" (honzoku) and their relative distance and proximity still apply across all teachings, it is necessary to return to this specific teaching to manifest the "is" by contrasting it with the "non-is.

Although the Trace Gate (Jikimon) has not yet clarified the original and the traced or the revelation of the truth, once that revelation is complete, these traces all descend from the Original Ground; those who descend as these traces do so by relying upon [the Original].
Because it is necessary to reveal the fundamental (the *ben*), one must clarify the fundamental by means of each specific trace (*ji*).

If the traces were not clarified, and the fundamental were only revealed later, one would merely understand the general meaning without discerning the distinct meanings of the fundamental. Furthermore, if the teachings were not clarified, the meaning of the perfect identity of fundamental and trace would not be fully illuminated;
therefore, it is necessary to clarify them by means of the common [principle]. From the preceding section, one has understood the general based on the common.
To explain the meaning while preserving both the literal and contextual senses, and to grasp both the general and specific aspects, is to achieve the highest excellence.

If one attains this insight, all other matters can be understood by analogy; there is no need for further elaboration. Only when one understands these general and specific textual meanings without obstruction may one discuss the subtle ultimate;
otherwise, one is not yet fit for such deliberation. Someone might say: "The myriad dharmas are mind-only; one should directly perceive them."

The general purport of the sutra clarifies that the mind is inherently endowed with all dharmas; by observing them with a single sublime contemplation, one’s practice is self-sufficient, being both concise and easy.
Why must one necessarily perform such distinct and sequential tasks? Is this not exceedingly cumbersome and difficult? The commentary states:
This is merely a delusion arising from the common sentiments of ordinary people; they have failed to understand the intent of others. Worldly people—
I shall now clarify this to prevent confusion and error. What is meant by "contemplating the mind" (guānxīn) refers to interpreting the sutras by means of contemplating the mind.
This involves explaining the sutras through four general principles; the first three explain them in terms of external phenomena, while this one explains them in terms of the internal mind.
That is to say, by discerning and manifesting within one's own mind, the principles of the aforementioned phenomena are revealed, thereby providing a comprehensive synthesis of the sutra text.

The meaning of this is intended to cause practitioners at the initial stage to constantly perform such observation and cultivation within their own minds, thereby advancing toward and realizing that path.
As explained previously, the reason for clarifying this here is to designate it as "contemplating the mind" (*guānxīn*) when interpreting the sūtras;

it does not mean that one discusses contemplative practice solely by referring directly to one's own mind. Since you do not understand the intent of these terms at all, how can you [presume to] act so hastily?

If one raises this objection—that if one were simply to take up the mind to cultivate contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), it would suffice to follow a single work such as the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (or *Mohe zhiguan*), since its intent is distinct from this [text] and thus this doubt should not arise;
or if one takes the "wondrous" (*miao*) in its entirety, it is already contained within the *Xuan yi*—others might say:
"Since the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* exists, it should be sufficient to explain that one directly relies upon it; why then this further prolixity? This is still a partial view. One...

If one has not yet grasped the meaning of "round" and "square," what is the reason? It is because the dispositions of beings are not uniform: some delight in contemplating the meaning and practicing cultivation, while others delight in propagating and elucidating the scriptural texts.
Since both preferences are preserved and neither is different in their common adherence to the holy teachings, how can one be partial toward one and disparage the other without slighting them?

If those who propagate the teachings today are exclusively devoted to these [scriptural] matters, they are like those previously mentioned who were solely intent on counting the recitations of others.

The Treasure Store [Sūtra] has no self-interest; throughout ancient and modern times, this deficiency has been particularly prevalent. Now, our school possesses these two gates and there is nothing it does not encompass.

Furthermore, as for the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) which, in terms of contemplative understanding, explains the names of the sūtras by means of the mind—herein, the mind is clarified in order to explain the scriptural text.
Thus, these names, phrases, generalities, particulars, and boundless matters and meanings are all originally within one's own mind.
If it arises from the mundane, yet one does not speak of it, it will ultimately not manifest from within one's own mind. Now, to clarify and demonstrate this:

it does not exceed a single thought-moment and can be contemplated with joyful vigor, free from weariness or lamentation. How could one then claim that it is cumbersome and difficult? Someone may ask:
"If the contemplative understanding must be thus, why did the Tathāgata not explain it at that time? It was simply because at that moment, [the conditions for] such a response were not met.
If all that is appropriate were inherently inconceivable, one would attain the wondrous sound upon the mere appearance of its shadow and echo; why then wait for such elaborate detail?

At present, various [teachings] have been fully explained and guided, yet people still do not understand. Although they do not understand, it is nonetheless impossible not to provide a detailed exposition.
Thus, what in the sutras constitutes the discourse on shadows and echoes? It is as briefly cited in the preceding scriptural evidence.

This is what is meant by the aforementioned analogy. Furthermore, as in the following passage, the three—Tathāgata, robe, and seat—are all based upon external phenomena to manifest the meaning of the internal mind.
Since the Tathāgata possesses these three external phenomena, they are used metaphorically to reveal the three meanings of the internal mind;
these should all be interpreted according to the *Guānxīn* (Contemplating the Mind) commentary and must not be explained merely in terms of external objects. This relies upon the Buddha.

I have specifically refuted this being incorrect; later generations should instead understand it solely as a matter of practice (*vastu*). Furthermore, one must not claim that the Buddha was entirely devoid of external phenomena.
When certain individuals see that the Buddha possessed such internal realization at that time, they discard the external altogether and focus exclusively on the internal.
Both of these approaches are errors—either going too far or falling short—and thus lose the meaning of the Middle Way. It is also like...

In the "Chapter on the Buddha-way of Vimalakīrti," the Bodhisattva Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana, seeing that Vimalakīrti’s room was empty and devoid of all possessions, asked where his parents, wife, children, and retinue were. Vimalakīrti answered him in full detail, as extensively recorded in the sūtra.
Such passages all describe the external to reveal the internal; how could one interpret the Tathāgata by focusing exclusively on the internal or exclusively on the external?
There are many such sūtras of this kind that cannot be described in full; thus, the meaning of how external objects are fully manifested by means of the mind is extremely clear and evident.
How could it be merely a matter of shadows and echoes? Furthermore, it is not only taught by the Buddha; the Confucians also possess it. As the records and biographies state:
