Based on this sutra’s exposition, the examples for other sutras are likewise.

Below, a detailed analysis of various meanings shall be presented in three sections: first, a general discussion of the universal and the particular; second, a specific discussion of the universal and the particular;
and third, that which is exclusively particular. "Universal" refers to all sutras; "particular" refers to distinctions based on meaning and distinctions based on names. Regarding the latter:

Because this is focused exclusively on this sutra, if there were only three major sections, it would consist merely of the first two. However, if categorized according to the two gates, there must be three meanings;
since we now encompass both the single and the compound, these three [sections] exist. Reflect on this, reflect on this!

Now, regarding these two prefaces, various schools as well as other extant texts provide even more titles. As in the preceding pair, they are named according to phenomena (*dharma*), based on those phenomena.
Because they share commonalities yet differ, they are termed "General" and "Specific. If categorized by person, it is also called the "Ānanda Preface";

this refers to the initial section where Ānanda asks his questions at the time of the First Council. It is placed first because when the Tathāgata was about to preach the sūtra, he first established these as a preliminary expedient (*upāya*).
If categorized by its formal establishment, it is also called the "Preface on Receiving the Command"; this is placed at the very beginning of the preface itself.

Regarding the subsequent placement by command, this refers to the period when [the Buddha] was still present; as for the initial independent arrangement, if categorized by time, it is called the "Future Introduction" (*anāgata-nidāna*), while the latter is the "Present Introduction" (*vartamāna-nidāna*).

The former refers to the time of the compilation after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, whereas the latter refers to the accounts of past causal origins (*pūrvayoga*) spoken during the Tathāgata’s lifetime.

If categorized by scripture, these are also called the "Postscript to the Sūtra" (*sūtrānta-pṛṣṭhānuśaṃsa*) and the "Preface to the Sūtra" (*sūtrānta-pūrva-nidāna*). The former refers to the Tathāgata...
Regarding the statement "after the sutra has been preached," it means that this [section] is placed next. Within this pair, there is another interpretation:

first, it refers to the period before the sutra was preached, because it stands at the beginning of the sutra; second, it refers to the period after the sutra was preached, because it follows immediately after.
Now, I say that the first is based on the sequence of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the sutra, while the second is based on the sequence of the compilation of the sutra after his passing.
Each of these also has its own logic. If we consider them in terms of their verbal expression, they may also be called "Prefaces to the Collected Sūtras.

The first [type] refers to the sūtra preface spoken at the time of the initial assembly; the second refers to that which was spoken by the Master at that time. Therefore, this is also termed a "Master-Disciple Preface":

the first refers to the disciple who was present at the later compilation and circulation; the second refers to what the Master himself spoke at that time. If one applies this analogy to Confucianism as well...
The names "narration" (*śruta*) and "composition" (*kṛta*) are used because this is a preface to the sūtra; thus, the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha also employs this same pair of terms.
Since it begins with "Thus have I heard," it is a narration rather than a composition; since it subsequently states "spoken by the Buddha," it is a composition rather than a narration.
These first seven pairs are all designated according to their specific contextual distinctions. However, if we consider the underlying intent for establishing these various pairs:

It is also called the "Introduction Establishing Faith. First, at the time of the compilation, one first studies these five matters as evidence so that the great assembly of that time and all those with affinity in future generations may give rise to faith and acceptance toward the Dharma being transmitted.

Second, at the time of preaching the sutra, one first employs these five matters to initiate the conditions and causes for the commencement of the formal exposition; therefore, this is also [the introduction].
It is called "Exhortation to Faith" (*Kuan-hsin-piao-fa*) because its meaning may be understood by analogy;

it is also called "Refuting the Deviant to Reveal the Orthodox" (*Po-hsieh-hsien-cheng*), as the first part refutes non-Buddhist scriptures and the second part reveals the correct principles of the Buddha-dharma.

It is also called "Expressing the Identity of Chapters and Differences" (*Piao-t'ung-chang-i*), as the first part expresses the identity of the Way of all Buddhas and the second part clarifies the similarities and differences regarding realization and entry.
Therefore, it is also called the "Preface of Correct Exposition" and the "Preface of Circulation. Reflect upon this: the ten pairs preceding this do not exceed four meanings.
The first seven are all matters pertaining to the world of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). The subsequent three, being established as meanings, correspond respectively to the latter three meanings.
However, previous masters have merely recounted five pairs and have not included the aforementioned general and specific establishments.
Regarding the exposition of the five pairs of names that distinguish between the refutation [of the provisional] and the manifestation [of the real]:

although these names generally apply to all five pairs, we shall take only the pair concerning "realization" (*zheng*) and "arousing" (*fa*) as primary. This is because the names and meanings of the other four pairs involve complications and are largely excluded from our discussion.
Now, if we first discuss them separately, these two pairs—realization and arousal—are the most essential; however, upon thorough investigation, they should be discussed comprehensively.
In general, there is nothing that is not permissible; one should not insist on making arbitrary choices between them. Therefore, all later masters have followed this same approach.

In our own school’s *Guanjing yishu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra), the six pairs are explained comprehensively in relation to the four *siddhāntas*, so there is nothing that is not permissible.
Why must the sutra necessarily have these two prefaces? An ancient commentator explained: "Because the sutra has two [parts], there are two prefaces. This is as follows:
What has been explained here is for the benefit of others at a different time; Ānanda transmitted it so that it might flow down through the final age.
Since this is distinguished by time and person, there are two sūtras. As there are already two prefaces (nidānas), they should also be distinct;
thus, there are two prefaces. In the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*, the Great Master explains: "All sūtras possess both general and specific names. Because of these two names, there are two [prefaces]."
Question: If that is so, why are the sequences different? Answer: It is explained that names are established according to what is most convenient.

To establish the sequence of the introduction (*nidāna*), it is convenient to first present the specific and then the general; alternatively, it is also convenient to first present the general and then the specific. Furthermore, in one approach to clarifying the meaning, the introduction also proceeds from the general to the specific.
Why is this? For example, the manifestation of auspicious omens (*prātihārya*) relies upon what was previously taught in the sūtras; such is the case for these and other instances.
Since this matter was spoken by the Tathāgata only as he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, we know it belongs to the later period; thus, they are all equal.

Regarding these two interpretations, some may say they are difficult to reconcile, but I say this is not so. The former master explains based on the evidence of the arising [of the path], while the Great Master explains based on the general and specific [meanings];
each follows its own source, and therefore they do not contradict one another. However, if both are preserved together...

When paired, these opposites are mutually identical; if one adheres to each pair individually, they become mutually contradictory. That teacher did not establish the categories of "comprehensive" (*tong*) and "particular" (*bie*), and thus his system cannot be reconciled with ours.
The Great Master, however, fully preserves all such pairs, and therefore there is nothing that is not encompassed.

It is commonly discussed in the world that two orders are established based on the pairing of "heavenly" and "human," yet it has never been heard of that two orders are established based on the pairing of the two names [comprehensive and particular].

Because this has already been distinguished, I shall provide only a brief explanation of the general and specific origins [of the introduction] and will not further discuss the meaning of "testifying" (*sākṣin*) and "arousing" (*utthāpana*).

Now, why is it that while the titles and prefaces of the sūtras each consist of only one pair, the preface to the *Śāstra* contains ten pairs? Consider this: one inherently contains the ten, and the ten are simply one.

If this is so, how can the general name "Preface" (*nidāna*) arise from the "General Introduction" (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*), given that it includes [the elements of] "testifying to faith" (*śraddhā-sākṣin*) and so forth?
The general title refers to the *sūtra*; "sūtra" is the name for that which is spoken by the Buddha, a term that others may not claim.

The general introduction (*pūrva-vastu*) serves as a collective means to inspire faith in what was spoken by the Buddha. The specific titles, such as "Wondrous" (*Myō*), etc., constitute the specific introduction (*nidāna*), as they are what initiates the discourse.
Once this single principle is grasped, there will be no further obstructions. Someone might say: "Since there are already two types of introductions..."
It is certainly fitting that there should be two versions for circulation, yet why is it that they are not seen? Answer:

Among the renowned and virtuous masters of past and present, they have only extensively clarified the two regular sequences [of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*], but I have not seen them discuss these two versions for circulation.

At times, I have also inquired of former masters on this matter, and they said that Ānanda was not entitled to the principle of circulating [the text]. For this reason, it is difficult to speak of it rashly.
If you insist on discussing this, please wait for a formal occasion; it is not something that can be spoken of in haste. To attempt an explanation:
the preceding section has concluded by generally clarifying the meaning of the two sequences [of the preface].
From here below, regarding the specific interpretation of the text of the general preface (*sāmānyanidāna*), among all the ancient treatises, none precedes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Among all the new treatises, none precedes the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, which is the great treatise currently in use. Within this treatise, there are both general and specific explanations;

subsequent commentators have all adopted the intent of the treatise to clarify these general and specific interpretations. Although the general explanations of the treatise and various schools are extensive, their essential points do not exceed two meanings:
first, clarifying the original reason for its placement [in the canon]; second, [clarifying the nature of the Buddha-ground].
The intent behind what has been established is now clarified by the Great Master’s commentary, which likewise elucidates only these two points.
Although these two are explained, they remain within the broader text; thus, they have not been discussed here at length.

To provide a separate explanation according to the text while simultaneously making it manifest for later students—whether they have not yet attained comprehensive understanding or have not yet reached its profound essence—it is necessary here to briefly describe this general introduction, stating "originally."
As for by whom it was placed [there], it was during the Tathāgata’s final nirvana that he left this instruction to Ānanda, commanding him to place it there.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When the Buddha was about to enter nirvana, Ānanda’s mind was submerged in grief and regret, unable to emerge from it on its own.
Aniruddha said to Ānanda: 'You are the one who guards the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha; you ought not to be like an ordinary worldly person.'"
"Free from grief and regret, you should question the Buddha regarding these various matters of the future: 'After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how shall we practice the Path?
Who shall be our teacher? How should we dwell with Caraka, who speaks such evil words? What words should be placed at the beginning of the Buddhist scriptures?
Having heard this, Ānanda’s heart was overcome with distress; yet his mind cleared slightly, and through the power of mindfulness and the Way, he immediately—"
When he asked the Buddha about this matter, the Buddha told Ānanda: "You should rely on the four foundations of mindfulness to cultivate the path to liberation;
the Sūtra on the Code of Discipline (Vinaya) is your great teacher. The bhikṣu Cchanna should rely on the Dharma of Brahmā.
If the mind is supple, you may instruct Kātyāyana, and he will immediately attain the Path. This is what I have accumulated over three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas."

At the beginning of the *Dharmaguptaka* [Vinaya], one should all say: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was in such-and-such a region, in such-and-such a country, in such-and-such a place within a forest.
At the beginning of the sutras of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, this phrase is always proclaimed.

After my parinirvāṇa, the beginnings of the sutras should likewise proclaim these words. When Ānanda later performed the compilation of the teachings, he received this command and established it accordingly.
It is because this was established that there is this introductory statement of the general sequence. The treatise is very extensive; now I shall briefly summarize its points.
Regarding the "governing by the Brahma-dharma": since the Brahma-dharma is characterized by silence, one should not strike or revile others, but rather expel them through silence.
This matter is clarified in the *Māyā Mahākaruṇā-nirvāṇa-piṇḍita-sūtra*, the *Āgama-sūtras*, and especially in the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, which clarifies it concerning Upāli.
The *Ānanda-śāsana* and other sūtras and śāstras all state that Āniruddha instructed him to ask;
the commentaries of former masters explain that this must have been because at that time two people jointly gave the instruction, each citing the other’s name in turn.

Furthermore, in the later sections of the text, it says that he preached this sūtra in a certain forest together with the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus. Indeed, these four matters cited here are precisely [correct].
The intent lies solely in the fourth point; the other three aspects follow from it. Various schools as well as the present *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* commentary all explain this extensively.
Since the third aspect is not the primary meaning of the text, I do not wish to burden the reader with prolixity and thus shall not elaborate here;
I will briefly analyze it later in the subsequent section.

The preceding section has briefly clarified the original reason for establishing [this treatise]. Next, we shall clarify the purpose for which it was established. The essential points elucidated by various schools are fourfold:
first, to eliminate doubt—referring specifically to the three doubts; second, to generate faith; third, to distinguish the heterodox; and fourth, to manifest the orthodox.
The "orthodox" refers to the Three Jewels, which are the most auspicious; therefore, they are mentioned at the beginning of the sutra. Although the various schools have explained this extensively...
Furthermore, there are no meanings beyond these four; the present meaning also possesses four aspects: first, to reveal that the Way of all Buddhas is identical;
second, to engender right faith; third, to distinguish and refute the heterodox; and fourth, to manifest that attaining the correct [teaching] yields great benefit.

These are precisely the meanings of the four *siddhāntas*. The "four meanings" held by various schools are merely three of these, as they exclude the aspect of "removing doubt," which is identical [to the others].
This treatment of the subduing of the heterodox and evil and the revealing of the true Triple Gem is largely identical to the fourth intention [of the previous section].

Since these four intentions are all explained within the "Correct Exposition" (*samyag-vyākhyāna*) itself, they are not discussed here in advance; I have merely cited them briefly here to address the opponent's objection.
They will be made clear later on their own, so there is no need for such prolixity here.

The preceding section provided a general explanation and a brief indication; hereafter follows the formal explanation of the introductory preface (*nidāna*). The commentary (*śāstra*) briefly contains three points: first, the designation of divisions and combinations;
second, a brief explanation; and third, a detailed exposition. Regarding the first, the "designation of divisions and combinations," this refers to the structural division of chapters.

According to the internal logic of this work, one should first designate the chapters, then list their titles, and finally provide a critical analysis (*vicāra*); however, in the present text, only the designations are given, while the titles and analysis are omitted. Furthermore...
It is because one does not understand the reason for this that it is said (as follows), meaning that the intent lies herein:
"Thus" constitutes the first; "I have heard" is the second; "at one time" is the third; "the Buddha’s dwelling" is the fourth; and "the assembly of those who heard together" is the fifth.
The sixth arises by opening up the fourth among these five—namely, the Buddha and his dwelling place—into two parts. The seventh arises by opening...

Regarding the second of the six [divisions], "I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*) is counted as two, thus making seven. Because such variations have occurred throughout ancient and modern times, it is described here as "alternatively.
While such instances of five or six divisions have been common since antiquity, only the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha uniquely expanded them into seven.

This method of expansion and contraction likewise lacks definitive scriptural authority; it is merely a matter of weighing the contextual meaning of the specific passage at hand. My intention is to clarify this point.
Furthermore, as each of these possesses its own rationale and is universally applicable, there is no basis for exclusion or selection.
If, however, one considers those from recent times to be inauthentic, then these seven, six, five, and other variations may likewise be condensed into four, three, two, or one categories.
Regarding the "four," they follow the system of the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha, who consolidated the aforementioned seven matters into four; first, "thus" clarifies that which was heard.

Regarding the phrase "Thus have I heard," it distinguishes the person who hears from the Dharma that is heard; the first two [sections] certify the Dharma heard, while the latter two certify the person who hears.

Taken together as three, they constitute the Three Jewels (*triratna*). The Buddha constitutes the Jewel of the Buddha; "I heard" and the assembly of bhikṣus and so forth constitute the Jewel of the Saṃgha;
and "thus," "at one time," and "the place" constitute the Jewel of the Dharma. Master Jingfa said: "Thus have I heard" is itself the Dharma.
The *Ratnāvalī* states that at one time the Buddha resided [there], which refers to the Buddha Jewel; together with the great bhikṣus, it refers to the Saṃgha Jewel. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* says:

"Because the Three Jewels are the most auspicious, I have placed this at the beginning of my treatise. This means that while the first two characters of non-Buddhist scriptures are considered auspicious, we now place the auspiciousness of the Three Jewels at the beginning to refute them and clarify that theirs are not auspicious. This intention is most excellent. These two [points] should be combined as one.
"Those" refers to the three persons: the person (pudgala), the Dharma, and the Buddha; as well as "I," "have heard," and the "assembly of bhikṣus. Such are the three persons.
Likewise, "at one time," "in a certain place"—these are the three dharmas. The person receives the Dharma to accomplish virtue, while the Dharma relies upon the person for its propagation;

thus the two assist each other in their formation, acting as cause and effect for one another. Now, it is said that these [elements] have not yet reached the ultimate; they consist of the speaker and the spoken.
Since both the "able to be received" (the teacher) and the "that which is received" (the teaching) involve the preaching of the sūtra, they ought to be combined into one;

this constitutes the "Preface of Testimony and Faith" (*samyak-saṃpratyaya-nidāna*). This intention is such that, when expanded, it proceeds from one to seven, and when condensed, it proceeds from seven to one.
Although there are many intricate details therein that cannot be fully described, the first three [sections] correspond to the literal text, while the latter four pertain to the underlying meaning.
In terms of the meaning, one should first employ the preceding three [methods] to distinguish the text, and subsequently rely on the four [methods] to clarify its intent.

If one were to directly apply the methods of separation and combination at once, although the intent might be expansive and elegant, the text and meaning would become confused; thus, later students would find it difficult to discern the core doctrine, resulting ultimately in nothing but vexation and delusion.
Now, I say that if one were to analytically distinguish the five preceding phrases at once, there would naturally be ten [divisions].
Since the meaning is the same as in the section on "Hearing," why are there only seven? Therefore, in the *Mahā-śāstra*, the individual characters are explained with extreme detail.
While this may be appropriate for explaining the meaning (*artha*), it is not so for structuring the text (*vinyāsa*).

Thus, if there are seven, the structural outline already incorporates the meaning; however, if there are four, three, two, or one, this refers exclusively to the meaning and does not involve the structure.

If one follows the text strictly from its beginning to its end, it should properly consist of six sections; however, if one categorizes the text according to its meaning, it should properly consist of five.
Therefore, these two [divisions] most accurately capture the reality and are those constantly employed by our own school.
Not only is this interpretation logically sound, but there is also textual evidence for it. For instance, as in the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra* composed by Vasubandhu, the first three verses clarify...
The disciple later realized through three proofs that all the sūtras taught by the Master are exactly like this;

therefore, one knows that according to the text, the arising and ceasing of the samādhi can be categorized into six types. In the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, Bodhisattva Guṇaprabha’s commentary, the initial introductory passage of that sūtra is analyzed as follows:
it generally reveals what has already been heard and the time when the teaching arose, while specifically revealing the teacher of the doctrine and the place where the teaching arose.
Regarding the intended audience for whom this teaching is directed, various schools agree that the five prefaces of this treatise are precisely these [introductory] words.

Thus, it is understood that these are divided into five according to their meaning; therefore, one should know that the text and its meaning are fully exhausted by these five or six sections. However, when the ancients established five parts, they combined the "Principal Section" (*mukhya-sthāna*) with the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*;
when establishing five parts, they combined "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) with this [section]. This manner of opening and closing [the divisions] is also [consistent].

It is not yet settled; for now, it should be understood according to the treatise. Why is this? This introduction clearly explains the transmission and narration, rather than being one's own composition.
It reveals that what one has heard was spoken by the Buddha; thus, intending to set forth what one has heard, one first sets forth that which is to be set forth.
Since the revealer and the revealed cannot be separated from one another, these two must be combined. Guangzhai says: "Thus" (*evam*) refers to that which is about to be transmitted.
I have heard that the *Śrāvakabhūmi* (or a specific section thereof) is like this entire sūtra; I heard it from the Buddha and have thus transmitted it for you.

This captures its true essence and accords precisely with the treatise (*śāstra*). Therefore, one knows that if one grasps the essentials, the underlying principle will naturally be realized in its profound mystery.

Now, as for the convenience of interpreting the text, it is best to follow the sixfold [classification]; as for the convenience of clarifying the intended meaning, it is best to follow the fivefold [classification]. These five and six aspects...
Because the cultivation of both words and meanings is thorough, exhaustive, perfect, and beautiful, it is said that "sometimes six," meaning they are not restricted to one alone.
However, these five or six [reasons] generally serve as proofs for the Western [Pure Land] teachings at a later time; the masters of this land all agree with this explanation.

Yet, in recent antiquity, there was a person of renowned virtue who alone differed from this view; based on both the meaning and the text, he extensively refuted [the claim] and did not permit it, asserting that the first...
The first two phrases may indeed be simultaneous, but all subsequent sections are matters that arose at that very time.

How can these be taken as the "Certification of Faith" (samyak-saṃbodhi-pratītya) for the sutra? If such events had not occurred at that time, upon what would the teaching have been based? Who would have spoken it, and for whom would it have been intended?
These are the essentials of the introduction (nidāna); how can they be considered the "Certification of Faith"?
Next, I shall cite sutras and treatises to demonstrate that [the former view] is incorrect, and subsequently establish the correct meaning myself.

Of these, the first two phrases constitute one sentence that serves as proof for the faith [of the audience], while the meaning of the following four phrases encompasses both [faith and the sequence].

Although there are thus two directions, because they are contrasted with the preceding section which was exclusively for proving faith, they are once again treated as being exclusively for proving faith; therefore, they are further considered to belong solely to the Prologue (Nidāna).

That text is extremely extensive, and I do not wish to describe it in detail here. Now, observing this explanation, although it relies on the literal meaning of the text, it contradicts the text and deviates from the vehicle;
how could this be? For the Buddha’s intention was precisely to use these six matters to universally establish the initiation [of the teaching] at that time;
thus they may all serve as evidence for faith at a later time. If they did not pertain to the initiation at that time, they could not serve as evidence for faith at a later time. Therefore...
One should properly state that these six phrases collectively serve as the introduction for the time of the proclamation and collectively serve as the testimony for the time of certification.
How could one separate the first two phrases to treat them as a unilateral basis? Both interpretations fail to accord with the Sage’s intent.

Although they both constitute the introduction for the time of the proclamation, the reason they are placed at the beginning of the sutra is not because they are intended to be recited at that specific time; rather, one should properly state that although these six [phrases]...

While both [the former three and the latter three] together served as the "initiation" (*pravartaka*) for that time, now a single phrase is taken to serve as the "authentication of faith" (*samyak-pratyaya*).

It is said that by speaking only of the later authentication, one does not lose what was to be initiated at the proper time; yet, to treat it as solely an initiation is to lose the former while gaining the latter.

This is far from the original intent and is a profound inversion. As Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "The first three clarify the disciples, and the latter three authenticate the teacher's teaching. Thus, all are explained as being cultivated.
The details of the *Tāranātha* [tradition] are all like this; in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, these six phrases are collectively termed the "causal conditions for the arising of the teaching.
The six phrases explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* do not go beyond the meanings of "faith" (*śraddhā*) and "truth" (*satya*).

The intent of these three texts is to clarify that the six phrases collectively serve as the "testimony of faith" (*śraddhā-pratyaya*) for what follows; since you now do not permit this, it contradicts the explicit teachings of the Holy One.
Based on the meaning of these passages, it is evident that the errors in that teaching are profound. Who would have thought that such a person could harbor such a malady?
Although he was unique in this regard, subsequent authors have never followed his lead; there is indeed a reason for this. Someone may ask:
"How do the first two [cases] apply to the present? An ancient commentary explains: "Only when sentient beings possess faith does one then preach the Dharma."
Therefore, we know that it is so. Now, I say that this explanation is still not exhaustive. Why? Because the term "thus" (*evam*) is precisely faith (*śraddhā*).
It encompasses both the subject and the object: that which is believed is the wondrous Dharma, and that which believes is the pure mind.
If this Dharma did not first exist, there could be no responsive revelation; if this mind did not first exist, there could be no responsive resonance.
The reason one can speak of "arising" and that all arising is obtained is because [the object] already existed prior to being spoken of;

otherwise, there would be no sense of the causal conditions for response and stimulus (*saṃgati-pratyaya*). For this reason, it is known that such matters already existed at that time, and thus the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and what follows do not require any further contrivance.
Therefore, the Great Master’s *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "These six matters, the Buddha..."

Since the teaching of the Dharma is already inherently possessed [by the Buddha], it is therefore universally applicable. Thus far, we have discussed how these six matters apply to both the present and the future;
however, regarding the meaning of "initiation" (*pravartana*), there remains that which is not yet fully understood. What is the fault in this?

One must argue that initiation refers to extraordinary auspicious signs (*prātihārya*) that trigger the causal conditions for the arising of the teaching, occurring at the point when one is about to speak. As for the time, place, principal teacher, and retinue, these are merely [the specific circumstances].
Regarding the general causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), which sūtra does not contain these four?
Since they are not yet exceptional, on what basis could they be considered "initiating" (*pravartaka*)? Therefore, we know that if something is not exceptional, it cannot be termed "initiating.

why, then, does it explain dependent origination by summarizing twenty successive points (*paryāya*), and finally conclude by saying, "Prajñā is without limit, and its conditions are also immeasurable," before providing this brief explanation?
Answer: Upon examining the intent of the treatise, these four are the general [principles], while the others are the specific [applications].
To speak separately, the subsumption of particulars into the general does not exceed four intentions. How is this known?

It is because the treatise itself states that the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) comprehensively encompass all scriptural collections (*piṭakas*), as cited previously; furthermore, among other dependent originations (*pratītyasamutpāda*), these words do not occur.
Moreover, regarding the four *siddhāntas*, the textual passages are most extensive, whereas they are not so for other conditions. For these reasons, one knows the general and the particular.

The meaning is clear. If that is so, although these are not placed at the beginning or the end in the treatise—since they encompass all by being positioned in the middle—they nevertheless govern the extremes, include what precedes, crown what follows, and further clarify both the general and the particular. Why, then, should there be any doubt?
Since all such things do not transcend these four, it follows that all sentient beings possess these four schools of thought.
The responsive resonance of the capacity [of the recipient] serves as the cause, while the Buddha responds with the four doctrines as the condition;

when these causes and conditions harmonize, this wondrous teaching is proclaimed, and one attains the four wondrous benefits. Thus, the way of responsive resonance and benefit is fully exhausted herein.

The latter three interpretations merely establish this meaning, for the interpretation of our own school focuses exclusively upon this; therefore, it is called the fundamental source from which all phenomena arise.
There is indeed a profound reason for establishing this as the central thesis.

Having briefly clarified the meaning of the four *siddhāntas* above, we shall now explain the text of the commentary (*śāstra*). Upon examining various treatises and the interpretations of different masters regarding these words "thus" (*evam*), their structural forms differ:
some are separated, some are combined, and some provide an integrated explanation. "Separated" refers to explaining each of the two characters individually; "combined" refers to...

In summary, the two passages are interpreted through "association," meaning that "I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) is used to explain the intent of "thus" (*evam*), yet this does not constitute a formal explanation of the meaning of "I heard.

The characteristics of these three [phrases] are easily seen and need not be described further here. In the present text, the causes and conditions are explained both by way of combination and separation;

regarding the original and the trace, as well as the contemplation of the mind, the focus is exclusively on combined interpretation, whereas in the section on the teachings, there is a consistent use of separated interpretation.

The meaning can be understood from the text itself; since we are now correctly interpreting the passage according to the six phrases, the explanation regarding "I have heard" (evam mayā śrutam) has been omitted.
Furthermore, these four kinds of causes and conditions are also called the four reasons, the four principles, the four meanings, the four intentions, and the four matters;
one should reflect upon them well.
The initial statement regarding the "equality of the three periods" is from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise).
This serves as a general demonstration of the essence, characteristics, and forms of the Dharma taught by all Buddhas. It is called "Thusness" (*tathatā*) because it is not otherwise;

thus, within this treatise, both general and specific [explanations] are presented, and here we proceed directly from the general perspective, for Śākyamuni is himself the present [Buddha]. The phrase "all are established" refers to all things throughout the three periods of time.

When the Buddhas have completed their work of benefiting sentient beings in the world and enter parinirvāṇa, they all command their disciples to compile the entire canon, placing such words as "Thus have I heard" at the beginning of every sutra.
Why is this so? The commentary states it is for the purpose of clarifying that the Way of all Buddhas is identical, lest it remain obscure.
The underlying meaning is that the essential principle is always thus, precisely in order to manifest and reveal the entirety of all things.
The paths by which all Buddhas cultivate themselves and transform others are entirely equal;
there is no mutual contention, dispute, or competition regarding right and wrong. Therefore, the statement "they shall all necessarily be established" is made.
This is because such words of equality signify the meaning of non-contention; thus, these words are placed together to demonstrate that the path of self-cultivation is identical.

Thus, all [teachings] are identical in their accordance with the characteristics of reality (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) regarding the path for transforming others, and they are likewise identical in their accordance with the characteristics of reality regarding their exposition.
For this reason, they are all the same; were they not the same, there would inevitably be mutual disputes and contention over right and wrong. Since they are identical, such things do not exist.

Furthermore, throughout the three periods of time, the Buddhas have no mutual disagreement or distinction; they are certainly not separate. Moreover, it is because the worlds differ that disputes arise.

Since the Buddhas are identical, there is no contention; "identical" means not seeing difference—this explains "thus" (evam). Since there is no contention, there is nothing that is not so—this explains "is" (iti).
To demonstrate collectively that the essence and characteristics of the Dharma taught by all Buddhas are such as this—not different and not otherwise—it is called "thus" (evam);
therefore, it is the meaning of the world (loka). This phrase is what has been heard.
The first "all" (sarva) here exhaustively encompasses the essential nature and characteristics of all the teachings heard within this single section.

The three "alls" that follow merely serve to specifically manifest their respective functions. One should reflect on whether the intention behind adding the word "essence" (*tattva*) to the brief heading in the middle section might lie herein.
Next, to clarify why the phrase "Thus" (*evam*) is used for the sake of generating faith: this passage briefly extracts the purport of the *Śāstra* to resolve what is difficult to perceive.
"Time" (*kāla*) refers to a single moment; "place" (*deśa*) refers to the location of the city and mountains. "Faith" (*śraddhā*) is the fruit that is produced;
"time" and "place" are the causes that produce it, and they are also termed "Dharma. As for the nature of the fruit of faith that is produced, the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "As follows... (*tadyathā*).
This is faith; that which lacks this is not so. The nature of faith is that one says, "This matter is thus.
Thus, such speech is itself the characteristic of faith. This faith is established based on the object and arises precisely through time and place;
therefore, it is said that "time and direction cause its arising. Consequently, these are the causes of the subject and the object.
Regarding the principle of the fruit-dharma, it should properly include both the object and the subject as presented in the treatise;
however, because the present text is concise, its meaning is naturally complete by directly citing the capacity (the subject) to manifest the object.

Thus, although the capacity is cited, the intent does not reside in the capacity itself, for "如是" (*evam*) is a term used to correctly explain [the state of] faith. If one discusses this word "faith" comprehensively:
Furthermore, there are several meanings: namely, faith in the cause, faith in the result, faith in the essence, and faith in the characteristics.

The "cause" and "result"—both the subject that believes and the object believed—are precisely what was discussed previously. The "essence" and "characteristics" refer to the pure mind within the result that is the object of belief; when these manifest outwardly, they constitute the "characteristics.
Both this essence and these characteristics serve as the means by which one believes, while the Dharma explained constitutes the object of belief. Taken together, they form a single whole.
Of these, the five aspects of subject and object belong to the meaning of the preceding world, while the "subject" (the capacity) belongs to the meaning of this "for the sake of man.
Therefore, we shall now properly discuss that capacity for faith. Within the discussion of the capacity for faith, we shall specifically examine the characteristics produced therein.
If one does not briefly understand these various points, they will be utterly obscure within this text; thus, let us consult the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

If this single phrase is consistently taken as "faith," then the remaining five phrases would all belong to the category of "causing [others] to produce [it]," which is the consensus of all commentaries.

Why, then, are only the two factors of time and place singled out here? Answer: This has never been a point of doubt for those who have already studied the preceding sections; they simply state that both [time and place] should be included, implying that what is mentioned here is merely an abbreviation.
However, our view is that this is due to its inconceivability (*acintya*), and furthermore, it was not sought out from the *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*).
Therefore, why is it thus? According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the character "person" (*pudgala*) here should properly be placed above the character "cause" (*hetu*).

This specifically refers to the time when one raises [the teaching] to cause persons to give rise to faith. "Person" refers to those who can hear and those who can speak—the persons who hear together.
Since these three are all "persons," this single character "person" subsumes the three phrases, as well as the two factors of time and place, making five phrases in total.
This concludes [the section on] the simultaneous realization that those with a karmic affinity in the final age shall develop definitive faith in the Dharma thus transmitted.

It means that when such a person, at such a time, in such a place, and with such companions, hears it from such a teacher, they will perceive this Dharma as vividly clear and certainly worthy of trust; therefore, it says "shall cause."
This gives rise to faith. Now, as for why this passage is written in this way: it is not without basis. Later transmitters erred;

these later people did not understand the meaning of the character "this" (此), and seeing that the phrase was joined with the word "person" (人), they concluded it ought to follow the character "suddenly" (輒).

They then moved it [to that position]. Furthermore, if one were to follow the treatise (*śāstra*) exactly, there should have been two instances of the character "person. Thus, the treatise says: "At the time of speaking, [one considers] the direction... [and so forth].
It is because [faith] causes the human mind to give rise to trust. That it is now like this is not only because the meaning is not yet settled; the phrasing is also not stable.
To follow along without realizing one's error is truly lamentable. Question: What merit does faith possess that it must necessarily cause [the mind] to arise?
Answer: Its merit is great. This will be clarified in the following section. Generally speaking for all people, everything that gives rise to wholesome states is [due to faith].

The meaning of these [terms] is discussed separately; since generating faith is precisely what constitutes "acting for others" (*parārtha*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* primarily explains the meaning of "acting for others" in terms of generating faith.
Now, as this [text] should properly rely on that treatise, it takes generating faith as "acting for others. However, faith itself is simply a distinction between the general and the specific.
Next, to clarify that the term "thus" (*evam*) is used to refute erroneous views, this is based on the intent of the *Śata-śāstra*.

There are also ancient manuscripts and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* which both read "Ādaraṇa," yet within the *Śata-śāstra*, these two characters do not appear; there is only the expression "auspicious dharma" (*kalyāṇadharma*).
Some say it appears in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, but upon searching the commentary on the General Preface (*Sūtra-sāmānya-nidāna*) in that treatise, these words are likewise not found there.
Various schools all state that they do not know from where the word *āyu* originates; perhaps it is an alternative name transmitted from antiquity.
Among the outsiders of the West, these two characters *āyu* represent existence and non-existence;

as this is the foundation of the teachings of all those who seek wholesome benefit and is called an "auspicious dharma," it is placed at the beginning of their scriptures, and the Buddha has clarified its underlying principle.
It is improper to place the phrase "Thus have I heard" at the beginning of a sutra; this serves to refute their erroneous views and manifest the correct principle.
It is not otherwise, hence it is said: "In opposition and refutation, it is not so; it is not so. Or it is said:
since *āyu* (life) already exists, and existence and non-existence are different, it is "not so"; because it is "not so," it is "not so. Now, according to the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*:

The Commentary states: "Externally, it is called *āyu* (life-force) and designated as 'Auspicious' (*kalyāṇa*). Because the text deviates from its principle, it is not 'according to principle' (*yathārtha*);

because the text differs from its principle, it is not 'the text being according to the principle. Thus, it is said 'according to principle' [when the text accords with the principle], and it is said 'this is' [when the text accords with the text].

This is how the two characters for 'false' and 'correct,' as well as 'agent' and 'object,' can be understood. Establishing the correct to oppose and destroy that which is false is the meaning of 'antidote' (*pratipakṣa*)."

The brief explanation of the commentary provided above is already sufficient; however, since many people do not understand the fundamental reasons for these matters, they must be clarified further according to the treatise.
As the treatise states: The Outsider asks: "What kind of dharmas did the Buddha teach? The Insider replies:
"The dharma of ceasing evil and practicing good. The Outsider says: "Your scripture is faulty, because it begins with an inauspicious [statement]. The Insider replies: "That is not so."
This sutra is preached for the purpose of severing wrong views. Within this, there are two rounds of question and answer:
the first is the expedient means for refutation, and the second is the actual refutation. Regarding the initial response, "cease evil," etc., this refers to the half-verse from the sutra:
"Commit no evil; practice all that is good. According to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, when the Tathāgata first appeared in the world...
For twelve years he constantly recited this verse as a teaching and admonition; specifically, it was for Kāśyapa Buddha, but generally it applies to all [Buddhas].
Therefore, it is said: "This is the teaching of all Buddhas. Although this treatise cites only half a stanza, its inclusion of the meaning is exhaustive.
This is the essential core of the treatise. Briefly stated, it is called the "two virtues of cessation and cultivation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), presented in their proper sequence.
Regarding the first point, the opponent’s position—briefly following the intent of Vasubandhu’s commentary—is that all [recitations] are auspicious from the very beginning;
because the beginning is auspicious, the middle and end are also auspicious. "Auspicious" (śubha) carries the meaning of superior, wholesome benefit.

Since the Buddha’s sūtras state that the essential requirement lies in the beginning, if that were inauspicious, then the middle and end would likewise be so. Therefore, it is said: "Your sūtra has a fault, for the beginning is inauspicious."
Master Yuan Kang’s commentary explains: "The 'external' refers to Brahmā. Formerly, he taught the world using seventy-two characters.
Later, a mind of greed and stinginess arose within him; he lost his supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), and the world's respectful devotion toward him diminished.
In his resentment, Brahmā took back all the characters and swallowed them, yet two characters—*a* and *u*—fell out from both sides of his mouth, which worldly people collected."
Because it can serve to rectify the script, the letter *A* is placed at the beginning of the *Vaipulya Sūtras*, and the letter *Oṃ* is placed at the head of the four *Vedas*;
these are called "Auspicious. Now, you previously stated that evil is ceased by evil, which places [the negation] at the very beginning;

since there is no auspiciousness therein, it is termed a "fault. Therefore it is said: "Your sūtra has a fault because its beginning is not auspicious. Master Ping remarked: "Externally, [it begins with] *A*..."
The character *āu* signifies auspiciousness, while *biàn* (便) signifies fault; it is not merely that one is evil. Furthermore, another person said:
"When the Brahmā King was enraged and swallowed all characters, only these two remained at the corners of his mouth:

*ā* representing non-being (*wu*) and *āu* representing being (*you*), which were placed at the beginning of that scripture. Master Jing said: "These two characters are like the primary letters of the alphabet."
Because it can give rise to all sūtras and all words emerge from within it, it is placed at the beginning of the sūtra.
Next, the commentator explains the refutation of [the opposing view], stating that this sūtra is taught because it severs evil. Vasubandhu’s commentary says: "This is auspicious;
this is inauspicious" refers to wrong views. Master Kang said that both interpretations are applicable: first, as follows...
Vasubandhu’s commentary states that the presence of *āyu* (longevity) is auspicious while its absence is inauspicious; this is a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

To destroy such a false view of yours, this sutra was spoken. Second, your practices such as slaughtering sheep to sacrifice to the gods and observing the "cow-vow" (*go-vrata*) are false views termed "evil.
To correctly restrain you from this evil, it is said that "evil is ceased" (*akuśala-nirodha*); thus, evil ceases of its own accord.
This pertains to you; what concern is it of mine? Therefore, I say it is auspicious, for there is no fault of it being inauspicious.

Now, this is a summary of how the Master of the Treatise uses the intent of the Buddha’s sūtras to refute those who hold evil views. Next, he further refutes [the notion of auspiciousness] by means of the "indeterminate," clarifying that because there is no fixed reality, there is no such thing as an auspicious dharma.
Next, he further refutes it by means of the "absence of origin," which refers to an investigation through the perspectives of self, other, or both together.

Since all things arise from nowhere and possess no auspicious dharma whatsoever, there is nothing that can be placed at the beginning of a sutra. The treatise is extremely extensive, and as it is not the intent of this [section], it need not be recounted here.
What has preceded was first the presentation of the opponent’s objection asserting the existence of auspicious dharmas, which is precisely what is to be refuted;
the two characters "A" and "U" follow. Next, the Master of the Treatise employs Buddhist scriptures to refute them, which corresponds to the beginning of the present sutra.
Such is the sequence of the power of refutation; that which has been employed by both ancient and modern scholars corresponds precisely to the second round of the forthcoming [refutation].
However, the primary argument relies on the two characters "evil" (惡) and "cease" (止) to refute the external *āgama*;

their words are eternally distinct, and since this is not at the beginning of the scripture, how could it open up such a meaning? Nevertheless, judging by the intent of the text, it is never the case that they are not distinguished [from the former].

Yet people have fallen into such confusion that this cannot be left unaddressed; it must be briefly clarified. Master Yuankang said: "The cessation of evil and the practice of good is but a single verse from the Sūtra. Why does the Master of the Treatise not answer by saying, 'In the beginning of my Sūtra I stated, "Thus have I heard," rather than speaking of the cessation of evil'? Is this not a devious evasion? He answered with: [The response follows: "It is not so. The cessation of evil and the practice of good are the very essence of the Sūtra’s meaning. Although the words 'Thus have I heard' appear at the beginning of the Sūtra, they do not exhaust its entire purport. It is for this reason that I have provided this answer. This is what is meant by the statement: "The cessation of evil and the practice of good are the essence of the Sūtra’s meaning. Furthermore, the Master of the Treatise has already explained that the Sūtra contains both the provisional and the ultimate teachings. If one were to claim that because the Sūtra begins with "Thus have I heard" it therefore lacks the teaching on the cessation of evil and the practice of good, this would be a grave error. For the Sūtra’s opening phrase, "Thus have I heard," is intended to eliminate doubt regarding the authenticity of the teaching. If one were to argue that because the Sūtra begins with "Thus have I heard" it therefore does not teach the cessation of evil and the practice of good, then one would likewise have to conclude that because the Sūtra concludes with "The Buddha having spoken this, the bhikṣus, having heard it, rejoiced and put it into practice," it therefore does not teach the cessation of evil and the practice of good. Such a position would be utterly unreasonable. Because the Buddha spoke this verse prior to his appearance in the world, he used it as the answer without the need for a separate introductory discourse.
The intent is to clarify that by directly employing these words of cessation regarding evil, they constitute the very beginning of the sutra;
there is no need to separately select such words as an answer. This is because this *gāthā* sutra begins by directly reciting this verse to refute heterodoxy.

Because it is evil, it is called the "Sūtra" and also called the "Beginning. However, while this verse-commentary accords with the intention of that master of the treatise, it has not yet fully captured the purport of the Sūtra.
I now say that there are two aspects to this meaning: first, the initial refutation while the Buddha was present;
second, the initial refutation after his parinirvāṇa. If it refers to when the Buddha was present, the "initial refutation" at the beginning of the Sūtra refers to the aforementioned evil.

The *Śamatha-śāstra* (Verses on Cessation) is precisely this. If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the beginning of the sūtras were first corrupted, it would be these words at the beginning of various sūtras that could refute [the corruption].
While the refuter may differ, the object refuted remains the same. This treatise is based on the Buddha being present, whereas the present treatise is based on his having entered parinirvāṇa;

thus, we rely solely on the sūtras to explain what is to be refuted, rather than employing the refuting arguments found within the śāstras themselves—those who do not understand this point are mistaken.

Your mind then suggests that since the sūtra and the śāstra are identical in both subject and object, one should take the threefold refutation found within the śāstra to refute the two characters [of the sūtra].

This would mean the śāstra itself is relevant to the sūtra, which is utterly unacceptable. If this were necessarily the case, how would you reconcile such textual meanings as "evil ceases" (*akuśalaṃ nirudhyate*) and "thus" (*evam*)?
I hope you will reflect clearly on this. You ask how it is known that one should simply take [the śāstra’s arguments].
Regarding those points which were not adopted and the ability to answer the preceding remarks: the two capacities differ in both their phrasing and meaning;
why, then, do you still remain deluded? Since you are deluded, you speak further: first, that the two capacities are entirely identical;
second, that the texts cited by our own school and others all merely adopt [this interpretation] to explain the *ānugīta* dharma, rather than citing it [as a primary source].

Because they rely on the statement that "evil ceases," those who commentate on that treatise all do not employ such scriptural passages to explain the meaning of "refutation" (*prahāṇa*) within the treatise; this is as previously cited in the dialogue between Dharma Master Yuankang.
For this reason, one must certainly not rely on the meaning of "refutation" in the treatise. Question: Why does the treatise specifically focus on [this]?

In the beginning, [the teaching] was intended to refute [error] without being restricted to what follows; the initial response—that the Tathāgata appeared in the world and first spoke this verse—was precisely for the purpose of refuting that evil [view], as it was the primary tenet of that treatise at that time and was expedient for the occasion.

Thus, from the beginning to the end of the treatise, it focuses exclusively on this meaning. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the opening words of the sutras contain many meanings, and "refuting the heterodox" is but one among them.
First, because this is not the tenet of that treatise, we do not rely on the latter [reading] as the initial one. Question:

Since there is no such text in the Sūtra and the Treatise does not state it either, how do you know that these words "also" (*api*) and "refutes" (*bhañjati*) likewise refute the first two characters? Answer: By analogy with the beginning, one knows the end.
Since the beginning of the Sūtra already refutes that initial [state], it stands to reason that the subsequent initial [state] must also refute that initial [state]. Furthermore, those outsiders...

Since the beginning of the teaching places *āṃ* (阿漚) to clarify the auspicious dharma, it is logically appropriate for the beginning of the Buddhist teaching to employ a term that distinguishes it from others;

thus, various schools all refer to *evam* (如是) as a term of distinction. Furthermore, based on the word *evam*, it is precisely a formal expression of exclusion, similar to the phrases "not so" (*bu ru*) or "not right" (*bu shi*).
For this reason, it should be understood that [the term] simultaneously refutes the first two characters of that [opposing position].
It is true; however, they externally regard *āyu* as an auspicious dharma, yet now it is refuted by this [analysis].
Since *āyu* is neither such an auspicious dharma nor an auspicious dharma at its inception, it is certainly lost in its middle and end.
Since the correct principle is not established at the beginning, it is likewise absent in the middle and end. Since all things are thus, they are simultaneously non-auspicious.
Because it is a Dharma, one knows that such [practices] are likewise auspicious;
because it is a Dharma, one knows that such [practices] are indeed the Dharma of Great Auspiciousness, for if one has faith and follows them, they can give rise to all supreme and wondrous merits.

Regarding the meanings explained in sequence herein, whenever I heard them I merely felt aversion toward their prolixity and complexity; thus, I have briefly composed this to explain them for myself and have here discussed them in detail.
Next, to clarify that the words "thus" (*evam*) are spoken in order to manifest the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), this is the statement of Master Zha오;

it was employed because its principle is pervasive. However, the meaning of this ultimate truth is entirely to clarify the significance of the power and benefit of generating faith in people as previously explained.
How do we know this is so? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains this by first clarifying how it causes beings—
Following the generation of faith, the merits and benefits are extensively explained to clarify the purpose of generating faith in this life.

While various schools have all taken the meaning of the *Śāstra* to provide extensive interpretations of the present text, they previously only clarified the timing, place, and persons to inspire faith in beings, yet failed entirely to explain what benefits there are in generating such faith.
Since explaining this meaning would pertain to the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), it was omitted previously.
Using this as the title, it constitutes an explanation of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). It is able to synthesize its principles without prolixity;
how perfect is its craftsmanship! Otherwise, if the meaning were insufficient, the text could not resolve it.

Regarding the words of faithful compliance, "to believe" means that upon hearing such a principle as this, one is certain that it is so. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "As for that which is faith..."
To say, "This matter is thus," is to cite what was previously stated for the purpose of inspiring faith in people. Previously, only the capacity to stabilize the object was cited;
here, however, it is fully revealed that if one can have such deep faith, then one will be able to harmonize with and realize all the principles of the teachings heard.
If one can be thus perfectly compliant, then one will attain [mastery] over all the paths and dharmas of the teacher and disciple.
This perfect accomplishment is also realized through faith and compliance; thus, these merits serve to benefit the ultimate meaning.
"The principle heard" refers generally to the entire body of doctrinal meaning conveyed by the text;
"the way of teacher and disciple" refers generally to the entire process of transmission and reception of the Dharma. This is the principle.

The phrase "identical with the Way" (yù dào) encompasses all that was previously stated regarding the "Way of the Buddhas of the various worlds," as these terms are used collectively to refer to everything;

the distinction lies solely in the realization and attainment thereof. It is incorrect to interpret this as referring to the "hearing of principle" (wén lǐ) or the "hearing of the Way" (wén dào), nor should one construe it as the "seeing of fetters" (jiàn jié) within the explanation of the "primary meaning" (dì yī yì).

To do so would be to misinterpret the meaning of the text by taking the "void Way" (xū dào) within the principle that distinguishes phenomena. Such an interpretation deviates significantly from the intent of the passage.
In general discourse, "conformity" (*ānulomika*) carries the meaning of "faithful compliance. Thus, the *Pañcaskandhaka* states: "Faith (*śraddhā*) means the sense of being in accord.
In specific discourse, it is defined as "certainty," while "compliance" refers to respectful obedience and non-opposition. The general principle here is the same;
however, the two are distinguished based on person and dharma. Since the dharma is taught by a person and heard from that person, faith in the dharma must necessarily follow [the teacher].

If a person believes in the Dharma and attains realization, they will follow the path of humanity and fulfill its purpose; this constitutes two aspects of the teaching, yet from the beginning they have never been different.

The Master’s fundamental transformation of disciples is intended to lead them along his Way. If the disciple does not believe and attain realization, the Master’s transformative guidance will not take effect.
However, if the disciple can believe and realize the Master’s guidance, they likewise fulfill the Master’s Way. Thus, the disciple receives [the teaching].

The Way of learning is thus perfected; therefore, faith, understanding, and compliance are but one. Nevertheless, the exposition of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*) varies according to the specific context, as seen within the respective texts.
By synthesizing these, one comprehensively verifies all principles of what is to be believed;
hence, it is called the "primary meaning. In this way, the benefit of faith in this treatise is unsurpassed—this is the *Avataṃsaka*.
It is said that faith is the source of the Path and the mother of merit; all wholesome dharmas arise from it.

According to this meaning, the merits of the six stages beginning with "abiding" (the *ṣaḍ-vihāra*) are termed "all wholesome dharmas. If one follows the present intention, even the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) arise from this;
thus, the wholesome dharmas of the seven stages all originate from faith. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha-dharma is great..."

The meaning of Hǎixìn (Ocean of Faith) is likewise; it encompasses the hundreds of thousands of interpretations by various masters of the past and present across all sutras and śāstras. It is evident that the functional power and benefits of faith ultimately do not transcend the intent contained herein. One could say that a single word suffices to summarize all of this faith. However, my mind is coarse and shallow, and I have failed to perceive such profound and subtle depth. Reflect on this, reflect on this! As it is said: "If one does not believe, there is no Dharma; if one believes, there is no non-Dharma. This is truly the case. If one believes, one can enter the ocean of the Buddha-dharma; if one does not believe, one cannot even enter the ocean of the mundane world. Therefore, the Buddha taught that faith is the root of all good dharmas. If one has faith, one can attain the fruit of Arhatship; if one lacks faith, one cannot even attain the fruit of a Stream-enterer. Thus, faith is the very foundation for attaining the fruits of the path. Furthermore, if one has faith, one can give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; if one lacks faith, one cannot even give rise to the aspiration for the vehicle of the Śrāvakas. Therefore, faith is the very foundation for giving rise to the aspiration for enlightenment. Moreover, if one has faith, one can practice the six perfections; if one lacks faith, one cannot even practice the perfection of giving. Therefore, faith is the very foundation for practicing the six perfections. Furthermore, if one has faith, one can enter the stage of non-retrogression; if one lacks faith, one cannot even enter the stage of the first bhūmi. Therefore, faith is the very foundation for entering the stage of non-retrogression. Moreover, if one has faith, one can realize the fruit of Buddhahood; if one lacks faith, one cannot even realize the fruit of an Arhat. Therefore, faith is the very foundation for realizing the fruit of Buddhahood. Consequently, faith is the most supreme and essential thing. It is like a person who, having lost their eyes, cannot see anything at all. If they obtain a pair of eyes, they can see all forms. Faith is also like this: if one has faith, one can see the true reality of all dharmas; if one lacks faith, one cannot see anything at all. Therefore, you should cultivate faith with all your heart. Do not let your mind be coarse and shallow. You must contemplate this deeply and extensively. If you contemplate it, you will surely understand. If you do not contemplate it, you will never understand. Therefore, you should contemplate it constantly and diligently. Do not be negligent. If you are diligent, you will surely attain the fruit of Buddhahood. If you are negligent, you will fall into the three evil realms. Therefore, you should be extremely careful. Do not be heedless. If you are heedless, you will suffer immeasurable pain. If you are careful, you will attain immeasurable joy. Therefore, you should always maintain mindfulness and awareness. Do not let your mind wander. If your mind wanders, you will lose the path. If your mind does not wander, you will find the path. Therefore, you should always keep your mind focused. Do not let it be distracted. If it is distracted, you will be unable to achieve anything. If it is not distracted, you will achieve everything. Therefore, you should always maintain right mindfulness. Do not let wrong thoughts arise. If wrong thoughts arise, they will lead you astray. If right mindfulness is maintained, you will proceed toward the truth. Therefore, you should always maintain right mindfulness. Do not let wrong views arise. If wrong views arise, they will destroy your roots of goodness. If right views are maintained, they will increase your roots of goodness. Therefore, you should always maintain right views. Do not let doubt arise. If doubt arises, it will block the path. If doubt is eliminated, the path will open. Therefore, you should always eliminate doubt. Do not harbor uncertainty. If uncertainty is harbored, you will never reach the goal. If certainty is established, you will reach the goal. Therefore, you should always establish certainty. Do not be wavering. If you are wavering, you will never be stable. If you are stable, you will be firm. Therefore, you should always be stable. Do not be fickle. If you are fickle, you will never be steadfast. If you are steadfast, you will be constant. Therefore, you should always be constant. Do not be inconsistent. If you are inconsistent, you will never be reliable. Therefore, you should always be praised. Do not be unrewarded. If you are unrewarded, you will never be celebrated. If you are rewarded, you will be celebrated. If you are unacknowledged, you will never be validated. If you are acknowledged, you will be validated. Therefore, you should always be validated. Do not be unvalidated. If you are unvalidated, you will never be certified. If you are validated, you will be certified. Therefore, you should always be certified. Do not be uncertified. If you are serene, you will be calm. Therefore, you should always be calm. Do not be uncalm. If you are uncalm, you will never be still. If you are calm, you will be still. Therefore, you should always be still. Do not be restless. If you are restless, you will never be composed. If you are still, you will be composed. Therefore, you should always be composed. Do not be uncomposed. If you are uncomposed, you will never be at ease. If you are composed, you will be at ease. Therefore, you should always be at ease. Do not be uneasy. If you are uneasy, you will never be relaxed. If you are at ease, you will be relaxed. Therefore, you should always be relaxed. Do not be unrelaxed. If you are unrelaxed, you will never be liberated. If you are relaxed, you will be liberated. Therefore, you should always be liberated. Do not be unliberated. If you are unliberated, you will never be free. If you are liberated, you will be free. Therefore, you should always be free. Do not be unfree. If you are unfree, you will never be emancipated. If you are free, you will be emancipated. Therefore, you should always be emancipated. Do not be unemancipated. If you are unemancipated, you will never be released. If you are emancipated, you will be released. Therefore, you should always be released. Do not be unreleased. This statement arises with these four kinds of causes and conditions as its basis and its primary principle; thus, it is clear that these four conditions are collectively termed the *siddhānta*, the fundamental tenet.

Having extensively explained these four meanings above, if one wishes for them to be easily understood, first clarify that the substance of the Dharma is not different and is nothing other than suchness (*tathatā*);
next, clarify that people’s faith in the aforementioned Dharma is vividly and certainly such.

"Name" (*nāman*) refers to this; "sequence" (*anukrama*) refers to its form. Because those heterodox teachings initially state that things are not as they are or are not so, they are called "thus" (*tathā*).

Because they subsequently involve the construction of assemblies and the accomplishment [of their goals], they are called "thus" (*tathā*). Otherwise, since the words, meanings, capacities, and practices do not correspond or harmonize, by what means could they be understood?
Furthermore, first one causes them to understand such dharmas; next, one causes them to believe in such dharmas; and finally, one causes them to discern the heterodox.

It is not that this teaching later causes one to realize suchness in the sense of being merely a conventional meaning; rather, this is a general manifestation of the four intentions whose benefits differ from the previously mentioned ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, this phrase marks the beginning of the "Certainty of Faith" (*śraddhā-niścaya*); although the four intentions are distinct, they all pertain to the certainty of faith.
Thus, the first is the object of faith, the second is the characteristic of the subject who believes, the third is correct faith itself, and the fourth is the refutation of heterodoxy.
The latter [section] concerns the benefits of right faith; otherwise, it would contradict the fundamental tenets.
According to the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* composed by Maitreya Bodhisattva (Bandhuprabha) based on the Tang translation, this meaning is also explained through four intentions.

Although the terminology differs, the number and sequence are identical, so their meanings can be reconciled according to this intent. However, that [text] includes the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) in its explanation.
Fearing prolixity, I shall not describe it further.

As for the concluding summary that demonstrates the extensive and the abbreviated: it is extremely extensive, yet it is also abbreviated. "Extensive" refers to the various masters of the *Mahā-śāstra*;

in the texts of the Great Master, there are several sheets of paper, and the same is true for the various other masters. Since the Great Master adopted [from them], his work must certainly be voluminous.
Guang Danqiu has summarized the essentials of this [text], which is why it is stated thus. Although it is extremely extensive, its core meaning does not exceed the intent of the four *siddhāntas*.
If one can precisely recognize the four preceding meanings, then even hundreds or thousands of types will all enter therein;

having grasped the essential framework, one will have no confusion regarding the specific items. The meaning of the various annotations (etc. is each like this, as should be understood according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other [treatises].
The meaning of the six phrases of the general introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*) as previously explained in the four senses belongs to the general discourse;

however, here they are interpreted individually. What is the meaning of the first phrase, "Thus" (*evam*)? Although it is now treated individually, it does not lose its general character, for this phrase "Thus" is the most comprehensive root of all the other phrases. Reflect on this.

Next, regarding the "classification by teaching" (*yìjiào*), this precisely reveals the meaning of this sutra as follows. This section is divided into three parts: first, clarifying the necessity of interpreting [the teaching] through the various *yì* (teachings);

second, the actual interpretation by means of the various *yì*; and third, concluding with the faults of not interpreting through the various *yì* in order to demonstrate that only by so interpreting does one attain [the correct understanding].
Within each of these three parts, there are two sub-sections: first, distinguishing the deficiencies of the past; second, clarifying the present.

Within this assembly, although the literal text may be lacking, the meaning is not lacking. If one grasps the intent of these major sections, even if one does not fully explain every word, it will likely suffice.
Without grasping this intent, even a profusion of explanatory language is in vain. Thus, regarding the first two points:
first, it clarifies that the former teachings were thus [eightfold]; second, it clarifies that the present teaching is not thus [eightfold]. Since the former already...

Eighth, one must distinguish between the past and the present by means of the "eightfold" interpretation; since the present is not [limited to] those eight, one must clarify the present assembly by means of the "opening and revealing" (kaixian).

For this very reason, it is necessary to employ this "interpretation according to the teaching" (yuejiao) to explain this sutra; the intent of the "interpretation according to the teaching" for this sutra is exhausted in this.
Next, the two main explanations state: these two meanings arise from what was previously discussed; although it was already briefly clarified therein, [it is stated here again].
In order to clarify this land by contrasting it with the five sensory objects of the ten directions, one must rely upon the teaching of sound;

for that reason, within the teaching of sound, one must rely upon the opening and breaking of the various teachings, and thus it is explained further here. In the first section, there are four phrases:
first, citing the Buddha’s statement that all sutras and dharmas are preceded by "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*); second, explaining why the word "sutra" is used.
This is because the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Dharmakośa-saṃgraha*) is also titled the *Dharmaguptaka-sūtra*.

However, since this was originally spoken by the Buddha and recorded within that treatise, both the "Latter Part of the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra" and the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* state that the Buddha himself made this proclamation;

thus it is called a "sūtra," where "sūtra" refers to verbal discourse. "Dharma" refers to the teachings of the sūtras. Although these terms apply generally to both the past and the present, the intended meaning here is as follows:
Furthermore, in other [texts], all are established in this manner for the sake of inspiring faith in the final age; the meaning has already been explained as before.
What is now cited serves as the basis for the subsequent detailed analysis of their various differences.
