Upon hearing it, the Licchavis described their own state and reproached themselves, saying: "We know ourselves to be heedless people; had we not been so..."
"O kings of the *Ṛṣis*, when the Tathāgata was about to depart from our country, there was among the great assembly a son of a Brahmin named Ajita.
He spoke to the Licchavis, saying: 'Excellent, excellent! It is as you have said.
King Bimbisāra has already attained great benefit. That the Buddha has appeared in his country is like a wondrous lotus blooming in a great pond.'"
Those who are themselves deluded and addicted to the five desires, not knowing to approach and go to where the Tathāgata dwells, are called "persons of negligence.
It is not that the Buddha appears in the world for them alone that they are called negligent. How is this known? The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is like the sun and the moon;
he does not appear in the world for the sake of only one or two people. Furthermore, the intent of the sutra is to clarify that the Buddha universally acts for all.
To depart from all [worldly things] yet remain mired in self-delusion and fail to go forth to draw near [to the Dharma] is called negligence;
it is not merely leaving them behind that constitutes negligence. Even if you have departed your own country, if you do not draw near, this too is negligence.
Conversely, even if you have already left those [worldly things], if you can believe and aspire to go forth and draw near, this is likewise called non-negligence. All that is cited in the text...

These words, "Incomparable One" (*anuttara*), are now divided into two persons because they are established according to their respective meanings and examples; thus, they do not entirely coincide with the sūtra.

Furthermore, the first phrase serves as an example to demonstrate that there was previously an occasion and location where [the Buddha] possessed the capacity [to teach], whereas the subsequent phrase serves as an example to demonstrate that there was no such occasion or location where he lacked the capacity;
therefore, it is not mentioned. As for the term "Licchavi," this refers to a distinguished clan of the country of Vaiśālī.
It is said that the Buddha’s lineage is like the lake in the kingdom of Magadha, as explained below; the metaphor of the lotus flower represents the response [of the Buddha].
The lotus is a marvelous object, cherished and utilized by all; this represents the marvelous beauty of the Buddha’s merits, which are cherished and valued by all sentient beings.
From these, benefit is derived. That which is equal and non-dual is as previously cited: like the sun shining universally, it does not favor one over another.
The second point concerns "emergence. This clarifies that if there is a responsive capacity for awakening, one may see and hear [the Buddha] in any location;

therefore, the outflow of the untainted (anāsrava) occurs throughout all lands. What is clarified here—that emergence occurs at a specific time and place—is precisely because it depends upon the resonance between the responsive capacity and the stimulus.
Furthermore, general sūtras and śāstras clarify that the Buddha must attain enlightenment at the summit of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu); therefore, within the Form Realm...

Those who attain the Way while in the midst of transcending desire in the heavens are indeed categorized as a distinct class of karmic conditions; it is only in terms of the meaning of sequential progression that such a statement is made.

It is erroneous for people to claim that the Nirmāṇakāya transforms [beings] of the Small Vehicle, or that the Mahāyāna Saṃbhogakāya must necessarily be realized within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Therefore, although the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* elucidates the Lotus Treasury Ocean, one must ultimately...
This teaching given within the Bodhimaṇḍa in the kingdom of Magadha is the discourse of ultimate definitive meaning (*nītārtha*);

other teachings are therefore of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), which one should contemplate well. This passage directly clarifies that [the Buddha] appeared in the world in response to the karmic conditions of sentient beings, and is not the primary truth; thus it is called the "Worldly Explanation."
Furthermore, the reason for appearing in the world is precisely to give rise to the goodness of sentient beings.

As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, within the analogy of the "conjunction and union," it cites the example that if the sun does not appear, two things cannot produce growth; conversely, it is shown that if the sun does appear, those two things can produce growth.

The same logic should apply to the conjunction [of the Buddha’s appearance]. If the Buddha did not appear, then the two types of goodness—namely, that which has already arisen and that which has not yet arisen—could not exist.
The generation [of the analogy] proceeds by way of two [contrasts], yet it is able to establish the meaning through the reversal of the analogy and its subsequent application;
this is because there is no desire for excessive textual elaboration. *Kṣatriya* is translated here as "Sun-Lord of the Earth," which refers to the royal lineage of that country.
*Brāhmaṇa* is also called *Brahmacārin*, translated as "Pure Conduct," or "Pure Resolve," or "Tranquil One," or "Tranquil Offspring. It is also... [text continues].
The *śūdra* is the lineage that cultivates pure conduct; the *vaiśya*, which in this [language] is translated as "merchant," refers to the lineage of merchants who deal in wealth and goods.

In antiquity, it was also translated as "householder" (*jushi*); "householder" (*ju*) means to accumulate, referring to one who dwells amidst accumulated wealth and goods and acts as a gentleman (*shi*).
Of the four castes, three have been briefly mentioned; one should further mention the *śūdra*, which in this [language] is translated as "farmer."
"Karma" (karma) is like sowing the seeds of the five grains; it is also called "the common people" (*sūdras*) because their occupations are minute and they descend early [to labor].
Among the clans of the Western Regions, these four are the most preeminent.

It is similar to how, in this land, the four classes of scholar, farmer, artisan, and merchant are roughly analogous; here, the human realm is presented first, while the various heavens are clarified below.
This refers to the twenty-eight heavens, which can be understood as follows: for those among humans and devas who have not yet been born, he causes them to be born;

for those already born, he causes them to increase and expand. This is the meaning of the passage below concerning the time before the Great Penetrating Buddha appeared, when humans and devas were diminishing.

Since his appearance is for the purpose of generating such goodness, it belongs to the category of benefiting others (*hitārtha*). Next, to clarify that his appearance is also for the purpose of extinguishing evil, it is said: "For..."
This is because it eliminates the evils of the world and causes one to transcend it.
If it were not for the response of the three vehicles to transcend the world, the Buddha-body would not manifest; it is precisely due to such karmic conditions that the Buddha appears.

Thus, he cuts off the stream of all birth and death within the triple realm—the delusions known as the four floods (*catur-ogha*), as will be explained later—and the Tathāgata’s remedial activity never ceases.
Therefore, it is said that "skillfully severing this" is also a passage from the sutra. Because this [state] arises by removing these evils, it is presented as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Next, the application and essential nature are clarified: this is also the twenty-eighth passage of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.

The dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is precisely the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which pervades all places like empty space. How could there be movement or emergence within this Buddha-body? This is its nature.

Therefore, there is likewise no movement or emergence; it is merely the result of responsive resonance. Thus, the *Yì* says: "Tranquil and unmoving, yet upon being stimulated, it immediately penetrates.
If even the Way of the *Yì* is thus, how much more so for the Buddha-Dharma, which reigns supreme and is sovereign over all phenomena?

Movement and emergence are simply its functioning; the three preceding meanings refer to this. To arise momentarily is "movement," and to manifest clearly is "emergence"—this is the nature of the essence.
There is fundamentally no such beginning or end; it is because there is this subtle manifestation that there may be movement and response.
Thus, the Confucians explain "response" (*gan*) as "movement. Among all natures, there is equality and non-duality;

there is neither response nor non-response, yet one moves in accordance with response, manifesting through appearance. This interpretation is also acceptable. That which is non-existent yet exists is precisely...
To exist while being non-existent means that it is truly non-existent. It is like a bright mirror manifesting images; does the mirror have any intentionality toward manifesting them?
Yet it is able to cause those images to appear. This is because it manifests by acting as the reality itself. This clarifies that within the non-duality of non-existence, one is able to be dual;
it causes one to realize the essence of non-duality. It also clarifies that the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is precisely the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), for this is the essence of non-duality.

Therefore, this is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Although these four meanings differ according to the distinctions between phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*), they are collectively presented for the sake of sentient beings so that they may obtain benefit from both phenomena and principle.
Furthermore, as this is a general discourse on the meaning of transcending the world, it does not yet touch upon specific intentions;

thus, it is explained as being entirely based on causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*). While this principle applies to all Buddhas, the present intent concerns specifically the reasons for the appearance of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Question: Regarding this, it is said that the four intentions (*cetanā*) exist only among humans in the world of Jambudvīpa, while the cultivation of goodness exists only among humans and devas;

yet, when discussing the three realms (*tridhātu*), [it is said they exist] everywhere. How is this to be understood? Answer: Superficially, it may be as you say; however, if one seeks deeply into the ultimate principle, there is no contradiction. Why?

Since it is said that all things are equal and non-dual, such that a response occurs whenever there is a resonance, how could it be that [the capacity for goodness] is restricted solely to this place? Furthermore, since...
If that which is pervasive can equally give rise to and extinguish everything, why then speak only of the virtues of humans and devas and the evils of the three realms?

Thus, although the words follow specific matters from the subtle to the manifest and appear distinct in meaning, in reality they are all equal. Now, for the sake of relying on the treatises, we shall provisionally follow these distinctions;
because they are mutually relative and are cited in relation to one another, it is so. One should reflect upon this well.

The preceding general discussion concerning the origins and causes for the existence of the name "Buddha" is thus concluded. From here on, the distinctions and reconciliations are clarified according to the teachings, specifically revealing the intent of the present sutra.
This section consists of three parts: the formal exposition, the citation of evidence, and the conclusion. First, regarding the four teachings, there are four distinct categories.

Within the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching, we first translate the name; it should be rendered in full as *Buddha*, or in its newer transcription, *Fo-tuo* (or *Bo-duo*). In this land [of China], it is preferred...
Because it is a concise [expression] for generating wholesome states, only the single character "Buddha" is retained;

as for the translations such as "Awakened" (*jue*) or "Aware" (*zhi*), other sutras and treatises often use "Awakened," while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Wisdom Treatise) often uses "Aware. Here, because they are combined in this general discussion, it is called "Awakened-Aware" (*jue-zhi*).
This means that which is capable of awakening and knowing; that is, the principal subject, who is the person, in contrast to the ignorant and deluded.
That which does not perceive or know is called "non-awakening," while that which perceives and knows is called "awakening"; though they differ in name, their meaning as awakening and knowing is one.

If one applies this analogy to the various schools, it can also be understood in terms of the two obstacles—the afflictive and the cognitive. Furthermore, it is precisely the meaning of wisdom regarding phenomena and principle.
Consider this, but fearing that the text does not intend this meaning, I have not employed it here. This awakening and knowing should all possess the three [natures].
This means that it is distinct from those three types of persons—ordinary beings, followers of the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas—and thus fulfills both self and others.
These three meanings are inexhaustible and can only be grasped through the mind; there is no need for further prolixity. Our own school also fully elucidates these three meanings;
although in this passage the text appears to explain only the two meanings of self and others, the meaning itself actually encompasses all three.
What is this? Since it clarifies the meaning of self and other awakening within the ultimate fruit, it constitutes the perfection of self and other awakening.
As previously cited from the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it is likewise so; this principle extends throughout the three lower teachings.

Within the section on the "Awakening Site" (*bodhimanda*) below, there is a formal explanation of the characteristics of awakening-knowledge in the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), which includes the locus of awakening-knowledge, the aspect of awakening-knowledge, and the form of awakening-knowledge.
To know life, to perceive form, and to perceive the ultimate characteristics as well as the fetters collectively constitutes the meaning of the "Initial Teaching" (*ādikarmika-bodhi*).
Regarding the mention of the "site of practice" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and so forth: this refers to the *bodhimaṇḍa*. At that place there is a tree called the *bodhi* tree;

it was formerly termed the "site of practice" (*daochang*) and the "tree of the path" (*daoshu*), because it is the location where the Buddha first attained the Way, and he sat beneath it. The new [translation] calls it...
The "site of awakening" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and the "tree of awakening" refer to the place where supreme awakening was attained. The *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciations) to the *Hanshu* states:
"To pile up earth and make it high is called a *tán* (altar); to clear the ground until it is level is called a *chǎng* (field/pavilion). Both are places where deities and spirits dwell.

This [site] is precisely a level and upright location brought about by the power of the virtues of the Buddhas, not the work of human labor. This is clearly explained in the *Xiyu Zhuan* (Account of the Western Regions).

Whether provisional or ultimate, they are all identical in their single statement regarding the general and specific characteristics of the mundane and supramundane. The Master said: "General" refers to the fact that nothing is not impermanent;

"specific" refers to the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness—that is, the three realms and the four noble truths. There is nothing among these specifics that is not contemplated as impermanent.

This is still difficult to perceive. Now I say: the mundane consists of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*), while the supramundane consists of the path and its cessation (*mārga* and *nirodha*).
It is generally said that contemplating the Four Noble Truths as nothing but impermanent is because this teaching uses them to correctly observe the arising and ceasing of the Four Truths;

this is fully explained in the *Fochengxuan* (Profound Meaning of Attaining Buddhahood) and the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation), where it is stated that "suffering" consists of the three characteristics and so forth.

Specifically, this is because within each of the Four Truths, there are sixteen aspects of contemplation (*ṣoḍaśākāra*), each having four distinct modes of observation. Reflect on this. Some say that beneath each individual Truth...

The four practices are all one, which is the general [category], while the remaining three are the specific [categories]; this is because the first is named "sameness" (the general), while the names of the remaining three are "distinctions" (the specific).
Because he himself produces such realization and causes others to produce that same realization, it is said that he is also able to awaken others.
His physical form was sixteen feet tall, as he was the most excellent among the people of Jambudvīpa at that time; his lifespan was eighty years during that period.
Among humans, he was neither of superior nor inferior, but of middle lifespan. The old bhikṣu’s appearance was identical to that of the ordained monastic community;

as clarified in the Āgamas, when approaching the time of parinirvāṇa, such as when the old bhikṣu went to Cunda’s house to beg for food before entering extinction, the person of ultimate realization has no fixed form—sometimes appearing the same and sometimes different.
Thus, while his physical stature was entirely different, his countenance was entirely the same, and so too was his lifespan.

Thus, regarding the thirty-four moments of mind that are half-similar and half-dissimilar: the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*) pertain to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*);

the nine paths of non-inquiry (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) pertain to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). When these two paths are combined, there are thirty-four. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is clarified that the causal stage of this Mahāyāna differs from that of the Hīnayāna;
whereas [the latter] spans three great aeons (*kalpa*) and one hundred aeons, these merely suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*) without severing them until the final birth and the path [of the fruit].

At that time, whether in the state of realization (*darśana-mārga*) or through cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), [the afflictions] are severed instantaneously; this is stated to distinguish [this path] from that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Furthermore, it is said, "under the Bodhi tree," and so forth. This differs from what is explained in other treatises regarding the severance and suppression [of afflictions], which is the same as that of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

The explanations provided by various masters all rely on the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā*, and other such works, and thus differ from this [text]. Students should understand this well and discern each respective position.
One must not base oneself on superficial appearances to falsely dispute matters of right and wrong; if one seeks to harmonize these perspectives now, it can indeed be achieved.

Why is this? There are two kinds of cessation: contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Other [texts] refer to the contaminated, while the *Mahā-śāstra* refers to the uncontaminated when speaking of "grasping" (*upādāna*).
How is this made clear? As Master Huī explains in his "Chapter on the Path of Vision": "When a Bodhisattva is at the stage of an ordinary person..."
By means of the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*), he exhausts the afflictions of the eight stages from the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) downward;

however, he alone cannot sever the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) because he lacks the path without outflows (*anāsrava-mārga*). Subsequently, beneath the Bodhi tree, he first gives rise to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) without outflows, culminating in the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
These thirty-four moments of mind are purely without outflows, and he does not give rise to this resolve [to seek further] until that point.
By attaining Buddhahood while seated, one realizes and knows [the truth], thereby clarifying the distinction between the two types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
Reflect on this: this phrase corresponds precisely to the meaning of the fulfillment of awakening (*bodhi-pūraṇa*).

Since the meaning of "realizing and knowing" in these [passages] differs from that of the latter three [vehicles], it should be understood that wherever various sūtras and śāstras present such an explanation, they all belong to this teaching (the *Śrāvaka-yāna*).
The meaning of "Buddha" is next explained according to the *Zhongguan* (Madhyamaka) school, interpreting it through other texts as the awakening to the non-arising of the Four Noble Truths.

Because the capacity of the teaching's recipient (*śrāvaka*) is superior to what precedes it and inferior to what follows, its form still manifests with residual traces. Furthermore, although skillfulness and clumsiness differ, the essence realized is one;
thus, the superior remains inferior. Regarding the phrase "a single thought-moment," this clarifies that the final awakening is itself [the realization of] the self.

The meaning of "fulfilling the realization of others" (paravijñapti) should be understood by analogy with the rest of the text. Fourth, because all meritorious practices are fulfilled, one becomes a Buddha; this is what is meant by "relying on the ultimate Bodhisattva ground."
Because it can eliminate all ignorance and bring dreams to an end, this stage—from the tenth bhūmi through the final thought-moment of Equal Enlightenment—enters into Sublime Enlightenment;

this is precisely the ultimate *ji* (identity). In the treatise, the initial discussion of original enlightenment (*benjue*) corresponds to the "true mind" in the sutra and the "Buddha of Principle" (*liri ji fo*);
they do not meet, for their self-identity is already established. Although the four types of *shijue* (initial enlightenment) lack explicit names in the text, [their meaning is implicit].

The meaning of the term is not without basis. Why is this? As clarified at the outset, within the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), although one possesses awakening and cognition, it is still termed "non-awakening" (*abodha*).
Since this cannot be definitively determined as either right or wrong, these are merely persons of designation;

thus, the *Benye jing* (Sutra on the Original Karma) names those in the ten levels of faith "Bodhisattvas by Name. They may properly be called "bodhisattvas by name" (*nāma-bodhisattva*), yet they still contain [the potential for realization].
There are two kinds of names: first, because one has already heard that the original self-nature is itself the name of awakening;
second, because although coarse delusions have not yet been eliminated and shallow principles have not yet been realized through investigation, there is nonetheless the name of "possessing awareness.
Thus, we know that from the very beginning there is the stage of Name, followed by the stage of Practice-and-Contemplation, and then the stage of Similar Awakening.
Next, there are the stage of partial awakening (*anupūrva-bodhi*) and the stage of ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*);

these three stages correspond to the names and sequence of the latter three Buddhas as explained in the preceding sutra. Since they are identical in this regard, they may be elucidated by analogy with the latter three explained here.

However, since the explanations in the sutras and treatises do not necessarily define the meaning of "perfect" (*pariniṣpanna*), such an interpretation is permissible; how much more so in the present case of the Perfect [Teaching].

Because it is subtle yet does not explicitly clarify the "six identities" (liu ji), it can also serve as an illustration to manifest the meaning of the six identities, thereby making them even more credible.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*’s discussion of the three types of bodhi (*tri-sambodhi*) is also of this nature. However, when explained in terms of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), it may be either extensive or concise.

If extensive, it fully clarifies the four types of contemplation as previously described in the *Zhonglun* (Treatise on the Middle); if concise, it directly addresses contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*). In this present text:

Taken together, these three meanings constitute the contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*), for the essential points of the preceding three explanations do not transcend this most sublime [meaning].
If one insists on opening them up to include all four, there is indeed a basis for doing so; however, as it is neither urgent nor essential, I shall not elaborate further with prolixity.

Next, regarding the explanation of the meaning of the character *zhù* (abiding), various treatises differ. Although the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* provides an explanation, it does not specify its classification;

the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* does not explain it at all, instead incorporating it into the explanation of the phrase "the locus of abiding" (*chǔjù*). The discrepancies among the commentaries of various schools are likewise similar.

In our own school’s *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-śāstra*, it is classified under the category of the "subjective phrase" (*zhǔjù*). Jiaxiang [Jizang] was also like this, as were the various schools of recent times.

Most of these are included within the category of "place" (*sthāna*), yet this [category] may also be considered non-existent at present; for now, following the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*, they are entered into the category of "subject" (*pramātṛ*).
The Buddha is the person who dwells, "dwelling" (*sthiti*) is the dharma that enables dwelling, and the city and mountain are the places where one dwells.

Since these are dharmas that enable dwelling, they have already been grouped together; it is therefore appropriate that they now be classified together with the person who dwells. Thus, [they are placed here].

The phrasing [of this passage] falls under the fourth category; other sūtras also contain such statements, differing only in terminology. Some say that "being present" (*zài*) refers to a temporary state, while "abiding" (*zhù*) refers to a long-term duration;

this is merely a provisional interpretation. In the commentary on the initial section on causes and conditions, it clarifies that there are four meanings of "abiding," all of which are from the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
However, as the treatise is somewhat extensive and this text is extremely concise, it is difficult to perceive [the full meaning]. Now...

First, I shall briefly set forth the essential outline of the treatise, and subsequently provide a detailed commentary on the text. Now, observing the commentary, there are five sections of meaning, which may also be considered as six;
first, the fivefold textual divisions are: (1) an explanation based on the four postures of the four directions; (2) an explanation based on various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*);

(3) an explanation based on the three modes of abiding of the gods, Brahmās, and sages; (4) a further explanation based on the aforementioned three modes of abiding; and (5) an explanation based on...
The Buddha’s dwelling explains its meaning; the sixth [point] is that within the five sections, it is known that these are all manifested within the explanations themselves.

Thus, these five or six essentials do not go beyond the four intentions. Therefore, the commentary here explains the treatise by means of these four meanings, such that no sound of the text remains unexhausted. Why is this?
First, regarding the "worldly" (loka), this refers to the initial section of the treatise which explains based on the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*). Next, it is explained for...
The two explanations regarding the "human counteragent" correspond to the second chapter of the treatise; the third and fourth chapters concern the three dharmas;
and the fourth [explanation] regarding the resolution of meaning through the ultimate truth corresponds to the fifth chapter of the treatise concerning the Buddha’s abodes.

Thus, it is clear that these four categories encompass all [interpretations]. Although various masters of the past and present have provided extensive exegeses, none transcend these four; the treatise speaks of the "four *siddhāntas*."

It is appropriate that this encompasses all [aspects]; however, among the five sections of the treatise, the first primarily explains "abiding" (sthiti) by way of the subject who abides, while the subsequent four all explain "abiding" by way of the locus in which one abides. The four points in the present text are likewise:

the first provides a general explanation of abiding, and the following three provide specific explanations. Their meaning is identical to the intent of the treatise, which can be considered accordingly. Now, as for the initial heading:
Regarding "subject and object" and so forth, this is because the term "abiding" (sthiti) is used universally. "Abiding" carries the meaning of dwelling or residing;
"that which is dwelt in" clarifies the location, while "that which is able to abide" clarifies the functional dharma. What, then, is that location and dharma? The commentary explains:

"The Land of Endurance" (*sahā*)—in Sanskrit, *sahā*, which is translated as "endurance" (*kṣānti*). The meaning will be explained later. This [passage] cites both the general and the specific categories together, and both are indeed [the subject].

The place where the Buddha’s transformation-body resides is called the "place of residence" (*sthāna*). The four modes of physical deportment (*īryāpatha*) are collectively termed the "means of residing" (*sthātṛ-dharma*), as they constitute the methods by which he dwells.

This means that the Buddha’s body, through its four dignified postures, abides in the Sahā world, royal cities, and various worldly locations to teach those with whom he has a karmic connection until his entry into *nirvāṇa*.
For this reason, it is called "residing. However, the initial explanation in the treatise refers only to—
This is because it further elucidates the meaning of how the world is established; it corresponds to the third explanation in this treatise, which concludes with the passage:
"Out of compassion for sentient beings, he dwells in Rājagṛha. However, since the manner of dwelling is not restricted to a specific location, it is appropriate to discuss it generally;
thus, although the treatise treats it separately for the time being, [it must be understood in this broader sense].
The royal city must be situated in a place that is even more luminous and pervasive so that the means and the end may correspond;

therefore, it is further described as the "Land of Endurance" (*Sahā-lokadhātu*), for this is the realm of a single transformation. Yet, since the Perfected One is without fixed location, how could there be any dwelling?

It is only to transform those who dwell within fixed locations and have attachments to such locations, leading them back to the state of no-fixed-location and non-dwelling, that he is said to "dwell. This is precisely...
"This is the inconceivable dwelling. This is the general explanation; it is called "dwelling" because the Buddha dwells in the world to teach and transform those with whom he has a karmic connection.
Thus, this is an explanation in terms of the causes and conditions of the world. Next, regarding the clarification of "dwelling in wholesome dharmas":
it clarifies that the Buddha's so-called "dwelling" does not merely refer to his physical presence in a worldly location; furthermore, dwelling within all wholesome dharmas is also termed "dwelling."

This is precisely the method for the two abodes of devas and Brahmās within the *Śāstra*. The *Śāstra* states that the six classes of desire-realm devas possess what is called the "abode of devas" (*devasthāna*).

A subsequent commentary explains: "The three matters of giving, precepts, and a virtuous mind are called the abode of devas. The *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* (*Guanjing shu*) explains these as cause and effect.
What is here termed the "ten wholesome actions" (*daśakuśala*) is a brief enumeration of the causes; among the three matters, it refers specifically to the single factor of the virtuous mind.
The *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* states: "From the Brahmā realm up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, abiding in the Dharma is called the 'Brahma-abodes' (*brahma-vihāra*).
Later, it further explains that the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*) are called the Brahma-abodes. The commentary on the *Śāstra* also states this refers to cause and effect.

What is now mentioned as the "four dhyānas" appears to be a brief enumeration of the dharmas abiding within the result. Question: In the *Śāstra*, the higher realms are universally cited in reference to the result. Why is this so?
Regarding the two realms, why is it that only the four *dhyānas* are mentioned in terms of their causes? Do not answer; it should simply be understood as an abbreviation.
Since the heavens and the Brahma-realm are free from human desires and evils, and are thus all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), they are combined into a single dwelling.
Within these wholesome dharmas, in order to cause wholesome states to arise collectively, this is designated as the "dwelling for humans. Next, the dwelling in the three samādhis is explained.
It clarifies that the Buddha does not merely proceed through worldly wholesome dharmas, but further abides within the supramundane noble dharmas;

this refers to the "noble abidings" (*āryavihāra*) discussed in the treatise. The treatise states: "The dharmas in which the various *pratyekabuddhas* and *arhats* abide are called 'noble abidings'. Later, it provides a further explanation, stating:
"Abiding in the three *samādhis* is called the 'noble abiding'. The commentary (*śū*) also explains this as cause and effect; here, the term "abiding" (*vihāra*) is used.
The three samādhis are precisely the dharmas of abiding in the causal stage that have been raised here;
both this cause and its fruit are the dharmas in which the noble ones of the Three Vehicles abide, and are therefore called "noble abodes" (*āryavihāra*).

However, to enter and realize the true path of the noble ones, one must first, by means of these three concentrations, destroy the three kinds of attachment to signs and the chaotic, evil states of abiding; it is within the destruction of these evil dharmas that [the noble abodes are realized].
Because it causes beings to shatter all attachments and evils, this antidote is called "abiding" (*sthiti*). Question:

Regarding the explanation of the three abidings in the *Śāstra*, are they presented as cause or as fruit? Answer: This is merely an alternating citation intended to fully encompass the purport of the treatise without excessive elaboration;
therefore, the *Sūtra Commentary* employs the entire text of the *Śāstra* for its explanation. Next, the term "abiding" is discussed.
Regarding "Śūraṅgama and so forth," this refers to the explanation in the treatise concerning the Buddha’s dwelling (*buddhavihāra*).

It clarifies that the Buddha does not merely dwell within the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*), but further dwells within all the Buddha-dharmas; therefore, it is called the Buddha’s dwelling. While "noble" (*ārya*) applies both generally and specifically—generally to the three vehicles and specifically only to the Great Vehicle—the treatise explains the Buddha’s dwelling after the noble dwellings for this very reason. Thus, the treatise says: "The Buddha’s dwelling."
The *Śūraṅgama* and other immeasurable samādhis, as well as the immeasurable merits of all Buddhas, constitute the dwelling place of the Buddha;
because the Buddha dwells therein, it is called the "Buddha-dwelling. *Śūraṅgama* translates here as the "Samādhi of Valiant Subjugation," or the "Samādhi of Heroic Aspect";
it is newly translated as the "Samādhi of Valiant Action. Because it is the greatest and most supreme among all samādhis, it is cited [as the foremost].
To begin with, these are the secret treasury of the *dharmadhātu*; therefore, they are the dwelling place of all Buddhas.
Since they are the dwelling place of all Buddhas, they are the supreme path of central reality; thus, they are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This is the ultimate dwelling place. To abide within it oneself and cause all beings to likewise return to it—this is what is meant by "abiding in the ultimate truth."
Regarding the Buddha’s abiding (*sthiti*): although the four meanings explained above clarify what is termed "abiding," they remain scattered and difficult to perceive.
To summarize: first, he dwells in the world for the sake of others’ happiness, so as to cause sentient beings to transcend the world;

second, he dwells in worldly locations so that all sentient beings may abide in wholesome dharmas, and thus he himself abides within those wholesome dharmas; furthermore, this serves to counteract and destroy...
Because sentient beings abide in all manner of attachments to signs and various evils, they are able to abide in the breaking of evil dharmas within the three concentrations;
furthermore, because they cause all sentient beings to enter together into the ultimate path of all Buddhas, they abide in the primary truth of the Middle Way.
Taking these four meanings in total, abiding in these four dharmas constitutes the four *siddhāntas*.

Because he dwells by means of causes and conditions, it is called the "Buddha-dwelling. However, in the second section of the treatise, the current text is explained by way of dwelling within the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Although no specific citation is provided here, the meaning is already subsumed therein;

for among the three dwellings—the Brahma-dwelling, the Noble-dwelling, and the Buddha-dwelling—all contain the term "meditative concentration. To speak of them individually, this [Buddha-dwelling] is precisely the Noble-dwelling (*āryavihāra*).

Because it is subsumed within the category of "counteractives" (*pratipakṣa*), the Treatise states: "In order to terrify the armies of Māra and to cause all disciples to rejoice, he dwells in the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
This is identical in meaning to the sense of "correctly counteracting and destroying evil," differing only in being a general versus a specific formulation;

therefore, it is subsumed within the counteractives. For this reason, it is not cited separately. Thus, one should know that the Treatise explains "dwelling" through five aspects, primarily manifesting the various [meanings].
The meaning of "abiding" (*sthiti*) is now explained through four points; these encompass the intent of the treatise without omission.

Although the terminology of the two masters—Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha and Dharma Master Jiaxiang—regarding the eight types of abiding differs slightly, their underlying meanings are identical and there is no difference in their sequence.
Since neither of them departs from the present four points, and as the remaining texts have already been reconciled, I fear that further elaboration would be redundant and thus omit it.

To restate: The previous judgment of the text stated that while "abiding in clarity" refers to the subject who abides (*nirdeśa*), why does the commentary here answer by referring to both the subject and the object of abiding?

The judgment states that in response to the scriptural text, the explanation follows the specific meaning of the passage; thus, where the meaning is distinct, it must be explained separately, and where the meaning is universal, it must be discussed universally. Such is the case here.

Question: Since the explanation of the Buddha’s dwelling (*buddhavihāra*) has already been fully established, what is the purpose of explaining the three dwellings of the devas, Brahmās, and noble ones (*ārya*)?

Answer: These three are all distinct locations for the Buddha’s dwelling; therefore, they are explained. If that is so, why does the treatise, at the conclusion of the explanation of the three dwellings, state, "dwelling within the noble dharmas" (*āryadharmeṣu viharati*), yet at the conclusion of the explanation of the Buddha’s dwelling, state, "dwelling in the place of the Buddha’s dwelling" (*buddhavihāre viharati*)? This is because the treatise merely... [text fragment] ...provides these distinctions.

Regarding the specific distinctions made according to their names: if one were to follow the argument strictly as it was presented, one should only speak of "dwelling in the Buddha-dwelling" (*buddhavihāra*).
However, since it is possible to say one "dwells in the noble dwelling" (*āryavihāra*), it follows that one may also dwell in the celestial and Brahma dwellings.

Moreover, the treatise itself states: "Dwelling amidst all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*). This clearly indicates a general sense. Furthermore, because the Buddha-dwelling encompasses all dwellings, it is known that [all are included].
This is the meaning of the Buddha’s dwelling; alternatively, it may be understood as citing the general to reveal the specific meaning. Consider this:

regarding the formal explanation of the location where the sutra was preached, the text merely states that he dwelt in the city of Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak, without mentioning the Buddha’s celestial abodes or other such places.

Why not explain directly according to the literal text rather than speaking circuitously? When the text reveals the profound within the profound, reaching the ultimate profundity, how does this fail to open up the intent of the sutra?
Therefore, modern authors not only do not employ this interpretation, but they even more severely condemn the errors and excesses of those who have used it throughout the past and present.
What is the reason for this? The answer is: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin jing) speaks of the "stages" (*vihāra*) in the same manner as this sutra;

furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Zhilun), in its commentary on that sutra, does not merely explain the text literally but extensively elucidates the various stages such as the "Heavenly Stages" (*deva-vihāra*), thereby leading later generations to follow [this expanded understanding].

Why is this so? That school explains it thus: "In the treatise (*śāstra*), the term 'abiding' (*sthiti*) is explained; following its characteristics, the meaning of abiding is elucidated in a general sense.
It is not that the Sūtra contains this specific meaning, but rather that the treatise provides this explanation and interpretation.

It is only later people who, failing to grasp the intent of the treatise, have misapplied the textual authority of the treatise and lost their own way. How can they claim the fault lies with the Sūtra and the treatise? Now, I say: as for this...
It is only natural that those people do not understand the profound intent of this teaching. *Jiashang* (Excellence and Auspiciousness) summarizes the eight abodes into two categories:

first, the four abodes concerning the transformation of the dwelling place while not yet having relinquished the lifespan—namely, the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*). These four abodes are called the "abodes of the body" and also the "external abodes.
Next, the four abodes concerning the heavens, Brahmā, the sages, and the Buddhas. These four abodes are called the "abodes of the mind" and also the "internal abodes."
Because the Tathāgata abides by means of these eight internal and external modes of abiding, he is called "Abiding. Although that Master made this determination, he did not clarify the reason for it;
thus, the intent of the sūtras and śāstras remains unmanifest, and the preceding points of confusion have not been systematically resolved.

Therefore, although there are many such determinations, they remain insufficient. I maintain that the Buddha’s abiding is twofold: first, the Abiding of the Essence (mūla-vihāra), and second, the Abiding of the Trace (nirmāṇa-vihāra).

Abiding is also called "abiding externally," and abiding externally is also called "abiding of the mind. Thus, among the four preceding meanings, the first is the manifestation (*traces*) of the world, while the remaining three are the source (*root*).
Since there can be no manifestation without a source, the manifestation-abiding exists by virtue of the source-abiding;

since there can be no convergence with the source without the manifestation-abiding, the source-abiding is revealed through the manifestation-abiding. As the *Śāstra* says: "One abides in the noble abiding because of compassion."
Residing in the royal city is analogous to the other three residences; this is why, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, after explaining the four residences, compassion is clarified.

For how could these residences not be the manifestation of the fundamental [nature] through its traces? It is precisely for the purpose of using these manifested traces to lead sentient beings back to the fundamental source that they are established.
Thus, although it is not explicitly stated, the meaning is naturally revealed. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies that he dwelt in the śāla grove.
Having transformed and guided all sentient beings to establish them within the secret treasury, one then dwells therein oneself;
is this not relying on a provisional trace to realize the fundamental source? Therefore, the Sūtra directly cites these traces. Although they dwell in these traces, they possess a fundamental basis.
The Master of the Treatise, having deeply perceived this intent, extensively elucidates the meaning of these various dwellings in order to clarify it; thus, the traces dwell herein.

To dwell and teach is solely to cause sentient beings to return together to their original place of dwelling. If there were no three original dwellings, there would be no way to manifest these provisional traces;
if there were no these provisional traces, there would be no way to reunite them with the original dwelling.

It is like form and sound being related to shadow and echo, each serving as the counterpart to the other; if one is absent, the others cannot exist. Thus, the three dwellings must necessarily be complete.
Thus, these two mutually manifest one another and cannot be lacking even for a moment; how could one abandon the fundamental while remaining in the traces?
Not only does one lose the fundamental, but one also loses the traces. This is truly because, by failing to recognize the traces, one becomes confused about the fundamental;

by judging the near as merely a means (the fish-trap and rabbit-snare), one remains dark regarding the distant goal. To simply disregard it is already a grave error, yet to further disparage its application is a transgression of no greater magnitude.
Where one has gone cannot be blamed; what comes next can still be pursued. Reflect on this, reflect on this, lest you bring ridicule upon yourself.
Yet, since my own translation, although various masters have used it to explain [the text], they have distinguished its underlying meaning;

thus, it was inevitable that such confusion should arise. Some may say: "This commentary also does not yet appear to provide a comprehensive interpretation; why then do you still claim otherwise? Now...

This means that this text is extremely clear; it is simply that you yourself do not see it, not that it is unclear. Moreover, in the *Jingming guangming shu* (Commentary on the Radiance of the Pure Name), these same judgments appear side by side.
It is not only others who do not understand this intent; even those who expound this text have abandoned its meaning within their own school.

If such is the case even within one's own tradition, how much more so regarding other schools? If this were not clear, then from here on, all explanations concerning the "abiding place" would be utterly futile.

As for the statement that "no one has ever been able to harmonize these texts," one should reflect upon them well. The commentary (which says... has already largely clarified the aforementioned points. Someone may ask:
"Since the relationship between the fundamental and the phenomenal (*honji-suijaku*) will be addressed later, why is it discussed here?

This person has not at all understood the meaning clarified above; they still cling to ordinary interpretations and thus fall into this confusion. This was written as a response to others who were judging the text.
This delusion arises from failing to understand that the meaning of these four abidings should be interpreted in terms of essence and function, as well as reality and manifestation;
it does not mean that this section is explicitly clarifying the reality and manifestation of the remote past. Therefore, your doubt is erroneous.
Next, regarding the classification by teaching (*yōkyō*): although the name "Śūraṅgama" appears within the first four meanings, it does not extend to the first two teachings;

furthermore, the terms "Buddha" and "the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) are common to all teachings. Therefore, while the first four meanings serve as a general explanation of the meaning of "abiding" that applies across all teachings, they have not yet correctly revealed the specific intent of this sutra.
Consequently, one must distinguish between the various teachings to clarify their relative and absolute status.

This is because the intended meaning of the present sutra is now being revealed. As for the explanation in the text that it concerns the "secret treasury of nirvāṇa," this is precisely because it is explained in terms of the Buddha abiding in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, since the ultimate truth itself has four distinct aspects, the remaining three meanings are self-evident without needing to be explicitly stated.
Moreover, the fact that the term "nirvāṇa" is mentioned first and "secret treasury" is mentioned later in the text is entirely due to the Buddha’s [pedagogical intent].
The names for the abodes of fruition (phala-sthāna) are established as four based on differences in the causal path of teaching;

however, when categorized according to the fruit, that which is abandoned, and the locus of realization, they are reduced to two. Since we are currently explaining the abodes of fruition, we shall rely solely on these two.

Nevertheless, while the terms "remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa), "without remainder" (nirupadhiśeṣa), and "nirvāṇa" are all general, the term "secret treasury" (guhyakośa) is distinct; therefore, it is designated by a general name.
The first two are specifically named as causes because they refer to the causes and effects of birth and death within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*);

whether these are identical to or non-identical with the truth is termed "breaking the substance" (*zhētī*). The latter three refer to the causes and effects of birth and death both within and outside the realm of phenomena; whether these are identical to or non-identical with the truth is termed "gradual" or "non-gradual.
This is also distinguished according to the Two Truths and Three Truths, as previously explained in the section on the Explanations by Teaching (*jiàoshì*). Thus it is.

The meaning of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) and "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*) as explained in the *Madhyamāgama* can be understood as usual. The "Secret" (*guhya*) refers to the treasury of the secrets of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), as it appears in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*;
this is discussed in detail in its commentaries and in the text of the present *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).

Regarding the different meanings of "abiding" (*sthiti*), there are briefly four types, as mentioned above; the first three are categorized as coarse or subtle according to the preceding preliminary discourse on the relationship between subject and object.
That this capacity does not arise apart from body and mind is as previously stated: the four types of locations are to be known as being either coarse or subtle.
Next, [the text] concludes that the present sutra is precisely the perfect and subtle, yet it does not clarify the absolute. Fundamentally, dharmas have no duality;
it was only because of two conditions in the past that there were two [teachings]. Now, with these conditions, there is no duality—how could there be two? It is simply non-dual.

Because the outflows (*āsrava*) lack coarseness and are inconceivably perfect and wondrous, they are immediately severed. One should know that the meaning of the "abiding" of this sutra—both the subject and the object—is such that it abides in this manner;
therefore, it is called "wondrous. Next, regarding the "original and the trace":
although the preceding discussion based on the teachings was distinct, it was essentially horizontal rather than vertical; now, we wish to discuss it vertically.
Therefore, this is an explanation based on the provisional and the ultimate (honji-suijaku). Within this, there is first the formal exposition and subsequently the summary of the essentials.

In the former, the provisional and the ultimate are clarified by means of the four teachings; this is to clarify the vertical through the horizontal. There is surely an underlying intention here which shall be explained later.

Although the four types of provisional and ultimate are clarified, each directly discusses the manifestation of the trace (*suijaku*), yet the meaning of the fundamental (*honji*) is naturally revealed. Since...

Because the traces [of the Buddha's manifestation] exist, one knows their fundamental nature; thus, there is no need for elaborate phrasing, and the meaning is naturally revealed, thereby capturing the essence of the Sūtras. It is for this reason that it can be so.
Within the initial *piṭaka* (Tripitaka) teaching, when terms such as "corresponding" (*ying*) are mentioned, the character should be pronounced with a level tone (*ping sheng*).

The fruit of Buddhahood elucidated by this teaching is likewise impermanent and subject to extinction into ashes. Since all afflictions were severed beneath the Bodhi tree, [the Buddha] should then be reduced to ashes.

Although his physical body has perished and his wisdom has entered into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, he does not yet enter it because he dwells in the world in a manifested body (*janma-kāya*) to transform those below who have not yet been delivered.
Thus, though he should have entered [nirvāṇa], he remains; therefore, he is called "Worthy" (*arhat*). Compassion is precisely the reason for manifesting traces and dwelling in the world;
subsequent passages follow this same principle. As for the term "manifested body," in this teaching there is no such thing as a [substantial] dharma.

This is because [the Buddha] possesses a body that is by nature unborn; furthermore, it is because he possesses only a body born of out-flowing retribution (*sāsrava-vipākaja*), a body born of parents, and a body subject to arising and ceasing.

From this subsequent statement, one may infer that this Buddha fundamentally abides in *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, yet through his great compassion, he remains in the world to transform and benefit others, manifesting the appearance of not having entered *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Next, regarding the universal [Buddha]:
This teaching begins from the stage of the eight persons and the stage of seeing, where one immediately severs delusions and realizes the truth.

From the sixth and seventh stages onward, although residual habits (*vāsanā*) remain, the primary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) have already been exhausted and the power of the Path has already been perfected.

One then intentionally retains these residual habits—either through the power of compassion and vows or as an auxiliary condition for manifesting in the world to deliver those with whom one has a karmic connection—until attaining Buddhahood and remaining in the world to teach and transform beings. This is that teaching.

Furthermore, because there is no application of the dharma-nature, one retains the practice; or, with compassion acting as an auxiliary condition for its arising, since the cause within the storehouse consciousness is never severed or realized, this teaching is explained in terms of the fruit.
Because the fruit exists within the cause and cause and fruit are identical, this teaching is also explained in terms of the cause.
Moreover, it takes abiding in *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* as its basis, with compassion acting as an auxiliary to maintain practice while remaining in the world to benefit sentient beings.
Not yet having entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, it serves as a trace; its distinction from the preceding lies simply in the fact that it provides a common cause.

Next, the paths of the two teachings—Distinct and Perfect—are explained: although they differ, their realization of the Way is largely the same. They are identical in that the Middle Way, the Dharma-nature, and its functional application are present.

Now, because the text focuses on the aspect of this commonality in realization, it treats them together. In the phrase "all are perfumed by compassion and the Dharma-nature," "perfuming" (*vāsana*) refers to striking and stimulating [the potential].

The meaning of this is twofold: first, while within the causal stage, one should constantly give rise to great compassion based upon the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), perfuming, striking, and touching the impartial *dharmatā* to universally serve as the conditions for the deliverance of all beings;

second, having already realized the *dharmatā*, one should constantly perfume, strike, and activate the realized *dharmatā* with the same great compassionate mind from the original stage, causing its applications to arise everywhere.

This is because it is without end or limit; the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is precisely the locus where the traces (*vyañjana*) should reside, which is the dharma-realm of differentiated phenomena (*bhāva-dharmadhātu*).

Since the functions of the former two traces are narrow, they are simply called "the world" (*loka*); since the functions of these latter two traces are vast and boundless, they are called the "dharma-realm.

Having thus completed the explanation of the fundamental and the trace across the four teachings, and since the reconciliation has already been established within the previous section on the teachings, then herein—
The fourfold aspects of origin (*hon*) and trace (*soku*) are in fact but a single aspect of origin and trace; whether one or four, they are freely manifest and inconceivable.

Nevertheless, because the internal realization of the principle-body (*ri-tai*) constitutes the origin and the external arising of phenomenal function (*ji-yū*) constitutes the trace, these constitute the origin and trace of essence and function.
Next, as for the summary: all of this refers to the explicit clarification of the origin and trace of the remote past.
It should be understood that the abodes of the four preceding Buddhas are all identical to the abode of the Primordial Buddha of the distant past;

this is called the "Abiding of the Fundamental" because it is the compassion of the fundamental [Buddha]. From that distant fundamental source, he manifests a proximate trace, abiding today in the royal city of the Sahā world as its sovereign;
this is called the "Abiding of the Trace. Now, upon examining this interpretation, it still cannot yet be reconciled with the former point. Why? Because...

1. Regarding the statement that "the coming [of the Buddha] has not yet been clarified" and that one should know the "distant origin and near manifestation over a long period," upon what does this depend for its inclusion? 2.

As previously stated, since the four types of distant origins and near manifestations apply universally, for what reason is it that, regarding the near manifestation, it speaks only of the King’s City in the Sahā World?

3. This is the concluding passage on the Buddha’s dwelling from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Within that treatise, there is no discussion of the meaning of distant origins and near manifestations over a long or short period. 4. [End of section.]

In both the *Jingming* (Pure Name) and the *Guangming shu* (Commentary on the Radiance), this passage is cited to conclude [the discussion], and both state that the provisional traces (*ji*) and the ultimate meaning (*yi*) do not involve distance or proximity.
For this reason, it is said that the distant origin and the near trace cannot yet be reconciled.

Now, I clarify that this is merely a conclusion toward the previously explained fourfold meanings of essence and function regarding origin and trace. Why is this? That which was explained above is merely general.

The meaning of the relationship between the fundamental and the manifested has not yet been precisely clarified; their names and essences are unknown, nor is it known where the fundamental abides or from where the manifestations descend.
Now, to summarize and clarify this, it says: "One should know," and so forth.

This means that one should know that each of the four Buddhas dwells in its own respective fundamental dwelling place, and out of compassion, each descends from that fundamental dwelling place to manifest traces.

The "traces" (迹) abide in the royal city of the Sahā world; this refers to the abiding of the traces of the four modes of deportment which have not yet ceased. The meaning of the "original Buddha" (本佛) abiding is as clarified previously and subsequently.

With this single interpretation, there is no contradiction with the four [preceding] points, and it is very easy to understand; how could one say it is otherwise? Furthermore, regarding this specific passage, should it not be understood in this way? If we were to discuss it more broadly, this interpretation... (Note:

The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on Buddhist doctrine, likely concerning the distinction between the *nirmāṇakāya* (trace body) and the *dharmakāya* (original body). The translation reflects the philosophical nuance of the original Chinese.)

By following what has been clarified above, it need not be spoken of further for it to be self-evident. Why is this? It is because, by taking the fundamental and the manifested as our standard, we should clarify the long and the near;
yet, why do we instead clarify essence and function? I have privately examined this text and find that it possesses a profound and correct illumination of the causes and conditions.

This is because, within the commentary on the "Exposition of Causes and Conditions," four meanings from a treatise are cited to explain the essentials of "abiding. Thus, the Great [Nirvana Sutra] was previously cited...
This treatise establishes four meanings; the first, the worldly, corresponds to the provisional dwelling (迹住), while the subsequent three correspond to the fundamental dwelling (本住).
This constitutes the meaning of the essence and function, as well as the fundamental and provisional dwellings, which were briefly explained previously.

Although the meaning is thus, the text has only addressed the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold purposes) without yet discussing the significance of the fundamental and provisional. Since the meaning is profound and far-reaching, it cannot be fully realized without further analysis and explanation.
The distant and the near are fundamentally distinct in essence, while the provisional and the real are necessarily interpenetrating.

Since this applies to the four teachings as well as to the long and the short, and as it concerns the meaning of the provisional and the real, it is appropriate to clarify it within the section on the provisional and the real. If one clarifies this, the previous intent will naturally become manifest;
there is no desire for prolixity, which is why it was not mentioned during the previous explanation of causes and conditions, but is clarified only here in this section.

For this reason, if this passage did not exist, the preceding passage would be useless—just like something discarded by others—and if the preceding passage did not exist, this passage would have no basis to follow.
Therefore, my previous explanation was immediately established as the primary meaning of "original" (ben) and "trace" (ji).

Nevertheless, within this context, one should first clarify essence and function, and subsequently clarify remoteness and proximity, before the full significance can be exhausted. As explained previously regarding the Buddha, this is based on the distinction between the original and the trace.
This is indeed the case here; however, since the essence and function, as well as the fundamental and the manifest, constitute the essential tenets regarding time, they must be clarified.

While the distinction between the distant and the near—the fundamental and the manifest—is discussed throughout this entire work and is thus not difficult to understand by analogy, the text here is brief and merely clarifies essence and function without further discussing the distant and the near.
From this point on, we shall explain the "abiding," continuing until the very limit of all that is abided in.

These passages do not at all distinguish between the long and the near; rather, they are all contained herein. By this, one should know that these texts explain the "knot" without involving distance or proximity.
That the distinction between the fundamental and the manifested is self-evident is already clear.

Such an intention is truly essential and subtle, transcending the divisions of past and present, and is found exclusively within this school. Yet, those who discuss this school generally [fail to see it] within these very texts.

Since it has been clarified that the provisional and the ultimate are distinct— as previously established through the analysis of the teachings— then the distinction between the fundamental and the manifested,

as well as the provisional and the ultimate, is naturally clear. Once the relationship between essence and function, and the fundamental and the manifested, is thus understood, the distinctions regarding the distant and the near, as well as the provisional and the ultimate,
can likewise be known without the need for further elaboration.
Next, having previously established the wondrous meaning of the practitioner’s method of dwelling in the homes of others, this clarifies the wondrous nature of dwelling within one's own mind.
How is the contemplation of this dwelling performed? There are five phrases below that clarify it;

these five phrases of contemplation are explained according to the teachings, with the first serving as a general heading and the following four providing specific explanations based on the Four Teachings.

This is the clarification of contemplation (*guan*). Some say that this is a clarification of contemplation based on the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold teachings) from the preceding causes and conditions;

however, we now maintain that it is generally applicable and may be used according to its function. For now, we shall clarify contemplation based on the teachings. The reason for using the teachings to clarify contemplation is also because the coarse and relative are employed to manifest the subtle and absolute.
The first phrase provides a general heading for the object of contemplation, which serves as the basis for the four subsequent specific sections.
The clarity that is able to abide by means of abiding in that which is to be abided in is called "abiding" (*sthiti*); this is the general explanation of the meaning of abiding.
Now, because the observing subject abides within the observed object through the act of observation, it is termed "observing-abiding" (*sthiti-darśana*).

This explains, in summary, the ritual of abiding and the mind as the three [factors] regarding the royal city of the land of the three patiences (*kṣānti*) and the three internal dharmas as the subject and object of abiding.
Fourth, to now abide by means of these four contemplations upon these four objects is called the "subject and object of abiding.

All thoughts that arise, take objects, and dwell upon them—being born and ceasing moment by moment without constancy—are illuminated by the wisdom of contemplation; this is termed the "object of impermanence.
Because this wisdom contemplates and realizes the objects as they are, it is called "abiding. Since this mind lacks any constant stability, it is therefore...
Because emptiness is not obstructed by arising from conditions, it is "provisional" (prajñapti); because it is non-dual and equal, it is "the Middle" (madhyama).

Each serves as the object illuminated by its respective contemplation, and thus they are all termed "objects" (viṣaya). Each contemplation, in accordance with its object, illuminates and realizes that object, and thus they are all termed "abidings" (sthiti).

Therefore, it is said that "they are equal," and so forth. It is simply one contemplation that, according to what it illuminates, encompasses four objects; it is one contemplation yet four contemplations, and one object yet four objects—all of which are simultaneously present.
Because it is indeterminate, the word "or" (huò) is used. One should know that the two characters "or...

abides" (huò zhù) apply throughout the following sections, while the two characters "equal objects" (děng jìng) are gathered back to the preceding section; that is, they equalize what precedes rather than what follows, in order to avoid prolixity.

By stating "there is no abiding" below, the meaning of "abiding in contemplation" (zhù guān) is established. Why does one abide in contemplation within these four objects? It is precisely for the purpose of refutation.
This is because all who abide in attachment to phenomena do not truly abide; that is to say, they do not abide because they perceive the world as being subject to false permanence;

they do not abide because they contemplate impermanence yet remain attached to existing phenomena; they do not abide because they contemplate emptiness yet remain attached to the phenomenon of emptiness;

and they do not abide because they dwell in the provisional yet remain attached to the phenomena of the two extremes. Since the Middle Way is likewise without fixed abiding and lacks priority or posteriority, it is said that [the Buddha] "sometimes" [teaches one way and sometimes another].
It is said that "abiding" means not dwelling in attachment to any phenomena while contemplating these various objects;

therefore, it is said to "abide in the realm of impermanence" and so forth. If one does not contemplate and illuminate while abiding in these various objects, one is indeed dwelling in attachment to phenomena.
This very abiding is non-abiding; to abide in non-abiding is the inconceivable abiding. For this reason, it is so named.
Because abiding in such an abiding is itself the sublime abiding (*pranīta-vihāra*), this explains and establishes the contemplation of the sublime abiding;
this is precisely the gate of contemplation on the word "abiding" (*vihāra*) in this sutra, namely the gate of contemplation of the sublime abiding.

If one can practice in this manner, then all phenomena of clinging and attachment to objects of perception (*ālambana*) will themselves become sublime; thus, the aforementioned sublime abiding of the original and the trace...
Although the Dharma is profound and vast, how could it be distant? It is simply that the mind is uniform throughout.
However, one must further regulate it by means of the six [perfections], whereby high and low will be orderly and there will be no fault of transgression or excess; thus it is utterly sublime.
