It is extremely rare; it exists only in the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), because [the Buddha] intended to specifically attract and guide those with the karmic conditions of this final age according to the exigencies of the time.

As for the assemblies from other directions, they should likewise exist based on the subsequent sūtra text, but since they are not essential to the meaning of "ultimate faith," they are also omitted here.
Therefore, in most other sūtras, the assemblies are gathered separately through specific invitations.
The intention for clarifying that [the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*] is not included in the general introduction (*sūtra-nidāna*) is as follows:

although the *Ratnarāśi* and other sūtras include it, this is done to encourage those of later learning; thus, it is merely listed in the general introduction in brief. One should further examine this in detail. Someone may ask:
"If this is so, why does the sūtra not say 'opening the assembly' (*saṃgha-avakāśana*), but rather 'monks' (*bhikṣu*)? The answer is: "Monks" refers to...
Why must this śrāvaka be subject to such confusion? If that were so, then later in the text it says "bodhisattvas and bhikṣus," referring exclusively to śrāvakas;

yet if that were the case, the text further states, "truly a śrāvaka. How could he ever not be a bodhisattva? However, while the term "śrāvaka" applies generally to all four assemblies, the term "bhikṣu" is specific to one.
Since other sūtras list them according to their specific categories, they say "bhikṣu"; here, however, we follow the general classification.
The meaning of the "miscellaneous assembly" following the śrāvakas is likewise so; this shall be clarified later. That which was appropriate to explain here has been briefly addressed as above.
As for other matters that require further discussion, they will appear at the beginning of the section on the miscellaneous assembly later on;
therefore, I shall not elaborate further here. If one grasps this intent, there will be no confusion regarding the interpretations of various schools.
Regarding the precedence of monks over nuns, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* also sets forth eight reasons: first, because of the distinction between male and female and their respective ranks;
second, because of the sequence in which they entered the Path; third, because of the status of teacher and disciple; fourth, because of the capacity to transmit the Dharma;
fifth, because of the protocol for advancement or retreat during the Councils; sixth, because of the attainment of co-residence; and seventh, because of the greater number [of monks].

Regarding the "eight [qualities] due to being few," these eight meanings are primarily for praising the virtues of existence and non-existence; thus, while they are numerous, they essentially consist of three *siddhāntas* (intentions).

They also apply generally to other sūtras, though in the case of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the latter two meanings do not apply, as the number [of qualities] exceeds those of the *Saṃgha* and the praise of virtues is likewise extensive.
Furthermore, this is explained according to the majority of cases. As for the old [translation] using terms such as "great" and "small renown," etc.:
This means that the first refers to "great renown," which is heard everywhere like the clouds; because its fame is universally known, it is called "great.
The second refers to "small renown," where what is heard does not travel far; therefore, it is called "small. According to this interpretation, both types of renown belong to oneself.
However, if one says there is "great renown" in the sense that it is heard by others, then the name [of the renown] resides in others.
Regarding the statement that [the name] belongs to another, I shall now follow the refutation of that view and rely on the previous explanation. As for why the ancients gave this name:
they saw that there was previously a *mahābhikṣu* (great monk) who spoke and praised his virtues; since these two conditions were absent here, they gave it this name.
I do not permit this, for although they applied this name based on their own interpretation of the meaning, it contradicts the literal text and must therefore be set aside.

Therefore, it is said, "Although," and so forth. For this reason, we shall now judge directly according to the text. Why? Because since the initial passage states, "known by the multitude," it refers to many;
since the latter passage lacks these words, it refers to few. By judging directly according to the text, both the letter and the meaning are preserved.
What need is there to deviate from the text and incur two errors? Or it may be said: in the initial passage there are "great bhikṣus," and it also says "the multitude."

Regarding the sequence of what is known through scriptural knowledge, if there is no such [sequence], then each [point] relies solely on the literal meaning of the text. What, then, would be the basis for [determining] what is non-existent?

Furthermore, as for the few and the many, the great and the small—how could one of these be considered right or wrong? That being so, although the "great" and "small" may have names upon which to rely, by what means can one take those names as a basis?

Although the meanings of "great" and "small" may be reconciled, the meanings of the names and reputations are entirely divergent. Why is this so? It is because of what is known through personal acquaintance.
Regarding the statement that "fame belongs to him alone, and since it belongs to him alone, what concern of his own is there with greatness or smallness?
As for others, they themselves [speak of it]; what does it have to do with me?"—the meaning of the text does not reside in the self, yet it is judged from the perspective of the self.
Therefore, why would this be disparagement rather than praise? Thus, the text has no basis for such a claim, and the meaning cannot be reconciled; one must certainly be free of doubt.
The meaning will become even clearer when the text is later explained. Jiaxiang calls them the "Assembly of Those with Manifest Names and Secret Practices" (Xián míng mì xíng zhòng);

the Master of Zhongjing calls them the "Assembly of Those Beyond Training and Those Still in Training" (Wú xué yǒu xué zhòng); and Ci'en calls them the "Assembly of Those with Renowned Virtue and Those of Great Virtue Without Name" (Yǒu míng gāo dé wúmíng dàdé zhòng).
However, the first term, "those with manifest names," is overly mundane; the second, "those who have or do not," is insufficient for praise; and those [other] terms are merely grandiose.
The phrasing of this passage is not straightforward; it generally relies on indirect expression, which results in a lack of clarity.

If one were to rely directly on the principles of the text, the meaning would be fully exhausted. Furthermore, since the number of these [qualities] naturally establishes their own sequence, there is no need for further separate discussion.

Regarding the listing of six chapters concerning "many knowledges" (*bahu-vidyā*), according to the treatise, this collectively clarifies that there are four kinds of accomplishment within this assembly.
First, enumeration; second, practice; third, the merit of inclusion; and fourth, abiding in accordance with the Dharma through dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Regarding the accomplishment of enumeration, it refers to the fact that the great assembly is innumerable. Regarding the accomplishment of practice, there are four types: first, those śrāvakas who cultivate the practices of the Hīnayāna;
second, those bodhisattvas who cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna; and third, those bodhisattvas who engage in provisional and indeterminate practices.

Fourth, regarding those who have left the household life, their majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) is fixed, and they are accomplished in the merit of conduct; this refers to the various praises of their virtues.
Their abiding in accordance with the Dharma in majestic deportment includes such things as being surrounded by the fourfold assembly and receiving offerings.

Master Jingfashi said: "According to their enumeration, they are called 'many'; according to their practice, they are called 'stages' (*bhūmi*); according to their virtue, they are called 'fruits' (*phala*; *guǒ*); and according to their majestic deportment, they are called 'karma' (*karman*; *yè*). These constitute one [section].
Each of the fifteen assemblies possesses these four meanings; the difference between the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings lies merely in whether they are explicitly mentioned or not.
Ci'en states that among the fifteen assemblies, they can be grouped into three categories: Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas possess all four accomplishments (*siddhi*);

those who are neither learners nor non-learners (*śaikṣa-aśaikṣa*), as well as the Bhikṣuṇīs, possess three accomplishments because their virtues are not extolled; and the remaining assemblies, such as the devas and others, [possess only one].
Because they lack both the two types of conduct and virtuous qualities, the treatise states that among the various assemblies there are four meanings combined,
rather than saying that each individual assembly possesses all four kinds. Now, according to the *New Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and other scriptures,

which list for each assembly that there are hundreds of millions [of beings] and praise their virtues while concluding with their majestic deportment, although the present text is brief, its meaning is [the same].
The Master [Hui]lin did not merely discuss the meaning; he comprehensively addressed the intent of the various sutras, discussing both the text and its meaning.

He did not, however, immediately divide the text according to topical sections (*kojie*). If one were to insist on fixing the text, the passage concerning *vīrya* (diligence) and *śīla* (conduct) would be found collectively at the end;

how could they have been sought separately earlier? Thus, we know that the text and meaning were discussed together. If this is so, then Master Jing’s discussion of both text and meaning is indeed comprehensive.

The *Cien* [commentary] is close [to the truth], yet its separate explanation based on the phrasing is somewhat superficial. However, since this treatise does not precisely define the essential nature [of the text], its structural division (*ko-wen*) remains somewhat inconvenient for exegesis;
moreover, as the passage concerning "dignified deportment" (*veiyi*) belongs to the separate introduction (*bie-xu*), it is not adopted here.
Now, these initial six chapters exhaustively cover the text; these six are also fully contained within the "Bodhisattva Chapter," with the remainder following suit.

If the various texts were abbreviated, they would not be complete; however, if one seeks them through their meaning and accords with the substance of the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* (Renwang jing) and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Guangming jing), then each and every assembly may possess these six [aspects]. Thus, we know that these six, from the perspective of their meaning, are universally applicable.

Furthermore, if these six chapters were considered directly according to their textual form, they could also be reduced to three pairs. Why? Because they correspond to categories, numbers, and connections.

Therefore, because the positions and virtues are praised both collectively and individually, and because the enumeration and conclusion share the same name, we know that from the text, the beginning and end can be broadly divided into three pairs;
yet, for the sake of simplicity in terms of meaning, they are immediately treated as six single units. This is also the case within the text concerning the Bodhisattvas;
thus, both the meanings of three and six are universally applicable—reflect on this, reflect on this.
First, regarding the explanation of its category: all previous masters have referred to this as a general designation (*sāmānya-saṃjñā*) rather than a specific name (*viśeṣa-nāman*).

Now, it is called a "category" (*jāti*) because it refers to a class of similar types (*prabandha-jāti*). This has two meanings: first, in contrast to other groups, these individuals constitute a single class of ordained men;
second, while the term "bhikṣu" is used generally for all such persons, here it specifically denotes this particular class.
As for what kind of category [of person] he belongs to, it refers precisely to those who are "great. Therefore, he is called a "Category-Holder" (*rùhán*), which encompasses these two meanings.
In the text, the explanation is based directly on the latter meaning, precisely because the significance of the word "great" (*dà*) refers to a person of lofty and noble character and resolve.
As the *I Ching* says, "Those of the same sound respond to one another; those of the same breath seek one another"—this is exactly that principle.
Next, I shall cite an illustration to clarify this point: for example, within a gathering, whether noble or humble, each person belongs to their respective class and rank.
Now, regarding the *I Ching*, it is said that "things are gathered by their kind and divided by their groups; thus good fortune and ill fortune arise.

"Kind" (*fang*) refers to those with similar spiritual natures who, through identical arts and calculations, dwell together in one place without being intermingled—just as in the aforementioned example.
This refers to the correspondence of sounds and so forth. Wenzi says: "Beasts with similar feet follow one another in their wanderings; birds with similar wings follow one another in their flight.
The commentary on this states: "Things of the same kind gather together. Therefore, it is said that things of the same category assemble.
"Things" (wu) refers to those lacking conscious intelligence; they are merely individual entities, each following its own suitability to dwell together in a single place.
As it is said in the passage concerning "clouds and water flowing to moisture, fire and heat burning," and as Wenzi states, "The orange grows in its native region;

the plantain and reed grow in their clusters," his commentary notes: "Things are divided according to their kind; therefore it is said that things are divided by their groups. If they gather in their proper places, there is auspiciousness;
if not, there is misfortune; thus it is said that "auspiciousness and misfortune arise. This clarifies how, within the realm of heaven and earth, the myriad things [arise] of themselves...
It is simply because of their numerical nature. Now, I have briefly borrowed these words as an analogy; thus it is said that "the various quarters" (qun fāng).

The meaning here is that, for example, when things are divided into groups and gathered according to their respective quarters, they each have their own rank and category according to whether they are noble or base, and do not become confused or intermingled.
This is also the natural law (dharmatā), and therefore it must be so; it cannot be otherwise. This refers to the order of ranks and categories.

The meaning of this can be understood through the following synthesis: it clarifies that these are all categories of the supremely high and supremely great, as fully explained in the subsequent section on "Greatness.

As for why they must necessarily be of this category—it is because were they not so, the preceding meanings of "original" and "traces," as well as those clarified subsequently, would not be possible. Therefore, there is a profound reason why they are first merely listed as such.

Next, the main text is formally explained. The text consists of five characters, whose meanings are distinguished into four categories. The first character applies to both the subject (the giver) and the object (that which is given);

the subsequent three apply exclusively to the object. These are explained in sequence. First, the explanation of "giving" (*yù*): this scripture’s term "giving" (*yù*) and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*’s term "together with" (*gòng yù*) are synonymous;

that is, they are combined and identical in meaning. Furthermore, "together with" (*gòng*) and "common" (*gòng*) share the same sense, as does "identical" (*tóng*). As for the question "Who gives?"—if it refers to the Buddha...
In the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), "bestowed upon" (*suo bei*) signifies the capacity of the recipient; it refers to the meaning of the Buddha bestowing [the teaching] upon others.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is raised to mean causing people to believe and serving as a testimony for those who heard together; this refers to Ānanda and the rest.
Although the term "with" (*yu*) contains these two meanings, in reality they are identical. However, the "with" used in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* has a distinct and profound significance. This is because—

By means of the final desire, [the text] generally summarizes that from the beginning, the monks were all identical in their initial aspiration, identical in their practice, identical in their realization of the fruit of the Path, and identical in their transformation of these various capacities and conditions;
thus, it specifically states "Buddha and [the monks]. How is this known? It is because "and" (*yu*) has the same meaning as "identical" (*tong*);
for unless they shared the same Way, how could they have reached such a state of mutual attainment? The word "and" (*yu*) is used here in the sense of being identical to the Buddha.

Because they are identical, the text states: "In order to manifest the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings of skillful means and to ensure that the various modes of preaching are not interrupted," and so forth;
all these are members of the assembly who initiate [the teaching], and thus their basis is the same.

Otherwise, why would this statement alone be set apart while other sūtras are not? Therefore, it cannot be spoken of separately; the subsequent sections of this sūtra will themselves extensively reveal and clarify this.

Therefore, there is no need for this separate [explanation]; this intention is already present within the commentary on the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. Furthermore, because Ānanda praises the Buddha’s virtues therein, the meaning of "giving" (*yǔ*) is established.
Regarding the *Śāstra* and so forth: the treatise directly cites the seven items to explain the meaning of "shared" (*gòng*) as it appears in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Since the Sūtra does not mention "giving," the treatise cannot explain the meaning of "shared" without it; thus, the text [of the Sūtra] should properly correspond [to the treatise].
Regarding the phrase "yún yǔ zhě gòng yì" (云與者共義), the *Śāstra* explains it as "sevenfold. First, "common purity" (*gòng jìng*):

if one were to follow the *Da jīng shū* (Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra) directly, it simply says "thus" (*ěr*). The fact that this current text provides this specific explanation is likely a scribal error.

This is because when one interpretation is given for "common," "one" (*yī*) carries the sense of "not different" (*bù yì*); and "not different" is precisely the sense of "identical" or "shared" (*tóng gòng*). As for the citation of "seven," it serves to distinguish [the categories].

This is because it demonstrates the limits of the dharmas that are shared. Thus, one should reflect upon the dharmas that are shared by means of the sevenfold interpretation, combining the "shared" interpretation with the "single" interpretation.
Next, the seven names are listed according to the sequence of the treatise (*śāstra*), positioned above "time" (*kāla*); the other passages cited are all consistent with the treatise.
Here, they are placed below either for the sake of linguistic convenience (*yathā-prasanga*) or for the sake of their meaning (*artha*), because time was prioritized there.
Furthermore, in the treatise, "mind" (*citta*) is positioned above; that it is now moved below is likewise due to the sequence of meaning. In the treatise, it may be [arranged] provisionally...
Perhaps there is another meaning, or it was transmitted differently; in the treatise, these are listed directly without explanation, and this passage is likewise.

Many different versions of the explanation exist, so for now I shall interpret the first two based on other texts: they simply refer to the time and place where one simultaneously attains the vision of the Buddha and hears the Dharma.
The sequence of the next three refers to the simultaneous attainment of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
The latter two are simply the same in realizing the principle of *nirvāṇa* and being equally free from fetters and karma.

They may also be understood as identical in their wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), and thus identical in the cause and fruit of *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, regarding these seven [aspects], the first two are understandable;

the subsequent five may likewise be identified with the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*), namely the path of liberation-knowledge-and-vision (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*), because it is through this that one can penetrate the One.

It is because [the path] is complete. Alternatively, that which is visible is precisely what is known; seeing the path is itself wisdom (*prajñā*). Because one penetrates through it by means of wisdom, it is called the "path" (*mārga*).
These seven are all one, and thus they are called the "seven. Each one among these seven is also called "one," and "seven" is their common meaning.
This means that at that time, Ānanda was not only identical to the assembly of bhikṣus, but was also identical to these seven factors.
This is because both the person (*pudgala*) and the phenomena (*dharma*), whether provisional or real, are entirely identical; therefore, they are said to be "one.

For this reason, the treatise condenses what was stated earlier and later into a single location, which is indeed for a good purpose. Otherwise, it would not suffice to call them a "single assembly of listeners" (*ekasabhya*).
If that were the case, why would only the bhikṣus alone receive the designation "one"? All those in the enumerated assembly who participate in the gathering would equally be called "one."

These seven [categories] are all designated as the "assembly of those who have attained the Dharma and heard it together"; thus, while the text treats them separately, their underlying meaning is universally applicable.
However, by speaking of these seven as "one," the encompassing meaning is fully exhausted, for there is nothing that transcends them—this principle should be understood.

Consequently, if these seven are one, then they are one with all dharmas; how much more so when considering the successive teachings, the provisional and the ultimate (honji-suijaku), and the contemplation of the mind?
The meaning and intent of the dharmadhātu regarding the horizontal and vertical, as well as self and others, are left without the slightest omission; reflect upon this, reflect upon it!

Furthermore, since it is stated that this is "according to the teaching," it should correspond here to the *nidāna* (causal conditions), and thus it is also appropriate to explain it through the fourfold intention (*catuḥ-prayojana*), though there are differences. Now, I say:

"place" refers to the world-realm (*loka-dhātu*), and "timeliness" refers to the person-teaching (*pudgala-vinaya*). As the *Sūtra on the Original Karma* says: "Precepts eliminate physical transgressions, while concentration is not absent."

When the mind is undisturbed, wisdom is awakened, and perceptions are realized as empty, then the three pairs of antidotes serve as the path of cultivation; liberation from these rigid attachments is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, being identical to these seven [factors] is to be identical to these four meanings; thus it is said, "it is the same as."

Next, the seventh section—distinguishing the differences and reconciling them to reveal the true significance of this sutra—is analyzed according to the teachings. Within this, first, the differences are distinguished by means of the four teachings;

second, the reconciliation is clarified through the contrast between the ancient and the present. Regarding the first analysis by means of the four teachings, each one possesses the aforementioned seven points.
First, concerning the Tripitaka (Śrāvaka) teaching, the mention of "one set of seven" is made because it is the most inferior, and is discussed from the perspective of its own specific level.

Regarding time and place, they are all identical to those of his previous manifestation as the Inferior Response-body (Hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya); the time and place of his seeing and hearing can be understood through inference and need not be described separately.

Furthermore, they are identical in that he simultaneously attained the unmanifested discipline (*avijñapti-śīla*), the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), untainted knowledge and vision (*anāsrava-jñāna-darśana*), and the path to *nirvāṇa*;
and they are identical in realizing the liberation with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-vimukti*). Because these seven aspects are identical, it is so stated.

The "seventy-one" [days] here are all based on the explanations found in the Master Danqiu’s other writings. Regarding the general statement of "two seventies," the Master says that this is because he distinguishes between the sharp and the dull faculties; for those of sharp faculties, who include both the Separate (Pratyekabuddha) and Perfect (Bodhisattva) vehicles, it should be stated as "three seventies. However, since this is a general and comprehensive exposition, they are treated as a single uniform example. Now, I venture to say that the superior capacity includes the inferior, and the "comprehensive" includes the Tripitaka; thus, in the *Great Sutra Commentary* (*Dajing shu*), within the explanation of the "Great Meaning" (*Dayi*), it is stated: [...text omitted... Thus, it is said that the "thirty-seven" [factors] are the path of the Śrāvaka, while the "seventy-one" are the path of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, the "thirty-seven" are the path of the two types of tranquility, while the "seventy-one" are the path of the three types of tranquility. Furthermore, the "thirty-seven" are the path of the two types of extinction, while the "seventy-one" are the path of the three types of extinction. Furthermore, the "thirty-seven" are the path of the two types of Nirvana, while the "seventy-one" are the path of the three types of Nirvana. Furthermore, the "thirty-seven" are the path of the two types of wisdom, while the "seventy-one" are the path of the three types of wisdom. Furthermore, the "thirty-seven" are the path of the two types of knowledge, while the "seventy-one" are the path of the three types of knowledge. Furthermore, the "thirty-seven" are the path of the two types of insight, while the "seventy-one" are the path of the three types of insight. Furthermore, the "thirty-seven" are the path of the two types of realization, while the "seventy-one" are the path of the three types of realization. Furthermore, the "thirty-seven" are the path of the two types of attainment, while the "seventy-one" are the path of the three types of attainment. Furthermore, the "thirty-seven" are the path of the two types of entry, while the "seventy-one" are the path of the three types of entry. Furthermore, the "thirty-seven" are the path of the two types of penetration, while the "seventy-one" are the path of the three types of penetration. Furthermore, the "thirty-seven" are the path of the two types of transformation, while the "seventy-one" are the path of the three types of transformation. Furthermore, among those outside the category of "all-knowledge" (*sarvajña*), there are those who cultivate wisdom alone; this is termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and is narrow, whereas the "without outflows" (*anāsrava*) is vast and expansive—hence it is "great.

As for "shared," it refers to the simultaneous cultivation of both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom, as well as both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*); by attaining realization through this, one is named "liberation of mind" (*ceto-vimukti*). It is also [the case that]...
This is called "liberation through both parts" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukti*). Furthermore, because its untainted (*anāsrava*) merit is superior, it can overcome those inferior tainted states.
As for the object of focus (*ālambana*), it is based upon concentration and wisdom, further augmented by universal mastery over all internal and external teachings.

That is to say, one again takes external phenomena as objects of focus to serve as support. At the time of fruition, concentration and wisdom are fully perfected, enabling universal penetration of both the internal and the external.

To know all things without exception is called "doubtless liberation" (*asaṃśaya-vimukti*); because its supernormal knowledge, eloquence, and discernment exceed those [of others], it is multiplied fourfold.

As for the four *Vedas*, these are the external scriptures of that region; within the "Practice of Peaceful Bliss," they are explained as such. Among the non-Buddhists of the West, these three are the greatest.
The Buddha, within the teachings of the Three Piṭakas, established three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) to bring them to completion in three types.
The Great Arhat, who has vanquished those three external schools, now expounds the treatise; herein, the three meanings are specifically intended to manifest this [title].

The *Zhiguan* and its commentaries explain this extensively, so I shall not elaborate further here. Because these three sets of three constitute nine meanings, it is called "Great," "Much," and "Superior.
Some scholars have extensively cited the six meanings from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* to explain the term "Great" according to the text.

There is no need to exhaustively elaborate on the meaning, as it would otherwise become overly prolix; later students should understand this well. Regarding the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) based on these causes and conditions:

"Great" (*mahā*) refers to the world-view (*loka-dṛṣṭi*), "many" (*bahu*) refers to the benefit of others (*puruṣakāra*), "remedy" (*pratipakṣa*) refers to the therapeutic (*prātipākṣika*), and "supreme" (*viśeṣa*) refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Although such a correspondence has been established, its underlying meaning remains unclarified; I shall now provide another interpretation: "Great" refers to the world...

The *dhātu* (element/realm) is placed first because it is great as it encompasses the person, its essence, and its characteristics; furthermore, it is superior because it is revered by heavenly kings and great beings.
Regarding its "victory," the treatise states that it can destroy the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*).

Thus, one knows that it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which universally knows the two truths, the three truths, and all phenomena. As for the sequence in the commentary (*śāstra-vṛtti*), it has been rearranged from the order in the original treatise.
Therefore, for now, we shall follow the sequence of the commentaries (*śāstra*) to correlate [the text] with the four intentions; thus, these three are precisely these four intentions.
Furthermore, if one proceeds through the preceding general exposition, this may also be understood by analogy.

After Jiāxiáng has extensively described the great meanings as interpreted by various masters, he further directly explains this according to this very sūtra, stating that this passage consists of six sections: the first marks the heading, and the following five are...
The commentary explains that "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the designation for the enumeration of qualities; these five are all called "great" (*mahat*).

This master, relying on the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, interprets "many" (*bahu*) through the term "number" (*saṃkhyā*), taking "many" to mean "great. He then applies this principle analogously to explain the remaining five [faculties].
Subsequent schools have followed this interpretation and further elaborated upon it, which cannot be fully recounted here. Now, I shall simply discuss them in a general overview.
While there is nothing that does not reach ultimate beauty, if one does not grasp the beginning and the end to clarify its ultimate purpose,

then even if it reaches far, it cannot be said to be fully perfected. As for the previously explained meaning of "three times three equals nine," which converges into the perfect and subtle to achieve Great Nirvana—
namely, the three Dharmakāyas, the three Liberations, and the three Prajñās— which are neither sequential nor simultaneous, this is the secret [teaching].
If one examines this through the lens of the *pitaka* (teachings), how could it be compared to the exegeses of other schools regarding their relative distance from the truth?
Students of later generations should carefully examine and elaborate upon this.

Next, as for the "approximation by teaching" (*yōkyō*), it is precisely because it reveals the three meanings of this sutra—Greatness (*dai*) and so forth. First, the preceding is designated as the *pitaka*.

Based on the treatises and in accordance with the three mindfulnesses and three liberations, these correspond to the three types of non-Buddhists and are all situated within the Initial Teaching (Āgama).
Therefore, among the common [teachings] of the Three Piṭakas, those referred to as "Arhats of Great Power" are those who possess no doubt regarding the Piṭakas;

because their skill in the Path surpasses that of others, they are revered by those great beings. This teaching praises them collectively as belonging to the seventh stage, the Stage of the Accomplished (Kṛtāvibhūmi).
Regarding "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) and so forth: internally, it refers to the thorough penetration of the two types of dharma-gates regarding essence and analysis;

externally, it refers to the thorough penetration of all worldly scriptures. Regarding "superiority": the four gates of the essence-dharmas integrate both principle and phenomena, and thus they are superior because they transcend that which is not integrated.

Within the specific [explanations], the great power of the essence-dharmas may be understood according to what preceded; "Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" is a metaphor for the immeasurable.
The Buddha-dharma consists of four teachings and sixteen gates; because each gate proceeds from cause to fruit, it is an infinite dharma.

When speaking of "those of the Two Vehicles," this refers generally to those of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). If one were to praise their qualities as those beyond training (aśaikṣa), they would all occupy the rank of the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi);
in reality, they even surpass the Three Vehicles. Why then speak only of the Two? It is perhaps merely a brief way of putting it.
This may be an error in the transcription. Regarding the statement "all the great bodhisattvas" within the *Yuanzhong* (The Round Center):

if one takes those who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), then those distinct from the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) are called great bodhisattvas; if one refers to those of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), then all those prior to Equal Enlightenment (*sam-bodhi*) are collectively called all the great bodhisattvas.
This is roughly the case. The details are found in other texts, for the dharmas of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are immeasurable and cannot be fully encompassed.
Because it is able to measure and know things exactly as they are measured, it surpasses all the Bodhisattvas of the four gates of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekadeśanā*).
Since these three meanings are most subtle and ultimate, it is "Perfect" (*pariniṣpanna*). When the Perfect is contrasted with the preceding three, the names "Partial" and "Perfect" are established;
from this, the meaning of "Inclusive" and "Subtle" can be understood, as can the sense of "Shared" and "Exclusive. This is thus... [the end of the passage].
The sutra contains many passages concerning the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).

Next, it clarifies the vertical discourse on the fundamental and the manifested (*honjaku*), demonstrating the distance and proximity of their application regarding the three meanings of the Perfect [Teaching].

Within this, first it clarifies that the three meanings of the long-attained, perfect, and subtle [nature] manifest the fundamental [teaching], and then it provisionally indicates the three meanings of the five periods to clarify the manifested [teaching].
The subsequent summary of the traces to harmonize with the original source clarifies what constitutes the great meaning of that original [source].
The statement "these great virtuous ones" refers collectively to twelve thousand people; this phrase continues to pervasively encompass the meanings of the three originals and five traces.
Regarding the phrase "for a long time," it correctly explains the great meaning: for a long time, such great persons...
The expression "zu jiē" (咨嗟) clarifies that the fundamental basis of his Way and Virtue has long been established, as explained in the section on Fuṇa’s realization (*Liǎngjiě*).

In the *Ěryā*, "zī xùn" (咨訓) refers to deliberation and consultation, which is not the intended meaning here. Furthermore, the *Ěryā* states: "Zī jiē, jiē tàn" (咨嗟嗟歎), meaning to sigh with admiration;

this precisely accords with the present context. It signifies that because his essence and function are profound and vast, benefiting both himself and others, he fully embodies the aspirations of all Buddhas, and thus [he is so praised].
The Buddhas praise and extol him; thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states, "The Buddhas praise [him]," and so forth.

This is because it employs the exact words of that sūtra, as well as the meaning of what is praised by the Buddha later in this sūtra and the respect and veneration expressed by great beings in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Within the treatise, for the sake of his immediate manifestation, it is simply said that he is esteemed by the great beings of the world.

It is said that this is what the Heavenly Kings revere; now, to clarify its remote origin, it is the ultimate state of the Great Man, and because it is praised by all Buddhas, it is said to be "that which all Buddhas extol.
Were it not for a Way that is most great and most enduring, how could one reach such a state?
Indeed, it must be so. The banner symbolizes victory; this samādhi can surely overcome adversaries, just like a banner of victory.
It is so named because Śakra possesses a banner that can crush his enemies, the asuras; upon seeing it, they naturally retreat and are defeated.
This samādhi is likewise able to overcome all demonic hordes and adversaries, and is therefore so called. Furthermore, regarding its fundamental nature:
if it were not originally the basis for the attainment of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowing wisdom), how could there be such traces of universal knowledge? Its profundity is indeed profound.

Without the fundamental (hon), there would be no way to manifest the traces (jaku); without the traces, there would be no way to reveal the fundamental. Since these three are already present within the traces, we know that the fundamental has long possessed these three.
Next, regarding the manifestation [of the Buddha], they are categorized into five periods; through these three meanings, the benefit of sentient beings is clarified, thereby explaining the traces.

This employs the text of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* as well as the intent of the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (*Śraddhābhūmi-parivarta*), for the Buddha's transformation indeed possesses the distinctions of five periods.
Because he manifests traces to assist in transformation, there are these five differences, as explained in detail in the "Chapter on Resolute Belief" (*Adhimukty-adhikāra*).

Among these five, each has its basis in the "Correct" (*samyak*) and the "Middle" (*madhya*); when categorized by analogy, they are entirely names of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, and when categorized by dharma within the "Correct and Middle," they are names for the gradual [teachings].
While their meanings differ, their essential intent is no different; one may infer this based on the subsequent text.

The initial statement regarding those who "assist the Buddha in his transformative activity" means to provide support and aid. This is because, as with a sovereign of the world, there must be ministers and assistants to aid him in governance.
Although this phrase is distinct, it remains connected to what follows, as all subsequent instances involve assisting in the transformative work.

As for those spoken of as having "afflictive views," these refer to the mundane world; generally speaking, although non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are numerous and differ from one another, they do not transcend [this category].

Regarding "affection" (*tṛṣṇā*) and "view" (*dṛṣṭi*): because they possess both the sharp and dull types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), [the former] specifically refers to all *māras*, while [the latter] specifically refers to all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). This meaning is also applicable to the Confucians and Daoists of this land;

Confucianism is characterized by much greedy attachment, while Daoism is characterized by many dogmatic views. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, these two are capable of [obstructing the Path].
Because they obstruct concentration and wisdom, one desires to eliminate their craving and views so that they may transcend the world;
thus, one should first employ "sameness of purpose" (*sādharmya*) as a support for being their teacher.

Following this principle, this phrase should state that it "demonstrates the three meanings within milk," yet the analogy of milk is not used because people might fail to understand its underlying method. "Milk" refers to the aforementioned "craving."

Regarding the person who sees [this], the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are like milk. This is because, among all flavors, the initial state is entirely raw and has not yet undergone transformation;

it is thus compared to those of gradual capacity (*anupūrva-yāna*), whose initial stage likewise remains entirely untransformed. "Curd" (*dadhi*) represents the next flavor, which is somewhat more concentrated;

this is likened to the *Tripiṭaka* teaching, wherein ordinary beings are transformed into sages, just as milk is transformed into curd. The Vaipulya [teachings] involve censure and reproach to induce a sense of shame.
Because the small admires the great and its flavor becomes increasingly more intense, it is likened to the third flavor, fresh butter (*navanīta*).

Because the *prajñā* has been refined through successive purifications until it flows freely and the conditions of the faculties have become even more excellent, it is the fourth flavor, the essence of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), which is the ultimate among flavors and possesses incomparable utility.

Since the Dharma Flower Sūtra (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) is the most supreme within the teachings and its essence and function are boundless, the previous metaphor is changed. As for the "knot," it is as follows:

These five kinds of threefold meanings gradually culminate in the ultimate reality; they are all provisional and near traces for the benefit of beings, whereas their fundamental reality—the threefold meaning—is exceedingly vast and ancient.
How is this known? First, according to the text, it is as the subsequent sutra itself declares.
Second, according to the meaning, were it not for long-term abiding, how could this source possibly possess such far-reaching and near-reaching [efficacy]? Third, by way of analogy.

The principal and its attendants are firmly established; since the principal has existed for an exceedingly long time, its assistants likewise cannot have been present for only a short duration. Thus one knows this to be so.

While the three fundamental [bodies] have already existed for a great length of time, the five traces certainly do not belong to a single age, as is detailed below in the passage concerning the teachings given in five periods by ninety billion Buddhas.
Although they do not belong to a single age, in the end they do not transcend these five [periods].
Therefore, by clarifying these five traces alone, one knows that both the distant and the near are likewise so; these three meanings may be called most subtle and wondrous.

Even if it were said that [the truth] has been attained, the world of the three teachings would still not consider it the reality; how much more so when these seven instances are all merely provisional traces—what benefit could there be other than this?
As previously stated, to exhaust their ultimate meaning is precisely what this sutra’s "Great" and so forth refers to.

"The three meanings constitute the second sense of 'wondrous' (myō)," as noted in the commentary (*yū*)—the details of which have already been briefly indicated above and will be explained extensively in the subsequent text.
Next, regarding the practitioner (*kanja*): because the currently attained superior dharma has become wondrous, although its essence (*tai*) is difficult to fathom, it is fundamentally wondrous;

thus, the application of the precepts (*yōritsu*) and the conditions (*en*) therein contain the essential wondrousness of contemplation (*kan*). Within the text, there are two layers, the first of which concerns the three contemplations (*sankan*).
To clarify that the Middle Way is superior among the three direct observations of emptiness: "Great" refers to emptiness itself, for it is void, empty, and without limit;
"many" refers to the provisional, for differentiated quantities are all limited; and "superior" refers to the Middle, for it transcends the two extremes while simultaneously encompassing them.
Previously, these were explained by means of the three [emptinesses] to illustrate the three [aspects]; now, one wishes to explain them directly through the One.
To possess these three is precisely what was stated previously; that these three are present can be seen in the text.

The nature of the mind (*cittatā*) is the true nature (*bhūtatā*), and the true nature is the absence of nature (*abhāvatā*). Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "Knowing that phenomena are eternally without nature, one observes that all phenomena are non-existent.
This is identical in meaning to the "ultimate emptiness" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. This actual absence of nature pervades all things.
Because its locus is as vast and expansive as space, it is called "Great. This refers precisely to the essential nature of the middle object (*madhyama-viṣaya*) within direct contemplation.

Although the middle object is thus, one must rely on constant illumination and non-dual realization to construct it; only then can one attain union with it. Therefore, it is said that both extremes are negated, and so forth.
The "Ocean of Quiescence" (*śānta-samudra*) is none other than the aforementioned vastness of the mind-nature (*citta-prakṛti*); although its essential nature is quiescent...
The extinction of the two aspects does not obstruct their constant functioning as two; thus, while the two vanish, they persist. Therefore, it subsequently illuminates both truths simultaneously.
Because it illuminates them simultaneously, there is nothing it does not encompass or contain. "One" refers to the true mind, and "all" refers to the provisional mind.

By presenting these two minds together, it reveals the manifold containment within the former, thereby clarifying its many meanings. Alternatively, "true" may be understood from the perspective of the provisional existence.
It is taught that because all things are directly empty and non-existent, they are not one, yet because they are the single mind of all, they constitute the manifold.
To be able to cultivate this contemplation—that one's own mind is the source of all benefit, vast and supreme—is truly marvelous. One should well understand these six points;
do not err by treating those of superior capacity as merely those of inferior capacity.
Next, regarding the explanation of "bhikṣu": this refers to a person possessing the three virtues, such as great virtue (*mahā-vitta*) and so forth.

However, the term "bhikṣu" is still a Sanskrit word; what is its name and meaning here? The text clearly elucidates that there are differences between ancient and modern interpretations, which consist of four sections:

first, citing Master Zhao’s translation; second, presenting Master Kumārajīva’s explanation; third, describing the interpretation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*; and fourth, synthesizing the meaning through a comprehensive analysis.

The first [section] merely translates the names; the subsequent three explain the meanings. Furthermore, the first two instances contain four meanings, while the latter two explanations contain only three;
these may be sought within the text. Why was the commentary not presented first, yet the interpretations of the human masters (puruṣācārya) were placed at the beginning?

It is precisely because one wishes to contrast the two previous schools—which were not yet correct—with the present correct explanation as its basis. Regarding the initial phrase "in the Qin language":
The two masters, Sengzhao and Kumārajīva, both lived during the time of Yao Xing of the Later Qin; this was precisely the period of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin’s orthodox line.
When it says "one who begs for food," it refers to a "beggar" (bhikṣu). However, while the four translations of the name are provided, their etymological explanations are not given;
this must be because the meaning was identical to that which followed later. One should therefore adopt the translation by Master Kumārajīva and the explanation by Master Sengzhao.

Why is it that these inversions follow their respective origins? Examining this further, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* explains that when translating from India and other regions, the intention was to preserve the original sounds within the commentary while still providing explanations;

because this land [China] lacks such inclusive names, they were translated by using opposing terms, hence it says "there is nothing that can... and so forth—this is the meaning of preserving the original sounds in various cases.
All cases are similar to this. In recent times, it has been said that the correct Sanskrit term is *bhikṣu*. Because it possesses five meanings, it is not translated [into Chinese]. These are:

terrifying Māra, mendicant (*yācanaka*), one who maintains the precepts, pure livelihood, and destroyer of evil. This refers to the first of the four meanings established by Master Daokai, which is divided into two, thus making five in total.
That is to say, having already left the household life, one sustains oneself by begging for food; therefore, he is called a "mendicant" (*yācanaka*).
Once a śramaṇa has received the precepts, the three types of karma he generates rely upon non-greed and do not rely on greed for a wrong livelihood;
therefore, it is called "pure livelihood. Because there is a distinction between the general and the specific, this is divided into two.

According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, "freedom from wrong livelihood" is combined with "the seeker of alms" (bhikṣu); thus, Master Sengzhao lists only four. Therefore, we know that these are all Sanskrit terms.

Because the term contains many meanings, it cannot be translated [directly]. In antiquity, some translated it literally as "the one who removes hunger" (chujinshi), meaning that because he is able to remove himself and others from the hunger and deprivation of the five desires, he receives this title.
This, however, simultaneously captures the two senses of "destroyer of evil" and "beggar," yet it is clear that it remains insufficient, as it lacks other meanings;
therefore, it is evident that it cannot be translated [fully]. Others say that *bhikṣu* is the name of a plant, which possesses five meanings used as metaphors.
The disciples of the Buddha also possess five meanings; however, these are merely secondary meanings and not the primary ones, as they cannot be described in detail here.
Next, regarding the interpretation provided by the Master Fu, he explains the preceding four meanings by condensing them into three, which is intended to follow a sequential order.
As for the reason why the first is called "pure alms-seeking" (*piṇḍapāta*), the meaning is that it refers to the initial stage of renunciation (*niṣkramaṇa*).
While one has not yet attained the fruit of the household way characterized by the affection between husband and wife, the body still remains subject to dependence.

Since one has just recently departed from such ties, it is not fitting to return again to the household for sustenance; nor can one seek relief through improper means. Therefore, one should for the time being support the physical body through alms-seeking.
Freeing oneself from the defilement of desire for sensory form, one maintains the life granted by past karma through purity. For this reason, this is the very first [practice].

That which is called "pure livelihood through begging for food" begins with the physical departure from the home of human affection and ends with the necessity of further departing the house of the three realms through the mind.
How can one depart? It must be by breaking the afflictions (*kleśa*) and maintaining the precepts (*śīla*) through self-restraint;
only then can it be achieved. Therefore, next comes the ability to maintain the precepts by breaking the afflictions, which arises from possessing the aforementioned [qualities].
The two types of abodes—the physical body and the mind—are such that the celestial Māras fear and dread them, as they transcend the Māras' own realm;
it is precisely because of this that fear arises, and for this reason, he is finally called "one who terrifies the Māras" (*bhīṣma-māra*).

Because these four meanings follow this sequence from beginning to end, one who possesses them is called a *bhikṣu*. This master explains [the term] specifically by way of its vertical progression from beginning to end.
Regarding the four meanings, the first is named "bhikṣu" because one attains it through pure alms-seeking; the second is attained through breaking evil by maintaining the precepts;

and the third is attained through the fear of Māra. Since these three occasions are discussed together, there are four meanings for the name. The subsequent general explanation is precisely applied to this point.

Next, based on the commentary (*śāstra*), only three meanings are clarified. Within this, first the three meanings as explained in the commentary are set forth, followed by the explanation that the sūtra contains only one.

Regarding the first part (the exposition of the three), there is the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion. First, the introduction of the three: although this cites the commentary, there remain three differences from the commentary itself.
First, a difference in number, because there are five [meanings] in the commentary. Second, a difference in names, because one name in the commentary is "Destroying Afflictions" (*kleśa-bhañjana*).
Therefore, the sequence of these three is distinct and not identical to this [present] order; thus the treatise asks, "What is meant by 'bhikṣu'?
A bhikṣu is called a mendicant (*bhikṣu*), and is also called one who destroys afflictions (*kleśa*);

furthermore, it is a name for a renunciant, a name for one who has undertaken the precepts through self-vow, and is also called one who terrifies Māra. This is precisely the sequence of names enumerated within the treatise. Therefore...

Regarding these designations, there are three differences from those established in the treatise (*śāstra*). Commentators of both ancient and modern times have often employed either three or four categories;
as in the case of the two aforementioned masters, their four names are identical to the four found in the treatise, though they lack the single name "renunciant" (*pravrajita*).
The interpretations of recent times merely divide the four into five, yet none of them include the "renunciant" mentioned in the treatise.
First, regarding the present school’s practice of relying solely on the three [categories] at various points:
although previous masters did not provide an explicit interpretation or reconciliation, it cannot be that they failed to do so; therefore, I shall now briefly reconcile them. Why is this?

Because "the one who has left home" (*pravrajita*) is a general designation without a separate essence, being merely the four remaining meanings, all of which are matters pertaining to leaving home. Among these four:
Furthermore, the meaning of upholding the precepts within the [three] distinct categories is subsumed under "destroying evil.

Since the meaning of destroying evil would remain incomplete without the precepts, this treatise on the three essentials—which discusses the general and the specific in detail—actually contains five points.
However, for the sake of the essential core, only three are taken here; moreover, these are praised as a comprehensive synthesis from the perspective of the correspondence between cause and effect.
Because provisional [teachings] enter into reality to achieve the great parinirvāṇa—the secret treasury of the three virtues—this single school uniquely regards these three as essential.
Other schools merely follow whatever appears in their respective texts and do not follow the intent of this essential convergence; therefore, they are not what is accepted here.

This will become clear later on its own, so there is no need for further elaboration. "Evil" and "afflictions" share the same underlying meaning, though there is a slight difference in their significance. Why is this?

Afflictions reside in the mind, while evil permeates the entire body; this also reflects the meaning of "root and branch. While the discussion here specifically addresses their root, it now speaks generally of both root and branch.
Furthermore, in order to establish a convenient nomenclature, afflictions are all expressed using two characters and thus referred to as "breaking the fetters" (*pójié*).
Alternatively, they may be termed according to their specific functions based on the treatises. However, there is no fixed order among these three.

Therefore, the sequential order varies in different places, and since all are equally valid, there is no fixed position. Thus, although there are three differences, they do not contradict the sequence of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Furthermore, among these three explanations, while I have not followed the text of the treatise in its entirety, though there are minor discrepancies, the major points do not differ in intent.
Now, I shall provide a brief explanation according to what appears before me and cannot further cite the full text of the treatise. First, the explanation of the meaning of "frightening the Māras."

Because Māra is the lord of worldly craving and desires only that himself and others remain perpetually within the tainted cycle of birth and death, whereas those who have gone forth from home do so for the sake of themselves and others escaping from birth and death; thus, they act contrary to his intentions.

He attempts to use force to compel those who oppose him to comply, yet he is not merely unable to do so—on the contrary, he is instead constrained by them. For this reason, his grief and fear increase all the more.
Thus, issuing commands oneself and being able to cause others to frighten Māra, and furthermore counteracting him, is precisely what constitutes "frightening Māra.

Because this summarizes the meaning, one who has left the household life is called a "Frightener of Māra" (*bhayabhairava*). Regarding the "five fetters," it refers to binding five locations with five corpses.

Alternatively, it is said to be the corpses of a dead person, a dog, a snake, a rat, and a pig; these should be verified in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation) commentary, which uses them as symbolic representations.

This refers to the five kinds of impurity contemplation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Alternatively, it is said that one is bound in five places, namely the head, hands, and feet. However, this may be understood in two senses:
first, if one has recently left the household life, it occurs due to the power of the Three Jewels stirred by the sincerity of one's devotion, yet because of one's unwholesome mind;

second, according to the ordinary interpretation, it is simply stated that when one first leaves the household life, the palace of Māra trembles. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states directly: [the palace of Māra shakes].
It is said that when this person first leaves the household life, Māra speaks thus: "This person will certainly enter nirvāṇa.
If they later attain the fruits of sainthood, they possess their own supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to subdue him, just as the noble one Kūṭadanta did.
Although the text states that they can subsequently transform others, this should be understood according to the latter meaning; yet in truth, it also encompasses the former. Next...
The *Pó è zhōng lùn* (Treatise on Breaking Evil) states: "One who can break afflictions is called a bhikṣu.
Since he is now addressed as "one who breaks evil," it should be said that he is so called because he can break the three karmas and the ten unwholesome paths;

yet the text mentions only seven. This may be because the treatise and this [text] cite them alternately; while the treatise refers to the mind, this [text] cites body and speech, doing so specifically in terms of the precepts. Alternatively, it may be...

Regarding the "seven" and the "ten characters": because the characters are easily confused and prone to error during transcription, and furthermore because people saw that the words for body and speech were not fully expressed while the textual phrasing was already complete, they omitted the intended characters and changed "ten characters" (*shi zi*) to "seven" (*qi*) to accord with the meaning of body and speech;
this seems plausible. However, if the meaning of the "ten characters" is correctly understood as being comprehensive and sufficient, it is easy to comprehend.

Next, I shall explain the term "beggar" (*bhikṣu*). In secular society, there are four occupations—scholar, farmer, artisan, and merchant—which are known as the livelihoods of the four classes of people.

However, the mention of only three [occupations] here may also be an error in the oral tradition. In secular life, these four matters are used to obtain one's livelihood, and they all accord with the Way of the King’s governance;

therefore, it is said that they are "in accordance with the Dharma. Those who do not permit them [the four occupations] argue that while these four are permissible for householders according to secular law, they are not so for those who have renounced the world.

One leaves the household life for the sake of the Way and must differ from the mundane; therefore, [worldly occupations] are not permitted. Since worldly activities are forbidden, one’s physical existence and life depend on others.
How, then, can one provide for these needs? Only begging is the resource. Because it benefits oneself and benefits others, one is further called a "beggar" (bhikṣu).

According to the treatises, one who does not rely on the four wrong means of livelihood and seeks a pure way of sustaining life is called a beggar; "begging" (bhikṣ) is the term for seeking and striving.

The term "shi" (士) is an appellation for the extraordinary; all those who leave the household life seek provisions in order to practice the Way as distinct from the secular world, to break through arrogance, and to bring benefit and merit to sentient beings.
Because these purposes are entirely different from ordinary seeking and acquisition, they are called "shi.

This is because, in the world, the term "shi" is likewise an appellation for those who differ from the common masses. [This is found] in the fourth of the five filial pieties and the fifth of the five meanings.
Regarding the twentieth person, it corresponds to the twenty-fifth; this refers to the matter of "instruction" (*xùn*) and "illumination" (*míng*).

Because one hears of one thing and knows ten, the character for "instruction" (*xùn*) is composed of the numerals one and ten. Now, if hearing of one thing fully encompasses all causes and effects, this already exceeds the scope of the ten realms—how much more so the meaning of the beginning and end of heaven and earth?
(etc. Question: Since you have cited the treatise to establish [the point], why not rely directly upon it?
The commentary answers that since it cites the treatise to indicate the point, the meaning of the treatise and its commentary is already self-evident;

however, because one wishes to provide a comprehensive understanding by reaching across to different versions, other texts are employed to assist in the explanation of what precedes and follows—examples of this are numerous.

Next, regarding the explanation within the sūtra, it merely presents a single meaning as explained above; yet since there are actually three meanings, why do those two sūtras present only the single point of "destroying evil"?
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is explained according to the text. The *Wenjing shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) states: "To destroy evil is the primary [meaning], while the rest are auxiliary.
Why is this so? Maintaining the precepts destroys the evil karma of body and speech; terrifying Māra destroys the evil of craving; and being a mendicant (*bhikṣu*) destroys the evil of arrogance.
This is because the sūtra briefly cites these essential points. Next, he provides his own explanation.

This is explained through three meanings based on both the initial and final stages. Previously, Master Kumārajīva provided a vertical explanation, defining the initial, middle, and final positions as fixed in their respective order.
Alternatively, according to the treatise, these may be either initial or final. For this reason, it is now clarified that these three meanings apply universally to both the initial and final stages;

thus, both the horizontal and vertical dimensions are fully complete. This is because for those who have left the household life, there are three matters present at both the beginning and the end that share the same name.

This is because it concerns the bhikṣu. Within this, first the meaning of the general application is indicated; second, the characteristics of that general application are distinguished; third, the general name is concluded;

fourth, the textual intent is distinct, stating that the term "should" applies to both the beginning and the end. The brief explanation has already been provided as above. Next, the characteristics of the meaning’s general application to both the beginning and the end are distinguished.
Furthermore, the reason for not following the previous sequential order here is to reverse the sense of the preceding discussion regarding sequence.
Furthermore, the sequence of the primary and auxiliary, the fundamental and the derivative, is clarified as previously explained.
Each point is discussed in relation to the three trainings (*triśikṣā*), which may be sought within the text. Moreover, each passage should consist of a proposition, an explanation, and a conclusion;

however, because the following two [passages] lack a cause and possess only the manifestation, it is said that "the cause produces" and "the unmanifested is manifested. Thus, it is like the initial recitation and so forth, wherein the unmanifested (*avijñapti*) arises.

This is because it functions spontaneously once it has been performed; prior to receiving the precepts, one spontaneously and constantly gives rise to evil toward all objects, but once the precepts have been received, one vows to prevent such actions entirely toward all objects. Thus, it is able to spontaneously reverse all former non-volitional (avijñapti) evil karma.
Although evil karma is manifold, it does not exceed the seven branches of body and speech, which are fixed.

The precepts associated with the Path (*mārga-sahabhū-śīla*) may be understood according to the usual interpretation. Regarding the greed and anger of the mental level (*manobhūmi*), they correspond to the three [karmas] of the body and four of the speech;

it is clear that the three of the mind can also suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*). These likewise correspond to the three previously mentioned, and when stated collectively, they comprise all ninety-eight [afflictions].

The term "also" (*api*) serves as a concluding censure of Master Kumārajīva, for he restricted his analysis exclusively to the subsequent mind (*paścāt-citta*). This is according to the principle explained above.
Thus we know that the initial mind is also capable [of this], not only the subsequent ones; how could one definitively state that it is only the subsequent mind that can destroy [the afflictions]?

Although these [subsequent minds] suppress [them] without yet destroying them, because they ensure that [afflictions] will never arise again, they ultimately bring about their destruction; for this reason, they are also termed "destruction.
Next, the meaning of the initial [mind] being able to "frighten Māra" may be understood by analogy. Regarding the term "mendicant" (*bhikṣu*), "one who has abandoned wrong livelihood" means:

This is because one must live out one's life by avoiding unlawful and perverse means of seeking sustenance. As previously mentioned, these four types constitute wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*) within the Sangha.

According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, one should instead abandon the four perversities, namely the four modes of seeking food: looking upward, looking downward, looking toward the intermediate directions, and looking toward the four cardinal points.

These are explained in the treatise as follows: looking upward at celestial phenomena, looking downward at terrestrial resources, acting as a messenger throughout the four quarters, and the practice of incantations and divination—all of which, according to the commentary, are forbidden for those who have left the household life.
Because these are not truly pure, they must be abandoned. Furthermore, according to another teaching, there are five further types of misconduct:

first, altering one’s usual deportment and feigning extraordinary appearances for the sake of gain and offerings; second, speaking of one’s own merits; third, raising one’s voice to manifest an air of authority;
fourth, proclaiming the gains and offerings one has received to incite others to give; and fifth, seeking... [the text continues].

For the sake of profit, one must forcibly seize the good or bad fortune of others; such things are perverse and contrary to the Dharma and must be abandoned. To seek one's livelihood through begging is considered correct and pure.

Not only does one maintain the precepts to distance oneself from perversity and seek food and drink from others externally, but one also internally examines one’s own mind to seek the food and drink of meditative concentration and wisdom—the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of *dhyāna*. Master Jiaxiang said: "From above, [one follows] the Tathāgata..."
One is called a "beggar" (bhikṣu) because they come to beg for the Dharma to nourish the spirit and follow worldly people to seek food to nourish the body; thus, they are named "beggars.
This is already the case when one seeks from others outside while failing to clarify what comes from within oneself; how much more so for those who beg for the Dharma?
Not only this person, but all who are truly "beggars" are so called because they obtain [nourishment] through all three types of seeking—both internal and external.
The meaning of this is not that the name "Bhikṣu" (one who begs) applies exclusively to the initial stage.
If even the three types of seeking at the initial mind can already be termed "Bhikṣu," how much more so when the subsequent mind accords with the Way? At that later stage, one is truly a Bhikṣu;
why then should it apply only to the initial mind and not extend to the subsequent? This is because Master Kumārajīva focused specifically on the initial stage.
The mind concludes this section and critiques this sutra’s conclusion as being fundamentally different from the preceding one;

it does so precisely because it provides a comprehensive explanation of the three meanings within this inquiry, all of which pertain to the Three Studies (*tri-śikṣā*). Why do other schools not agree with this? The answer follows: since these are subsequently concluded as the Tripiṭaka, they constitute the essential practice for renunciants according to this teaching.
Not only is this the case for this teaching, but the Perfect Vehicle (*pūrṇa-yāna*) is likewise so; thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra states: [text omitted].
In this context, these three gates are called the "Noble Practices of Great Nirvāṇa" because they constitute the fundamental source of the myriad virtues of Great Nirvāṇa.

While various commentators have demonstrated its profundity by each specializing in a single aspect, what is here termed "comprehensive" (tong) is so designated because it serves as a general conclusion that fully encompasses these three meanings from beginning to end; therefore, one is called a *bhikṣu* based on this comprehensive sense.
The heading applies to both the beginning and the end, yet the commentary speaks only of the beginning; how then can it be said that the "bond" (saṃyojana) applies to both the beginning and the end?

The first two bonds state that they do not apply solely to the latter, clarifying that the latter applies to both the beginning and the end. The single bond states that it does not apply solely to the beginning, clarifying that it applies to both the latter and the former.

The meaning of this application is as clear as one's palm—what room is there for doubt? Although the meaning of the *bhikṣu* has been thus discussed in general above, if we rely upon the present sutra...
That which is praised by the householders is all a separate praise of the final mind, as it does not extend to the initial explanation;

the stage of enlightenment is defined here as the meaning of an Arhat, for he is one who attains realization after [the Buddha's] passing and inspires confidence. Therefore, this is not a general [definition], but rather refers to a Bhikṣu who possesses the three ultimate meanings.
Thus, these general and specific [explanations] differ from other interpretations.

The four preceding sections all explain the meaning of "bhikṣu" (monk), which corresponds to an explanation by way of causes and conditions (*nidāna*). Such an explanation should fully embody the intent of the four *siddhārtha* (purposes).
At first glance, the text appears to establish only the purpose of "remedying" (*pratipakṣa*). However, the Master said:

"Taking the terrifying of Māra as the worldly purpose (*loka-saṃvṛti*) and renunciation as the ultimate purpose (*paramārtha*)"—this is extremely difficult to comprehend. Now, observing the intent of the text, since it takes the [remaining] three purposes as primary, [the former interpretation must be reconsidered].
In the subsequent section on "Exegesis through Contemplation," the meaning of renunciation (*pravrajyā*) from the *Śāstra* is again employed;

that is, by combining the general and the specific, the significance of the four *siddhāntas* is present therein. Why is this so? The *Śāstra* states: "One who has renounced the world is called a *bhikṣu*.

This is a general statement [encompassing] three meanings, for all three are modes of practice for one who has renounced the world; thus, they correspond to the Worldly (*loka*), which is the general [category].

Regarding the three [meanings]: first, because he begs for alms, he is a "beggar" (*bhikṣu*); second, because he destroys evil, he is a "destroyer" (*bhikṣu*); third, because he opposes the fear of Māra, he is a "fear-opposer" (*bhikṣu*).
This is the primary meaning, as both himself and others seek the supramundane. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Māra says this because this person will certainly enter *nirvāṇa*.
It is precisely because he and others seek the path to *nirvāṇa* that Māra is terrified; thus, this is the primary [meaning].
The intended meaning is clear. In the "Contemplation of the Mind" (Kuan-hsin) section, the sequence is likewise based on these four meanings;
this precisely manifests these four intentions, leaving no room for doubt. Therefore, the three aspects—general and specific—are these very four meanings, which are termed "bhikṣu."

Next, regarding the classification by teaching (*yōkyō*), this primarily clarifies the meaning of the "bhikṣu" in this sutra. First, directly concluding the preceding causes and conditions constitutes the meaning of the initial teaching.
The phrase "these are all," etc., refers to the passage that points back to provide a comprehensive explanation.

The term "letting" (*ryō*) likely serves as a general conclusion pointing back to the four previous layers of interpretation, rather than being a unique explanation for the present one; for the four previous interpretations were all based on the phenomenal (*shi*).

Since the three trainings (*śikṣā*) differ from the latter three [collections], they all embody the intent of the Three Piṭakas. That which takes the middle as its object is precisely the phenomenon (*vastu*);

thus, begging for food belongs entirely to the category of phenomena. Yet, according to each phenomenon, one is able to immediately realize the principle; by taking the substance of the phenomenon to seek the food of the principle, it differs from the Three Piṭakas where phenomena and principle are eternally separate.
That which obstructs the principle is either affliction or evil; this [realization] may arise when one is deluded regarding the principle.
Because the very substance of the obstacles to evil is non-existent, it is called "shattering. This refers to the practitioner; these are the two aforementioned practices.
Once these two practices have been cultivated, one then fears the three Māras. Since the three Māras are feared, the celestial Māra (devaputra-māra) is startled; therefore, it says "fearing the four.

Although the Tripiṭaka should also speak of four, the *Anraku-gyō* (The Practice of Peace and Bliss) states, "with the affliction-māra and so forth," following the conventional explanation and omitting [the fourth] for brevity.
It does not mention "three" because within this realm, the causes and conditions of birth and death, as well as their karmic retributions, are all exhausted here.
