For this reason, one lacks the benefit of the wondrous path of the past, the Dharma-body, and the life of wisdom. This clarifies that such destruction and harm constitute the causes and conditions for obstructing the Path.
This refers to the indeterminate stage of the Perfect Vehicle (Yuan-sheng). It is because one has lost what ought to have been attained, and the matter cannot be restored. Furthermore...
Previously, I merely explained the preceding citation from the Vaipulya sutras; now I shall directly explain the preceding citation from this very sutra.

However, the conditions for benefit primarily concern food and clothing, while the conditions for harm do not exceed those of destruction and injury. Therefore, these two explanations are mutually related;

one should contemplate this well. For this reason, there is great loss or gain; because such loss or gain is so immense, both the transgressions and the merits are grave. This is the essential point herein.

It is said that this person is worthy of being a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) and should be venerated; the reason why the passage on "Contemplating the Mind" is the most extensive is briefly due to four intentions:
first, to distinguish between harm and benefit; second, to exhort and encourage people according to the ease or difficulty of their dispositions;
third, to comply with the Buddha’s words; and fourth, to encourage its widespread circulation. It is for these four reasons that this statement was made.
Because this intention is clear, the commentary states [at length]. This refers to the person by way of their virtuous conduct; one should reflect upon it well.
The preceding brief explanation of the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Essentials) is now complete.

Furthermore, there was once another school whose name is not recorded, consisting of people from the Chen and Sui periods who provided a broad threefold explanation of the phrases for this stage within the brief [treatise], stating: "As for the Arhat, there are briefly three [types]."
Within the meaning [of "Arhat"], there are six meanings; broadly, there are fifteen meanings; briefly, there are three meanings, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:

"the slayer of thieves," "the one worthy of offerings," and "the non-arising. Regarding the middle meaning, as explained in the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā*, it is called "the slayer of enemies" (*vairi-sūdana*);
"enemy" (*vaira*) takes transgression as its characteristic, and since all sufferings arise from afflictions, this person is the ultimate enemy.

Because he has severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) without remainder, he is said to have "slain the enemy. Although the three preceding fruits also eliminate afflictions, they do not do so exhaustively;

therefore, they are not called "slaying the enemy. Second, he is named "one who breaks the wheel" (*cakrabhedin*). All ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) give rise to the wheel of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*) across the three periods of time, which revolves through birth and death;

this is the nature of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*). This person, by means of the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*), [overcomes] both the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

The Arhat who has destroyed the twelve links of dependent origination so that they are entirely exhausted without remainder attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

Because he is free from the ten wheels of the past and present, he attains the knowledge of exhaustion; because he has destroyed the two wheels of future birth, death, and illness, he attains the knowledge of non-arising.

The Arhat who has attained these two knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) Arhat; the one who attains the two knowledges [alone] is a conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) Arhat.
The Arhat has two names. First, "Non-arising" (*anutpāda*): just as seeds that have been stored for many years cannot sprout even when external conditions are present, so it is with the Arhat;
although karma and its retribution exist, because the afflictions of both seeing and cultivation are exhausted, they do not arise.
Because they do not arise, they are called *Arhat*. Fourth, "Not ascending": this means not ascending the vehicle of birth and death, due to the perfection of the two trainings.
Fourth, because the four floods (*ogha*) are forever severed and he does not enter into birth and death, he is called "One Who Should Be Honored" (*arhat*);

fifth, because he is endowed with perfected knowledge and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), and as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) is most excellent, he is called "One Who Should Be Honored. Sixth, he is called "One Who Should Be Taught" (*śaikṣa*);

since he has himself extinguished evil and produced good, he is able to instruct others according to what he himself has attained, leading them to reach that which he himself has attained; thus he is called "One Who Should Be Taught. All *arhats* possess these [qualities].
Regarding these various meanings, "fifteen" refers to what is stated in this treatise: because an Arhat is said to possess fifteen meanings, they are termed "possessing.
There is a heading, an enumeration, and an explanation. In the explanation, the fifteen meanings are first grouped into four categories, which are then explained according to their respective types.
As for the four categories: the first is the "Arhat who ought to cultivate meritorious fields," and the next five...

The first five [stages] are those that should be practiced as the cultivation of the field of wisdom; the latter four are those that should be practiced as the cultivation of one’s own portion, followed by the cultivation of superior progress.
As explained extensively in that text, I cannot describe it all here. Now, I maintain that such an interpretation is indeed very rich;
however, the reason this particular passage is not adopted here is that it does not correspond with the explicit wording of the sūtra, and thus it is not the sūtra itself.
Because it accords with the correct intention and is not merely incidental, the current text relies directly on the three meanings from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*;

this is because the passage praising the general and specific aspects within the stages corresponds precisely [to those meanings], and because these fourfold explanations constitute the fundamental intent of this sūtra.
Ultimately, they converge upon the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), wherein no meaning remains unexhausted and which represents the ultimate pinnacle of essential significance.
Therefore, those who study by means of the interpretations found in various sutras should examine this thoroughly.
This preceding section of the old commentary may also be moved to the end of the "Causes and Conditions" (Nidāna) chapter above. This concludes the explanation of the meaning of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Private Notes on the Words and Phrases of the Wondrous Sutra, Scroll Four;
Private Notes on the Words and Phrases of the Wondrous Sutra, Scroll Five (from the passage praising the virtues of the Arhats up to the end of the section on Maudgalyāyana).
Compiled by the Stone Drum Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyun.
Next, the following explains the praise of virtues, which briefly clarifies two points: first, it praises the merits possessed by the aforementioned individuals within the preceding six chapters;

second, it explains the preceding—namely, it explains the general statement mentioned above. When viewed from the perspective of the single phrase [of the general statement] in relation to the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), it clarifies their respective stages;
yet when viewed in relation to what follows, it remains a general praise of virtue. Thus, the aforementioned single phrase constitutes both the stage and the praise.

This is a general summary and a specific analysis; regarding the stages, it is specific, while regarding the virtues, it is general. This is because it is not any of the first three fruits, yet it contains the meanings of the latter three—reflect on this.
Furthermore, it serves both as a heading and as an explanation. If one were to treat it solely as a praise of virtues, one would lose one aspect of the meaning;

the same applies to the subsequent section on Bodhisattvas—reflect on this. In the commentary, there is first a general explanation, followed by a specific explanation; within the general explanation, there is...
First, the general indication of the textual divisions and the qualities worthy of praise; second, the citation of treatises to establish the proof;
third, the conclusion that these constitute the praise of the three qualities. First, it is explained that although there are five meanings based on the text, they are in fact only three.

This is because the preceding section used a single phrase to encompass all three meanings generally, whereas here the text is specific; thus, these five phrases specifically praise the three meanings.
Some say that "Arhat" (羅漢) is translated here as "one who is worthy" (應). There are three meanings of "worthy": first, being worthy because one has eternally destroyed the thieves of the afflictions;

second, being worthy because one will no longer undergo birth-and-death within the realm of segmented existence; and third, being worthy because one is fit to receive the sublime offerings of the world.
Now, I maintain that these [three] are selected from among the fifteen meanings found in the root treatise to explain this passage; thus, it is consistent with the meaning.

This does not contradict the meaning established here; however, since there are both general and specific [aspects], one should know that the general is fully present within each particular, and each particular is fully present within the general.
This correctly clarifies that this stage possesses such virtues. These virtues exist within that stage to manifest the excellence of the former person’s majestic power (*vibhūti*).
Because these two [general and particular] reside herein, they reveal such meanings as the provisional and the real, and the fundamental and the manifested.

This is because it concerns the meaning of "beginning" and "end. Since the treatise has already stated this, and because [the subject] does not depart from these three meanings, I now provide this explanation.

Next, the individual explanation of the three meanings consists of three distinct parts; first, the general restatement of the present topic serves as a heading, which will be contrasted with what follows below.
To explain further: first, it is clarified that outflows (*āsrava*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) are identical in being harmful; therefore, they are all "thieves.

Since it is said that they are "exhausted" (*kṣīṇa*) and "non-existent" (*abhāva*), this means they have been completely "slain. This is because it refers to the ultimate stage. Although outflows and afflictions differ, they share the common meaning of being "thieves";

thus, they are combined into one [category] and given three names. Although the names differ, they are collectively one. As for how these three names are obtained, they shall be explained in sequence below.
In the subsequent detailed explanation, the first phrase is explained first; according to the meaning herein, there should be a distinction of four or five [sections]:

namely, indicating the number, listing the names, identifying the essence, and explaining the meaning of the names. Since within the meaning of the names there are both specific and general aspects, these constitute four or five [sections].
Within the indication of the number itself, there are further three [subdivisions], namely three, four, and seven. Now, this text...
In this section, only the general enumeration and the explanation of the term are indicated; the rest has been omitted because it is commonly discussed in the world.
May later students take note of this (the subsequent chapter on the meaning of "outflows" [āsrava] is provided separately).

Furthermore, regarding the reliance upon the *Śāstra* (commentary), this clarifies its essential purport. Within this, first, in the section on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), there is first a general explanation, followed by a specific explanation, and finally the explanation according to the treatise.

Regarding the initial general explanation, it consists of three sentences: first, citing the text to indicate the heading; second, providing proof and establishment; third, concluding the correct meaning. These do not differ from the initial [explanation]. As for the first:
although the text contains five points, their essential meaning is only threefold; thus it is said "thus" (*evam*). These five are easily understood in meaning.
The *Commentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* by the Master of the Three Wisdoms (Sengzhao) states:

"The Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci, wishing to translate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra* in the second year of the Jingming era, was unable to do so due to minor disturbances in his native country; he merely produced one fascicle titled 'Essential Meaning' (*Yàoyì*).
[And so forth. Now, I say that this may be called a mere excerpt from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra*; it cannot be called a complete discourse, for it lacks a beginning.
The "Tail" (the concluding section) and the "Rare Record" (the commentary) explain these three meanings in sequence;

collectively, they represent the general meaning of the "stages" (*bhūmi*), while individually they are praised as excellent qualities, hence the term "eulogy. Next, the treatise (*śāstra*) is cited to present both the general and the specific.
The treatise contains three sections, of which this is the second: the section on the general characteristics and the specific characteristics. Within the treatise, there are sixteen [points].

Regarding the "phrases" (*pada*), the Sanskrit manuscripts differ; this is a common feature in many sūtras. However, in this treatise (*śāstra*), the section is intended solely to praise his virtues through a general heading followed by specific explanations;
thus, it is structured as a "general and specific" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) gate. The treatise takes the first phrase as the general heading and the subsequent fifteen phrases as the specific details.
"Arhat" is the general name for one who is "worthy" (*arhat*), while the following fifteen phrases specifically elucidate the aforementioned [qualities].
Regarding "should" (*yìng*), there are fifteen meanings in total, all of which are termed "should"; it is not only the first meaning that is "should.
"Should" refers to the very first of these meanings. Now, we shall discuss this based on three meanings regarding the general and the specific;

it is not necessary to adopt the specific sense of "general and specific"—one should simply know that these are three meanings among them. As for "concluding" (*jié*), because of this, one knows that the first is [the primary].
The three in general and the five in particular constitute the three distinctions.

In the subsequent detailed explanation, there are likewise three distinctions; first, the text cites the passage and indicates that "the two" refers to the two categories of outflows (*āsrava*) and afflictions (*kleśa*), as both are thieves and are therefore mentioned together.
The meaning of "killing" is still broad, but here it specifically takes the sense of "exhaustion," because [they] are exhausted.
Next, we shall explain the term "outflows" (*āsrava*). Herein, the structure should likewise consist of five parts:

stating the number, listing the names, defining the essence, explaining the etymology, and providing a detailed analysis. Within these five, this commentary contains only the statement of the number and the general explanation of the term;
the remainder is omitted. The text says: "Outflows" (*āsrava*) is a collective reference to the various outflows mentioned in the Sūtra. (3)
"Outflows" (*āsrava*) is a general designation for their number; speaking briefly according to their essential categories, there are only these three outflows.

Because these three universally encompass everything, they are "all. What are the three? They are the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
This is the inquiry that introduces and enumerates their names. What constitutes these three in total? It refers to all afflictions (*kleśa*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Excluding ignorance, all afflictions of the desire realm constitute the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*); excluding ignorance, all afflictions of the form and formless realms constitute the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*);
and the ignorance of the three realms constitutes the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). This is the essential nature [of the outflows] as briefly set forth according to the sūtras.

According to the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*, it is exactly like this. However, according to the various masters’ interpretations based on the sūtras and śāstras, the explanation is extremely extensive, as fully detailed in the preceding text.
One must summarize the essentials to explain what has not yet been addressed. Now, although "outflows" (*āsrava*) and "afflictions" (*kleśa*) differ in name, they are identical in substance.

Since the meaning of "torment" (*upāyāsa*) was explained previously with a brief text, it is not discussed here in this summary. However, the "dharma of outflows" presented in the sūtras and śāstras varies;
in its broad outlines, it does not exceed three categories: namely, the three outflows, the four outflows, and the seven outflows. As for these three, they are as described above.

The fourth consists of the three aforementioned [leaks] with the addition of the leak of views (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*). The seventh refers to the leaks of proximity (*saṃsarga*), reception (*parigraha*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*) that are abandoned through both vision and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*).

Although these are fully set forth in the *Mahā-sūtra*, although the meaning of the *Mahā-sūtra* is complete in its three textual passages, there are only two categories mentioned—namely, the third and the seventh.
Therefore, the commentary by Danqiu, in its topical outline (*vibhāga*) of the passage concerning those leaks, states: "First, it clarifies the three leaks; next..."

This clarifies the seven outflows (*āsrava*). Because the seven outflows are further distinguished into three categories, other teachers say that there is a different school which speaks of four outflows;

this is based on the textual essentials, which comprise these three sections. However, when analyzed according to their meaning, there are many further subdivisions, as previously mentioned by Master Jingying, ranging from one up to the infinite.
Explanations by ancient and modern scholars have sometimes addressed them individually.

Regarding the first three [categories], although they may fully rely upon the three aggregates (skandhas), here we speak only of three. If one discusses their essential nature (*tattva*), then each of the three aggregates individually and collectively encompasses all outflowing phenomena (*āsrava-dharma*).
However, if one takes into account both the essential nature and the completeness of causes and conditions, the seven outflows are the most comprehensive and complete;
thus, it is for good reason that the Buddha himself provided an extensive explanation of them in the Mahāyāna Sūtras. Yet, in the present context, they are not seven.

Regarding these three [categories], various treatises and scholars have mostly explained them based on this "one and three"; therefore, I shall also briefly follow this essential point and speak only of the three.
Furthermore, within the commentaries (*śāstra*) on the present Great Sūtra, there are already detailed analyses and exegeses;
those who study this school may seek them out for themselves, so I shall merely provide a brief indication here. If one wishes to understand their beginning and end, one must rely on what precedes.

The arrival at the assembly of the Śākyas is not covered in this present text. Below, the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*) is explained; there are three types: specific outflows and general outflows. What are these three? Why are they called "outflows"?
Why are they called "outflow of desire" (*kāmāsrava*), and so forth, up to why are they called "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyāsrava*)?
In this passage, only the general name is explained and not the specific ones. Within this, first the meaning of "outflow" is explained, followed by [the explanation of the specific ones].

Regarding the explanation of the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*) following the refutation of the meaning of "thief": first, three passages are cited; finally, the conclusion is that their intent is the same.

First, this clarifies that the term "outflow" possesses these three meanings: first, it clarifies that "outflow" has the sense of "leaking away"; second, it clarifies that "outflow" has the sense of "flowing out"; third, it clarifies that "outflow" has the sense of "falling down.
The first refers to losing the truth by following delusion—that is, following delusive afflictions and thereby losing the true path.
This is because it is the principle. Thus, the *Great Sūtra Commentary* (*Dajing shu*) states: "The masters of the treatise call this a 'leakage of principle' (*lou shi daoli*).

Next, since these are people of ignorance and delusion, they are called "fools. As for karma, that is, "active karma" (*xingye*), since it cites the Vinaya texts and pertains to body and speech, the present meaning must encompass all three [doors].
Karma is the cause most capable of bringing forth its fruit; karma itself is the gate through which one enters, according to whichever single karma one performs.
Because various karmas arise in competition, it is said that "all gates are opened. Since the gates are the cause, the outflows (*āsrava*) should be the fruit.
Reflect on this, reflect on this; this meaning is even more evident than before, for they flow forth as outflows.
Since the cause must inevitably reach its fruit, the fruit of birth-and-death with outflows is inferior here, and because one falls into it, it is called "falling" (*pāta*).
The *Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The numerical schools refer to 'leaking' as falling into birth and death; this is the proof.

The next phrase concludes the judgment and explains the meaning of "leakage" (*āsrava*). "Treatises" refers to the two treatises, and "vinayas" refers to the various vinayas, because such words of censure are found throughout those vinayas.
"Different terms" refers to the three distinct expressions—lost, leaking, and fallen—all of which explain [the same concept].

In terms of the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*), they are identical. Here, one ought to distinguish and harmonize the various explanations of the meanings of these names, though that has not yet been done.

This is because, following the previous discussion on the meaning of "outflow," the meaning of "thief" is now explained; by means of the meaning of "thief," the extreme severity of the faults and afflictions of the outflows is revealed.
One should know that "outflows" and "afflictions" are the phenomena, while "thief" is the metaphor. The essential point here is precisely this.
It is clarified that these outflows (*āsrava*) are as extremely harmful as those enemies and bandits. To clarify the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*), there must necessarily be these three aspects;
although each is mentioned individually, all possess the three meanings because they are inseparable. The "bandit" refers to the aforementioned afflictions (*kleśa*):
because they fail to understand false objects, they follow after delusion, lose what is real, and thereby deviate from the truth. Because the Path (*mārga*) is most venerable, it is so named.

Because this delusion is cherished as the very essence of the thief, it alone receives the name "thief. Furthermore: because there is no merit, one is poor; because there is no wisdom, one is destitute;
because there is no companion of wholesome dharmas, one is solitary; and because there is no covering of shame and dread of blame, one is exposed.

By means of these conditions, one commits various evil karmas—namely, the out-flowing karmas within the three realms of existence. The following phrase clarifies that karma invites retribution, whereby one falls [into the miserable states].
The meaning of "falling" (*luò*) is assisted by this; "causing to arrive" (*zhì*) refers to the manifestation of response through extreme clarity.

Although this clarity possesses these three meanings, it is precisely because of the first meaning that it leads to the second, and because of the first two that it leads to the third. Thus, the first [meaning] has two aspects: first, causing one to lose the principle; second, causing one to create karma.
The second [meaning] has one aspect, which is the "loss," namely, causing [one] to reach the fruit. Below, the single meaning of "causing to arrive" is clarified.
If, at the time of the fruition of outflows (*sāsrava*), one immediately loses the three untainted fruitions (*anāsrava-phala*), why is this?

Because once one has brought about an outflowing body of suffering, there is no longer the untainted Dharma-body; there is no longer the untainted life of wisdom; and there is no longer the untainted True Path.
Thus, when one [quality] is present, the other three are absent. This is all said because one fears that these three might be lost in the Mahāyāna; yet, I suspect this may not yet be the case. Why?
This is the general principle of causal conditions, which is still largely found in the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*).

If this is so, then the *dharmakāya* refers to the fivefold *dharmakāya* as a whole, while "the life of wisdom" (*prajñājīvita*) specifically refers to one among those five. "The precious treasure" refers to the truth of reality (*tattva*). Previously, it was explained that having one necessarily implies having three;
now, it is shown that losing one necessarily means losing all three. If one explains it in this manner, it accords with the various teachings of the ancient past.
Fearing that a detailed explanation as previously given might deviate from the intent of the text, the conclusion states that they are all "thieves" in meaning.
Since the scriptural term for these outflows (*āsrava*) has already been explained as the virtue of "slaying thieves," they are called thieves.

Because these outflows are themselves the thieves, this current explanation of outflows is used to clarify the thief-nature in order to harmonize it with the meaning of the Arhat; thus, the conclusion says so. This is precisely because the various afflictions (*kleśa*) constitute the thieves.

The two meanings are that causing one to lose the Path, creating karma, and bringing about the fruit of suffering all stem from delusion; thus, it is precisely on this basis that [delusion] is treated as a thief.
There are three general harms caused by thieves in the world, and since the thieves of affliction possess these three calamities, they are said to have the full sense of being "thieves.
The phrase "this bond of outflows is itself the thief; one should not [view it] as equal [to other things]" is a refutation of ancient misconceptions.
This is because it is the cause for birth; once it has been exhausted, there is no longer a future fruit of birth.
Below this, one ought to explain the specific names and identify the essential nature (svabhāva), as well as provide a detailed analysis and resolve doubts, but there is no time for that at present.

The following explains the subsequent phrase "absence of afflictions," which should likewise be treated in five parts: (1) the heading, (2) the teaching, (3) the enumeration of names, (4) the explanation of names, and (5) the determination of essence and the resolution of doubts.
In the text, there is only the heading, the teaching, and a brief explanation of the names; the conclusion serves to refute errors, while the other sections are omitted.
First, the text cites the passage, indicates the number, and briefly presents the five determinations; these are all afflictions, and they also concurrently present their essential natures.

However, among these five categories, the first is a general designation while the remaining four are derived from specific [sub-classifications], all of which originate from the section on afflictions (*kleśa*).

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Afflictions refer to all fetters (*saṃyojana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), outflows (*āsrava*), bonds (*bandhana*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*);

because these are all severed and eliminated, it is said that there are 'no afflictions. The ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are thus established by combining those abandoned through the two paths of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)."

It is said that the number [of afflictions] in the sūtras and śāstras is not fixed: they may be ninety-eight *anuśayas*, or one hundred and eight, or one hundred and twenty-eight, or eighty-four thousand, or even an immeasurable number. Regarding the ninety-eight, the verse says: "In the stage of suffering (*duḥkha*), all [ten] are present;
in the stages of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*), three views are excluded; in the path (*mārga*), two views are excluded; in the higher realms, anger (*pratigha*) does not function."

There are eighty-eight [afflictions] to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and ten to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Regarding those to be abandoned by insight: within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the category of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) possesses all ten;

for the two truths of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*), three views each are excluded; and for the path (*mārga*), the view of self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) are excluded. Thus, there are thirty-two in the desire realm.

In each of the two upper realms (*rūpa- and ārūpya-dhātu*), four [of the ten]—specifically anger (*pratigha*)—are excluded. Thus, there are fifty-six in the upper realms. These constitute the eighty-eight [afflictions] to be abandoned by insight.
Regarding those to be abandoned: those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) consist of four types in the desire realm and three each in the higher realms, totaling ten;

when added to the preceding [nine] categories, they constitute the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*). As for the term "one hundred and eight," it refers to the ninety-eight plus the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).

As for the term "one hundred and twenty-eight," according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (Great Commentary), it is said that there are one hundred and twenty-eight [proclivities] to be abandoned through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), combining the three realms.

Regarding the one hundred and twelve [defilements] to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), when the three realms are combined and stated as a total, there are sixteen. First, concerning those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*):

in the four truths of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are ten types for each, totaling forty; in the two higher realms, four types of anger (*pratigha*) are excluded from each, resulting in seventy-two.
This can be understood from the preceding [table]. Regarding those to be abandoned by cultivation: the desire realm possesses all six [types], while the two higher realms each possess five.

Taken together, there are sixteen such [categories]; when combined with the preceding, they total one hundred and twenty-eight. Regarding the mention of "eighty-four thousand" and so forth, these are fully explained as they appear in the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Bhadrakalpika Sūtra*;
fearing prolixity, I shall not describe them here. These various enumerations apply universally to all vehicles, both Great and Small.
When it is said that something is "non-existent," it means that such a thing does not exist at all. Furthermore, when it is said to be "flowing," it refers to the four [streams].

The "floods" (*ogha*) refer to the flood of desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. The "yokes" (*yoga*) are these same four floods, which are also termed yokes.
The "envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*) refer to the ten envelopments: torpor, drowsiness, restlessness, remorse, stinginess, envy, lack of shame, lack of dread, anger, and concealment.
The "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*) refer to the five hindrances: sensual desire, ill-will, torpor-drowsiness, restlessness-remorse, and doubt.

Regarding the term "etc. (*ādi*) used to briefly indicate these five [afflictions] and others: it is called "etc. because it refers to all remaining [afflictions] as well. The section above [the heading] concerns the names and essential natures (*nāma-svabhāva*);
the section below explains their general meaning by way of the term "oppression" (*pīḍana*). They are called "afflictions" (*kleśa*) precisely because they oppress and disturb the practitioner;

they are also called "messengers" (*dūta*) because they drive the practitioner about, depriving them of autonomy. The single character "oppress" (*pīḍa*) at the beginning [of the title] refers to this.
Furthermore, this also explains the meaning of "affliction" (*kleśa*); it clarifies that the latter four [categories] are all afflictions because they invariably cause oppression and distress.

Because they can sweep away and flow with great speed, they are called "floods" (*ogha*). Because they agitate and move the practitioner so that they cannot attain mastery, they are called "yokes" (*yoga*).
Because they entwine and bind, they are called "fetters" (*paryavasthāna*). Because they cover and obstruct the right path, they are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*). One should also say:

The text on the "outflows" (*āsrava*) is abbreviated because it summarizes the general meaning of the afflictions (*kleśa*). "Afflictions" is the general term, while the others are its specific instances;
furthermore, they mutually subsume one another. Since the previous [section on] outflows is no different from this, that section merely indicated their number, whereas here they are listed in brief.
In this way, both the names, the categories, the essence, and the meaning are contained therein, so there is no need for further prolixity. Now, regarding the outflows...

Since "outflow" (*āsrava*) and "affliction" (*kleśa*) are one and the same thing, why are they mentioned twice? An ancient commentary explains: according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, "outflows" are specific while "afflictions" are general.

This is because within the classification of the three outflows, specific categories such as the yokes (*yoga*), floods (*ogha*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), and impurities (*mala*) are all subsumed under the general term "afflictions.
Thus, it is a case of praising both the general and the specific. Furthermore, it is said that the outflows are the root, whereas the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the afflictions.

This is because both the branches and the roots are presented together. Furthermore, it is said that if one were to explain this solely according to the literal text, it would mean that since all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, they can no longer cause the mind to be afflicted.
Another explanation states that "outflows" refers to active manifestations (*samudācāra*), while "affliction" refers to seeds;

thus, both seeds and manifestations are eliminated here. The commentary on our own school (*sva-naya*) explains that "outflows" encompass both cause and effect, whereas "affliction" is distinct, referring only to the cause.

This is because both the general and specific [aspects] are excluded. Furthermore, another explanation states: "The 'outflows' (*āsrava*) are also afflictions (*kleśa*), but the term 'outflow' encompasses karma as well.
Since the sūtra contains two phrases that cannot be repeated, we now separately interpret the first phrase in terms of outflows and karma.

This interpretation from the marginal commentary still does not fully clarify the meaning. Now, since there are various differing interpretations such as those mentioned above, the text remains... [incomplete].
It may be said that while "outflows" (*āsrava*) are difficult to comprehend and "afflictions" (*kleśa*) are easy to eliminate, their names differ while their essence is one.

If one knows they are one in essence, then upon hearing that the outflows are exhausted, one immediately knows that afflictions are likewise absent. For those who do not know this, even when they hear that the outflows are exhausted, they believe that afflictions still remain;
it is for those who are confused by these different names that this further statement was made, specifically to reconcile these distinct designations.
Furthermore, regarding the summary below: first, one summarizes the correct principle, which precisely reveals that the afflictions have two primary functions: first, they initiate karma;
second, they moisten rebirth. "Initiating" refers to the very first arising [of karma], while "moistening" refers to what follows immediately, whereby [the afflictions] irrigate and cause [rebirth].
Because causes produce effects, what was previously called "creating karma" is here termed "moistening birth. This merely reveals that afflictions possess this functional power;
it does not mean that different people hold erroneous views. Below is the conclusion which rebuts the faults of the ancients, as the meaning of "both being thieves" cannot be taken as "non-arising.
When the ancients offered this interpretation, their intention was to take [the term] as meaning there is no cause capable of producing [birth].

Furthermore, since these three names exist, what is their distinction? "Outflows" (*āsrava*) possesses all three meanings; "afflictions" (*kleśa*) possesses two, namely affliction and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
In their broad sense, they include many others such as floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and so forth—all of which are different meanings of "affliction.

"Thieves" (*caura*) subsumes the two preceding meanings of outflows and afflictions. To state it briefly: they are so called because they kill and plunder the cause and fruit of the True Path, leading them to ruin.
This is because of the causes and effects of birth and death; the absence of these two types [of causes and effects] is precisely the meaning of "exterminating them completely.
Since this refers to having already eternally destroyed the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*), the first of the three meanings has been concluded.

Next, the explanation of "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat) proceeds by first citing the heading and indicating its meaning, followed by the formal explanation. "Worthy of Offerings" refers to the benefit of others (*parārtha*).
As the Sūtra says: "One takes one's own benefit as the benefit of others; if it were not for oneself, one could not benefit others. This implies that one possesses the capacity for self-benefit.

The Sūtra uses the term "attaining" (*prāpta*), which means "reaching" or "including"; it merely manifests these two meanings—neither being secondary nor primary—because "self" is a designation established in relation to "others," and thus it is explained first.

"Manifesting oneself later" refers to the initial emergence of the two things belonging to others; these are the aforementioned bandits (the cause). "Obtaining oneself later" refers to the subsequent existence of this [result];
because this is not produced by the causes and conditions of clear understanding (*vidyā*) nor by the true Path, it is entirely due to others.

As for what was said previously regarding which bandit loses the profit, since they have already been killed, one obtains one's own profit. "Wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to true knowledge and vision (*yathābhūta-jñānadarśana*), which is capable of severing all [afflictions].
The "object of delusion" refers to the afflictions that are to be severed; the "place where there is no delusion" refers to the state in which those severed afflictions have been exhausted.
Taken together, these two factors are both attained through one's own cultivation and are not derived from another; therefore, it is called "one's own benefit.

As explained extensively in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, although that text is voluminous, its essential points do not exceed this. By means of this personal benefit, one is further able to enable others to attain benefit as well.

Because he is worthy of being a field of merit, he is called "Worthy of Offerings" (*Arhat*); this means he is worthy of receiving the sublime offerings of the world, which is the second of the three meanings of "Worthy.
Next, regarding the explanation of the meaning of "Non-arising": the preceding two lines praise the faults abandoned and the merits attained during the causal stage.
Regarding the two lines below "Virtue" (*guṇa*), these are an encomium based on the fruit (*phala*) concerning that which is abandoned and that which is attained.

If one grasps this meaning, one will know that the five phrases manifest three [aspects], which simultaneously manifest four meanings. First is the general restatement and indication; second is the detailed explanation of the two lines.

Within the first, there is first the explanation of "all existences" (*bhava*), then the explanation of "fetters" (*saṃyojana*), and finally the explanation of resolving doubts and obstacles. The first refers to the fruit, while the second refers to the cause.

Regarding the subsequent double explanation of the two [sections], in the first part one should indicate the number, list the names, and explain the meanings; however, the text here merely indicates the number.

While the *Mahā-śāstra* and various other treatises explain "all existences" (*sarva-bhava*) solely in terms of the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*), we follow the *Mahā-sūtra*, which is why it speaks of twenty-five.
Indeed, the *Mahā-sūtra* fully explains the meaning of all existences by means of ten types, the first of which corresponds to the single existence (*eka-bhava*). Thus it is.
The increasing numbers up to the ninth clarify the nine *bhavas*, while the final tenth clarifies the twenty-five *bhavas*;
each of these exhaustively encompasses the meaning of all that exists. Now, the final tenth is employed to explain the number of *bhavas* for the sake of clarity and convenience.
Next, the names should be listed; the verse says: "The four evil destinies, the four [dhyānas], and the four emptinesses."
Together with the four dhyānas, the realm of non-perception (asaṃjñi), the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa), the Brahmā kings, and the six heavens of the desire realm—these constitute the twenty-five names.

Next, regarding the explanation of their names: while it is impossible to detail them individually, one must briefly understand that these twenty-five are all mundane phenomena of segmented birth-and-death (*pratisaṃdhi-jāti-maraṇa*) characterized by outflows (*sāsrava*). They are not the supramundane principle of true emptiness; therefore, they are so named.
Regarding what is called the "place of birth," this refers to the location where the retribution of a specific karmic cause is manifested;
it clarifies the primary fruit (*maula-phala*) by means of its supporting fruit (*niśraya-phala*), which is the same meaning as that previously discussed under the heading of causes.

As for the "fetters" (*saṃyojana*), there are nine names, natures, and meanings. Regarding the names, they are: attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, grasping, doubt, envy, and stinginess—these are the nine.

Regarding those who explain that the essence of these [fetters] consists of the afflictions (*kleśa*) according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are both general and specific meanings. The specific meanings cannot be described in full;
as for the general meaning, all nine of these are able to bind a person within the various states of existence (*bhava*) in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), preventing them from attaining liberation;

therefore, they are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*). They were also formerly called "interlocking bonds" (*kṣepa*) because they are difficult to break. There are three meanings to this term "interlocking": namely, [The text continues with the three meanings.]
The meaning of "bondage" (*bandhana*) is as follows: it refers to craving (*rāga*), which is capable of binding.

"Conjoined with suffering" (*duḥkha-saṃprayukta*) means that the sensations (*vedanā*) of the three realms are conjoined with the suffering of the three realms and are not conjoined with pleasure. "Mixed with poison" (*viṣa-vimiśra*) means that all sensations produced by birth are impure conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) mixed with the poison of afflictions (*kleśa*);
this is because the Noble Ones (*ārya*) have abandoned them. As for the term "generative cause" (*janaka-hetu*):
"Causes" refers to the conditions, specifically that by which the retributive fruits of the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) are brought about;

hence it is called the "cause of birth. This single phrase contains three meanings: first, "existence" (*bhava*), which refers to the fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*) and the fetters themselves.

The objects of such binding are no more than two kinds: namely, the self and its fruit. If one speaks of "that which is immediate," it refers to the fruit. If one speaks of "that which is expressed," [it refers to the cause].
If one says that the "fruit" (phala) reaches the "son" (putra), then indeed the fruit reaches the son. Now, this very case corresponds to that statement;

yet, since the previous killing of the thief already removed the son's fetters while the fruit had not yet been removed, it is now being discussed in relation to the latter. Therefore, one should not further speak of the "son.
However, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks in the same manner, whereas the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* fully discusses both meanings of cause and fruit.

Therefore, all ancient and modern commentators have relied upon the meaning of the treatise; I shall do the same here. However, if one were to provide an immediate commentary directly on the text, it would be easy to understand and there would be no difficulty.

Yet, although my current approach—commenting by way of "reaching" [the meaning] (*ji*) and "explaining" (*shi*)—accords with the meaning of the treatise, it is nonetheless difficult to comprehend when applied to the sūtra itself.

There must be a profound significance to this, for not only have the various schools of the past and present failed to see this point, but even within our own school, it has not previously been explained.
Since I have also not yet seen a comprehensive synthesis of these points, this remains difficult; I shall now attempt to state it briefly to dispel my own accumulated doubts.
Specifically, within the previous explanation of "slaying the thieves," there are two phrases containing two meanings:
first, to explain and reconcile different names as before; second, to demonstrate that they are not merely "thieves" but are all to be completely slain, thereby praising the Arhat.

Because the virtue of the Han [dynasty] lies in the eradication of delusion, this [state] here also possesses two meanings: first, it is to manifest that which is attained, namely the meaning of the mind attaining mastery.

This is because, being free from the two bonds of cause and effect, it is fully endowed with all meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and is separated from the two obstacles of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*) and nature (*svabhāva-āvaraṇa*), thereby possessing both types of liberation (*vimukti*). Second, it is primarily to manifest the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*), as there is no cause...
Because the two kinds of fruits arise, they are called "non-arising"; because this praises the virtues of an Arhat, it is called "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*);
because the two kinds of dharmas of arising are both exhausted, it is called "exhaustion. To manifest these two meanings, both the cause and the fruit are fully expressed as "exhaustion.
You should contemplate this well. Furthermore, the previous mention of "slaying the two thieves" refers to the two [types of] non-... [text fragment].

The two "born" and the two "unborn" are precisely the two who were previously killed; thus, when the ancients referred to them in the preceding text as "unborn," they likely adopted this same meaning.
The same applies to the meaning of "Arhat" (One Worthy of Offerings). Consequently, whichever one is mentioned, it inherently possesses all three [qualities], because they have no separate essence.
This is the general principle; one should examine it closely. Next, the doubts shall be resolved.

Regarding the "obstructions," one should understand that they are presented first to raise doubts; their explanation involves two meanings, both of which follow the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The treatise states:

"To say that food is the life-force is like a person falling from a cliff," and so forth—these constitute the two meanings. Below, the text explains that the mind attains mastery: if there are bonds, one cannot attain it;
since the two bonds are absent, one attains the two kinds of mastery. First, the two [bonds] are clarified; second, [mastery] is clarified.
There is one who possesses one fetter and one who does not; subsequently, one who possesses four fetters is established as two types of liberation.

The meaning of "five fetters" is certainly that they will not arise again. Some say: "Upon careful examination of the intent of the sūtra, this may be a case of citing the name of the fruit to designate the cause—meaning that the fetters which exhaust existence are called 'fetters of exhausted existence'.
If this is so, then this [type of practitioner] also abandons delusions, just like the aforementioned "slayer of thieves."

If they were thus established as non-distinct, then the refutations in both places would fail to establish their intended meaning. The previous response merely addressed the cause, whereas the intention regarding the cause was exhausted therein;
this present passage cites the effect to clarify that once the intention regarding the cause has been fulfilled within the cause, the effect subsequently does not arise.

This, then, establishes the refutation of the meaning in the commentary while avoiding the objection regarding the exhaustion of all existence (*bhava*) in the sutra. Now, I shall comment upon this interpretation.
This is not yet sufficient to dispel doubts; the general outline has already been explained as before. Consider this:

those liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*) do not cultivate the mundane dhyānas associated with the outflows-free state, and thus possess mastery only over wisdom. Those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*) possess mastery over both.

As for the text stating that "one is born into certainty and exhaustion," I now say that such a person is fully endowed with both the mundane and the outflows-free aspects of concentration and wisdom.
This is because all hindrances have been eliminated.

Next, the commentary below cites a treatise to explain this, stating that there are three gates for explaining this "Praise of Supreme Virtue": first, the gate of the progressive arising of the supreme among the supreme;
second, the gate of the general and specific characteristics; and third, the gate of the inclusion of matters. The above concludes the second gate. Furthermore—
Because there is the significance of this first gate, I shall now further employ it to explain why the second gate was used first:
it is because it is convenient for following the sequence of the thematic momentum. If one were to use this second gate at the outset, it would also be acceptable;

however, the intention behind citing the treatise at the beginning to state the meaning and subsequently explaining the preceding section is to clarify that each subsequent stage is the meaning of each preceding stage. Thus, it is "superior and superior" (shang-shang) in relation to what precedes it.

It is said that "the highest-high corresponds to the lowest-low. Here, "highest" refers to the preceding and "lowest" to the subsequent. This means that the highest-high arises dependent upon the lowest-low;

the highest-high is the "object" (*sādhyamāna*) and the lowest-low is the "agent" (*sādhana*). Because the agent and the object are not identical, it is called "highest-high. Within this gate, there are three meanings:
namely, the preceding cause giving rise to the subsequent effect, the subsequent cause giving rise to the preceding effect, and the agent [giving rise to the object].

The objects distinguished may be known as either mutually serving as the agent and the object, or as established independently within their own respective categories without depending on what precedes or follows;
thus, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are formed, each possessing its own meaning. However, as this is not the primary point [of the current discussion], it is not described in detail.

Below, following the treatise, the characteristics will be presented, briefly citing the first and last permutations. In both cases, the word "by" (*yi*) signifies "due to" (*yōu*). Furthermore, in the latter permutation, there is also mutual interaction.
The meaning is that because the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted, the mind attains mastery; this can be understood from the intermediate passage. Regarding the term "transmission" (*paramparā*):

while the *Saṃyojanasūtra* contains sixteen phrases, here we obtain only five; thus, it is the transmission of the treatise (*śāstra*). The two gates of the treatise have already been briefly explained above.
As for why the third gate, the "Gate of Comprehension" (*saṃgraha-vastu*), is not employed here, it is because it does not pertain to this [context].
Because it is the primary focus of the middle section, it is not mentioned there. An ancient commentary states: "The 'Gate of Arising from Above' (shang-shang qi-men) clarifies the sequence;
the 'Gate of General and Particular' (qian-hou zong-bie men) clarifies the meaning; and the 'Gate of Gathering and Releasing Affairs' (juan-shu she-qu shi-men) clarifies the extent of virtue.

As for the statement in the *Śāstra* that "one is called an Arhat because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted," this refers to the sequential arising of the lower [stages] leading to the upper [stages], specifically as a single, independent progression.
One is called "one whose outflows are exhausted" because the mind has attained mastery; this refers to arising from below to above, skipping over intermediate stages and arising individually.
One is called "one whose mind has attained mastery" because there are no further afflictions; this refers to arising from below to below, proceeding in immediate succession and arising individually.

One is called "one whose mind has attained mastery" because one has well attained liberation through wisdom of the mind; [this refers to arising from below to above, skipping over intermediate stages and arising individually].

From this point downward, the subsequent sections arise in sequential succession. Regarding the statement "it is called 'no further afflictions' because it is far removed from the seer and the seen," this is a case where the meaning following the text gives rise to the text itself; the rest should be understood accordingly.

As for the section on the general and specific gates, the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) specifically clarifies that the skillful means of preaching the Dharma possess six characteristics: namely, the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
The characteristics of sameness, difference, formation, and destruction are explained extensively in that treatise; here they are summarized briefly.

For instance, it is said that among ten dharmas, the first serves as the general [characteristic] while the remaining nine serve as the particular [characteristics], and so forth. Therefore, that treatise states: "The general characteristic is the root;
the particular characteristics are the remaining phrases, for they fulfill that root. The characteristic of sameness is the root; the characteristic of difference is the augmenting characteristic."

Therefore, the characteristic of formation (*saṃbhava-lakṣaṇa*) is explained briefly, while the characteristic of destruction (*vibhava-lakṣaṇa*) is explained extensively. Thus, according to the formation and destruction of the world-system:

the first [characteristic] corresponds to the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of sameness (*sabhāga-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of formation; the remaining nine correspond to the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of difference (*visabhāga-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of destruction.

The gathering of the characteristic of formation is like the formation of the world-system, while its dispersal is like the destruction of the world-system; this is a general summary regarding destruction.

The commentary clarifies that "rolling up" (concealment) and "unfurling" (manifestation) take "one" as the root and "nine" as the branches; thus, identity and difference are explained in terms of wisdom:

one knows the root to be identical because the number decreases, and one knows the branches to be different because the number increases. Furthermore, formation and destruction are explained in terms of teaching:

the root is said to be "formation" because it is concise, while the branches are said to be "destruction" because they are extensive. This is why it is said that the teaching possesses the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*).

Because the establishment of the thesis has a basis, the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is required; because that basis must be explained, the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) is required; because one must realize that the basis is non-dual, the identical characteristic (*tulya-lakṣaṇa*) is required;

because one must facilitate the increase [of understanding] regarding the branches, the different characteristic (*bhinna-lakṣaṇa*) is required; because one must briefly establish the basis, the establishing characteristic (*siddhi-lakṣaṇa*) is required;

and because one must extensively explain the destruction of the basis, the destructive characteristic (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*) is required. Herein, the general and specific characteristics are briefly cited to clarify the meaning of contraction and expansion, as well as identity and difference.

"Formation and destruction" refers to contraction and expansion. The first phrase serves as the general [heading], while the subsequent phrases serve as the specific [details]. The same applies to identity and difference, as well as formation and destruction.
Regarding the "gate of encompassing matters," the *Mahāvyutpatti* explains that fifteen phrases encompass ten kinds of merit.

This demonstrates both the manifestable fruit and the unmanifestable fruit; thus, it connects to the matter. "Matter" refers to the essence of merit, while "encompassing" refers to the sense of accomplishment. It is expressible.
Regarding the "fruits": because the ten matters are clearly manifest, they are called "explicable fruits.
Because the remaining virtues are hidden, they are now shown through fifteen phrases as the "ten matters," which constitute the meaning of "explicable fruits";
this also implies that the remaining virtues are "inexplicable fruits. Thus, it is said that the explicable and inexplicable fruits are demonstrated; the ten matters are as described above.
This has been explained extensively; it is not necessary to describe both the general and the specific, as the essential points of this section have already been briefly stated.
All that precedes constitutes the causal conditions (nidāna) by which the four *siddhāntas* should be clarified. Previously, the exposition was complete according to the stages (*avasthā*);

here, although the presentation is distinct according to the text, the meaning does not differ from what preceded, and thus it need not be repeated. This also applies to the meaning of the essential teaching (*yukti*).
Nor is it stated again; however, because the phrasing differs between the provisional (hon) and the real (jaku), it is restated here to clarify them.

Within this, first is the separate section on the three aspects of the Real, followed by the general clarification of the three aspects of the Provisional. Regarding the former, there are three initial points.

First, within the section on non-arising, the text first cites a passage from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. These two types of non-arising universally encompass all things, and their meaning refers to both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*).

Regarding the severance of cause and effect and so forth, here we specifically take cause and effect; this is because Nirvāṇa is termed "non-arising. As for the section on afflictions (*kleśa*) below, it explains the first point:
that the fundamental cause does not arise, which corresponds to the meaning of the Sūtra’s phrase "the fetters are exhausted. The two characters "source" (*yuan*) and "long" (*jiu*) clarify this:

"source" reveals the two extremes, while "long" correctly reveals that the fundamental [nature] does not recur. Furthermore, the following clarifies that the fundamental fruit does not arise, which corresponds to the Sūtra’s phrase "there is... [existence].
"Exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) means that the causes and fetters of the five abodes have been completely exhausted, and thus one does not fall into the realms of the two deaths;
this is why it is so described. "The source is eternally dried up" means that within this state, there may be either the ultimate stage or [a stage] from which much or little remains;

this refers to the fact that "afflictions" (*kleśa*) corresponds to the sūtra’s phrase "no further afflictions," while "outflows" (*āsrava*) corresponds to "the outflows are already exhausted. This is precisely because these two names function both as general and specific designations. Below is the explanation.
Master Jili says: "In these two phrases, the former clarifies cultivation (*xiū*) and the latter clarifies nature (*xìng*).

Cultivation and nature correspond to wisdom (*zhì*), severance (*duàn*), and the Dharma-body (*fǎshēn*), which are the three virtues (*sāndé*). The two characters 'real wisdom' (*shízhì*) refer to the Dharma-body of nature;

the two characters 'merit and virtue' (*gōngdé*) refer to the two virtues of nature. Furthermore, another interpretation states: "This refers to the virtue of wisdom and severance upon entering the stage of the Dharma-body; thus it is this wisdom."

Since the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa*) accords with the Middle Way, it is a merit of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Now, it is said that the three—body, wisdom, and abandonment—are all treasures within the storehouse of Great Nirvāṇa;
because they are all attained through cultivation based upon the nature (*dharmatā*), they are called merits of true reality.

Because they have been accomplished through long-term cultivation, they are called "one's own original benefit. Next, the explanation of "slaying the thieves" refers to attaining the King Samādhi, which is capable of slaying [the afflictions].
It is precisely because of this that it is called "King" (*rāja*), which has two meanings: first, there is a specific samādhi named "King," as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;

second, it refers generally to the twenty-five concentrations, collectively termed "King," because each individual concentration is subsumed within the samādhis of the three truths, and thus they encompass all concentrations—therefore, they are called "King. If it were not for this [method], how could one possibly break through?
This thief was intentionally raised [for discussion]; the full details are set forth in the Great Sūtra (*Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*).

This single statement "existence" (*asti*) carries a specific meaning that must be applied to both types [of views], as both are fundamentally bonds that deprive one of autonomy; thus, they must be shattered, as previously explained.

The explanations provided in the *Xuan-yi* (Profound Meaning) regarding the four points to be refuted and the twenty-five names of the refuting agent are extremely extensive; they are not the primary intent here, so there is no need for further elaboration.

The *Sūtra on the Great Vehicle of the Exposition of All Dharmas* (*Shu ju da jing*) clarifies that by cultivating wisdom through noble practice, one enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), attains twenty-five samādhis, and is able to destroy the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
Since the statement in this present sūtra—that "all fetters of existence are exhausted"—corresponds precisely to this meaning, it is cited here.
While the aforementioned sūtra does not clarify the method by which these fetters are exhausted, this [present] text explains it; thus, the word "exhausted" is used.
Now, this statement refutes both the general and the specific exhaustively; since it is stated that [the self] is fundamentally non-existent, it directly refutes them all and has long been so.

because only the Buddha possesses ultimate mastery, it is called "I. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the twenty-five states of existence, there is a self."

The Buddha replied that both [views] exist. By clarifying the refutation of "existence," it simultaneously clarifies that if one can refute the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), one can manifest the true, eternal self-nature (*ātman*) within those twenty-five realms.

Upon seeing Mahādeva, this single interpretation brings together the meanings of two sutras; how wondrous! Throughout antiquity and the present, who has ever heard of such a principle? The "self-nature" is the essence. (8)

The two lines of the sutra also reveal that one can contemplate the wondrous contemplation; the nature of mind is the wondrous object.

For those who cultivate this contemplation, it is called the "Supreme Samādhi" among the three concentrations—this is the text of the Great Sutra. The following passage also reveals the capacity [of the practitioner]:

this concentration is itself the Great Quiescent Concentration (Mahāśānti-samādhi). Why need one seek elsewhere? Within the robe lies a priceless treasure-store; one who can cultivate this concentration [attains it] in a single moment.
Because all inherently existing merits are fully manifested, it is for one's own benefit. In the third contemplation, the two phrases of the sūtra text contain three meanings;
furthermore, the first phrase leads to the three capacities below. Because of the absence of right contemplation, the three [defects] arise.
By first cultivating one right contemplation, the three virtues are attained. Since there is no fruit without a cause, it says "also. [This refers to] the two extremes.

This means that both the causal and the resultant aspects of the nature of phenomena (*vastutva*) are freed from their two respective obstructions. Next, citing the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, he explains the three preceding meanings:

the first phrase explains the severance of the aforementioned fetters; the second phrase explains that although it is said "afflictions have been severed," they actually remain present in a latent sense;
the final two phrases provide a comprehensive explanation of the meaning of "mastery," which also simultaneously explains the meaning of the first two phrases mentioned previously.

One should also say that because the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are severed, the two extremes and so forth are equal; this is because they are unified by the single phrase of "right contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*).
By contemplating afflictions as being *bodhi* and realizing that darkness and delusion are themselves clarity and understanding, one regards what exists as non-existent.

By comprehending that arising and ceasing are themselves quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), one is able to enter [the truth] without severing [phenomena]. This is entirely due to the power of wondrous contemplation. Although they exist...
Because there is nothing that does not enter [this realization], this is sovereign mastery; one must fully understand that the six [realms] are likewise so.
The subsequent explanation relies on the treatise’s extensive exposition of faith through sixteen propositions and three gates, which is indeed vast and rich.
Now, I say: though it is rich, it is not yet noble in itself. Why? Because it is entirely limited to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and does not open up [to the Greater].
Though there be many subtle points, what would they avail? Now, based on the five phrases of the current text, I shall explain the three virtues individually through four methods:
first, by way of causes and conditions (*nidāna*), which corresponds to the four *siddhāntas*; second, by way of the teaching, which is both horizontal and vertical;

third, by way of the fundamental and the trace, which is lofty and vast; and finally, I shall harmonize these with one’s own mind, so that the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—are without distinction and all return to the One.
If one does not diverge from this sublime path, one may truly be called wealthy and noble; how could those with aspirations for the Way not admire such a person?
As for the names listed below, the first four chapters are general discourses on their virtuous conduct, and their specific identities remain unknown.
For what reason must their names be enumerated? Within this, there is first a general and concise explanation, followed by a detailed and specific exposition. The former consists of five parts:
(1) the enumeration, (2) the intent of establishing the names, (3) the evidence for the intent, (4) the explanation of the intent, and (5) the application of the meaning.

For now, we shall treat these as three: first, the general presentation of the enumerated categories; second, a general clarification of the method of interpretation; and third, the actual [explanation].
Regarding the initial explanation of the numerical meaning according to the text: "Twenty-one" refers to the number enumerated; "briefly" (*saṃkṣepataḥ*) is its meaning.
Since the ten thousand and two thousand [followers] mentioned above cannot be cited in full, only the twenty-one principal figures are cited.
This is the case in all sutras; therefore, the single word "briefly" indicates the number of those enumerated. Furthermore, this...
Although the number of the assembly of śrāvakas mentioned in the sūtras should naturally be the greatest, the fact that only twelve thousand are cited here serves to manifest those whose name,

virtue, fundamental and manifested traces, and depth and breadth are sublime and vast. Furthermore, the reason why only these twenty-one individuals are listed now is that they are the most exalted and eminent among them.
Regarding the disciples of the Buddha, what follows is the general method for providing explanations. This section has two parts: first, the general method for providing explanations;
second, the specific revelation of the number of this present sutra. Within the first part, there are three sub-sections:

first, clarifying the names and the source from which they are obtained; second, citing scriptural passages as evidence; and third, clarifying that once these numerical categories are obtained, there is nothing that cannot be explained. First:
It is clear that their names are all established based on their virtuous conduct (*śīla-guṇa*) and possess both square and circular aspects.

The "square" aspect refers to their own practice (*sva-caryā*), while the "circular" and complete aspect arises from the perspective of others. We know they are all complete because these praises are made in reference to their previous stations;

we know they are established based on virtuous conduct because, for instance, Kāśyapa was called "The One of Great Virtue" (*Mahākāśyapa*) and Ājñātakauṇḍinya was called "The One Who Knows the Unarisen" (*Anujñātakaunḍinya*).
Śāriputra’s practice manifests great wisdom, Maudgalyāyana displays great supernormal powers, Ānanda is renowned for his joy, and Rāhula is known for removing obstacles;
these names were all established based on their specific virtuous practices. We know they are "complete" because the preceding section praises them as such, indicating their fullness.
We know they are "partial" because, as cited in the sutras, each is said to be "foremost" in a particular field.

They are called "partial" because each represents a single virtuous practice that is collectively praised by the world; this is the meaning of the partiality of the hidden versus the manifest, and the partial versus the perfect.
Next, after citing the scriptural passage concerning the three types of people, the conclusion serves to establish that the preceding meaning of "proceeding from the partial" is clear.
As for the term "one dharma," it means that their respective virtuous practices are each a single dharma; "one" here refers to the partial. This exists within things themselves...
The essence is eternally perfect.
The preceding section clarifies the origin of its name; if one wishes to proceed below with the formal elucidation, having already known the name, one follows it to explain its meaning.
Since this is where they converge, it is said that there is nowhere it does not penetrate. Names are used to summon the essence, and characters [are used to]...

Virtue is manifested through titles to glorify one's meritorious deeds; yet, while names and titles may sometimes coincide and sometimes not, because these refer to sages, they are all mutually inclusive and are cited interchangeably.
The preceding section on clarifying the stages and offering praises is now complete; as for why this matter is clarified once again, is it not redundant?

However, since the general and the specific together constitute the entirety of *nirvāṇa*, how could such confusion arise? To provide fourfold explanations for each item is precisely what constitutes the correct elucidation.

This is the essential method for understanding the names of these various sages. The "fourfold explanation" refers to the four types of explanation, such as those based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The reason each name is explained through these four methods is precisely to demonstrate that while the names may be partial (*pian*), their meanings are complete (*yuan*).

Although the names themselves are partial, the virtuous conduct is always complete; if one does not provide the fourfold explanation, one cannot even manifest its completeness, let alone understand its profundity.
Since one must cause oneself to reflect upon the application and the reasons for it, one must necessarily rely on the four intentions.
If these intentions are attained, one will know that each and every name and meaning is itself the Dharma-realm; all without exception become perfectly marvelous and absolutely transcendent.
How much more so for the Śrāvakas, up to the most extreme variety of assemblies—all are exactly like this. That is to say, everything is thus.
All people shall become wondrous persons; once they have long attained mastery of themselves, they will likewise all immediately succeed. Contemplate this, contemplate it!

Thus, the sequence of the names [of the bodhisattvas] varies across the various sutras, and there are generally two types of ordering: first, according to the superiority or inferiority of their virtuous conduct.

This is as intended in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, where the Buddha dispatches [bodhisattvas] to inquire after his illness; they must possess wisdom, eloquence, and so forth, and thus they are ordered according to the superiority or inferiority of their virtuous conduct.

Regarding the second point, "clarifying the sequence": herein, these twenty-one individuals are all arranged in order according to the chronological sequence of their renunciation and attainment of the Way.
As stated in the *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings*: "First, he converted the five men," and so forth, as clarified below.
While ancient and modern commentators have collectively explained this meaning in such a manner, it may now also be further elucidated through another principle, namely:
The letter *A* is the root of all letters, all meanings, and all Dharma-gates;

it represents this Dharma-gate as descending from the fundamental to the phenomenal, proceeding from the real to the provisional, revealing the real by opening the provisional, manifesting the fundamental by disclosing the phenomenal, and returning all to the ultimate pinnacle of non-arising.
By diligently cultivating wondrous practice based upon this wondrous essence, one will attain wondrous wisdom, supernatural powers, and wondrous functions.
Up to the passage on "the vast learning, the dhāraṇī, and the unimpeded secret writing," it says: "Because ultimate nirvāṇa is the mark of eternal quiescence.
Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "I place all my children within the secret treasury. This is the essential core of this sūtra;
to manifest this meaning, the sequence is established in this manner. This is the most vital principle, which you should contemplate well. Furthermore, these various...
Among these, there are those with surnames and those with given names; some list both together, some state only the given name, and some take the surname itself as the name.
Some derive from the mundane, some from the supramundane, and some directly express transcendence through worldly terms.
As for the subsequent passages, their patterns can be understood through reflection rather than being fully detailed in words; reflect upon them again and again to further explain this.
Regarding the twenty-one names, with the exception of the three Kāśyapas who are combined into one, the others may also be arranged as two or one in the text according to individual preference;
there is certainly no fixed standard—consider this.
First, regarding "Cunda," it should be understood that this refers to both his personal name (*nāma*) and his clan name (*gotra*). The old translation states:
