"This name has a root and a branch; Cunda is its root-clan name, while 'A' is the name acquired after he attained the Way.
Now, it is said that this refers to both his name and clan, encompassing both the secular and the monastic, as well as the mundane and the supramundane. This is the opening of the commentary.
Within the section on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), there are four sections of commentary; while the phrasing appears simple, the underlying meaning is profound.

Those who do not study it merely understand it according to the four [sections], yet they never reach its essential point. Although they may have an understanding, it cannot be called true comprehension.

I now say that the first section provides a general explanation of the names, while the subsequent three provide specific explanations that clarify and establish one of the meanings within those names. If one directly grasps this intent, one will attain the essential point.

This has been understood. In the initial general explanation, there are two parts: first, the clan name (*gotra*), and second, the personal name (*nāman*). Now, the clan name is the original, while the personal name is acquired later.
Although in the sūtra the personal name is mentioned first and the clan name last, all ancient and modern commentators have placed the clan name first and the personal name last.

This is because the sūtra sometimes follows local dialectical usage, sometimes correctly highlights the excellence of his virtues, or sometimes employs the clan name for the sake of distinction; thus, the commentary further explains the clan name.
This follows the local dialect and further clarifies the sequence in which he attained [the title]. In the initial explanation of his clan name (*gotra*), there are five phrases;
first, regarding the indication of his clan name, the world explains it thus: "Clan" (*xing*) means birth; it is that from which a person is born.

In antiquity, there was a divine and sagely mother who conceived a son through a response to Heaven; therefore, he was called the Son of Heaven (*tianzi*). Based on this birth, [the title] was established as...
Regarding the surname: surnames and given names originate from women; since "birth" (*sheng*) is also a phonetic element, this is a "form-and-sound" character.

Next, the term translated as "fire-vessel" refers to the implements used for seeking the Way; its meaning is evident in the subsequent [explanation], as ancient scholars have likewise provided this interpretation.

Next, clarifying the clan lineage serves to manifest that its lineage is most supreme and excellent. In the Western Regions, surnames are generally noble, and there are four such types as follows: [text continues].

It is always known that among these, the practice of purity ranks first; thus they reckon that [the fire-ritualists] were born from the mouth of Brahmā, while the other three [classes] gradually became inferior.
Now, to clarify their preeminence, it is said: "This lineage is complete," as explained in the *Xiyu zhuan* (Records of the Western Regions).
Regarding the interpretation of the "fire-vessel" below: "The former" refers to his remote ancestor of a previous generation. "Practicing fire to seek the Way" means serving the Fire-God (*Agni*).
The deities burn various objects as offerings in order to seek the Way; such practices abound within the *dhāraṇī* gates of the Buddhist tradition.
However, these are entirely contrary to their own fundamental tenets: what they regard as the "Right Path" is here considered "auxiliary to the Path.
What they offer to gods and spirits, we here offer to the various Bodhisattvas and those manifested in provisional forms.
The *Śrīmad-bhāgavata* states: "All dharmas are either false or all dharmas are true"—this is precisely what is meant here.

One should understand that the first four phrases [of the verse] employ surnames to distinguish names; "fire-worship" distinguishes those who do not serve other deities; "pure conduct" distinguishes them from the other three *varṇas*;
and "their ancestors" distinguishes those who are not of their own [immediate] lineage. Reflect on this, and below I shall further explain the meaning by summarizing what they represent.
Since his virtuous conduct was so lofty, the reason he was entrusted with this seed to be born therein was precisely to manifest something significant;
that is, by relying on the secular world to manifest his supramundane virtue and wisdom. First, it clarifies that the fire of the mundane world has its traces:
when it acts, it can dispel darkness, and when it burns, it can consume material objects. This serves to symbolize that the fire of supramundane wisdom can eliminate birth.
Death is the result, and cause and effect are two distinct entities. "Obscurity" does not mean the absence of cause, nor does "entity" mean the absence of result.
"Absence of cause" refers to the prior exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*); "absence of result" refers to the prior exhaustion of all modes of existence (*bhava*).

Furthermore, because the worldly lineage is used to represent the supramundane lineage, one is born by relying upon this clan; thus it says, "This, etc. However, within the Secret Essential Gate, fire...
Because the Dharma is the most swift, the five [stages]—such as quelling afflictions and increasing the Path—are all brought to their efficacy with the speed of the number of fires.
It is precisely by the power of the fire of wisdom that birth-and-death is first eliminated and non-arising is realized; thus it is represented in this way.

Such an interpretation is profound, and only through exhaustive inquiry can its meaning be fully exhausted. It is also like the subsequent sense of "covering and obstructing," which may be described as mysterious.

There is nothing that he does not penetrate; yet as for why this is so, if we discuss it according to reality, it is because his father accumulated the path and established great vows, which reached the Tathāgata in the unseen realm, and his own virtuous deeds moved the holy spirits to provide swift protection, thereby bringing it about.

However, if we discuss it according to its outward manifestations, it is certainly appropriate, and there is no need for further words, whether from the perspective of skillful means or ultimate reality.
The meanings herein do not differ; they are all comprehensively reconciled without any contradiction.

Next follows the explanation of its name. Within this, many phrases first state the name, then provide a phonetic transcription, and thirdly clarify that the explanations in the sacred teachings vary.
Below that, the four sections clarify that it is named "Ekottara" (*Zengyi*) according to the majority of cases. The final five sections cite scriptural evidence and provide a conclusion. First:
The indication of the name of the direction corresponds to the preceding surname; for while the surname is general, the name is specific and restricted to the individual self.
"To translate" means to render it according to the local dialect, and thus it must be translated so that its meaning may be manifest in the subsequent words.

As for the absence of the term "ignorance," this is because the letter *A* exists as its condition. Furthermore, since such phrasing might be misconstrued as an erroneous interpretation, it is necessary to clarify and distinguish it. Moreover—
The reason for using [the term "limit"] is to manifest that the capacity [to transcend] is not non-existent; it is not called "non-existence" because the designation is derived from that capacity.
Below, two sūtras and one śāstra are cited to demonstrate that while the translated names differ, their underlying meaning is not distinct.

"Original limit" (benji) refers to the aforementioned "truth" (*tattva*) and subsequent "cessation" (*nirodha*). Below, it is again based on what is manifested by the capacity: that which is known is the object, which is the truth (*satya*).

As for the object (*viṣaya*), if it were not the principle of cessation (*nirodha-tattva*), it could not be considered non-existent; this cessation is precisely the aforementioned Reality (*bhūtatathatā*) and the Ultimate Limit (*koṭi*).
The following clarifies that various sutras are mostly identical to what precedes, because they primarily take the letter *A* as their object; they are mostly identical for this reason.

It is called "the attainment of the Way" because it is attained for the first time; thus, in the past, it was also translated as "Initial Wisdom" (*ādi-jñāna*), precisely because [it occurs] at this point below.
The "citing of evidence" refers to the evidence-bearer’s verification and exposition of the various meanings previously stated; it is also a general praise of his virtuous conduct.
The text consists of three phrases, praising his three kinds of virtues: namely, great compassion, great wisdom, and [the realization of] the path of non-arising.
The sequence of the text makes these clear as being, respectively, knowledge (*jñāna*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and their underlying principle (*tattva*). He is endowed with these.

Because it is not the case that the three virtues (triguṇa) lack any virtue, it is given this name; yet when the stage of "opening and revealing" (kaixian) is reached, it becomes the Great Nirvana of the Three Virtues.
This is set forth in advance to serve as the foundation for what follows. Regarding the previous explanation, all traditions from antiquity have been the same;
however, a recent interpretation states: in Sanskrit, it is *Ajñāta-kauṇḍinya*. *Kauṇḍinya* is a Brahmin clan name, and *nya* is a masculine suffix.

Ājñāta means "one who has understood the meaning," as he was the first to attain realization. Since the clan name Kauṇḍinya comprised many members, he was designated by this title to distinguish him from others.
To differentiate him from females, the masculine suffix *na* was added, hence the term *nā*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refers to him as "Ajñākauṇḍinya.
It is said that this arose because the sounds *ā* and *a* were similar.

The general explanation of the meaning of "name" (*nāman*) and "surname" (*gotra*) above is now complete. From here on, the text provides a specific, detailed explanation regarding three matters to further establish the meaning of the aforementioned names.
As for what is meant by "specific": whereas previously there were both name and surname, here we only explain the meaning of the name; thus it is "specific.

Furthermore, while in the previous section on "name" it was spoken of generally as "ignorance at first birth," here there are additionally these three matters, and for this reason it is called "specific. Moreover, as explained previously...
It may be asked: since they have attained the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), this is used as their name;

yet one might doubt this, thinking that as in the previous stage it was praised that all noble ones (*ārya*) attain non-arising, how could he alone receive this name? To address this, the proof already provides a brief explanation:
because he is the first to attain it, other sources refer to it as "initial knowledge" (*prathama-jñāna*); therefore, he alone receives this name, while others do not.
It is not so because it was not the first; furthermore, a doubt arises as to why that person alone obtained this at the very beginning.
Below, this doubt is resolved by separately examining three matters, which serve to clarify and establish the preceding point.

These three matters consist of his prior vow (*pūrva-praṇidhāna*), prior practice (*pūrva-caryā*), and prior realization (*pūrva-siddhi*). It is on account of these three matters that he attained it first. First, the vow is explained.
The *Caiguojing* (Sūtra on Cause and Effect) further explains that there are two reasons for this: first, because [the Buddha] was a bodhisattva at that time;
second, because that person made a vow of their own accord. For these reasons, he first attained the old understanding.
There is a citation from Paramārtha’s commentary which states: "In the past, Cunda had six brothers; five were the five bhikṣus, and the sixth was Subhadra. In their former household..."

Being poor, they engaged in agriculture together. At that time, coinciding with the appearance of a Buddha in the world, when it was time to sow grain, the five of them took up seed-grain and together pounded it to prepare food to offer to the Buddha, making this vow:
"In a future life, may we encounter a Buddha and be the first to attain the Holy Path; may we be the first to leave the household life.
When the grain ripened and its juice was like milk, they again pressed it to extract the juice, boiled it into a gruel, and offered it to the Buddha, again making this vow.
He made this vow: "When the first grain ripens, I shall prepare food beforehand to offer to the Buddha. Subhadra also made this vow:

"I shall prepare it only after [the others] have ripened, to offer to the Buddha; may I encounter the Buddha in a future life as the very last to attain the Holy Path, and may I be called the 'last to leave the home-life.
May the Buddha deliver me and immediately enter parinirvāṇa. For this reason, when Śākyamuni appeared in the world, these five were the first.
After obtaining [enlightenment], Subhadra was attained; subsequently, among the five men, Cunda was attained first, followed by the other four.
Therefore, Cunda alone is named Ajñāta. This, moreover, is a distinct and most excellent vow, and thus it is recounted.
Next, the practice is elucidated. Regarding "first among the first," the previous vow clarified the capacity to continue past wholesome roots;

this practice clarifies the capacity to manifest the extinction of all evils. Within this, first both the essence and the function of the practice are indicated together; next, they are explained individually.

In the explanation, there is first wisdom and then abandonment, each with a simile, its application, and a conclusion. Regarding the first of these, the initial phrase serves as a general simile for the absence of all wisdom.
Because it clarifies the dark and obscure places of birth and death, it is called "night. Because it comprises the three realms and the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), it is called "great.

Because beings have rested therein since beginningless time, it is said they are "long asleep" within it. Since there has been no one with the light of primordial wisdom to illuminate it, no one is able to awaken;
thus, the metaphor of the sun not yet having risen represents those among the various sages of the Three Vehicles who have not yet attained enlightenment within this single transformation.

The "Morning Star" (Mingxing) refers to the star Venus (Jiqiming), which rises before the sun and subsequently merges with it; here, it signifies that the Morning Star appears first among all luminaries.

The "assembly of those with illumination" (zhongming) refers to the assembly of those who have attained realization through the Three Vehicles. The "illumination of the wisdom of all people" refers to this aforementioned assembly of luminaries.

Regarding the lower [explanation], the commentary states that in severing conduct and destroying darkness, none precedes the Morning Star; by analogy, in extinguishing and eliminating delusive ignorance, none precedes Kauṇḍinya.
Because he was the very first to be able to illuminate and to shatter [ignorance], he alone receives this name.
Next, it clarifies that this person was the very first to realize the Way, and thus obtained this name. Within this, there is further an explanation to resolve two doubts:
first, as previously vowed, all five wished to attain realization first; since they all attained it first, why is it said that this person alone attained it first?
If one considers the transformation of one person, all five are attained simultaneously as the first;

yet among those five, there is also a "first" because both [the first and the subsequent] are considered the beginning in relation to two different perspectives. Second, this clarifies by whom this was originally established at the very beginning.
This meaning is fully explained within the text; therefore, this passage serves to explain both of these meanings simultaneously. This text is somewhat...
The long summary consists of four points: first, it clarifies that when the Prince abandoned his position to practice the Way, five men followed and attended him;

second, it clarifies that because the Prince attained the Way, he was the first to deliver them; third, it offers three praises stating that in all matters he was supreme and foremost; fourth, it cites evidence to conclude that he alone receives this title.
The first point explains the reason for his being the first to deliver others, as they were the ones who first served and attended him; the second is the formal clarification of this matter.

First, the characteristics of those to be delivered; second, the three points of extensive praise; third, the reliance on the words of the Sage to definitively establish that it is so. Within the first [section], there are five sentences:

first, the designation of the number of persons to be sent away; second, the enumeration of their five names; third, the identification of these individuals as belonging to the two types of lineages, internal and external;
fourth, the clarification that the natures and conducts of these two classes differ; and fifth, the clarification that the conduct they serve is contrary [to the Dharma].
Because of what they cherished, they all abandoned [their former lives] and departed. As for the initial mention of "renouncing the kingdom to study the Way" and so forth:

the causes and conditions for studying the Way, as well as the specific characteristics and manifestations of the actual practice of that study, are as extensively explained in such works as the *Śrī-mālā-devī-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (or *Prasannārtha-sūtra*). These can be understood through reflection;

since they are not essential to the present context, there is no need for further elaboration. The five names listed above may be understood as being summarized into two categories according to various explanations.
A different master says that the three [ancestors] on the father’s side are Aśvajit, Maṇibhadra, and Kauṇḍinya, while the other two are from the mother’s side.
For now, we shall follow the sequence of the commentary: the first two correspond to the first two listed above, and the third corresponds to the third name listed below.
Since this is the established order, we shall rely upon it, provided it accords with what is found in the *Buddhavaṃsa*. Let us verify this.
This is so; Rāmaṇa was the elder brother of Aniruddha, the eldest son of King Amṛta.

Regarding the difference between the two types of conduct—namely, the conduct of views (*dṛṣṭi-carita*) and the conduct of craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*)—these are the afflictions to be remedied by the paths of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and they correspond respectively to the paths of Māra and the heterodox (*bāhya*).
Since the Prince [Śākyamuni] was intended to counteract the former rather than manifest the latter, he abandoned them in their respective order.

Since both [extremes] deviate from their respective inclinations, they are both abandoned; as the Sūtra says, "There are two kinds of practice: namely, the suffering of the five desires and asceticism.
To depart from these two extremes is called the Middle Way—this is precisely the proof.

The following is the explicit clarification of the characteristics of those whom he first delivers; "attaining the Way" refers to attaining the Way of the Four Noble Truths—namely, departing from Suffering and Accumulation and realizing Cessation, as previously analyzed regarding the meaning of the character for "Buddha" (*buddha*) within the context of the teachings. As the Sūtra says:

"In the past, at Vārāṇasī, he turned the Wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths," which refers precisely to the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing. Regarding the two types of persons in the Initial Teaching:
Because there were three who begged for alms, he next instructed three others in the same manner. Thus, in the morning six people ate together, while in the evening there were only five;
this was because the rule against eating at improper times (*vikālabhojana*) had been established from the beginning, as all Buddhas by nature abstain from eating at improper times.

The reason begging for alms is divided into two parts is that there are two classes of people: one to demonstrate that the task has already been accomplished, and the other to demonstrate the teaching of the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "because it is not in vain," the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (Póshā) states that this period is either three months or four months; indeed, it cannot be fixed definitively.

The "five people" and "eighty thousand" collectively refer to those who received the teachings and attained benefit. The following two sections specifically clarify the path through which benefit was attained, namely the fruits of the beginning and the end.
However, the words of Yuan [Daoxuan] indicate that the "manifest" refers to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), while the "esoteric" refers to the final fruit.
The teaching is that they abide in the stages (*bhūmi*); for now, this is merely being made manifest. Regarding the statement "the three have replied, 'We already know,'" Dinglin says:
"The five persons [know] by means of knowing; they realize the principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). The Earth Deities and others know that [the five] have already realized it.
This interpretation completely misses its fundamental tenet, as this passage explains the reason why [the deities] spoke with such inconceivable words. However, this section of the commentary also...
It appears somewhat obscure, causing commentators to fail in their understanding; for this section specifically clarifies the origin of Ājñātakauṇḍinya’s name and his initial attainment.
According to the commentary and the preceding explanation, those of the fifth and eighth classes are all named "Ājñāta" (One-Who-Knows);
why then is it applied to Kauṇḍinya alone? Now, I say that while the syntactic flow of the text is general, the intended meaning is specific. Why? Because it applies generally to the beginning.

If, later on, one were to pose a question regarding the beginning of the first eon, it would be entirely appropriate for Cunda—who had already realized the first fruit—to answer that he "already knows.
However, if the question were posed from the perspective of the third [fruit] or thereafter, then Cunda alone would be the respondent, and this would have no bearing on the others;
since these two cases both pertain specifically to Cunda, he alone receives this title. Therefore, others [do not].

In the section on "The Person" (*pudgala*), the commentary states: When the Buddha first turned the Wheel of Dharma, among the five disciples he questioned as to whether they had understood, Cunda was the first to report, "I have now understood.
The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens also declared that they had understood; for this reason, he was named "Understanding" (*Ajñāta*).
This explanation applies to both meanings [of the name]. Both of the aforementioned meanings are applicable here, and the text of the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) also supports this.

It would not be otherwise; there is nothing to which one can become attached. When one contemplates what is spoken of as "knowing," this is precisely the realization of the name of the True Way, which is not like what is commonly spoken of.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "At the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), having known. The recent translation renders this as "already understood" (*jiejie*).
"Understanding" (*jie*) has the same meaning as "knowing" (*zhi*); it is not a different term. Furthermore, it is called "realization" (*liǎo*), yet it is no different from the former.

Because there is this exchange of questions and answers transmitted by those who chant [the teachings], it clarifies that the Way can be attained; it is not in vain, for it possesses great benefit in inspiring study.

The intention of what follows is this: although it was previously stated that [the truth] is already known, the words were general and the meaning implicit, so its specific characteristics had not yet been revealed.

Therefore, from here on, [the text] extensively traverses various objects of perception to manifest that which is already known; that is, it extensively explains the reasons why [this knowledge exists].
This is because it manifests capability. Regarding the phrase "the initial vision of the path and its characteristics," it was previously stated that the initial vision occurred in Cunda;
for later people, this serves as a precursor. Furthermore, it was said that the Buddha is like the mechanism of a drum, conditions are like the mallet, and the Wheel of Dharma is like the sound;

all five people were at the beginning, yet Cunda was the first to awaken, which is why it is called "initially hearing the fragrance" in the *Dharmapada* (Verses on the Path). In the past, the mechanism was like the body and the Wheel of Dharma was like the fragrance.

The first "transcendence" is named "drinking the nectar," which refers to the stream of the Dharma of the principle of cessation; it is the realization of the first fruit, wherein one directly perceives the Truth (*satyadarśana*).
Now, examining this specific explanation, it does not entirely accord with the original text. Why is this? Because these six phrases here expand upon the previous meaning.

Previously, it was simply stated that "already known" pertains to the sense of the mind; although this generally encompasses the whole, it is difficult to comprehend. Now, by unfolding it through these six meanings, they are all fully clarified.
"Containing both the subject and object" refers to the six sense organs confronting the six sense objects. "Manifesting the benefits obtained" means that all [benefits] are prior to all [conditions].
The first two lines concern the internal and external as subject and object; "object" refers to the Buddha’s form and voice, while "subject" refers to the eyes and ears of Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
The four lines of the following text directly address the aforementioned subjects to discuss subject and object, which is based on the preceding vision.

Regarding the meaning of "hearing, possessing, practicing, and realizing," these correspond to the objects of the four faculties (*indriya*); this meaning is clear in the text. Having grasped this intent, even if the literal phrasing were not fully resolved, it would already suffice.
"Seeing" refers to the capacity to see; "the marks of the Buddha-way" refers to that which is seen. From here on, one should understand by analogy:
it means that upon first seeing the physical appearance and deportment of the Buddha, one recognizes these as the signs and characteristics of having attained the Way. If one says [this is] too...
As for the son’s transgression against the letter, although the term “five people” is generally applicable, there are differences in what those of the sharpest faculties perceive;
because the general is subsumed under the particular, it belongs to that first stage. The Dharma-drum refers to the sound of the Four Truths of arising and ceasing heard at the very beginning;

although it generally applies to two types of persons, since one of them does not yet awaken, the general is again subsumed under the particular, and thus it belongs to that individual. Fragrance refers to the essence of the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*), which is pure.

Because it is pure and can also distance one from the foul stench of afflictions, it is called "fragrance" (*gandha*); this refers to the initial realization of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

Since this object is apprehended by the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*), it corresponds to the objective sphere of the nose. Because the principle of extinction (*nirvāṇa*) is like nectar (*amṛta*) and because that principle of extinction is eternal, it is used as a metaphor;

since tasting sweetness allows one to know flavor, this carries the sense of the tongue (*jihvā*). It may also be correlated with the aforementioned abandonment, representing the extinction manifested through realization (*pratisaṃvid-nirvāṇa*).
"Principle" (*li*) refers to the stream of the Dharma; "stream" (*liu*) has two meanings: the sense of "category" (*lei*) and the sense of "conformity" (*shun*).

Entering the category of the noble ones (*ārya*), one proceeds according to the Path, which also clearly establishes the meaning of the "fragrance of the superior Path. This is now called the initial stage of entry, which is the stage of wisdom (*jñāna*).

Since one has entered and dwelt within the sphere of the noble ones, it naturally accords with the meaning of the "body" (*kāya*); the True Truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is thus the principle of cessation (*nirodha*), which is once again manifested as the superior state above.
"Amṛta" (Ganlu) signifies the meaning of "attaining realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*), which is itself the meaning of "directly encountering the mind.

Furthermore, since the former two [the path and its fruit] consist of wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), this [nirvāṇa] is the principle of cessation within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). One should know that these four meanings apply throughout both the beginning and the end, for they are present at the outset during all three stages.
Reflect on this, reflect on it again; one should know that these four are the dharmas pertaining to the stages of wisdom and abandonment. Reflect on this; one should know.
The fact that the four who followed Śāriputra all attained realization is due to their having previously heard the drum of the Dharma;

thus, the latter four all attained it by means of the former two. This clearly demonstrates that the initial benefit of receiving the Buddha’s form and voice is the foremost among the three categories of those who attain the Way, which is why he alone receives this name.
Furthermore, these three categories are those among the three happy realms who most frequently attain the Way.
Below is the fourth [section], which cites evidence; while various editions all use the character "yóuyóu" (遊行), this manuscript uses "yóuyóu" (由行).
It is unknown which is correct, but from the perspective of the meaning, it may well be the character "yóu" (由), referring to the *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*. However—

It should be understood that there is no need for amendment. Furthermore, while various traditions state that five people were ordained in the second year, all extant versions of this text read "the first.

I have not yet had the leisure to examine the cited evidence, but it contains two meanings: first, it specifically takes the initial section as proof that although Cundin (Ajñāta-kauṇḍinya) was among the five, he was explicitly mentioned as being at their head.
Thus, even though the text generally speaks of "five people," it specifically singles out Cundin as occupying the foremost position.
Furthermore, these two [points] also comprehensively take up the sequence of the three sections to establish the reason for the order in which the names are listed herein.
That the names of Cunda and the others are listed first is precisely due to this; therefore, it concludes with "It should be known," etc.
This means that both the meaning of the names and the significance of listing them first must come first; it is precisely because of this that one attains this.
The name is again listed at the very beginning. Regarding the phrase "these causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*), this is a summary of the four preceding meanings;
it is an explanation based on causes and conditions. First, the name is generally considered as a worldly phenomenon (*laukika-dharma*);
such a name exists in accordance with the world, for it is not the supramundane ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The following three [sections] provide specific explanations of its names.

In this matter, because it causes the arising of past wholesome roots, it is "cause" (*hetu*); because it enables a person to practice and thereby extinguish present evils, it is "condition" (*pratyaya*);

because it serves as the prior realization of the principle of cessation (*nirodha*), it is "reason" (*yukti*); and because it encompasses these four aspects, it is "basis" (*āśraya*). Thus, the reasons for manifesting his name have been stated;
however, the meaning of its specific application has not yet been discussed. It is called "cause" because it is named in contrast to the latter three [conditions].

This is the commentary on the "Conditions" (Pratyaya). Below, regarding the classification of teachings, the differences and convergences in the meaning of "non-arising" (anutpāda) are distinguished from the preceding general discussion in order to reveal the meaning of the causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya) of this sutra.
Within this section, the sequence and structure differ slightly from the usual; all state that [the truth] is revealed by means of relying upon contemplation (vipaśyanā).
The current teaching is precisely intended to manifest the doctrine by means of its practice;

for the doctrine is that which is expressed and practice is that by which it is expressed, and since the dharma-gate of non-arising is the essential core of these, it is manifested through practice at the end. Since all other gates can be understood by this same principle, it is specifically discussed here.
Furthermore, the primary intent is that while the sutra clarifies how [the Buddha] receives his name from the fruit, the present [treatise] seeks to reveal [this].
The "non-arising cause" clarifies the cause by means of the fruit and reveals the fruit by means of the cause, because both cause and fruit are non-arising;

this is because, in the subsequent [section], they are opened up and unified as the wondrous identity of non-arising cause and fruit. However, the teachings differ in being either horizontal or vertical;
here, we only discuss them horizontally according to the fourfold clarity, whereas the subsequent discussion of "original and trace" is discussed vertically according to the five periods.

These are presented interchangeably according to the convenience of their respective meanings. There are four distinct aspects to the explanation of these four marks (*lakṣaṇa*); within the first section on the "Treasury" (*kośa*), there are further three parts:

the heading, the arousal, the explanation, and the conclusion. The first two meanings can be understood as they stand. Regarding the "investigation" (*vicāra*) section, all refer to the object and contemplation;

now, for the sake of distinction, the general framework of the practice (*pratipatti-dharma*) is established. From the section "Opening" (*apara*) onwards, the specific characteristics of the practice are clarified.
Regarding the terms "general" and "specific": they are so named because practice (*caryā*) is distinguished by its mutual relationship with phenomena (*dharma*).
"Phenomena" refers to the objective domain of wisdom (*jñāna*), which serves as the basis for cultivation. "General" refers to the universal statement that all things are unarisen (*anutpāda*);

"specific" refers to the distinct aspects of practice as one proceeds through each of the three categories (*triskandha*) individually, and thus they are called "specific. Herein, both the doctrinal expositions and the analogies briefly summarize the contents of the Tripiṭaka.

Regarding the textual and doctrinal meanings within the teachings of the Four Āgamas, it is sufficient to explain them by relying solely on the text itself; there is no need for further extensive citation of the original passages, which would result in prolixity.

As for the examples established at the beginning, they are appropriate [for the context] (and so forth). At the outset, when the Dharma and the analogy are explained together, there are generally four meanings:
the analogy refers to spectacles and reflected images; the Dharma refers to the objects of wisdom, as well as cause and effect. This is the opening [of the section].
Regarding conceptualization, there is the arising of cause and effect; regarding cessation, there is neither opposition nor conceptualization, and thus no arising of cause and effect.

By means of this opposition, the meaning of "non-existence" is clearly revealed; therefore, it is raised as a metaphor. One should understand that cause and effect are phenomena that are produced, whereas if they are opposed by non-arising, they are phenomena that do not exist.
This must be carefully considered. Why is it that one does not speak directly of the "eye," but instead speaks of [the eye] in another way?
The "blind and blind" metaphor clarifies the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Why is the mirror used as a metaphor?

Because it is perfectly capable of manifesting images, and these images are what is observed. The inclusion of the three categories (*triskandha*) within all phenomena means that they are collectively the objects of observation;

this universally reveals all objective realms—that is, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-fields (*āyatana*) of the six destinies. These are precisely the objective realms. Whether one observes through the partial or the perfect [teachings], the objects of observation do not transcend these.

This is currently situated within the initial teaching—what was formerly called the "aggregates" (*skandha*) and "bases" (*āyatana*), and newly termed the "heaps" (*khandha*) and "spheres" (*āyatana*) [and so forth].

The body, head, four limbs, and six parts constitute the manifesting essence; therefore, they are used as a metaphor for the present cause. The distinct manifestation of the master of karma is like the image in a mirror—sixfold, empty, and unreal.
Since the retribution still exists in the future, it is used as a metaphor for the arising of the fruit. As for "arising,"...
They do not arise nor do they emerge simultaneously; this is merely due to the sequence of opening and closing, as the text itself clearly reveals.

What follows below specifically clarifies the modes of activity (*ākāra*), which is divided into two parts: first, a brief indication based on a simile; second, a detailed explanation based on the sūtra.

Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the exclusion of what is incorrect; second, the revelation of what is correct. Both passages employ similes to manifest the Dharma. Herein, five points serve as metaphors for delusion.
The mind discriminates and grasps objects, creating karma that serves as the cause and brings about its fruit;

all this arises from ignorance (*avidyā*), which fails to understand the continuity of the causes and effects of birth and death, thereby preventing the realization of non-arising. Next, it is shown that within this there is nothing seen—namely, the two matters below, which are the mind and its objects.
Because one does not see these, one attains the non-arising of cause and effect. Not seeing the six parts is the capacity for this.

When illumination does not perceive the mirror, it is because there is nothing with which to confront it; this is precisely because one does not grasp at sense organs (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) to create karma.
Because the cause does not arise, the effect does not arise. For this reason, "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) is termed "unborn" (*ajāta*).

What follows is a detailed explanation: whereas previously only the direct indication was given, here the characteristics are extensively clarified according to that sutra, fully categorized into three [aspects].
The sections are again condensed into two: first, based on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); second, based on the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*).

Regarding the first [section], it is explained by means of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) to clarify the practice of non-arising causes; this is precisely the core doctrine of the Hīnayāna. Within this, there are further two parts: first, distinguishing what is not [the correct method];

next, employing the fivefold contemplation to correctly manifest what is. Regarding the first of these, there are three parts: namely, the teaching (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the synthesis (*yoga*). First...
In the middle [section], it is shown that by giving rise to the four inversions based on the five aggregates, there is indeed arising and not non-arising.

It is also said that the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) consists of four modes: contemplating the object collectively while the contemplation is specific; contemplating the object specifically while the contemplation is collective; contemplating both collectively and specifically; and contemplating both collectively and specifically.
The first mode refers to collectively contemplating the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena as impermanent, or collectively as suffering, up to impurity, employing any one of these contemplations.
First, one contemplates the four objects, wherein the objects follow the contemplations; because the four are combined into one, the objects are termed "comprehensive" (*sāmānya*).

Second, it means that the comprehensive application of the four contemplations follows the contemplation of each individual object; because the objects are correlated with the contemplations, the contemplations are termed "comprehensive.

Third, at a single moment, one comprehensively uses the four contemplations to universally contemplate the four objects. Fourth, the objects and the contemplations correspond; since the contemplation already knows this to be so...

The same principle applies here. Now, it is said that this meaning is explained extensively in the Great Master’s *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* (*Catuḥsmṛtyupasthāna*), which one should consult; however, I have not yet had the leisure to do so.
For now, it is said that there is no error in following the sequence of this very text directly. It need not be restricted to a fixed pattern.

The text briefly explains the arising of the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*) based on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and thus there are four distinct categories. Within each of these, one first cites a single [aggregate] as a representative.
First, regarding the remaining three [aggregates], one calculates them as being as pure as the form-aggregate; thus, all four are calculated as pure. Next, one calculates feeling as pleasure;

thus, all four are calculated as pleasure. Next, one calculates perception and formations as self; thus, all four are calculated as self. Finally, one calculates consciousness as permanent; thus, all four are calculated as permanent.
These four modes of calculation across the four aggregates all deviate from the true principle; therefore, they are called the "four perversions" (*catur-viparyāsa*).

Therefore, because there is indeed the fruit of karma, all things are within birth and death and are not non-existent. As for the next analogy, the metaphor of holding a mirror represents the inversion;

the metaphor of seeing one's face while performing an action represents the arising of cause and effect. There are five aggregates involved in holding the mirror, and it should be understood that all these constitute the seeing of the face.
Next, the text correctly reveals this very point, which means overturning the aforementioned inversion to manifest correct practice.

Within this, there are also three parts: namely, the Dharma-exposition (dharmanirdeśa), the Simile (aupamya), and the Conclusion (nigamana). Regarding these two [the first two], there is first the explicit clarification of the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) from the words "Since one knows...

onwards; second, the clarification of its function (vṛtti). Within the first of these, there are three sentences. First, the initial sentence is specific, while the subsequent sentence is general. Now, regarding the specific [first] sentence:

although the wording is brief, one should understand that it fully reverses the four types of perversion (viparyāsa) mentioned previously to manifest what is correct. As for the text of the subsequent sentence...
Regarding the statement "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) in the middle [of the passage], it was previously said that one should know that the word "selflessness" (*anātman*) is missing from the text;

however, I now maintain that it is not merely a matter of these two characters being missing, but rather that the character for "emptiness" is superfluous. Why? Because in other texts, the meanings of the two terms are distinguished:
in the "Five-Gate Contemplation," both emptiness and selflessness appear, whereas in the "Four Foundations of Mindfulness Contemplation," there is only selflessness.
Regarding the statement "emptiness": this current phrase may have resulted from a scribal error during transcription, leading to a general explanation that emptiness is identical to non-self.
The final sentence cites an analogy to clarify this point. Because correct contemplation is itself correct, there is no cause or effect;
therefore, it is not "arising. This follows from the knowledge already established; as for the subsequent text, it first explains the accomplishment of contemplation and the destruction of delusions.

The *Mingzhun* [commentary] explains that while the first section clarifies the accomplishment of contemplation and its freedom from faults, and the next clarifies the functional power of employing contemplation, this section as a whole constitutes the second part, which correctly reveals the function of the Middle Way. Within this, there are four points:
first, a brief clarification of the ability to shatter all views; second, a comprehensive clarification of the ability to shatter all causes, effects, and phenomena of arising.
All are entirely non-arising; the three "raisings" (uddhāra) are non-arising, which serves as an analogy to apply to the fourth [point].

This concludes the demonstration of the characteristics of the non-arising of these aggregates. As for the various views, there are twenty types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity). Since all five aggregates are each associated with four [aspects], they constitute twenty types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*.

These constitute the root of all views; when the root is destroyed, the branches collapse. Therefore, all views are demolished. Not only are all views [demolished] through this contemplation— *Note: The original text contains a structural outline (1. Introduction, 2. Detailed Explanation, 3. Conclusion) and specific technical categories (the three uddhāras, the twenty satkāyadṛṣṭis). The translation above reflects these elements directly.*
If one can awaken to the ultimate path within this very life, then both the sharp and the dull faculties are entirely transcended;

because all things are non-arising, one cannot be restricted to the view of cause and effect. Next, regarding the analogy of the "unborn" (*anutpāda*): having realized that path, one does not falsely cling to or create karma;
thus, there is no connection between the causes and effects of birth and death. Such practice is itself the realization of the aggregates (*skandhas*).
Within the objective realm (*viṣaya*), one attains the practice of non-arising (*anutpāda-gati*).
The following is the second section, which clarifies the dharma-gate of the practice of non-arising by means of two categories: the sense bases (*āyatana*) and the elements (*dhātu*).

Because there are differences in the ways of awakening through these three categories, it was necessary to explain them further. However, for the sake of convenience in accordance with their meaning and to avoid prolixity, they are stated together here. Nevertheless—

The previous section discussed the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) by way of the aggregates (*skandha*); now, this section discusses them by way of the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*). These are merely presented alternately as causes and conditions.
Furthermore, in the initial teachings, practice is mostly clarified through the truths (*satya*) and conditions (*pratyaya*). The previous section treated the arising of cause and effect;

"non-arising" refers to the contemplation of the Four Truths, while "arising" refers to suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), and "non-arising" refers to the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*). This was still a horizontal, general treatment. Now, we treat it vertically by way of the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions.

Because it is the most essential and complete among the practices regarding the causes and effects of the three periods of time, the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) is elucidated by means of this [text].

Within this, there are two parts: first, the exclusion of what is incorrect; second, the revelation of what is correct. Regarding the first, there are three sections: first, an analysis of the sense-bases (*āyatana*); second, an extension of this to reveal the elements (*dhātu*);

third, a dual conclusion that demonstrates the non-arising of both types of error. Regarding the first section on the sense-bases, there are two further parts: first, an analysis of the two bases of the eye and visible form.

Next, the remaining ten *āyatanas* are illustrated by way of analogy. This section has three parts. First, it is stated that the great ocean of the world is not considered deep or vast when seen with the eye;
next, it clarifies that the two *āyatanas* of the eye and form can bring about the endless cycle of cause and effect across the three periods of time, which is termed "seen by the eye";
finally, it concludes that this [cycle] is the most profound and vast. The first part is easily understood; from here on, the main point is clarified.

"Profound and vast" clarifies the meaning of being able to give rise to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). Although the text contains many phrases, the essential meaning is simply these twelve.
Why is this so? The first two [links] belong to the past; the next eight belong to the present; and the final two belong to the future.

Now, within the commentary (*śāstra*), it should be understood that there are three [factors] in the past and six in the future; furthermore, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is still ignorance (*avidyā*), and karma (*karma*) is still volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, these three names are merely the past [forms] of two meanings; the eight types of names and meanings in between are identical to those of the future members.

The remaining [members], namely birth (*jāti*) and old age (*jarā*), belong exclusively to birth; the other three are common to both old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Thus, one should know that although there are six meanings, they are in fact only two.
Depending on the text and depending on the meaning, there are many phrases. The initial explanation of ignorance (*avidyā*) simultaneously explains formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
The reason why karmic activities arise is precisely because of ignorance (*avidyā*), which lacks clear understanding. The first phrase refers specifically to this ignorance;

because one cannot comprehend the faults and perils of form (*rūpa*), one greedily delights in creating karma. Since karma results in the bitter fruits of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is described as a "great ocean.
This passage from the *Āgama* explains that one sinks into the three miserable destinies (*durgati*), thereby establishing the aforementioned meaning. This clarifies [the nature of] non-existence.
This is because clarity (vidyā) is endowed with all manner of faults; one should know that what follows below further elaborates upon the meaning stated above.
That the great ocean of the world possesses these various faults is also taught in this sutra. The female ghost (nārī-rākṣasī) refers to the female rākṣasa;

in the Great Sutra, she serves as a metaphor for the two delusions of views and craving, and it should be understood that the general outline here is the same. From "craving" onwards... [text continues].

These are all the meaning of "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*). This serves as the concluding summary for the lower [link]. It is the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*) that this very arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is itself volitional formation;
it is a mental formation (*manosaṃskāra*), and for this reason, it is further called "karma. Karma is both general and specific:
the former refers to craving as the formation, while the latter speaks of karma because the three types of karma—body, speech, and mind—are initiated by the mind. Herein, "mind" refers to...

This is explained by summarizing two lifetimes: because ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are mentioned together in the present, these two—ignorance and craving—are both causes and both results.
The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) refer to the head and the hands and feet; the six bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) refer to the six sense organs.

In relation to the six objects, they are called the six contacts (*ṣaṭ-sparśa*). Because karma necessarily has a result, it is called "existence" (*bhava*); that which is to be experienced is what will certainly be received.
The remaining meanings and the conclusion can all be understood accordingly. Next, regarding the other ten locations based on this precedent:

when the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) correspond, each possesses the twelve [links]; taken collectively, these constitute six layers of the twelvefold dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Next, to illustrate the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) by precedent: the two sets of six—faculties and objects—are the same as before; however, while the six consciousnesses were omitted previously, they are detailed here, which constitutes the difference.
The faults and calamities that arise are no different from those previously mentioned; therefore, they may be understood through a brief illustration.
In the previous section, two items were paired against two, whereas this present section requires three items to be paired against three. Otherwise, the conclusion could not be established.

Furthermore, since the characteristics of the faults and calamities that arise are as described above, one might ask: "What are the characteristics of their non-arising? This is precisely what is clarified below. Within this [section], there are also two parts; first—

Regarding the summary by way of the middle [category], there are also two parts: first, the eye and visible objects; second, the analogy for the remaining ten. Within the first part, there are again two: first, the summary by way of the headings; second, the explanation according to the phenomena (*dharma*).
Each of these two further has two sub-sections: first, the interrogation, and second, the explanation. The general interrogation at the beginning may be understood [by itself].

Within the explanation, there are again two parts: first, the presentation of the four phenomena; second, the clarification that if even one is absent, then all four are non-existent. However, as for the preceding...
Although it was previously established that there are twelve [links], we now again rely on these four dharmas because we wish to harmonize with the statements found in the sūtras.
This is precisely because we intend to cite the essentials to clarify the preceding twelve; furthermore, those twelve are themselves the meaning of these four.
To clarify that without one there are none of the four: as explained above, if there is even a single instance of ignorance (*avidyā*) or craving (*tṛṣṇā*), then all four are present.

Regarding all causes and effects, it is now clarified that if there is no arising, then [the subsequent three] have already arisen; if they have arisen, they must necessarily possess the latter three. Non-arising is likewise.
However, if there is only non-arising, then the latter three do not exist, just as in the previous discussion on the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*).

This clarifies that where there is one arising, there is the arising of all; the same applies to non-arising. The primary intent is to manifest the essential principle of being able to contemplate these two modes: arising and non-arising.

In the actual commentary, within the subsequent explanation, there is first an explanation of the meaning of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*), followed by an explanation of the meaning of the non-arising of the four dharmas.
Within these two sections, each contains three elements: an inquiry (*pṛcchā*), an explanation (*vyākhyāna*), and a conclusion (*nigamana*).

In the text, only the first section fully possesses these three; the remaining three sections possess only two, as the inquiry is omitted for brevity. Furthermore, within each of these explanations, there are likewise two elements.
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to both the essence (*svabhāva*) and the significance (*artha*). Regarding the first inquiry: what is the "seed of suffering," and what constitutes this "seed"?

These are the two meanings; the following three examples are likewise so. Among the three—greed, aversion, and discursive thought—the new terminology for "investigation" (*vitarka*) and "analysis" (*vicāra*) is as explained previously.

Within the seven outflows (*āsrava*), this is clarified as the seed of suffering because it is capable of producing the fruit of suffering; thus, the single character "arising" (*utpāda*) is itself the seed. The "seed" is directly applied [to these].
The "seeds of the suffering of dharmas" can be understood as a collective description of persons; it is also a description that combines the subjective (agent) and the objective (object).

The remaining four [categories] follow this same analogy. The "five desires" (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) are the dharmas themselves. The "five thoughts" (*pañca-saṃjñā*) are what give rise to them, causing them to arise through constant mental ideation.

The "six sense objects" (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are the putrid fluids. "Taking" refers to their flowing out. Because of these external conditions, "good and evil" are like the maggots and flies that compete to emerge from a festering sore.
In this context, both the arising of thought and the grasping of objects are instances of "origination" (*jāti*). However, with the presence of the first alone, all four [links] are present.

What was previously stated—that all four are metaphors for causes and conditions—means that initial craving is "attachment" (*tṛṣṇā*) and mutual ignorance is "ignorance" (*avidyā*); these two are both ignorance.
The subsequent two [links] both belong to "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*). Because these two do not arise, the twelve [links] do not arise; such is the meaning.
The four [factors] are treated as two, and these two encompass the twelve. Now, it is said that this is still difficult to perceive;

one should know that the first two are both craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which are divided into internal and external, and thus constitute two. Both arise from a lack of clear understanding and therefore belong to ignorance (*avidyā*).
Of the next two, the first is the preceding activity (*pūrva-karma*), and the second is the preceding karma itself; they are distinguished as two because of their general and specific aspects.

Therefore, these are collectively subsumed under the meaning of one or two branches of the formations (*saṃskāra*). This is precisely the meaning of two branches across two lifetimes. Since there are two causes, there are likewise two fruits;
thus, "two" refers to both [the two branches] and the twelve [links]. As for "non-existence" (*abhāva*), it is as explained above.

The preceding section concludes the explanation of the meaning of "arising" (*utpāda*); the following explains the meaning of "non-arising. When one fully understands the five meanings of form (*rūpa*), the four kinds of arising do not exist.
The meaning of "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) is to be understood as explained previously; it refers to clear comprehension and thorough penetration.

It is not that there is no clear awareness of the fact that form (*rūpa*) is subject to arising and ceasing, is oppressed by suffering, is false and unreal, lacks self-mastery, and is exceedingly defiled. Therefore, these four types [of perceptions] do not arise, which is precisely what is meant by "non-arising.
This constitutes the five-gate meditation (*pañca-dvāra-bhāvanā*). In the text, the impurity (*aśubha*) is omitted for brevity, but it may be understood through the intended meaning.
Since the eye and form are thus, and the other five pairs likewise possess the fourfold sense of arising and non-arising, it is said that "it is also thus" regarding the bases (*āyatana*).
Since the observation of the bases is thus, the same applies to the elements (*dhātu*) and formations (*saṃskāra*); therefore, it is said that "the elements are also thus."

The second section, which correctly establishes the characteristics [of the practice], is now concluded. Below this begins the third section, which concludes by identifying the source from which that person derives their name.

When that person first heard [the teaching], they immediately attained such knowledge, understanding, and realization regarding all phenomena—the aggregates, bases, and elements—whereas others did not; therefore, they alone receive this name.

Next, the following section clarifies the universal contemplation (*sāmānyālambana*), which also consists of three parts: the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion. First, regarding the introductory heading:

the single character "one" (*eka*) initiates the subsequent explanation of its characteristics. Here, the text directly clarifies the practice (*pratipatti*) without first establishing the method universally;

it previously stated that because the objects (*viṣaya*) are identical, one does not first establish the objects. Now, it is said that while the objects are the same, the contemplations differ, being the same sixfold [contemplations].

Because the Path consists of three categories, and because their essential natures differ in terms of skill and clumsiness, I shall now distinguish them directly by means of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) without needing to further clarify the objects of cognition (*ālambana*).
I maintain that there are three points of difference here compared to the previous Tripitaka: first, it clearly elucidates practice;
second, it does not point out what is wrong to reveal what is right; third, it clarifies non-arising and non-ceasing. The first point is as explained above; next, I shall explain...
There is nothing that can be discussed [in this regard], for since the three knowledges (*vidyā*) are without arising, they are without cessation; thus, they differ from the previous meaning.

Within this, one first relies on the aggregates (*skandha*), and subsequently on the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). The Master says: "In the beginning, there are again two parts: first the general, then the specific. The general refers to the analogy of the five mirror-images;

the specific refers to each of the five analogies individually illustrating the five [aggregates]. Some say: "The first [analogy] generally illustrates the mirror-image, while the subsequent ones are divided."

Regarding the five similes, there are two aspects: the general, which applies the similes collectively to the five aggregates as a whole; and the specific, which separately cites five distinct objects to correspond individually to the five aggregates.
Within the first of these, there are further two parts: first, the application to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); second, the extension by analogy to the remaining four.

Here, the teaching directly employs the similes to reveal the nature of phenomena without providing a separate synthesis. This section contains two parts: first, a brief presentation of the characteristics of contemplation; second, a detailed explanation establishing its validity.
Regarding the meaning of the first section, there are five phrases. The "three persons" refer to the practitioners who are able to contemplate according to this teaching.

The "mirror" refers to the objective realm that is contemplated; as clarified previously, this encompasses the three categories [of the Abhidharma], specifically the form-aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*) among them.

The act of looking at one's reflection in a mirror represents the characteristics of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). This is because the wisdom of contemplation through this teaching is skillful.
Since persons, phenomena, causes, and effects are all devoid of fixed reality, they are all like illusions.

Although it is said they are like illusions, it is not yet known how this very state constitutes non-arising; therefore, the following provides an extensive explanation to clarify this, which consists of four parts:

first, clarifying non-arising; second, clarifying non-ceasing to manifest non-arising; third, showing that it is not produced through cultivation, as its nature is inherently non-arisen from the beginning; and fourth...

Because of this, it is "non-arising. Regarding the two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) at the beginning, the Master says: "The two emptinesses are precisely the two—nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The meaning is that emptiness is non-arising; the first set of four [propositions] concerns the non-arising of nature, while the latter set concerns the non-arising of characteristics.
Each of these two sets of four propositions should individually state and refute [the opponent's views], yet in the concluding text, they are simply stated together and both are omitted.
The remaining two [positions] involve a shift in the force of the arguments, and thus scholars understand them;

these are all the meanings of the four propositions—self, other, both, and neither—from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*. "Combined" means "both"; "separated" means "without cause. "In between" also refers to "both.

Furthermore, regarding "neither arising nor ceasing," this is explained by way of non-ceasing to reveal non-arising: if there were cessation, there would be arising; since cessation does not exist, arising certainly does not exist either.

The passage beginning with "Also, nature is fundamentally... explains that it is not through cultivation that nature is manifested; if nature were inherently subject to arising and ceasing, then even cultivation could not extinguish it.
Thus, present cultivation merely manifests the original state; it does not mean that something new is acquired. It concludes by stating:

"Precisely because one realizes that this [nature] is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, it is called 'practice of non-arising' (*anutpāda-caryā*). Subsequently, the four aggregates (*skandha*) may be understood by analogy; that is, all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).
All are like illusory appearances; since illusory appearances are fundamentally non-existent, how could there be true arising and ceasing? Therefore, they are all precisely non-arising.

Next, regarding the specific [classification], because this specific meaning exists within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is further reconciled here. However, since the beginning and end of the text are identical, if one relies on this analogy, there would be only four;
why then are they called five? Furthermore, since these include both the general and the specific, why are they treated exclusively [as such]?
Although the individual and the collective are not explicitly stated here, they are implied; thus, there is a profound significance. Why is this?

Within this context, although the five [aggregates] are individually distinct, they must all simultaneously be understood as illusory. This is because the five aggregates are precisely what this teaching intends to illustrate through metaphor. Therefore, the text states:
"illusory form," where the single character "illusion" (māyā) pervades all that follows, from "illusory images" down to "illusory... [sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness].

For this reason, some say that form (*rūpa*) is like a reflection in a mirror because it possesses spatial dimensions; sensation (*vedanā*) is like a reflection because it arises only momentarily; perception (*saṃjñā*) is like a reflection because it consists merely of mental noting;

formations (*saṃskāra*) are like a reflection because they are coarse and manifest as the movements of the mind; and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is like a reflection because it is capable of producing all phenomena.

Now, I [the author] say that this passage also contains two names which are the same as those previously mentioned: form is like a phantom and like a reflection in a mirror, being momentarily perceived by the eye.

Because it is seen, feeling (*vedanā*) is used as a metaphor for being like an illusion or a bubble, as it lacks any real accumulation; perception (*saṃjñā*) is like a mirage, as it does not abide even for a moment;

mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are like a plantain tree, for although they lack any solid core, they consist of many layers of false and provisional accumulations, and since the phenomena of mental formations are most numerous, they serve as a metaphor.
As for consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is directly stated to be "like an illusion"; thus, its creation is like the creation of an illusion. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The mind..."
The master of illusions is this very thing; since consciousness is the sovereign of the mind, it is used as a metaphor.
In the preceding *Pitaka* teachings, whether taken collectively or individually, all observe actual objects; here, both collectively and individually, the metaphor of illusion is adopted.
Otherwise, why would it differ from what preceded? Next, in the section establishing the proof, only the first [part] consists of four propositions; the rest are all [the same].
The preceding section may also be sought therein.
The passage beginning with "Contemplating the faculties and objects" explains practice by way of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).

However, since the bases and elements differ slightly in their brevity and detail, and because the explanation of the bases can be understood by analogy with the elements, the text refers only to the bases and does not mention the elements again; this should also be inferred from what precedes.

This is because it is known. Within this, first one contemplates the emptiness of the twelve *āyatanas*, and next one contemplates the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Because delusion regarding the *āyatanas* gives rise to the causes and effects of the three periods of time, one clarifies "emptiness of emptiness" by means of these two; thus, there is non-arising.

Furthermore, both the textual phrasing and the meaning herein are derived from the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, the *Prabhāsa Sūtra*, and other such scriptures, either using their texts in full or adapting them.

Regarding the meaning, I have merely summarized the essential intent; knowing that there is a basis for this is sufficient. There is no need to laboriously cite every single source, for that would be far too tedious.
Here, I simply clarify that the dwelling place of those evil, fettering thieves is such that both person and phenomena are empty.

I shall briefly point this out according to the text, as I cannot further elaborate on all the various explanations one might find therein. Among these, I first clarify the emptiness of the sense faculties and their objects.

Next, the emptiness of causes and conditions is explained. Regarding these two points: the first is a brief explanation of the emptiness of the fruit, while the second is an extensive explanation that both cause and fruit are empty;

because they are empty, there is no arising. The first section contains three phrases with two meanings: first, contemplating the emptiness of the sense organs and their objects; second, correctly explaining fundamental emptiness.
The passage beginning with "deluded thoughts" explains the reason for this emptiness. These two meanings simply clarify the nature of emptiness.
Regarding its meaning: the reason this analogy is presented in the opening sentence is precisely to clarify emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

One contemplates these sense-faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) as being like that desolate village or hamlet. The "hamlet" is a metaphor for where the bandits—the fetters of the six sense-faculties—dwell;

this clarifies that the desolate village is devoid of people, which precisely illustrates the emptiness of the six sense-faculties. That the bandits of the fetters gather in a crowd and collectively harm things clarifies that [the faculties] are not [inherently existent].
"Subhūti, this is like the emptiness of the six sense-objects above; it is derived from the Great Sūtra. Thus the Sūtra says:

'One does not see people at all, nor does one obtain the objects they seek,' which clarifies the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*). Below, the meaning of emptiness is clarified: it is empty by its very nature from the beginning, not merely now;

this correctly clarifies that its nature is inherently empty. Within the Sūtra, the term 'outflow-free' (*anāsrava*) is explained; while the literal meaning of 'outflow-free' is emptiness, the underlying intention is distinct while the general principle remains consistent."
Now, following the general principle, this teaching may be cited as proof. The next phrase explains the reason why it is empty: it is empty because it arises from causes and conditions.
What are these causes and conditions? They are afflictions and karma. "Afflictions" refers to ignorance and delusive conceptualization; "karma" refers to various karmic actions.
This passage appears in the *Guanfo Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Samadhi of Contemplating the Buddha), where it says that the power of karma is like... [as follows].
Those "triggers" (*ji*) and "levers" (*guan*) are both essential principles rather than subtle meanings;

the trigger is the master that initiates movement, while the lever is the gatekeeper who controls opening and closing—it is precisely in this sense that they are called "pivot-triggers. Since the faculties (*indriya*) are already like this, how could their objects (*viṣaya*) be otherwise?
They are not substantial entities at all; they are entirely illusory.
From "Ignorance" (*avidyā*) onwards, this next section clarifies the emptiness of dependent origination; that is, it extensively explains that both cause and effect are empty.

Within this, first there is a brief explanation of the emptiness of the single dharma of ignorance; next, there is a general discussion of the three paths, which collectively clarifies the twelve links of dependent origination—that is, that both cause and effect are entirely empty.
The intent of explaining it in this way is to show that if ignorance alone is empty, then [the remaining ten links are likewise empty].
Because both are empty, they are collectively explained in terms of the three paths, as the twelve essentials are nothing other than these three.
For instance, in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra*, the first three phrases provide the heading, the explanation, and the citation of evidence.

This citation refers precisely to the third verse on the elucidation of emptiness within the "Four Impermanences" section of the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā-sūtra* (the *Renwang jing*). Since its meaning is identical to that found here, it is cited.
This is like a whirling firebrand; it carries two meanings: first, to clarify that there is no end, and second, to clarify the meaning of emptiness.
Thus, a verse from the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra* says: "Afflictions and karma give rise to perception; perception in turn gives rise to afflictions;
therefore, afflictions again produce karma, and perception exists by virtue of karma. This clarifies the sense of cause and effect revolving in succession without end. Since...
Because these causes and conditions revolve without end, they must be empty; thus, the Verse on Dependent Origination says:
"In the cause there is no fruit, and in the fruit there is also no cause; that which arises within the cause is empty. This clarifies that all four positions are eternally empty.
Next, to summarize and clarify the three paths, the first, eighth, and ninth verses of the *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa* state:
The afflictions constitute the second [truth], karma the tenth, and the remaining seven are all suffering; thus, the twelve factors are subsumed within these three.

Therefore, one knows that the twelve essentials are merely these three, as explained above. As for the manner of direct pointing: because I do not wish to burden the text with excessive detail regarding the meaning of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) already clarified through enumeration, I have pointed directly to it.
Regarding the conclusion: by realizing this essence in such a way, one understands that all arising phenomena are, from the very beginning, non-arising.
The Three Piṭakas differ [from this] because they attain non-arising only after having extinguished what has already arisen;

therefore, this is the Universal Teaching (*pāryāptika*). Next, the Contemplative Practice of the Distinct Teaching (*prātibhedika*) is explained. Within this, there is the introduction, the exposition, and the conclusion. The initial section contains two meanings, which may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

In the subsequent exposition, it is stated that "first, the metaphor for the object and wisdom is presented"; from the phrase "if one desires" onwards, the arising [of contemplation] is explained next.

Regarding "practice" (*caryā*), it refers first to the method for establishing practice, followed by the actual clarification of the characteristics of practice. Within this, there should be four meanings:
namely, object (*ālambana*), wisdom (*jñāna*), arising (*utpāda*), and non-arising (*anutpāda*). The present text mentions only three, yet these already encompass the four meanings.

"Practice" refers to cultivating the practice of non-arising; it destroys arising to manifest non-arising. However, the reason why [things] arise is due to delusion regarding principle (*tattva*); as for non-arising, it is due to...

This explains the principle. Herein, the reason why "Dharma" and "Practice" are established first and distinguished from the preceding two is that they differ in terms of deficiency versus completeness and shallowness versus depth;
