these distinctions may be sought in the text. The text contains three meanings: the mirror’s ability to manifest images serves as a general metaphor for the One Mind giving rise to the myriad dharmas.
Regarding the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), briefly stated, there are three meanings: the meaning of cause, the meaning of nature, and [the meaning of essence].
The locus of meaning (*artha*) refers to the basis for all phenomena and principles, serving as the cause and support for both delusion and enlightenment.

Because the eye can discern and illuminate everything, it is used as a metaphor for the wisdom of this teaching and contemplation (*dṛṣṭi-vipaśyanā-jñāna*). The passage beginning with "blue and yellow" explains the images appearing within the mirror above;
it clarifies that within the mind of the *dharmadhātu*, all phenomena are fully present. This is the mind of the *dharmadhātu*.
Although they are vast and boundless, they do not transcend the causes and effects of the ten dharma-realms. Within this, there are three parts: first, a combined heading;
second, individual correspondences; and third, a summary. Regarding the first, the heading uses eight colors to correspond to the ten fruits.

Through the distinction of combining and separating, one opens up two from within the "white" and "small" categories, thus forming ten. These may be interpreted according to their respective meanings.
There is no need to wait for further elaborate explanations; the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* and its extensive commentary will be cited in full later.

However, since those teachings of the Hīnayāna clarify the meaning only in relation to the six realms of existence, the present exposition adds the analogy of the ten realms (*daśadhātu*). As for why the *Tripiṭaka-bodhisattvas* are not mentioned here:
it is because their initial stage has not yet severed the afflictions, and thus their tainted virtues (*sāsrava-kuśala*) are the same as those of humans and devas. Nevertheless...
These ten kinds of colored images that can appear within a mirror are a metaphor for the mind’s dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which possesses ten causes and effects.

Due to delusion there are nine; due to liberation there is one. When delusion and liberation are combined, they are said to constitute ten. However, within the nature of the mind, there is neither delusion nor liberation, neither nine nor one.
It is only through causes and conditions that there is delusion and liberation, nine and one; it is because causes and conditions differ.
Because this is discussed by synthesizing the fundamental with the derivative and nature with habit-energy, there are ten [categories].

However, because one cannot yet realize that the one is identical to all, nor realize that delusion is itself nature, nor realize that the arising of the nine realms is identical to the non-arising of the Buddha-realm, it differs from the Perfect [Teaching].
This is roughly the case; reflect upon this, reflect upon this.
From here below, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are clarified; within this, first there is a preliminary distinction and manifestation, which also serves as a summary of the general meaning.

Next is the actual clarification. Regarding the first [of these two parts]: it is distinguished from the previous two to manifest the excellence of this one. The previous two merely concerned oneself, whereas this one possesses both self and others;
the previous two merely extinguished the arising of the six elements (*dhātu*) to manifest non-arising (*anutpāda*), whereas now the non-arising of the nine elements is brought about.
This causes the birth of a single Buddha-field. For this reason, it is described as a "great difference.

To speak of "birth" here means that by eliminating the obstacles and delusions of beginningless time, one allows [the nature] to unfold in accordance with wisdom. Next, based on the following passage, the actual mode of practice is clearly explained in three parts:

first, clarifying the sequential cultivation of the three types of practice so that the causes for the three types of birth do not arise; second, clarifying that one immediately attains the three types of birth-realms.
The final summary of "Non-arising" begins with the first line, which generally indicates the fundamental tenet of its practice.

What is called the "Dharmadhātu" (Dharma-realm) is the Middle Way, the essential nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). It is that upon which both delusion and enlightenment depend; through delusion regarding it, there are the nine [realms of] existence, and through understanding it, there is the One [Vehicle].
Since this treatise clarifies the practice of understanding, it first establishes this to manifest its central tenet. Those of the initial resolve receive...

The teaching reveals that this principle exists; relying upon it, one initiates practice. This practice functions with respect to this object-condition (*ālambana*), yet it is not identical to it, and is therefore distinct from it, because the teaching does not [immediately] fuse them.
This is the principle of the *dharmadhātu*. It is neither cause nor fruit, yet it serves as the basis for what is practiced. Practice is the cause, while Bodhi is the fruit.

This principle is not only difficult to practice, but also difficult to understand; as was previously distinguished: [...]* *Note: The original text contains an ellipsis marked by "向既簡於" (xiàng jì jiǎn yú), indicating a prior section has been omitted.*

The *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings also differ from the *Yuan* (Perfect) teaching; therefore, this phrase constitutes the essential body (*zongti*) of this specific teaching—reflect on this, reflect on this!

Regarding "the sequential [teachings]" and so forth, this precisely clarifies the characteristics of practice (*xingxiang*). Since the principle (*li*) is not yet integrated, the practice is likewise not integrated; this is why they differ from the "prior" and "subsequent" [teachings].

First, the analysis of contemplation (*cheguan*) is clarified as being like the three *Zang* teachings regarding the characteristics of practice; subsequently, the contemplation of essence (*tiguan*) is applied.
As previously stated, this is the mode of practice for universal contemplation; because one’s faculties are dull, it is necessary to proceed in this manner.

Whether [the stages] come before or after, or whether they serve as the primary or auxiliary, they need not be strictly confined to fixed positions. One should understand this through faith and abide within it through reflection, for by means of these two types of contemplation, one is able to eliminate the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*).
This corresponds to entering the stage of emptiness, the tenth *vihāra*. Next, one immediately emerges into the provisional (*upāya*) to illuminate the conventional world.

Wisdom is also called "non-knowing" and is termed the "delusion regarding the obstacles of the sands of phenomena" (*rajas*) to distinguish it from that which obstructs the principle through identity with it;

thus it is said to "contain dust. This refers to the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). True wisdom is that which is cultivated during the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) and is attained at the time of entering the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*).

At that time, one partially attains the fundamental [wisdom] wherein non-arising is primary. This "fundamental" is simply ignorance (*avidyā*), for it is that upon which all delusions depend. Furthermore, it is the root...
The "Fundamental" (*ben*) refers to the Middle Way (*madhyama-pratipad*); because one attains this Middle Way, ignorance (*avidyā*) does not arise—this is what is meant by those words.

These three correspond to the five stages (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*), which emerge from within the delusions of ignorance; they are established as three based on the distinctions between hindrances to phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*) and hindrances to principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*), as well as their coarseness and subtlety.
Since these names and meanings exist in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, they are cited here from the commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. [They are] found elsewhere as well.

The passage "For the most part, these do not exist" and below clarifies that the three fruits do not produce further fruits; since causes produce causes and do not produce fruits, there are certainly no three kinds of fruits.
Since these three fruits do not exist, they are merely the absence of two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

Within the *nirmāṇa-cyuti* (transformation death), the provisional means (*upāya*) are distinguished, thus forming three. However, the term "actual retribution" (*vipāka*) has both partial and ultimate senses; here, we follow the latter.
This is stated thus as a general explanation; if one were to explain it in detail and specifically, that would not be the intent here, as it is addressed in other teachings.
Since this will be further clarified in the subsequent text, there is no need for further words. The phrase "arising and also... serves as a concluding summary of the names.

Some say that because birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) in the world is contrasted with *nirvāṇa*, and because these two are not [ultimately] existent, it is called "arising and non-arising. However, I maintain:

Furthermore, one may contrast the *paricchinna* (segmented) and the *pariṇāma* (transformative) births, as both are forms of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Because these two types of birth do not arise [in this state], it is called "non-arising.
Thus, by subsequently taking segmented birth as a point of comparison, the meaning of the transformative birth is revealed.

Moreover, it can simply be said that there is no arising of the threefold cause and effect; therefore, it is called "arising-non-arising. Since it does not arise within arising, it is also not non-arising.
Regarding cessation, because it accords with the previously explained meaning of neither arising nor ceasing, it is said that "non-arising does not arise either.
These various meanings are termed "non-arising. As for the conclusion: what has been explained here differs from what precedes it and is distinct from what follows;
therefore, this is the specific pedagogical method (*pṛthag-upāya*) of this distinct teaching (*pratyekadeśanā*).
The following is the fourth [section], the explanation according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). This also consists of the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion.

Within the explanation, because the first two methods of teaching involve both the same practice and different teachings, they directly clarify the contemplation (*guan*) while distinguishing it from the previous two. Therefore, the establishment of the method (*fa*) comes first, followed by the clarification of cultivation (*xing*).
Now, since the Perfect Teaching shares the same method as the Separate Teaching (*bie*) yet differs in its practice, it likewise directly clarifies cultivation without further establishing a method.

Within this, there is first the general and then the specific. The "general" refers to the universal contemplation that the causes and effects of the ten realms are identical to the single true reality (*dharmatā*).

The "specific" refers to the three obstructions being precisely the three virtues (*triguṇa*). Whether general or specific, all are without spatial direction; therefore, they constitute the perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*).

Within the initial [section] on the general, there is a metaphor and its application. In the metaphor, spatial direction is excluded to reveal perfection; this consists of a heading and an explanation. Within the heading, there are three parts.
The first phrase of the verse directly demonstrates the perfect contemplation; the subsequent two phrases negate the limited to reveal the perfect and the limited.

The latter refers to the specific aspects mentioned previously. The mirror possesses three meanings: essence, function, and non-duality. Essence refers to its physical form; function refers to its capacity to contain all phenomena;
non-duality means that both essence and function are non-dual. This serves as a metaphor for the Dharma-body, which is without spatial limitation yet contains all things.
All dharmas are without exception the one true mark; all produced phenomena are identical with the single dharma of non-arising.
The following two phrases distinguish and clarify the two contemplations, showing that the Perfect is distinct from the Separate because the two are not identical to the Perfect;

thus they are distinguished and clarified. What follows is the explanation, which comments on the preceding two points. It first explains the distinction from the Separate and subsequently explains the clarification of the Perfect. Initially, there are four [sections].

The "phrase" (*jù*) explains the preceding two [terms]; the first two [explanations] clarify the preceding initial phrase. "Darkness" (*míng*) refers to delusion (*mí*), and "clarity" (*àn*) refers to awakening (*jiě*).

Delusion and awakening have both general and specific aspects: specifically, they refer to the six realms of existence and the four classes of noble ones; generally, delusion refers to the nine realms and awakening refers to the Buddha-realm.

Because the perfect contemplation (*yuánguān*) views them as non-dual, they are not two. The term "form" (*xíng*) explains the preceding character "form" (*xíng*); the term "image" (*xiàng*) explains the preceding character "image" (*xiàng*). Thus, these two...

The phrase "together" explains the very last line of the preceding [verse]. It describes the causes of the ten realms as the "frames" (or "reflections") and the effects of the ten realms as the "images.

Because there is delusion and awakening, there is the distinction between the causes and effects of the ten realms; yet, because they are thus perfectly identical within the single reality (*ekadhātu*), there is nothing to be grasped, and therefore they are neither [delusion nor awakening].
In the text, the character *jìng* (frame/reflection) is mistakenly written as *yán* (word); it should be *jǐng* (to warn/alert), referring to the ancients.
Some people borrow this term to mean "the image of an object" (*viṣaya-bimba*), arguing that it is the object (*viṣaya*) because it can be perceived and confronted.

However, if one relies on the phonetic reading of the character *qíng* (pronounced *chén-jīng* in the fanqie system), its meaning completely deviates from the intended sense. I maintain that this interpretation is far too convoluted.
It should properly be read as *jìng* (with the same tone as above), where *jìng* is glossed as "to lift up. It refers to a stand used for holding up a mirror, and it also...
Just as in common parlance a lamp-stand is also called a "lamp" (*dīpa*), because both are mostly made of wood, this character is used by extension.
There are many such instances in the world; furthermore, among these extensions, there are those who borrow "stand" (*jìng*) for "to lift/sustain" (*qíng*).

Some who are ignorant might take "alerting" (*jǐng*) for "object" (*jìng*) and surely consider it an error, yet they also say it should be read as "reflection" (*yǐngxiàng*); when contrasted with the preceding term "description" (*xíngmáng*), this meaning is quite elegant.

When these two interpretations are taken together as essential points of convergence, they differ from the previous [explanation] which was circuitous; thus, later students should evaluate them accordingly.
However, observe that the preceding initial interpretation marks "round contemplation" (*yuánguān*); this means "wondrous and without direction.

"Round and perfect" (*tuányuán*) refers to its wondrous nature, while "without boundaries or limits" (*wújiànpàn*) manifests its wondrous state—that is, being "without direction. The four pairs and eight items are all "directions."
Furthermore, because there is nothing with which to observe or penetrate it, it is without direction (*an-uddeśa*). Being circular, it has no boundaries; thus, it is without limits. To summarize:

it is neither horizontal nor vertical, neither delusion nor awakening, neither Buddha nor sentient being. This precisely clarifies that all such phenomena are themselves without direction, and therefore are universally circular.
Next, in the section on the correspondence of the Dharma, the two preceding points are integrated. First, the correspondence:

"Previously there was no sequential order; now we combine them to reveal their completeness. Regarding the first of the three sections [of the initial part], the first phrase provides a general combination, while the following three provide specific combinations.
Since the previous metaphors did not exclude the ten realms, although this current combination is presented through both general and specific aspects, it likewise does not go beyond these ten.

This phrase cites the specific details of the latter three to clarify good and evil; that is, within the ten [realms], the first six are those of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). "Deviant and correct" refers to...
The six [realms] of the previous life and the four supramundane realms—small and great—are distinguished directly by means of the four supramundane noble ones (*ārya*).

"Small" refers to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), while "great" refers to the Bodhisattvas and Buddhas. Although there are these distinctions, they ultimately do not limit or exclude any of the ten realms within the supramundane;

thus, the "square" (the distinct) and the "round" (the inclusive) differ from the previously mentioned fixed distinctions. Below, this is combined with the preceding "round contemplation," which is solely one.

Reality is indeed the markless nature of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāva*); the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is indeed the naturelessness of phenomena. As for "Buddha-dharma," this markless nature is that which the wondrous person—the Buddha—has awakened to and realized, and it is also the teacher and model of all Buddhas; therefore, it is called "Buddha-dharma. This refers to the person to manifest the Dharma. Furthermore, to clarify that the natures and marks of the nine realms are all the Dharma of the Buddha-realm: The nature and marks of the nine realms are all the Dharma of the Buddha-realm. Why? Because the nature and marks of the nine realms are identical to the nature and marks of the Buddha-realm. What is the reason? It is because the nature and marks of the nine realms are originally non-existent. Since they are originally non-existent, they are not subject to arising or ceasing. Because they do not arise or cease, they are beyond increase or decrease. Because they are beyond increase or decrease, they are neither defiled nor pure. Because they are neither defiled nor pure, they are neither conditioned nor unconditioned. Because they are neither conditioned nor unconditioned, they are neither existent nor non-existent. Because they are neither existent nor non-existent, they are neither one nor many. Because they are neither one nor many, they are neither coming nor going. Because they are neither coming nor going, they are neither near nor far. Because they are neither near nor far, they are neither internal nor external. Because they are neither internal nor external, they are neither self nor other. Because they are neither self nor other, they are neither mine nor not mine. Because they are neither mine nor not mine, they are neither grasped nor abandoned. Because they are neither grasped nor abandoned, they are neither attained nor lost. Because they are neither attained nor lost, they are neither birth-and-death nor Nirvana. Because they are neither birth-and-death nor Nirvana, they are neither samsara nor cessation. Because they are neither samsara nor cessation, they are neither bondage nor liberation. Because they are neither bondage nor liberation, they are neither cause nor effect. Because they are neither cause nor effect, they are neither beginning nor end. Because they are neither beginning nor end, they are neither past, present, nor future. Because they are neither past, present, nor future, they are neither temporal nor spatial. Because they are neither temporal nor spatial, they are neither form nor mind. Because they are neither form nor mind, they are neither subject nor object. Because they are neither subject nor object, they are neither knower nor known. Because they are neither knower nor known, they are neither perceiver nor perceived. Because they are neither perceiver nor perceived, they are neither seer nor seen. Because they are neither seer nor seen, they are neither hearer nor heard. Because they are neither hearer nor heard, they are neither speaker nor spoken. Because they are neither speaker nor spoken, they are neither teacher nor taught. Because they are neither teacher nor taught, they are neither master nor disciple. Because they are neither master nor disciple, they are neither high nor low. Because they are neither high nor low, they are neither superior nor inferior. Because they are neither superior nor inferior, they are neither right nor wrong. Because they are neither right nor wrong, they are neither true nor false. Because they are neither true nor false, they are neither good nor evil. Because they are neither good nor evil, they are neither merit nor demerit. Because they are neither merit nor demerit, they are neither wholesome nor unwholesome. Because they are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, they are neither tainted nor untainted. Because they are neither tainted nor untainted, they are neither with outflows (*sāsrava*) nor without outflows (*anāsrava*). Because they are neither with outflows nor without outflows, they are neither mundane nor supramundane. Because they are neither mundane nor supramundane, they are neither worldly nor transcendental. Because they are neither worldly nor transcendental, they are neither samsaric nor nirvanic. Because they are neither samsaric nor nirvanic, they are neither delusion nor awakening. Because they are neither delusion nor awakening, they are neither ignorance nor wisdom. Because they are neither ignorance nor wisdom, they are neither darkness nor light. Because they are neither darkness nor light, they are neither obstruction nor clarity. Because they are neither obstruction nor clarity, they are neither hindrance nor penetration. Because they are neither hindrance nor penetration, they are neither concealment nor revelation. Because they are neither concealment nor revelation, they are neither covering nor uncovering. Because they are neither covering nor uncovering, they are neither veiling nor unveiling. Because they are neither veiling nor unveiling, they are neither obscuring nor illuminating. Because they are neither obscuring nor illuminating, they are neither darkening nor brightening. Because they are neither darkening nor brightening, they are neither dullness nor sharpness. Because they are neither dullness nor sharpness, they are neither coarseness nor subtlety. Because they are neither coarseness nor subtlety, they are neither gross nor fine. Because they are neither gross nor fine, they are neither large nor small. Because they are neither large nor small, they are neither long nor short. Because they are neither long nor short, they are neither square nor round. Because they are neither square nor round, they are neither straight nor crooked. Because they are neither straight nor crooked, they are neither level nor uneven. Because they are neither level nor uneven, they are neither even nor odd. Because they are neither even nor odd, they are neither dual nor non-dual. Because they are neither dual nor non-dual, they are neither manifold nor singular. Because they are neither manifold nor singular, they are neither differentiated nor unified. Because they are neither differentiated nor unified, they are neither separate nor combined. Because they are neither separate nor combined, they are neither distinct nor identical. Because they are neither distinct nor identical, they are neither different nor the same. Because they are neither different nor the same, they are neither various nor uniform. Because they are neither various nor uniform, they are neither diverse nor homogeneous. Because they are neither diverse nor homogeneous, they are neither scattered nor concentrated. Because they are neither scattered nor concentrated, they are neither dispersed nor gathered. Because they are neither dispersed nor gathered, they are neither expanded nor contracted. Because they are neither expanded nor contracted, they are neither wide nor narrow. Because they are neither wide nor narrow, they are neither broad nor thin. Because they are neither broad nor thin, they are neither thick nor thin. Because they are neither thick nor thin, they are neither deep nor shallow. Because they are neither deep nor shallow, they are neither bottomless nor surface-level. Because they are neither bottomless nor surface-level, they are neither profound nor superficial. Because they are neither profound nor superficial, they are neither subtle nor coarse. Because they are neither subtle nor coarse, they are neither minute nor gross. Because they are neither minute nor gross, they are neither fine nor crude. Because they are neither fine nor crude, they are neither delicate nor rough. Because they are neither delicate nor rough, they are neither smooth nor rough. Because they are neither smooth nor rough, they are neither slippery nor dry. Because they are neither slippery nor dry, they are neither moist nor parched. Because they are neither moist nor parched, they are neither wet nor dry. Because they are neither wet nor dry, they are neither humid nor arid. Because they are neither humid nor arid, they are neither damp nor parched. Because they are neither damp nor parched, they are neither cold nor hot. Because they are neither cold nor hot, they are neither warm nor cool. Because they are neither warm nor cool, they are neither feverish nor refreshing. Because they are neither feverish nor refreshing, they are neither burning nor extinguished. Because they are neither burning nor extinguished, they are neither inflamed nor quenched. Because they are neither inflamed nor quenched, they are neither blazing nor extinguishing. Because they are neither blazing nor extinguishing, they are neither radiant nor dim. Because they are neither radiant nor dim, they are neither luminous nor obscure. Because they are neither luminous nor obscure, they are neither bright nor dark. Because they are neither bright nor dark, they are neither clear nor murky. Because they are neither clear nor murky, they are neither transparent nor opaque. Because they are neither transparent nor opaque, they are neither lucid nor turbid. Because they are neither lucid nor turbid, they are neither pure nor impure. Because they are neither pure nor impure, they are neither clean nor dirty. Because they are neither clean nor dirty, they are neither stainless nor stained. Because they are neither stainless nor stained, they are neither white nor black. Because they are neither white nor black, they are neither light nor heavy. Because they are neither light nor heavy, they are neither buoyant nor sinking. Because they are neither buoyant nor sinking, they are neither floating nor drowning. Because they are neither floating nor drowning, they are neither rising nor falling. Because they are neither rising nor falling, they are neither ascending nor descending. Because they are neither ascending nor descending, they are neither moving nor stationary. Because they are neither moving nor stationary, they are neither shifting nor fixed. Because they are neither shifting nor fixed, they are neither changing nor constant. Because they are neither changing nor constant, they are neither impermanent nor eternal. Because they are neither impermanent nor eternal

This is because it is explained as cited later. Furthermore, the following citation serves as proof to clarify that the causes and effects of all ten realms are entirely the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is the cause and effect of the one Buddha; that is, the nine directions are all perfect.
This generally clarifies that all phenomena of birth are precisely the dharma of non-arising.

The following section specifically addresses the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*) and the elimination of birth through the Dharma-clarity, which is precisely the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-darśana*).

This is also like the aforementioned meaning of the general and specific contemplations of non-arising. Within this, there are two parts: first, the elimination of birth within the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence); second, using that as a comparison to reveal the elimination of birth within *pariṇāmi-bhava* (transformative existence).
Regarding the first part, there are four distinct points: first, the general indication of the elimination of birth through the Dharma-clarity, which is itself non-arising; next...

The commentary separately clarifies that the three obstructions (*trividha-āvaraṇa*) are themselves the three virtues (*triguṇa*) and the three insights (*trividyā*). Since these are identical to the three virtues, they are identical to the non-arising of the four fetters (*catuḥ-saṃyojana*).

First, because there is no fixed direction, this is the meaning of the perfect non-arising (*pariniṣpanna-anutpāda*). Regarding the beginning of the first [fetter], the former masters said: "Arising is itself suffering.

Some say the word "suffering" (*duḥkha*) has been omitted from the text. Now I say: the meaning of the omitted word corresponds to these three [virtues/insights] arising and ceasing in alternation, as previously described.
Because they are luminous, all are dharmas of arising. Since they are dependently originated and conditions have no fixed nature, arising is itself non-arising.
Since arising is non-arising, how could there be anything that arises? Thus, non-arising also does not arise; the total absence of these two is called "non-arising.

Regarding the next three distinct points, their intent is to clarify that because of delusion, the three are what is "not" [the truth]; because of lack of understanding, the three are "not" [the truth]. This "not" is precisely the reality.
Knowing that the ultimate principle is quiescent and transcendent, there is neither right nor wrong; it is only in the latter two causes that right and wrong exist.
First, it clarifies that non-dharma is itself dharma; next, it clarifies that ignorance is itself enlightenment; third, it clarifies that bondage is itself liberation.

If this were according to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), since it does not accord with the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), these points would not be manifest; however, because this is according to the Perfect Teaching, it is so. Below, it clarifies that since the three are themselves [liberation].
Because of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), the three kinds of arising are precisely the three non-arisings; they are identical with Great Nirvāṇa as a single dharma.
Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* names it "Nirvāṇa" and "Non-arising. The fourth [verse] concludes by synthesizing the four lines to reveal the meaning of the Perfect (*pariniṣpanna*).

It should be understood that the profound meaning of the secret treasury of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is exhausted here. One should move the subsequent conclusion [of the verse] to serve as an illustration.

Next, regarding the provisional and the real (honji-suijaku) within the third section of the "Explanation of Non-arising," which clarifies the long and the near: although the text is not difficult, [it requires careful consideration].

"This sutra opens the gate of expedient means and reveals the mark of reality. This refers precisely to the horizontal and vertical dimensions.

what follows now corresponds to that second intention. If one were to rely solely on the preceding section, its meaning would not be exhaustive, nor would it accord with the scriptural text; therefore, this explanation is necessary.
Furthermore, although the Buddha has not yet revealed his origins, the disciples first manifest their own fundamental nature, acting as a preliminary gradual stage for the sake of the Teacher.

Therefore, the subsequent text contains its own detailed analysis (*viniścaya*), so there is no need for such prolixity here. The text is divided into two parts: first, the formal elucidation of the fundamental and the manifested;
second, the citation of scriptural evidence to establish the initial meaning. The first part has five sections: first, elucidating how the fundamental manifests as the trace;

second, elucidating the trace itself; third, showing that the trace is identical to the fundamental; fourth, elucidating that the essence and function of the fundamental and the trace are boundless; fifth, elucidating the cessation of function and return to the source.
The "Essence" (ti) first indicates its fundamental source; "fundamental" means that which has existed for a long time, in contrast to the "traces" (ji).
From oneself to others, it manifests traces for the sake of sentient beings. How is this known to be so? It is known by the textual evidence cited later;

although one knows the text, how is it known that this section specifically uses the traces to verify the essence? Regarding the similarities and differences between this [teaching] and that of the Buddha, this is not...
It can be understood that while one knows its origin exists, its length cannot be fixed; this will become clear from the subsequent text.

Next, the traces [of the teaching] are clarified, which refers to the five periods for the sake of sentient beings. The first four and these five appear as horizontal and vertical manifestations of one another.

As for why the text mentions only four, it is because the four are indeed the five. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Ordinary persons are like milk," which indicates that they are shown to be ordinary persons at the very beginning and do not yet receive [the teaching].

The Great Transformation is as explained later in the section on Faith and Understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*). Since the manifestation of traces is fundamentally for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings, each instance first clarifies its underlying cause.
This meaning of gradual progression has already been fully discussed above within the analysis of the teachings (*yōkyō*);
it can be understood through reflection, so there is no need to elaborate further. As for "its basis" mentioned below, this refers to the three [aspects] which are the traces (*jaku*).

To manifest its source, one follows the traces to clarify that they are identical to the source; thus it is said, "and yet they are equal. This means that what is fundamentally abiding has not begun only now.
The passage beginning with "If one hears... clarifies that its essence and function are boundless, non-dual yet dual.
To explain this meaning, the text first cites scripture to clarify the reason why: the letter *A* is the expression of non-arising.
Yiwen [states]: "To know that the one is non-arising is to understand that the four meanings are clear; for one is four, and four encompass all. To understand one is to understand all.
This means that knowing arising is itself non-arising, and non-arising is yet arising; they are both negated and both affirmed.

Since this is so regarding non-arising, it applies equally to the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (ji). That is to say, the fundamental is the manifested, and the manifested is the fundamental, and so forth.

Regarding the fifth section below, it clarifies that if sentient beings are able to enter the perfect non-arising (*anupapatti*), their individual capacities for transformation and benefit are returned to the essence.
This perfected path of convergence is precisely that which is directionless within the aforementioned four propositions.
If beings have not yet converged upon this wondrous state, the Great Matter remains unfinished; once they have converged, it is completed. Thus, the text says: "Now it has already..."

Since the Master [the Buddha] was thus satisfied, it is only natural that his attendants were likewise so; this is precisely why, after the three cycles of teaching, they all immediately revealed their origins and manifested their fundamental nature.

The above concludes the first section, which clarifies the fundamental and the derivative (honji-suijaku). What follows is the second section, which cites scriptural evidence. This section contains two parts:

first, citing the relevant passage from the current text to verify the derivative aspect; second, citing the *Āgama* to corroborate the fundamental aspect. Within the first part, there is the initial chapter.
In the initial prose section, because Pūrṇa requested [the teaching], his traces were first extensively revealed; in the verses, the traces of all the bhikṣus are revealed in general.
For now, let us cite the meaning of the text concerning the primary cause: the underlying intent actually lies in the general clarification that Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya is included therein.
Since the subsequent text clarifies how he benefited sentient beings during five periods under ninety billion buddhas, we shall now clarify this.
The worldly affairs of that single lifetime cannot be recounted in their entirety; by this, one knows that his fundamental and manifested traces are vast and remote.
Without relying on this interpretation, how could they be made manifest? Next, the citation from the *Āgama* serves to further establish the meaning of what preceded;
it refers specifically to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. Thus, that sutra says: "When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī during a light drizzle at night, he addressed [the monks]."
"Ānanda, cover the lamp with a canopy and follow behind me. Ānanda received these instructions and went to a certain place.
The Buddha then smiled. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "It is not without cause or condition that you now hold a canopy and follow me.
I see the Brahmā King holding a canopy and following behind Cundabhadraka with a lamp. This is merely a manifestation of his outward traces, while secretly expressing his fundamental practice."
One knows that its origin is lofty and vast; this is why Brahmā-king holds it and subsequently conceals it. Although it was not previously explained, it may be inferred through reasoning:
for according to those scriptures universally esteemed by the world, Brahmā-king is taken as the source of birth, and he himself likewise claims this to be so.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The father of all sentient beings. Furthermore—
The sutras clarify that those of the four castes are all born from the Brahma King; thus, it is evident that he is the source of birth.

Now, Ājñāta-kaundinya has long dwelt in the source of non-birth (*anutpāda*). Since there is nothing in the world—neither the existence nor the cessation of birth—that does not depend upon this, although he is the lord of birth, he must inevitably revere the Lord of Non-birth. By this, one further knows that his origin is supreme.
Although the previous explanations of the textual characteristics may be roughly understood, they still lack the most essential points; one must understand what these are.
Regarding the teaching of the original and the trace (*honjaku*), both equally reveal the essential purport of the sutra. The methods and structures of the exegesis are likewise identical.

Within the essentials of the teaching, there are four aspects as previously clarified; within this current commentary, one must also know these four. What are they? They are the divisions... [text ends].

In this section on the Distinction between the Origin and the Trace (*benji-pian*) regarding the Opening and Closing of the Assembly, the first part establishes the Origin and the second clarifies the Trace;

thus, it distinguishes between the Origin and the Trace. Once these names are established, the meanings of provisional versus real and coarse versus subtle naturally manifest, which constitutes the judgment of their relative dependence.
Having clarified how the Trace is manifested from the Origin, the text next concludes the Trace to return to the Origin, thereby elucidating the mutual identity of Origin and Trace.
The four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) have no fixed substance, and both their essence and function are quiescent; this is precisely the meaning of "opening the absolute" (ka-jeol).
Such a principle is the essential point of non-arising (anutpāda) in this sutra, and it corresponds to the fourth intention [of the Buddha]. (etc.)
Next, regarding "contemplation" (*guan*): this clarifies the basis for those who have already attained [realization] and serves as the cause for those who have not yet attained it to bring it about.

Once the assembly has been opened, there is only the contemplation that is singular and beyond dependence. However, if one can understand that the causes and effects of the ten realms within the single mind are themselves emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle—then the three causes and three fruits, as well as all phenomena of arising, are all non-arising; this has already been fully explained as previously clarified by others. Thus, it is already established.

Therefore, it is said that one need not trouble oneself with further elaboration, as the principle can be understood. For one who attains such realization, how could the person of "All-Knowing" (Ajñāta) be far off?
One may immediately designate them as such. If this is the case for "All-Knowing," then all other instances may be understood by analogy.
Although they are known, one must realize that these six cases are not so; otherwise, the fault of overstepping and presumption is not far removed. Reflect on this, reflect on this!
Next, regarding Śākyamuni Kāśyapa: one must first understand this name and title before one can comprehend the commentary.
It should be known that "Kāśyapa" is his personal name, while "Mahā" is an exalted praise of his virtuous conduct; thus, the name and conduct are combined in speech.
Furthermore, it is because the former and the latter are joined together. Moreover, it is because the mundane and the supramundane are combined.
This is for the sake of explanation; the sequence of name and surname follows the same pattern as previously mentioned regarding Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya. Within this text, there are two major distinctions:
first, his name and surname are explained through three meanings; second, the great significance of "Mahā" is extensively explained in relation to his virtuous conduct.

As previously stated, according to the *Cūḍapanthaka Sūtra*, the name is given first and the surname later, whereas in the explanation here, the surname comes first and the name later—each following what is most convenient.
Regarding the three meanings explained previously: first, his clan name (*gotra*) is explained; second, his personal name (*nāman*) is explained; and third, his title (*upapada*) is explained.

Moreover, those who follow the lineage of the immortals are the foremost clans of that region; those who speak of studying the Way refer to studying the Way of the immortals, which responds to one's resonance.
This region also has such matters, as the *I Ching* says: "The River produced the diagrams and the Luo produced the writings;
the Sage took them as his model. When Fu Xi governed by binding himself to Heaven, he was moved by the River Diagrams and drew the Eight Trigrams to manifest [the Way].
When King Yu of Xia was regulating the floods, a divine tortoise emerged from the Luo River carrying a book; this is the *Hongfan Jiuchou* (The Nine Categories of the Great Plan).
Both were brought about by the resonance of virtue, and thus they belong to the same category. Regarding the term "shi" (clan), some refer to it as a "xing" (surname) and others as a "zu" (lineage);
however, when first acquired, it constitutes a surname, whereas later it is called a clan. "Shi" refers to that which follows after one's original surname.

The character for "shi" (氏) lacks a dot; if a dot were added, its pronunciation would be identical to that of "jing" (精). The name of the commandery or town has been frequently corrupted during transcription—be aware of this.
Next, regarding the explanation provided by Paramārtha, which constitutes the second interpretation, it states:
"As for 'other light' (yuguang), some explain it as the light of Kāśyapa, calling it 'other' because it is distinct from the ancestral sage's light. I maintain that this explanation is erroneous.
The extreme absurdity [of the objection] is precisely this: to claim that the light of other persons and other things is called "other" (yu). Therefore, another commentator explains:
"In ancient times there were sages whose bodies possessed radiance that eclipsed the light of the sun and moon; since this holy one is of their lineage, [he possesses such light].
Alternatively, the character *yin* (飲, "to drink") may have been erroneously written as *yu* (餘, "other"). Thirdly, this [explanation] contains the following meaning:...
The two meanings are as follows: first, it refers to his ancestor, indicating that he is a descendant of him;
second, it refers to his own person, using "also" (*api*) because he is being contrasted with his forebear. Therefore, others say:
furthermore, this Sage himself possesses light and is able to drink the light of the sun and moon; thus it is said. These three preceding meanings all refer to his clan name.
To take one's clan name as a personal name; if one says "Self-Luminous" (Svayamprabha) or "Drinking Light" (Rasmi-pāna), it further incorporates his virtuous characteristics to form the name.
Thus, an ancient commentary states: "Furthermore, his own body also possesses the quality of 'drinking light.
When Jambūnada gold lies at the bottom of the water, its radiance penetrates through the surface; the light of this gold 'drinks' up all other golden lights so that they do not [shine forth]."
Furthermore, he manifested the body-light of Kāśyapa and drank up the light of that [Kāśyapa] so that it would no longer appear; thus he is named "Drinker of Light" (Pītabhāsa).

Alternatively, the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* translates this as "Great Tortoise. According to the Sanskrit original, *kacchapa* is translated as "tortoise," while *kāśyapa* is translated as "Drinker of Light" (*pītabhāsa*).
The former is merely an error in translation due to the similarity of the sounds. This is based on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Regarding the commentary on the *Aṣṭabhāga-śāstra*: if that were so, the second interpretation cited in this text—that it refers to "light-waves" (*prabhā*)—is also not correct.

This is because the word "wave" (*p'o*) is still a transliteration of the Sanskrit term, which here means "remainder" (*avaśeṣa*); therefore, it does not yet constitute the actual meaning of the word.
Consequently, all modern translations state that *Kāśyapa* is the correct Sanskrit form, and they take "Drinking Light" (*Ābhāsvara*) as its correct translation.

The name and meaning of Kāśyapa Tathāgata are identical to those here; based on this principle, the two meanings of "Drinking Light" (Yǐngguāng) derive respectively from his ancestry and from his physical body.
That which is stated in the text as "thus" (ěr) is mostly a scribal error from later transcriptions.
Next follows the explanation of the names; that the initial names differ is likely due to variations between the sutras and the śāstras.
Because he emerged from it; the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (付法傳) also briefly clarifies its origins.
Although the name of that tree has not yet been translated [into Chinese], ancient commentators all say that because he was born beneath this tree, he was named Piṇḍola-bhadra (畢鉢羅童子).
Others say his parents prayed to the heavenly deities, whereupon a Brahmā descended to take birth [in their womb], as is explained at length in other sūtras. This should indeed be the *Dharmapada*.
This is because the *āgama* (transmission) is also called a *sūtra*. Such differences cannot yet be definitively determined.
The next phrase explains its title; as for this name, it has not yet been seen translated [into Chinese].
Since a "village" (*grāma*) refers to a place where many people dwell together, the reason he alone bears this title is that his virtue is so holy and sublime that he is revered by the world.

Although there are many meanings above, they all pertain to the explanation of Śākyamuni’s name;

therefore, although "Mahā" was mentioned first, the current explanation proceeds from the pair [of names] to reveal its three meanings of the true and the conventional. Now, based on other texts, the explanation of "Great" possesses ten meanings. Why is it that the meaning of this current passage specifically possesses these ten?

This is as explained in Danqiu’s *Commentary on the Attainment of Buddhahood*, where the passage praising Śāriputra’s great wisdom clarifies that there are ten aspects of the "Great Meaning.

sixth, the greatness of authorization; seventh, the greatness of stage; eighth, the greatness of compilation; ninth, the greatness of upholding the Dharma; tenth, the greatness of compassion.

Since these ten meanings are clearly distinguished, as for the fact that three among them do not establish the designation "great" within the text, it may be due to abbreviation, omission, or because they follow the pattern of the others.
This is because one knows it through reflection; reflect upon it, reflect upon it! Thus, among the ten meanings, there are essentially only two:
namely, name (nāman) and virtuous conduct (guṇa), as briefly discussed previously. Within virtuous conduct, there are again essentially only two:

namely, selection and excellence (viśeṣa-śobhā), which are also manifestation (vyakti) and negation-indication (pratiṣedha-vyañjana). If this is so, then among the nine [meanings], one is selection, manifestation, and negation, while the other eight are...
"Beauty" means manifestation and expression. If this were the case, then the fourth textual unit should properly be placed at the very beginning of the ninth;
doing so would accord with its sequence. As for the remaining eight, they all manifest beauty and naturally follow their own order; once this is understood, there is no need to move them further.

Next, we shall now follow the text to provide an exegesis. First, regarding the explanation of renunciation (*tyāga*), there are two parts: first, clarifying the characteristics of renunciation; second, concluding by correlating the names.
Regarding the first, the clarification of the three types of renunciation, there are three distinct sections, each of which first clarifies that which is renounced and concludes with a summary.

Within the first section, there is first the heading on "great wealth," followed by the citation of a sutra to explain its characteristics. Within that, there is first a praise of his family and kinsmen, briefly clarifying the greatness [of his lineage].
The reason why the affairs of wealth cause one to involve their entire clan and kin is that they are all matters resulting from what has been relinquished.

The names of the sixteen great kingdoms appear in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra*, the *Rājāvavādaka Sūtra*, and various other scriptures; as they are numerous, I shall not describe them here. The *Dharmatrāta-parivarta* (付法藏) explains the essentials of household affairs in detail below.

To summarize, these do not go beyond the "reliant" (*niśraya*) and the "supported" (*adhiṣṭhāna*). By citing the causes, the manifestations of the fruits can be investigated; as for the name "Gold," it is as follows:
"Floating and so forth" refers here to superior gold (*suvarṇa*). Regarding the *yojana* and other measures, the smallest is sixteen [units];
