As for that which already exists, whether it is identical to or different from the Buddha—while we may discuss its existence, we cannot discuss its identity. Desire, hatred, and pride are the three fundamental poisons of affliction (*kleśa*).
This is the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Next, the citation of scriptural evidence refers to the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Awakening of Faith).

The first phrase praises the mind, which is both wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*). The following two phrases praise the body, specifically praising the virtue of its observance of the precepts.

Thus, the treatise states that the thirty-two marks have no distinct causes other than the attainment of purity through the observance of the precepts; this praises the merit of his compassion. He regards all things as he does himself.
This also praises the excellence of their primary retribution (*vipāka*), which arises from the correct perception of the environment;

thus, the secondary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*) that serves as their support is entirely brought about by the accumulation of superior karma over a long period. As for "Golden Lady," her wife’s body was identical in color to gold because she had previously offered golden beads to the Buddha.
Although they were husband and wife, they were entirely free from desire; from the very moment they were first united, they...
They made a pact, saying: "In this room there is now only one bed; you shall sleep while I practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), and if you fall asleep, I shall practice walking meditation.
Later, during the middle watch of the night, as his wife slept with her hand hanging down from the edge of the bed, a venomous snake intended to bite her hand.
Kāśyapa wrapped her hand in his robe and lifted it onto the bed; the wife woke up in a startle.

And he rebuked him, saying, "We originally made a vow together; why have you deceived me? Kāśyapa explained everything in detail and showed him the snake, whereupon his wife’s mind was finally enlightened.
Next, it can be understood that she abandoned the subtle for the coarse. Finally, the summary concludes by clarifying the three things she was able to renounce:
first, she renounced her family inheritance as one who has severed worldly ties; second, she renounced her rare and beloved wife; third, she renounced her precious bedding. These are all...
Because these three matters are extremely difficult such that ordinary people cannot endure them yet he was able to accomplish them, there is no one in the world who can match or equal him.
Because he was able to do these things while the world would rather lose their lives than ever be willing to abandon them, his greatness is manifest.
This meaning collectively reveals the depth of his resolve for the Way; therefore, he is worthy of praise.

Next, regarding the "reception of the great," it is so named because one receives [the teachings] by renouncing them before the [Teacher]. Although there is "equanimity" (*upekṣā*) in the world, this is distinct from that because it pertains to a different realm;

therefore, the Teacher is clearly identified as the one who bestows this equanimity upon oneself. Regarding the perception of the Teacher as one's own teacher: the Buddha is indeed one’s teacher because he has bestowed [the teachings] upon oneself.
As for the stūpa, it is the place where the Buddha’s body relies; as for the robes, they are the garments worn by the Buddha’s body. Therefore, with respect to the Buddha—
One should always regard the robe as the body of the Buddha; by venerating it in this way, one can generate great merit for both oneself and others.
Furthermore, it is capable of receiving what is bestowed by Great Beings. Moreover, among the robes received by Great Sages, this is rare and unique;
thus it is called "Great. From the passage beginning with "from the disciples of the Buddha" downward, there are one and a half lines of text [composed by] two former worthies.
Furthermore, you have ordered that it be moved and placed within the "Great Text" (dàwén) of the subsequent section;

however, your intention was likely to place it there because the "Great Section" is broad and expansive, thereby manifesting its status in contrast to the various disciples. This, however, is entirely untenable for two reasons:

first, you do not understand the structural flow of the text; second, you have missed its essential purport. Why is this? Because this [passage] first simplifies its name, while the subsequent text clarifies it.

Regarding their positions and stages (*bhūmi*), since the names and locations differ, the meanings of "distinguishing" (*jian*) and "excellence" (*mei*) are distinct. Where there is similarity, one distinguishes the difference;

where there is nothing [to distinguish], it reveals existence. How could these be considered of the same class? If one insists that what is distinguished must be manifest, then even that which is "immediate" (*ji*) would become "absolute" (*jue*);
therefore, this is untenable. The *Chengfo shu* clarifies that among the ten greats, the seventh is simply named "Great Disciple" (*dizi da*), meaning "great" in relation to all other disciples.

It is called "Great" (*mahā*) because it is the greatest among [the ten powers]; this is also to manifest its wisdom as being the greatest in contrast to the wisdom of the various disciples, and thus it alone is named "Great.

Furthermore, while this is a manifestation rather than an exclusion, it is not a case of identical names. However, the essential purpose of establishing "Great" lies solely in exclusion and manifestation:
within the ten [powers], the first one’s meaning encompasses both exclusion and manifestation, whereas the second excludes the remaining eight.

This merely clarifies that if one follows the underlying intent, it should be placed before the major section on "Abandoning" at the very beginning; if one follows the meaning of "awakening to the principles," there is no fixed position as one attains it accordingly;
and if one were to move it within the major section on "Positions," there would be three faults: first, it would not be of the same category; second, it would lose its essential purpose;
and third, the number would be insufficient, as has already been clarified previously. Therefore, this [placement] is entirely unacceptable; we shall now adopt it as follows.
To distinguish this from others, this single name was established; it not only avoids the three aforementioned faults but also possesses three virtues—reflect on this, reflect on this!
In the text, the term "most eminent" explains the meaning of being able to distinguish [himself], precisely because his virtue and reputation were the highest.
Next, regarding "Great Practice" (*mahācaryā*): it is so called because it is the highest among all forms of practice. What constitutes this practice? Why is it called "Great Practice"?
It refers to the twelve ascetic practices (*dhūta*), which are able to eliminate faults and manifest virtues; because they advance oneself and benefit others, they are called "practice.

Since even practicing them for a short time is difficult, how much more so to practice them constantly throughout one's entire life? To find contentment within such practice—is this not truly "great"?
Because the Confucians regard the Way of Filial Piety as supreme, Kong Anguo’s commentary on the *Classic of Filial Piety* states: "Filial piety is the highest conduct of humanity.
Now, in Buddhism, since the dhūta practices are the highest conduct for transcending the world, they are considered the greatest.

Next, regarding "seal of approval" (*anumodanā*), this refers to the Buddha’s definitive praise and authorization of the various merits of Kāśyapa before the assembly. Within this [category], there is...
Third, first it clarifies what was approved by the Buddha; next, it clarifies Kāśyapa’s recounting of what the Buddha approved;
third, it concludes by summarizing these two as "great. Within the first [section], there are three parts: first, the individual approval and praise of his long-standing practice of *dhūta*;
next, the general praise of his manifested merits, which are all identical to those of the Buddha; and finally, the monks’ hearing [of this] and their subsequent praise of his past [conduct].

Because he shares with the Buddha a common beginning, as explained in the text, the following section clarifies how they manifest identical meritorious qualities. Within this, there are three parts: first, the manifestation of the assembly's pride;
second, the Buddha’s command for them to sit together in order to eliminate that pride—wherein Kāśyapa, fearing the increase of suspicion, did not immediately sit;
and third, the extensive praise of his merits in order to completely dispel all suspicion. This initial part proceeds from two matters, or alternatively, from three.
This is because one conceives pride by grasping at these as being superior to others; the following extensive description of virtues is precisely intended to eliminate such pride.

There are six sections: first, the four dhyānas; next, compassion and loving-kindness; third, the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*); fourth, the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*); fifth, the five concentrations (*samādhi*);

and sixth, a general summary of all mundane and supramundane states, which are identical in their initial foundation. Regarding the first—the four dhyānas—these refer solely to the fundamental four dhyānas, from which both the mundane and supramundane arise.

Among these, the four divine abidings (*ṛddhipāda*) are simply the concentrations of the four bases of psychic power; because their function is subtle and unfathomable, they are called "divine" (*ṛddhi*);

because their transformations are manifold and unrestricted, they are called "formless" (*arūpa*); because they can universally know all things, they are called "immeasurable mind" (*apramāṇa-citta*);
and because their untainted (*anāsrava*) merits are perfected, they are "pure. They are able to transform the tainted (*sāsrava*) so that it attains the untainted.
Therefore, for one who is non-retrogressive and possesses the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the four dhyānas follow in their usual order; first, they attain certainty regarding four dharmas:
namely, having already realized all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), they possess the knowledge that can definitively discern all conventional truths (*saṃvṛtisatya*);
wisdom (*prajñā*) can definitively resolve the principles of all phenomena (*dharmatā*); and ethical discipline (*śīla*) can either restrain or perform all that is wholesome or unwholesome. This...
Regarding the four dharmas, because they are all realized to the ultimate degree, they are called "fixed" (*niyata*).
Since this is the sixth [section], everything supramundane is equal to this; that is, it is the state of an Arhat free from doubt.

The passage beginning with "The Bhikṣus" (the Buddha’s citation below) is the third [section], which describes past causes in order to eliminate doubts. Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying the assembly at that time.
Pride has been removed, yet there may still be doubt. Previously, pride arose because his mind and demeanor were not reverent;
now, that his hair stands on end and his heart is struck with awe, it is clear that pride of mind and demeanor has been removed and he is now respectful. Yet, there is still doubt as to why:

"If merely recounting his merits were sufficient to startle the assembly and remove their pride, why was it necessary to command him to sit together? Therefore, the Buddha immediately proceeded to cite further precedents.
This is because, in order to eliminate these delusions, this illumination is not merely a direct result of the present, but is also identical to past causes.
How is its nature clarified? It is known to be so by referring to the concluding text later on. It is precisely because of this doubt that there is this further explanation;
otherwise, it would not accord with the concluding text. The Master said: "Mendhaka is the crown of the head."

Regarding the birth of the King: the *Ekottarika-āgama* states that when Kāśyapa heard heavenly beings call the Buddha the "Teacher of Gods and Men," he rose, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said, "The Buddha is my teacher;
I am his disciple. This is the second section. Herein, Kāśyapa describes three matters for which the Buddha gave his approval, in order to shatter the arrogance of the various *nirgranthas*.
First, it concerns the Threefold Training (*tri-śikṣā*), which possesses the principle of daily renewal.
The next two [points] refer to the great merits of the Buddha previously explained; that is, these six kinds.
This is because the Sage does not bestow [merit] privately upon himself, but accords only with what is real; it is for this reason that it is so. The final summary states:

"If there are such vast and great merits, they constitute a great praise and approval by the Great Person, the Buddha. It is on account of these three meanings that this is the Buddha’s seal of approval (*buddha-mudrā*).
It is "great.

Regarding the greatness of the successive stages (*krama*), it should here differ from what preceded; that is to say, within the Buddha-dharma, this refers to the ground of functional office (*adhikāra-bhūmi*) rather than the ground of self-realization (*svasaṃvedana-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, while the former [section] treated the essence (*tattva*), this treats the function (*vṛtti*); therefore, among these, it is "great."
This is due to the latter two matters. The *Chengfo shu* (Commentary on the Attainment of Buddhahood) states:

"Regarding the term 'great disciples' (*mahāśrāvaka*), they are called such because they are the elders among the assembly of *śrāvakas*, because they uphold the Dharma, and because they serve as objects of reliance; it is by virtue of these three meanings that they are termed 'great disciples.
Regarding the 'four great disciples,' [they are] Kāśyapa, Rāhula, Piṇḍola-bharadvāja, and Kuṇḍopadhānīya; this is according to the traditional explanation."

According to what is clarified in Xuanzang’s new translation of the *Ārya-Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* (specifically the section on the Arhats’ Praise of Nandika and the Record of the Dharma’s Abiding), the Buddha commanded sixteen great Arhats to protect the Buddha-dharma;
the first four among them are included within this group, though I have not yet had the opportunity to correlate them in detail.
Among these, they are further distinguished as "Great" ones, whereas other individuals merely protect the Dharma under the leadership of Kāśyapa.
Because they uphold the Tathāgata’s robe and attend upon the future Buddha, they are the greatest; yet the text simply states "the four great disciples" without specifying the basis for this.

We know they are those four either because they are the very ones from the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" who, through the turning of the wheel of Prajñā, taught others—these same four who heard the Dharma and attained realization, being the foremost among them—or perhaps it refers directly to these four here. However...
Among the two sets of four, one refers to the present and the second to after his parinirvāṇa; since he is the greatest in both of these, the meaning is likewise applicable.

However, in the *Chengfo Shu* (Commentary on Attaining Buddhahood), when praising Śāriputra’s greatness through ten points, the seventh is titled "The Greatest Among All Disciples," which is identical to this [text].
It simply lacks the final two matters—the robe and the seat—regarding their similarities and differences.

Why is it that in the former case wisdom is revealed through the person, while here the rank is revealed through the person? It is for this reason that they differ. To summarize the greatness of this rank:
first, one briefly clarifies receiving the Buddha’s entrustment; next, one transmits the Dharma and appoints successors;

while the Buddha is present, one manifests the capacity to uphold the fundamental framework; after his extinction, one secretly acts as a guardian. Abiding in these four matters constitutes the office of the position.
In this land, people possess nothing at all; even if they do have something, it is not complete. Therefore, its status is great. Next, to clarify the compilers:
the Great Sage, at that time, spoke various teachings according to the capacities of his audience, which differed from one another.

Yet, he was able to categorize and classify them into three or four essentials; hence it is said they were "compiled. Within this, there are three parts: first, a general discussion; second, a specific analysis.

The third section, the conclusion of the treatise, reveals its greatness; this itself has three parts: first, raising the heading to indicate the collection; second, correctly revealing what is collected;

and third, concluding by manifesting its merit—this is the "Possession of Many Trees. Although the specific source from which this is drawn has not yet been seen, it must certainly have scriptural authority.
Some say that the tree possesses the function of providing shelter, used here to symbolize the three councils (*saṃgīti*).
The *piṭaka* exists for the sake of benefit. If that is so, why must it consist of these four? This remains to be examined.
Now, it is said that the bark and leaves of this tree are the very materials used for transcribing the teachings in that region, just as paper and silk are used here in our own land;
therefore, their production here signifies the compilation and circulation of the holy instructions. Since those instructions consist of four parts, they are further [classified accordingly].
Because they are expressed by means of the number four, there are four;
yet since four is but one among the three, why not express those three directly to include the four, rather than expressing them indirectly through four and omitting the remaining two?
However, because these four are the basis for the remaining two and were also spoken first, following the basis and the beginning—namely...
It is summarized and represented by taking the very last [section]; this lacks the aforementioned faults, yet it is difficult to believe and hard to comprehend.

Next, citing the Preface by Sengzhao, he correctly clarifies what was compiled: first, he clarifies the Tripiṭaka, and next, he clarifies the Four Āgamas. Within the former, there are again three parts:

first, a general clarification of the reasons for preaching the Three; second, the actual clarification of the Three; and third, the conclusion that they constitute the Three. This is the "Extended" [version].
This is the preface to the Āgama Sūtras. The first two lines clarify silence; the subsequent two lines clarify speech. One remains silent because one has personally realized the ultimate principle;
one speaks out of compassion for those who have not yet realized it. Here, "silence" refers to the absence of words, while "bringing forth the teaching" refers to the initiation of speech.

This correctly raises the concept of "no-speech" to elucidate the nature of speech. Although that which is spoken is manifold, it essentially rests upon three points; it is not that the guarding of the mind is neglected.
Regarding the body and speech, these constitute the seven branches; regarding good and evil in terms of cause and effect, there are three for each;

"subtle and profound" refers to nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), meaning the nature and characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*). The preceding section establishes the sequence of these three meanings; what follows below is the conclusion and demonstration of those three names in relation to their respective entities:

"Precept" (*śīla*) corresponds to the aforementioned prohibitions and rules; "Concentration" (*samādhi*) corresponds to the aforementioned sūtras; "Wisdom" (*prajñā*) corresponds to the aforementioned... [text fragment].
The definition of "explanatory wisdom" (*vyutpatti-jñāna*) refers to the *Abhidharma*, which is the aforementioned "Dharma-characteristics" (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). This has been stated specifically;
however, in a general discussion, each [of the three baskets] possesses all three meanings. Below, this text specifically clarifies the meaning of the four Āgamas within the Sūtra-piṭaka.

Although the aforementioned introduction also contains an introduction to the four [baskets], it does not mention what is explained therein; therefore, that is set aside here to manifest this [specific point].
"Existence" (*sāṃ*) refers to the fact that the causes and effects of the three periods of time are all far-reaching; thus, it refutes all heterodox and deviant views.

"Profound meaning" (*gambhīrārtha*) refers to the meaning of the two truths and the four truths. These are discussed both specifically and generally, as each clearly elucidates the four truths because this is the Tripitaka Teaching.
Such circulation of these three and four [truths] throughout the world is due to their respective powers. Below, the specific and the general are clarified.
Regarding the discussion of Kāśyapa’s distinctness: although there were three individuals, Kāśyapa was the principal among the three essentials;

therefore, it is said that he presided over the compilation and that the Great Dharma thus compiled brought about great benefit. Furthermore, he served as their leader for these three reasons, and for this reason he is called "Great.
As for why he was the leader: it was because he was the first to receive the entrustment to succeed the Buddha in his place. However, the general compilation...

Regarding the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, why are the Three Piṭakas mentioned separately? It is because the Mahāyāna is common to all Bodhisattvas and is not restricted solely to Kāśyapa;

therefore, for now, we shall speak according to the specific [Hīnayāna] tradition. Furthermore, the meaning of the compilation (saṃgīti) is vast and extensive, and it is not the primary essential point here; thus, I have merely provided a rough summary.

Next, regarding the "Upholder of the Dharma," this refers to one who, after the passing of the preceding Buddha, is able to compile the teachings so they do not fall into disarray, and further, is able to maintain them so that they circulate perpetually without decline or loss;
thus, it is called "Upholder of the Dharma. The text consists of four phrases: first, clarifying his capacity to uphold;
second, explaining the person’s capability to uphold; third, clarifying the maintenance of one's own portion of the teaching; and fourth, concluding the section.
Therefore, this is the greatness of upholding [the Dharma]. The initial statement regarding "acting as a refuge" reveals its stage and position and clarifies its essence and function.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* asks: "How does one attain vastness and act as a refuge for the multitude? This questions the person who serves as the four refuges after [the Buddha's] passing.
"Attaining vastness" refers to the internal realization of the vast Dharma; it questions its essence. "Acting as a refuge for the multitude" refers to its function.

To stop here is merely to inquire about his external utility for benefiting others. Now, since Kāśyapa has already attained the ultimate fruit, he belongs to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna as a person of the fourth reliance (*caturtha-āśraya-pudgala*).
In the Mahāyāna, this corresponds to the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*), reaching the limit of *Samyaksambodhi*, because such a person is next in line to occupy the seat of a Buddha.
Therefore, the Tathāgata subsequently cites the Buddha’s praise to explain the reason for his ability to uphold [the Dharma], which is due to his virtuous conduct.
Therefore, it is said: "It is man who can broaden the Way, not the Way that broadens man. This applies even to Confucian scholars, let alone to the Awakened One.
Thus, only those who possess virtuous conduct are capable of such a thing. As for the statement that [the Dharma] may abide for a long time:

from the initial reception of the Buddha’s entrustment until his final entry into *parinirvāṇa* after transmitting the robe, although there were many powers at work, he remained its master; therefore, he maintained it.

Regarding the merit of those who say that the Dharma was transmitted and the robe bestowed, or who say that the Dharma was transmitted to Ānanda and the robe bestowed upon the Compassionate One (Maitreya):
this interpretation is incorrect, for both [the transmission of the Dharma and the robe] occurred together with the Compassionate One. How is this clarified?

According to the *Sūtra on the Attainment of Buddhahood*, after Maitreya has attained the Way in the future and finished preaching the Dharma in three assemblies, he will lead the great multitude to Mount Kukkuṭapāda and arrive at Kāśyapa.
By means of various skillful expedients, he awakened him; Kāśyapa arose from his meditative concentration, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and offered his robe to the Buddha.
After Maitreya World-Honored One had praised Kāśyapa in various ways, he then accepted the robe and performed eighteen miraculous transformations.
He entered the Lapis Lazuli Cave and, with a Brahma-voice, recited the twelve divisions of the Sūtras of Śākyamuni and paid homage.
The Buddha returned to his original place, emitting fire from his body and entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; thus it is clear that these two matters both reside within the Compassionate Honored One.
The reason for transmitting these two is to manifest that his entry into compassion is infinite in its form, voice, and benefits. Why is this?
Clothing is the adornment of the physical body (*rūpakāya*), which signifies what is manifested from the *dharmakāya*; thus, it is the *dharmakāya* itself.
The benefit of this is the Dharma; as it is the teaching through sound arising from Prajñā, it signifies the benefit of being able to give birth to Prajñā.
These two both arise based on Great Compassion, which signifies the benefit of liberation. "Transmission" signifies the benefit of the three virtues.
The self-benefit and benefit-of-others of all Buddhas of the three periods of time reside solely in this, O Śākyamuni Buddha.

Since it has already been transmitted and shown, and will likewise be so in the future, it is therefore called "transmission" (den); this is the second [meaning], which is also the third. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
"I have placed my children within the secret treasury, and I myself also dwell therein. This is precisely that meaning.

Although the instructions of the Supreme Sage are distant, even when we strive to look up to them through concrete matters, they will likely reach such a state. Regarding the term "conclusion" (ketsu), there is... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
The Great Virtuous One is able to uphold the Dharma entrusted by the Great Being and perform great benefit; for this reason, he is the greatest among those who uphold the Dharma.
From here on, the text does not establish specific titles; the Master says that the "Great Intent of Compassion" refers to the pity and protection found within the text.
Regarding the meaning of "protection" (*rakṣā*): if we follow the example of the various devas, who give rise to extreme affection and longing, it may also be called "great benefit.
When the gods in the heavens preach the Dharma, they honor those above and take pity on those below; this is precisely what constitutes the matter of benefiting others.

Because the devas give rise to such profound admiration, sentient beings obtain its benefits. Thus, they are able to benefit both humans and devas, enabling them to attain both worldly and supramundane [attainments].
The interim benefit is its greatness. In the text, the character is sometimes written as "cave" (kū) and sometimes as "secret" (mitsu).

If it is written as "cave," it refers to the hidden place and belongs to the end of the preceding phrase. If it is written as "secret," it refers to his supernatural power of traveling incognito such that others cannot know;
this belongs to the beginning of the following phrase. Although both meanings are logically possible, observing the context, it seems more appropriate to take it as "secret. (Note says...)

The phrase "it is said" clarifies that the preceding text contains multiple meanings as well as the remaining implications of the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold standards of truth), which have been briefly explained above.

Regarding the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*, the Master says: "Name and the faculties of sensation and perception constitute the Worldly (*loka*) [standard]; the three and four great elements constitute the Personal (*puruṣa*) [standard];

because hearing the name and observing the conduct are both wholesome, this constitutes the third; and the fifth, the seal of approval, constitutes the Therapeutic (*prātipakṣika*) stage, which is associated with compassion."

This is because one enters the stage of the "Entrance through the Principle" (*li-ru*) by means of seeing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Thus, both the "Gathering of Dharmas" (*ji-fa*) and the "Upholding of Dharmas" (*chi-fa*) involve those who have entered this stage.

Some say that within the "Explanation of the Greatness" (*shi-da-zhong*), the first [section] on the Four *Siddhāntas* concerns the worldly (*loka-vyavahāra*); that which follows "at Vaṃśa" concerns the person-oriented (*pudgala-artha*); that which serves as "confirmation" (*anumodana*) concerns the remedial (*pratikāra*);
and from the section on "the Great" (*da*) onwards, all concern the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Now, regarding these textual meanings, I fear it may not be so. Why? Because...

In principle, this cannot yet be accepted, as the preceding and following passages would otherwise contradict one another. Now, it is clarified that there are ten great meanings, as previously explained.
First, within the "Greatness of the Spiritual Lineage" (*gotra-mahattva*), the inclusion of names and titles refers to the worldly dharma of the world-realm (*loka-dhātu*).

The two greats of "Abandoning" and "Receiving" represent the ultimate excellence of generating the wholesome; thus, they constitute the "human" aspect (*puruṣa*) to distinguish them from those of the same name. Furthermore, "conduct" (*caryā*) eliminates the twelve kinds of evil.
The seal of approval (*anujñā*) removes all forms of contempt; since these three represent the ultimate destruction of evil, they are all positions of antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Because the four [stages] from "Great" downwards internally attain the Great Essence and externally possess Great Function, they are all the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha*).

The meaning of the text is very clear; why should there be confusion? The passage distinguishing them should appear before the section on "Renunciation" (*tyāga*); it is precisely for this reason that it is placed here.

At the beginning of this composition, this intention was not apparent; it was only after [the text] had been completed that it became necessary. Therefore, students should apply themselves deeply to its meaning.

Although there are ten essential points regarding the Great Meaning, they are summarized in these four types of discourse: because they accord with the great clans of the world, they can greatly produce goodness;
because they can greatly remedy evil, they can greatly awaken one to the Path. Thus, while there are ten applications, they possess these four great causes.
It is called "Great" (Mahā) because it is based upon conditions (*pratyaya*).
Next, regarding the classification by teaching (*yāna*), this specifically clarifies the meaning of the greatness of this sutra.

To discuss the teaching directly in terms of *dhūta* (ascetic practices) is precisely the practice of the Great Vehicle (*mahācaryā*) among the ten preceding meanings; it explains the meaning of "counteractive" (*pratipakṣa*) among the four meanings to manifest this [sutra].
Regarding the causes and conditions of this sutra: the reason for summarizing these into one is that their meaning is most essential and convenient.
Why is this so? Because among all dharmas, practice (*caryā*) is supreme; how much more so is the *dhūta* practice, which is even more distinguished—let alone when compared to inferior things.
Therefore, because it is the most essential and convenient, it is specifically summarized here; furthermore, it subsumes everything. When worldly people merely see something unusual...

Regarding the practice that is called the Path, one should fortunately examine this explanation to discern its rightness and wrongness; furthermore, there are four distinctions based on the Four Teachings.

First, within the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) Teaching, there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Regarding the initial part, it should be stated that "according to the teaching" means distinguishing the teaching by means of the *dhūta* (ascetic) practices.
First, the enumeration of the twelve kinds of faults is clearly explained, which simultaneously presents two meanings.
That is to say: for what reason is this used as the basis for clarification? Because it is able to contemplate faults. For what reason are there twelve based on the twelve faults?

Because they are the most profound and extensive, encompassing all things. Why are there exactly twelve? Because these twelve are that which is to be abandoned (*heya*); "abandonment" (*hāna*) is itself the act of abandoning (*prahāṇa*).

Since the object of abandonment and the act of abandonment are discussed in combination, one abandons the twelve faults. What was formerly called *dhūta* (ascetic purification) [is here explained in this way].

The new translation says *duṭo*, while the old translation says *dǒu dòu* (to shake off). The new translation says "removal and abandonment. However, "shaking off" (*dǒu dòu*) carries the meaning of vigorously tossing away dust and grime;
it is for this reason that it is used here to clarify [the practice]. The phrase "those who are fond of... and below is the subsequent explanation. Within this, there are two parts:
first, it is said that the initial section relies on objective phenomena (*vastu*), and then, from "furthermore relying on... onwards, it relies on the contemplation of the truths (*satya*). Now...

This means that, first, we shall provisionally discuss this in terms of phenomena (*vastu*), and subsequently in terms of the principles of the Truths (*satya*). Furthermore, the initial section provides a general explanation, while the subsequent section provides a specific explanation based on the teachings (*śāsana*).
Within the initial section, there are again two parts: first, a direct application to the twelve [links], and second, their condensation into three dharmas.

The former follows the latter’s requirements, which consists of three distinct parts. Generally speaking, in explaining these twelve, each should include a heading (*uddāna*), an interrogative inquiry (*praśna*), an explanation (*vyākhyāna*), and a conclusion (*nigamana*).
Exhausting the full extent of their enumeration, [the text] first addresses the two types of robes; the second clarifies that one should not keep fine ones.

Why does it designate this [category] rather than that? The commentator explains: "Fine [robes] have three faults, whereas worn-out [robes] have none. Therefore, for this reason, it designates this rather than that;
this single point is precisely what enables one to remain free from these three faults. Among the five [categories], the "evil son" is omitted.
Although there are five [factors] here, they merely explain what was previously obtained: at that time, there is much fear, and this "much fear" refers precisely to these five.
The others are easy to understand and thus are not explained; they can be grasped by means of one's own intellect. Furthermore, they are not numerous, but only three.

Next, the reason is questioned three times, and the reasons are explained threefold because of three faults. Fourthly, it is concluded: for this reason, they are not many, but only three; therefore, it is so.

There is no fault [in this]. Regarding the first of the six types of alms-seeking, there are also three faults: it obstructs the right path, leads to much contradiction, and causes distress to oneself and others.
For this reason, one begs; by begging, one immediately abandons the aforementioned three faults. Next, the sequential begging (sāvadāna-piṇḍapāta) should be explained, but the text is missing.
This also has three faults: it is uneven, it causes others to suspect [one of ulterior motives], and it breaks one's own greed.
Because of the mind, one is able to abandon [faults] in succession. Next, regarding eating at a single sitting (*ekāsanika*), there should also be three points;

however, since there are only two, there is still the fault of being cumbersome. One is the abandonment of the three [faults]. Third, clarifying moderation (*mātrajñatā*) means causing one to attain the middle way;
having much has three faults, having little has one fault, and the middle way abandons the former four. One bowl also abandons three faults; this is the text.
Since the emergence of these two is also accompanied by weariness and toil, "one" is thus distinct from "three. Not drinking the gruel makes it easy to see;
next, regarding the four abodes, the first two are free from craving, the third is free from sorrow, and the fourth is free from both faults—it is also the freedom from delusion.
Knowing these twelve [abodes] as being free from immeasurable faults, one who is free from these twelve is free from all faults. Thus it is said.
Because one knows these various faults, one practices the twelve [precepts] to depart from them. Next, these are summarized into three;
the reason for this summary is twofold: first, to clarify the essentials, for among the twelve essentials, there are only these three dharmas;
second, to establish the essential practices for the three subsequent teachings, namely clothing, food, and dwelling. These three are all...
The fault of depending [on the body] is that the dependent itself—namely, the body—is entirely due to a failure to comprehend the body.
If one can deeply penetrate the defects of the body, then one will be able to abandon them all. Laozi said: "The reason I have great affliction is that I have a body;
if I had no body, what affliction would I have? These words are close to the truth, yet the cause of that existence or non-existence lies with him [the practitioner].
This is not yet all. What has been discussed above has merely been an examination of detachment within the context of worldly affairs;

however, as various sacred teachings differ in their details, they have not yet been fully reconciled or understood. From here on, we shall discuss detachment in terms of the practice of the True Path.
Why is this? Although the previous section clarified the capacity for detachment from all faults, that which is capable of detaching itself was not yet considered truly real.
If one follows the path of correctness, one will merely undergo toil and hardship that ultimately proves useless;

therefore, by summarizing the aforementioned twelve factors of detachment (*vairāgya*) to clarify the Four Truths and the factors of the Path (*mārga*), it becomes clear that these factors of detachment themselves constitute a great affliction and are thus objects to be abandoned.
The path itself is what brings about detachment; only in this way does one truly shake off and forever leave behind all faults and calamities.

Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying the avoidance of faults by means of the method regarding food; second, using that as an analogy to illustrate the remaining two. Within the first part, there are three sections:
first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Regarding the first [heading], the word "for now" (*tāvat*) indicates that it is not yet exhaustive.
Among the twelve [categories], we first clarify the very first one; among the three dharmas, we first address the method regarding food, specifically within the context of the method regarding food.

Within these six, the term "for now" (*qiàn*) is used because alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*) is first discussed in contrast to the others. The two characters "shaking off" (*dǒu shòu*) encompass both the agent and the object:
the "object" refers to the faults within alms-gathering, while the "agent" refers to the practice of observing them with discernment. Next, in the formal explanation, there are two parts:

first, distinguishing the characteristics; second, citing scriptural evidence. Regarding the first, the characteristics are clarified by means of the Four Noble Truths; this is why the Four Truths are employed.
Regarding the Truths (*satya*): the first two are the knowledge of faults and what is to be abandoned; the latter two are virtuous conduct and that which is capable of abandoning.
Among these, the former two constitute the mundane cause and effect, while the latter two constitute the supramundane cause and effect.
Therefore, there are four. Since these four are precisely the mundane and supramundane causes and effects, all meanings subsumed within the categories of subject and object are encompassed therein.

If one fully understands its essential outline, the explanation is already complete; otherwise, it would be overly prolix. Within this, there are four distinctions. First, regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*):

even a single act of begging for alms encompasses the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). These three realms do not transcend the primary and secondary environments, all of which are results of karmic maturation (*vipāka-phala*).

Because they constantly oppress and scrutinize [the practitioner], and because they are real and not false, they are called the Truth of Suffering. Next, the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is explained.

The Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) consists of the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), which—when fully enumerated—comprise eighty-eight, ninety-eight, or one hundred and eight afflictions, as explained in detail in the preceding text.
Here, the text briefly clarifies that even within a single act of begging for alms, such afflictions are present and are capable of summoning the aforementioned fruits of suffering;
because they are real and not false, it is called the Truth of Origination. First, there is the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
The first is called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because it erroneously conceives of a self within the body. Next is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*);

because one adheres to either of the two extremes—existence or non-existence—it is a view of extremes. Next is the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), because one erroneously regards what is not a cause as a cause.
Next is the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), because one erroneously regards what is not a fruit as a fruit. Finally is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which is like the preceding four.

All these types are erroneous and not correct; because they are mistaken calculations taken to be true, among the subsequent five [afflictions], joy gives rise to delusion, greed and hatred arise from craving, the sense of "I can see" is pride, and being rebuked yet unable to resolve it constitutes doubt.

While the *Dṛṣṭimārga* (Path of Seeing) consists of eighty-eight [afflictions] and the *Bhāvanāmārga* (Path of Cultivation) adds nineteen, with eighteen plus ten further *paryavasthānas* (envelopments) totaling one hundred and eight, the text here is abbreviated and concerns itself only with the Path of Seeing.

The fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that constitute the origin (*samudaya*) are as explained in the preceding text. These aforementioned causes and effects—the great afflictions—are all things to be shaken off and eliminated.
What follows below correctly clarifies the means by which they are shaken off and eliminated: namely, the sevenfold path of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
This very path is able to shake off and eliminate those afflictions of suffering and its origin that are not the Path; it is certain that [it will do so].

Because it is empty, it is called the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). Within this, the first section clarifies the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), beginning with the objects and followed by the contemplation.

First, regarding the distinct characteristics of the objects: since the consciousness-mind, whether good or evil, is of a similar kind and flows on uninterruptedly from moment to moment, it is said to be "similar.

Next is sensation (*vedanā*), then perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and finally form (*rūpa*). All of these are called "concealed" because they are obscured by delusion and fail to realize their true nature.

From "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) through the fourth [aggregate], the text correctly clarifies contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). By realizing that the four [aggregates] are not real, one knows them to be impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;

thus, the six practices that overturn the four inversions are all preparatory stages. This is precisely the clarification of shaking off and removing the characteristics of the faults of the previous suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*).
Next, the term "consciousness" clarifies that which is capable of extinguishing [the afflictions]. The preceding section clarified the agent of extinction.

This clarifies that what is extinguished is precisely the cessation of suffering, its origin, and the path, thereby attaining extinction. Within this, first it clarifies the extinction of the cause, which is the aforementioned extinction of the origin (*samudaya*);

next, it clarifies the extinction of the fruit, which is the aforementioned extinction of suffering (*duḥkha*). These all successively clarify how each subsequent cause relates to each preceding one, with each having two meanings.

Regarding the first [the extinction of the cause], there is first an explanation according to the Dharma, followed by a single application of a simile; the explanation according to the Dharma can be understood.
The subsequent analogy of the "seed" refers to the "bondage of the seed. "Seed" carries the meaning of "germ" (*bīja*) and "cause" (*hetu*);

this is another designation used in the Noble Teachings, which is established by way of metaphor. However, because the seed can produce a fruit, its meaning is identical to that of "accumulation" (*samudaya*).

"Bondage" (*bandhana*) means to restrain the practitioner so that they do not attain autonomy; thus, the seed is itself the bondage. This is a designation based on the essential nature of the thing itself. Since [this] already exists...
Because of these two meanings, they are further analyzed to clarify the significance of "accumulation" (samudaya) and "cessation" (nirodha). "Fruit" refers to the fruit of suffering;

it is called a "fruit" because it can bind the practitioner, preventing them from attaining autonomy—it is, therefore, a bondage. Within this, the first phrase refers to the cause [of the previous section], which serves as the analogy for the following phrase.

The twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) are the actual phenomena (*dharma*); although one speaks of the cessation of the fruit, if one does not recognize it, [the meaning remains obscure].

Because it is the demarcation of the fruit (*phala*), twenty-five [factors] are further enumerated to manifest it; these are collectively termed the "outflowing" (*sāsrava*) fruits of suffering, consisting of both the primary and secondary [receptacle worlds].
This is precisely the extinction of the causes and effects of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), wherein one realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nirvāṇa of quiescence.

Because it is authentic and not false, it is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). This is the complete abandonment of all worldly afflictions, their total exhaustion, and universal pervasion.
This is indeed a thorough investigation. From the following passage onward, the Great Sūtra is cited to establish the preceding meaning.

The first four lines demonstrate that because the Four Truths are not perceived within the realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there remains the great affliction of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).

The subsequent four lines demonstrate that because one is subsequently able to perceive them, there exist the great merits of the Path and Cessation (*mārga-nirodha*). The final section concludes by using the analogy of food to clarify this point.
It should be understood that the wisdom of the remaining two contemplations (*vipaśyanā*) is precisely the method for shaking off [defilements]. However, this text is still brief;
since there are six aspects to the practice of eating (*bhojana-vidhi*), and we have treated two of them, it should be stated: "Just as it is with begging for food, so it is with the other five.

Since the wisdom of contemplation regarding the practice of eating is thus, so it is with clothing and dwellings. Therefore, this is an abbreviated treatment. As for the term "thus" (*evam*), it applies throughout the twelve [aspects].

The power and numerical sequence of each dharma are all as previously described. If one grasps this meaning, then regarding all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), one should understand and perceive them in this same way.
Otherwise, it cannot be called the cultivation of the path (*mārga-bhāvanā*). Reflect upon this:

that which takes the fetters (*saṃyojana*) as its storehouse is neither the same as the former [shallow] matters nor identical to the latter [deep] ones; this is precisely the interpretation of this teaching.
Next, the explanation of the "Pervasive" (tong) is also threefold: namely, the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion. Within the heading, the question is raised:
what are the characteristics and manifestations of this teaching? Within the explanation, there are three parts, each of which further contains three sub-sections.

First, its object is indicated; second, its practice is clarified; third, its excellence is praised. Regarding the object, it indicates the three essentials; regarding the practice, it clarifies the cultivation of the three; and regarding the praise, it extols them.

Since all things are empty, they differ from what preceded; therefore, this is established as the objective realm (*ālambana*) for contemplation.

As for the phrase "conditioning the Truth" (*tattva*), it refers to the principle of emptiness that is both the object of focus and the realization. Just as food nourishes the body, the wisdom of emptiness supports the manifestation of the principle of emptiness;
thus, it is called the "practice of food. The various virtuous practices of the three karmas are used to adorn the body of the principle; thus, they are called "clothing."

However, both merit and wisdom serve as practices and both serve as adornments; now, following worldly convention, they are explained individually, with the former alone receiving the name "practice" (*caryā*) and the latter being termed "arousing" (*utpāda*).
Next, its contemplation is clarified, which likewise consists of three parts: first, the objects of contemplation—the nature of the myriad phenomena is fundamentally empty;
second, the wisdom that contemplates—this too is entirely empty; and because the objects are empty, [the subject is likewise empty].
The wisdom of contemplation is also illusory and transformative; though it can be seen, it is ultimately unattainable, and is therefore emptiness.

This clarifies that the practice capable of detachment is itself emptiness. Next, the passage beginning with "deluded thoughts" clarifies that the practice is empty because wisdom is illusory, and thus the practice is empty.
Therefore, it says: "Deluded thoughts do not arise; the sovereign mind and its mental factors all cease to function. This is the sentence.
This explains the preceding [section] on the non-arising of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*). It explains that all evils do not arise;

it explains this non-arising by means of the single phrase "because they are unobtainable" (*anupalabdhi*), which generally establishes the former while giving rise to the latter. This is because everything is entirely unobtainable due to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Thus, there is no time when anything is not empty; all things are like illusions and transformations, quiescently non-arising. This constitutes the final establishment of the argument.

The preceding section clarifies that both the subject and the object are entirely empty. It is precisely because of this emptiness that all three are "foremost"; this serves as the introduction to what follows.
The subsequent concluding praise states that they are all foremost by virtue of being empty in general.
First is the praise for the emptiness of the objective sphere; next is the emptiness of practice; and finally is the emptiness of wisdom. Regarding the phrase "all three are foremost," it means...
The former three sections of the Tripiṭaka are not "victorious" (śreya), because they do not encompass these three matters.

First, it is clarified that since all things are identical with emptiness, there is nothing that is not a place of dwelling; likewise, there is nothing that is not an adornment; and likewise, there is nothing that is not fully understood.

Thus, all things are mutually identical (*paraspara-aviruddha*), which differs from the previous [sections] where they were not mutually identical. Although the three are the same in being one emptiness, their manifestations differ.

Regarding the conclusion for the sake of victory: hitherto, we have explained by means of the three dharmas that all are *śūnyatā* (emptiness) and can thus distance one from all faults and afflictions.
Although the phrasing is extremely concise, the meaning is complete; this is an essential summary rather than a mere abbreviation. Therefore, the conclusion states:
"The brief explanation is finished."

Next, regarding the specific [explanation] within the text, there is a heading and an exposition. As for the heading: this teaching’s subject and object possess natures and characteristics that differ from those previously mentioned;
this will be self-evident in the subsequent exposition. Within the following exposition, there are four distinct sections: first, the heading of the objective phenomena (*ālambana-dharma*);

second, the clarification of the practice; third, the elucidation of the faults to be abandoned; and fourth, the summary of their differences. The initial objective phenomena are precisely the aforementioned three.
To summarize: the distinct dharmas share the same essence as the originally existent *dharmakāya*, for it is that upon which they depend and for whose sake they exist; thus, it serves as their abode.

One cultivates the two adornments of merit and wisdom for this purpose, yet from the very first moment of the resolve, these are not yet real entities possessing the characteristics of subject and object.
Therefore, wisdom establishes the *dharmakāya* just as food sustains life; this is explained in terms of the capacity established through cultivation.

The nature and conduct (*śīla*) have two meanings: they can adorn and they can restrain. This is because conduct exists to preserve the good and eliminate the evil, just like the two functions of clothing.

Since both [nature and conduct] can adorn, "clothing" receives its designation from one specific aspect; following the logic of the preceding two passages, these two [subsequent] passages should also state "for the sake of clothing," though the two characters [for "sake"] are omitted—know this to be the case.
Now, since these three are all objects, they are collectively that upon which one relies and that which is cultivated. However...

The *dharmakāya* is fundamentally of the nature of the innate seeds (*prakṛtisthagotra*), while the other two are both of the nature of cultivated seeds (*samudānītagotra*). This is like [the distinction between] the dwelling place, the robes one wears, and the alms one begs.
Furthermore, because the substantial entities of these three are each distinct and do not merge, they are considered separate; this should be carefully examined.

Next, it is explained that the practitioner cultivates three types of practice in order to eliminate three types of faults and evils; this constitutes the non-merging of practice. Initially, it merely speaks of "removing" them.

For those whose karma is evil, what was previously described as "adornment" is actually "obscuration"; these are one and the same meaning, though for the sake of brevity they are treated separately here.

To eliminate the darkness of afflictions and delusions, one cultivates wisdom and practices the Dharma-body. In this regard, contemplating the suffering of the *rūpakāya* (form body) as being the *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body) is the third of the three types of knowledge (*traividyā*).
This also generally demonstrates the efficacy of spiritual practice; that is to say, by practicing the aforementioned...

Because the three practices can eliminate two kinds of the three paths, and since these three paths pertain both to the internal and external, although the three were previously clarified, they were not yet divided into two;
now, by dividing them into two sets of three, the meanings of "comprehensive" (*sāmānya*) and "specific" (*viśeṣa*) are established—reflect upon this.

Because [these practices] can eliminate these two, they differ from the preceding sequence and differ from what follows. Why, then, are the three [practices] of the "expedient means" (*upāya*) not mentioned? Since the holy teachings already...
There are two explanations; since the former has already been clarified several times, I shall now briefly follow the latter two.

Regarding the four points that distinguish this [section] from the preceding, the term "Middle Way" (Madhyamaka) begins with the section on *dhūta* (ascetic practices), which separately identifies the transcendence of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*).

Although the text is missing [explicit statements], the meaning must necessarily be present. Why? Because by eliminating the *pariccheda-bheda* (segmented existence), one immediately enters [the path].

The contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) eliminates the coarse delusions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges within *pariṇāmi-vedanīya-karma*; the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) eliminates the subtle delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*);

and the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*)—though their sequence differs—necessarily requires all three, for without the former two, the latter would not exist; this is why it is said so.

As for "the practitioner of suffering" (*duḥkha-cārī*), this refers to the practice of *dhūta* (ascetic purification). By relying on the three objects to cultivate the three practices, one abandons the three afflictions and shakes off the duality of subject and object.

"The meaning lies therein"—these two phrases also serve as a commentary on the preceding heading and explanation; that is, they constitute the third section, which concludes by indicating the specific distinctions.
Regarding the note "(and so forth)," it contains several essential points, a brief summary of which is provided above.

Next, regarding the Perfect [Teaching], there is also a presentation and an explanation. This teaching—whether in terms of its objects or its practices—is able to transcend that which is to be abandoned;

everything is both present and complete, as it differs from the previous distinct [teachings], and is thus called "Perfect. Within the explanation, there are four parts: first, clarifying the perfection of the object;

second, clarifying the perfection of practice; third, the perfection of transcending faults; and fourth, the conclusion on the perfection. Regarding the perfection of the object, the first phrase refers to the three [realms].
Because the One is identical to the wondrous Way, the second phrase takes the One as the Two to serve as the causes and conditions for sentient beings to give rise to understanding;
this meaning should be understood through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), and its lack of fixed direction is called the "perfectly wondrous realm. Next, regarding the perfection of practice:
one cultivates wondrous practice based on the aforementioned wondrous realm. Herein, too, the four permutations are complete; because the realm is wondrous, the practice is perfect.
It is called "perfect and wondrous practice" for this reason. All previous editions contained the words "shaking and tossing," but because later practitioners preferred brevity, these were omitted;
however, one must certainly know them, for otherwise, one would not understand that this is the cultivation of practice.

Some take this to correspond to the first phrase of the three contemplations as the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita*), while the second phrase corresponds to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). This is discussed in terms of clothing. Next, it concerns... [the contemplation of the middle].
The discourse on food is neither [one] nor [many]; this refers to the "Middle" in terms of location, while "shaking off" (抖藪) refers to the removal of extremes.
How strange! How strange! One must discern this, one must discern it! Now, regarding the expressions "one" and "all," one should know there are three levels:

the brief, which refers to the "three"; the intermediate, which refers to the "twelve"; and the extensive, which refers generally to the "ten thousand practices. In each of these, there is both "one" and "all."
This is because of the meaning [of the preceding]. This is the essential method for those who have truly renounced the world according to the meaning of this sutra;
therefore, one must understand it well. "Reflect upon it, reflect upon it"—the phrase "at the bottom of all" serves as a conclusion that distinguishes the function by departing from faults.
This is because all afflictions and calamities are themselves the wondrous Way. "That which all Buddhas practice" and so forth is below.

The fourth section concludes by distinguishing the complete from the partial through the first phrase. It praises and reveals that this is the person and dharma of one who practices the complete path, surpassing all bodhisattvas and thereby distinguishing it from the person and dharma of those who practice partially.
"Bodhisattvas" refers to those of a partial nature, while "the Buddhas above" refers to those of the complete nature.
"Pure conduct" distinguishes this from non-partial conduct that has not yet reached ultimate purity; it reveals that the conduct of the Tathāgatas above is precisely that of the perfect and wondrous.
"Exhaustive purity" (the commentary states "and so forth") clarifies that there are four meanings as previously explained;

it now reveals and manifests that the preceding three are all, in themselves, the perfect, wondrous, and absolute practice of shaking off [all defilements]. This chapter is the most essential among the gates of cultivation.
For now, this is merely a brief summary; I have not yet had the leisure to provide a detailed account.

Next, regarding the distinction between the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku): although the previous discussion concerning the Perfect Teaching (enpō-e) already reconciled the near [manifestation] with the distant [fundamental], it did not yet exhaust its potential nor reach the ultimate purport of the Sūtra;
therefore, this further explanation is provided so that its meaning may be fully realized. This section consists of two parts:

first, clarifying the five fundamental [bodies], and second, clarifying the five manifested [traces]. Furthermore, while the general clarification of the fundamental and the manifested is found in the subsequent text, each of these five [categories] is treated individually here.

Furthermore, by examining its traces, one may know its fundamental basis. That is to say, since it already possesses a fundamental basis, and these five matters are now present within its traces, one should know that it has long possessed these five matters.
The first four clarify the capacity of the fundamental basis to be detached from both the general and the specific;

the fifth clarifies what the fundamental basis is detached from internally—namely, the absence of craving for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*)—which means it has long been detached from all semblances of the Path and from grasping.

Therefore, while possessing the aforementioned four internal merits, one is externally free from defilement; this refers to the previous abandonment of the golden wife, which was due to the absence of internal craving for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).

Thus, by internally possessing the four merits and being externally able to remain undefiled, these five factors together constitute the ability to abandon that which is to be abandoned, both internally and externally.
"Fundamentally" (*ben*) means "for a long time. It simply means that one has known [the truth] for a long time, yet...

One may determine the distant and the near, and subsequently clarify their traces. Although four meanings involve five matters, some say that the first clarification of the twelve matters and the departure from the twelve errors refers to this;

we maintain that "matters" refers to the initial teaching. Although there is contemplation of the truths (*satya*), when compared to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), these are all substantial matters;
therefore, the subsequent texts refer to them as the "two truths of reality. This is precisely the meaning.

The single phrase "also desiring" (yù yù) runs through the following four sections. First, it refers to [the milk] being transformed into curd; next, it refers to the curd being transformed into cream;
the latter two cases should be understood by analogy as also possessing these four meanings and four propositions, which may be inferred from the preceding examples.
Below, regarding the practitioner: although they know its resultant virtue, they must also know its causal practice.

Since such a result is brought about by this cause, if one desires to obtain this result, one must practice this cause. Now, because the practitioner admires the result and cultivates the cause, the explanation is provided in terms of contemplation.
First, the three contemplations are clarified; next, the unification of the single mind is shown, wherein that which is abandoned and that which abandons are both contained therein. If one can...
For one who practices in this manner, how could their virtuous conduct be far from perfection? Thus, the subsequent passage states:

"One who can uphold this sutra is called one who maintains the precepts and practices *dhūta*. This is precisely the proof. If one does not properly understand the six identities (*ṣat-tathatā*), then praising such a superior person would actually fail to constitute a skillful removal of faults;
therefore, one must examine this matter with care and caution. For these various reasons, it is said [in the commentary]: "The commentary notes..."

(As stated above). In the explanation of the initial causes and conditions regarding the three Kāśyapas, there are three points, which comprise four sections: first, explaining their names and residences;
second, explaining that they were brothers and describing their activities; third, explaining how they were collectively able to abandon heterodoxy and return [to the True Dharma].

Regarding their lineage within the True Path, they are collectively called Kāśyapa; their names are the three superior ones. As for the three distinct residences where they dwell together, they are like brothers sharing a single gourd.
This explains the common saying that these three abandoned heterodoxy to return to the Right Path; it demonstrates their ability to cast away false sentiments and follow the True Way.
Thus, the three texts contain four meanings. First, in the initial section, we first explain their lineage and then point to...
The preceding section merely explains that Pindola is of the same Brahmin lineage as the ancient seers; the following explanation of his name contains three distinct points.
First, the Sanskrit term for "person" (pudgala) has three variations, likely due to differences between earlier and later translators, yet all are translated as "Pomegranate Grove" (Dāḍima-vana).
Traditional commentaries all state that he practiced the Way beneath this grove, and thus it was so named.
The current text refers to this as "Yitong" (意同), while the *Zhengfajing* (正法經) names it "Shangshi" (上時), yet neither explains its meaning.
The new translation calls it "Ulūpila," which means "Papaya" (*kapittha*), though it does not mention a grove.
The commentary states that upon his chest there arose a tumor shaped like a papaya; furthermore, because he lived near a pond where there was a dragon also named "Papaya," [he was so called].
He was given this name because of his voice; the source for this meaning has not yet been found, so for now it is explained according to the traditional interpretation.
As for *Nadi*, this text is out of order; according to the sūtra, it should follow *Gayā*. The new translation provides the correct Sanskrit as *Nadika*, which is the name of a river;
its meaning will appear later. Next, regarding the explanation of *Gayā* in the text, there appears to be an error that should be corrected.

It is called "Cloud" (Yun), it is also called "Elephant" (Xiang), and it is also called "City" (Cheng). The commentary explains that "Elephant" is the name of a mountain, namely Mount Elephant Head (Xiangtou Shan).

As for "City," there was a city near this mountain; therefore, it is called Elephant Head City (Xiangtou Cheng). Since "Elephant" is a term from this region [of China], one should not further say "also" (yi) in reference to it.
Thus, the Correct Text states: "The former 'Elephant' and 'Jiang'—these three are all terms from this regional dialect. According to this...

In the *Caigu jing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect), it is said that these three individuals all practiced the Way near a riverbank. The Buddha employed his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to transform them and lead them into the Dharma;
they were subsequently given distinct names based on their respective circumstances, hence the differences such as "Pomegranate River" (*Dūguā shān*).
When it says they "practiced the Way," it refers to their former heterodox paths. Furthermore, when it mentions "their families," it clarifies that they were originally people of this very country.
The following commentary explains the meaning of their being brothers; it clarifies the significance of their number as three.

Furthermore, it explains why they are constantly addressed as "brothers" within the Holy Teachings, why it is said they practiced external dharmas together, and why they collectively abandoned the heterodox to return to the orthodox—all of which were previously unknown.
Now, based on the Holy Teachings, I shall clarify their causes and conditions, as well as manifest their karmic activities.
This is because it commemorates the past and present roots of goodness and the origins through which one may likewise attain the Way.

Regarding the term "kṣetra-stambha" (刹柱), the full Sanskrit is *kṣetra-stambha*, which translates as "field" (*kṣetra*); it refers to the sacred field of the Triple Gem. Specifically, it refers to a Buddha-field;
generally, it refers to any location. Here, it is used in the general sense. "Stambha" (柱) means a pillar or marker; a pillar is erected to mark out that specific territory.
This single phrase establishes the former [state] and further gives rise to the latter three; it is because they are like-minded brothers who serve as the pillars of the *kṣetra* (buddha-field).

Because they have entered the Way but have not yet emerged from it, they were, in previous lives, those who transcend the world. This is named by combining the "subject" (*sādhana*) and the "object" (*sādhya*), for it is the pillar of this *kṣetra*-family.
Those who rely upon this are the practice (*caryā*). At that time, there must have been a vow (*praṇidhāna*); thus, vow and practice are mutually interrelated.
It is because of these [past] conditions that he was able to bring this about; since the time of the Buddha is so remote, they were brothers not merely for a single lifetime.
Bimbisāra is the father of King Ajātaśatru. Because his learning encompassed non-Buddhist scriptures, he used them to convert others before the Buddha appeared, and thus served as a teacher.
One should understand that this passage establishes what precedes and initiates what follows, encompassing everything.
There are three reasons why this thought leads to such karmic conditions from the past: first, because they were brothers who erected it together;
second, because they obtained the conditions for liberation by means of this pillar; and third, because they shared both their deviance and their renunciation, as a result of the former two.
Thus one should reflect upon them.
From here below is the third section, clarifying how they were all able to abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox, discarding the false and following the true.
Since they previously established their practices and vows within the supreme realm, they already possessed superior causes;

however, because they had not yet encountered powerful conditions, they remained on the heterodox path. Now, as the time has come for these various conditions to mature, they are able to abandon [the false] instantaneously.

Thus, they all equally return to awakening and entry [into truth]. Although the Buddha’s transformative benefits reach their ultimate expression in the three mysteries, the resulting gains do not exceed two kinds:
that which is produced by the transformer is called form and sound, while that which is received is called hearing and seeing.

However, their application differs—sometimes both are used together, sometimes only one, and sometimes they appear in various combinations—as described at the beginning of the Great Sūtra regarding the initial transformation of the various beings.
In the Way, when employing supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) at the very end to transform the ten immortals, one applies them exclusively through wondrous eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Because their respective capacities for awakening differ, these are treated as distinct and individual cases. What is clarified in this present passage consists of two meanings:

first, it clarifies the extensive employment of supernatural powers while still not having abandoned [the physical form]; second, it clarifies the abbreviated use of sound to awaken, which is instantaneous.

To submit and take refuge in this is the meaning of employing both the primary and the auxiliary methods. Within the first [section], there are again two parts: first, the explicit clarification of extensive transformation;

second, clarifying that [beings] are still unable to immediately abandon [their attachments]. Within the first of these, there are three sections: first, a general indication of the directions and numbers;

second, a brief listing of their names and characteristics; third, a general reference to the detailed exposition of what was briefly indicated. Regarding the term "spiritual transformations" (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*): the word "spiritual" (*shen*) refers to its...
The essence is without direction and unfathomable; its transformations describe its function. That its movement is not constant is precisely what constitutes "pervasion" (*tong*).

Since this speaks of both essence and function together, although the numerical categories of its functions are indeed many, it mentions only ten as they represent the essentials. The names are listed next;

these texts refer back to themselves, such as the *Śrīmatī-sūtra* (*Ruìyìng jīng*), which first provides explanations or cites the *Āgama* and the *Buddhacarita*, though they extensively elaborate upon those sources.
Although this meaning is essential, it has not yet been fully reconciled; for now, I shall briefly explain this passage without extensively addressing the former point.

As for the statement that "poison does not strike," it means that [the poison] cannot cause harm, as clarified in the Sūtra: when the Buddha was about to subdue [the dragon], he entered the cave of the poisonous dragon;
the dragon became greatly enraged and attempted to inflict extreme harm, but the Buddha subdued it and placed it within his alms-bowl (*pātra*).
Because he spoke verses in praise of the Buddha, it was said that fire would not burn him in the midst of flames;
thus, when he spat fire at a venomous dragon to harm him, it was instead burned by the Buddha’s fire, causing the dragon to submit without dying.

When the waters of the Ganges surged in a great flood, fearing he might drown, the Buddha sent him to look at it, yet he did not drown, walking upon the water with his feet. Regarding the three types of equality, this refers to his request.
When the period for making offerings during the Buddha’s three-month residence had arrived and it was time to invite him for a meal, the Buddha said, "Go ahead.
He then went to the Jambu tree in Jambudvīpa to take jambu fruits; to Pūrvavideha in the east to take bilva fruits; to Aparagoyānī in the west to take harītakī fruits;
and to Uttarakuru in the north to take naturally grown non-glutinous rice. He further proceeded to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to fetch ambrosia (*amṛta*). This is also clarified in the Sūtras.
Every year there was a great sacrifice, and the sovereign, his ministers, and the common people would all assemble there. Kāśyapa thought to himself, "Gautama is handsome;
if the kings and nobles come to see him, it will cause me to lose my reputation. If he does not come tomorrow, it will be a great blessing for me.
The Buddha, knowing this, went to Lake Anavatapta the very next day to eat, returning only at dusk.
Kāśyapa asked, "Why did you not come yesterday? The Buddha said, "I knew your mind, and therefore I did not come.

Thus it is said that [the Buddha] knew [their] aversion, and so on, up to his manifest appearance. Or it is said that knowing their thoughts, he manifested his arrival; these are distinct matters, though no separate account has been seen for them.
