Furthermore, when he commanded his disciples to light a fire and they did not, or when he wished to extinguish a fire and it would not go out, he questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha in both cases ordered him to light it.
Regarding the passage "Because it is extinguished, it is said that the fire is extinguished and does not burn," although the text is brief, it contains these four meanings which should be understood.

Furthermore, he had his disciple split a piece of firewood; [the disciple] was unable to lift the top part once the bottom was held, nor could he lower the bottom once the top was held. He also questioned the Buddha about this, and the Buddha likewise had him attempt to lift it.
The subsequent passages follow this precedent. These items listed above constitute ten matters. The following section provides a summary and demonstration.
The extensive sources for these points have been cited here merely as a summary; furthermore, the specific timing and scope of these ten matters remain undetermined.
What has been presented above is but a brief explanation of the extant text, and one must consult the sūtras in detail for further clarification.

The above concludes the extensive clarification of the circumstances of the True Transformation (*saddharma-vinaya*). Although one observes what follows below, this next section clarifies that [the beings] were still unable to abandon their heterodox assemblies and undergo transformation.

This refers to both the brief and the extensive; the brief is as previously stated, while the extensive is as shown in the Sūtra. Therefore, it says "the various transformations" (*saṃvarta*) in the Sūtra. The two phrases beginning with "etc.
(*ādi*) rely on what is taught in the Sūtra to manifest the state of their fundamental reformation, just as observed in the ten matters previously mentioned.
Each individual event contains these words; however, as I do not wish to burden the text with excessive detail, I have presented them here collectively in this single statement.
According to the sequence of the *Buddhacarita-sūtra*, five hundred miraculous transformations were manifested, and upon witnessing each one, these words were spoken; it is the same as in this case.
The Buddha then proceeds below to clarify how, by means of these words, he immediately awakens and enters the Right Path. As the *Sūtra of Past Deeds* (*Pūrva-yoga-sūtra*) states:
after witnessing the various transformations, [the disciple] further says, "Even though it is thus, I am unable to attain the fruit of Arhatship as I do today.
The Buddha then says to him: "You are not an Arhat, nor have you yet entered the Path; indeed, there is no Path [for you]."
Previously, through mutual comparison and further results, they were awakened by this cause and returned in submission; they left the household life and attained the fruits of *śrāmaṇya*.
As for those who had cast themselves into various heterodox arts and implements, they followed the current downstream; when the second group saw these signs, they likewise returned in submission.

[The Buddha] commanded them all, "Come hither" (*ehi bhikṣu*), and they all attained the fruits of *śrāmaṇya*. This is the transformative function of the two wheels of form and sound, whereby those who receive them obtain the fruits of seeing and hearing.
This is doubly beneficial. The term "huòrán" (霍然) describes an appearance of extreme swiftness;
it may also be borrowed for the sound of "shù," and its meaning remains consistent. It is precisely what is meant by "bèirán" (悖然).
The above is based on the essential conditions (*nidāna*), which must number four: first, the world; second, the people (symbolized by the erecting of the pillar);
third, the remedial measures (*pratipakṣa*); and fourth, the Buddha’s words regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Some say that in this text on the *nidānas*, there are four major sections:
first, the clan; second, the name; third, the dwelling place; and from the section on Vipaśyin onwards, the fourth clarifies the conditions for entering the Path.

In this passage, it is precisely the four *siddhāntas* that are clarified: first is the *loka-siddhānta*, next is the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (for the sake of others), then the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the Buddha’s remedy), and finally the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate truth).
Now, considering the intent of this text, one should examine these two interpretations; both have their merits and drawbacks. Why?
Because in clarifying the first three among the four, there is a fear of contradicting the text. For the text states: "False attachments have not yet... [and so forth].

If one were to revise it to say, "Seeing the Buddha immediately eliminates evil," this would contradict the meaning of "counteracting" (*pratipakṣa*). Since the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) is thus not established, it is likely that this is not a valid precedent.

Furthermore, regarding the four [types of causes], if the first three were not in the sense of being "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*), then all preceding instances should likewise follow suit.
Since they cannot be so generalized, why should this case alone be an exception? In every instance, this is precisely what brings forth wholesome causes, yet it is instead...

If one considers the world to be a realm of perversion and engages in such evil, yet conversely produces good through the transformative power of spirits, this is because the application of the remedy has not yet been abandoned.
Since the meaning of the remedy has not yet been established, how could such "sudden" (霍然) discourse constitute the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?

Therefore, this subsequent explanation does not accord with [the views of] later students; it is indeed necessary to examine this in detail. Now, regarding the preceding text, I shall briefly explain its three parts.
The four meanings are precisely these meanings. First, the explanation of his name and place of residence is a general discussion of his origins;
these are all worldly matters, which are the fruits of the mundane world. Since they together manifest the supreme realm, they are like branches joined together.

Although he practiced in heterodox directions, he shared the same aspiration for the Way; this was the condition for turning toward the Right Path. Therefore, this is for the sake of people beholding the ten transformations.
Yet, without abandoning what was heard, upon hearing a single word, one becomes vast and open;

this term "vast and open" clearly demonstrates that through a single word, the darkness of delusion is suddenly removed and the clarity of understanding is suddenly manifested—hence it bears the name of "swiftness.

Therefore, these two meanings are identical to the sense of "treatment" (therapeutic remedy). How could one separate them? For if both the text and its meaning were not aligned, both would remain obscure. This is the general demonstration.
Because this person has these four kinds of causes and conditions, they possess this name and number; how could it be for no reason?
As for the character "Huo" (霍) therein, it is also said that one may pronounce it simply as "Huo" (豁); since the meaning is the same, it is merely a matter of phonetic convenience.

Next, regarding the classification by teaching (*yàojiào*), we distinguish the convergence of the provisional and the real within the causes and conditions of the three types of persons. This is further clarified by means of the five flavors;
it is not that we disregard the teachings and rely solely on the flavors, for the horizontal and vertical dimensions manifest in mutual correspondence.

By relying on four flavors, one immediately encompasses the five, which thus possesses four distinct divisions. Within these, there are two initial distinctions: first, the specific clarification of the virtues and conduct of the three persons; second, the summary conclusion thereof.
In the initial teaching, there are three distinctions from the very beginning, each of which possesses two meanings.

First, it clarifies the ability to benefit others, specifically the capacity to ensure that the fourfold assembly is free from discord and lacks nothing in the four requisites; this constitutes the instruction, the external protection, and the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Second, regarding one's own practice, it clarifies the ability to eliminate evil and diligently advance toward good. Third, it clarifies the ability to practice for oneself while simultaneously benefiting others.

The benefit of others, which is also the instruction for those of knowledge, is likewise summarized as the first teaching. Since the *Āgamas* have already been cited, it does not involve other stages;
this corresponds to the initial stage. The initial transformation from delusion to awakening is just like milk transforming into curd.

Next, by traversing the *Vaipulya* (Vaipulya-sūtras) through censure and rebuke, one develops a sense of shame and aspiration; this should be explained below according to the meaning of "producing cream" (*maṇḍa*), based on its flavor.
Because it gradually becomes more profound, the analogy implies that those who know [the truth] are of a similar class throughout the preceding and succeeding stages.

Next, upon entering Prajñāpāramitā, one should immediately understand that they are capable of [realizing the ultimate]. Generally speaking, from the beginning until this point, Śrāvakas possess this very meaning; they cannot be distinguished [from Bodhisattvas], nor can their underlying significance be questioned.
It is the same with the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras): having received the prediction of Buddhahood and completed the utility of their practice, they are like the ultimate state of flavor.
These serve as metaphors: first by deconstructing, second by refuting, third by purifying through washing, and fourth by revealing.

When one reaches this stage of revelation, even deconstruction itself becomes a metaphor; how much more so when considering the detailed application of these methods. This is why the *Lotus Sūtra* is thus:
it is entirely due to this revelation that, at this point, all persons and dharmas are fully opened up and harmonized.

It must be understood that this refers exclusively to the matured ghee (*pakva-sarpiḥ*); this is based on the meaning of the single benefit arising from the gradual stage. I hope you will not be confused by this, as it is explained in detail in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).

Next, regarding the provisional and the real (*jia-ji*), first the provisional is used to manifest the real, and then the real is used to clarify the provisional. Within the former [the provisional manifesting the real], there are... [text fragment].
The initial heading, explanation, and conclusion: the reason for the heading is that one knows by verifying the traces (*liǎo jì*).
This is because within these traces, the numerical meanings are inseparable; they correspond precisely to the numerical meanings and essential nature (*tǐxiàng*) of the Three Virtues (*sāndé*).

Thus, we know this is a case of using traces to manifest the fundamental. Therefore, we know its fundamental nature is such. Some say: "The nature of the forest is pure and cool, warding off the various oppressive heats."
The *Biao* states: "Because *prajñā* has 'discrimination' as its meaning, it is like a forest formed by many trees;
this takes the sense of dispersing many branches and trunks. Now I say: if all forests are thus, why must this specific forest take 'discrimination' as its meaning?
Furthermore, how does this differ from the conventional world? Now I say: this is a forest that possesses the power to cure illness.

Merit has flowers and fruits that can adorn and manifest its ground; now, the realm beloved by all things represents the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) of *prajñā*, which can eliminate the maladies of the tainted (*sāsrava*). It can manifest the *dharmakāya* as the root of all virtues;
therefore, it is used as a representation. A city serves as a refuge for people and things, representing the *dharmakāya* as the basis upon which these two rely. Water can purify.
Because it excludes impurity and can sever defilement and evil, it is manifested through this; as for the statement that "it is called secret (*guhya*) and so forth," these three are in fact one.
Because the four lines have no fixed direction, they are called "secret" (*guhya*); because they encompass all virtues, they are named "treasury" (*kośa*);

and because it is that which has long been realized and dwelt in, it is named "root" (*mūla*). As for the statement that "the three persons together manifest the three," this refers to the first [of the three].
One virtue is entirely identical to the three, and the three are each fully possessed of the three virtues; this should be understood. One is the three, the three are the one;
one-three is the three, and the three-three is only the one. The term "contemplation of the Way" is called the "inconceivable";
the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* calls it the "Secret Treasury," while this sūtra is named the "Sublime Dharma. This is explained in detail as clarified in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).

Regarding the initial section on the three names within the contemplation (*guan*), it clarifies the meaning of "brothers" following the contemplation. First, the Master said: first one attains the Middle Way;

next, one negates the extremes and inversions; finally, one illuminates the truths of the extremes. Some say that "immovability" purifies the extreme of existence (*bhava-anta*) while "movement" purifies the extreme of emptiness (*śūnyatā-anta*).
Now I say: the Middle Way within the contemplation of the mind can prevent the enemies of the two extremes, just as a city provides defense; subsequently, one proceeds to the two [extremes].

Because it can purify the delusions of the two extremes, it is like water; this refers to its activity (*caryā*). Because it simultaneously illuminates both self-benefit and benefit for others, it is like a forest;
these two meanings refer to the two types of wisdom (*jñāna*). Regarding the first, it refers to the essence (*svabhāva*); regarding the latter two, they refer to the activity.

The purifying function is like water; this refers to virtuous conduct (*śubha-caryā*). The illuminating function is like a forest; this refers to how wisdom can manifest the principle (*tattva*), which is like a forest that is majestic and manifest.
Furthermore, that ground is also able to remove obscurations and darkness, which is in accordance with the meaning of the "Forest of Medicines" (Bhaiṣajyavana).

Even according to the proximate interpretation, it does not lose these two meanings. As for the explanation of the "brothers" below, since each one possesses the other two, they are mutually supportive rather than eternally distinct.
Next, regarding the explanation of Śāriputra: although the initial causal narrative is very extensive, in explaining this name one must first understand its essentials.
There are two aspects to these essentials: namely, the name and the conduct;
either the name itself reveals the conduct—as in "Ārya" (Noble One)—or the conduct is manifested separately from the name—as in adding "Mahā" (Great) above Kāśyapa—or neither.
That which is neither distinct [from the preceding] yet still implicitly contains its meaning is, for example, the title "The Three Sages" (Sanskrit: *Tri-satva*) used heretofore.
Alternatively, that which is neither identical nor different, and does not implicitly contain the meaning but must be explained with clarity, is the title "This Sage" (*Ayaṃ satva*).
Although it lacks the textual or semantic content of the former, all the various sūtras extensively praise this sūtra, as it establishes the beginning and end of the correct teaching.
To propagate and circulate [this teaching], one must provide testimony for its credibility; if one does not recount [the circumstances], how could one possibly grasp this intent?
By what means then could its origin be revealed? The expounder has never understood that this intent is the basis by which the meaning of the text can be recognized.
If one grasps this intent, then all that follows can be sought through it. Reflect upon this, reflect upon it!
Although there are no explicit headings in this current text, it nonetheless contains ten instances from beginning to end, the first of which is the passage concerning Mahākāśyapa.
I shall first explain them here. Some passages directly synthesize and clarify the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*, while others treat the subject with excessive detail;
I fear that both the overly elaborate and the overly concise would deviate from the text and lose its essential, moderate intent. Therefore, I shall now follow the text as it proceeds.
The general outline consists of ten sections, which are then consolidated to clarify four essential points.
Having already provided the overall heading for the first [section], we now clarify that all ten are "the foremost. Furthermore, regarding the first ten: the first explains the present name;

the second, from "In the past" onwards, manifests his ability to employ skillful means (*upāya*) regarding unwholesome matters in former times; and the third, from "First, as for the womb" onwards, elucidates...
First, his power regarding the womb was foremost; second, from Nanda downward, fourth, it clarifies that after birth he was early able to become a Confucian scholar and master;
third, from the first [section] downward, fifth, it clarifies that subsequently he was further able to be broadly proficient in the arts of the Way (*dào-shù*);
fourth, from the first [section] regarding the Way downward, sixth, it clarifies that he was foremost in the swiftness with which he could awaken to and enter the Buddha-way.
Section Seven (from *Tishatuo* [Devadatta] onwards) clarifies that he was not only able to awaken to the truth himself and rectify his own being, but could also subdue heterodoxy.
Section Eight (from the first part of the *Zhong ahan jing* [Madhyama Āgama] onwards) clarifies that he was further able to propagate and exalt the True Dharma.

Section Nine (from the first part of the *Fo shuo* [Buddha-spoken] section onwards) clarifies that he was further able to discern and expound the Right Path. Section Ten (from the first part of the *Zhong ahan jing* onwards) clarifies that...
The first major section, "The Divine Power Manifesting the Correct," consists of ten chapters; their subtle intentions are to be discerned according to the text.
Regarding the distinctions of wisdom, ten types are briefly explained; because he is the most excellent among the śrāvakas, he is in every case "foremost" (*prathama*).

However, at the beginning of the *Maitreya-buddha-sūtra*, it is praised as "the Great Wisdom Śāriputra. In the commentary by Danqiu, the character "Great" (*da*) is explained as follows: [text continues].
There are ten meanings. First, the greatness of lineage (*gotra*) is roughly equivalent to the first meaning here [of the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*].

Second, the greatness of auspicious signs is equivalent to the third meaning here, "dwelling in the womb. Third, the greatness of fame is equivalent to the fourth meaning here, "the power of youthful illusion.
Fourth, the greatness of ease of awakening is equivalent to the sixth meaning here, "swiftly and thoroughly awakening to the true path."

1. The greatness of being foremost in swiftness is identical in meaning to the fifth [greatness]. 2. The greatness of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is identical in its primary sense to this tenth [greatness], the greatness of spiritual power (*ṛddhi*).
3. The greatness of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) is identical in meaning to the ninth [greatness]. 4. The direct name "Disciple" refers to the Great Illumination;
among all disciples, he is the greatest, which corresponds to this sixth [greatness], the first in awakening to the Way at the end of the fifteenth day of the month.
The subsequent passage of praise regarding the meaning of the text is largely identical to the eighth [section], titled "Respectful Veneration.

This is immediately followed by the eighth [section], which clarifies that it is identical to the first passage on "Manifesting the Right Path. The ninth is titled "The Great Illumination of the Field of Merit":

"If humans or devas make offerings, they shall obtain immediate retribution. This text is slightly abbreviated; one may also take the passage from Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra’s eulogy, which states: "Those who encounter you shall attain greatness."
To "benefit" is also its meaning. Tenth, he gives rise to the great illumination of wisdom, attaining mastery over both internal and external scriptures;

that he is now able to penetrate the internal while knowing the external can be understood even from his childhood, when his extensive studies were peerless—how much more so when he has realized the ultimate fruit of sainthood and possesses unimpeded knowledge?
Therefore, this single term "penetration" (tong) encompasses all the preceding meanings, as it collectively and correctly praises his wisdom.
That [text] is called "Great," while this is collectively called "First.
However, those ten points are merely contained within these nine sections here, as they still lack the second point which clarifies his marvelous skillful abilities in the past.
These nine sections herein encompass those ten, because that [text] specifically praises his present virtues; thus, it briefly explains the ten points in this manner. If...
The four essential points will be explained later.
First, regarding his name, he is the foremost among all names because he accords with the Buddha’s original vow and can assist his parents.
This section has three brief parts: first, explaining his name; second, explaining his clan name; and third, briefly indicating his virtuous conduct. Within the explanation of the name, furthermore—
Regarding the first of these three [sections], there are three parts:
first, a direct translation without explaining the meaning, which still lacks the term *cu*; second, a re-translation with an explanation of its meaning;
third, yet another re-translation that precisely explains the meaning of the initial translation. This is to be understood accordingly.
This meaning should have been explained immediately following the initial translation; yet here it has been translated again as the four characters "shēn zì" (身字).

These latter four characters should be removed, as they were already examined and not fully understood in the preceding explanation. Next, to clarify that the name was derived from the father, there are two further sentences.
The first provides a direct translation and explanation: because of engaging in doctrinal debate, he obtained a wife and had a son. This is...
"This son brings glory to his father" is the correct interpretation; here we are precisely explaining that the son should be described by means of his parents, as all ancient commentaries state.
Why then do some say "bringing glory to his parents," or allow for mutual application? Now, it is precisely this [son's] capability that is being highlighted:

because he is capable of bringing glory to his parents, he is called "greatly filial. Thus it is said, "To establish oneself and spread one’s name in order to bring glory to one’s parents. Therefore, this is indeed the proper sequence.
Furthermore, citing another commentary, there is yet another interpretation: first, the name is derived from the mother’s virtue; second, the name is derived from the father;
third, the name is obtained based on both parents—this can be understood. It has been said since ancient times that one name is derived from the teacher’s original vow;
this refers to Śākyamuni Buddha, who in the past was a potter and encountered a disciple of the previous Śākyamuni named Śāriputra.
He made offerings and vowed to become a Buddha in the future; thus he was named Śāriputra.
His mother’s eyes resembled those of the śāri bird, so she was named Śārī.

Because she was the most intelligent among women and was highly esteemed by people, her son was called Śāri-putra (Son of Śārī). If his name were derived from his father, it would accord with the current text.

The same source further states that the Sūtra records that when the Buddha first saw him, he ordered his name "Tiṣya" to be changed so that it would return to its original form, "Śāriputra," in accordance with his original vow;
therefore, in the sūtras and śāstras, everyone speaks of Śāriputra and not by his former name. In recent times, another interpretation has been offered:
the correct pronunciation is *Śāriputradatta*; *śāri* refers to the śārika bird, which is the hundred-tongued bird (*śata-pattra*).

It is also called *Chun-ying-fu-dan-lo* (Spring Cuckoo Not-at-Dawn), which means that the son is distinguished by his mother’s eloquence; it is like the *śāri* bird, where the son is designated by the name of his mother.
Thus, he is called the "Son of the Śāri" (*Śāripūtra*). Furthermore, he is named *Upadeśa* because he is capable of debating doctrine and thus shares that title.
Now, those who interpret it in this way do not grasp the meaning of the "body-jewel" (*kāyamaṇi*), as it merely follows its own [literal] derivation.
The ability to discuss [the Buddha] as not being the "Father" serves as his name; for now, we shall follow the traditional interpretation.
Having finished explaining the meaning of his name above, the following section on "clan" (*gotra*) explains his lineage. This should be the name of a tree, namely the *Nyagrodha* tree.

According to ancient interpretations, it is called the "vertically and horizontally spreading tree" because this tree is the tallest and largest; thus, it was likely due to this tree that his ancestors [were named].
He acquired his clan name because he was a distant descendant of a sage; furthermore, among the four castes, he belonged to a lineage of pure conduct and was thus the most excellent of lineages.
The above explains his name and clan; the following phrase indicates his virtuous conduct.
Since it is not known what kind of virtue such a person possesses, [the text states] "this wisdom is inexhaustible," and so forth.
The characteristics for resolving doubts are briefly explained as follows. This phrase should properly belong to the subsequent section on conditions;
however, because the word "formerly" (昔) appears in the question that follows, it is provisionally assigned here to the preceding general heading, which governs the nine meanings that follow.
Next, regarding the nine matters concerning the practice of Śākyamuni’s conduct: there are those of the past and those of the present; there are mundane and supramundane aspects;

and there are those for one's own benefit and those for the benefit of others. Although these differ, they are all manifestations of his wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). Among these, the first clarifies the past:

it shows that his marvelous and skillful application was not merely manifest in the present, but existed long ago; furthermore, it was not limited to virtuous deeds, but was also exercised within unwholesome circumstances.
To be foremost, this does not reside apart from the foundation of wondrous wisdom; how else could the meaning of the eternal essence and its manifested traces have become increasingly clear?
Herein, first ten kinds of skillful capacities are elucidated, followed by a concluding synthesis of ancient and modern teachings.

Regarding what is called the *Sheng jing* (Sūtra of Birth), it refers precisely to this *Sheng jing*. These ten matters are summarized into three parts: first, it clarifies that through great theft one obtains a vast reward; next...
Eighth, they could not be captured; tenth, even if they were captured, they were not simply executed—on the contrary, they were rewarded even more heavily.
Thus, although this is indeed a great artifice in the world, the Sūtra says: "When a thief steals without limit and is caught, he informs the King.
Next, those who strictly guard [the property] may say that they have adorned their daughters and established dwellings by the water's edge, or they may say 'strict' as if it were a state of alert."
The prepared meanings are all appropriate for the long-standing master of cakes; therefore, he was made free from doubt.

As for the statement regarding "five hundred riders," there were two hundred and fifty each in front and behind, with those in the center not less than the King himself. The King then examined them closely, and among them, he seized one and questioned him.

He prostrated himself and requested that his remaining life be spared. The King said: "You are exceedingly clever and discerning; I grant you your wish. The rest of the text may be understood without further elaboration.
To elaborate further: from the passage "The fetus... onwards, it has already clarified the capacity [of the karma] in past lives; this section clarifies its function in the present life.
Although it pertains to the present life, it is nonetheless the power inherent within the fetal stage. What kind of power is this? Essentially, there are four capacities, the first of which is:
First, he was able to manifest his father’s wisdom; second, he enabled his mother to possess great eloquence;
third, he allowed his maternal uncle to achieve great renown; for were it not for him, how could they have been moved to such exertion as to attain such fame?
Thus, by the power of his wisdom, fourthly, he manifested his own great intelligence, his vast wisdom overflowing even from his armored belly.

Furthermore, the fire-crown symbolizes his lofty brilliance and his ability to shatter all darkness. As for the phrase "setting forth what is old" (*cén gù*): "setting forth" (*cén*) is equivalent to "old" (*gù*).

This means that since he has served as the National Preceptor, it was naturally expected he would defeat his adversaries; however, reflecting on his own declining years and long-standing career, he realized he was no longer a new appointment and that the younger generation was formidable.
He felt certain his mission would not succeed, and thus the signs were inauspicious. These inauspicious signs originated from within his own household.
While heading toward the site of debate, he encountered two oxen fighting; he took this as an omen for determining which side would prevail.

He considered one ox to represent the opponent and the other to represent himself, intending to discern their relative strength. Since he was unable to know [the outcome] beforehand, it must have been unfavorable; thus it is said that "the signs were inauspicious.
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly. As for the term *brahmin* (*fan-zhi*): *brahman* means purity, and *citta* (here translated as *zhi*) refers to conduct or resolve.
Because both [meanings] are cited here and there, it is said that *brahman* is the same as *brāhmaṇa*, which in this [Chinese] context means "Pure Conduct" (*jingxing*).

Since it encompasses these four meanings, it is the foremost among those dwelling in the womb of wisdom; for the other meanings are explained extensively in the subsequent text, hence the annotation "(and so forth)."
Next, the fourth section clarifies that after his birth, even during his childhood, he was able to discern and propagate the essential tenets of the Confucian tradition.
This section also has two parts: first, it clarifies how he was able to discern and propagate [the teachings] at a young age;

second, it clarifies how, even in his infancy, he was able to investigate and master their profound meaning. If these two qualities were considered in that land, they would be said to have been divinely bestowed.

This is precisely what constitutes innate knowledge (*jñāna*); if one is near to the Buddha’s teaching, it is the perfection of past cultivation, and if far, it is the manifestation of the fundamental through its traces.
Otherwise, who could have brought about this? First, it clarifies that even from youth and obscurity, one was able to discern and propagate [the truth]. Within this, there are five points:

first, a general clarification of the causes and conditions, which refers to the resolution of matters such as the "celebration" (*qing*) leading to this auspicious assembly; second, the clarification of how he immediately transcended...
To go forth and still uphold benevolence while treating minor illusions as secondary is what is meant by "surpassing the multitude.

In this context, even Jia Yi, who was able to respond to the Emperor at the age of eighteen, is considered one who has surpassed his station; how much more so for this eight-year-old who can surpass the assembly?

How could he be compared to the Three-Vidyā scholars of long standing, who were unwilling to remain [in their positions] and yet simultaneously clarified the reasons for it? As for the Four-Vidyā masters, they merely allowed him to engage in incidental dialogue in response.

All [the questions] were exhausted and submitted; as for the "Table of Questions," it was produced because the questions went beyond what was expected, clearly showing that the inquiries were still shallow and near-sighted rather than profound and far-reaching.

Formerly, the biography of Master Zheng of Beihai in this region stated that he was profoundly learned and thoroughly investigated the Confucian tradition, such that when various scholars constructed difficult challenges, he answered them all, exceeding their expectations.
Although the matters mentioned in the "Table" are similar to this account, we are separated by both age and status.

It is sufficient to say that, just as in Western traditions of debate, one establishes a banner to manifest the signs of victory—hence the name "Victory Banner" (*jaya-dhvaja*)—if one is not victorious, it should immediately be toppled;
for when Śakra fought with the Asuras, the Asuras were defeated upon merely beholding the banner.

Thus, Master Shentai composed the *Dichang lun* (Treatise on the Imperial Banner), taking this very point as its basis; hence the statement that "all fall under the banner. Regarding the five sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*):
The entire nation celebrated, calling it a "Blessed Response. Next, to clarify that even in his childhood he was already able to investigate thoroughly and expound extensively:
by this time, he had already investigated the texts broadly and elucidated their essential meanings. The five regions of India constitute the center of Jambudvīpa;
the sixteen great kingdoms are mostly located within these five regions, specifically in Central India. All [of these] are present.
In the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra), these passages collectively clarify that his wisdom among Confucians was preeminent; thus he is named "The First Among Universal Confucians.

From here below, up to the fifth section, it clarifies that he did not merely investigate and expound the Confucian tradition, but was also able to extensively master the various arts and techniques (*shu*), being the very best among them.
Within this, there are three essential points: first, clarifying how he attained the Way and arts of his teacher and received the transmission from him.

Next, it clarifies that regarding the Way of the Master, there was still a small portion not yet fully realized; subsequently, it clarifies that although he had not yet attained [full mastery], he had already exhausted most of what remained, and for this reason he is ranked first.
Regarding the "beginning" (the initial stage), he served the same teacher as Maudgalyāyana, though it does not state what the fundamental tenets of that teacher were.
Next, concerning the term "joyfully" (*xīrán*), the ancient editions have the character "listen" (*tīng*) with the phonetic *yǔ* and the radical *jǐn*.
The character *fǎn* (反) means "to break off" and thus conveys the appearance of a joyful laugh; the character *tìng* (聽) simply denotes the act of laughing.
Although both meanings are applicable, the sense of *tìng* is more appropriate. Thus, Sima Xiangru’s *Shanglin Park Rhapsody* states: "Master Wushi laughed *tìngrán* (聽然).
This likely expresses a sense of profusion and strangeness. These two characters are easily confused; current editions all read the character *xīn* (欣), which is indeed its proper meaning.

The secrecy does not mean that the person was deemed unworthy, nor that there was doubt regarding their capacity to uphold the lineage; rather, it was kept secret so as not to bestow the teachings in their entirety.

Since it was said that no other teacher could be found, this was established as the foremost existence (*bhava*). This clearly indicates that there will subsequently be another foremost person who will surely be able to enter [the path].
For this reason, there arose the vow: "If I obtain the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), I swear that I shall certainly share it with you. Thus it is.
Next, the following section is the sixth, which clarifies that his wisdom is foremost in its ability to swiftly awaken to and enter the Buddha-dharma.

This passage is from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise). Within it, there are two main points: first, clarifying self-benefit; second, clarifying benefiting others. Each of these two further has two parts:

the first concerns the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*); the second concerns being without a master and having companions, where the "companions" are as follows:
It assists in transformation; furthermore, it serves as both teacher and resource, meaning one acts as the teacher for two people and as a disciple for one person, thereby transforming others.

For these four reasons, it is called the foremost. As for "dignified decorum" (*xiángxù*), it refers to a deportment that is moderate and conforms to the laws of propriety, without any haste or recklessness.
Laozi said: "The manifestation of great virtue follows only the Dao"—this refers to external demeanor.

If it is necessary to follow the person and the Dharma, one asks about the teacher and the Dharma taught by that teacher. In the treatise, there are three rounds of questions and answers: first, the question and answer regarding the teacher;
second, the question regarding the Dharma, to which the teacher replies with humble words, stating that he cannot explain it in full and requesting a brief exposition.

The answer is as found in the current text. Some say this refers to a brief exposition of the Four Noble Truths, while others say it refers to the exposition of the Three Truths, because [the text] states: "By knowing..."
Because the hearing is clear, when observing the text, it appears that there are generally these two meanings:

if there are four [phrases], the first phrase is suffering (*duḥkha*), the second phrase is origination (*samudaya*), and "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*).

If there are three [phrases], the first two phrases are origination, and the third phrase is both the path and cessation. Because of these two versions of four and three, this is the foremost among those who enter the right path.

Next, the following section is the seventh [part], which clarifies that its essence is capable of refuting heterodoxy. Since the first [section] has already been able to harmonize with the correct [teaching], the essential method for refuting heterodoxy likewise possesses three parts:
first, refuting internal heterodoxy; second, refuting external heterodoxy; and third, reiterating and establishing the primary meaning.

Regarding the first, the refutation of internal [heterodoxy], it is as explained later in the section on Maudgalyāyana, hence the commentary states (*etc.*). Next, regarding the refutation of external [heterodoxy], there are many [points].
The phrase "various [qualities]" refers to all the supreme endowments as described in the *Laudu jing* (Sūtra on Rādhagupta);

they need not be recounted here at length. The subsequent sentence offers praise to manifest and establish the preceding meaning. Some say that because the Dharma was preached to him by Śāriputra, right understanding (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) arose;

thus he is called "the one born" (*jāta*). Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana used his supernatural power to lead him back to the Buddha’s presence so that he might achieve accomplishment; thus he is like "the one nurtured."
This is one interpretation; since it mentions the "fourfold assembly," it applies universally (as indicated by the note *yúnyún*).
For a general outline, refer to the detailed discussion in the subsequent text. Because of these three meanings, this [treatise] is the foremost among those that refute heterodoxy.
The following is the eighth section: it not only subdues the heterodox, but is further able to strike forth and manifest the True Honored One as the most supreme.

Although this passage is extensive, its essential points are twofold: first, clarifying that one can manifest [the truth] to others; second, clarifying that one can cause others to manifest it for oneself.

Within these two aspects of self and other, both of which constitute the manifestation and exaltation of the True Honored One, there are two further divisions. First, the clarification... [text ends].
The subsequent section below clarifies the formal proclamation (*saṃprakāśana*). First, regarding the word "by means of" (*yena*):
it refers to the profound reflection upon what has been seen and heard based on the praise of others; thus, the practice of praise does not arise apart from the two benefits of self and others.
Within the following formal proclamation, there are three parts: first, the initiation of his virtuous conduct, as Śāriputra asks; next, the manifestation of his name, as Śāriputra [speaks].

From the passage beginning with "Praising and extolling" below, there are two pairs that praise their names and deeds. Within these, there are sections on the Dharma and sections on the subversion of the Dharma.

Regarding the text, there are seven rounds of question and answer; however, according to the underlying meaning, there should be eight, as the eighth section contains only an explanatory response following the previous point and lacks a formal question.
This section is extremely difficult to comprehend; its essential points may be summarized into two parts.
The first section provides a general discussion, while the subsequent seven sections provide a detailed analysis. "General" refers to the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*);
"detailed" refers to the seven purities (*saptaviśuddhi*), which constitute the very essence of the Brahma-conduct.
Within the initial section on Brahma-conduct, there are three parts: the first three instances distinguish the cause to reveal the fruit; the next three... [text continues].

Section Three: Distinguishing Causes to Reveal Causes, and Distinguishing Effects to Reveal Effects. First Section: Distinguishing Causes to Reveal Causes. The cause refers to the seven purities (*sapta-viśuddhi*); the effect refers to the state of being without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

It is not that there are seven [paths] as such; rather, it is for the sake of the state of being without remainder. Second Section: Distinguishing Effects to Reveal Effects. The effect here distinguishes the state with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) to reveal the state without remainder.

Third Section: Distinguishing Specific Causes to Reveal Universal Causes. "Specific" means that within the seven [purities], one takes each individually; "specific" does not mean they are distinct from one another. It is not that they are separate.
It is also generally said that possessing all seven constitutes the "counter-correspondence" (*pratipakṣa*), wherein both existence and non-existence together constitute the fruit.

Regarding these three [categories], the fact that each individual exclusion is stated in terms of both the general and the specific indicates that neither the general nor the specific alone is sufficient.
As for the reason they are collectively called the "Seven Purities," the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "Spread with the flowers of the seven purities, one bathes those stainless people."
The meaning applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings; his commentary explains: "Precepts" refers to right speech, action, and livelihood;

"mind" refers to right effort, mindfulness, and concentration; "view" is right thought; "crossing over" (tara) is also called the purity of severing doubt; "purity" (śuddhi) is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), where one knows the path and what is not the path;

it is also called the purity of discernment (*vibhakti-śuddhi*); "trace of the path" (*mārgapada*) and "knowledge and vision" (*jñānadarśana*) are also called the purity of practice (*caryā-śuddhi*). These two constitute the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

The knowledge of the tracks (*vaja-jñāna*), the abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and the purification (*viśuddhi*) are also called the purity of *nirvāṇa*, which is precisely the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).
The reason these seven are all termed "pure" is that they are able to remove the defilements and delusions of the two paths. Regarding the phrase "all together," one might ask:

"Is it not the case that one practices for something other than this? The answer is "no," which clarifies that it is not for anything else. The preceding two [sections] have finished distinguishing what is not [the goal]; the following one...
This explicitly reveals that which is intended; for within the teachings for Śrāvakas, the intended purpose reaches its limit here, and thus it is "for this.
The three subsequent sections below distinguish what is not [the case] to reveal what is, following the same sequence as before; however, they differ only in that they take two fruits as their basis.
As for the term "if" (設), some say that "if" (設) is synonymous with "conjunction" (合), meaning that if one were to conjoin [the practice] solely through precepts and so forth.
That worthy one has not yet fully realized those dharmas he has encountered, for Nirvana without remainder is not achieved through the convergence of a single dharma alone.
How could it be said that this principle does not yet exist? Why would it be limited to a single [dharma]? This has never been heard.

Even if such a principle were to exist, it would also contradict this text. This is not so; rather, "only" (zhi) should be understood as having the sense of "provisional application" (shishui), and "not only" (bu zhi) implies "immediately."

"Is this [the case] such that there is no remainder, and so on, up to each of the remaining six being likewise? He replied, "None of them are so. This is a general refutation of what is not [the case].
The question asks: "What is it? For what reason is it not taken as such immediately? The explanation clarifies the reason why it is not [the case]:
whether individually or collectively, these are merely "with remainder," and therefore they are not "without remainder. This is because they are only able to eliminate the cause.

Therefore, all of these are merely "with remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa) and not "without remainder" (nirupadhiśeṣa). If one were to depart from what follows, this would constitute the third section, which clarifies the distinction by discussing the causes.
According to the meaning of the subsequent analogy, it means that what was explained previously is not the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, but rather the cause of *nirvāṇa*.
If that is so, is the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*) the cause? No; [this applies] up to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Is it that "severance and purity" (*prahāṇa-viśuddhi*) serve as the cause? No. Is it that apart from these seven [factors], they constitute the noble cause?
That too is not so. This clarifies that neither individually nor separately are they sufficient. One should ask: "What is the meaning of this? The answer is:
"If each were to act as such individually, none alone could bring about the result. Below this, the reason is explained: "It is not [the case that they are sufficient individually]."
Because it arrives without cause, the following section clarifies that it is only by being endowed with the seven dharmas, starting from "not being separated," that this is so.
This text is likely an abridgment of that sutra; since the previous explanations did not state this, it makes the meaning difficult to comprehend.

For now, I have provided a brief account rather than a detailed one. Next, regarding the analogy: according to this analogical text, the "True" (Zhen) indeed constitutes the third [section], which concerns the cause.

This concise and manifest composition is not merely a textual elaboration of the preceding two dharmas. Regarding the initial essential meaning of the analogy and its application: it correctly clarifies that [the factors] serve as causes;
whether they are taken individually or in isolation, they are both inadequate, and only when fully assembled do the seven [factors] attain the status of being causes.

The text contains three sections: first, an analogy for the practitioner seeking the Way; second, an analogy for the seven dharmas acting as causes; and third, the analogy regarding their individual or isolated states.
Neither can it be reached, nor can it be manifested; only when the seven [factors] are fully present can it be realized.
"Sāvatthī" is the name of the place Vajjī; its distance from here is unknown. This analogy is for the purpose of sequential application.

As briefly explained above, based on this metaphorical application, one does not compose the previous explanation; otherwise, faith would be unable to accord with it. This concludes the initial correct arousal of those virtuous qualities.
The section below is the second, which clarifies his name; the section below that is the third, which offers a double eulogy of both his name and his conduct because both have been heard.
Thus, there are two praises, consisting of six phrases. The first phrase is a general eulogy of the person’s excellence, which is to say, it is the praise of his name.

The subsequent five phrases are the eulogy of his virtuous conduct (*guṇa*); they do not go beyond [the categories of] wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*), as well as [the benefits for] oneself and others. The next phrase...

The sequence of supreme wisdom leads decisively to fearlessness; the sequence of supreme abandonment leads to great eloquence. These two lines further clarify the virtues of the aforementioned supreme wisdom, while the subsequent lines further clarify the virtues of the aforementioned supreme abandonment.
These four clarify the two aspects of one’s own practice. The words praising the benefit of others describe the manner of wearing the robe:
"wrapping the robe" means to coil the robe and place it upon the crown of the head, symbolizing that his virtuous conduct is lofty and representing the utmost degree of reverence.

This is also because the wisdom previously attained enables one to benefit others. From the question of the Compassionate Son (*maitrī-putra*) downward is the second section, which demonstrates how he attains others in order to exalt himself;
herein there are also three parts: first, his name; second, his virtuous conduct; and third, the praise of his virtues. First, regarding the name:
it was given by his parents, and through it one recognizes the person. Next, the praise of his virtuous conduct: his virtue is praised as being equal to that of the Buddha.
Because they are uniform, they are said to be "equal. Next, because they seek the Buddha, they are called the "second. Thirdly, regarding the principal and the associates:

because they assist the Buddha in subduing Māra, restraining outsiders, and manifesting the true and correct Dharma, they are called "Dharma Generals. Following the Buddha in their preaching and being his disciples, they are called "further turning [the wheel].
As for the disciples' perfection of wisdom and abandonment, as with the preceding [section], the text is abbreviated; therefore, it is annotated with "and so forth" (*yún yún*).
The following is the ninth [section], which clarifies that his discernment was foremost; this is from the *Śāriputra-siṃhanāda-sūtra* within the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
It relates how the Buddha spoke of the meaning of a single phrase three times to Śāriputra, yet Śāriputra was unable to answer three times.
After a short while, the Buddha had entered his quiet chamber. Śāriputra then assembled the bhikṣus and said: "The Buddha has not yet shown me the starting point of the matter..."

He was unable to answer; whereas I have now expounded this Dharma for seven days and seven nights without reaching its end, the present text extracts the essentials to illustrate his eloquence by using the few to represent the many, whereas others cannot do so—therefore, he is ranked first.
The following is the tenth section, which manifests its divine function. First, it is said that there is no meditation without wisdom; thus, this is the capacity of wisdom.
Herein, the primary focus is on the spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) of Śāriputra, while the extensive exposition regarding Maudgalyāyana serves to illustrate the perfection of Śāriputra’s realization.
Now, it is said that this primarily clarifies his capacity: by manifesting his own power, he is further able to manifest and inspire others. Therefore, this is categorized under Wisdom.
The first [section] is also as in the separate text; its essential purport is this, so do not entertain other interpretations. Why would it not be essential?
Within that, the first clarifies the cause by which one reveals oneself through others; the "Dragon King" below demonstrates the ability to reveal to others.

Regarding the first of these, there is the preliminary and the formal; now there are five sentences: first, the Dragon King’s invitation; second, the Buddha’s command to go and call him; third, the [response of] receiving [the command].
He sent a messenger to summon him, ordering him to arrive immediately; this was done to stimulate his spiritual power, which is the underlying reason.
The passage below concerning Śāriputra refers to four causes for the manifestation of his supernormal powers. As for why they are linked in succession:
it is because Maudgalyāyana’s supernatural power shook [the seat] incessantly. Thus the Sūtra says: "I have heard the Buddha say that the Tathāgata’s seat cannot be moved."

Dong now uses this belt to tie it [the head], so that he can no longer act as a teacher. The Master says: "What is now called 'the foot of the Buddha’s seat in another realm' is merely a slight variation.
I now say that these different versions arise from either taking the general meaning or providing a specific explanation;

the passage from "his ears and eyes are connected" onwards is the fifth section, which summarizes the essentials to manifest its excellence and clarify its benefits, though the text contains them without explicitly stating them. This is what is meant.
The four *ṛddhipādas* (bases of psychic power) are explained as before. From here on, the text further demonstrates the power of others;
within this section, there are five phrases, which together with the preceding [section] constitute five points in total: first, clarifying that the minds of the assembly were light;

second, clarifying that they were all equal [in capacity], yet the Buddha’s power assisted them; third, commanding them to manifest [the powers]; fourth, their manifesting [the powers] in obedience to the command; and fifth, concluding by clarifying their excellence.

Benefiting those who receive his commands, Mingmu (Clear Vision) followed the command to pay homage to the Buddha and immediately traveled to the east, across worlds as numerous as the sands of seven Ganges Rivers.

There, the Buddha was named Qiguang (Marvelous Light). At that time, he placed the alms bowl upon the tip of a blade of grass; when the assembly saw it, they took it to be an insect and showed it to that Buddha.
That Buddha said, "To the west, across worlds as numerous as the sands of seven Ganges Rivers, there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni; this is his."
The Buddha’s disciple of supernormal powers addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying: "Manifest your spiritual power so that these bhikṣus do not give rise to thoughts of inferiority.

Maudgalyāyana placed five hundred bhikṣus in his bowl, stepped with one foot upon the Brahma Heaven and with the other foot upon Mount Sumeru, and recited verses that filled the Jeta Grove. When the bhikṣus heard this, they did not know where [the others] were; they questioned the Buddha.

The Buddha said that in that world, it should be understood in full according to that sūtra; this text provides only a brief summary of the essentials for one to know, as the details are explained extensively below, hence the note (云云). One should know that herein, too, it is by the power of the Buddha.

The ten meanings mentioned above all explain the significance of his being foremost in wisdom; since these are all based on causes and conditions, one must clarify the four *siddhāntas*. The Master says:
the first is the *loka-siddhānta*, which clarifies [the events] from his past lives and within the womb; "Nanda and others" refers to the production of goodness upon his birth;
"the people of the present kingdom" refers to the arising of faith; and "seeing Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya" refers to the ability to produce goodness well; "Devadatta and below" refers to...

Because it counteracts both the [two types of] evil—the object to be countered and the counter-agent—and because the *Madhyama Āgama* and those following it praise him as equal to the Buddha in terms of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), we now say that there are ten kinds of "firsts.
The first refers to his name and birth, which both pertain to the mundane world, just as in the previous cases of Kāśyapa and others; all were likewise so.

Next, regarding his past entrustment to the womb, his birth, and his subsequent seeking of the Way, he was always born as a human being, and because he always gave rise to wholesome states, this is called the "Way" (*mārga*).
Regarding the five matters from the jaw downward, both the primary meaning (*paramārtha*) and the remedial meaning (*pratipakṣa*) are intended for the attainment of the Way.

The manifestation of the Right Path and so forth constitutes the primary meaning; the destruction of internal and external evils and the tenth divine function are all intended as remedies for destroying evil.

By means of these, one passes through the present and past, [undergoing] conception in the womb and birth, encounters the teachings of Confucianism and Daoism, meets the Buddha, abandons heterodoxy, and enters the orthodox path.

Because the essence gives rise to function, thereby refuting the heterodox and manifesting the orthodox, the sequence of the four [stages] differs from the ordinary. Why is it that the arising of wholesome states is exclusively mundane?
As with the previous three Kāśyapas, so it is here; among the three Kāśyapas, the supreme meaning of the antidote is likewise the same.
It is not the case that all [three] are not so; thus, the first [stage] is the mundane, while the first [of the latter two] is the supreme antidote for the arising of wholesome states.
It is called "foremost" (*agrya*) for four reasons: it is foremost in its evil and foremost in its realization of the Way; it is for these four meanings that it is termed "foremost.

Next, regarding the teaching, this distinguishes the common [teachings] to reveal the specific, correctly clarifying the intent of this sutra. Furthermore, by relying on the four clarifications, one simultaneously encompasses the five meanings.

The ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) reveal its essence; the severing of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth clarify its function. As for the "ten knowledges," they are: knowledge of suffering... [and so forth].

The ten types of knowledge are: the conventional knowledge of the aggregates, their cessation, and the path; conventional knowledge of the world; knowledge of others' minds; and the knowledges of exhaustion, non-arising, and dharma, as well as inferential knowledge. These constitute the ten.
The realization of abandonment demonstrates its function for one's own benefit, while assisting the Buddha demonstrates its function for the benefit of others.

Next, the treatise is cited as proof, stating: "Regarding 'the right side,' this is a designation relative to the left, signifying its superiority. However, the commentaries differ; some state that "the left side" is based on the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
The statement that "the right face and eyes are joined to form the left face" is a later alteration made by subsequent generations.

The reason for this is that in this region, the left is esteemed as superior; furthermore, according to local dialects, both sides are referred to as "left" and "right," so they arbitrarily changed it.
Now, I follow the original treatise as correct: in Buddhism, the right is honored as primary because its essence accords with [the natural order], and thus its application is superior.
This is because, as in various sūtras, the left is used as a metaphor for concentration (*samādhi*) and the right as a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*);

this is precisely its meaning. Thus it is said. This, therefore, constitutes the meaning of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*). Next, regarding the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), there are four points:

first, examining the sūtra to clarify the speaker’s own view; second, clarifying that the words of the Sage differ from those of ordinary people; third, clarifying that since they differ from the mundane, [they are extraordinary].
Therefore, it is precisely because one can be free from the two views of ordinary and sage that the four sutras differ;
since ordinary and sage are not the same, this is the meaning of this teaching. The initial reference to the *Prajñāpāramitā* refers specifically to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
It correctly clarifies that within the latter sutra, Śāriputra himself made this statement, thereby manifesting his own actual realization of such a view. It is not [otherwise].
Indeed, all worldly dharmas of ours are like illusions and transformations, and all supramundane dharmas are likewise like illusions and transformations.
Since they are all like illusions, the two extremes of real existence are refuted;
it is only in this way that one attains the title of "Great Bodhisattva. The following is the Master’s own statement regarding the intent of the sages. Because these words involve...

This is because of constant doubt; that is to say, ordinary people are called "constant people" because they act according to their own emotions for their own sake and thus engage in much false speech, whereas the Sage acts according to the Way for the sake of all things and is not so. Since this is the case, what was previously explained precisely clarifies that my reality is truly such as I have realized.
To conclude: those who are like this are still like two distinct things that cannot attain self-mastery. However, this differs from—
The former [teaching] merely refutes the dharmas of the person that arise, but cannot refute the dharmas of the person in *nirvāṇa*;

furthermore, in the former, both the subject (the means) and object (the goal) were real, whereas here both the subject and object are empty. Therefore, this differs from the initial [teaching] and correctly accords with the meaning of "wisdom" (*prajñā*) in this teaching.

Next, regarding the section on the distinct [teachings], there are four points: first, the presentation of its method; second, the exclusion of the two preceding [teachings] as being non-[ultimate]; third, the correct elucidation of the five [dharmas]; and fourth, the conclusion.

The four characteristics are established to manifest that this initial heading must refer to the five [vehicles], because the sequence of the meanings clarified by this teaching is identical to that [of the other systems];

thus, it refers to them. Next, regarding the exclusion of two [vehicles]: the "Treasury" (Āgama) refers to the Deer Park and the Vaipulya; the "Common" (Sādhāraṇa) refers to both the Vaipulya and the Prajñāpāramitā.
In all these, one first clarifies hearing the teaching and subsequently clarifies practice. Because these two differ, neither is [the intended subject].
Furthermore, hearing "curd" (*dadhi*) refers to "breaking," and hearing "milk" (*kṣīra*) refers to the fifty wholesome dharmas and so forth that are to be destroyed by the world;

thus, "curd" signifies the power that breaks and destroys. When it says "the essence of curd" (*dadhy-ātman*), it means that cultivation is likewise explained in this way. The phrase "curd does not depend on...

and so forth uses the same two names to distinguish them from what preceded. Next, the specific characteristics of these five are correctly revealed, and the hearing of the teaching is also clarified.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that through practice one "attains hearing the *amṛta* (clarified butter)": this refers to fully hearing the five flavors, of which *amṛta* is the ultimate.

It is said that one "attains hearing" because this experience of hearing is different from what was previously not heard. As for "seeking by means of sound," this refers to being moved by the Buddha’s teaching of the wholesome dharmas of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*).

"Curd" (*dadhi*) refers to entering the reality of the ten abodes (*bhūmi*). "Fresh butter" (*navanīta*) refers to the ten practices (*caryā*), and "matured butter" (*ghṛta*) refers to the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*).
“Ghee” refers to the stages from the first bhūmi up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*). “Concluding” means that the preceding and succeeding sections differ.
Therefore, next, regarding the Perfect [Teaching], the clarification of hearing the teaching and practicing it is precisely this conclusion; this is found in the text of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
It possesses both essence and function, which can be understood therein. To act as such is to practice while attaining such essence and function; this is the conclusion.
Because both its teaching and its practice are entirely without deficiency or diminution, it is "perfect" (*yuan*). Herein, one should clarify the provisional and the real through the lens of wisdom.

Since it is called "perfect," it stands in contrast to the partial; since it is said that all medicinal herbs enter into it, this is the perfection that transcends the partial. This is how this teaching is to be understood.
Next, regarding the distinction between the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku), this also concerns the manifested to know the fundamental.

First, it clarifies that the "son of the body" (*shinshi*) refers to the *prajñā* of ultimate reality (*shōsō hannya*) as the mother and the body, and the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*kanjō hannya*) as the son.

Just as the body-mother can give birth to a child, the observation of ultimate reality can produce contemplative observation; the object can produce wisdom. Therefore, he is named "Son of the Body," which is his original ground (*honji*). This is also...

By examining the traces, one knows their source. Second, the traces are clarified; they are threefold. First, there is the general indication of the reasons for manifesting traces and their boundaries.
Second, there is the specific explanation that reveals their manifestations. Finally, there is the conclusion regarding the traces in order to reveal the source.

Regarding the term "compassionate pity" (*karuṇā*), it means pitying those who lack the five kinds of wisdom pertaining to both the provisional and the real. However, these five kinds must all be understood in terms of wisdom.
What is meant by "discourse" refers to unwholesome wisdom, tainted wisdom, provisional wisdom, wisdom of the two extremes, and wisdom of the Middle Way.
Within this context, the fourfold negation (catuṣkoṭi) and its lack of fixed direction are both as explained previously.
Next, by means of the practitioner, his past causes are revealed so that he may measure his own capacity and practice accordingly;
herein there are three parts. First, the general indication of essence and function: "One" is the essence, and "three" is the encompassed function. Is this not a concise and essential approach?
To speak of "one" and "three" is merely to cite the object and the contemplation alternately; one must understand this well without falling into error. All...
As for those [categories] listed separately below, they are next revealed individually as three distinct types, each of which possesses both essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*).

First, "curd" (*nǎi*) refers to the two teachings [the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings]. Second, "butter" (*sū*) refers to the stages prior to the [Shared] Grounds (*diqián*), while "worldly" (*shì*) refers to the aforementioned "pores" (*kǒng*).

This [category of "worldly"] subsumes the beginning and end of the Middle Teaching (*zhōng*) and the Perfect Teaching (*yuán*), as well as the separate [stages of] the Ten Dedications (*shíxiàng*) and above the Grounds (*dìngdì*). This [classification] subsumes all that has been discussed previously, both horizontally and vertically.
When wisdom is exhaustive in every respect and subsequently the knots are resolved into luminous, perfect fusion—this is because emptiness is identical to the provisional and the middle;
the provisional is identical to emptiness and the middle; emptiness and the provisional are identical to the middle; and the middle is identical to emptiness and the provisional.
Thus, one is three and three is one; yet one, three, and one are not one, three, and one. That which can be three and can be one is called the "perfect, wondrous, and non-referential contemplation."
How could such wondrous wisdom be far away? It may be sought within oneself; there is nothing that is not it. Although it is indeed within, one must know its six aspects.
If one does not know them, one reverts to being a coarse entity; how could this be wondrous?
The second section of the Commentary explains "Mahāmaudgalyāyana. It should be understood that this name of the Noble One contains both his designation and his conduct.
The first character is used to distinguish his name and to praise his virtuous conduct; the subsequent three characters directly indicate his personal name.
Regarding this explanation, there are two distinct parts: the first explains his name and lineage, while the section beginning with "The Explanation of the Treatise" below explains his virtues.
In the first section of the "Practice" (xing), there are five sentences: first, an explanation of his clan name; second, an elucidation of his father’s name; third, an explanation of his eye-name;
fourth, an elucidation of the different names he held; and fifth, a brief explanation of his "Great Name" (dazì).

Among these five, the first four explain his personal and family names to manifest his parentage, while the fifth sentence briefly clarifies the great significance [of his name]. Regarding the first of these, from ancient times until now, all...
It is said that they recited [the scriptures] together without clarifying their meaning. Next, there are two versions combined into a single explanation:
it states that "hu-dou" (hemp beans) refers to mung beans (*mudga*); thus, all new translations refer to them as mung beans.

As for "naming the clan after this," it refers to the family name of this noble one’s distant maternal ancestor; therefore, the ancient commentators all state that his mother was of this ancient lineage.
The lineage of seers (ṛṣi) takes the mother’s surname as its name; therefore, it is so called. Furthermore, the new translation renders it *Mahā-maudgalyāyana*, which means "Great Mung-bean Clan.
In ancient times, there was a seer who dwelt in a secluded mountain retreat and constantly gathered mung beans (*mudga*) for food;
consequently, he took this as his clan name. The Venerable One’s mother belonged to that lineage, and thus [the clan name] was taken from the mother’s surname.

Regarding his name "Upatiṣya" (上): the first part is derived from his mother’s clan name to serve as his given name (*nāman*), while the latter part is explained in the *Śāstra* as being derived from his father to serve as his family name (*gotra*).
The master of divination belonged to his father’s lineage; thus, "Son" (*putra*) refers to the Venerable One’s personal name.

Because he was the son of that man, people used this as his title to honor both father and son equally. The following section provides the formal explanation, clarifying that his name is properly called *Kauṇḍinya*.
The old interpretation by Eṣa-lu-to (Li-duo) is as previously stated; because this tree is the highest and the great deity dwells within it, people offer prayers there.

The two lines below further clarify its name. Regarding the phonetic differences, the Master says that according to the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is correctly written as *mukalinda* (目伽路子度);
some versions abbreviate it to *xi* (兮), which is an error resulting from transcription. Next...

Furthermore, the addition of *nyāya* is also due to their being distinct. While the meaning of the first three characters of each [term] is certainly not different, the meaning of the last two characters of each ought to be distinct;
yet no commentary has been seen that clarifies this essential point. For instance, as previously mentioned, some say that the five characters of the preceding phrase should be moved to the front;
this is because they do not realize that both phrases are alternative names for the same thing. Below...

This first phrase provides a brief explanation of the general meaning. "Great" (*mahā*) has two senses: namely, exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) and manifestation (*prakāśana*). The meanings are as previously stated;
here, for now, it is explained by way of exclusion, while its sense of manifestation will be clarified in the following sequence.
The following should now be explained as the virtues that clarify the meaning manifested by the "Great Characters" (*da-zi*).
Although these manifestations are all "great meanings," though their specific names are not established in the text, by inferring from the preceding principles, they likewise number ten.
What are they? First is the distinction [from others]; second is the greatness of its category; third is its divine function.

The first [of these ten] is based on the names; the remaining nine are based on the meanings. First, it can subdue wrong views; second, it can crush the poison of hatred; third, it can subdue the poison of delusion;
fourth, it can eliminate the filth of greed; fifth, it can subdue all forms of pride; sixth, it can manifest the Buddha’s vocal karma; seventh, it can reveal the Buddha’s mental karma;

eighth, it can manifest the Buddha’s body-karma; ninth, it can manifest the Buddha’s wisdom-karma; tenth, it can manifest the Buddha’s power-karma. The first is based on the names, while the latter nine are based on the meanings.

Regarding the practices, the first is based on the essence (*tī*), while the subsequent eight concern the essential aspects of practice. To summarize, these are merely the names for the great majesty of the essence and function of practice.
As for the four *siddhārtha* (purposes), they will be explained there. Regarding the initial explanation of "just as soon as" (*cái míng*) and so forth:
it refers to being noble and spirited according to one's wisdom; because of one's majestic power and capability, one is seen as noble and spirited, and thus [the path] is taken up.
The repeated "shuang" (爽) is not intended here as a listing of noble qualities; rather, it refers to those that are mutually comparable and similar, where there are instances of nasalization.
Now, we simply take the meaning of "comparison" (*bi*) to correspond with what follows. The first two lines present them alternately, while the latter two clarify that they are identical.
In reality, these are merely *samādhi* and *prajñā*; there is no wisdom apart from concentration, and no concentration apart from wisdom. Wisdom... [is thus established].
Without concentration (*samādhi*), there is no means to exhaustively perfect its illumination; without wisdom (*prajñā*), there is no means to deepen its stillness (*śamatha*).

Since one can possess both deep concentration and wisdom, they are equally balanced, and thus all are identical. As previously explained, when Śāriputra’s spiritual power was manifest, it was because his clear wisdom possessed penetration;
when he preached the Dharma for Śakra, it was because that penetration possessed wisdom. Therefore, they are identical. This is based on their internal identity.
Therefore, externally they form homogeneous groups; as the *I Ching* says, "Things of a kind gather according to their category," which expresses this same meaning.
Internally, their essence is thus; externally, they adapt to what is appropriate for things, each promoting its own capacity. This generally describes the greatness of their person.

The addition of one [character] below signifies that they obtain the divine power (*śakti*) to assist in greatness. Flying to the ten directions—whether before or after—as previously described, can be understood accordingly.
This refers to the aforementioned matter of his noble and spirited character. The mention of the "left side" is because it is in contrast to Śāriputra’s position on the right.
The commentary (shū) does not provide a fixed interpretation, but as previously summarized based on the sūtra text, the "left" is a term for assisting the primary transformation.
Thus, the *Erya* states that "left and right" mean to assist; here, it specifically employs supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) as the assistance. This is determined by...
The essence is concentration (*samādhi*), while its function is supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). Next, the subduing of the heterodox is explained; "the great" refers here to external heterodoxy.
The seven matters below all manifest the activities of supernormal powers as aids. Regarding the term *pò'é*, some editions read *pǒ'é*, which denotes a state of swaying, tilting, and instability.
Next is the ability to subdue the poison of anger; this matter appears in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*.
In the first *Āgama*, it is explained that the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother and was passing over [the palace] from above;
therefore, [the Nāga] gave rise to anger and said, "How can this shaven-headed man pass over me as I ascend? This refers to the period before he had yet attained faith.
As for why he did not permit the bhikṣus [to enter], it is first to clarify that the power of the dragon and the intensity of its poisonous anger were great, and secondly... [the text continues].
