To manifest Maudgalyāyana’s great power, the Buddha first asked him for the means to subdue and convert [the beings], namely:

first the coarse, then the subtle, and finally the manifestation of his ordinary body—these being the three modes mentioned in the text. Subsequently, as they were approaching the Buddha’s presence, he commanded him to return to his original form;
he then manifested himself as an upright human being. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and having attained faith, he became a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
Next, Sezi again became angry with the King; while the King remained unmoved, Sezi gave rise to great wrath within the royal palace and performed great, monstrous transformations.
Maudgalyāyana, through his supernormal powers, transformed them all into great auspiciousness so that no harm was done.
Fearing that the text would become too prolix, I cannot cite it in full here. What follows below clarifies the greatness of being able to subdue the poison of ignorance.

From the *Ekottarika Āgama*: As for those who, being both brothers in the secular world and likewise disciples who have left the household life, suddenly hold such divergent views—this is indeed the height of foolish malice.
The reason such people hold these divergent views is that the Sūtra clarifies that at first they requested to leave the household life three times, yet the Buddha did not grant permission;
they then became angry with the Buddha, claiming it was out of a jealous heart.

He then went forth into homelessness and studied under other bhikṣus, where he attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and was able to perform extraordinary feats; his fame spread far and wide, and he received great offerings.
Later, he requested the Buddha for a following of disciples. The Buddha rebuked him, saying, "I would not entrust my assembly even to Śāriputra or Maudgalyāyana, let alone to you, a foolish man.
Thereupon, he harbored a grudge and separately organized an unlawful faction to entice the Buddha’s followers. At that time—
There were five hundred newly initiated practitioners who did not yet know [the correct path] and followed him; he took them to Mount Gayā to perform religious rites together.

Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana went there to convert them and brought them back. As recorded in the *Pṛthakcaryā-pañcadharma* (The Five Dharmas of Separate Practice), these five dharmas are as stated in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*:
first, not accepting the five flavors; second, abstaining from meat; third, abstaining from salt; fourth, not accepting cut-and-sewn robes; fifth, not...
He resided in a monastery on the outskirts of a village; the rest is as explained in the commentary. Kokālika was one of his followers.
Those who trampled him did so to cause him to awaken; yet that he still did not awaken was due to the power of the Venerable One.
Because of this, he later committed various heinous acts, was consumed by fire, and finally entered the Avīci Hell, as described in detail in the Sūtra.

It is said that although this one individual remained deluded and had not yet returned [to the path], the five hundred had already reformed; the great assembly was harmonious and free from folly or confusion.
Therefore, this is capable of exercising the function of subduing ignorance and delusion. Next, the following passage clarifies its capacity to eliminate the functions of greed and defilement.
The reason it is not mentioned here is that the Buddha’s virtue is so sublime that he does not answer when there is no inquiry, lest it cause harm.
Therefore, it is not mentioned; others are not sufficiently qualified to be so described, and the Venerable One is likewise, which is why he also does not serve as the *karmadāna*.
In this way, he can eliminate [faults] at that time and further exert himself for the future; thus, he is able to remove the poisonous evil of greed and defilement.
Below, this clarifies his ability to subdue all forms of pride, wherein there are three meanings, the first being "stopping."
1. The chariot; 2. Burning the two [palaces]; 3. Using the small to contain the great. Regarding these three intentions:

first, it clarifies that he was made to realize the absence of self because he had not yet attained mastery; second, it causes him to awaken to impermanence so that his attachments may be immediately extinguished;
third, it causes him to eliminate pride entirely. Regarding the first point, the commentary on the "Chapter on Solid Life" states: "Prince Bimbisāra..."
When the daughter was first born, she was abandoned on the road; everyone around her said she was already dead, but she immediately declared, "I am indeed alive," and thus she was given that name.
Because she was skilled in medical treatment, [the Buddha] went to consult her. Since she was already a holy person, why would he need to ask her?
It was merely to conform to worldly custom and to serve as a cause for converting her. Next, it speaks of engaging in battle.
Because Śakra possesses the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*) while the asuras possess beautiful women, they constantly harbor mutual jealousy; for this reason, they battle.
"Victory Hall" (*Jiētáng*) is the name of the hall constructed [for this purpose]. Among the thousand worlds, this hall is the most excellent, and is thus named the "Victory Hall.
This is from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. Following this, the passage clarifying that one can know the marks of the Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice is cited here.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that this Brahma-sound is one of the Buddha’s thirty-two marks.
Among these thirty-two marks, the sūtras declare this mark to be the most excellent; its sound can pervade the worlds of the ten directions, and wherever it is heard, all who hear it understand it.
Because Maudgalyāyana heard this, he sought its distance and proximity; the treatise summarizes this briefly.
The third section on clarity has three parts: first, hearing [the Dharma] as if before one's eyes upon reaching the summit of Mount Sumeru;

second, by means of supernormal power, going to the edge of the great trichiliocosm to the summit of the Great Iron Ring Mountains, where what is heard is likewise no different from being before one's eyes;

and third, again by the Buddha’s supernormal power, traveling to the west to a buddha-field ninety-nine Ganges-sands of worlds away, where the land is named Radiant Banner and the Buddha is named Radiance.

The King, having heard that voice from afar as if it were face-to-face, learned that the body of that Buddha was forty *li* tall, the Bodhisattvas were twenty *li* tall, and the alms bowl was over one *li* in height, as recorded in the commentary.

That Buddha further addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying, "The Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas of this land see that your body is small and may give rise to thoughts of contempt; you should manifest your supernatural powers. Maudgalyāyana then immediately—
He leaped into the void to a height of more than a hundred million *ren*, sat upon a transformed throne, and adorned himself with various radiant precious jewels and necklaces.
Those bodhisattvas marveled at this unprecedented occurrence. [This section] clarifies the meaning of "one who can know the Buddha's mind," which refers to where the Buddha’s intention resides.
The Sūtra states that when the Buddha was fifty years old, he sought an attendant; among his various disciples...

The Buddha requested that he [Maudgalyāyana] act as his attendant, but the Buddha accepted neither; Maudgalyāyana entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and perceived through observation that the Buddha’s intention was fixed solely upon Ānanda—just as the sun shines directly upon one's face when facing a wall, meaning it is straightforward—as explained at length in the sūtras.
Therefore, this is evidence of his power to know the mental activities of the Buddha. These seven preceding matters all clearly demonstrate the state of his supreme supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

The section beginning with "Coming from cause and effect" (來因果) below explains the reason for the term "Great Word" (大字); the section beginning with "The fourfold commentary" (四釋論) extensively demonstrates the divine function.

Within this extensive text, there are naturally four parts, which correspond to the Fourfold Beneficence (四悉): first, the Worldly (世界); second, "Increasing [merit]" (增一) and so forth, for the Satisfactory (為人);
third, "Non-Buddhists" (外道) and so forth, for the Remedial (對治); fourth, "The Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice" (如來梵聲) and so forth, for the Ultimate (第一義). This person discards the first three.
It is not that there are four separate categories; rather, the fourth alone is divided into four. This accounts for the structural integrity of both the preceding and following sections.
Now, it is said that the first [section] clarifies his name and title, which pertains to worldly affairs; thus, it constitutes the "worldly" (loka) aspect.

Next, the "class of beings," "supernatural powers," and "attendants" constitute the "human" (pudgala) aspect, as they are capable of uprooting evil and the most severe greed, hatred, delusion, and pride; therefore, this is the "Buddha-sound" (*buddha-ghoṣa*) as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Because the Buddha-mind enables people to know the ultimate sage’s wondrous essence and function, it is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
It is from these ten meanings and four causal conditions that this name is obtained; since these meanings are clearly present, the commentary states [“and so forth”].

Next, regarding the classification by teaching (yào jiào), this means distinguishing the provisional and the ultimate to reveal the subtlety of the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of this sutra’s Dharma.
According to the four teachings, there are four distinct types of supernatural power.

As for the "four dhyānas," they are also called "fundamental dhyānas" because they arise from the same causes as the mundane and supramundane states. Regarding the "fourteen," the first dhyāna has two kinds of transformation; that is, the first dhyāna...
The first dhyāna transforms as the first dhyāna; the desire realm transforms as the second dhyāna; the third dhyāna transforms as the third dhyāna; the fourth dhyāna transforms as the fourth dhyāna;

and the fifth dhyāna transforms as the fifth dhyāna—thus there are fourteen. Regarding the statement that "transformation is a different name for the supernormal power of action (*ṛddhi-viṣaya-vidhijñāna*) based on contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and so forth," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are three kinds of dhyāna, namely the mundane (*laukika*) and others; these four [types of transformation] are the supramundane (*lokottara*) dhyānas.

The four kinds of dhyāna encompass all matters of dhyāna; the six subtle gates, the sixteen special victories, the nine contemplations of impurity, the eight reflections on repulsiveness, and so forth, which cultivate the contemplation of the provisional and the real, are called "contemplative dhyāna" (vipaśyanā-dhyāna).
Using the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) to further refine and train the preceding contemplative dhyāna is called "refined dhyāna" (prahāṇa-dhyāna).
By means of the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (Lion’s Stretch Samādhi), one is able to eliminate even the most subtle obstacles within meditative concentration.
Furthermore, it can cause the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) to enter and emerge from various dhyānas with such swiftness and continuity that it perfumes and ripens the preceding dharmas;

therefore, it is called "perfuming dhyāna" (*vāsita-dhyāna*). By means of the *vyutkrāntaka-samādhi* (the samādhi of leaping over stages), one is able to transcend the various stages and enter and emerge from them with mastery, thereby augmenting the previously cultivated practices;
therefore, it is called "cultivation dhyāna" (*bhāvanā-dhyāna*). The ten *kṛtsnāyatana* (totalities) refer to blue, yellow, red, white, the four great elements, space, and consciousness.

To recognize these as the ten is to understand that each individual characteristic enters into and pervades all places; it is in this sense that they are called the "ten universal bases" (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*).

Thus, the new translations refer to them as the "ten universal bases of meditative concentration" (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana-samādhi*), which carries the same meaning. They are also called the "ten universal entries.

Some say that these already belong to the preceding category of contemplative dhyāna (*vipaśyanā-dhyāna*), yet they are mentioned separately because the essence of contemplative dhyāna is this [state].
When the essence is accomplished, there is the function of arising activity; because this explains the power of transformation and adaptability, it is mentioned separately.
One should further consult the *Dharmadhātu-krama* and the ninth section on the "Meditative States" (*dhyāna-viṣaya*) in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Among the fourteen supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) common to the first four dhyānas, these four are distinct, and thus they are called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, they differ from the subsequent [state] because they manifest as emptiness.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that there are eighteen transformations of the physical body (*kāya-vikurvaṇa*), these are the applications of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-prayoga*).

These applications consist of both general and specific types; they are generally fourteen, but specifically eighteen. Thus, when one speaks of fourteen or eighteen, some say: first, water issues from the right side;

second, fire issues from the left side; third, water issues from the left side; fourth, fire issues from the right side; and fifth and sixth, water and fire issue alternately from above and below the body—these constitute four [additional] transformations.
10. Walking on water as if on land; 11. Disappearing from mid-air and reappearing on the ground; 12.
Disappearing from the ground and reappearing in mid-air; 13–16. Walking, standing, sitting, and lying down in the four postures; 17.
Manifesting a massive body that fills the void and then manifesting it again as small; 18. Manifesting smallness after being small.
The *Dayi danqiu yuchu* (Great Commentary on the Remaining Passages) explains: "Water and fire [manifest] above, below, left, and right, two in each direction, making eight.

Entering the earth as if it were water, treading upon water as if it were earth, the earth sinking to reveal space, and space sinking to reveal the earth—then the great manifests as small, and the small manifests as great;
these combined constitute the eighteen transformations. It is likely that some portions here are insufficient due to omissions in the transcription. This may be compared [with other versions].

The aforementioned four modes—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—are permeated throughout the void. Furthermore, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are eighteen transformations, namely:
first, trembling, up to the eighteenth, emitting light. These are fully detailed in the verses within the *Shiji* (Record of the Master); they cannot be described here in detail.
It concludes by stating that the "Initial Teaching" is so called because it is composed based on phenomenal dhyāna; therefore, it is the initial [stage].

Furthermore, because one realizes that phenomena are identical to principle and cultivates practice based upon this, there is no distinction between earlier and later stages; therefore, it is "universal" (pervasive).
As for the "particular," the fundamental substance upon which one relies differs: first there is merely phenomena, next there is the truth, and now one relies on the three truths.
Because each subsequent stage is deeper than the preceding one, it is said that one "progressively enters ever more deeply. In reality, however, this also transcends the two previous teachings.

Regarding the three vehicles, I have briefly mentioned only two. Within the Perfect [Vehicle], the wondrous essence inherently possesses wondrous function; by simply contemplating the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), one spontaneously possesses supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

Just as myriad images naturally appear in a clear mirror free of dust, one does not employ dualistic characteristics to draw forth the "Pure Name" (Vimalakīrti) as a separate realization of the divine eye power (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*).
Because both do not possess dualistic characteristics, they are the essence of formlessness (*animitta*). Thus, when seeing the various Buddha-lands, one is able to see them.
This refers to all aspects and functions, even up to the four propositions; it is without fixed direction, arising from the True as a response.

This universally explains and clarifies the subtle essence and function of the three karmas. The limit of truth (*bhūtakoṭi*) is precisely the absence of dualistic marks; pervading the ten dharma realms, there is nothing that does not interpenetrate.
Therefore, having attained this wondrous essence, one can spontaneously and effortlessly manifest wondrous functions. The matter is exhausted here; furthermore—

Because there is nothing superior to it, this is the wondrous meaning of perfect penetration that transcends all relative distinctions; since the present sutra still contains such an intention, the commentary states [as follows].

Furthermore, another point is that the mundane world is obtained through retribution, the Initial Teaching is obtained through cultivation, the Common Teaching is obtained through manifestation, the Distinct Teaching is obtained through both cultivation and manifestation, and the Perfect Teaching is obtained solely through manifestation; now that the teachings have been opened and unified.
All are wondrous functions; all dharmas are exhausted within this gate. Next, the explanation of past vows:

since these were causes from the past, they ought to have been placed within the section on "Causes and Conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) under the passage concerning "Foremost in Spiritual Powers" (*ṛddhi-vidhijñāna*).

However, as for their placement here, the Master said: "They may also be understood as collectively representing the four [bases of miraculous power], and thus they are placed here. Nevertheless, there is a slight discrepancy between the preceding and following sections.
This is because such examples are often out of sequence. The reason for making this vow was that, although the Sages frequently manifest themselves, they rarely preach;
thus, he manifested supernatural powers to repay the kindness of his tonsure and ordination. From this aspiration and joy, the cause was initiated;
when the cause is invoked, the fruit is inevitably attained, and reaching such a state is nothing short of marvelous. This is a brief indication of its meaning.
Therefore, the commentary states (as follows).
Regarding the provisional and the ultimate (*honjaku*): since the sutra has already clarified that there is both a fundamental and a manifested aspect, it is necessary to clarify this;

however, while the sutra speaks of it only in general terms, we must now explain it specifically—namely, the duration of the fundamental and manifested aspects of his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Within this, first, [the duration] is explained in terms of two factors: essence and function.
The text displays the "Original" (hon) horizontally and clarifies the "Trace" (ji) vertically according to the five flavors; thus, one knows its essence by cross-verifying the Original and the Trace.
The "True Limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*) is the meditative concentration of the nature-merit (*prakṛti-guṇa*), while the "Śūraṅgama" is the meditative concentration of the cultivated merit (*bhāvanā-guṇa*).

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is translated as the "Concentration of Vigorous Characteristics" or, in the new translations, the "Concentration of Vigorous Action. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that these are alternative names for Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Thus, cultivation and nature are [one].

Because they are united, it is called the "Samādhi of the Ultimate Reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*); this is precisely the fundamental substance (*tattva*). Regarding "the ten directions," etc., this refers to the vast and remote;
it correctly discusses its function, which is horizontal [pervasive]. The manifestations and activities do not go beyond the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind].
The reason one must take up this samādhi is that without this substance of great vigor, there would be no such function of great vigor. Therefore, it is praised in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

All manifestations of supernatural power and function arise from this power of meditative concentration; thus, it is shown that the divine efficacy relies upon this concentration. This demonstrates the perfect and wondrous essence and function.
As for the term "compassion" (*karuṇā*) used in reference to the traces [of the Buddha’s manifestation], it refers to the reason for manifesting these traces.

All are for the purpose of uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness; yet, as they pass through the five periods, there are differences in their depth and shallowness. Within the various scriptural teachings, all clearly elucidate this.
Because of the matter of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), there is both immediate and gradual introduction. "Ultimate" means entering together into the wondrous essence (*tattva*);
once the wondrous essence is realized, the wondrous function (*vṛtti*) ceases. In the various sūtras, both small and large, the accounts of these supernatural powers are frequently mentioned;
this is precisely the intent behind the introduction. Since the text directly and briefly indicates them without further detailing their specific forms, the commentary states: "[...]".
Next, regarding the contemplation: it is not merely that within one's own mind there exists the principle of "otherness" distinct from external others;

rather, for this very reason, the wondrous function of the ultimate ground (*bhūmi*) is brought to completion herein. The essential point here is precisely to clarify that the three truths of the nature of one's own mind are non-localized;
through this, the wondrous essence is realized and manifested, just as supernatural powers attract beings and lead them to the ultimate. Therefore, it is thus.

This is the contemplation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). This text [states] that "one and three are contained within two and three," meaning that one and many are non-dual, and existence and non-existence are non-dual;
thus, it contains the meaning of two and three. The reason for practicing these suddenly is that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) has no fixed order.
Although there appears to be a sequence here, it is merely the supernormal powers drawing in sentient beings toward the ultimate; it does not refer to a fixed, sequential progression.
Some say that because the three contemplations contemplate the mind and bring the mental object into union with the mind, they are said to "penetrate" to the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).

This is because contemplative wisdom is taken as the "spiritual" and the object as the "penetration"; thus it is called the "contemplation of spiritual penetration. Now, I say: "spiritual" (*shen*) means "wondrous" (*miao*).

Wondrous cultivation brings about union with the wondrous nature, just as those wondrous functions cause sentient beings to realize the wondrous essence; therefore, the contemplation of spiritual penetration is explained first.
"The three contemplations are without fixed direction" explains the meaning of "spiritual" (shen); "they penetrate to the ultimate reality" (shixiang) explains the meaning of "penetration" (tong).
This is because, by means of wondrous cultivation, one is able to realize the wondrous nature;
thus it is said. *Miaojing Wenju Sizhiji*, Scroll Five.

Regarding Śākya-Kātyāyana, it should be known that the first two characters of this five-character name specifically distinguish and praise his virtue.
The three characters "Xing-xia" (行下) are his name. The commentary on this passage has two distinct parts: first, a general and concise explanation;
second, a detailed and specific analysis. The first part contains six phrases: the first five explain his name, and the last one indicates his virtuous conduct.

Although there are five points in the first section, they comprise only four phrases. Regarding "ornamented" (*wen-shi*): it refers to beautiful and exquisite words that adorn and manifest [the meaning].
The Way and its Virtue (Dàoyì) is the merit of expounding the principles; it is adopted as the name because it constitutes a grand literary adornment.
In terms of its meaning, it is truly the most essential and appropriate. As for the name Shànshéng (Fan-String), his father died early, and his mother, out of affection for her son, did not remarry;
she was like a string tying a fan, hence the name. Furthermore, Hǎoshuān (Good Shoulders) was so named because his physical form was beautiful.
Regarding the name *Koṭivīsa*, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha translated it as such. The commentary explains:

this is the name of an ancient ṛṣi; because he possessed a "victory over thought" (*koṭivīsa*) superior to that of others, and because [the author] now belongs to his lineage, it was taken as his name.

Since this is a name derived from a clan (*gotra*), it does not reflect the merit of his treatise and should not be counted among his intellectual qualities. Regarding the four names mentioned here, they are direct [designations].
These merely list [the names] without explaining their meanings, yet conclude by stating that "all are names derived from their surnames.
This suggests that only *Siṃha* (勝一) is a name derived from a surname; the preceding ones are names, whereas the current statement likely contains a scribal error for the character "皆" (all).
Thus, while one is a name derived from a surname, the remaining three are simply names. This has been the case since antiquity.
The explanations are all the same in this regard. In recent translations, it is said that Mahākātyāyana means "Great Shaver-Male" (*mahā-kṣurakāraka-puruṣa*).

This refers to a member of the Brahmin caste who, having lived for a long time in a secluded place within the mountains where many sages dwell, had his beard and hair grow somewhat long because no one shaved them.
According to the dharma of the Brahmins, shaving the hair is considered an evil act; thus, one sage—
There were two brothers among his sons who both came to visit their father; the younger one had his hair shaved by various seers (*ṛṣi*).

These seers vowed to protect him so that he would later attain the path of a seer. Because those of this lineage all have their hair cut and trimmed, and because the men of this clan possess a particularly venerable majesty that distinguishes them from others, they are called the "Great Shaving Clan" (*Mahā-keśakambala*). Furthermore, there was also [a tradition] in ancient times...

Regarding those who take their mother’s surname, it is now clarified that they are actually [the offspring] of the father; therefore, they are called "men" (puruṣa). Previous translations and interpretations were all incorrect.
I maintain that in translation there are both literal renderings and interpretive meanings; thus, it is not contradictory that various causes and conditions may lead to the adoption of such a name.
The first line of the second section is a general heading that characterizes his virtuous conduct; this is precisely the meaning of *mahā*.

Because it is most excellent and greatest, it is termed "foremost" (*prathama*), which subsumes and clarifies two meanings therein. "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to that which is explained, while "teaching" (*dharma*) is that which explains;
since these two are most excellent in this context, it is called "foremost. What follows below is a detailed and specific exposition of those virtues.
Regarding the characteristics of this practice, there are four parts therein: first, gathering those with wrong views and causing them to give rise to right faith;

second, clarifying skillful means and bestowing upon them the good path; third, clarifying the ability to refute various heterodox treatises; and fourth, clarifying the ability to discourse on profound meanings so that those with wrong understanding may enter [the truth].
Within the first of these, there are three sections: first, a general indication of the number of methods for both the agent and the object; second, the actual manifestation of their characteristics.

Regarding the third section, the summary conclusion on faith and submission: first, as for the general introduction, the Master says that this borrows the passage from the aforementioned sutra concerning the bhikṣuṇī Kāśyapī and her refutation of Pāyāsi, using it to illustrate the nature of the doctrinal discourse of Cāṭiyāyanī.
How is this known? At the beginning of the text it says, "As at the final conclusion," and it concludes by stating, "The nature of Cāṭiyāyanī’s doctrinal discourse is likewise so."
Therefore, we know that it is capable of being borrowed to manifest [the truth], as the Sūtras already desire to praise the primary meaning of the treatise.

Since its matters are scattered throughout various sūtras and difficult to describe in full, I shall now select its relevant categories to illustrate the excellence of this virtuous discourse; because it possesses the beauty of turning away from heterodoxy and believing in the correct path, it is virtuous, and thus it is borrowed here to manifest the categories.
As for the term "annihilationist view" (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), it refers to the cessation of the body and the extinction of consciousness.

When body and spirit are both exhausted, there is no longer a future life; because one perceives neither what precedes nor what follows, one concludes that things were originally non-existent and now exist, and having existed, they return to non-existence.
Since there is no future life, one gives rein to one's passions and commits evil. This is a foolish sentiment, and its transgression is particularly grave.

Because many in the world hold this erroneous view, it must be thoroughly refuted. Furthermore, since ancient times there have been those who held such a calculation; thus, [the text cites] Xian of the Liang dynasty...
*The Treatise on the Immortality of the Divine Spirit by Xiufu* (and so forth). [The author] asserts that there is no other world (*paraloka*) as his primary thesis, and proceeds to refute it.
There are ten points of inquiry; these represent the opponent’s heterodox attachments, while the ten responses constitute this author’s correct refutations.
Among them, the first inquiry establishes the thesis, and the subsequent nine inquiries establish the arguments to substantiate that thesis. This is also known as...

Regarding the ten responses, the first establishes the reason (*hetu*) and is termed "establishing the principle" (*yukti*). The first [response] refutes their thesis (*pakṣa*), while the remaining nine refute their reasons (*hetu*).
Within these subsequent nine, each first presents their argument and is then subsequently refuted.

Of these, the first six rely upon logical principles (*yukti*), whereas the final three lack such principles; they merely stubbornly cling to their deluded sentiments, which are thus directly refuted.

Furthermore, by directly addressing matters of delusion and folly, when principles are exhausted and events reach their limit, one must take refuge in the Right Path. Initially, it was stated that there is no other world;
subsequently, its meaning was explained, as the significance lies in what follows. Thus, the Master of our school said: "The initial response through counter-questions is as follows:
Is the sun and moon established by themselves, or are they established by another? If they are established by another, is it by Heaven?"
To act for others is solely because there are devas and humans; therefore, there is tomorrow. If there were no future lives, there would be only today.
If there were no tomorrow, there would also be no yesterday, for today is precisely the "tomorrow" of yesterday.

It is said that the first two tones of the character *wei* (to act) are pronounced in the departing tone (*qushēng*), meaning that the sun and moon exist universally for the sake of humans and devas. One who wishes to employ [this principle]...
Since these constitute parallel cases, I first describe their respective positions so that they may serve as a reliable standard; next, I establish the following inquiry:
"Is there only this world, or is there also another world? This takes the rising and setting of the sun in a single day to represent one "world.

If there were no other world, once the sun had set today, it should not rise again; yet since it does indeed rise again, there must be another world, just as there is the birth and death of human beings.

It is likewise thus: having abandoned [the previous view], one returns to accept it; how can you say there is none? Now, regarding the initial "ji" (即), these three characters are read together as a single breath.

Because this is used to counter-verify [the argument], "zhì" (質) refers to definitive interrogation. The subsequent meaning differs from this; these two interpretations have their full textual basis herein.
It is unknown whether the scriptural text is exhaustive or not; even now, I am unable to fully comprehend it, for those born later are truly formidable.

One should be able to resolve this; however, initially there are fixed difficulties, and within those, all contain three pairs of challenges that likewise require three [responses], all based on the sun and moon as the primary texts. This is extremely brief; one should pose the challenge as follows:
"Since there is now a tomorrow, we know for certain that there cannot be no other world. One should reflect well upon this. Below this are six rounds [of debate].

Furthermore, he establishes a separate thesis to prove that [the intermediate state] definitely does not exist. First, he relies on the fact that a dead person does not return; thus we know it does not exist.

Since this is the case for most people in the world, he cites the living as an analogy for the dead in his refutation. As for *dhāraṇī*, it is like a horse being restrained by a bridle and bit so that it cannot act freely;
this illustrates how after death one is constrained by the suffering retribution of evil karma and cannot attain freedom.

Next, the rebuttal begins by granting the opponent's premise and then providing a response in two parts. First, it refutes the analogy of the latrine to demonstrate the impurity and foulness of the lower realms.
Second, it grants the reason for the objection; the "granting" consists of raising a suspicion regarding the possibility of attainment, stating:

"Since he possesses superior power and mastery, even if he does not return permanently, if he were to return for a brief moment, would he not attain [the goal]? Therefore, this explanation is provided. Within this, first, he has no leisure.
Following this, regarding the statement that he died one day after a hundred days had passed, this is based on the account of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

however, the actual event was that Vasubandhu and his brother vowed to be reborn in Tuṣita, returned to report their success, and then departed. His younger brother, Siṃhabuddhi, went once and did not return—this was the original meaning.
When Vasubandhu arrived there, he paid homage to Maitreya, circumambulated the palace once, and then returned; it had already been three human years since he left.

The year corresponds to the later meaning [of "yi"]. As in that commentary, "huáng" means leisure or opportunity. The next question concerns those whose grave crimes merit death; therefore, they are boiled.
One waits to see if their spirit emerges, for if it exists, the spirit should immediately emerge when being boiled.
Thus, one watches for its emergence. If it emerges, then it exists. Since none is seen to emerge, there is no spirit. Because there is no spirit, it is certain that [the soul] does not exist.

Regarding the other world, this has already been covered by ten thousand words. As for the spirit (*ātman*) and the other world: the spirit occupies the physical body, while the other world pertains to its functional application.
If the spirit were substantially real, it would be able to flow into the other world; however, since its substance is non-existent, how could there be such efficacy?
In the response, an analogy is cited to demonstrate that during sleep, the spirit travels and experiences various places; thus, the *Liezi* clarifies how King Mu sat [and traveled].
While asleep, the spirit wanders to the heavens; thus, the spirit is able to go forth on its own while bystanders do not see it.

Therefore, one might boil such a person in hopes of finding the spirit emerging from them, yet none can be found. This makes it clear that the spirit has no form and cannot be produced as something with form.
To seek it through its own nature and to investigate its numerical patterns is not to say it does not exist. As for the next questioner, he previously sought it outside of form.
If one seeks that spirit within the living body itself, even there it cannot be found; how much less so within a dead body? This is utterly impossible.
This point has already been explained at length. To answer this next with an analogy for clarification:
fire-nature certainly exists within firewood, yet it is not found by breaking the wood apart; to seek the nature of fire in such a way is incorrect.
The spirit within the body is fixed and cannot be sought by setting aside the body; the principle for seeking the spirit is certainly not otherwise.
How does this answer differ from the previous one? It is because it says to seek it among the dead and fail to find it—this should entail two criticisms:
first, since you call them "the dead," their spirits have already departed; how can you still seek [the spirit] therein?
To seek the spirit by these means is to be doubly foolish; it is a total deprivation of it.
Furthermore, as for those who employ reprimands—assuming that one could seek the spirit within the body of a living person, this would already be impossible; how much more so for a dead person?

To seek the spirit through methods that are fixed and limited, when the spirit is wondrous and boundless, is to use the coarse to seek the subtle. How could this possibly succeed? To seek its numerical patterns in this way is not incorrect.
This means that because [the opponent] wishes to hold the Spirit (shen) as non-existent and intends to level two charges with a single statement, they have simply done so;
you should reflect upon this well. The subsequent question further relies on a separate principle, which is likewise a metaphorical expression.

In the response, there is both an analogy and its application, because [the opponent] does not know that the Spirit is a subtle and wondrous entity; therefore, this analogy is used to enlighten them. Fire is the analogy for the Spirit; this is the application.

It should be understood that this arises from a failure to comprehend the divine principle (shenli), not because it does not exist. Regarding the seventh question: previously, you referred to those already deceased; now you speak of those at the point of death.

One who is already dead cannot be seen, whereas one at the point of death can indeed be seen; therefore, it is not the case that [the spirit] does not exist. The answer uses a metaphor to clarify its solemnity:
though formless, to seek it by turning away from its true nature is not the correct method. The spiritual consciousness (shenshi) is formless, yet it follows the conditions of karma (ye-yuan).

How could coming and going be brought about by the existence of a substance through transformation? It is because you do not recognize its spiritual essence and activity that you are unable to bring it about;
it is not said that it does not exist. Regarding the subsequent question: the preceding section has finished refuting the heterodox basis upon which [the opponent] relies;

the following section directly refutes their ignorant sentiments and stubborn attachments. Because their underlying principle is exhausted while their emotional attachments have not yet been uprooted, [the text] proceeds to refute and uproot them accordingly.

Regarding the initial statement that it has been "for a very long time," this is intended to ensure that a good beginning leads to a successful conclusion. The respondent provides a metaphor to rebuke him;
the meaning here is that by citing the wise who are able to abandon the inferior for the superior, it conversely reveals that the foolish are unable to do so—this being the constant way of the world.
The final conclusion should be the same as that of the wise. What, then, is meant by "stubborn adherence" and "desiring to be the same"?
"It is not appropriate for a fool. Regarding the phrase "the entire multitude": if it were only I who am thus, I might be considered a fool;

but since it is not the case that the entire multitude is so, why should I alone be excluded? Here, he refers to his own followers as "the multitude. What does this mean? It is a compound censure, a formal objection intended to refute [the opponent].
The answer consists of an analogy and its application (*upanaya*). Within the analogy, there are three parts: first, clarifying the deception of the ghost; second... [text fragment ends]
Regarding "the two people": first, one person is deceived; second, one person is not. The Master says these represent the two views of the heterodox and the orthodox.
However, according to the intent of this chapter, they may also be used as a metaphor for the two types of people—the ignorant and the wise. Within this, there are four meanings:
namely, the person, the ox, the rice, and the grass. The person is able to ride; the ox is the vehicle upon which the person rides, which is the cause. The rice and the grass are... [the result].

This refers to the result. The metaphor of a ghost appearing in human form illustrates the false teacher who propounds the view of annihilationism; this corresponds to what was previously called "those people.

Regarding the phrase "speech and so forth," the former refers to the false person, while this metaphor illustrates the preaching of false dharma—namely, what was just mentioned as "speaking in such a manner.
The "path ahead" refers to the next world. Just as rice and grass provide sustenance for humans and oxen, so too is the fruit of peace and happiness mistakenly [attained through such views].
Because false non-action (*mithyā-asamskṛta*) brings about great peace and bliss, it is said to be "abundant. What does this mean? It is a metaphor for not accepting the preceding correct teaching.
Next, the metaphor of a person being struck refers to the fool who, by believing in and clinging to false non-action, falls into the evil realms.
Next, the metaphor of one not being struck refers to the wise person who is able to believe that both the mundane and supramundane are uninterrupted and unceasing, thereby attaining the Way.
The result is eternal peace and happiness. Next, combining the previous three meanings, it is shown that deceptive speech lacks any basis in reality.

Like fools who discard grain for straw, one will surely fall into the evil realms. Why not discard such [speech]? Because they are like the wise, who seek to attain the fruit of the Path and abide in constant peace and happiness.
The intent of the final question is as previously stated: although all the various objections have been refuted, they are still not [fully] resolved.
Because one is able to follow the right path yet merely succumbs to ordinary emotions, it is called "anger. The answer also employs a metaphor to rebuke him; the text consists of five sentences:
the first metaphorizes his adherence to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); the second metaphorizes his establishing [that view] through extreme means;
the third metaphorizes how he, through this perverse attachment and madness, invites evil retribution for himself; and the fourth sentence metaphorizes... [the remainder of the fourth sentence].
The final phrase, "not accepting the present correct exhortation," serves as a metaphor for the state of not accepting correct exhortation; it means that you do not accept what I have seen.
This is also a reprimand for their suffering. The ten preceding sections have refuted their thesis, refuted their doctrine, and refuted their deluded sentiments;
this concludes the refutation of the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*). As for the doctrine of permanence (*śāśvatavāda*), [it is addressed as follows]:

One refutes [the notion of permanence] by means of the two types of impermanence—the coarse and the subtle—both internally and externally; this applies likewise even to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Next follows the second section, which concludes the subduing through false faith; it is also termed "benefit" and serves to manifest its efficacy.

By breaking down and shattering false attachments and extensively expounding the correct meaning, the false is destroyed and the correct is revealed. Because one thus accords with and follows the true path, there is faith and submission, followed by praise.
The exclamation "Excellent! (*sādhu*) below clarifies the characteristics of his faith and submission;

it is beautiful because it accords with reason, and it is a sublime discourse that praises his words, for both word and meaning are exquisite. The conclusion below follows the same pattern as before and may be understood through a brief explanation.
Next, to clarify the skillful instructions: for now, they are explained through the categories of the simple, the weighty, and the skillful employed out of absolute necessity;
their characteristics are thus made easy to understand. Because the following section would involve prolixity, the commentary states: (and so forth).
Furthermore, the third and fourth sections of the World Scripture (Jièdiǎn) are now combined into one, which is the third [section]:
"Capable of Refuting Various Heterodox Treatises to Reveal This Profound Way. Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying the request for the treatise by a different person;

second, clarifying the formal granting of the treatise. Regarding the reason for requesting the treatise: it is because heterodoxy was about to be refuted and the capacity for the Correct [Dharma] was about to arise.
This is because it was [merely] initiated. From the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the following clarifies the granting of the debate;
therein are two parts: first, clarifying that the debate was not granted immediately at that time; second, clarifying that the debate was granted only later.

Regarding the reason why it was not granted immediately at first, there were many intentions: for the sake of slighting and despising him, and for the sake of obstructing and suppressing him. As for "that which should destroy the heterodox and manifest... [the text continues].
Since the truth does not reside in this person, it must reside in that other person at a later time and place;

for these four reasons, we temporarily cite the two individuals mentioned in the source text as the lowest examples to contrast with them, yet without engaging in debate—this is precisely a skillful deployment of strategic pressure to lay them low. As the Sūtra says: "That person, having already..."
Having heard and reflected upon this, fearing that [the interlocutor] might be acting on behalf of another, he said, "I am not fit to discuss this now.

This explains that at a later time he would indeed engage in the discussion. Within this section, first Pūrṇa is addressed, followed by Pūrṇa-śāṭyāyanīputra. Regarding the former, there are three rounds of question and answer.
The reason for asking about his name first is that even if one does not yet know the person, they may have long been familiar with their name.
Therefore, although he raised the question first, he did not answer it; seeking to conceal his own lack of ability and his shortcomings, he failed to respond.

On the second turn as well, he intended to heighten his momentum so that [the opponent] would be cowed by his reputation and fail to perceive the truth. Thus, he proceeded to debate the expediency of his position. Consequently, [the opponent] accepted this and raised an objection.
Since there was no clever sophistry, he simply manifested his spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*). Even a wise person follows principle and does not prize eccentricity; therefore, he did not believe him.

Since he is already without discursive thought (*vitarka*) and possesses both meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), he must be endowed with all perfect virtues; why then would he be unable to respond?
However, because there are also those who do not fully possess both concentration and wisdom, there are three different types of *arhats*. Furthermore, it is not that he is incapable of responding;
rather, this is intended as a skillful means (*upāya*) for the subsequent discussion.
Next, the actual exposition according to the *Candraprabha-paripṛcchā-śāstra*: first, he manifests his form through supernatural powers;
second, during the actual discourse, he immediately conceals his own form and manifests himself as that other being’s body. Within the actual discourse, there are two parts:

first, a preliminary inquiry regarding the shallow meaning established previously; second, the main discussion on the profound meaning to follow. Regarding the first, the Sūtra says: "Having manifested his form..."
After a while, he said to him: "If you say that I possess only supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and am not fit for discussion, I shall repay your argument by employing a metaphor for you.
What is your honor’s title? He replied, "I am a Brahmā. He asked, "Are you a man? He replied, "I am a man.
He asked again, "Are you a person? He replied, "I am a person. He asked once more, "Since a person is also a man, is this not redundant?"
The meanings of "blind" (*andha*) and "eyeless" (*acakṣus*) are not the same. A scripture asks: "What is meant by 'blind'? It answers:
"It is like one who does not see this world or the world beyond, nor the arising and passing away of beings, nor know as they truly are wholesome and unwholesome karma;

being forever without any abiding [wisdom], such a person is called blind. "What is meant by 'eyeless'? It answers: "It is precisely the absence of the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) described above. A secular treatise says: "Stop."
"Ceasing as explained in the commentary" means suppressing what is shallow before and initiating what is profound after;
because the capacity for the Way arises in due time, one suppresses the preceding mundane, shallow, and mixed discourse to purely discuss the supramundane, profound, and pure *nirvāṇa*.

Within this, there is first a question-and-answer session, followed by the attainment of the fruits of the Way. The initial word "頗" (*pho*) is a term used to grant permission or allow for something. Since all worldly [beings]...

Because one grasps at [the notion of] real existence as being the Path, this question-and-answer is established; it contains both "two" and "one. First, having provisionally admitted that there are two, he further asks:

"In dependence upon what dharma? He answers: "Not in dependence upon the five aggregates (*skandha*)," because these five are the very things to be eliminated—being neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa—in order for them to be transcended.
According to the sūtras, he further asks: "Is the arising of the five existences (*pañca-bhava*) with conditions or without conditions?"
He replied, "Birth has conditions; it is not without them. He asked again, "What are its conditions? He replied, "Craving. He asked again, "What is craving?
He replied, "Birth. He asked again, "What is birth? He replied, "Craving. The preceding section clarified that one does not rely on the dharmas of the aggregates (*skandha*);
this section clarifies that one relies precisely on these dharmas to attain [liberation]. Since all eight types are correct, they are able to sever the false.
The *Piyajātika Sutta* is complete in its textual form; as the preceding commentary briefly sets forth its essentials, it is presented here directly.

Having heard the secular account, [the Buddha] attained the fruit [of Arhatship]; at the end, Cūḷapanthaka informed the Śākyas, who then prepared the wood for his cremation and erected a stupa for him.
Regarding the four purposes (*catuḥ-saṃgraha-hetu*) within the preceding causal conditions (*nidāna*), the Master said: "The first is for the world; the *Ekottarika-āgama* says it is for people.

It corresponds to the 'remedy' (*pratipakṣa*) and the 'ultimate meaning' (*paramārtha*), as each—whether refuting heterodox views or secular classics—serves both to destroy error and to attain the Way.
Others say that within the subsequent exposition of virtues, the four purposes are clarified: first, for the world; and so forth.
In the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the lower [teachings] serve as antidotes to the Vinaya; the middle [teachings] serve as secular treatises for human beings. Regarding the "First Principle" (*paramārtha*) here:

first, names and surnames belong to the world of phenomena (*loka*). Next, the ten stages and the wholesome refuge and precepts cause those two groups of followers to give rise to deep faith and goodness—this is the "human" [teaching].
The miscellaneous treatises that refute secular works are the "antidote" [teaching]. The profound meaning of the causal treatises that enables them to attain the Path is the "First Principle."
The meaning of this single passage is very clear; there is no need for confusion.
Next, regarding the analysis of the differences and convergences of the methods of debate according to the teachings: first, "impermanence and so forth" refers to that which can refute;
next, "the refuted, such as eternalism and nihilism," refers to everything up to the sixty-two views. Since these are matters of refutation and dismantling, they belong to the initial stage.

Furthermore, within the "General" (sāmānya) category, there is also a distinction between the agent and the object of refutation, whereas the object to be refuted itself has no differentiation; thus, the wisdom of emptiness refutes both views and attachments.
Since this constitutes a refutation of their very substance, it belongs to this teaching. To cite the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* as proof is precisely for this reason.

Next, within the "Specific" (viśeṣa) category, there is also the distinction between agent and object, which differs from the former case. In the former, both the agent and the object were treated as the objects [of refutation]. In the latter...

Having merely refuted the conventional to enter emptiness, one now further refutes emptiness to reveal the provisional; furthermore, by refuting both extremes, one reveals the convergence with the Middle Way—thus it is forever distinct from what preceded.
*Dhāraṇī* refers to the four types of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), namely those concerning words and meanings, and so forth;

these two constitute the essence of this teaching and its treatise. "Observing the capacity" means knowing the illness; "illuminating the provisional" means recognizing the medicine. To apply the medicine according to the illness is...

Administering medicine to shatter [views of] permanence and annihilation is precisely the correct administration of medicine. Because it is thus profound yet not yet fully integrated—differing from what precedes and follows—it is "distinct" (bie).
Next, within the Perfect [Teaching], there is also the marvelous interplay of the agent and the object, whereby the coarse is shattered and nothing remains that is not marvelous;
because everything is immediately suchness, this is the perfection of the Perfect, which is itself the marvel.
Next, regarding the sequence of the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku): first, the manifestation of the fundamental substance (*dharmakāya*) refers to the two adornments (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*);

next, the fundamental function refers to the two bodies (*dvaya-kāya*). The text of this Great Sūtra is as explained later in the section on Avalokiteśvara. Now, when discussing doctrine, it involves the exchange of words;

such exchange must necessarily involve both parties, and for both to be complete, they must possess the two adornments. Only when one has attained the two adornments within themselves can they manifest them to others. This is how the manifested traces are brought about.
As for the reason why what was originally a single sublime trace is divided into five: it is because [the Buddha], out of compassion for sentient beings, gradually led them [to the truth].
The first four and this fifth are mentioned interchangeably.

Within contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one employs contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) to maturely observe and illuminate the mental object according to reality; as with the question regarding the object, the object itself can bring forth the contemplation.

Wisdom responds thus, and such illumination arises; through long practice, one is able to realize the non-duality of the Thus-Come One. By rectifying the heterodox and exhausting the correct, all contemplations can be stilled.
This is precisely what is discussed in this *Miaoguan Lun* (Treatise on Sublime Contemplation). Thus, within one’s own mind, the cultivation of the sublime path is brought to completion.
Next, in explaining the primary causes and conditions for Nārada, there are four sections: first, a brief explanation of the name; second, a detailed explanation of the clan name;

third, a detailed explanation of the personal name; and fourth, an elucidation of his virtuous conduct. Regarding the first of these, the Sanskrit term is first presented with its three phonetic variations;

next, the corresponding terms in this land [China] are translated, which likewise have three differences; and finally, among the three names briefly explained, their single underlying meaning is stated, noting that they are all equivalent in their Sanskrit pronunciation.

This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the three "differences" (*san-yi*) in the Sanskrit term *śramaṇa* (the character *sheqie* [奢切] means "deceitful," and "also" implies "prolixity"). Next, I shall briefly explain one meaning;

within it there are further meanings that can be understood from the internal text. Although only one meaning is briefly explained, it inherently contains all three, as will be evident from the subsequent text and can be grasped through reflection.
Next, I shall explain his clan name (*xing*); this is intended to manifest the Buddha’s younger brother.

Because this is the origin of the clan, this text is somewhat more detailed. However, those who have now left the household life all call themselves "Sons of Śākya," yet they do not know the fundamental origins of their lineage.
Is it because they are his descendants that this account of Śākya is more detailed than others?

According to the *Fosong* (Buddhist Genealogy) by Nanshan, one first clarifies the ancestral race and subsequently clarifies the clan name; among the Western [Indic] nobility, there are four such types.
"Dependent upon" refers to the Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. "Buddha" refers to the Buddha-lineage (*kula*), within which there are further five types:
Gautama, Ikṣvāku, Śākya, Śāyi, and Āditya-bandhu. As explained extensively elsewhere, the present text contains two meanings;
first, it distinguishes his clan, specifically clarifying that he was a Kṣatriya. (See *The Twelve Years of Wandering*, Part II).

Next is the explanation of his clan name, namely Śākya-Gautama and so forth. First, regarding the Great Śākyas, one must clarify the original cause by which they attained their status, as well as the remote and proximate origins.
At the beginning of the kalpa, when the world was first formed, human sentiments were gradually becoming corrupt;
as people vied with one another in greed and plunder, a ruler was established, who was distantly titled *Kṣatriya*. Thus, the *Buddha-pǔ* (Buddha Genealogy) says: "Kṣatriya..."
*Di-li* (帝利) is translated into Chinese as "Field Lord" (*tiandi zhuzhu*). Because there was initially much dispute and litigation, a lord was established to manage affairs;

thus, this name arose. As for the mention of "great waters" and so forth, these are the signs at the beginning of the formation of this *Bhadrakalpa* (Auspicious Aeon), as fully explained in the *Dīrgha Āgama* and in the chapters on the Great and Small Kalpas.
"Ābhāsvara" refers to the second dhyāna heaven. Regarding the term "multitude" (*zhong*)...

That sentient beings are born together in the intermediate state is one of its many meanings. Regarding the statement that "those with desire" refers to men and women and so forth, the *Buddha-piṭaka* says:

"Those who have desire for food possess both male and female organs; thus, through this process, they become husband and wife, and are consequently born via the womb. The *Loutan jing* (Kāraṇḍavyūha-sūtra) states:
"There is naturally growing non-glutinous rice, which ripens by evening after being harvested in the morning. The *Madhyama Āgama* states: "The rice grows [spontaneously]."
People vied with one another to preemptively adopt such signs; this is what is meant by "preemptive adoption. Later, Master You remarked:
"Once the corrupt wind has stirred, the pure source is thereby exhausted; when spiritual resonance and response prevail, striking back becomes an act of rebellion.

I have personally investigated the era of the Two Han dynasties: when Donglai added the bare shoulder (the *tan*) garment, the sea fish swam in hidden depths; when Hepu increased its tribute, the pearls [were recovered].
The tadpoles were then moved closer together; since time immemorial, there has been no breach of this covenant.
That rice would not grow was not enough to cause wonder or doubt. Changhan says: "At that time, because sentient beings saw that rice no longer grew, each harbored fear and distress.

They demarcated their fields and dwellings with boundaries, and consequently, the practice of hiding one's own rice and stealing grain from another's field arose. From this, the matter began. No [other source].
One capable of making decisions was established as a single person and titled the "Lord of Equality.

He rewarded the good and punished the evil, and when he provided for all equally, there was a man of magnificent appearance and dignified bearing who commanded the respect of everyone. The multitude then collectively requested him to take charge;

having accepted, he subsequently acquired the title of "Lord. The *Loutan jing* (Lokadhātu-vibhāga-sūtra) states: "The multitude all said, 'Act as our leader,' and thus he was called the 'Elder' (*dīrgha*)."
On the day [of his consecration], the King took the ancestral land by means of the Dharma; therefore, he was named Kṣatriya, which refers to the lord of the fields and the earth.
What is now called "Lord of Men" (Janādhipa) is a title derived from the King. The *Buddhapuṭa* states that the original title of the Lord of Men was Mahāpuruṣa (Great Man).
The preceding section concludes the account of the origins of his lineage. From "The Lord of Men had a son" onwards, the succession of his descendants is described in detail; within this, first—
Having clarified the succession of the Golden Wheel-turning Kings, the text next clarifies the lineage of the Iron Wheel-turning Kings, concluding with a summary of their total number.
According to the *Buddha-pu* (Genealogy of the Buddhas): "Now, counting from the beginning, there were a total of eighty-four thousand two hundred and fifty-three kings.
From the time the Bodhisattva first emerged as a Cakravartin King down to King Śubhamati, there were thirty-three kings; these were merely minor rulers (śūdra-kṣatriyas). Thereafter...

There are eighty-four thousand two hundred and ten lineages of Cakravartin kings; these are no longer [ordinary] wheel-turning monarchs, but rather lords of the Ten Wheels (*daśacakra*), and their number is thus the same.
According to the genealogical records, among these there are both sages and ordinary beings, so one cannot uniformly refer to them as "Golden Wheel Sage Emperors" (*suvarṇacakravarti-rāja*).
However, according to the *Loutan jing* (Lokasthāna-sūtra), it is said that they are all sages; the Nanshan school relies upon this.
The patriarchs do not distinguish between races; for now, we shall rely generally upon the scriptures.
In the genealogical records (*pǔ*), it is directly stated that during the era of the Iron Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*), only four generations are mentioned as Iron Wheel-turners.

Furthermore, among the enumerated figures, the thirty-three minor kings (*kṣudra-rāja*) and the ten patriarchal holy kings (*śāstra-rāja*) are not specified; therefore, there are only eighty-four thousand two hundred and ten kings. This clarifies the origin.
This concludes the explanation of the Kṣatriya lineage of the Śākya clan, which has been extremely long-standing.
Hereafter follows the explanation of their family name (*gotra*). There are five such names as previously listed;

this text specifically explains two while implicitly including four others, omitting the remainder as they are not essential to the primary purpose. There are two distinct parts to this initial explanation: first, the explanation [of the first name].
"Gautama" possesses both the meanings of "sugarcane" (*ikṣvāku*) and "Śākya. Next, regarding the explanation of "Śākya," there are initially two meanings:

first, it is derived from the teacher's command; second, it is derived from the teacher's dharma. It is by means of these two that this single surname was obtained. As for the statement that he served the Brahmins:
since Gautama belongs to the Kṣatriya caste, the origin of this [claim] remains unknown; therefore, the Buddhist genealogies cite this [passage] in common.
The Sūtra states: "In the past, during the first incalculable aeon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), the Bodhisattva was a king whose parents had passed away early.
He abdicated the throne to seek the Way. His teacher’s surname was Gautama, and because he succeeded him, it is feared he might not be a Brahmin.

As for the words 'You should be equal,' these two phrases appear to be mentioned interchangeably to cause [the king] to cast off his royal robes, change his royal surname and status, and don the teacher's own garments."

Because it follows his own clan name, it is "mutual" (interchangeable); because it follows a designation from another person, it is "initial. It was bestowed by his teacher, through whom he obtained this clan name.
As for "dwelling in the Ikṣuvāku garden," this clarifies that he dwelt within this garden to cultivate the Path;
because it refers to the place where he resided, he further received this name as his clan name. Thus, this single phrase simultaneously explains this Ikṣvāku clan.
This is the meaning [of his name]. Thus, the *Buddha-pu* (Sutra on the Lineage of the Buddha) states: "The Bodhisattva went to dwell and practice the Way within a sugarcane grove;
because the grove was owned by the clan of Ikṣvāku, he was also named Sugarcane. Therefore, the *Buddha-benxing-zan* (Praise of the Buddha’s Original Deeds) says, "He is of the lineage of Sugarcane.
The section beginning with "robbers and thieves" is the second causal condition, clarifying that he later received his surname from a master through the recitation of dhāraṇīs. Thus...

The *Fǔ* (Genealogy) of the Buddha states: At that time, while the Bodhisattva was contemplating the Way in the grove, he was captured by bandits due to his past karma and impaled upon a wooden stake, his blood flowing onto the ground.
The Great Seer Gautama, possessing pure divine vision, saw that the Bodhisattva had reached the limit of self-restraint and that no other Buddha could intervene;
he flew from the mountain, gathered the corpse with compassion, took the blood from within the earth, kneaded it into a clay ball, and placed it [upon the stake].
Within the vessel, by the power of his divine incantations, they remained in their respective places for ten full months;

the one on the left transformed into a male and the one on the right transformed into a female, and thus the clan name Gautama was restored. Regarding the term "Gautama," this is translated as "Śākya" (釋);
its meaning is purely refined and unadulterated. "Śu" (淑) is a designation for goodness and beauty, signifying that which is most noble and supreme.

It appears that this translation has existed since antiquity, yet its meaning was never explained. The *Fopu* (Record of the Buddhas) states that it is the name of a star, just as in this land there are those surnamed Zhang [named after] stars;
thus it has been handed down through the ages. As for the term "Gautama," some say it means "mud" (*nìtǔ*).
However, this is merely a matter of the translator’s choice regarding the weight of the phonetic rendering. When I questioned a Brahmin monk, he said that "Gautama" means "mud."
"Qiutan" (求曇) is the name of a star; thus we know that his clan name was derived from a star and certainly does not refer to "mud.

The phrase "also named [X]" clarifies alternative names. Although it is translated as "Noble Clan" (貴姓), this is merely a figurative expression of praise and is not a literal translation, nor does it explain the original meaning.
The *Buddha-pu* (佛譜) states that according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the Buddha was of the Śākya clan.
Regarding the name "Śākya," the Nanshan [Master] was broadly learned yet still said he did not know its meaning; who else could possibly know it?

Among the predecessors within our own school, someone has rashly offered a false explanation, claiming that "Śā" means "level" (平) or "tranquil" (靜), and that it refers to the tranquility of the essential nature.
I say this person does not understand that this is a Sanskrit term and thus provides a gloss based on the conventions of this land [China]. How utterly ignorant! Furthermore—

This also serves as an explanation for the clan name Śākyamuni. Regarding "Renxian" (仁賢) and others, their temporal distance [from the Buddha] is determined by consulting the *Buddha-pu* (Buddha Genealogy).
This eon is that of Kṛkī Buddha; in the Tang translation, he is called "Tathāgata who Abandons and Destroys the Aggregates" (*skandha-vināśaka*).
The present reference to him as "Dangbao" (當寶) should be due to differences in older translations. Thus, men and women from the surrounding areas were subsequently reborn there.

This refers to the period of his birth; however, I do not know from which scripture it is derived. Since those such as [Daxi] and others state that it was at the beginning of the kalpa, we know it to be so.
This clarifies that Mahāgautama attained his nature.
The above concludes the primary explanation of Gautama, which also encompasses the other two meanings. Below this, the clan name Śākya shall be explained in turn. This section contains three parts:
first, a general clarification of the original cause for obtaining [the name]; second, a specific clarification of what is currently inherited, beginning with "Now, pure...";
and third, a concluding eulogy, beginning with "...is precisely...". Since his ancestral lineage was originally that of the Gautama clan...
For what reason is his clan name now Śākya? This clarifies that there are two causes and conditions for this: namely, it was obtained through both virtue (*guṇa*) and a grove (*vana*).
The *Fǔpǔ* (Buddha-pu) cites the *Dīrgha Āgama*, which states: "In the past, there was a king named Yima (Yìmo).
The Southern Mountain [Commentary] says he was the tenth Cakravartin, one hundred lifetimes and four thousand years prior to the Buddha's own body."
The names in the sacred teachings may differ slightly, as the *Sūtras* and *Vinayas* vary; regarding those who were "suspicious," this refers to suspicion.
Because he was born of the second queen, the designated mother (*jyeṣṭhā-mātṛ*) became jealous and slandered his father, the king, causing him to be exiled.
The *Buddhapurāṇa* states that the four sons were banished to leave the country; having received the king’s command, they arrived at the Northern Snow Mountains and resided there.

In the forest of Ṛṣipatana, vast and expansive in the four directions, vegetables and fruits flourished; for several years, people flocked there to submit to his virtue like to a marketplace, until it became a powerful state.
His father thought of summoning him back, but he declined the invitation and did not return. The father-king sighed three times, saying, "My son possesses great capability," and thus named him Śākya;
this was derived from his virtue. Below, to clarify the location, the *Buddhavaṃśa* quotes the Mahīśāsaka school as stating that [the Buddha] resided there.
There was a grove of trees also named Śākya; according to the Sanskrit pronunciation, it is simply called Śākya.

Since many things and events in India have multiple names, this [clan] name was likewise derived from the grove. Furthermore, it is said that according to other traditions, there was a tree in that land named Śāka, which possessed lush roots and trunk.
Those skilled in physiognomy declared that a sovereign would surely emerge from it, and thus they moved [the seed].
Although the establishment of states and the adoption of clan names by the four sons is not part of the canonical teachings, I have briefly appended these as unusual accounts.

This clarifies that this surname was obtained through two conditions. The preceding section correctly explains the meaning of the two surnames; including the other two, these constitute the four meanings, which concludes the explanation.
As for the "Solar Lineage" (*sūryavaṃśa*), it is not essential to the present context, and since its origins are few, it is omitted here without further discussion. Thus, the *Buddhapurāṇa* says:
Regarding the term "Solar Lineage" (*Sūryavaṃśa*), the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that his father’s personal name was "Sun.

Master Nanshan remarked that the circumstances of this origin are not clearly detailed, and thus he omitted further discussion. Furthermore, it is said that while the five lineages are unified under a single clan, they are distinguished according to their various manifestations throughout history;
thus, although the Śākya clan is extensively clarified in many scriptures, other names appear or disappear according to specific conditions.
Therefore, Vinaya Master You said: "I look up with reverence to the prediction of Dīpaṃkara, which conferred upon him the title Śākyamuni; he profoundly bore this mandate to proclaim the Truth.
Thus, he took birth within the Śākya clan, manifesting his signs before his physical form had yet taken shape, and leaving his traces in characters after he was born.
His radiance has shone upon devas and humans throughout the succession of vast kalpas; such is his origin."

How sudden it is! To distinguish clearly from below the succession inherited by the present Buddha, we shall follow the *Buddha-pu* (Genealogy of the Buddhas) to enumerate the Buddha’s seven ancestral generations.
The seventh ancestor was named Mahāsammata; the sixth was named Ikṣvāku;
the fifth was named Upama, also known as Ulumpa; the fourth, the great-grandfather, was named Kula, also known as Nimi.

According to the *Qiúluó* (Seeking the Lineage), the third ancestor was named Nibula; the second ancestor was named Siǎnzíjiá (Lion Cheek); and the first ancestor, his father, was named King Śuddhodana.
Based on this, it should state that [Śuddhodana] was born from Siǎnzíjiá; the current reading is likely a scribal error.

Furthermore, it should state that he was born from Sìfàn (Four Meals), so the mention of "three" is also likely an error. Thus, the *Fófǔ* (Buddha Genealogy) states: "The ancestors of the Bodhisattva..."
King Siṃhahanu had four sons: the first was named Śuddhodana, the second Śuklodana, the third Droṇodana, and the fourth Amṛtodana—these are the four characters [for their names].
Regarding the phrase "the two names and so forth," the *Fǔpǔ* (Buddha-pu) states: "King Śuddhodana had two sons;
the elder was named Siddhārtha and the younger was named Nanda. King Śuklodana had two sons; the elder was named Devadatta and the younger..."
Ānanda’s father, King Droṇodana, had two sons: the elder was named Mahānāman and the younger was named Aniruddha.
King Amṛtodana had two sons and one daughter; the elder son was named Vāsabha, the next was named Bhadrika, and the daughter was named Amṛtā.
Each of these [other brothers] likewise had two sons. Since the present explanation concerns Aniruddha, only his second cousin (the son of Amṛtodana) is mentioned here.
The phrase "it is precisely these" serves as a summary, praising his noble status and his ability to diminish it in order to follow the Way.

Second, Rāhula’s paternal uncle was named Wénlè (文略), taking the character *lè* from the name of the Duke of Zhou (*Zhōu Gōng*). Thus, the Duke of Zhou and others are cited as analogies to illustrate this point.
After the Duke of Zhou assumed regency, King Cheng enfeoffed his son Bóqīn as the Duke of Lù (*Lù Gōng*). As he was about to depart for his post, the Duke admonished him.
This was said so that they would not treat the great ministers and high officials with disrespect;

these words are found in the *Shiji*, where it says, "King Cheng," and while the remaining texts mostly refer to the "present king," it should indeed be so. As for the matter of holding and spitting, it is easy to understand and need not be described in detail.
Regarding the honoring of the worthy and so forth, if this is the case even when my own courtesy is directed toward ordinary virtuous people, how much more so [in the case of those of higher merit]?
As for those of high standing who hold superior positions, he causes them to reflect with reverence and humility at court, ensuring they are free from arrogance or haste.

He says: "If even those who are upright in this world and esteemed by the worthy act thus, how much more so should those who follow the wondrous sages beyond the world not exhaust their minds and bodies to follow them?
This was to demonstrate that although Nanda was exceedingly wealthy and noble, he was able to renounce it all at once to follow [the Buddha].
This is the Buddha-way.

The above constitutes the second section, which concludes the extensive explanation of his family name (*śīla*). From here below is the third section, which provides a further extensive explanation of his given name (*nāman*).

Regarding this, former predecessors have all remarked that the sequence of this text is incorrect; it should be moved to the preceding section and placed immediately after the brief mention of the name. Now...
