This means that while one aspect of this has been seen, the second remains unknown; for now, we shall proceed directly according to the sequence of the text, and its underlying meaning will be revealed later.

Within this, first is the explanation of the meaning of "Free from Poverty" (Akiṃcana), which also includes the absence of hunting; subsequently follows the explanation of "As One Wishes" (Yathākāma). Regarding the first, the essential point is as follows:

because he gave even coarse grain (*śyāmāka*) as an offering, he attained the status of a precious rabbit due to the long-standing establishment of his vow; thus he received this name. Although this food was small...
This is because the mind is weighty and the object is superior. Since this gift does not result from what has been hunted, it is said that there is "no hunting";

this simultaneously clarifies its meaning. Regarding the explanation of the meaning of "as one wishes" (*yathā-kāma*) below: this appears to have no separate cause, as it is simply the previous karma;

however, while the former was a general explanation regarding the past, the present one is specifically concerned with the present, thus manifesting them reciprocally. The text consists of three parts.
The mind first clarifies that it is empty within yet substantial; next, it clarifies that it goes out and enters back in; finally, it clarifies that joy arises spontaneously and manifests itself.

Because these three meanings are present, it is called "Yathāmanas" (As One Wishes). Among the various commentaries of past and present, this interpretation is most frequently used to explain the origin of the term, as it is the most excellent and elegant.

Next, there are two conditions that clarify his virtuous conduct. His name is already known as previously stated, but because the essentials of his virtuous conduct are not yet known, they are briefly explained here.
First, it clarifies how he can personally attain the superior divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); second, it explains how he can cause others to obtain the path-eye (*mārgacakṣus*).
Regarding the first of these, there are five phrases: first, it clarifies the loss of the physical eye; second, the mindfulness of cultivating the divine eye; third, the offering thereof...
Cultivating and attaining the four great powers, and employing the five [faculties] for the sake of being praised by the Buddha—this first clarifies the reason why the deceased [should not sleep]:
it is because of diligence and the absence of sleep. As for the reason for not sleeping: because indolence and sleep prevent one from hearing the Dharma, and thus one is rebuked by the Buddha.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: When the Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park preaching the Dharma to the assembly, that person alone fell asleep. The Buddha...
The Buddha addressed him with a verse, saying: "Alas! Alas! Why do you sleep? You are like a snail, a clam, or an oyster.
He asked, "Are you fleeing from kings and bandits to go forth into homelessness? He replied, "No; it is because I am weary of birth, old age, sickness, and death that I seek to go forth.
The Buddha said, "Since this is so, why do your eyes sleep while the Buddha himself is preaching the Dharma? Thereupon, Aniruddha rose and said to the Buddha, "From this day forward..."
In the past, when my body was dissolving and decaying, I never slept before the Buddha; because I did not sleep until dawn, I lost my faculty of sight.
The Buddha said, "The eye has sleep as its nutriment," and so on, up to, "The mind has dharmas as its nutriment, and Nirvana has heedfulness as its nutriment.
When he urged me to rest and sleep, I replied, "I dare not disobey your wish. For this reason, the Buddha commanded me to cultivate the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

Following the Buddha, he was taught to cultivate the pure form of the first dhyāna. Regarding its manifestation within the realm of desire, it emerges from half the head if one is an ordinary person, whereas if it is the Buddha, it emerges from the entire head;
thus it is said to emerge from "half the head. Based on this, there are three types of initial [manifestation]:

the first is as seen by ordinary people, while the second involves the distinction between half and whole; these distinctions are explained according to the Hīnayāna teachings. This refers to the cultivation through diligent practice in the present life.
This is due to past conditions, as explained in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*. The citation of the *Vimalakīrti* serves to demonstrate its scope.
Next, the citation introduces the concluding praise of its supreme excellence. Regarding the section on "causing others [to attain it]," this is indeed something that was lost and not yet attained;
although one has not personally attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), by causing others to attain the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*), one achieves this through them.

The four meanings of name and lineage and virtuous conduct discussed above are concluded. Regarding the four essentials, the Master says: the first is the worldly [level], as in "the Benevolent and Worthy Kalpa" (*Bhadrakalpa*);
the second is for the sake of humans, as in "Narada"; the third is for remediation, as in "the Buddha’s Broad [Teachings]"; and the fourth is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). Now, I say:

the initial explanation of name and lineage is the worldly level, because it arises from the most excellent [nature] inherently present to inspire the desire and aspiration of sentient beings; the subsequent re-explanation of the name is the ultimate level.
Because it gives rise to goodness, it is for the sake of humans; this desire is explained extensively again after the mention of "lineage" (gotra) and cannot be shifted to precede it.
To govern one's own sleep is the remedial application (pratipakṣa), while enabling others to attain the Path is the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Due to these four causal factors, there is the practice (caryā) that bears this name.

Regarding the provisional teaching (*kyōkyō*), this clarifies the convergence of the causes and effects of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Within this, there are two stages: first, regarding its arousal; second, regarding its cultivation.
The reason both are termed "arousal" is that the intention is to take the perfected essence as the arising of function; thus they are collectively named "arousal.

Generally, outsiders also obtain this function, but it is based merely on mundane, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). As for the out-flow-free (*anāsrava*) meditative concentration of phenomena, it is as previously described.

This brief explanation is because all [faculties] rely upon the principle of the Truths (*satya*). Since untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is the root of all virtues, that which "arises" is the wisdom of the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Next, within the detailed [explanation], the stages are traversed; the initial cultivation encompasses both the preceding and the subsequent. Therefore, there are these five.

Regarding the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) in this primary treatise, why is the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*) discussed in full? Some say it is to clarify them collectively, while others say it is by way of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Following this, it may be explained through two causes; you should reflect further upon this. Because true virtue is perfect, subtle, and boundless, all things are identical [to it].

In terms of cultivation, the manifestation of its function differs: scattered virtues have not yet attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), whereas these are the pure physical eyes (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) which rely on emptiness for their cultivation.
Cultivating one is to cultivate both. As for the sequential method, it is as explained above.
As for "non-sequential," it means that within a single mind and through the threefold contemplation, both the subject that sees and the object that is seen are entirely complete;
thus, it is "perfect" (*yuan*). To correctly discern the characteristics of cultivation is as extensively explained elsewhere and is not the subject of this discussion.
Here, whether it be the arousal [of the aspiration] or the cultivation [of the path], it all pertains to the eye of the absolute, non-dual, and peerless convergence of the non-sequential.

Next, regarding the "Original and Traces" (honjaku), within the Original there is both essence and function; within the Traces it is very brief. The underlying intent clarifies that by guiding sentient beings, one causes them to realize the Perfect Original.
Regarding the "Contemplation," because the wholesome mind has not yet minutely sought the principle, the "fleshly eye" (nikkō) is not mentioned as the "wisdom eye" (chiken).
The Master said this was an omission; one should rather say that the concentrated mind contemplating causes and conditions is the "heavenly eye" (tennō), and the empty mind is the "wisdom eye."
This is likely due to omissions during transcription rather than being missing from the original text.

Although it is written thus, since this discernment is already perfect and subtle, one must contemplate that the mind is itself goodness, concentration, and emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; one must not interpret the text according to the literal words alone.
Because there is this underlying meaning, the commentary states: (and so forth).
Next, regarding the explanation of Piṇḍola: although this chapter is difficult and there have been many previous interpretations, none of them can be reconciled with the text.

Now, observing the meaning of the passage, although there are names and practices, these are all explanations of the name and do not follow the structural patterns of the preceding sections on the various *dharmas*.
Following the three conclusions in the text, this is the name of a single sound derived from three meanings; first, it is established as a name based on worldly convention.
Next, regarding the three general meanings derived from "transcending the world," they are established by name through two principles: first, [the name] is derived from one's parents;
second, it is appropriate to derive it from the individual themselves, which is to say, from their own virtuous conduct. Within this, there are two parts:

first, the inversion of the names, and second, the explanation of their meanings. First, as for the inversion: this single word, when viewed in relation to what follows in the explanation, contains three meanings. The first is...
This is because: first, it is one of the names for the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*); second, it is simply a name for a dwelling or lodging;

and third, it is a general term for all the stars and celestial phenomena. Although these three meanings share the same phonetic sound, and while the initial [term] is common to the *xiù* (秀) pronunciation, there is no reason to exclude it from the specific textual commentary; this was likely the personal opinion of a later person.

Regarding the phrase "the cause was not originally so," this explains the first meaning. Within it, the mention of the *fáng* (房) star refers specifically to the *Tiān sì* (天駟, Celestial Charger) star;

thus, the *Ēryá* states, "The *Tiān sì* is the *fáng*," and Guō Pǐng’s commentary notes that the Dragon is called the *Tiān sì*, referring to the fourth star among the seven lunar mansions of the eastern quarter.

[The sages] did not dare to claim it as their own possession, but rather attributed the merit to its source and named it accordingly. As for the term "birth-body" (*shēngshēn*), it refers to the father.
This is because the body born of a mother is contrasted with the subsequently attained Dharma-body. Furthermore, this explains the second meaning:
since the capacity for this path has matured, they meet by chance; thus, it results in "staying overnight" (*sahavāsa*).

All previous commentators say that within the monastic quarters, there was a monk of inferior status who stayed with him overnight; however, this case is somewhat different, and therefore it should be treated separately.
There is that which emerges; when it is said that one "sees the Dharma-body," this refers to the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*).

Just as through cultivation one attains [the Dharma-body] in contrast to the previously existing physical body, which is not the Dharma, it is therefore called the "Dharma-body. Next, the following passage explains the third meaning, which serves as a general explanation to establish the previous two meanings.
Why? Previously, it was clarified that the parents sought one star and obtained it; now, it is clarified that its body is capable of universal penetration.
Previously, it was shown that his body was born from the constellations; now it is shown that his mind is able to penetrate all celestial phenomena.
Therefore, the text says he is named "from understanding. Within this, there are three points: first, it clarifies that the Heavenly Kings attend upon this bhikṣu;
second, it explains the reason for this attendance, which arises from his penetration of all the heavens.

Because the text encounters [teachings] that are common to those [other traditions], it is respectfully upheld; furthermore, among the three Arhats, this refers specifically to the Great Arhat *Anāthapiṇḍada* (Vasumitra), who internally possesses the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) and externally is able to penetrate all worldly phenomena and signs.

Since he is endowed with both internal and external brilliance and clarity, he is respectfully upheld. Following this, the Buddha’s praise is cited as proof: "The stars are the five celestial bodies; the lunar mansions are the two."

The eighteen lunar mansions and the sun and moon constitute these two luminaries; thus, one penetrates the three lights within the palm of one's hand—how could this be achieved by means of a single star alone?
Please examine the words and phrases of my explanation further to solidify the meaning of the character *fáng* (house/abode). Reflect upon it, reflect upon it!
This follows the four essential points of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); because previous exegeses have failed to provide a comprehensive synthesis, they are not accepted here.

I shall further elaborate on my current view: the three meanings explained above actually encompass four meanings. The first is the worldly meaning (*loka-saṃvṛti*). Within the second, two meanings are contained:
from "he sat upon the ground" up to this point, his goodness was unsurpassed, and thus he is the foremost among men;

hearing the Dharma at midnight and attaining the Way constitutes the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). Within the third meaning, since he has already attained broad mastery and is free from doubt, he is the Heavenly King.
Serving and honoring the Buddha brings joy; who would say it is otherwise? The remedies are clear, and the four meanings are very evident;
there is no need for confusion. It is named for these four meanings. Next, regarding the "teaching" (yàojiào), this distinguishes the convergence of the common and the Buddha’s prior dharmas.
Specifically, among the first three meanings, one focuses on the second single meaning because it is the most stable. This is the first [point].
This Buddha takes this ultimate truth as his eternal dwelling place; to now cultivate this and realize this principle is equivalent to "dwelling" there.

Since sense faculties and objects are the twelve *āyatanas*, by citing the middle to encompass the beginning and the end, the aggregates (*skandhas*) and elements (*dhātus*) are included therein—the meaning of this can be understood.
As it says below, "resting in the true" refers to the supramundane, while "the two" refers to birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Nirvana also extends through the Middle Way; it does not differ from what preceded, but its capacity to act as a distinction does. Within the Distinct Teaching (*bie*), both the object (*suo*) and the subject (*neng*) differ from the preceding.
In the initial stage, one discriminatively knows the ten realms—the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and the dwellings (*gṛha*).

Through the three successive contemplations (*krama-vipaśyanā*), one successively attains the vision of the three Buddhas dwelling together. In the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), one immediately perceives the three truths (*satya*); the dwellings are also perfect, and one perceives the three [truths] simultaneously.

The Buddha therefore says that "all" refers to this very teaching, which cuts off coarse meanings. Within the context of the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku), it is not without this fundamental that this manifested trace can be bestowed.
To cause all beings to return to the wondrous fundamental, he displays this trace and speaks of "the various [buddhas]," referring to the four mentioned previously;
this is precisely to cause them to return to the final one. Within contemplation, the transformation buddha is the inferior response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya*) that accords with conditions.

The middle verse is called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) because it is neither fixed in time nor fixed in words; "retribution" (*vipāka*) refers to the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), which is also termed the "excellent response" (*vaśitā-nirmāṇa*).
From the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) upward, this meaning applies universally. Because these are provisional, that which is "middle" is such that all phenomena are the true mark (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the term "Dharma-Buddha," it is so called because the sublime object and sublime wisdom are, in their suchness (*tathatā*), non-different; thus it is named "Dharma."
The reason for relying on these four [methods] is further to employ contemplation (*guan*) to clarify the meanings of the provisional teachings (*jiao*) mentioned previously.
By attaining this contemplation, one can explain the four meanings within the teachings; this is roughly the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "It is clearly stated that... (云云).

In the initial explanation of the causes and conditions for the name Kauṇḍinya, first the name is explained, followed by his virtuous conduct. Regarding the first [the name], there is first the transliteration, then the explanation.
Both the old and new translations are identical here; the new translation renders it as *gopapada*, which means "ox-sign.

This is called a "sign" (*lakṣaṇa*) because it takes the two characteristics of rumination and hoofprints, both of which resemble those of an ox. "Hoofprint" refers to the heel of the foot, because it has the mark of an ox's hoof; furthermore, "hoofprint" refers to...

"Traces" (*zōngjì*) refer to the marks (*xiàng*) [left behind]; thus it is called "the mark of the ox. The first and last [of the three] derive their names from manifest characteristics, while the middle one receives its designation from past causes.
In the commentary, only two of these are explained and not the "traces"; the term "unlevelled" (*yí*) means to flatten or to annihilate.
Thus, in the state of Qin there was the "Qin punishment" (*yíxíng*), which meant the total extermination of one's clan. Furthermore, the text does not explain the character "wen" (pattern/ornament).
Regarding the causes for his former existence as an ox, all the Śākyas say that in the past he was once a bhikṣu who passed by another’s field of millet.
Because he plucked a few grains to observe whether they were ripe or unripe, several fell to the ground. Consequently, for five hundred subsequent lifetimes, he was born as an ox.
Although he has now encountered the Buddha and attained the Way, his feet remain like those of an ox, and even after eating, he still chews the cud; it is for this reason that he is so named.
This is why, at the very beginning of his renunciation, he was given this name; how could it have been for nothing? Indeed, there is profound significance that will later manifest itself.

From "Formerly, five hundred... onwards, his virtuous conduct is revealed. Within this section, first, he relies on the teaching to provide a general heading; next, he explains its meaning and intent.
In the first part, there is the cause and the fruit, as well as the citation of beautiful evidence: the five hundred geese and the king.
Regarding the three people whose subsequent retribution can be known, four people can be known.
As for King Ajātaśatru, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that the Brahmin Vairaṇyā invited [the Buddha]; this differs from what appears in the sacred teachings.

At that time, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha and being filled with joy, that man invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to observe the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*). The Buddha then accepted his invitation.
There was once a man who, having been led astray by Māra, failed to make offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha despite being invited to do so.

At that time, there was a horse merchant from another country who drove five hundred horses near the Buddha’s residence for ninety days. During this period, the bhikṣus were unable to obtain almsfood and went to the merchant’s place to beg.
The man then ceased giving fodder to his horses and instead offered five *śī* of barley to the bhikṣus each day.
The World-Honored One had Ānanda have one *dō* (a measure) ground into groats (*śaktu*) to offer to the Buddha and the bhikṣus, who each cooked barley to eat;
thus it is said that they all ate "horse-barley. How could it be that the Buddha’s cultivation of causes was inferior? The *Baiyuan jing* (Sūtra of a Hundred Karmic Causes) states:
"In the past, when the Tathāgata was the leader of five hundred brahmins, he saw the assembly making offerings to Kāśyapa Buddha..."
The fosterer spoke these words: "Such excellent food should be offered to me; these śramaṇas ought to be given horse-barley.
Therefore, this retribution was brought about. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that the karma of good and evil does not perish;
thus, these words are indeed true. Next, the Buddha’s praise is cited as proof. The following commentary explains the meaning; it is for this reason that it is explained.
What was said previously—that what is induced by the causes of merit is but a single intent—was followed by a citation from the scriptural testimony which states:

"Pleasure and non-pleasure, though their meanings are indeed twofold, cannot be known by oneself; therefore, they must be explained. This clarification that there are four intents further comprises two layers.
First, it is said that the meaning of "desire for pleasure" applies to both sides, as both are based on the principle of the resonance between past conditions and present response.
Since there is such a principle as this, dwelling in the heavens is not for nothing; thus the commentary says [as follows].

The second part, which provides a further explanation, first directly explains the meaning of "governing" (*zhi*) mentioned previously, and subsequently separately reconciles it with the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).

Because the previous explanation of "governing" merely presented the heading without yet articulating its meaning, it is explained again here to clarify the reason why. It is only because people possess merely the physical eye that they do not...
Knowing that he possessed virtue, they smiled at him; because they smiled, they incurred the offense of others. Not wishing for people to incur such offenses, he did not remain among them.

Furthermore, he intended to lead [them] to the heavens so that they might awaken to the Way; therefore, he resided in those heavens. Regarding the statement about the assembly of one thousand *arhats* and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"At first, when they were about to hold the council, they deliberated together, saying: 'Who is capable of compiling the *Vibhaṅga*?'"
The Bhikṣuṇī Dharmakośa Āniruddha said: "Kauṇḍinya (Gavāmpati) is gentle, harmonious, and refined;

his mind is tranquil and settled, and he always delights in dwelling in seclusion. This man is most capable. Kāśyapa is the bhikṣu who sits in the lower seat (the *Fu fa zhuan* states he is the bhikṣu Śilabhadra).
Go to the Śiṃśapā Grove in the heavens and say to Gavāmpati: 'Mahākāśyapa and the others are now...'"

"All must assemble at Jambudvīpa; there is a matter of great importance, so come down quickly. Thereupon, the bhikṣu flew through the air to that place and related the aforementioned matters in detail.
Upon hearing this, the man’s heart was moved by both wonder and suspicion, and he asked him, "Has the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa?
He replied, "Indeed it is so. He asked again, "Where is my preceptor Śāriputra now? He replied, "He has already..."
Having spoken thus, he said, "The Upādhyāya and the Mahāśramaṇa have both already entered parinirvāṇa; what more is there for me to do remaining here?
I shall no longer descend to Jambudvīpa. Having said these words, he leapt from within the eight dhyānas into the void and manifested various supernatural transformations.
Fire issued forth from his own heart and consumed his body, while water emerged from within, flowing down in four streams.
The verse spoken by Kāśyapa says: "Kauṇḍinya bows his head in homage to the Great Virtuous Saṃgha, the foremost among the wondrous assembly.
Hearing that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, I shall follow him, just as when a great elephant departs, the elephant calf follows.

Where the current text and the treatise differ slightly, these are either citations based on the general intent or alternative versions; all of these capture the essential function of the teaching, which is now summarized here.

Because it takes the substance of consciousness as its cause, it is also the ultimate (paramārtha) mind. The preceding section, titled "The Requisites of Practice," has completed its explanation of the four meanings according to the text itself.
Hereafter, regarding the teaching, we shall distinguish the convergence and divergence of this dharma-gate. "Divergence" consists of four types, while "convergence" is non-tripartite;
because there is both good and evil, this teaching is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Therefore, the *Xuanyi* states: "It is substantially existent."
"To be conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*) is precisely its meaning; as for the term "manifestation" (*darśana*), it means to reveal or display.

This refers to revealing this meaning within the gates of teaching (*śāsana-mukha*), and does not refer to the "original and the trace" (*honji-suijaku*), nor to "essence and function" (*tathatā-vyāpāra*); one must avoid such confusion. Since all that is pervasive is not fixed reality, the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) states:
"That which exists as an illusion is the conventional. Internally, this refers to the three wholesome and three unwholesome [karmas]; externally, it refers to transformation.
Even the causes and effects of evil can be rectified by right wisdom; when causes and effects accord with the Right Path, they are good.

Not a single form or scent fails to be the Middle Way; internal and external, good and evil, are all non-dual. The meaning of this sutra may be understood through this. Next, regarding the "Original and Traced" (Honji-Suijaku):
the Original resides in the Bull-King, the First Principle Heaven; the Traced manifests these matters to lead sentient beings [to enlightenment].
This refers to returning to the source. Regarding the four fearlessnesses: (1) fearlessness regarding omniscience; (2) fearlessness regarding the teaching on the obstacles to the path;

(3) fearlessness regarding the path that exhausts suffering; and (4) fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "First, he declares of himself: 'I am a perfectly awakened one (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).

Second, in accordance with the truth, he declares of himself: 'I have eternally exhausted all outflows. Third, for the sake of his disciples, he teaches the dharmas that constitute obstacles to the path. Fourth, for the sake of..."
In the *Sutta on the Path Leading to the Exhaustion of Suffering*, the various disciples have extensively explained its meaning; here it is briefly stated:

whether they be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or any other beings, none are able to raise an objection based on the Dharma, saying that this is not perfect enlightenment, that outflows are not eternally exhausted, that these are not factors obstructing the path, or that this is not the path leading to the exhaustion of suffering. Because of this, I have attained peace.
Dwelling in seclusion, free from fear, the True Teacher lets out the lion’s roar and turns the sublime Brahma-wheel;
none among all others are able to turn it in accordance with the Dharma. This [text] is largely the same as the old translation with only minor differences.

Herein, it clarifies that the "Original Abiding Ox-King Dharma-gate" means that one has personally attained fearlessness and is further able to cause all others to attain fearlessness; thus, it is named after that ox-king.
"The Bull-King who dwells securely as the Holy Lord" takes its meaning from the latter part of the scripture which speaks of the "Holy Lord, God of Gods.

Just as the Bull-King achieves the supreme state of fearlessness, so too does the Holy Lord achieve the supreme state of being a holy lord; the commentary states that he dwells in the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Thus, it says:
"That Great Man, the Bull-King, the Holy Lord, the King of Gods, dwells securely in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This means he abides in the ultimate reality.

People say that the character "ju" (居) is missing below the character "wang" (王), but I maintain that because the term "an-zhu" (安住, dwelling in peace) from above governs the passage, there should be no further [character needed].
In this middle contemplation, the meaning of the "great carriage with white oxen" from the subsequent text is taken up. This matter has two meanings:
first, being without partiality; second, being swift. Because one who can practice Madhyamaka-śāstra regards all things as immediate, it is both without partiality and swift.
The contemplation of King Swift-Ox is capable of reaching this Way; how could his fundamental essence and its manifestations be far removed? Reflect upon them to fully comprehend them.

Regarding the initial causal conditions for Śāriputra (here rendered as Shi Li-po-duo): first, the names are translated; second, the meanings are explained; third, scriptural evidence is cited. First, the names are translated: "Shi" (釋) refers to him... [text continues].
Regarding the statement that there are "only two," although four distinct items are mentioned, their meanings are actually three, because the first two share a single meaning.
Furthermore, when discussed according to their actual substance, they are merely two. The first two derive from the parents, while the latter two derive from virtues and conduct.

Within the first two, the lunar mansion *Chamber* (*Mṛgaśiras*) should be considered the primary one; it is the name of a star in the northern quarter among the twenty-eight lunar mansions. The following section provides an explanation.
Regarding its meaning: the preceding four passages are fully explained [as follows]. There are only three [sections], for the first two meanings are identical and thus combined in their explanation.
As for why one follows the root by means of the stars: both parents and children proceed from the root; because one attends to the root, the Way arises, and thus it is not swift.
The new [translation] says *Hye-rye-bat-da*, which here means the "Lunar Mansion Star" (*Śatabhiṣaj*). This Lunar Mansion Star is the star of the Northern Quarter.
He also made offerings to them and thereby obtained a son; for this reason, the boy was named Mi (Obtained). The *Vigraha-vyāvartanī-ṭīkā* (*Mishé jiāhé lùn*) states:

"Suppose a man travels far away and stays alone in a room or pavilion. A ghost arrives carrying a corpse and places it before him. Another ghost follows behind and becomes angry, reviling the first ghost, saying:
'This is my corpse! The first ghost replies: 'It was originally my property; I myself carried it here.'"
The two ghosts each grasped him with one hand, contending for him. The ghost in front said, "You may ask this man.
The ghost behind immediately asked, "Who are you? Who brought this dead man here? The man reflected, "These two ghosts both possess great power;
whether my words are true or false, neither will spare me from death. I should not answer falsely now," and he spoke to them, saying, "The ghost in front brought me here."
Afterward, the latter ghost became greatly enraged and pulled out its hands and feet, placing them upon the ground; the former ghost felt ashamed and took the corpse to replace them.
Once the hands, feet, and limbs were restored, the entire body was changed. The two ghosts then ate the body together, wiped their mouths, divided the head, and departed.
Next, as for the one who constantly made sounds, he previously merely harbored doubts in his mind that it was not truly his own possession, and thus it was a mere provisional combination.

Because he manifested his intent through his speech in seeking a resolution for his mind, he constantly uttered sounds and arguments to clarify his state. At night, filled with doubt, he sought the path until dawn;
upon reaching a Buddhist stūpa, whenever he saw any monks, he spoke of nothing else but asking whether his own person existed or did not exist.
Each time, the bhikṣus would all ask him, "Who are you? and he would reply, "I am also not [existent]."

Knowing whether this person was human or non-human, he explained the aforementioned matter in detail to the assembly of monks, saying that they were easy to deliver, and so forth. The *Śāstra* states:

"The assembly all said, 'This person knows for himself that there is no self, and is thus easily converted. He then spoke to him, saying: 'Your body has been eternally devoid of self from the very beginning;
it is merely a collection and aggregation of the four great elements. Your present body is no different from your former one.'"
He subsequently left the household life to become a śramaṇa, exhausted all afflictions (*kleśa*), and attained arhatship;

as this text is a concise summary, it merely provides the annotation (as indicated by "etcetera"). Regarding the mention of Śāriputra and others, these are instances where the Buddha praised their virtuous conduct, citing them here to corroborate the preceding argument.
This, then, refers to the path previously realized; since he was already able to enter realization as described before...
How could there be anything further that can reach such disorder? This refers to the path realized and the delusions abandoned.
Within this, there are four points: first, the world of parents; second, relying on truthful speech to influence things and assist others, which constitutes the "human" [realm];

third, the meaning of attaining the Way through constant practice and thereby overcoming [delusions], which is the sense of "governance"; fourth, being clearly free from confusion; and finally, the point concerning the provisional teachings.
This refers to the discrimination and convergence based on these dharmas; it specifically concerns the discussion of the aforementioned virtues and conduct.

First, because the phenomena and their principles, as well as the subject and object, are not identical in their establishment, it is said that they "are not my own. Second, because they are all identical, they fundamentally have no distinction.

Within this, although the Buddha-realm is true, it also arises dependently upon conditions; thus, the ten stages of dedication and the ten stages of ground are precisely this realm. Therefore, the treatise says: [The Treatise].
Within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of phenomena, there is no self and no agent. Since this is so for the self, how could one firmly cling [to it]? Therefore, all things are not one's own.
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), "self" refers to the individual. Because these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arise from ignorance, they are not one's own;

because they are ultimately empty, they do not belong to another. Being able to realize this such that the two characteristics do not exist is itself the true reality. Thus, the following passage states:

It is said that contemplating all phenomena as empty according to reality—this meaning also simultaneously involves contemplating the aforementioned "settling" (ning), thereby manifesting the capacity [of this samādhi].
Since there are no further phenomena external to this, it is within this very "Ultimate and Sublime Essence" (*jìmíàoběn*) that this name appears in the following text.
Because this concentration is able to embody the three wisdoms and penetrate the three lights, it bears this name; its traces are thus demonstrated here.

The name "Ning" (Peace/Rest) signifies that by taking one's resolve as the foundation, one causes all beings to return to the same source. "Contemplating within contemplation" refers to cultivation; "beholding the ten directions" refers to the signs of realization.

By contemplating the three bodies of a single Buddha, one immediately perceives the three bodies of all Buddhas; thus it is called "many. This is as clearly explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation);
this is precisely the appearance of the cultivation and realization of the Pratyutpanna Samādhi. This samādhi has three names.
The subsequent text will clarify that there is intentional meaning [in this], hence the commentary states (and so forth).

The reason for focusing specifically on the practice of virtue and taking the fundamental contemplation as the basis while still employing these names is because each follows the convenience of its respective meaning; it is intended to comprehensively encompass the full significance of both name and practice.
In the initial causal account of the explanation of Piṅgala, there are two parts: first, the translation and interpretation of the name; second, the manifestation of his virtuous conduct.
Within the interpretation of the name, there are again two parts: first, clarifying his habitual nature (*śīla*); second, clarifying his habitual characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
"Nature" refers to the internal mind, while "characteristics" refer to external speech. Since the Brahmins are the most noble among the four castes, he is said to have descended from them.

The remaining three classes were born from the mouth of Brahmā, gradually descending from above; how much more so would they have been prone to arrogance had they merely perceived themselves as high and remote?
Since their habitual tendencies had accumulated over time, they could not be eradicated instantaneously; thus, even though the Way reached its ultimate limit, the residual force still remained.
"Qi" (氣) refers to their essential nature (*svabhāva*). As for their characteristics: the deity of the Ganges is no ordinary being, yet he now speaks these words.

That one dares not disobey [the teacher] must indeed be true; the reason for saying this is that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that by the power of his past lives, he saw that the river deity had once been a maidservant in his own household. This is merely one example cited; others can be inferred accordingly.
Thus, a scripture is quoted stating that when the Buddha was in the world, this person would descend from his seat before the Buddha and all the bhikṣus.

Everyone addressed him as "Sir" (bhadra), even when they scolded the deity of the Ganges; the Buddha therefore admonished him, saying, "From this day forward, do not address the Venerable One with the word 'Sir'.
Because he recalled the Buddha’s words, he subsequently changed his manner of address. This clearly illustrates the characteristic of residual habit (*vāsanā*).
The new translation renders *piliṃdavatsa* as "residual habit," the meaning of which does not differ from the former [explanation]. Next is the section on virtuous conduct.
This clarifies that his integrity and resolve are lofty, far-reaching, and preeminent beyond the common crowd; this may indeed be called the ambition of a true man (*zhàngfū*).
Therefore, it constitutes the virtuous conduct (*déxíng*) of this person. Regarding the four meanings within the middle section, they have traditionally been viewed differently.

Now, I shall explain them directly: the first is simply the mundane world (*lokadhātu*); the second, within virtuous conduct, encompasses all three meanings. Why is this? Because one perceives and hears of such conduct.
Who would not admire this? Even as a human being, if one disregards outward form and can encourage those who are timid and weak, this is itself the "antidote" (pratipakṣa);
it is not merely a matter of achieving victory over others. Because this is a unique capability, it constitutes the ultimate truth (paramārtha).

Next, regarding the classification by teaching (yāna), we distinguish between the coarse and the subtle within the dharma of pride to manifest the meaning of this sutra. In the former two [vehicles], what they share is the same while their capabilities differ.

It should be understood that while the latter two [the object and the subject] are identical, the capacity [of the subject] is distinct. Regarding the terms "high" and "low," pride (*māna*) is defined by the sense of elevating oneself and looking down upon others;

this meaning here is likewise so. To explain this in terms of the ten realms (*daśadhātu*), one must first distinguish these levels of high and low before realizing their entry into a state where there is neither high nor low.
Someone has said: "If one discriminates between high and low, then there is honor and subordination."
Because there is deliverance, the interpretation that this is the meaning of "governing pride" (*māna*) is erroneous; it is rather the virtue within the true, wondrous nature of the Perfect Middle.
Thus, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Within the selflessness of dharmas, there is a true self. This refers to the meaning of "self-pride" (*asmimāna*).

Next, regarding the fundamental and the manifested (*honji-suijaku*), the four eights of the Brahma-voice clarify the two kinds of virtues, internal and external. The first [of these] is that which possesses the four.

Therefore, the traces manifest two matters, which are precisely the aforementioned two habits of nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). The intention behind manifesting these coarse traces is to cause them to return together to the wondrous source.
Within contemplation, "coarse" and "soft" refer to good and evil; they encompass both the internal and external, as well as the provisional and the real.
Now, observing that these two emerge from the same single mind, their essential substance is non-dual; therefore, they are all the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). This is what is meant by "emerging."

This is the passage from the eighteenth fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*) in which King Ajātaśatru praises the Buddha. Because the intent of the sūtra is somewhat remote, it has been annotated [as follows].
A brief reconciliation and explanation of this was already provided previously in the section on "Manifesting the Characteristics of Instruction," as can be understood.
In the first causal account of the explanation of Vakkula, first the name and age are explained; next, his virtuous conduct is clarified.
First, although there are three variations in the translation, they consist of only two meanings. The commentary explains only the first, as it is the essential point.

The new [translation] renders *Vakkula* as "Good Appearance" (*Shanrong*). The subsequent two [terms] merely signify being large in stature; since they are easy to understand, they are not explained here.
Next, within the section on virtuous conduct (*śīla-guṇa*), first there is a specific clarification of the two excellences of his body and lifespan;
next, a general clarification of his existence and cessation, characterized by few desires and contentment; finally, citations of the holy teachings are introduced to provide proof.

Regarding the first [of these], there is first a general clarification of the two fruits, followed by a specific clarification of the two causes, and thirdly, a specific explanation establishing the meaning of one cause. His age was one hundred and sixty years, which generally clarifies his body and lifespan.

Regarding his excellence in being free from illness, it specifically clarifies that his physical body was not subject to untimely death; regarding his excellence in longevity, it specifically clarifies that his life-force was not subject to premature end.

There are five types of "non-death," which further explain the aforementioned freedom from untimely death. As cited from the *Dharmaguptaka-avinaya* (or *Dharmarājika-vinaya*), concerning the last birth in a Brahmin family:
his mother died early, and his father remarried. When the boy Kula was young, he went to his stepmother to ask for bread; the stepmother, out of jealousy, seized him and threw him away.
Although the oil on top was extremely hot and scorching, it could not burn him; when his father came from outside, he immediately took him down and held him.

Later, while the meat was being boiled, the boy again asked his mother for some. His mother became greatly enraged and threw him into the boiling cauldron. His father, unable to find him, called out to him;
from within the cauldron, the boy responded to his father, whereupon he was taken out, his body appearing as it had been before. Afterwards, he followed his mother toward the river.
The mother threw it into the river; it encountered a large fish which immediately swallowed it.
A man who caught this fish took it to the market to sell it. The father saw it at that time and purchased it, bringing it home.
He slit open its belly, and [the child] inside the fish’s stomach cried out, saying, "I pray my father be careful not to injure me. The father opened the fish’s entrails and embraced him.
This is the fifth [point]. Having left home at the age of one hundred and sixty, from birth until old age, he never again experienced bodily fever or headaches;
this is because every effect must have a cause. Below, these two causes are explained individually. The first, the cause for not dying prematurely, is understandable.
Regarding the second, the cause for being free from illness, some say that this passage should be moved to [the following section].
The phrase "previously there was no premature death" (前無夭) is placed below [the term for illness] precisely to explain the absence of disease; the remainder explains the absence of premature death.

Now, following the literal text: regarding the "one who administers medicine," the *Dharmakośa-śāstra* (付法藏) states that after the Buddha Vipaśyin entered nirvāṇa, there was a bhikṣu whose headache was extremely severe. At that time, a poor man saw him and took a single *harītakī*.
A *bīja* fruit was joyfully offered by a layperson to a bhikṣu; upon consuming it, his pain was immediately cured.
Because he had given this medicinal gift, for ninety-one kalpas he experienced the happiness and bliss of gods and humans, never suffering from illness.
To explain separately the cause of not meeting an untimely death: as explained above, by observing even a single precept against killing, one can obtain such a result.
I have not yet ascertained what the characteristics of this retribution are; if it were otherwise, such a karmic result could not be brought about.
Regarding those who say they can maintain even a single precept, the Sūtra states: "Kuṇāla fully received the five precepts, yet his observance of them was uneven.
Regarding the single precept of non-killing, he made it his primary focus; regardless of whether it involved personal gain or loss, he ensured its total adherence, while the others..."

Regarding the fourth precept: if one encounters difficult circumstances or acts for the sake of benefiting others, provided it constitutes a permissible exception (*anujñāta-pratyaya*), then temporary relaxation or relinquishment is permitted;

this is all for the purpose of adorning the precept against killing. Thus, although one upholds only a single precept, its manifestation is as described above, and therefore the resulting retribution is difficult to obtain [in full].

Although the five transgressions are categorized differently, the excellence or inferiority of their retribution is as noted in the commentary. The meaning is roughly as explained above; for details, refer to the section on the five precepts.
That which is elucidated within one fascicle of the sutra is further explained in the commentary on the Great Sutra (*Mahāsūtra-ṭīkā*) among the section concerning the *upāsaka* assembly;

however, it has not yet been fully integrated for understanding. What follows below provides a general clarification of the virtuous conduct of having few desires and being content, both regarding their survival and their passing away.

Within this, first the survival of those with few desires and contentment is clarified, followed by the state of having few desires and contentment after death, wherein there is nothing [to be grasped].
"Seeking little" refers to having few desires for the sake of sustaining the body; "contentment" refers to the two practices following the cessation [of desire] mentioned below.
That he was able to fly out precisely symbolizes the virtue of fewness and contentment.
One who can act thus does so through the power of their lifelong virtuous conduct and by the inspiration of protective deities; this is fully detailed in the Sūtra.
There is a king and his ministers who praise him as one who is truly of few desires and content with little; the following citation of praise serves to establish this through the text.
The three virtues therein correspond to the meanings of the three sections explained previously. Within this, there are four points: the first is the worldly perspective (*loka-saṃvṛti*);

the next two concern cause and effect, which is for the sake of others (*puruṣakāra*); and the ability to firmly maintain the precepts is the remedial practice (*pratipakṣa*), which constitutes the virtue of conduct regarding existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, the ultimate truth (paramārtha) subsequently establishes what preceded it; by means of these four conditions, their names and practices exist.

Next, regarding the teaching, one distinguishes the coarseness or subtlety of their virtuous conduct; this is precisely to manifest the meaning of "no fixed direction. As clarified previously, this is the first intention.
That the six sense faculties are detached from sensory objects is entirely the principle of leaving clamor for tranquility; this is to follow the extremes.
The first three of the middle [sections] all embody the meaning of the "Perfect Opening and Unification" (yuán kāihuì); this is the intended purport of this sutra.
The fundamental Great Quiescent Samādhi is itself the Great Nirvāṇa, and the cave of profound meditative concentration is the Secret Treasury. These three necessarily possess the four virtues;

just as the manifested body (traces) possesses the four merits, those who manifest these traces cause sentient beings to realize this same fundamental nature. Although the text is concise, one should understand that this is also the case here.

The preceding [explanation] is fully detailed as in the four [meditations], such as the Longevity Meditation (*āyus*) and so forth. Regarding the mention of the "Middle Way" (*madhyamā pratipad*) and so on within the contemplation: because the nature of the mind is perfectly pervasive, it is the Middle Way;

because the Middle Way is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and so forth. To cultivate these three contemplations is to cultivate the four [noble truths]. Because it is empty, it is pure and free from defilement and accumulation;
because it is provisional (*prajñapti*), the functions of the self are sovereign; because it is the Middle Way, it is eternal bliss.
Because he is not moved or oppressed by the two extremes, this is precisely the "Sublime Virtue" (Mañjuśrī) contemplation within this sutra.

Regarding the initial causes and conditions for Śāriputra, his first name was "First Practice" (*prathamacaryā*); it is merely translated as "not" and not explained, yet its meaning manifests of itself to others.
Others say his name was *Mahākauṣṭhila*, which is translated here as "Great Knee," because his kneecaps were large.

This meaning is consistent with the subsequent explanation of "original and trace" (*honjaku*). Because he possessed these characteristics that distinguished him from ordinary people, they were used as his name;

it was surely intended to manifest the greatness of his dual practice of meditative concentration and wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*). As for the mention of Śāriputra, this is to highlight the uncle by citing the nephew, thereby initiating the subsequent argument.
His father was also a great master of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. From the phrase "from of old" (*yurai*) onwards, [the text] clarifies his...

Regarding the section on "Virtuous Conduct" (*śīla*), first the principle is clarified and subsequently supported by citations. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, clarifying the ability to be extensively versed in worldly matters;

second, clarifying the ability to awaken to the supramundane path. Within the first of these, there are again two parts: first, clarifying extensive learning; second, clarifying the fulfillment of one's resolve.

Each of these two passages has its own underlying rationale. This is precisely the meaning of the "stimulating penetration" mentioned by the ancients. Regarding the phrase "first, by means of the text," the note below states "as before."
He is the "Bright One" (*Prakāśa*) among the sons of Śāriputra; his name does not appear among the eighteen great sūtras, as this region’s largest numbers only reach half of that.
As for the term "Brahmacārin," it refers to one of the Brahmin caste; he was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra and the son of the National Preceptor.
Since his conduct in worldly studies was already such, his resolve regarding the supramundane must surely have been firm.

Furthermore, it is truly believed that upon merely hearing a single word, one immediately attains awakening and enters [the path]. Having completed the study [of this], the following clarifies the ability to awaken to the supramundane way (*lokottara-mārga*).

Within this, there are cases where one attains it through correctness or through seeking; for instance, his nephew Chang (Chang Shih-huai) ultimately attained the vision of the Buddha and awakened to the supramundane way.
"Directly" (*ching*) means swift; it refers to how, because of his indignation and arrogance— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

Because of his accumulated past afflictions, he went there with the intention of destroying the Buddha and seizing his nephew; however, he did not expect that he himself would immediately become a disciple of the Buddha.

When he said, "I have not attained a single dharma," he meant it according to his own emotional views, asserting that all dharmas are non-existent, intending to use this momentum to destroy the Buddha.
Thus, he first relied upon this thought and then spoke these words; this is what appears to be the case.
Even the non-Buddhist outsiders who hold the view of emptiness cannot endure these words; "endure" refers to what follows here, which is now explained as its meaning.
"To establish" (*an*) means to cause something to exist or stand firm; "to refute" means to cause it to have nothing upon which it can stand.

However, how could there be anything to subsume within another? Upon hearing this, the Buddha immediately counters with a question: "Do you rely on such knowledge and vision to establish this, or do you not?"

This is precisely what is meant by "speaking in two directions": because one is endowed with intelligence and is moreover quick-witted, one immediately realizes that one has fallen into a position of double defeat (*ubhaya-pakṣa-nigrahasthāna*).
This is his own reflection on the explicit meaning of falling into both [contradictions]: first, there is the contradiction of one's own words;
second, it results in the negation of that which was intended to be established. As for what the predecessors have said, it accords with what is clarified in the treatise.

Although he knew this in his mind, he did not yet immediately submit; he continued to reflect on it. Where he was patient, everyone knew it, but where he was impatient, even the multitude found it difficult to perceive.
When asked by the Buddha, "Do you see anything that you do not tolerate? he replied, "I see things that I also cannot tolerate.
The Buddha said, "If that is so, you are the same as the multitude. How then will you refute others? At these words, he immediately submitted and attained awakening. He spoke again:

Regarding "Kāśyapa": first, it clarifies the cause by which Kāśyapa attained ultimate realization; second, it praises his virtuous conduct, noting that he was able to realize the Path for himself and further enable others to attain ultimate realization.
The citation below serves as evidence of his virtue in benefiting others after attaining ultimate realization; the preceding section concerned his virtue in self-cultivation.

The "four analytical knowledges" (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ) refer to the analytical knowledge of phenomena, meaning, language, and eloquence; in the new terminology, they are called the four [analytical knowledges].

The "unimpeded analytical knowledges" (*pratisaṃvid*) refer to the essence and function of these [knowledges]. To speak of their source, they consist in being extensively proficient in worldly matters and deeply penetrating the supramundane.
Generally speaking, their essence is both merit and wisdom; specifically, their essential point is simply *jñāna* (insight).
When defining their excellence, they are the Arhats who possess liberation free from doubt. The subsequent citation of the King of South India is intended to illustrate this.
This is because he revered their morality and virtue; one cannot know this man’s conduct as being "high and great" merely through his status.

It is indeed true that among these four essentials, the first concerns the world, the second concerns establishing one's resolve and achieving mastery in study, and the third concerns engaging in a single exchange of words with the Buddha, wherein one falls into two points of defeat.
However, the first meaning—the primary principle—is clearly understood through the contemplation of the Path as the antidote.

Fortunately, there are no errors here. Regarding the "subsequent summary of the teachings," this clarifies the common and specific aspects of his altruistic virtuous conduct and reveals the meaning of this sutra.
As for the name and meaning of the four Vedas, they are explained in the later text.
Because they can subdue the three external paths and penetrate the Tripitaka, and because they can subdue the two types of Arhats, they are the greatest among the initial teachings.
Regarding "that which is non-apprehensible": if one can explain it according to principle, both the speaker and the spoken are unapprehendable.
"Name" refers to the names upon the phenomena of the ten realms; "meaning" refers to the reason for those names beneath the phenomena of the ten realms.

Briefly citing two of these, one should further state that "phrasing" refers to the words and sounds of the ten realms, and "eloquence" refers to [the speech] that accords with the words and sounds of the ten realms.
It is taught that within the single true reality (*ekasatyalakṣaṇa*), one distinguishes the four "all-encompassing" categories of name, meaning, and so forth;

or, within the true reality that is neither provisional nor ultimate, one distinguishes the provisional and the ultimate—all of which are fully elucidated. Because their fusion and identity are without fixed direction, it is the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*).

Within the three secrets of the fundamental [Buddha], this corresponds to the secret of speech; the three wheels correspond to the wheel of speech. It is the wheel that grasps the one and the many, yet remains unfathomable.

"Taking up that which can revolve, crush, and grind in an infinite succession" refers to the inconceivable; this general praise of the aforementioned two [aspects] transcends the reach of both mind and speech.

Next, regarding the "Original and Traced" (honji-suijaku), first the "Original" is clarified by means of vocal karma (*vākkarma*), and then the "Original" is clarified by means of mental karma (*manaskarma*).

Furthermore, the first clarifies function (*kāritra*) and the second clarifies essence (*svabhāva*); the first clarifies benefiting others (*parārtha*) and the second clarifies self-cultivation (*svārtha*). The first is... [end of fragment].

Below "virtue" (guṇa) is "practice" (caryā); this refers to the merit of the stage of fruition consisting of the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid). Concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā) constitute the essential practice;

among practices, nothing surpasses concentration and wisdom. Among these essentials, the most excellent is the "Great" (mahat). The significance of these two "Greats" is the same as the aforementioned "Superior" (uttara).
The knees and feet represent practice, while the two [knees] represent concentration and wisdom. Furthermore, the presence of the Great Marks (mahālakṣaṇa) represents...

Because the essentials of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are preeminent, he possesses these marks that distinguish him from ordinary people; thus, his name is not given in vain.

Although the previous names distinguished him by virtue (*guṇa*), here the name also constitutes a virtue, as it serves as a general designation for the virtues of his fundamental stage (*mūla-bhūmi*).
He manifests this through his traces (*śeṣa*) so that, by relying on the traces to reveal the fundamental, sentient beings may cultivate this great practice.

Therefore, by taking the whole substance and subsuming its functions, the mention of only "concentration" (samādhi) and "wisdom" (prajñā) already includes the four aforementioned analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).

Furthermore, the aforementioned verbal karma is merely the "eloquence of joyful speech" among those four; since joyful speech consists of explaining the preceding three [analytical knowledges], the one [term] possesses all four.
This is because the text is extremely concise. In the contemplation [section], the discussion is focused exclusively on names and practices to explain the contemplation; here, it is based on...
Because there are two aspects of practice, one speaks only of emptiness and the provisional; furthermore, taking the sense of "adornment," it further says that one uses these to adorn the mind.
This is not merely conceptualizing emptiness and the provisional; rather, they are themselves great samādhi and great wisdom.

Taking these as the means to adorn the mind is precisely the true mind, and the true mind is the Dharma-body, which is that which is adorned. Thus, through cultivation one manifests the inherent nature, wherein both self and other are included.
The phrase "the note says... indicates that the meaning is presented in brief.
In the explanation of Nanda’s initial causes and conditions, although the text is very concise, it contains both the meanings of name (*nāman*) and conduct (*carita*).

Regarding the first [meaning], the name, the text says "also called," because this person was not fixed [in one state]; thus it says "also. According to the various ancient commentaries, they all simply or... [text ends].

The Master [Paramārtha] now likewise translates it as "wholesome" (*śubha*) and so forth; however, based on this Sanskrit term, since it carries no sense of "wholesomeness," all previous commentators simply rendered it as "joyful.
Furthermore, since the term "delight" (*abhirati*) mentioned below also lacks the meaning of "wholesomeness," we know that it refers solely to "joy.

This meaning appears frequently throughout the preceding and following sections and can be understood by analogy; therefore, I shall not explain it further. Nevertheless, the meaning of these two names is as follows:
It should be understood that this applies equally to himself and others. There is a commentary which states: Originally a cowherd, he asked the Buddha about the matter of tending cattle.
The Buddha answered him with eleven points; realizing that the Buddha possessed all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*), he subsequently attained the fruit of Arhatship.
He was exceedingly brilliant, and his voice was most exquisite. According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, King Bimbisāra invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
During the three-month *varṣā* retreat, the King issued an edict to the cowherds, ordering them to reside nearby and deliver milk and curd daily until the end of the three months.
The King was greatly pleased by this and, having been granted a special audience with the Buddha, he subsequently resolved to leave the household life and attained the fruit of *aśaikṣa*.

This account of King Śuddhodana’s subordinates serves to manifest his virtuous conduct; for were it not so, how could such an edict have been issued? Therefore, this person relies directly upon this text.
Yi still found it difficult to discern the auspicious signs. Ji said, "Some say that among the ten thousand people who have left home from the Śākya clan, this is one of them;
his nature is extremely light and frivolous, yet he is very intelligent and his voice is exquisite. Based on this, he is not a cowherd.
Furthermore, there was another Śākya who previously stated directly that he is indeed one of the ten thousand, and moreover, he is a younger brother of the Buddha.

Since they are listed in succession, it is certain that this is one among the [four] Śākyas. Next, there is the statement "there are other masters," etc.; this merely represents a different tradition and should not be considered the primary one.
Within this, four intentions are fully contained: first, the translation of the two names; second, the proper selection from the world to cause him to leave the household life;

third, the intention to manifest the Buddha’s virtues and eliminate the contempt of the people; and fourth, that all [who encounter him] attain the Way. These three points constitute the detailed analysis.

The four intentions are fully possessed and require nothing else; there may be this name because they practice accordingly, hence the listing of these persons. Next, regarding the classification by teaching (*jiao*), this correctly clarifies the meaning of this sutra and its dharma.
The term "dwelling" (*zhu*) in the context of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*) means dwelling in that which is called "joyless," for it covers the meaning [of joy].

By analogy with the Distinct Teaching (*bie*), one only perceives the Middle Way upon reaching high stages and still feels joy; how much more so in the ultimate stage of the Perfect Teaching, where the initial mind immediately perceives the Middle Way?
Yet they do not rejoice, for they are likewise so; whereas those who rejoiced previously—referring to the first three [weeks]—now experience the supreme joy of the revelation of the One Vehicle.

Therefore, it is said that in the latter three weeks, upon attaining realization, they all "leap for joy and rejoice," as these are individuals who have already ascended to the stages of the *shō* (abodes) and above.
Next, within the sections on the Original and the Traces, each should possess the essence and function of the Three Truths; however, the text primarily emphasizes only...

The essence and its traces are one, and their functions are identical; these are merely mentioned alternately. Alternatively, [the teaching on] long-abiding in the perfect path of the Three Truths shows the preceding four stages so that all beings may return to the same goal.
Reflect upon this, reflect upon it! Regarding the contemplation of the Middle Way, we distinguish between the two stages of the "semblance" and the "true.

Since both of these two stages possess the meaning of "joy," I have briefly mentioned two of them; however, one should understand that they fully comprise the six levels of "identity" (*ji*), which can be considered by analogy.
Next, in explaining the initial causes and conditions regarding Sundara, there are first his name and then his virtuous conduct.

Regarding the former, it should be understood that this name was established for the sake of distinction and clarity: "Sundara" refers to his wife. While this is primarily an explanation of Nanda, the mention of his wife serves two purposes:
first, to distinguish him from others who share the same name; second, to manifest his virtuous conduct, which will be explained in detail later.
By means of these two meanings, his wife is introduced; therein, Sunda is explained first, followed by Nanda.
Within the initial section, the two names mutually clarify and manifest their respective meanings, which will be evident later.
Next, in explaining Nanda, there are two parts: first, a direct translation and a reference to what was previously stated—namely, "toward joy and delight";
second, a clarification that it should possess both meanings. First, it signifies the sense of being extremely good and beloved, arising from his mind.
Second, it arises when others see him, referring to his physical form. It is because of these two meanings—pertaining to both mind and body—that [the name is used].
The meaning of "Joy" (Nanda) is manifested in the text; there is no need for further elaboration.
Regarding the second meaning, four matters are briefly cited to provide an explanation: first, lineage; second, time of birth; third, physical stature; and fourth, deportment.
Because these four matters are all different from the ordinary, those who see or hear of them all give rise to joy. Thus, it is by virtue of others that this name is obtained. Therefore...
The second meaning explained above will be manifested later; "clan" (*gotra*) also refers back to the former, namely the Kṣatriya clan of Gautama Śākya.
Because he was the biological younger brother of the Buddha, born of Māyādevī, he is referred to as the "former. Regarding the time of his birth, the *Dvādaśayātra-sūtra* states:
"The Buddha was born on the eighth day of the fourth month at the time of the rising of the morning star, and his body was tall."
The Buddha, one *zhang* and six *chi* tall, had a younger brother named Nanda, born on the ninth day of the fourth month, who was one *zhang*, five *chi*, and four *cun* tall.
What is now referred to as "four fingers" should be stated as "six *cun* shorter" according to the sutra.

As for the term "distinguished" (*tingte*), "distinguished" (*ting*) means to stand out from the crowd, while "unique" (*te*) means solitary; it refers to his appearance being exceptionally prominent and standing alone. Regarding these four matters, who [could surpass him]?
There are those who, upon seeing or hearing [this], do not rejoice; this concludes the preceding explanation of its name.

From here on, the text next clarifies its virtuous qualities, which are broadly divided into two parts: first, it clarifies how it can cause even the most perverse individuals to look toward its form and return to the fundamental school;
second, it clarifies how it can sever extreme craving and evil, leading to awakening in the path of purity. First, "Mīśāsaka" refers to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
Regarding the term "naked-form" (nirgrantha), this refers to those among the heterodox paths who lack a sense of shame (*ahrīka*), the most debased of the wicked.

As for the "wife," it refers to the second meaning listed below. Some people say that this subsequent passage should have been moved to follow the preceding section on "explaining the names" (*nāmavyākhyāna*);

however, I maintain that these individuals do not understand the intent of the text at all. To speak thus of the author himself is certainly improper; this [passage] clarifies that such a person is capable of refutation.
The path of purification for extremely heavy desire and evil is used here to manifest one's virtuous conduct. How could one be so deluded as to hold such a view?

Now, in order to make known the essential meaning of this passage, it should be understood according to its beginning and conclusion. There are three main points: first, clarifying the heavy desire that is to be remedied;
second, clarifying the path of purification that serves as the remedy; and third, concluding by clarifying both meanings. This is the first section.

There should be four propositions: the first indicates [the offense], the next three distinguish its characteristics, the section beginning with "The Buddha" and following clarifies its specific manifestations, and the final proposition concludes its meaning.
Regarding the first, it is precisely because the object is superior that the emotion is grave. Next, within the section on the manifestations, there are roughly five parts:
first, it clarifies the temporary departure to welcome the Buddha while making an appointment with his wife; as for the term "traveler on the road," "road" (tu) refers to—
The character for "road" (*dao*) is also written with the characters for "mud" and "to smear," which has been used since antiquity as a homonym for "path";

thus it remains so today. Regarding the passage beginning with "Next, he said to the Buddha": fearing that his life span was limited, he was unwilling to leave the household life. Leaving the household life involves departing from affection and reverence, which would contradict his deluded sentiments;
therefore, he was unwilling. As for the "King of Jambudvīpa," the Buddha was destined to be a Golden Wheel-turning King (*Cakravartin*) who ruled over the four continents.
Rāhula was a Wheel-Turning King of Jambudvīpa, and since he has now likewise renounced the world, his rank corresponds to that [of the Buddha]; this is why it is said so.
When the Buddha urged him to come down, Rāhula had no choice but to comply; although his outward appearance and dress have changed, his feelings remain entirely earnest.

As for those who say he fled, it is because when the Buddha was about to travel to the heavenly realms, Rāhula resented his wife’s love for the celestial maidens and made a vow to be reborn in those heavens.

When the Five Buddhas first traveled to the hells, they finally understood the root of suffering and realized the path of purity. Regarding the statement that they "traveled through heaven and hell," the text is very brief;
according to what is clarified in the sūtras, the Buddha first led them to travel to Mount Gandhamādana.

On this mountain there was a fruit tree, and beneath it was a female macaque who lacked one eye and had been scorched by fire. The Buddha asked, "What kind of person is this? [The answer was: "Sundarī."

Li replied: "How can this be used as a comparison? Furthermore, when he was led to tour the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, being shown the sights until he reached the Nandana Grove and the Miśrakāvana Grove, he saw various heavenly maidens and all kinds of music. At one place, there was a heavenly maiden who had no husband;
when asked about it, the deity answered: 'The Buddha’s younger brother, Nanda, has been born here by virtue of maintaining the precepts; he shall be your husband.'"
The Buddha then asked the goddess, "How does she compare to Sundarī? She replied, "It is as if one were to compare Sundarī to a blind monkey.
The Buddha said, "Since you now maintain the precepts, you shall be reborn in this heaven; yet you still long for that celestial palace and practice the holy life [for its sake].
The Buddha then led her to tour the various hells, where he saw all the hells being governed by people, though some places were devoid of them.
When people asked this, the warder replied: "The Buddha’s younger brother, Nanda, practiced the holy life for the sake of being born in heaven;
though he dwelt briefly in the heavens, he will soon return here to undergo suffering. Upon hearing this, Nanda shed tears like rain.
The Buddha then returned to the Jeta Grove and extensively explained the characteristics of the remedy. Consequently, Nanda resolved his mind upon liberation and began to practice its cultivation.
The Brahma-faring further attains Arhatship; the details are as described at length in the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*, so the matter is summarized here (as indicated by "and so forth").

Of the five stages mentioned above, the first four clarify the characteristics of being deeply attached to and receiving sensual desires—this is the primary meaning of "joy," and it is precisely what is to be eliminated.
The fifth stage clarifies the characteristics of the path that serves as the antidote. It is supreme.
The following sentence is the conclusion; it is placed at the beginning specifically to manifest that which is capable of counteracting the most cherished objects of attachment.
The preceding word-by-word commentary has been brief. As for the essential meaning, various interpretations differ;

I am currently unable to reconcile them, nor can I provide a further exposition. First, the explanation of name and lineage follows worldly convention; next, [the text] returns to the account of Sujāta.
To turn the mind toward the monastic life is for a person to be able to shatter the most heavy desires and evils and awaken to the path of purity; this is the meaning of "treatment" (治).

The second and fourth [meanings] clarify that there is no difference between them. Next, regarding the classification by teaching (*jiao*), it correctly clarifies the meaning of this sutra as "joyfully receiving the Dharma.

Taking the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* as a reference, it takes up the meaning of being able to shatter "joyful attachment" (*xi'ai*). The former [shattering desire and evil] is to break away from the conventional and realize the ultimate truth.
Next, the clarification of "identity with reality" (jìzhēn) is explained through three aspects according to the sequence of the Perfect (yuán) and the Middle (zhōng).

First, "one is all," meaning that the conventional (sú) is identical to the real (zhēn), yet it is neither conventional nor real, and yet it is both conventional and real. Since this applies to each and every aspect, it constitutes the meaning of the perfect and subtle (yuánmiào).
As for the original contemplation, since it refers back to the preceding text, its meaning and characteristics are also explained as before; reflect upon this.
