Regarding the initial causes and conditions for the Śākya Pūrṇa, there are two parts: first, his name; second, his conduct. Within the section on the name, there are two further points:
first, the transliteration of the name; second, the explanation of its meaning. Regarding the transliteration, the single character "zi" (子) is itself the local dialectal term [for *putra*].

Some commentators state that he was of the Brahmin caste in the city of Rājagṛha; according to the subsequent explanation of the meaning, this refers to his parents. Within the explanation of the meaning, there are three points, the first of which is the individual [meaning].
Regarding the three types of "following"—the first following the father, the second following the mother alone, and the third following both—the first refers to the fulfillment of one's intent;

it is so named because the aspiration is realized through these three causal conditions. Since the aspiration is called "fulfillment" (*suī*), it is designated by that name. The first is the external sign:

having made a prayer by the riverbank, one encounters this omen which signifies that what is sought will certainly be realized. The second is the internal auspicious sign; the third is the correct [realization].

The matters sought have been accomplished; what was requested refers precisely to the three aforementioned points. Next, regarding "following the mother": the mother received her name because of what she recited;
since he was born of this woman, it is described thus. Following this, the text clarifies how he received his names from two venerable figures:
if named solely after the father, he is called "Fulfilling-Wishes Son" (*Pūrṇa-putra*); if named solely after the mother, he is called "Compassionate Son" (*Maitreya*).
Since he is called Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, this indicates that he is derived from both [his father and mother]. Ancient commentaries all reached this conclusion.
A recent commentary states: "In Sanskrit, *Pūrṇa-Maitrāyaṇī-putra*. *Pūrṇa* is his personal name; *Maitrāyaṇī* refers to the maternal lineage (*mātṛgotra*).

To speak fully, he should be called Ānanda, the son of Śuklodana and the younger brother of Daḍḍa;

The meaning of joy (*prīti*) and the meaning of being untainted (*anāsakta*) are both manifested therein; this will become clear later on its own. First, regarding the explanation of the mother, there are two types of joy:

first, the joy of the paternal uncle, and second, the joy of the parents. Each of these has two meanings. Regarding the two types of joy for the paternal uncle: first, because his son has attained the path of awakening;

Since these four positions are already established in this way, would one not feel profound sorrow and distress? Māra [uses this]...

Because he was jealous and distressed that the Buddha could not be moved to his will, he did not cease until he had caused distress to his parents, seeking to cause them to lose their rank and status;

since this suffering is even more severe than the former, these signs of weeping and lamentation are called the "omens and traces at birth," as fully described in the *Buddhapurāṇa* and various sūtras, which I have been unable to recount in detail here. Compared to the great sorrow mentioned previously, this [sorrow] is greater.

The reason for the words "the entire nation rejoices" is that there is no one—whether among the sovereign’s parents, kinsmen, ministers, subjects, or those of the court and the commonalty—who does not feel moved with gratitude and celebration;
this is because, in total, the first two matters were so extraordinary. The phrase "following his parents" is explained as before.

This concluding statement is made to distinguish [this case] from instances where [rejoicing occurs] simply because of manifesting virtuous conduct. An old commentary states: "There is joy... [and so forth].

There are three meanings: first, his physical form was upright and handsome, and all who saw him rejoiced; second, he was born on the night the Buddha attained the Way, which is called the time of "rejoicing" (*pramuditā*);
thus he is named "Rejoicing. Third, he made a vow, and the term for the vow is "Rejoicing Friend. Daolin says it means "extensive learning," while others say it means "untainted";
the latter meaning comes later. Regarding these three meanings, the first corresponds to the sequence [of the stages], while the subsequent two correspond to the following [stages].
The meaning is as previously stated in the third section; this particular passage is missing from the text. According to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, there are three meanings:
first, "parents," which refers to what people perceive; second, "original vows," of which there are two—namely, those made during the Buddha’s causal stage and those from his previous lives;

and third, "vast learning," which pertains to his virtuous conduct, as the Sūtra calls Ānanda a "man of much hearing" (*bahuśruta*), as will be explained in the subsequent section. Furthermore, according to ancient traditions...

There is an interpretation which states: "The name 'Joyful' (Nanda) refers to the time when he first gave rise to his vow based on causes and conditions accumulated in previous lives; it refers to the night he attained the Way upon being born;
and it refers to his face being like the full moon and his eyes resembling blue lotuses, which cause those who see him to rejoice in spirit and bring celebration to his father, the King.
Because he possesses these meanings, he is called 'Joyful'. Now, I say that this interpretation provisionally possesses three meanings, as previously [stated].
The three meanings are identical. The new [translation] states that Ānanda means "Joyous Celebration" (*Prāmodya*);

because he was born at the time of celebration when the World-Honored One attained enlightenment—feeling both internal and external joy—he is named "Joyous Celebration. This may be understood as one among the three [meanings].
From this point onward, all [sections] manifest his virtuous conduct; first, it generally clarifies that all who see him give rise to joy. This is the opening.
This is precisely its reason: namely, the first of the three meanings mentioned above. To briefly cite one person as an example serves to manifest the aspect of extreme delight;
however, because the woman’s verse regarding the rejection of desire does not pertain to the present context, it is not recounted here.
Next is the second [section], which specifically clarifies how the fourfold assembly, upon seeing and hearing of his deeds, all gave rise to joy.

Regarding the matters performed [for this purpose], three points are briefly enumerated: speech, the act of speaking, and the four modes of physical deportment; these constitute the two categories of form and sound.
This being so, because of the power of past merit and karma, and because one’s current conduct is refined and appropriate, such results are brought about.

Following this, the third section specifically clarifies how it causes the five hundred [disciples] to rejoice, stating that on the eighth day of the fourth month and other such occasions—this is based on the *Buddha-pu* (Buddha-sūtra), citing ten [instances].
The *Eryou jing* (Sutra on the Two Wanderings) states: "Devadatta was born on the seventh day of the fourth month at the time of the morning meal;
the Buddha was born on the eighth day of the fourth month when the morning star appeared; the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda was born on the ninth day of the fourth month;

and Ānanda was born on the tenth day of the fourth month. Their heights were one zhang, five chi, and three cun. This differs from [other accounts], which should be understood as different versions of the sacred teachings that cannot be reconciled.
When it was time to appoint an attendant as requested, [the Buddha] mentioned Ānanda and others; these accounts are all found in the thirty-sixth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
When he requested someone to serve as an attendant, the Buddha did not accept anyone else, his intention being fixed upon Ānanda.

The reason for this was that it accorded with [Ānanda’s] original vow, and his capacity and character were appropriate. Since the other people understood this, they collectively submitted to and followed the Buddha’s will.
He exhorted them, and because they were able to comply and act in accordance with the inclinations of the assembly, all were filled with joy.
Below this is the fourth section, "The Tathāgata’s Joy," which has two causes and conditions for the Tathāgata’s delight: first, he praises their ability to protect the minds of sentient beings;

second, he extols their capacity to uphold the Dharma. It is for these reasons that he rejoices. The following passage, beginning with "I pray that the Buddha... and so forth, is the expression of this wish; there will certainly be benefit.
To benefit sentient beings, one must be able to come and go with mastery; this mastery refers to the capacity to speak for the sake of benefiting others.
As for the phrase "surpassing those of the past" and so forth, it praises the capacity of the physical vessel (the body).

It suggests that the attendants of the past should have been the attendants of the superior Buddhas of the past, rather than referring to their specific physical forms. Reflect on this, reflect on this! Herein there is the heading and the explanation.
In the commentary on the *Sūtra*, first the past [events] are explained, and next Ānanda is explained; this indeed demonstrates his virtue of being intelligent and capable of discerning the subtle.
The *I Ching* says: "The son of the Yan family did not have two errors. Because he had one error, it was still considered an error; however, that was merely in reference to his own person.
Now, being able to understand the intent of the Ultimate Sage—how could he be compared to that? Within this, there are two points, the first of which states:
The minds of the multitude can know the Buddha’s mind; if he can even know such things, how much more so those that are manifest—could he not know them?

This is intended solely to show that the people’s intent lies therein. What follows is the fifth section, clarifying his virtue of joy (*prāmodya*). Previously, his capacity to receive was praised; now, his capacity to uphold is praised.

Regarding the previous capacity to receive, there are two aspects: first, being capable of receiving [the teaching] to serve as the Buddha’s attendant; second, [being capable of serving as the Buddha’s attendant].
Those capable of receiving the Dharma taught by the Buddha are now able to uphold it; herein there are two types: first, being able to uphold the Buddha’s vessel for food;
second, being able to uphold the Dharma spoken by the Buddha. The former is "bearing and upholding," while the latter is "reciting and upholding"—the phrasing is clear.
The former is the power of one's own merit and virtue, while the latter is the power of wisdom, intelligence, and *dhāraṇī*. Both of these are difficult to achieve.
The subsequent passage states: "Deeply rejoicing that one has obtained great and wholesome benefit, one therefore experiences joy.

Regarding the text on the Four Heavenly Kings offering the alms-bowl, this appears in the *Āgama*. What follows is the sixth [section], clarifying the reasons for the joyful delight of devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits;
because it is untainted (*asaṃkliṣṭa*). This text simultaneously explains the meaning of being "untainted," and thus others [have said so].

People say that this person is one who has fully realized the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and has cultivated [the path] such that they do not give rise to defiled thoughts upon seeing celestial maidens, *nāgas*, or others;

thus it is said they are "undefiled. Yet, while the essence of defilement is not yet exhausted, they are able to remain free from conceptualization amidst this challenge because the power of their mindfulness is so intense that even if [defilements] exist, they are as if non-existent;
therefore, they can cause others to rejoice. The following is the seventh among these virtues: the ability to cause all beings to be born [in the higher realms].
Regarding the joy within this [context], there are three main points: first, clarifying that the assembly rejoices when the physical remains are collected;

second, clarifying that the entry into *parinirvāṇa* brings equal benefit, causing joy in four places; and third, clarifying that after his passing, the stupas cause people to feel longing and provide joy through their offerings.
As for the first, the great assembly selects a capable person and requests them to collect the scriptural treasury (*sūtrapiṭaka*), because of his physical form...
Because his vessel was deep and he was worthy of his task, the multitude joyfully praised him with verses. First, they praised his physical form—the features and contours of his face;
next, they praised his mind, which was able to receive and uphold the ocean-like waters of the teachings he had spoken. Next, he entered into the equality of parinirvāṇa to benefit all equally.
As he was about to enter nirvana, he went to King Ajātaśatru’s assembly while the king was sleeping during the day; leaving a message with the gatekeeper, he then departed for Vaiśālī.
King Śreṇika immediately dreamed that the stalk of his parasol snapped; startled awake, he informed the gatekeeper, who then reported it to the king.

The king arrayed his fourfold army and went to the banks of the Ganges, requesting that [the Buddha] enter parinirvāṇa within his own domain. However, because the Licchavis also requested that he remain there, and since both groups would have harbored resentment, he entered the river to attain parinirvāṇa.
Desiring to manifest his body in various parts, he entered this samādhi. These four [events] are the most significant regarding the Buddha.
Because it was the dwelling place of Fa-sheng, he left it for him; because such equal benefit was bestowed, all were filled with joy.

Subsequently, after his passing, they yearned for his virtue and made offerings with joy. Although these kings lived in different eras and did not meet one another, they were moved by his profound and flourishing virtue, and thus offered this joyful worship—namely, that both presented jewels and offered praise.
Within the praise, first the excellence of his flourishing virtue was extolled, thereby manifesting their offering.

Next, in "Nurturing the Will," he praises the mind and mouth for their ability to uphold and transmit [the Dharma] as Buddhas; he praises them as beautiful and worthy of the love and respect of humans and devas.

These three, combined with the preceding six, constitute nine meanings, all of which pertain to the meaning of virtuous conduct (*guṇa-dharma*). Finally, he cites a sutra to collectively substantiate the preceding nine meanings, stating:
"To know the time" means to recognize the appropriate capacity and occasion; "to clarify things" means to discern the characteristics and forms of the Dharma. These two are essential.

Because he has discerned [the truth], he is free from all doubt; because he is not deluded, he is able to uphold it; because he has heard much, he is able to receive it; and because he is broad-minded and thorough, he has mastered its principles and meanings.
Due to these three aforementioned factors, he is capable of reverently upholding [the teaching] and is without equal, thus he is declared the foremost.
For this reason, the preceding meaning is collectively verified. Within this, the ten points are condensed into four essentials: first, prior to his renunciation, due to his father...
Establishing names constitutes the world-realm (*loka-dhātu*). Next, when all people see [the teaching] with joy, the fourfold assembly is delighted;

this constitutes the person-realm (*pudgala-dhātu*), for it enables one to receive and uphold [the teaching] without defilement. These three are the remedies [for the three poisons]. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, these three matters all abide in the middle way;
their essence is functional utility, and they are equal, all being the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Because these four points constitute the essential meaning, [they are taught].

The name "Joyful" (*pramuditā*) is next explained according to the classification of teachings (*yōkyō*). This distinguishes the provisional from the ultimate, clearly revealing the meaning of the name "Joyful" in this specific sutra.

That is to say, by means of four names, the four teachings are revealed; thus, while the preceding ten meanings were all equally termed "joyful," they specifically correspond to the meaning of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).
"Worthy" (*bhadra*) carries the sense of being superior; because it is skillful in contrast to the previous clumsiness, it correctly corresponds to this [teaching].
The scriptural teachings are the royal office of this Dharma; as they are profound and vast, if one were to house them before oneself, one should regard them as this ocean.
This ocean is profoundly vast, gathering the confluence of the hundred rivers, all of which share a single flavor, being perfectly interfused and non-dual.

Thus, its name is self-manifested and does not require further distinction between the three provisional means and the one reality. If one arrives at this point, the three are precisely the one, just as was explained previously in the section on "Thus have I heard."
Tracing this to the primary meaning of this sutra: that which is neither born nor extinguished, neither good nor evil, is the Dharmakāya, which is like empty space.
Relying upon this realm of the body, one possesses great wisdom, just as a great cloud can hold and receive a great rain;
this is the essence and function of the fundamental nature. It is because it receives and upholds all the Buddha-dharmas of the ten directions.
The reason I have composed this commentary is that the ten meanings previously discussed do not go beyond the relationship between the object (*viṣaya*) and the wisdom (*jñāna*).

Therefore, I shall now take the essentials and directly clarify [the truth] by means of these two, so as to encompass the previous meanings entirely. From these two fundamental aspects, they descend into the two provisional traces;

by relying on the traces to manifest the fundamental, I cause sentient beings to attain [realization]. (As stated... Regarding the "traces being equal," it is for the sake of enabling those at the end of the age to attain [it].

Therefore, the four types of joy are shown to demonstrate that the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual. Since these observations correspond to both the semblance and the true aspects, all are "joyful.
This is as stated in the following text: "A single thought of sympathetic joy" refers to the semblance, while "exultant joy" refers to the true.

The realization and understanding throughout the three assemblies are all described as "exultant joy," which is true joy. Generally speaking, this meaning applies to all six [aspects]. Regarding the phrase "Note (云云)," there is... [text continues].
The meaning is roughly as follows.
In the explanation of Rāhula’s initial causes and conditions, the preceding account given to Ānanda is also largely similar; it likewise contains ten points.
The first concerns his past causes and present fruits, which is simply an explanation of his name. The remaining nine points are directly based upon his present state.
The meaning of the name clarifies his virtuous conduct; thus, they are roughly the same. However, the significance of this "virtuous conduct" is somewhat difficult to grasp.

It is like understanding that poison becomes medicine, or realizing that what is not [the cause] is precisely the cause. This is not something easily understood; one must examine it carefully and not act with haste.
Regarding the first name, there are two causes and conditions. As for the first condition, some say that in a previous life, Yaśodharā caused her child to block [the Buddha’s path].
A rat died after being trapped in its hole for six days; this was a residual retribution for that sin. For six years, his pregnancy lasted; this refers to Rāhula.
Because he blocked the opening according to that teaching, he was punished for six years. This was brought about by karmic retribution due to such an obstruction.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states that the *Nidāna-sūtra* clarifies that he received this retribution because in a previous life he blocked a rat's hole. Furthermore, it is not [the case that] he did not [attain enlightenment].
Regarding the term "etcetera," the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* quotes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states: "In the past, he was once a king who desired to wear the robes of a rishi.

Having become attached to pleasure, he forgot [the time] for six days until he remembered them. When he went out to put on the robes of the rishi, he remained outside for six days in a state of distress;

therefore, he dwelt in the womb for six years. The present text says "six days," referring to two sets of six. As for the phrase "due to these conditions," this refers to the synthesis of the two aforementioned conditions.
It is named "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*). All previous explanations were identical to this. The new [explanation] states that *Rāhu* means "retribution" (*vipāka*), yet its meaning is not explained;
it is also the same as the old explanation. The ancient commentary also names it "born in the palace. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* says:
"When the Prince was about to leave the household, he pointed to his consort and said, 'In six years from now, you shall give birth to a son,' [referring to] Yaśodharā."
Because she became aware of her pregnancy, they all began to suspect that she had conceived while in the palace;
it was only later, through various corroborating circumstances, that they realized she had truly given birth to the Prince in the palace, which is why he is named "Palace-Born" (Kung-sheng).

Since this passage intends to clarify the meaning of the ten obstacles, this specific name has been omitted, yet its significance is contained therein. The nine subsequent meanings are metaphorical designations.

To manifest his virtuous conduct, although it is titled "Concealment" (*paryavasthāna*), the true intent lies precisely in its revelation; that the words are proximate while the meaning is profound is well illustrated herein.

Of these, the first two [verses] manifest the virtues of his father, the next one manifests the virtues of his mother, and from the fourth verse through the end of the text, all together manifest the virtues of his father.
Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of the father’s virtues in the first two [verses], there are two parts, the first of which is as follows:
Within this, there are two further points. First, it clarifies that his father’s virtue of filial piety was such that he could comply with and honor his ancestors;

thus, the virtue of supreme filiality shielded him from impiety. Furthermore, it demonstrates that filial piety across different lifetimes ensures that impiety does not lead to the extinction of one's lineage, thereby resulting in a son who is filial.
This is brought about by the power of the Way and its Virtue (*mārga-guṇa*), which differs from worldly causes. This is how his son attained such a state.
This negates that which is non-conforming and non-different in order to manifest the virtues of being conforming and different; the primary intent lies herein.
Furthermore, the mention of "six years" is because the meaning of the "six days within the middle" mentioned previously has not yet been clarified, so it is mentioned here by way of this occasion.
The text appears in the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*. Next, the first [section] is a subtle manifestation of how his father was able to relinquish worldly affection and love.
This explains the virtue of concealment and obstruction; it clarifies that one whose aspiration is for the world-transcending, pure path abandons the defiled and turbid dharmas of the mundane world.
Some say that between the characters "xiū" (修) and "luó" (羅), the character "xiū" (修) must be added again;
since the original text is already abbreviated, there is yet another who says that what Paramārtha (Zhēndì) has explained is not in accordance with the Buddha’s words below.

Now, our school’s attachment to that text for the purpose of explaining the meaning of "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) does not mean we entirely adopt its underlying intent. We maintain that this is not the case;
it is sufficient simply to be able to discern its meaning, so why need one further trouble oneself with its source? This particular passage is used in its entirety as the correct interpretation.
How could it be said to be inappropriate? Therefore, both [the source and the interpretation] are acceptable. Within this, the first part clarifies that the names are identical.
Regarding the statement "the title contains an explanatory gloss on the original name," it should be said that this is originally the name of an asura, namely Rāhu-asura;
this is translated as "Obstructing the Moon" or "Seizing the Sun. The following section is the explanation:

that deity is able to seize and obstruct the sun and moon with his hands, and thus he is named accordingly. This [section] first translates and then correctly reveals this name and its meaning. First, the translation:
Next, regarding this meaning, Rāhula should also be said to "obstruct the moon. The Buddha’s words below explain this meaning; it has two aspects:

the agent and the object. First, the two obstructions are clarified by saying "like the moon," because its light is pure and cool, and it is capable of providing great benefit—this refers to the object obstructed.
The passage beginning with "this child" below explains the obstructing agent, meaning that he causes [the father] to possess affection and attachment.

The following clarifies the two types of relinquishment (*tyāga*). The first phrase indicates that which is relinquished; the second phrase indicates that which relinquishes. It is not merely for a single lifetime, thereby manifesting the greatness of its virtue.

The concluding statement regarding "obscuring hindrances" (*āvaraṇa*) explicitly refers to that which is capable of relinquishing such heavy and thick obscuring hindrances. By mentioning the object to be manifested, the capacity [of the relinquisher] is revealed;
otherwise, it would fail to demonstrate its skillfulness, loftiness, and greatness. Next, the first [section] reveals the virtue of the Mother, whose power is as described above.
The preceding passage further implicitly reveals the mother’s virtue of chastity to dispel doubt and slander. This section consists of two layers:
both first present the obstacles that concealed her virtue and subsequently reveal her magnificent excellence. Regarding the slight difference in wording, the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-vyūha-sūtra* states:
"That person said, 'I have traveled and stayed together with Yaśodharā; never has there been any transgression. Because of this testimony, the assembly [was convinced]."
Although his doubts have not been entirely eliminated, they can be known to have become somewhat lighter; therefore, it is said that they are "small.

As for the mention of the "Jewel Woman," she should not be the "Jewel Woman" among the seven treasures of a Wheel-Turning King, because when one is about to receive the rank of a Holy King (*cakravartin*), these [treasures] arrive in succession within a single day;
it is impossible for this one alone to have arrived first and remained for so long. Rather, she was summoned solely by the merit of the Crown Prince.
A woman of noble and eminent status is called a "jewel" (*ratna*). Since your doubts have not yet been dispelled, please wait for her arrival to verify this.
After she has given birth, we shall test the matter against our previous vow; once the vow is fulfilled and she is offered up, there will be no such obstacle.
This serves to manifest the virtue of her chastity; thus, it is clear that what appears as a covering obstacle is actually the manifestation of her virtue. Here is another matter.
This is intended to manifest that his virtue is utterly perfect and complete. "Serving the Buddha" and so forth refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
At the time he was serving the Buddha, he transformed himself into five hundred arhats who were indistinguishable from the Buddha;

because Rāhula, while still a child, went directly to the Buddha to miss his meal, he was thus able to quell slander. This is the fourth meaning. This passage contains three meanings; if one relies on this...
The current text reveals that the Buddha’s father was able to cause [the Prince] to leave behind obscurations by enabling his renunciation and departure from secular life;
therefore, it concludes by stating that through renunciation, he lost his station. According to the *Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra*, however, this reveals the virtues of his grandfather and parents;
for that sūtra clarifies how his mother initially refused to release him, and his grandfather, the King, had to provide exhaustive exhortations to persuade her to let him go. This is...

This manifests his ancestry; that the Buddha transformed himself into a human and proclaimed a voice from mid-air, whereby [Rāhula] awakened to his past roots of goodness and relinquished [the throne], demonstrates the virtue of his parents.
Possessing these three meanings, yet because he is the *dharmakāya* (True Cause) Buddha, it is said to be the virtue of his father.

Regarding the "Golden Wheel," according to the *Nanshan Fopu*, all state that Rāhula corresponds to the rank of the Iron Wheel-turning King; this and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* [also support this].
The commentaries all state that the "Golden Wheel" (Suvarṇacakra) must refer to the different traditions within the sacred teachings, each employing the divine treasures according to its own source;
these are the Seven Treasures of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*): first, the Golden Wheel Treasure; second, the Elephant Treasure; third, the Horse Treasure; fourth, the Woman Treasure;
fifth, the Mani-Jewel Treasure; sixth, the Minister-Treasure of the Treasury; and seventh, the Minister-Treasure of the Military. These seven are the most precious and rare among human things.

Because they are supreme, they are all called "treasures" (*ratna*). As for the term "divine" (*śen*), it means "wondrous. Because their power and function are subtle, wondrous, and boundless, such that the world cannot fathom them, they are named "divine.
However, their essential form and the extent of their power and function are as widely described in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtras*.

Furthermore, there are other similar seven treasures which have not yet been fully detailed. Regarding the phrase "Buddha’s begging bowl" (*bō suǒ děng*) and so forth, the *Adbhutadharma Sūtra* states that the Buddha...
In the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden, he addressed Maudgalyāyana, instructing him to go to Kapilavastu to comfort Prince Yaśodharā and Rāhula.
"Rāhula is now nine years old; though mother and son have shared the joy of mutual affection, today they must suddenly part forever.
You may release Rāhula to become a śrāmaṇera. If he attains the Way, let him first deliver his mother. Maudgalyāyana received these instructions.
When the order reached the city of Kapilavastu, Yaśodharā heard it and took her son up to a high multi-storied pavilion, closing the doors and shutting the windows.

Maudgalyāyana, by means of his supernatural power, flew up onto the high pavilion and related the Buddha’s words in full. Having heard them, Yaśodharā felt deep resentment, thinking the Buddha lacked compassion;
she spoke most vehemently and refused to comply. When the father-king heard this, he was greatly astonished at her folly and thus sent Prasenajit to go and thoroughly explain the matter to her.

The metaphorical meaning is that she was unwilling to acknowledge the Buddha’s kindness, thereby severing the lineage of his succession. At that time, the Buddha immediately dispatched a manifested being who proclaimed from mid-air:
"When Śākyamuni Tathāgata was a bodhisattva, he purchased flowers to offer to Dīpaṃkara Buddha. You then made a vow, saying:
'In every life I am born into, may we be husband and wife; may our kingdoms, cities, men, women, and even my own person [be yours] in accordance with your wish.'"
"You have made a vow to give [your children] away without any stinginess; why do you now begrudge your son and not allow him to go forth?
When Yaśodharā heard this, she was suddenly enlightened and recalled her original vow. She took Rāhula and entrusted him to Maudgalyāyana.

This differs from the wording in the *Sūtra*; it is actually the text of the *Vinaya*. Because of these differences, the *Fǎngzhōng Lìdài Fǎbǎo Jì* by Sengyou of the Liang dynasty states: "The *Buddhapǔ* (Chronicle of the Buddhas) compiled by [the same author] harmonizes [these accounts]."

Yǒu specialized exclusively in the Vinaya and the scriptural matters; his approach differed from that of Xián because their respective dispositions were not the same, and thus both of their teachings have been preserved.

Although there are these differences, they secretly reveal how the Buddha Father’s great compassion provides the causes and conditions for removing the pleasures of worldly karmic retribution and bringing about the fruits of supramundane bliss. Below this, there are two sections concluding on the existence and non-existence [of these fruits].
This secretly reveals that they share the same task: to admonish them to eliminate the karma of falsehood and to perform the karma of truth.

For this reason, these two sections first present what exists and subsequently clarify its elimination. It is precisely for this purpose that the former contains a concluding summary while the latter does not.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When he was young, he did not yet know how to guard his speech; when someone came to ask whether the Buddha was present..."
He answered immediately: "It lies in the words, not in what is not in the words; it does not lie in the words so as to prevent others from obtaining the benefit of seeing and hearing.
Thus, he speaks of "delighting in much [speech]" and so forth. To obstruct others in this way is precisely what is called the karma of continuous delusion (*santāna-mṛṣāvāda*).

By citing that which is to be severed, the power that can sever it is secretly revealed. The Tathāgata acts as an obstacle-severer to cause them to cultivate the karma of true reality. From this point downward...
This is precisely what the Tathāgata warned against as an obstacle. Within this, there is the introduction, the main body, and the conclusion.

In the main body, there are both the facts and the words. Regarding the facts, although there are three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) and three types of concealment (*mrakṣa*), these manifest the extreme wickedness of the deluded act;
alternatively, they may also signify that one lacks the three benefits of hearing, reflecting, and meditating upon the Buddha-dharma.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites [the case of] Rāhula covering [the Buddha’s feet], yet it does not say he jumped over them three times; the commentary (*śū*) states that the "three" are unknown as to their source.

Now, I suggest there must be a separate source for this. As for the "knotting" (the binding of the feet), it should now be understood as an exhortation not to speak falsely—it is a warning against such.
Some say the meaning of this translation is that because of false speech, one obstructs oneself, and thus it is so named.

Regarding the phrase "as for 'obscuration' (*saṃvṛti*)," although it is not explicitly concluded in the text, its meaning is fully established. I maintain that you have failed to understand the intent of the passage and do not comprehend the meaning of "obscuration," which is why you have reached such a conclusion.
What was stated previously—that "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) refers to obstructing others—was intended to clarify that one is obstructing one's own path;

this current passage correctly clarifies that [the teaching] is called "obscuration" because it serves to remove those obstructions. How could this be a false interpretation? Please reflect upon this.
The eighth section following this [preceding] passage explains the "unifying thread" (*tongyuan*); it is the essential core among the ten meanings.
The preceding seven [sections] all constitute obstructions, as they obscure the Way by means of non-Ways;
therefore, this one [section] also constitutes an obstruction, for it severs the aforementioned non-Ways by relying upon the Way. The text consists of five phrases: first, the formal request; next...

This consists of five parts: first, the formal presentation; second, the threefold explanation; third, the exhortation; fourth, the conclusion and fulfillment; and fifth, the summary of the title. First is the reason for not obtaining [the teaching] as requested;

next is the question to the Buddha regarding the actual cause for not obtaining it, which—as previously stated—is due to the karmic obstruction of false speech, and because although he was taught true speech, his realization of true speech was not yet complete.
Because he strove diligently yet did not obtain it, he raised a request, to which the Buddha replied by instructing him to speak.
The Dharma is this correct teaching that brings its true words to fulfillment. Although what preceded was true speech, it was merely true regarding specific matters;

although what preceded was a prohibition against falsehood, it was merely correct regarding specific matters. Now, by relying entirely upon the principle of the Truths (satya), these are for the first time the words of reality concerning what is to be ceased and what is to be practiced.
These three encompass all dharmas; to speak of these three is to speak of all, and it is also to refute all.
"Because it is false, it possesses the meaning [of being deceptive]"—this explains the exhortation regarding the "gate. "Gate" has the meaning of "cause" and the meaning of "essential";
since it is both the cause for attainment and the essential, it must be explained. The phrase "if one desires," etc., exhorts that it must necessarily be explained.

Next, to clarify how one may achieve fulfillment through following [the teaching]: "How can one attain it? This is explained in the subsequent section of this sutra, which clarifies reliance upon the three dharmas.
To bring about great peace and happiness, for now we shall follow the general path, which possesses three essentials:
first, because of compassion; second, because of non-self; and third, because of repaying the Buddha’s kindness. Non-self is wisdom; compassion and repaying kindness are merit.

Because one can thereby accomplish wisdom and abandonment, one is able to attain the Way. This is the essential core of all faith. To conclude this: [The original Chinese text concludes with "結是為者" (concluding this as such), indicating the end of a section.]

The meaning contains two layers of subject and object; here, it concerns the subject and object as discussed in the context of the Path (mārga). From the seventh stage up to this point, these have all been severed;
because this is its subtle subjectivity, it is called "concealing and obstructing. This refers to the Path, which is the wisdom of the ultimate truth of the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
The next three meanings refer to the functional activity upon the very substance of the aforementioned eighth stage, and yet there is...
Second, some say it refers to the absence of both cause and effect; others say it refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Furthermore, the former may refer to "action" (*karman*), which is to say, karma; the latter refers to "vow" (*praṇidhāna*).

Since karma has been exhausted, even if there were prior vows, they could not give rise to rebirth, for in this teaching there is no rebirth through vow. This is because [the practitioner] possessed grave and solemn vows in previous lives. By reason of these...
Since these two do not exist upon the attainment of the Way, they are the power and function inherent within the essence itself;

that is, because they are able to eliminate both practice and vows, they are called "obscuring veils. For this reason, they constitute a single meaning in their entirety—reflect on this, reflect on this.
Regarding the final meaning: the obstruction of non-remainder manifests its non-abiding; the obstruction of wisdom-manifestation manifests compassion; the obstruction of its own [nature]...
The virtue manifests its benefit for others, while obstructing solitary thoughts so that they may repay their debt of gratitude;
because it contains these many meanings, the commentary states (at length). Regarding the four great arhats, as briefly explained previously, the Master says:

according to the seventh fascicle of the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*, the Buddha prophesied that sixteen arhats would uphold the Buddha-dharma until the appearance of a future Buddha, at which time they would enter parinirvāṇa; among them was Piṇḍola-bharadvāja.

Regarding these many kalpas, the names of Kāśyapa and others are not mentioned here; rather, one should now refer to the *Mahā-Ārya-Aṣṭadaśa-Ārya-Sthiti-Sūtra* (Great Record of the Abiding of the Dharma by the Eighteen Great Arhats) translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty, which extensively clarifies the names, retinues, dwelling places, and beneficial activities of the sixteen holy ones as commanded by the Buddha.
Although this [present text] mentions them, it has not yet provided a full account as detailed in that work.
The intention of these four points lies in Rāhula, being the first. Regarding the ten meanings mentioned above collectively termed "obscuration" (*paryavasthāna*):
to block, obstruct, and sever is the meaning of obscuration; to conceal so that nothing is known is the meaning of obscuration.

All [these] are manifested through profound secrecy, serving to obscure, block, and sever the ten types of non-path practices while giving rise to the ten types of path-practices; therefore, all ten are correctly named "obscurations."
Taking this sacred mystery as the core of his practice, the text below states that these secret practices can only be known by a Buddha; it is from this that he derives his name.
Thus, it is said that he is "concealed and shielded. Now, in order to discern the beginning and end of this matter, there are these ten points.
The reason he is able to act in such a way is due to his fundamental, profound, and weighty great vows, just as Ānanda previously derived his name from his own original vow. This is indeed so.
Why is he not called "Guhyaka" (the Secret Practitioner)? The name "Guhyaka" is used specifically to manifest the sense of universality.

Some explain that while for the previous twenty individuals the name "Guhyaka" refers solely to their conduct (*caryā*), for this one individual alone it refers solely to the meaning (*artha*) and does not concern his virtuous conduct;
this is because the sense of "concealment" (*āvṛti*) is not itself a virtuous quality. This is certainly not something that can be understood in a superficial manner.
To be able to know and penetrate that which is not the Path as being the Path is surely no easy matter! How could there be a son of the Buddha who lacks virtuous conduct?

Yet, when the teachings concerning the provisional and the fundamental, and the manifest and the trace, are condensed, how can one deal with the texts? The Sūtra says that his secret practices are foremost; how then can it be said that he has none?
The Sūtra says, "Only a Buddha can know this"—to believe otherwise would certainly be incorrect. To take poison for medicine is something only Jīvaka could do.
Is it not the case that by penetrating the non-path, one reveals the Buddha-path through what was previously concealed?

Thus, first, the karmic obstacles of others are manifested in their present retribution; those obstacles being secretly revealed, the causal relationship between good and evil is entirely fixed and cannot perish.

Second, his father’s ability to practice filial piety is secretly revealed, thereby obstructing unfilial conduct, while his own actions further reveal what is extraordinary compared to worldly customs.
The third [chapter] secretly reveals his father’s practice of filial piety, which obstructs worldly slander and transgressions;
it reveals how he was able to purify his moral virtue and sever the bonds of worldly affection.
The fourth [chapter] secretly reveals his mother’s extraordinary and chaste virtue, free from even the slightest flaw. These preceding sections manifest the virtues of his parents.
The fifth [point] reveals the power of the Buddha-father’s great compassion in secret:

by removing obstacles to worldly virtues, it manifests the happiness of karmic fruition in this life and serves as the cause for supramundane, supreme bliss. The sixth and seventh reveal the power of the Tathāgata’s great compassion in secret:
by removing obstacles to them, it eliminates the extremely grave fault of fabricating false speech through the karma of the mouth in this present life. Eighth.

The following ten points clearly manifest the Tathāgata’s power of great compassion, which causes one to sever the suffering of birth and death in the world and bestows upon them the bliss of supramundane nirvāṇa;

furthermore, they secretly reveal that the Buddha acts as a protector to remove their obstacles and eliminate their solitary anxieties, thereby making it manifest that one must guard [the teachings] to repay the Buddha’s kindness. How could these ten meanings not all be his secret practices? How could they be otherwise?
To say that one person alone has failed them—how could such a failure be so extreme? It is simply because they have not yet fully understood the meaning of "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*).
One should know that while there are eleven textual categories and ten names, in terms of substance there are only three, and in terms of intent there are only four.
The three are: the parents, and the Buddha’s great compassion. The four are the Fourfold Accomplishment (*caturvidha-sampad*), which were presented previously.
Each [of these] possesses the sense of both negation and affirmation. Regarding the essential meaning clarified herein, the *Jì* (Record/Commentary) states:
"The 'past world,' 'present world,' and 'ancestral joy'—these are mostly for the sake of persons (*pudgala*). The various objects of negation are mostly for the sake of counteracting [afflictions].
The subsequent attainment (*prsthalabdha*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Now, I say that the first one is the mundane world; it is general and worldly.

The second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth chapters clarify the virtues of the parents; through the power of the Buddha’s great compassion, they cause them to leave the household life, which is most excellent and beautiful.
Therefore, for the sake of human beings, the seventh and eighth chapters are dedicated exclusively to eliminating deluded karma and evil; thus, they serve as a direct antidote.

From the ninth chapter downward, since the principle and its application have both attained the essence of the Way, although their meaning includes the aspect of antidotes, they follow the preceding form.
These all belong to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), and since there is no contradiction in the sequence of their principles, one cannot claim that this is not so.
Furthermore, these four are secretly manifested; thus they are designated by these names. The commentary on this chapter is extremely extensive and has not yet been fully edited;

next, regarding the classification according to the teachings (*yāna*), the distinctions of benefit are subtle and wondrous, serving to reveal the meaning of how this sutra secretly manifests the Dharma. Based on this:
The meaning of what was previously explained as "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) can thus be understood. If it were not as previously explained, how would the text for these four obstacles be interpreted?

According to the traditional explanation, the word "obstacle" (*āvaraṇa*) should be placed beneath each of the words "abiding" (*sthiti*), and the word "removal" (*apanaya*) must be added above each of the four terms.
One should understand that the first two terms refer to the Truths (*satya*), while the latter two refer to Wisdom (*jñāna*).

They mutually acknowledge this; however, since the Truth of the Path takes the three—precept, concentration, and wisdom—as its essence, this is the meaning of "pervasive" (*tong*), which follows the convenience of the principle.

Regarding the three types of knowledge (*trividya*)—namely, the knowledge of all [phenomena] (*sarvajñā*) and so forth—they also correspond to the true, the conventional, and the middle; and to the empty, the provisional, and the middle. As for the five types of destruction:

conventionally, both [the true and conventional] together destroy ignorance; conventionally, they destroy the "dust-sand" [afflictions], which are the coarse ignorance that deludes regarding phenomena; and the middle [knowledge] destroys...
This refers to those who obstruct the principle of the subtle.
Although one who clarifies the fundamental and the manifested has already realized the Perfect [Teaching], this is merely the trace-manifestation of a single lifetime.

Because it was attained long ago, when discussing its fundamental basis, one considers what dharma it originally abides in that allows it to manifest such traces. Regarding the duration of these manifestations—whether long or short—the text provides only a brief explanation thereof.
The Dharma does not speak of time or seasons; it abides in the three fundamental wisdoms while manifesting ten traces. The text consists of five phrases:

the first clarifies the fundamental essence, and the subsequent four clarify the fundamental function, with the traces contained therein. "Middle" refers to the Middle Way of All-Seed Wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*);
this is the absolute, non-relative middle, which is the essence of the fundamental. This is also understood by way of the traces. This is the designation of the fundamental essence.
"Furthermore, it obstructs and blocks the two extremes. The following clarifies the fundamental function (*mūla-vṛtti*) of the text, which consists of four phrases.

The first is the thesis (*uddiṣṭa*), and the subsequent three are the explanation (*nirdeśa*). This first phrase explains the essence (*svabhāva*) while also serving as the thesis for the function (*vṛtti*).

Why is this so? It is said: "Neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa. This explains the aforementioned characteristic of the essence. If one says that it can [function] with respect to both, that is the meaning of "function"; thus, this single phrase [serves both purposes].
"Identity-in-essence and identity-in-function"—these two meanings of "identity" (ji) refer to the two obstacles that block and obstruct;

these two sides are what is blocked, as indicated by the latter two meanings below. The subsequent explanation has three parts, yet although there are three, they are merely the meaning of the two sides, still relying on the ten previous meanings to manifest these three kinds of "identity," which correspond to what preceded.
The first eight [of the ten] are these; all say that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) can act as an obstruction, preventing one from entering *nirvāṇa*.
This interpretation is not only inconsistent with the present text, it is also impossible to reconcile with the various preceding meanings.

Now, I maintain that the eight kinds are the obstructing dharmas, while *nirvāṇa* is that which is obstructed. These eight capacities are precisely the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), which constantly abides within the world.
Because benefiting and bringing joy to sentient beings differs from the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) who abide in nirvāṇa, it is said that [the latter] constitutes an obstruction;
herein, the two meanings of "concealing" (*bì*) and "blocking" (*sè*) are implicitly revealed. One type is the "capable dharma," which refers to true wisdom (*tathatājñāna*);
this combines the preceding ninety-two items into one, namely the ninth. Birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is the "object obstructed," which refers to the fundamental nature.

By means of true wisdom, one cuts off all birth and death and attains mastery; this differs from ordinary people who, being attached and fettered, lack such mastery—therefore, it is called an "obstruction.
Within this, there are both the meanings of negation and affirmation. Next, regarding the third meaning:
one type is a faculty that is not an obstruction, while those below are what are fettered. Furthermore, as for one type of faculty, it may be [the faculty of] vision.
To claim that being "neither" constitutes the "Middle Way" is incorrect. This refers to the dual application of the essence, not merely the essence itself;
it specifically denotes the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional, which are employed together to maintain the long endurance of the Dharma.

Because they differ from other śrāvakas, they are not burdened by worldly ties and have attained mastery; because they differ from ordinary beings, they employ both [wisdoms]. This dual application is precisely the tenth [ground].
The passage below clarifies that which is "in the middle. First, it distinguishes this from the previous two types of birth-and-death;

the ninth corresponds to *nirvāṇa*, which refers to the aforementioned eighth *nirvāṇa*—namely, *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. The obstacle to *nirupadhiśeṇa-nirvāṇa* is precisely what reveals the object [of the teaching].

Furthermore, regarding the "trace," it means that he was commanded to remain in the world for a time to protect the Buddha-dharma and await the appearance of a future Buddha, rather than immediately extinguishing his physical body; thus it is so called.
There are no remaining obstructions; however, while the preceding [section] clarifies their mutual dependence (*pratītyasamutpāda*), this passage elucidates their mutual identity (*samasattva*).

Reflect upon this—reflect upon it! This very point contains within it the two meanings of negation and manifestation. Regarding the previous discussion of essence and function, as well as time and duration:
since the aforementioned text establishes him as the eldest son of all past Buddhas, he is certainly not "near"; furthermore, it can be known because only a Buddha can know it.
This text does not state what the "traces" (ji) are; it merely proceeds from the eight kinds below to clarify those traces.

Although this heading is established, its meaning has not yet been clearly explained, and thus it remains difficult to comprehend. Furthermore, there are several points where the phrasing and meaning contradict what was stated previously.

I maintain that in the preceding enumeration, one first establishes the essence and the function before clarifying the traces; here, however, the discussion is directly situated within the traces themselves.
The ten meanings manifest the fundamental function; this very fundamental function, in turn, reveals the provisional traces. Thus, by explaining one meaning, both are simultaneously clarified.
What could be more concise and elegant than this? Why add anything further?

In the *Guan* (Contemplation), the statement follows the precedent of the previous section; however, when seeking such precedents from both near and far, none exist except for the Perfect Wisdom (*yuan-zhi*) within the Provisional Teaching (*jiao*).

Thus, it refers solely to that. Regarding the meaning of "contemplative wisdom" (*guan-zhi*), there are both general and specific senses; here we follow the general sense, and therefore it can be understood by analogy:
by practicing the three contemplations within a single mind alone, one is able to manifest the virtues of the three wisdoms and eliminate the faults of the five abodes of obstruction.
All these points must be understood through six meanings; if one can do so, how could the ten kinds of esoteric applications be far off?
Next, the explanation of the concluding chapter: thus, in total, twenty-one items have been briefly listed to point toward them.
"Known by all" indicates the manifestation of his virtues in general. The word "etc. includes other extensive details not listed here, which number approximately twelve thousand.
In this passage, the term "equal" (*sama*) is placed above [the word "assembly"] because its meaning of virtue extends broadly.

"Assembly" (*gaṇa*) refers to those who possess knowledge—namely, the Arhats and others—who are the objects of that knowledge. The text merely explains the two characters for "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and does not analyze the person who possesses that knowledge;
however, since "assembly" implies a multitude, it is superior to the three aforementioned categories of persons, as explained previously regarding "greatness."

Since this has already been explained within the commentary on the definitions of the terms, it will not be discussed further here. All the various schools cite the explanation from the *Mūla-śāstra* regarding this point, stating:
"First, those known by the assemblies of human kings and celestial kings; second, those known by the assemblies of noble ones, such as śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.
Recently, someone has remarked: "The first interpretation refers to being known by assemblies of both the noble and the humble, while the latter interpretation refers to the Great [Assembly]."
"Known by the minor assembly of holy ones"—this concludes the meaning of "known by the assembly. Regarding the two characters *jñāna* (knowledge/awareness), are they identical or different?
If there are two meanings, what are their characteristics? The text explains that they possess both meanings. As for their identity, the two characters form a single compound with but one meaning;
below, its twofold distinction is explained as being through hearing-and-seeing (*śruta-dṛṣṭa*) and through physical form (*rūpa*).
Regarding the mind (*citta*): first, it refers to both self and others; second, it refers only to the self. This is the distinction based on the internal and external, or the coarse and the subtle.

As the aforementioned school cited from the treatise, first the various interpretations clarify the meaning of "knowing" (*jñāna*), and subsequently they clarify the meaning of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
This is the distinction between knowing being shallow and consciousness being deep; therefore, that [treatise] does not separately explain the meaning of consciousness. Some say:

To know their inner virtues while recognizing their outward forms; furthermore, to know those who are distant while recognizing those who are near—there are four permutations regarding "knowing" and "recognizing.
These three explanations are as follows: the first involves knowing what is deep while recognizing what is shallow; the second involves knowing what is coarse while recognizing what is subtle;
and the third set of four permutations should be understood by applying the meanings of the preceding two cases. This is the sense.
Since the middle [section] involves causes and conditions, it should likewise possess the fourfold explanation (*catuḥ-prakāra-vyākhyā*).
It is not said here that the two sets of four meanings within the text need not be sought far away; rather, they constitute the most immediate and mundane phenomena of the world.

Having heard its name and further personally beheld the form of the Sage, one immediately gives rise to faith and reverence; this is what is meant by "seeing the person" through their physical appearance.
One immediately knows that there is virtue and no fault, just as when Śāriputra saw Aśvajit and immediately sighed in admiration and submission;
thus, it serves as an antidote for the minds of noble ones, allowing them to rest in the true path. Therefore, the four intentions of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) are clarified.

As for those who do not rely on the teachings, the knowledge of the four types of capacities and conditions constitutes four distinct categories; this principle appears frequently throughout the preceding and following sections and may be applied by analogy.

Because this is already understood, it is omitted here. Regarding "root and trace" (*honjaku*): it is simply because his virtue is perfectly complete and he is capable of acting as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for all beings;
because he is known by ordinary people, sages, and great men, this explanation is necessary. One should reflect well upon these words.

"The full letter" (*manji*) refers to the perfection of the essential substance; the "root" is so called because it is the self-realization actually attained, while the "trace" is so called because it manifests that realization.

The reason it is said that "half" [of the text] is thus is because both the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku) aspects pervade the four and five stages; the wording follows a concise, alternating style, and for this reason it is stated here.

To cause one to know this meaning, the original commentary states (*etc.*). Regarding the practice of contemplation (*kan-gyō*), as previously briefly cited and explained from the *Shōyō*, to put it succinctly:
if one can skillfully penetrate the single mind and the three truths, such a knowledge and vision—which exhausts principle and exhausts nature—is precisely true and good knowing.
One who understands this has reached the ultimate limit for both self and others; how much more so for those on the stages prior to the grounds, let alone those following other teachings?

The subsequent explanation of the various texts concerning "slight understanding" is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the headings and the display of the text; second, the explanation of the headings and the explanation of the text. First, [the presentation]:
This is the second category among the monks. Below is the explanation of the preceding two [categories], which consists of two distinct parts:

first, explaining the establishment of this title and its meaning according to the structural divisions (*ko-chang*); second, providing a general explanation of the intent of both chapters based on their essence (*ti*) and function (*yung*).

Regarding the first part, as for why it is called "Lesser Knowledge" (*shao-shi*) based on its specific meaning: because it is contrasted with what precedes it, there are six [points] that precede it.
The meanings of these four names are most prominent; therefore, they are called "many" (*bahu*).
Now, because these two forms precede the "many," they are called "few" (*alpa*). Since there are only these two, the other four are omitted.
Why, then, does it only say "not praising virtue"? Although the text omits the other four, stating only "not praising virtue" is the most essential point. Now, I maintain that this alone...
A single phrase encompasses four meanings. Why? Because within the category [of "great"], the term "Great" is first cited;

then, by mentioning "non-arising" and the other six [perfections], the concluding text itself makes it manifest. Thus, all four possess the sense of praising their virtues. It is clear that one phrase encompasses four meanings;
for the sake of clarifying this point, these words were spoken. For this reason, the former [section] is extensive while this is concise.

If the preceding section primarily describes those who are "beyond training" (aśaikṣa), why is the name "learner" (śaikṣa) established here? Why not establish the name "learner" for the preceding section and the name "beyond training" for this section?
To a certain extent, there is indeed such a principle; therefore, since ancient times, several schools have likewise established these names.

However, as the meaning of these names is insufficient to be praised and they do not represent the refined style of exegesis, they are not adopted here. This concludes the first division of the chapter.
The brief explanation of the "abiding" has already been completed above.

This section clarifies how the two chapters relate to one another to establish their positions; the following section provides a comprehensive explanation based on essence and function to clarify the intent behind the naming of the two chapters.
Within this, first it is clarified that the self-essence is non-dual, and second it is clarified that because of its functional utility, there are two. Subsequently...

The concluding exhortation clarifies that its essence and function are boundless and cannot be fixed by adhering to its name; otherwise, one loses its fundamental substance. The first two phrases clarify this:
the upper phrase correctly demonstrates that its essence is boundless. To "sever ties" (juejiao), one must first have had ties before discussing severance;
this means that initially their wills were identical and their voices in harmony, with no interval whatsoever—this is called "tying. Later, because circumstances arose...
To cause estrangement and abandonment is what is called severing [a relationship]. For this reason, there exist compositions in the world titled "Severed Friendships" (*jiejiao*).

However, the Sage takes only the Dao as his position, while ordinary people take only their emotions as their position. Thus, from the very beginning, no such friendship ever truly existed; so what is there to discuss regarding its severance?
Yet, when one speaks of "severed friendships," there are two meanings: first, that while their natures are identical, their cultivation differs; second, that their natures...

Because they are the same, it is said that they "interact" (*jiao*); because they are different, it is said that they are "severed" (*jue*). It is precisely because of this identity and difference that they are said to be severed yet interacting.
Thus, the Confucians say, "Natures are similar; habits differ. This statement is indeed close to the truth.

These two [terms] directly express that the realized essence of the sage and the unrefined state of the ordinary person are fundamentally different; therefore, it is said they are "severed," not that they first interact and then...
Later, when [the connection] is severed, it is called "severed friendship"; furthermore, although this term encompasses two meanings, its intended sense lies precisely in the second meaning.
This clarifies that the sages are not subject to the measure of quantity or number; because they are ordinary in terms of numerical quantity, there are two [categories].

This clarifies that both assemblies are equally sages, as their essential nature is entirely uniform. How do we know this is so? Because they equally receive the provisional and the real, and likewise...
To reveal that they are of the same class as the Buddha’s disciples and sons, receiving the same prediction and attaining Buddhahood at the same time—how could this be a trivial matter?
Thus, their equality is evident. Since both their essence and virtue are equal, their function is necessarily identical.
Because both essence and function are equally balanced, it is impossible to speak of them in terms of more or less.
It is specifically for this reason that the origins of these two names—“High” (gāo) and “Far” (yuǎn)—are explained; they are derived precisely from these two meanings.
“High” refers to one’s own practice (*sva-caryā*), as one seeks upward toward Buddhahood; thus it is called “high.

“Far” refers to benefiting others (*parārtha*), as one transforms sentient beings downward throughout the bounds of the future; thus it is called “far. “Specifically” (tè) means “only” (dàn). “For” (yǐ) means...
Regarding the phrase "to lead" (*yin*): this refers to those who preside over the world, namely human beings. Furthermore, the term "by means of" (*yi*) signifies "using.
This specifically means that because such a class of people are particularly fond of [learning], one uses words of extensive knowledge to lead them;
therefore, they are listed first. Moreover, for another distinct class of people, one uses words of limited knowledge to lead them.
Because he was brought forth [to this position], he is listed in the sequence; that is, within this text, it is not said that he has "vast knowledge" (*bahuśruta*).

Because his name is kept in concealment, his name is not listed; because his virtues are hidden, his virtues are not extolled; and because he practices humility and deference, he is placed at the end of the list. Thus, the designations of "many" and "few" arise naturally from him;
they do not pertain to the actual substance of the Sage. Therefore, the conclusion states "in accordance with," etc. "Several" (*jiǎnrúan*) refers to what was mentioned above.
Second, as for "it is not permissible to equate them": it is not permissible because clinging to names results in losing the reality.

Zhuangzi said, "The sage has no name"; if this is so even for him, how much more so for this case? Regarding "traces and the fundamental," these refer to the provisional and the real, essence and function, name and reality, and also to the long and the near.
This meaning precisely clarifies that while both essence and virtue are complete, the function is expressed through names alone; it relies directly upon this.

Regarding the second name, there are various interpretations: "Liberation" (*śāstra*), "Elevating," "Transcending Loss," "Pervasive," "Perfect," "Way," and "Reaching the Unrestricted. Only when one reaches this state of being unrestricted can it be considered exhaustive.
Although various interpretations provide diverse titles, if they do not cultivate the perfectly luminous Way (*pariniṣpanna-mārga*), they have not reached the ultimate excellence.

This clarifies that if one wishes to grasp the essential meaning, one must accord with the world; thus, there are various [teachings] to suit the dispositions of beings within the world. Since these already accord with them...
That each clan is able to give rise to past goodness is what constitutes being human; that each is able to reform their unwholesomeness is the application of antidotes;
and through awakening to the essence of equality, one reaches the primary meaning (paramārtha).

The above concludes the general discussion on the intent of establishing the chapters; what follows is the specific analysis of the text. Regarding the structural divisions of the text, there are two distinct parts.

First, concerning the analysis by way of stages (*sthāna*), the reasons for not analyzing by way of causes and conditions have already been fully explained in the commentary on the title of the subsequent chapter;
as we do not wish to burden the reader with redundant text, they are not analyzed here. Within this section, there are two parts: first, a direct and concise explanation of the two phrases.

Following this passage, the text extensively clarifies the meaning of the five phrases. Within the first four categories, each must comprise three aspects: essence (*tattva*), meaning (*artha*), and position (*sthāna*).
In the current text, the first [category] merely presents the essence, while the subsequent three merely clarify the positions; the meanings are not explained, as they have been mutually abbreviated.
The *Madhyama Āgama* records that a householder asked the Buddha: "How many kinds of fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) are there? The Buddha [replied].

It is said that there are eighteen types of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and nine types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding the eighteen types of those in training: they are the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the one liberated by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), the one attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), the body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*), the one who goes from family to family (*kulaṃkula*), the one with only one interval (*ekavīcika*), the candidate for the first fruit (*srotāpattipratipannaka*), the one established in the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), the candidate for the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*), the one established in the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the candidate for the third fruit (*anāgāmipratipannaka*), the one established in the third fruit (*anāgāmin*), and the five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*):

namely, the one reborn in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), the one reborn upon arrival (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), the one who attains nirvana with effort (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), the one who attains nirvana without effort (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), and the one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*). As for the nine types of those beyond training, they are as follows: [the Arhat who attains nirvana] in this very life, upon rebirth, with effort, without effort, in the intermediate state, upon arrival, with effort, without effort, and the one who flows upwards.

This refers to those who possess the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), application (*prasthāna*), non-retrogression (*anivartana*), immovability (*aniñjya*), abiding (*sthiti*), and protection (*ārakṣā*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Those who possess the wisdom of retrogression, protection, abiding, reflection, death, non-retrogression, and non-destruction are persons of unbreakable dharma (*abhedyadharman*). This constitutes their essential nature.

Regarding the various commentaries on those who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they are all agreed that these refer to those who have attained the fourth fruit. As for the explanation of those still in training (*śaikṣa*), there are two views: first, some say that those who have attained the three fruits are persons in training.
Second, the seven types are designated as those in training (*śaikṣa*), namely the three fruits and the four candidates.

If one says that the three fruits belong specifically to the true sages (*ārya*), and if one says that the seven types pertain generally to the stage of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*), this present explanation is made in accordance with that sutra;

it is said thus because both of these two types of persons are included within the Middle Way. However, these [distinctions] are all made in reference to the persons who are capable of training. If...

Regarding the dharmas to be studied, their essence consists of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). However, because practice has not yet reached its ultimate limit, they are designated as "learning" (*śaikṣa*) and "no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣa*).

The explanation provided above encompasses both the meaning of the essence and the stages (*bhūmi*). As for the meaning of the names [of the stages], it is as explained later in the section on the "Chapter on Names.
Within the "Common" (*sāmānya*) category, there are two layers, both of which are defined according to the stages (*bhūmi*); this is because this teaching primarily focuses upon the stages.

The "Ten Grounds" (*daśabhūmi*) clarify their respective stages. Regarding why they are explained in two layers, the Master said: the first is based on the Two Vehicles, while the latter is based on the Bodhisattvas;

furthermore, the former concerns the common stages shared by the Three Vehicles, whereas the latter concerns the exclusive stages of the Bodhisattvas alone. Moreover, the sixth ground is named the "Ground of Freedom from Desire" (*vītarāgabhūmi*), which corresponds only to the level of the *anāgāmin* fruit;
it is only upon reaching the seventh, the "Ground of Having Accomplished What Was to Be Done" (*kṛtāvibhūmi*), that one becomes a person beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
A commentator explains this as being based on the correspondence between the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the ten perfections (*pāramitā*);

it is claimed that upon reaching the sixth stage, wisdom (*prajñā*) is perfected and thus becomes equal to an Arhat, which is why it is called "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). However, I fear this is not the case.

Since there is no doctrine of a general correspondence between the ten stages and the ten perfections, it is possible that the characters "five" and "six" are errors in transcription and should instead be read as "six" and "seven."

If an Anāgāmin attains realization upon reaching that [stage], they are subsumed under the "candidate" (pratipannaka) category; the remaining intentions are not yet detailed. The ninth is named the Bodhisattva, and the tenth is named the Buddha;

the two meanings are self-evident according to their names and do not require further explanation. Others say that from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) downward, there is effortful practice (*sābhisamskāra*), which constitutes the state of training (*śaikṣa*);
from the eighth stage upward, there is effortless practice (*anabhisamskāra*), which constitutes the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). This is a distinction.
Regarding the meaning: if we take the present "perfect meaning" (yuan-yi), from the first stage (chuzhu) upward, one is already beyond effortful application (wugongyong).
As for "possessing" and "not possessing," both teachings are encompassed within the two stages of Equality (deng) and Subtlety (miao).
From the *Āgama* downward, the first two phrases are self-evident; they inherently contain the remaining three phrases, thus completing five phrases in total.
Regarding the meaning within this, there are four parts: first, explaining the third phrase by reference to other sutras; second, illustrating the fourth phrase by citing sutra passages;
third, clarifying the fifth phrase in contrast to the preceding four; and fourth, applying the fifth and fourth phrases across the four teachings to demonstrate their twenty phrases.
This explains that because the textual structure and numerical progression of the sutra naturally give rise to these various meanings, [the author] first cites [other scriptures].
The Sūtra asks: "Is he one who trains (śaikṣa) or not? If he trains, then he is a person in training; why then is he called "one beyond training" (aśaikṣa)?
If he does not train, for what reason does he constantly follow a teacher? The Buddha’s intended answer clarifies that while he is indeed one in training, he differs from [ordinary] learners.
This single response answers both questions and simultaneously distinguishes him from the two simple categories; thus, it constitutes the third alternative. Some people hold this view.

"Cloud" refers to the dharmas to be practiced within the fruits of training (*śaikṣa-phala*); for example, a person liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*) further cultivates the cessation-of-perception-and-feeling samādhi (*nirodha-samāpatti*), while a person doubly liberated (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*) enters only the various untainted dhyānas such as the "leap-over" (*vyutkrāntaka*).
