Now, the text says:

"Not committing evil, abiding in the good"—this clearly indicates the abandonment through wisdom (*prajñā-prahāṇa*). "Perfect" (*yuan*) refers to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who act spontaneously to assist the Buddha in benefiting others.
Because one studies for the sake of repaying the Buddha’s kindness, it is called "study"; it does not mean that what is termed "study" refers merely to the act of cultivation.

Therefore, this is "studying while being beyond study. If such is the case, this passage from the Sūtra clarifies the four propositions—introduction, explanation, conclusion, and so forth—which are easy to understand.

Below this, in contrast to the preceding, the fifth proposition is revealed; the first four all pertain to the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*), whereas the preceding [stage] opens up the stage of the worthy ones (*śaikṣa*).

Since the status [of the practitioner] is not among the four noble ones, it spontaneously constitutes the fifth category. The third [category] is derived from the Sūtra’s section on the "Non-learner" (aśaikṣa);
the fourth is derived from the Sūtra’s section on the "Learner" (śaikṣa); and the fifth is established in contrast to the preceding four noble ones.
Thus, it is clearly shown that twenty categories are not limited to the four vehicles alone. Why would this meaning not be fully present? It can be seen in various commentaries.

By this analogy, one should know that there is no leisure for a full textual exposition; however, when it comes to this sutra, which consists solely of the five phrases of the Single Wonderful [Vehicle], one must not exclusively follow the literal text to construct analytical distinctions.

Next, regarding the "Original" (hon) and the "Trace" (seki): the term "Original" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which distinguishes itself from the birth-body (*janmakāya*) that is not the Dharma, and further distinguishes itself from the Small [Vehicle].

"Half" refers to the affairs of one who is "full," for in worldly convention, serving those above is called "attending. Now, taking the Great Way as the business of oneself and others is what is meant here.
Furthermore, the Confucians say: "The scholar (*shi*) is clarity; distinguishing right from wrong and knowing principle and duty is called being a scholar.
One is the beginning of numbers, and ten is the end of numbers; having heard of the beginning, one knows [the end].
In the end, they are called "Śrāvakas" (Sō); thus, the character for "Śrāvaka" (Sō) is composed of the numerals ten and one.

Now, these people all, by means of this very cause, know the ultimate fruit; therefore, they are called "Mahāsattvas" (Daisō). The "full" character (Manji) signifies that it opens up and encompasses the "half" (the Śrāvaka level).

Do not interpret this as a mere correspondence between opposites, for this is because [the Bodhisattva] has truly attained it through their own practice, whereas sentient beings [perceive it] through the manifestation of traces.

Regarding the two aspects of the twin trees—withering and flourishing—as well as that which lies between them: first, the four withered branches are adorned; next, those same four withered branches are used to adorn the four flourishing ones;

finally, the space between them is adorned. It is not without the withered that the flourishing can be manifested; thus, the withering is presented first. It is not without the flourishing that the withering can be rejected;
thus, the flourishing is explained next. It is not without both the withering and the flourishing that the intermediate state can be manifested; thus, they are treated in this sequence.
The "neither" [of the two extremes] refers to neither decay nor flourishing; "decay" refers to impermanence and so forth, which refutes the world’s false conceptualization of permanence and so forth;

"flourishing" refers to the permanence and so forth of the supramundane, which refutes the supramundane notion of impermanence and so forth; and "the middle" refers to that which is neither permanent nor impermanent, which expresses the realization of the Middle Way.

The Buddha's work reaches its ultimate here. This is because, starting from the fulfillment [of the full teaching], it provides a partial opening and a partial manifestation [of the half-teaching], thereby bringing the great matter to completion.
This refers to the adornment of the twin trees.

Although there were five phrases in the previous contemplation, they were merely for the sake of the argument; now, in this contemplation, we shall rely on the literal text and thus there are only two.
"Not taking the two extremes as objects" means that all things are entirely the Middle, with no further extremes remaining; what, then, could be taken as an object? This is called "naturalness."
Because the middle is boundless, it is incapable; because all are compliant, this is the study. Since this is an observation of the object, it is "study";

since the *Śaikṣa-aśaikṣa-sūtra* follows the convenience of the terminology, "study" comes first; now, following the convenience of the meaning, "non-study" (*aśaikṣa*) comes first. The three preceding sections conclude the textual explanation of the meaning of the stages.

"Contemplate this; contemplate this. As for 'the trace is identical' (*jì jí děng*), here the primary intent is an explanation based on contemplation (*guān*), yet it is used metaphorically to clarify the fundamental (*běn*).

Next, regarding the reason why the *bhikṣuṇī* community is mentioned after the *bhikṣu* community, there have been many ancient expositions and analyses;

I shall briefly clarify them here as they have already been addressed previously, so I cannot elaborate further now. First, I shall refute the errors of the old scholastic divisions, and thereafter provide the correct interpretation.
At the beginning of this section, the two "non-[monks]" are first refuted individually, and subsequently both are demonstrated together to clarify their non-monk status.

At the outset, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are refuted, followed by the refutation of the "many" and the "few. The initial example follows the previous discussion on the Mahāyāna, which is here termed "Hīnayāna"; it was Master Jiaxiang who coined this name.

As for the term "not used," it lacks scriptural authority and contradicts the meaning; since the definitions of Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna established by the preceding monks are untenable, this [designation] is certainly not [valid].
It may be argued that one need not rely on what was previously clarified, or take the preceding as an analogy for determining "many" or "few. This too is incorrect;
for while there were six passages at the beginning of the prior section, all of which contained multiple meanings, those subsequent passages can be analogized by way of meaning.

However, since there is no such text in the preceding part and no such meaning in the subsequent part to serve as an analogy, it is said that "meaning is also untenable," because the subsequent passages all contain the designation "great sound" (mahā-śabda).

This passage generally clarifies the present intention and critiques the two previous errors. Since the former *saṃgha* already had two establishments with two names, and the present *bhikṣuṇī* community likewise has two assemblies, if one does not permit [the use of these], what could serve as the title? This is now explained, hence it says, "It is simply," and so forth.
These two individuals serve as the primary teachers for this transformation; it is sufficient to rely directly on the text itself.
There is no need to further contrive a separate title, which is why it says, "Why is it necessary," and so forth.
Next, regarding the sequence of these two in the actual explanation, the ancient commentators state: "In the mundane world, there is the distinction between mother and wife;

in the Path, there is the distinction between those born earlier and those born later. This constitutes their order. Although within this [text], the first two names are translated... [the passage continues].
Do not take the following passage. Previous scholars all translated it in this same way, yet none provided an explanation of its meaning;
thus, it remains unknown what the original name was. Furthermore, if one were to become a renunciant later on, the meaning would be easy to understand.
If the new translation says *mahā-bhārājapatnī*, this means "Great Mistress of Beings. This is originally the name of the Brahma King, as all sentient beings...
Born from her and having received [the name] from her as its cause, it was used as a name; because the traditional way of speaking had not been precise, this discrepancy arose.
The correct name should perhaps be *Mahāmāyā*, which means "Great Illusion" (*mahāmāyā*) or "Great Artifice" (*mahāmāyā*); that is, she dwelt in the dharma of great illusory artifice.

This is the Buddha’s maternal aunt. Her mother was the Buddha; [she is] *Mahāmāyā*, which here is translated as "Great Artifice" (*mahāmāyā*) or "Great Illusion" (*mahāmāyā*), meaning she abided in the dharma of great illusory artifice.

At the gate stood a great and wondrous attendant, as described in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, who was one among the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) encountered by Sudhana.
Regarding Gautamī—newly transliterated as Kautama or also as Jotama—this likely refers to her family name;
she is thus the same person as the previously mentioned Gotamī. Therefore, when outsiders address the Buddha in the sūtras, they most frequently do so using this [surname].

The statement "it is thus its nature" clarifies four essentials herein: first, "love" (愛) refers to aspiration and desire, which constitutes the worldly aspect; second, "enabling others to love" constitutes the human aspect;

third, "governing sentient beings" and "governing things" constitute the aspect of subduing non-ways by removing them so that they may awaken to the right path; fourth, "governing meaning" (治義) is the second [essential].

This intention signifies that the great task has been fully accomplished. As for the phrase "redeeming one's life," it refers to entering extinction after having finished preaching the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

The application of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury is likewise so: for the sake of future evil bhikṣus who store impure things and preach to the fourfold assembly that the Tathāgata has ultimately entered parinirvāṇa, and who study worldly treatises while showing no reverence for the Buddha’s sūtras—

if one preaches this sutra to extensively clarify the Buddha-nature, extensively refute impermanence, and clarify that the Buddha is eternally abiding, this redeems the Buddha-Dharma.
The body is the life-force of wisdom; the Vinaya extensively elucidates the precepts that destroy all evil dharmas, enabling those in the final age to abandon what is wrong and follow what is good.
That it causes the Buddha to abide long and not perish quickly is what redeems the life-span of the Buddha-dharma.
Thus, the statement that "the Piṭaka of Vinaya is the life-span of the Buddha-dharma" and so forth conveys this very meaning. This clarifies the significance of the two forms of redemption.
As previously cited from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, these two meanings are fully present; this is the essential point.

First, two thousand [Buddhas] are mentioned; throughout the three periods, they are all the same as those mentioned later.
This clarifies that the final Buddha is like this, and by this analogy, all twenty thousand are likewise so. Therefore, it says "thus" (*er*). This is from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
It is said that during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, sentient beings had very slight craving and abundant wisdom;
the bodhisattvas possessed great majestic power, and the world was pure. All sentient beings knew that the Tathāgata does not undergo ultimate extinction, but dwells eternally and remains unchanging.
Although such scriptures existed, there was no need to expound them. Since it is said that he did not preach [the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*], then [nirvāṇa] is—
Because the ultimate meaning of the Lotus Sūtra’s teaching of transformation penetrates both gates, this [section] establishes what precedes and initiates what follows;

it requires the distinction between the "original" and the "traced" (honji-suijaku) to clarify that the great matter of the single transformation is fully exhausted in this sūtra. Of the three phrases, the first pair designates the teacher and disciple, while the subsequent two phrases cite the sūtra to provide proof and explanation; these are easily understood from the text itself.
With this, the third section concludes by demonstrating the circumstances of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). "With this" refers collectively to the preceding eight and three [sections].
The *dharmakāya* is the very essence of the *Śūraṅgama*; it is that which bends its shadow to manifest traces and arises in response according to conditions.

As for those traces appearing, they pervade all places where there are sentient beings with whom one has a connection—both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), comprising the two assemblies of bhikṣus mentioned previously.
"Male" refers to the two groups of monks mentioned above; "female" refers to the two groups of nuns mentioned next; "clergy" (dao) refers to the aforementioned monks and nuns;

and "laypeople" (su) refers to the two groups of laymen and laywomen mentioned above. According to the underlying principle, the two groups of laymen and laywomen should follow the two groups of clergy;
although the text places them later within the section on miscellaneous assemblies, the meaning remains consistent [with this order].
For this reason, the sūtra is constantly referred to as being for the fourfold assembly of śrāvakas; it is precisely these four assemblies of śrāvakas who are praised in this sūtra.
It would certainly be inconsistent to now take them as referring to other sūtras. Those who study later must reflect upon this with care.

Regarding the phrase "the first *Lengyan* [Sūtra]," etc., this cites the previously mentioned extensive and remote skillful means; regarding the phrase "etc.," this concludes the preceding matters of provisional, near, and expedient teachings. One discusses from the perspective of the near.
The general characteristics are briefly as follows. Regarding the note (云云), there is an underlying intention as clarified above.
Next, the section on the general explanation of the contemplation has two parts: first, clarifying the purpose of its introduction; second, the actual explanation of the contemplation.

As for the first part, although it was already explained previously, it is explained again here because the previous explanation was made in contrast to specific cases, whereas this present explanation is made in contrast to the application of the fruits already attained.

How does this differ from what was previously explained regarding the beginning-mind practitioners of the final age? Later, in the general discussion of the entire work, this section specifically addresses the assembly of *śrāvakas*;

you should understand this well and not confuse it with other points. As for that which is said to be performed by the *dharmakāya*, this refers entirely to the manifestation of function (*vṛtti*) by one who has already attained the *dharmakāya*—that is precisely what was previously termed "original" and "traces. If one does not clarify the cultivation of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), [the distinction will remain obscured].
As previously stated, if such wondrous functions do not provide benefit to the practitioner, two analogies are presented below:
the first analogy illustrates the lack of benefit from one's own merit, and the second illustrates the lack of benefit from wisdom. For this reason, it is necessary to further clarify contemplation.

However, in the section on "The Mind and Mental Factors" (*citta-caitta*), the text clearly elucidates contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Some say: "How can a person who possesses a mind be separated from mental factors?
Therefore, by attaching this to the Buddha’s transformative ritual, it reveals how [the practice] assists and accomplishes benefit.

As for settling the mind within the objects of consciousness, this is a topic particularly subject to debate; one should skillfully apply the meaning found in the various teachings on the contemplation of mental factors to this context.

Regarding the three [sections]: first, the number and characteristics of the initial kings are clarified to manifest the path of contemplation; next, this contemplation is performed, followed by the reliance on the five flavors (*pañcarasa*) to distinguish the stages of gradual entry according to the depth of realization;
third, reaching the *tīmadhu* (ghee), the culmination of contemplation and the forgetting of emotional attachments are explained to establish the marks of the resulting benefits.

Since we are currently unable to provide a detailed analysis, we shall proceed directly according to the text in two parts: first, discussing the principal and attendant [elements] based on the virtuous mind.

Regarding the general discussion of the primary and secondary (主伴) [factors] of the mind, there are five initial points: first, comparing the external primary and secondary factors to establish the number of primary and secondary factors of the contemplative method;
second, listing their names according to that established number; third, clarifying that the function of the internal primary and secondary factors is identical to the external ones;

fourth, clarifying the mutual correspondence between the internal and external persons and phenomena based on the number of faith-factors and so forth; and fifth, [the explanation of] the fifty factors.

The lower [level] simulates the traces [of the Buddhas] to clarify the completion of the path of contemplation. Regarding the "beginning" and "middle," they are explained generally and specifically, as was done in the preceding text;

this is because we set aside the distant for the sake of the proximate. As for the statement that "the mental factors (*caitta*) are numerous," it is intended to clarify the specific [classification];

therefore, having first indicated them generally as being very many, and because they are so numerous, we shall for now follow the essentials according to the *Mahāyāna Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*, wherein the mental factors are fifty-one and are subsumed as follows:
There are six categories: first, the universal mental factors (1); second, the object-specific mental factors (5); third, the wholesome mental factors (11);

fourth, the afflictions (6); fifth, the secondary afflictions (26); and sixth, the indeterminate mental factors (6). Since these total fifty-one, they are said to be "very numerous. This refers to their general classification;
however, if we consider them according to the number of wholesome factors, they are further divided into sub-categories, which comprise six classes.

Regarding the third section within [the second chapter], it says "skillful enumeration. There are ten such skillful enumerations, listed in sequence below. These numbers do not exist apart from the King;

this is precisely the meaning of observing the principal and its attendants (*sahāya*). The phrase "like disciples, etc. clarifies the internal by means of the external to explain the ten purposes used herein.
This is because most sūtras and śāstras clarify those who can assist the sovereign primarily through these ten types of persons.
However, these two sets of ten encompass all disciples; now, with reference to this, we shall clarify the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Since if these ten are transformed, everything is transformed and perfected into the sublime path, we shall treat them solely in terms of these ten. The "new eleven" refer to:

faith (*śraddhā*), shame (*hrī*), dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), non-attachment (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), non-delusion (*amoha*), diligence (*vīrya*), serenity (*praśrabdhi*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and non-harming (*avihiṃsā*).
Next, regarding the enumeration of the ten mental factors, the Master says: "The names follow the old translations, while the new [explanations] are as follows:

faith (*śraddhā*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), shame (*hrī*), dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), the two faculties (*indriya*), non-harming (*avihiṃsā*), and diligence (*vīrya*).

These exist only in wholesome minds. The first three phrases consist of single characters each, followed by four characters that conclude them. Regarding the first term, 'faith,' its name and meaning are identical to the old translation. As for 'heedfulness,' the name differs but the meaning is the same."

"Lightness and tranquility" (praśrabdhi) has the nature of being light, agile, comfortable, and capable; its old name was "joy" (prīti), which refers to delight and ease, though the meanings differ slightly. "Equanimity" (upekṣā) has the same meaning as its name.
"Moral shame" (hrī) and "moral dread" (apatrāpya) differ from "tranquility" (praśrabdhi) both in name and meaning.

The two faculties refer to non-attachment and non-hatred; their old names were "concentration" (samādhi) and "wisdom" (prajñā), which differ in name and meaning, yet their underlying principles are largely the same. This is because...

Without these two, concentration and wisdom cannot achieve non-harming (*avihiṃsā*), because there would be no absence of injury or affliction. The old [translation] calls this "precept" (*śīla*); the name differs but the meaning is the same.

As for the term "diligence" (*vīrya*) used in contrast to the old [translation], the names and meanings are largely the same, though in some cases they differ entirely. This reflects the different intentions of the translators and need not be reconciled.
Now, the priority here lies in entering meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*) by following the names; thus, wholesome kings and wholesome numbers together lead away from all evils.
To establish these as sublime virtues (*kuśala*), we now follow the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* of the Mahāyāna in enumerating the eleven wholesome factors:

namely, faith (*śraddhā*), shame (*hrī*), dread (*apatrāpya*), non-attachment (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), non-delusion (*amoha*), diligence (*vīrya*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and non-harming (*avihiṃsā*). These are the eleven.

Now, it is said that there are four points of difference between this [text] and the older [tradition]: first, the difference in number, which should be due to the distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.
Second, there are cases where the names differ but the meaning is the same, due to differences in the translator or the period;

third, there are cases where both name and meaning are entirely different, whether due to the original text or the translator; fourth, there are cases where the names are conflated with general enumerations, which should be distinguished as separate productions.
Now, because this [text] belongs to the Minor Vehicle and is also a Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), it speaks of "ten. The treatise itself explains: "Faith (*śraddhā*) means..."

Its nature is a state of mental purity that is profoundly and correctly in accord with karma, its results, the truths, and so forth. "Karma" refers to the three types of action, such as bodily movement;
"results" refers to the four fruits; "truths" refers to the Four Noble Truths; and "reality" refers to the Three Jewels.

Being in extreme conformity with these and similar objects is also termed "purity" and has the sense of "aspiration. Its function is to serve as the basis for the mind. Regarding *hrī* (shame): it is that which takes oneself as the primary authority.

And *hrī* (shame) has the nature of being ashamed of the transgressions one has committed due to the influence of the Dharma; its function is to serve as the basis for preventing and ceasing unwholesome conduct.
*Trapā* (embarrassment) has the nature of being ashamed of the transgressions one has committed due to the influence of others; its function is as previously described for *hrī*.

Non-attachment (*alobha*) is the antidote to attachment; it has the nature of profound revulsion and non-clinging, and its function is to serve as the basis for the non-arising of unwholesome conduct.

Non-hatred (*adveṣa*) is the antidote to hatred; its nature is loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Its function is as previously explained for non-attachment (*alobha*). Non-delusion (*amoha*) is the antidote to delusion (*moha*);

its nature is correct practice according to reality (*yathābhūta-pravṛtti*). "According to reality" refers briefly to the Four Noble Truths and extensively to the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Application toward these is the meaning of correct knowledge (*saṃprajanya*). Its function is also as explained for non-attachment. Diligence (*vīrya*) is the antidote to laziness (*kausīdya*).
The nature of *pratipakṣa* (counteractive) is diligent exertion toward the manifestation of wholesome qualities; its function is the perfect accomplishment of a virtuous nature.

*Praśrabdhi* (pliancy) has the nature of being the antidote to *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness), characterized by the physical and mental harmony and capability [to act]; its function is the ability to abandon the ten unwholesome actions and other hindrances.
*Apramāda* (heedfulness) is the antidote to *pramāda* (heedlessness); it consists of [the absence of] greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as diligence.
That which is called "heedlessness" (*pramāda*) relies upon the three preceding roots of goodness and diligence;
because these four factors serve as its antidotes, they constitute "heedfulness" (*apramāda*), whose function is to serve as the basis for the world. Regarding "equanimity" (*upekṣā*):

it refers to the attainment of mental evenness, mental rectitude, and mental effortlessness based upon such non-attachment, non-hatred, and so forth, up to diligence. Its function is as follows: ... [as above] ... its function is as follows.
Regarding "non-harming" (*avihiṃsā*): its antidote is compassion (*karuṇā*), which is its intrinsic nature; it is non-aversion (*adveṣa*) and has the function of not inflicting injury or distress.
These ten [factors] are explained somewhat extensively in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*; here they are briefly described below.
The third point may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

The following is the fourth [section], clarifying how the person and the dharmas are mutually related by relying on external principal and attendant figures to manifest the principal and attendants of practice.
Within these ten [points], each first establishes a correspondence and then explains the reason for it. First, the eye is directly correlated;
furthermore, it is explained that the eye occupies the foremost position among the sense organs, and as it presides over the East, it is the beginning of all directions—this is done by analogy.
Faith is manifested as the beginning of all enumerations and the primary entry point into the Buddha-dharma; thus it is designated as "the source of the Way and the mother of virtue.
It is through these traces that one enters the Way from this enumeration, and by means of these traces, its corresponding virtue is made manifest.
Since *dhūta* (ascetic practice) is the most refined form of diligent effort, it is assigned to this category. As for mindfulness (*smṛti*), it arises precisely from recollection and maintenance.
Only by clearly memorizing and not forgetting can one uphold the Vinaya; therefore, it corresponds to this [term]. The Master [Vasubandhu] intends to unify these with heedfulness (*apramāda*).

Concentration (*samādhi*) is the essence and penetration is its function; since the essence encompasses the function, it corresponds to this. Both of these have their meanings naturally manifested through their names, so all may be understood.
"Joy" (*prīti*) is contrasted with the explanation of meaning for ease of observation; the Master intends to unify these with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and tranquility (*passaddhi*).

Those who pair [this factor] with "shame" (*hrī*) all do so because they believe it accords with the meaning of shame; however, this is likely inconsistent, for it should properly be paired with "pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*).
Why? Among the seven factors of enlightenment, what was formerly called the "factor of discrimination" (*prahāṇa-sambodhyaṅga*) is translated in the new version as "pliancy.

Regarding its meaning, the treatise states that the Venerable Śāriputra’s mind was characterized by being "tamed, supple, and capable," which means its nature is to abandon the ten unwholesome courses of action and its function is to eliminate hindrances. This...

The text states that "leaving evil to obtain good" and "releasing suffering to obtain happiness" carry exactly the same meaning. *Āśraya* (猗) signifies the sense of being relaxed, at ease, and thoroughly delightful;
it has no connection whatsoever with the meaning of "releasing shame" (*hrī-vinirmukti*), so one should examine this carefully. The meaning of "abandoning" (*prahāṇa*) is as explained previously.

Here, we directly take the sense of abandoning [distractions] to abide in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is precisely its intended meaning; therefore, this is used to represent it. As for "awakening" (*saṃbodha*), the intention is to grasp the mental state.
This is because speech arises from vitarka and vicāra; all [these] converge upon the meaning of "shame" (hrī).

If one asks how this meaning of "precept" (śīla) differs from the aforementioned "discipline" (vinaya): the former is general, while the latter is specific, being exclusively concerned with the esoteric.
All these converge upon the meaning of "non-harming" (ahiṃsā), which may be understood as applicable to both. Such is the general outline; it should not be interpreted too narrowly.
The following section constitutes the fifth category, which concludes the exposition on the power of the path of contemplation through the primary and attendant aspects of external transformation;
it refers to the primary [nature] as the wondrous goodness (*sukṣema*) realized as the single essence of the Three Jewels, which are the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

To enter deeply into the wholesome dharmas is "wondrous goodness," which carries the same meaning as previously explained regarding entering the secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*). The text consists of five phrases; the first provides a general heading for the perfection of what is accomplished.
The next three phrases separately explain [the preceding], while the final phrase summarizes the meaning of external transformation (*bāhya-vineya*). This can be understood.
Next, the second section clarifies contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) by way of the universal mental factors (*caitasika*), because it comprehensively encompasses all phenomena (*dharma*).
It also adopts the principle of the principal and its attendants (*saparivāra*) regarding external transformation to clarify this; herein, there are five initial pairings.

First, the general heading distinguishes the universal enumeration; second, the names are listed in sequence; third, these are correlated with specific individuals; fourth, the commonalities and distinctions between the external and internal are clarified.
Regarding the fifth section below, which clarifies the benefits of the path of contemplation: each point is examined by contrasting it with external phenomena. First, as for the heading:
because these ten pervade all things, they are called the "great ground" (*mahābhūmi*), and each one is associated with the mind.
When kings arise together, if there is a king, there must necessarily be his domain; and if there is a domain, there must necessarily be a king. This is also the case with the "one" and the "many.

Although the two treatises differ slightly regarding this, we now follow one of them and thus say they "arise together. Entering into the wholesome and unwholesome clearly explains the general principle (*sāmānya-artha*).

Next, ten names are listed: among these, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*) are precisely the first five of the five aggregates (*skandha*) mentioned at the beginning of the *Śāstra*.

The five [mental factors] of application (*prayoga*) are as follows: within this context, desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—these five are precisely the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*) explained next in the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*.
As for why the first five are called "universal" (*sarvatraga*), the treatise itself states: "Because these pervade all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate minds, they are called universal.
As for why they are called "object-specific," it is because each of these five functions toward a distinct [object].

Regarding the mutual determination and inseparability of objects: within this [process], the presence of one necessarily entails the presence of all. Therefore, these two sets of five are both universal meanings;
thus, they are now collectively termed "universal mental factors" (*cittasādhāraṇa-caitasika*). It should be understood that herein there are three differences between the new and the old:

first, what was formerly one is now divided into two; second, what was formerly two is now combined into one; third, the sequence is not as it was before. These three are named "possessions" (*samanvāgama*).

Regarding "sameness and difference" (*sādharmya-vaidharmya*): "recollection" (*smṛti*) and "new name" (*nāma-nava*) refer to *manasikāra* (attention); "liberation" (*vimukti*) and "new" (*nava*) refer to *adhimokṣa* (resolute confidence).

Since one now wishes to manifest their common meaning, they are combined into one. Because they are combined to reveal this commonality, they do not correspond to the sequence of the three categories;

furthermore, within the subsequent pairings, they constitute a distinct sequential order. Although the names differ, the meanings are not distinct; although the names are similar, [the meanings differ].
The full meaning of these ten names is explained in detail within the *Arthaviniścaya-śāstra*;
here, I shall briefly clarify them according to their respective correspondences. As before, each correspondence will be presented along with its explanation.
First, regarding "perception" (*saṃjñā*), the treatise states: "It is the wisdom that excels in apprehending the characteristics of various objects. Thus, perception is the excellence of wisdom.
"Apprehension" (*udgraha*) refers to the capacity for superior grasping; it is called "superior power" (*balavat*), just as one of great strength is said to possess superior power.
This is precisely because, for that person, it functions through the power of perception (*saṃjñā*). "Desire" (*chanda*) has the nature of longing for objects that are pleasing and desirable;
this refers to things such as what has been seen or heard, and it serves to manifest the meaning of seeking with joy. It provides the basis for diligence (*vīrya*).

Regarding the statement that for such a person there is no worldly desire (*kāma*): although things such as a former wife or wealth are all worldly desires, it is certainly not the case that one lacks the desire to renounce them.
Because one seeks *nirvāṇa* through the ascetic practices (*dhūta*) and austerities, this is the desire for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
this is the truly sublime desire. "Contact" (*sparśa*) refers to the nature of discrimination arising from the conjunction of the three; that is, the eye and form.

Because consciousness and such [mental factors] arise from the conjunction of these various [elements], it is called "contact" (*sparśa*); its function is to serve as the basis for sensation (*vedanā*).

Regarding the term "person" (*pudgala*), first, the meaning of contact is explained below: briefly citing the engagement of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), and briefly taking consciousness (*vijñāna*) as an illustration for the sake of clarifying the doctrinal discussion, it is stated that there are "two.
Since the meaning of "person" applies here, it is contrasted with that. As for "wisdom" (*prajñā*), it means...

"Discernment" (prajñā) has the nature of investigating phenomena; that is, because one attains certainty by means of wisdom through the discernment of the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, its function is the severing of doubt.
Since a person who has attained certainty regarding phenomena possesses this very capacity, it is designated as such.
"Mindfulness" (smṛti) refers to the non-forgetting and clear recollection of familiar objects within the mind.
Its nature is non-distraction, and its function is to serve as the basis for that [non-distraction]. Regarding the meaning of "toward that person," it is explained as before.

"Volition" (cetanā) refers to the mental karma that causes the mind to engage with virtues, faults, or that which is neither; its nature is to form [the mind]. Its function is to direct the mind toward what is wholesome or unwholesome.
Regarding the meaning of "toward that person," it may be understood accordingly. To distinguish it from "separation" (viveka), one should say "secret composition" (saṃdhāya-bhāṣita).
Regarding "yathābhūta" (as it truly is), there is concern that it may have been misinterpreted through scribal error. "Vimokṣa" (liberation) is newly translated as "adhimukti" (resolute conviction);

this refers to having the nature of confirmation regarding a determined object, exactly as it has been understood. Although this name shares some slight similarity with the old [translation], its meaning is entirely different.

As for the person [referred to by this term], the name and meaning correspond precisely to those of the old [tradition], because they resolve emptiness most excellently. Regarding "smṛti" (mindfulness)...
"Newly translated as *manasikāra* (attention), its nature is that which causes the mind to awaken; it functions to bring mental states (*citta-caitta*) into manifestation and to stimulate them.

It has the meaning of 'recollection' and the function of maintaining and elevating the focal object. Regarding the phrase 'previously cultivated to achieve the divine eye' (*divyacakṣus*), this is the correct interpretation.
*Samādhi*, newly translated as *samādhi* (equipoise), means 'equal holding,' referring to that which is neither too high nor too low."
"Below, 'equanimity' (*samāhita*) refers to holding the mind steady; it was also formerly called 'right concentration' (*samyaksamādhi*), and is synonymous with 'equipoise' (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, there are two other names for it that have similar meanings, which I cannot describe in detail here. The treatise states:

'It is the one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) regarding the object of observation,' referring to the five aggregates and so forth, as well as impermanence, suffering, and so on. This 'one-pointedness of mind' is the meaning of the term 'object' (*vastu*); it is the union of the object and wisdom."
Its function is to serve as a basis, because through the stabilization of the mind, one understands things as they truly are (the old translations also say "right concentration").
Regarding this person, the meaning has already been explained previously. The "feeler" refers to this aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), which is the experiencing of consciousness.
There are three kinds of feeling: pleasant feeling means that when it ceases, there is a desire for reunion; painful feeling means that when it arises, there is aversion.
The desire for neither suffering nor pleasure refers to the absence of duality; it refers to the absence of both conjunction and disjunction.

For one who encounters such a person, to uphold the meaning through extensive learning is precisely what accords with its significance. Thus is the brief explanation of the principle of correspondence.

Regarding the fourth section, "Ten or Fewer People," which clarifies the commonalities and distinctions between the persons and the dharma, there are two parts: first, clarifying the commonalities and distinctions of the persons; second, clarifying the commonalities and distinctions of the contemplative dharma.
Within the first part, there is a general heading followed by specific correspondences that conclude the intent. First, "each being complete" indicates their own fundamental nature;
therefore, "to lead others" and so forth indicates their traces for the purpose of transformation. Next, within the specific section, the first and last of the two [categories] are cited.

The "intervals" (khaṇḍa) can be understood as the single office that governs each; this refers to the individual distinct dharma-gates. Next, regarding the contemplation of dharmas, there are two parts:

first, the initial phrase provides a general analogy similar to the preceding [section], and second, the subsequent phrases provide specific analogies based on the preceding general and particular [categories].

Next, the analogy for the particulars is also briefly cited by way of two examples, while the remaining cases may be inferred. The section beginning with "according to suitability" (yathāyogam) serves as an analogy for the third [section] of the preceding [text].

This summarizes the intended meaning. "According to what is appropriate" refers to what kind of sphere is appropriate. Regarding the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and mental factors (*caitasika*), let us speak briefly of these ten dharmas;

the "mind" here refers to all mind-kings and mental factors. "The six govern together" means governance, which refers to cultivation and regulation, as well as striking and breaking [through obstacles].
Within this context, it refers to *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). As for the three types of sounds of the root-syllable: first, all-encompassing sounds; second, tongue-sounds.

When "dong" (冬) is pronounced with three departing tones, it correctly corresponds to the second tone; its meaning is as explained by the predecessors. Although people generally employ the *qie* (cutting) pronunciation, it is not entirely correct.
In reality, it is just like the examples of "gùshǒu" (故手), "yìduān" (異端), and "zhèngchéng yězhàn" (政城野戰), where the phonetic meanings are identical.

One should know that within these cases, the visual characteristics (*guānxiàng*) are not explicitly clarified; this principle pervades the preceding and following sections and may be understood through a comprehensive grasp.
Because the intention was not to produce excessive textual complexity, it is not stated again; for in this sutra, right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) is itself sublime practice (*pratipatti*).

Sublime practice necessarily arises based on a sublime object (*ālambana*). If one recognizes the sublime object, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) constitutes right contemplation, while the mental factors (*caitta*) constitute the sublime object.
Just as mental factors assist and perfect the mind-king, so too can the sublime object give rise to sublime contemplation.

Since what applies to one king applies equally to all kings, it is said that the various mental factors (*caitta*) collectively attack the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and perform the work of a Buddha (*buddhakārya*).

The "work of a Buddha" refers to the attainment of Buddhahood; the "mental factors" refer to all sentient beings. To "govern" them means that the mind-king performs right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), which is to reveal and manifest.
The "work of a Buddha" is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). As the Sūtra says: "In order to..."
"To reveal and manifest the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to all sentient beings" is precisely its meaning. One must thoroughly understand this intent.

Having established this contemplation, what follows is the fifth section, which concludes the matters of external transformation and clarifies the cultivation of the benefits derived from this contemplation.

The Bodhisattva’s own severing of delusions and the myriad practices of the six perfections are all outflowing wholesome dharmas; the true intent lies precisely here.
Since this differs from the Two Vehicles and is distinct from what follows, it alone receives the specific designation of "partial" (or "separate"), and is therefore termed the Initial Teaching.
Regarding the characteristics of the fulfillment of the six perfections, they are explained very extensively in the treatises; here I shall provide only a brief summary.

To point out those individuals: King Śibi, who cut away all the flesh of his own body to save a pigeon without any resentment or regret, is an example of one whose perfection of *dāna* (generosity) is complete;
King Sutasoma, who faced death with truthful speech without any fear or trepidation, is an example of one whose perfection of *śīla* (ethical discipline) is complete;
and the seer Kṣānti, who was mangled by King Kali in the forest, is an example of one whose perfection of *kṣānti* (patience) is complete.
To have a physical body yet be free from anger is the fulfillment of patience (*kṣānti*).

As in the case of Prince Sudāna, who drained the ocean to seek the jewel and gave it to all beings, persevering until his goal was achieved without ever flagging, and moved by his sincerity so that the heavens sent assistance—this is the fulfillment of diligence (*vīrya*).
As in the case of the Śravaṇaka-jaṭila rishi, who attained the fourth dhyāna, whereby inhalation and exhalation ceased; while sitting beneath a tree, there was a bird’s nest [upon him].
The sage Keṭī, while raising his son, entered meditative absorption (dhyāna) out of fear that his mother would be startled and fail to come.
He remained in this state until his son had flown away, at which point he finally arose from his concentration; thus, his meditation was perfected.

Furthermore, when the great minister Gopaka, in order to settle a dispute, divided Jambudvīpa into seven parts—ensuring that cities, towns, and villages were all distributed equally so that no further contention existed—this is called *praśama* (pacification).

If one were to fulfill both of these simultaneously, it would not accord with the principle of the stages of practice (*bhūmi*). Next, regarding the statement in the *Sūtra* that "it is associated with," this refers to "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñā*), which is the wisdom of entering emptiness;
it means realizing that all phenomena are entirely identical to emptiness, thereby being in accord with the principle of emptiness.

The intended meaning is that from the stage of milk, one enters the abbreviated [path], wherein contaminated virtue (*sāsrava-kuśala*) is integrated with the uncontaminated reality (*anāsrava-tattva*), such that the phenomenon is itself the principle.

Furthermore, within the specific [classification], this refers to the arising of the resolve from the provisional name (*prajñapti-nāma*). It means that based on the essence of the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one gives rise to functional utility;

this refers to the Lord of Transformation in the Pure Land. Moreover, regarding the citation of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, some say it is because the realization of the Way is identical in its perfection and because it is the teaching of the inconceivable (*acintya*).

However, I now maintain that emerging from emptiness into the provisional is like milk being transformed into curd to bring sentient beings to maturity. Next, the reliance [on the environment] and the correctness [of the body] are clarified.

It is stated that although they have already realized the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), they further receive the formal instruction; this is because those with a sudden initial resolve cannot immediately realize it.

The primary intent here is to lead them toward maturity; therefore, the conclusion states: "Maturity follows birth. This refers to the arousal of the mind within the Perfect [Teaching] (*pariniṣpanna*).
"Arousal" means from the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) upward. These are individuals who hear the Perfect and realize the Perfect. These three passages follow one another in sequence.
Because it is taught [in this way], the latter serves as the basis for the former. Regarding the citation of three passages from below, some say this is for the purpose of resolving a doubt.
The doubt is as follows: "If one seeks to attain Buddhahood with a resolute mind, the principle should be one and only true;

how could there be many paths? Therefore, these are cited to explain it. Since the doubt is eliminated once heard, it is clear that there must be various explanations to resolve such doubts. Now, I say: the former...
It is said that there are many types; next, the sequence is listed and explained by means of both the treatises and the sūtras.

Since it has already been stated in this way according to the treatises, we know that there are indeed many types. Thus, we know that within the teachings of the past there are these four distinctions: three are provisional (*upāya*) and one is real (*tattva*).
This is the meaning of "relative" (*sāpekṣa*); the "absolute" (*anapekṣa*) has not yet been clarified. Below, three passages are cited in succession to establish this point.
This sutra reveals that there is only the single, absolute reality beyond which no other three exist;
thus, it is certainly improper to hastily interpret its primary intent by forcibly constructing alternative explanations based on the three provisional [vehicles] of the Bodhisattvas.

Hearing this Dharma—the wondrous Dharma of absolute transcendence—those whose doubts are removed come to know with faith that there are no three, but only the one perfect and wondrous reality, and they enter into realization together. Furthermore, it says:

The preceding section was based on the teaching (*śāsana*), while this section is based on practice (*caryā*); the subsequent passage is termed the "cause" (*hetu*). This current text provisionally contains three meanings identical to those mentioned above.

Furthermore, the preceding section clarified that the person of provisional means (*upāya-pudgala*) is the person of reality (*tattva-pudgala*), whereas this section clarifies that provisional practice is identical to real practice.

Next, by citing examples from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it reveals that provisional principle (*upāya-tattva*) is identical to real principle; thus, the teaching is included therein, providing a comprehensive clarification.
The fourth is the single meaning; this also has three aspects, which are the same as those mentioned previously, because the provisional has not yet reached the real and thus involves aspiration.

To summarize: the "four" are merely enumerated and explained in contrast to the preceding [three]; thus, while there are generally four types in the brief discussion, according to the three specific texts distinguished above, there are actually none.
Next, regarding the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku): although both are perfect, they differ in terms of being distant or near; therefore, this explanation is structured accordingly.

Within this, first there is a general clarification of the high and vast nature of the fundamental and the manifested, followed by a specific clarification that dispels the near to reveal the long duration of the fundamental. Regarding the first of these, there are two distinct parts:

first, the fundamental height is clarified through a general indication of its unfathomability, which is precisely the "inconceivable" (acintya); below, it is further clarified through two specific positions that demonstrate its unfathomability.

Because the state of "one who is to be succeeded" (kṣetrajña) exists within this meaning, it is called "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksambodhi). Alternatively, because there may be ancient Buddhas [among them], it is called "Dharma King.

Next, citing scriptural evidence to demonstrate the status of Equal Enlightenment, it is said to be "adjacent to the Buddha" (*buddhasāmantaka*) yet not yet a Dharma King; this will be made clear later in the explanation of the names.
Regarding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* cited here, some say the text does not contain these words, while others say this refers to the old translation and cannot be accepted.

Regarding the statement "there is no present," since it is said that [the teaching] emerged from the past, why was it not cited? If there were necessarily both the old and the new, they should not be two separate things;

this has not yet been fully understood and shall await further investigation. However, the meaning can be reconciled with the text as it is not of urgent necessity. Thus, this is the essential meaning of the High [Teaching];
to clarify the Extensive Trace [Teaching], the three karmas are employed without fixed direction to assist in transformation; this refers to the mind of samādhi.
The "dispersed shadow" is the body; that which is below it is the mouth—this refers to the assistance provided by the three mysteries (*triguhyāni*).

This matter is extensively elucidated in various sutras and śāstras; how could this [text] fully express it? Therefore, it says "inexpressible eloquence. The reason for what follows is to clarify the intent behind manifesting traces (*avataṃsaka*).
The purpose of manifesting traces is precisely to lead those of provisional capacity (*upāyapuruṣa*) into the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*). When beings attain entry into reality, then the trace...

The transformation has ceased; there is a method for this. To use an analogy: when one works with uncut jade, it is still in its raw state. Once it has been fully worked and polished, so that there is no longer any need for further hammering or chipping, this is called "stopping" (*ting*).
This meaning is also applicable to the state where it is entirely unworked, serving as a vessel for ritual use; thus it is called a "vessel" (*qi*).
Now, this general term does not necessarily refer to jade, because it speaks of "hammering and chipping. It refers generally to all things that can be forged and refined.
To "polish and refine until it becomes a vessel" is a general metaphor for how the four flavors of karmic conditions are tempered and refined into a single flavor.
As for the phrase "the transformation has ceased," this refers to the ultimate limit of its manifest function. However, by brushing away what is near, it reveals what is far.

Previously, only the height and breadth were generally clarified, while the duration and proximity were not yet revealed; now, these are precisely elucidated. First, the text correctly clarifies that the origin is fundamentally eternal and ultimate.
This was likely the Dharma King of former times; how could it be that today’s [teaching] contradicts the traces of the recent past?

It is not that there are two distinct periods; both the sudden and the gradual are but recent traces. To speak of "sudden" and "gradual" refers to the independent practice of the past and the non-duality realized in the present assembly.
This single phrase encompasses the meaning of both the ancient and the modern; to interpret it as referring solely to one [period] is a grave error.
If even those who study the ancient teachings are still confused by this, how much more so should later students of other schools pay deep attention to it!

Within "contemplation" (*guan*) there are three meanings, which constitute the Great Bodhicitta. Because the contemplation of the three truths—both central and peripheral—is all-encompassing, it is called "Great.
Because one takes this as the cause and reaches the ultimate fruit of the Great, it is called "that which can lead to penetration" (*neng tong*). Five.
Abiding is itself affliction (*kleśa*) and is also the dharma of mind and consciousness; because it causes people to undergo birth in every place, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*).
When the wondrous cause and effect are perfected, the causal and resultant states of the five abidings no longer exist, which is why it is said they are "destroyed.
This is precisely the contemplation of the category of the wondrous Way. One must understand the six levels of identity (*liu ji*); thus the commentary says [as follows].

Next, regarding the enumeration [of dharmas], there is no distinct meaning here; furthermore, since it was already clarified by the previous enumeration, this section simply analyzes the quantity.
This question is from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Therein, the *Large Sutra* (*Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā*) was contrasted with other sūtras to show that their scope is identical;

now, this sūtra is being clarified through its contrast with other sūtras. The intent of the initial question is as follows: in the enumerations of other sūtras, there are even cases reaching down to the number of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Regarding the term "numerous" (*bahu*), it is said to mean "very many. Since what is taught in this sutra is extraordinary and distinct from ordinary assemblies, why is their number so small?
This is explained by two points, both of which are major arguments in the treatise (*śāstra*). As for the phrase "a large number," it refers to a complete total;
even if there were some excess or deficiency, the full figure is cited, hence it is called a "large number. Thus, the text below says "large."
The number is eighty thousand; the *Book* says "the *Shi* has three hundred," and the commentary states that this is the approximate total of its chapters, including its various branches.
This is merely one general sense and does not yet clarify the meaning intended here. Furthermore, the latter sense is as follows:

in that [previous] case, the profound and far-reaching nature of the principle of *prajñā* was termed a "mysterious matter" (*mi shi*); now, in this case, the most profound and far-reaching aspect is the unification through the two gates, which is termed "mystery."
The subsequent passage states that being "profound, firm, remote, and far-reaching" refers to the most esoteric matter;

it must be one who has transcended the ordinary who can [comprehend this], and such a person must necessarily be one who has long since realized the ultimate identity of the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku).
However, these [preceding descriptions] all cite the ultimate of the Master; thus, while this passage mentions eighty thousand, the following passage mentions eight million billion nayutas.

Regarding the other [interpretation]: furthermore, in the "Original Gate" (Honmon), the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth are initially said to number sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (sands of the Ganges);

yet, by the beginning of the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (Jinziritoku-hon), they are said to number as many as the atoms (*paramāṇu*) in a thousand worlds. Other commentators explain this by saying that "a thousand" refers to the atoms in a trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*).
Since it was thus in the original [text], even though the "traces" (Jikimon) state eighty thousand based on the analogy of the original, it is not [the case that the original meant only that].
The number can be understood through reflection without requiring prolixity; this refers to the fourfold nature of causes and conditions.

"Number" is a worldly phenomenon (*loka-dharma*), conforming to the world—that is, the realm of existence (*loka*). As clarified above, since numbers differ from the ordinary, hearing them gives rise to faith and respect for the person [who teaches them].
"Secret matters" refers to the disclosure of what was concealed, which corresponds to the latter two intentions. Thus, the four meanings are clear; the explanation here is brief.

For this reason, the commentary states [as follows]... Since the examples for those who do not rely on the teachings can be understood by analogy, the fundamental [reality] is not explicitly explained here;

rather, from these numerical fundamentals, the numerical traces are suspended, such that through the traces one knows the ultimate fundamental. Next, regarding the reliance on contemplation, it clarifies that within one's own mind there are these eighty thousand numbers.
Since the mind possesses all things, how could it be limited to only eighty thousand? It is simply that they are not spoken of and not known.

To clarify this: first, within that [total], one uses the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) to clarify the ten thousand; next, one uses the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) to clarify the eight. Taken together, they constitute eighty thousand.
Regarding the initial ten wholesome actions, there are two ways of application, both of which are valid. First, one uses a single wholesome action to clarify the thousand;
next, by using all ten wholesome actions, the ten thousand are established. Furthermore, regarding a single wholesome action, there are ten realms, and within each of those ten realms...

Possessing the ten [virtues] means that each of the hundred realms possesses ten; thus, the hundred realms constitute one thousand suchnesses (*tathatā*). Since one good [quality] is thus, ten are likewise so, thereby forming ten thousand.
As these are applied to each of the eightfold right path (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*), each becomes ten thousand; thus, there are eighty thousand [qualities]. The "eightfold right path" consists of:
right speech, right action, right livelihood, right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right [concentration].

This is concentration; it is precisely the perfect, wondrous, and unconditioned Eightfold Noble Path. Now, these eighty thousand [precepts] are "mindless" because they are necessarily fully possessed by the mind.
Since the mind possesses all things, how could it be merely eighty thousand? Nevertheless, although they are fully possessed, they are not spoken of or known; therefore, they are clarified here.
This refers to the number of wondrous persons after the revelation and manifestation—that is, the "wondrous number. It is thus.
The wondrous number is precisely the mind-dharma; because one has never known it from the beginning, understanding it by relying upon this is called "contemplation" (*guan*).

Because the object and the contemplation are spoken of in union, it is said that "one contemplates the mind" (*guanxin*), for this clarifies the point. The meaning culminates here; one must not seek further clarification of the three truths and three contemplations beyond this.
This is a meaning implicit in the text rather than a direct commentary on the words of the scripture; it pertains to the true essence of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
The explanation of the methods for cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is not intended as a commentary on the scriptural text;
therefore, it should not be taken as a precedent—such is the general meaning of the note (etc.).
Next, regarding the stages (*bhūmi*): "Bodhisattva" is a general designation for those who are on the path of the Mahāyāna. Since the causal ground is general...
Because one knows which stage this belongs to, its position is clarified; that is to say, these are all the stages of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).

Within this, first the text is cited to mark the heading, and then it is translated and explained—one should know that regarding the text being cited, the preceding phrase is still in the original language, and thus it must be translated.
The old [translation] says: *a* means "non-"; *nuttara* means "supreme" (the three upper [realms]); *saṃyak* means "correct."

"Samyak" (perfect) means "pervasive," and "sambodhi" (complete enlightenment) means "knowledge of the path," or alternatively, "awakening. It refers in general to the unsurpassed, perfect, and pervasive knowledge-awakening and the path thereof.
As for its meaning: by means of the fourfold perfect equality (*samyak-samatā*), one sequentially corresponds to the principle and the measure;

through non-conceptualization and the attainment of those four types of wisdom, one contemplates suchness according to the principle, and as it is, one contemplates the conventional according to the measure. Thus, it is "perfect" because it is non-conceptual and all-pervasive.
Because one has severed the two types of ignorance, it is called "knowledge. Because non-conceptual subsequent knowledge emerges beyond the state of sleep and dreams, it is called "awakening.
These four wisdoms constitute the true essence of bodhi. Regarding the meaning of "unsurpassed," there are two [ways of categorizing] and seven [types].
Briefly stated, there are two: first, in relation to other vehicles; second, in relation to one's own vehicle. Regarding the relation to other vehicles, the bodhi of the śrāvakas is of two kinds.

Regarding the enlightenment of the Pratyekabuddhas, there is one that is superior; regarding the enlightenment of the Tathāgata, there is none superior, and thus it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).

From the perspective of one's own vehicle, there are five types of enlightenment; the generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) has four levels of superiority; the subduing of the mind has three levels of superiority; the clear mind has two levels of superiority;
and the emergence and arrival have one level of superiority. Because there is nothing further above it, it is called "unsurpassed. If it is complete...
It is explained that there are seven unsurpassed aspects, as stated in the subsequent text. Furthermore, another interpretation says:

*anuttara* means "unsurpassed," *samyak* means "correct," *saṃbodhi* means "perfectly equal," and *bodhi* means "awakening. Thus, it is "unsurpassed, correct, equal, and perfect awakening" (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
This consists of four types of awakening; the first is "unsurpassed awakening," which is the general term and reveals the pure *dharmadhātu* of *bodhi*.

1. "Perfect" (*samyak*) distinguishes it from the false awakening of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). 2. "Complete" (*sam-bodhi*) distinguishes it from the limited awakening of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), who only realize the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
3. Furthermore, "perfect" (*samyak*) distinguishes it from the bodhi of Bodhisattvas, whose causal awakening is not yet fulfilled at the stage of fruition;
thus, this reveals that the path to bodhi consists of the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*). The single character "awakening" (*bodhi*) below governs all that precedes it.

Fourth, because it possesses the three lower [qualities]—namely, that nothing surpasses it, that it transcends all, and that it is universal—and because it is realized through the principle of truth (*tattva*), it is called "unsurpassed awakening" (*anuttara-bodhi*).
However, since most sūtras and śāstras refer to the principle of truth itself as the essence of unsurpassed bodhi due to its being the fundamental basis, here both are taken together:
the fruit of Buddhahood and its wisdom-principle (*jñāna*) are both termed "unsurpassed bodhi. In these two fruits, there is no regression whatsoever.

Regarding the transition [from the past to] the present, although there are many differing interpretations between the ancient and modern scholars, no historical record has emerged that distinguishes these two.

However, this text encompasses five meanings in total: four general and one specific. According to the first school, the first [meaning] serves as the general [principle], while the latter four are the specifics.

According to the second school, the former four are the specifics and the last one is the general. From the perspective of rational contemplation (*yili*), the former is not as [convincing] as the latter. Furthermore, according to the first school...

The first three are the "correct" (*samyak*) and the latter three are the "knowledge" (*jñāna*); yet since both are said to consist of "three," why is it that the latter are immediately called "knowledge"? This, too, is untenable.
Now, this commentary simply says "unsurpassed path" (*anuttara-mārga*), which merely cites the beginning and the end while abbreviating the middle three.

To state it fully, it is "unsurpassed, correct, equal, and right path. The first four are specific, while the last one is general; that is to say: [The full title is] *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-mārga*. The first four terms are distinct [attributes], while the last one is the common [designation]. That is to say:
The Unsurpassed Way, up to and including the Right Way—this "Way" is itself awakening (*bodhi*).

However, since the Way arises from that which is awakened to, and because there must necessarily be both the subject (the capacity) and the object (that which is penetrated), the subject must necessarily have what is called the "Way" as its object of awakening.

The passage beginning with "As for the subtle [state] of the object" (*yathā-viṣaya-sūkṣma*) is an explanation of the meaning; this should be understood. In the sūtra text, the first part refers to the essence (*tattva*), which is the basis (*āśraya*), the object of seeking (*paryeṣya*), and the object of cultivation (*bhāvya*).
The three characters following it refer precisely to the stages (*avasthā*), which are that which manifest [the essence]. Now, within the present text, there are three phrases:

the first correctly explains the path (*mārga*) for the sake of which [the practice is undertaken]; the next two explain the stages upon which one relies. The first phrase provides a general explanation of the meaning of the stages. Below...

In the initial passage of the section explaining the stages (*bhūmi*) by analyzing the phrases, it says, "As for the 'Excellence of the Object' (*viṣaya-prakarṣa*)," which means that the meaning of this unsurpassed path is as explained in the first of the "Ten Excellences" (*daśa-prakarṣa*) within the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), namely, the Excellence of the Object.

Since the object is precisely the path and the basis upon which these stages rely, and because the textual meaning is so extensive that it would become cumbersome to elaborate here, the author refers back to that explanation. The Master said: "The Great Object comes first."
The four types of *bodhi* (awakening) are these; they are all objects that the sublime path tends toward, for it is by means of what is manifested that the manifestor is known.
Therefore, one must point to the object. Some say that *bodhi* is the path sought; the *Dharmajñāna-śāstra* states: "All the qualities of the Buddhas are called *bodhi*.
Because this serves as the basis for the mind that seeks, the object itself is designated as *bodhi*. This is its [meaning].
Master Mi explains that because there is no fixed [subject] for a person, the text states: "These are all that upon which the Buddhas rely; this is the Way sought.
Now, although this interpretation is general, it has not yet clarified the meaning of "the Middle" as the path corresponding to the three concentrations (*samādhi*) within the one fixed object.
Second, an explanation by way of the general; third, an explanation by way of the specific. (1) [General Explanation]... [End of Section 1]

Because the realm of the path must be determined as one, those two can be pointed out; since these paths are both fruits of merit, they are called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*), yet this still encompasses four types.
Although the dharmas of the clarified realm are numerous, each possesses three meanings: namely, differentiation (*vibhāga*), judgment (*nirṇaya*), and opening (*apavarga*).
Differentiation refers to the distinctions among the four types; judgment refers to the three provisional and one real; and opening means that all coarse [phenomena] are... [subsumed].
That is to say, "wondrous, sole, and unsurpassed" means that there is no second, third, or fourth; this is the meaning of this sutra.
Although it is thus, this is merely a general explanation of the meaning of the "unsurpassed way," for the meanings of its four specific distinctions have not yet been discussed.
Since the sutra is so detailed and thorough, it cannot be in vain. If it were merely a general explanation, I fear it would not fully satisfy what is sought as a result.

The Way of Virtue likewise has not yet reconciled its textual meanings as in the two previous interpretations; although each has its own points of correspondence, neither is what we now take as our primary authority.

According to what our own school currently takes as its primary authority, the fruit-virtue (*phala-guṇa*) does not exceed three kinds, just as the Threefold Profundity of the Dharma was explained in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
Since both of the previous schools possessed both general and specific [explanations], we shall also take "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) as the general [definition].

Taken collectively, the three [preceding] are the general; taken individually, they are the specific. Regarding the word "equal" (*sama*) therein, its interpretation has varied between ancient and modern scholars. If one takes it to mean "truly pervasive" (*satya-vyāpin*) or "equally pervasive," then it can indeed be understood as such.
However, it is certainly not permissible to take the three bodies collectively as the meaning of "equal. Specifically, the name "Buddha" refers to the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*).

Individually, the Dharma-body is the primary retribution (*vipāka*), while the Enjoyment-body is "equal" because it is the primary transformation for others, and thus it is also considered "primary. Finally, there is the single character "Way" (*mārga*).
By penetrating and subsuming these three, one raises this "one-three"; even the general and specific aspects of the remaining triads can be understood by analogy.
Within this, there should be the meaning of causes and conditions; regarding the general and specific aspects of the three, there are thus four meanings.
If one proceeds through all four teachings, they all possess this meaning, which may likewise be inferred accordingly. Thus, with respect to the sacred teachings and the school’s own doctrine:
All gates may be entered through this; otherwise, one will encounter obstacles at every turn—reflect on this, reflect on this!
The following two lines correctly explain the meaning of the stage (*bhūmi*). First, they explain the sense of "penetration" (*tong*):

because one has proceeded toward that unsurpassed *bodhi* and has already reached the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), this clarifies the stage itself. Furthermore, it serves to distinguish it from the preceding stages. It also refers to...
This is explained in the fourth section of the tenth part of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), within the "Excellence of the Explanation of the Stages.

Since the names and meanings are identical, I do not wish to repeat the text; therefore, I refer back to that explanation. That explanation of the stages is most extensive, but to summarize it, it does not go beyond three points:

first, a general differentiation of the four types of distinctions; second, a judgment regarding the provisional and the real; and third, the revelation that there is only one perfect and wondrous [truth], with nothing else being partial.
The essential point here is that "this" and "that" are identical; "that" is precisely "this. Otherwise, it would be merely prolix and of no benefit.
Having already explained the meaning of the "stages" (*bhūmi*) above, we shall now analyze the text concerning the stages—namely, the three characters [of the title].

Within this explanation, there are four distinct sections: first, the enumeration of their names within the section on causes and conditions; second, the explanation of their essential meanings according to the teachings. Regarding the first of these:

There should be a numerical designation for its essence, meaning, and phrasing; however, as this is a brief summary, only the names are listed. Regarding the number, various masters of ancient and modern times have proposed either three or four;
in this present text, only three are clarified. As for the names, they are as stated in the text; the three names of ancient and modern times are mostly identical to those given here.
If one were to posit four, the two traditions would differ: the first [tradition] adds "Realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*) to the aforementioned three.

The three stages of regression and their respective sequences are all identical to those mentioned previously; this is precisely the interpretation of the Master of the *Dichijing* (Treatise on the Stages) in the present text.
Next, another school states that there are four types of non-regression: first, faith; second, position; third, realization; and fourth, practice.

This school’s enumeration is the same as the previous one, though its names and sequence are both similar and different. Now, it is said that since the sūtras and śāstras differ, each follows its own [system].
Because [the master] relied on this [tradition], he held these differing views; yet despite these differences, the current text provisionally follows the three types.

The reason for limiting it to three is that their meaning is essential and convenient, as they encompass the other two. If one grasps the intent of the four lower explanations, then although various divergent meanings may not be fully harmonized, there will be nothing that is not penetrated.
However, since a single statement was used to definitively establish the stage of the śrāvaka above, here too it should likewise be so.

To speak of them separately results in differing meanings; however, the meaning of "Śrāvaka" is specific and is explained directly from the ultimate perspective, whereas the meaning of "Bodhisattva" is comprehensive and cannot be definitively determined.

Thus, while other sutras may state that they are all in the stage of the "Final Birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*) or that they are all on the "Tenth Ground" (*daśabhūmi*), how could these not be distinct?
Nevertheless, this [text] intends to reveal the specific by means of the comprehensive, and to clarify the comprehensive by means of the specific.
This is the teaching for the opening of the assembly, the wondrous Way that is without fixed direction, because from beginning to end it is entirely non-retrogressive;

one should examine this well. The above constitutes the meaning of causes and conditions (*nidāna*). As for the four intentions (*catvāraḥ saṃdhāya*), the sequence of the three meanings—general and specific—is precisely these four intentions.
Someone asked: "What is the difference between 'non-retrogression' (*avaivartika*) and 'not turning back' (*apratyudāvartana*)? The answer explains Maitreya’s question.
