The Sūtra states: "Attaining one's own portion of merit constitutes non-retrogression; attaining merit beyond one's portion constitutes non-reversal.
Furthermore, it is because one attains wisdom and attains merit, and because one attains *prajñā* and attains skillful means (*upāya*), that there is non-retrogression and non-reversal.
It is also said: "Why is there non-retrogression? Because by possessing the ten causes listed below, one is non-retrogressive and is thus able [to attain] the fruit of Buddhahood."

Regarding "retrogression" (*parihāṇi*), one will certainly realize [the goal]; regarding "non-retrogression," it is called the progressive cultivation of every thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*). "Retrogression" means loss; "retrogression" (*parivarta*) means movement. There are four types of non-retrogression:
first, non-retrogression of faith (*śraddhā-aparihāṇi*), which is the sixth stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) called the "Mind of Non-retrogression" (*aparihāṇi-citta*);

from this point onward, one no longer retrogresses into the arising of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Second, non-retrogression of position (*avasthā-aparihāṇi*), which is the seventh stage of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) called the "Abiding of Non-retrogression" (*aparihāṇi-vihāra*). From this point onward...

Fourth, because they do not subsequently regress into the two vehicles, there are three types of non-retrogression: first, "non-retrogression by name" from the first bhūmi upward, because the dharmas realized therein are not lost;
second, "non-retrogression by practice" from the eighth bhūmi upward, which is called the "stage of non-retrogression" because one is able to cultivate both conditioned and unconditioned dharmas;
since these bodhisattvas today are all at or above the eighth bhūmi, it is said that they abide in the unsurpassed.
Because one realizes the certainty of non-retrogression, that which is "non-retrogressive" is not merely the absence of turning back; furthermore, there are two types of non-retrogression:

first, having already attained non-retrogression upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*); second, attaining non-retrogression for the first time at the eighth stage, where one subsequently attains unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Because these are dharmas to be attained later, from the eighth stage upward, one is able to be non-retrogressive regarding the mind of the perfectly realized awakening of sentient beings.
Because one advances within the swift current of the immovable dharma, moving spontaneously without turning back, it is called "non-retrogression.
This non-retrogression—this "not retreating"—is precisely "not turning back. These two explanations, as well as all other interpretations, do not go beyond the general and specific [meanings];
thus there are such differences. If the perfect path were revealed, everything would be without fixed direction; how could this [state] be fixed?
Because they are distinct, they are not discussed here.

Next, regarding the classification by teaching (*yàojiào*): the term "non-retrogression" (*avivartana*) encompasses three meanings and further extends through four types of assemblies, as they ultimately converge into the single Threefold [Assembly].
Within this, first the four types are designated, for the sūtras and śāstras state that these three contain these four distinctions.
In accordance with the intent of the Noble Teachings, there are four types [of benefits]. First, regarding the *Mahā-śāstra* within the *Piṭaka*, it states:

"By remaining far removed from five things, one obtains five merits. As for the five things: first, the three evil destinies; second, birth into a poor or lowly family (the *Vyākhyā* notes that "borderlands" should be mentioned separately, or else it follows directly from the meaning);
third, deficiency of the sense faculties; fourth, the female body; and fifth, a disposition prone to forgetfulness. As for the five merits, the first is...
One will always obtain the bodies of gods or humans; second, be born into wealthy and noble families; third, have all sense faculties complete; fourth, always be a male;
and fifth, constantly remember past lives. These five matters constitute the abandonment of unwholesome causes and the cultivation of wholesome causes.

These five merits are the attainment of wholesome fruits through the abandonment of unwholesome fruits. Now, having attained these five wholesome fruits, one stands in contrast to the three [unwholesome] states.
Regarding the first pair of stages, because one has departed from the three unwholesome grounds and dwells in the wholesome ground,
never again falling back into unwholesomeness, humans and devas [regard this] as being still like ordinary beings; therefore, next, through the three pairs of practices,
because one constantly performs these practices and does not perform other practices, one knows past lives— that is, one possesses constant mindfulness— and thus there is no regression.

Possessing these [characteristics] is called "non-retrogression," which refers to the three types of non-retrogression. Some say that, according to the *Saṃkhyā-śāstra*, Śrāvakas attain "non-retrogression in position" (*avasthāna-avaivartika*) at the stage of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*).

Now, the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) judges that for Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections, from after completing the three great *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas until before sitting at the site of enlightenment, they all attain "non-retrogression in practice" (*caryā-avaivartika*) through middle patience (*madhya-kṣānti*), and "non-retrogression in mindfulness" (*smṛti-avaivartika*) through superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). These two patiences...
The *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) judges that Bodhisattvas obtain these [three non-retrogressions] only after ascending from their seats at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) in successive order.

This meaning should be further investigated in the explanations within the *Sìjiào* (Four Teachings). The *Shìjì* (Record of Explanations) states: "During the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, one horizontally attains the three non-retrogressions;

therefore, when departing from the five obstacles, one maintains all three meanings simultaneously. This means that the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa extends through to the hundred kalpas, and thus encompasses all three types of non-retrogression. Upon reaching this point—
This is because it is called "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). Next, regarding the statement that "six minds" are common [to both teachings], the *Jì* (Record) states:

"In this teaching, there is no distinct stage prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) to discuss; thus, one borrows the names of distinct stages to encompass its own stages, specifically referring to the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*) and above in the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), which enters the stage of 'dry wisdom' (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

Therefore, it is said that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the sixth stage, one is termed "non-retrogression of position. Alternatively, it may refer to the provisional stages prior to the [true] stages.
The establishment of the Seven Sages takes the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) as the sixth mental state.

Although it is said that within the stages of the Hīnayāna this is the "stage of non-retrogression" (*avivartika*), when compared to the Bodhisattva vehicle, it is still termed "retrogression. Some say that the various stages of this teaching have not been clearly established in their sources, and thus they dare not speak of them;

their intention is that because these matters are rare and they have not seen the original sources, they do not dare to speak. Now, I shall address this: *Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "今謂" (Now, I say). A complete translation would require the subsequent argument.*
This is an alternative interpretation by an ancient master; because it accords with this teaching, it is now cited here to correspond to it.

Kaku says that there are four explanations regarding the three stages of non-retrogression (*san-futai*). First, it is said that prior to the ten abodes (*jūjū*), during the first six mental states, provisional understanding has not yet been established, and thus one may retrogress from the bodhicitta to become a follower of the two vehicles (*nishō*).
From the seventh mental state upward, provisional understanding has already been established, and one is therefore named a Bodhisattva.

Regarding the stage of solitary accomplishment (*ekāntika-bhūmi*), there is freedom from these two types of regression. First, "regression of practice" (*caryā-hāni*) occurs from the first stage up to the sixth stage;
herein, when practitioners occasionally fail to progress in their cultivation, it is called regression of practice. At the seventh stage, such regression no longer exists.

However, at this seventh stage, because the habituation of craving may still arise and effort (*prayoga*) is still required, it is called "regression of mindfulness" (*smṛti-hāni*). From the eighth stage upward, one enters the state of non-effort (*anābhoga*).

First, because one employs the Way and is forever free from the three types of regression, it is called "non-regression" (*avaivartika*). Second, the six minds of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) are termed "regression of stage" (*avasthā-vyāvṛtti*);

from the seventh mind upward, it is called "non-regression of stage. The remaining two [types of non-regression] do not differ from the previous explanation. Third, the nature of the seeds of practice (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*) is termed "non-regression of stage";

the nature of the seeds of the Way (*mārga-bīja-gotra*), wherein understanding and practice are fully matured, is termed "non-regression of conduct" (*caryā-avaivartika*); and from the first ground (*bhūmi*) upward, one attains [non-regression].
The patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is called "non-retrogression through mindfulness" because one no longer gives rise to mental activity or discursive thought;

this is the third specific interpretation within the present text, which explains non-retrogression by means of the four [aspects]. Since it is identical [to the previous], it will not be further described here.

Having already presented these four schools, [the author] states: "I now say that since the sutras and śāstras differ, they are difficult to reconcile in detail"; subsequently, he extensively presents the sutras.

In this treatise, I cannot describe all the variations for fear of excessive prolixity. Now I say that these various differing explanations exist solely because the sutras respond to different conditions;

the masters employ them according to their differences, yet none are ultimately able to synthesize them. Although the differing views cited previously are numerous, they ultimately do not transcend the two meanings of the general and the specific.
If one grasps the four points of the present text, then even though they differ, they are easily synthesized. Furthermore, as for the old...
Regarding the four meanings, the first is seemingly specific but is mostly general; the second is a single explanation that corresponds to the general meaning in the present text;

the third and fourth explanations correspond to the specific meanings in the present text. Because the latter master lacked these four points of intent, he said it was difficult to reconcile in detail;

yet if one grasps this intent, it will not be difficult to believe. The text states that "light hair" refers to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) among the external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).
The first six minds, if followed by seven or more, constitute the seventh stage of the Ten Abodes, named the "Abode of Non-retrogression.

This is because it employs the framework of the Ten Abodes to clarify the meaning of the Ten Faiths. According to the accounts of others mentioned previously, one should also say that from the seventh mind upward, one is termed "non-retrogressive in rank," whereas from the first stage (bhūmi) through the sixth stage, one is termed "retrogressive in practice," while the seventh stage is termed "practice" [itself].
Non-retrogression from the eighth stage and above is called "non-retrogression through mindfulness. Here, it is referred to as the "contemplation of the path" (*daoguan*);

this means that the transformation of the path is the contemplation of emptiness (*kongguan*), while the path itself is principle, which is the contemplation of emptiness, and the contemplation of the [sentient] capacity is the contemplation of the provisional (*jiaguan*).

However, among the ten stages of the three vehicles, the eighth is the stage of the *pratyekabuddha*, and it is not yet called "the dual flow. If others say that one enters the state of non-effort (*anābhoga*) here, then—
The "Immovable Ground" (*acalā-bhūmi*) is another name used by other schools; thus, the meanings of both teachings are not established [in this context].
The intended meaning is that one takes the eighth ground and above as the primary reference, which then universally encompasses the sense of the Bodhisattva grounds.

Alternatively, it may be that the intention of the ancients was to correlate the "Ground of Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*) with the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), the "Ten Faiths" (*daśa-śraddhā*) with the stage of nature (*prakṛti-bhūmi*), and the "Eight Persons" (*aṣṭamaka*) and "Second Ground" with the distinct [stages].

The three types of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) within the stage of inner cultivation (adhyātma-pratipannaka) are equated with the stages from the "ground of seeing" (darśana-bhūmi) upward in the separate school (Vijñānavāda), because they correspond to the first ground and so forth up to the eighth immovable ground of effortless practice (*anābhoga*). This is likely what is intended here.

However, this is merely an assertion made by ancient scholars who, failing to recognize the distinctions between the various systems of teaching, sought to forcibly harmonize them; they considered such a synthesis to be a sublime reconciliation.
Now, although it is granted that this also merely represents the three meanings common to the Three Vehicles, it is not the specific intent of this sutra;

rather, it is because the particular [teachings] are employed to establish the general meaning. Although there are slight differences within it, it is called "common" based on the majority of its content.

Next, by attaining realization and merging with the True [Suchness], one leaves behind the four abodes of affliction and no longer remains an ordinary person; therefore, it is designated as the "initial manifestation of realization."
The verification [of this stage] is presented at the beginning; reaching this ground, one will certainly not become a follower of the Two Vehicles.

Therefore, within the practice of this stage, one does not proceed toward the two extremes; only then is there non-retrogression in practice. Having realized the Middle Way, one is not moved by the two extremes;

therefore, there is non-retrogression in mindfulness. To summarize these distinctions: even the "use" (the third stage) is not yet attained, let alone the two preceding stages. This is the interpretation of the Master who distinguishes the persons.
Below, the teaching of the holy scriptures regarding "spontaneous inflow" (svayam-pravṛtti) is examined as having the meaning of non-retrogression;

this comprises three aspects, which apply only when one has reached a high stage and thus represent a distinct [interpretation] rather than the intended meaning here. Next, within the Perfect Teaching (yuan), first, that scripture is cited to clarify the Perfect [nature], followed by a reconciliation of the subtleties of this present scripture.
Third, the intended application of this meaning is concluded. The first [aspect] is the possession of the three bodies (trikāya) and the three wisdoms (trijñāna).
The object and wisdom are merged as one; the three bodies (*trikāya*) abide in their respective positions without regression; the three wisdoms (*trijñāna*) are non-regressive in their activity;
and this merging into one is such that there is no external differentiation, allowing for non-regression in every thought-moment. Because this one is precisely the three, it is "non-retrogressive.
How could there be any further separate meaning of "non-turning" (*avivarta*)? In this regard, what is here taught is the single reality itself, which is also called the "most real."
The "matter" (*shì*) is also called the "one great matter. To speak in summary, these are all different names for the one wondrous matter.

This meaning applies equally from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) upward through the entire bodhisattva rank; it is precisely because this principle is being manifested that no distinction is made. Reflect on this, reflect on this:
it is used as a criterion because it signifies the ultimate transcendence of all relativity (*atyanta-apekṣā*).

Next, regarding "Original and Traces" (*honjaku*), this clarifies the long duration of the non-retrogression of the Perfect [Teaching]. Within this, first is the direct clarification of the Original and the Trace; second is the refutation of various errors.
In the first section, there is first the designation of the Original, which is the wondrous enlightenment of the patience of quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*).

Because it is neither beginning nor end, neither Perfect nor Partial, it is the Original of Quiescence. From the Distinct and Shared [teachings] downward, its traces are clarified; this clarifies the manifestation of the trace.

In the past, the partial and the perfect were treated as identical; now they are distinguished, existing only in the wondrous perfection as previously discussed. [The text] successively refutes those who do not understand the traces, showing four types of distinctions.

Herein, because one takes the single, wondrous, perfect awakening of the present as a distinct interpretation of the general and the specific, it is said that such a person does not recognize [the truth].
They do not even know the number of the wondrous traces of the present, nor can they manifest the wondrous origin of the fundamental; they merely praise what is biased and coarse.
Since these traces [of the teaching] are already present within it, the record states that this single error incurs two faults:
because the sutra contains no mention of the three vehicles, one who wishes to forcibly add them—by suppressing the Perfect and diminishing the Partial—commits a fault no greater than this.

Some say that [the practitioner] was originally at a high stage or even at the ultimate fruit, but because they do not recognize their own fundamental nature, they diminish themselves to a lower stage; this is called "diminution-heresy" (*apavāda*). Since they have added [themselves] to a lower stage...

To name this again as "increasing slander" is what I now mean by "the essence is neither partial nor perfect. The essence is fundamentally neither partial nor perfect; it is only in its manifestations that it shows partiality and perfection.

To speak solely in terms of the partial and the perfect is to lose the essence; to speak solely in terms of the essence and the manifestations is likewise to lose the partial and the perfect. The first interpretation was merely the correct [view of] the manifestations, while the subsequent explanation rested only on the essence.

Even if one were to explain them in relation to one another, I fear it would still not be correct, let alone when one relies exclusively on either the singular [essence] or the singular [manifestations]. Now...

This means that from the beginning, the descent of the trace was intended to manifest the fundamental reality by relying upon the trace; yet now, some do not understand this and take the trace to be the ultimate reality—this is the slander of superimposition (*samāropa*).
Others fail to speak of its fundamental reality—this is the slander of denial (*apavāda*). Furthermore, the provisional was established based on the real, using the partial to manifest the perfect;

yet now, some do not understand this and cling to the provisional as being the ultimate reality—this is the slander of superimposition. Others fail to speak of the actual reality—this is the slander of denial. It is thus.
Now, consider that these two passages can be understood independently; reflect upon this, reflect upon it. The intent of the sutra is to manifest the fundamental by relying on its traces.
For instance, the introduction clearly states that Mañjuśrī’s path of transformation has been long-distant; he is the disciple of the ninth-generation patriarch of Śākyamuni Buddha.

If one individual has already been established as long-distant, how much more so for those of even more remote generations? Since this is the case for one, the same principle applies to all others. Furthermore—
If even the śrāvakas manifest the inconceivable fundamental [nature], how much more so the bodhisattvas?

Thus we know that while the fundamental is universally wondrous and the traces are shown as either partial or complete, upon arriving at this assembly, they are entirely of one flavor. Since the partial and the complete are employed specifically without speaking of their fundamental or traced aspects, what further could there be of increase or decrease?

Next, the explanation of "contemplation" (*guan*) is presented by way of three meanings—clarity, mystery, and wondrousness—pertaining to one's own mind. First, these three are explained because their wondrousness has not yet been manifested;
therefore, below, they are further discussed in relation to the single mind (*ekacitta*) in order to reveal that wondrousness. The sequence of these numerical meanings can be understood accordingly.

Although [the nature] is fundamentally and inherently such, one does not know it oneself; thus, this teaching is now shown so that one may come to know it. Fundamentally, it is the clarity of nature; knowing it is the realization of suchness.
The "one cultivation of nature" (*xing-yi-xiu*) and the "five cultivations" (*wu-xiu*) combined constitute six; if one does not understand this, it remains a coarse and general [explanation].
This is because the intention is to manifest that these exist, hence the commentary states "[and so forth].
Next, the explanation of the "praise of virtues" (*tan-de*) clarifies the merits possessed within this stage. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* says:
For what reason is the merit of the bodhisattvas praised? It is for the purpose of causing sentient beings to abandon thoughts of contempt.
Thus it is said: "The assembly of śrāvakas has long practiced the holy life; the assembly of bodhisattvas should be revered. Furthermore, it is to cause sentient beings to give rise to pure faith:
"If even the bodhisattvas possess such merit, how much more so the Tathāgata? Within this, there is skillful means.

The two meanings of "treatment" (*cikitset*) should likewise each possess four aspects. Since one has already praised the śrāvakas and now aspires to hear of the bodhisattvas' merits, this arouses joy;
and because one awakens to the Path by means of such praise, it thus possesses all four. Others have explained the intent of this praise at length, which I cannot recount in full here.
In the text, first the boundaries of the sections are established according to the traditional scholastic divisions (*pūrvapakṣa*), and next the actual [exegesis] begins.

Regarding the resolution of the intentions of the ancient masters of both the earlier and later periods: their texts contain two directions, yet they capture only one and do not exhaust the full meaning of the text.

Now, by establishing these two directions, we manifest the two intended meanings. Furthermore, there are two further aspects—namely, whether this refers to the "stage" (*avasthā*) or the "eulogy," and whether it is "general" (*sāmānya*) or "particular" (*viśeṣa*).
Only when these are fully accounted for in accordance with the sutra and its commentaries, and when they accord with the nature of the preceding text, can it be considered truly excellent.

From here below is the formal commentary and explanation, which consists of three parts: first, the presentation of the ancient interpretation; second, the refutation of it; third, the formal explanation itself.

Regarding the initial statement of "twelve phrases," this is because the general is established based upon the particular; the text merely provides a brief outline of its topical divisions (*koṭa*), while the meaning of the structural analysis is implicitly contained therein.
First, the presentation of the major divisions is fourfold, which also reveals the sense of the general and the particular. This refers to Master Zang’s major divisions.

Regarding the four intentions, they are the same as this [previous section], though there are slight differences in wording: "practice" (*xing*) is changed to "cause" (*yin*), and "internal" (*nei*) is changed to "substantial" (*shi*).
The fourth is named for the sake of "beauty" (*mei*) and "reputation" (*yu*); thus, the meaning does not differ from this. Most of these are the interpretations of Guangzhai.

As for the reason why the four names therein should be understood according to the text, they are easily known. Regarding the phrase "the four intentions, etc.," it is used to resolve doubts and complete the preceding discussion of the general and specific [meanings].
Master Yi praises the virtues as being distinguished into these four categories; since virtue is placed first, citing the beginning encompasses the subsequent ones.
Master Ji says that the first praises both cause and effect, while the latter praises both essence and name, thus briefly encompassing the merits of a bodhisattva.
Next, he further elaborates by dividing the preceding four into ten, which also possesses its own significance; within this, one should simply follow the text of the sūtra.

Since the details would become too numerous, I shall not further describe how the Master of the Tripiṭaka (Vasubandhu) divides each of the four previously mentioned categories into two, resulting in eight sections in total;
as these variations are merely minor and do not constitute the essential points, there is no need to recount them further.
The above concludes the account of differences; what follows below is the discernment of errors, clarifying that their meaning is not to be employed.

The reason for this is as follows: herein, first there is a general concession followed by a refutation; next, there is a critique that challenges the concessions. While the textual divisions (kēwén) are distinct, the refutations address the underlying meanings (yìyì).
Although the texts may be broadly categorized and explained, the meanings may diverge; if one does not understand this, one will fail to reach a convergence of understanding.

For what reason is it not permissible? Furthermore, "granting" means to allow the topical division (*ko-p'an*) of the passage as it stands; "seizing" means to refute its deviation from the preceding meaning.

To speak of "eyebrows and eyes" is because nothing surpasses these two in representing the beauty of a countenance; likewise, the metaphor of the "two-layered topical division" suggests that the text is exceptionally beautiful.
Yet, when one exhaustively examines its underlying intent (*tzu*), there is ultimately nowhere for it to lead—it merely possesses a general applicability.
This is because their words are merely superficial and ultimately lack any concrete reality. Regarding the claim that there is no "essence" (*tīti*) or "substance" (*tāi*), the *Jì* states:
"That which is the basis of a position is called the 'basis of the position' (*wèiběn*); this 'basis' is itself the essence, and the 'position' is the thesis. Others say:

"The thesis (*zōng*) refers to that which is the primary focus of the meaning; this thesis is the essence. Upon examining these notions of thesis and essence, they are entirely contrary to the intent of the various teachings. Therefore, [they are rejected].

It is said that there is no "tending toward" (*qùxiàng*). Now, it is held that "principle" (*zōng*) has the meaning of "tending toward," for it is that which can tend toward; "essence" (*tǐ*) is that which is tended toward.
Although one may thus analyze and explain the text in this way, one does not know where the ultimate destination of its meaning lies;

because it lacks any definitive reality, it is said to be "different. The first two characters, "principle" and "essence," speak separately of the subject (*néng*) and the object (*suǒ*), while the following phrase combines them.
Regarding the statement that "the subject and object are combined" and "the subject and object are appropriate," one should reflect well upon this;

it is a refutation of the three teachings from below, establishing the meaning of their absolute difference. First, these three meanings are used to demonstrate that they are not the tenets of this teaching.

Second, these two meanings clarify that the tenets of this teaching are not established. Third, it shows that they contradict the single meaning [of this teaching], and therefore [the former] cannot [be accepted].

This meaning is presented here because it was already manifested in the preceding text during the explanation of the meaning of the "stages" (*avasthā*). Whether one advances or retreats, the reasons for not employing [these stages] are clearly established:

advancing does not constitute the Perfect [Teaching], and retreating does not constitute the Separate [Teaching]; neither accords with the truth, which is precisely what was previously termed the "absence of a fundamental essence" (*mūlatattva*).
Even if they were to apply to all three [teachings], they would still not accord with the intent of this sutra; therefore, they are not employed.
From this point downward is the third section, the formal explanation. Within it, there are four parts: first, the presentation of the basis and the method of explanation;

second, the detailed exposition of the reasons for its meaning; third, the actual word-by-word commentary; and fourth, the citation of treatises to establish what was previously stated. Regarding the "thirteen phrases" mentioned earlier:

because the previous [section] dealt with others from specific perspectives, there were twelve; now, as it includes both the general and the specific, it is said to be thirteen. Thus, they are made thirteen.
"Horizontal and vertical" refers to the method upon which this text relies for its exposition. The following two phrases explain the reason for employing these two methods of interpretation.
This contains three points: first, what constitutes the "vertical," which refers to the ten stages (*bhūmi*);
second, what constitutes the "horizontal," which refers to the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*); and third, why the ten stages are called "vertical."

Because there is a sequence of shallow and deep stages, why is the first dwelling (prathamā-bhūmi) called "horizontal" (*tiryak*)? It is because all meanings are suddenly and simultaneously prepared therein.

Why is it explained by means of such horizontal and vertical [distinctions]? It is because each is convenient according to the specific textual meaning. How is it that this convenience of meaning precisely accords with the textual meaning?

Furthermore, by citing the partial and gradual [teachings], one intends to title [the work] after the complete and sudden (*yuganaddha*). This is merely the intent of the various ancient and modern commentaries.

This meaning of sequential progression is not the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden; therefore, it is precisely for the purpose of titling this sutra that it serves as the meaning of "opening and merging.
It may also be combined with the two meanings within the treatise, as the second meaning is contained within the third.
Thus, the term "meaning" (義) conveniently encompasses multiple senses, which should be carefully examined. For this reason, the explanation is provided by means of these two methods. Below is...
The third section, the formal explanation, has two distinct parts. First, regarding the vertical progression (*ūrdhva-madhya*), there are further two sub-sections:

first, the formal explanation; second, the summary that clarifies its intent. Within the formal explanation, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) each have ten distinct points, and each contains three meanings:

namely, citing the text, correlating it [with the principle], explaining the reason for this, and concluding by establishing the meaning. Although the text may occasionally lack explicit wording, the meaning is always present.

The first [section] correctly uses the three characters "non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*) to correspond to the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*). Below the name of the First Ground, the following explains the reason for its designation.
Within this, it first presents the name of the ground and then clarifies its meaning. The "New Translation" calls it the "Ground of Supreme Joy" (*pramuditā bhūmi*);

as for its meaning, it refers to the initial attainment of the nature of a noble one (*ārya*), because one has severed the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and attained the nature of a noble one. Now, this [text] correctly employs the terminology of this very sutra.
The text clarifies its meaning without contradiction and does not fall into the two extremes; it severs the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and enables entry into the Middle Way.
Thus, one attains the nature of a noble one (*ārya*). Speaking in terms of completeness, this refers to being initially free from the three faults and obtaining the three virtues;
extreme joy and delight arise precisely because one has attained non-retrogression for the first time. By this principle, one should know for certain that this is so.
The phrase praises the virtues of the first bhūmi. Next, in the explanation of the second bhūmi, its name is likewise presented first.
Regarding this name, the "new" (modern) interpretation states that it is called the *Vimalā-bhūmi* (Stainless Ground) because one is able to abandon the stains of subtle transgressions.

Now, I say that this is so because this ground is contrasted with the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). If we follow this same logic, the preceding [ground] should have been called the "Able-to-Abandon" ground.

Because it is free from the stain of stinginess in contrast to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), although this was not explicitly stated in the preceding text, the meaning is nonetheless fully present;

for being free from the two extremes and the three types of regression is precisely the meaning of relinquishment (*tyāga*). Since the precepts possess both the aspects of restraint (*saṃvara*) and active cultivation (*pravṛtti*), they share the same two meanings as the dhāraṇī.

Thus, one should know that this phrase praises the virtues of the second bhūmi. Next, the third is named "The Radiant" (*Prabhākari*); the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states: "It is called 'The Radiant' because of the arising of the light of wisdom."

"Ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to that which can accomplish the great dharmas of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and total retention (*dhāraṇī*), and can give rise to the light of boundless, wondrous wisdom.
Now, according to this text, the meaning is revealed by means of the external based on the internal; furthermore, it is cited as proof that the internal is known through the external.

This "new and old" [distinction] seems to derive its name from the internal essence (*svabhāva*). Since the Sūtra cites the external function precisely because of the internal essence, one perceives the capacity for external function through the external.
Regarding the statement "explaining knowledge of the internal, knowledge of clarity," the following commentary explains the specific intent behind mentioning "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*).

To clarify that internal wisdom is profoundly clear, it states that "speech has various kinds," which distinguishes the four types of eloquence: namely, *dharma-pratibhāna*, *artha-pratibhāna*, *nirukti-pratibhāna*, and *pratibhāna-pratibhāna*.

Since *pratibhāna-pratibhāna* (eloquence regarding eloquence) is the last, it is capable of explaining the preceding three; therefore, it is called "various. Because it can encompass the previous three, it is called "supreme."
The *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* states that while there are various kinds of *pratibhāna* (eloquence), the term "discourse" (*vyavahāra*) is somewhat difficult to comprehend;

it is explained as follows. Regarding what is called "joyful discourse" (*pratibhāna*), there are two meanings: first, because one takes joy in speaking for the sake of others based on the Dharma attained by oneself;

second, because one speaks for their sake according to their inclination to hear. Since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* contains these two meanings, it is termed "joyful discourse. Some say that *pratibhāna* is simply—

Regarding the four types of discrimination (*pratibhāna*), there are both general and specific distinctions. When these are clearly distinguished according to their respective objects, all four are termed "discrimination. To be clear when in the eye is called "clarity" (*prakāśa*);

to be acute when in the ear is called "sharpness" (*paṭu*); to be wise when in the mind is called "insight" (*jñāna*); and to be discerning when in the four [senses] is called "discrimination. This is the specific sense of discrimination.

To respond with speed to the capacities of beings is called "discrimination"; to possess the brilliance of phrasing and literary elegance is called "talent" (*pratibhāna*). It is also said that to speak without stammering or haste when addressing the capacities of beings is what is meant by "discrimination within the midst of capacities."

Regarding the principle of *pratibhāna* (eloquence), there are references to "fourfold eloquence" and "sevenfold eloquence. As for the fourfold, the new [translation] calls them the "four *pratisaṃvid*s" (unimpeded analytical knowledges);

the first three names are identical [to the old], while the fourth is simply called "unimpeded eloquence in preaching" (*dharmapratisaṃvid*). Regarding the sevenfold eloquence: first, "swift eloquence," because speech is immediate and free from stammering or obstruction;
second, "rapid eloquence," because it is neither slow nor hesitant; third, "timely eloquence," because it neither exceeds nor falls short of the occasion.

Therefore, it is (4) free from error, for whatever is spoken accords with reality and is without mistake; (5) it is inexhaustible, for its continuity is like a linked chain that never comes to an end;
(6) it is rich in meaning and eloquent, for every single word and phrase possesses both the conventional and ultimate truths;
and (7) it is the most supreme and wondrous eloquence among all worlds, being profoundly deep, resonant as thunder, clear, and far-reaching.
Because there are five kinds of sounds, such as those heard [by the ear] and so forth, it is now said that these seven, when compared to the preceding four, are all subsumed within the fourth.
Furthermore, the statement that "there are various kinds" refers generally to all seven, while the statement that "the musical sound is most excellent" specifically refers to the seventh;
this is not the case. This passage is difficult to interpret—reflect upon it, reflect upon it! To summarize: "discernment" (*bian*) means clarity, and "talent" (*cai*) means capability.

This phrase is correctly interpreted as such because it clarifies the meaning of the "Stage of Manifest Wisdom" (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*) by elucidating its discernment and capacity for correct understanding.

The fourth stage is newly termed the "Blazing Wisdom Stage" (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), so called because one dwells in the most excellent factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and the flames of wisdom increase, thereby burning the fuel of afflictions.
In this text, the meaning of this stage is first clarified in two parts: first, the explanation of the stage’s significance; second, a reconciliation with the scriptural passage.

Since the meaning is identical, it is certain that this phrase refers to that ground. Regarding the meaning of the "Wheel of Dharma," as explained later, the fifth ground shares the same name in both the new and old translations.

As for the meaning of the "new" [translation], it states that while in the preceding grounds one contemplates the ultimate and the conventional separately, in this ground alone the ultimate and the conventional are reflected upon simultaneously;
because this simultaneous reflection is superior to the former, it is called "Extremely Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*). As for the explanation in the present text, regarding this ground...

Because it is precisely the perfection of dhyāna, it is said to "attain the name of meditative concentration" (*dhyāna-samādhi*). This is named according to its function; the Sūtra speaks of its essence as well, which refers to its state of being difficult to surpass.
It is named here from the function of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), whereas it is designated by the function of concentration (*samādhi*) in this context.

Since it possesses many meanings, each statement expresses only one aspect. For this reason, it is known that this phrase refers to this stage [the Fourth Ground]. As for the matter of making offerings:
The meaning is as follows: regarding the sixth bhūmi, where the new and old names are identical in meaning, the treatise states:

"Because the wisdom of dependent origination abides and draws forth the most excellent non-conceptual prajñā, which now manifests before one. This means that by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, there is the most excellent contemplation;
because it is neither defiled nor pure, it is called "non-conceptual. The intent of the present text is that since merit serves as the support for wisdom, this [wisdom] is manifest.

This is easy to understand. The meaning of "the root of virtue" (*kuśalamūla*) will be explained later. Next, regarding the new name for the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), it shares the same phonetic sound;

it is pronounced either level (*ping*) or departing (*qu*), but is mostly called by the departing tone. The *Śāstra* states that because one reaches the limit of effort at the stage of signlessness (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*), one transcends the worldly path of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
Thus, the sixth stage and below are characterized by signs (*sanimitta*), whereas the seventh stage is signless (*animitta*) and is also characterized by effort (*prayoga*).
Regarding "the ultimate": this refers to reaching the final consummation of one's spiritual effort; thus, it is called "the ultimate.

The present text says "transcending," meaning that one transcends both the mundane world and the paths of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). Because one can initiate practice within emptiness, it is said to "transcend.

The preceding phrase explains the name of the stage (*bhūmi*), while the subsequent phrase harmonizes the meaning of the present text: that self-benefit and benefit for others are profound, and thus they accord with the Buddha.
Because of the mind, it is praised by the Buddha; furthermore, since this stage corresponds to the *upāya-pāramitā*, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
As for the term "constant," it means that its practice is always thus. For this reason, one knows that this phrase is a praise of this stage.

Next, regarding the eighth stage, its new name is no different [from the previous]. The *Treatise* says: "Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) continues spontaneously; its characteristics and functions..."

Because afflictions cannot disturb it, its "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refer to its marks and its "function" (vṁśa) refers to its efficacy; since these characteristics and functions cannot disturb the mind, it is called "immovable.
In the text, the first part explains the meaning of the "ground" (*bhūmi*): "correct wisdom" (*samyag-jñāna*) is precisely the aforementioned non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*).
For this reason, it cannot be moved or displaced. The phrase "but merely by... and following explains the present passage: [the Buddha] moves by means of objectless compassion (*apraṇihitā maitrī*).

Third, because benefiting sentient beings involves movement yet is non-movement, it embodies the meaning of immovability. Although the text mentions only the movement of the body, it already encompasses these three meanings;
how much more so when they are explicitly explained in full! For this reason, we know with certainty that this phrase praises this stage.

Furthermore, the name for the ninth stage is no different from its new designation; as the *Treatise* says: "One achieves the subtle and wondrous four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), which can pervade the ten directions."
Because he skillfully expounds the Dharma, it is called "Excellent Wisdom" (*suvijñā*); Bandhuprabha says that because this wisdom is wondrously excellent, it is named "Excellent Wisdom.

An-hui says it refers to the realization of the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), for this knowledge is the most supreme wisdom, which is precisely what is meant by "wisdom. In the text, "profoundly entering" means to penetrate wondrously;

"thoroughly penetrating" explains the skillful entry into the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); and "original source" explains the Buddha-wisdom. Both of these refer to the ultimate realm of the Buddha-wisdom.

Because it is also capable of doing so, it is called "skillful" (*kuśala*). Regarding the phrase "most appropriate," since two characters therein are identical, the *Śāstra* explains only "skillful wisdom" (*kuśala-prajñā*).
While the term "entry" (*praveśa*) is here interpreted in terms of oneself and others, for the sake of this [verse], it is treated as self-realization;

however, the meaning of "skillfully entering" applies to both self and others, and thus they are one. "Thorough" (*cheda*) means penetrating understanding. For these reasons, it is known that this phrase is a praise.

This section now explains the three phrases below, which involve both separation and synthesis. "Synthesis" refers to the entirety of the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*), while "separation" refers to the final two [phrases] in relation to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Regarding the first phrase: there is a name that possesses both a designation and a meaning, where the name and the meaning coincide.

The treatise states: 1. The great dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) is like a cloud containing the waters of manifold virtues; 2. "Obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) is like space, and the "coarse heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) is called the "cloud"; 3. It is "fully pervading."
Because the Dharma-body is like a cloud pouring down water, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Having attained the Great Dharma-body, one possesses complete mastery;
on the Dharma-cloud stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one is like a cloud that pervades everywhere, for like a crown prince, one has attained sovereignty. Asamga says:

"By attaining all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and taking all teachings as its object, it does not depart from True Suchness (*tathatā*); the knowledge of all phenomena is like a great cloud of *dhāraṇī*."
The doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) and the doors of meditative concentration (*samādhimukha*) are like pure water; wisdom (*jñāna*) is able to store them within, just as clouds hold water.
Furthermore, it is like a great cloud covering and obscuring space; wisdom is like that cloud, covering and obscuring coarse hindrances.
Moreover, it is like a great cloud pouring down pure water that fills space; this wisdom gives rise to all merits and fills the *dharmakāya*. Contemplate what has been explained here.
It appears that the name "Dharmameghā-bhūmi" (Cloud of Dharma Stage) possesses four meanings; however, in this passage, only three meanings are employed, and these are illustrated by three analogies:

clouds depend upon space, they provide shade and protection, and they contain and sustain rain. These serve as metaphors for the three virtues of the Dharmakāya—namely, the Dharma-body itself, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Next, regarding the two characters *hui* (convergence) and *zhi* (meeting), worldly exegesis holds that these two characters have many meanings, yet there is also [a sense in which] they are identical.
There is a different interpretation of this single point: that the essence itself gives rise to its function, which is both self-originated and other-originated.
The term "mutually cited" (*huju*) indicates their equality. The name is established based on three meanings; the present text cites one of these three, yet it inherently possesses all three.
For this reason, it should be understood that this is a praise of the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*).
The following two sections clarify the internal and external virtues; what precedes was the general overview, while this section below provides the specific details.

That is to say, the Way of the Three Truths is named the "other shore" (*pāra*), and its ultimate realization is named "reaching" (*gata*). Since these praises are made while still at the causal stage of a Bodhisattva, the latter two meanings are used to explain them.
Now, it is said that this is the tenth pair concerning the *jñāna-pāramitā* (perfection of wisdom): the first phrase is "wisdom," and next—
The phrase "the other shore is the pāramitā" precisely clarifies this meaning; therefore, these words correspond exactly to the textual meaning of the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), which is clearly evident.
Regarding the expression "inner and outer are in accord," this means that name and reality do not differ.

As for "in relation to Equal Enlightenment" (*samyaksambodhi*), the title "Bodhisattva" extends even to Equal Enlightenment, and this stage is also called the "Stainless Stage" (*vimalā-bhūmi*). This is indeed present in the *Mūla-karma* [Sūtra].
Since the *Renwang bu li jing* (The Benevolent King’s Scripture on Non-Establishment) is not definitive, both the progressive and regressive approaches are acceptable here.

Regarding the "remaining stages," they may be nine or ten, depending on whether two positions are added or subtracted; this is because these positions are most excellent for the utilization of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).
The meaning of these ten stages is as extensive as the numerous explanations found in the *Benye jing* (Scripture of Original Action); I shall now provide a brief commentary.
This passage cannot be fully understood [without further context].
From the various stages (*bhūmi*) downward, the meaning of the vertical explanation is clarified again because this sutra represents the perfect stage; thus, all possess the manifold merits.
As for these "manifold merits," each and every one is endowed with the thirteenfold meanings. This is because they take the wondrous essence of the Middle Way as their basis.

This is why, while each [of the ten stages] now presents one specific meaning and omits the remaining twelve meanings, we know that this "appearing and disappearing" within the commentary is intended to highlight three points of distinction.
This refers to the method of sequential differentiation (*pṛthak-bheda*). Both ancient and modern masters have favored this mode of explanation;
thus, even here, in order to accord with human sentiment amidst non-differentiation, I likewise provide this explanation, just as was done for the *Daśabhūmika*.

In the sutras, the ten perfections are established in correspondence with these; this also accords with human sentiment. For now, I have merely borrowed the wondrous Way to follow human sentiments as a provisional approach;

it does not yet exhaust the ultimate principle. Therefore, "conforming to sentiment" is termed "expediency" (*upāya*); as stated previously, "expediency of meaning" clarifies that both the text and the meaning are in accord.
This is just as in the text, where names or meanings correspond to the explanations found in the sutras and śāstras.

Because all [the aspects] correspond, and because it is easier to illustrate the difficult by citing [the easy], and because they are treated individually, the single character "one" (一) from above permeates these three.
For the sake of these three meanings, this one type of principle is employed to explain and resolve the text.
Next, regarding the horizontal [perspective], there are four sections: first, the dual presentation; second, the dual explanation; third, the dual proof; fourth, the dual analysis.
The error regarding the "Five-Seeking" (Wǔxún) treatise has not yet been reconciled in the correct interpretation of the fourth section of the analysis.

At another time, during our deliberations, we shall cite the explanations from that treatise to provide a dual interpretation of the first two meanings. Regarding the first [of these], it first establishes the initial stage (*ādikarmika-bhūmi*) and then, by analogy, reveals the remaining stages.

As for the phrase "directly concerning," etc., "horizontal" (*heng*) signifies the meaning of perfect completeness; "directly" means that within the single stage of the initial dwelling (*prathama-bhūmi*), one already possesses all thirteen [stages].
Regarding the phrase "by way of the meaning of the term, one cites other stages," this refers to the two stages above up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

Next, in the double explanation, first the transverse characteristics of the initial dwelling are clarified, followed by the explanation of the transverse characteristics cited for the other stages. Within the first part, there are two sections:

first, the commentary on the present text; second, the elucidation of the broad meaning. Within the first section, there are thirteen phrases. Within these, there are three meanings, the first of which is the explanation of "arousing" (*utpāda*).
The meaning of the mind abiding: this mind is explained below according to the text. Regarding the meaning of non-retrogression, there are three points for concluding [the section].
As for why this name is explained first: among the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*), the very first is named the Abiding of the Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*);

it is precisely the principal subject here, and because it is the general [foundation], its meaning must be explained first. The remaining phrases below all belong to this [section], and thus the first four [points] are not discussed further.
The five characters following the title explain the meaning of "development" (*fa*). This refers to abiding in the true stage and developing it;
it does not mean that "development" consists of establishing one's resolve by taking an object as a condition. First, regarding the general statement:
when the single true mind develops, all true merits are fully developed. This should be understood according to the explanations provided in other passages.
To summarize, it is simply because these three virtues encompass all things. This phrase serves as the foundation for the various subsequent phrases.
First, the explanation of their names serves as the basis for the following explanations of "transcending faults" and so forth.

The explanation of "separating from the ordinary and surpassing the holy" establishes the meaning of "surpassing the two extremes" mentioned above. The phrase "entering the Middle Way" precisely clarifies the meaning of "abiding," as stated in the Sūtra.

The phrase "entering the principle" (*praveśa-tattva*) refers to *prajñā*, which signifies abiding; that is, entering the wondrous principle of the Middle Way. The above explains the meaning of the "Abiding of the Arousing of the Mind" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*).
The section beginning with "his mind" (*tasya cittaṃ*) below serves to harmonize with the meaning of "non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*) in the present text.
In this stage, one is able to personally enter the ocean of all-aspect wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*); for this reason, it is called "non-retrogression. This...
It is called "Dhāraṇī" (Total Retention), also translated as "Obstructing and Holding. This first stage is able to obstruct the three delusions and hold the three virtues;
it is precisely because this capacity exists in this stage that it is said one "attains Dhāraṇī. The meaning of Dhāraṇī is explained extensively in the subsequent text.
Next, by citing a semblance to illustrate the reality, it is shown that this stage further possesses this attainment. [This concludes the section on] Eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
The meaning of this has been briefly explained above; in other sutras and treatises, there are similar explanations, though most other texts focus on the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).

In the *Avataṃsaka*, however, there is this specific textual passage. Here, we bring together and reveal the perfect, wondrous, and non-local nature; thus it is said to be the "actual place" and the "place of actuality. This actual place is the wondrous essence and the wondrous vow.
One should know that while its own essence is non-local, its manifestation through other conditions is likewise non-local. It should be understood as being without direction or location.

It is also said that "turning" (*vartana*) is the act itself, and the Dharma taught is the wheel (*cakra*). Regarding the term "Dharma-wheel" (*dharmacakra*), the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha stated that there are three kinds of wheels:
the military wheel, the wealth wheel, and the Dharma wheel. The military wheel refers to the fourfold army consisting of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry.

The wealth wheel refers to the four types of wheels—gold, silver, copper, and iron—employed by the four classes of Wheel-Turning Kings (*cakravartin*). The Dharma wheel, however, belongs to the Buddha.
It is that which the Dharma King employs; in contrast to the two wheels of the army and wealth, it is called the "Dharma Wheel" (*dharmacakra*).
Furthermore, regarding the term "non-retrogression," the True Truth (*tattva*) is also spoken of. It is said that there are three wheels of the Dharma: namely, turning, illuminating, and maintaining.

"Turning" refers to the Four Āgamas of the Deer Park; "illuminating" refers to the various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras; and "maintaining" refers to the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and others. These are also termed the Small Vehicle and the Great Vehicle, respectively.
Because the small vehicle is broken to become the great, there is regression; because the great is broken into one, that breaking also involves regression;

but because the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) cannot be broken, it is called "non-regressive. It is for this reason that these present Bodhisattvas are said to turn the non-regressive wheel of the One Vehicle.

Regarding the names of the three wheels of Dharma: the names of the three wheels appear in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, while the turning of them at three times appears in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
The *Tou jing* (now known as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*) has a separate commentary by Paramārtha titled the *Yìzhāng* that provides an extensive explanation.

Regarding the meaning of "non-retrogression" elucidated by our own school, there are four types, as previously explained; the textual meaning is clear. Now, all bodhisattvas are generally able to transform these four types.
However, since this sutra specifically discusses only the single type of "perfectly subtle" [non-retrogression], both [the general and specific meanings] are opened up here.
Since all things are realized as being free from dependence and external to themselves, with no further phenomena existing outside this, how could there be any ground for regression?

Therefore, it is said that one "turns the non-regressive wheel. As the subsequent text states, "turning the unsurpassed Dharma-wheel," and further, "now again turning the most wondrous, unsurpassed, great Dharma-wheel"—this is precisely its meaning. Furthermore, the second [type of] offering also possesses these virtues. II.

The phrase "the sentence is itself the essence and function" refers to the three pairs of meanings: attaining the wondrous essence of meditative concentration internally while being able to employ wondrous functions externally;
and the internal and external aspects of essence and function regarding principle and phenomena. Attaining this path within arises from the power of the Buddha;

because one seeks to repay his kindness externally, one offers worship and service. "Service" is synonymous with "worship," meaning the respectful compliance of the three karmas. This is because the Buddha is all-encompassing.
The true spiritual friend has now attained this wondrous path; therefore, one makes offerings.

The reason one is able to make universal offerings is that, internally, one possesses great meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and great power of meditation, thereby enabling one to universally offer to all at once.
Others say that "offering" refers either to material wealth, the Dharma, or the three types of action (*trikarma*); in total, these are called offerings. Some say that "offering" means...
The practice of making offerings has three aspects: being able to uphold, being able to practice, and being able to explain.

Because these three can bring joy to the Buddha, they constitute true offering. Therefore, when the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, humans and devas made offerings to him, and the Buddha said:
"Ānanda, this offering is not the foremost. There are three kinds of people in the world who can truly offer to me: those who can uphold, those who can protect the True Dharma..."
One who can practice the Dharma protects the true meaning (*artha*), and one who can expound it protects the true Dharma (*dharma*) and the true meaning.
This is the foremost offering, which accords with the intention of the Tathāgata and causes the Tathāgata to rejoice; this is called the true offering.
There are further extensive explanations, but they cannot be fully recounted here. Furthermore, it is said that there are ten kinds of offerings according to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
1. Offering in the presence: making offerings directly before the Śarīras of the present Buddha, Caityas, and all other members of the Triple Gem;
2. Offering in the absence: performing offerings in the absence of others by conceiving of other Buddhas and their Caityas as being the Buddha himself;
3. Offering both in the presence and in the absence: when one is currently facing [the object of worship].

Later, he formed this thought: "Because the dharma-nature of the reliquary (caitya) of one Buddha is the very same dharma-nature as the reliquaries of all Buddhas of the three times and ten directions, my present offering to the reliquary of one Buddha is itself an offering to the reliquaries of all Buddhas of the three times and ten directions.
Thus, he cultivated the practice of making offerings both to those present before him and to those not present before him. Fourth, regarding the Tathāgata...

1. This refers to making offerings based on one's own resources (sva-pūjā). 2. If one gives rise to a compassionate heart and gives whatever items one can afford to those who are poor and suffering, wishing for their peace and happiness, this is called "offering through emulation" (anupūjā).
3. When one performs an offering oneself and further exhorts and instructs others to do so, this is called "joint offering" (sahapūjā).
4. Material and reverential offering (lābha-satkāra-pūjā) consists of offering flowers, incense, and so forth, as well as respectful greetings, prostrations, and even precious gems.
The eight vast offerings consisting of material wealth and reverential service— namely, making offerings of material wealth and reverence over a long period of many kalpas,
dedicating them toward enlightenment with a pure mind, gathering wealth through one's own efforts and seeking it from others, and making vows and visualizations—
result in manifesting hundreds of thousands of bodies to perform respectful prostrations, and each transformed body emanates hundreds of thousands of hands holding flowers to scatter.
With hundreds of thousands of voices, they sing praises of their true virtues and further produce hundreds of thousands of exquisite ornaments as offerings.
They universally rejoice in all offerings made throughout Jambudvīpa and the ten directions;
though employing little effort, they perform boundless and vast offerings. These nine untainted offerings are free from contempt, hypocrisy, and negligence.
One practices undefiled offerings with impure objects and so forth through the ten types of correct practice.

If necessary, one further cultivates the four immeasurables, up to a brief period of dwelling in non-conceptualization within the ineffable true nature (*dharmatā*) of *tathatā*, having attained faith and patience;
this constitutes the guarding of the pure bodhisattva precepts and the cultivation of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and so on.
When performing offerings, one should reflect that this is the most supreme and wondrous, surpassing previous offerings by hundreds of thousands of millions of times beyond all comparison.
One should correspondingly contemplate the ten meanings as found in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (Treatise on the Holding of the Ground), as follows.

When practicing offerings according to the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*, one should reflect that the Tathāgata is a great field of merit, possesses great benevolent virtue, is difficult to surpass, and uniquely transcends all others.

As it is with the Buddha, so it is with the Dharma and the Sangha (as explained extensively in the "Praise on the Upper Section" and the "Nurturing in the Middle Section" of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*). Regarding offerings, there are no more than two kinds:

first, material offerings; second, Dharma offerings. As stated in the "Chapter on Dharma Offerings" of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, material offerings consist of the three types of action (*trikarma*), the four requisites (*catuḥpariṣkāra*), and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
These [Dharma offerings] are of four kinds: first, following the Buddha’s instructions and commands to propagate and transmit the Buddha’s teachings.
The first is the offering of Dharma, which consists of teaching the Dharma for the benefit of all;

the second is the offering through ritual action, which refers to the offering of Dharma as described in the sutras—performing mudrās, reciting mantras, and visualizing sublime objects as the offering of Dharma;
the third is the offering in accordance with the Dharma, meaning that each and every aforementioned offering is performed without contradicting the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
To practice in accordance with the Dharma is called the supreme offering; furthermore, because all offerings performed are for the sake of the Dharma, they are termed "Dharma-offerings.
Among these seven types of offerings, the latter two are the most excellent. Regarding those not yet mentioned, one should reflect upon what is most essential:
that within each and every specific matter, throughout the course of practice, there is the principle of reality—the true mark of suchness.

This means that, for instance, the burning of one's body by Bhaiṣajyarāja is called the "true Dharma-offering" (dharmapūjā), and the inexhaustible offering of jewels is called "Dharma-giving" (dharmadāna);
such is their meaning. If one wishes to understand the meaning of these matters, it is as explained at the beginning of the separate introduction [to this chapter].

If one wishes to understand the meaning of the practice of the Dharma, it is as described in the *Ratnakoṭi-parivarta* regarding the five kinds of offerings for the propagation of the sutra to all beings. Thus, when the matter is identical to the principle, it is as in the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*.
In the "Universal Gate" (Pumen) chapter, the offering to all Buddhas is explained as being the most essential and subtle; since this will be made manifest in the subsequent text, it is omitted here.
Next, it clarifies that one is further able to possess the root of all virtues. What was previously called "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is here termed "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
To speak according to the actual substance: wisdom arises in dependence upon the object; while wisdom belongs to the various virtues, true reality is the fundamental planter of the seeds.

Furthermore, at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), the principle of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is manifested and all virtues are fully prepared; this is what is meant by "planting," not that seeds are being sown for the first time.

This is as explained previously regarding the meaning of the "Stage of Resolving the Mind" (*cittotpāda-bhūmi*). Moreover, if while making offerings one further hears the Dharma and one's wisdom becomes increasingly clear, this constitutes planting new roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*).
Regarding this, it is said that "virtue" refers to the three virtues: namely, wisdom (*jñāna*), severance (*prahāṇa*), and [the nature of] the dharma (*dharmatā*).

The "Original Gratitude" refers to the three causes, namely that which should be attained and so forth, as set forth elsewhere. Furthermore, my current intention is as follows: next, regarding the praise, there are also these merits.

Originally, the Buddha merely intended for [beings] to attain the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; now that they have attained it, he praises them in accordance with his original intent and grants his seal of approval.
Therefore, he offers praise. Next, it clarifies that they are further able to benefit others through the wondrous application of the three karmas.
This is also as previously explained. Next, regarding the virtue of entering the secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*): the three virtues are the three *prajñās*, which are termed the Buddha’s wisdom.
Because one wondrously penetrates the three delusions through these three *prajñās*, it is called "skillful entry.

The reason the secret treasury is named the Buddha’s wisdom is precisely to clarify that the Buddha’s wisdom encompasses all virtues. Because one realizes they are not identical, it is called "skillful entry. Next, [the text] clarifies...

Furthermore, regarding the perfection of the qualities of the cognitive object (*jñeya-pariniṣpatti*): the first phrase explains "great wisdom" (*mahājñāna*), and the second phrase explains "thorough penetration" (*prativedha*).
Some say that "one mind" (*ekacitta*) refers to the object; however, we maintain that this is from the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*, which simply clarifies wisdom in its general and specific aspects.

This precisely means that one wisdom is itself the three wisdoms. At the beginning of the "Chapter on Expedient Means," these are fully explained as both horizontal and vertical illumination, all of which is unobstructed.

Regarding the second phrase, "penetration because of hindrance": since the preceding [phrase] was discussed in terms of wisdom (*jñāna*), this refers to the objective realm of phenomena and principle (*dharmatattva*).

Since the preceding [section] mentioned the three types of wisdom, this refers to the three truths (*trisatya*). As previously stated in the text, the three virtues (*triguṇa*) are raised interchangeably.

This phenomena-and-principle is precisely the inconceivable realm of means and reality (*upāya-tattva*) and the object and wisdom (*viṣaya-jñāna*). As for the term "partial attainment," it refers to the very beginning of the stage of partial realization.
This is the subsequent section on the inconceivable; do not let it be judged by ordinary sentiments. Next, since the essence is already perfect and complete, its fame is universally heard;
this refers to the virtue of pervasive renown. The next phrase clarifies the virtue of external transformation (*paravivartana*).

Previously, under the term "compassion," only the essence of transforming others was clarified, but the extent of that transformation was not yet discussed; therefore, this is explained here: the liberation of the ten realms serves as an infinite basis for reliance.
This explains how [the Buddha] is able to deliver sentient beings: although their classes and groupings are infinite, they do not exceed the ten realms. How is it that he is able to deliver them?

By means of great compassionate wisdom (*mahākaruṇā-jñāna*), he provides them all with a place of reliance; through great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), he bestows happiness, and thus it is said "he establishes" them;

through great compassion, he extracts them from suffering, and thus it is said "he rescues and protects" them. For this reason, it is said he is "able to deliver. Furthermore, "reliance" is synonymous with "instruction" (*avavāda*).
"Also providing peace" refers to internal practice; "providing protection" refers to external support. The preceding section clarified reaching the other shore for oneself;

this section clarifies acting for the sake of others. Because these three kinds of wisdom of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) cause [beings] to ultimately reach the place of great peace and happiness, it is said that they "are able to deliver.
The thirteen preceding lines have distinct names according to the treatise; now, one may likewise rely on them.
I have not yet had the leisure to establish names based on the meaning of the current text; this concludes the separate explanation of the thirteen phrases above.

Below is the summary, which demonstrates the relationship between the extensive and the concise. Since the concise version clarifies the extensive, it says "furthermore," for [the extensive] is without limit or measure, transcending words and thought.
To know this, one relies upon the holy teachings and accords with the principles of reason, as seen in the *Avataṃsaka* and other such scriptures.
Because the majestic reputation and the praise of all his merits are equal to those of all Buddhas, it is by principle that this is so perfectly wondrous;
because it is thus, it is also vast and manifold. To speak briefly of "equality" is to manifest the brief in contrast to the vast;
since the vast is already such as this, one knows that the thirteen [categories] are its brief summary. It should be understood that this brevity is an essential abridgment, not a deficiency.
Briefly stated, these thirteen phrases encompass all extensive meanings.

Having completed the explanation above regarding the horizontal meaning of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), what follows is the explanation of the second example, which demonstrates how the subsequent stages likewise possess the full meaning of all these phrases horizontally.

From the beginning up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), it is shown that the subsequent stages are also like this, demonstrating the sense of complete possession through analogy.

This is also as previously explained. To clarify that within this intermediate stage there are forty positions, each possessing the meanings of the detailed and abbreviated explanations mentioned above, it says, "it is likewise.
The reason for this conclusion is that if even the first dwelling is already like this, how much more so those above it; thus, one may have confidence.
Next follows the third citation, which provides dual proof for the two preceding meanings. The letter *A* is pronounced with a short vowel as "Mu" (無).
Some say that the text is found in the fifth fascicle of that sutra and also in its twenty-second [fascicle]. It further states:

"The single character enters all forty-one characters, and the forty-one characters also enter the single character. This refers to the equality of the letters (*akṣara-samatā*). It also says: [and so forth].
All languages enter the first letter-gateway, and likewise enter the second letter-gateway, up to the forty-second letter-gateway;
this is what is meant by "language and so forth. Regarding the phrase "and so forth," the *Commentary on Stopping and Contemplation* (Zhiguan ji) states:
"As Vajragarbha spoke of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), when the Ten Grounds are spoken of in the ten directions, both the person who speaks and the name [of the ground] are called 'Vajragarbha'."
The equality of names refers to the teaching of the ten stages; the equality of speech refers to the non-differentiation of their qualities.

This is the horizontal perspective. Now, it is said that one name is all names, which is the equality of names. For example, the first dwelling is named the "Gate of the Letter A," and all forty-one positions are likewise named the "Gate of the Letter A"—this is the equality of names.
Furthermore, the letter *tu* (荼) is the name for Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), which is the ultimate—this is the equality of names.

The remaining forty-one stages are all termed "ultimate," and the intermediate stages are likewise so; therefore, those referred to as "names" and so forth, or "speech-sounds" and so forth, all consist of the sounds of the forty-two letters.
Those referred to as "merits" and so forth all possess the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*);
these are termed "merits" and so forth. This is because they differ when viewed from the perspective of the vertical progression [of the stages]. Now...
This means that first, there was merely an explanation of the second [set]; second, although the third was fully explained by citing the *Vyākhyā*, it was not yet understood here;

and third, although the third was also fully explained, the meaning still could not be reconciled. Now, I say: the first three phrases correctly clarify the three types of meaning, while the latter three conclude them as the three types of meaning.
Why? Because within the first [set], each individual syllable further possesses the meaning of all the other syllables.
These characters are equal [to their meanings] in these three respects: to speak any single character among them is to speak the meaning of all characters;
this speech and so forth enable each individual character to allow the listener to realize and understand the principles of the meanings of all characters;
and the benefit of these merits and so forth is the utility of manifesting the characters. This concludes the discussion of these three.

Because the matters are uniform, it is said that "the characters are equal.
