Since the text explicitly clarifies the merits of the various characters and then explains that they all possess the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth—how could this not be an extreme error?

By using this passage as evidence, one knows that both of the previous two interpretations are clearly horizontal (*tiryak*) in their possession of all [qualities]. One should understand that although these are horizontal here, they are vertical (*ūrdhva*) from the very beginning.
Because all [aspects] further extend to the subsequent [stages], although they are vertical, they are horizontal;
since each and every one possesses a single merit, even the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) that are difficult to conceive constitute what is called the meaning of "perfectly wondrous" (pariniṣpanna).

Although the preceding [classification] was vertical and already possessed horizontality, it was termed "vertical" merely to conform to common human understanding. Although these four propositions are difficult to conceive, they are provisionally named [horizontal] in contrast to the preceding verticality.
One should reflect upon this thoroughly.
What follows below is the fourth section of analysis, which contains two rounds of question and answer. In the first round, both the transverse and the vertical are discussed together;

this also serves to eliminate the partial and reveal the perfect. In the second round, the discussion focuses exclusively on the transverse, which likewise focuses exclusively on the perfect contemplation (*yuan-guan*). One should contemplate this meaning.
The "intention" (*yi*) also seems to be based on the meaning of the provisional teachings. The two preceding explanations—horizontal and vertical—correspond to the *nidāna* (causal conditions);
this meaning should be contemplated according to the provisional teachings. Furthermore, in the initial question, the school’s tenet is first established;

this is because the questioner, wishing to raise an objection, first seeks to ascertain the tenet. Since both [the preceding and current sections] are praising the virtue of true realization, it is said that [ignorance] has been "severed. This...

Within this [section], there should be a refutation that exhausts its full force; next is the formal objection (*paryanuyoga*), which involves a Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka citing a Śrāvaka of the Tripiṭaka as an analogical precedent to serve as the basis for the formal objection.

Since both of these teachings involve the severance of delusions from the very beginning, this intent should equally apply to praising [the Buddha’s teaching] in general. Why, then, do both the horizontal and vertical [explanations] praise only the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*)?

This is because it manifests and establishes the meaning of the Perfect (yuan). As for what is called the "trace" (ji), one should know that following these two gates, the meaning of the trace has two aspects.
In the answer, it first provisionally grants the general [meaning] and subsequently refutes it to manifest the distinction between the Separate (bie) and the Perfect (yuan).

"The person" refers to the two roots, namely the two realities of long and short [practice]. One should also understand that the conclusion of the objection follows. The subsequent question concerns this preceding meaning.
Having completed the explanation, [the author] speaks further because he wishes to contrast the former partiality with the present perfection.

In the response, first the horizontal and vertical lack of fixed direction are clarified to challenge the questioner’s fixation on direction; next, the former is contrasted with the present to reveal the latter.
Within this, first the former partiality is used as a foil for the present perfection, and then the former is used to illustrate the latter—reflect upon this.
Next, this application of the text is the first explanation; the section on "Citing Evidence" (the fourth) was mistakenly placed here [below].

What follows is the fifth section, "Citing the Explanations from the Treatise," which provides a dual explanation to establish the two preceding meanings. Regarding the thirteen phrases of this passage that praise his virtues, the treatise offers two general interpretations:
first, the "Gate of Upper and Lower Branches," and second, the "Gate of Encompassing Matters. Both of these exhaustively praise [his qualities].
Regarding the text: "Now, this first section describes the exposition of the primary upper and lower gates; next, it describes the exposition of the gate of encompassing matters.
Within the first of these, there are three parts: first, the description of the treatise’s heading; second, the description of the treatise’s exposition; and third, the summary that reconciles them.

Regarding the first of these, concerning the phrase "upper branches, etc.," some say that "branches" (śākhā) means "to uphold," implying that the upper and lower sections each uphold their respective meanings. However, I maintain that this refers to the whole.

"Indivisible" (*abhedyam*) refers to the divisions; "upper and lower" refers to front and back. They receive their names through mutual dependence. "Division" (*bhāga*) carries the meaning of a distinct limit or demarcation.
To clarify this, the text praising its attainment contains the sense of two divisions, upper and lower, just as the preceding text contains the sense of the "gate of successive arising.
Next, the explanation within the commentary should consist of three parts, namely: first, the dual designation of...
The meaning is presented in pairs, and the text is explained in pairs. Regarding the characteristics of the indicators: what are the "upper" and "lower" members?

They refer to the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Because the general comes first and the specific follows, they are termed "upper" and "lower.

The following is the presentation of the text; since it should be presented in pairs accordingly, the treatise states: "All [of them] do not regress from Bodhi" is the general characteristic, while the remainder...

"This is the distinct characteristic" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) is the passage that simultaneously indicates both [the general and the specific]. Now, because it is presented here in an abbreviated manner, it is shown only singly;
for "non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*) comprehensively encompasses the meaning of the twelve subsequent phrases. Therefore, it is called "general" (*sāmānya*).

Because these distinctions are analyzed and revealed below within the twelve phrases, they are called "specific" (*viśeṣa*). What follows is the explanation of the characteristics of these general and specific meanings. First:
This first phrase explains the general meaning and also serves as the heading for the detailed explanation. Why is this so?
The treatise states that there are ten meanings of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*); since it explicitly says these ten are the reasons why one does not retrogress, it explains the general sense.
Because there are ten meanings of non-retrogression, it serves as the heading that introduces the detailed explanation. Thus, this single phrase is both the heading and the explanation.
What is called "meaning" (*artha*) refers to the cause and the reason. It is precisely because of these ten reasons that one attains non-retrogression in unsurpassed *bodhi*;
thus, ten meanings are established based on these ten reasons. What is called "manifestation" (*saṃdarśana*) means "to reveal.
This refers to the grouping of the twelve phrases to reveal ten kinds of meanings; specifically, the fourth and tenth [sections] each contain two phrases.
Therefore, the twelve [links] are treated as ten.
From "Hearing the Dharma" onwards, the following section describes the detailed explanation of those ten within the treatise (*śāstra*). There are ten distinct sections;

in each one, the treatise first establishes the name and then presents the scriptural text (*sūtra*). Furthermore, regarding the expressions "one or two" up to "nine or ten" found within the treatise:

The current text abbreviates this because it is easy to understand. Furthermore, since one first attains *dhāraṇī* through hearing the Dharma, one is able to attain non-retrogression regarding the unsurpassed path;
thus, the meaning of cause and effect, as well as agent and object, can be understood. The patterns of the subsequent nine instances may be inferred accordingly.
Some say that this translates as *dhāraṇī*, and that there are four kinds of "holding" (*dhāraṇa*): namely, the holding of Dharma, meaning, mantra, and patience (*kṣānti*).
"Dharma" refers to the name; "meaning" refers to the principle; "mantra" refers to the words; and "patience" refers to wisdom. Dharma is the gateway; meaning is the explanation;
mantra protects against obstacles; and patience brings about liberation. Furthermore, some say that dhāraṇī is twofold: first, gathering, and second, scattering.
"Gathering" means to hold. This is "retention through hearing"; it means hearing the text and its meaning and retaining them without forgetting—that which has been heard.
The method by which one is able to maintain [the Dharma] is called "transcription" (*chao*). "Hearing" (*wen*) is the essence of *dhāraṇī*, which consists of mindfulness and wisdom.
"Dispensing" (*san*) means bestowing; there are four kinds of this: first, the Dharma; second, its meaning; third, the ability to attain the Bodhisattva's patience (*kṣānti*);

and fourth, the bestowal of mantras upon sentient beings. Among these, there are two types: the former is that which maintains, namely "hearing and maintaining" (*wen-chi*); the latter is that which is maintained.

The remaining four types are further categorized into two: first, those for one's own benefit, such as hearing and retaining [the teachings]; second, those for the benefit of others, such as the Dharma and its meaning.
Because cause and effect are distinct, the subsequent [section] should follow the previous pattern, with the character "all" (*jie*) being applied here as well.

Regarding the meaning of "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*), which was previously placed elsewhere, it should now be moved from that prior text and inserted here. This is what is meant by "discrimination" (*vibhāga*).
Regarding the four [types of] *saptaka* (groups of seven), because one has previously attained this, one is able to delight in eloquent speech (*pratibhāna*);

because one has attained such eloquence, one is able to be non-retrogressive. Among the seven types of eloquence, the seventh refers to the possession of the five kinds of sounds—being the most supreme and wondrous eloquence in all worlds, being profound like thunder, and being clear and heard from afar—and thus some explain that there are five.
First, it is as profound as thunder; second, it is clear and heard from afar; third, those who hear it find joy; fourth, they enter into it with deep reverence and acceptance;
fifth, listeners never grow weary—these are the five kinds of vocal sounds of the Buddha. Third, regarding "the teaching of non-retrogression": "retrogression" (turning back) refers to speaking;
thus, it is called the "teaching of non-retrogression. Non-retrogression is that which is turned toward and that which is spoken. Some say:

Because the essence of the correct contemplation of non-arising can be grasped and modeled, it is called the "Dharma-stream" (*dharma-srotas*). Because its perfect penetration unfolds without being restricted to a single person, it is termed a "wheel" (*cakra*).

Furthermore, because the correct contemplation of non-arising is free from entanglements and cannot be destroyed, it also carries the meaning of a "wheel. Since once attained it is never lost, it is called "non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*);
and because it revolves from oneself toward others, it is called "turning" (*pravartana*). It is said that this refers to what is taught as the "Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*).

Because it constantly teaches this Dharma of non-retrogression, it is called the "turning of the wheel of non-retrogression," referring to the two kinds of non-retrogressive Dharmas in the four aforementioned stages.
Furthermore, the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "To teach the virtues of one's own level is called turning the wheel of non-retrogression;
to teach the virtues beyond one's level is called turning the wheel of non-retrogression. It also says that wisdom does not...
To speak of "receding" while referring to merit is called "non-reversal"; to speak of "wisdom" (prajñā) and "skillful means" (upāya) is called "non-retrogression" and "non-reversal.

Furthermore, to speak of conditioned activities (saṃskṛta-caryā) and the unconditioned principle (asaṃskṛta-tattva) is called the non-retrogressive and non-reversing Wheel of Dharma. This wheel has three meanings: first, the meaning of perfection;
second, the meaning of indeterminacy, because self-benefit and benefit for others enter the Noble Path and proceed inexhaustibly from one to another; third, [the meaning of turning].
The meaning of "crushing" (*cakra*) refers to the Noble Path within the mind: it can crush the afflictions, it can subdue them, and having subdued them, it can settle them.
Because it is like the wheel-treasure of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), it is metaphorically called a "wheel. "Turning" (*vartana*) means to move, to manifest, to transport, and to arise.

It moves by proclaiming the teachings, manifests the sublime principles, transports the Noble Path through sound, and gives rise to true wisdom after words. Thus, it completely crushes all obstacles and afflictions.
Regarding the title "Turning the Wheel of Dharma," it will be fully explained below in the "Chapter on Expedient Means. As for the life-span, it has already been discussed in the preceding text;
alternatively, it may be moved here to be combined with two lines of text within these four meanings to form this single meaning.
Because both lines speak together of the Buddhas as the most supreme spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), by relying upon and making offerings to them, one attains non-retrogression.

Making offerings is itself the planting of the root; it can also serve as an offering because hearing the Dharma enables the arising of wisdom, and thus constitutes the planting of the root of virtue.
This has already been explained as before. Regarding the next five meanings: because of this praise, the doubts of oneself and others are definitively exhausted;
by means of this, one attains non-retrogression. This meaning is established as the bestowal of a prediction (vyākaraṇa) as described in the subsequent text.

Regarding the meaning, the preceding text also provides a brief explanation, stating: "To act" means to cause, to enable, or to obtain; this is brought about because one's practice meets with the Buddha.
It is also said that this refers to severing doubts regarding both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*);

there are two types of doubt: the afflictive (*kleśa*) and the cognitive (*jñeya*). The cognitive is the obstacle to the two principles within the conventional, while the afflictive is the obstacle to the principle of emptiness. Furthermore—

The objects of knowledge are the dust-like and infinite delusions; the afflictions are the delusions of views and thought. When combined, these constitute the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*); when separated, they are the three delusions.
Regarding the principles of phenomena and reality, one should reflect upon their sequence. The *Six Meanings Treatise* states: "The sixth [meaning] is: for what purpose?
For what matters does one preach the Dharma? One enters into each respective Dharma so as not to regress. As the Sūtra says: 'One cultivates body and mind through great compassion.'"
Some say that while the *Sūtra* lacks [the discussion of] the mind and the *Śāstra* lacks [the discussion of] the mouth, the authentic scripture possesses all three karmas;
thus, although there are omissions in the wording, their meanings are all contained within one another, merely being hidden or revealed alternately. Now I say:

furthermore, this *Sūtra* contains only "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*), while the *Śāstra* adds "greatness" (*mahat*) and "compassion" (*karuṇā*); these are mutual omissions in the text, but not omissions in the meaning. Whether taken individually or collectively, they are equal. Moreover, it says:

This explains the reason for this: because Bodhisattvas perform various deeds—teaching the Dharma to others externally while internally entering into the realization of all phenomena—they perfume their body, speech, and mind with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

They manifest various forms, preach various Dharmas, and employ various skillful means (*upāya*) to extract various sufferings and bestow various joys, thereby revealing both the benefit of others and one's own benefit. "Externally" refers to benefiting others; "internally" refers to self-benefit.
Because one realizes all dharmas for the dual benefit of self and others, one speaks them to others externally; now it is said that these two are themselves the practice (*caryā*).
Because one unites with these two, it is called "entry" (*praveśa*). For this reason, one attains non-retrogression in the unsurpassed path.

Next, the seventh meaning is that "entry" is realization (*sākṣātkriyā*); the cognitive object (*jñeya-viṣaya*) is the Buddha-wisdom, which is that which is realized and entered, while "entry" is the agent.
As for "entering through non-entry," it is precisely because one does not act as if entering that one attains non-retrogression.

Some say this statement is inverted; they argue that one should instead say: "Entering the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of the realm of reality (*yathābhūta*) is non-retrogression," which would distinguish it from the subsequent ninth stage, the wisdom of contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). However, according to the treatise itself, there is no difference. Others say: "Now..."

This means that realizing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is called "entering the conventional" (*saṃvṛti-praveśa*). The person who realizes it is the "one who enters," while the object and wisdom realized together constitute the "object of entry.
Furthermore, regarding the eighth meaning: because one realizes the two kinds of emptiness—of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)—one attains non-retrogression.

Although this includes both the subject (the agent) and the object (the goal) as before, the former [preceding] intention focused on the subject, whereas this present intention focuses on the object. Reflect upon this. Some say it refers to the "self of phenomena" (*dharma-ātman*).

The insight into both types of emptiness constitutes the Middle Way, which differs from the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-śāsana*). Now, I shall first explain this according to the text of the treatise; it does not refer here to the sequential stages of the ten meanings.
This is because one has reached the ultimate realization of principle and thus does not regress. Others say it is because one has exhausted the nature of reality (*tathatā*);

however, I maintain that the exhaustion of principle and the perfection of nature belong solely to the Buddha alone, whereas the present stage is merely "adjacent to the ultimate. Next, below this, is the tenth [stage], based on...
The treatise should state: "One should perform what is to be done so as to maintain [the Dharma] without falling back. The commentary is incomplete here.
Regarding the two characters *zhuchi* (住持, "to maintain"), the treatise establishes two meanings for this name, whereas the scriptural text presents only one meaning. Others say:
these two phrases should be combined into a single phrase, because the name is heard throughout immeasurable worlds; thus, one is able to maintain the Buddha-dharma. Now...
The Dharma does not diminish; when sentient beings hear its name, they believe and practice it, thereby able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
For this reason, it is called "that which should perform its function" (*kāryakara*). What the Bodhisattva ought to do is to benefit sentient beings; thus, two meanings are contained therein.
The treatise on the sutra mentions only two functions, omitting "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*). The term [in the treatise] corresponds exactly to the text of the present sutra. Alternatively...
Because of non-retrogression, one is able to perform these two functions; precisely because of these two capacities, one never retrogresses.
These ten points in total constitute the meaning of the specific characteristics of non-retrogression.
The following is the third summary, which brings together two phrases from within the initial conclusion: first, it brings together the two characteristics of the two branches;

second, it brings together the current text through a horizontal interpretation, which is identical to the general and specific [distinctions] in the Treatise. First, the single phrase "non-retrogression" corresponds to the first dwelling;

this is the general [aspect] within the horizontal [interpretation], and it is also the aforementioned branch. Next, the twelve phrases constitute the [specific aspect] within the horizontal [interpretation].
The term "also" (*api*) refers to the fact that this is likewise a member (*aṅga*) of the passage below; reflect upon this, reflect upon it.

Next follows the second section, which presents the commentary explaining the second door of the summary of matters (*vastusaṃgraha*). This also consists of thirteen phrases. Within it, there are two parts:

first, the presentation of the commentary’s explanation, and second, the reconciliation [with other texts]. Regarding the first, it says: "As for 'the matter of grasping' (*vastugrahaṇa'), it means..."

This treatise on the "Comprehension of All Meritorious Deeds" (Sarvaguṇālaṃkāra-saṃgraha) further provides two interpretations; within these two interpretations, each likewise consists of fifty-three phrases.
In the first interpretation, there is first a general enumeration followed by a detailed citation and explanation. The treatise says:
"It demonstrates in which pure stages (*viśuddhabhūmi*) the various bodhisattvas abide, by means of what skillful means (*upāya*), and for what purpose..."
Because one must perform what is to be done within the objective sphere (*viṣaya*), this serves as the general heading.
In the commentary below, the thirteen phrases are divided into three parts: first, the phrase "not regressing from unsurpassed enlightenment" indicates in which pure stage one abides;
next, ten phrases indicate by what means one practices; and finally, the two phrases on "regression" indicate what [is to be understood].
Because one must perform what is to be done within the sphere of activity (*viṣaya*), the treatise cites and explains [the verse];
therein, it only interprets the first two phrases of the heading and does not explain the third phrase: "In what sphere of activity should one perform what is to be done?

Regarding "the purity of the ground," this refers to the three stages from the eighth ground upward, where practice is signless (*animitta*) and tranquil and pure; herein, the principle of signlessness is termed "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
Because of perfect enlightenment, the final three stages are all spontaneously tranquil in signless practice, purified and free from hindrances;

thus they are called "non-retrogressive," for they cannot be retrogressed by any defilements or signs associated with conceptualization. Regarding the second phrase, "by what means [is this attained]?
there are four kinds: first, the means of grasping the sublime Dharma, which consists of upholding the sublime Dharma.
Because one teaches others by means of the power of eloquence, these three phrases encompass the "upholding of the sublime Dharma. Those who uphold the sublime Dharma all attain *dhāraṇī*.

By attaining *śrutadhāraṇī* (retention of what has been heard), they uphold the sublime Dharma so as not to abandon it; because they maintain the sublime Dharma within their own minds without forgetting it, it is called "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*).
Regarding "by means of the power of eloquence": it is because of the analytical skill of eloquent speech that one teaches others.
First, by turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma and preaching this irreversibility for the sake of others; second, by embracing spiritual friends and performing what ought to be done.
These three phrases are subsumed [under the category of reliance]: because one who relies on spiritual friends makes offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, they perform what ought to be done;
"what ought to be done" refers to planting the roots of merit in the presence of all Buddhas, and these roots of merit are precisely the wholesome.
The faculties (*indriya*) are that which ought to be cultivated; for this reason, they are constantly praised by all Buddhas. Third, the skillful means of gathering sentient beings:
because one does not abandon sentient beings, this is subsumed in a single phrase. Fourth, purifying the body through loving-kindness (*maitrī*):

because one cultivates and perfumes the body and mind with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one is able not to abandon any sentient beings and can constantly rescue and deliver them. These constitute the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Taking up the skillful means of wisdom to teach and transform sentient beings so that they may enter that wisdom—this comprises three phrases.

Skillfully entering the Buddha’s wisdom, penetrating great wisdom, and reaching the other shore: because one possesses these three types of wisdom oneself, one can cause sentient beings to take up the three wisdoms;
thus, becoming a possessor of the three wisdoms oneself is the primary cause for sentient beings to take up the three wisdoms.
The first wisdom is the knowledge of reality as it is, which is the wisdom for one’s own benefit; the next wisdom is the knowledge of phenomena, which is the wisdom for the benefit of others;

and the final wisdom is the wisdom of the ultimate truth, the true nature. Some explain that the first is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the second is the seed of the wisdom of the path (*mārgajñatā*), and the last is the wisdom of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Others say that within this treatise, only the first [of these] is explained, while the initial two phrases are merely presented without further commentary.

In what sphere does one perform what is to be done? This is comprised of two phrases: "renown and so forth" refers to the sphere, while "being able to deliver [beings] and so forth" refers to what is to be done.
Because the Bodhisattva possesses the three types of knowledge and so forth, his fame resounds far and wide throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
thus, within the sphere of these immeasurable worlds, he performs the work of delivering all sentient beings.
That which ought to be done for the sake of delivering sentient beings is precisely what all Bodhisattvas must do;

the above summarizes how others explain the headings and their meanings within the treatise. Now, in this present text, we shall directly state the headings from the treatise itself without stating its explanations.
Regarding the initial explanation of the headings, there are only three [points]; what are they? This is the present text.
Regarding the four [points], all were stated in the *Śāstra* as errors; however, upon examining the explanation of the meaning, one finds that within the third phrase there are two actual meanings:

"What is the objective sphere? refers to the locus, which is the textual passage of the first two phrases; "that which is to be done and what is done" refers to the functional activity, which is the textual passage of the latter two phrases.
The *Śāstra* deeply perceived this intent, wishing to manifest its meaning so that future generations might know it. Therefore, [I have] clarified this here.

To add to this, it is certainly not an error; I hope you will reflect upon it deeply. The subsequent variation in the explanation within the treatise is not the essential point here, and thus it is as described in the text.
The passage beginning with "If one were to allow... is the next section, which serves to synthesize and establish the meaning of the initial vertical explanation. The intent therein is as follows:
Taking the first phrase correctly, the subsequent three stages correspond to the preceding seven stages, which together constitute the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Furthermore, as their shallow and deep aspects differ, they properly accord with the vertical (*ūrdhva*) principle, which is consistent with the intent of the treatise; therefore, it is said there is no contradiction.

To summarize the essential points, the two explanations cited from the treatise are precisely intended to confirm and establish the two preceding explanations; thus, it was previously stated that citing the treatise’s dual explanation establishes the two preceding meanings.
This is precisely that meaning. The significance of the aforementioned causes, conditions, and so forth has already been fully explained within the preceding general statement on non-retrogression;

therefore, they will not be discussed separately here. Regarding the essential points for contemplating the mind and maintaining [the practice], the previous text was brief, so they are clarified further here.

The former section concerned others, while this concerns oneself; the former concerned the fruit, while this clarifies the cause; the former concerned the middle and the end, whereas now we address the beginning.
For this reason, the beginner’s mind is further clarified: it is said that if the beginner’s mind can perform this contemplation, it is immediately able to possess all these merits.
Thus, this praise of its virtues does not pertain solely to the present moment, but also extends to the subsequent stages;
it intends for the very beginning of the present moment itself. Herein, the tenth and eleventh [contemplations] are combined into one, and thus there are only twelve contemplations. Regarding this:

Among the twelve [sections], the second and the fifth each have two layers of meaning, while the others are explained directly and simply. Within these, one must understand each point through six aspects:
the principle is profound and requires careful attention; do not fall into error. However, everyone says this text is easy and thus no one explains it.
I maintain that it is actually not easy; let me briefly clarify it. First, regarding the phrase "as before," it refers to the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
This refers to the three kinds of non-retrogression. Regarding the second phrase, there are two sections: the first corresponds to this sutra, and the second corresponds to other sutras.

Because they can transform the provisional (prajñapti) into the ultimate emptiness (śūnyatā), there is nothing that can intervene; because they can transform the ultimate into the possession of all qualities, the dharma-nature of the Middle Way is both absent and present simultaneously.
Thus, the text, meaning, characters, and principles are all that which is heard and maintained. Because one hears and is able to maintain the teaching, it is the mind.
All that arises in the King’s mind are *dharmamukhas* (gateways to the Dharma), for they are both what is practiced and what is maintained;
because one can maintain them within this very practice, existence is transformed into emptiness. Because one can transform within non-existence, one is immediately endowed with all things.
Because the *dharmatā* of the Middle Way is both simultaneously absent and present, the contemplation of emptiness realizes that all phenomena possess only names and are in reality unattainable.
Because one maintains [the teachings] immediately upon hearing them, this is established as "retention through hearing" (*śrutadhara*).

To realize that all mental factors (*cittadharma*) are themselves gateways to the Dharma (*dharmamukha*) and are the very objects of practice, and to be able to maintain this realization immediately, is "Madhyamaka," which is the ability to maintain the ultimate meaning (*tattvārtha*).

Thus, these three are also equivalent to hearing, reflection, and meditation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*). Other sūtras further speak of four types of retention as previously mentioned; however, for the sake of convenience regarding the meaning, only [these three] are treated here.
Regarding these three: because they are all intended for the ease of practicing the perfection of the rational nature (*dharmatā*), "designation" (*prajñapti*) is placed first.

This is because it follows the convenience of its meaning; wondrous contemplation is not restricted to a single direction. "Dharma" refers to the names that express [things] upon all phenomena, which are one's own mind.

"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the principles and meanings that are expressed. "Phrases" (*vyañjana*) refer to the various different sounds and languages of diverse classes. "Emptiness" (*śūnyatā*)... [is the absence of intrinsic nature].
This is the thorough realization that all things lack fixed reality and exist only as sounds and speech; therefore, next, one delights in explaining the synthesis of the preceding three.
Now, regarding the three aspects of observing the mind: first, the one and many of the [three] realms are all endowed with multiple phrases, which is the *dharma*;

second, all are the principle of true reality, which is the *artha*; third, they exist only as names, which is the *nirukti*; and fourth, their unimpeded rotation is the *pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid* (unimpeded eloquence).
These two characters summarize and penetrate the preceding four, because all four are termed "unimpeded": by realizing that existence is itself emptiness, one does not regress from the stage;
by realizing that principle is itself phenomena, one does not regress from practice; and by realizing that the extremes are themselves the Middle, one has no divergent thoughts.

Next, regarding the offering clarified by means of contemplation: first, clarifying the meaning of making offerings to the Buddha—complying with the Buddha’s words is precisely following his instructions, which is to say, it is complying with the Buddha’s intention.
Below, the actual clarification of making offerings to the Buddha: he is the person who can expound the three contemplations;
seeing the ultimate principle of what is expounded is the ultimate intention of the Buddha. To practice in accordance with this is the ultimate reception [of the teaching].

This is the offering of the "Excellence of Accordance. The intention behind making offerings to the Buddha is to manifest the Path; that is, it is an offering to the Dharma, for it is able to accord with the principle of the Three Truths.
Therefore, it is an offering to the Sangha. Although the sutra clarifies only the Buddha, the present text mentions the "three" because one is identical to the three.

Thus, the purpose of making offerings to the Buddha is to destroy delusions and to manifest the principle; the true intent of offering to the Buddha lies precisely here. Therefore, it is... [the same].

To possess these three is precisely the identity of the one essence and the three aspects. Regarding the subsequent re-explanation: whereas the preceding [section] still involved both the phenomenal and the noumenal, this single phrase refers to the mind of the practitioner.
Here, the mind of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*) is the Buddha; the mind of various practices is the "provision" (*sambhāra*), which is the act of making offerings.

Thus, the primary and auxiliary practices function as the subject and object respectively. As for "Dharma," it unifies the aforementioned subject and object to serve as the objective realm (*ālambana-dharma*); the *dharmadhātu* is that which is offered. The capacity [to offer] is the subject.
Causing the mind that savors the object and wisdom to be the very offering to the Sangha—this is the true offering of contemplative practice.
As the Sūtra says, "This is the true Dharma-offering," which refers precisely to this meaning. Next is the contemplation on the planting of merit; the text contains three phrases:

the first two clarify the basis of virtue, and the last one explains the meaning of "planting. First, taking the real object as the basis for contemplative wisdom is the foundation of all virtues; next, they are combined.
The former [two phrases] constitute the foundation for the virtues of all practices, both subjective and objective; the latter phrase encompasses these two meanings.

To cultivate the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) based upon the true nature (*dharmatā*) is to plant the root of the virtues of contemplative wisdom; to cultivate various practices based upon correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) is to plant the root of the virtues of all practices.

Because these two fundamental roots of virtue are established of themselves, it is said that they are "established. The Confucian tradition also says: "Devote yourself to the root; once the root is established..."

Now, as for the arising of the Way, one must not fail to apply oneself to the various practices, which constitute the myriad practices of merit and virtue. Next, the explanation of the Buddha’s praise of this matter:
because practice and the Way have merged, it is certified by the Buddha. Now, through contemplation, one accords with the object; the object accords with the contemplation;
and the wisdom of contemplation takes the object as its basis. To be in accord with contemplation in this manner is what is meant by "praise."

To say that "observing in accordance with the object" refers to the state of darkness (*mīng*) is not to say it is realization (*zhèng*). "Seal" (*yìn*) has the meaning of conformity. That wisdom possesses these [levels] below is the sense of being constantly practiced;
this very observation is what is constantly praised by the Buddha. Contemplation of phenomena (*fǎyuán*) can attain the true Dharma-joy;
contemplation of conditions (*néngyuán*) can bring about the attainment of conventional Dharma-joy; and contemplation without conditions (*wúyuán*) can attain the joy of the Middle Way. Next...
Those who enter the Buddha-wisdom find that the three Buddhas are of one essence, the three contemplations are of one mind, and the three wisdoms are themselves the other shore.

The three contemplations serve as the cause, and the three wisdoms serve as the fruit. If one speaks of the fruit within the cause, the three contemplations are themselves the three wisdoms—contemplate this through the "six identities" (liu ji).
Regarding "universally heard" (pu wen), it means that the three contemplations act as the faculty of hearing, such that one's reputation is heard everywhere; the three truths are... [the object].

The "places where it is heard" refers to immeasurable worlds. To speak of it again with greater emphasis: whereas previously the True and the Conventional were not spoken of as universal, they are now spoken of universally.
Next, regarding the capacity to deliver, one should know that within the three contemplations there are both the subject (the capacity) and the object (that which is delivered).

Finally, the conclusion clarifies the broad demonstration and the brief opening: all dharmas are none other than the Three Truths; if one can contemplate them according to principle, there is nothing that cannot be realized.
Because it is not for the sake of mere excellence, nor because it exhaustively praises [the teaching] according to the literal text, these thirteen phrases are briefly explained;
reflect well upon how they fully realize the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Regarding the subsequent listing of names: although this serves to praise their virtues in general, as the specific individuals remain unknown, it is necessary to list their names.
The commentary consists of four parts: first, a general explanation of the origin of the names; second, an explanation that the names contain multiple meanings;

third, an explanation of the methodology for interpretation; and fourth, the actual word-by-word exegesis of the text. "Great Being" (*mahāsattva*) refers to those previously mentioned who seek the unsurpassed [enlightenment] for both themselves and others.
Because he is a person of the Way, he is called a *mahāsattva* (Great Being). The name "Great" (*mahā*) signifies that his name is endowed with all meanings.
Regarding the three [categories], the "Dharma-gate" refers to the essential means for initial awakening and entry; "virtue and conduct" refers to what is accomplished and what is practiced.

Whether these three are taken individually or collectively, as explained in sequence below, they may be understood by oneself. The phrase "although these are... refers to the meaning of the aforementioned "Great Name."

It is also said that because of the three [aspects] mentioned previously, as well as the partial (*prādeśika*), the perfect (*pariniṣpanna*), the original (*mūla*), and the trace (*nirmāṇa*), there are prepared immeasurable [meanings].

The intention here is that while the name is partial, the meaning is perfect; this will also be seen for oneself in the subsequent explanation. Regarding "relying on the sutras," it means relying on what is found within various sutras.
This, in brief, encompasses three meanings, and thus only two methods are indicated, yet they encompass four. It is not the same as sound.
Since the deeds and characteristics of the bodhisattvas are limitless, I have merely provided a brief account based on the scriptural teachings.

Next, in the formal explanation, it is said that the sequence in which bodhisattvas are listed in various sūtras follows their respective causes and conditions rather than following a fixed uniform pattern.

For instance, they may be ordered according to the relationship between host and guest, as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, where the host is mentioned first and the guest later; or they may be ordered by the scale of their greatness, as in...

In this sutra, Mañjuśrī’s rank is high while the ranks of others are low; however, it is now said that each should be understood according to the specific causes and conditions of the time, and thus cannot be fixed as a universal standard.
Here, Mañjuśrī occupies the first position for two reasons: first, the factual (vastu), and second, the doctrinal (artha).
As for the fact, it is because this Bodhisattva was the very first to initiate the propagation of this sutra, just as he was among the twenty thousand lamps of the past.
Having clarified the causes for which it was taught, I now transmit it so that it may circulate. The present Buddha likewise teaches based upon these causes;
this is a brief enumeration of how it first entered the Dharma and circulated. There should be many more such instances, as this matter is practiced accordingly.
As for the meaning of its initial listing: the name of this sutra is *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; in the past he was named *Prabhāpāla*, and in the present he is named *Guṇadharana*.
Mañjuśrī is specifically represented as the sublime Dharma; therefore, he is placed at the very beginning of the list as the most sublime person.
For example, because the *Avataṃsaka* is named "Great Vaipulya," it places Samantabhadra at the beginning. Thus, that sutra also places him first for two reasons. Someone might ask:
"Why does this person alone possess these two meanings? It is because he was the very first to attain this sublime Dharma.
Therefore, by virtue of my original vow and because of the manifestation of the Dharma’s subtlety, I alone contemplate it thus—contemplate it again and again.

In the first section on Mañjuśrī, there are two meanings, which comprise four textual points; these two correspond to what was previously indicated as "relying on the sūtras" and "relying on contemplation.
As for the meaning comprising four points, the first—relying on the sūtras—possesses the sense of three types of exegesis. First, relying on...

In the Sūtra, the first three phrases are translations of names, while the subsequent four phrases explain their meanings. Regarding the first of these three, the first is a translation of the name, and the second is an alternative designation.
As for "Mañjuśrī," its meaning is explained according to the sequence [of the preceding terms]:
"Mañju" signifies "wondrous virtue" (*guṇa*). Next, regarding the alternative designations, both of these are still in their original Sanskrit forms.
This is not the local dialect; the original term for "Ju" (儒) is sometimes written as "Ru" (濡) or "Ruo" (濡), which is a phonetic abbreviation of Mañjuśrī.
"Shou" (首) refers to Śāri, which is a conjunct sound from two syllables in the Western [language]. In Sanskrit, it is a single character, namely the letter *Śa*, with the *Ri* portion abbreviated.
Many people do not understand this and instead provide explanations based on local dialects, which is a grave error. Next, the explanation follows.

Within the section on the meaning (*artha*), the first three [sections] correctly explain the name, while the fourth is the source for the explanation of the "Original and Traces" (*honji-suijaku*). Each of these three explanations clarifies "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*);

however, the first two concern the virtues of practice (*xingde*), while the latter one concerns the virtue of vows (*yuande*). Furthermore, the very first refers to the virtue of self-realization; the next refers to the virtue of benefiting others;

and the Buddha-nature (*foxing*) is the wondrousness of the nature-virtue (*xingde*), because it is seen with perfect clarity, which constitutes the wondrousness of the cultivation-virtue (*xiude*). As for the remaining [categories], they are the nature.

Because the Buddha-nature is not [intrinsically] wondrous, this nature is wondrous; although it is seen, it is not clearly perceived. Because the perfected virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*) is wondrous, it sees clearly.
Furthermore, because the perfected virtue and the nature are identical (*lakṣaṇa-samāveśa*), they are wondrous in their fourfold lack of fixed direction;

thus it is called "Wondrous. It is named "Wondrous Virtue" (*Guṇākara*) based on the meaning of this perfected virtue. This follows from the virtue of self-realization (*svasaṃvedana-guṇa*); next is the benefit for others (*parārtha*).
"Virtue" (*guṇa*) refers to preaching the Dharma to benefit others; "wonderful" (*miao*) refers to the non-arising of the two marks of being and non-being, or right and wrong.

Because he is named after these qualities, he is called "Wonderful Virtue" (*Guṇākara*). This means that while he is skillfully able to discern all phenomena, he remains unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This explanation follows the sutra; however, speaking in terms of the essential meaning, he may also be said to be the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

Neither vertical nor horizontal, he is named "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*). The preceding two lines of his conduct serve as his name, while the following one establishes his title based on his fundamental vow.

Within this, there is the making of the vow and the Buddha’s seal of approval. Regarding the vow, there are three parts: first, that those to be transformed before him shall first achieve the ultimate fruit;
second, that once he has achieved it, all others within his realm shall abide in the most perfect and complete state; third, [the vow concerning] what is to be transformed...
The practice of this conduct is vast and far-reaching; these three vows are themselves merits, none of which are not wondrous. Contemplate them, contemplate them!
Among the Buddha’s seals of approval (*mudrā*), there are those that seal and those that record. These merits are profoundly deep; they are wondrous merits.

The profound depth of these merits seals the first vow, while the wondrous land seals the latter two vows. Contemplate them! Because the name of this collection is derived from the totality of these practices and vows, it is thus named.
Wondrous Virtue, since these herein constitute causes and conditions, they should fully possess four meanings: the general establishment of names through practice and vows is the world;
the wondrous essence of self-realization is the primary meaning (paramārtha); the transformation of others by shattering appearances is the remedial meaning;

and the fulfillment of past vows is for the sake of others. These are all perfect and real, not subsequent, partial, or provisional; as they are the teachings and their meanings, they are not discussed separately hereafter. Next, the fundamental...

The "trace" refers to the manifestation of the essence and its function without fixed direction, adapting to conditions to transform beings according to the distinctions of the ten realms; briefly stated, these are the provisional and the real.

If one considers the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, where he attained Buddhahood long ago under the title Dragon Seed Supreme Honored King, and looks toward the present in the northern direction, this constitutes the fundamental and the trace in terms of the distant and the near.
In the contemplation of the three virtues, the secret of these virtues is neither vertical nor horizontal.
The nature of the wondrous mind is inherently thus; such is the wondrousness of its intrinsic virtue (*dharmatā-guṇa*). To contemplate and realize this is precisely the cultivation of the wondrous.
Because that wondrous name arises from this, how could the ability to practice it now be far off? This is precisely the essential practice of this sutra.
Because it subsumes the three [aspects] into one merit, it is called "secret"; because all merits return to these three, it is called "essential."
Because there is no before or after, it is not vertical; because it is not simultaneous, it is not horizontal. Furthermore, because it is three while being one, it is not vertical;
because it is one while being three, it is not horizontal. It is therefore "wondrous."
Regarding Avalokiteśvara, first the transliteration and then the explanation: the complete Sanskrit term should be *Avalokiteśvara*, though it is also directly rendered as *Valkiteśvara*.
The upper *va* is pronounced with the sound *fang* (as in "fangke"), and the lower *va* has the same pronunciation;
however, when combined with the character *shi* (濕), they are now pronounced as a single syllable. The character *lu* (路) is sometimes written as *lu* (魯).
In some versions it is written as "Lu," but it should correctly be "Lu. The middle character is pronounced "Ji" (with the *jiyi* rhyme); it is also acceptable to pronounce it as the character "Ji.

This is because the old translations were extremely corrupt and abbreviated, which is why it was written thus. "Va" means "to contemplate" (*guan*). "Lo-kite" means "world" (*loka*). "Śvara" means "sovereign" (*īśvara*).
Taken together, it is correctly translated as "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. [This was translated during the] Northern Wei dynasty.
Tirunātha considered this to be a translation; if one were to speak of "sound" (*śabda*), it should be called *Ghoṣa*, which is also called *Ghoṣan*—this means "sound.

Since it is called *Śvara*, it refers to "sovereignty" (*īśvara*). This is precisely because in ancient translations *śva* was rendered as "tax" (*śe*) or "tribute" (*shou*), and the letter *ra* was omitted;
thus, the two sounds "tax" (*she*) and "tribute" (*shou*) are phonetically close to "Ghoṣa" (*sha*) and "Ghoṣan" (*shan*).
It was then translated phonetically; in the subsequent scriptural text, its meaning is explained by itself, yet only one of its meanings is obtained while two remain lacking.

If one says that "sovereignty" (*īśvara*) possesses all three meanings, or if one follows the meaning according to the region such that one [meaning] inherently contains the other three, then there will be no objection regarding the significance of the oral mechanism (*mukha*).
This will become clear later in the section on the explanation of the meaning. First, regarding virtuous conduct (*guṇa*), there are two meanings; the first is...

Regarding the contemplation of the world’s bodies, this is first the contemplation of Avalokiteśvara. Initially, there is great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) that bestows happiness; subsequently, there is great pity (*mahākaruṇā*) that uproots suffering.
Within the body, the meaning is also contained. Taken separately, these are three names; taken together, they constitute the "perfect contemplation.
Because he perfectly responds to the three types of karmic stimuli in the world, causing all beings to leave suffering behind and attain happiness, he is named Avalokiteśvara. Next...

In the section on the "Clarification of Vows," although the meaning of responding to stimuli and uprooting suffering is addressed solely in relation to the two treatises, the principle of bestowing happiness is also fully present within them.

Since the original vows are such that one receives names based on these vows, all subsequent virtues and practices are the planting of these very vows. Next, the text points to the following passage where it explains this itself;
the commentary (*shu*) also provides an extensive explanation. However, there are four essentials: first, practice and vows constitute the world; second, seeing [the truth] constitutes the Way.

The "extracting suffering from the primary truth" (paramārtha-duḥkha-niḥsaraṇa) is the remedy; the "original vow" (pūrvapraṇidhāna) is for the sake of others. These, too, are all the circular application (pariniṣpanna-prayoga) and cannot be achieved through partial means—this is the intended meaning of the teaching.

The distinction between the "original" (hon) and the "traced" (jaku) is easy to understand, as it will be explained in the following text. Because these various meanings are summarized here, the commentary states "(clouds/clouds)" [indicating an extensive explanation].

Regarding the statement "the three wisdoms" (tri-jñāna) within the context of contemplation (vipaśyanā), one should properly have said "contemplation"; the use of the term "wisdom" (jñāna) seems to indicate a search for [the ultimate].

Whether it be due to errors in transcription or because they are explained through mutual correspondence, the phonetic glosses (*shiyin*) provided for the contemplation are also difficult to understand. Why is this?

For while the phonetic glosses for external phenomena belong to the mechanism of speech and thus still pertain to the realm of the thirty-six sense bases (*ṣaṭtriṃśat-kṛtsnāyatana*), the worldly sounds (*shiyin*) within the subsequent extensive explanation all belong to the objects of contemplation, the truths (*satya*).
Now, since we are discussing this in terms of contemplation (*guan*), how could it not be difficult to comprehend? The intended meaning is that the mind is speech.

The fundamental wisdom of contemplation takes the mind as its root and subsumes the derivative; thus, contemplating the realm of the Truths is itself the sound of speech and voice. The *Commentary* states:
"The explanation of the first two characters is no different from what follows, yet the third character differs slightly from below.

Below, the explanation is based on phenomena (*vastu*), taking that which is addressed as 'sound' (*svara*); here, it is based on the contemplating subject, taking that which is proclaimed as 'sound'. By reason of this...

Because it is through contemplation that the teaching is established, it is said that "contemplation" is the root of speech; as it is also said, "it is only by means of wisdom that verbal expression exists.
Reflect on this, reflect on this!
As for "Mahāsthāmaprāpta," throughout the beginning and end of this sutra, it is stated that he has attained great power (*mahāsthāma*); both the ancient and the current texts state this.
If one were to interpret "Mahāsthāmaprāpta," its meaning is essentially the same; however, because many sūtras frequently mention Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the term is used according to that majority usage.

If one were to analyze it specifically: "attaining greatness" likely refers to self-realization regarding the essence (*tattva*), while "great power" likely refers to the manifestation of function (*vṛtti*).
At the beginning of the text, based on the two sūtras, this refers to both practice and vow. First, the phrase "where I set my foot" is explained as reaching [the goal].
"Shaking all that is supported and its support" explains the meaning of Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
it should be understood that this name is established based on the sense of his power and function—namely, that wherever he goes, he is able to exercise such immense majesty and power.

One should know that this applies not only to Māras and non-Buddhists, but likewise to those both within and outside the realms. One should reflect well upon this, for it arises from his very essence.

It is because both the primary and secondary [realms] are interfused that this is possible. Next, regarding the vow: based on the meaning and momentum of this vow and its prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), it refers to the "present world" reaching the ultimate;
this is what is meant by "aspiration. It is called by the name "Great World" because it takes the great aspiration as its essence.
What was previously stated—that a single name contains manifold meanings—refers precisely to this category. To synthesize these points, it is through the power of the great aspiration and vow.
This is because one seizes the great world-system through power; however, since it is formed by the character "zhi" (志) with its immeasurable meanings, it is clear that it contains two senses.
Among these, the four essentials constitute the totality of practice, vows, and the world-system. The locus, the basis, and the substance are the primary meaning.
The shaking and so forth are the remedies (*pratipakṣa*). The vow is for the benefit of others. The sequence is also the same as before.
This means that one should know, by analogy from what precedes and follows, that the names and teachings are established based on these four essentials.

Furthermore, since the gates of teaching have possessed distinctions from antiquity, whereas now there is only this single, wondrously transcendent [teaching], it is not explained extensively; the subsequent sections should be understood by analogy.
Next, regarding the section on contemplation (*guan*), this refers to clarifying contemplation prior to the aforementioned conduct and virtue. Within contemplation, what is taken as sufficient?
This refers to "stopping" (*śamatha*). The place where one settles is the principle of the Truths (*satya*). There are three types of stopping: (1) stopping as the essence of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*;

(2) stopping as a skillful means that follows conditions; and (3) stopping that ceases the conceptualization of the two extremes. Although there are two kinds—namely, the single [stopping] and the twofold [stopping]—here both are referred to as "three.

However, the sutra merely speaks of the "place where one settles" and does not mention "two" or "one"; it is only because we are considering the meaning of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) here that this must be so.
Furthermore, the three matters to be practiced are merely two, namely the two of provisional and real, and the two stages of cessation and contemplation. These two and three are not fixed;

one should not dogmatically insist on a specific location as their basis. This is because wondrous contemplation follows whatever object is contemplated, yet all such instances are transformed into the wondrous Way.
Since everything herein is wondrous, this may be called the "Explanation of the Great Contemplation. It is clear.
For this reason, the commentary states (at length): "The others [take] the three aforementioned sages as a pair, namely, Great Compassion bestowing bliss and [Great Compassion] extracting suffering;
Mañjuśrī possesses Great Loving-kindness bestowing bliss, while Avalokiteśvara possesses Great Compassion extracting suffering. Śrī-Ārya [Amoghasiddhi] possesses both.
Now it is said that Samādhi and Prajñā [are the two]; since they are named according to the three virtues, Avalokiteśvara represents Prajñā through his contemplation."

This refers to the power of wisdom and the power of Samantabhadra’s meditative concentration; because it arises based on meditative concentration, it is designated by the name "Wondrous Virtue" (*Mañjuśrī*), which combines both [wisdom and concentration] for one who possesses great compassion.

The meaning of the subsequent two [names] can be understood individually. Furthermore, regarding merit and wisdom, the first [name] combines both because he is able to answer and ask questions in this sutra;
the subsequent two are distinguished accordingly. All of these are established for the sake of sentient beings according to their specific capacities.
Since his actual virtues are perfectly complete in every respect, this present text does not discuss them further; hereafter, all cases shall follow this same principle.

Below, the term "constant diligence" (*nityodyukta*) should be explained; however, as it is largely identical to "unremitting effort" (*apratiprasrabdha*), it can be understood by analogy and is therefore omitted.
Some say that because sentient beings are inexhaustible and must always be rescued and delivered, it is called "constant diligence. [It is also said that] one cuts off one's own...

Regarding the statement "evil is like saving one's head from fire," others say that these two—self-benefit and benefiting others—are contrasted such that one constantly exerts oneself in self-cultivation while never tiring of benefiting others.
Now, I maintain that both schools take these two benefits as their respective contrasts, yet differ in their sequence;

this is easily seen in the text. This is merely a matter of human interpretation; according to the scriptural exposition, the first follows from benefiting others, while the subsequent section concerns self-cultivation, encompassing both the general and the specific.
To know this by example and to always practice with diligence is as stated in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*:

"This bodhisattva, for the sake of a single sentient being, pursues them through immeasurable eons without abandoning them; even if the other does not accept [the teaching], he does not have a single thought of forsaking them.

Therefore, it is called 'constant diligence' (*nityavīrya*). This also involves both practice and aspiration; therein, the general and the specific, as well as the underlying intention, are intended to lead others into [the path].
Because it is the Way, it inherently possesses the four intentions; this is the perfect vision of the wondrous principle, which cannot be attained by partial views.

The two types of origin and manifestation (*honji-suijaku*) may likewise be understood by analogy. For the practitioner, the objects of mind and mental states are boundless; through wondrous contemplation, one must strive to bring them all into complete union with the wondrous Way.
Therefore, this is called "constant diligence."

Next, the term "without rest" (*anirantara*) is explained: previously, for the sake of sentient beings, one has firmly resolved to diligently seek this vidyā-mantra, vowing that once it is attained, there shall never be a cessation.
This is easily understood from the text. "Brahmacarya" refers to pure conduct, namely the two benefits [of self and others].
"Merit" (*guṇa*) refers to both fortune and wisdom. The essential meaning here is simply the desire to transform those below through compassion for a long duration.

This is because he has already repaid the Buddha’s kindness and does not yet wish to accept offerings from others. Herein, both the practice and the vow are included, whether collectively or individually;
that which serves as their basis is the essence of perfect virtue (*pāramitā*), whose body and function are inconceivable. These three meanings are fully present.

Regarding the statement "not dwelling" within the contemplation, the intent clarifies that because they are identical, this applies to all states of mind. Dwelling is itself rest, for it is by means of non-dwelling that one dwells.
To constantly engage in this contemplation without ceasing is precisely what defines such a person; they are certainly not far from it.
Sixth, regarding the explanation of Ratnapāṇi (Precious Hand): other commentators all state that his hands produce various jewels which he bestows in inexhaustible charity.
This is but a partial meaning and does not accord with the perfect intent of the sacred teachings. In the scriptural explanation cited within this present text, two meanings are contained.
This does not share the same interpretation as that provided by others; although it contains two meanings, the commentator within our own school essentially does not recognize these two.
The first meaning is "to guard and protect precious jewels," where the agent (the hand) and the object (the jewels) are combined into a single term.

The second meaning is "to hold jewels and bestow them upon others," where again the agent and the object are combined into a single term. The former refers to "guarding" (*shou*), while the latter refers to "hand" (*shou*). These are the two aspects of the object.

"Jewel" has two meanings: first, it refers to the jewel of the sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna; second, it refers to the sense of "palm," where the meaning differs while the essence remains the same—namely, "protecting and upholding.
Both of these refer to wisdom. In the text, from the beginning up to "the two vehicles," it is annotated as "holding the jewel";
from "always with... onwards, it means bestowing the jewel through wisdom. The former refers to personal realization.

Next, "benefiting others" (lit. *li-ta*, pronounced with a departing tone) refers to the act of donning [the armor]; the character is correctly written with the radical for "hand," though it is commonly used in its borrowed form.
This single character metaphorically represents one's own cultivation and realization, as well as the arousal of the great vow.
This means that based upon the essence, one arouses the great vow to protect the Great Dharma Jewel. The phrase "and so forth" (*nǎi zhì děng*) reveals that the vow is firm and unyielding.
It is capable of destruction; even a Buddha cannot [destroy it], let alone others. Therefore, it is said "even unto this," which refers to its protection.

This single phrase, in total, is the same meaning as the previous statement regarding non-retrogression from unsurpassed bodhi. As for the character *zǔ* (in the phrase *zhù zǔ*), its pronunciation here is *zǔ*;
it is the name of a ritual vessel and is not the intended meaning here. There are those who change it to *zǔ*, but that also is not the intended meaning. Correct.

The term *jǔ* (沮) should be pronounced like *zǔ* (咀), meaning "to destroy" or "to ruin. Regarding the current interpretation of "guarding" (*shǒu*), the commentary states that it distinguishes [the practitioner] from the profane use of the Dharma-treasure.

This interpretation establishes the preceding point, which still belongs to the initial sense: externally, even the Buddha cannot destroy [this state], and internally, even in dreams, one does not conceive of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Thus, it serves to complete the previous argument; as for the instruction to provide this explanation, it is for this reason.
Some say that this is the Buddha causing a Bodhisattva to preach the Mahāyāna Dharma for the sake of humans;

those who do not aspire to the Two Vehicles cannot preach the Mahāyāna because their mental dispositions (śīla) are such. Therefore, even in dreams, he does not cause them to aspire to either [vehicle].
This has yet to be reconciled, as it merely explains the meaning of those names. Now, I fear these two characters are erroneous, or perhaps they are *shou* (to maintain/guard).
The character "she" (攝) should be further verified against that sutra; furthermore, the character "zhi" (志) may be written as "zhi" (至).
"Zhi" means to arrive at, while "zhi" (志) means to aspire to with devotion—meaning to protect the Mahāyāna so that even in dreams, body and mind are not bound, but reach that [state].
Furthermore, one's mental focus is not bound to that [worldly object] either. Next, it clarifies holding jewels and bestowing them upon others; first, by means of two...
The mind is the hand that is able to hold; preaching and proclaiming it for others is the bestowal of right wisdom.

The precious treasure is the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure that is bestowed; it is the treasure previously realized and held in one's grasp. To speak of the two minds is to refer to the two wisdoms of means (upāya) and reality (prajñā);
using these two wisdoms to proclaim the wondrous path of the Mahāyāna for others is like holding [the treasure] with one’s hands.
The giving of jewels to others should be understood as merely provisional; why, then, is it called real? For in the subsequent passage, both types of wisdom are termed "expedient means" (*upāya*).

Here, too, the inclusion of both practice and vow, as well as the general and the specific—attaining [enlightenment] for oneself and causing others to attain it—possesses these four meanings, all of which are wondrous and not merely provisional.

Since this matter was already explained in the preceding sutra, the distinction between the fundamental and the manifested is clear; thus, the meaning of the threefold interpretation may be understood.
Next, regarding the contemplation of the three truths within the Middle [Truth], these are the ultimate treasures revered by all Buddhas;
the three aspects of the one mind are precisely the inconceivable contemplation (*acintya-vipaśyanā*). If it were not as explained previously, how could it accord with this text?
Therefore, it is certain that all interpretations hitherto offered do not accord with this passage. Truly, truly so!

Next, I shall explain the passage concerning Bhaiṣajyarāja. While the following section provides an extensive explanation, this brief commentary clarifies only that he received his name through a prior vow.
Within these vows, there are four: the first two are vows to repay kindness; the next two are vows of great compassion to save sentient beings, and great benevolence is also included therein.
These four are the essentials among all vows. Regarding the phrase "one thousand and four," some say it means "among one thousand."
To separately cite these four, or to speak of them "along with the four," is both unclear and remains to be verified through other texts. Furthermore, regarding these four vows:

the first two are offerings to the Buddha, and the next two are likewise offerings to the Dharma and the Sangha; thus, they constitute offerings to the Three Jewels, which are most essential and supreme.
Next, concerning the Buddha’s prediction that those who are "purified by fire" (huo jìng) all derive their name from burning the body, I now fear... [text ends]

The meaning of this [term] contradicts its intended sense, making it difficult to reconcile; if even the first four meanings seem somewhat problematic, I suspect there is a textual error, perhaps that the character "da" (大) should be "ru" (如).
This is because, as in the previous four vows, both the present and the future attain purity—thus it carries the meaning of "great.
Furthermore, the first two meanings refer to fire-purity (*agni-śuddhi*), while the latter two refer to Bhaiṣajyarāja. Consider this.
Although the text is concise, it fully possesses four meanings. Taken as a whole, the first two [meanings] concern repaying kindness for the sake of humans; the latter two concern remedial measures.
The final point—attaining Buddhahood so that sentient beings may realize the Way—is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The meaning of the teaching follows the previous examples;

the relationship between the original and the manifested (*honjaku*) is as explained in the following two chapters and can be understood there. As for the contemplator, through the threefold contemplation within a single mind, one can eliminate the defilements of the five abodes (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*), which are like filth.
The purification by fire can eliminate the suffering of two kinds of fruits, just as the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta* speaks of the two ailments of body and mind (and so forth).
The essential meaning is roughly thus (and so forth).

Regarding the omission of the seven Bodhisattvas in the future [section], the underlying causes and conditions have not been seen; since they are common to the direct meaning [of the text], they are omitted for now.
As for "Vīradatta" (Courageous Bestower), some say it refers to a Mahāsattva who, having realized ultimate emptiness, does not give rise to cowardice even when relinquishing body, life, or wealth.
These [names] all explain the union of aspiration and practice; this is for the sake of benefiting others and for the purpose of destroying one's own delusions.

Because they are attached, all serve to manifest the Way; thus these four intentions are all for the sake of the Dharma. To practice according to the Dharma is for the teaching and its meaning to abide long.
Taking the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as neither abandoning nor not abandoning, one preaches "abandoning" for the sake of sentient beings.

The observer who wondrously penetrates the principle of the three truths of the mind-nature may observe at will. Others take the three sages mentioned above as means to relieve poverty and rescue [the destitute].

The names "Swift Response," "Treasure Hand," "Medicine King for the Relief of the Poor," "Healer of Illness," and "Courageous Bestower" each encompass a portion of the meaning of the preceding two [names].
As for the current interpretation, each one is itself the Dharma-realm. Regarding the previous statement that "One Name is Equipped with Immeasurable Meanings, Treasure Moon":
some say that his wisdom and virtue are as precious as the moon and worthy of veneration. "Moonlight" refers to the function of wisdom that cuts through [delusion].
Delusion is like darkness that the moon dispels. "Full moon" refers to the perfection of the characteristics of wisdom, just as the moon is full.
The commentary states: "These three guides of illumination dispel darkness. In contrast to the "Jewel Moon," the "Guide of Wisdom Illumination" is like the moon and is worthy of veneration;
its light dispels all the darkness of ignorance, just as moonlight does. Just as the full moon can perform two functions, the meaning of the current passage can be understood by analogy.
It is called "Jewel Moon" (*Ratnacandra*) because it is able to shatter birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and attain *nirvāṇa*, which is truly precious.
Furthermore, it is called "Moonlight" (*Candraprabha*) because it does not abide in *nirvāṇa* but instead reflects back upon the world to dispel the darkness for all beings.

It is called "Full Moon" (*Pūrṇacandra*) because its dual limits coexist and its wisdom-function (*jñāna-prayoga*) is boundless. Taken as a whole, these are the three types of wisdom; taken together, they accord with the inclinations and desires of the world.
Furthermore, the three successive stages correspond to the latter three meanings; these four essentials are sufficient.

This meaning extends to the present context, where each individual stage possesses the threefold perfect and wondrous significance. What originally abides as the three wisdoms is manifested in its traces as partiality.
Contemplation is precisely the three contemplations, which are three-in-one and one-in-three. Regarding "Great Power" and so forth, others say that these two are divine powers.

Regarding the penetration of the small and the great through transformation and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): by means of these powers, one awakens those with whom one has a karmic connection, causing them all to resolve their minds [toward enlightenment].

That which can shake a hundred worlds is called "Great Power" (*mahābala*); that which can shake countless worlds is called "Limitless Power" (*apramāṇabala*). Now, it may be said that although this specific passage does not provide an explicit explanation, it can be understood by analogy:
the ability to personally shatter extremes and reveal the Middle Way is called "Great Power," while the ability to transform both extremes is called "Limitless Power. This is the sense here.

Both possess practice and vow; collectively they constitute the world, while individually they serve as remedies to lead [beings] back to the non-dual essence, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
All these are the traces manifested by those who are perfectly realized and have long since attained the ultimate, yet show such marks for the sake of others.

For the observer, this is the contemplation that directly perceives the Middle Way while simultaneously illuminating both extremes. Regarding "transcending the three realms," some say it means wisdom surpasses birth and death (*utpāda-nirodha*).
The Way transcends the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), which are what must be eliminated; "transcending" (*yue*) carries the meaning of departing and crossing over.

Now, it is said that these two interpretations are insufficient to manifest its essential nature and virtues. It is said that it surpasses and excels both kinds of *tridhātu*. This is, for the time being, a virtue;
there should also be a vow, and through their conjunction or separation, the traces of the essential teaching can be known. As for contemplation, it is precisely emptiness.
The virtue of transcending the three realms of分段 (duḥkhavipāka) is both provisional and middle; therefore, it is able to transcend the three realms of 變易 (pariṇāmika).
As for why the [first] seven were not explained, most commentaries do not sufficiently address them; thus, one may briefly adopt this from the perspective of the 宗門 (zongmen) school. It is thus.

Next, I shall explain the term *Bhadra*. In the new translations, it is simply called *Bhadra*; however, because the word lacks the vowel *a* and the syllable *dha* is pronounced with a light tone, it is combined with the letter *ra*.

Thus, in Sanskrit, it is a single syllable, and for this reason, it is here translated as "Worthy Protector" (*Xiangu*). One should know that "good" (*shan*) and "worthy" (*xian*) share the same meaning, while "guarding" (*shou*) and "protecting" (*hu*) are synonymous.

This is because "good" refers to the name of one who is capable of goodness, rather than having the sense of "being good and compliant"; therefore, the character "worthy" (*xian*) serves as its gloss.
