It is indeed so; all the Śākyas refer to those adjacent to the Sages as "Worthy Ones" (*bhadra*), and they firmly maintain that this refers to "guarding.
However, this merely captures the meaning of practicing it oneself and does not fully exhaust the intent of the sūtra. As for the commentary on the sūtra cited here:

if one hears this name and is able to have deep faith, then the Sages will skillfully guard them, causing them to reach certainty and arrive at the Unsurpassed Way. This refers to skillfully guarding others.

To act for the sake of reputation is not to practice exclusively through one's own conduct. Within this school, it is said that to maintain these virtuous deeds is called "virtuous maintenance," which is erroneous.

Others say that the former is the departure from defilement while this is the advancement toward goodness; to treat them as a single pair is extremely shallow and narrow, failing to fully extol the sutra’s illumination of the virtues of practice and the excellence of conduct.
This [practice] encompasses both the original vow and the joy of hearing the name, leading to faithful acceptance.
Severing doubt and being certain of attaining Bodhi constitutes the four essential meanings; these are all perfect and real, not the partial or expedient teachings of other sutras.

Since various sutras already extol them highly, they certainly do not merely suit those at the beginning of their practice. Within the contemplation, the first phrase indicates the essence of the contemplation (*guan-ti*), while the subsequent section explains its name and meaning.
The intent clarifies that one who skillfully maintains this contemplation is precisely the Middle Way and Right Contemplation (*zheng-guan*). For what reason is this contemplation so named?
Śaoshou’s commentary states that this is because, among all skillful modes of guarding, it is the most preeminent;
thus, he explains "skillful" (*śubha*) by means of "preeminence. This is because the Middle Way is the skillful means that is most capable of manifesting and protecting the principle of the Truths.
Regarding "Next, Maitreya": the correct Sanskrit term is *Maitreya*, also written as *Maidreya*. Translators did not transcribe it precisely;
they changed *mai* to *mi* and *drei* to *le*, and added the character for "compassion" (*ci*) to form the name. The following citation from three sutras explains this etymology:
first, his virtuous conduct; second, his past causes, which also include his making of vows; and third, his fundamental vow. The first is dependent upon the latter.
Second, by the power of his original vow, he abides in himself and causes others to do so as well. As the *Sarvajñāprabha-ṛṣi-sūtra* states: "In the past, he was a seer named Sarvajñāprabha;

having encountered the Buddha Maitreya and heard him preach the *Maitrī-samādhi-sūtra*, he made a vow, and for this reason he is called 'Maitreya' (the Compassionate One). The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says:
"Because he first attained the *maitrī-citta-samādhi*, he is called Maitreya. [This is illustrated by] the account of seeing the tamed elephant.

At that time, as the king was riding an elephant, he saw one of its kind running away recklessly and beyond restraint. He then rebuked the elephant trainers, who replied, "Its lustful mind is burning fiercely;

it cannot be disciplined by physical means alone. Three days later, once the lustful mind had subsided, the king took seven iron balls, heated them until glowing red, and made the elephant swallow them.
Having swallowed them, the elephant died. The ministers asked, "Such is the nature of desire..."

When it was asked, "Who can tame the mind? a great minister replied, "The Buddha’s teaching can tame it. Upon hearing this, the king resolved his mind, vowing, "I shall become a Buddha to rescue and deliver all beings.
From this, he received the name [Śākyamuni]. This is explained in detail according to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*.

Next, to clarify how this original vow differs from the previous one: the former was a resolution made in response to a state of suffering, whereas this is an aspiration aroused in response to a sublime object.
The two matters mentioned above are both the extraction of suffering; this is compassion (*karuṇā*). Why, then, are they both called "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*)?
This clarifies that the perfect and wondrous [state] possesses all things: the myriad practices and myriad virtues are all contained therein. There is no need for forced, divergent interpretations.

Taken as a whole, these vows and practices are what is seen in the world and through which one attains concentration; they are the primary meaning, wherein the noble and the ignorant are in opposition.

Cultivating the Flower of Compassion means that within a single practice for the sake of others, all things are fully perfected; this is what is extensively discussed in the various sutras of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Regarding the virtues of the primary and secondary manifestations (benji), they are not sequential. Next, concerning the Great Compassion within contemplation, there are three types.

If one brings forth the "unconditioned" (wuyuan) compassion, it subsumes all three kinds. Abiding in this unconditioned compassion, everything is non-active (*wuwei*), yet there is nothing that is not done.
Those who have the karmic affinity will all follow others in practicing this contemplation;

because this wondrous [contemplation] reaches the realization that all mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) are without exception wondrous, it is said that one is "separated from all unwholesome [states]," and the meaning of compassion (*karuṇā*) is contained therein. Next, another interpretation explains by correlating this with the subsequent text.
Master Mitian (Sengzhao) said: "Nothing can surpass it" means "nothing is capable [of surpassing it]"; this is precisely the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Because it is most excellent. Some say that this passage should have been moved to below the preceding section on causes and conditions (*nidāna*).
However, we maintain that this follows as a secondary consequence (*prasaṅga*) rather than being a formal explanation of the name; for this reason, the various masters likewise do not mention it.

To discuss it in full detail, the fourfold explanation (*caturvidha-vyākhyā*) regarding the meaning of this name should naturally be included here, which is precisely the intended meaning; thus the commentary states "and so forth" (*yathā-prapañca*), the details of which are found elsewhere.
I have not yet had the leisure to explain the remaining passages.

Next, regarding the explanation of "Jewel Accumulation" (*ratnakūṭa*): since its meaning is not found in the sūtras, it can be understood through other sources. All commentaries state that it refers to the accumulation of both material wealth and the Dharma;

furthermore, it is said to be "comprehensive" because the cultivation of causes is perfected, such that all the virtues of the *dharmadhātu* are fully and exhaustively detailed. Thus, it is so called.

Since the Jewel Accumulation (Ratnakūṭa) is fully complete, all practices and vows are contained within it. Having attained personal sufficiency, it can further universally inspire faith, dispel doubt, and lead the world to realize the Way;
thus, the four benefits are complete. Once these are fully provided, the meaning of perfection naturally manifests, and its functional traces naturally become evident.
Being able to contemplate the three truths such that the truths are revealed and wisdom is perfected is the meaning of the Jewel Accumulation.

Next, regarding the "Guide" (*śāstṛ*): he is called a Guide because he himself is able to realize the right path and is further able to lead all those who have not yet realized it so that they may all attain realization.
In the text, the first phrase refers to those who have not yet attained realization and whom he leads. Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is the essence of that which leads;
because it causes them to enter the right path and so forth, it is [the basis for] the metaphor of wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, it is compared [to the guide].
Not seeking a reward for the teacher’s virtue is precisely because one has attained the Way oneself and has no further needs;

it is solely out of compassion for those who have not yet reached it that one guides them to realization. If one were to seek a reward, it would instead reveal that one has not yet attained [the Way] oneself, which is not true compassion.
It is based on this principle that the name [of this practice] is established. The scriptural commentary explains it thus; most other commentaries are largely the same.
The mental formation [of this vow] is not yet complete; this is virtuous conduct, yet it should also involve a vow.

In general, it is for the sake of great compassion for all beings in the world, leading them to enter the Path of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*). It is not seeking gratitude or recompense; it is the antidote [to self-interest].

Great Compassion without object (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*) and the All-Knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) are both perfectly sublime. This has existed for a long time; it is merely now being manifested to attract and guide sentient beings. (3)
Contemplation is the capacity; the myriad practices are its locus; non-duality is the detachment from existence; and all that enters is the convergence upon the True Path.

Since this is wondrous contemplation wherein all things are fundamentally as they are, what further could be sought? As for the phrase "not yet explained," it refers to the eight names not yet being explained.

Because the principle of dependent origination has not yet been seen, one relies on the sutras to perform contemplation; since the explanation in the sutras has not yet been seen, it is likewise [not yet explained].
The lack of contemplative understanding has now been briefly appended to the refutation of slander as explained previously.
The reason all previous explanations cited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Bèihuá jīng) is that the vows of the various bodhisattvas are mostly expounded therein.
Sixth, regarding the summary: "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to those previously listed, while "etcetera" (*ādi*) refers to those not listed.

The term "etcetera" is used because one should understand the categories in brief rather than enumerating them exhaustively. This serves as an example; even when the number eighty thousand is listed, it likewise indicates the primary subject.
As has been briefly clarified above, this concludes the second section among the three types of assemblies, namely the assembly of Bodhisattvas. Below, the third [assembly] will be explained.

Third, regarding the "Mixed Assembly," there are four sections: first, the initial heading; second, the general explanation of the intent; third, the detailed analysis of the text; and fourth, the comprehensive examination.
First, the mixed assembly reiterates the headings of the preceding individual chapters. The word "this" (*zhè*) serves to introduce the subsequent general explanation of the terminology.

Within this section, there are two parts: first, a general comparison with the old [commentary] to briefly state the present intent; and second, the section beginning with "That which is called... and so forth.
This is the formal explanation. At the beginning, we first describe the partial errors of the three schools, followed by the correct presentation of our own position.
Regarding the term "ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*) used here inclusively: Master Zang established this name through contemplation to contrast them with the two preceding categories of "sages.

Thus, within this category there are sages, for various sutras extensively describe their sagely virtues; moreover, they have all already attained the opening and manifestation [of reality]. As for the term "worldly" (*loka*), it refers to those who have previously seen [the truth].
The old commentary did not reveal the names; these names have been supplied here with the intention of pairing them with the preceding two, as they represent the Path (mārga).

This is because all who possess the Path attain it. Since this section follows the initial arrival [of the text] and precedes the "Circulation" (liútōng) heading, it is said that according to the extant text of the sutra, there should be no mention of the five groups of the ordained (pañca-varga);
this must be a scribal error by Zhǎn'ān. Now, regarding the commentary’s statement that "among them, some have attained the Path," [it refers to those who have realized the fruit].

Those who have attained the Way are equal; why should one need to debate their outward form or attire? Thus, they merely delude themselves. Because gods and humans mostly seek victory over others, there are those who [cite] dragons and ghosts.
The first two [cases] contradict the meaning, and this one contradicts the text; all such instances are "inconvenient," referring to the names established by the three previous schools.

All of these lack skillful essentials and do not exhaust the reality of the matter. Ci'en [Master Kuiji], from here on, [discusses] five... (Note: The final character "五" (five) indicates that this is likely the beginning of a list or a section heading.)
Regarding the classification of names and meanings for the protection of the assembly, this is somewhat acceptable; however, compared to the previous [classification], it is considered "internal.
Furthermore, because it is not yet convenient, it is not as good as opening the previous [classification] into three: first, the general name "Internal Assembly";

second, the name "Assembly Equipped with Both Internal and External," because within it there are also renunciant bodhisattvas; and third, directly naming it the "External Assembly" in general. This terminology is slightly [better].
How regrettable that those who seem to have attained [this teaching] fail to employ it! Now, the preceding text’s explanation based on the three truths already encompasses this meaning.

Next, to explicitly state the present intent: by citing the single character "miscellaneous" (雜), it comprehensively subsumes the three pairs of both textual expression and meaning mentioned previously.
Because there is nothing that is not fully exhausted, it is said to be "comprehensive" (*jian*). This may be called the essential truth and is indeed convenient;
it is like the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā), which, by explaining according to the middle way, is termed the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.

From this point downward, until the end of the sequential sections, although the various commentaries within the tradition differ in many respects, they cannot be reconciled as far as their fundamental tenets (*zongzhi*) are concerned; this is also the case here.
I am unable to provide a detailed commentary on the characteristics of the "mixed and combined" meanings previously indicated;

herein, there are two parts. First, the section concerning causes and conditions, starting from "furthermore, mixed," and so forth. Second, the section concerning the teachings. Within the first part, two meanings are clarified, which is why it is called "mixed":
namely, because the categories and types are numerous, and because they do not follow a sequential order. There are two further subdivisions within this first part; first, the direct explanation.

Next, to harmonize the existence and non-existence [of the realms]: although the categories and numbers at the beginning and middle are many, they do not exceed three types—namely, the paths (*mārga*), the realms (*dhātu*), and the classes (*nikāya*).
Speaking in terms of the paths, among the six, there are only five, as the single hell realm is excluded.

Speaking in terms of the realms, among the three, there are only two, as the single formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is excluded. Speaking in terms of the classes, there are eight. Herein, whichever one of these is cited, it is immediately [the same].

The remaining two [aspects] are subsumed within it; however, these three must necessarily be complete in order to exhaust its essence. If only one were mentioned in isolation, it would reveal that the reality is not firmly established;
therefore, all three are enumerated together. Since these three meanings necessarily encompass a multitude of factors, they cannot be designated by a single name alone.

To name it according to any one of them would result in losing the true nature of the whole. Thus, a single term is used to cover all meanings, as this is more effective for managing their complexity.
This is the correct explanation of the miscellaneous meanings; below, the reconciliation of existence and non-existence explains the previous points regarding the single path and the single realm.

It addresses the difficulty posed by other sutras which claim that this sutra lacks the "constant mind of the world. In the various paths and intermediate states (*antarābhava*) of the Vaipulya [sutras], the matters within the realms are as described in this text.
The explanation of the *Antarābhava-sūtra* clarifies in detail how the Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers, reaches the non-... [non-perceptual realm].

The gods of the Realm of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) receive beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and lead them to that heaven, where they preach the Dharma for them so that all attain the paths of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as explained extensively in those scriptures. Furthermore, it is not only that [the Buddha] goes there;

as clarified in the *Benye Renwang Da jing Houfen* (The Latter Part of the Great Benevolent King Sutra on Original Karma), the assemblies of the Formless Realm descend to listen to the Dharma. Thus, these various sutras fully demonstrate the transformation of the three [realms].

The meaning of the existence or non-existence of the six realms within the equality of the *dhātu* (realms) is as analyzed below; however, because this is an abbreviated version, it lacks the details found in the extensive version, which may be immeasurable.
Alternatively, all [realms] may possess transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), just as in the first part of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* they are absent while in the latter part they exist.
These "equalities" are now explained and reconciled: according to the capacities of beings, they appear or do not appear as appropriate to the time, yet they exist there.
Because this [latter case] does not exist, it cannot be treated as an identical example. Furthermore, although [the Buddha] does not go there in person, his light nonetheless shines upon them;

thus, while in one case he transforms through sound, in this case he benefits them through light. This, too, cannot be categorized as the same. Below this, the second miscellaneous meaning is clarified:
not only is it diverse and manifold, but its sequence is also indeterminate. Because it is disordered, it is further termed "miscellaneous. To clarify this further...
Because this principle applies, the word "furthermore" (又) is used. Within this section, there are four parts: first, the presentation of non-sequential [teaching];

second, the refutation of the old masters' forced sequentialization; third, the exposition of the characteristics of non-sequentiality; and fourth, the conclusion which, for these reasons, designates it as "mixed" (雜).

First, regarding the "indefinite": as will be shown later, this refers to King Ajātaśatru. Second, regarding the exposition of the old masters' intent: they maintain that [the teaching was given] to the Buddha’s śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
All of these are human beings; immediately following them, they should have been listed among the kings of men.

That they are placed last for this very reason is precisely because they are the local inhabitants of that place and are the sovereigns of the land; thus, it is said that the etiquette of the "Lord of the Soil" (Tuzhu) should involve yielding out of deference.
This refers collectively to the devas, nāgas, and spirits, all of whom are treated as guests. Next, he cites a sutra to clarify this point.
This is not unreasonable; for that sūtra also enumerates the three assemblies in a sequence identical to the present one. Within the miscellaneous assembly, there are four categories:
first, the eight classes of devas and nāgas; second, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; third, the three assemblies [of the śrāvakas];
and fourth, the various wheel-turning kings (cakravartin), such as those of gold and silver, as well as kings, princes, state ministers, commoners, and officials.
The women of the kingdom and the great elders of the kingdom each arrived before the Buddha with their retinues numbering in the hundreds of thousands and tens of millions.
The purpose of listing these individuals is precisely to clarify that the four wheels [of sovereignty] and the various kings are all outsiders and are not the original lords of the land;

thus the text says, "Furthermore, there are ten thousand billion kingdoms. If they were to be accorded precedence, they should have been listed first; however, since they are all placed at the end, this confirms the point.
The fact that there is no mutual yielding is further clarified. From here on, the intent will be briefly explained.

Since they were all present at the same time and place during the assembly, yet the events unfolded in this manner, it simply arose from the circumstances of the compilation; it was merely a matter of the occasion.

It was not something intentionally arranged by the King of Men—what need is there to discuss the meaning of "mutual yielding"? Therefore, one must not forcibly impose a sequential order upon it. Some say: [end of quote]
I fear that the words regarding "taking" and "seeking" may not yet be excellent; now, I maintain that these words are entirely excellent, yet people do not understand them.
Next, I shall explain "removing" and "taking. Now, it is said that there must be a distinct meaning here, as in various previous explanations, though I am currently unable to examine them in detail.
This contains a profound meaning and does not rely on those various explanations. Since the principle is not yet subtle, how can one examine it thoroughly?
Some may say that this is simply because [the assembly] gathered according to the sequence of their arrival at that time;

however, judging by the *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (Wuliangyi jing), this too seems unlikely. In that sūtra, the assembly of nuns is placed after [the monks], whereas in this sūtra, they are placed before.

Furthermore, in that sūtra there are the four wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*), while here there is only a single sovereign. It cannot be that those who had already arrived there have not yet assembled here.
This is not so. Regarding those who claim that the preceding scholars have organized this into three sections—first the heading, then the enumeration, and finally the conclusion—I ask:
if this were indeed a formal structural division (*ko-wen*), please examine how the concluding remarks at the end read.

Furthermore, if it were merely an enumeration, why would there be only seven items, while the subsequent explanation establishes distinct titles for each of the preceding ones? I consider this as follows:

This reveals the characteristics of the disordered and mixed meanings. Regarding the eighth [point]: it refers to the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), nāgas, kiṃnaras, and humans.

To say simply "the assembly of the desire realm" or "the assembly of the form realm" without interspersing the word "gods" (deva) is what must first be refuted by the student, because such usage leads to confusion and over-extension; this should be understood. How are these eight points to be treated?
This is the section on "Confusion"; below, the text correctly distinguishes its characteristics as they appear in the four phrases of the passage, which precisely set forth those characteristics.
Former scholars all agreed that it should be stated that the Sanskrit text says "four," but this is an error. Now, I say that such a view misses the essential point:
if that were so, this would simply be a sequence; how could it be called "non-sequential"? Now, I say that if one proceeds from the inferior toward...
According to the sequence of superiority, one should first list the human kings, followed by the four heavenly kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*), then Śakra, then Brahmā;
the various nāgas, spirits, and so forth all belong to the jurisdiction of the kings and devas and are therefore listed last. If the sequence were arranged from superior to inferior, it would be:
first Brahmā, then Śakra, then the four heavenly kings, then the nāgas and spirits, and finally humans. If, however, it is according to the realms of existence (*gati*)...
Regarding the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), the sequence of their superior and inferior paths is as previously explained.

If one speaks in terms of the realms (*dhātu*), the sequence of the superior and inferior paths within those two realms is likewise as previously explained. Now, since this is not the case here, it constitutes the meaning of being "non-sequential" and "disordered.
First, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is clarified; within that, first the upper [levels] are presented, then the lower ones are returned to, and finally the upper ones are returned to again.

Therefore, although the textual description of the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is brief, it nonetheless follows a sequential order; thus, one should not claim that the text is erroneous based on human ignorance of this meaning.

This is an error on the part of the person, not an error in the text. Furthermore, since dragons (*nāga*) and birds (*pakṣin*) belong to the same realm (*gati*) yet are listed interspersed, this too constitutes a lack of sequential order;
hence the mention of "before and after. Moreover, when compared to other realms, these [dragons and birds] are inferior to the *preta* (hungry ghosts).
Because they are listed at the beginning, it is said later that the spirits of the front and back appear in three cycles.

If one considers the common discourse regarding the Eight Divisions (*aṣṭa-nikāya*), the celestial spirits (*deva*) are usually placed first and the *kinnara* spirits last; yet here, the *kinnara* are placed foremost, which differs from common discourse and is also not in sequential order.

Generally speaking, there are two reasons for this: first, the realms and destinies (*gati*) do not correspond in their sequence; second, within their own respective divisions, [the order] is not fixed.
Next, because this order is not sequential, it is called "miscellaneous" (*zā*); one cannot insist upon its specific sequence.

There is an ancient master’s explanation that the worldly multitudes are arranged in three groups: first the celestial multitudes, next the divine multitudes, and third the human multitudes, according to the order of their power.

Thus, the celestial multitudes are divided into two layers: first the multitudes of the desire heavens (*kāmadhātu*), and next the multitudes of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), based on the distance [from the human world].
Because they follow a sequential order, the heavens of the desire realm consist of three tiers: first, the assembly of Śakra; second, the assembly of the Four Great Kings;

and third, the assembly of the Sovereigns (Īśvaras) together with their ministers. Since this sequence is superior to those of other schools, it remains merely one path that does not exhaustively capture the essential meaning.
Now, to clarify the essentials, there should be four [points], as none of the aforementioned systems explicitly state the sequence; thus, they are summarized here as a concise outline.
Regarding this first teaching, it corresponds to its causal conditions (*nidāna*). Why is it that [the text] speaks of what was not previously mentioned? It refers to the eightfold distinctions;

these worlds—comprising devas, humans, as well as humans, ghosts, animals, and other sentient beings—are the means of remediation (*pratipakṣa*) for attaining the Way and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Now, if one considers the intent in this way, how could it manifest a "mixed" meaning? I now say that there are two senses to this "mixed": the first concerns the three [vehicles].

The multitude of meanings gathered together is called "miscellaneous" (*saṃkīrṇa*), which refers to the world (*loka*). Next, that which is not in sequential order is called "miscellaneous," which possesses three meanings:

First, "not in sequential order" reveals that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) lack a fixed nature (*niyata-svabhāva*), causing beings to recognize this principle; this is for the purpose of destroying deluded attachments to a fixed nature (*pudgala-vinaya*). Because the single ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is equal and devoid of any hierarchy, superiority, inferiority, or sequential order, it is precisely the "First Meaning" (*paramārtha*).
To clearly manifest this meaning, the text is arranged without sequential order and termed "miscellaneous" (*miśra*).

When the scripture says it "emerges from the compiler," the intended purpose lies in this very arrangement; it is not a term of definitive restriction, for its meaning clarifies that all may attain this perfect and wondrous Way.
Therefore, regarding such miscellaneous matters that manifest the subtle meaning, who is able to know them? Students of later generations should be deeply vigilant;
do not seek after them with ordinary views or common ears. There are those who resent these seemingly casual words; they have clearly not yet attained faith in the boundless and wondrous Way.

Next, regarding the classification by teaching (*yōkyō*), this refers to the previous "mixed intent. Since even the distinct [teachings] still involve commonality regarding phenomena (*ji*), we shall further examine them through the teachings to distinguish them.
First, there is a general discussion of the mixture of the two classes of people—ordinary beings and sages—which also concerns the mind.

In terms of the path and the individuals, there are two types of mutual admixture; in terms of karmic retribution, physical appearance, and attire, there are many forms of admixture. This is as follows:

The teachings and meanings of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) school are next; those of the *Tong* (Shared) school follow; then the Bodhisattva [vehicle], which refers to the three distinct stages, specifically the stage of emerging from the conventional world (*chujia*);
and finally the Perfect [Teaching], which refers to the meaning of the mutual identity and interpenetration of the one and the many, termed "intermingled" (*za*).

The first three all involve a gathering and intermingling, which corresponds to the former initial meaning from the past; the latter one corresponds to the previously mentioned meaning of "indefinite sequence," which is precisely this sutra.
Because its opening and assembly are wondrously without fixed method, it is called "miscellaneous" (*zā*). Next, the summary of what precedes refers to the three previous schools mentioned above.
As for the "root" (*běn*), it means that while one already dwells in this wondrousness, one now establishes the "traces" (*jì*) in order to lead sentient beings to return to the same [truth];

this meaning applies to both the distant and the near, which should be contemplated. Furthermore, the "contemplator" observes that the mind is itself empty; thus, all phenomena and even a single phenomenon are themselves provisional (*jiǎ*).

The eighth section is as before, consisting of eight distinct parts. The first, the listing of the assembly of the desire-realm heavens (*kāmadeva*), has three sub-sections:

(1) the assembly of Śakra, (2) the assembly of the Four Great Kings, and (3) the assembly of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods. Regarding the first two, there are two types of dwellers on the earth; regarding the third, there is one type of celestial being.
The initial text contains four expositions. First, within the causal conditions, there are two parts: first, a general explanation of the four meanings, and second, an explanation based on the sutra.

Regarding the detailed explanation of his names, the first four meanings are as follows: first, the correct explanation of the person's name; second, the explanation of the name of the heaven in which that person was born;
third, the explanation of the name of the mountain upon which that heaven rests; and fourth, the explanation of the meaning of the person listed at the beginning.
Regarding the first name, it should simply be called Śakra Devānām Indra; the character "Indra" (or "In") is redundant in the text.

The Sanskrit name has been translated and explained, yet it remains generally erroneous and abbreviated, making it impossible to reconcile with previous interpretations. Some have said that it should properly be rendered as *Śakradevānām-indra*;

*Śakra* means "able," *deva* means "heavenly being," and *indra* means "lord. Because he governs and transforms [the gods] in the Hall of Good Dharma (*Sudharmā*), his conduct accords with the will of the heavens;
thus he is called "Able" and "Lord of the Heavenly Beings. While this may be acceptable, it is not entirely new.
Regarding "Śakradevendra": *Śākya* is his clan name, which translates as "Able" (*neng*); *deva* is "Heaven" (*tian*); and *indra* is "Emperor" (*di*).

The full term is "Able Heaven Emperor. It is called "Śakra-devānām-indra," meaning "The Able One among the Heavenly Kings," or "Śakra-devendra," which means "Sinking into and Reaching [the State of] the Heavenly King.
If one were to state it precisely according to modern phonetics, *Śakradevendra* would be transliterated as *Shijia Tiewo Yindala*, and its translation and meaning would be identical to the above.

Previously, there was someone who, while extensively comparing Chinese and Sanskrit, stated that he did not know the origin of the character "Huan" (桓). Now, according to the character *va*, its original form is *bha*.
When pronounced in Sanskrit, it is very light; the sound of "he" (*he*) is close to it, and the sound of "he" is also close to "Huan.
Thus, it changed into "Huan," and this is its origin. For example, the name of the Bodhisattva Lokāloka is called *Vasuprabhāsa* in Sanskrit, yet the old [translation] used "Shi Guan" (世觀).

Vāsudeva is also called Heshouxiu (和和修); these are general examples of such cases. According to the actual principle, this is a name and title combined, referring to the "Capable Heavenly Lord" (Neng Tian-di).
"Di" (帝) means "lord" (zhu). Because it is unknown which celestial lord this refers to, it is [the lord of] the Cāturmahārājakāyika Heaven.

As for this character "Cai" (切) in the term Cāturmahārājika: if written with the "heart radical" (心), it is the character "cai" (裁); if written with the "ten" (十), it is simply the character "qie" (切). If...

The term "from seven sides" (*qībān*) refers to the phonetic transcription of the word *cetiya*. Since it is said to be "cutting" (*qiè*) and "beneficial" (*lì*), yet its specific name and meaning were unknown, it was therefore translated and explained.
Regarding the term "Joyful Sight" (*Xǐjiàn*): this is the place where Śakra, the Lord of the Gods, resides.

Various traditions all call it "Good Sight" (*Shànjiàn*) or "Good Manifestation" (*Shàxiàn*), yet throughout this text, both above and below, it is consistently referred to as "Joyful," perhaps because it is sacred.

This [passage] appears in a different version or is a scribal error; as for the mountain where he resided, since it is already stated that he dwelt upon its summit, yet it is not known what the name or meaning of this [mountain] is, it was therefore explained later.
That it is deep and broad is its stability (*āśraya*); that it is high and prominent is its clarity (*prabhāsvara*).
The subsequent explanation is self-evident. Regarding the mention of "high, broad," and so forth, some say it is based on [the following].
*Acama*. This Bodhisattva questioned the Buddha, and this was the answer he received. However, many of the points currently employed here do not accord with the *Abhidharmakośa*;
since the scriptures and treatises differ, there is no need to reconcile them.

"Sumeru" is newly translated as "Wondrously High" (*Miaogao*), because it is composed of the four precious substances, is wondrous, and rises above all other mountains. The phrase "this is [the explanation of]... serves to explain what was previously listed.

Regarding the phrase "Lord of the Desire Realm" (*kāmadeva*), an ancient commentary explains that among the three heavens of the desire realm, Śakra is the sovereign while the other two are ministers;
my current intention follows this general sense, hence the term "Lord of the Desire Realm.

Others say it does not refer to the lord of the six desire heavens, but rather specifically denotes the lord of the second heaven. Still others say his original name was Magadha, an old man of that land.
Therefore, regarding the various previous explanations listed at the outset, I have cited them extensively from sources such as the *Abhidharmakośa*;

however, as these are not the primary essentials for this context, I do not have the leisure to describe them in full detail here. Following this, I shall rely on the sūtras to provide a detailed exposition of the meanings of these various names through a series of questions and answers, totaling nine sections.
Of these, the first eight all consist of questions and answers; the first section concerns the preceding cause (*hetu*), whereas the previous [section] only clarified the result (*phala*).
To distinguish its cause, this is clarified: because one gives everything one possesses at once without hesitation, it is called "sudden giving" (*tun-shi*).
Next, regarding the name "Unseen" (*wei-jian*), when translated back via logical inference (*hetu-pratyaya*), it simply means "numerous givings.

Third, this is originally the name of a person from the country of Magadha, used as a title based on his origin. Fourth, "Unseen" has likewise not yet been translated; it should likely mean "superior and exquisite garments."
Furthermore, among these five, we have not yet seen [the term] translated; it is common in the Western Regions (India) for this to be used as a name based on one's original clan name (*gotra*).

The sixth and seventh [categories] can be understood accordingly. How does the eighth differ from the preceding? The preceding is based on the original cause, whereas this refers directly to the present fruit.
The ninth merely presents alternative names rather than explaining the meaning of the names; this is precisely the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Great Jewel Garland Sutra), which accords with the Dharma.
The Master said: "Wuyi (物翼) is actually *Kauśika*. Originally it was *Kauśika*, but when it was translated here [in China], as this land did not understand it, they took 'shì' (翅) to mean 'yì' (翼).
It would have been better to leave it as 'yì' (翼). Because those who translated the Sanskrit did not understand it, they followed the local dialect and changed 'Kau' to 'Wu' and 'shì' to 'yì'.
This error arose precisely because of that lack of understanding at the time; the principle of the matter is indeed thus."

This is so. Within this, there are four essentials: first, the explanation of the name "world"; second, the clarification of past causes such as the practice of giving, which constitutes the capacity for human benefit;

third, the ability to destroy afflictions and obscurations, which constitutes the capacity for remediation; and fourth, the contemplation of the thousand meanings, within which the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is contained.
It is for this reason that past causes are extensively cited; it is because these four kinds of causal conditions exist.

Regarding the name [of this teaching], according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, various schools cite it as saying: "In the Tripiṭaka, it is said that such a person attains the stage of Srotāpanna;
in the Mahāyāna, they are described as Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas. Now, following the words of that treatise, within the Small Vehicle one merely attains the first fruit (Srotāpanna);
yet here, citing the sūtra, it is said that one directly attains the third fruit (Anāgāmin). Furthermore, the term "Dharmakāya" used in the treatise also applies generally to this very context.

The difficult questions regarding the meaning are explained through three modes, and for now, they reside in this general explanation. This samādhi is named "Valiant Subjugation" (*vīra-vijaya*) and is also called "Heroic Aspect" (*vīra-lakṣaṇa*) or "Heroic Practice" (*vīra-caryā*).
There are both general and specific attainments, as has already been stated previously. Regarding the differences in internal realization:

although those who realize it equally may differ in the degree of their realization, because one intends to manifest that there is difference within the same state, the explanation is given collectively first, and subsequently it is said that they are "not the same. If one considers them according to the ten [stages]...
The earth is for the ten heavenly kings; this heaven corresponds to the second stage (*bhūmi*). Now, it should not be understood according to this [literal] meaning alone.
Furthermore, regarding the bestowal of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), this is the previous teaching which, by following a certain partial condition, speaks in such a manner.

If, within this teaching, one has already realized the reconciliation (*samavaśaraṇa*) and finds that the essence and function of the wondrous Way are without fixed direction, how much more so when the fundamental and the manifested (*honjaku*) are difficult to conceive, as they follow in sequence?

The commentary (stating "and so forth") is provided to ensure that this meaning is understood. Within the context of the provisional and the fundamental (*honjaku*), even the teachings of the past had already attained this samādhi;
however, it is now at its ultimate peak through the opening and unification of all teachings. Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, there is the wondrous ambrosia, the medicine of immortality. This is a case where the provisional traces are employed to manifest the fundamental reality. Those who dwell in these traces are led by skillful means.

In reality, they all converge upon the same source. The two aspects of "long" and "near" can be understood through contemplation. Next, regarding the ten wholesome actions within the context of contemplation:

these are the causes for celestial rebirth because they are dharmas pertaining to the heavens. However, if these thirty practices are merely worldly causes for heaven and not the ultimate cause of heaven, then when they are all realized as empty, provisional, and the Middle, they become the wondrous realm of the Three Truths, which is the ultimate [cause].
One should understand that the meaning of "principle" (yi) is such that it is none other than emptiness, the provisional, and the middle;

do not merely recite these words, for they are the wondrous Way of Heaven, which simply allows all things to be as they are and shines upon them naturally. This is the contemplative path of the Heaven of the Thirty-three according to this sutra.

Next, in the explanation of the causes and conditions for the three lights and four kings, regarding the term "inner minister" (*naichin*) mentioned within the section on the first three lights: the intention is first to indicate and then to enumerate them.

They are called "inner" because they face outward [toward the world], and "ministers" because they look toward the sovereign; the sovereign is the one who explains [the Dharma]. The commentary states: "They are the ministers who assist Śakra.
Because inner ministers are close to the sovereign, they are listed first. Alternatively, it is said that the following sections sequentially explain what was previously mentioned.
These three correspond to the Three Luminaries; the subsequent assembly corresponds to the three sages who manifested as traces.

While various schools simply refer to them as "stars" (*xing*), here they are called "luminaries" (*ming*) because this is a distinct or superior explanation, as they illuminate and shatter what is most supreme.

Some directly state that there is a sutra [on this], while others say it appears in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*. All commentaries state that it appears in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* under the name "Moon-Jewel" (*Candraratna*).
"Śrī-sarva-candra" is the name of a Devaputra; the two following examples should be understood in the same way.

That which binds [the teaching] as the "original and the trace" (honji-suijaku) is precisely this causal condition (*nidāna*), and it is also the meaning of the original and the trace. Herein, one ought to distinguish its essence, magnitude, and causes, but I have not yet had the leisure to do so.
Others say that the "three lights" are subsumed under the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and that there is no separate heaven; if [it were] the four...
In essence, the three luminosities (triloka-prabhā) are fundamentally one. That which manifests as the penetration of the world (*loka-vyūha*) illuminates all;

that which manifests as the penetration of humans (*puruṣa-vyūha*) can shatter darkness; and that which manifests as the penetration of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-vyūha*) can cause beings to firmly awaken to the Way.
These are the original three Great Sages, who should manifest these three traces. This is the most perfect [teaching], capable of corresponding to the other three.
In the present sutra, since this same perfectly wondrous teaching is easy to understand, it is not mentioned in detail;

however, the causes and conditions of these three lights should be sought thoroughly according to the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Origin of the World) as translated. In the contemplation (*guan*), the three wisdoms (*trividya*) are taken as the three lights, and the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) are taken as the three wisdoms;
this is an explanation in terms of their universal characteristics. These three contemplations are able to shatter the darkness of the three delusions.
Because it manifests the path of the three truths, it is the three lights (*trimaṇḍala*).

The above explains the meaning of the three lights; below is the explanation of the meaning of the "Heavenly Son" (*devaputra*). The first phrase generally presents the meaning of its essence, while the subsequent phrase specifically indicates it.
Thus, the meaning of the Heavenly Son of the Three Lights of One’s Own Mind according to this sutra is clearly elucidated. It is clear that there is [this meaning].

first is a general explanation, followed by a specific explanation. Within the general explanation, first the items are listed and their significance indicated, then the dwelling places are clarified, and thirdly, their physical dimensions.

Next, in the separate explanations below, there are first the separate explanations of the Four Kings, followed by the separate explanations of the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*).

Regarding the first four, for each one, there is first the translation of the name, second the place of residence, and third the retinue they command. These four names all originate from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
This is a direct translation without an explanation of the meaning. Furthermore, while the initial section identifies two types of ghosts, the subsequent explanations all refer to them as *piśācas*;

it is unclear which is the definitive reality. The names of the Four Kings should be as stated in the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" of the new *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* and as explained in the old commentaries.
The specific names of each pair of ghosts are fully detailed in the *Mahādāna-bhūta-āhāra-sūtra*. [The term] *akṣi-pāpaka* (Evil Eye) has been newly translated.

Regarding the "Cloud-Ugly-Eyes" (*Yúnchǒumù*): the first two names of the ghosts are explained in sequence as follows. They are also simply called "Fragrance-Eating Ghosts" (*Shíxiāngguǐ*) and collectively known as "Extraordinary Stench Ghosts" (*Qízhòuguǐ*).
Their bodies are like scorched bones, smelling of putridity. *Pīlíduō* (Piśāca) is translated here as "Hungry Ghosts. *Jiūpántuó* (Kumbhāṇḍa) is translated as "Palace-Guarding Ghosts.
*Bīshèshā* (Vetāla)—newly translated as *Bìshèzhā*—is translated as "Toilet-Guarding Ghosts," so called because they guard toilets and watch for people.
This purifies the food. Next, the term "World-Protectors" (*lokapāla*) is explained: "world" refers to the people of the four continents who are protected;
"afflictors" refers to various spirits and ghosts; and the "Four Kings" are those who provide protection. Because they are discussed collectively, they are called the "Four World-Protecting Kings.

It is commonly said that there are eight classes of beings, all of which refer to the eight categories beginning with devas and nāgas. However, some say this explanation is incorrect; it is actually based on...
These Four Kings each lead two groups of eight; these are not the same as the eight [classes] such as the devas. Now, it is said that the "eight" applies to both [categories].
If one follows the general explanations found in various sutras, the eight are taken to be the devas and so forth;

however, if one follows what is explained within the *dhāraṇīs*, they specifically refer to these [eight classes of spirits] as the eight. Since this discussion concerns the eight [classes] among ghosts and spirits (*bhūta-graha*), [the former list does not apply here].
The various heavens are repeatedly governed by the Four Great Heavenly Kings;
if one further subdivides them, there are twenty-eight divisions, all of which are under the command of Senāpati (Saṃjñeya), who is the one formerly known as the Great General Vaiśravaṇa.
This is explained in detail in the ten-fascicle *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. Since this is a causal narrative, it should possess four essential points; however, there are three types of protection.

"Yi" (義) means to obstruct, to preserve, and to manifest; collectively, these three are called the "World-Protectors" (*Lokapāla*). "Obstructing" refers to remedial counteraction (*pratipakṣa*); "preserving" refers to benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha*);

and "manifesting" refers to enabling them to attain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Regarding the provisional teaching (*kyō*), since all Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles speak of these four, one knows they apply universally to both the provisional and the real.
As for the four types [of worlds], if the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) correspond to the ten heavenly kings, this...
The "Heaven" (deva) corresponds to the meaning of the first stage (*bhūmi*); this interpretation—encompassing both the distinct and the perfect—is what was previously taught.
However, according to the present sutra, all are opened and reconciled into a single, ultimate, and most perfect circle, such that there is nothing that is not consummated in its wondrousness.

Thus, the subsequent passage states: "We, too, are like this; we shall certainly attain Buddhahood. This serves as the proof for this meaning. Since this point is easy to understand, it is treated briefly here. Next is the meaning within the context of the fundamental and the manifested (*honjaku*).
This is precisely the meaning taught in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which relies upon these provisional traces (*jì*) to manifest the fundamental reality (*běn*).

Within the sūtra, it first clarifies specific protection (*bié hù*) and subsequently clarifies universal protection (*tōng hù*). Now, this [text] correctly employs these two meanings from the sūtra: first, it clarifies the fundamental and the trace by specifically applying them to the four [aspects];

second, it clarifies the fundamental and the trace by universally applying them to the four. Regarding the first [section on] the specific, it first briefly indicates the fundamental and the trace according to the intent of the sūtra.
Next, relying directly upon the sūtra, we correlate [the subsequent section] with the initial heading; "that which is called 'the fundamental'" refers to this very thing.
This fundamental entity is the sovereign of these four virtues. Since these four masteries encompass all virtues without exception, it is termed "sovereign.

Although each of the four persons possesses all four virtues, they are here distinguished for the sake of pairing the four [virtues] respectively against the four [persons]. The full text explicitly states that each one possesses all four.

This is a brief summary. How is this known? It is known by means of the traces (*likeness*); thus one knows the fundamental source. Why is this so? If it were not for this fundamental source, how could there be these traces?
That these traces can exist is precisely because of this fundamental source. Therefore, from this fundamental source, these traces are suspended;
and by relying upon these traces, this fundamental source is manifested. Furthermore, in the Great Sūtra, the four trees symbolize the four virtues as the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings.
It is known because [the Buddha] is protected by them. Below, the text clarifies that since his original essence (*honji*) is thus, his manifesting these four kings is merely a trace (*kegyō*).
In this passage, the reason for the descent of the trace is directly explained without a formal conclusion;

one should understand that the meaning of the character "to act" (*u*) above the character "to protect" (*go*) is what makes its intent clear. "The Buddha-dharma" is precisely that which is protected; this is stated briefly.
To speak of the four virtues being fully possessed is, in truth, to speak of the eight kinds of exhaustion; yet, in essence, it refers to the three and the four. One will see this for oneself below.
Outsiders falsely calculate the world to possess these four virtues; [the teaching] not only prevents outsiders from grasping them, but also prevents insiders from grasping them.
If outsiders grasp them, they destroy the "four withered" (the four elements); if insiders grasp them, they destroy the "four flourishing" (the four nutriments). This is now a brief summary.
To clarify, what is termed "external grasping" refers to false attachment; it possesses three meanings: negation, preservation, and manifestation.
If one were like the "protectors" discussed previously in the section on causes and conditions, they would be merely worldly beings.

[The Buddha] was able to manifest his wondrous function precisely for the sake of protecting this Dharma-world, and thus displayed these traces. Below, according to the sutra, the specific correspondences are as follows: [toward...]

What has been discussed thus far concerns the meaning of the primary and secondary manifestations (*honji-suijaku*) of the Four Heavenly Kings; however, the meaning of the four directions and the two obstructions has not yet been clarified, and therefore it is explained here.
Previously, the four virtues were correlated with the four persons; now, the four persons are correlated with the four directions.

Furthermore, whereas previously only the external was mentioned, here both the internal and external are addressed; thus, each one fully possesses the protection of both, as the trees exist [to provide this].
The four pairs and eight classes, the four withered and four flourishing, represent the "constant";

the eighth method, in which the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa, represents the "neither-of-the-two" Middle Way, which is the Dharmakāya and the three virtues (*triguṇa*). The preceding section clarified that there are three meanings to protecting the world;

now, the refutation of internal and external erroneous attachments constitutes "obstructing and protecting," while the preservation of these eight methods constitutes "guarding and protecting. This is the eternal.
To know that their essence is non-dual is precisely to manifest the Middle Way; this is the protection of the Dharma (*dharmarakṣā*).

Now, although only "two" are mentioned, protecting these two is equivalent to protecting the three [realms], because by relying on their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), one manifests their true nature (*svabhāva*). This is just as protecting the world (*loka*) enables the manifestation of the meaning of transcending the world.

This explains the characteristics of the previous discussion regarding the manifestation of traces and the act of protective maintenance. The preceding section has provided a complete and detailed account.
Although the previous explanation was somewhat extensive, it was essentially distinct [from the present one] and its underlying principle was not yet fully exhausted;

therefore, the sūtra text provides this further interpretation to clarify its universal principle, whereby the principle is finally complete. Thus the sūtra says: "These four pairs of trees are presided over by the Four Heavenly Kings," which refers to the aforementioned meaning.
It further states: "The flowers and fruits of the twin śāla trees are luxuriant and can constantly benefit immeasurable multitudes."

The production of flowers is a metaphor for the self; the fruit is a metaphor for bliss. Although the scriptural text briefly mentions only the first two, since the first two exist, it follows by principle that all four should be complete;
thus, by analogy with the meaning, the latter two are added here. "Uprooting the substance" is a metaphor for permanence, because it is the foundation and the beginning of virtues.
The term "roots" is not mentioned because this is explained in terms of cultivated virtues, and roots belong to the trunk. "The self" refers to the sovereign flourishing of blossoms.
Therefore, "joyful" (*nandana*) means it provides the resources for enjoyment and comfort; "pure" (*śubha*) means it is flourishing and radiant.
Since each [of these] possesses these four virtues, they constitute the "common" (*sāmānya*). As the object of protection is thus, so too is the subject of protection.

The following clarifies the subject of protection that manifests these four virtues, so that all who have not yet attained them may attain them. Having previously explained the dual protection, now...

Why, then, do you exclusively protect that which is flourishing? It is because one protects the withered in order to destroy false flourishing, and protects the flourishing in order to destroy the withered.
Now, it is explained that this refers to the greatness of the benefits of the four virtues of the Middle Way;

thus, the *Eighteen Emptinesses Treatise* clarifies that all four virtues are established as names upon the substance of the Middle Way—which is the "neither-nor"—just as, for example, it is said to be "neither coarse nor subtle."

The name "Miao" (Wondrous) signifies this. Regarding the concluding statement, "Thus, the traces are equal," the Middle Way and its four virtues, as well as persons and dharmas, constitute the world that is to be protected.
Reflect upon this, reflect upon this! By contemplating the four kinds of knowledge within the Middle Way, one is able to protect the principle of the Four Truths;

this is the protection of what is to be protected. The removal of the two delusions constitutes the protection of the traces. To be able to cultivate this contemplation is the self-protection of the world.
The following is the third [section], which explains the two highest heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Within this, it first explains the reason why the two intermediate heavens are not listed, and then provides the formal explanation of the two that are unsurpassed. The initial part has three sections: first, a brief explanation of the two heavens;

second, an explanation of the reason for not listing them; and third, a detailed explanation establishing the first heaven. Regarding the phrase "the time of goodness" (*kṣema-kāla*), the text does not explain its meaning.

In one place, it is explained that this is because one practices wholesome dharmas according to their respective periods. Regarding the term "Exquisite Endowment" (*miāozú*), its meaning is not explained there either.
In another place, it is explained that the dwelling place of a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood is fully equipped with the superior cultivation of precepts, concentration, and wisdom;

it excels those above and below, and is thus called "Exquisite Endowment"—this is merely an abbreviated statement. The phrase "briefly stated" (*yánlüè ěr*) precisely explains the reason for not listing [the details], since they have already been listed.

The superior, inferior, and intermediate [levels] can be known by oneself and do not require elaborate textual exposition; therefore, it is said to be "abbreviated. Below, this is further explained and established:

those who are "inferior" refer to the inhabitants of the lower realms who possess only mundane wholesome states (*vyavakīrṇakuśala*). Those who "delight in the superior" aspire to the heavens of the upper realms because the objects of desire there are superior;

furthermore, the various devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are attached to the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyānasukha*). For these reasons, one should know that this is merely an abbreviation. Next...

This is the formal explanation of the two aforementioned heavens. If one were to list these two names according to the usual order, they would be the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*) and the Heaven of Mastery over Emanations (*Vaśavartin*).
Now, because these names appear here unexpectedly, they lead to a different interpretation. Regarding the phrase "self-emanated and other-emanated," this explains the meaning of the two names;
it is precisely the meaning of those two usual names. Both of these heavens create instruments of pleasure through emanation and enjoy that pleasure, yet they emanate [it].

"Delighting in this pleasure" refers to the self-transformed [heaven], while "receiving pleasure above" refers to the transformed-pleasure-of-others [heaven], because they have already enjoyed the objects of pleasure manifested by others;

thus it is called "self-and-other-transformed. Some say that the first heaven should properly be called the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (Nirmāṇarati), and that calling it the Heaven of Transforming Pleasures (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) is incorrect.
This above has merely explained the names of the two "transformations"; it has not yet explained the meaning of the two types of "mastery" (vaśavartin). That is to say:
This is because one attains mastery over both the transformations of oneself and others; it is called "Great" (*mahā*) because it excels what is above and below.

Regarding the note "and so forth," one should clarify the causes and conditions according to the teachings. Now, I say that this very "desire for joy" contains four meanings: if one desires the mundane, it is the Worldly Vehicle (*laukika-yāna*);
if one also desires the supramundane, it is the Human Vehicle (*mānuṣya-yāna*); and if one desires that which transcends the mundane, it is the Supramundane Vehicle (*lokottara-yāna*).
There is indeed weariness with the world as the antidote to delighting in the supramundane truth, which is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*);

all sūtras speak of these various devas as having access to both the provisional and the real teachings. Now, in this present sūtra, they have all been brought together and reconciled, none of them being anything other than perfectly wondrous.
It is precisely to manifest this meaning of perfect wonder that both [the devas and the bodhisattvas] are equally given the name "Sovereign" (*vaśavartin*), which carries profound significance.
Below this, [the author] further refutes divergent interpretations. The intention of this master is that "Mastery" (*vaśitā*) refers to both the *Kāmadhātu* and the *Brahmaloka*;
these two realms are both termed "Mastery," and because they are both "summits" (*mūrdhan*), they both receive the name "Mahāvaśavartin.
As for the refutation, it is certainly the case that there is no such principle as "non-existence. There is an old citation from a commentary which states: "Mastery is the Emperor (*Indra*)."
The Lord of the Śakras, the Great Minister, Maheśvara, is the teacher of Śakra; some say he belongs to the latter two heavens of the Desire Realm.
Now, according to the commentary, this is taken as the correct interpretation. The *Paramārtha* [translation] also calls him Viṣṇu, who assists Śakra in battle with the Asuras.
When the Asuras swallowed him, the gods were filled with grief, believing they had lost their great general. According to this meaning:
Therefore, Īśvara and Maheśvara, along with Śakra and his ministers, do not belong to the latter two heavens;
others hold that Īśvara belongs to the two heavens of Yāma and Tuṣita, while Maheśvara constitutes the two heavens of Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmitavaśavartin.

Thus, these two [classes of beings] comprise the four celestial abodes (*kāmāvacara-antarīkṣa*) of the Desire Realm. As previously cited from the *Vyākhyā*, the author first provides an explanation as before, and then offers his own interpretation, stating:
In the preceding list, Śakra, the first Heavenly Lord of the Desire Realm, was designated as the sovereign, while the Three Luminaries and the Four Guardians were designated as ministers.

Now, the two heavens of the Desire Realm—Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin—are listed; these are the two heavens in question here. It is said that this third Śakra accords with our present intention;
however, we cannot help but omit the intermediate two heavens, for their significance remains incomplete [this passage is adapted from the other four *siddhāntas*].

[Insert before the title: Next, regarding the "Original and Traces" (honji-suijaku), these two fixed names refer to the samādhis among the twenty-five that are capable of destroying these two forms of existence (*bhava*).
If one relies on the *Daśabhūmika*, they correspond to the fifth and sixth stages; how much more so since they are both perfectly wondrous—this is certainly the case.
Because the five desires originally depend on others and are not self-existent, whereas now one is able to exercise mastery over them, this is a case of manifesting the Original through the Trace.

This is understood as follows: observing the Middle Way leads into Emptiness because it is not obstructed by any phenomena; thus, the Middle can simultaneously be said to exist in both [Emptiness and Provisionality].
Because it preserves all things without obstruction, and in order to eliminate the duality of the two names, "Provisional" is not mentioned.
Furthermore, since it is immediately subsumed within the Middle Way through the simultaneous illumination of both [aspects], there is this general intention; hence the commentary states: "[...]".
Next, the listing of the deities of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) constitutes the second section. Within this, there are three parts: first, the explanation of Śikhin;

second, the explanation of Ābhāsvara; and third, the explanation of the word "etc. The first of these has three parts: first, the explanation of Sahā; second, the explanation of Brahmā-rāja; and third, the explanation of Śikhin. The first [explanation of Sahā] consists of four phrases.
Regarding the two meanings of its name, the first two explain "patience" (*kṣānti*), and the next one explains "mixture" (*miśra*). First...
Regarding "affliction" (*nirṇāmanīya-karman*) and "patience" (*kṣānti*): next, we clarify affliction alone. Furthermore, since the cause should also encompass the fruit, the Sūtra says:
"Even when encountering great suffering, one does not regard it as a calamity. This refers precisely to the Path (*mārga*), because it relies upon the correct name. Next, regarding "mixed" (*miśra*):
the old translations say "mixed evil" (*miśrākuśala*) or "mixed encounter" (*miśrasamnipāta*), yet neither provides an explanation. The current explanation follows the text as annotated.
(As stated above) other passages further state that both the cohabitation of the pure and the impure, and the cohabitation of ordinary beings and sages, all share this same meaning.
As for what are called the "nine paths," they refer simply to the sentient beings of the nine realms. Some say these are the "nine abodes of sentient beings" (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*);

the new terminology calls them the "nine abodes of sentient beings" (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*), referring to the humans and devas of the desire realm as one, the three lower dhyānas of the form realm as three, and the lower [three] of the formless realm...
The three emptinesses constitute three [realms], while the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception constitute the remaining six; thus there are nine.

Among these, the first seven are the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), to which two instances of the fourth dhyāna are added to make nine. This enumeration does not exhaust all realms of birth (*upapatti-dhātu*), but that is not the intent here.
The new term *Sahā* means "Endurance" (*Kanshin*); the commentary explains that it refers to the Bodhisattvas and others who practice for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to others.

At that time, because he was able to endure and patiently accept the many afflictions and oppressions of resentment and jealousy, as well as physical fatigue and exhaustion, it was for this reason that he was given this name;
thus, the name was derived from the seeker of the Way. There is an old citation of Paramārtha’s commentary which states: "Kṣānti" (Patience) is the name of the Brahmā King;
because he is able to endure the superior achievements of others and does not give rise to jealousy, malice, or delusion, he is called "Kṣānti. This [is his name].
Regarding the derivation of this name from its presiding lord, there must be a basis for it; its meaning is superior to the previous explanation.

Now, I maintain that the name should be derived from both the general and specific senses. The general sense is as previously explained, while the specific sense refers to the primary manifestation within the general category.

Because they are mutually illustrative and must necessarily possess both meanings, the term "Lord" (*Brahmā*) is used. Regarding the subsequent explanation of "Brahmā," the text contains both translations and etymological interpretations.
The term "Exalted Purity" (Viśuddha) refers to the Desire Realm being inferior and defiled; thus, it signifies ascending from that which was previously excluded.
However, the full name should be *Brahmapurohita* (Heaven of Ministers of Brahmā), also called *Brahmakāyika* (Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā).
Here, "Brahmā" is *brahma*, and "kāya" is *kāya*; this is a concise designation that omits the middle two characters by citing only the first and the last. This is [the meaning].
Essentially, the ancient translations were extremely abbreviated, merely stating "Brahma. The new translation renders it as "Quiescence" (*śānti*), also called "Purity.

The meaning is the same as before: because one is free from the turbidity and filth of desire, one is pure; and because one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) through this purity, one is quiescent.
Following this precedent, there ought to be the character "Great" (*mahā-*) here; thus, all the commentaries of the various schools state "Great [Brahma]."
The intent of the *Brahmādevarāja-sūtra* is precisely to reveal that this [being] is Śikhin; thus, the title "Great" (*Mahā*) is placed at the end. Reflect on this, reflect on it!
There is a citation from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* which states: "Because he is produced by extensive virtue, he is named Brahmā. This Brahmā is 'great,' therefore he is called Mahābrahmā.
Because he has attained the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), because he was the first to be born, and because he is the last to pass away."
He is called Mahābrahmā because his majesty and power are preeminent; he is called Brahmakāyika because he governs others and is governed by others;
he is called Brahmapurohita because he stands in front of Mahābrahmā to serve and protect him. Next, regarding Śikhin, there are two parts:

first, the direct explanation, and second, the reconciliatory explanation. In the first part, there are two names; the first does not explain the meaning, while the second provides an explanation, stating that there is fire upon his crown.
Because his light is like a topknot, he is called "Cūḍin" (Topknot); alternatively, because there is a great topknot upon his head, he is named "Cūḍin.
The second meaning refers to Mahābrahmā himself. One who cultivates this meditative concentration is reborn in this heaven; thus, the name is established based on the virtue of its cause.

There is an old tradition stating that when this king entered the *tejo-dhātu-samādhi* (fire-element concentration), fire emerged from his crown; therefore, he is called "Agni" (Fire). Furthermore, according to an old [tradition]...
Some say that while all other Brahmā heavens are consumed by the calamity of fire, this king alone is exempt; therefore, he is called "Fire" (*agni*).
Others say "Fire-Crest" (*agnicūḍa*) refers to the Lord of the First Dhyāna, as it is the highest point of the calamity of fire.

Now, if we follow the Tathāgata Śikhin, which is translated here as "Jewel-Crest" (*ratnaśikha*), we know that "Śikhin" carries the meaning of a "top-knot" or "crest. Thus, the new translation is correct.

All say it is the *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance). Some say the *māṃsa-uṣṇīṣa* (fleshy cranial protuberance) resembles a conch shell, such as the large topknot on the crown of the head mentioned previously;

this refers to the *Śrīvatsa-uṣṇīṣa* of the Brahma King Śikhin in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. However, from "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) below is the introductory assembly (*nidāna*).

Because the sūtras and treatises differ and the commentaries of past and present vary, it is necessary to provide a brief reconciliation of these points. Of the six phrases [that follow], the first clarifies that the sūtra says "resembles."
The second section explains the treatise as one and three; now, by means of the treatise, it is reconciled with the sūtra as two and four.

First, it clarifies the dwelling place and the reason for attaining kingship; fifth, it distinguishes its causes; sixth, it clarifies the elevation of the leader to encompass the assembly of subjects. In summary, this forms four parts.
The first three correctly clarify that Śikhin is the leader and is the king of the first dhyāna; next, it clarifies the dwelling place and the attainment [of sovereignty].
The reason the Master [Sengzhao] provides three general explanations and four specific clarifications is to demonstrate that the primary subject subsumes the other two.

Regarding the first three, Master Xuchang says: some claim that Brahmā Devarāja is the king of the first dhyāna, Śikhin is the king of the second dhyāna, and Prabhāsvara is the king of the third dhyāna;
as for the fourth dhyāna, the Brahmā King is the one employed by Guangzhai. Furthermore...
It is said that the Lord of the World is Maheśvara, the Brahmā King of the Fourth Dhyāna;
Śikhin is the King of the Third Dhyāna; Prabhāsa is the King of the Second Dhyāna; and so forth refers to the Kings of the First Dhyāna. His own commentary explains:
"Now, according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the name of the Brahmā King who is the Lord of the Sahā World is Śikhin. This cites his location in order to clarify [his identity].
That he is the Brahmā King Mahābrahmā refers to his office; "Śikhin" indicates his name.
The new translation, *Prabhāsa*, also provides this same explanation, which accords with the meaning of the present text. An old questioner asked:

"The *Saṃyukta Āgama* speaks of ten billion Brahmā kings, while another *Āgama* states that Śikhin is the Brahmā king of the First Dhyāna, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also speaks of the Brahmā king."
Regarding how to reconcile this discrepancy concerning the Lord of a thousand-world system (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*), there are two traditional explanations.

One says that ten billion Brahmā kings mutually communicate and share the sovereignty of their realms. Another says that, just as with the four classes of wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*), it is the same for the Brahmā kings;
namely, the lower, middle, upper, and upper-middle grades constitute one small-thousand-world system, and thus there are ten billion middle-grade [Brahmās].

He becomes a lord of a thousand worlds (sāhasralokadhātu), a supreme lord of two thousand worlds (dvisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu), and a supreme lord of three thousand worlds (trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu).

As stated in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages): "In the eighth stage, one acts as a Brahmā-king, a lord of a thousand worlds; in the ninth stage, one acts as a Brahmā-king, a lord of two thousand worlds;
and in the tenth stage, one acts as a Brahmā-king, a lord of three thousand worlds. This is also the case here, as explained in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.
Within the three thousandfold world-system there are ten billion Māras; there is another Māra named King Pāpīyān, and within this three thousandfold world-system it is likewise.
Whether collectively or individually, these kings all abide in the intermediate dhyāna, just as the four wheel-turning kings all abide in Jambudvīpa.
An old tradition states that Śikhin is a Brahmā of the dhyāna realm, also named Kumāra.

*Kārttikeya* is translated here as "Child God" (*Dāraka-deva*). This deity is so named because his countenance resembles that of a child; he holds a cock in his hand, carries a bell, and raises a red banner while riding upon a peacock. Question: The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states that Maheśvara is the lord of the three realms. Why, then, is it said here that the Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna is the lord of the trichiliocosm? Answer: There are four kinds of Brahmās. The Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna is the lord of one thousand worlds. The Great Brahmā (*Mahābrahmā*) is the lord of two thousand worlds. The Sublime Brahmā (*Brahmapurohita*) is the lord of three thousand worlds. Furthermore, there is the Great Brahmā who is the lord of the four continents.
