Regarding the first [type] of Brahmā King, a sutra states that there are ten billion suns and moons, ten billion Brahmā Kings, and ten billion [beings in the realm of] Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception;
this refers to the lower grade of Small Brahmā Kings. Second, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Brahmā King is the lord of a thousandfold world-system (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*);

the *Dīrgha Āgama* is likewise, referring to the middle grade. Third, it is said that a Bodhisattva of the ninth stage acts as a Brahmā King presiding over two thousand worlds; this is the upper grade. Fourth...
This refers to the highest grade of sovereignty over the trichiliocosm. There are also two types of Māra-Cakravartins;
as stated in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the Māra is as previously described, while the Cakravartin—as stated in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*—rules over the three thousand worlds.
Therefore, one cannot judge them according to a single path. Now, it is said that if one attains the meaning of the "present trace" of our own school...
Question: All [realms] can be assembled; where does Śikhin, as the lord of a great trichiliocosm, abide in the intermediate dhyāna? Answer:
He currently abides in the center of ten billion intermediate dhyānas, just as the Buddha abides in the center of a great trichiliocosm.

Another commentator explains: "The size of the first dhyāna is equal to one set of four heavens within the desire realm; one thousand such [first dhyāna realms] constitute a single intermediate dhyāna."
The first dhyāna and the like constitute the limit of the fire calamity; one thousand [worlds] have the second dhyāna and the like as their limit.

The third dhyāna and the like constitute the limit of the water calamity; one thousand [worlds] have the third dhyāna and the like as their limit. The fourth dhyāna and the like constitute the limit of the wind calamity.
This is the trichiliocosm known as the Sahā world, where the Great Brahmā Deva King is the sovereign; he is the lord of the fourth dhyāna.
Śikhin (Yaśi-qi) is the Lord of the Fire Disaster at the Summit, which is the primary ruler of the First Dhyāna; because he is the pinnacle of the fire disaster, he is called "Light.

He is the Lord of the Second Dhyāna—the Sovereign of Parīttābha (Little Light), Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Light), and Ābhāsvara (Utmost Purity of Light). By this, the Lords of the Third Dhyāna are also included.
However, the *Prajñāpāramitā* states that he is the Brahmā King Śikhin who holds the topknot as the Lord of the Sahā World; thus, Śikhin refers to the topknot (*śikhā*). That is to say—

The Brahma King Keśin is an alternative name for the Brahma King who presides over the Sahā world-system. According to this interpretation, the "Lord of the World" refers to the king of the fourth dhyāna;
Śikhin is the lord of the first dhyāna; Prabhāsa is the lord of the second dhyāna; and so forth, with Ābhāsvara being the lord of the third dhyāna.
While there are various differing explanations such as these, the present text follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which identifies Śikhin as [the relevant figure].
Master Xiang’s interpretation is the same as this. Here, one should cite the verses and commentary of the *Śāstra* to clarify and establish the preceding meaning.

Regarding the reason why the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is considered primary: as for what is called "intermediate," the *Mahāśāstra* states—as previously explained by various commentators—that it is named "intermediate" because it lies between the first [dhyāna] above and the second [dhyāna] below.

"Applied thought" (*vitarka*) and "sustained thought" (*vicāra*) are two of the five factors (*pañcāṅga*) of the first dhyāna; the new terminology calls them "investigation" (*paryeṣaṇā*) and "analysis" (*pravicaya*).
Because of these vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), there is speech;

because of this duality of internal and external, they attain the status of sovereign leaders, namely the two classes of devas—the Sovereign and the Retinue—and the Universal [Kings], who are the lords of the Sahā world-system.
Regarding the phrase "practicing them individually," this distinguishes their differing causes. Some sources state that by adding these four minds to the fourth dhyāna, one becomes a Caturmahārājika.
If one practices meditation alone, it is solely for the sake of the assembly; here, the general is cited to reveal the particular.
Regarding "the first dhyāna and so forth," this dhyāna comprises three heavens, yet here only the primary one is mentioned, which subsumes the other two.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states that the three heavens of the first dhyāna differ because the three grades of practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are distinct. [The first heaven] is the Brahmakāyika (Assembly of Brahmās).

Serving as a subordinate to the Brahma-purohita heaven and ascending to become a Brahmā King—by this analogy, the rest may be understood. Now, observing this passage, it appears to contain the fourfold intention (*catuḥ-saṃgraha-vastu*).
The first three phrases together clarify that he is the sovereign of the world. That both the internal and external attain the status of a king is the "remedy" (*pratipakṣa*);

that the distinction in causes is for the sake of human beings is the "discrimination" (*vibhajana*); that he leads the multitude by taking charge of the sovereign is the "benefit" (*anuśaṃsā*); and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is as follows: this is the first [intention].
The causal conditions for this heaven may be understood by analogy; the remaining three meanings will be explained later.
Next, regarding the explanation of "radiance" (*ābhāsvara*): first, its general position is indicated; second, its distinctions are analyzed to clarify its meaning.

If one merely says "radiance," it is not known what is being designated; this refers to the King of the Second Dhyāna Heaven. How is this known? Because there are three such heavens that share this name.

Because of light, one knows that "luminosity" (*ābhāsvara*) refers to the second dhyāna. Its third [level] was formerly called "Light-Sound" (*ābhāsvara*), but is now termed "Utmost Luminous Purity" (*parittābha*).

Within the heavens of its own stage, its luminosity is the smallest, hence it is called "Limited Light" (*parittābha*). As its luminosity becomes increasingly superior and its measure difficult to fathom, it is named "Immeasurable Light" (*apramāṇābha*).
Because it universally illuminates both itself and others, it is named "Utmost Pure Light" (*ābhāsvara*); alternatively, it may also refer to the luminosity of the second dhyāna.

It is precisely from this that the name is derived. Since there are three distinctions herein, they are further called "kings"; by analogy with the preceding principle, the meaning can also be understood.
From here below is the explanation of the devas of the third and fourth dhyānas; the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the main text is explained as follows. Therefore, the old [commentary]...
The commentary states: "Briefly citing the first two" refers to the latter two [of the four dhyānas]. Herein, no general name is established;

by analogy with what precedes, they may also be called the "Universal Purity Great Brahmā" and the "Ultimate Great Brahmā," both names derived from their supreme excellence. If categorized according to the factors of dhyāna, the first is applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*);
the second is the dhyāna of joy (*prīti*); the third is the dhyāna of bliss (*sukha*); and the fourth is the dhyāna of equanimity (*upekṣā*). There is [a distinction].
The pleasant sensation of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) is called "Pure" (*śubha*); because this purity is the most inferior within its own level, it is named "Limited Purity" (*parītta-śubha*).

Because it increases further and is difficult to fathom, it is named "Immeasurable Purity" (*apramāṇa-śubha*). Because this stage is most pervasive, it is named "Universal Purity" (*śubha-kṛtsna*). These three have the same names in both the new and old [Abhidharma] systems.
Since the superiority and inferiority of these three fruits are established, their causes can be known by analogy. Next, there are four levels in total for the Fourth Dhyāna.
Regarding the initial statement that the Nine Heavens are "subtle" (*mi*), this is a new designation for "cloudless.

Furthermore, as for being "subtle," it refers to the fact that the abodes of the gods within the space below the clouds are like dense, gathered clouds; thus they are called "Cloud-bodies. Because they dwell in these places, they are called "Subtle-bodies" (*mi-shen*).

Now, in comparison to the coarse bodies of the lower realms, the bodies in this realm are fine and exquisite, hence they are named "Subtle-bodies. Since they are so fine and exquisite, what [is there] to [be seen]?

Regarding the ability to obstruct this, the meaning of the old name should be understood as follows: as for "Cloudless" (*Anabhraka*), some say that above these heavens there are no further grounds with clouds, and because they are at the head of those without clouds, they are called "Cloudless.
Next, regarding "Immeasurable" (*Apramāṇa*) and so forth, the new [translation] says "Born of Merit" (*Puṇyaprasava*);

others say that only when one possesses superior merit as an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) does one attain birth there, and thus it is called "Born of Merit. Now, I maintain that this [explanation] is still not [final].

The *Xiaoshu wen* (Commentary on the Elucidation) also anticipates that there may still be "measurable" [realms] prior to this; because this [realm] is even more subtle and wondrous, it is called "immeasurable.

It is understood as receiving merit because it is the excellence of the fruit. Next, regarding "Vipākaphala" (Fruit of Maturation): some say it is the "Vast Fruit" (*Bṛhatphala*), while others say it is the most distinguished among the fruits of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and is thus called "Vast Fruit.
As for "Asaṃjñin" (Non-percipient), it is so named because it is the deepest and most subtle within the state of non-perception.
The new translation states directly that "non-conceptualization" (*asaṃjñin*) refers to what non-Buddhists reckon as *nirvāṇa*, which is produced through the cultivation of dhyāna.
Regarding the preceding four names, the word "also" (*api*) is used; this distinction between two versions arises from differences in earlier and later translations.

I shall now describe them in full, and thus all are said to be "also. Next, the five heavens above are listed; these are the abodes of the five types of persons who have attained the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Regarding the place where they dwell, it is newly called the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*). Some say that because the various noble ones who have abandoned desire wash away the stains of afflictions with the water of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), they are called "Pure" (*śuddha*); and because this is the dwelling place of those with pure bodies, they are called "Pure Abodes.

Furthermore, it is said that because those who dwell here destroy the limits of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they are called "Pure Abodes"; the meaning is the same as before. Moreover, there are no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) born there.

They are called "Pure Abodes" (*śuddhāvāsa*) because they are inhabited exclusively by noble ones (*ārya*). Regarding those who are "free from affliction" (*anāsrava*): "affliction" (*āsrava*) refers either to being "mixed with afflictions" (*sāsrava*) or to being "broadly afflicted" (*vistṛtāsrava*).

Since this [first] heaven is the very beginning among them, it is called "Free from Affliction" (*Anabhraka*). Furthermore, among the "Broadly Afflicted" heavens (*Vistṛtāsrava*), this one is the most inferior; thus it is designated as "Free from Affliction.

Having already well subdued and eliminated the obstacles to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)—both the mixed and the concordant, whether of medium or superior grade—their mental disposition (*āśaya*) is tamed and free from attachment.

Because it is free from all burning afflictions (*paridāha*), it is called "Without Affliction" (*Atapa*); alternatively, because it prevents the arising of afflictions, it is called "Without Heat" (*Atapa*).

Having already clearly manifested the name "Without Heat" through this initial distancing [from defilement], the excellence of its fruit—the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) cultivated through intermingling (*vyavakīrṇa*) in its superior degree—is easily revealed; thus, it is called "Well-Appearing" (*Sudṛśa*).

Because the obstacles to the concentration of intermingled cultivation have become extremely subtle in its remaining degrees, and because one sees with extreme clarity, it is called "Good Vision" (*Sudarśana*). Beyond this, there is nothing further.

Abiding within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there is nothing that can surpass this; thus it is called "Akaniṣṭha" (Ultimate). Alternatively, because it reaches the final limit of the body which is the basis for all suffering, it is called "ultimate.
In this present text, according to the proper sequence, it should appear below [the description of the heavens].
The name of the supporting location for Akaniṣṭha is what is referred to here as a colloquial term; that is, the term "Akaniṣṭha" found in the subsequent sutra text.

"Deva" means "Great Īśvara"; this is the name for the Lord who is the support, which is the local vernacular term. The following four characters are that [Sanskrit] vernacular term. As for the "place," it is ultimate;
as for the "person," Great Īśvara is the most honored and supreme among all forms within the three realms.

The following concludes by clarifying the meaning of these terms. However, since there are still many retinues in the lower realms, what will he bring forth now that he has attained such supremacy above?
Some [passages] follow existing scriptures, some are brief enumerations, and some list each dhyāna with its respective number of retinues; these texts are generally concise.
As for these various heavens, they are fully described as explained in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, though I have not yet had the leisure to do so here.
Within each of these, there should be the fourfold meaning (*catuḥ-saṃgraha-vastu*), which has already been briefly clarified in the preceding section on the World Rulers (*lokapāla*).
This can be understood by analogy, so I shall not elaborate further. Regarding the "Teaching" (the *kyōmon*):

these various heavenly hosts have all passed through the assemblies of the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings, and thus have fully heard the explanations of the provisional and the real; having now arrived at this assembly, everything is opened up and unified into the single, perfect, and wondrous [truth].

This meaning is easy to understand and does not require extensive textual citation. Regarding the "Trace and the Source" (*honjaku*): both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras extensively expound upon them.
Because of their merit, it is known that all have an origin. Within this, there are those that are distant and those that are near.

Speaking from the perspective of the distant, as in the sequence of the Mahāyāna’s four Brahmavihāras, these are the traces of the final four stages among the ten bhūmis; the four stages are the essence, while the four Brahmavihāras are the traces.
This meaning can be understood. If one approaches it from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanmen), one cannot fix their positions, for all stages have long since attained the reality.
Taking the purity of the marks as the foundation, he manifests these traces of purity; by dwelling in this heaven, he leads all beings to return to the same state—this is his far-reaching intent.

Once one reaches this assembly and the two gates are opened and revealed, that which was previously cited as "real" refers to those whose positions are adjacent to the ultimate, for whom all the defilements of the causes and effects of birth and death have been exhausted, becoming one with perfect purity.

The Way is like that lotus flower; this is its fundamental reality (*mūla*). To dwell in this Pure Heaven so as to cause those who are not yet pure to become pure is its provisional manifestation (*traces*, *śeṣa*).
This is discussed in terms of the recent [manifestation]; it is thus the fundamental and the provisional, the reality and the trace.

Therefore, the "fundamental and trace" (*honji-suijaku*) of this sutra contains these two meanings, which can be understood through the mind rather than through prolixity; the words are concise, yet the contemplation is vast.

There are some who, regarding each of the eighteen heavens, first provide an interpretation based on the "original and the trace" (*honji-kempon*) and then offer an explanation based on the contemplation of the mind (*kanjin*).

This is far too prolix. The *Sūtra Commentary* (*sho*) instructs one to reflect upon this for oneself; it merely requires that one exercise discretion according to one's own inclination, adhering to the essential tenets of our school rather than following any fixed standard.
I do not wish to be overly wordy here, but shall directly and concisely state the essential points of the teaching.

The traces [of these practices] are roughly as observed above: if one can cultivate the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), one is able to depart from the turbid defilements of the three delusions and manifest the pure principle of the three truths (*trisatya*).
This is the "contemplation of purity through the departure from desire. Furthermore, the Sanskrit name for this is *śānti* (quiescence);

the three contemplations can depart from the clamor and confusion of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three delusions, and thus they constitute the "contemplation of great quiescence" (*mahāśānti-vipaśyanā*). Moreover, there is the "contemplation of emptiness in its general characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
To be able to transcend all states of existence (*bhava*) and attain mastery is the *Cūḍāmaṇi* (Topknot) contemplation;
to thoroughly illuminate and understand the characteristics of all phenomena through the provisional contemplation of universal characteristics is the *Prabhāsa* (Radiance) contemplation;

and within the contemplation of universal characteristics, to have no attachment whatsoever toward any extremes is the *Viśuddha* (Universal Purity) contemplation. Furthermore, even the craving for the Dharma that accords with the Path does not arise at all.
If both the contemplation and its object are entirely without direction, this is the ultimate contemplation of Great Sovereignty (*Maheśvara*);

it is also the contemplation of the four Brahmās. Although there are eighteen assemblies of Brahmās, only these four are mentioned because one wishes to clarify that the superior encompasses the inferior;
by citing these essentials, the meaning is complete and can be understood. What need is there for prolixity? Nevertheless, one should deliberate well upon this.
Reflect upon this meaning in relation to the six [stages].

The subsequent explanation regarding the dragon hosts constitutes the third section. Regarding the old tradition that dragons belong to the class of animals and are inferior to the other paths, yet are listed after the heavens, there are generally four reasons:
first, because their power is the greatest; second, among the five inconceivables, the dragon is [the foremost]...
First, their power is one and the same. Second, according to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, evil nāgas assist the asuras while virtuous nāgas assist Śakra;
since these are the virtuous ones, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that when the gods fight with them, the nāgas first join the side of the gods, thereby assisting the devas.
Third, they bestow grace upon both heaven and humanity by harmonizing yin and yang. Fourth, they protect and maintain the scriptural treasury of the thousand Buddhas. Next...

The *Tiānliè wàishū* (Heavenly Array of External Writings) and the *Shuowén* (Explanations of Words) state that the dragon is the sovereign among scaly creatures; it can become small or large, and can manifest in darkness or light.
It ascends to heaven in spring and enters the springs in winter. Guangzheng states: "Those with scales are *jiāolóng* (coiling dragons);

those with wings are *yìnglóng* (responding dragons); those with horns are *qiúlong* (curved-horned dragons); and those without horns are *chīlóng* (hornless dragons). This is the Buddhist perspective.

The middle section clarifies that there are four types of birth for nāgas, which is the same as the subsequent text. In this land [of China], they are regarded as the foremost of the Five Spirits, presiding over the East;
in Buddhism, they are considered the vanguard of the Heavenly Emperor and the foremost among the celestial deities who protect the Dharma on earth.
Because this is most essential, it is placed at the beginning. The scriptural text has three parts: first, the enumeration of the categories; second, the explanation of their names.
The subsequent explanation of the retinue and all the following assemblies is identical to this. Within it, the first two are explained together because they are brothers:

first, the names are translated; second, their meanings are explained; third, the beginning of their reception of the Way is clarified; and fourth, their dwelling place is explained. Regarding "Śubha," many say it means "Worthy" (Xián);
"Worthy" and "Excellent" (Xiànshàn) are one and the same. A new interpretation states it is "Joyful Worthy" (Hǎnxí Xián). As for the meaning of "Joyful" (Hǎn): because...
Because those who contemplate the King’s bounty find joy throughout the land, he is thus named. This merely explains the meaning of *Nanda* as "virtuous" (*bhadra*) according to the preceding text;

there is no separate explanation for other interpretations. It is said that while the former [aspect] causes people to rejoice, the latter nature is virtuous and causes them to rejoice, hence the name.
As for "the one who has been subdued," it is because faith and compliance began at this time, marking the start of the era of *Māyā*.
Although he is reported by this country to reside within the ocean, there are four intentions herein:
first, benefiting the world and causing all to rejoice, which constitutes the two meanings of "World" (loka) and "Person" (pudgala);

second, subduing them so that evil may be eliminated, which is "Counteraction" (pratipakṣa); and third, dwelling beyond the ocean, which is the "Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha) of abiding in the great ocean of wisdom, the *dharmatā*.
Below this, the teaching is not further explained; however, by merely recognizing the names of the past and present, the meaning of their relative coarseness and subtlety is naturally revealed.

This can be understood by analogy with what precedes, so the text is not burdened with further elaboration. As for the original term "ground" (*bhūmi*), it is because these grounds possess such names that one may know the fundamental through the phenomenal traces.

Because the virtues and functions within these stages are profound and vast, they are established as dwelling places to guide and lead sentient beings toward a common return [to the source]. Contemplation.

The middle three contemplations observe the three truths; because the contemplation accords with the object, it is said to be "the Middle Way. Since the object can give rise to contemplation, one generates the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*).
*Sāgara*—the syllable *ga* is pronounced lightly—and this is translated as "ocean. It is named after its place of habitation, namely, the [Nāga King] below.
The name "Wén" (文) refers to the father of the Dragon Girl; others say it refers to the dragon of the salt sea. The term used for the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—namely, "shèng" (稱)—means to praise or extol;
it refers to that sūtra’s praise of her ability to raise various clouds and so forth, bringing immeasurable benefits both horizontally and vertically.
Regarding the term "jiù" (舊), the old [commentary] states: "This country is near the Immortal (Rishi), and the King attained awakening through contact with the Immortal."

The immortals incanted this land so that it became an ocean, and because this dragon dwelt therein, it was named after him; this is likely based on a legendary account rather than the definitive meaning.
Regarding the four meanings of the causal conditions (*nidāna*) herein, since they refer to what is termed in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, these four meanings are naturally complete within it.

To point to that [Sūtra] is precisely because these can be understood through the power of intention here, without relying on the proliferation of literary teachings; this may be known by analogy with the gate of instruction.
Regarding the "Original and the Traces": it is because the Original is not otherwise than this that the Traces can be as they are; one who understands these Traces knows the Original as it truly is.
This is precisely for the purpose of leading sentient beings back to this Original. Even those who do not clearly understand the regulations may infer the principle:
to contemplate the three truths through the three contemplations is itself the contemplative wisdom abiding within the great ocean of the Dharma-realm.
Regarding the term "many-headed," both ancient and modern commentators state that this refers to a nine-headed dragon.

As for the name "Precious Call" (Bao-cheng), it is an alternative appellation; it likely arose because he was adorned with many exquisite jewels, or perhaps because he was praised on account of his jewels.
Regarding the phrase "in the water," various explanations suggest either "at the bottom of the water" or "born from the water," yet none [of these] are definitive.
Regarding his dwelling in the water: it is because he possesses the four intentions, which are worldly dharmas of retribution, that he has many heads.

His precious title and beautiful name signify that he is a human being; yet he constantly dwells in the water and rarely appears among humans. "Resting from evil" expresses the fundamental [principle], which constitutes the four meanings.

The pedagogical model can be understood thus: the provisional manifestation (traces) is used to express the fundamental reality. Based on a single body, he manifests many heads to symbolize reliance [upon the one].
It is from this certainty that many bodies manifest; these traces are intended to lead beings to realize this fundamental reality.
"Immeasurable within contemplation" refers to the dharma-gate of the three truths and three contemplations. This is the universal elucidation of the inconceivable provisional (the *prajñapti*);
it means that this provisional is precisely the provisional within emptiness. Therefore, the meaning of the commentary [“... is roughly as follows. It should be understood thus.
Examine this carefully.

Furthermore, among the three names for the Kāśyapa clan, the Śākyas simply refer to them as "the garrulous. This likely reflects the fact that the sacred teachings were transmitted through different lineages, though they all agree on this one point:
regarding those who look with poison, as other sūtras state, nāgas possess four poisons, of which looking is one.

Because it is also capable of harming others, it is called "many-tongued" (*bahujihva*). Other commentators explain that it is so named because it possesses many tongues, or perhaps because it delights in speech.
It is also called "double-tongued" (*dvijihva*), either because it has two tongues, or because it is one of the four types of unwholesome verbal karma.
The old translation says it dwells upon the earth; as for the four meanings, they are found in the world of poison.

When beings are fearful, they dare not commit transgressions; this is the worldly antidote. To be able to follow the inclinations of various types of people through eloquence is to act for their benefit.

By means of divisive speech, one distinguishes between the mundane and the supramundane, leading them to return to the non-dual ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The pedagogical precedents can be understood from this;

as for the provisional and the fundamental (*honji-suijaku*), it is clarified by taking one instance from the intermediate stage. This discernment constitutes the four [methods]. This manifestation of the provisional is precisely intended to lead beings [to the truth].
This text is the same as that [previous one], though it does not explicitly clarify that speech arises based on the mind;
rather, it simply states that if one can clearly comprehend the three truths within one's own mind, that constitutes the foundation of all verbal expression.

Next, regarding the term *Anavatapta*, first the name is translated, followed by an explanation of its meaning. In the first section, there are three sentences: first, it indicates the source from which the name is derived;
second, it provides the actual translation, adding the two characters "Shèngzhòng" (剩重) and "Wúrè" (無熱); third, it clarifies the location of the lake.

According to ancient traditions, some say it is on the summit of Mount Gandhamādana, some say it is on the summit of the Snow Mountains (*Himavat*), while more recent translations all state it is on the summit of Mount Gandhamādana.
The *Western Regions Biographies* (*Xiyu zhuan*) also describes this in detail: from this lake emerge the four great rivers, and the Yellow River of this land is the river on its eastern side.
Since ancient times it has also been called the Kunlun Mountain Lake; because the lake is situated atop the mountain, Guo Huo’s *Eulogy on the Illustration* states:
"Kunlun has three tiers and is known in the world as the Pillar of Heaven; it is truly the source of the rivers and the numinous treasury of waters."
In this passage, the four characters "also seemingly superfluous" (亦似剩) [should be read as] "derived from the pool to establish the name" (從池為名).

Following this, the text clarifies that there are no three afflictions, which is the direct explanation of the meaning of the pool's name, "Heatless" (無熱). First, it explains that others have these three afflictions;

subsequently, it clarifies that this [pool] lacks them—this is to manifest the absence by citing the presence, for the name is established based on its absence. Regarding the initial mention of the "three afflictions," these are precisely the torments of heat (*paridāha*).
This is because it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of karmic retribution; that which is absent here is because this superior place was summoned and manifested by meritorious karma.
An ancient commentary states: "This lake is situated on the summit of Mount Gandhamādana, beneath the constellation Tiānqí (the Heavenly Equalizer) to the north of Jambudvīpa.

Because its waters are cool and refreshing, it is called 'Without Heat' (*Anavatapta*). This refers to the causal conditions. Regarding the four meanings [of the name], they are collectively not three.

"World" (*loka*) refers to the realm of names; this is brought about by the maturation of wholesome karma. That which exists prior to human birth is brought about by the maturation of unwholesome karma.
Because this world exists as an antidote to that [unwholesome state], it is through the realization of its non-existence that one attains the supramundane path;

this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). From these four causal conditions, this name arises. As for "teaching" (*śāsana*), it refers to all teachings that are free from feverish affliction and are cool and refreshing.

Those who possess this [teaching] shall hear it; if within this assembly there is but one wondrous [being], then within both the provisional (迹) and the fundamental (本), the provisional reveals the fundamental.
The provisional abides in the world as a "Cooling Place" (清涼) to lead sentient beings to return together to the wondrous fundamental Four Virtues.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) are the dragons of this pond, and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* likewise speaks of Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage regarding this matter. Herein they give rise to a great...
The Dharma-gate of the Cloud of Compassion, which shelters all sentient beings and enables them to be free from suffering, is that by which self-mastery is attained;
this collectively refers to its fundamental basis. The "wondrous wisdom within contemplation" is that which is capable of making non-existent what previously existed.

The "five abodes and two deaths" are the heat and afflictions that are thereby made non-existent. The five abodes are as previously described; the two deaths—the death of the segmented and the death of transformation—differ in their causes and fruits.
The *Furen jing tonglun* (General Treatise on the Sutra of the Lady) explains that the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) are identical to wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*).

While the three contemplations may be discussed in terms of the cause and wondrous wisdom in terms of the fruit, the three contemplations can purify the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*), whereas wondrous wisdom can bring liberation from the two types of death (*dvividha-maraṇa*). Reflect upon this:

the character "sa" (唼) has two pronunciations and is easily understood as referring to both afflictions (*kleśa*)—which are like violent winds—and insects or birds; the two deaths refer to the suffering of the resultant fruit.
Therefore, because the category of "burning with heat" carries this significance, the commentary states [as follows].

Within the causal conditions for *Manas*, there are first three translated names; these three characters contain these three meanings, and as the translation was produced according to their respective emergence, such differences arise.
"Great body" (*mahākāya*) refers to the physical form; "great mind" (*mahācitta*) refers to compassion.
"Power" (*bala*) means "benefit" (*hita*). Regarding the term "equal" (*sama*), it is also said to mean "pleasing conduct" (*manojña-caryā*) and "compassionate mind" (*maitrī-citta*).

The following explains its meaning: at first glance, this seems merely to explain the meaning of the "Great Body" (*mahākāya*), but in reality, it encompasses all three—namely, the [Three] Powers (*bala*) and Compassion (*maitrī*).
It is because of these three great qualities that such is possible. By verifying this matter, one knows the meaning of the Three Great Qualities (*trividha-mahattva*).
"Enveloped" (*ying*) means winding and twisting; "obstructing" (*e*) means stopping. This refers to the dragon coiling its body around the city to ward off and stop the seawater.

All the commentaries state that this is a dragon of compassionate heart. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says that when it wishes to send down rain, it first raises clouds for seven days to wait until all construction work is finished, and only then does it pour forth the rain; this is proof of its compassionate heart. This...

This refers to the meaning of "Great" (*mahat*) in the preceding text, which should possess four meanings. Briefly stated according to the explanation provided: "The world exists" corresponds to the first meaning;

"preserving cities and stopping waters" corresponds to the two meanings of benefiting humans and removing harm; and "the World-Protecting Devas" refers to the first meaning among the four meanings of the *deva* (Heavenly Being).
If one takes it in the sense of "compassion," then compassion protects the world and causes the world to be happy; this is the "world."

The "realm" (dhātu) refers to waiting for the task to be accomplished without causing harm; this is the meaning of the two distinct [aspects]. The "intention" is to enable the attainment of the bliss of supramundane nirvāṇa; this is the primary meaning.
Regarding the "teaching gate," compassion penetrates both the Great and Small Vehicles; in terms of the true doctrine, it is exclusively the Perfect [Vehicle]. Now, this is the "absolute great.
As for the "original," it is the Boundless Body (*Anantakāya*), as in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding the Bodhisattva Anantakāya.
This general designation for all names is "Dharma. By relying on provisional traces to manifest the fundamental, it shows the world that returning to the Dharma-nature is the peerless greatness.
For the observer, the equality of the three truths is called the "Middle"; its nature being vast and extensive is the meaning of the Great Sutra’s text.
The Sutra says: "Its nature is vast and extensive, like empty space," because the three truths are one and the same, being without self-nature.
Because they are equally non-existent, it is as vast as space; this is the contemplation of the Great Body (*mahātman*), and so forth—this is the general meaning.
As for the term "dark blue" (*nīla*), it refers to a greenish-blue color; that lotus has four colors, and this is its blue aspect.
Others say that because the red lotus dwells in the pond, the pond is named after it, and this dragon is likewise named after that flower.
It is because it receives its name from being like a pond. Regarding the four meanings: "World" (*loka*) is named after its place of abiding;

"Good" (*śubha*) refers to the ability to produce such beautiful names through virtuous causes; "Peaceful" (*praśānta*) refers to the remedial capacity to extinguish other remaining unwholesome causes;

and "Pure" (*śuddha*) means that dwelling in this beautiful and pure world is precisely for the sake of the supramundane path of purity, which is the primary meaning. Thus, the teaching is one of beauty and purity.
The Way penetrates both the provisional and the real; it is now solely the one true, wondrous, and pure Way.

As for its "root," this samādhi is such that within the provisional and real ways, there is no limit to its horizontal or vertical reach. Its "traces" reside in the realm of phenomena to manifest that root and lead all beings to the same destination.
Because his original vow was profound and weighty, he alone received the name [of the Buddha]. His wondrous fruit is like a lotus, and his wondrous cause is like...
The three wisdoms are the sublime fruit, and the three contemplations are the sublime cause; because they are like the flower of a lotus, they are precisely those contemplations.
Next, regarding the intent of citing the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, it clarifies the sequence of the heavens in general.

The principle of the order should have been at the beginning of the text, as in the four interpretations previously cited. Although there is no fixed position for them before or after, [the current arrangement] is appropriate.
One should know that it possesses the fourfold meaning of the *siddhāntas*. It belongs to the realm governed by the devas and can bring great benefit to them;
it also possesses great power to protect humans and devas and acts as their antidote.

Furthermore, it can protect the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma and cause one to attain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of the supramundane path. These four meanings are such that no other [teachings] can possess them.
Because they possess these [qualities], they are listed next in the order of the heavens.
Regarding the four *kiṃnaras*, first, within the section on causes and conditions, the numerical categories are explained; the traditional commentaries state that what follows explains these four.

At the beginning of this section, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states that they are subsumed under the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*). The initial presentation of their two names also reflects the sequence of earlier and later translations.
Although their substance is one, their manifestations differ; thus, when explaining their meaning, they appear as distinct forms.

Because this gives rise to doubt in people, it is said that they are "doubtful spirits" or "doubtful forms. One wonders whether these are human beings or non-human beings; therefore, they are also called "human-non-humans.
According to the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, "human-non-humans" has another specific meaning, which should be verified by consulting the *Devendra-sūtra*.
This clarifies their respective affiliations and reveals the intention behind their sequential arrangement. "Dharma" refers to the deities who chant and praise the Buddha-dharma;
because dragons are able to provide protection, they are listed first, and because they are able to offer praise, they are listed next.

Next, it clarifies their dwelling places and the reason for the performance of music above. Regarding the "ten mountains," as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: first, Snow; second, Fragrance; third, Kāśa.
1. Ilā; 2. Caturṛṣi; 3. Āryaka; 4. Pañcaśikha; 5. Gandharva; 6. Aśvakarṇa; 7. Nimiṃdhara; 8. Cakravāḍa; 9. Jāmbūdvīpa; 10. Sumeru—each of these is called a "jewel.
Regarding their distinct characteristics, they are manifested through the merit of the devas. Next, the actual performance of the Dharma music is clarified:
first generally, then specifically. The *pañcavīśatikā* (or *pañcaviṃśati*) is the name for the music of that region.
Alternatively, the single character "se" (瑟) refers here to the local dialect for what this region calls the *qín* and *sè* lutes; it refers to singing accompanied by the upper strings.

In this context, one should cite the account of music from the *Mahāvṛkṣa-sūtra*, as found in detail in the *Shuji* (Commentary). Next, regarding the explanation of the individual names, this clarifies the four names.
According to the intention of the ancients, these four are all aspects of the Buddha-dharma, yet they possess degrees of superiority and inferiority. The former [refers to...]
The sequence follows this order for subsequent reasons. Regarding the term *dhāraṇī* (持), the old interpretation treats it as a general term, encompassing the preceding three categories;
all ancient and modern commentators have held this view. However, my own intention is that while the old explanation is firm, its terminology is not actually as elegant or appropriate as it could be.

According to the old sense, it still does not transcend the *zàng* (Tripiṭaka) or *tōng* (Shared) teachings. The new interpretation states that *kiṃnara* (緊捺洛) is translated here as "song deity" (*gēshén*). At first...
First, one sings of the Four Noble Truths; next, of Dependent Origination; next, of the Six Perfections; and finally, of the One Vehicle.

Alternatively, one may first sing of the three types [of teachings] regarding the practice of the Three Vehicles, and subsequently sing of the principle and fruit of the Five Vehicles; for this reason, it is called "upholding the Dharma.

Or, one may sing of the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit of the One Vehicle, assigning them respectively as follows. Among these, the four intentions concern the causes of doubt, the world, and the meaning of the universe.

Furthermore, the Dharma-joy that is simple and distinct serves as an antidote to the mundane. To dwell upon the mountain and perform music for the sake of humanity is the foremost meaning of the Dharma-gate.

The text consists of four phrases, and the primary intent lies therein. However, regarding the passage in the commentary which addresses the former explanation of performing the four Dharma-teachings:
while this may have been appropriate in the past, how does it apply to this present assembly? The text consists of four phrases, and the primary intent lies therein.
Regarding this, some say: "Let us follow the ancient explanations for now and not yet discuss this point. Now, I maintain that this must indeed be discussed; otherwise, it remains unresolved.

If one says that arriving at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Lotus Sūtra) means the principle should be purely wondrous, although this possesses the meaning of one aspect of "wondrous," it does not yet possess the meaning found in the four names of the sūtra.
As cited previously from the final section, according to the three interpretations of another school, the third is specifically...
If one discusses these four according to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), although their underlying intent is universal, it does not lose its specific meaning within this sutra.

If one follows the present intention, they are the "Fourfold One Dharma" (*catur-eka-dharma*); these four are also called the "Four," and they are also called the "Four Sublime Ones" (*catur-praṇīta*), which precisely accords with the sense of praise and magnification, as these four alone exist within this single section.
Furthermore, they are also the "Fourfold Opening" (*catur-vivaraṇa*) and so forth. These are the [teachings] of all Buddhas.
This is because the four wisdoms are the essential core of the Great Matter of world-transcendence; thus, the meaning of this sutra’s provisional teaching is fully exhausted.

If one were to rely solely on the explanation provided above, it would not yet be reconciled with the fundamental intent. When the text speaks of "inconceivable," it refers to the long-realized wondrous essence.
The passage beginning with "does not arise" clarifies its wondrous function. That which does not arise yet is able to act is precisely the essence itself.
"Functioning without arising" refers to the teaching on the name "Pure Name," which pertains to bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
"Peaceful meditation" and so forth are what this sutra teaches; this pertains to verbal action (*vākkarman*). "Relying upon wondrous concentration" refers to mental action (*manaskarman*).

Because these three actions are non-localized in their offering of praise, they are inconceivable; thus, the inconceivable is the wondrous source. Yet, because he now externally manifests these matters, this is a provisional trace.

This is used metaphorically to reveal the fundamental source and lead sentient beings to assemble together within the boundless fundamental essence. Among the Buddha’s merits, the ten powers (*daśabala*) are the most sublime;
they are spoken of here from the perspective of their excellence. The meaning of the ten powers will be explained later.

However, as for the meaning of "sublime" (*miao*), it is now further elucidated through another interpretation: "doubt" is named after its physical form, while "delight" (*le*) receives its designation from sound; thus, it is the "fundamental abiding" that is sublime.

Wisdom cuts through the two doubts and gives rise to the two faiths; because it serves as the trace for severing [doubt] and producing [faith] for the sake of sentient beings, it manifests in these forms and sounds.
This meaning is extremely vital—reflect upon it, reflect upon it! For the observer, the Three Truths are the Teacher of the Buddha and are also the Buddha himself.

To manifest them by following the principle of these truths through the three contemplations is precisely what constitutes praise. As for their ultimate essentials and subtleties—reflect upon them, reflect upon them! Thus it is said.
This text should include both general and specific explanations; each must employ four modes of interpretation to fully exhaust its essence.
For the sake of brevity, however, consider it here according to the general explanation.
Next, regarding the explanation of the four *khandhas*, first the general category is explained, followed by the specific names. First, the translation-explanation has two layers. First:

Regarding the term "olfactory" (*ghrāṇa*): "olfactory" means "eating. Thus, the ancients said it is "eating fragrance. As for the "fragrance-aggregate" (*gandha-skandha*), "aggregate" refers to the body;
by using fragrance as food, one sustains the life of that body. Since they eat fragrance, they are able to emit fragrance, just like the musk deer and similar creatures in this region.
This is simply the nature of their retributive dharma (*vipāka-dharma*). All ancient explanations are identical to this. The new [exegesis] says "vigorous" (*kṣetra*).
*Dāva* has two pronunciations, namely *dā* and *vā*. This is translated as "Fragrance-Seeking Traveler" (*gandharva*), which refers to the deities who provide music;
they travel seeking the scent of incense while performing music and making requests. The phrase "these are [the... serves to distinguish, clarify, and list them in sequence.

As for what deity this is, it refers to this specific deity. This clarifies their affiliation. If one were to follow the common classification of the eight classes of spirits, there are four *kiṃnaras*...
Previously this deity resided at the end, but now it is listed after the four *kṛtaka* [deities]; because it pertains to worldly music (*laukika-vādya*), it is placed in that subsequent position.

Regarding this, the Dharma and the secular are, for the time being, said to be directly in accordance with the secular meaning; however, a further detailed analysis must be made, which I have not yet had the leisure to do.
Nevertheless, this also requires a comprehensive understanding of each of the four; for now, I shall merely provide a general overview, and will cite and resolve them in detail below.
Regarding the name "Nánshān" (Southern Mountain), its phonetic transcription is pronounced with a departing tone (*qùhū*); all other schools agree on this.

There are those who pronounce it with the tone of "Yuè" (Mount), which is incorrect, as it is distinct from the Sanskrit original. Some say that in the current commentary (*shǔwén*), the character is definitively pronounced with an entering tone (*rùhū*), but this is not so;

the text merely presents its four radical components and does not provide a phonetic gloss or semantic analysis—how could there be such a fixed restriction? It has been said of old that the first and third [tones] are "toneless" (*wúshēng*).
Regarding "joyful lower-upper" (樂下上), the second and fourth [categories] involve music with sound as the lower-upper; this differs from the current text.

The new explanation states that *manu* is equivalent to *sāvara*, which is translated here as "pleasing sound" (*kē-yì yīn*); it is also called "music according to one's wishes" (*rúyì yīnyuè*), meaning it causes people to feel love and joy.
Within these joys, there are two categories: first, those not involving stringed or wind instruments, such as the sound of drums and the like; second, [those involving such instruments].

These categories such as the silk and bamboo instruments—the *xiao* and *zheng*—are not merely types of silk and bamboo; among these, the lower grade is called "music" (*yue*) while the higher grade is called "musical sound" (*yinyue*).

Among these, the lower grade is termed "beauty" (*mei*) while the higher grade is termed "beautiful sound" (*meiyin*). Alternatively, this may be the same as the previous discussion regarding the divine songs and melodies.

As for the subsequent questions concerning these, they differ slightly from the current meaning. This is because the ancients composed their commentaries based on the presence or absence of specific characters in the musical notation.
Because these new compositions follow a sequential order, they are all provided with commentaries; furthermore, as each possesses its own rationale, both [the old and new views] are preserved here.
It was formerly said that this belongs to the realm of ghosts (*preta*), while others say it belongs to the realm of *asuras*. Within this context, if one considers the four essentials:

eating fragrance is the retribution for the world of dharmas; the emergence of fragrance is for humans, serving as an antidote to inferior worldly pleasures and dharmas, and it is also capable of manifesting the truth.
Regarding the "Supreme Meaning" (*paramārtha*), there are four types of teachings manifested following the "Joyful" (*rati*) [assembly], as previously described for the former and latter periods.
The first two are both termed "joyful" because they correspond to what is enjoyed by worldly beings;

the latter two are both termed "exquisite" (*śubha*) because they are perfectly suited to the capacities of Mahāyāna practitioners, surpassing the former two. When one reaches this assembly, there is only the single, wondrous fourth.

The text is concise regarding the latter three examples because the preceding ones can be understood by extension. Furthermore, it further clarifies the relationship between the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku).
"Fragrance" refers to purity; "bliss" refers to joy. The fundamental [truth] abides in the supramundane Middle Way, possessing the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The manifested [truth] displays the four mundane matters to lead sentient beings to equally attain the original four virtues. The meaning and logic are the same as before and are fully established.
Reflect upon this, reflect upon it! Regarding the meaning of "contemplation" (*guan*), there is one sense that is the same as before; another sense is that it refers to contemplating one's own mind.

If the four aspects of both the mundane and supramundane extremes are identical to the four virtues of the Middle Way, that is contemplation. One should verify this through the six identities (*liu ji*).
Next, the four types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) are explained. Within this, first the general name is explained, followed by the specific names;
"general" refers to their category, while "specific" refers to their number. "Category" refers to the asuras, and "number" refers to the four—that is, there are four.
Herein, the sūtra and the commentary are both consistent; however, regarding those sections where the sūtra and the commentary do not coincide, one should examine them in detail.

At the beginning, first the names and meanings are translated, followed by an analysis of their categorical inclusion. There are three ways of translating names: namely, "no wine" (*amadya*) and "not unupright" (*amṛṣā*).

These explain two meanings; the explanation of the first is easy to understand. The character *A* is pronounced with a short vowel. According to the ancient explanation of "no wine," there are two meanings:

first, it is identical to this [meaning of non-intoxication]; second, it refers to having maintained the precept against drinking alcohol in the past, whereby one has obtained this body as a karmic reward.
This means that the principle stated here is not necessarily universal. Next, regarding the term "text" (*vyañjana*), it does not explain the meaning because the meaning is easily understood;

this refers to its lack of formal correctness. For instance, although a man may be ugly and a woman beautiful, the name is derived from the man. As for Master An’s interpretation: *ā* signifies "non-" and *sura* signifies "substantiality" or "reality";
thus, it is derived from "lacking substantiality. The current text explains and establishes this meaning below, which should then be concluded accordingly.

Therefore, it is said that they lack "substantiality and integrity" (*asāra-śraddhā*). An old commentary cited this, explaining that because they are full of flattery and crookedness, this term was established for them so that they might become upright;

here, *śraddhā* means faith. There are those who do not understand this and claim that the text is erroneous—that the word *asa* means "no" and *sura* means "substantiality and integrity," thus forming the name *asura* ("lacking substantiality and integrity")—but this is not a case of a mismatched name, as it is based on this very principle; [the other view] is what constitutes the error.
Previously, it was said that Master An had erred, or it was said that this current text refutes Master An’s translation of the name as being improper;
however, his translation was actually correct, and thus the critique was mistaken. Now I say: these people do not understand the meaning of the text at all.

If this is so even for a passage that is extremely shallow and easy, how much more so for those that are deeper and more difficult! Formerly, there was one translation of the name which was... [text fragment ends].
The meaning of "non-gods" (asura) is as explained later in the *Nāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, where they are called "deities lacking virtue" because their actions are contrary to reason and unwholesome.

In the old tradition of Vasubandhu, they are called "those who do not engage in wholesome play," for while the various devas delight in play through wholesome dharmas, these beings mostly engage in unwholesome play.
Explanations from antiquity do not go beyond the five or six meanings mentioned above. The new [translation] calls them *Asura*.

"Ruo" (洛) here means "not" (非). "Suluo Tian" (素洛天) is an alternative name for Ābhāsvara (光音天). "A" (阿) signifies "not" (非), because due to excessive flattery and deceit, they lack the conduct of devas;

thus it is called "Non-Heaven" (非天). This concludes the explanation of the names. Below, the inclusion within the destinies (*gati*) is distinguished. This passage from the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* contains two meanings:
first, inclusion within the destinies; second, their dwelling places. According to the standard method, these should be combined into two sections; however, in the present text...

Although the matter is treated briefly here, its meaning is extensive; I shall now provide two explanations. First, regarding the general classification: the interpretations of various masters, both ancient and modern, differ. I shall briefly describe them here.

According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it is included within the celestial realm (*deva-gati*). The *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* classifies it as belonging to the hungry ghost realm (*preta-gati*).

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* includes it among the realms of hungry ghosts and animals (*tiryagyoni*). Furthermore, the *Gāthā-sūtra*, cited in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, states that it exists within three realms: hungry ghosts, animals, and devas.
It is said that Rāhu, the asura, is a son of a lion and is thus categorized among the animals; such is what is taught in the sūtras and śāstras.
In this present text, for brevity, only his inclusion within two destinies (*gati*) is clarified. No other explanations fall outside of this.

This is the meaning of his inclusion within a destiny. Next, regarding his dwelling place: while the general principles of the various explanations on this section are largely the same, I shall now briefly describe them according to others.
It is said that there is a class [of beings] described in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* as being extremely weak, dwelling among humans in mountain forests;

these are the great, deep stone caves found today in the West (the majority of which are inhabited by non-gods (*asura*), such as those where the Bodhisattva Prabhākaramitra manifested his presence to await the appearance of Maitreya). Second, regarding the four classes below this, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* speaks of Mount Sumeru.
1. Beneath the great ocean to the north of the mountains, at a depth of twenty-one thousand yojanas, is the palace of the asura Rāhu;
2. Further down, at a depth of one hundred and twelve thousand yojanas, is the palace of Śūraṃjaya;
3. Next below, at a depth of twenty-one thousand yojanas, is the palace of Mālādhāra; 4. Next below, at a depth of twenty-one thousand yojanas, is the palace of Virocana.
The palace of Vemacitra is, according to this [text], eighty-four thousand *yojanas* deep, surpassing Mount Sumeru;
(whereas current traditions all claim it is twelve thousand *yojanas*, and some say forty-eight thousand—this text says eighty-four thousand; it is unknown which is correct).

This contradicts the *Lokotpāda-sūtra*, which states that one thousand *yojanas* to the east and west of Mount Sumeru, there is the palace of Vemacitra, measuring eighty thousand [yojanas] in length and breadth.
There is no contradiction in considering the sevenfold city-walls and so forth as separate settlements; this is their dwelling place.
The present text states that "by the seaside" refers to the first of the five [classes], the inferior one. Other masters also say it is "upon the earth.
Next, it mentions "the seabed," which refers to the following four types. The four names listed in this sutra are precisely those four who dwell within the sea.
Following this principle, they should be listed in ascending and descending order; first Rāhu, second Bhañji, third Khara, and fourth Vemacitra.
If proceeding from the bottom upward, it should begin with Citra and so forth.

That they are not arranged thus here is because even within their respective categories, there is no sequential order. They are called "miscellaneous" precisely for this reason. The significance is as explained previously.

If, within this context, one acts for the sake of the four *siddhāntas*, then the names derived from all meanings, as well as the inclinations, the subsumptions, and the abodes, are all worldly retributive dharmas;
these constitute the *loka-saṃvṛti* (the worldly). Furthermore, hearing the Dharma from the Buddha, receiving it with faith, destroying delusions, and attaining the Way involve three meanings.
Having traversed through various sūtras of both the Small and Great Vehicles, they are now all opened up, reconciled, and unified into the Single Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*).

In the Way of the Single Reality, how could there be anything further that is not celestial or not upright faith? The Primordial Abiding is the Celestial of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*), which is neither a celestial of the mundane nor the supramundane extremes.
Its manifestation as "non-celestial" is intended to lead all beings back to the source. The observer observes the mind:
all phenomena are identical within the true mark (*dharmatā*), the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is devoid of the two extremes.
Having already explained the four general meanings above, we shall now explain its four specific names. Although one may know the general [meanings], one does not yet know the specific ones;

therefore, they must be explained. However, since this type of matter is extensively discussed in the sūtras and śāstras and its traces are manifest, each individual name should possess all four meanings.
In the present text, however, only three are clarified, and these are all presented concisely according to the teaching (*yathāśāsana*). Only those that can be obtained are included.

The intent of the present sutra is that once its discrepancies are scrutinized and reconciled, it is sufficient to revise it; therefore, the initial title is omitted. According to the sequence, it should correspond to the second [section], "From the Sublime Path.
Within the first section on causes and conditions, there are two translations of the commentary. The first translation concerns being bound:
according to the ancient commentary, this refers to the vanguard of the asuras fighting with Śakra, who were bound and subsequently released by virtue of a vow. Therefore, [it is so titled].
Regarding the explanation of the meaning within the present text, the phrase "five places" refers simply to the five unwholesome objects: the hands, feet, head, and neck.
According to the *Dharmatāsaṃgraha* (or *Fufa zang zhuan*), Guḍu tied a dead person, a dead snake, and a dead dog to the neck of Māra;

thus, what is here called the "five unwholesome objects" refers to these five corpses. Some say they refer to a dead person, a dead snake, a dead dog, [a dead horse, and] a dead... [text fragmentary].
The pig and various foul bones constitute the fifth; that is, these five objects are bound to its five locations.

Because the "bound" (the object) and the "binding" (the agent) are combined into a single name, it is said to be "bound. The use of the terms "either" or "or" indicates that the sources of this account are not uniform.
As for the term "possessing power," it refers to being brave and robust; by virtue of such valorous strength, he acts as the vanguard and fights alongside Śakra.
Because he possesses power, he is released from the bonds by which he was bound; furthermore, since this is spoken from the perspective of being bound, it does not explicitly mention "liberation.

According to the actual reality, it should properly be translated as "valiant" (*vīryavat*). In other sūtras, the term is correctly rendered according to its actual meaning as *vāyaka*, which means "round" (*pūrṇa*);
in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is translated as "most excellent," which refers to being valiant rather than being bound. Now...

This means the sense of being perfectly complete in terms of its mass, shape, or function; "supreme" (*parama*) refers to the greatness of its power and efficacy, and carries the meaning of being courageous and robust.
This etymological explanation is most appropriate. Because it is based on the meaning, it is listed first.

This [term] corresponds to four meanings: it is the world of worldly courage and robustness; it is the ability to hear the Dharma from the Buddha; and it is the ability to give rise to great valor and heroism.
To give birth to all that is good, to extinguish all that is evil, and to attain the Noble Path—these are the four meanings.

Since one has already attained mastery over the single transformation and fully heard the convergence of its various aspects, one now leaps forward with joy and attains transcendent realization within this single, wondrous Way.

Thus, immediately following the first cycle [of teaching], the asura hosts attained understanding; this is precisely the meaning of the "valiant" ones mentioned in the present sutra, who possess this from the very beginning.
The distant [objects] reach both the present and the future, while the near reaches only the future. Because one attains the nature and form of purity and subtlety, this capacity exists.
To bind the Māra is precisely the five kinds of impurity contemplation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) which destroy the five desires;
furthermore, the five gate contemplations externally destroy the five types of false attachments. This is solely to cause one to depart from craving and views and return to the Right Path.
The traces follow the fundamental source, so their distance can be known. Now, let me provide another explanation:

"Śūraṅgama" (首楞嚴) means the Samādhi of Valiant Subjugation, or the Samādhi of Solely Vigorous Practice; this spirit fundamentally abides in this samādhi, and thus its traces receive this name. This interpretation is most convenient.
The "three contemplations" (三觀) are the capacity, the "five abodes" (五住) are the place, and the "limit of reality" (實際) is the site where one is established—namely, emptiness (空).

Contemplating the bonds of the four abodes, the provisional bonds within the sands of phenomena, and the bonds of ignorance—through the threefold contemplation of the single mind, one simultaneously binds the five abodes.
All are immediately the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*); this means that afflictions are immediately enlightenment.

Furthermore, for one who can contemplate in this way, the delusions and hindrances of affliction are instantly and completely dissolved, leaving nothing to oppose them; this is the contemplation of great valor and strength.
Regarding "Khara": the character *kha* is pronounced with both the second and fourth tones, not the level tone; the character *da* is likewise.

This character is formed by attaching the radical for "horse" (*ma*) with a large shape, representing a phonetic component, and it is not attached to the radical for "dog. Those who see transcribed scriptures should be shown this:
as for "bhrū-karṇa," it is also called "Broad-Browed Shoulders"; as for "vikaṭa-gātra," his physical appearance is most extraordinary. Therefore...
His commentary explains that "his appearance was even more magnificent" refers to the previous instance of surging seawater that submerged the city of Priyaṃkara.
Next, "the Valiant" (Vīryavanta) is none other than Puṣpamāla. The text cites the original source as stating he was "truly adorned with brocade";

this means his body was embellished with various kinds of precious jewels, resembling flowered brocade, and for this reason he was named Puṣpamāla. This is precisely what is meant by "flower-garland."
The meaning here should properly be translated as "flower garland" (mālā), or alternatively as "beautiful flower garland.
It may also be that the character is an error; it should correctly refer to "jeweled ornamentation," which is highly elegant and appropriate. These are all names derived from worldly conventions.

That which is "constantly hearing the Dharma from the Buddha" refers to the subsequent three [aspects] and the fourth: the "complete" (paripūrṇa), the "sufficient" (sākalya), the "teaching" (śāsana), and the "manifestly clear" (vibhakti). This signifies the perfect, wondrous, and majestic adornment.

Intrinsic virtue is like a jeweled flower garland adorning the body; the two wisdoms within the fundamental [nature] constitute its essence and function, which are employed by sentient beings to transport them out of birth and death.
Because it is revealed that this essence and function exist inherently from the beginning, these traces are manifested.
Furthermore, while the fundamental [nature] is already capable of adorning the Dharma-body with merit and wisdom, the traces manifest worldly flower garlands to adorn the physical body. From...
This is stated because the names are established based on the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku).

In the contemplation, the "drum-covering" is immediately overturned, transforming that cause and effect into the cause and effect of Great Nirvana. Since both cause and effect are profound and vast, they are like the ocean.
Furthermore, being able to cultivate the cause of the three contemplations and manifest the fruit of the three wisdoms is precisely the contemplation of the flower garland.

Regarding the first part, two names are presented, but only one is explained.
