This [term] is free from various doubts. Although the current text also contains three [instances], one of them is likewise in the "repetition" (punar) section.

Furthermore, none of the older versions contain the term "pure mind" (viśuddha-citta). This indicates that while this explanation existed in the older versions, its meaning was not elucidated; therefore, it is also omitted here.

If one were to claim that these four characters directly constitute the "pure mind," it would be incorrect, because since there are still two characters, *tatra*, following them, they cannot be the pure mind.
Regarding this meaning, because the old translations from the Sanskrit were incomplete, such various doubts arose. Although these names existed in the old versions, their meanings were not explained.
Now, the explanation beginning with "waves and sea" means that when water produces this sound, people do not understand it, and thus they call it "doubt.
This, too, is not yet clear; according to this, it is precisely an explanation of the "height of resonance."

According to the old commentary on the meaning, it is said that because he emerges from the great waters and utters a great sound, proclaiming for himself, "I am Vemacitra," he is called *Ghoṣavat* (Resounding).
Based on this, it is sufficient to correctly explain the name *Ghoṣavat* while simultaneously resolving various points of doubt;
for when people hear this, they do not understand its underlying intention, which gives rise to all manner of doubts. This is based on that [commentary].
One should have first indicated that "the resonance is also high and manifold," and then explained it accordingly;
since the explanation exists while the indication is absent, this is an omission. As for the term *taraṅga*, it refers to the drum-straps.
As for the term *Śacīpati*, it refers to the father of Śakra’s wife, used here as a figurative epithet of praise. This begins the detailed explanation. Within the detailed explanation:

First, the meaning of "echo" (*pratiśrutkā*) is indicated; next, the meaning of "Father of Śacī" is explained. Regarding those who observe the Buddhist scriptures, it is said that the *Āgama* (or perhaps both sūtras) state:
"One daughter was born"—this refers to the female Asura whose body is like Mount Sumeru. "One son was born"—this refers to Viśvāmitra. Among the Śākyas... [there are... (Note:

The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on a specific passage concerning the etymology of "Śuddhodana" (Pure Rice), likely from a Chinese exegetical work such as the *Fahua xuanzan*. The translation reflects the technical terminology of Buddhist scholasticism.)
It is said that its form is four times that of the Mother Great Ocean; its name is derived from the place where it is bound beneath the waters.
Although the creature existed, its name did not yet exist; it was because of the ocean’s waves and billows that this sound emerged, and thus it was named accordingly.
Before this name existed, people might have seen its form but, not knowing what deity it was, they applied various doubtful names to it.
In the Sūtra, Śakra is subsumed within the celestial realm precisely because he is praised there by way of metaphor;
the subsequent explanation regarding the causes and conditions of Śacī is that he took her as his wife because she was originally of celestial lineage.
As for those who slandered his father, it is said that Śakra had many wives and, due to jealousy, such things occurred. Regarding the term "Yanjū" (燕居), none of the various schools have this name.

All say that "dwelling in caves" (*xuéjū*) is likely a scribal error; however, upon further inspection of the original manuscript, it is stated that those who dwell in caves—just as those previously mentioned who dwell in the sea—constitute the fourth category, and because they reside at the very bottom of the ocean, they are called "cave-dwellers.

Alternatively, because their dwelling place is most profoundly secluded, they are called "nest-dwellers" (*yānjū*). The new term is *Vemacitra*, which is translated here as "Exquisite Pervasion" (*qǐjìn*), so named because its patterns are ornate.
Regarding the body, some say it refers to using precious ornaments to adorn one's clothing; this is considered the most significant aspect.

This meaning implies that one adorns both the body and the head with rare jewels. Since these are the four essential points within the causal conditions, there appear to be four corresponding intentions according to the text:
first, a brief explanation of the world; second, praising the excellence of its species, which is the "human" [realm]; third, [the response to] slander; and fourth, [the response to] flattery.
Having long engaged in military affairs, his mantra-power remains unimpaired; this is precisely the remedy for the root problem. His dwelling in seclusion manifests his supreme commitment to the Way.

His practice of living in caves is identical in meaning [to the former]; observing the text, it is evident that it is so. As for the meaning of your new interpretation—that he entered among humans—this can be understood by analogy with the previous case.
However, because he possesses the power of the Prajñā-mantra within him, he is not to be treated as a mere parallel.
The teaching has both differences and convergence; having converged, it can unify through a wondrous sound that pervades the entire Dharma-realm, which is why it is called "the resonance is lofty.

As for "primordial purity" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), this refers to the long-term cultivation of virtue being termed "primordial," rather than referring to an original nature. Please do not misunderstand this as being the fundamental nature itself.

This "primordial" refers to long-term purity manifested as a trace for the sake of sentient beings to demonstrate how they may attain purity; its merit is clarified herein according to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.
Because they emerge as the greatest among all the heavens, it is known that they have long since entered the Lotus Dharma-gate;

this is clear. To "contemplate" is precisely to cultivate and manifest the nature; contemplate this most wondrously! Thus, those whose resonance is lofty are those who wondrously penetrate the principle of the two truths of mind-nature;
this is what is meant by being "lofty and profound. That the Dragon Girl deeply penetrated was precisely this contemplation. As for those of "great body":
To be able to cultivate wondrous contemplation so as to manifest the Dharma-body of inherent virtue is the "Contemplation of the Great Body.

Next, in the explanation of Rāhu, within the initial section on causes and conditions, there are three parts: first, the presentation and explanation of the name and meaning; second, the discernment of past causes; and third, the clarification of alternative names.

Within the first part, there is first a brief explanation along with the discernment of the categories, types, essence, and measure; next follows the extensive explanation beginning from the "Contemplation of the Heavens" below. First:
Previously, in the brief explanation of the translation, *āvaraṇa* (obscuration) refers to veiling, and *dhara* (holder) refers to grasping;

that which can obstruct and hold is "his hand," while that which is obstructed and held refers to the sun and moon. As for the term "the one who speaks" (*vaktṛ*), it means that he is the person [who speaks].

Since merely saying "obstructing-holder" does not clarify what object it is, the so-called "sun and moon" are further specified. The new translation says *Rāhula*, which in this language [Chinese] means...
Regarding the "Seizing of the Sun": when the Asuras fought with the gods, the gods of the Four Great Kings first engaged them in battle.
The Sun and Moon Devas emitted intense radiance and struck the Asuras; these were the vanguard of the Asuras. They seized the sun and moon with their hands to obscure their light;
therefore, it is called "seizing the sun. Now, as the fourth [category], it should logically follow the initial listing. The reason for its placement here is its connection with the gods.

Regarding the combatants, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* traditionally states that the asuras possess beautiful women but lack fine food, while the devas possess fine food but lack beautiful women;
because they harbor mutual hatred and jealousy, they constantly fight. Now it is said that slandering their father is also one such cause.
As for identifying them as belonging to the class of animals, this [creature] is a lion.
The phrase "the child is likewise" and so forth distinguishes its physical dimensions;
that it is able to obstruct and sustain the sun and moon of the various heavens is precisely because its physical magnitude is such that its power rivals that of the gods.

To explain and establish the meaning of "obstructing and sustaining," the section from "observing the heavens" downward provides a detailed exposition. Furthermore, there are two senses of "obstructing and sustaining": first, obstructing and sustaining others.
This refers to the sun and the moon; the two being obstructed and supported by others constitutes the three powers (*trivīrya*).

Because it combines these two meanings, it is called "obstructed and supported" (*āvaraṇadhāraṇa*), which is identical in meaning to the previous definition. Therefore, the citation from Paramārtha’s commentary on the name Rāhula was established based on this.
Now, as explained above, this text refers to being obstructed and supported by others; what follows below clarifies how one is obstructed and supported by others. If...
If one does not grasp these two meanings, how can one interpret this passage? Within it there are two parts: first, the elucidation of the three powers; second, the summary.

Regarding the first, there are three sections: first, being sustained by the power of human merit; second, being sustained by the obstruction of celestial power; third, being sustained by the obstruction of the Buddha’s power.
The first concerns being assisted by the power of human merit. As for "observing the heavens" and so forth, it refers to envying others.

The gradual emergence of conflict over superior realms is as follows: if a person can be filial and obedient toward their two parents and make offerings to the Triple Gem, they shall, by virtue of these causes of merit, be reborn there.
Although they have not yet departed for that place, their merit already provides remote support, strengthening their power so that those who would oppose them are rendered unable to act.
Therefore, this constitutes a protective barrier against obstacles to one's meritorious power. Furthermore, day by day...
The latter three matters are all obstructed and sustained by celestial power; the first two are forms, while the last is sound.

Since they are obstructed and sustained by the sun and moon, one becomes enraged and emits a great sound; yet because the hands are unable to act and the voice likewise cannot cause harm, this is due to the power of celestial merit.
This clarifies that when people of the world do not understand the underlying cause and regard these events as calamities or portents, there is indeed a degree of reason for their doing so.
The world does not entirely agree with this, holding instead that it is simply the operation of the cycles of yin and yang;

yet, even though it is a matter of those [celestial] forces, it does not preclude that human beings must also invite their own karmic retribution through their own actions. It is like a person facing the light who cultivates the roots of goodness:
it is not for the sake of Heaven that Heaven brings them blessings, nor is it because they obscure Heaven that they suffer harm; rather, they bring about their own calamity. The same applies here.
When Duke Qi perceived the omens of a hegemon and instead promoted the doctrine of the "sick Prince," his illness was cured as soon as he heard it;
yet this was not the case for others who did not understand the underlying reason and instead formed a one-sided, fixed interpretation—it was certainly not entirely so.
If one can penetrate deeply into the matter, then there will be no cause for concern. It is also like hearing of battles.
Fearing death, they hear [the teaching] and become even more courageous; originally they were not dualistic, yet it is not that they do not act as if dualistic.
This passage is stated here for the purpose of refuting fixed assertions. From the section "From the sun and moon" downward, it clarifies being sustained and protected by the Buddha’s power.

The text appears in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which contains five parts: first, reporting the situation; second, the Buddha’s admonition and exhortation; third, extreme terror; fourth, the Buddha’s consolation; and fifth, the restoration of their original state.

Fearing that the four *pācī* (female spirits) would come to inquire about the cause, he answered fully the reason why; this is contained in detail within the treatise (*śāstra*) and cannot be described at length here.
In the present text, there are only the first three [sections] and not the latter two questions and answers.

Regarding the phrase "he appealed to the Buddha," it means that he was being harassed and troubled by them, and thus requested the Buddha’s protection. Regarding the phrase "the Buddha told him," it refers to the full exposition of the merits of the sun and moon.
"Dispelling darkness, illuminating, cool, lovely, beneficial, and profound"—this means that they shall not be afflicted or harmed. The following clarifies their great terror;

the following is a summary of how the causal conditions of the three powers cannot obstruct or maintain [the state], whereas for those [beings], it is inverted and becomes an obstruction to their maintenance.
Herein, the "three powers" refer to the aforementioned three [powers], and the "sentient beings" refer to the aforementioned first four heavens.

This refers to the power of the lower beings cultivating goodness; the other two [categories] may be understood accordingly. It is commonly said that one merely reads the text directly without understanding its meaning;
thus, the two texts proceed in opposition. The following clarifies their causes. As for "knowing," the preceding section clarifies their physical strength and bodies.

Their bodies are as large as previously described, and their power is capable of obstructing and supporting the sun and moon. Furthermore, their forms are twice as large, and they all delight in fighting and battle. Why is this so?
The causes that have brought about this state are now fully elucidated; these are the two causes. The first is the cause for obtaining a great body and great power:
namely, practicing great giving toward vast and superior objects and generating great vows. Because of these three "greats," one obtains a great body and power.
However, because this is driven merely by a worldly mind of pride and competitiveness, rather than being guided by supramundane right faith, it results in a constant fondness for [worldly things].

Engaging in battle is the second cause. Furthermore, it is clarified that by virtue of performing great acts of giving with joy, one brings about a superior environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) as its dominant result (*adhipati-phala*), and becomes its sovereign. "Radiant" (*Prabhāsa*) is the name of the city where he dwells, as previously explained.
Although the first three [causes] should likewise have their respective causes, they are not mentioned in the sutra and thus are not described here. As for the term "inhaling breath":

Various schools also cite this name but do not explain its meaning; they simply state that after being admonished by the Buddha, [the people] were terrified and, holding their breath and swallowing their voices, did not dare again to gaze upon the sun and moon or raise a loud cry, and thus it was named accordingly.
Since these four essential points constitute the causal conditions, the first—obstructing the maintenance of others—is the *loka-dhātu* (worldly realm), wherein people cultivate merit and goodness.
The various devas possess power over humans; the power of the devas and the power of the Buddha are precisely the antidotes.

Suppressing their breath and swallowing their voices, they believe that the power of the Buddha is great and dare not again act as the primary principle. Thus, the sequence of the text correctly reveals this.

"Teaching" (jiao) means that it sustains understanding while obstructing delusion; "delusion" refers to the two obstacles of phenomena and principle, while "understanding" refers to the path of the two wisdoms.

It is like the sun and moon: "penetration" refers to what is common to all teachings; now, in this assembly, there is nothing coarse, only the sublime, which is why it is called "obstructing and sustaining.

Regarding "the fundamental obstructs and sustains the provisional": the fundamental obstructs and sustains all things in order to manifest the three powers. Regarding "the provisional serves as the three obstructions that sustain": [this refers to the same].
As for "contemplation," it is the threefold contemplation within a single mind; it obstructs all delusions and sustains all sublime understandings (and so forth).
The general meaning is roughly as follows.

Next, regarding the explanation of the four *kārikās*, there is only the section on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), with no other three explanations. Within this section on causes and conditions, there are two parts:

first, the explanation of the general and specific names; second, the comprehensive discussion of their resultant retribution and functional efficacy. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the general, and second, the specific. First [the general]...
This section consists of two parts: first, a correct explanation based on the authoritative scriptures; second, an account of the differing interpretations of various masters.

Within the first part, there is an explanation of the name through its translation, followed by the location, dimensions, and a new interpretation. Regarding the name: *Kāruṇḍa* (迦路荼) is translated as "Wondrous-Winged Bird" (*Miaochi*).
Its wing feathers are wondrous not only because they are golden, but because this meaning is beautiful. As for its location, it lies twenty-four thousand [yojanas] east or west of Jambudvīpa.
The distance from north to south is two hundred and eighty thousand *li*; how could one dwell upon such a tree?
If it were through the sovereign power of his spiritual faculties (*ṛddhi*), that might be possible, though it remains unknown where this statement originates.

As for the mention of the "two wings" and so forth, all ancient and modern commentators have explained this phrase in reference to his "great body," rather than as a description of his actual physical dimensions. It may be that these terms were used merely for the sake of convenience or to follow established convention. Next...
The following clarifies the differing interpretations of human masters. Zhuangzi says: "In the Northern Ocean there is a fish whose name is Kun;
the magnitude of the Kun is known to be several thousand li. It transforms into a bird named Peng; the breadth of the Peng's back is unknown, perhaps several thousand li.
When it rises in a rage and flies, its wings are like clouds hanging from the sky. Because the descriptions of these two beings are somewhat similar, the ancients [relied upon this].

This is called the *péng* (Peng); the subsequent passage explains the meaning of this *péng*. The following section also provides an account of the *fènghuáng* (phoenix), because when it flies, the various birds and *péng*s follow it;
thus it is named *péng*, and the *fèng* is likewise so called. Therefore, this *péng* bird is the *fènghuáng*.
The *Xiāngyún Lóngwáng jīng* (Cloud-Summit Dragon-King Sutra) translates it as *fènghuáng*; the intent is to clarify that it is the Golden-Winged One (*garuḍa*).
This is the phoenix; it is one of the five clouds of the sovereign, specifically the cloud of the south.
It is also called Zhuque (the Vermilion Bird) and Chique (the Red Sparrow). Furthermore, as it is the leader of the *yue* clan, all follow and assist it.

When a sovereign is able to fully implement the rituals and patterns of propriety, this is the spiritual response. The character for "phoenix" (*feng*) is a *sheng* (phonetic) character containing the form of a bird within its structure.

This refers to internal form and external sound. The character *huáng* (皇) should simply be written as the character for "Emperor" (*dìhuáng*); it should not follow the [夙-歹] radical added by secular convention.
All commentaries from the *shūběn* (draft manuscripts) follow this [夙-歹] radical, yet scholars must understand that these were all unilaterally altered and modified by later people.
As for why Danqiu did not permit it: it is because the phoenix possesses the three virtues, whereas the golden-winged bird (*garuḍa*) does not; therefore, it is not [the same].

The secular classics of the Three Virtues (San De) frequently discuss this, and there is indeed a basis for what they say. According to Prince Zhaoming of the Liang Dynasty’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi*:
"Peng is the same as Feng; there is no separate Feng other than Peng—this is merely a different name for Peng, not the 'Feng that comes to pay homage' (the auspicious phoenix).
As explained therein, based on this meaning, he [the commentator] harmonizes them by treating them as identical. However...
The general meaning is roughly as follows: because there are no authentic scriptures, human sentiments cannot serve as a basis for reliance, and thus they are not employed (and so forth).
Below, the distinct names are explained; initially, there are two meanings as in the text. "Majesty and virtue" (*vaibhutva*) refers to power and influence. "To be intimidated" (*śatha*;

*zhàn* being pronounced *jiē*, meaning timid, fearful, or submissive) is another reading for *dié*, and the character is also written as *shè*. It describes the appearance of being terrified. This is complete.
Because all these matters are vast, they are "complete" (*pūrṇa*). "Great body" (*mahākāya*) refers to that which is the largest in form among its own kind.
All various commentaries explain this meaning by stating that the distance between its two wings is equal [to the universe]. This means that Jambudvīpa can only accommodate one of its feet.
"Immovable" (*acala*) has the sense of being as one pleases and acting with sovereign mastery. All commentators of both ancient and modern times have [explained it] thus.
The section beginning with "The same applies here" below serves to comprehensively distinguish the differences in the power of their karmic retribution.

Within this, first it clarifies that there are four distinctions regarding the food that sustains the material basis of retribution; next, it clarifies that there are further three temporal distinctions. Regarding the former, there are two parts:

first, it clarifies that although the power of retribution possesses the capacity for provisional transformation, its actual retribution necessarily relies upon the substance of food; second, it clarifies the [nature of] that which is consumed.
Regarding the distinctions among the objects of their food, there are four aspects. First, the phrase "those who must eat the *nāgas* as retribution" identifies their actual retribution;
since they previously manifested through the power of transformation, whereas this is not a manifestation, it is the actual power of the natural law (*dharmatā*).
Below this, the specific characteristics of what they consume are distinguished, as described in the Sūtra: there are birds of the four modes of birth.

This refers to those who eat the four types of birth-dragons (*catur-yoni-nāga*), casting themselves into the ocean and parting the waters with their wings to seize those born from wombs, eggs, and so forth.
Another source cites the *Ekottarika Āgama*, which states: "Those born from eggs can eat those born from eggs; those born from wombs can eat those born from wombs;
those born from moisture can eat the previous three; and those born by transformation can eat all four. This differs from the first two [categories] mentioned here, as stated in the sutra.
Furthermore, according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, one should first mention the egg-born and then the womb-born; thus, among the four classes of beings, each receives what it is destined to eat.
If one forcibly takes that which is not its due portion, the bird will perish—such is the natural law of causes, conditions, and karmic retribution.
The sutra further states: "Even if there are those with dragon bodies who are able to serve the Buddha, birds cannot devour them."

Because the Buddha possesses the four great powers of equanimity, the text is abbreviated and does not elaborate; below, it clarifies that there are still distinctions of three periods, which are as follows:
first, it clarifies the quantity of food consumed and the timing; second, it clarifies that when the retribution is exhausted, one can no longer consume food;
third, it clarifies the characteristics of the residual power after exhaustion. The first is due to the natural law (*dharmatā*) of karmic force; the next is...
The exhaustion of retribution is the natural law (*dharmatā*); these three are the natural laws of residual power. Regarding "chán sān" (啖參):

the upper character is pronounced *jiào*, meaning to speak in a loud voice; the lower character is pronounced *shuàn* (with the phonetic *huò*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the collective chirping of birds;

the correct character is *sào* (喿), and this character *shuàn* is merely a vulgar variant. If one uses *zào* (譟), it means clamorous speech that disturbs and binds others. From "the flesh tears apart" onwards, it clarifies his death.
Regarding the later description of the mind as a pearl, we know that the substance of this pearl is likewise not singular. Now, if we consider the four essentials:
first, the general and specific names and meanings, as well as the dharma of karmic retribution, pertain to the meaning of the world (*loka-dhātu*).

Second, the two middle sections provide a comprehensive analysis, which serves as the remedy for the two [extremes]. Furthermore, being able to hear the Dharma from the Buddha and attain the Way constitutes the possession of all four. Thus says the text.
There is no fourth [category] that surpasses the first three; this is the most powerful and influential among the classes of the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*).
It is capable of swallowing all poisons and evils, as various sutras clearly explain its nature. Thus, it encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate.
Upon reaching this assembly, after the single gate has been unified, they share one wondrous essence and function, such that there are no longer any coarse things to be called by name.

The *Garuḍa* has exhausted its essence. As for the "Root," it refers to the fundamental abiding of the Great Heroic and Valiant Samādhi, which is able to subdue all demons, outsiders, and various poisons;

it manifests these traces merely for the sake of eliminating all poisonous evils. For the observer, the perfect and wondrous Threefold Contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) can cause all the various poisons of affliction (*kleśa*) to be completely dissolved and absorbed;
this is precisely the contemplation of "devouring the poison. [This is not explicitly stated] in the text.
The examples provided are thus brief; reflect upon them, reflect upon them in detail.

Next, regarding the explanation of the assembly of human kings: this is the eighth section. The King of Magadha is listed last because he is the sovereign of the land and, according to the sequence of worldly power, he comes at the end.
The full text contains three types of explanations, with the sole exception of that which concerns the teachings (*yàojiào*).
In the initial section on causes and conditions, the sutra text mentions the mother to indicate the son; this is precisely what reveals the identity of the mother.
The translator rendered it as "She Who Contemplates" (Sīlavatī). Although this has been the standard translation throughout ancient and modern times, its meaning has never been explained.
Alternatively, as in the *Amitābha Sūtra* where it says "teach me to contemplate," she is given this secret name because she is able to initiate this gate of contemplation (*dhyāna*).
Therefore, in the *Bhadrapāla-sūtra*, he is called "Manifest Contemplation" (*Santimukha*) and so forth.
In some places it is said that he was originally a native of the kingdom of Vaiśālī (and so on). The new [translation] says: *Vetadhyipura*. *Veta* means "supreme meaning" (*paramārtha*);
*dhyi* means "body," which is the name for the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha. *Ha* is the masculine form of address, and *hi* is the feminine form of address.
This is the name of that mountain, and it is also the name of the deity within that mountain; because he obtained [the name] by requesting it from that deity, it was used as his name.

Next, the father’s name is presented. Although it has been translated, its meaning has not yet been seen. Alternatively, seeing the image allows one to know the reality, hence it is called "molding the real" (*moshi*);
or it is called "shadow-solidity" (*yōkan*), the meaning of which is the same. The sutra mentions only the mother; now, wishing to ensure that both are known, it is presented again. Why?
Therefore, it is not by means of the father that the son is designated; Master Xuan says this is because the father had already been killed at that time, and thus the father is not designated.

Another interpretation further states that because he killed his mother, the mother is used to designate him. Now, I say that as previously mentioned, there are many instances where both parents are used to designate their son;
why must it necessarily be so in every case? Therefore, this [interpretation] is incorrect. Next, the name of the king is correctly explained.
There are two interpretations of this term. In the first, the full Sanskrit is *Ajātaśatru*.
*Aja* means "unborn" (*amita*) and *śatru* means "enemy" (*du-lu*). Because he already possessed enmity even before being born, he is now called by these two meanings.
First, it refers to his past enmity, as explained in the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra*. Second, it refers to the present, even though...

This is because the signs of enmity and harm already existed even before they had arisen. Regarding the name *Varuṇi*, some write it as two characters beginning with "婆" (*ba*), which is largely confused;

it should likely be the character "娑" (*sa*). As for the statement that he was "without fingers," various schools all say his fingers were severed, meaning that when he was first born, an astrologer divined that he bore the marks of a rebellious and malevolent nature, so his father-king ordered him to be cast from a high tower; yet he did not die.
It is merely because of the injury to a single finger. Regarding those who act with malice and harm, there are briefly four causes and conditions:
past lives, present injuries, greed for royal rank, and evil associates; it is for these reasons.

It is said that one "guards against" [the harm] because one fears that in the future, tracing back the origins of such matters, they will become a great affliction; thus this name is provisionally applied. Furthermore, it may also be...

"Good Manifestation" (*Sukhāvatī*) is the opposite of the aforementioned "Evil Manifestation. Regarding this, one should consult the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra* (*Guanjing shu*) and the *Miscellaneous Records of the Bestower* (*Nengshou zaji*).
This refers generally to the world of worldly cause and effect. Showing that there are enemies and oppositions is intended to prevent people from engaging in such things;
it serves as an antidote. "Protecting those within" refers to acting for the benefit of others, which consists in hearing the Dharma from the Buddha.

Attaining the Way is the primary meaning (the ultimate truth). Alternatively, it may be understood that the first two meanings pertain to the mundane world (*loka*), while the subsequent [meanings] within the context of the fundamental and the manifested (*honjaku*) encompass the remaining three meanings.
As for not explicitly clarifying the teaching, its meaning is naturally clear within the context of the fundamental and the manifested;

thus, there is no need for prolixity. Next, below, the fundamental and the manifested are clarified: first, the names and meanings from the preceding section are used to designate their fundamental and manifested aspects; next, they are clarified by means of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

This present provisional manifestation of the ultimate and the remote is followed by the provisional manifestation of the Lotus Sūtra and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which reveal and perfect the original ultimate and the remote.
Regarding the initial statement that "the name 'Good Vision' (Sudarśana) is the original," this secretly reveals that his original nature has long since wondrously realized the Dharma-nature;

because it is neither contrary nor compliant, "Good Vision" is his original name. However, in order to lead those of evil disposition, he manifested the appearance of contrariness and thus assumed this [present] name.

Therefore, regarding these traces, there are two layers within the section following the "Fundamental" (ben). In the first of these two layers, there is both separation and combination. Within the combination, there is the knowledge of the inverse and the direct;
this knowledge is that the *Ajātaśatru* (A-jie-sheng) is not as he was previously. Thus, "She-du-lu" (which is translated here as "enemy") is now rendered as "she" (world);
the last two characters are omitted, and furthermore, the character for "family" (*jia*) is omitted, leaving only "enmity" (*yuan*). What follows is the section on combination.
The commentary states that there is both opposition and conformity, which can be understood; furthermore, the successive combinations and separations can also be understood.

Regarding the "eight dharmas," the record says they may refer to the eight perversions (*aṣṭa-mithyātva*), the eight winds (*aṣṭa-vāyu*), or the eight inversions (*aṣṭa-viparyāsa*). It is certain that they correspond to the "eight impure riches" (*aṣṭa-aśuddha-dhana*) elucidated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Now, I ask: why are these called "eight dharmas"? Why is it known that they are these specific eight? Moreover, this original precept was issued for those who have left the household life (*pravrajita*); why does it mention kings?
Why do worldly people say this? It is because it cannot be [affected] now; it is precisely by means of the eight winds that we speak thus. How is this clarified?
These eight consist of four adversities and four prosperities, which clarify that its fundamental abiding is neither adverse nor favorable—the path of wondrous purity.
Therefore, although its traces manifest as adversity and prosperity, these eight cannot wound or repel its fundamental purity; for this reason, it is further named the "Immovable Bodhisattva."
The meaning of being unmoved by the eight winds is thus clearly established; "this is the equality" serves as the conclusion.

As the sutra says, "This explains that he has long since attained the true, perfect, and wondrous Way," which clarifies his fundamental realization (*mūla*). Next, regarding the clarification of his traces (*vyañjana*), some commentators explain that there are two different locations:
either the tenth stage of Dedication (*daśamī pariṇāmanā*) or the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmi*). However, I say: how could there be ten? [The text here implies a critique of such a division.]
The previous statement that he still fell into hell was a provisional teaching (*upāya*) from the preceding sutra.

It first clarifies that his fundamental nature had long since been seen as pure, yet subsequently describes how he committed rebellious acts and, despite repentance and forbearance, still fell into hell;

these are all manifestations of his traces. These traces are used to reveal the fundamental reality. Since the traces appear as such—whether rebellious or compliant, vast or narrow—one may gain great faith and understanding.
Its foundation profoundly penetrates the inconceivable; the following citation from two sutras serves to manifest and establish the preceding two points.

"Pure" corresponds to the subsequent "adverse evil," which is precisely the "good" that accords with the multitudes. This is as detailed in the eighteenth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Its foundation is non-dual, yet it can function dualistically;

therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is used for the "good" that accords [with the multitudes], while the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* cites "adverse evil. Furthermore, Kāśyapa is raised as an example. It is not so.

In the "Chapter on Longevity" (*Dīrghāyuṣka-parivarta*), it is clarified that those who are capable [of receiving the teaching] are all ultimately impermanent and unable to give rise to [the realization of] the Great Nirvāṇa, the eternally abiding Dharma;
nor can they be entrusted with it. Based on this meaning, it is made clear that Kāśyapa, during the two assemblies, likewise manifested as a trace for the sake of sentient beings.
Because he had long since entered the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), he was used as a parallel example to reveal that King Śibi was likewise [a trace].

He also asked: "Since these two [teachings] are equal in their function, why does this [sūtra] not follow the *Lotus Sūtra*? It should logically follow the sequence of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which is pure;

for it responds according to what is perceived and adapts to the timing and suitability of the occasion. Thus, this sūtra properly constitutes the great event of the entire dispensation (the 'Opening and Convergence'), while the subsequent sūtras are for gathering up residual conditions.
Therefore, the former serves to purify, while the latter serves as a gradual guidance—first harmonizing their virtues and subsequently [leading them forward]."

To "shatter their evil" means that each [of the three] has its own intent and each possesses four meanings; although there are many explanations of these in the past, they are not the essential point.

The essential point lies in the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku); therefore, I shall not clarify them here. This is because [others] do not know this essential point, and thus the conclusion of the reprimand says, "One must not be deluded.
In this way, the meaning that the fundamental and the manifested do not give rise to resentment is clarified. As for the fundamental, it is solely the wondrous; as for the manifested...

Because it penetrates both the provisional and the real, the teachings regarding the fundamental and the trace are naturally clarified; this is the intended meaning behind not treating the doctrinal classification separately.

Next, regarding the contemplation, this statement is made in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. Since it perfectly accords with the meaning of contemplation, it is cited here, as explained in the separate commentary (*biechao*).
It is said that these two are "also" [the same] in order to correspond to the parents; or, they are like past karma.

To eliminate these two branches is to subsume all afflictions of the three poisons. When one contemplates according to reality and perceives that these [afflictions] no longer exist, this is what is meant by "harming.
Regarding "contrary" and "conforming": to be contrary to the deluded sentiments of birth and death is to conform to the correct path of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, citing the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* to establish the proof: practicing what is not the Path is "contrary," while realizing the Buddha-path is... [conforming].
"Conformity" refers to that which is not the Way, namely the three paths of affliction, karma, and suffering within the nine realms; "the Buddha-way" refers to the three virtues of the Buddha-realm.

The practice of the three contemplations is the cultivation of these three paths. To proceed from contemplation toward the realization of the virtues is "thorough penetration. This is precisely the contemplation free from resentment and harm.
The preceding section clarifying the miscellaneous texts concerning the assembly consists of four parts; this concludes the third section, the "Exegesis of the Text.

What follows is the fourth section, which analyzes and elucidates the meaning established previously. Within this, first there is a specific discussion of persons, followed by a general examination of the various realms of existence (*gati*).

First, the question: why is it that [the Buddha] should have been many, yet instead fewer are mentioned? Regarding the statement that he was preaching the Dharma among humans: this is precisely where he should have been numerous, rather than few.
Because the human realm is superior to other realms in terms of receiving the path, and because it is proximate to this very place, one should not say "few.
As for the phrase "only one king and his retinue," the answer consists of four points: first, it clarifies that the assembly of people is not few;

second, the text is abbreviated and incomplete, referring to the passage currently cited; third, below, two further passages are cited to show that "few" does not apply; and fourth, the initial point refers to the present text itself.
"This is the introductory text; 'and so forth' (et cetera) refers to the subsequent passage which says:

'Furthermore, the wheel-turning sage-kings from the many billions of lands arrive here,' which is extremely extensive. Next, the preceding sutra is cited: in that sutra, after first listing the four types of wheel-turning kings, it further states:
"Kings, princes, citizens, and royal women, as well as great householders, each with their retinues of hundreds..."
Ten million [verses] have come forth from the Buddha; it is by this that one knows they are exceedingly vast and not few.

As for why the text is abbreviated, it is because one can know its vastness through the preceding sutras and the subsequent passages that follow; since its breadth does not depend on prolixity, it has been abbreviated.
Next, regarding the general analysis below: the text listed here within the three realms (*tridhātu*) and six destinies (*ṣaḍgati*) completely lacks the upper realm and the lower destiny;
there must be a reason for this, as its cause was not previously discerned, and it is clarified here.
First, the question follows the intent of the response, which should also contain four points: first, a general inquiry concerning the three realms and six destinies.

The reasons for the distinctions are as follows: (1) two general inquiries regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within this realm; (2) three specific inquiries concerning the seeing and hearing [of beings] within this realm;
(3) one inquiry regarding the complete absence [of such states] in other realms and lower destinies within this realm, as found in other sūtras;

and (4) two further inquiries regarding the presence or absence [of these states] within the two sets of five, which constitute both the general and the specific. These are the four points concerning "this realm" and its various locations.
Because seeing and hearing cannot be separated from one another, they are mentioned together in what follows; this will be evident in the response itself. Within the response, there are two parts:
first, the preliminary concession and analysis, and second, the formal analysis of this meaning. Since it is essential to distinguish them next, it says "it should be analyzed.
Within the formal analysis, there are three initial points. Regarding the first, the causal conditions, there are two parts: first, the response to the preceding general and specific [questions].

The final summary consists of an exhortation based on the initial response, which contains two distinct parts: first, the clarification of the two causes; second, the explanation of its essential nature and characteristics.
Within the first part, there are again two sub-sections: first, a general overview; second, a detailed analysis. The general overview is as follows: if one upholds [the precepts], one ascends;
if one violates them, one sinks. If one is diligent, they are seen; if one is lax, they are not seen. Following this general overview, the detailed analysis concerns the manner of upholding them.

There are coarse and subtle [distinctions]; since the brief enumeration includes both, there are the three higher realms (*gati*). As it is with upholding [the precepts], so it is with violating them; thus, there are the three lower realms.
Speaking broadly, the first three [realms] generally provide a brief enumeration of names, wherein the small and the great are contained within them.
Only the Perfect [Vehicle] is called "Great," because it is the reality (*tattva*); this is briefly explained here, as will be seen below in due course. Next, the two [aspects] are clarified.
Although one may know their names based on their essential characteristics (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), because their actual nature has not yet been identified, they must be distinguished.

Within this, there are three parts: first, the establishment of the three categories of phrases; second, [the discussion] regarding their essence, starting with "If [one practices] the precepts and the vehicle" (*śīla-yāna*); and third, the explanation of their characteristics. Regarding the first part, there is both a heading and a listing;
each initially consists of three categories, which are easy to understand in sequence. As for the single phrase, it refers to the "Four Reliances" (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).
The text states in this chapter: "To be lax regarding the precepts is not called laxity; rather, to be lax regarding the Vehicle is what is called laxity.

This is expanded into four points because a single phrase from the sutra possesses four meanings. It is not treated as four separate sentences, for that would fail to exhaust the full purport of the meaning. Why is this?

The fundamental intent of the sutra lies precisely in the principle of being "lax regarding the precepts but urgent regarding the Vehicle. If one were merely urgent [in practice], that would indeed be the Dharma.

If you abide by the four reliances (*catuḥpratisaraṇa*), you should primarily emphasize the urgency [of practice]. If one’s observance of the precepts is urgent, it does not accord with the true intent of the sūtras; this is unavoidable.

As for the fourth phrase, its principle follows the natural course of things and does not depend on human intention. Thus we know that the sūtra text already contains the meaning of two phrases, which applies to all four intentions;
yet the primary point lies in one. Now, I have comprehensively exhausted the principles, and I shall now correctly employ the comprehensive meaning.
Next, four phrases are listed, which take the "Vehicle" (yāna) and "Precepts" (śīla) respectively and, through their mutual inclusion, form four [categories].
This constitutes four interpretations based on the three [aspects]. Next, below, their essence is revealed: first generally, then specifically.

Generally speaking, the Vehicle is also called the Precepts, and the Precepts are also called the Vehicle, because both serve to cease evil and bring about transcendence. Furthermore, by citing scriptural evidence, it can be known that they are shared.

The term "and so forth" refers to the latter four precepts. Next, regarding the specific [classification], there are two parts: first, the presentation of their essential nature (*svabhāva*); second, the reason for this.
In the first part, these six enumerated precepts are grouped into three categories. The first four constitute the lay precepts;

because their dharmas are not yet complete and their karmic fruit is still inferior, they are classified as the lower. Although the next one (the fifth) encompasses the former, it does not yet reach the level of the latter (the sixth). The dharma... [text ends].
Because it abides between the [causes] and the retribution, it is called the "middle. As for the "one that follows," it can encompass the preceding three;
thus, it is said "up to" (乃至), because the dharma and the retribution are supreme and ultimate, which is precisely the meaning of the "superior grade" (上品).

This is merely a discussion based on the dharma and has not yet addressed the practice of upholding [the precepts]; therefore, it says "the three grades of upholding" (持品三戒) without yet discussing the three grades of upholding.
If one discusses the precepts (*śīla*) solely in terms of their observance, they do not accord with the meaning of the vehicles (*yāna*); this should be carefully considered.

That all such [factors] are collectively termed "precepts" because they can prevent what follows below is the explanation thereof; this is the specific discussion on the meaning of the dharma of the precepts.

Next, the specific discussion of the essence and meaning of the vehicles follows, citing scriptural evidence to clarify the two essences of the three and four [vehicles], as well as the truths, conditions, and perfections (*pāramitā*).

The essence of the Three Vehicles is still limited by this meaning; therefore, it is further elucidated through the four kinds of wisdom—such as that of arising and ceasing—to fully reveal its essence.
The reason these are all termed "vehicles" (yāna) is explained by their capacity to shatter [samsara]:

because they can destroy the causes of suffering and enable one to transcend the fruits of suffering, the essence of these causes and fruits must be understood in terms of both the pervasive and the specific, including the immeasurable and the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra).
This must be discussed in terms of that which lies outside the realms (*dhātu*). Below, citations are introduced to distinguish the general from the specific, thereby clarifying the particular;

this refers to the two natures, general and specific, and the present intent follows the specific. Having identified these two interpretations, what follows explains the characteristics of the "two" and "three" in relation to the four consciousnesses.
Within those, there are four distinct explanations for the four lines; first, regarding the line on "both being urgent," there are three [points].
Regarding the categories of afflictions and the three vehicles, each category of precepts possesses the three vehicles, thus constituting nine meanings.
Within the second phrase, "the precepts are lax while the vehicle is urgent," there should likewise be nine [meanings], though they are briefly summarized as three.
The third and fourth phrases each contain only one meaning. Among the initial nine, the first one fully presents all three [aspects], whereas the other two each present [only] two.
As for the first [of the four], the remaining three follow the same pattern as previously discussed and are easily understood from the text.

Within the initial section concerning those who are "swift in the vehicle" (*yāna-śīghra*), the term "Shared Teaching" (*pītaka-sāmānya*) refers to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya/ Fangdeng) teachings, as they universally accommodate the four types of capacities. Regarding the phrase "retaining the provisional means" (*sopāya*), this refers to the Prajñāpāramitā teachings, which retain the two types of provisional means.
Following the logic of the second sentence, there should likewise be nine categories; however, the text here is abbreviated, treating the general precepts as one and the specific ones separately.
Regarding the three explanations of "vehicles" (*yāna*): the first two are easily understood from the text.

As for the third phrase, since there is not even a single person among those with the retribution of the precepts who belongs to the Three Vehicles, it consists of only one sentence. This precept is said to be the cause for wandering through future lives.

Regarding the "three hundred million," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī for twenty-five years, there were nine hundred million households in Śrāvastī; three hundred million saw [the Buddha]."
Three hundred million hear it but do not see it; three hundred million do not even see it, because they lack the seed of the vehicle (*yāna*).
The Sūtra says: "To be lax regarding the vehicle is what is called laxity. This refers precisely to this point—how could one not practice?

Regarding the fourth phrase, before the period has expired, the preceding phrase refers to the present, while this phrase refers to both the present and the future. How could one not exert oneself? This concludes the preceding section.

The general explanation concludes the answers to the two preceding general questions. What follows below is the second part: the specific answer explaining why this sutra is non-dual while other sutras are dual;
this simultaneously answers the two specific reasons. Consider the following: first, it answers the reason for the presence or absence of a single destination (*ekāyana*);
next, it answers the reason for the presence or absence of the realms (*dhātu*). Within each of these, its respective basis is set forth.

Therefore, in the *Wen* (Text), it is easy to know that the initial [portion] refers to the Vaipulya (*fangdeng*) sutras, while the subsequent [portions] refer to the *zhongyin* (intermediate state) sutras;
as for other remaining [portions], they are explained as before. "If one attains [this]" and below constitutes the second section, which is a summary exhortation.

It clarifies that there are three functions to encourage later students to apply diligent attention. That is to say, if one deeply understands the meaning of what has been explained above and employs it...
By investigating all sentient beings, one attains thorough penetration into their causal origins; whether those origins are lax or urgent, they all pertain to the two types of karmic fruition.
The distinctions in these original causes arise from the laxity or urgency of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the distinctions in hearing the Dharma, and the distinctions in the vehicles (*yāna*).
Because of this, all can be understood and exhorted. Not only is this recognized here, but other sutras also know it; the following passage points to the extensive explanation of that in other texts.

The miscellaneous explanations from the *Shizong lü* are analyzed and expanded into seven sections: (1) differences regarding the One Vehicle and the precepts; (2) faith in the Dharma versus faith in practice;
(3) the Great and Small Vehicles; (4) the gradual and sudden capacities; (5) responsive traces; (6) contemplating the mind; and (7) transforming others.

Although that text is lengthy and its meaning extensive, the present text, while brief, is extremely concise and essential. One should simply study this text thoroughly to grasp its core significance.

It may be sufficient to consider that these [teachings] assist in its accomplishment; furthermore, from the stage of consciousness (*vijñāna*) onwards, their efficacy also consists precisely in being able to know the provisional and the real, as well as the fundamental and the trace.
Since the preceding explanation of causes and conditions—whether general or specific—has already established the meaning according to the four teachings, it will not be discussed further here.

Instead, we shall proceed by analogy to clarify the fundamental and the trace. There are two kinds of reality: the slow and the urgent; the provisional follows accordingly. One need only grasp the essential meaning of the real.
Thus, as the provisional traces naturally manifest, it is said that they "turn to become clear. Third, the conclusion of the contemplation concerns the practice of one's own cultivation.
Within this practice, there are two types—observing others and observing oneself—concerning both cause and effect: namely, the mundane and the supramundane.

If one knows the superiority or inferiority of mundane retributions, it is due to the laxity or urgency of past precepts; if one knows the presence or absence of differences in supramundane causes and effects, it is known through [the observation of] the past.
Observing that there are differences in habitual tendencies, one verifies past causes through present effects and future effects through present causes;

thus, there is nothing that is not known. Therefore, it is said that the causes and effects of the three periods of time are thoroughly understood. This general outline is as such. One should reflect upon this in detail and repeatedly contemplate it.
Furthermore, regarding the concluding summary of the commentary (*śāstra*), it may be omitted from the preceding section, or it may be included within the enumeration of the three.

The preceding section on the various assemblies is broadly divided into two parts: first, the listing of the three assemblies; second, the general conclusion. This present passage constitutes the second part.

Alternatively, at the beginning of the second section concerning the miscellaneous assemblies, it may be broadly divided into two: first, the listing of the eight assemblies; second, the general conclusion.

The current text corresponds to the second part. Both of these divisions are acceptable; there is no fixed preference. As for the phrase "the assembly has gathered," this refers to the audience listening at that specific time.

The assembly gathered in this manner because they paid their utmost respect to the Buddha’s supreme virtue; thus, they prostrated at his feet. They withdrew to sit because it was the protocol for receiving the sublime Dharma.
They are said to be "on one side" because each sat according to the direction from which they had come, and again because they gazed with single-minded devotion upon the Honored One’s countenance.
This, too, is the ritual procedure for the compilation [of the scriptures]; it should be understood as summarizing the gathering of the assembly.
The Ritual Manual. Although the preceding introduction clarifies five points, its ultimate intent lies in explaining that the Way originates from Virtue, which is the Mother;
since the foundation is established and the Way arises therefrom, one must not fail to apply oneself to this contemplation. Thus ends the General Introduction.
Private Notes on the Words and Phrases of the Wondrous Sutra, Scroll Seven;
Private Notes on the Words and Phrases of the Wondrous Sutra, Scroll Eight.
Compiled by the Stone Drum Śramaṇa, Śākyamuni Zhìyún.
The general preface concludes; here follows the commentary on the specific preface. This section consists of two broad parts:

first, a reiteration of the topical headings, which is divided into five sub-sections; second, the formal analysis and explanation of the text itself. Regarding the term "specific preface" (*bie xu*):

although it has already been explained in the preceding text, various predecessors have further elaborated upon it. Nevertheless, despite such extensive discussion, the essential core remains difficult to grasp. Therefore—

Knowing that further elaboration would be merely vexing and of no benefit, I shall not describe it further now; I will simply append it to the meaning of the preceding and following context to briefly express its intent.
This is divided into three parts: first, a general clarification of the five meanings; second, an explanation of their underlying reasons; and third, a conclusion to manifest the present subject.

Regarding the first part, what is called "distinct" (or "specific") is a term used in contrast to "general"; that is, while the general introduction universally establishes the proof of faith for all teachings, the distinct introduction pertains to specific [teachings].

This is because the general introduction (sūtra-prologue) initiates the entire section [of the sutra] as a whole, whereas the specific introduction (nidāna) initiates the particular meaning within that section.
Furthermore, while the name of the general introduction is universal yet its substance is particular, the matter of the specific introduction is particular yet its meaning is universal;

it is spoken thus from one perspective. Moreover, since the general introduction and the certification [of the teaching] apply universally to the entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the specific introduction [is distinguished].
Because there are four excellences within the "Distinct Introduction" (bīe fāqǐ bù), it is distinguished from the [General] Introduction and thus termed the "Distinct Introduction.

Furthermore, the General Introduction encompasses both the "Gate of Testimony and Faith" (zhèngxìn mén) and the "Gate of Distinct Arising" (fāqǐ mén). The Distinct Introduction specifically concerns the Gate of Traces (jìmén), as the Gate of the Origin (běnmén) lacks the "Gate of Testimony and Faith" and possesses a distinct "Gate of Arising.
Therefore, the first three [sections] explain this generally in relation to all sutras, while the latter two sections explain it specifically in relation to this sutra alone.
The reason it is so is that the force of the meaning requires it; it is intended to distinguish the general from the particular.

Thus, there are two distinct sections of meaning precisely because, according to the previous classification, this sutra contains three types: the single, the double, and the triple. The first repetition is the single-distinct, and the second repetition is the double-distinct.
Although the meaning of "distinct" (*bīe*) mentioned here encompasses five aspects, since we follow what is essential, it consists of two parts and three sections.

The explanation of the text properly accords with the latter two meanings; however, when the fourth pair arises, all three preceding treasures are entirely subsumed within it, no longer possessing separate entities.
Thus, there is nothing that is not a wondrous object. It is based on this meaning that it is called "distinct" (*bie*).
If it were not explained in this way, it would not correspond with the text of the preceding two sections; therefore, [this is the correct interpretation].
Because it is able to reveal this essential and subtle meaning, those previous ordinary explanations are insufficient to manifest the Buddha’s intent;

therefore, this is the core significance of this sutra. Although various ancient and modern commentators have failed to discuss this single school [of thought], and though some may clarify it, their explanations remain unrefined and obscure.
Thus, although I now understand it briefly, I am still unable to fully elucidate it; for now, I shall provide a concise summary.
This constitutes a ground for reflection; those of later generations should examine it thoroughly and exhaustively. Jiaxiang says:

"From here below is the second [section], clarifying the Introduction (nidāna), which also consists of six chapters: namely, the assembly of the multitude, the preaching of the sutra, entering meditative concentration, manifesting auspicious omens, raising questions, and answering questions—these are the six.
Together with the preceding six chapters on the 'Certification of Faith' (samyak-pratyaya), there are twelve introductory sections. Because the multitude has assembled, the sutra is preached."

Because the sutra is preached, one enters meditative concentration; because of entering concentration, auspicious omens appear; because the omens are not understood, a question arises; because of the question, there is an answer.

Through these six matters, the main body of the teaching is developed; therefore, it is called the "Development Introduction" (*kai-fa xu*). Now, I say that in discussing these three meanings, [this approach] surpasses that of Guangzhai;
however, regarding the opening and closing, or the concealment and manifestation [of the teachings], it is far from being appropriate. This shall be examined in detail.
I have not yet had the leisure to analyze this (and so forth).

Next, regarding the formal exegesis of the main body of the text, there are three sections: first, the analysis of the textual structure; second, the general explanation of the meaning; and third, the specific explanation.

The analysis of the textual structure has two parts: first, stating the number of items; second, listing their names. As for the "five," these refer to the five matters found in the preceding General Preface.
This preface also contains five matters, which can be understood by listing their names.

Next follows a general explanation of the intent behind these five; within this, there is first a preliminary exposition and then the formal explanation. Regarding the initial exposition, there are two distinct parts:
first, the presentation of the two [points], and second, the description of the characteristics of those two. First, the presentation: [The text continues with the specific points.]

Regarding the arising in direct and reverse order: "arising" (*utpāda*) refers to that which produces, while "origination" (*samutpāda*) refers to that which is produced; these constitute the causal conditions and the sequential order. Because the former gives rise to the latter, it is the direct order;
because the latter precedes the former, it is the reverse order. In the initial presentation of the sequence, the first is the direct order and the second is the reverse order.
Although these two aspects are not two distinct entities in terms of their textual meaning, if one considers the subsequent arising from the preceding, [the reverse order is established].

The preceding section may be understood as containing a distinct line of thought; what follows below is a differentiation of that which remains uncomprehended, resulting only in divergent interpretations.

This passage comprises three points: first, a judgment regarding what is granted and what is rejected; second, a general and total rejection; and third, the actual explanation. First, regarding the provisional granting:

"reversal" refers to the inverse order of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), while "concealment" refers to the direct order of dependent origination. Furthermore, this is illustrated by analogy, such as a hook or a chain. Next, its lack of comprehension is clarified.
This commentary clearly explains that this passage must possess two meanings: first, the specific context (*prāsaṅgika*), and second, the indicative and retributive (*naimittika-vipākaja*).

The latter is the primary intent, as it initiates the formal exposition. If one were to merely describe the causes and conditions of the specific context without clarifying where the primary intent of the indicative and retributive lies, it would be called a separate introductory sequence; therefore, for those who have not yet understood, this is done directly.

The following uses the correct intent of the sutra to completely refute [the opponent's view]; however, since even their own specific causal origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) has not yet been fully understood, it is therefore a complete refutation (and so forth).

Why is this? Because these five [factors] of the first [set] must first clarify the five causes for the second and fourth [sets], and subsequently, by binding them together, clarify the meaning of the manifest action (*vijñapti*) and its retribution; whereas now, although there is the cause for its arising...
The intention regarding the non-informative (*avijñapti*) within the four conditions has not yet been understood even for one of them, let alone the other three;

since its meaning is not stated at all, this error results. This merely discusses the meaning of one among the four conditions, and thus it is not established, let alone being able to encompass all four.
Therefore, the character "condition" (*pratyaya*) is added below the "three" and "four. If the "two," "three," and "four" are taken as the remainder, [the same applies].
Regarding the three interpretations, the lowest one—which relies on the character "yuan" (緣)—is difficult to reconcile;

such an interpretation lacks any distinct meaning for the "Introductory Section on Origination" (*nidāna*) and thus concludes that there is no direction toward it at all, making it entirely untenable. One should know that the phrase "these five" contains three meanings:
first, the five [aspects] of the Introductory Section on Origination; second, the five as being distinct [from the other four]; and third, because origination is the functional capacity (*śakti*).

Therefore, the introduction (*nidāna*) is established in contrast to the formal discourse (*samyag-deśanā*); it is established in contrast to the general [teaching] to reveal the specific; and the fifth [the "Thus have I heard"] is established in contrast to the proof of faith (*śraddhā-prasāda*).

It is called the "Introduction" because it stands in contrast to the formal discourse. Although that [introductory formula] arises in both reverse and direct order, it lacks even one of these three [characteristics];
therefore, it cannot be considered so now. One should reflect that a single word alone already encompasses these three.

The following is the formal explanation, which fully relies upon the four conditions (*pratyaya*). Within the first condition, the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*), these four [aspects] are simply different names for the four *siddhi* (purposes);
because they do not accord with the views of the Guangzhai school, I speak here directly from the primary meaning. What is called "one" (*eka*) means "same.
It initiates the correct teaching and brings together the four differences, causing them all to return to the same; therefore, it is called "one. It is also called "reality" (*bhūta*).

It is also called "wondrous. However, when speaking of only four, this is based on a general discussion according to the sutras; there are three in the abbreviated version, ten in the intermediate version, and all [dharmas] in the complete version.
Yet, as the sutra text frequently speaks of four, it follows the essential abbreviation. Now, following the essentials of the text, it is stated thus.
Within each of the four, there are both the subjective (agent) and the objective (object); the first three characters are the agent, while the latter... [is the object].

Within these two characters, both the essence and the function are present; "narrate" (*xu*) is the function that serves as the capacity to act, while "multitude" (*zhong*) refers to the various individuals who have gathered.
Because they are diverse, they are brought to the state of being one person. The auspicious omen manifests the single principle. To summarize:
the manifestation of the omen precisely symbolizes the opening of the provisional and the revealing of the real. The real is the revelation of the principle of original existence; therefore—

The Sūtra’s purpose of causing [beings] to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) and so forth refers to the unity of principle; doubt and hesitation refer to the diversity of practice.

Because one attains unity through these, the questions and answers manifest that which is to be expounded as the wondrous; because one thereby obtains the wondrous teaching, it is described as the unity of the teaching.

Generally speaking, "narration" (*xu*) carries the meaning of the origination of causes and conditions. "Person" refers to the world, for the person is the fruit of retribution within the mundane world.
The *Mahāśāstra-saṃnipāta-nāma* states that because the world exists, there are persons; this is precisely its meaning. Principle (*li*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which is easy to know;
practice (*xing*) is for the sake of humans, intended to lead them toward the cultivation of goodness.

If one follows other texts, practice is most often presented as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*), as each is applied according to the convenience of the specific context. Thus, the teaching itself is the remedy, for it is precisely through this that doubt is eliminated.

This indicates that the four [aspects] should become one fourfold unity. As for what is called "these causes and conditions," it means they are fashioned in response to the four types of sublime capacities, so as to enable them to obtain the four kinds of sublime benefits.

This is discussed from a general perspective, wherein each [aspect] possesses all four meanings, just as in the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning), each item is fully endowed with the four. One should know that five is precisely four.

The "four" refers to the causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), while the "one" refers to that which is produced by them. Since this expresses the "one," both the agent (the cause) and the object (the effect) are wondrous.
Furthermore, to explain this in terms of the teachings (*śāsana*), it is done to distinguish and clarify [the truth] in contrast to what is different.

Moreover, because it is explained in terms of mutual dependence (*apekṣā*), it is said to be "not the Perfect" (*na pūrṇa*); in reality, it is precisely the fourfold one. Regarding the distinction between the original and the trace (*honji-suijaku*): if we consider the time [of the Buddha's appearance],...
This refers to the implicit meaning (samdhāya-bhāṣita) when speaking of "extinction after [the Buddha's passing]," which is based on the explicit teaching because the characteristics are identical;

that is, because the fundamental (hon) is identical with the derivative (jaku), and the derivative is identical with the fundamental. As stated in the preceding topical outline, although one speaks of "following the proximate" to interpret the text, all [explanations] possess fourfold interpretations;
while the literal text is specific, the meaning is universal. Here, we follow the universal sense of the meaning, as it is the essential point regarding the three periods of time.

This is because there are no more than four "ones. Next, regarding the practitioner, the *Ji* (Commentary) states: "The single mind and the three truths are the oneness of principle; the single mind and the three contemplations are the oneness of practice;
the person who performs this contemplation is the oneness of the person; and the teaching that can express the object of contemplation is the oneness of the teaching.

There are many other interpretations which I cannot describe in detail here. I maintain, however, that it may simply be understood as being able to cultivate the one perfect and wondrous contemplative practice.
This constitutes the fourfold unity. What are these four? First, the realization that all mental phenomena are the single true reality (*ekasatyalakṣaṇa*):

although the objects thus realized differ, they are not different [in their nature], which is the unity of principle (*li-yi*). Second, the non-differentiation of the mind capable of such realization, which is the unity of practice (*xing-yi*).

Third, the person who is capable of such realization, which is the unity of person (*ren-yi*). Fourth, the ability to perform this contemplation, which correctly accords with the purport of the Initial Teaching (*shijiao*), which is the unity of teaching (*jiao-yi*).
Furthermore, because one can realize that the minds regarding all karmic retributions are identical to the true reality (dharmatā), this is the oneness of principle;
because one can penetrate that the minds regarding all conditioned activities are identical to the single true reality, this is the oneness of practice;

and because one understands that the mind which clings to a sovereign controller is identical to the mind of all sounds and speech, which is the single wondrous speech—this constitutes a single section.

That is to say, "The person" is the essential point for thoroughly understanding the mind; "Teaching" is the essential point for universally penetrating this and the preceding three [sections]; "The former" is the essential point for initiating the correct exposition;
and "This" is the essential point for giving rise to the realization of the wondrous Way—one should reflect well upon these, as they have not yet been fully detailed.
The section beginning with "Regarding the assembly" (*jù zhòng*) is the third part, which provides a specific explanation of the five introductory passages.

Since both passages speak of the gathering of the assembly (*zhòngjí*), and both likewise possess their respective protocols (*wēiyí*), how are they to be distinguished? Some say that in contrast to the former, one should speak of "gathering the assembly"; however, I maintain this is not the case.

The former was for the purpose of extinguishing [doubts] and briefly explaining the certification of faith (*zhèngxìn*); the present [passage], being the main treatise, initiates a detailed explanation of what is currently occurring. Furthermore...
Reflect on this: whereas previously it was stated that this sutra could be specifically bound [to a single meaning], here it is universally applicable to immeasurable meanings.
If one follows the *Anantārthasūtra*, at the end of the listing of the assembly, the sutra says:
