Regarding the phrase "There is an analogy; although there is none below," this explains how this assembly is unable to know [the Buddha].
Because it is not known who these members of the assembly are, two categories are raised to reveal them: namely, those of the two types—perfect cause and perfect fruit.

Next, the text correctly clarifies that the various Buddhas of influence and response conceal their fundamental fruit and manifest the forms of various causal traces; thus, they hide their ultimate state.

When a Bodhisattva conceals their perfect and sudden [teaching] to manifest the partial and gradual, this is to hide the essence (the form and voice) while manifesting the trace (the shadow and echo).
This is precisely to conceal the ultimate perfection and fundamental source while manifesting the partial causes as traces.

Alternatively, the ultimate perfection may be explained universally without necessarily assigning it specifically to two individuals; reflect on this, reflect on this! Thus one assists the Dharma King and correctly clarifies the manifestation and concealment [of the teachings].
The reason why the mind conceals or manifests itself is precisely for this purpose: it conceals its own form and sound to manifest the transformative influence of the true forms and sounds of others.
This is the meaning of being mutually principal and attendant. "Kuang" (匡) means to rectify; "zhuang" (助) means to assist.
As the Confucians say, "to follow along with what is beautiful and to rectify and rescue what is evil," this refers to employing the Way of uprightness and integrity.

To assist the primary teaching in its transformation of the world, this [text] now manifests in various provisional stations, employing the path of equality and rectitude to aid the Buddha-Dharma Lord’s transformation within the Dharma-realm. This follows the principle of correctness and meaning, while also concurrently assisting the other three [teachings].
The analogy of the many stars illustrates how the hidden, perfect essence manifests various essential traces as it revolves.

The "sun" is a metaphor for the support and guidance [of the state], while the "moon" is a metaphor for the Dharma King. Although there is no deliberate activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*), this distinguishes it from form and sound;
this is the function of the transformative master. Yet, there is great benefit, which precisely clarifies the efficacy of the shadow and echo.

Alternatively, although there is no deliberate activity—distinguishing it from the initiation of thought—the term "thought" refers to the "great benefit," meaning that it can cause the wondrous... [to arise].

Thus, the assembly gathered through the opportune connection will attain accomplishment. Therefore, Confucius said, "If I have Yan Hui, my disciples will become even more intimate," considering him a friend who was willing to attach himself to him;
if this was so even in that case, how much more so in this one? Hence, the Treatise says:
"When the transformative teaching is about to proceed, it must await its companions"—this is the first point.

Regarding the term "forming a karmic bond" (*kemyō*), the commentary states: "Bond" (*ketsu*) refers to the beginning of establishing the capacity of the practitioner; "condition" (*en*) refers to the final stage of enabling completion through supportive conditions.
Thus, it is the first sprout for attaining the three virtues (*santoku*) in the future. Now, I explain: "bonding" (*ketsu*) means to tie or fasten, and it also implies attachment.
Therefore, the subsequent passage says: "To fasten a priceless jewel within one's inner garment. This is the condition (*en*).
This refers to the name "condition" (*pratyaya*) given to the cause in relation to the subsequent accomplishment of the fruit.

Specifically, the initial hearing of the sublime Dharma and the resulting faith and understanding—which belong to the essence of the sūtra—are termed "binding knots. Because these knots serve as the conditions for attaining liberation through a single further hearing at a later time, they are called "karmic conditions" (*pratyaya*).
These knots are also "seeds," as they function as the causal conditions for maturation and liberation.
It is said that "karmic affinity" (*kyōen*) refers to this class of many people, hence it is called "the multitude" (*shū*).

"The one who is ready" (*tōki*) refers to those currently manifesting [liberation], whereas "karmic affinity" refers to those who plant the seeds for what is to come. This is fully as explained in the preceding text. Within this, first the meaning of the absence of the three aforementioned types of assemblies is clarified;
subsequently, it is clarified that by lacking the three aforementioned types, one merely achieves karmic affinity. Regarding the first point concerning "power," it should possess three aspects.
Power (*bala*), wisdom (*jñāna*), and the power of spiritual faculties (*abhijñā*) and voice—these constitute the power of the three secrets (*triguhyabala*).
While the preceding passage fully encompasses these three, the current text mentions only two of them by combining them as form and voice. The subsequent passage refers to the body;

since these two must necessarily possess all three, and the preceding passage refers to the discernment of wisdom (*jñāna-vicaya*), this function relies upon the essence (*tattva*). How could one employ such a function without having attained that essence? Therefore, it is said that they do not [possess them].

"Leading [the assembly] to the Buddha’s presence, striking [the ground] to manifest auspicious omens," and so forth—these are the three. Regarding "virtue is not [the case]": previously, this was discussed strictly in terms of function, hence it was called "power" (*bala*);

here, it is discussed in terms of essence, hence it is called "virtue" (*guṇa*). "Virtue" (*guṇa*) means "attainment. Since one attains the function of the Path, how could such a capacity exist before the Path has been attained?
Therefore, it is said to be "not [the case]. As for the phrase "subduing things" and so forth, there should be three meanings within this context: first...
It cannot subdue things (1); it cannot suppress phenomena (2); and it cannot adorn [them] (3). Because all evils are eternally exhausted, it can subdue;
because all virtues universally assemble, it can manifest the Way; because its essence is pervasive, it can suppress. Evil being exhausted is the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*);

virtues assembling is the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*); and the essence being pervasive is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*). Since these constitute the three virtues, they are called "virtues. This refers to what was mentioned previously.
The "hidden" refers to the ultimate perfection (*pariniṣpanna*). Now, people of this class entirely lack the status of abiding in the three paths;

how then could they possess the function of these three virtues? Therefore, it is said that they are not [qualified]. Furthermore, they can cause others to feel awe or love with single-minded devotion and without distinction.

Yet, since these people themselves have not yet attained these three qualities, how could they cause others to do so? Therefore, it is said that they are not [qualified]. There was a former master who lectured on this...

This work was originally composed for the purpose of serving as a talisman against the *rāga* (passion/demons); it is thus said to be like the two fruits of *jambu* and *kovidāra* mentioned in the Mahāyāna sūtras—eternal life and the complete extinction of evil.
It is claimed that this alone captures the essential core, and while it is not merely a direct oral teaching, it has nonetheless been transmitted through the brush and ink.
Who among later students would say this is not so? Now, I must say it is certainly not so, as briefly indicated above.
The explanation proceeds by first distinguishing those who lack the capacity for the teaching; this sequence follows the convenience of the commentary’s logic.

First, it clarifies that because their past habitual causes were inferior, they did not become vessels for the three types of wisdom. Next, it clarifies that because they lacked the three [types of wisdom] in the past, they currently lack the four benefits.

Regarding those said to have "shallow faculties," this means they lack deep faith and understanding in the perfect and wondrous Way; this serves as a contrast to reveal those who have planted profound roots in the past. It further addresses the issue of concealment and leakage.

The following section correctly clarifies that there is no capacity for the three types of wisdom; this stands in contrast to the previous point regarding the "ripening" when conditions coincide, which constitutes having such capacity.
One lacks the capacity for *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing) because they are incapable of receiving the correct teaching, like an overturned vessel.

One lacks the capacity for *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from reflection) because they cannot engage in careful deliberation, being like a leaking vessel; thus it is said they are "leaking. As the subsequent text states: "Yet in searching, he forgot the Confucian classics."
It is said that if one does not contemplate, there is no wisdom; without the faculty for cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), one cannot eliminate faults.

This is like a vessel that is defiled, impure, and filled with evil things; therefore it is called "defiled and mixed. Because the three faculties are absent, the three types of wisdom do not arise. Wisdom is understanding;

hearing without understanding is merely "hearing" and not "wisdom," and the same applies to reflection and cultivation. Since the three wisdoms do not arise, it is clear there is no benefit corresponding to the capacity of the practitioner.

Although one may obtain seeing and hearing, because there is no understanding, it is not called the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Since the wisdom of hearing is absent, how can there be the [other] three wisdoms?
Because they are absent, the four benefits do not exist. If one were to speak only of the "three," it would not fully encompass the benefits appropriate for those in the stage of the five ranks;

therefore, the word "four" is added so that their meaning is complete. The *Commentary* states: "The 'universal' refers to the six sense organs, while the 'distinct' refers to the arising and departing [of the five ranks]."

Following this principle, these stages are all designated as "appropriate to the capacity" (*yathābhavyatā*) because they correspond to the four *siddhāntas*. From the stage of the five ranks (*pañca-varga*) onward, there is the benefit for the world (*loka-siddhānta*).

From the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) onward, there is the benefit of treatment (*pratipakṣa-siddhānta*). From the first dwelling (*prathamā bhūmi*) onward, there is the benefit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-siddhānta*).

That which is without hearing, reflection, or cultivation is called "sequential"; it lacks the benefit of the three *siddhāntas* because there is no cultivation, and it lacks the benefit of the ultimate truth because [the conditions for it] are absent.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) also has both general and specific meanings: it is general in relation to the five stages and specific in being located in the first dwelling (*prathamā bhūmi*).

Thus, the term "attaining deliverance" likewise has both general and specific meanings, which correspond to the general and specific aspects of the ultimate truth. Now, observing this intent, if taken specifically, the three [conventional] satisfactions (*siddhi*) pertain to ordinary beings while the one ultimate meaning pertains to the sage;
if taken generally, all four meanings apply universally to both ordinary beings and sages. The present text contains these two meanings.
Now, it is said that generally speaking, from the stage of "names" (*nāman*) onward, all belong to those who are "responsive to the occasion" (*tatkālārthin*);

specifically, from the stage of "right determination" (*samyaktvaniyāma*) onward are called "responsive to the occasion," while those in the indeterminate stage are termed "establishing a connection" (*pratyaya-bandha*). Therefore, following the general explanation, the benefits of the three types of wisdom (*trividya*) and the four means of integration (*catuḥsaṃgrahavastu*) are collectively designated as "responsive to the occasion," with the intention that they lead to the attainment of faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*). This is what is explained below regarding the mind harboring regret and remorse.

It is said that one repents of past immovability and enters the stage of the ordinary person within (the stages of sanctity); this "ordinary person within" is precisely the stage of the fixed group of those destined for enlightenment (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Furthermore, the meaning in the *Guānxīn wén* (Text on Contemplating the Mind) is exactly like this. Thus, "name" corresponds to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), "contemplative practice" corresponds to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), and "resemblance" corresponds to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
If one were to say that "name" is not the wisdom of hearing, how could it be called "correspondence"? If hearing can bring about understanding, [then name is indeed the wisdom of hearing].
If all these are identical, for what reason do they brush aside their mats and withdraw? This clearly illustrates the meaning of right and wrong.

However, the phrase "merely performing [the acts]" precisely clarifies the meaning of establishing karmic conditions (*karmapratyaya*). Because what was practiced in the past does not constitute the three causes, and there are no four benefits in the present, one merely creates the future conditions for the third and fourth causes; therefore, this category as a whole is designated by the term "establishing conditions" based on this principle.
This concerns the conditions for the assembly.

Next, the following section concludes the analogy by explaining one instance to illustrate the remaining three, and demonstrates their total number. Previously, it was stated that based on the single [category], it is further divided into four;

thus, all four [categories] consist of four [subdivisions each]. Having already explained the first set of four, this section now concludes the analogy to demonstrate the remainder; hence, it says "the rest."
The same applies to the third [vehicle], and the other three as well. If one were now to cite the scriptural evidence for each case, the details would be too numerous;
it suffices to know that all possess both the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku), as well as the provisional (gon) and the real (jitsu).
Now, regarding why these four are mentioned while the other two are not: some say that by mentioning these four, the other two are already subsumed within them. If that is so, then what?
Therefore, what was previously stated as "the name is restricted" refers here to the Śrāvakas; since this is the case for them, it applies by analogy to the other two [vehicles].
This meaning is self-evident and does not require further elaboration, which is why it was not explicitly mentioned. If one wishes to know specifically, it may be illustrated by this example:

if one briefly discusses the two assemblies with four each, that makes eight; adding the previous sixteen, that makes twenty-four. If one considers the eight rounds of the mixed assembly with four each, then...

The thirty-two and the twenty-four together constitute fifty-six groups. If one further adds the four wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*), along with various kings, state ministers, and elders—these being another six groups—and each of these also has four [subdivisions], resulting in twenty-four groups;
when added to the previous fifty-six, they total eighty groups. This is merely a rough approximation; were one to discuss this in detail, the number would be beyond reckoning.
If one grasps this meaning, then the various fourfold names found in all the sutras will never exceed these four categories.
Since this is such an essential and subtle point, what person of wisdom could claim it is otherwise? To say it is otherwise is surely the mark of one lacking wisdom.

The following section cites past analogies to illustrate the present; it consists of two parts: first, it clarifies that there was one "fourfold category" at that time to manifest the single "fourfold category" of the present;

second, it clarifies that the meaning of those [past] events also comprised four sets of four, which serve as analogies to manifest that the Buddha-way of the present is identical, and thus there are likewise four sets of four.
As for why the term "echo and shadow" (yǐngxiǎng) is not used: since the other three [analogies] are already present, this one must necessarily exist.
By means of this "shadow" [of the text], one knows that the wording is not redundant. Initially, it should have said "requesting the exposition," yet all versions say "re-explaining" (*fùjiǎng*);
regarding this, some masters of antiquity claim it is a textual error. However, I maintain that this is likewise a case of mutual clarification through elliptical abbreviation.

This has two meanings: namely, the Teacher who transforms and the receptive conditions (*pratipattṛ-pratyaya*). If one says "requesting the exposition," it refers to the initiation by the Teacher; if one says "re-explaining," it is... [the response of the recipient].

Regarding the "Sutra on the Occasions for Arousing [the Resolve]," there are two textual versions; however, I do not wish to elaborate further here. I shall merely cite the occasions for arousing [the resolve] to indirectly manifest the Teacher who transforms others.

This is because, when the occasion for arousal is established through a review lecture (*fujiang*), those who already possess the capacity (*yijian*) immediately attain the wondrous Way, while for those who do not yet possess it, this serves as the causal condition for its arising; therefore, these are called the "assembly of those who arouse [the resolve]. This is what is meant.
At that time, there was this present "fourfold" [assembly]. Since it existed then, it certainly exists now; how much more so for those who manifest it?
At that time, since there were śrāvakas and furthermore the four groups of followers (catur-parṣad), each group possessed both the provisional and the real, making two of each;
thus, there were four. The subsequent mention of "the four divisions of the assembly" refers precisely to these four groups of śrāvakas. Therefore...

Because there is one set of four within each of the four [sets], it is directly based on these four to clarify the sixteen; this text contains two meanings: first, to cite the inferior to illustrate the superior;

second, to clarify that the path of all Buddhas is identical. Regarding the illustration: at that time, in those places, for those beings, the three factors were all superior and yet they still possessed the sixteen [qualities];
how much more so now, when the three are inferior and not even present? Second, to clarify that the path of all Buddhas is identical to that.
Since there is a present Buddha, it is not non-existent. "Ning" (寧) means "peaceful" (安). What is meant by "peaceful"?
If one were to clarify a single meaning, one should not speak of "time"; yet, because the Way is the same, we know this is again a shadowy manifestation (*yǐngxiǎn*).

One should know that within this single phrase there are four shadowy omissions (*yǐnglüè*): first, a general clarification that cites three shadows to manifest one; second, the beginning and the middle...

Regarding the three points—raising [the topic], commenting on the concealed, and requesting the exposition—it is sufficient to raise the former to imply the latter by analogy; how much more so for the fourth?
It is sufficient to raise the present case as being identical to the former to manifest that all these [points] exist;
therefore, although this single passage is brief, it possesses these four exceptional characteristics. Scholars must not fail to know this. This follows from having already clarified the teaching.

These three [explanations] clarify the preceding [section]; thus, the four meanings of "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) should be understood as they were briefly explained before, as clarified in the section on "forming karmic connections according to the capacity of the recipient.

One should reflect upon how these four [aspects] initiate the influence, how the four recipients properly obtain the benefit, and how forming the connection is the causal condition for all these four.

The five preceding layers of explanation regarding the causes and conditions of the fourfold assembly are concluded. Regarding the direct teaching of the Perfect [Vehicle], this is because the previous explanations were made by directly applying the five prefaces of this sutra;
since all of these initiate the "Correct" and "Sublime," it is said that the three examples are likewise so. This refers to the relative [teachings] of the past;
however, when one reaches this assembly, after the cessation [of the Buddha], there are no longer any remaining three—this is precisely the meaning of the Perfect in this sutra.

Next, regarding the *Benji bu shi ji* (The Record Explaining the Origin and Trace), it says: "If we provisionally consider this in terms of essence and function, the 'origin' (*ben*) is the eternally abiding, most honored, or profound stage of the *dharmakāya*;
the 'trace' (*ji*) consists of the four teachings and sixteen assemblies. Now, I say that one may also rely on the explanation below:

since it clarifies that the attainment of enlightenment occurred long ago and that he constantly preaches the *Lotus Sūtra*, then in each instance of preaching, there are all sixteen assemblies within the past.
The sixteen assemblies previously mentioned are the "root," while the sixteen assemblies encountered today are the "trace.

Since this meaning is easy to understand, the text does not provide an explicit explanation, but simply states that it can be understood. If one were to offer any other interpretation, it would remain unintelligible.
As for those who contemplate the names, upon hearing of the wondrousness of the root, they will certainly know its reason; such is the stage of this [text]. As it says:

Regarding the phrase "the principle-observation is uninterrupted," this refers to the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*) prior to the aforementioned explanation of specific meanings; it is precisely based on this that [the text] speaks thus.
Among those for whom the teaching is intended, one should know that this applies generally to the stages above, yet because we begin from the starting point of the stages, it says "this.

Within the stage of partial realization (*viśeṣa-bhūmi*), having attained the wondrous essence, one is immediately endowed with the two functions; therefore, one can act as these two. One should know that within this stage there are two meanings, the first of which is...
The meaning is roughly as follows: "The two [aspects] corresponding to the occasion" refers precisely to these two stages (and so forth).
Regarding the term *parivṛta* (surrounded), the previous explanation concerned the assembly that had gathered; this current explanation concerns the deportment (*īryāpatha*) of that assembly.

The *Śāstra* explains this passage by stating: "1. surrounded by the assembly; 2. preceded and followed [by others]. Others say: "Since the current scriptural text lacks the phrase 'preceded and followed,' it should be stated as such."

In the fourfold assembly, the text was only complete when they surrounded him from both front and rear; now, it is observed that there are many discrepancies between the treatise and the sūtra, leading one to suspect that while the text may be deficient, the meaning is already complete. Why is this? "Surrounding" does not refer solely to the two sides, but inherently includes the sense of front and rear.
Furthermore, since the *Anantaparyāya* (The Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings) also lacks any mention of front and rear, the matter is already exhaustive and nothing further can be added.
In the text, there are four explanations; the first explains only the original cause, while the middle two explanations each incorporate one of its meanings.

Since the initial [explanation] states that the causal conditions require these four meanings, the *Ji* (Record) says: "The descent from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven is the world-meaning (*loka-artha*); transforming into human form is the person-meaning (*pudgala-artha*);
being taken as a model by people is the remedial-meaning (*pratipakṣa-artha*); and having paid respects and heard the Dharma is the ultimate-meaning (*paramārtha-artha*). Now, I fear...
This deviates from the meaning of the text; my current interpretation is as follows: The world is spoken of in general terms as the essence and characteristics of phenomena.
When heaven sends down its manifestations and humans take them as models, this constitutes the "world. Turning to the right symbolizes faith and compliance, which is the human way.

Reverent salutation is the antidote to arrogance. Hearing the Dharma and awakening to the Way is the primary principle. Following the sequence of the text, the meaning is further clarified; I dare not differ from it.

Next, regarding the analysis of the teaching (*yōkyō*), within the initial section on the complete commentary on the text, among the four modes of deportment (*shii*), this includes three: walking, sitting, and standing. This refers to what was previously mentioned:

having arrived, one circumambulates and bows, then sits—these are the three. Now, explaining from the beginning to clarify their significance: what is "circumambulation" (*sen*)? It actually applies to both.
To turn back is "encircling" (*i*), and to move around in a circle is "revolving" (*en*). When combined with the proper measure of ritual (*reido*), it constitutes dignified deportment (*iigi*).
The customs of different lands vary: in this land, ritual propriety (*li*) is esteemed; in that land, circumambulation is valued—whether three times, seven times, or even a hundred thousand times.
Thus, the *Anantamukha-sādhaka-nirdeśa* states: "Circumambulating a hundred thousand times is a matter of ritual decorum. What is the underlying intent here?

Some cite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which says it is to manifest the Buddha’s virtues and show that people receive the Way just as the devas do. My interpretation of the meaning is that it serves to symbolize...
The Perfect Principle (yuan-li) is circular, and thus represents the four gates; because it is circumambulated by practice, it is that which is surrounded by movement.
This represents the Buddha’s perfectly wondrous body, signifying that one shall hear the correct teaching and perceive the wondrous Way at each and every gate.

The four phrases beginning with "opening and revealing" correspond to these four gates, all of which converge upon the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—this is the Perfect Principle. As for the statement regarding the contrast with the partial, it is based on...

When the provisional is contrasted with the ultimate, it is said that there is only the one and no longer the three; this is stated because the ultimate is revealed by means of waiting upon [the provisional] for its manifestation.

Yet, since both the partial (p’ien) and the perfect (yüan) possess four aspects, why are they distinguished as "square" and "round"? Consider this. Next, regarding the contemplation of circumambulation:

it is placed first because it clarifies the sequence of the fundamental and the trace. First, it explains the reason for circumambulating and gazing, stating that "to go around" (*chou-chuan*) means...

The perfection of the primary and secondary marks is the "wondrous contemplation" that observes in four directions. As stated in the verses of the Dragon Girl below, it is by means of this that one circumambulates and gazes with reverence.
Because of this circumambulation and reverent gazing, one attains profound samādhi; *pratyutpanna-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Direct Encounter) is precisely what is termed "walking samādhi.
This is the contemplation of circumambulation. The intended meaning within the original text is to realize the nature through the marks.

This means that function is identical to essence, and essence and function are identical to the fundamental and the derivative. Because this is the power and function of perfect contemplation (*yuan-guan*), it is explained here following the section on contemplation.

The above concludes the explanation of the ritual procedures; below is the explanation of the matters concerning the gathering of offerings. Within this section of the commentary, there are three parts: first...
This consists of three parts: first, a brief explanation based on the text; second, a detailed clarification of the essence and characteristics by citing the *Anantamukha-sūtra*;

and third, an elucidation of the underlying intent of both [the sūtra and the commentary]. Regarding the first, the sūtra contains four phrases, which the commentary explains through two interpretations: the general and the specific. First, regarding the "three kinds" in the general sense:

this means that the intent of these four phrases applies generally to the text on making offerings; they do not go beyond the three types of action (*trīṇi-karmāṇi*). If discussed generally, all of them constitute offerings.
Thus, the first phrase appears to be a general heading without a distinct individual essence. However, if discussed separately, each of the four phrases has its own distinct essence and meaning;

since they all generally constitute "making offerings," yet do not fall outside the three types of action (trīṇi karmāṇi), the first two phrases refer to bodily action (kāyakarma), the next to mental action (manaskarma), and the last to verbal action (vākkarma). For this reason, it is said to be "general. Below follows the specific explanation.
The term "zhě" (者) indicates humility and prudence; "shì gōngqián lǐ" (釋恭虔禮) means to explain the reverence and devotion of ritual. This is a separate explanation followed by a combined conclusion.

Some say that "xiū jǐn" (修謹) refers to being reverent (*gōng*), while "chóng yǎng" (崇仰) refers to being respectful (*jìng*). Others say that being modest and shrinking from difficulty is *gōng*, while inferring [the Buddha's] wisdom and virtue is *jìng*.
Next, regarding the phrase "zhìxīn" (至心) and so forth: it means to exhaust one's mind and direct it with single-minded intent toward the wondrous realm of the Buddha. Some also say: one...
"Among all beings, there is none equal to the Buddha," is called *zun* (venerable). The mind that relies upon him as one's protector exceeds [the protection of] heaven and earth;
his name is so weighty that it is said with profound reverence: *zun-zun* (venerable-venerable) and *shen-zhong* (profoundly weighty).

Regarding the two characters used when speaking of such equality, although their meanings differ slightly, they are both sufficient as terms of praise. Since the citations from the scriptures following this all refer to a single meaning, I shall now proceed directly.
It is said thus because it is spoken of in combination. Some say that to praise (*praśaṃsā*) is to extol its excellent qualities;

yet even this is insufficient, so one further lauds it, which is called "eulogy" (*udīraṇa*). There is indeed this principle: to speak of beauty is "praise," while to discuss virtues in relation to specific matters is "eulogy.

Regarding the statement of its *upabhoga-pratyaya* (enjoyment-retribution), the three preceding phrases are distinct in expression but universal in meaning; this phrase, however, is universal in both name and meaning, and its essence is as follows:
Having already previously established the general meaning of "offering" (*pūjā*), we now further clarify its specific nature; therefore, it is discussed here once more.

Regarding the objects of the *niśraya* (support) and *upabhoga* (enjoyment), they are produced in the sequence that follows. The character "shī" (施) may also be pronounced level-tone (*ping sheng*), which refers to the actual practice of offering:
that is, employing the various objects of support and enjoyment for the purpose of making offerings. Some say that things such as celestial flowers and incense are termed "offerings."

The *Buddhamātṛkā-śāstra* defines "nourishment" (*yǎng*) as providing sustenance; some say that the act of offering material wealth is "offering" (*gòng*), while the inclusion of material resources is called "nourishment.

Alternatively, it is said that according to the *Yìdì lùn* (Treatise on the Stages), there are three types of offering: first, material gain (*lìyǎng*), referring to the four requisites; second, respect (*jìngyǎng*), referring to incense, flowers, and so forth;

and third, practice (*xíngyǎng*), referring to practices such as faith and precepts. Now, in general terms, it is as previously stated in the section on the virtues of a bodhisattva; in specific terms, however, it is as follows.
As stated in the passage cited above, it is also called "the matter" (vastu) and "the two" (dvaya), both of which are dharmas;

because they are all in accordance with the Dharma, the treatise is titled *Yúfǎzhùlùn* (Treatise on Abiding in Accordance with the Dharma). Thus, the title of the treatise fully encompasses these two meanings.

Next, the following passage is cited to extensively reveal their essential characteristics. First, it presents the characteristics of the objects of offering; although that text is extensive, it does not exceed five categories.
Heavenly flowers correspond to form (*rūpa*); heavenly music corresponds to sound (*śabda*); heavenly incense corresponds to fragrance (*gandha*); the hundred flavors correspond to taste (*rasa*);
and heavenly garments and so forth correspond to touch (*spraṣṭavya*). Thus, there are five. The external objects used for making offerings do not exceed these five categories.

Because the mental visualization of these [objects] immediately constitutes the dharma-object (*dharmaviṣaya*), they are complete as six; here, the text briefly cites two or three, while the term "etc.
(*ādi*) takes up five or six in total, which is why it says "etc. These are all the essential forms of bodily worship.

Next, regarding the *Gongjing jing* (Sutra on Reverence), it mentions only kneeling and joining the palms (*añjali*), omitting the term "crossed hands" (*kṣiptahasta*); however, since the meaning necessarily requires it, the term is included here.

This is the essential form of bodily veneration (*kāyakarma*). Although the sutra merely says "with one mind" (*ekacitta*) and does not mention the words "gazing up with reverence," the meaning necessarily requires it;
therefore, they have been omitted. Simply being "one-mindedly gazing up" constitutes honoring and respecting [the Buddha];
this is the form of mental offering (*manaskarmapūjā*). As for the seven phrases, they are "How great! Great awakening," and so forth.
The text consists of fifty-one lines; the initial verse comprises only twenty-five and a half [lines].
Commentators claim there are fifty-one verses, taking it that one line constitutes a verse (*gāthā*). This interpretation is likely incorrect.

Since the Sūtra states, "He spoke in verse (*gāthayā*) with words of praise," the term refers generally to expressions of admiration and is thus called "praise" (*praśaṃsā*). This, then, is the manifestation of the offering of verbal action (*vākkarma*). (6)
How can the requisites for offerings be obtained? How can one perform these offerings as distinct acts of the three karmas?
How is it that such offerings constitute those distinct acts of the three karmas? It is thus: an offering consists of providing what is required.
Since the Buddha has no worldly needs, the requirement lies solely in the object [of devotion]. If one can thus serve with sincerity through the three karmas, then this is indeed [an offering].
Because they have attained the conditions for the Way and are honored as sages, they should be venerated with sublime offerings; thus, all such acts constitute offerings.

As for the five sensory objects being called "heavenly," this refers to the most excellent and beautiful things in the world. Since there are both provisional and ultimate aspects among sentient beings, it is appropriate to call them all "heavenly.
Yet, since there are those who surpass heaven, how could they merely be equal to heaven? This is simply in accordance with worldly convention.
Next, regarding the explanation of the meaning of "this" and "that," there are two sūtras—one with inquiry and explanation, and one with conclusion—which differ and agree.

Those who have attained realization find no discrepancy between them; however, many fail to understand this. Because doubts arise based on their differences, this explanation is provided. It should be known that the two prefaces of the two sūtras both have points of agreement and points of difference:

the five elements of the general preface (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*) are entirely identical, while the five elements of the specific preface (*asādhāraṇa-nidāna*) differ. Among these, the gathering of the assembly is the same.
One matter is the same as that [other sequence], while the remaining four matters differ from it.

Regarding their distinct introductory sequences (*nidāna*), they consist solely of the assembly of the multitude and the initiation through the three types of karmic offerings; thus, the distinct introductory sequence of initiation is exhausted by this assembly of the multitude.
Therefore, the remaining four differ from this distinct [sequence]. Since the first of these differs entirely from that [other] in substance, it is abbreviated here.

That [extensive version] explains this [concise version] extensively; since it is firmly established by reason that it is thus, what fault could there be? According to the end of the sutra, which states:

"When the great assembly had heard the Buddha’s teaching, they rejoiced, prostrated themselves, and departed having received and upheld it. Since it says they "departed having upheld it," how could one say they did not disperse?
Now, it is said that in this single assembly, there are two kinds of benefit from the teaching: first, the benefit of generating [realization]; second, [the benefit of...]

Although there are two aspects to the benefit of inclusion, the primary intent lies in inclusion; having already explained the benefit of production, this [section] exhorts the transmission [of the teaching].
It reflects the intention of the assembly to respectfully disseminate [the Dharma] after receiving the mandate.

Furthermore, it clarifies the essential substance of a single exposition from beginning to end, and for those with the karmic affinity to focus on a specific portion during the final age. Since these are the words of the compilers, it says: "Take this back to the original."

Because his correct intention regarding this sutra had not yet been fully expressed, he entered that meditative concentration; as the earth-lord rained flowers and shook the ground, and since [the Buddha] did not arise from it, how could the assembly have dispersed?
Now, because he follows the correct exposition, it is said that he remains "dignified. For this reason, it is known that the introduction to that [sutra] is also the introduction to this one.
Since that correct exposition looks back to its own introduction, and this correct exposition likewise looks back to this [introduction], [it is established].

The introductory sections of those [other works] serve as introductions because they precede their respective main bodies; yet, from the perspective of this present work, they also function as introductions because they lead toward its correct exposition.

Thus, it is clear that each of those parts possesses the threefold structure [of introduction, main body, and conclusion], and when viewed in relation to this [present work], they all constitute the meaning of an "introduction. Reflect on this, reflect on this!

The following explains the sequence of the "Manifestation of Signs" (xiànxiàng). The commentary consists of two parts: first, indicating the scope of the scripture and setting forth the topical headings;

second, the detailed explanation of the textual divisions. Regarding the first, the reason for specifically indicating the limits of the textual divisions is that, in ancient and modern traditions, some do not treat these as the text concerning the manifestation of auspicious signs;
since our current intention differs from theirs, we precisely indicate their beginning and end, treating them as such.
This is because it manifests and brings forth [the teaching]; it is also called the "Sequence of Manifesting Auspicious Omens" (*prātihārya-nidāna*). The sūtra text possesses these two names;
it is also called the "Sequence of Manifestation," which will be explained in detail within the text itself. To state the essential point:
the former [sequence] is the stimulus that evokes this luminous response, thereby causing the stimulus to become even more profound. Those three matters together constitute the second part.
Next, regarding the formal analysis and explanation, there are two distinct parts: first, the analysis, and second, the explanation. Within the analysis, there are two sections:

first, the presentation of differing views, and second, the critical assessment of those views. Regarding the first view, there are two schools. The first school indicates that while the two lands are opened, they are discussed as a unified pair; thus, it says "seven.
According to this other [view], only the *Prabhāsa* (Emanation) is primary, while the rest are all secondary illuminations resulting from what is seen. This is the subsequent formal explanation.
Since the meaning is self-evident, the text does not explicitly state the sequence. This master first describes the headings and enumerations, opening each of the two lands into six parts;

this enumeration is correct. Below is the description of their respective explanations. For now, the six divisions of this land and the six divisions of the other land will be seen later on their own;
within these six, they are further grouped into three pairs, each of which is...

There are three meanings, namely: name, phrasing, and meaning. First, the initial movement is the "name. Expounding the Dharma to save sentient beings constitutes its "phrasing" (its textual body), and it is also its "meaning.
This refers to the first three [of the six characteristics]. The same applies to the five subsequent matters; they may be analyzed accordingly, so I shall not elaborate further to avoid prolixity.
Next, regarding the critique of differing views, I have only critiqued the first interpretation of Guangzhai; as it is easy to understand, I have not [further] discussed it.
Fán [Seng]yè, within the Guangzhai Monastery, permitted certain points while not initially permitting others;

he evaluated their numerical counts and the sequence of their textual passages, and either rejected their names, meanings, and the intended implications they express, or permitted their numerical counts. Regarding the permission of the numerical counts, this refers to positing "two" and further dividing each into "six.
As for the textual passages, he ensured that the beginnings and endings of these two and six passages were each properly established. Because these were appropriate, he permitted them.
"Seizing the names" refers to the six names established; "the meaning" refers to the meanings explained beneath those six names.

As clarified previously, what is meant by "ease"? It means that while the intended meaning of what is to be explained has been made manifest and the purport of the correct teaching has been indicated, the [underlying] principles have not yet been fully elucidated. Therefore, it is improper to seize upon and refute them.
Since the general meaning is thus, what is the specific intent?
From here on follows the formal exegesis of the main section, which consists of two parts: first, the listing of the six names; second, the explanation of their meanings.

As for the text and its numerical sequence, they are identical to those of Guangzhai, and therefore need not be discussed further. However, regarding the names and their meanings, they differ from that [previous school].
Therefore, I shall list the names directly and explain their meanings; this is precisely the sense of the preceding "giving" and "taking.
It should be understood that the initial listing of six names is entirely different from those six names [previously mentioned], as they are all names established through paired correspondences.
One should know that while it would be possible to establish these names by relying directly on the literal text, they do not rely directly on the text but are necessarily...
The reason for establishing this title is precisely to arrange the six names so as to manifest the six correct meanings.

The name "Guangzhai" (Light-Abiding) lacks entirely the meaning of manifesting correctness; since it manifests nothing, how can it be called an "arrangement of the correct"? Furthermore, it contains both meanings simultaneously [and thus cannot serve as an orderly sequence]. (And so forth.)
Next, in the explanation of the meaning, there are three parts: first, the explanation of the specific names; second, from "these six" onwards, the explanation of the general name;
and third, from "briefly clarifying" onwards, the combined explanation of both the general and specific names. Alternatively, it may be treated as having only two intentions:

the first two explain the meanings of the names, which are convenient for correlating with what precedes them, whereas the negation of those names and meanings is not so convenient. The final one refers to that which is manifested as the retribution.

The meaning [of this passage] counters the previous [view] by negating the notion that it does not manifest the sense of retribution. Furthermore, one may first explain the two names—specific and general—and then consider what the subsequent section explains regarding the meaning of manifestation and retribution.
Initially, within each of the six [categories], both meanings are present; that is, the meaning of essence (*tattva*) and the meaning of wisdom (*jñāna*).
As for the phrase "the discourse of wisdom," this specifically refers to the auspicious signs (*nimitta*) of preaching the sūtra. Since preaching is the function of wisdom, it is said to be [wisdom].

Regarding "Wisdom" (*jñāna*): it refers to the teaching of the One as being many; this is indeed "Sublime Wisdom. "Referring" (*nirdiś*) is also "teaching" (*deśanā*), meaning the teaching of the principle of how many phenomena emerge from the One.
This is the same as the preceding [point], for it focuses exclusively on the single essence; thus, it is "Sublime Samādhi. Because these two mutually support one another, they constitute a pair.
Regarding the "cause," namely the raining of flowers: since the fourth [point] involves both flowers and their descent from the heavens, it is therefore [the cause].
The four sublime causes, to which two are added, constitute the fruit—that is, the sublime fruit. Because cause and fruit are mutually dependent, they form a pair.
"Eliciting" refers to the arousal of joy, for it is through delight that the sublime capacity is activated.
Because this elicitation manifests this light, it constitutes the sublime response. Since response and elicitation are the harmonious union of cause and condition, they likewise form a pair. This...
The sixth title, "Renowned for Understanding the Meaning," indicates that the celestial manifestation will preach the six dharmas; thus, it is convenient and differs from previous versions.
Why not simply rely on the names in the text as they are, rather than necessarily establishing this specific name? It is to manifest the intent of the orthodox teaching.

If it were not so, what would be called the "separate introduction"? If it were like the Guangzhai school, where there is no underlying reason at all, one could only say it belongs to its own section.
The text contains no sense of "arising" or "correctness"; rather, what is now termed the "Preface" (xu) and the "Correct Meaning" (zhengyi) are both fully understood therein.
One should know that this single [term] and the six [sections] must contain three meanings: namely, these six, their sequence, and the contemplation from which they emerge.

The following explains its general name, which refers to "auspicious signs" (*nimitta*). Since these two names appear in the scriptural text and their usage has been inconsistent throughout past and present, it is necessary to distinguish them;
this serves as an introduction to the subsequent explanation regarding manifestation and response. Within this section: first, the identity of their essence is clarified;
second, their differences in meaning are clarified; third, the reason for these differences is explained. First, according to the scriptural teaching, since it says "as it was originally,"...
It is simply one thing, namely the six kinds. Next, to clarify its meaning through provisional differentiation, it may also be said to have two senses.
Regarding "human sentiment" (*jénqíng*): previously, based on the words of the Sage, the ultimate principle was one;

now, because this is a provisional differentiation according to worldly human sentiment and terminology, it is again provisionally made into two. The following sets forth these two senses, which exist upon that single thing.

The two meanings of "mystery" (*mi*) refer to the praise of the Dharma of correct teaching regarding retribution, which concerns its merit; and "extraordinariness" (*ki*), which refers to the essential nature itself—that is, the substance of the six matters is all non-constant.

Because this state of extraordinariness can mysteriously signal [retribution], it is called a "portentous mystery" (*sui-mi*); because the substance of the mysterious retribution is extraordinary, it is called a "mark" (*sō*).

This is a case of being different yet constantly the same, and being the same yet constantly different. What is the basis for these marks? [Note: The term *sō* (相) here refers to the physical or phenomenal manifestations of the Buddha’s presence, often associated with the thirty-two major marks.]

This explains why the auspicious signs (*śakunāni*) have a basis for their manifestation. Regarding the standard for interpreting the resolution of doubts based on the initial inquiry into that resolution:
it should state, "Since the assembly has already gathered, one should simply preach immediately; why is it necessary to first manifest through extraordinary signs before preaching?

To speak briefly, one should ask, "What is the purpose of these signs? Below, this is explained by means of interpretation and verification; yet, [the current explanation] does not at all accord with [the requirements].
If one were to follow the logical sequence, this inquiry should properly appear immediately before the brief explanation of the six auspicious omens (*ṣaḍ-prātihārya*).

However, it is said that this inquiry seems to contain two meanings: first, to inquire into the reason for the auspicious signs—that is, for what purpose these signs are employed to manifest and report;
second, to inquire what these signs signify. In the commentary, the first meaning is explained briefly at the outset.
The explanation below clarifies the subsequent meaning; as it appears to contain this sense, it is stated thus.

Within the explanation of the first meaning, the first two lines clarify the cause of the auspicious signs. The first line clarifies that the Way being taught transcends ordinary discourse and cannot be bestowed in vain upon those who are not worthy.
Those who receive it are not ordinary or commonplace people who can merely accept it through faith; they are extraordinary individuals.
For this reason, the Path proceeds by means of the next two phrases to clarify that one must first manifest extraordinary signs to startle and transform [the audience];
subsequently, because they develop a sense of alarm and reverence, one may then preach the Dharma. It is for this reason that these two meanings exist;
thus, these two serve as the explanation of the "wondrous principle," which is the Path that is preached—the principle of the wondrous Dharma. Xuanyi sighed in admiration of its subtlety.
The principle of the Dharma is profound and far-reaching; it transcends form and sound and lies beyond the realm of the ordinary.
The *Book of Changes* says, "To probe the jaws and seek out the hidden, to summarize the profound and reach the distant"—these are all designations for the ultimate depth and distance.

Among the most difficult things to explain is that, had we merely praised the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings would have remained submerged in the suffering of their transgressions for over forty years before the reality was revealed; is this not indeed the most difficult thing for human sentiment?
The term "etc. explains the reason for the objection. "Ordinary" (*youyou*) refers to that which is not urgent regarding matters;
it signifies the commonplace and the casual. To summarize this meaning: the Way is extraordinary, while the conditions and opportunities are ordinary.
Because the ordinary cannot receive the extraordinary Way, one first uses extraordinary matters to awaken and stir them, causing their habitual and constant will to shift.
It is only then that one may be granted the extraordinary Way. For this reason, it is explained through two meanings:

first, the explanation of the "manifested retribution" (*pratibhāsa-vipāka*), which discusses specific similarities to startle the minds of sentient beings; second, the "omen as a manifested retribution" (*praṇidhāna-pratibhāsa*) which refers to the manifestation that initiates the formal exposition of the six matters.
These two intentions are summarized here.

Having previously explained the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), we now explain and establish the auspicious signs (*praśasta*) based on what they represent; this also serves as the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion. To briefly clarify:
according to the exposition in the following text, if expanded, it comprises all [the categories], while in summary, it consists of the four "ones" within the ten "wonderfuls.

Although these three are distinct, each one individually pervades all others. Previously, in contrast to Guangzhai, five were used to represent four; now, regarding the auspicious signs, six are employed.

Manifested in ten, each of the four [categories] individually possesses the ten, and likewise possesses all meanings; this clarifies the six auspicious omens (*ṣaḍ-prātihārya*) as they are extensively discussed to manifest all wonders.
Now, for the sake of brevity, we shall briefly discuss how they manifest the ten; thus it is called "brief.

This is said in contrast to the extensive treatment of all [the categories], not because the four brief [categories] themselves are called "brief. The first five manifest the four [categories], and these auspicious omens correspond to those four.
The "middle" refers to the expression of the primary meaning; this is the ultimate abbreviation. Next, it is expanded into six to express the six aspects of the correct teaching;
this is the "middle. Now, expressing ten is the "extensive. Because one wishes to reveal that these ten encompass all things, they are called "abbreviated" despite being extensive;
thus, they constitute the sense of "repeatedly abbreviated, middle, and extensive. Contemplate this when correctly expounding the sublime Dharma.
This is an exquisite omen signifying the preaching of the wondrous Dharma; since the Dharma has ten aspects, it signifies the ten wonders.

In the *Correct Explanation of the Profound Meaning*, within the section on the "Wondrous" (*miao*), the characteristics have already been explained in detail as clarified therein. Therefore, this refers back to that record, which states: "The text is found within the 'Wondrous' section on Supernatural Powers (*abhijñā*).
The phrase "furthermore says" (*geng dao*) is synonymous with "moreover"; it means to speak further. Many later students do not understand the meaning of "dao" [in this context].
To alter the meaning of a single character in order to make it "comprehensive," and then further add characters upon it, is improper; one must be cautious of this.

The reason for revising the text is that the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) summarizes the meanings and sequence, and its "comprehensiveness" draws from both the prose and verse sections of the two lands (*zītǔ* and *tātǔ*).
This treatise on the Ten Profound Subtleties (*shímiao*) combines these; herein, I shall directly follow the sequence of the prose sections concerning our own land (*zītǔ*).
The sequence of the textual meaning differs between these two sections because the former treats them comprehensively while this one addresses them individually;

thus, the ten [categories] are contrasted with the ten [points], and here, since they are treated separately, the ten are represented directly by six matters, resulting in the distinction between the inclusive and the single.

To ensure that later students do not fail to understand the underlying reason for this presentation—showing both the comprehensive and the specific—it is necessary to explain it further. Therefore, [this statement is made].
To speak further of their differences, they are roughly as follows.

Below, the text correctly clarifies their characteristics: the "Preface" (序) is that which can manifest [the meaning], while the following two sections are that which is manifested—the "Proper Exposition" (正說).
First, because a function must have a substance, and because these two are not separate from one another, the two [sections] manifest the two [meanings], and thus they are the manifestors.

Because they are impermanent, they are all wondrous; because concentration is itself practice, it is manifestation. It also encompasses both cause and effect, possessing both the agent and the object;
since this practice of concentration is impermanent, it likewise manifests the wondrous. Because the flowers are of four kinds, they manifest the four stages.
Because the rain falls from heaven, they are all wondrous. The single event of the earth’s trembling manifests two things.

This term precisely indicates that, because it pertains to the aspect of what is revealed—namely, the destruction of delusions and the manifestation of principle—it belongs to the objective realm (*viṣaya*).

Since both the destroyer and the destroyed, as well as that which is manifested, each possess six aspects, and these encompass the beginning and end of the movement of self and others, it is called a "Vehicle" (*yāna*). However, because principle and delusion are mutually identical and their beginning and end are not different, they are all "Wondrous.
In the *Miao-xuan-wen*, these are termed the "Three Dharmas": those previously mentioned are called the "fruit," while those herein are called [the cause].
The reason there are three vehicles is that they are intended to manifest the multiplicity of meanings. If one relies on the text here, the meaning becomes clear:

"vehicle" (*yāna*) may indeed refer to the fruit; "assembly" (*gaṇa*) refers to the provisional person and the ultimate person—the provisional person who shall become an ultimate person, and the provisional dharma which shall become the wondrous dharma.
These two are the reasons for joy; thus, this single joy represents both.

The "Emission of Light" (Raśmipramokṣa) is a response-granting bestowal, performed precisely as a supernatural power (*ṛddhi*); thus, it represents these two. Since both are the Middle Way, they are both wondrous.

Some say that "response" (*gan*) belongs to the joy of the assembly; however, in this context, it should properly be said that it is called "response" because it comes from following the signs (*nimitta*).
Now, I maintain that while the single essence has two meanings, there is no contradiction in presenting them both. This is the correct conclusion.
Because these ten meanings are manifested, the six are collectively termed "equal" (*sama*).

Above, the general explanation of the intent of the six chapters is concluded. Below this, the second section is the specific analysis of the text concerning the six auspicious omens, which consists of six distinct parts.
First is the explanation of the "Introduction to the Teaching," which contains two meanings: first, to extol the preceding introduction; thus, it is the actual teaching itself.

The second [purpose] is to introduce what follows; thus, it serves as the introduction to the five phrases of the sutra text. The first phrase identifies the person for whom the teaching is intended (*deśanā-viṣaya*).

The subsequent four phrases identify the Dharma that can reach them (*deśaka-dharma*). These two constitute "response and stimulus" (*saṃgati*). The text only explains the latter four phrases and does not explain the first phrase.
To distinguish this person from those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), it says "Bodhisattva. Although this sutra is fully intended for all three vehicles (*triyāna*),...

Regarding the various differing explanations concerning the bodhisattvas, for whose sake were they formulated? They were intended to distinguish them from those of the two vehicles; thus it says "bodhisattvas. I cannot elaborate further here.

Now, if we consider the primary meaning as it is presented in its own context, although three vehicles are mentioned as an introductory framework, this is solely for the purpose of teaching the Dharma to bodhisattvas.
The intent of the *Lotus Sūtra* encompasses these two meanings, which is why it is stated thus. Next—
Regarding the four phrases of the summary, some say they consist of essence, name, cause, and result; others say that the first is general while the latter three are specific.

I, however, maintain that since the second is called "name," the first must be the "essence," and the subsequent three are all names applied to that essence—namely, the three among the seventeen names mentioned in the treatise.
Furthermore, since the first is proclaimed as being for the sake of all bodhisattvas, it is necessary to explain "Great" (Mahā).

Because the term "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle) is used throughout the sūtra, it is further distinguished; since this section recounts a single period of teaching, there are three [aspects]. The commentary consists of three parts: first, citing the sūtra to provide an explanation; second, summarizing the essential points of the sūtra to clarify that the names follow the sequence from the end [of the text]; and third, correlating the explained meanings with the significance of the sūtra. First, the "Mahāyāna" is explained. Regarding the meaning of Mahāyāna, sometimes the sūtra itself provides the explanation, while at other times it clarifies what is interpreted in the treatises. As for the explanation provided by the sūtra: [The sūtra states: "What is the Mahāyāna? It is the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas who have set out on the path, who have generated the thought of awakening, who have practiced the perfections, who have entered the stages, who have attained the powers, who have reached the ultimate limit of the Dharma-realm, and who have realized the equality of all phenomena. This is the explanation of the Mahāyāna according to the sūtra. Furthermore, there are four types of explanations for the Mahāyāna: first, the explanation based on the vehicle; second, the explanation based on the practice; third, the explanation based on the result; and fourth, the explanation based on the nature. These are as follows: 1. Explanation based on the vehicle: This refers to the vehicle by which one proceeds. Because it is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. 2. Explanation based on the practice: This refers to the practices undertaken. Because they are vast and great, they are called the Great Vehicle. 3. Explanation based on the result: This refers to the fruit attained. Because it is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. 4. Explanation based on the nature: This refers to the intrinsic nature. Because it is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. These are the four ways of explaining the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, there are two types of vehicles: the vehicle of the Śrāvakas and the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas. These two are collectively termed the "Lesser Vehicle" (Hīnayāna). The vehicle of the Bodhisattvas is termed the "Great Vehicle. Why? Because it surpasses the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Therefore, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because it carries all sentient beings across the ocean of suffering, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its provisions are vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its wisdom is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its compassion is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its vows are vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its skillful means are vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its power is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its liberation is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its knowledge of all modes is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its realization of the equality of all phenomena is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its entry into the realm of all Buddhas is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its mastery over all dharmas is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its transformation of sentient beings is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its adornment of the Buddha-lands is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its attainment of the Buddha-way is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its turning of the wheel of the Dharma is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its parinirvāṇa is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its legacy after parinirvāṇa is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its preservation of the True Dharma is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its establishment of the community of disciples is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its protection of the True Dharma is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its subduing of Māras and adversaries is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its manifestation of various bodies is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its mastery of all transformations is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its penetration of the realms of all sentient beings is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its entry into the realms of all Buddhas is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its non-abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its non-duality of birth and death and nirvāṇa is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its non-duality of self and others is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its non-duality of subject and object is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its non-duality of existence and non-existence is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its non-duality of permanence and impermanence is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its non-duality of purity and impurity is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its non-duality of emptiness and non-emptiness is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its non-duality of signs and signlessness is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, because its non-duality of wishes and wishlessness is vast and great, it is called the Great Vehicle. Regarding the seventh treatise on the explanation: here, based on the meaning of the sutra, we shall first further describe the introductory gate and the treatise itself.
Nāgārjuna himself explained it by means of six meanings, after which he correctly interpreted the present text. As for the initial six meanings: first, because it emerges above the two vehicles;

Now, to summarize the essentials here: it does not go beyond person, dharma, essence, and function. Because these are "great," it is named "Great."

Riding upon this, I shall briefly describe it because its interpretation differs from that of the sūtras and other treatises, as it clarifies both the meaning and the method. Following the commentary text:

In the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this is termed "Greatness of the Object" (*ālambana-mahattva*), corresponding to the *Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra*'s "Greatness of the Sphere" (*viṣaya-mahattva*). Since the former takes the great teachings of conversion as its object from which [the mind] is aroused, their meanings are identical.
"Greatness of Mind" (*citta-mahattva*) refers to the arousal of the bodhicitta based on the aforementioned dharmas as objects. This is [the meaning of] *Prajñā*.

Regarding the greatness of practice (*pratipatti-mahattva*): it refers to the name of the opponent in debate; this is different from the others because it possesses both benefits for oneself and others. Third, regarding the greatness of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā-mahattva*): "understanding" (*adhi*) means to uphold the great earth;

The perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is called the greatness of resolute belief (*adhimukti-mahattva*); its meaning is entirely identical [to the previous]. The antidote to the impure mind is called the greatness of knowledge (*jñāna-mahattva*).
Because it realizes the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*), its nature is roughly the same as the four purities.

Regarding "great," the *Bhūmivastu* (Section on the Grounds) states that the "greatness of the pure mind" refers to the Bodhisattva of the first ground, which is identical to this path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). The name "Prajñāpāramitā" is also the same.

As for the "greatness of vigor" (*vīrya*) in the name *Abhidharma*, it refers to the practice of difficult deeds over three great incalculable eons; therefore, this is not the same as the "five adornments of the great ground."
The "Greatness of Possessing All Requisites" refers to the twofold endowment of merit and wisdom; while the names differ slightly, the meaning is entirely the same as the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

The "Greatness of the Provisions for Wisdom" corresponds to the *Abhidharma*, which is named the "Greatness of Skillful Means. This nature arises from being endowed with both compassion and wisdom, thereby abiding neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa.

Seventh, regarding the "Greatness of Endowment" (*samanvāgama-mahattva*), the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* calls it the "Greatness of the Fruit," meaning that because one is a great bodhisattva, the names differ while the meaning is the same. As for the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, it is called the "Greatness of the Vehicle" (*yāna-mahattva*). This is because the vehicle is superior to all other vehicles; it is not merely a matter of the name being different. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains this "Greatness of the Vehicle" by stating that the Mahāyāna is superior to the Śrāvaka-yāna and Pratyekabuddha-yāna because it possesses eight kinds of greatness. What are these eight? First, the greatness of its object (*ālambana-mahattva*); second, the greatness of its practice (*pratipatti-mahattva*); third, the greatness of its wisdom (*jñāna-mahattva*); fourth, the greatness of its skillful means (*upāya-mahattva*); fifth, the greatness of its activity (*karma-mahattva*); sixth, the greatness of its result (*phala-mahattva*); seventh, the greatness of its duration (*kāla-mahattva*); and eighth, the greatness of its ultimate goal (*niṣṭhā-mahattva*). Among these, the first five correspond to the "Greatness of the Vehicle" as explained in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. The sixth, the greatness of the result, corresponds to the "Greatness of the Fruit" in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* establishes eight kinds of greatness to encompass the "Greatness of the Vehicle" of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. It is called "Great" because it is superior to the Śrāvaka-yāna and Pratyekabuddha-yāna. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains the "Greatness of the Object" by stating that the Mahāyāna takes all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) as its object, whereas the Śrāvaka-yāna takes only a portion of phenomena as its object. The "Greatness of the Ultimate Goal" refers to the fact that the Mahāyāna ultimately achieves the state of perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), whereas the Śrāvaka-yāna ultimately achieves only the state of Arhatship.
