thus, while the two treatises differ in name from the Sūtra and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, they are identical in meaning. Since the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* accords with the Sūtra, I shall provide this explanation based on these two.
The following concludes the essential points of the sūtra and clarifies the basis for its established title; the meaning of cause and effect can be understood thereby.
If one follows the explanations of the other two treatises, the summary of the conclusion is very convenient and easy to understand.

As the sūtra states, the seven points, when summarized, are simply cause and effect—namely, the former six and the latter one—and thus they can be known. If one follows the other two treatises, this conclusion...
The reason this conclusion is placed here, rather than following the sequential order of the text, is to introduce the ten wonders of the subsequent assembly.

One should know that both the seven [aspects] and the two [aspects] constitute its essence; since their meaning has not yet been fully manifested, one does not yet know why they are called "Great" or "Vehicle.
One should know that these seven terms refer to the cause, which encompasses all myriad practices (*caryā*), while the terms for the fruit are fully endowed with all myriad virtues (*guṇa*).
Therefore, it is called "Great" (*mahā*); because it carries oneself and others, it is called a "Vehicle" (*yāna*). When essence and function are discussed together, it is termed the "Mahāyāna.
Since the essence of this Mahāyāna is explained through its function to instruct bodhisattvas, and because the subject and object are combined in name, it is called a "Mahāyāna Sūtra.
What follows is the application of the subtle meaning one has interpreted to harmonize with the great meaning of the sūtra; the reason for doing so is precisely to clarify [the following].
Because both "wondrous" (*miao*) and "great" (*da*) possess ten meanings, the Sūtra says: "The preaching of the Mahāyāna sūtra is called the Wondrous Dharma Lotus.

Although the meaning of "vaipulya" (*fangdeng*) applies generally, here we take the sense of "perfect" (*yuan*) to apply to the term "Great" (*da*). Therefore, "wondrous" can be used to explain "great. Regarding the character *shu* (捒) used by the commentator:

it is pronounced *so* (反). It means to adorn, to arrange, or to correlate. Although there are ten [meanings], they are subsumed under seven; though the numerical count differs, the essential meaning does not.
This is precisely why the preceding [five] are first grouped together as cause and effect;

because the latter five are functions based upon the fruit, the seventh chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* (the *Dharmaparyāya-śāstra*) refers to them as the "great nature of karma" (*karma-mahattva*), stating that they establish the Buddha-work throughout the limits of the future.

Thus, they possess the latter five. However, it is sufficient to follow the essential points of the commentary (*śūtra-vṛtti*) for a proper understanding; there is no need for further elaboration by providing separate correlations, hence it is said: "it may be."
If one understands these characteristics in this way, what is the distinction between the Introduction (Nidāna) and the Proper Exposition (Saddharma)?

If one follows the meaning of "Introduction" as it pertains to that specific time, one takes the ten *mahā* (greats) to represent the ten *myō* (wondrous), because while the meaning of *mahā* is general, the meaning of *myō* is specific. However, once one reaches the stage of the Proper Exposition and beyond, the characteristics of *mahā* and *myō* are identical, possessing both meanings;
thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, one should know that *mahā* is the essence (*t'i*) and the vehicle (*sheng*) is the function (*yung*). Now...

In the explanation of the essence (*tattva*) of *nirvāṇa*, both the essence and its function are treated together; however, in the case of the *Mahāsannipāta* (Great Assembly), the essence and function are explained separately, as can be understood from the commentary on the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.

Regarding the subsequent explanation of the names based on the aforementioned essence: while the term "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle) is general, names such as "Immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) and so forth are specific; therefore, [the former] precedes [the latter].
Because these three names below constitute the specific [explanations] while this [preceding one] is the general, all commentaries treat them as general and specific.

In the first explanation regarding the "Infinite Meanings" (*Anantārtha*), there are two parts: first, the analysis of the ancient interpretation; second, the citation of the correct understanding. Within the first part, there is first the specific and then the general.
Regarding the specific, there are six points concerning persons and five points concerning meanings; for each, the principle is clarified by first stating the position and then refuting it.
Among the five types of exegesis (*pañca-vyākhyāna*), each necessarily consists of two parts: the explanation of the title of the scripture and the introduction of its meaning.

This title was originally intended for the purpose of introducing the work; if it serves as an introduction, the meaning is naturally established. If it does not so serve, then it does not constitute an introduction.
Whether the text provides merely an explanation of the title or merely an introduction is precisely due to this principle; one must not [assume otherwise].
These essential points would become needlessly prolix if explained exhaustively; ultimately, they are not the primary intent—reflect on this, reflect on this!

Although the first master directly clarifies the meaning of the "Preface" while simultaneously including its terminology, this master specifically uses the "signless" (*animitta*) to explain the "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) and the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), thereby clarifying the meaning of the word "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*): because this sutra correctly teaches the signless principle of emptiness.
It is titled *The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings*. Why is this spoken first, followed by the *Lotus Sūtra*? The commentary explains:

"This principle of signless emptiness is the foundation of the Mahāyāna teachings and practices. Since one intends to bring the branches back to the root, one must first discuss the root and only then bring [the branches] back to it.
Thus, because the *Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings* discusses the root, it serves as the introduction; because the *Lotus Sūtra* brings the branches together, it serves as the main body.
Some say that this is not the essential purport of Master Sheng’s own words, but rather a transmission of another person’s interpretation of Master Sheng’s meaning;
however, I maintain that this is not so. First, I shall fully set forth the text of that commentary, and then I shall synthesize its essentials with the present [work]. That commentary states:

"Those who expound the Great Sūtra [but] externally comply with the traces while contradicting the principle, and cling to the literal text while deviating from the intent—how can they [be said to understand it]?"

To verify the proclamation of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), because he was about to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he first led them by addressing their dispositions through the preaching of the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (the *Wuliangyi jing*).

Since their lingering attachments had persisted for a long time, they were suddenly startled upon hearing that there was no [distinction between] the three vehicles, which abruptly contradicted their former preferences.

If those former preferences were thus contradicted, they would have recoiled in fear, like those who turn back at the sight of a precipice; and had they turned back, there would have been a great failure in the mission. Therefore, a gradual approach was necessary, which is why it is called "Immeasurable" (*ananta*).

"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the fact that all characteristics are non-existent; there is neither more nor less, neither shallow nor deep—it merely explains the practice that accords with the Buddha.
To speak of existence as reality is called "meaning. The commentary (*śāstra*) explains the text up to this point; herein, it does not exceed two intentions:
first, explaining the meaning of the introductory statement, which serves as the preface; second, the necessity of correctly explaining the names [of the chapters]. That text is extensive.
Now, this present text bypasses the literal wording to directly extract its essentials; it takes the principle of formlessness (*animitta*) as its immediate focus.

Furthermore, it extracts the subsequent [sections] by looking up at the essential titles, having long since extracted the initial [sections]. It addresses the stagnation regarding the traces below the text, asserting that while that sutra clarifies the fundamental dharma, at the conclusion of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly, when one is about to clarify the end of the assembly characterized by forms, one must first clarify the root of formlessness (*animitta*), and only then bring them together.

I have returned here to discuss the original purpose for which this preface was composed for the *Huìmù* (Meeting at the End). What has been presented here exhausts its essential meaning rather than reproducing the full text; therefore, it does not transmit the words of others.
As for the observation that [Dao]sheng and I studied under the same teacher, Kumārajīva, my understanding of the meaning and intent is identical to his. Next, regarding the sense of the objection:

since these various sutras all clarify the principle of formless emptiness (*animitta-śūnyatā*), I have raised this challenge based upon them. Furthermore, as for "next" (*cì*) and "that" (*pǐ*): "next" refers to the sequence of the arguments, while "that" refers to the preceding point.

Furthermore, regarding the "Universal Meaning" (Tongyi): although it universally clarifies the signless (*animitta*), because the preceding two [periods] are remote, they do not constitute the meaning of "Infinite Meanings" (*Ananta-artha*);

because this [period] is adjacent, it alone is designated as the introductory statement. Regarding the "Five Periods": according to ancient masters, the initial period was not fixed—some took the *Tiwei* [Sūtra] for humans and devas as the beginning, while others took the *Āgama* as the beginning;
the rest may be inferred accordingly. Furthermore, regarding the difficulty of the meaning: then the "Infinite Meanings" and the preceding...

This reasoning is certainly not so, for because the explanation of the title is incorrect, the meaning of the preface is not established.

If one asks, "In that case, how does this differ from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* of the second period? the answer is:

"The former teaching clarifies emptiness as the foundation for the practice of the three vehicles, and thus it cannot serve as a prologue; here, emptiness is clarified as the foundation for the practice of the Mahāyāna, and therefore it can serve as a prologue.

Although such a distinction is made, it provides no basis for proof. This is because the explanation of the title does not accord with the meaning of a prologue, and thus the point remains unestablished.
Next, regarding the Master’s commentary on the initial phrase "signless goodness" (*animitta-kuśala*) and so forth, the *Ji* (Record) states:

"The meaning is that for twelve years prior [to the *Lotus Sūtra*], there was only teaching with signs (*sanimitta-dharma*), which is not the cause for attaining Buddhahood; it indicates that signless goodness possesses the principle of attaining Buddhahood.

The meaning is that by the time of the *Lotus Sūtra*, there is nothing among all things that does not attain the path of Buddhahood. What is called "principle" (*artha*) here refers to that which can be accomplished; therefore, it is established [as such].

Regarding the statement in the *Sūtra Preface* that "the meaning of Buddha is the One Vehicle," it further says: "If that were so, since the *Vaipulya* and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras also clarify the signless (*animitta*), they too should serve as the preface and seal for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Since this *Dharmaparyāya* has not yet been translated, there are three errors: first, a mistaken interpretation that the *Dharmaparyāya* does not speak of existence or non-existence;
second, the erroneous claim that the sūtra has not been translated; and third, the reckless refutation of the ancient masters.

Regarding the claim that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dapin) is the primary source for the *Anantārtha-sūtra*: since that sūtra already states that the two and three [categories] emerge from the signless (*animitta*), why is it said that it does not mention the distinction between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?

Question: "By what Dharma-gate can a bodhisattva quickly attain unsurpassed bodhi? The Buddha replied: "There is one Dharma-gate;

What is its meaning? How is it practiced? These were three questions, which the Buddha answered in full, beginning with the first.

The answer consists of three parts: first, the answer regarding the name; second, the answer regarding the practice; and third, the extensive answer regarding the meaning. First, the answer regarding the name:
"This one Dharma-gate is named 'Infinite Meanings' (*Ananta-artha*). Next, the answer regarding the practice:

"One who practices and studies the Infinite Meanings should observe that all dharmas, from their very origin until now, are empty and quiescent in their essential nature and characteristics; they are neither great nor small, and they are without arising or ceasing."
Movement is not non-movement; there is neither advancing nor retreating, just as space has no dualistic phenomena.
Yet all sentient beings give rise to various views regarding this principle, creating all manner of evil karma and cycling through the six realms of rebirth to undergo the poisons of suffering.
Having contemplated this with keen insight, the Bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of compassion, desiring to rescue and deliver them, and further enters deeply into all things.

Furthermore, one contemplates that all phenomena possess various distinct characteristics and natures; having contemplated them in this way, one enters into the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of sentient beings.
Because these faculties, dispositions, and inclinations are immeasurable, the teachings are immeasurable; because the teachings are immeasurable, their meanings are likewise immeasurable.
The following is the detailed explanation of this meaning, which correctly elucidates the title [of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*]. Regarding "immeasurable meanings," it proceeds from...
That one dharma gives rise to another dharma is precisely the signless (*animitta*). Thus, signlessness is not signless; that which is not signless is signless.
This is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). When a bodhisattva dwells securely in such a true mark, the compassion they generate is clear, certain, and not false;
it is truly able to extract suffering and bestow happiness through the teaching of the Dharma. If a bodhisattva can practice in this way...
Regarding the first point—that a single dharma-gate has immeasurable meanings—one will necessarily and swiftly attain unexcelled bodhi.

From this point downward, through the extensive presentation of questions by Mahāvyūha and the Buddha’s broad explanations and clarifications, up until the attainment of the ten merits, the text extensively elucidates the meaning of the previously mentioned term "immeasurable meanings.

The answer to his question is that because the names, meanings, and manifest power of this sutra are exceptionally distinct from other sutras, it is said to be taught directly.
This person has become confused by the meaning of the single word "directly" (zhíshuō) and has failed to grasp the sense of the introduction and the main body [of the teaching]. How lamentable!

Reflect on this, reflect on it! That different names constitute an introduction is easy to understand; how could they not also function as an introduction? Thus, the various names are fully endowed with this quality.
Explaining their meanings, it is not merely that the names differ, but their meanings also differ; thus they can collectively constitute a preface.
When names are identical, one simply indicates the name itself without discussing its meaning, and so it may also serve as a preface.

Therefore, what precedes the text is called "explaining" (shuo), while what follows is simply called "reciting" (chang); this is why each is contained within a single phrase. Failing to grasp this principle constitutes a textual error.
How obscure this is! Within it there are two parts: first, citing three preceding sutras as analogies; second, citing the present sutra across past and present times to clarify their commonality.
Regarding the first part, the three sutras are mentioned in their prefaces with the chanting of names fully recorded in those texts, so I shall not recount them here again.

As for the statement that "there is no hindrance," the act of chanting differs from the act of explaining; one first chants the name and subsequently explains the meaning. This is the sequence of the introduction and the main body.

Because the meaning of this is well-established, there is no contradiction. Next, to clarify that [the *Wuliangyi jing*] is identical [to the *Lotus Sūtra*], the text again cites the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*.

The above constitutes the completion of the introductory section, which discusses the interpretation of the title and clarifies its purpose as a preface. Below follows the main body, which provides a formal explanation of that title and its purpose as a preface according to the sutra;

Within the first part, there is the heading and the actual exposition. The heading refers to the Buddha’s own explanation of this title within that sutra.

Therefore, although I have previously harmonized these with the general treatises, I shall now separately rely on the Buddha’s own correct explanations.

Although both the sutras and the śāstras provide explanations, I have not seen their convergence across ancient and modern contexts or among various practitioners; thus, I shall now first provide a detailed commentary.

Following this, within the explanation of the sūtra, it is further stated that the first phrase establishes the title to indicate the core thesis, while the subsequent four phrases explain its meaning.

however, since this name is correctly derived from two meanings, the heading should have stated: "That is to say, immeasurable dharmas arise from a single dharma.
Only in this way would it accord with the explanation provided below. As for the commentary on the sutra, it is stated thus simply for the sake of brevity and directness.

Although the wording refers to only one aspect, the meaning always encompasses both; otherwise, it would be difficult to reconcile. Thus, two chapters are presented together, followed by four lines that separately explain these two meanings.

Regarding the former, the Sūtra says: "That which is the One Dharma is precisely non-suchness (an-evaṃ)."

This characteristic must be the absence of characteristics; where there is no characteristic, there is no non-characteristic, and this absence of non-characteristic is called the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Second, in the previous sutra’s commentary there were three phrases, and the present text likewise has three phrases;

however, they collectively explain the middle phrase of the previous sutra. Although in wording it is but a single phrase, in meaning it fully encompasses the sense of two phrases—this is extremely concise and expedient.

Because it is named "signless" (*animitta*), the two phrases of the sutra merely express the meaning of the two extremes. Now, by explaining the first phrase, the meaning of the second phrase is implicitly included.
This was because the translator did not fully exhaust his skill, resulting in two phrases; now that the essential point is exhausted, one is sufficient.

That which cannot be characterized is named "real characteristics," meaning there is nothing it does not characterize. This is what is meant by "non-... [the negation of all conceptualization].

Now, observing his interpretation, it is affirmative rather than negating; and as for the conclusion, it functions as both negation and affirmation alternately, which is not optimal.

Next, I shall explain the immeasurable meanings arising within the sutra. That is to say, the aforementioned three categories are themselves the immeasurable dharmas.

this is termed "immeasurable meaning" (*apramāṇārtha*). Next, it clarifies that the Tathāgata, having personally realized the single dharma of signlessness, preaches immeasurable teachings according to the capacities of beings.

For over forty years since the Dharma was taught, its true reality has not been revealed; because there are these distinctions of two, three, and four [teachings], it is of "Immeasurable Meaning" (*Ananta-artha*).
Within this, first the two names are presented, then the two texts and their meanings are individually shown—these are easy to understand.

Both the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Vaipulya* are what the sutras themselves call the "Three Piṭakas. Although the name "Three Piṭakas" does not appear in the sutras, their meaning is indeed fully present within the text.
Since the text clearly explains the three—Truth (*satya*), Condition (*pratyaya*), and Means (*pāramitā*)—[these constitute the Three Piṭakas].

The meaning of the "Vehicle" (yāna) is thus clarified. Furthermore, by clarifying the truths, conditions, and perfections, as well as the profound principle of emptiness, the distinction between the partial and the perfect is made manifest.
Moreover, by clarifying that four kinds of benefits are obtained upon hearing [this teaching], the realization of the four fruits is proven.

In the first two [sections], the term "all" is used together precisely to clarify the sense of the immeasurable meaning; although the various distinctions produced are many, they do not go beyond this.
These two [categories] possess these two [subdivisions], which together comprise eight sets of eight; because they encompass all distinctions, "all" refers to the meaning of the immeasurable.
Although the initial statement spoke of the sudden [teaching], since this section fully discusses all the various manifestations of transformation, it encompasses all three [vehicles].
This is explained in terms of the cause (the fourth) and the fruit (the third), even though it concerns a Bodhisattva who has heard from me.
Because their benefits are realized, both are treated as fruits; since these two are both dharmas included within the gradual [teaching], they are not mentioned again.
If one says that both possess all [dharmas], this is incorrect because such a statement would lack substantial basis.

If one says that what is contained within also possesses both the subject and the object, this contradicts the fundamental tenet. Therefore, the Sūtra explains a single dharma by saying it has neither "great" nor "small."

The previous statement that "all are for the sake of the single reality" was met with some who said: "In the Chinese version of the sutra, the words of the *Avataṃsaka* appear after the *Vaipulya* and *Prajñāpāramitā*;

how can it now be considered the beginning? I say this is not so. Within the sutra, it is taught that from the past until the present, the teaching is divided into three periods—beginning, middle, and end—and that these teachings all contain both the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as the sudden and gradual methods.
The benefit gained upon hearing [the teaching] is likewise without fixed priority or sequence;

it is now explained that these two meanings are presented first as "sudden" and later as "gradual," rather than being restricted to a specific initial stage, which would contradict the meaning of the text.

Jiaxiang also stated that regarding the two dharmas of gradual and sudden, the "sudden" refers to the *Avataṃsaka*. Some say: "The Sūtra speaks of the three dharmas, four fruits, and two paths. Regarding this, according to the commentary:

"Three" refers to the teachings of the Three Vehicles; "four" refers to the four fruits of the Śrāvaka; and "two" refers to the fact that each of these four fruits has both a stage of progression (*pratipannaka*) and a stage of attainment (*phalastha*).
My current explanation not only differs from those in terms of terminology and meaning, but also reverses their sequence relative to the sutra. How should this be reconciled?
I maintain that this is the correct explanation of the *Anantārtha* (Infinite Meanings) [Sutra], which has only now, for the first time since before today, been fully articulated.
The transformations of the final three periods and the distinctions in the benefits obtained serve to manifest the characteristics of the "Infinite Meanings.

If one were to interpret it directly according to that [previous] understanding, it would be merely a minute portion within the gradual teaching; how could it suffice to reveal the essence and characteristics of the "Infinite Meanings"?
Therefore, based on the meaning of the scriptural text, it must be explained through such a definition and interpretation of the name. For this reason...
Furthermore, the meaning must be established in this sequential order; only in this way can the subtle purport of the sutra be fully exhausted. Thus the sutra says:
"The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma, the faculties and natures of sentient beings, the Dharma-gates, and liberation—these three matters are all inconceivable.

How could it be appropriate to definitively state that this is merely a conceptual understanding? Is it not inconceivable? It is fortunate that you have set aside ordinary sentiments to accord with [this truth].
The Way that is without direction is precisely the meaning of the immeasurable.

The following constitutes the third section, which concludes the exposition of the meanings and correlates them with the names, while simultaneously explaining the significance of the characters used in these meanings. The phrase "these [etc.

concludes the reference to the meanings of the three categories (triskandha) produced by what was previously explained, returning them to the name "immeasurable"; these three categories universally encompass the four periods of time and extend horizontally.
Because it establishes distinctions and benefits for all beings, it is "immeasurable. This clarifies that this name is established based on this essence (*tattva*).

Regarding the phrase "its reality, characteristics, and so forth," this concludes the preceding explanation of the meaning of how a single dharma is produced; it returns to the point that the name "meaning" (*artha*) is also established upon this very essence.
Although both are names for the essence, the former refers to the essence itself, while the latter refers to its functional activity.
(As stated above) This clearly explains that the name is derived from the synthesis of these two aspects; hence it is called "Immeasurable Meanings" (*Ananta-artha*). Question:

Why is it that for "Meanings" (*artha*) the capacity [the cause] is mentioned first and the object [the effect] second, whereas for "Names" (*nāman*) the object is mentioned first and the capacity second?

Answer: Regarding "Meanings," it is an explicit discourse on how many names emerged from a single [teaching] in the past; regarding "Names," it is a subtle indication that in the future many [teachings] shall be subsumed into a single name. Thus, the mutual clarification of these meanings constitutes the intent of the sequence.

Therefore, reflect upon this; it will become manifest within the subsequent commentary. Some say: "According to the interpretation provided by the Sūtra, the meaning belongs to that which is produced, and this has been so throughout all time, both ancient and modern.
To now consider it as the single producer—would this not contradict the Sūtra and oppose the consensus of the faithful?
Is this acceptable? From this point on, the root text is missing; here we shall provide a general overview of the various interpretations of past and present.

All [scholars] agree that the character "yi" (義) belongs to the objective [aspect], yet there are differences in the explanations provided by Master Jiexiang. He maintains that the character "yi" applies to both locations;

this does not contradict the meaning of the sutra text, as it also applies to both the subtle and the proximate. This school, however, holds that while it is acceptable for the general names "subject" (*neng*) and "object" (*suo*) to apply universally, it is not permissible for the term "immeasurable" (*wuliang*) to do so.
Nevertheless, among the scholars of this school, there are none who do not state that the character "yi" belongs to the objective aspect.
Since the "immeasurable bases" (*apramāṇa-āyatana*) pertain to that which gives rise [to the meditative states], the sūtra names it "entry into concentration on the immeasurable bases.
Therefore, the term "bases" (*āyatana*) should not have been inserted here; or, if one insists on using the word "bases," it should be taken from the subsequent phrase and placed here.

However, I maintain that both of these approaches contradict the meaning of the text and are entirely untenable. I further maintain that the term "object" (*artha*) actually applies to both the subjective and the objective.

What is the meaning? The preceding sutra speaks of "the teaching of immeasurable meanings" and also "immeasurable [meanings]"; the subsequent sutra speaks of "the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena," and further, "the meaning that assists in bringing forth the true reality.
Based on these two passages, the meaning is certainly applicable to both. Furthermore, according to the commentary, the interpretation of the meaning applies to both;
yet, regarding the phrasing, the principle is restricted to one. Regarding the intent of establishing the names, it is generally applicable to both, though it follows the specific [designation].
Regarding the term "meaning" (*artha*), it should properly be able to generate [the understanding of] that [reality]; why then is this not so? It is because names do not exhaust their reality;

while the substance has two aspects, the name only invokes one, and thus it is insufficient. The Buddha first proclaimed the names and then elaborated upon their meanings, so that beings might know that both names and substances encompass both meanings.
In the formal sequence, they are established as such; if one were to follow only one aspect and lose the other, it would be a failure.

From the perspective of meaning, this is not permissible. As deluded attachments accumulate daily, let us further substantiate this with examples. For instance, both "permanence" and "impermanence" possess their respective meanings:

arising and ceasing are the meaning of impermanence, while non-arising and non-ceasing are the meaning of permanence. These also involve the relationship between subject and object, applying in both directions.
To take the meaning of permanence as the meaning of impermanence is precisely to say that it is the meaning of impermanence; it does not mean [that permanence itself is impermanence].

This is precisely the meaning of impermanence (*anitya*). "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to that by which something is brought about or reached; how could it be that arising and ceasing themselves bring about arising and ceasing?
It is precisely because of non-arising and non-ceasing that they can be brought about. Therefore, one acts through non-action. Now, this case is also like this:
it is precisely said that within the past, this is the meaning of the source from which the immeasurable emerges, and thus it is secretly manifested. Therefore, it is appropriate.

The meaning of "converging and returning to a single place" is that once the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* has been fully expounded and its entirety revealed, it is named as such because all things have converged into this one point of meaning.
As for its capacity to be immeasurable, how could it be brought about by means of the immeasurable?
It is precisely because it is not [brought about] that it can be brought about; this clearly demonstrates that the "one" is incapable of being the cause of the "immeasurable."

Therefore, regarding the meaning (*artha*): if one considers it in relation to the immeasurable, it is the locus of that meaning; if one considers it in relation to the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is itself the locus of that meaning.
Since this meaning is itself the locus, how can one forcibly divide them into two distinct meanings? Furthermore, "meaning" refers to the object (*viṣaya*);

because it is precisely the locus upon which that [object] relies, meaning is itself the locus. Thus, name and reality do not differ, and the ancient and the modern meet in perfect accord. This is the correct sequence.
The principle is exhausted in this; what more could be added to it? (etc.).
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the title (*shiming*). The following is the second part, clarifying the meaning of the introduction (*weixuyi*).

Since the explanation of the title was originally intended to manifest the introduction, and the title has already been completed above, the following section now correctly elucidates the introduction. This section contains three parts, namely: the Dharma, the Simile, and the Synthesis (*fayuyihe*).
The meaning is as follows: for what reason is this presented as the introduction? To explain it thus:

since there is no way to gather [the manifold] apart from the One, the sequence describes how the One is the source from which all is gathered. Within the four analogies of the sequence, the first analogy represents the Buddha;
the second represents the past, where the One becomes many; and the third represents the subsequent gathering of the many back into the One.

The final phrase serves as a metaphor for the present immeasurable [teachings] which can be known (and so forth). From the first [phrase], there are three phrases that correspond to the preceding three;
this may be understood accordingly. Because the *Immeasurable Meanings* (*Wuliangyi jing*) describes these open and closed [sections], it serves as the introduction (and so forth).
This concludes the summary of the assembly. That is to say, as explained previously, whether it be a Sūtra or a Śāstra, each possesses the meaning of establishing a name as its introduction;
therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, because it secretly indicates the manifest, it does not conflict with the previous two [categories].
If it is purely manifest, it serves as a remedy; thus, this commentary on the Sūtra [is appropriate] (as stated in the *Yùzhù*). Such is the general intent; reflect upon it accordingly.
The above concludes the explanation based on the sutra; next, we shall harmonize it with the explanation in the *Śāstra*.
Now, while the general intent of the *Śāstra* is indeed thus, its specific explanation of the term "Immeasurable Meanings" (*Anantārtha*) appears entirely distinct. How can this not be contradictory?
Since neither ancient nor modern commentators have provided such a reconciliation, I shall briefly state it here. In short, although the phrasing differs, the meaning is no different. Why?
The treatise states: "First, it is named 'Infinite Meanings' because it accomplishes the meaning of its title;
for by means of this Dharma-gate, it explains that most profound and wondrous realm of phenomena. This "most profound and wondrous realm" refers to the supreme realm of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
The treatise's explanation of this name is exhausted by these points alone. Now, observing the text of this explanation in the treatise, there are three phrases.

The meaning consists of only two [aspects] which are subsequently transmitted. In the initial phrase of the commentary, "teaching" (*jiao*) refers to the doctrine, while "meaning" (*yi*) refers to the principle (*li*).
This means that there are immeasurable teachings and immeasurable principles; this is an explanation based on what is produced.

Next, the following two phrases separately explain based on the producing teaching and principle: "teaching" refers to the doctrine, and "wondrous object" (*miaojing*) refers to the principle. This means that there are no...
The "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*) is the single true mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*). The third phrase is a re-explanation of the principle of "that which is produced" mentioned in the second [phrase].

Since it is not known what this "wondrous principle" (*sūkṣma-nyāya*) refers to, it is explained by way of analogy: this is precisely the Dharma realized by the Buddha himself, the Dharma awakened by wondrous wisdom;
therefore, it is extremely profound. As for the reason why "previously" (*pūrva*) was used, it is to accord with the title of the sutra. Thus, it should be understood.

The title of the sutra is named according to both the agent and the object; it is also known that what was previously [discussed] pertains solely to the agent, yet its meaning extends to both locations because it clarifies the meaning of the "introduction" (*nidāna*).
Therefore, while one follows the two characters of the "object" (*ālambana*) in their general sense, one specifically follows the "agent" (*kartṛ*) in its specific meaning.

Since this object is the sphere of experience and the basis upon which it arises, one knows that the character "meaning" (*artha*) specifically refers to the agent that gives rise to it. For this reason, it is known that all [elements] are integrated.
Reflect upon this: there is no contradiction.
The section above concludes the correct explanation of the name "Innumerable Meanings" (*Ananta-artha*) and its function as a prologue.

The section below refutes the errors of the old interpretations regarding the intermediate main exposition by means of the meaning of what was taught in the preceding prologue and the subsequent section on circulation (*pravartana*).
The "Old Commentary" refers to that of Guangzhai; one should know that from this point downward, the entire section constitutes a refutation of Guangzhai.
This is because its biased interpretation that the *Lotus Sūtra* lacks the teaching of impermanence is as fully set forth in the subsequent text. Within this, there are two parts:

first, citing the introduction to reconcile the two interpretations and thereby critiquing the errors in the commentary on the main exposition; second, refuting the difficult arguments used to rescue the interpreted meaning. First, it cites the preceding scripture.

The section on "The Permanence of the Body" next cites the subsequent sutra to clarify the permanence of the land; this clarifies that both the primary and secondary [receptacle worlds] are permanent.
The first part is the passage from the introduction of the preceding sutra where the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha praises the Buddha, consisting of four and a half stanzas in seven-character verse.
The first three stanzas extensively praise the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body as being free from all marks, which corresponds to what is stated in the text.

The "one hundred negations" (*śata-apavāda*) thoroughly dispel [all conceptualizations]. Next, the three phrases praise the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body); the text is abbreviated and does not explicitly state this.

Following that, there are three phrases praising the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), which refers to the "equality" (*samatā*) mentioned in the text. This clarifies that all three bodies are eternally pure.

Because the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya*—which has thoroughly dispelled the one hundred negations—is in profound accord with the realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), its responsive manifestations are inexhaustible; therefore, all three are eternally pure. One hundred.

The statement that it is "not so" applies generally to all cases; one should not fixate on a definite number, for in reality, this is the single body of non-characteristics (animitta-kāya) manifesting as infinite bodies, just as a single dharma manifests as infinite dharmas.

Next, regarding the *Sūtra of Contemplation* (*Guan jing*), that sūtra was compiled later to ensure the circulation of this *Lotus Sūtra*; thus, that sūtra refers to [the Buddha] by the name Śākyamuni.
Vairocana pervades all places. His dwelling place is named the Light of Eternal Quiescence (*nitya-śānti-prabhā*).

It is a place established by the perfection of permanence (*nitya-pāramitā*), a place founded by the perfection of self (*ātma-pāramitā*), a place where the existence of marks is extinguished by the perfection of purity (*śubha-pāramitā*), and a place where the marks of body and mind do not abide due to the perfection of bliss (*sukha-pāramitā*).
This clarifies that the Dharma-realm and its manifestations are non-dual, both being fully endowed with these four [perfections].

The virtue [of this section] next summarizes and rebukes [the opponent] by refuting them. Previously, it was clarified that arising from the True Body (dharmakāya) to manifest the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) means that a single body produces immeasurable bodies;
here, it is clarified that the Response Body is itself the Dharma Body, such that immeasurable response-bodies all enter into a single body.

Thus, both the preceding and following sections are entirely and simultaneously eternal; how could the central, orthodox doctrine in between possibly be non-eternal? It would be like having beautiful hands and feet, while the trunk [is deformed].

If one’s mind is evil, one cannot be called a good person; this case is likewise so. Since the Prologue and the Circulation (Pravartana) are both permanent and correct, yet the Main Exposition (Saddharma) is impermanent, how can it be termed the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma)?

Furthermore, by way of analogy: if the preceding and succeeding parts—which serve as the primary context for the middle—are themselves permanent and correct, while the middle itself, which is the very foundation, is merely a provisional means (upāya), it would still be permanent and correct; yet here it is further impermanent. Therefore, such a principle does not exist. As for what is called the "middle," it is in contrast to...
The "before" and "after" constitute two [contradictory positions]. To speak of the span of life (*āyus-pramāṇa*) implies permanence throughout the three periods of time.

As the Sūtra says: "If even the characteristics of the world are provisionally eternal, how much more so the Tathāgata? The original text itself states that he is "eternally abiding and indestructible.
To claim he is impermanent is to openly disparage the Buddha; how could this be called the most subtle art of "suppression and exaltation"? This fault is so great that it must be refuted.

This is precisely what Guangzhai used as his judgment regarding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, following the intent of the *Dajing shu* (Commentary on the Mahāyāna Sūtras).

Since both sections of the sutra text already clarify permanence, although this [objection] challenges the other, it conversely establishes its own difficulty.

This error is even more severe than [the claim that] the "Non-dual" explains the Middle Way, whereas the *Gandhavyūha* (Fragrant Accumulation) and the Bodhisattvas do explain the Middle Way.
As for this person’s ingenious interpretation—that the attribution of merit belongs solely to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* while all others are not so—it is not a sound explanation of the passage.
It fails to comprehend the principle of the *Nirvāṇa*. As for the refutation [of this view], it was initially unreasonable;
thus, I previously pursued the matter extensively. Now, however, I shall withdraw that pursuit and no longer accept it. Furthermore, regarding the inclusion of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*...

if the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* truly clarifies that [the Buddha-nature] is eternal, then both the introduction and the main body of the text would be eternally true; the *Lotus Sūtra* is likewise so—why then must you be confused?

Even those who do not accept the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* or the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* might establish [this position]. Someone says: "Since all three clarify permanence, how can there be any difference?
One may ask this question: "If they are different, they should not both be permanent; if they are not different, [the distinction between them] should not exist."
The third distinction states: Since these meanings have already been enumerated previously, why are they mentioned again here? They must necessarily be further distinguished.
In the *Preface*, the "relative permanence" (*xiāngdài cháng*) is clearly revealed, while the "absolute permanence" (*juédài cháng*) is subtly indicated.

The *Lotus Sūtra* (*Fǎhuá jīng*) correctly expounds the absolute permanence, and the subsequent scriptures for its circulation also convey the absolute permanence. This single interpretation harmonizes both aspects; all other cases should be understood by analogy.
This does not involve prolixity.

Because this reveals the dharma that is capable of [manifesting] the power, it is now explained directly from the perspective of the dharma itself; there is no separate dharma, as it is simply the object previously designated by the name.
Thus, we know that this specifically clarifies the meaning of the "object-locus" (*artha-sthāna*) of the immeasurable *praveśa* (entry) and *niṣkramaṇa* (exit).

The first phrase indicates the title, which is simply the aforementioned dharma. The subsequent explanation has two meanings: what is the meaning of the "object-locus" dharma, and for what reason is this used?
When the Dharma-Transformation Bodhisattva first explains and brings forth his Dharma-truth, it is the principle of ultimate reality, the most supreme truth.

Since this principle is the division of the primary extreme, its locus of meaning is precisely that Dharma. This refers to the stage where, having already completed the opening and convergence [of all teachings], the infinite enters into the single locus of meaning.
Later, because he reiterates this and places it at the beginning of the sutra, he provides this distinct explanation. Below, he explains the second...
The reason why these two intentions necessarily employ this method to transform bodhisattvas is due to their original vows and the manifestation of those original aspirations;

the sequence of the two cited passages corresponds precisely to these two intentions. One should understand that the locus of meaning here is that the path of the Buddha and the [bodhisattva] path are one and the same.
Next, the third phrase is explained according to the treatise. The aforementioned alternative names are now further elucidated to clarify their significance and complete the meaning of those names.
The treatise states: "The five names are 'protected by the Buddhas' because these dharmas exist by virtue of the Buddha-Tathāgatas.
This commentary explains that the intent of this treatise clarifies that these are the dharmas belonging to all Buddha-Tathāgatas.
Now, the commentator of the present text correctly clarifies that this very "Place of Immeasurable Meanings" is the Dharma protected and remembered by the Buddha.

There are two meanings to "protecting and remembering": first, because it is what one has personally realized through one's own practice; second, because it involves protecting and remembering the conditions and capacities of others for the sake of transforming them.
These two meanings are combined, hence the name "protecting and remembering. Within the text, these two meanings are used as the basis for the explanation, beginning first with the former.

Next, all [the preceding passages] contain citations that are easy to see in the text. The phrase "long remained silent" (*jiumo*) means that the self-realized, dark essence has been so; hence it is called "long silent.
The phrase "this essential" (*siyao*) refers to the single point of meaning from which the immeasurable teachings proceed.

If one takes the *Lotus Sūtra* as the point of convergence, it is the place where the meanings are opened and unified. Because the one encompasses the immeasurable, it is called the "essential. "Matters" (*wu*) refers to the destination or the direction toward which one proceeds.
Furthermore, in the past, I never acted with recklessness by rashly explaining these matters to others, lest they should fall into suffering.

Thus, from what has been said above regarding the twelve [names], it is evident that the principles of the immeasurable and wondrous Dharma are revealed; one should know that the names and meanings of the remaining fourteen are likewise so.
Their meanings all pertain to both the esoteric and the exoteric, and can be understood through the power of intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) without the need for further verbal elaboration.

Next, the following explains the second section, the *Sūtra on the Auspicious Omens of Entering Samādhi*, which consists of four points: namely, time (*kāla*), ritual procedure (*vidhi*), name (*nāman*), and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
"Time" refers to the conclusion of the preceding [section], indicating that this is the appropriate time. "Ritual procedure" refers to the method by which [the samādhi] is entered;

there are four such procedures, among which sitting alone is the most excellent part. "Name" indicates which specific samādhi is entered. "Characteristics" refers to the signs manifested after having entered it. (And so forth.)

Clarifying its characteristics is also a functional application. The commentary consists of four parts: first, the sequential order of the intent; second, the meaning of the sequence beginning with "those who doubt";
third, the explanation of the text beginning with "body and mind"; and fourth, the explanation establishing the meaning of the auspicious signs beginning with the questions and answers.
Now, it is said that in discerning the essentials herein, there should be four points: first, for what reason is it called "entering"?
Regarding the two aspects of meditative concentration (*samādhi*): first, the sequence; second, the subsequent re-entry; third, the non-entry into the latter after the former.
First, within the initial intention, the first three are explained; subsequently, the latter two are clarified as part of the sequence. Within this, the entry into concentration is first explained;

the phrase "that which is wisdom" and below explains the meaning of the sequence. Within this section, there is both a heading and an explanation. Ancient and modern commentators have interpreted this as follows:

Regarding the statement "The mental hindrances are many; now they are directly designated as 'mutually accomplishing,'" this means that the two support and perfect one another to manifest non-duality.
The commentary states, "It is not [the case of] dhyāna, etc.," because without tranquility there can be no illumination, and without illumination there can be no tranquility.

Other texts explain: "Without dhyāna, wisdom has no means to exhaust its illumination; without wisdom, dhyāna has no means to reach the极致 (ultimate limit) of its tranquility. Thus it is said in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
To reprimand Śāriputra through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and to reprimand Maudgalyāyana through wisdom (*prajñā*) is precisely this meaning.

Now, in order to establish that the preceding wisdom is profound, [the Buddha] again gives rise to the subsequent discourse on the marvelous; thus, he enters meditative concentration. Regarding the explanation here of "entering concentration" while using the term "dhyāna," there is both a general and a specific sense.

Specifically speaking, "dhyāna" is general while "samādhi" is specific; however, when spoken of in terms of the perfect and pervasive interpenetration, they are mutually fused. Here, we follow the general sense.
It is said thus because it is perfectly pervasive (*pariniṣpanna*). The meaning of "entering" is as follows; how is the sequence of before and after?

The passage beginning with "that is, wisdom" (*ji zhi*) and below explains this. The first phrase clarifies that the essence and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are not without a sequence—there is no "before" and no "after.

The second phrase clarifies that because its function (*vṛtti*) is sovereign, it is able to manifest before and after without interval or obstruction. By this, the essence of wisdom is also without emerging or entering; it is function itself.

To speak of "entering and exiting" according to conditions is the third meaning. Taken as a whole, within the sequence of manifesting auspicious omens, there are no more than two things, namely concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Why? Because the raining of flowers, the shaking of the earth, the joy of the multitude, and the emission of light all arise from the power of concentration;
these are the essence and function of concentration. Thus, there are only these two. The subsequent passage on "abiding in oneself while saving beings" is also based on this.
Secondly, in terms of the Dharma, they are called Samādhi and Prajñā; in terms of metaphor, they are called hands and body; in terms of vows, they are called spiritual power and the power of wisdom.
As for the Buddha’s attendants—Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta—all are Samādhi and Prajñā.
These two are non-dual, yet they constitute the three entities. Self-benefit and benefiting others are fully encompassed within this. Therefore...
This treatise alone takes it as its essential thesis that these two categories universally encompass all things; reflect on this!
Jiaxiang [Jizang] considered them to be like a garment, a basket, a desk, and a stand—this is a grave contradiction; reflect on this, reflect on this!

The following section provides a sequential explanation of the meaning of "preface" (*nidāna*), while also explaining the latter two meanings. First, it explains the re-entry into the prior meditative concentration; second, it explains the non-entry into the subsequent concentration.

In the initial part, one may understand that a question is first posed. Within the explanation itself: first, it clarifies that entering [the concentration] beforehand serves as the preface for what follows, which is easily understood.
Next, it clarifies that one returns to enter [the concentration] precisely because it serves as the preface for the subsequent sutra. This is the text.

There is a heading, an explanation, and a concluding summary; the heading can be understood [as it stands]. Next, the subsequent section consists of a reverse explanation followed by a direct conclusion, both of which are intelligible.

If one were to proceed as follows, this would be an explanation that does not explicitly state the purpose for entering the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. If one were to first expound the meaning, the sūtra should require an initial entry into the "meaning-concentration" (*artha-samādhi*);

if one were to next expound the "wondrous" (*miao*), one should next enter the "wondrous-concentration" (*miao-samādhi*). Why, then, does one further enter the "meaning-concentration"? As for the commentator’s explanation: if one discusses...
The sequence of the principles ought to be exactly so; yet, for what reason is it not so now? The following section explains this meaning. What is that meaning?
It is precisely because this single name for the samādhi contains two meanings: it is manifest as the "correct" [teaching] for the former [part] and esoteric as the "sequence" for the latter.
The words are not prolix, yet the intent is fully exhausted—truly it may be called "sublime. Regarding what is contained within the text...
"Clarifying" (ming) refers to the meaning of explaining the esoteric through the exoteric as an introduction. It first involves a reverse explanation and only then concludes with a direct sequence.

This means that if the "wondrous concentration" (miaoding) were explicitly stated, the great assembly would not be greatly startled or doubtful; since the assembly would not be greatly startled or doubtful, Maitreya would not be so earnest;
and since he would not be so earnest, Mañjuśrī would have no reason for his reluctance. Without these three matters, [the discourse would not unfold].
It was unable to manifest the Dharma of the True Teaching, nor could it bring about the most sublime benefits for the assembly of the present age.

That it was able to manifest and bring about these results is precisely due to the merit of this title. For this reason, we know that directly stating this title serves as a profound and subtle introduction;
how could one not believe this? Matters concerning its concealment and preservation will be seen later on their own; there is no need to wait for further elaboration.
This is an elaborate text.
What follows below is the third section, which explains its meaning; the text consists of four phrases, which are briefly correlated as before.

Now, I shall only explain the latter two phrases—name (*nāman*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)—and not the former two. The reason for not explaining the former two is that their meaning regarding time is easy to understand.
Regarding the meaning of "knowledge of deportment" (*īryāpatha-jñāna*), its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are presented later in the section on emerging from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*).

This will be explained subsequently when the two following lines are commented upon; therein, the characteristics are first explained, followed by the name, and finally the meaning of it being the "introduction" (*nidāna*) is clarified.

First, regarding the characteristics: the meaning is that body and mind are unmoving. This manifests the functional power of this meditative concentration (*samādhi*). There is an explanation of this as follows:
The first line of the three [sections] provides a general heading for the two reasons why there is no movement;

it means that because the body and mind correspond with the phenomena of this meditative state, they are identical to the single true reality (*ekalakṣaṇa*). Next, there are six lines that provide a detailed explanation.

Among these, the first four lines specifically explain the characteristics of the meditative object (*ālambana*), including both its interpretation and its verification. The final two lines specifically explain the subject—the body and mind that take the object as their focus.

The final phrase of this section summarizes that it is because of their respective "objects" (*āśraya*) that they are able to achieve such capacities. The "source of the body" (*shen-yuan*) is the *dharmakāya*;
the "nature of the mind" (*xin-li*) is the innate nature (*prakṛti*) of the mind. Both are equally primordial simplicity (*tianzhen*), the locus of abiding, and there is no duality between them.
Next, regarding the proof of these two: when those two enter meditative concentration at different times, this [present case] is the entry at the initial time.
The names of the concentrations are clearly distinct, yet their essential natures and characteristics are identical, and their meanings are likewise so; therefore, they are taken as proof.
Next, the two [types of] objects of cognition have such characteristics that they are appropriately subsumed under the body’s form and the mind’s function, for their natures are mutually compatible.

Thus, the summary reveals the underlying cause and conditions, which may be understood. Next, regarding the explanation of the names: since the dharmas of concentration are universal, it is necessary to demonstrate them.

The name is identical to the essence, and from it function follows; what was formerly considered as "name" is, in the present context, identical to illumination yet eternally quiescent—this is the convergence into one.
This name has both general and specific meanings; this text explains only the specific meaning and not the general one.

The old tradition calls it "the sphere of right mind-action," also "harmonized and straightened concentration," or "right concentration. The new tradition calls it "samādhi" (equanimity-maintenance); its meaning is thus clear.

In this passage, the inclusion of the two characters "shìjiān" (worldly) seems superfluous. Furthermore, according to the sequence of both the text and its meaning, one should first explain these names and phrases, followed by the explanation of "immovability" (*acala*), which serves as the sequential order for the section on "manifestation" (*prabhāvanā*). Thus, the current text appears to lack proper sequential order.

Next, regarding the meaning of "manifestation" as sequential order: previously, it was explained in general terms that entering meditative absorption constitutes the sequential order; here, [it is explained] specifically.

This is a distinct clarification of the sequence based on the meaning of the immobility of body and mind. Regarding the mention of "movement," "discrimination," and so forth: previously, this was discussed in terms of the capacity that manifests the object;

here, it is discussed in terms of the capacity that integrates with the object. Furthermore, while the previous section clarified that which has already entered [the state], this concerns that which has not yet entered;
thus, it differs from what preceded. Moreover, this represents the principle of illumination-and-function being quiescent, signifying the gathering of all [phenomena] back into the One.
Since the meaning of the "Preface" (xu) seems to derive from this [present] sense, I do not follow the sequential order of the preceding text.

Next, regarding the analysis of the meaning of the two auspicious signs (*śakuna*) that herald the preaching of the *Samādhi*, the interpretations of both ancient and modern scholars have all failed to take the three factors—the preaching, the stabilization, and the joy of the assembly—as the auspicious signs;
rather, they have taken only the other three. However, both the Guangzhai [School] and the present [author] take all six as such.

The commentary on the two [points] regarding auspicious signs (*śakuna*) is now concluded. Regarding those who do not consider [certain things] to be such, the explanation clarifies that all [of them] are indeed auspicious signs.
First, the question establishes the definition of an auspicious sign by taking up the meaning of "extraordinary" (*visiṣṭa*) as being applicable to all such signs.

Below, it clarifies that the two [specific cases] are not extraordinary and therefore cannot be considered auspicious signs. In the response, the two meanings are first explained individually, followed by a general summary citing scriptural passages.
Since these manifest as both extraordinary and marvelous, they are all auspicious signs; it is certainly not right to claim they are not such signs. The *Erya* states:
"Susu denotes reverence," referring to the appearance of the utmost respect. With physical deference and mental veneration, I especially hope to hear your subsequent explanation.
As for those who speak of "ordinary sentiments," this refers to ordinary people who follow their own inclinations in choosing and rejecting, thereby deviating from the Way of the Sages.
Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the auspicious signs (*praṇidhāna*), the first two signs among them are common to both sūtras;

therefore, the preaching of the Dharma constitutes the "Correct" [portion], while the entry into meditative absorption (*samādhi*) constitutes the "Introductory" portion—these together form the two introductory sections. The four signs following these, however, exclusively serve as the introduction to this specific sūtra.
Within these, the scriptural text contains six phrases, yet in meaning there are eight; six are readily understood, while one additionally explains the "time," and the remaining six are complete.
The commentary on the text clarifies that one should understand this through the following points: first, the time of the rain; second, that from which it proceeds; third, its number;

fourth, the distinction of its names; (and so forth). There are eight meanings: first, the time of the rain; second, that from which it proceeds; third, its number; fourth, the names of its distinct positions;
fifth, its color; sixth, that which is rained down; seventh, the general name "flower"; eighth, scattering [the flowers] upon the Buddha and the assembly. Furthermore, within these eight points:
However, it does not explain the "one" [vehicle] at this time; the remaining seven points are explained in the text, so one should know them from there.

Jiaxiang says that this is precisely the time when the fourfold assembly hears the sutra and awakens to the One Vehicle. Now, I say this is a grave error. It is impossible for either of the two preceding cases to be so;
let those with discernment know this. It cannot be said now that as soon as the explanation of the meaning of the sutra is finished, he immediately enters this samādhi.

Because this is the time [for such an event], the subsequent scriptural passage states: "When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, he immediately [ascended] upon the Dharma-seat," and so forth;
since these clear words are present here, how could they be erroneous? Regarding the seven meanings below, the text itself provides the explanation. Within this, there are two parts:

first, distinguishing the flowers that serve as the signifiers (the "old" tradition says "and so forth" below); second, explaining the dharmas that are signified. The first two auspicious omens apply commonly to both.

Because it is based on the *sūtra*, this exposition of the Dharma is correct; it is the introduction (*nidāna*). Entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) constitute two types of introductions.
What follows below—the four auspicious omens—is exclusively the introduction to this specific *sūtra*. The first [section] has four meanings: 1. Translating the name; 2. Citing alternative names; 3.

Generally manifesting its essence and function as "wondrous" (*miao*); 4. Specifically clarifying the number of its colors, which remain numerous. Regarding the first [point], the ancient translations were as follows; concerning the color, it is only...
Secondly, regarding their forms, they are distinguished as four; among these, because two of the sounds are *mahā*, there is a distinction between "great" and "small.
It is the same in the subsequent translation of the differences. Master Xiāngyún said that the first two are white flowers and the latter two are red.

Furthermore, he cited Dàolǎng of Hexi, who stated that these are all names for celestial flowers: the first two are red flowers and the latter two are white flowers. This explains the initial [classification].
The second [set] has a color like vermilion yet yellow, like azure yet purple, like green yet red. The next two white ones are a brilliant white, for which no other white can serve as a metaphor.
The commentary on the Sūtra states: "The first two are the *ruci* (as one wishes) and *mahāruci* (great as one wishes) flowers;

the next two are the *mṛdu* (soft), *mahāmṛdu* (greatly soft), *ghoṣavat* (resonant), and *mahāghoṣavat* (greatly resonant) flowers. (I now suggest that there may be omissions or errors here, and it should perhaps read: "the *mṛdu* and *mahāmṛdu*, and the *ghoṣavat* and *mahāghoṣavat* flowers. Radiance.
The *Zhai* [Commentary] states: "The first two are red circular flowers, small and large; the latter two are white circular flowers, small and large.

This is what Jiaxiang described, and the old tradition follows this directly without further analysis or interpretation. The *Xin* [Commentary] states: "The first two are 'pleasing' (*shiyi*) flowers, small and large;
the next two are 'soft' (*roumian*) flowers, small and large. The commentary explains that "pleasing" means they can cause the hearts of those who see them to be joyful and satisfied.
This is derived from its function; as for "soft" (*mṛdvī*), since the body of the flower is soft, it also causes the three karmas of those who see it to become harmonious and supple.

Thus, it is named according to both its essence and its function. Regarding the translations of names mentioned above, such differences between ancient and modern versions are due to the fact that these are wondrous flowers of the heavens, which inherently contain many meanings.
Each may be taken according to what is emphasized, or perhaps due to transcriptional errors, the various translations of the names differ as clarified in the scriptures.
The initial term "yi" (意) means "to accord with one's wishes"; the text omits the two characters for "accordance. The subsequent term "boxiang" (博響) refers to "broad renown":
"bo" means extensive, and "xiang" means universal resonance; this is the "Great Sound" (*mahā-ghoṣa*) mentioned previously, which signifies "accordance with one's wishes.
As stated before, "boxiang" means that the fame of this flower’s supreme sound is widely heard. All older editions read "boxu xiang" (博浦響), but [the correct reading is as given].

To change [the term] to "resonance of the harbor" (puxiang) is not considered beautiful; to call it "wondrous" (miao) means that its celestial flowers (tianhua) are immeasurable, for this is the most supreme and unsurpassed.
Its essence and function are without fixed direction, as explained previously; thus, it is called "wondrous" because no other wondrous object can manifest its wondrous Dharma.
Next, to clarify that the number of colors is still many, it is not merely like the previous two, red and white.
Furthermore, there are five types [of colors]. If one refers to the ordinary five colors of this region, they are the colors of the five directions;
alternatively, purple may be substituted for black. If it follows the translation by Master Lang mentioned previously, there are six colors, with white still placed at the end.
The reason for citing this sutra is to establish that the preceding two colors are expanded into four; thus, it does not simply state "four" directly.
The statement that "five and six are simply two, yet they constitute four" is what is indicated by the shadow, as will be explained by the author himself later.

Above, the explanation of the names and characteristics of the flowers that serve as the indicators is complete; below, there follows the explanation of the phenomena indicated, which consists of three parts:

first, the presentation of the ancient interpretation, followed by the critique beginning with "I [now] say"; second, the analysis of why the ancient view was incorrect, followed by the current explanation beginning with "the words [of the ancients] were not appropriate."
This is the third correct explanation. Within the initial description, the first part clarifies what is signified by the two "twos" and four [categories];
the following single phrase clarifies what is signified by the "combined flowers. The primary intent correctly explains that, based on form (*rūpa*), there are two things signified;
therefore, it signifies the place of emergence. Because the two names possess both small and large [dimensions], they signify the four combined. Thus, these two have already been explained.

This is manifested in the four dharmas. The reason the sequence of the two forms of matter (*rūpa*) is thus is that it intends to clarify that in the first two, form and dress have not yet changed and the defiled dharmas are not yet deep;
the next two are the reverse of this. Because the first [two] possess the distinction between male and female, there is "great" and "small";

the next two are likewise so. Regarding the subsequent mention of "causes not yet having borne fruit," it is because of the flowers that these four assemblies are spoken of, even though they existed in the past.
Since the attainment of the fruit is not yet the actual fruit but is merely its cause, it is represented by this;
herein there are three meanings, namely, the three dharmas symbolized by the two [types of] fourfold flowers.
From here below, the next section distinguishes that which is not yet appropriate; herein there are two parts: first, indicating the deficiency, and second, explaining the reason for it.
The indication of the deficiency has two aspects: "narrowness" refers to the fact that the phenomena represented by the number are not comprehensive;

"inadequacy" refers to the fact that the flowers represent what is not the past cause, and thus they do not correspond to the three meanings previously represented. These are the three meanings represented by the preceding three [flowers].
This is not yet correct; the subsequent explanation contains two meanings, each with its own conclusion, which is easy to see in the text.

As for the phrase "discussing directly," it means that one discusses the four [categories] such as bhikṣus directly. As for the phrase "sixteen," it means that within each of those four, there are four sub-categories such as "setting out" (prasthāna) and so forth.
This is because the direct discussion mentions only the four such as bhikṣus, whereas the [sub-categories] such as "setting out" are not mentioned therein.
Since it cannot be fully subsumed, it is provisionally discussed according to the Three Teachings, resulting in forty-eight [categories].

This is because there is no meaning of "provisional teaching" (yàojiào) here; furthermore, as for the assembly of Bodhisattvas and various others, all can be understood through the mind and cannot be manifested through words.

Next, if one were to speak of "retribution fruits" (bàoguǒ) and so forth, such terms do not exist here; rather, these words are now spoken as a provisional concession, and thus it should rain accordingly.
Furthermore, if it were said that the present fruit manifests past causes and future fruits are revealed, then both flowers and fruits should rain down together, rather than flowers alone.
Huìquán says: "Since this does not accord with the correct principle, it is improper to explain it thus. Sēngxiāo says:

"That only four kinds of flowers rain down precisely symbolizes that the four assemblies shall attain Buddhahood; the first two flowers symbolize the attainment of Buddhahood by the two assemblies of those who have left the household life."
The latter two flowers signify that the two assemblies of the householders manifest the attainment of Buddhahood; therefore, only four flowers rain down.

The first two are white flowers, signifying that those of the Two Vehicles attain Buddhahood through untainted (*anāsrava*) realization. The latter two are red flowers, signifying that humans and devas, though possessing tainted (*sāsrava*) suffering, will likewise attain Buddhahood after a long time.
That all proceed from the Small Vehicle to the Great Vehicle signifies that their cultivation proceeds from the small to the ultimate.

This proceeds from the shallow toward the profound. Now, examining this commentary, it correctly explains that while the four flowers can symbolize the "one" (the Buddha), there are two "fours" that they symbolize.
That is to say, the first four represent the various assemblies, and the subsequent two represent the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, devas, and humans.

As for the claim that these flowers directly symbolize the attainment of Buddhahood, this principle has not been applied at all; they remain as previously explained, being held in a manner that is inappropriate and should not be counted among the [primary] numbers.
It is not merely that one or two [points] are explained; rather, much more is elucidated, none of which falls outside the scope of the two faults you have raised in your critique.
By grasping the essential intent previously established, there is no difference in the capacity to evoke [realization], and so forth.
Next follows the present formal exposition, which consists of four parts: first, the formal exposition; second, the citation of scriptural evidence;

third, the resolution of doubts; and fourth, the repeated clarification and manifestation. Within the first part, there are further four sub-sections: first, the explanation of the four flowers; second, the explanation of the rain from heaven;

third, the explanation of scattering [the flowers] upon the Buddha; and fourth, the explanation of [the scattering] by the fourfold assembly. Regarding the first of these, because the previous established interpretation was not yet appropriate, its correct meaning is now revealed; thus, it is called "correct."

The meaning is that the three [vehicles] of the past were all partial causes and not the perfect cause; this reveals that the present opening and revealing shows that all equally enter the one perfect cause.

The text is divided into two parts: first, it indicates that the three of the past were not the middle [truth], because they relied on the perfect cause as a relative contrast, and thus only spoke of the three as being partial.
Regarding the "two vehicles," while the Flower [Garland Sūtra] is extremely pure, the bodhisattvas of this teaching have not yet severed [all afflictions].

Because their delusions are the same as those of humans and devas, they are said to be "two vehicles. Because they share the commonality of severing [delusions], they are the causes for all three vehicles.
Because their specific stages differ in sequence—being prior or posterior—they are the exclusive dharmas of Bodhisattvas. Thus, these are all partial causes and not the perfect cause;
nor are they the single, true, wondrous cause. If all three teachings were to attain the fruit, it would be as previously explained in the sutras.
This is the meaning of the four fruits. Why, then, is it now said that they are explained by way of mutual comparison? It is because of the principle of the "gate of skillful means" (*upāyamukha*).

Next, to correctly reveal what this refers to: although the flowers are rained down as one single rain, they are able to be so distinct and manifest because those that are coarse are due to this rain of celestial flowers, while those that are subtle are likewise so.
Even the mere raining down of celestial flowers already transcends the realm of insentient things.

How much more so when considering the wondrous past, where the forms were both manifest and perfect, and the numbers naturally revealed themselves. First, regarding the contrast with what was previously non-existent, the designation "the Buddha as the cause" is explained below.
