First, the term "retribution" (*vipāka*) means that all have equally attained it; the Buddha is a person of the Perfect [Teaching] (*yuan*), and thus naturally shares in this Dharma, which is borrowed here to represent the wondrous perfection of the Perfect.
Because these are the wondrous flowers of the heavens, they represent the Buddha as the cause; this, for now, provides a general clarification.

The meaning of the four distinct [stages] indicated by the "celestial flowers" has not yet been clarified. Although the subsequent explanation carries the sense of "flowers," it is precisely an exposition of what those four represent.
Within this explanation, there is a general heading, a detailed analysis, and a concluding summary. As for the heading:

since they represent the perfect cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*), and yet there are four, these four positions of the cause represent the causes of the four stages. The "wheel" is a metaphor for these four stages; that is to say, copper... [and so forth].
The *Silver, Gold, and Lapis Lazuli Wheel* is also not outside the *Bodhisattva-ābharaṇa-sūtra*. However, there are two versions:
one titled *Bodhisattva-ābharaṇa-sūtra* in ten fascicles, and another titled *Bodhisattva-mūla-karma-ābharaṇa-sūtra* in two fascicles.

Because their titles are identical, ancient scholars distinguished between them, referring to them as the "Small" and "Large" *Ābharaṇas*. For the sake of convenience, they may simply be called by their abbreviated names.

The *Xiǎoběn* (Small Version) serves as the primary source for the text of the *Běnyè jīng* (Sūtra on the Original Acts). In what follows, I shall cite directly from it according to its current title; one should understand it by this name alone.

This present work is precisely that "Small Version," which is the *Běnyè jīng*. Within the sūtra, the six wheels (*ṣaḍ-cakra*) are fully elucidated; to the preceding four, two more—*maṇi* and *sphaṭika*—are added.

These correspond sequentially to the metaphors for the stages of practice: *xiū* (practice), *zhù* (abiding), *xiàng* (orientation), and the various *bhūmi*s (stages), up to the ultimate wondrous state.
The "six stages" (ṣaḍ-bhūmi) and the "wheel" (cakra) express the meaning of the essence and function of what precedes them; that is, the essence and function of the six stages.

This refers generally to cause and effect. Because their depths and shallows differ, there are seven [stages], yet the distinction between six and seven arises from the fact that within the perfectly wondrous [state], they are non-different while appearing different.
That sūtra also mentions the iron wheel, but in its commentary only the six are clarified; furthermore, there are many other varieties.

The six meanings are numerous and have not yet been fully described; now, regarding the fourfold rain of flowers, because their fruits are not discussed based on the four stages, only those four are taken up.

Although the six meanings are inherently present within the causes, they are not discussed in terms of their sequence, as these represent the true cause while simultaneously manifesting other meanings.
As for why only the true cause is taken up: the pervasive delusions were already severed in the past and will not arise again.
This refers to causing [beings] to enter the stage that resembles [the ultimate]. Regarding the detailed explanation of the four [stages] below, there are four distinct sections.
Within each of these, there are five meanings: the first always cites the flower that serves as the signifier, while the subsequent four clarify the dharmas of the stages signified.
Within those signified dharmas of the stages, the first three meet with what is clarified in the *Original Karma Sūtra*, and the final one meets with this present sūtra.

Regarding what is explained in the subsequent text, among those three [categories], the first in each is the metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the latter two are the dharmas illustrated by the metaphor (*dārṣṭāntika*).
Since that sūtra explains this across six stages through various types of "sixes," I have here briefly cited the three essentials; these should be fully set forth [in detail] (etc.).

Next, regarding "nature" (*prakṛti*): the nature of both innate (*prakṛti*) and acquired (*paribhāvita*) natures appears inconsistently in the sacred teachings (*āgama*), with their sequence being interchangeable depending on the cause.
Nature is formed through habituation, and habituation completes nature; therefore, it is not fixed, as this refers to its formation through causes and habituation.
Next, regarding the statement "the path" and "relying on that sutra": it is because one who can cultivate the Middle Way is able to penetrate and enter the nature of the sages.

According to this underlying meaning, within the path of the three truths, they are harmoniously integrated and become increasingly profound. As for the "nature of the sages," it is that which can [employ] the three wisdoms and the three...

Because they are created with the equality of the truths and are supreme, they are called the "Noble Nature" (*āryatva*). The four meanings, such as "opening" (*vivaraṇa*) and so forth, will be explained in detail later;

there is no need to discuss them here. Regarding the four stages within the cause of the concordant example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta-hetu*), the sequence of white, red, small, and large has already been explained previously;
it differs only in that [the former] uses a circle (*vṛtta*). (etc. As for the concluding summary below: these four wheels are used as metaphors by him.
Because of the four stages [of the cause], one knows that the current four flowers precisely symbolize these four stages;

since their meaning is identical to that [cause], one knows that the four flowers are symbols of the four stages of the cause. This is the sequential meaning based on the two colors and the four names.

If [the order] were first white and then later yellow, the meaning would seem inconvenient; however, if one follows the sequential names such as "pleasing to the mind" (*rucira*) and so forth, it may also be acceptable.
The summary of this section consists of four points, which explain the four flowers. Regarding the subsequent explanation of the meaning symbolized by the rain falling from the heavens:

first, the dharma symbolized is presented. There are many kinds of heavens; here, the "worldly heaven" (*laukika-deva*) is used to represent the "supramundane heaven of the ultimate truth" (*lokottara-paramārtha-deva*).

It should be understood that this [supramundane heaven] is able to represent what the worldly heaven represents: namely, it is the locus upon which the perfect and wondrous cause (*pariniṣpanna-kuśala-hetu*) relies.

Because it is manifested here, the character for "heaven" (天) is explained by "rain" (雨), and the character for "rain" (雨) is explained by "heaven" (天). The pronunciation of the character for "rain" (雨) admits of both readings; its meaning can be understood accordingly.

Here, we specifically follow the departing tone (*qùshēng*), which carries the sense of descending and emerging; therefore, it is explained by the character for "birth" (生). The phrase "by these means" (*yóushìděng*) indicates that these characters are used in conjunction to provide a layered explanation.

Below, the meaning manifested by the Buddha's subject and object is explained through the term "dispersion" (*sàn*). Regarding "dispersion of the Buddha" (*sàn fó*): *Note: This passage appears to be a commentary on a Buddhist technical term, likely *vairocana* or a related concept involving the manifestation of light or rain from heaven. The text discusses the phonological and semantic interplay between the characters 天 (heaven), 雨 (rain), and 生 (birth).*
This is that which expresses the attainment of the fruit; the Buddha is the person who has realized this ultimate fruit. Therefore, it indicates that [the practitioner] shall attain it.

Because it arises from its source, it is named "Heaven of Meaning" (*Arthadhatu*). The essence of this ultimate Heaven of Meaning is termed the "Fruit. This Fruit is the Sublime Enlightenment (*Sambodhi*);
its original function is named the "Crystal Wheel," signifying that its essence and function are pure, wondrous, and supreme, as well as being pervasive.
The "affairs of the great assembly" (mahāparṣad) are that which expresses; these people of the great assembly are the "dharma expressed" by the realization of cause and effect.

"Realization" (kē) means to pursue and attain. Regarding the three phrases beginning with "the heavens rained," although various commentators have generally stated what they express, most explain them in terms of concrete events (*vastu*), saying that the various devas made offerings because they had heard the Dharma. Thus, even though it is peripheral...
Because these meanings are not the primary focus of the text, they are not discussed here; rather, only the ultimate essentials are stated.

To summarize them now in order to highlight their core significance: the various preceding meanings do not exceed three pairs—namely, nature and cultivation (*xing-xiu*), cause and effect (*yin-guo*), and person and dharma (*ren-fa*).
The rain falling from heaven symbolizes that cultivation is clarified by relying upon nature, yet it scatters [in diverse ways].
The "Buddha" indicates the cause by which one proceeds toward the fruit; "cause and fruit" are the Dharma, while "the great assembly" refers to the people.

This indicates that the Dharma of cause and fruit is that which has been brought forth through the realization of these people. If this is so, is it not essential to exhaustively investigate this meaning?
To leave it unexamined would mean that all the interpretations of past and present are of no practical use. Someone may ask: "Is the Buddha not a human being?"

It may be said that this Dharma is entrusted to a person of wondrous virtue to manifest the fruit of the wondrous Dharma; one should know that the meaning of the single character "san" (to scatter/dispense) applies to both contexts.
Therefore, at the beginning of the text, it is first explained as "tending toward" (*qu*) and subsequently as "eliciting and attaining" (*ganku*).
Reflect upon how the essential significance of such a principle is indeed beyond doubt. Contemplate this.

Below, I shall next cite three passages from this sutra to corroborate the essential points of the formal exposition, which previously explained the four meanings of the "perfect cause" (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*) by means of four stages.
Since this is so, it is clear that the auspicious omens in the introduction specifically manifest these [meanings]. How else could they be reconciled with faith?
As for the phrase "section by section," it refers to the three sections; in the *Avataṃsaka*, all [sections] are based on the four directions.

This is manifested in four stages; the current mention of "wandering through the four directions" and "leaping forth from the four directions" is identical to that [previous description], and thus refers to the four stages of the true sages (*ārya*).
As for the three textual passages and their meanings, they shall be clarified by themselves as the text proceeds.
The following two rounds of question and answer constitute a threefold critical analysis intended to resolve doubts and remove obstacles. The intent of the first question is as follows:
In the *Benye jing* (Sutra on the Original Vows), the sequence [of stages] is not harmonized, and other passages all explain the meaning of distinct positions (*bie wei*).

Here, however, the opening and unification (*kaihui*) is used to clarify the meaning of the perfect position (*yuan wei*). How could using that [text] as an explanation be appropriate? It appears close but is actually remote.
Because it is necessary to provide an exegesis, this question and answer are presented. Although the commentary [of Tiantai] is extremely concise and clear, its principles are profoundly subtle;
here, the inferior is used as an illustration for the superior. As for the term "universal" (*tong*), it refers to what the Sūtra calls "true śrāvakas" and "true arhats.
While the Sūtra text briefly cites these two universal and specific names, in their full form, the four specific types should be mentioned collectively. This is why they are so named.

The text of the True Scripture itself explains this as encompassing the two preceding teachings; thus it is called "the meaning that encompasses" (*tongyi*). Since it exists solely within the Perfect [Teaching], it is called "the perfect meaning" (*yiyuan*).

If even that which is named "inferior" yet distinct can still be harmonized with the Perfect Principle, how much more so for that which is "distinct and superior," where the names are identical yet the meanings cannot be considered perfect?
Herein, this is the introduction; for now, I shall borrow these names to manifest the underlying meaning. If...
Having already explained the opening [of the teaching], the arrangement of the stages is precisely that which you all practice: this is the Bodhisattva path.

There is not a single person or phenomenon that is not ultimately wondrous. If even such names as "human" and "deva" are themselves the Perfect [Teaching], how much more so are names such as the "Distinct" (Pratyekabuddha)?

As explained in the *Commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, if even names such as "all evils" are identical to the wondrous meaning, how much more so are names such as the "Distinct"? Next is the question and answer.

This section distinguishes between the "perfect" (yuan) and the "distinct" (bie). Previously, the distinct was used as the perfect; now it is clarified that there remains a difference from the distinct.

First, the distinct existence is raised to question the perfect sameness; this is not yet correct, as it serves to initiate the discussion on sameness and difference. The answer contains two parts: first, clarifying that although they are equally existent, there is further difference;

second, explaining "sameness" as the existence of both the worthy (xian) and the sage (sheng), and "difference" as the further presence of four propositions. Thus, sameness and difference are discussed in combination.

There are thus six propositions; their meanings and characteristics have already been analyzed in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). Previous commentators have interpreted this in three different ways (*etc.*).
In explaining this, one should proceed in three stages: first, the *Xuanyi*; second, the ancient interpretations; and third, the present intention.
Although these three or four [approaches] exist, the two texts have not yet been fully reconciled. Now, it is necessary to briefly describe the *Xuanyiwen* (Text on the Profound Meaning), and then...
To synthesize this meaning, the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), fascicle nine, establishes two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) to examine the sense of the gradual perfection of cause and effect.
The first set—gradual, perfect, gradual-perfect, and perfect-gradual—is not the intended meaning here and is not described in detail.

The second set employs six propositions to clarify the stages of the worthy and the sage; since there are two for each of the single, mutual, and double [combinations], they constitute six propositions.

Although the thirty minds (the ten abidings, ten practices, and ten transferences) all share the meaning of "worthy" (*xián*) and "sage" (*shèng*), they are termed "worthy" because they suppress [afflictions] more and sever them less;

thus, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are termed "sages" because they suppress them less and sever them more—this is the distinction between the two. Furthermore, the ten abidings are called "worthy sages" (*xiánshèng*) and the twenty minds are called "sage worthies" (*shèngxián*)—this is their mutual interchangeability.

The ten stages and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāyogi-bodhi*) are "sages," while the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) is the "supreme sage"—this is the distinction between the sages themselves.

This is important; it is what is explained in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). One should not rely on the previous four commentaries, as they do not follow the sequence [of the text] and thus constitute six points rather than four.
For now, I shall provide an exegesis by correlating [the text] with the *Xuanyi* and the various earlier commentaries.

However, even if one were to rely directly upon the text of the *Xuanyi* and the aforementioned commentaries, one would still be unable to fully comprehend the essential purport herein. Nevertheless, since the *Xuanyi* is not entirely identical to this [text], it refers to...
That [text] merely takes that [passage] as an analogy; its explanation does not mean they are identical. If they were indeed identical, there would be two impossibilities:
first, while the number of phrases would be exactly the same, the names would be inconvenient; second, the meaning would also be inconvenient.

This is because it uses those [phrases] precisely to separately manifest the Perfect [Teaching], for that meaning is different from this one. Since it is already stated that "the present usage employs those phrases," [the distinction is clear].
By means of the shifting and reciprocal application of these meanings, it is made manifest that all things herein are universally pervasive and unimpeded.
What are they? First, the worthy; second, the sage; third, the worthy-sage; fourth, the sage-worthy; fifth, the sage-sage; sixth, the worthy-worthy.

The first refers to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*); the next refers to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) and above, up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*tathāgata-bhūmi*). The third and fourth phrases refer to... [text ends]

The three stages of worthiness (san-xian) correspond to the first stage [of the ten abidings], while the five stages from the first ground up to the wondrous enlightenment (miao-jue) constitute the sixth stage.

This is because, although the provisional and real teaching gates (quan-shi jiao-men) clarify many levels, their essential points do not exceed the two distinctions of worthiness (xian) and sagehood (sheng).

The Perfect Teaching (yuan) is likewise; by merely designating these two names, the essential substance of the levels is fully exhausted. As for the thirty minds (san-shi xin), they pertain to their respective divisions.
That is to say, while they are "sages" (*ārya*) within the "worthy" (*bhadra*) family, they are distinct; yet, while they are "worthy," they are "sages" within the "perfect" (*pariniṣpanna*).

Because these two are discussed in combination, they are called "Worthy-Sages" (*bhadra-ārya*). Furthermore, although their essence is identical to the perfect, the designation does not abandon its distinctiveness.

Moreover, in contrast to what follows, this "sage" is also called "worthy"; because name and essence are discussed together, they are called "Sage-Worthy" (*ārya-bhadra*). From one's own stage upward, all have always been sages; furthermore, in contrast to [the preceding], [they are so designated].
The preceding section also involves a partial classification based on a combined discussion of the "sages" (ārya); thus, the ten stages of faith are also partially "worthy ones" (bhadra).

Furthermore, when these worthy ones are discussed in combination with those sages, they are called "worthy-ones-of-the-worthy," because they represent the gradual progression toward those sages and worthy ones.

Since there are already sages, the sages must necessarily include this stage. Moreover, according to the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), since there is both the gradual and the perfect, and since the perfect is itself perfect, this stage must necessarily exist.

The phrase "venerating the worthy" (*xianxian*) is a direct citation from the *Zhengtun* (Treatise on Rectifying the Confusion). However, only the first two phrases specifically manifest the interpretation of our own school’s exposition of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Thus, there are those four phrases; precisely by means of these four phrases, they represent the four stages.

This is because the three levels of the Worthy (*sanxian*) are all designated as "sages" (*sheng*), hence there are the middle two phrases. Since there are already the middle two phrases, there are consequently the final two phrases.
There are four [categories], which together with the preceding ones make six. These six phrases encompass all textual meanings, both general and specific;
therefore, one should refer to the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) to apply this analogy for comprehensive understanding. One must not rely exclusively on that [text].

If one were to rely solely on it, why would the ten levels of faith not be called "worthy" (*xian*)? How would the distinct teachings differ from one another, and how could the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) be fully revealed?

The meaning of "perfect" (*yuan*) in that *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning) is intended to clarify the revelation and manifestation [of the truth], and thus it does not entirely coincide with this [text].
It may, however, be appended as an analogous case to elucidate what is presented here; therefore, that work is cited precisely because it has not yet fully harmonized with this.

The interpretations offered by predecessors are threefold, yet they do not entirely coincide with that [work] either. Although they do not entirely coincide with it, that work concludes by ultimately harmonizing with this.

Now, by employing their names, numbers, and meanings, and through the principles of opening, closing, and harmonizing, one can clearly manifest the intent within this [text]; thus, both the general and specific textual meanings will be fully understood and integrated.

Reflect upon this, reflect upon it! Further seek the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), the section on the "Stages of the Sublime," and the text on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (*catur-smṛtyupasthāna*).

From this point downward, the text further refutes what is not that [the subject] rather than explicitly demonstrating what is this [the subject], because there have been those in the past who have offered such an interpretation;

therefore, it is refuted again. Within the text, each of the three layers contains both the "expresser" (nirdeśaka) and the "expressed" (nirdiṣṭa). Each of these two—the expresser and the expressed—possesses two meanings that may be investigated.

Furthermore, within each of these two, there are again three types: those that fall into the middle, those that precede the middle, and those that follow the middle. Each of these three also possesses its own internal subdivisions.

Because humans share the same cause, they are distinguished within the middle [category]; although the term "bodhisattva" is used universally to exclude the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), it does not yet exclude those who follow the gradual stages (*anupūrvika*). Therefore, the following summary does not establish this as being distinct, as previously stated—referring to the causes of the four aforementioned positions. As for the absence of the fourfold explanation in the text, it is not that the meaning is lacking; rather, there was no desire for prolixity. If one were to speak of it in general terms: [The passage continues with the summary: "Humans are the same because they share a single cause. This distinguishes them from within the intermediate category. Although the word "bodhisattva" is employed universally to set aside the two vehicles, it has not yet excluded those who proceed by stages; thus, the subsequent summary does not clarify this as being distinct. This refers to the causes of the four positions mentioned before.

Regarding the fact that the fourfold interpretation is not present in the text, it is not that its significance is absent; it is simply that the author did not wish to burden the text with excessive detail. If one were to express it in summary fashion:
The signifier and the signified constitute the world; the perfected cause and effect constitute the human realm; that which rains down from heaven constitutes the manifestation of the Middle Way;
and the principle manifested therein is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). These six phrases of the perfected stage are non-spatial and transcend all attachments;

this is the application of antidotes. Thus, both the signifier and the signified are wondrous rather than coarse. Furthermore, the manifestation of the coarse becomes the wondrous; this is the fundamental and the derivative aspects of the teaching’s meaning.
The principles and precedents can be understood from what has been stated before and after.
Since the meaning of the "wondrous contemplation" (*miao guan*) when the Deva Śakra sent down rain can be inferred by these same precedents, it need not be elaborated upon further.

Next, regarding the auspicious sign of the earthquake: following the previous sequence, the former sign indicated the cause of perfect enlightenment (*yuan*), while this indicates that perfect enlightenment is about to be realized.

If it is for this reason that the former four and these six [are distinguished], then there should only be one or two; since these [six] apply to both cause and fruit, the former four should also apply to both.

As for the previous statement that [the flowers] were scattered over the Buddha, they also apply to the fruit because they fell as rain-like blossoms. Thus, while they are spoken of as causes, they are also fruits;
yet, although the meaning applies to both, the intent is distinct, and we follow the specific distinction here. There are two parts to the scriptural text.
The phrase contains three meanings, which the commentary explains in full detail; the text itself also has three parts: first, the citation of the old interpretation;

second, the refutation of that error; and third, the correct explanation. First, regarding the meaning of the old interpretation: it indicates that the meanings of both subject and object are contained within this sutra, and thus there is no need for further elaboration.
Because the three types of people each cling to these as being real, they are called "fixed"; yet, because they are not actually real, they are [referred to as such].
Since the point was already stated and would naturally be included in the formal citation, the text uses the expression "three sixes" as a shorthand;
thus, the statement is made by way of ellipsis. It restates the previous point precisely to serve as the introduction to the following refutation, meaning that if one interprets it in this manner...

The following section concerns "giving and then taking away," which serves to break down [the previous understanding]. Because the underlying principle expressed was not yet appropriate, and because one must follow its literal meaning, it is called "giving.
This "giving" refers to the Three Baskets (Tripitaka); the "taking away" refers to the fact that the universal and particular aspects have not been fully exhausted.

This is why this auspicious sign appeared. First, regarding the universal aspect, there is first the heading and then the explanation. Ten pairs are presented as headings for "giving and taking away. In the explanation, although only the meaning of "taking away" is explicitly explained.
The Master Xushì explains that these are "hidden" (zàng) but not yet "penetrated" (tōng), because the three attachments regarding persons and dharmas are each fixed as distinct;
furthermore, since the latter two meanings have not yet been established, it is known that this refers only to the first [meaning]. Next, he explains "unmanifested" (wèi):

both refer to the two types of *nirvāṇa*—the substantial (*tǐ*) and the phenomenal (*fǎ*). The intended meaning is whether the three dharmas—the fundamental afflictions, the secondary afflictions, and their exhaustion—are exhausted or not exhausted; they are both.
That which is refuted is not real; therefore, the refuter does not know that it is identical [to the refutation], but speaks only of the three differences.

This is because the former [the refuted] is subsequently sublated by the latter. First, it clarifies why that [the former] is not refuted; next, it clarifies why the present [the latter] must be refuted. As for the reason one knows it is not refuted:
first, since they do not even understand the general [principle], how much less could they understand this specific expedient means? Second, [they do not understand it].

Since these [three] lack the designation of "three" or "six," yet the term "three and six" is used, we know that the established doctrine is certainly not being subverted. Next, it clarifies that even now [the opponent's view] is being subverted:

since there are neither three nor six, by what means would one express the number of things being subverted? Furthermore, for what reason is it necessary to refute and explain them? The commentator replies:

although there are no three persons or three causes and effects, there is the principle of the three dharmas and their causes and effects; therefore, they are expressed in order to indicate what is being subverted.

These numbers are not deficient because they are arranged both vertically and horizontally; thus, they would otherwise violate principle and contradict the teaching. To "contradict the teaching" means that the Sūtra states they are neither vertical nor horizontal.
To "violate principle" means that since they are already vertical and horizontal, they are coarse and not subtle entities, and therefore must be refuted.

Regarding the terms "vertical" and "horizontal," according to the interpretation of the Confucians, south and north are vertical while east and west are horizontal, which refers to length and breadth. According to the doctrine of this [Buddhist] school, the former...

Subsequently, the sequential [development] constitutes the vertical, while the simultaneous possession [of all factors] constitutes the horizontal. At the time of the cause, the *dharmakāya* is primordially present;

the conditions for cultivation—namely, *prajñā*, merit, and liberation—are the vertical aspect. Within the consciousness, the seeds of these three dharmas are contained; this is the horizontal aspect at the time of the cause.
First there is the *dharmakāya*, next one attains *prajñā*, and finally, that which was previously bound becomes capable of liberating others; this is the time of the fruit.
"縱" (vertical) refers to the fact that once these three substances are obtained, they always abide in the same place; "橫" (horizontal) refers to this at the time of fruition.

This also applies equally to both teaching and principle (*jiao-li*), for there are no non-spatial, wondrous objects that do not require being broken through and revealed. Thus, movement is used to signify the great scripture of retribution (*biao-bao*). (The *Da-jing-su* [Commentary on the Great Scripture] says... [etc.])

The preceding section concludes the alternative explanations regarding "seizing," "taking away," and "destroying. From here on follows the primary explanation. According to various sacred teachings, there are three aspects to the six movements:
namely, the six times, the six locations, and the six characteristics. The "six times" refer to the six occasions:

entering the womb, birth, renunciation, attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa. When the earth shakes during these six times, it is the events of these six times that constitute the movement.
Regarding these conditions, two are excluded from among the eight distinct characteristics. "The six directions" refers to the mutual rising and subsiding of the six directions.
"The six characteristics" refers to movement, leaping, and so forth; this constitutes the movement of the three sets of six.
What is now mentioned is one of those six at that specific time, namely the time of turning the wheel of Dharma. That which moves at this time generally clarifies its fourfold *siddhānta* (purposes).
Regarding the causal conditions (*nidāna*), the other two [sections] consist of six lines each; though the text is abbreviated, their meaning should be understood as complete.

Furthermore, according to the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, there are also three types of movement, though the enumerations differ: first, six movements; second, twelve movements; and third, eighteen movements.
These correspond to the three types of movement in that sūtra; however, while it mentions these three movements, it does not distinguish them individually.

Regarding the names and characteristics, I shall now briefly explain them. If one speaks of "six," this is said in a general sense, referring to the six movements that occur when the Dharma is being taught;
these are precisely those two [movements]. Next, regarding "twelve," this refers to the aforementioned six directions surging and subsiding alternately to form twelve.
Regarding "eighteen," this means that within each of the six characteristics, there are three further characteristics. One should further examine the sutra.
The meaning expressed will be evident from the text itself. In the present commentary, there are three sections: first, a general explanation of the six movements;

second, a specific explanation of the six movements in relation to the six directions; and third, a specific explanation of the six movements in relation to the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*). The first is the general [explanation], while the latter two are the specific ones.
Although the text mentions only "six meanings" (*ṣaḍ-artha*), it omits the other two; thus, there is both a general and a specific explanation. Regarding the first of these, following the text:

Regarding the three instances where "two" is mentioned: since it is stated that the first instance is the primary contemplation (*mūla-vipaśyanā*), the meaning should not be discussed within the first instance;

rather, it corresponds to the meanings of the first two [instances]. The *Ji* (Commentary) states: "The first seems to concern the teaching (*shè jiào*), and the second seems to concern causes and conditions (*yīn yuán*);

because the text is not explicit, both are termed 'seems'. Here, we directly establish two [sections]: first, the formal explanation (*zhèng shì*), and second, the citation of evidence (*yǐng zhèng*). Within the first, there is the heading and the explanation; herein is the heading.
The first phrase generally cites the three things that can manifest; next, it manifests the "Perfect Family" (yuanjia), followed by a general indication of the three dharmas manifested.

There are six rounds of explanation and six rounds of refutation. These explain the movement of ignorance and the stages (di). Because the Perfect [Family] does not have six [stages], it is called the "Perfect Family. The six are as explained there.
Opening these six rounds results in forty-two positions, which is precisely the breaking of the forty-two grades of delusion.

The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Great Commentary on the Clarification) states that because the categories of ignorance (*avidyā*) are extremely numerous, the "Samādhi for Destroying Ignorance" is discussed in various places by citing forty-two [categories] as a general outline;
how much more so when it simply speaks of destroying the ten obstructions to reveal the ten true suchnesses (*tathatā*).

Even if the latter two [obstructions] were added, they would still only amount to twelve factors, because [the practitioner] has not yet fully realized them. As the text says: "Riding the Great White Ox Vehicle, the Jewel Vehicle, one travels..."
From the four directions extending all the way to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the sixfold elucidation of the perfect meaning based on these four passages is thus made clear;

this interpretation is unprecedented throughout past and present. Regarding the section "Ignorance" (*avidyā*) below, the commentary consists of three parts: first, a specific explanation of the reason for the shaking of the earth;

second, a specific explanation of the meaning of the universal shaking of the Buddhas' lands; and finally, a specific explanation of the reason why it shakes at the very beginning of the six [stages]. This is the "Manifestation of the Earth."
What is meant by "shattering ignorance"? To explain this, it is said as follows: First, the term "vast and expansive" (*panbo*) describes a state that is broad, thick, and extremely firm.

Now, regarding the expression "ignorance" (*avidyā*), there is both a general and a specific sense. If spoken specifically, the three teachings have already shattered the four abidings (*catur-vāsabhūmi*) since ancient times;
this is the specific usage of "the ground of the abiding of ignorance" (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*). However, speaking generally, this [ground] has not been shattered until now.
This refers to the entirety of the five abodes; in general terms, "ignorance" (avidyā) is precisely like the initial ignorance within the twelve links of dependent origination.
Now, this [term] fully contains five meanings, which indicates that all shall be opened up and refuted. Why is it said that the entire Buddha-world shakes?
Regarding the phenomenal aspect, some say it means shaking throughout this single Buddha-land, while others cite the subsequent passage concerning "all."

Regarding the equality of all Buddha-lands, there is currently no need for forced debate over their universal or limited scope; it suffices to take the meanings of "movement" and "light," by which they may be aligned.

As for interpreting the meaning of the text, it is not easy to comprehend. Although the concluding passage here is general, its primary intent explains the meaning of the Buddha-world and does not explain "universality" and "movement.
Why? Because this [passage] clarifies that the cultivation of merit within these Buddha-lands has reached its ultimate perfection.
The purity is as previously explained in the *Śrīmaladevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, where it is clarified that the fundamental essence of all sentient beings inherently possesses this luminous and pure body.
Yet, through delusion, their entire being has become entirely obscured by the defilements of ignorance.

Now, in order to reveal and manifest this for them, so that these obscurations and impurities are seen to be entirely identical with luminous purity, one first moves within the realm of luminous purity to signify that what is to be transformed is itself entirely such.

First, movement is used to signify it; having already explained its six meanings below as previously understood, the following citation of scriptural evidence serves to demonstrate the meaning signified by the earth’s trembling at the time of birth, thereby corroborating what is signified by the trembling at the present time of turning the Wheel of Dharma.

Since it was so even at the time of birth, how much more so when preaching the Dharma? Thus it is said that the earth trembles because afflictions are extinguished; therefore, what is now moved signifies this.

Since it destroys [the view that] there is no clear understanding, it is said that this refers to the very same meaning. Within this, there are also the agent and the object, as well as the self and the other, which can be understood;
because these correspond to what follows in this section, there are two interpretations. That is to say, the first is the teaching, and the second is the causal condition.
Now, since this is an exegesis establishing the path, these two meanings cannot be separated. Why? Because the first is general...
The "heading" refers to the world; the next three "distinctions" refer to the remedies; and the "ultimate meaning" refers to the person. It should be understood that the sequence is likewise so.
Furthermore, although the realization merely extinguishes delusions to manifest principle, it nonetheless possesses the four meanings—both general and specific—which are the causal conditions.
The *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) fully contains all four in each instance; here, it is precisely the "remedy" that inherently possesses these four intentions. Since they are all perfect (*yúan*).

The wondrous is without direction and its sequence is also not fixed; these all pertain to the meaning of the perfect and the non-referential, which is explained according to the teachings (*yàojiào*).
Next, regarding the section on the fundamental and the manifested (*běnzhì*), it says that those who "secretly grasp this meaning" refer to the intention of Mañjuśrī.

All that Mañjuśrī cites contains both the manifest and the secret meanings. If one were to directly cite such instances from the Buddhas of the past to show that the present is likewise, [it would only be the manifest].

It is evident that just as in the past when the Buddha was about to speak of the matter of manifestation, so too was it at the time he was about to speak long ago after his attainment of enlightenment;
Śākyamuni Buddha’s case was likewise. This is Mañjuśrī’s secret intention at that time.
If one can deeply penetrate this intention of Mañjuśrī, one will know that by citing the past to manifest the present, the present is also secretly indicated by citing the past.
This is because it reveals the manifest in order to know the hidden, and uses another to represent the fundamental; thus it says "thus.

What was previously stated—that the introductory section has both manifest and hidden meanings—is precisely this. This single interpretation universally clarifies that all six auspicious omens are like this, not only the earthquake.
However, while explaining the six omens, the reason for clarifying the fundamental and the trace specifically here is to indicate the retribution.

The meaning of the refutation and revelation of cause and effect reaches its ultimate point here; therefore, the text fully elucidates the matters of the three and the six, being most comprehensive and complete.

Furthermore, it is because one wishes to manifest the preceding and succeeding stages by means of the middle category so as not to burden the text with excessive detail. Next, in the section on contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), there is a statement and an explanation.

Although the statement is brief, it also contains the three meanings of the signifier (*vyañjaka*) and the signified (*vyaṅgya*) respectively. That is to say, regarding the six movements of the earth:

The "manifestation of movement" (biao guan xing dong) breaks through the attachments and stagnations of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). The explanation of the "earth phase" (*pṛthivī-lakṣaṇa*) below follows this principle:
the meaning herein should be stated as follows—the attachment to the water of the six sense faculties has never yet entered the path of the Mahāyāna;

it is like the earth-phase, which is firm and difficult to move, yet now moves that which was difficult to move. As for the present text, one should consider whether it follows the occasion or is not in sequential order; thus, it speaks of "moving that which was difficult to move."

The "ability to manifest" refers to the meaning manifested by that which is pure or impure; this is still a matter of phenomena (*vastu*). What, then, is meant by "contemplative practice" (*vipaśyanā-caryā*)?
It refers to the manifestation that, having already heard [the teachings], one has entered true cultivation—the practice of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*).
Because there is such a meaning as described above, the commentary states [“...”].

Next, regarding the explanation of the "movement of the six directions": the previous four interpretations were general explanations of the six movements and did not yet specify their names, essences, or characteristics;

therefore, it is in these two subsequent interpretations that they are finally revealed. As for the "six directions," these refer to the four cardinal directions along with the center and the periphery.
This is derived from the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. These six, when combined with one another, constitute ten.
Because there are two [aspects], it is verified that in the Mahāyāna sūtras they are referred to as the "twelve movements. However, what do these signify?
None of the commentaries clarify this, nor is it known for what purpose they are employed within the Prologue.

Even if they were explained in other sūtras, such would only be a general meaning (*sāmānya-artha*) and not a specific meaning (*viśeṣa-artha*), and furthermore, it would not be the intended sense here. Although there is no explicit textual evidence in the sūtras or śāstras, [the meaning must be inferred].
It cannot be that there is no meaning in the statement "the six realms and the six stages shall attain Buddhahood.

Now, [if one were to say] this merely refers to the sixty and the twenty-eight, it would be entirely devoid of meaning. What is explained in the current text clarifies each point regarding the subject and object of manifestation and retribution;
within these, it is precisely through the perfect and subtle that the intended meaning is realized. Herein, all things manifest the assembly of the time.
That one may obtain these benefits is not merely a matter of the understanding derived from contemplative practice; I request that later students reflect upon this.

Regarding the explanation of the first six [verses], there is first the explanation of the east and west, followed by the remaining four directions. Within the initial section on the east and west, there is first the explanation of the east and west, followed by the explanation of the emergence and submergence.
Within these two passages, each has its own signifier and signified, and each possesses its own meaning, which may be sought within the text; the word "arising" (*jìng*) refers to this.
"Cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the two characters "leaping up" (*yong*) and "submerging" (*mo*). Since they leap up and submerge alternately, this constitutes alternating arising and ceasing.

Otherwise, what would be the purpose of these empty words? Next, regarding the other directions: since the east and west are paired with the eyes and nose, it is logical that the south and north are paired with the ears and tongue;

the center represents the mind (*manas*), and the four directions represent the body (*kāya*). Since the body possesses four sense organs and the mind universally takes all four as its objects, [the arrangement is thus established].
Regarding the center and the directions: the four directions serve as the indicators (*lakṣaṇa*), and the four sense-faculties (*indriya*) are that which is indicated (*lakṣya*).

Since this relationship between indicator and indicated holds for the four directions, how could the emergence and submergence (*utkṣepa-apakṣepa*) not likewise apply to their mutual arising and ceasing? Although the meaning of the six directions is thus established, what is the meaning of the twelve?
The indicators of the twelve consist of the six emergences and six submergences of the six directions; that which is indicated consists of the twelve.

Thus, one generally attains six [realms] for both arising and ceasing. If one follows the subsequent text—which indicates the eighteen pure realms—this also indicates the twelve pure bases (*āyatana*), and these represent the purity of both faculties and objects. One must also consider their mutual arising and ceasing;
otherwise, there would be no sense of "surging and submerging."
Next, the explanation of the six sense organs consists of three parts: first, the enumeration of the six; second, the clarification of the eighteen [elements];

and third, the synthesis that reveals the capacity to manifest the objects. Regarding the first part, the new [commentary] states: "stirring, surging, shaking, striking, roaring, bursting, and clashing.

This corresponds to the old [text], where "arising" is the same as "stirring," and "bursting" is the same as "shaking," while two are identical and two differ. Following the old text, the current commentary explains: "to sway unsteadily is 'stirring' (dòng); to be pitted with depressions and protrusions is 'shaking' (zhèn)."
To leap (*pluta*) means to rise and submerge in the six directions; this is called leaping. To rise from below and ascend to a height is called rising (*utthita*).

According to the new [translation], to strike or beat something is called striking (*āhata*). To produce a deep, resonant sound is called vibrating (*pragarjita*). To emit a crashing and thundering roar is called roaring (*nirghoṣa*). To cause the multitude to awaken is called awakening (*buddha*).
According to the new [translation], to produce a sound that causes wonder is called bursting forth (*sphoṭa*). Next, regarding the eighteen [qualities], it refers to each of the aforementioned six.
Furthermore, there are three characteristics, namely movement and so forth. The "New" [commentary] states: "Movement, equal movement, and extreme movement;

even up to 'awakening' (bodha), it is likewise. Next, the meaning of these three movements is explained according to the text. The "New" [commentary] states: "Slight movement is called 'movement'; movement pervading all locations is called 'equal movement';
pervasive and great overturning movement is called 'equal extreme movement. All other cases should be understood accordingly. The present text is extremely general, but...
The "six movements" are named after the "trembling" among the eighteen [dharmas]; this is the summary below which clarifies the phenomena manifested by the capacity [to manifest].
Precisely because it manifests this, there are further three within each one. What is the method for purification?
It is that within each and every object, all are the Three Truths and the Three Contemplations; thus, they are the eighteen perfect [dharmas].
The subtle realm contemplates its essential principle, which can be fully exhausted therein; as this intention is manifested, the commentary states [as follows]. Master Xuan says:

"In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, within the section on the 'Leaping Up' (踊), six modes are established—namely, moving and so forth—and each of these six realms has six further aspects, totaling thirty-six.
The present text briefly cites only two of these: 'shaking' (震) and 'moving' (動). [As follows].
Next, regarding the auspicious sign of the assembly’s joy: according to the general principle, it should logically follow the auspicious sign of light;

thus it is so in the verse. This is because there are two intended meanings: first, if one intends to manifest the sequence of the response and its resonance, as well as to avoid prolixity when referring to other lands, it must be placed here.

Second, if one intends to comprehensively clarify the underlying cause and the significance of the auspicious sign, it would be appropriate to place it later. It is for these two reasons that it is situated here.
The two texts differ; reflect upon this, reflect upon it! Xuanzang says: "The four assemblies represent the four flowers previously mentioned;
the eight classes of beings represent the shaking of the earth; and the attainment of Buddhahood by those in the six realms of existence represents the intent of the two kings.
As for the joy of the bodhisattvas, since they have already been described as becoming Buddhas from time immemorial, there is no need for an auspicious sign to represent them."

Therefore, it is not that the Bodhisattvas are not clear about this; rather, I say that people’s reasoning is excessively convoluted and fragmented. There are two explanations for the text and three meanings for its content.
First, what constitutes the great assembly? What constitutes their joy? And what constitutes the auspicious omen? The scriptural text contains two parts, yet there are three meanings within them.
Among these, the "three assemblies" refer to the fourfold, the eightfold, and the twofold; furthermore, the Bodhisattvas are omitted from the latter two. This, then, is the great assembly.
The phrase "also rejoices" (*yě huānxǐ*) refers to the joy of the mind; this very joy of the mind is the meaning of an auspicious omen (*ruì*).

Because these elements are combined to form the statement, it is said thus. Alternatively, one might move this text to precede the current point, but I maintain that since there were previously three groups, by citing the first and the last, the middle can be understood of itself. Being concise yet complete, why resort to such forced conjecture? (etc. First.

Regarding the "Upāsaka" and so forth mentioned among the four [categories of disciples]: they are called *qingxin nan* (male faithful ones) and *qingxin nü* (female faithful ones), or alternatively *qingxin shi nü* (male and female faithful ones).
This refers to those who, while remaining householders, possess pure faith in the Buddha-dharma, thereby distinguishing them from the aforementioned ordained [monastics].
In the new terminology, they are called *upāsaka*. *Upa* means "near," *ka* means "to serve," and *saka* is the masculine suffix; *sikā* is the feminine suffix.

Regarding the term *upāsaka* (lay follower) and *upāsikā* (lay follower): because those who have perfected the precepts among men and women are capable of drawing near to, serving, and attending upon the community of *bhikṣuṇīs*, they are called "male lay followers" (*upāsaka*) and "female lay followers" (*upāsikā*).
Next, concerning the eight classes [of supernatural beings], those previously explained shall not be discussed; those not yet explained shall be briefly defined here.

As for the *yakṣa*: formerly translated as "Swift" (*jiéqí*), now translated as "Valiant and Strong" (*yǒngjiàn*), and in recent translations as "Yàchā," this is rendered here as "Majestic and Fierce" (*wēiměng*).
Because their power is most fierce and robust, they are also called *jin* (exhaustive), meaning they can completely devour and consume whatever they eat;
thus, the term *rākṣasa* is omitted for brevity. These are all from the north, so it is logical that the official [title] should be present here.
To speak fully, they are called *rākṣasa*, which means "violent and evil" or "terrible"; the meaning is clear. *Mahoraga* means "large intestine-crawler."
"Deities" refers to such beings as great pythons and snakes; the new translation calls them *mahoragas*, which is the same name as the old translation.

Regarding the phrase "humans, non-humans, and so forth," the old commentary states that this summarizes the two preceding groups of four assemblies as humans and the eight classes (*aṣṭa-nikāya*) as non-humans.
Others say that while the eight classes of spirits and ghosts are fundamentally all non-humans, they manifest in human form to come and listen to the preaching of the Dharma.
Therefore, this is what is said. However, according to the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, there is another distinct meaning that emerges (as detailed in the following passage).
The explanation below regarding the two kings is exactly as described in the preceding text and corresponds to the number found within the *Anantarya-nirdeśa*.

To clarify the "joy of mind," the *Xiaoyun* commentary states: "Joining the palms expresses a physical form that is no different [from the state of concentration]; with a unified mind, one clarifies the intent so that there are no other conditions.
Celestial joy and reverence converge, truly containing a sentiment of longing and yearning. Extraordinary omens arise together, leading one to suspect there is an extraordinary teaching.
Now, regarding "attaining what has never been attained before," this is a general statement for attaining the encounter with extraordinary omens; it refers to the joy thereof.
The act of joining one’s palms by Yu expresses a most extraordinary reverence; the state of single-mindedness gives rise to a most extraordinary veneration;

and the gazing upon the Buddha is a response of most extraordinary longing and aspiration. These manifestations signify that what is about to be wonderfully expounded shall, in its entirety, constitute the One Vehicle and the Threefold Virtue.
Why is this so? What is the great assembly? What is the joy of heart? And what is the auspicious omen of the sutra?

The text has two parts but contains three meanings. Among these, the "three assemblies" refer to the four, the eight, and the two; the latter still omits the Bodhisattvas, which constitutes the "great assembly.
From "rejoicing" (*pramuditā*) onwards refers to the mind. Since this mental joy is itself the meaning of the auspicious omen (*praśasta*), they are combined in this way;
therefore, it is said thus. [Question: What is the great assembly? What is the joyful mind? What is the auspicious omen? [Answer: This is according to the Sūtra.
There are two [aspects] yet three meanings within them; therein, the "three assemblies" refer to the four, eight, and two [assemblies], while the Bodhisattvas are the "great assembly.
From "Joyful" (*pramudita*) onwards refers to "joy"; since this mental joy is itself the meaning of an auspicious omen (*praśasta*), it is spoken of by combining these factors.
There are two explanations for the text; in the first, regarding the causal conditions (*nidāna*), there is a person who clarifies the four *siddhānta* (the four purposes) herein.

The first meaning concerns the distinction between the internal and external; this is the world’s question-and-answer for the purpose of removing doubt, which serves as an antidote. The joy that is not [of] permanence is for the sake of others.

The single-minded contemplation of the Buddha is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). Now, as for the question-and-answer regarding "who," this constitutes three intentions on the part of the sūtra compiler.
If this is so difficult to believe even when it is easy, how much more so for that which is difficult? Now, I say that the first is the cause.

Following the sequence of questions and answers, the significance of the auspicious signs (*śubha*) is explained and established. First, the capacity to signify is clarified through its basis and its connection;

since this is discussed from a specific perspective, it is said that "the flowered ground is nectar," which refers to the sublime teaching and the sublime principle. "Rejoicing" (*prīti*) is the mind’s exultation, while "leaping up" (*utpluti*) is the physical manifestation.

The aforementioned joy that signifies points toward what is below—the signified—which still belongs to the mundane. By briefly employing the mundane to clarify the supramundane, it is shown that the world itself is [the supramundane].
What is expressed in the underlying intent of this passage is that although it consists of a single phrase, it contains three meanings:

the arousal of the great capacity (*mahā-vimukti*) signifies the arising of great goodness and the extinction of great evil, and the manifestation of the Great Principle (*mahā-dharma*) corresponds precisely to the meaning of the threefold purpose (*tri-siddhi*).

The "response to the stimulus" (*kō-jō-ō*) refers to the person endowed with the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) who is able to cause the three greatnesses (*tri-mahat*) to be developed; this constitutes four meanings—so what need is there for further elaboration?
Regarding the refutation of the erroneous views that follow: first, it is because none of the various schools consider these three to be auspicious omens; this is the first point.
Although the second point—that they are not ancient precedents—has already been refuted and explained, we shall explain them further here to clarify that they are indeed all auspicious omens.
As for what is called "the common understanding of people": since auspicious omens are by nature extraordinary events, how could these be considered ordinary worldly matters? How could they...
Regarding this as an auspicious omen, the Confucian school clarifies that there are six or seven manifestations of the emotions; joy and anger are two among them, which is why it is said so.
This is simply because joy and anger follow one another in succession. In the response, it is clarified that the cause of joy is not an extraordinary event, and that it is not an extraordinary joy.
The following concludes the censure by stating that one cannot claim it is "not [joy]" simply because it does not arise from an extraordinary cause.
Therefore, this joy is not ordinary joy; because it is not ordinary joy, it signifies that one shall hear the Dharma of impermanence and obtain extraordinary benefit.
This is surely the profound meaning of an auspicious omen; how could it be otherwise? Thus, it is not right to think so.

When it says, "Although there were [teachings] in the past," it means that prior to the preaching of the Three Teachings, even if they existed, they were not [the true teaching]. Therefore, the text...
It is said that the fourfold assembly was filled with joy, their bodies and minds refreshed, having attained what they had never experienced before.

The phrase "now, etc. explains this as an auspicious omen (*śakuna*), signifying that the great capacity for awakening is about to be aroused. The subsequent section on "teaching" (*yāna*) distinguishes the differences and convergences;

these four distinctions constitute the differentiation. One should know that within each of these four, there exists both the subject (the capacity) and the object (the teaching). Furthermore, one must understand the relationship between the present and the past. If, regarding...

Now, the fact that all these sutras move the mind toward the true mark (*dharmatā*) indicates that those who hear them shall equally realize the one perfect and wondrous [Dharma]. Since it is already called the "true mark," why is it further said to "move"?

This is explained in terms of the mental capacity of the practitioner (*citta-kalpa*), not as a description of the realized essence itself (and so forth). The original contemplation (*mūla-vipaśyanā*) and the subsequent contemplation (*anuvipaśyanā*) may both be understood by analogy with this principle.
Next, the sixth auspicious sign of emitting light is explained. Other [commentators] say the text consists of three parts: first, the emission of light; second, the illumination of objects;
and third, that which is seen. For now, based on the text, it shall be briefly divided into two: first, the emission of light; second, that which is illuminated.

However, although the meaning of "that which is illuminated" applies generally to this text, it specifically pertains to other lands; therefore, it cannot be treated as a separate part. Later, one will see for oneself that the sūtra text contains five points, namely:
The "time" and "person" mentioned in the phrase "the time and person who emit [light]" refer specifically to these five points, which ultimately reside within four:
first, "time," which Master Xuanzang explains as the time of emitting light; I now take this to mean precisely the moment of entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

This is also simultaneous with the raining of flowers and the shaking of the earth. "Buddha" refers to the person capable of emitting [light]; "emitting" means responding appropriately to the capacities of sentient beings.
"Shu" (舒) means to unfold. That which is below the space between the eyebrows is precisely the light that is emitted. There are two parts to the textual explanation: first, the emission of light;
second, the explanation of the textual divisions. Regarding the first [the emission of light], there are two sections: first, a brief statement of the general meaning; second, the formal explanation.

Regarding the first of these, the *Ji* (Record) states: "Responding to capacities marks the causes and conditions; establishing the teaching marks the provisional teaching for the destruction of delusions."
The following clarifies the intent behind these two matters. The manifestation of light fundamentally signifies these two; possessing both aspects, it removes doubt and confusion.

Now, the preceding [phrase] cites that which manifests, while the following clarifies the meaning of that which is manifested. "Responding to the capacity of beings" refers to the intent of manifesting that which is signified;

"establishing the teaching" refers to the intent of the light itself as that which is signified. The four characters below clarify the utility of the teaching manifested by the light—namely, the light itself.
This is the meaning of "light" (*ābhāsa*). There are two meanings to light: first, it can destroy darkness; second, it can reveal things.
Destroying darkness means destroying delusions so that beings may give rise to understanding. Revealing the true nature of things means causing beings to eliminate doubt and give rise to faith.

The primary intent is precisely to destroy the provisional and manifest the real, enabling beings to attain the wondrous faith and understanding; this is the ultimate limit. As for "capacity" (*tūṣṇī*), it refers to what was mentioned previously.
This refers to that very point.
Below the white tuft (ūrṇā-kośa) is the second section, which correctly explains the scriptural text. Excluding the introductory section, there are only three meanings in total;

the textual explanation consists of four parts: first, the correct explanation of emitting light; second, clarifying the differences among what is emitted; third, clarifying the reason for not withdrawing [the light]; and fourth, [the conclusion]. If... [text continues]... if.
Regarding the four explanations of the person capable of emitting [light] following the "six-foot" [measurement], this simultaneously explains the character *buddha*.
This section has two parts: first, the causal conditions (*nidāna*), and second, the analysis according to the teachings (*śāsana*). Within the causal conditions, there are three parts:

first, explaining the white hair (*ūrṇā*) that serves as the symbol; second, explaining the Dharma that is symbolized; and third, a general clarification of the meaning of what is symbolized. Within the first of these, there is first a general [introduction].
Regarding the title "Endowed with Virtue," its explanation begins as follows: As for the mention of the "eyebrows" (*bhru*), some say it is the place from which light is emitted.
However, I maintain that this refers to the location where the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair) resides, and is not the actual point of emission of light.
Regarding the term "between the eyebrows" (*bhrumadhya*), some say that "eyebrow" (*bhru*) signifies "grace" (*maitra*); that is to say, it represents the grace of the face and head. To indicate...
What has been stated is the superior essence of the Mahāyāna school. Now, it is said that the eyebrows represent the two extremes; by eliminating these extremes, the Middle Way is revealed.
If this were merely intended to express the sectarian tenets of the school, why would one further speak of the "middle"? You should reflect upon this.
Next, I shall explain the brief enumeration of three matters to clarify their various aspects. Regarding the first, all commentaries state that [the tree] was [planted] during the time of the Prince.
When lowered, it is one zhang, four chi, and five cun; after attaining Buddhahood, it is one zhang and five chi.
In neither case is its symbolic significance stated; this is a general explanation of its physical form. The following is a specific explanation of its white characteristic (*śvetavarṇa*).
As for the *ūrṇā-lakṣaṇa* (white tuft mark), "white" distinguishes and reveals it—distinguishing it from others and revealing this very mark. This is one among the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata.
Regarding "marks" (xiàng), it refers to the thirty-second mark; "háo" refers to long hair. Nanshan says it is "extraordinary hair.
The scripture also uses "háo," taking the sense of "exquisite hair"—that is, the most extraordinary among all hairs.
Both characters are acceptable, though the original text correctly uses "háo. It is said that ten facets appear, penetrating both the interior and exterior; when released, they curl into a circle.
It is like the full autumn moon, bright, pure, and distinct, its color reflecting off white jade and snow; it is as round as three inches.

In the sūtras, it is sometimes said that it spirals to the right, winding like the sun at its zenith; this is also as explained in the latter part of this sūtra and in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* (and so forth).
The following explanation is a general interpretation of the merit of the text; by citing these three instances, all [merits] are subsumed.
This is indeed the merit of the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). The characteristics of this [mark] are as explained below.

Furthermore, first the essential nature and form are clarified, which explains the *ūrṇā* (the tuft of hair between the eyebrows); next, its whiteness is explained; thirdly, there is a general explanation of its meritorious functions.
This is the meaning of the preceding statement regarding "various merits. The above concludes the explanation of that which expresses [the mark]; below is the specific manifestation of it.
This refers to what is signified; it is explained by way of the four virtues, which signifies that the teachings to be expounded herein clarify the meaning of these four virtues.

In each case, first the meaning of the capacity [to signify] is presented, followed by the manifestation of the dharma signified. Because there is no beginning or end within it, it is eternal (*nitya*);
because it is supple and perfectly accommodates all, it is blissful (*sukha*).

The above concludes the specific explanation of the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft) mark. Below this is the general explanation of the meaning of emitting light from within it and illuminating the two lands;
within these two aspects, there are likewise both the signifier (*vyañjaka*) and the signified (*vyaṅgya*).

The reason for emitting light from within it is that "within" excludes the two extremes, and "light" is able to destroy darkness; this signifies that when the teaching of the Middle Way is expounded, sentient beings will be inspired [to realize it].
This gives rise to the light of wisdom that perceives the wondrous realm of the Middle Way. However, there are three differences between this passage and others:

first, in other cases, the subject that hits [the object] is simply called "light," whereas here, that which is hit is called "the Middle. Second, regarding the emission of light, there are two meanings:
destroying darkness to reveal objects, and destroying non-manifestation to manifest wisdom. In the present text, both subject and object are each mentioned only once, as they are raised alternately.
Furthermore, the two characters "zhongdao" (middle-way) must be understood as applying to both locations; as explained previously, the text merely cites one instance by way of abbreviation.

One must carefully contemplate these three differences. Next, regarding the two [realms] illuminated therein, because they are the spheres where self and others mutually reign, this is used here as a representation;
that is to say, it represents what is to be taught herein, instructing sentient beings to awaken within this middle-way teaching.

"Because of self and others, and for this purpose, he emits light here that illuminates two lands. Since these preceding [statements] constitute the causes and conditions for the four *siddhāntas*, the Record states:
"The first is the world-view (*loka-saṃvṛti*); the light emitted from beneath the brow is for the sake of humans; the light emitted below as a remedy is for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Although these belong to the category of correspondence (*pratipakṣa*), their meaning has not yet been clarified. Now, I shall first explain that which can represent it.

This also possesses four aspects in relation to what is signified: first, because it corresponds to the four virtues signified by the Worldly Truth; second, because it is the sublime virtue (*guṇa*) that is the object of expression;
third, because it clearly manifests the object and wisdom within the Middle Way; and fourth, because it dispels the two types of darkness and attains the two types of awakening.
It is a counteractive measure (*pratipakṣa*), for through this function of subject and object in self-realization, it benefits both oneself and others.

This is because it gradually and subtly differs from the ordinary, further manifesting the perfect and wondrous. Next, within the section on the classification of teachings (*jiao*), the four teachings are fully elucidated;

by specifically distinguishing the presence or absence, and the possession or lack thereof, in the first three, the meaning of the perfection of the *yuan* (perfect) teaching is revealed—namely, that it is both present and complete.
To summarize, the reason for expounding this wondrous and correct [teaching] is precisely to distinguish the partial and manifest the perfect. This concludes the first two [sections].

That is to say, the two preceding teachings do not expound the Middle Way in these two respects; therefore, they both first clarify the "object" (the Middle) in order to indicate this "subject" (the teaching), as this [Middle Way] is truly present in the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).
Although the Distinct Teaching (*bie*) does expound the Middle, because its horizontal and vertical dimensions are not integrated, it is not what is ultimately indicated here.
Now, the specific mention of this light from between the brows is precisely for the purpose of manifesting the Perfect Teaching. Interpret it according to this explanation.

The sequence of the preceding section explained the white tuft (ūrṇā-kośa); next, this explains the light emitted from it. Following this, the teaching is categorized according to the four teachings; this explains the difficulty of understanding [the phrase] "between the eyebrows. Reflect upon this.

Having finished explaining the emission of light above, the following clarifies that what is emitted is not uniform; this is merely to manifest and establish the intended meaning within this context. To cite:
Regarding these three, their significance is threefold: first, they signify the utility of the Three Mysteries.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the face represents the mouth; in this sūtra, because it is situated between the eyebrows within meditative concentration, it represents the mind.

Second, the *Mahāprāpāramitā Sūtra* symbolizes the practice of Prajñā as the foundation of the myriad practices, leading from cause to the ultimate fruit; therefore, it emits many rays of light. Furthermore—
From the feet up to the crown of the head, this sutra symbolizes the convergence of the teachings of the five periods; thus, it emits light of five colors from its mouth (and so forth).

Because this sutra correctly symbolizes the principle of the Middle Way and the True Mark (*dharmatā*), it emits a ray of light from the hair-tuft between its eyebrows. These three [emissions] symbolize the Three Virtues:

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* Sutra symbolizes the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*), the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sutra symbolizes the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*), and this sutra symbolizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The teaching begins by showing that each [of these three] possesses the other two; since the same applies to the following two, the three virtues (*guṇa*) are likewise so.

Although the conditions (*pratyaya*) extend across them, this distinction is made because what is signified is the same. Within each of these three meanings, there are nine aspects, as they mutually possess one another.
It is precisely for this reason that these three are specifically singled out. As for the final phrase, which explains their distinct significance: since...

Since that which is indicated is identical in all cases, why is there this distinction? It is because the objects of cognition extend universally; thus, while there is this difference in the phenomena, the meaning indicated remains the same.
One should understand that the Prajñāpāramitā is spoken of here in terms of its unique [unshared] characteristics (as it is said, etc.).

Next, the following section clarifies the intent behind the reabsorption of light. Since that which is emitted must necessarily be reabsorbed—and as the preceding section has already described the emission, the following section explains the reabsorption.

This is because the emission represents the teaching being proclaimed, while the reabsorption represents the bestowal of predictions (vyākaraṇa). Furthermore, this serves to precisely indicate the beginning and end of the events within this single assembly.

Although it indicates the beginning and end of the transformative activity, the specific nature of that activity varies, and thus its beginning and end are distinct; for this reason, the other sutras are first recounted.

Next, the actual meaning of the present passage is revealed. Regarding the distinctions within the first section, there are thirteen points. The first three are general predictions concerning the three periods of time;

the fourth is a textual passage on the present that was omitted [in some versions], which Danqiu added according to his interpretive principles. The next three are predictions regarding the three evil destinies. The following three are predictions regarding humans and devas.
The subsequent four are predictions regarding the four noble classes; the asuras are not mentioned because the text speaks only of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*). As for the... [text ends].
Regarding the statement that the five destinies and the three vehicles are predicted, this merely records the fact that each shall receive such specific retributions within their respective domains;
it does not mean that they are predicted to become Buddhas. The reason for this can be understood through reflection.

Below, the sutra explains the meaning of "no inclusion," which is divided into two parts: first, the brief presentation of this summary; second, the explanation of the intent behind the summary. First, the words:

That which is abbreviated is necessarily collected after being released, yet because there is no explicit text, it is "abbreviated. This is a brief enumeration; if expanded, it must necessarily exist.

Furthermore, the following section explains the reason for the abbreviation by further analyzing the meaning. "The present" refers to that which is manifested and revealed in the introduction (*nidāna*).

"The future" refers to that which has already been granted a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) during the formal teaching (*samyaksaṃbodhi-deśanā*). Since these are both incidental and primary, the primary is now being presented.

Knowing that the surrounding text would become overly prolix, I have omitted it here. Regarding the subsequent passage where every single phrase speaks of "summarizing the teaching" (*yàojiào*), I do not understand why this one specific phrase is treated with a double-layered summary of the teaching.
