Doubts accumulate and remain unresolved; how much more so for those who are in a state of haste!
Now, I maintain that the Sūtra says, "The Buddha emits [light]," wherein "Buddha" refers to the person who is able to emit it, and the light emitted has already been explained previously.

Those who have not yet understood how this "capable person" can be released are now correctly explained herein. However, since this capable person is universally applicable to all, we shall now distinguish that universal application to reveal the specific;

thus, it is clarified by means of the teachings (*yàojiào*). Otherwise, one would not understand the meaning of the "explanation of the initial teaching" and so forth, which has already been concluded according to the [fourfold] classification.
Although what follows here appears to be based on the four teachings, it is in fact precisely based on the four [periods].
At that time, first there were the *Āgamas* (Four Agamas), followed by the *Vaipulya* (Vaipulya Sutras);

because the four capacities [of sentient beings] were all present, these were followed by the *Prajñāpāramitā*, which does not accord with the Tripiṭaka, as it reveals the Universal Form (Vairocana) to all alike; therefore, it is called "Distinct" (*bīe*). The latter refers to the present meaning.

Because of the opening and merging [of teachings], there are no longer two distinct aspects; thus the Sūtra says, "The name of Muni is Vairocana," which is why it is said they are "identical. This is the current capacity...

If one releases [the mind], this person is precisely such a sublime and venerable being. Recently, it has been said that the supernormal power of realization through knowledge of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-sākṣātkriyābhijñā*) possesses eighteen transformations:
first, trembling; second, blazing; third, streaming forth; fourth, manifestation; fifth, transformation; sixth, coming and going; seventh, contraction; eighth, expansion;
ninth, entering all forms into one's own body; tenth, approaching in the form of a similar class; eleventh, invisibility; twelfth, visibility; [and so on up to] the tenth.
Third is mastery over what is done; fourteenth is the supernormal power of subduing others; fifteenth is the ability to bestow eloquence; sixteenth is the ability to bestow mindfulness;
seventeenth is the ability to bestow peace and happiness; eighteenth is the emission of the six rays of light. Now, this raining of the four flowers is the transformation of mastery;
the shaking of the earth in six ways is the transformation of vibration; and this emission of light is the transformation of dissemination.
Regarding the transformations seen in the manifestation of the six realms and so forth, these will be fully displayed in the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (Ṛddhipāda) below.

Here, we clarify that the interpretation of our school is simply that utility arises from the essence; as for this sutra, it is as wondrous as described below in the "Expedient Means" (Upāya) and in the "Mysterious Meaning" (Xuan-yi) regarding response and resonance (ganying).

The preceding numerous points have already concluded the explanation of the "light that illuminates. What follows is the second section: the analysis of the textual divisions concerning the passage on the light’s illumination.
Within this, first the textual divisions are established, and next the text itself is interpreted. Regarding the former, there are three parts [and so forth].
In truth, according to the actual meaning, this applies to both lands; however, such was the judgment made by the ancients for a specific reason.
First, regarding the meaning: since it already extensively illuminates other directions, how could it fail to illuminate its own realm?

Furthermore, a verse states: "The Buddha emits a single ray of light, and this world-realm is seen in all its various wonders. If it did not illuminate [this realm], how could one see its various features?
Based on these textual meanings, this belongs to this land. My current intention is that since the text explicitly says it "illuminates the eastern direction," [it must include this realm].
This then belongs to another land; however, the first phrase alone pertains to this land as a manifestation of light and auspicious signs.

Yet, from the perspective of meaning, it must necessarily be universal, whereas from the perspective of the text, it is restricted to that [other] land. Since text and meaning are mutually complementary and cannot be separated, the present intent actually resides in both.

Therefore, the preceding passage states that "illuminating the two lands" signifies the awakening of both self and others. If one follows this specific passage, then it is restricted to the other [land].
If one follows the verse text, it applies to this land as well; thus it is said that "great light shines everywhere.

Moreover, since each side’s reasoning is accepted and we speak with composure, the meaning and the text may be taken either together or separately, allowing for whatever is appropriate; hence it is said, "it depends on the person.
However, if one follows the meaning according to the text, it belongs to this land. Thus, there are six passages concerning the emission of light, which constitute the light itself.
Regarding that which is illuminated: if one follows the literal meaning (wen), it belongs to other lands (and so forth). To say it depends on the person is also not entirely certain;
for this is a general omen corresponding to the six subsequent specific ones, and because it is that which manifests, it is the cause that brings about what is seen.
Thus, although the meaning of this single passage is universal, this passage must belong to other lands; yet for now, following the literal text, it belongs [to this land].
In general, other lands are all suitable for reliance upon this; this is for the sake of convenience in explaining the text.

Next, regarding the correct interpretation of the passage: "The light shines eastward to eighteen thousand [yojanas]" refers to the horizontal extent, while "from below up to the heavens" refers to the vertical height.

However, I maintain that this is not yet definitive. I maintain that the scriptural text consists of three parts: first, a general statement concerning the eastern direction; second, [the description] within the directions...
Regarding these numbers, among the distinctions within the three categories of numbers, the sūtra mentions "Avīci" and so forth; this is translated as "Without Interval" (Muzhuan).
Among the eight great hells, this one is situated at the very bottom; because the suffering experienced therein has no temporary respite, it is called "Without Interval.

It is also called *naraka*, which means "vessel of suffering," or "that which is not to be enjoyed," and it is also "not a place for practicing the Dharma. It is located... [in the midst of]... the world.
Regarding the various places mentioned here, the term "hell" (*naraka*) is spoken of from the perspective of its primary location.

*Brahmākaniṣṭha* is translated as "the ultimate limit of material obstruction" (*kaniṣṭha* meaning "ultimate limit" and *ākaṇiṣṭha* meaning "material obstruction"). It is also called "the summit of existence" (*bhavāgra*), the "limit of the peak," or the "heaven of the ultimate limit.

This is because it is the uppermost point of all that possesses form (*rūpa*), and light can reach this place; however, it does not illuminate the formless realms (*ārūpya*), for those [realms] are formless.
Therefore, it is explained in detail that "illuminating the hells" clarifies that suffering is to be pitied, while "illuminating the Peak of Existence" reveals that even pleasure is impermanent.

Since both suffering and pleasure are impermanent, this causes sentient beings to weary of worldly affairs and leads them to awaken to and enter the Buddha-dharma. Thus, some say it signifies that although there is suffering, all shall be uprooted;
and that those who possess pleasure are exhorted to seek the One Vehicle. His compassion is universally vast, illuminating the suffering of all who have a connection with him.
Although it is certainly easy [to understand], one cannot yet reach the ultimate assembly; nevertheless, the illumination causes suffering to cease.

Now, this is said to clearly demonstrate that the universal illumination of the six realms of existence explains that this teaching should universally open up all provisional means to reveal the aspect of the true reality.
Among the three types of scriptural exegesis, this commentary explains the first two. Within this, there are three parts: first, the description of the ancient interpretations; second...

This clarifies that the following shall be the threefold formal explanation. Regarding the beginning: the general indication provides a universal interpretation, while the specific section provides a particular one.
"Universal" refers to the fact that, according to principle, it should universally illuminate [all meanings]; however, the "particular" is precisely used to manifest this specific significance.

As for "significance," it is precisely because the East represents the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and "ten thousand" represents cause and effect; since the East is the foremost of all directions, it is taken as the symbol for the One Vehicle.

The meaning of the "Superior" (shàng) is that it represents the fullness and deficiency of the eighteen numbers; thus it serves as a table for cause and effect. Regarding the sequence of difficult inquiries:
the cause and effect of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) encompass everything completely. Since each is individually sufficient, why wait for further words?

As for the universal illumination of the ten directions, both [theories] are untenable. To ensure there is no error, one should correctly rely on the subtle words (sūkṣma-vākya), which should universally illuminate all ten directions.

Regarding the spatial orientation, why is it only the east? Furthermore, regarding the statement "eighteen thousand," the commentary explains only its limitation while simultaneously implying its universal application;
thus, the heading and the explanation contradict each other, and neither is established. Therefore, this [interpretation] is not adopted. A detailed explanation still contains three points:
first, to clarify that illuminating only one direction signifies the Single Vehicle Dharma (*ekayāna*); second, to clarify the reason for illuminating the east; third, to clarify...
The meaning of "eighteen thousand" and the meaning of the latter two [categories] are the same as those mentioned previously;
subsequent commentators who explain only these two meanings also share the same intent as the former, yet both differ from my present interpretation.

Next, in the formal explanation, the three passages are fully interpreted according to three modes of exposition. The first exposition treats the single direction of the East as simultaneously encompassing the meaning of the ten directions;

furthermore, the explanation of "direction" alone simultaneously encompasses the meaning of "number. First, the East is clarified by designating both the subject (the capacity) and the object (that which is manifested), each having its underlying reason.

From the "Trace Gate" (*jimon*) onward, that which is truly manifested is clarified, which is the act of opening and revealing. Here, "direction" symbolizes "position," and "East" symbolizes "beginning."
The beginning of the first position is like the head of the East; this applies to the subsequent text and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as well, which refers to the stage of the true cause (*bhūta-hetu*).

By citing the beginning, the following serves as an example: knowing the initial stage allows one to understand the subsequent ones. Quoting the text establishes that both the subject (*grāhaka*) and the object (*grāhya*) are all-pervasive.
"Subject" refers to the first and the ninth [positions]; "object" refers to the four positions opened by the first, namely: Manifestation (*darśana*), Realization (*avabodha*), and so forth.
"Opening" (*kai*) signifies showing, awakening, entering, and the single stage; thus, one stage is itself four stages, and each [of those] is likewise so.
These four are themselves eleven, for within each single stage there are ten. Therefore, there is no statement that is not all-pervasive, which secretly expresses two meanings.

Someone says: "This merely clarifies the meaning of the eastern direction; how then are the other eight directions? Although they are explained separately below, they are merely contemplative understandings (*kanke*). Who [is it that realizes them]?"

It should be said that this expresses the meaning [of the full moon]. Some say that the text omits this meaning; others say that although the commentary below observes it, it still refers to the phenomenon itself, and thus the text says "it expresses.

Others say that previously one only refuted the other's [view of] the One Vehicle, but did not refute the meaning of cause and effect, because the intended meaning regarding what is expressed by the number is the same. Now, I fear this is not the case. Why? Because these are both the full and the deficient...
The number specifically signifies the meaning of the "perfect cause" (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*) herein. How is this known?

Because all four are at the stage of the cause, and since they are all spoken of as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*), how could this not signify the perfect cause? If it were not the perfect cause, one could not possess the latter [the fruit] from the very beginning, nor could one have the whole within the single part.
What was said previously—that the explanation of the "directions" (*diś*) is itself the explanation of the "number"—its intent lies precisely here. Thus it is known.

"Directions" and "numbers" merely represent the beginning and end of the causes for circularity. Within this, if one speaks generally of the four intentions, they refer to the subject and object, as well as the beginning and end—that is, the Worldly [Truth].
If one speaks specifically, citing the beginning to reveal the end—that is, the Human [Truth].

The perfect subtlety that is directionless breaks through fixed attachments—that is, the Truth of Counteraction. By relying on the four constants to manifest the principle of the absence of four—that is, the Ultimate Truth.

This is the ultimate cause for severing [delusion] and perfecting [enlightenment], which is precisely the meaning of the teaching. Next, regarding the distinction between the original and the trace, this reveals the perfection of the ultimate cause.
First, it clarifies that which signifies: namely, that as the near is about to be opened to reveal the far, the Buddhas from the four directions assemble.

Below, it clarifies that which is signified: that is to say, one should understand that this causes the four stages to increase to their ultimate limit. As for the phrase "the Buddhas assemble," the *Ji* (Commentary) states: "The assembly signifies increase."

The Gate of the Traces of Meaning (*Gyōjimon*) concerns the illumination of light; the Gate of the Original Source (*Honmon*) concerns the gathering of people; the Gate of the Traces (*Jikimon*) concerns the One; and the Gate of the Original Source (*Honmon*) concerns the Four.

Now, it is said that the former [the *Gyōjimon*] was the Buddha’s illumination of light, while the present [the *Honmon*] is likewise the Buddha’s initial convocation; both are equal as matters concerning those who have attained the fruit.
Since the former clarified that "the One is precisely the Four," and having already concluded the reconciliation that "the One is precisely the Four," one can now speak of those "Four."
Although the emanated bodies pervade the ten directions, here only four are mentioned because [the text] speaks of the capacity [to manifest] based on what is manifested; thus it mentions only four.

As for why it says "Buddhas" rather than "Bodhisattvas": some say that "Buddha" is specifically taken to represent the meaning of perfect and wondrous [enlightenment], and thus Bodhisattvas are not included;

others say that "Bodhisattva" is specifically taken and Buddha is not, as this accords with the scripture’s statement that they emerge from the four directions. The sub-commentary below explains that this represents...
Because there are four positions, some say that both are Buddhas; others say that since both serve as the catalyst for arousal, they should be taken together.

I now maintain that taking them together is entirely excellent and beautiful. While the previous statement referred to the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and this present statement refers to the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*), the meaning is already manifest in the subsequent text.
As for why the fruit is not explicitly indicated here, I maintain that the "gate" itself encompasses this meaning. Why is this so? Although...
Furthermore, because the preceding light merely illuminates the location, the subsequent light summons the assembly of those who have realized the fruit.

Since this causal assembly is summoned by the central light and consists of those who have attained the fruit, it precisely represents the perfection of the causal stage reaching its ultimate height and the accomplishment of the perfect fruit.

The "summoning" by the perfect light symbolizes that the perfect cause is capable of evoking the perfect fruit; the "assembly" of Buddhas symbolizes the perfect fruit being offered in recompense for the perfect cause. This is the meaning of the sound.
The same applies to that which is summoned (and so forth). This interpretation, which accords with the meaning of the scriptural text, differs from the explanations of former scholars;
although there are many such divergent interpretations between ancient and modern times, I have reflected upon them and shall now elaborate upon them hereafter.

Furthermore, for the sake of convenience in the exposition, I will first explain the eighteen thousand [types of beings], followed by the ten dharma-realms. Within the first of these, I shall first...
If one calculates the number based on a single realm (*dhātu*), there are the following: first, by combining the ten realms, one establishes the eighteen realms;
based on this number, if one discusses each [realm] as possessing the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), there are one hundred and eight realms.
Furthermore, based on these realms, if one considers that each of the heavens possesses the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*), it becomes one thousand and eight hundred. This is as previously stated.
Since there are already one thousand eight hundred realms, when calculated according to the ten realms, there are eighteen thousand;
this illuminates that within each of these eighteen thousand realms, there are all such differentiated objects. The following section explains the meaning of what is illuminated:

"The Buddha-wisdom" refers to the threefold perfect and wondrous objects and the wisdom of the three contemplations (*trividha-pratyavekṣaṇā*). Although this is still an analytical understanding (*vipaśyanā*), it nevertheless manifests what is to come.
At that time, because he still entrusts [the teaching] to the matters and the objects of contemplation, this is the contemplative understanding of the Buddha-wisdom;

it returns to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby manifesting the perfect cause and fruit. This does not contradict the previous meaning. Since this is discussed in relation to the ten [realms], which ones are they? Therefore, the text is cited to demonstrate this;

this is precisely the explicit teaching on the ten realms (*daśadhātu*). Furthermore, regarding the citations as proof: the previous one proved the stage of this person, while this one discusses this [topic].

The person in this station possesses a single word that contains two meanings; therefore, both are cited. Xuanzang says: "The vehicle has ten meanings. First, the meaning of being supreme is represented by the head.
Second, the meaning of the Middle Way is represented by the space between the eyebrows. Third, the meaning of manifest clarity is represented by the white [tuft].
Fourth, the meaning of being free from obscuration is represented by the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft. Fifth, the meaning of destroying... [text continues]
1. The meaning of manifesting through radiance is represented by six; 2. The meaning of non-duality is represented by one direction; 3. The fundamental meaning is represented by the east; 4.
The meaning of the fulfillment of the resultant vehicle is represented by ten thousand; 5. The meaning of the causal vehicle being incomplete is represented by eight thousand; 6.
The meaning of the exhaustive explanation of the principle of cause and effect is represented by pervasiveness. (And so forth. East Breaks.
Although the ten meanings have not subsumed this for such a long time, the four virtues (and so forth) relate to purity and bliss (and so forth).
Next, this corresponds to its respective textual passage as previously discussed. When discussing the meaning, it must apply universally; when interpreting the text, it must belong to the other land.
Since we have already interpreted the text [in that context], it should not again be applied here. This appears to be inconsistent with the text.
Next, the auspicious signs in other lands are explained. What preceded was general; this is specific. "General" refers to the illumination by a single ray of light;
"specific" refers to the manifestation of six kinds of characteristics. Thus, the former is the agent (the general) and the latter is the object (the specific).

Furthermore, what preceded was the Buddha emitting light that illuminated; this is the great assembly seeing through the light. Therefore, the six chapters are all titled "Seeing. Moreover, what preceded—
This is that which manifests; this is that which is manifested. One should know that these two phrases combined constitute these three names.
The commentary (*śūtra*) explains this in two distinct parts: first, the formal analysis and explanation of the text concerning the six auspicious omens;

second, the clarification of what the six omens signify. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the presentation of the headings; second, the detailed enumeration; third, the explanation of their sequence.
Regarding the "classification and enumeration" (ke-lie): this refers to the topical headings that correspond to the numerical markers above, as well as the listing of names;
thus there are three. As for the six, they exhaust the various states of differentiation, hence there are six; furthermore, to re-emphasize their essential meaning, they are presented as three pairs.
One should know that the six [categories] of this land are likewise so; within each of the eighteen thousand worlds, these six are all fully present.
The first six lines of the chapter clarify the three phrases of the sutra text. First, "those who are able to see" refers to the great assembly gathered at this very assembly;
therefore, it says "at these [beings]. Second, "the objects seen" refers generally to the eighteen thousand [beings] and the specific numbers contained therein.
The *Śāstra* treats four among them as the Three Jewels; however, the meaning here is intended figuratively rather than being definitive.

Since the mind does not take this as its primary focus, the text does not restrict itself to it. Regarding the names, essences, and the classification and combination of the six destinies (*ṣadgati*), these shall be explained in the subsequent text.

"The two" refers to the transforming lord within those [destinies]; "lord" here denotes the Ultimate Sage. Within the destinies, there are also traces of the Sages, as they are contrasted with the transformations of the higher Sages;
therefore, it is said that the teaching for the lower ordinary beings has both general and specific meanings. The general meaning follows from the beginning.

This concludes the section on the provisional and initial sudden teachings, which will be manifested in the latter four assemblies. Within the text, there is mention of "practice," which refers to the cause; "attaining the Way," which refers to the fruit;
and "person and dharma," which refer respectively to that which covers and that which is covered. These are explained here according to their general application.

Regarding the person, they should generally apply to the subsequent sections, yet for now we follow the specific distinction. Within the sūtra text, there are four phrases concerning practice, which will be briefly explained later; this brief explanation does not clarify every detail.
It is said that the boundless [qualities] of a bodhisattva are briefly subsumed under two gateways that encompass all things. First is the gateway of causes and conditions:

past habitual tendencies serve as the cause, while meeting virtuous friends externally serves as the condition. Because internal causes differ and external conditions are not uniform, they are called "various faiths and understandings.
That which begins as faith and culminates in understanding is termed "faith" for those of dull faculties and "understanding" for those of sharp faculties.
Having explained above that entering the Way each has its respective causes and conditions, we now clarify that entering the Way each has its beginning and end;

because there are differences between the sharp and the dull, the Bodhisattvas are subsumed under the Gate of Faith and Understanding (*śraddhā-vimokṣa-mukha*). Regarding "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*):

when a Bodhisattva practices, there must be characteristics that manifest their conduct of body and speech, which are displayed outwardly as "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), while the conduct of mental action is made clear and is called "appearance" (*nimitta*); therefore, they are referred to by "characteristics."

The "Gate of Appearance" encompasses those who practice the bodhisattva path; because these three aforementioned matters collectively constitute what is called "practicing the bodhisattva path," the Treatise states:
"To gather in sentient beings by means of the four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu) is called practicing the bodhisattva path.

Furthermore, it is said that "causes and conditions" (hetupratyaya) carries the sense of "the reason why," meaning that by seeking birth [in the higher realms] and swiftly realizing the fruit of Buddhahood, one delivers sentient beings.

They give birth [to this resolve] for various reasons: some practice the bodhisattva path to cultivate the causes and conditions [for enlightenment]; some practice the bodhisattva path to adorn and purify buddha-fields and to bring sentient beings to maturity through the practices of awakening;
and some practice the bodhisattva path to cultivate the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

Such are the various reasons. As for "faith and understanding" (*adhimukti*), it refers to one who both has faith and possesses understanding while abiding in the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*), having not yet attained the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
Regarding the "aspect of the fruit" (*phala-lakṣaṇa*): it refers to the aspect of the conduct and demeanor of one practicing the Bodhisattva path.
Having already attained the fruit of the Path by abiding in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one enters the two positions because of having practiced the Bodhisattva path through various means.

The *Mūla-śāstra* states that "conditions" (*pratyaya*) refer to encountering external favorable conditions and meeting many virtuous friends; for a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is a great causal condition, and thus one has faith.

The "appearance" (*ākāra*) refers to internal cultivation; within this internal cultivation, mental activity is called "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*), while physical and verbal activity is called "appearance.
Contemplating the subtle principle with the mind is called "resolute belief," and the relinquishing of one's head, eyes, and so forth is called "appearance.

Regarding the practitioner of the Bodhisattva path, the treatise states that because they teach and transform sentient beings by relying on the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and skillfully gathering them in, it is termed "belief."

Understanding the characteristics [of this state] is the practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha-caryā*), while practicing the Bodhisattva path is the practice for the benefit of others (*parārtha-caryā*).
"Seeing the Buddha enter *nirvāṇa*" refers to entering it; it is also called *parinirvāṇa*. Sengzhao says it is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and is also named "extinction" (*mie-du*).

Ancient translations also called it "quiescent extinction" (*jimi*). Jingying says "entering extinction" means "resting. Modern translations call it *parinirvāṇa*, which is rendered here as "perfect quiescence" (*yuanji*). This means:

"Perfection and tranquility" (*parinirvāṇa*) means that virtues are perfected and afflictions are stilled. According to the common explanations of various schools, this indicates entering the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*;
what is clarified by our own school is the cessation of function and the return to the essence. Therefore, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are called "returning to the great abode.
The two phrases herein cause sentient beings to cultivate the seeds of the path and accumulate merit; as will be explained later, they also serve as the capacity for production.
The cessation [of all things] is entirely for the sake of providing the conditions for the deliverance of sentient beings who are ready to be delivered.
Although various commentators divide this into two sections, I now merge them into one; it is simply a single manifestation for the sake of sentient beings. As for the terms "beginning" and "end":
because the Bodhisattva first begins their cultivation, it is the beginning of this practice; because the Buddha is a person of fruition whose activity has ceased, it is the end of this practice.
It is appropriate to discuss this, hence it is said thus. Next is the third section on "Sequence. This single passage should be understood as having three meanings:

first, why does it speak only of the six? Second, why is the sequence as it is? Third, it means that the Way of teaching and transformation does not exceed the principle of response and stimulus (*ganying*).
Specifically, the first pair refers to the response (*ying*); the second pair refers to the correct response to the stimulus; and the third pair refers to the stimulus itself.
This response arises from the nature; this cultivation accords with the function of wisdom as it returns to the essence. This is also the meaning of the "subject" and "object.

These three and six are necessarily such that these six cannot be exceeded or omitted in their sequence. To summarize the ultimate point, it does not go beyond the mutual resonance of the Way between the stimulus and the response.

From this point onward, the following clarifies the "manifestation of the response" (*pratibhāsa*). Since it is said that there are six auspicious omens (*ṣaḍ-pratibhāsa*), although the meaning of these six omens was previously clarified, their significance as a "manifestation of the response" had not yet been explained;
thus, this section serves to manifest and respond to that significance. This manifestation of the response is precisely the correct interpretation of the meaning of the omens.

Within this, there are two parts: first, the brief [explanation], and second, the extensive [explanation]. The brief refers to the distinction between the two [the Buddhas and the bodhisattvas], while the extensive clarifies the five points of commonality. Now, regarding the first of these: [The text continues with the specific details of the manifestations.]
This section generally clarifies the intent behind the illumination of the two lands; for although the light that manifests is one, there are six types of phenomena manifested by it.
Of these, the first two phrases contain both the agent and the locus, which are easy to understand from the text;

in the preceding section, "Correctly Clarifying," this section specifically clarifies "Awakening" because it emits the central light. Reflect on this. The subsequent two sections specifically clarify the meaning of the six aspects within each of the two lands.

The initial statement regarding the "identity of the Way" refers to the identity of the way of teaching and transformation. This is because the Buddhas speak collectively of the three periods of time and the ten directions so that all beings may hear it and necessarily believe it.
Although this general statement of identity contains two specific distinctions—namely, the two types of identity—there should actually be three identities;
however, only two are mentioned because the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* (*Anantaparyāya-samudgata-sūtra*) has not yet been revealed within the text, and thus one is omitted.
Now, although only two [aspects] are clarified, when the assembly raises their doubts, Mañjuśrī answers them by clarifying the identity of the three;
for once they have seen that they are identical, they will know that they must necessarily be identical. Thus, he merely uses the mystery of phenomena to symbolize this.

Once the questions and answers are concluded, it is known that the great task of preaching this sutra is finished and the path of transformation is complete; its wondrous function is inconceivable, brought about through such means.
As for the preceding exposition of the meaning, one should clarify four points: first, the initial exposition of the two types of awakening pertains to the world;

since the previous exposition refuted the two extremes, it pertained to the remedial (pratipakṣa). This [present] exposition concerns the two lands—the environment and its inhabitants—and thus pertains to the world (*loka*).

(And so forth. Second, the collective exposition of their identity is intended to inspire faith in sentient beings; this constitutes the "person" (*pudgala*) aspect. Their shared state of being free from delusion constitutes the remedial aspect. They shall be identical.

That is to say, having first eliminated the general [meaning] and taken up the specific, and having already established the commonality for the person who has gained conviction, one proceeds to refute it and reveal the second meaning (and so forth).
Next, the extensive explanation consists of four parts:
first, the summary and heading; second, the formal exposition; third, the concluding summary and indication; and fourth, further analysis according to the text.

In the initial passage, the text contains the meanings of both "two" and "five," yet as it stands alone, it is not fully understood; therefore, it must be further expanded upon in order to exhaust its intended meaning.
This text thus possesses five aspects, all of which will be manifested in the subsequent verses. All that is explained here adopts the latter sense. Regarding "the first":
because the six are necessarily five, the ultimate truth is non-dual. The "second" arises from conditions; the "first" arises from immediate conditions.
Therefore, that which is non-existent yet exists, and its sequential progression is likewise so. In the second [stage], both the gradual and the sudden are fully present.
In the fifth meaning, "opening" and "gathering" constitute the two meanings of "opening and harmonizing. "Immeasurable" refers to the aforementioned gradual and sudden.
Thus, the previous explanations of the gradual and sudden all speak of "all," which is precisely the immeasurable Dharma. In the concluding summary below, first, it concludes that.

The former [period] corresponds to this [present], and this [present] corresponds to that [past]; beginning with what is called "appearing in the world" and ending with what is called "withdrawing and ceasing his transformative activity to erect a stupa.
Since these two passages in the *Sāṃkathya* (or *Saṃgīti*) are clear, the meaning is manifest.

Regarding this intent, although the present assembly already knows it must necessarily be so, they still keep the two [aspects] concealed; thus, although there are five [periods], they are effectively treated as two.
This causes them to doubt, so that they may request the manifestation of the three insights (*tisro vidyāḥ*) to clarify the excellence of his wondrous merit;
how truly marvelous is this faith! The above concludes the extensive explanation of the meaning of the manifested retributions.

Below is the fourth section, which further clarifies the text by correlating it with the fifth of the six preceding passages—the two phrases concerning the "bodhisattva practices" (*bodhisattvacaryā*). Because these contain manifold meanings, they must be further synthesized.
In the explanation of this [passage], first the three phrases of the sūtra are explained, followed by a conclusion clarifying the two similarities.

Within the initial section, there is first a separate explanation of the meaning of "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*), followed by a combined explanation of the two phrases. Within the former, there is first a general explanation and then a specific one. The general explanation applies across all doctrinal flavors;

however, while the meaning of causes and conditions has both general and specific aspects, here we explain according to the specific aspect. Therefore, it is divided into "present" and "past," as is the case with everything else.
Now, the current teachings state that what the Prince heard in the past—the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—served as the seed planted as the cause;

that which was accomplished through various intermediate skillful means served as the remote condition (*parapratyaya*); and hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* teachings now serves as the immediate condition (*sannikṛṣṭapratyaya*), whereby one immediately attains awakening and so forth.
This resulting phenomenon is called "liberation. Now, I say that this person does not contemplate at all, but is entirely in a dream.

Regarding the source of this passage: it is a general exposition on the meaning of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), for the flavor of all teachings contains the principle of causes and conditions, and thus it is the same in every case.
These four points are not to be taken as one: first, the land of transformation does not involve this world;
second, a general discourse should not be treated as a specific one; third, bodhisattvas do not hear the [teachings] of the two vehicles; and fourth, the text...
To claim that practicing the Path leads to the fruit of liberation while contradicting both the text and the meaning is utterly untrustworthy;

how could such a view even be entertained for a moment? This point precisely means that past habituation serves as the cause, while the current teaching of a virtuous friend can provide the necessary assistance;
with the former acting as the condition, one is thus able to hear, believe, understand, and practice, which constitutes the dharmas that are produced.
This explains that one practices the Dharma through hearing and faith as the causal conditions; it is called "various" because it applies universally to all.
Thus, this does not contradict the sutra—such is the meaning of the commentary (and so forth). Next, regarding the term "specific":

in contrast to the preceding universal sense, it refers specifically to those currently present, and furthermore, it refers specifically to the three types of people within the two flavors during the intermediate period; hence it is called "specific. Here, the Vaipulya (fangděng) is not mentioned, but...

Regarding the term "Prajñā," some say the text is abbreviated; however, I maintain that since it is called the "Collection" (Piṭaka), it necessarily encompasses both flavors (the *sādhāraṇa* and *asādhāraṇa*).
Furthermore, the phrase "common and so forth" (*sādhāraṇādi*) fully applies here as well. In the verses below, the distinction between the common and uncommon is clear;

it is stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* that "common" refers to what is shared with Bodhisattvas, while "uncommon" refers to the distinct and the perfect [teachings]. However, if one were to discuss this according to the ultimate reality (*tattva*), [the situation is as follows]:

"Common" refers to both the general and the specific; "uncommon" refers to the Perfect [Teaching]. This is because the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) serves as the primary and correct factor, acting as the cause;

it cannot be taken separately as merely the teaching of the *prajñā* vehicle. The other perfections—precept, concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth—are the five perfections that act as auxiliary factors, serving as conditions.

These two [aspects] exist only within the *prajñā* [vehicle]. The above explains the causes and conditions; below, the various three types of persons are explained. These are the three kinds of bodhisattvas.

Because the sūtra text refers specifically to Bodhisattvas of the *vaipulya* (extensive) teachings, although these apply generally to later stages, they are mentioned here to clarify a specific distinction;

furthermore, because the characteristics of the practice of Bodhisattvas in the *tripiṭaka* are entirely different, it mentions only three [types]. Next, regarding the combined explanation of the two phrases:

although both phrases are cited together, only the two kinds of "various" (*nānā*) are explained, and the causes, conditions, and characteristics are not further explained. "Causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) refers to...

Regarding the "intimate and distant aspects of past and present" as mentioned previously, this refers to the physical form and demeanor—that is, the physical form and demeanor of the practice of the three karmas.
Since these two meanings are thus established, how are their various types categorized? First, there are four gates;
second, when these are combined with the two [meanings], there are twelve. Within these twelve, each further contains numerous internal and external varieties.
What is this? The following citation from the sutra clarifies it. Regarding the phrase "the cause of the body," the body is the effect and the cause is the cause;

it is spoken thus because it refers to the cause that brings about the effect of this body. As stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the five hundred arhats each spoke of what they had observed regarding the cause of the body prior to their realization of the Way: some said ignorance was the cause, while others said it was afflictions or karma.
Taking these as causes, one attains liberation through such contemplation. Having spoken thus, he questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "There is nothing that is not the correct teaching.

This meaning is that because all have attained the Way, they are all correct. Although this belongs to the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teachings and is a shared doctrine common to one portion [of the teachings], it is temporarily borrowed here for the sake of providing proof.
This is a brief citation of what is common; below, examples will be used to clarify what is not common (*asādhāraṇa*). If...
Those who wish to realize this are those who enter the Gate of Non-duality through the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti); as the text is abbreviated, it is not cited here.

Thus we know that the concluding summary below mentions "various" (*vicitra*), which implies "immeasurable. Regarding the three phrases in the sutra, the middle one—faith-understanding (*adhimukti*)—need not be discussed further, as its meaning is clarified in many places in the subsequent text. As for the meaning of "various," it follows the same principle as the preceding sections.

On each gate there is faith and understanding; because these are of various kinds and easy to comprehend, they are not explained in detail. The concluding section below is the same as the first phrase above.

The first sentence concludes that what was previously given here is the same [as what follows]; the next two sentences conclude that what is to be given here will be the same as that, and what is here will be the same as that.
Because immeasurable meanings are hidden, there are only two types of "sameness. Within the category of "will be the same," there is only...

Because the manifestation through events had not yet been fully revealed, doubt arose, leading to a request for clarification: "Why do you not immediately manifest the three identities (*trīṇi samāni*)?

Instead, you first give rise to discourse while remaining concealed in common secrecy, causing others to inquire in doubt before finally speaking. The Sūtra states: "This is the most supreme, the most difficult to believe and understand, and the most difficult to expound.
It must be taught only when the Way of the present accords with that of the past; only then may it be spoken. Although [the Buddha] manifested in the East...
Since the present and the future are identical to the past, it was necessary to remain cryptic and wait for his doubts to arise before revealing the truth;

furthermore, there are two gates of correct teaching: the horizontal illumination toward the East represents the unmanifest traces (*traces*), while the vertical orientation toward the Origin represents the distant, hidden Root.
Thus, by first inducing his questions and then manifesting both [the traces and the root], only then...
How could the intent of this earnest exhortation be merely superficial? Reflect upon it, reflect upon it!

Now, since that which is manifested herein is both causal and conditional, it should briefly comprise four meanings. Briefly stated, these four are: illuminating the two lands to manifest the two types of awakening;

specifically, the preceding [section] represents what was manifested by the light received from within, while the subsequent [section] illuminates the two lands simultaneously to manifest the destruction of the darkness of the two extremes.

Therefore, while [the previous section] pertained to the counteractive (*pratipakṣa*), the present section directly serves to manifest the awakening within the self and others regarding the environment and its inhabitants;

thus it pertains to the world (*loka*). Each has its own reason. Next, the identity with oneself is clarified: once one’s own substance is realized, others will believe it without doubt; this constitutes the "Human" [Vehicle].

It secretly indicates that what follows shall break through the provisional to reveal the real; this constitutes the "Counteractive" meaning. Although the text is extensive, it consists of only these two.

The same three meanings apply to the subsequent sections of the text as well. Alternatively, because the sutra contains three textual passages, they correspond directly to the aforementioned three meanings:

(1) cause and condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)—the present and the past; (2) basis (*āśraya*)—the world and faith-understanding (*adhimukti*); and (3) for the sake of persons (*pudgala*)—the various characteristics of the practice of the three types of karma.
Since these three are already complete, one should rely solely on the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), even though [other levels] exist.
I fear that this interpretation may not be the intended meaning; for now, let us consider how the brief and extensive versions differ as previously discussed.
Furthermore, these points accord with the intent of this very sutra and not with other teachings. This can be understood by analogy through the *Ben guan* (Original Contemplation), and so forth.

Next, regarding the "Preface of Doubtful Thought": because it is extremely secret and constantly unfathomable, there is "doubtful thought. Doubt serves as a ford for liberation;
because it leads to the absence of delusion, doubtful thought itself constitutes the preface. This is because there is both doubt and thought. As for the presence of these two:
since the entire assembly was in doubt, Maitreya was the one who first initiated [the teaching]; therefore, he is first singled out, and the great assembly is likewise mentioned. This is the meaning.

Regarding the "doubtful thoughts" mentioned at the beginning of the three [stages] for the assembly in question: "attention" refers to the mind being directed toward the objective realm, while "not yet fathoming its cause" constitutes doubt.
As for the passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī’s arising of thought," although it clarifies the thoughts of the three [stages], it preserves the three insights (*vidyā*).
Based on this explanation, one should know that the first and second stages both possess doubtful thoughts, whereas the third stage possesses only thought and is free from doubt.

Knowledge (*jñāna*) pervades all three types of doubt, whereas mindfulness (*smṛti*) is restricted to the first two; here, we follow the comprehensive explanation and thus speak of "mindfulness" for all. It is said that mindfulness excludes only the intermediate doubt.
The first doubt and the subsequent mindfulness both remain without having yet given rise to a question, as the subsequent mindfulness has not yet ceased.

Thus, we know that only the single intermediate doubt is absent. Only after the subsequent mindfulness has questioned is the initial [doubt] removed, and only after the initial [doubt] has been answered is it severed.
First, regarding "recollection" (*smṛti*) and "doubt" (*vicikitsā*): since what follows consists only of recollection and not doubt, both terms are mentioned here.

To explain the first part of the sutra text, there are three phrases. The first is the introductory heading provided by the *śāstrakāra*; the latter two constitute the actual doubt and recollection. The first phrase is "recollection," and the second is "doubt.
The "spiritual transformations" (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) that are recollected refer collectively to the six aspects of the two lands; these are the objects of the recollection.
This is the origin of doubt. The subsequent phrase states that because its source cannot be fathomed, one therefore doubts.
At the outset, the names and essences are presented in pairs, referring to the names of the two entities: the internal and the external.
The following explains the meaning of its name. Regarding the term "Heavenly Mind" (*tianxin*), according to this location, the *Yi* (Book of Changes) states:

"That which cannot be fathomed through yin and yang is called the numinous" (*shen*); it also states: "The numinous has no fixed location"; and it further states: "The numinous is subtle and wondrous throughout all things.

Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) combines these two passages from the *Yi*, hence he says: "The numinous is subtle and wondrous, and without fixed location. Among the various interpretations of this location, some take [the former], while others take [the latter].
Whether it is "unfathomable" (*bùcè*) or "taking [forms] without fixed direction" (*qǔ wúfāng*), both follow the explanations in the *Yì* (Book of Changes).

If one were to look at the single character "spirit" (*shén*) from a superficial perspective, it might seem to be a praise for transformation. What is being said here, however, relies precisely on the explanations provided in the sutras; thus, the *Benye jing* explains supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as follows:

"Spirit" (*shén*) refers to the Heavenly Mind (*tiānxīn*), and "pervasion" (*tōng*) refers to being unobstructed. This means that the function of the truly real mind is immediately liberated and unimpeded.

Because it is unobstructed, it is called "supernatural power" (*abhijñā*). The four characters "Today, the Heavenly Mind" (*jīnrì tiānxīn*) precisely employ that sutra to explain the meaning of "spirit" (*shén*).
What follows below explains this meaning by correlating it with that sutra. Since the sutra speaks of "mind," it refers to "inner wisdom" (*neihui*), which is true and wondrous gnosis (*prajñā*).
It is appropriate that there be a wondrous object; since the object arises from gnosis, it is named "wisdom. This is the essence (*tǐ*). Transformation...

Because this matter manifests as a phenomenal appearance, it is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*), which is precisely its function. Since we are now speaking of the wondrous essence and the wondrous function, it is termed "divine transformation" (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*);
this essence is itself the function, and this divinity is itself the transformation. What follows is a citation of evidence:

the "non-dual dharma" refers to the aforementioned wondrous essence, while "the ability to act" and so forth refer to the wondrous function. The *Record* (the commentary) states: "Internal and external," etc.
This clarifies that they are distinct and thus requires this separate explanation; however, if one were to provide a general explanation, it would be as stated in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*:

"All dharmas are called spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*)," as fully recorded in the first commentary on the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Now, I say: the text of the sub-commentary clarifies that [the transformation] is the function while being the essence (*tattva*), whereas the Sūtra clarifies that it is the essence while being the function—reflect upon this.
The preceding section concludes the explanation of mindfulness; the following section resolves doubts. The first phrase correctly clarifies that which is unfathomable—the source of profound doubt.

The subsequent phrase concludes by stating: "For this reason, there is profound astonishment and doubt. The "Dharma King" refers to the Buddha, whose realized essence (*dharmakāya*) is sublime and wondrous;

his essence and function are lofty and vast, reaching the ultimate limit. "Transcending" (*chao*) means to surpass this ultimate height. "Pervading" (*gai*) means to encompass this ultimate breadth. This is the person who is able to manifest [this reality].
Using the ultimate of height and breadth, the intent of what is performed extends both horizontally and vertically without limit.
For this reason, how could those who have not yet reached the pinnacle of universality fathom it? Thus, one attains freedom from doubt; hence it is said that "the thought arises reaching this point.

"Reaching this point" refers to the auspicious signs manifested by the Buddha as divine transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*); it means that these are boundless and ultimately unfathomable. The *Jì* (Commentary) states: "At first..."

The meaning of the causal conditions of the text is complete through the four *siddhāntas*, as the internal and external differ; thus, seeing and hearing bring joy. The six auspicious omens manifest externally so that beings may behold them and give rise to goodness.
Relying on principle, they adapt and transform, universally harmonizing all things. Because the principle of the Dharma King is ultimate, there is nothing superior to it.
Now, I say this cannot be reconciled [with other views]; herein, one should discuss the matter strictly in terms of what is doubted, rather than further discussing what is merely contemplated.
This realm is explained through the "Correct" [Teaching] precisely because its underlying cause cannot be fathomed.

That which is called "its cause" refers to manifesting these boundless transformations to secretly indicate that the two gates of the Trace and the Origin shall open the Provisional to reveal the Real, enabling all beings to obtain the benefit of the fourfold unity and the fourfold intent.
This is the ultimate meaning of the highest and most expansive [teachings], known only by the Buddha; therefore, it is beyond the reach of other stages.
No one could fathom the reason for this, and they were greatly startled and filled with doubt (and so forth).

Although the following passage appears to summarize the *Provisional Teaching* (*jiao*), it actually employs specific events as metaphors to resolve and establish the meaning of the "unfathomable. There are seven categories of text that convey this in succession;

this is also the constant norm of the Dharma. "Ordinary" (*yongchang*) refers to common practice. "Arts" (*shu*) refers to worldly arts and calculations; "methods" (*shu*) refer to medicinal formulas and the methods of spirits and deities.
The laws of yin and yang enable one to accomplish what ordinary people cannot understand; yet this concentration (*samādhi*) is still worldly concentration.

This record briefly covers the ascetic practices of non-Buddhists, the attainment of meditative concentration by ordinary beings and those with faith, and how, if one attains supramundane concentration, one becomes a realized sage—just as when the Universal Eye of the *Avataṃsaka* confronted Samantabhadra.
Because he does not see [the Buddha], he does not know the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*sambodhi*) of the one in the position of succession (*upapadya-bhūmi*).
