Because one takes this giving as the cause to bring about that eternal fruit, it is said that "one attains the indestructible.

Since there is neither giving nor non-giving, and both the phenomenon and the principle are fully present, this is the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*). If these three factors are all empty, that is the general meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā*;

however, since we are now clarifying the specific meanings of the three, [this applies here]. Thus, regarding these three types of Dharma-gifts, if one is preaching the Dharma, they all apply universally.

If a person practices solely for the sake of the Dharma, they belong to the Separate Teaching (biejiao); if they practice in accordance with the Dharma, they are exclusively a person of the Perfect Teaching (yuan). This applies to both the beginning and the end.

Although those of the Separate Teaching may, prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), appear to be attaining the stages, upon reaching the stages they are immediately a person of the Perfect Teaching; from beginning to end, they are one and the same.

Those who interpret it in this way differ from various other schools regarding the wording of the commentary; our current interpretation differs from what is explained in other traditions, and among these, this is the most [authoritative].
One must not fail to apply focused attention (*manasikāra*), for by taking this giving as a cause, one brings about that eternal fruit; thus it is said that "one attains the indestructible.
Since there is no such thing as giving or non-giving apart from the totality of the phenomenon (*dharma*), this is indeed the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

These three types of giving thus subsume the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*): material giving subsumes *dāna*; the fearlessness [of giving] subsumes *śīla* and *kṣānti*; and the gift of Dharma subsumes the final three. Therefore...
[The text] subsumes [the practices] from six up to ten thousand; the same applies to the remaining perfections. Master Xuanzang says:
"Since there are already the six perfections herein, they should merely serve to support the single meaning [of the paramitas]. I say this is not so. A brief explanation is as provided above;
this meaning is most essential, yet it is not discussed in any of the commentaries. Although there are transmitted explanations for this passage, none of them mention it—what a pity, what a pity!

Regarding the meaning of the commentary (*shu*) within the section on the Perfection of Precepts (*śīla-pāramitā*): because the scriptural text directly illustrates the perfection of precepts by focusing specifically on the monastic life, the commentary provides this explanation.

It is precisely for this reason that [the previous section] did not mention precepts and [this section] does not mention giving. However, if one were to discuss their perfect inclusion (*parigraha*), what would not be complete?

For now, however, proceeding according to the literal text and its practical application, these two perfections are clarified by way of their respective spheres of activity—namely, the lay and the monastic—as [he] approaches the Buddha to inquire.
This explains the origin of leaving the household life to uphold the precepts; it is only by relying on this upholding of the precepts that one is truly called "crossed over" (*tīrṇa*).

This refers, as stated in the Great Sūtra, to drawing near to virtuous friends and hearing the True Dharma. Thus, one first possesses faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*), and only then does one resolve to uphold the precepts.

Otherwise, it would be merely fruitless asceticism. The same applies to all six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); therefore, we know that it is not the case that clear faith and understanding arise separately later on.

Following the previous section, the next single line concerns precisely the observance of precepts upon leaving the household life (*pravrajyā*). Now, regarding leaving the household life, according to the examples in the sūtras, there should be four permutations;

that is, because body and mind may be in combination with one another, there are four cases. Although their outward appearance and attire may be identical, those whose bodies leave the home while their minds do not—lacking both aspiration and practice—are termed "those without shame or dread" (*ahrya-apatrāpya*) by the sūtras and śāstras. There are also those whose minds leave the home while their bodies do not...
One who leaves home to embody the Way and establish their resolve for its ultimate goal is exemplified by Vimalakīrti’s exhortation to the Elder’s son;

such a person both "leaves" and "does not leave," which is easy to understand. Now, since this person has left home specifically for the sake of the Way, they are one who both "leaves" and "does not leave.

Although this applies generally to all teachings, the present text primarily concerns the Distinct and Perfect [Teachings]. However, if the mind itself is sufficient, why must one necessarily leave home? Yet, although the Way is without...
Now, we rely upon causes and conditions; these conditions are most excellent, as clearly elucidated in the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra.

How much more so when it is further stated that the various kings do not merely possess superior conditions, but also manifest the noble and admirable nature of the path they practice. Regarding the citation of the *Pañcarājaka-sūtra* here:
it is briefly of this same category, cited now so that one may recognize its specific characteristics and circumstances. This is the sūtra [referred to].
To speak briefly of the essential point of this single minor fascicle: In the past, there were five kings of neighboring states who were free from rivalry and were mutual friends.
One great king was named Puhuan (Universal Peace); he practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva. The other four kings were full of intense false views.
King An took pity on them and summoned them to come together for seven days of mutual enjoyment. When they took their leave to return, King An escorted them as far as...
Along the way, he asked them what their aspirations were. One said, "I wish for a spring day to roam and play upon the open plains.
Another said, "I wish always to be a king, adorned with all manner of finery, while the people turn their eyes toward me as we travel along the road.
Another said, "I wish to have a beautiful wife and son who are upright and handsome, to have many brothers whose wisdom is peerless, and to share fine food and music with my father."
Having thus entertained one another and each finished speaking, they turned to address King Anavatapta: "What is your wish? He replied: "I shall first speak of your wishes:
if you delight in spring excursions, you will wither in winter; if you delight in being king, your merit will be exhausted and another will succeed you;
if you delight in wife and children, one day you will suffer immeasurable pain through illness; if you delight in your parents remaining forever, one day they will pass away."
When the Four Heavenly Kings asked about the affairs held by others, they further inquired: "We wish to hear of that which the Great King delights in. He replied:
"That which I delight in is neither arising nor ceasing, neither suffering nor pleasure, neither hunger nor thirst, neither cold nor heat;
it is the sovereign mastery over existence and non-existence. The Four Heavenly Kings asked again: "Where does such joy exist? Where is there a teacher who dwells in peace? The King answered.
It is said that my teacher, titled Buddha, was recently at Jetavana; the various kings were filled with joy and each went to the Buddha’s dwelling.
The Buddha preached on the eight sufferings, and the kings along with their retinues—numbering hundreds of thousands of people—all attained the first fruit [of the path].

Here, we specifically take up the matter of abandoning their kingdoms to leave the household life and uphold the precepts, treating it as a parallel case for brevity. Other meanings are not necessarily taken in full; one should further consult that sutra.
Once a bodhisattva has left the household life, they should uphold the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) as clearly elucidated in the *Mūla-karma* [Sūtra].

It is said that there are three types of bodhisattva precepts: first, the restraint of all evils, which refers to the *saṃvara-śīla*; second, the cultivation of all virtues, which refers to the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*;
and third, the deliverance of all sentient beings, which refers to the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*. Since this text is an excerpt...
A family must necessarily receive all three precepts. Some say that the first precept takes the cessation of evil as its essence, while the latter two take the performance of good as their essence.
This is not so; rather, they all take the cessation of [the failure to] perform good as their essence. The first precept ceases the evil of non-dignified conduct;
the next ceases the evil of failing to practice good; and the last ceases the evil of failing to save others. First, one attains the fruit of being free from entanglements; next...

[The opponent claims: "After attaining the fruit of the Dharma-body, one causes both oneself and others to attain the fruit of the Dharma-body; however, this is not so" (and so forth). The Sūtra says, "those who wear the Dharma-robe.

All commentaries on the Śāstra explain that "wearing" (*bei*) means to scatter [the robe] over the body, but this interpretation is incorrect. It should properly be read as *bei* with the second tone (qùshēng), meaning to put on [the robe] such that it covers and binds the body.

Furthermore, many versions of the Sūtra text write this character with the radical for "clothing" (*yī*). Regarding this, I say: [The text continues with the author's critique of the opponent's view regarding the nature of the Dharma-body and the process of its realization.]

The character "bei" (披) has traditionally possessed both the second tone (*pī*) and the fourth tone (*pì*); it carries the meaning of "to carry" or "to wear. People simply do not understand this, or they disparage and attack it;

yet Nanshan was the most elegant and authoritative in his treatment of written characters, and that he remained hesitant and failed to reach a definitive conclusion in his *Yijing Yin Yi* (Phonetic Explanations of the Scriptures) is still not entirely satisfactory.
Next, the patience (*kṣānti*) is explained. Regarding the first two lines of the initial passage following the text, the first clarifies the person;

the second clarifies that for the practitioner, mind and form differ, and practice consists of both place and action. In the commentary, the first part provides a general indication of the number of patience-practices, which should be listed by name as the three names found in the explanation.
"In the secluded forest" and below constitute the second part, the detailed explanation, which first generally applies the meaning and then [proceeds further].
To discuss the three meanings collectively based on both the text and its significance: first, "birth" refers to sentient beings (*sattva*).

Because they endure the afflictive conditions of existence, humans and animals alike are considered sentient. Regarding their own bodies, they firmly establish their resolve for the Way and endure these difficult challenges;
thus, this refers to the patience of ascetic practice (*duṣkara-kṣānti*), which encompasses the meanings found in the texts concerning both superior and inferior patience.
Therefore, not being occupied with anything else but being single-mindedly settled in the path of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is called "patience regarding the ultimate" (*paramārthakṣānti*);

this is precisely the meaning of "delighting in reciting the sūtras. Since there is already the patience regarding sentient beings (*sattvakṣānti*), does it not also follow that there is patience regarding non-sentient phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*)?
This meaning also exists. Within the category of ascetic practices (*duṣkaracaryā*), these are subsequently explained again as three successive and distinct phrases.

Regarding the meaning of the three types of patience (*kṣānti*): because a monk who has gone forth endures various things, abandoning evil and transforming toward the good, this constitutes ascetic practice.

The [meaning of] the next two is the same as the preceding one; previously, two texts were cited for three meanings, whereas now it is explained that the three specific texts correspond precisely to the three meanings.
The new [translation] calls them: "enduring enmity and harm," "peacefully accepting suffering," and "thoroughly examining the Dharma. This is *dharmakṣānti*.
This is the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). These three names correspond to the sequence of the three stages in the current text; they differ only in name.
The *Benye jing* (Sūtra on the Original Acts) has the same three as the current text.

Next, regarding the explanation of progress: the first two phrases cite the person and indicate their practice, while the following two phrases correctly explain the characteristics of the practice. [End of] Commentary Text.

The explanation provided is precisely the meaning of the latter two lines. First, the preceding line is explained; for this reason, the stage of progress (*vīrya-pāramitā*) is elucidated by means of this point.

Next, the final line is used to explain the meaning of diligence (*vīrya*), still carrying over the previous point to initiate the clarification of the characteristics of the actual process of advancing.
Incidentally, there is no separate explanation for "mindfulness" (*smṛti*); from "念念" (*nien-nian*) onwards, it explains the reality of progress.
The Buddha-way and its concurrent objects of reliance are precisely that which is the locus of one’s prayers for deliverance. To speak of being "concave" (*wa*) is like a gourd resting in a hollow;
it is incapable of action, serving as a metaphor for the indolent who cannot be diligent. "Timidity" (*k'yak*) refers to those who are weak and unable to rouse their will.

"Courage" (*yong*) explains the aforementioned timidity, and "advancement" (*jin*) explains the aforementioned concavity—this should be understood. Originally there were three [categories]... (as stated).

It is said that there are three types of progress: first, the Great Vow, because of the emergence of great aspirations; second, the Accumulation of Wholesome Dharmas, because of personally cultivating all virtues;

and third, Benefiting Sentient Beings, because of delivering all beings. According to the *New [Commentary]*, there are also three: namely, "donning the armor," which means possessing the power such that evil objects cannot subdue one;
"gathering wholesome dharmas," which refers to non-retrogression in self-benefit; and "benefiting and bringing joy," which means being abundant [in altruism].
The meaning of "ever more without weariness" is the middle sense among the three [meanings] discussed here.

There are further explanations, but as they are not essential to this context, I shall not describe them at length. One should compare these three meanings with the original three meanings and analyze them in contrast with the present text (and so forth).
Next, in explaining the perfection of dhyāna, it is said: first, the cultivation and attainment of the fruit are clarified; second, the non-duality of movement and stillness is clarified.
Now, within this [section], the first two phrases clarify the preliminary application of cultivation, namely, "leaving" and "approaching. "Leaving" means departing from the objects of distraction;

this should include both the five objects and the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). "Approaching" means dwelling in a quiet place. The following two phrases correctly clarify the actual cultivation and its manifestation.

The first phrase clarifies cultivation, while the second phrase clarifies benefit. Next, within this section on the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, there are five parts: first, the title; second, the scriptural exposition;
third, the doctrinal interpretation; fourth, the correlation with the present sutra; and fifth, the commentary on the text. First, regarding the title:

"contemplative cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to stillness and concentration (*samādhi*), which is also "one-pointedness of mind. The scripture—the *Mūla-karma-saṃgraha*—states that there are three types: namely, the non-arising of distracted signs, the arising of various merits, and [the third].
Regarding the benefit of sentient beings through virtue, the subsequent treatise on consciousness also consists of three parts: abiding, eliciting, and accomplishing tasks.
First, "abiding" refers to the bliss of the present life (formerly translated as *dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), because the internal mind is tranquil.

Second, "eliciting" refers to the meditative concentrations that produce the six supernormal powers (formerly translated as "producing merit"), because they give rise to the four immeasurables and the six supernormal powers. Finally, "accomplishing tasks" refers to benefiting [sentient beings].
Sentient beings are able to accomplish the work of benefiting others—what was formerly called "benefiting sentient beings"—because they deliver all beings through the perfection of dhyāna.
According to what is clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are also three kinds; although their number is the same as before, their names and meanings differ.
What are they? They are: mundane dhyāna, supramundane dhyāna, and the most excellent supramundane dhyāna. Mundane refers to the dhyāna of attachment (*āsvādana-dhyāna*); supramundane refers to...
The supreme purity of dhyāna is the true mark (*dharmatā*); the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* is called the "Ultimate Meaning" (*paramārtha*), and the *Laṅkāvatāra* is called "Tathāgata-dhyāna.

Those who comprehend the text of this sūtra find that the first two phrases correspond to the beginning of the sūtra and its śāstra; the next two phrases correspond to the subsequent merits of the sūtra.

The following verse praises these virtues so as to inspire reverence and esteem in others, which corresponds to the benefit (*anuśaṃsā*) of the sūtra and śāstra. This is as in the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*.
The three meanings will be seen for themselves in the subsequent commentary; the three sub-commentaries rely precisely on the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Chizhi lun) for their exposition.
The first section has two parts: the first appears to be a general introduction clarifying the benefits of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), while the second concerns its sublime function alone;

however, since the meaning applies to both, the text consistently uses the term "cultivation" (*xiū*). Within the text, the first sentence generally indicates the fundamental meaning, while the section beginning with "detachment from desire" (*liyù*) provides the specific details.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning and characteristics of the cultivation [of the dhyānas], the initial mention of the "fundamental" refers to the four dhyānas. The commentary states that this is because all teachings involve their cultivation.

This means that whether mundane or supramundane, and whether characterized by attachment (*āsvādana*) or purity (*śuddha*), they are all universally cultivated, realized, and manifested based upon these;
therefore, they are called "fundamental."

Next, the individual explanations are presented in sequence to clarify their characteristics, which consist of three parts: first, one phrase concerning "detachment from desire" is used to clarify the four characteristics;

second, the passage on "profound cultivation" is explained; and third, the passage on "supernatural powers" is explained. Regarding the first part, there is first a separate explanation, followed by a general explanation.
As for the initial mention of the "Shared Teaching" (Tongjiao), the *Ji* states: "The 'separate' above refers to the Shared Teaching; furthermore, below..."
Regarding the general application of the preceding two teachings, it is now stated that the first phrase applies to both preceding teachings and is not a separate statement.

As the Sūtra says, "The cause of all suffering is rooted in craving"; therefore, it must apply to both [teachings]. Second, regarding the application through the meaning of being the root and the meaning of detachment:
it is applied because it generally explains both the mundane and supramundane, as these are all contained therein. As for the term "root-detachment" (mūla-viveka):
Because this is an ancient worldly dharma, it is said to be "originally separate" and not something produced by the appearance of a Buddha; it has existed from the beginning.

This refers to the practice of delighting in and loathing [the mundane]. Since the stillness and movement of ordinary worldlings and outsiders are mutually contradictory, one must become detached from them.

"Turning away and abandoning" (*pratisaṃvid*) refers to the pure meditations (*dhyāna*) of the supramundane, which are all cultivated based on the principle of the Truths (*satya*) to abandon the mundane. This thus encompasses both teachings, though specifically speaking, it includes both.

"Zhè" (者) refers to the provisional; it is called "jiān" (兼, inclusive) because one cultivates both mundane and supramundane two-fold meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) to advance toward the Middle Way.

To be free from attachment to the Middle Way is the Perfect [Teaching]; at the initial stage, one cultivates the Middle Way of the true reality (*dharmatā*). If one gives rise to craving and attachment at the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*), one will not enter the Truth;
therefore, this clarifies the meaning of "leaving" (*li*). Although the meanings of "leaving" differ, the words themselves are the same; thus, it is universal (*tōng*).
Furthermore, the intent here lies in the three Bodhisattvas and not in the Three Piṭakas or the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;

this is to distinguish and clarify by correlating them with the meanings of the preceding two "flavors" (rasa). Now, when these four phrases are combined with the five meanings, they exhaustively encompass the three types of dhyāna taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Why is this? Because the first [meaning] is the fundamental detachment from the world, while the next two teachings correspond to...

The distinct and perfect [stages] of the supramundane are the "supreme-supreme" (uttarottara) meditation of the supramundane; because the latter two share the Middle Way within the realm of existence (*bhava*), they are combined into one.

If one wishes to speak of them as they manifest their bestowal, there should be four types: the third should be called "superior" (*uttara*), which refers to the "distinct" (*pratyeka*) stage when viewed in relation to what precedes and follows it;
only the fourth is named "supreme-supreme" (*uttarottara*), which is the ultimate perfection (*pariniṣpanna*). Although the treatise speaks of three names, in reality [there are four].
These four meanings encompass the entire purport of the treatise; now, by explaining them through these four interpretations, the essential intent of the discourse is fully exhausted.

If one were to correlate these meanings with the three [categories] of previous sūtras and śāstras, then the three bodhisattvas would collectively possess these three meanings, for which the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Da lun) is most abundantly and completely equipped.
One should know that the treatise was established based upon the sūtras; it is not as if the treatise adds anything to the sūtras—the meaning is merely that there is some slight difference. Next...

Regarding the term "profound cultivation" (*shenxiu*): it is called "profound" because it distinguishes the specific from the general. Thus, in the text, the repeated use of the term "profound cultivation" serves to specifically clarify and distinguish [the subject].

It refers collectively to the latter two of the three dhyānas. Within this, first, there is a specific explanation of profundity based on the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).

Next, following the section on "turning away," there is a general explanation of profundity based on all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). This is why the initial explanation is restricted to the nine.
Regarding these nine, they are the meanings within the four dhyānas of refinement; let me explain them briefly. Some say the text is not in proper order; it should rather state:

the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), the ten totalities (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrva-samāpatti*), and the ten totalities (newly termed the "ten pervasive bases," *daśa-vyāpy-āyatana-dhyāna*).

As clarified in the remaining text, there are four types of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), namely: contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), refinement (*pariśodhana*), perfuming (*vāsana*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*). This is the passage concerning this text.
Regarding the statement that "the first three are contemplative dhyānas and the ninth is preparatory dhyāna," the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the cultivation through perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Thus, these four types are successively deeper. Since Bodhisattvas cultivate these various concentrations with great clarity, it is said they "profoundly cultivate" these dhyānas.

The detailed definitions and meanings are found extensively in other texts; as they are not essential to the present context, they are not described here at length. As for the term "dhyāna-samādhi," it is [derived from] the Sanskrit...

It is called *dhyāna*, or *jhāna*, or simply *ch’an*. This is translated as "calm concentration" (*ching-ting*), or "single-mindedness," or "cultivation through reflection," or "abandoning hindrances," or "a grove of merit.
Recently it has been called *dhyāna*, which is translated as "calm contemplation" (*ching-lü*).
Some commentators explain that "contemplation" (*lü*) refers to mental deliberation; because this [state] calms such laborious deliberation, it is so named. According to...
The formal explanation states: "Quiet" (*śamatha*) means tranquility; "meditation" (*dhyāna*) means contemplation. Because one contemplates within tranquility, it is so called.
It is also said that because one quiets away discursive thought, it is so called. The former is the primary meaning, while the latter is a secondary meaning;

together they do not transcend cause and effect, as explained extensively in other texts. Here, "dhyāna-samādhi" (meditative concentration) is used to encompass both. From "this concentration" below...

This explains that the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) arise from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), where it is said that "essence" and "function" are now described as being "identical to cause and effect.

First, the supernormal powers are explained; below, the fifth and sixth [powers] are explained. This "concentration" refers collectively to all the aforementioned concentrations. "Supernormal power" is the function of mastery, arising because of mastery over causes.
Regarding the phrase "all supernormal powers," this does not refer solely to the fifth and sixth, but encompasses all the various teachings (*śāsana*). As follows:

Regarding the "explanation below," this explains the reasons for the fifth and sixth [categories]. It proceeds through the various teachings (*śāsana*) to clarify that the "flavor-dhyāna" (*rasa-dhyāna*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—refers generally to all ordinary beings, both internal and external.
The term "shared by the Two Vehicles" refers to the *Tripiṭaka* and *Shared* [vehicles], wherein the three vehicles obtain it together;

this is easily understood. As for not mentioning them separately but speaking of them as "divisions," this refers to those from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward. Regarding the "Perfect" [teaching] speaking of "beginning and end," the beginning is...

Abiding in wondrous enlightenment, their essence is identical because they realize the same unity; thus, all possess the six [perfections], yet there is only a distinction between partial and ultimate attainment.
These six have no differentiation of beginning or end. Why is it that they do not precede the formal [stages]? Because they are distinct.
Next, the explanation of the "Superior-Superior" meditation text concerns the meaning of the three karmas: settling the mind is the karma of the mind; joining the palms is the karma of the body;

and praising with verses is the karma of speech. These constitute the offering of the three karmas to this meditation. One receives this meditation from the Buddha and thus uses this offering to repay his profound virtue.
It also causes others to hear of it and likewise admire it. Xian says: in Sanskrit it is called *añjali*, which in Chinese means "joining the palms."

This is a case where both the Sanskrit and Chinese terms are presented together. If that were so, this commentary would not represent the "superior-to-the-superior" (shang-shang) meaning; the ancient masters also refuted this interpretation.
This person remains stubbornly attached [to their view], yet the seven phrases at the beginning of the commentary first point to the "superior" among the three [categories] as previously explained;
next, they indicate the latter two of the four [categories]; third, they clarify that there is no fixed direction; and fourth, they cite the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* as proof. All of these...

The "pervasion of ritual" refers to the three karmas; the "five" are so named because they correspond to those [three] by category. This is the power of retribution, as it accords with the spontaneous functioning of meditative cultivation.
The sixth is categorized according to the Dharma, and the seventh summarizes its meaning; this can be understood.

Next, to explain the name of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*): in Sanskrit it is called *prajñāpāramitā*, which is translated here as "Wisdom Reaching the Other Shore" (*hui dao bi an*), also as "Wisdom Perfection" (*hui du wu ji*), or simply "Wisdom Perfection" (*hui du*).
If one says *jñāna*, it is translated as "Knowledge Perfection" (*zhi du*). If combined, it is "Wisdom-Knowledge Perfection" (*zhihui du*). Since this is currently [the case], it is *prajñā*.

The sixth is precisely the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); because one relies on the principle of signlessness (*animitta*) to cultivate sublime wisdom, thereby crossing over birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and reaching the further shore of bodhi and nirvāṇa, it is named by combining its essence (*tī*) and function (*yòng*).

Regarding its fundamental activities, there are three: illuminating existence, illuminating non-existence, and illuminating the middle way. Within the treatise, there are three: preparatory application (*prayoga*), faculties (*indriya*), and...
The fundamental and subsequently attained [wisdoms] are also called the non-conceptualization of the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena.
According to the root treatise, there are eight meanings (etc.). Now, to first reconcile the two sutras: the initial "profound wisdom" refers to the complete possession of the three types of wisdom.

The subsequent "complete possession" is likewise so because, by possessing the three types of penetration and the three truths, one's own practice is finally perfected; only when one possesses these virtues within oneself is [the path complete].
Regarding the statement that "the ability to transform others" refers only to the fundamental activity (*mūla-karma*) within its own essence:

in this sutra, the application concerns another school of thought where some have interpreted it by saying that the three wisdoms (*tri-jñāna*) in the *Mūla-karma* are merely the two wisdoms of the fundamental and the subsequently attained (*prsthalabdha*) from the treatise;

they claim that in this sutra, one's own practice is the fundamental [wisdom] while transforming others is the subsequently attained. However, I maintain that this disregards one’s own school and forcibly uses the sutra to harmonize it with the treatise.
Neither of the two sutras mentions this; the Master [Vasubandhu] criticized the ancients for claiming that the *Śāstra* is rich while the *Sūtra* is poor.
One who studies this school yet fails to reflect upon this warning brings calamity upon themselves. This is not merely a matter of disparaging the *Śāstra*;

it also suppresses and eclipses the Master’s own tradition, which ought not to be so. Now, as for the "Eye" (*cakṣus*) mentioned previously, its principle is essential for reaching the subtle realization of the single school, whereas the rest are not essential.
"Therefore, it is not employed" (and so forth). Regarding the commentary’s mention of "self and others": holding the sutra within oneself is for one's own sake;
preaching the Dharma to the assembly is for the sake of transforming others. These two together constitute wisdom. The three types of wisdom exhaust the principles of the three truths.

That one first attends to oneself and subsequently to others is naturally so. As for the statement that "wisdom exhausts [the truths]," this clarifies that wisdom is one—that is, the three types of wisdom [are unified].

To exhaustively penetrate the principle of the three truths (*triratna-satya*). If one does not exhaustively penetrate them, it cannot be called the profound principle. This principle is fundamentally the three truths;
this principle can give rise to the three wisdoms (*tri-jñāna*). Principle is the fundamental essence. "Solid" (*kū*) refers to the firm and stable substance, which is the vow (*praṇidhāna*).

If it were not vast, it would not be a firm and stable substance. This substance is the vow; because one studies all Buddha-dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings, it is called "vast. These two are—
The essence of being able to question and able to uphold [the Dharma] arises from wisdom for the former and from firm resolve for the latter; these two together constitute the adornments.

To vow to act for the sake of all beings is the adornment of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*); this refers to self-adornment. Furthermore, that which is questioned does not exceed the scope of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Although the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* possesses both the capacity to question and the capacity to answer, it is said here that [the Bodhisattva] "is able" because he acts as the one who poses difficult questions.

Question: Since it has already been explained that one must inquire about upholding what has not yet become deep and firm, why is it necessary to do so again? Furthermore, since this was only a partial explanation and not the ultimate one, why is it necessary to proceed in this way?
Answer: It is because one is about to reach the ultimate; therefore, it is necessary.

Next, regarding the first of the two aspects concerning transforming others, the essence consists of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); that is, the three concentrations and the three wisdoms are all fully possessed.

The subsequent one and a half lines explicitly clarify the transformation of others, namely, preaching the Dharma to destroy Māra; this is precisely because one is able to do so through the full possession of concentration and wisdom.

The commentary (*śāstra*) explains these three meanings in detail; as the Sūtra says, "fully possessed" (*paripūrṇa*) has the meaning of being "evenly balanced," which is why it is explained as "all."
Regarding the phrase "equality and so forth": because equality is contrasted with inequality, it is manifested through various [categories].

There are four sections in total: first, concerning the mundane; second, concerning the supramundane; third, concerning the Three Vehicles; and fourth, concerning the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, the first two concern phenomena (*dharma*), the third concerns persons (*pudgala*), and the fourth concerns practice (*caryā*).
Because it has not yet reached the threshold of the First Dhyāna, the *Xin lun* (New Treatise) calls it the "accessory concentration" (*sāmantaka-samādhi*).

Although they are proximate, because they have not yet been attained, wisdom (*prajñā*) predominates; since the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are collectively termed "flavors of concentration" (*samādhi-rasa*) and take emptiness as their object, concentration (*samādhi*) predominates.

Furthermore, because the factor of "one-pointedness of mind" (*ekāgratā*) exists within all four dhyānas, these are concentration; the remaining factors belong to wisdom. Moreover, *dhyāna* is translated as "calm contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), which is virtuous concentration;
since the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti*) involve the contemplation of liberation, all ten are collectively termed "concentration. Thus, there are ten.

Because they are universally pervasive and can mutually enter one another; or as it is said, "The first eight belong to wisdom (*prajñā*) and the latter two belong to concentration (*samādhi*)," and so forth.
Furthermore, among humans, the former two are partial when compared to one another, whereas for a Buddha, there is tranquil illumination and illuminating tranquility without partiality, and so forth.
Next, regarding contemplation, the Middle Way negates the two extremes—this is concentration—and it simultaneously illuminates both—this is wisdom—and so forth. Now, since this...
"Containing two flavors" possesses such meanings as these (and so forth). In this context, one should explain *samādhi* and *prajñā* directly;

why is it necessary to clarify them through various skillful means based on these dharmas? These various skillful means of manifesting [the truth] by teaching and transforming beings through immeasurable analogies can reveal the reality (*tattva*). What, then, is this reality—the principle of the dharma that is revealed?
Regarding these various [categories], what constitutes the provisional means (*upāya*) and what constitutes the ultimate reality (*tattva*)? The various teachings explain these three below:

the immeasurable explanations of the various teachings clarify the provisional means through the aid of diverse analogies; the explanation of the primary meaning clarifies the reality that is revealed.
Since the meanings of these two differ, one should carefully contemplate the sense of "aiding clarification" in the subsequent text and avoid conflating them.

Next, the "Subduing of Māra" is explained; "subduing Māra" refers to the subject (the subduer) and the object (that which is subdued). While the Sūtra directly indicates the subject and object without specifying their actual entities, this commentary fully enumerates them:
the two methods of subduing through the Three Contemplations, and the three categories of objects to be subdued—the Four [Māras], the Eight [Sufferings], and the Three [Delusions].

Regarding the "Four Māras," there are two types: first, the four such as the *skandha-māra* (aggregates); second, the four inversions (*viparyāsa*). Both of these belong to the realm within the triple world (*dhātu*).

Because these are objects that stagnate in existence, they are collectively able to be shattered by the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Regarding the "eight," this refers to the two [categories] outside the realms and the four [categories] within each of those two.

First, one shatters the four [categories] such as impermanence, and subsequently, one shatters the four [categories] such as the afflictions of the aggregates (*skandha*); hence it is called "sequential" (and so forth).
Since these are all objects that cling to emptiness, they are shattered by the contemplation of the conventional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*). The "eight" and the "ten" are as previously explained.

In the commentary on the *Bhikṣu*, it has already been clarified that because the Middle Way avoids both extremes and thus neither loses nor retains them, it is able to completely dismantle [all views].

Furthermore, the term "all" is used as a general expression for their various categories and lineages. For example, in the *Saṃyukta-piṭaka-sūtra*, the Buddha stated that the demonic armies consist of ten types:
namely, desire, sorrow, hunger, thirst, craving, sleep, fear, doubt, poison, and fame and profit.

"Those who are self-exalting and contemptuous toward others—such as your armies—none can destroy my wisdom-arrows. With the hammer of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), I shatter the earthen jars [of their delusions] like throwing them into water;

this is the gathering of all things. This passage concerns the celestial Māras within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) acting as the conditions for the preceding three [perfections], while also clarifying the means by which they are overcome:
namely, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). As clarified in the sūtras and śāstras, when the Buddha enters [the womb]:

The Immovable Samādhi (*acala-samādhi*) can destroy all hosts of Māras; if one now encounters it, one is both concentrated and wise, as it possesses the three types of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
Therefore, the text says that concentration and wisdom are fully perfected. This is stated here from a general perspective, hence the mention of the "three contemplations. In Sanskrit, *māra*;
in Chinese, this means "destruction," referring to that which can destroy the Buddha-dharma and its practitioners. This is its [meaning].
He is named Pāpīyān, which here means "the Evil One" (formerly translated as *Pāxún*, meaning "extremely evil").
Others say it means "one who rejoices in the benefits and pleasures he has obtained for himself," but we maintain that it refers to one who forgets his own self to benefit others.

When a Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma and causes people to attain the Way, they destroy the Māra of Afflictions and manifest the attainment of the Dharma-body; they destroy the Māra of the Aggregates (*skandha-māra*) and attain the Dharma of the Way.
By destroying the two matters of the body, one overcomes the Māra of Death;

by attaining the Samādhi of Immovability, one destroys the celestial armies of Māra, namely the Ten Armies, with Desire as the first and Arrogance toward others as the tenth. "Beating the drum" refers to preaching the Dharma.
Having thus subdued Māra, one realizes the path of Perfect Enlightenment and turns the Wheel of the True Dharma. This is the explanation according to the preceding text.
This Bodhisattva’s form and voice are the manifestation of the Buddha’s form and voice, for they transform others through these two matters;

as the subsequent text states, "One should [appear] in the body of a Buddha," and so forth. The passage cites a sūtra to explain this meaning, stating that this stage and ground possess such causal capacity, which is precisely what is meant here.
Moreover, it clarifies that from this point upward, one possesses this capacity; it does not mean...
What was perceived at that time must refer to this stage. Regarding the term "Brahma-wheel," it signifies purity;

it means that having personally realized the path of purity, one expounds it for the sake of sentient beings using pure and wondrous sounds to remove their defilements and lead them to realize the path of purity.
Its purity is its wheel, which is fundamentally and eternally pure. As stated later in this sutra: "It is able to turn the wheel of the pure Dharma."

The "wheel" (cakra) and its meaning are as follows: some say it refers to the preaching of the *Lotus Sūtra* to open up the provisional and reveal the real, which corresponds to the meaning of "beating the great Dharma-drum" found in later passages.
However, since the current text states that both "perfect" (*yuan*) and "Sanskrit sound" (*fan-yin*) are universal, they are not yet specifically distinguished here.

Nevertheless, the Sūtra speaks of the "wheel" and the "Dharma-drum," while the commentary speaks of the "Brahma-wheel"; these must be reconciled. The drum is spoken of in terms of its underlying principle (*yi-li*).
Striking according to principle and teaching like striking a drum to produce the wheel of sound briefly clarifies two meanings: the capacity to destroy and the capacity to transport.
"Destroying" refers to karma, while "transporting" refers to the movement from cause to fruit. Because this manifests the merit of teaching, the term "wheel" (*cakra*) is used to explain the "drum."
Next, the explanation of the non-sequential [questions] has four parts: first, showing the text and indicating the headings; second, the questions and answers for deliberation;
third, the temporal sequence and flavor to which they belong; and fourth, the formal analysis and explanation of the words. Regarding "according to what was seen":

because of the light, there were two aspects of what was seen. Following what was explained, the sequential questions were completed; now, these follow what was seen in a non-sequential manner, as there is no fixed order.
[The text] establishes partial names according to specific perspectives (and so forth). Next, it first raises a question regarding the preceding sequential meaning to resolve the doubt;

it does not repeat the sequence because it would be redundant. Since the essentials of the Bodhisattva practice do not exceed the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), and a single cycle does not go beyond them, [repetition] would be redundant.

In the explanation, it first clarifies two points, and then, based on the text, concludes by censuring the objection that it should not be resented as redundant. First, the two points: [text follows].
This passage clarifies that because karmic conditions are not fixed, there are these two paths; thus, the two aspects manifested and perceived are precisely intended to represent this.

Following the text here, even this statement already exceeds the duality [of the two vehicles], let alone merely clarifying the two while considering it redundant, for it serves to penetrate the meaning of the "two flavors" and the "four or three" periods. Therefore, it is said: how could it possibly conform to ordinary sentiment?

There are also those who say that because the Vaipulya (fangděng) section contains both of these practices, it is used to represent them. Next, regarding the meaning of the two successive representations:

according to principle, this should apply universally to both flavors (the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* teachings), yet the term "Vaipulya" alone is used; the meaning here has both a general and a specific sense, which shall be explained in due order.
This is stated thus for the sake of a single point. As the Sūtra says, one "cultivates practice," yet here we speak of a "section" (*piṭaka*); however—

Practice arises from the teaching; having understood that practice arises from the teaching, I shall now explain its meaning, and thus it must be stated as follows. The teaching and practice apply universally, yet how is it known that this refers specifically to the Vaipulya (fangděng)?
By examining the preceding and following contexts and the sequence of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, which clarifies this through mutual questioning, one knows it to be so.
While the terminology of "Vaipulya" applies generally, here we follow the specific sequence of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and state it thus. Some say that this passage should... [text fragment ends].

It would be appropriate to move the section on the various practices of Bodhisattvas in other lands from below to above, placing it there to provide a systematic correspondence between the sequential and non-sequential texts; however, it is not fitting to clarify this point here. Now, I fear this may not be the case. Why?
If the preceding [text] had simply divided these into two chapters, it would indeed be so; but since the preceding [text] has already been divided into three chapters, therefore—
Because it was not convenient to do so previously, I shall discuss this here in connection with the causal context; since I will treat it more extensively later, I shall state it briefly for now.

According to the *Vaipulya* (fangděng) sūtras, as there are both general and specific [categories] in multiple layers, it would be appropriate to explain them here as well—perhaps they were omitted during transcription, or the phrasing here is out of order.
There should be three meanings: first, that it does not follow the previous sequence; second, that there is an excess or omission.
As for the two types of auspiciousness, the meaning of "three" being further insufficient will be seen later by oneself, as there are three in total.

Others [interpret] from the beginning of the six perfections as having three major sections; following the previous sequence, the four verses starting from the second section on "transforming others" within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are called the second part, "the benefit of the three karmas," which is a verse summarizing what precedes it.
Various characteristics and appearances are manifested externally through body and speech as "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), while the mental karma is also revealed as "appearances" (*nimitta*).

First, there are two verses clarifying the noble one’s teaching of the Dharma, which is the benefit of vocal karma; next, there is one verse clarifying the noble one’s silence, which is the benefiting of beings through mental karma;
next, there is one verse concerning the emission of light while dwelling in the forest, which is the rescue through bodily karma. Furthermore, there are many other [instances].
This analytical distinction is not the intended meaning here, so it will not be further elaborated. Although there are many underlying intentions, the text does not exceed two [categories];

therefore, these two textual sections alone are used to reveal the multiple intentions. However, since the preceding section already provided a comprehensive explanation of the six [topics]—namely, the name (*nāman*), essence (*svabhāva*), and so forth, according to five intentions—I shall now briefly synthesize and explain this section, omitting anything that does not differ from what preceded.
There is no need to further discuss the initial statement that "abandoning dhyāna" refers to the fourth dhyāna.

According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, because it is easy to cultivate compassion (*karuṇā*) in the first dhyāna, joy (*muditā*) in the second, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in the third, and equanimity (*upekṣā*) in the fourth, this [equanimity] belongs to the fourth.

Alternatively, according to the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*, when cultivating the four samādhis, the stage of cultivating great equanimity is interpreted by others as being the sixth ground, the Ground of Equality (*samatā-bhūmi*).

Alternatively, according to the commentary by Danqiu on the eighth [chapter], from the first dwelling (prathamā bhūmi) and above, all equally realize the principle of the ultimate emptiness (paramārtha-śūnyatā).

Now, this passage precisely accords with that meaning; since it is neither one of the other three meanings nor identical to the subsequent text, it represents "abandoning" as part of self-cultivation (svayam-pratipatti).

Next, regarding "passing through the forest" within the section on compassion (*karuṇā*): this symbolizes the arising of function based upon the essence. Because it uproots suffering, it is compassion; because it is compassion, it is the transformation of others.
This is merely a brief indication of its characteristics and does not manifest them fully; therefore, it is shown to exist in other sutras. First, it possesses two meanings;

second, these meanings apply generally to all four [teachings], though they are mostly found in the Separate and Perfect [teachings]. I cannot describe them in full detail, hence the note says "and so forth" (*yún yún*). One should know this briefly.

Without waiting for further elaboration, this clarification of dhyāna differs from what preceded it: previously, it was explained through three aspects to clarify the two categories of universal and specific;

now, it is explained through four aspects to clarify the two categories of self and other. Although both the preceding and present sections possess these two capacities—the former being the capacity for supernatural powers and the capacity for praising the Buddha, while the latter being the capacity for relinquishment and the capacity for salvation—both are the essence and function of the pāramitā of dhyāna. Having thus clarified these two, it is also...

One should clearly understand the four dhyānas; here, two are briefly cited to illustrate meditation (*dhyāna*). Thus, while the four are specific meditations, they also represent the general category.
Next, regarding the inquiry into diligence (*vīrya*): from this point onward, the second section consists of verses on the six perfections practiced without fixed direction (*anupāya-kauśalya*).
Regarding the various modes of faith and understanding mentioned above, "without fixed direction" has three meanings, the first of which is being appropriate to the conditions encountered.
This is because there is no duality between the former and the latter, yet their root-natures are not one, and their own practices are different. The text consists of six sections;

"t'ang" (甞) means "formerly" or "previously," and it serves as a general exhortation regarding that which has never been bound by [delusion]. Although various treatises explain the meaning of sleep extensively, I cannot describe them in detail here.
In the Great Teaching, it is simply this: if one is entirely unclear regarding principle and lacks diligence in practice, the body...

The mind being left to its own devices is the meaning of "sleeping"; this is derived from the text to clarify its significance. It refers to this practice because it is practiced constantly throughout the ninety days;
thus, it is the most supreme form of diligence (*vīrya*). The old tradition says that the Buddha established meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

this [practice] is based on the attainment of cessation through the perfection of conduct. In the Nanshan school, one attains concentration by means of conduct; this is likely a case of naming the cause after the effect.
There is an interpretation of the *Bhadrapāla-sūtra* which names this "the meditative concentration on the visualization of all Buddhas before one.

This also takes cause and effect as its basis; "visualization" refers specifically to the mindfulness of the Buddha mentioned in the text. In summary, the diligent application of the three karmas constitutes its characteristic practice. The text says, "walking meditation (*caṅkrama*)";
while this appears to be merely physical karma, it actually includes both mental and vocal karma. Regarding the phrase "in the forest groves," it means a place that is secluded and pure.
This is a pure place. A detailed explanation is as found in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā-ācāra* (The Constant Practice of Calm Abiding and Insight) and the *Samādhi-prakāśa*.

Some say that those who travel between [realms] according to the *Vijñāna-gati-sūtra* (Sutra on the Transmigration of Consciousness) should rely deeply upon the meaning rather than adhering exclusively to the literal words. The preceding passage merely cited the body and its significance, yet the meaning also encompasses the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind].

The current statement, "never having... and so forth, differs from the previous one; therefore, while the former may be understood generally, this specifically corresponds to the cultivation of this samādhi.
It must be that all concentrations require diligence, for it is said that there are expressions regarding this specific concentration that have not been previously practiced;
nor is it restricted solely to concentration, which is why the term "etc. is used.

Next, the characteristics within the precepts are clarified. Regarding the phrase "the meaning can be understood," the intent is to clarify that since both the beginning and the end are cited, one must fully cultivate all ten [precepts].
These ten names originate from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:

(1) unimpaired, (2) unbroken, (3) unpierced, (4) unmixed, (5) conforming to the path, (6) unattached, (7) praised by the wise, (8) sovereign, (9) conforming to meditative concentration, and (10) complete.
The first six [precepts] lead from the conventional to the ultimate; the next two cast off the ultimate to enter the conventional; and the final two abide in the equality of the correct [path].

The current intent lies mostly in the Separate and Perfect [teachings], whereas the preceding text simply spoke of "leaving home. Here, the characteristics of upholding [the precepts] are fully elucidated; that was the general [explanation] while this is the specific one.

Furthermore, the meaning of these ten precepts also encompasses the three clusters (triskandha); thus, the subsequent text correlates them with the contemplation of the three truths and the emergence into the provisional.
"Benefiting beings" (*li wu*) refers precisely to the "benefit of sentient beings" (*sattvārtha*).

Next, regarding the explanation of patience (*kṣānti*): this differs from the previous [section]. The former directly addressed the meaning and possessed all three [aspects], whereas here the meaning is somewhat more explicit.

The first two lines provide a general heading; the next three lines offer an explanation; and the final line concludes by clarifying the intent of patience. As for the aforementioned three lines, they are as follows: [not provided].

The same applies to "lightness" (*laghu*). The commentary states that regarding the "two kinds of patience" (*kṣānti*), although patience is threefold, the mention here of "two" has two textual meanings and three logical meanings.

The first three phrases generate the meaning; the single concluding phrase combines these meanings. This refers to the second [category], the practice of the Dharma (*dharmācāra*). The Buddha-way is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); because one abides in this one and does not arise in the two, one thereby possesses all three. As for the term "power" (*bala*) used as a heading: [Note:

According to the Āgamas, there are six kinds of power: children have crying as their power; when they desire to obtain something, they must first cry.
Women have anger as their power; when they desire to obtain something, they must first become angry.
Kings have arrogance as their power. Arhats have diligence as their power. All Buddhas have great compassion as their power. Bhikṣus have patience as their power.

The power of patience now refers to the renunciant bodhisattva, who is precisely the bhikṣu. Others claim that "patience" (kṣānti) means suppressing internal emotions and abiding in the endurance of suffering;
here, however, we clarify that it specifically concerns the endurance of harm from others, based on the bhikṣu. Now, this applies universally to both monastics and laypeople.
Previously, it was designated as dwelling in forests and springs; now, it applies universally to residing in mountains or towns.
Next, regarding the term "further" (*geng*) in the subsequent inquiry: it is called "further" because meditation (*dhyāna*) is elucidated twice within the non-sequential [section].

The first one and a half lines correctly elucidate the cultivation of meditation, while the final two lines conclude by clarifying the intent regarding time. As for the explanation in the text based on the departure from the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*):

this is the skillful means; it may be called the correct cultivation. The intent clarifies that through correctness there is departure, and through departure there is correctness. Furthermore, it clarifies reliance upon principle (*li*).
To be free from expedient means is precisely right cultivation; as in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, both perspectives are clarified there at length.
As for the doubt raised—asking how one could see [the truth] through a mere temporary cause when this involves a long duration—I say: why do you not doubt that even sixty meals' time is sufficient?

If one speaks according to human sentiment regarding the beginning and end, or discusses the sincerity of one's resolve, why would one fail to understand the meaning of the text? Such is a misconception.
Regarding these doubts: some say that previously it was explained how others attain the fruits through the cultivation of dhyāna, whereas now we merely distinguish the causes for practicing it;
previously it was distinguished how those of sharp faculties perceive principle, whereas now it is clarified how those of dull faculties rely on a teacher;

now it is said that the previous section separately used the two types of concentration to clarify dhyāna, whereas now it directly and comprehensively distinguishes its cultivation; previously it concerned benefiting others, whereas now it clarifies one's own practice; previously it concerned essence and function.
Now, by focusing on the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the correct [practice], it is demonstrated that the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) possesses these various meanings.

Next, regarding the four items mentioned within the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), Kikai states: first, medicine and food; second, clothing; third, bedding and seats; and fourth, gardens and groves.

Others say that the text concerning giving consists of three parts: the first three verses concern the four items, the next one verse concerns the sublime gift, and the final one verse [concerns] the subsequent [gift].
The meaning of the verse concerns the practice of giving through the intention of joy: regarding food, drink, medicine, clothing, and bedding;

first one practices the first two matters, next one practices the third matter, and in the following two lines, the fourth matter. Jik says that meat served as a side dish and grain-based food collectively constitute "fare.
Since the prohibition against meat-eating had not yet been established at this point, [the text] clarifies the Bodhisattva’s giving of meat in the "Chapter on the Four Marks" of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Having already prohibited meat-eating, it was only upon reaching the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly" that Cunda brought forth his offerings;

this was because he had not yet heard the prohibition established in the "Chapter on the Lamentation for His Return Home" regarding the four marks [of existence]. How extreme is such a person's delusion!

Even the *Mahāyāna-jāla*, the *Brahmajāla*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra* establish these prohibitions all at once; how could they have been as lax as what you previously cited? If you claim that those were taught according to the gradual [teachings], [then...]
In the assembly at Laṅkā, how could there not be those of the two vehicles? Thus, it is not appropriate [to exclude them]. It is said that "that which is not grain but is eaten" refers to *yáo* (肴).
*Yáo* means pickled vegetables; it should be written as *yáo*, meaning food or what is chewed. It is also a class of vegetables, and is further called the fruit of beans.
*Shàn* (饍) refers to prepared food; even today, fine food is called *zhēnshàn* (珍饍). According to common interpretation, *shàn* also refers to meat.
Now it is not so; to write "zhàn" (膳) instead of "shàn" (饍) is incorrect—this interpretation is correct. [As] Nanshan says...
[regarding] "named garments," these are like the *kāṣāya* robe offered by Kāśyapa to the Buddha, which was worth one hundred thousand pieces of gold; such is their kind.

"Red" refers to ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*), "black" refers to red sandalwood (*raktacandana*), and "white" refers to white sandalwood and the like. This is the second verse on "Purity and Excellence."
Generosity is now, according to the general essentials of the sūtras, subsumed under the fourth category.
In the subsequent verse of the summary, "others" constitutes the third [point]. There are three types of intention for giving: first, joy; second, lack of satiety;
and third, excellence—that is, seeking the unsurpassed path. The present summary is intended to synthesize and establish the underlying intent of the preceding acts of generosity.
The first two lines conclude the objects previously offered; the next line clarifies the mind of the donor; and the final line clarifies the intent of the giving.
Regarding the similarities and differences with what preceded: others say that while the previous [verse] concerned the four classes of beings, the present one clarifies offerings to the Triple Gem;

whereas the preceding section fully explained both internal and external [offerings], the present one explains only the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣa-dāna*). This commentator says: the preceding section’s meaning implicitly contained all nine [types of giving], whereas here...
Among the three types of objects in the first category, there are only material things; among the three in the second, there are only the necessities of life;
