This is the matter [discussed] therein (etc.).
Next, the following clarifies the passage of praise concerning existence and non-existence, which may be understood from the sutra as it appears.

For this reason, it is said that "the cause" (*hetu*) does not refer to the specific interlocutor, but is certainly intended for the purpose of general circulation. Next, regarding the citation of an example, some say it was cited by the former Master Yao from his commentary.
Taking the *Jia* (Family) as an example, the commentary notes: "In the past, [the disciples followed] Miaoguang; now, they follow Yaowang.

Although Yaowang is not listed among the gate-disciples, the fact that Miaoguang introduces eight hundred disciples serves to manifest Maitreya’s role in seeking fame and profit within the sutra, while marking out Mañjuśrī as the one entrusted with resolving doubts.
Master Yao approved of this, hence he said, "It may be so," yet the question remains whether such gate-disciples actually exist or not.

The name "Xiao" (Minor) does not seem consistent with the present context; I fear it may not be so. Since [the commentary by] Yao dates to the Song dynasty while this [commentary by] Zhu dates to the Qi period, they should not be identical.

Perhaps Yao was the teacher of Zhu, or perhaps they represent two distinct schools whose views happen to coincide with those of Yao’s teacher. What I explained previously was merely an interpretation based on the meaning (*yi*);

now I shall further establish it through textual precedent (*wen-li*). Since this has already been circulated, and because its meaning is particularly significant in light of these words, I provide this further clarification.

I previously established this as a precedent and permitted the statement "it may be so. Furthermore, regarding the remark that it is "not analogous," this was because the passage concerning the cause for the circulation [of the teaching] accords with one portion of the meaning;

thus, I permitted the statement "it may be so. However, within this context, the citation of the past to establish the present meaning is not entirely identical, which is why it is called "not analogous.
Why is it not analogous? Because *Prabhāketu* possesses both meanings, whereas *Bhaiṣajyarāja* [possesses only one].
Because there is one [who exists], it was correct in the past and is now being circulated. Since the present is the correct occasion for requesting, I shall proceed with the correct exposition.

Later, this will be entirely superseded; for the time being, as we proceed at ease, it is called "small. Thirdly, the school below maintains that because this explains away doubts, it does not depend on the specific person being addressed;
rather, it uses the present day as a category to explain the ancient past, and thus it is called "the auspiciousness of Mañjuśrī."
It is said that the lamp-lighting [of Dīpaṃkara] was due to the teaching of Prabhūtaratna, while the [attainment of Buddhahood by] Śākyamuni was due to Mañjuśrī.

By citing the past through Mañjuśrī to verify the present, the doubts of the assembly at that time were resolved; only then did the Tathāgata arise from his meditative absorption to preach the Dharma. Thus, we know it was due to Mañjuśrī.
This interpretation is entirely identical to what is cited in the current text, as both take the response to the question to explain the "cause" (hetu), and thus they belong together.
This explains the meaning of the introduction and refutes those who claim it is inappropriate. The Record states that at the time of resolving doubts, the Tathāgata was in meditative absorption;

his emergence from absorption was triggered by the spiritual capacity (*gotra*) of the audience, not by Mañjuśrī. Since the text simply says he addressed Śāriputra upon emerging from absorption, how can one take the person who was in absorption while resolving doubts and equate him with the one who has emerged from absorption to address the assembly?
Now, I maintain that the Sūtra explicitly states that his emergence from absorption was triggered [by the capacity of the listeners].
Regarding the main exposition, if one were to instead rely on it as a resolution of doubts based on necessity, one ought to say that the Buddha arose from samādhi;
because [the current text] is inverted in this way, it is said to be "inconvenient.

Next, the formal explanation has three parts: first, a general refutation of the contradictions in the various previous interpretations; second, [the section beginning with] "From the past... and so forth; third, the manifestation of the correct view.
Regarding the "Doubts Concerning the Meaning": the subsequent section refutes the sentiments of the preceding text. First, it refutes the two prior errors;

second, it reveals the correct teaching of the addressed interlocutor; third, it refutes the persistence of those who still cling to their views. Within the first [of these], there is first a general refutation, hence the statement "it is not so.

Below this is the specific refutation of the first two schools, both of whom explain and respond based on the *Liutong* (Circulation). The phrase "you publicly resist" explains the original intent of the scripture.
To propagate and clarify the Buddha’s intent, you now specifically manifest a blatant rejection of the Holy Word; how could this be the conduct of one who provides an explanation?
Second, regarding the formal exposition, there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the simultaneous presentation of the causes for the agreement in the formal teaching;

third, citing three matters each from the past and the present to explain the reason for their agreement; and third, concluding by equally rebuking their false claim of difference. The first part is easily understood. As for the second...
In the commentary, it is first explained that in the past, all three matters were manifest together; this can be sought directly in the text.
It is clarified that now, of the three matters, only the first is not present in this sutra, while the remaining two are both included. Regarding the phrase "the Trace Gate is concluded":

although the text has already reached its midpoint, it is at the end of the formal parables that the middle is raised to encompass the beginning and the end. This is spoken according to the intended meaning, hence it says "the Trace Gate is concluded. This concludes the summary and the reprimand.

As for the question of why this [present teaching] is superior, the ancient intention was that because there are many differences between the superiority and inferiority of the past and the present, they are not the same.
To speak briefly, the past possessed four capacities: first, the ability to resolve doubts; second, the ability to ensure circulation; third, the ability to serve as a teacher;

and fourth, being the causal stage of a Bodhisattva. Since the present recipient of the teaching lacks these four capacities, whereas the past [teachings] possessed them, [the former is considered superior].
This is not addressed to a specific interlocutor; rather, it is now clarified that because all [beings] equally possess these three, they are equally subjects of this address.
Therefore, this reprimand concerns the fourth point, which will be explained next; thus, only these three are clarified here.

Next is the third assembly’s commentary on the fourth single point, which simultaneously refutes emotional attachments. At the beginning of the text, the doubts and attachments are first stated; next follows the formal commentary and refutation.
First, both the "already" and the "not yet" must be understood through two gates. To say "not yet" means that [the teaching] is still in the introductory stage;
*chan* (孱) also means "equal" (*qi*) or "manifest" (*xian*), meaning it is equal, distinct, and clear, and thus identical. As for "hidden and manifest":
The meaning of "containing distinctions" refers solely to Wondrous Light (Prabhāpāla), wherein his prior provisional [teachings] are concealed and his subsequent reality is revealed.
If this is so, then all are equal; how could there be superiority or inferiority such that they are made identical yet subsequently rendered different?

Next, regarding those with "identical names" within the formal exposition, the name is the same, being "Wondrous. However, while the sutra contains both names and texts, here we cite only the names directly.

It is said thus because the name is the same as the present name. Within this [section], there are both similarities and differences between the general and specific [names] compared to the *Anantārthika* (The Teaching of Infinite Meanings).
Regarding the specific names, there is one difference and two similarities; however, according to the current intention, all four are the *Saddharma* (Wonderful Dharma).

As for the various interpretations, they do not differ from those of other teachings (*yùnyún*). [Regarding the phrase "the meaning is complete" (*quán yì wèi shàng*)]: the portion beginning with "Maitreya" and ending here should be moved [to its proper place].
Regarding the first Buddha at the end of the text, it is judged to belong to the two preceding "identical" sections;

if this were not shifted, there would be great impediment—this can be easily understood upon reflection. Now, as for this point, one must examine whether it is appropriate or not, but I have not yet had the leisure to do so. Regarding the absence of objects after the practice:
following the two cycles of the six perfections, no further remaining realms are seen, and one immediately perceives the Buddha entering parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the matter of erecting the stupa, some say that those who see it later should say "immediately sees" (*biàn jiàn*); however, this is likely a scribal error for "directly sees" (*jí jiàn*).
Thus, the subsequent text says "immediately sees" (*jí jiàn*) and "immediately enters" (*jí rù*), where the meanings of *jí* (immediately/directly) and *biàn* (then/at once) are precisely equivalent.

As for the terms "this" and "that," some say that the past Lamp-Light Buddha is "this" and the one questioned by Maitreya is "that"; others say that the other land is "that" while Mañjuśrī is "this. Since the former [Mañjuśrī] is already [in] the subtle [state], [the distinction is made].
Because of the light, it is referred to by way of Mañjuśrī as the land of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna;
since this is a portent of another land concerning what Maitreya asks, there must have been entry into parinirvāṇa and the raising of a stupa prior to this.

Since the past Buddhas cited by Mañjuśrī already manifested the reality [of the teaching], one must know that after such manifestations there was necessarily entry into parinirvāṇa and the raising of stupas. Since both lands simultaneously preached the Lotus Sutra...
It is logically appropriate that all six auspicious signs appear; although the sutra is brief, taking its essential meaning, it reveals that the Buddha-way of all Buddhas is identical.

This serves as the answer to the intended meaning of the question, and thus it is said generally that "the six auspicious signs here and there" refer to the preaching of the sutra and entering nirvana.

Since the first Buddha cited is identical to the auspicious signs of other lands mentioned in the question, one knows that this is indeed the direct answer to that question; therefore, it says "this."
"Thus, they are clearly equal," and so forth. Next, regarding "time": this refers to manifesting the Dharma by means of time.

It is explained that time has no fixed direction (*amudha*) because it serves to express the supreme excellence of the Dharma being taught. Otherwise, even if there were clarity and even if there were sameness, what would be the purpose?

The Sūtra employs two [aspects] to manifest that time has no fixed direction; namely, the speaker and the audience. As for the statement that "sixty minor kalpas" passed, this is from another perspective.
It is said "as explained in the preceding treatise," hence it is stated thus. This is further analyzed through three propositions regarding the assembly:
first, clarifying the patron, the land, and the time; second, clarifying that it is not considered long; third, clarifying that body and mind are at ease such that fatigue is forgotten.

This explains the wondrous power of the speaker and the wondrous realization of the listener, which brings about such a state. In sum, the Dharma taught is so exquisitely sublime as to reach the ultimate limit.
This is because the assembly shall immediately hear and obtain wondrous benefit. The subsequent text states, "By the Buddha’s spiritual power, it is as if half a day has passed.

These instances of long and short times being mutually identical represent the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) without fixed direction; they manifest the two gates and reveal the inconceivable nature of the wondrous Dharma.
When it says "by the Buddha’s spiritual power," both gates should be understood in this way; this precisely represents the manifestation and revelation. This should be examined in detail.
The *Chū* (Commentary) states that although the citations from the various scriptures are slightly different, they all refer to the absence of fixed time at that moment;

this is not discussed here as it is briefly explained within the verses. Master Sheng says: "How could it truly be so? It is merely a metaphorical expression of the arrival of the mind intent on hearing the Dharma, using 'time' as a provisional designation.
This meaning uses words to express the state of mind; thus, the words do not possess actual reality. Even if that were the case, however...

The profound essence of the manifest object has not yet been fully revealed, nor has the ultimate subtlety of the Dharma been made clear; for this reason, I fear that what has been presented thus far is not entirely perfect.
The brief summary provided above takes the single principle of "subtlety" (miao) as its fundamental cause. All other elaborations are merely redundant and do not constitute the essential core.
Future students should firmly maintain this tenet and not follow the shifting currents, allowing themselves to drift and forget their point of return. Within this [treatise]...

Regarding why the four schools differ in their explanations of auspicious birth and compassion (as detailed in the commentary): although each is distinct, none of them provides a single word that encompasses all of them.
The Master says: "The five preceding explanations are all derived from the same source; they all arise because the Dharma is wondrous" (and so forth).
In the *Mahāsamnipāta Sūtra*, it is said that eight thousand kalpas are neither long nor short; this is likely an abbreviation. Furthermore, within this [text], the attainment is clarified.
Because it is wondrous, it is long yet short. They value the literary expression but do not realize its meaning; thus, he speaks directly of "long contemplation.
The chant of "extinguishing the same" clarifies that the past and the present are identical; this, in turn, manifests and perfects the wondrous. Why is this?
The beginning and end of the path of transformation both reside in the wondrous; the appearance of the Great Matter begins with the wondrous, and now it reaches fulfillment at the end.

Regarding "wondrous": it is now clarified that the wondrousness of the transformative path has reached its ultimate limit and its tasks are complete; as activity ceases and one returns to the essence, the Nirvana is proclaimed as profoundly wondrous and supremely luminous.
In the scriptural text, there are times when [the Buddha] addresses specific groups; here, he formally proclaims his extinction before the assembly.

Within the assembly, he first specifically mentions the fourfold assembly, and subsequently clarifies the eight classes of beings in general—namely, the Brahma gods who are lords of the form realm (also representing the lords of the three realms), and Māra, the lord of the desire realm.
The "Lord of the Realm" has been explained as before. As for the term *śramaṇa*, its full expression is *śramamano* or *śramana*;
this means "one who exerts effort and attains rest. "Effort" refers to cultivating all that is wholesome, while "rest" refers to ceasing all that is unwholesome.

It is also called "merit" (*guṇa-lao*), meaning that one possesses merit through the cultivation of the Path. A *brāhmaṇa* is called "one of pure conduct," which also signifies "pure resolve" or "tranquil resolve."

This refers to the four [periods] consisting of two for each of the devas and humans; the commentary directly explains the third section, the actual proclamation of extinction (*nirvāṇa*), which further contains three distinct parts:

first, it clarifies how [the Buddhas] proclaimed [their teaching] in the past and subsequently entered extinction; second, it clarifies how Śākyamuni retained [his teaching] and has not yet immediately entered extinction;

third, although there are slight differences regarding whether they did or did not enter immediately, the general intent behind proclaiming extinction is the same, and thus it is said they are "identical."

Master Ji said: Some claim that after the Buddha preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* by means of the lamp-lighting miracle, he also preached the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; however, because the text is obscure on one side, it is simply said that he did not preach it.
Now we clarify that this is not so. Since the sutra states that he entered parinirvāṇa at night immediately after preaching the sutra in the morning, we know he did not preach the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Furthermore, although there was a *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, it was not required because the faculties of people were sharp.

The Lamp of the Teaching is likewise: because Śākyamuni appeared in an evil age, those of sharp faculties attained awakening upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, as it is said in the *Lotus Sūtra* that eight thousand śrāvakas received predictions and achieved the great fruit, like the harvest of autumn followed by the storage of winter, requiring no further action.
However, because those of dull faculties did not yet understand, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* had to be preached further; this is what is meant by "the two [teachings] of the past."
The Buddha possesses three meanings: namely, that his time, place, and capacity are all superior, pure, beneficial, and lead equally to awakening and entry [into the truth].

Thus, although Śākyamuni entered nirvāṇa amidst three inferior conditions, he still awaits further fulfillment; therefore, he proclaimed [the teaching] but did not immediately enter [nirvāṇa]. In general principle, they are the same. Next, regarding the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*):

upon hearing the teaching, one awakens and enters [the path], thereby establishing the cause. Since the cause has a corresponding fruit, the bestowal of prediction is clarified. Master Sheng says: "From oneself... [text continues].
The disciples of Yaśas suddenly heard that the Buddha was about to enter *nirvāṇa* and, fearing there would be no more sages thereafter, ceased their practice on the path;

therefore, [the Buddha] recorded their future attainment of Buddhahood. Now, while this may be acceptable as an interpretation of the text, it cannot serve as the essential tenet, and thus it is not adopted.

The scriptural passage has two parts: first, the announcement of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), and second, the manifestation of the characteristics of the actual prediction. Within this, there are both specific names and general designations.
Now, it is proclaimed that delusions and entanglements are exhausted and all virtues are complete; thus he is called "Pure Body.
*Tathāgata* means "Thus-Come One" (*āgata*). *Arhat* was formerly translated as "Worthy of Offerings" (*yìnggòng*), while the new translation simply says "Worthy" (*yìng*);

the five characters below [the title] were formerly translated as "Perfectly All-Knowing" (*zhèngbiànzhī*), while the new translation calls them "Perfectly Equal Enlightenment" (*zhèngděngjué*). These constitute the first three of the Ten Epithets. [End of excerpt]
Regarding why there are only these three, others say that this sequence refers to the person (*pudgala*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and knowledge (*jñāna*).

Because the person possesses both abandonment and knowledge, and because the meaning is briefly complete [with these], there are only three. Others say that these three mostly rely upon the three virtues of abandonment, merit (*guṇa*), and knowledge, and are explained in their respective order;
therefore, the others are not mentioned. Now, I say: the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states [that the Buddha] possesses these three meanings, and even throughout kalpas... [they are inexhaustible].

The exhaustion of these three constitutes the most essential [teaching], as it is frequently expounded; it may also be understood as the meaning of the three virtues—Dharmakāya, liberation, and prajñā—and the three bodies (trikāya).

The textual explanation directly clarifies their identical meaning without distinguishing between them. First, the identity is established; next, the differences are raised to provoke inquiry by citing past events.
Below this, the reconciliation is explained: first through a direct exegesis, and then through a reverse exegesis, clarifying that this matter reaches its ultimate point.
The Great One’s transformation has not yet spoken; it should properly reside in the "Correct Exposition" (Zhengshuo) rather than within the Preface by Mañjuśrī.
It is precisely because [the Buddha] was about to speak that Mañjuśrī deferred the merit to Him, and thus [the Buddha] did not speak immediately.

Although these words appear in a separate record, they follow the general principle so as to cause the assembly to remain in doubt without alarm, thereby further clarifying the meaning of the Preface. Such is the general purport [of the passage]. (etc.)
Regarding the various explanations offered: some state that this refers to the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of the one who succeeds [the Buddha], given as a consolation to the assembly;

others say that Maitreya received his prediction prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, while Guṇakaraṇa received it after the preaching of the sutra. Since he had to wait for the opening [of the Dharma] before being granted it, he must certainly have been a śrāvaka manifested through transformation.
Nevertheless, whether recorded in ancient or modern times, there is no distinction between śrāvakas and bodhisattvas regarding those who occupy the position of the successor.

As for "the same," how could there not be some slight differences between the modes of transformation in the past and the present? Here, we take up the point that the two vehicles receiving their predictions is the same [in both cases] (and so forth).
Now, if this were so, then the latter part of the present sutra should also grant a prediction to Maitreya.

It is not only that this sutra does not mention *nirvāṇa*, but that event itself never occurred; although the matter appears similar, it is not the essential core of the introductory section of this sutra.
Since this sutra is currently revealing and bestowing predictions upon the śrāvakas, we shall now proceed directly from this essential point without employing other meanings.

Below, the clarification of the commonality with the *sūtra*’s circulation follows; the preceding section concluded the description of how the original teaching of the past accords with the present, while the following describes how the matters of the past’s circulation and its benefits accord with the present.
Together with the preceding "accordance with the present," these constitute the introduction (*nidāna*), such that all three divisions [of the sūtra] are complete.

They are identical in that all three parts are wondrous. Regarding the first, the "periods," various schools all claim that the former is the proclamation of cessation while this is the actual cessation;
however, our current view takes only the former proclamation of reduction as sufficient to express the intended meaning.

Since the actual cessation is not the primary intent, we follow it into the general classification of scriptural periods, yet the true intent resides solely in these four characters; therefore, it is called "direct."

To take the four characters and speak of "midnight": this refers to abiding within the cycle of birth and death while manifesting the Middle Way of the Dharma-nature—neither arising nor ceasing, the great quiescence.
To speak of "without remainder" (nirupadhiśeṣa) applies to both the Small and Great Vehicles and encompasses multiple meanings, as has already been briefly discussed above.

The previous account of leaving home and attaining Buddhahood was the manifestation of birth where there is no birth; this [present passage] clarifies the manifestation of cessation where there is no cessation.

This means that function ceases and returns to the essence. As for the mention of "after extinction," it refers generally to the three periods of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), and the Final Dharma (*antima-dharma*).

"Persons" refers to those capable of circulating [the teaching]. "Upholding" (*dhāraṇa*) is general and not specific; it encompasses the three karmas and many skillful means so that the wondrous Dharma may abide for a long time and benefit beings without quickly vanishing.
Therefore, it is called "upholding. This is as in the case of the Dharma Master’s "Practice of Peace and Bliss" (*Sukhavihāra-pratipadā*) for a long duration.
Regarding "near" (*antika*) and "time": since the previous discussion was general, it spoke of "after extinction"; since this [discussion] is specifically determined, it speaks of "long" and "near.

A duration of eighty years is "long" in relation to the Great [Vehicle], whereas for the Small [Vehicle], it is restricted to being "near. Alternatively, it may follow the presence of conditions, or it may simply refer to the time of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

Regarding the eight disciples to be converted: the previous [passage] concerned humans in general, whereas this specifically clarifies them; among the eight sons, there are those to be converted mentioned in the sutras.

The phrase "those who can transform these [beings] by means of the lower" refers to the accomplishment of practice and the attainment of Buddhahood. Among the eight hundred, one person’s name and the stages of their virtuous conduct and rank may be known.
The above concludes the separate explanation of the two passages; below follows the combined explanation of the two meanings, wherein the purpose for directly combining the two passages is explained.

First, the initial citation introduces the intended meaning, which is explained below. Regarding the first doubt within the middle section: the doubt is presented as in the text, which contains two meanings.

First, in terms of time, it refers to the Patriarch; in terms of successive transmission, it refers to the ninth. Here, we follow the sense of successive transmission, hence it says "nine generations.
Jik (吉) states that from the perspective of Mañjuśrī, Maitreya is the teacher of the tenth generation; therefore, the following passage is cited to explain how Mañjuśrī possesses these two meanings.
By contrast, it is revealed that Maitreya did not receive his training from him [Mañjuśrī] through direct address; therefore, Mañjuśrī should now be questioned and he should respond.
Thus, the resolution of doubts becomes clear. Next, regarding the "secret opening," first the manifest identity is clarified, followed by the secret opening.

The statement that the roles of teacher and disciple were not fixed in the past or present is precisely intended to secretly indicate that the manifestations of the Śākyamuni Buddha are all indeterminate—that is, they are all...
"It is neither arising nor ceasing, yet it arises and ceases"—this "double negation" refers to the ultimate principle (*li*). (And so forth.
It is called "esoteric" because it remains latent and has not yet been manifested at that time. That it can be believed later is due to this.
These two meanings constitute the pivot of the two gates of the Trace and the Source: the former definitively reveals [the truth], while the latter allows for both the near and the far.
Reflect on this: it is because of faith that one must come.
The following question and answer further clarify that Maitreya is not the actual [Buddha], for both he and the self act as initiators for the sake of sentient beings.
Now, I say that the arrival of this text has two purposes: first, to manifest the power and function of the sutra; second, to resolve doubts and secretly express [the truth].
Regarding the "Dispelling Doubts" section, there should be three parts: first, dispelling doubts concerning the precepts; second, exhorting diligence regarding fame and profit;

and third, the concluding synthesis, which serves to clarify the matter further and increase its credibility. As for the two individuals mentioned, both have ancient and modern [accounts], as can be understood from the text.

Regarding the "Judgment and Response," within it, there is first the formal explanation and subsequently the distinction between the incorrect and the correct. First, the general purpose of the coming [text] is reiterated and explained. Finally...

In the initial analysis of the text, the term "clearly" (*fēnmíng*) signifies "certainty" (*nièdìng*). The section beginning with "present and past" (*jīnxī*) explains the meaning of this certainty; for this reason, there is a definitive judgment.
Some say that although the text contains four sections, they do not go beyond the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion.

First, the introduction states the intent to expound the Great Dharma (*dàfǎ*). Next, citing ancient authorities to corroborate the present, it refers back to the previous explanation regarding the intent to expound the Great Dharma. Now...
This concludes the introduction to the preaching of the Great Dharma. Within this section, the four lines correspond to the four auspicious omens, while also encompassing the six.
Since it is the same teaching of the Mahāyāna, it signifies that the immeasurable is definitively gathered and enters into the One.

Since it is likewise the same flowers and fruits, it signifies that the heavens will certainly rain down and scatter upon the Buddha. Since it is precisely when one becomes a Bodhisattva, the assembly will certainly rejoice. Now, [the Buddha] shall turn the wheel of the Dharma.
Because they are manifest, these are the stages of meditative concentration and movement; the term "decisive" (*niyata*) is used because all are clearly and certainly fixed as such.

Since all four are based on concentration, their meaning is implicitly included even if not explicitly stated. As for the phrase "emitting light," since light also relies upon concentration, it need not be mentioned separately;
one should simply contemplate the five phrases in response to the auspicious omen (as explained at length). Some say [this refers to] the subsequent [section].
Regarding the first point concerning the judgment of the three [sections] in the preceding part: how can they be so judged?

The answer is that although, according to the preceding text, they do indeed constitute a judgment of the three, when it comes to resolving doubts and responding to questions, the principle and the wording are most clearly elucidated therein; therefore, this excellence is separately highlighted as a distinct response (as detailed below).

Furthermore, by subsequently refuting the old view—which divides them into two and thus contradicts the text—it is shown that the present interpretation follows the meaning of the sutra and its principles as three; only then can it be definitively established as three.
This is to clarify that this sutra discusses the beginning and end of the Buddhas' transformative path as being entirely a convergence, as seen in the subsequent chapter on the five Buddhas.
Having already discussed how their beginnings differ, we now distinguish the reasons for those differences in their beginnings and ends;
subsequently, we shall manifest their essential convergence. Since these three aspects must exist for the transformative path to be complete, none may be omitted.
In the subsequent verse, the Sūtra states that there is no [one] before or after [him] within the great assembly, which contains a profound meaning (and so forth).

First, it indicates the boundaries and the presence or absence; thus, among the four [cases], it only versifies the latter two. Regarding the third case, three [subdivisions] are treated such that only the preceding and succeeding parts are versified while the middle is omitted.
This is primarily due to the force of the requirements of the verse-text; this is one instance of such suitability.
Regarding the temporal sequence as previously explained in detail, the prose version at the beginning contains three [sections], and although this verse is concise, it likewise possesses all three.
One should understand that the first line and the third and fourth lines constitute the specific names, while the second [line] applies generally to all ten.
Next, one should speak of the third [section]; since the three are identical, and following the current text, it is referred to as the "second."

Regarding "speaking and preaching of its own accord," as stated in the opening passage of the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*: "Without being asked, he speaks of his own accord," and so forth. Is this not indeed without cause? It distinguishes [this teaching] from ordinary forms and sounds;
yet it is not that there is no responsive resonance with the capacities of beings (*indriya*). Because it manifests the ultimate profundity and subtlety, it is described in such a way.

Since ancient times, various auspicious signs have not been expressed solely through light; rather, they are summarized in verses that encompass other meanings, as has already been clarified previously regarding birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Regarding the term "place of karmic retribution" (*karmavipāka-sthāna*): others explain "place" (*sthāna*) as that which is grasped as the result, because it is the destination to which karma—the cause—returns;
or "place" refers to principle (*yukti*), because there is this principle that good and evil causes evoke good and evil results;
or "place" refers to the locus where one experiences the fruits of good and evil. The radiance of Śākyamuni is entirely golden in color, like the two jewels of the sun and moon.
To manifest that the Mahāyāna is pure, singular, and supreme, it is exclusively golden; because its manifold virtues are perfectly complete, various colors appear within one another.
Its full name is *vaiḍūrya*, which possesses various colors. *Sphaṭika* means crystal, also known as water-jade or white pearl.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states that it emerges from mountain caves and is formed when ice melts after a thousand years.

Now, following the *Mūla-karma* [Sūtra], lapis lazuli is used as a metaphor for the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the maṇi jewel for Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and rock crystal for Wondrous Enlightenment (*tathāgata-bhūmi*).

These are all employed to clarify the merits of the various stages and positions. Herein, both the ancient and the modern are metaphorically based upon this to manifest the Correct and secretly express the Revealed;
everything is entirely real, entirely pure, and endowed with manifold virtues, as briefly clarified above, which shall be further explained later.

Furthermore, upon further reflection, it is certain that the reason why the manifested colors of these auspicious omens differ throughout the ages is due to the varying degrees of the devotee's resonance (*kang*).
When light, they appear as crystal; when heavy, they appear as gold. This may perhaps indicate that the radiance of the Dharma is sovereign and free.
(And so forth.)

Next, the explanation of "seeing the Buddha as identical" refers to seeing the Teacher who attained enlightenment all at once (*tong-shi*). In the text, there is first a specific explanation of the phrase "spontaneously accomplished," followed by a general explanation.

Within the first part, there is initially an explanation that distinguishes and clarifies [the truth] by means of two paths; this is followed by a direct explanation of the meaning of realizing true attainment.
These two paths refer to the "semblance-true" and the "sages and worthies. The Sūtra distinguishes between the worthy and the semblance to reveal the true.

Because it is "sacred" (ārya), it is called "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*); this signifies the meaning of being effortless and without exertion (*anābhoga*). Since this meaning applies universally, one must explain it according to the teachings.

The *Ji* (Record) states: "Each of the four teachings has its own true path: in the first [the Śrāvaka], one sits and spontaneously traverses the thirty-four moments of mind with a single thought-moment of correspondence, without adding further effort;
in the second [the Pratyekabuddha], at the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), one originally attains spontaneity; as for the third [the Bodhisattva], it is said that under the tree..."

Through thirty-four moments of mind, one severs both the manifest afflictions (*vitarka*) and their residual habits (*vāsanā*) to achieve penetration; specifically, under the Bodhi tree, a single thought-moment severs the remaining habits.

In the particular case of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), it occurs after the final moment of mind; in the case of Perfection (*pariniṣpanna*), it occurs after the Vajra-like mind, when delusions are exhausted, wisdom is perfected, and principle is fully realized, thereby attaining Buddhahood.
Now, I maintain that the original commentary’s explanation of "spontaneous understanding" has failed to accord with the first of these meanings.
As for the three [stages] following the text, they all proceed from the initial realization; by simply allowing delusion to be liberation, one reaches the goal spontaneously.

Without severing [delusion], it is exhausted; without achieving [enlightenment], it is perfected. Because these are all reached spontaneously through the true Way without adding any effortful practice, they are called "natural.
Thus, the Sūtra says, "Entering without severing"—this is precisely its meaning. The general sense is roughly as stated above; for a detailed account, see [the full text].
The mystery of attaining Buddhahood can be sought therein.

Next, regarding the inquiry into the meaning of the manifestation of reality as spontaneous (*svabhāva*), the intent of the question is as follows: since reality does not depend on causes, this question is posed.

In the response, there are analogies and their applications. Within the analogies, four meanings are presented; within the applications, two examples are briefly clarified, while within the [subsequent] examples, they are fully elucidated.
The four meanings may be investigated; some say that "spontaneously [ending] in seven births" refers to the nine grades of afflictions moistening seven births:

the uppermost grade (upper-upper) moistens two births; the upper-middle, upper-lower, middle-upper, and middle-middle each moisten one birth; the middle-lower and lower-upper together moisten one birth;
and the three lower grades together moisten one birth. Now, I say that even if there were such an addition here...
Merit is also spontaneous, for it is through this true realization that one accords with the Way.

Next, the text is further interpreted through the three bodies (*trikāya*) so that the words and their meanings correspond; because there are established statements, this refers to the retribution body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Its fundamental purity explains the meaning of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and these words regarding the dharma-body combine the two [bodies] to form the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The fundamental is not the true nature; the fundamental is also that which is cultivated to accord with the fundamental. "The complete image as the response" refers to the two types of responses, the superior and the inferior.
As the Sūtra says, "The response is sixteen feet tall, with the luster of purple gold. The sixteen-foot form is the inferior response.

Regarding the Dharma in terms of persons, this explains and clarifies the meaning of opening the Sudden Teaching. First, regarding "persons and the Dharma," it means preaching the profound and wondrous Dharma.
Thus we know that this was the first teaching of the sudden doctrine (sudden *dharma*) preached for those of great capacity. Next, regarding the "person and the dharma":

while the preceding phrase spoke only of the profound dharma, this speaks only of two persons; knowing this to be necessarily so, he offers this explanation. Regarding the mention of "diligence" and so forth:
the previous [passage] generally cited the person, whereas here he specifically cites their practice. Since the previous text already mentioned the pratyekabuddhas, herein—

Regarding the statement "one," since one knows that there are two by implication, it is not explicitly mentioned. As for the phrase "equal to four," according to various commentaries, this simply means it is equal to the four preceding and following [categories].
However, in the present case, since two have already been cited, it refers to the remaining four. The *Ji* (Commentary) states: "It should say 'two,' as the verse lists six perfections;
that it says only 'one' is likely an error. Furthermore, the statement that it is "equal to the four perfections" is also likely an error.

It is an error to claim that *vīrya* (diligence) occurs twice in the second line and *dāna* (giving) and *kṣānti* (patience) occur twice in the third line, such that they would merely equal the other two, *dhyāna* (meditation) and *prajñā* (wisdom).

For now, let us examine this according to the text; it appears that neither case is so. Since there was originally not a single word [of *vīrya*] in the first passage, we know that both lines are fully taken into account.
Although the word *vīrya* does appear in the second line, it is merely used as a term of praise.

The accomplishment of upholding the precepts does not correspond to the first two [verses]; it is only within the third line that the two [first] perfections are raised, with the others being included by way of analogy;

thus, the fourth [verse] is not an error. Regarding the statement "the six perfections mentioned above," this refers to a brief citation of two [perfections], from which the remaining four are taken by implication, constituting one distinct category corresponding to the initial Mahāyāna teaching. The subsequent two lines correspond to the middle [teaching].
In the previous section, because the prose was long and the phrasing narrow, the six perfections were treated collectively as a general statement.

Now, since this current passage is somewhat more expansive, it separates them for the sake of corresponding to the various preceding points of meaning; thus, it says "versifying the above vision," which is precisely the verse response to that intervening section.
If one follows the usual commentaries, however, the final three lines are combined as a single unit.

The Six Perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) are the meaning of the Mahāyāna. If one were now to synthesize the three practices to clarify the meaning of the Six Perfections so as to correspond generally to the three samādhis, it would not necessarily be incorrect;
however, in various textual passages, the force of the meaning does not correspond, and it would deviate from the essential body of the doctrine;

therefore, this is not the case. Furthermore, regarding the intention to reveal the reality within the preceding prose section, that was not yet the primary intent, as has already been briefly indicated.
What was previously clarified;
here below is the clarification of the meaning of the missing response in the verse. There is both the heading and the explanation. It is said that this may be a scribal error by Zhǎng'ān;
herein, the auspicious sign of Dīpaṃkara in another land is correctly cited to answer Maitreya’s question regarding another land. This is its explanation.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* concerns the events within the land of Lamp-Light (Dīpaṃkara) itself; how could it be relevant to another land?

As for the objection regarding the entry into extinction and the raising of stupas, this is answered as follows: furthermore, that which is introduced later—the entry into extinction and the raising of stupas—is likewise an event within the land of Lamp-Light itself.
How could one use that to answer a question concerning another land by citing something from one's own [context] to answer another?
Because the guest and host have diverged, we know that the absence of mention here of entering nirvana in another land and erecting a stupa is merely due to an omission in the sutra.
Now, I maintain that within the initial question, such signs appear after the two periods of the Dharma;

yet in the current answer, both the prose and the verses lack a response to this point. Regarding the explanation of the reason, first the preceding question is restated, followed by the present reason.

The explanation of the former response [to the question] is why it was asked in such a manner; the present response to the former [question] contains both meanings of self and other regarding the two lands (*dvipṛthivī*).
Although each contains these two meanings, they are unified in one: namely, the "self" of the present.

Since each statement here subsumes the two, I suspect this is not an error by another hand, but rather what I have established myself. Consider this. Next, regarding the "retrospective verse," this refers to the twenty billion bodhisattvas mentioned in the preceding text.
The phrase "sa etc. (薩等) refers to this. The term *zhui* (追) has two meanings: first, to retreat from what precedes; second, to follow after what follows.
In other texts, it is used when there is a lack of sequential order, meaning to retreat from what precedes; this is called *zhui*. However, in the present case, there is no lack of sequence;

it simply means "to follow," and thus it is termed *zhui*. It would have been acceptable even without this character. Some say that the commentary (*shu*) may be incomplete and should instead read "precedes" (前).
Yixing’s *Verses in Praise* [of the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*] contains the latter half-verse of the "Auspicious Omens" chapter, which expresses the joy of the assembly in this land;

the subsequent verses concerning doubts and reflections [in the introduction] are as follows (*et cetera*). Next, regarding the six items that correspond to the prose text, these fully versify the six sections of the long prose.

First, concerning the person: the term "just now" (*shìcóng*) signifies the beginning and implies proximity. Although there is a variant reading "zhí" (石) with the phonetic value "fǎn," it is far more convenient to simply follow the common pronunciation.

Such is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding the reasons for the initial praise, since that which was taught is the most sublime and ultimate Dharma, and the one addressed is the very person capable of both illuminating and manifesting it, as well as penetrating it—truly, such a person is not easily found;

therefore, it was necessary to offer the highest praise. As for why the Buddha does not praise Śāriputra here, it is because this is an abbreviated version; the extensive original text is as follows: [text omitted].
The ocean must indeed possess [these qualities] within its successive seasons; here, the wise one who possesses inconceivable knowledge explains the difficult-to-imagine through two aspects.

Now, this also consists of two parts: the first two lines correctly clarify the inconceivability of the seasons, while the following three lines clarify the inconceivability with respect to the *vidyādhara* (knowledge-holder).
The text first explains the seasons and subsequently explains the *vidyādhara*, which is able to cause the characteristics of long and short durations to manifest.
Therefore, both prolongation and contraction are devoid of spatial dimensions; because they function through wisdom, they are called "inconceivable.
The *Inconceivable Wisdom Purity* chapter states: "A Bodhisattva can contract one kalpa into seven days. What I mean by "seven days" is precisely this meaning.
Some say that while this only involves contraction, the mention of "prolongation" (yán) occurs because the two tendencies follow one another. I maintain, however, that both should be present.
The commentary below states: "In this manner, fifty minor kalpas elapse"—this refers to extension. Now, it is said that [the same period] is but half a day—this refers to contraction.
Since the Buddha is thus now, he was certainly so in the past; one should not view this as partial. This is merely a matter of response, for response arises from resonance.
Such wondrous efficacy of response and resonance entirely results from attaining the essence, which is the Sublime Dharma (Saddharma). Therefore, it is...
This refers to the past and expresses the wondrous Dharma that is to be expounded here and now; the following is the explanation of the passage concerning "upholding.
Now, while Subhūti has the praise but lacks the entrustment, and Śāriputra has the entrustment but lacks the praise, these are cited alternately to manifest their equality.
The text says, "one who is able to receive and uphold it"; this is a phrase arising from the resolve to offer praise, not an act of entrustment. Otherwise, how could it be so?
Regarding the statement that "before it was proclaimed, he entrusted [the teaching]," and the subsequent phrase "the entry into extinction is the same," some say this is an error.
The Sūtra cites the entry into extinction in the Buddha’s own land by Dīpaṃkara to answer the question concerning other lands; how could this be called "the same"?
Since they are not the same, how could it answer what was asked? The meaning is roughly as explained previously. Now, I maintain that its meaning is also as stated above.
In this treatise, among the teachings on cessation (*nirodha*), the two great matters have been fully elucidated through the most detailed exposition, and their exposition is now complete.

Regarding the entrustment (*parindanā*) as taught in the *Śāsanānuśāsana-sūtra* (The Teaching of the Bequeathed Instruction), as extensively clarified therein, there are many exhortations to diligent progress and detachment;

yet none of these transcend the two meanings contained herein. The interpretations cited by various commentators have failed to capture this essential point, which I am currently unable to describe in full detail. As for the passage concerning "weeping," it refers to the text.
It requires two things: namely, compassion and longing. As for "like the *Nirvāṇa*," if one refers to the preceding section, it is like Cunda’s lamentation;
if one refers more broadly to the latter section, it likewise does not go beyond these two—sorrowful grief and yearning attachment.

Furthermore, regarding the *Śāsanāntima-sūtra* (The Teaching Left Behind), two phrases therein correspond to the text of that sutra: "the causes and conditions for attaining liberation" and "having already [attained] within the three."
The seeds of the jewels were sown; now I exhort you to cultivate them so that liberation may be attained at the proper time. Examples of this are found below;

the specific categories of such matters are fully detailed in the *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood* and its commentary, as indicated by the note "and so forth," which now cites the explanations from that sūtra. This too has not yet been reached [in the present discussion].
Next, within the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), the untainted true reality (*anāsrava-tattva-lakṣaṇa*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the wondrous Way;
thorough penetration is the Wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) of ultimate fruition; and "one shall next become a Buddha" is the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifested through the eight phases.

Thus is the meaning of the three bodies being fully possessed, whereby one awakens oneself and awakens others. "Becoming a Buddha" is the general designation, while "Pure Body" (*śuddhakāya*) is its specific name, for that body is pure.
"Purity is like a lotus flower" because it gathers the immeasurable into the one; thus it is said that "immeasurable multitudes are also delivered.

Although this refers to Bodhisattvas, the primary intent is to clarify that for Śrāvakas it is not so. This is because the purpose of the formal exposition is to initiate [the teaching], and therefore [the Bodhisattva stage] is not employed here.
Within the first two lines, there are two meanings which correspond to the sequence of the two lines; in the initial prose section, there is no arising.

This statement is based on what is inherently established by Tāranātha. The commentary fully explains two meanings. In explaining the first meaning, it first applies it to the Hīnayāna and then to the Mahāyāna.

Since there are both *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder) types of *nirvāṇa*, and this instance specifically refers to the *nirupadhiśeṣa*, the long passage states: "entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, because it applies to both vehicles, it is explained in this way according to these two; as for the Hīnayāna: [The text continues with the specific analysis of the Hīnayāna interpretation.]

The wisdom regarding the six fruits that are without cause remains as "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*); when the wisdom of the extinction of the body ceases, there is no further substance remaining, which is "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
Departing from those two states of existence and returning to the One Nameless is called "entry. Thus, just as fire is extinguished when fuel is exhausted, the Mahāyāna also possesses two meanings:

first, the exhaustion of the causes of birth and death through one's own practice and the consequent disappearance of their fruits; second, because these two are without before or after, they are like the exhaustion of fuel.
When the fire is exhausted and extinguished, if one approaches the response to transformation, the response perishes as its function is completed; thus it is said that there is no further remainder.
Its activity ceases and it returns to the essence, which is termed "entering. Now, this refers precisely to the Mahāyāna’s cessation of response, and is why it is described in this way.
Next, regarding the explanation of "benefit" and "non-extinction": because this benefit exists right here, it is not extinction; rather, its manifestation as extinction is precisely for this reason.
As will be explained extensively later, this merely clarifies the occasion of reciting the sutra; it does not mean that the propagation of the sutra itself brings about such benefits.

Therefore, the prose section simply states, "after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. Furthermore, among these people, one should know that while the words are general, the meaning is specific; lest there be fear... [text ends].
This is not the same as the present Buddhas, Kāśyapa, and so forth; therefore, it says below that this refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Next, regarding the phrase "the various sages" (*ṛṣis*) in the sutra, some say that this is a general reference to those who have transcended birth-and-death in its segmented form (*paricchinna-janma-maraṇa*), attained bodies of sovereign mastery (*vaśitā-kāya*), and have advanced from this point upward;
hence the term "various. Now, I maintain there are two meanings: first, those who have attained mundane dhyāna and possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

Because their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and lifespans are long-lasting, and because they were most excellent and beautiful before the Buddha appeared in the world, they are also generally referred to as "Buddhists" in accordance with worldly convention.
Furthermore, the master who transforms and the assembly he transforms are both collectively termed *ṛṣis* (sages). Thus, the *Mahāsamaya Sūtra* states: "There are many kinds of gods;
the Wheel-Turning Kings are gods among men; the various gods of the three realms are gods among gods. As for those who have attained the first fruit [of the path]...
The preceding passage refers to the Buddha as the "Ultimate God among Gods" because he is the ultimate *paramārtha-deva* (First Principle Heaven) who dwells above the pure heavens of the world.
Now, I say that this [previous interpretation] is extremely crude, shallow, and erroneous; how much more so would it be for something profound and subtle?
I maintain that when the preceding text says "the Honored One venerated by devas and humans," and the subsequent text says "the Holy Lord, God among Gods," these both refer to the Buddha.
It is considered so because it is the eighth among the eight; thus it is called "the last. Students should examine this thoroughly and not fall into error.
If one refers to the Great Sūtra, it says, "The Great Sage shall now speak," and again, "I only pray that the Honored Great Sage will analyze and explain this for me.
These are specific praises of the Teacher who transforms others. Herein, he addresses all those beings who are to be transformed.
Because he praises the Master, it says "the guide of all sages," which generally refers to all those who aspire to the sublime, yearn for the distant, and seek deliverance from the world.
Regarding the term "Lion of the Śākyas," this cites a nature as a metaphor for virtue: among beasts, the lion is the king;
it is majestic, fierce, fearless, resolute, sovereign, and capable of subduing all. The virtues of the Buddha are likewise such. These two passages together contain two meanings: first...

Thus, the two aspects of clarifying the sutra and benefiting [sentient beings] have been explained; the second part, which resolves doubts and secretly reveals the original gate, has already concluded its analysis of the structure and the intent behind its presentation as previously detailed.
Next, regarding the conclusion:
although one may have been indolent in the interim, one can still attain Buddhahood now—how much more so for those who are able to be diligent and manifest the power of the sutra!

Regarding "using this skillfully to urge beings toward diligent service": this refers to forming a conclusion that causes beings to look up with admiration for what follows after the preceding answer.
If that were the case, the prose (*gadya*) would also need to be so; otherwise, there would be mutual redundancies or omissions.
My intention is that since the meaning of the text is clear, it must indeed be thus. How could there be a direct verse (*śloka*) upon the preceding prose, and yet also be further interrupted?

Now, regarding the questions concerning the text, the explanation of these two [sections] involves two distinct differences. First, the prose section contains four meanings, yet it simultaneously encompasses five or six;

since this verse now summarizes the preceding [prose], it contains only three. This may be due to abbreviation or omission. Regarding the first [of the three], one should state that it simultaneously summarizes the two meanings of "speaking of great rain" and "flowers.
The subsequent two lines are identical in being exhortations to the assembly, intended to cause them profound joy. Thus, [the structure] is established.

This verse consists of four lines: the first line clarifies the Buddha, and the second line admonishes the assembly present at that time. Of these, the first two phrases refer to the past, while the latter two phrases refer to the present.

"Aiding and eliciting" (*jufā*) refers to the elicitation [of the teaching]; "the true aspect" (*zhenshíxiàng*) refers to the correct exposition; and "light" (*guāngmíng*) also refers to the skillful means that aid and elicit.
The two characters for "aiding and eliciting" apply generally to the aforementioned two meanings. "True aspect" (*shíxiàng*) is precisely that which is elicited from reality (*zhēnshí*). All...

The person addressed the entire assembly; "separately" means to form a karmic connection according to the specific capacity of each individual. Joining the palms with a single mind unifies both body and spirit. The latter two lines clearly reveal the intent of the address:
the Buddha shall descend with the great rain of Dharma, which means to reveal the ultimate reality by opening up the provisional teachings.

This satisfies those who seek the supreme Great Way. "Severing doubts" constitutes being protected and remembered by the Buddha, for it removes [delusions] so that one may realize the same principle as the Buddha.
Because of this knowledge and vision, and because he is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha, the preceding four meanings are fully expressed in verse;
the meanings of the fifth and sixth are also as explained before, which can be understood from the text itself, as was briefly indicated above.

Next, regarding the explanation that resolves four latent doubts, there are four sections: first, a general discussion of the purpose; second, a formal analysis of the text to reveal its characteristics;
third, a summary praising the capabilities of the two sages; and fourth, clarifying that the previous explanation of non-uniformity avoids the fault of disparagement or exaltation.

Within the first section, there are two parts: the first formally clarifies what is appropriate, and the second clarifies what is inappropriate. Regarding the first, the momentum and numerical categories are identical and harmonious.
Such being the case, since the force of the textual structure is also extremely clear, one cannot help but provide this explanation.

However, because the previous objections and doubts both reside within the mind, they are all referred to as "lying dormant" (*fu*). Both "resolving" (*shi*) and "severing" (*duan*) are likewise clearly manifest.

This [explanation] pervades the four subsequent sections; specifically, within each of these four sections, there are further distinctions. In each instance, one first sets forth the latent doubt, followed by...
The explanation of the severance of doubts: furthermore, within each individual doubt, there are both the causes and the actual state, which are easy to understand from the text.

Regarding the term "name" (myō): the Dharma and the parable constitute the name; these two characters refer precisely to the Dharma and the parable. The true aspect (shōsō) constitutes the substance (tai), which is the real entity existing from the beginning.

The marvelous cause and effect constitute the thesis (shū); this refers to the entity that manifests the thesis and manifests the substance. The beginning and end of seeking the Way are precisely cause and effect.
"Comprehensive" (*qià*) means pervasive; "moistening" (*rùnshī*) refers to the function of severing doubt and engendering faith, as is clear from the text itself.
An interpretation such as this not only resolves four latent doubts but also reveals four essential meanings; the quintessence of this entire sutra is exhausted herein.
These essentials consist of five layers. Whether one discusses the teaching (*jiào*) or the reality (*zhèng*), the essential points presented above do not reside in the expressive words themselves.

The subsequent scriptural passages of this treatise likewise conclude with a eulogy. The term "linked and translated" (*lianfan*) means that they fly forth one after another in succession without interruption;
this is because the present question-and-answer sequence continues up to the fourth [section]. "Matter" (*shi*) refers to names and so forth, while "principle" (*li*) refers to the essence (*tǐ*).

Alternatively, "name" (*míng*) may apply to both matter and principle, whereas "essence" (*tǐ*) resides solely in principle; "source" (*zōng*) pertains only to principle, while "function" (*yòng*) pertains only to matter. This treatise reaches its ultimate point through the convergence of these entities and causes.

The profound meaning is such that it is realized within one’s own heart; why then need further proof? It is excellent indeed. Were it not for the two aspects of ultimate perfection, how could this be achieved?
Therefore, both texts contain these passages from the "Lion’s Roar" chapter (*Siṃhanāda-parivarta*) of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, where the Buddha praises the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda.
One must possess both aspects to achieve this capacity; for the benefit of others is necessarily brought about through oneself.
The two adornments of merit and wisdom constitute the perfection of self-benefit; for how could one who has not reached the ultimate in self-benefit be able to benefit others well?

That one can now do so is indeed the culmination of both [merit and wisdom]. Next, it clarifies that the former [interpretations] were partial errors: not only do they fail to establish the force of the numerical sequence, but they also fail to exhaustively explain the text.
This is the intention of the Great Master (Zhiyi). The following points regarding this meaning are according to the intent of Danqiu (Guanding), as recorded by the Master.
Having already provided my own interpretation and the interpretations of others, it was necessary to include this chapter for detailed examination; hence these words.

However, the preceding prose and verses consist merely of four chapters whose phrasing and intent are densely layered, their essential purpose being to clarify that the Buddha was about to preach the wondrous Dharma and that the assembly had already attained it at that time.
The present commentary provides yet another layer of re-exposition; if one can believe in this, then [the truth] will surely become manifest.
This is what has now been attained. Furthermore, there are five general prefaces in total, beginning from the assembly of the multitude and concluding with the questions and answers;

though each is profound and extensive in its wording and reasoning, their essential intent does not exceed the manifestation of two meanings. First, regarding the "manifestation of the response," it refers to the marvelous path that is about to be expounded, which inspires a longing for the marvelous within the assembly at the time of its proclamation.

Now, if practitioners can investigate this explanation, they will [realize] the void... (Note: The final character "虗" appears to be an incomplete or truncated term, likely intended as "虛妄" (emptiness/falsehood) or part of a phrase such as "虛通" (penetrating emptiness). As the source text ends abruptly, the translation reflects the available portion.)
If those who come after desire to engage in correct discourse, they will grasp the intended meaning of its manifestation.
