Because it is half [of the full], it is "concise" (*saṃkṣipta*); because the Buddhas are persons, it is "general" (*sāmānya*) and thus "abbreviated" (*laghu*).

To reveal and clarify the essential meaning of this sutra, there are only two [aspects], and thus it is "abbreviated. The aforementioned "abbreviated" means that the meaning is manifested here. What follows is the clarification of the three "extensive" (*vistara*) aspects in contrast to the above;
the extensive meaning is manifested here. This is a combined explanation of the two types of "abbreviated" and "extensive. It is easy to understand in its textual form.
One should know that this meaning ought properly to have been stated previously, beneath the first "Repeated and Extensive Chapter" (*chóng'ěr guǎng zhāng*).
It penetrates through the three periods and four chapters, and the five Buddhas and six meanings exhaustively encompass the texts of the orthodox tradition. Why, then, is it listed here?

It is because it specifically addresses the aspect of being able to open and reveal [the teaching], and is presented as an expansion in contrast to the preceding brevity. Furthermore, the extensive text is further divided into...
The third chapter explains it at the beginning because the meaning is more convenient there; whereas [the previous section] explained it at the end because the meaning was not as convenient.

(etc. Next, the specific explanation of the reasons for the "Extensive Meaning" (*vyāsa*) follows, which consists of four parts: first, listing the six names; second, explaining the six; [third, etc.]...

The three knowledges of the mind (*manas-trividyā*) are mutually equal; the four [knowledges] and the one [knowledge] are likewise in accord, which is precisely what is permitted. Furthermore, there is a prohibition followed by a permission, and below there is also a distinction followed by a permission.
Therefore, regarding the first [category], there are two textual passages, and for each of the latter two, there are two texts and two meanings; these should be carefully considered.
Within the first [section], one first restates the request as that which is to be accorded with and permitted, which is also the reason for it. Next, the permission itself has two parts.
The commentary on the text explains this admonition with two intentions: first, to analyze the passage so as to give rise to the three types of wisdom;

second, to harmonize it with the four kinds of wholesome dharmas in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Regarding the first, there is a topical heading that correlates [the text] specifically for the purpose of causing these three benefits to arise.

Thus, this admonition is established: if one is not attentive and acts unskillfully, the three [wholesome states] will not arise, yet they would be merely [wholesome] states rather than wisdom. This is the name of the three wisdoms.
To penetrate this is itself the wondrous; one should use the character "good" (*śubha*) to unify these two meanings, namely, good and evil, and awakening and delusion.

Next, regarding the unification of the four: the subsequent sutra states that there are four dharmas that can serve as proximate causes for Great Parinirvāṇa—namely, drawing near to virtuous friends, hearing the true Dharma, reflecting upon its meaning, and practicing according to the teaching. These are the four.
Regarding how these three relate to the latter four: the Sūtra states, "I shall now instruct you," and "be attentive and equal-minded toward the Buddha.
This means to cause one to draw near to a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Since the remaining names and meanings are comprehensive, they are said to be easily understood.

These two [explanations] both clarify the intent of the instruction; it is not only that one can immediately give rise to the three types of wisdom by drawing near, but it also serves as a distant cause for...
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* establishes these as the proximate causes for the three supreme fruits; therefore, it sets them forth at the beginning as this admonition.
Furthermore, the Great Sūtra states: "It is impossible that one could attain nirvana through the practice of asceticism while remaining apart from these four dharmas of virtuous speech.
This means that if one practices asceticism without correct understanding, it is called useless, being no different from that of the heterodox.
Because there is no difference between persons, the subsequent passage states, "seeking to abandon suffering by means of suffering"—this is precisely its meaning.
It is also called "acting without cause. Since this is the most essential point, it is first admonished here so that a sublime understanding and practice may arise.
As the preceding text is easy to understand, it is not explained. Having previously requested the verse on the "perfection of the path," he now grants it, saying, "For you..."
The detailed explanation here permits [the teaching] to those who possess [the requisite qualities]. Next, regarding the explanation of the restrictions and permissions:

this clarifies that the wondrous Way must not be recklessly bestowed upon unworthy persons. It is like bestowing a *maṇi* jewel upon the son of a butcher; it would not only be of no benefit but would instead cause great harm.
To exclude such individuals through restriction, as stated in the verse, there are two commentaries which provide a thorough explanation; one should first consult them.
Following the headings, the second part provides an explanation. First, regarding the explanation of the "Selection" (*jiǎn*) section of the sutra text, there are six points:

first, stating the reason; second, stating the number and then withdrawing [the list]; third, explaining the reason for the withdrawal; fourth, clarifying that the selection was appropriate; fifth, praising the assembly present;
and sixth, extending [the praise] to those who withdrew. The commentary (*shū*) explains these latter five in detail. Regarding the reason, there are two aspects: the distant and the proximate.
"From afar by the three cessations (*nirodha*) and from near by the compliance with admonitions; the reason for citing the timing is precisely because of this...

[The commentary] explains that initially there were those who possessed the number [of attainments] but experienced regression. The text of the commentary explains directly and excludes them because such people are not the proper candidates;
thus, the three cessations are not discussed for them. Now, since we are about to explain it for those who are the proper candidates, [it is stated as follows].
Regarding the term "wei-shen" (威神), it refers to the latent exercise of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), as indicated by the subsequent verse;

it is so named because it distinguishes the non-true and causes [the obstacles] to depart. The first three periods of cessation were all for the sake of the two assemblies: first, to distinguish [them], and second, to manifest [them].

The three cycles of the *Māyājāla* (or the three weeks) fall within the category of manifestation. This manifestation has two meanings: first, to cause the three requests; second, to represent the three.

The present passage from the *Zhou* [Book of Documents] already contains two or three of these points (and so forth). The commentator says: "When the season of Vermilion Brilliance begins, the shepherd’s purse and wheat wither first;
when one speaks of the *Ekottara-āgama*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* immediately arises. This translation is uniform yet the objects differ. Below is the explanation for the withdrawal.
Since the text contains evidence, what is the purpose of explaining and concluding that evidence? Why is it that those who are summoned are ordered to withdraw?
The commentary states that because there are three faults, it concludes by saying, "Because there are these three errors," and so forth.
Some say that next, the reason for the arising and departing is explained through nine points, which have two meanings: first, the Mahāyāna... Exert yourself! Exert yourself!
Private Notes on the Words and Phrases of the Wondrous Sutra, Scroll Nine;
Private Notes on the Words and Phrases of the Wondrous Sutra, Scroll Ten (Exhausting the Explanation of the Title from the "Chapter on Expedient Means").
Compiled by the Stone Drum Śramaṇa, Śākyamuni Zhìyún.
The following section corresponds to the second part: the commentary on the main body of the text (*śāstra*). Within this, there are three sections: first, stating the intent of the sub-commentary;

second, determining the title of the chapter; and third, explaining the text of the sub-commentary. Regarding the first: the sub-commentary explains this by first presenting the headings and then the explanatory text.
The reason for doing so is twofold: first, to directly address the manifest text; second, to follow its underlying principles. First, the manifest text: [text follows].

Regarding the meaning of the sequence that is easy to understand: the previous explanation of the meaning of the "Chapter on Interpretation" (Shichu pin) contained four points, whereas this chapter contains two.
First, while the meaning of the chapter title is specific, the meaning of the section title is general, as seen in the preceding single and double-layered structural outlines (*kebun*).
From here below, both correspond to the second [point]: each of the main sections (*shōjū*) contains many chapters, yet this chapter is merely the first of them.
Second, although the title of this section is restrictive, its meaning is actually universal throughout the entire treatise.

If one were to categorize it solely as having the meaning of "expedient means" (*upāya*), the scope of that category would remain restricted and would not encompass the universal meaning of the whole work.

Therefore, this present text, for the sake of convenience regarding the subject matter and because the meaning is universal, first explains the title and subsequently provides a topical analysis (*vibhāga*) of the text. This precisely captures the essential core of the matter.
It is for this reason.
Next, regarding the origin of the chapter title: although the ways in which names are acquired differ, they have been briefly explained above.
Now, it is named after the various [aspects] of the teaching; in brief, it refers to the Dharma of skillful means and wisdom. Such is the meaning of this sutra.
Since it is necessary to exhaustively reveal the ultimate reality by opening up the provisional means, the introductory text states:

"The meaning of the true reality of all phenomena has already been explained for you in brief as 'the true dharma of the Buddhas after a long time must speak the truth,' and in detail as 'straightforwardly abandoning the provisional means, one speaks only the unsurpassed path.
Now I shall explain for you the most real matter. How could this not be the wondrous and true [reality]?
To place something at the very beginning of a work and title it "The Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paryāya*)—is there any greater discrepancy between name and reality than this?
What is the reason for this? An eminent predecessor who first grasped the essential point explained it thus:

"Since the three vehicles of the past were used as names to manifest the non-[ultimate] as the [ultimate], once the three vehicles of the past are designated as 'expedient means,' the truth of the One Vehicle is revealed of itself without needing to be stated."

Since this was first proposed, later scholars have not failed to follow it like shadows. Although there are indeed those today who do not employ what has been explained, the ultimate truth is quiescent and absolute, such that it cannot be spoken of at all;
yet because there are causes and conditions, it can be spoken of. Since both [the conventional and the ultimate] are what is spoken of, one intends to manifest the former through the latter;
however, if one does not directly follow the actual reality from now on, then that which manifests is not [the truth].
Truly, when one is completely free from doubt and confusion, how could it not be entirely excellent? Yet why must one take such circuitous routes to arrive at an error?
There is no precedent for this within our own school, nor is there even a trace of it in the various sutras; furthermore, there is no logical basis for it in the commentaries or exegeses.
This is all due to being ignorant of the specific and general meanings of technical terms; how could such a principle possibly be so? Human nature is indeed thus, and it is not to be trusted.

Furthermore, although later commentators who provide general exegeses claim that the names and meanings of "expedient means" (upāya) apply universally to both the ancient and modern, as well as the Great and Small Vehicles, they fail to realize that these two entities—expediency and reality—proceed in opposition;
they do not grasp the essence of this sutra’s two gates, which are non-localized and uniquely wondrous.
This shall be seen in the formal explanation that follows. For now, relying on the fundamental tenets, I shall briefly indicate them: such is the "localized" aspect of this sutra.
This is appropriate; thus, what the text refers to as "the foremost skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas" and so forth is precisely the skillful means of this sutra.

One should understand that by citing this single character, all [other meanings] are subsumed. Furthermore, the meaning of this title contains two layers: first, a pair of the general and the specific;

second, a pair corresponding to this particular section and the other chapters of the work. In the past, various sutras have treated the specific from the perspective of the general, and the general from the perspective of the specific, both [approaches being employed].
The skillful means of this sutra are what enable oneself and others to attain the wondrous essence;
if one first grasps this intent to stabilize the will and then practices it with dedication, how could it be difficult? Otherwise, the faithful will merely labor in vain.
Having understood how the chapters of the sutra proceed, one then explains the meaning of the text as commented upon in the sub-commentary (*śāstra*).
Within this, first the method of explanation is presented, and subsequently, one explains according to that method.

First, regarding the word "this" (*idaṃ*), it refers to the two characters of the title, "Expedient Means" (*upāya-kauśalya*), which are the very objects to be explained. The terms "concise" and "extensive" specifically indicate the method itself; that is, employing this [method].
It is explained by means of two dharmas; the reason for this is that the Sūtra contains these two meanings.
Since the Buddha himself spoke thus even at that time, how could it be otherwise now?

Having already taught the wondrous Dharma through these two gates, which have no beginning and reach to the end, with meanings profound and vast, one must first demonstrate their essential tenets before proceeding further.
To expound and clarify this—that is, to explain the essential points—is necessarily so.
Within the subsequent section on "Exegesis According to the Directions," there are again two parts: first, the headings, and second, the explanations. Regarding the initial headings, there are two:
namely, the "Direct" and the "Revealing the Hidden. As for the objects [of exegesis], there are briefly three types of exegesis; thus, one proceeds directly to the explanation.
To explain by first stating the names and numbers, one must first list them; according to principle, one should state: "A Brief Explanation in Three Parts.

Having thus listed their names, one then proceeds to the formal explanation. As for these three names, according to the literal text: the first is called "Dharma" (the teaching), the second "Function" (application), and the third "Secret Profundity" (mystery). If explained according to their meaning:
the first is explained in terms of the "capacity to employ," the second in terms of the "capacity to penetrate," and the third in terms of "opening up and unifying non-duality."
The commentary further explains that first, there is a section exclusively concerning the past; second, a section contrasting the past with the present to clarify the three aspects of the past;

and third, a section on the general integration of the past. Furthermore, within the first of these, there is a general explanation according to the meaning; second, a specific explanation according to the intent; and third, a general integration of the meaning and intent of the past.

Moreover, within the first of these, there is a general explanation regarding all provisional and real teachings across the four periods of the past; and second, a specific selection and clarification of all the provisional teachings across the four periods of the past.

The Dharma is explained here as the actual reality of the present, while the three types of knowledge (*vidyā*) of the past are explained as all being provisional means that are themselves perfectly real.

Furthermore, the first [explanation] is based on the essence itself; the second is based on function; and the third is based on the non-duality of essence and function. Moreover, the first [of these three] is based on the capacity to act; the second is based on that which is acted upon;

and the third is based on the non-duality of the agent and the object. Finally, the first two [sets of explanations] distinguish the inadequacies of the past, while the latter [set] establishes the truth.

The first [point] reveals that this is explained from the perspective of relative dependence; if the first two clarify what is transcended, the final one correctly clarifies the transcendence itself—this is explained from the perspective of absolute transcendence (*atyantāpekṣā*).
Although this interpretation is brief, it constitutes the essential method [of exposition], and therein all things are nothing but wondrous skillful means (*upāya*).
This is truly what is meant by "having no predecessor and transcending all successors," whether in terms of enumeration or otherwise.
Regarding the names and their sequence, both are contained herein; furthermore, as for the "sequence of names," the reason why they are collectively included therein should be examined in detail.

Below this, the formal explanation consists of three distinct parts. Within the first part, "The Dharma and its Function," there are again three sections: first, a general explanation; second... [text continues].
Following the characters, the essential nature and characteristics of the two meanings are distinguished; subsequently, this is concluded by excluding what is not [the case].

The first "convenience" (fang) refers simply to the meaning of the character *fang* (method), while the second "expediency" (bian) refers simply to the exclusion of what is not [the case] now, thereby manifesting what was [the case] in the past. Regarding the first, the "application of the Dharma" (*fayong*), Fazang fully explains it as follows:

first, it is explained according to its etymological definition (*xunshi*); next, it is explained according to its meaning (*yi*). It is called "expediency" (*bian*) because it skillfully employs provisional dharmas.

To clarify the definition: "Dharma" (fa) refers to the essence (ti), and "expedient" (bian) refers to the function (yong). To give rise to function based upon the essence is called "expedient means" (fangbian).

Because one gives rise to the functions of the partial and perfect teachings based upon the essences of the partial and perfect teachings, it is said that "the Dharma has [these aspects]," and so forth. Now, I say that both of these two explanations are untenable.

If the meanings of both "essence" and "function" are equally applicable to both the provisional and the real, why distinguish them? This [distinction] is precisely what defines the relationship between the capacity (neng) and the object (suo).

Since it is not possible for either [the essence or the function] to serve as the basis for the other, neither [position] is tenable. Regarding the interpretation of these two characters throughout antiquity and the present, there are both divergent and convergent views.
In this current text, there are three interpretations: the first and last rely on divergence, while the middle one relies on convergence.

However, because there is convergence only through divergence, if convergence itself lacks divergence, what would there be to discuss regarding convergence? Now, first, concerning "method" (*fang-fa*) and so forth, this is the explanation of the text.
This is the conventional meaning of the characters. This "method" (*fang*) refers to the methods that are employed; "employing" means being able to employ them.
The "methods employed" generally refer to all dharmas, while "being able to employ" generally refers to all capacities for practice and application.
Master Jing said, "Method is a term for technical arts and calculations. Now, as for what is called "method":
There are both general and specific [categories]; here, it is appropriate to distinguish them. "Fang" (方) is a general term for all names of arts and techniques;

therefore, since ancient times, those who possess arts and techniques have been collectively called *fangshi* (方士). Among those capable in these matters, they are specifically termed "expedient" (*bian*).
My current intention is precisely to clarify that one is skillful in employing methods and benefits all things, so that each thing may obtain its own benefit. This is what is meant by "ability."
Because they are spoken of in combination, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*); the text is abbreviated because they are separated rather than combined, and thus it simply says "thus.

Below, regarding the meaning of the distinction between the two characters [of the title], this section uses the "function" (*yòng*) to explain the "essence" (*běn*). This is a general discussion of the past period of teaching and transformation;

since that was the primary dispensation and their convergence had not yet been discussed, it speaks directly of their distinctions. Therefore, it is necessary to differentiate them in order to clarify and establish the differences of the past.

This is the demarcation of their respective portions. Within this, there are two parts: first, the designation of the two names and their differentiation; second, the explanation of their essential nature. Regarding the designation:

"square" refers to the differentiation of phenomena (*dharma*), while "round" refers to the convergence of function. Functioning through the square is "differentiation," while functioning through the round is "convergence.
The square represents following after things, wherein each portion is fixed according to its own category without yet having attained universal penetration; therefore, it is termed "differentiation."
"Yuan" (Complete) is used because it generally accords with one aspect of the original intent; thus, while the applications of this term are many, they do not exceed these two points.
Next, below, its essential nature and characteristics are explained. First, the explanation of "Dharma" contains two meanings: essence (*tǐ*) and significance (*yì*).
The "three" and the "one" constitute two aspects of the same essence; thus, they simultaneously possess two meanings.

As for the mention of the square and so forth, all say this is an explanation based on concrete phenomena (*dharma*). A "square" (矩) is the tool for drawing squares, and a "circle" (規) is the tool for drawing circles.

Now, some explain according to worldly convention, saying that the compass and square were the laws for rectifying sovereigns and fathers in antiquity. Formerly, in the time of Yao, there was a craftsman...
The name of the official was Shui; Yao employed him to create the four instruments: the compass, the square, the level, and the plumb line.

The compass can produce circles, the square can produce squares, the level can make things level, and the plumb line can make things straight. Now, borrowing from that analogy, these two [the Buddha and the Sage] are thus described.
The provisional methods of the Three Teachings are able to accomplish those partial and biased things; therefore, it is said that the square can cause things to reach toward bias.
Because it is compared to the "further" (the *bhūyaskṛt*), it is said that this "method" (*fang*) should be spoken of as being conjoined; thus it is so stated.

The three provisional means (*trīṇi upāyāni*) each abide in their own determination and do not interpenetrate or converge; therefore, this is "Method" (*fang*). The One Reality (*eka-tattva*) converges at the ultimate point; therefore, this is "Round" (*yuan*). (And so forth)—this is the meaning of "substance" (*ti*).
"If wisdom" and below is the next [section] explaining the function (*vṛtti*). In the previous explanation of the Dharma, there was the meaning of having an essence (*svabhāva*);

now this meaning contains three aspects, namely: essence, characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and function (*artha*). (As detailed in the original text). Within this, there are two distinct parts: the explanation of the Dharma and the explanation by means of analogies. Regarding the explanation of the Dharma, there are two further divisions:

the first and the last. These two consist of internal essence and external function; that is, their differentiation and convergence. "Wisdom" refers to partial wisdom, which is also expedient means (*upāya*).

"Also *yì* (詣) means to approach, to go toward, or to arrive at; here it means the present intention (*yì*) is illumination. 'Illuminating partial dharmas' refers to expedient capacities (*quán-jī*). This is the internal essence (*nèi-tǐ*).
'Then, goodness and below' correctly explains the external application (*wài-yòng*); this is precisely the differentiation (*chā*).

'Adjusting and stopping' (*dòu-zhǐ*)—the meaning is not yet entirely appropriate, meaning to cast or place [them] in their former positions; it is also a convergence (*huì*). It may also be pronounced directly as the sound *tóu-zhì*."

The subsequent meaning is also that the internal essence is itself the perfect and real wisdom; when this wisdom illuminates the perfect and real capacities [of sentient beings], then "the good" and below correctly clarify the external application—this is what is meant by "convergence.
Although this and the preceding section both speak of "convergence," their meanings differ: the former is specific while the latter is general.

For example, although "expedient means" (*upāya*) and "perfection" (*pariniṣpanna*) are both spoken of as "perfection," they differ in being general and specific, just as "expedient means" and "perfection" are distinct.

If one penetrates both the square and the circle, they are distinct; thus, although these two are spoken of together here as "convergence" (*hui*), the former is "differentiation" (*cha*) and the latter is "convergence.

One must discern this skillfully without acting precipitously. Next, regarding the analogies: the first analogy illustrates the preceding differentiation, followed by the illustration, the application (*he*), and the conclusion.

The first analogy and its application clarify the function of partial illumination mentioned previously; the analogy resembles what was previously able to apply, and the application resembles what was previously illustrated, appearing alternately.

... (as before) ... Regarding the term "eye" (*moku*), it refers to a designation or name. It specifically means observing by following the pointing finger. "The eye of wisdom" (*chichi*) refers to partial wisdom. The *Shō* (Commentary) states: "Partial" is like one finger pointing toward a single direction; "complete" is like five fingers pointing universally toward all directions. Furthermore, "wisdom" is so named because the capacity of the recipient—the sentient being for whom the teaching is intended—is able to receive the Dharma; thus, it receives the name "wisdom. As for its function: 1. The eye of the Buddha-body (*hosshin-moku*) is like the moon reflected in water, manifesting everywhere throughout the ten directions. 2. The eye of the Dharma-nature (*hōshō-moku*) is like the moon in the sky, pervading the entire universe. 3. The eye of the transformation-body (*hen'ō-moku*) is like the moon’s reflection, appearing according to the conditions of those to be transformed. 4. The eye of the principle of reality (*jissō-moku*) is like the moon’s essence, which is neither identical to nor different from the reflections. 5. The eye of the wisdom of the path (*dōchi-moku*) is like the moon’s light, illuminating both the near and the far. 6. The eye of the wisdom of phenomena (*hōchi-moku*) is like the moon’s radiance, shining upon all things. 7. The eye of the wisdom of equality (*byōdōchi-moku*) is like the moon’s sphere, which is equal in all directions. 8. The eye of the wisdom of wondrous observation (*myōkanchi-moku*) is like the moon’s clarity, penetrating all things without obstruction. 9. The eye of the wisdom of liberation (*gedatsu-moku*) is like the moon’s purity, free from all defilement. 10. The eye of the wisdom of non-obstruction (*mushōchi-moku*) is like the moon’s unimpededness, penetrating all dharmas without hindrance. These ten eyes are the functions of the Tathāgata’s ten powers (*jūriki*). They are called "eyes" because they are the means by which the Tathāgata perceives the world. They are called "powers" because they are the means by which he subdues and transforms sentient beings. Because these two aspects are inseparable, they are termed the "ten eyes and ten powers. Furthermore, these ten eyes are the fundamental source of the three bodies (*sanshin*). The first six correspond to the Dharma-body (*hosshin*); the seventh and eighth correspond to the Reward-body (*hōshin*); and the ninth and tenth correspond to the Transformation-body (*hen'ōshin*). Thus, the ten eyes encompass the three bodies. Moreover, these ten eyes are the source of the four kinds of wisdom (*shishochi*). The first six are the wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*hokkai-chi*); the seventh and eighth are the wisdom of equality (*byōdōchi*); the ninth is the wisdom of wondrous observation (*myōkanchi*); and the tenth is the wisdom of accomplishing tasks (*jōgyōchi*). Thus, the ten eyes encompass the four wisdoms. Furthermore, these ten eyes are the source of the three mysteries (*sanmitsu*). The first six are the mystery of the body (*shinmitsu*); the seventh and eighth are the mystery of the speech (*gomitsu*); and the ninth and tenth are the mystery of the mind (*ishinmitsu*). Thus, the ten eyes encompass the three mysteries. Furthermore, these ten eyes are the source of the three bodies of the Buddha. The first six are the Dharma-body; the seventh and eighth are the Reward-body; and the ninth and tenth are the Transformation-body. Thus, the ten eyes encompass the three bodies. Furthermore, these ten eyes are the source of the three bodies of the Bodhisattva. The first six are the Dharma-body; the seventh and eighth are the Reward-body; and the ninth and tenth are the Transformation-body. Thus, the ten eyes encompass the three bodies of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, these ten eyes are the source of the three bodies of the Śrāvaka. The first six are the Dharma-body; the seventh and eighth are the Reward-body; and the ninth and tenth are the Transformation-body. Thus, the ten eyes encompass the three bodies of the Śrāvaka. Furthermore, these ten eyes are the source of the three bodies of the Pratyekabuddha. The first six are the Dharma-body; the seventh and eighth are the Reward-body; and the ninth and tenth are the Transformation-body. Thus, the ten eyes encompass the three bodies of the Pratyekabuddha. Furthermore, these ten eyes are the source of the three bodies of the ordinary person. The first six are the Dharma-body; the seventh and eighth are the Reward-body; and the ninth and tenth are the Transformation-body. Thus, the ten eyes encompass the three bodies of the ordinary person. Furthermore, these ten eyes are the source of the three bodies of the Dharma-nature. The first six are the Dharma-body; the seventh and eighth are the Reward-body; and the ninth and tenth are the Transformation-body. Thus, the ten eyes encompass the three bodies of the Dharma-nature. Furthermore, these ten eyes are the source of the three bodies of the principle of reality. The first six are the Dharma-body; the seventh and eighth are the Reward-body; and the ninth and tenth are the Transformation-body. Thus, the ten eyes encompass the three bodies of the principle of reality. Furthermore, these ten eyes are the source of the three bodies of the wisdom of the path. The first six are the Dharma-body; the seventh and eighth are the Reward-body; and the ninth and tenth are the Transformation-body. Thus, the ten eyes encompass the three bodies of the wisdom of the path. Furthermore, these ten eyes are the source of the three bodies of the wisdom of phenomena. The first six are the Dharma-body; the seventh and eighth are the Reward-body; and the ninth and tenth are the Transformation-body. Thus, the ten eyes encompass the three bodies of the wisdom of phenomena. Furthermore, these ten eyes are the source of the three bodies of the wisdom of equality. The first six are the Dharma-body; the seventh and eighth are the Reward-body; and the ninth and tenth are the Transformation-body. Thus, the ten eyes encompass the three bodies of the wisdom of equality. Furthermore, these ten eyes are the source of the three bodies of the wisdom of wondrous observation. Reflect on this.

Thus, the three explanations collectively encompass the three meanings, which are fully exhausted herein (etc.). The commentary divides this text into six sections:

Because it is a realization, the following section concludes by returning to explain the underlying intent. This shall now be divided into five parts: first, the explanation of the two characters; second, the demonstration of their meaning and characteristics;

Regarding the first part, there are three aspects: first, the direction; second, the means; and third, the inclusion, which serve to manifest two meanings. First, as for the word "furthermore" (*yòu*), there are three types of meaning for "expedient means" (*upāya*), of which the preceding ones have already been discussed.
This explains the second [section] to manifest the present third; thus it says "furthermore" (*yòu*). Regarding the term "now the secret" (*fāng mì*), this is a citation used for exegesis.

One should first understand its general and specific applications: it applies generally to all [teachings], but since we have now provided a brief explanation, we shall point specifically to the three vehicles (*triyāna*), which are the two entities mentioned previously under the "directional gate" (*fāng mén*).
The exegesis of the character "directional" (*fāng*) has many meanings; although there are three primary ones here, they are treated as two.
First, explaining it as "Dharma" (fa) is one [interpretation]. Second, explaining it by directly following its meaning rather than its formal etymology is not a primary etymological definition.
Now, this explanation as "mystery" (mi) is yet another; thus, two are the standard secular definitions, while one is the essential meaning of the scripture.
Observing the intent of these three explanations: "Dharma" follows exclusively the ancient gate, while "mystery" clarifies the ancient in contrast to the present.
Thus, if we were to explain the single character "fang" (方) comprehensively from this point forward, there are eight meanings in total:

They are the "places where those of the three vehicles abide," fixed according to their respective divisions without mutual convergence, and thus "constant. They serve as a signifier for the ultimate reality at a distance.

The "text" (*mon*) is not a thing that is merely round and subtle or without direction; therefore it is "square" (*hō*). Because it is necessarily able to penetrate the reality (*shinjitsu*), it is a "gate" (*mon*).
Now, when this is opened and revealed, its very substance is itself perfectly complete and without direction; therefore it is "secret" (*hi*).
Regarding these eight meanings, the first seven pertain to the past, while the eighth pertains to the present. Once this one [eighth] is opened, the preceding seven are none other than this.

Now, because the meaning of this ultimate ability is revealed, it is termed "exquisite. This subsequently serves to clarify its significance through synthesis.

Now, regarding the explanation of names, there are indeed instances where terms are both separated and combined; yet when they are not combined and remain unattached, their meaning is not fully revealed.

To explain this strictly according to the text without further elaborating on external, ingenious insights would fail to reach the Dharma that is to be realized;

Because this is established as the title based on the union of the subject (the means) and the object (that which is reached), it is called the "Chapter on the True Expedient Means."
However, although these three phrases are few in wording and difficult to comprehend, they are nonetheless of the utmost importance.

Regarding the different sequences of the combined and separated interpretations of the two characters "Wén" (Text) and "Shì" (Explanation), I now maintain that there are two meanings:

Those who explain [the text] without understanding this intent merely claim that the former is "Mysterious" (Miào) and the latter is "Secret" (Mì), following the momentum of the sequence.
This error is indeed grave; those of later generations must reflect upon it deeply. Regarding what is called "true secrecy," the Record states:

Therefore, it is called 'secret and wondrous' because it is now revealed and manifest. I say: "True" means truly real, and "secret" means perfectly complete.
The substance is one while the meanings differ; it is precisely by confronting the two preceding directions that these two names are obtained.

To penetrate that square of the compass is itself the absence of direction, for it accomplishes this perfect circle; thus it is called "secret" (*mi*). To penetrate that door of skillful means is itself the locus of reality;
thus it is called "true" (*shin*). Although the subject and object each have two meanings, in fact they are one. Thus, all directions are fundamentally...

The realization of the perfect reality does not depend on subtle penetration alone to bring it about; rather, it is because the mind is deluded and fails to penetrate that the perfect truth becomes a mere expedient.
Now, by demonstrating how to reach the source within this very state of delusion, one realizes it is already so—this is why it is said thus.
The term "wondrous penetration" (*miaoda*) is another name for "opening and revealing. All commentators have taken this to refer to "things" (*wu*);

however, I maintain that its meaning extends to both self and others, as it primarily reveals one's own practice (*xing*). Thus, the extensive text refers to it as "the skillful means of one's own practice. Although it mentions both self and others, they are in fact but a single thing;
this is because the term "own practice" is used directly to distinguish it from the confusion that might arise from the phrase "transforming others by means of oneself. But what, then, is it?

Regarding the teaching on the profound mastery of self and others, there are both general and specific aspects. Generally, this refers to the revelation and clarification of an entire section of the scripture;

thus, by taking oneself as the object for others, one attains "opening, showing, awakening, and entering. To speak specifically of one's own practice, as it says in the passage where Mañjuśrī offers praise:
"He thoroughly understands the profound and subtle meaning of all phenomena. Furthermore, his own verse must state: "Profoundly penetrating the equality of sin and merit," and so forth.
The profound penetration achieved through one's own practice refers to the five Buddhas and six meanings; this is what causes others to achieve profound penetration.

The general characteristics of such profound penetration by oneself and others are as described above. This is precisely the opening of the provisional and revealing of the real for both self and others.

One’s own wondrous penetration means relying on the wondrous teaching to understand the wondrous principle, cultivate the wondrous practice, and realize the wondrous essence. Causing others to achieve wondrous penetration means relying on one's own [realization].

Taking the wondrous essence to explain it for others is to cause them to realize their own essence. If one uses the wondrous penetration of self and other to harmonize these two meanings, first, the direction arises based on the means;
second, the direction relies upon the means. This is precisely the fusion of the direction and the means—the nature of the direction and the means can be known.
Second, causing others to do so is likewise: because the direction arises from the means, one realizes the means of the direction.
This constitutes the expedient means for harmonizing others; the former refers to cultivation and nature, while the latter refers to essence and function—this is their distinction.

Although the previous detailed clarification of the seven sections—the first being the general [treatment of] the two characters and the subsequent six being the specific discussion of "wondrous penetration" (miaoda)—has not yet exhausted every detail, it serves as a rough outline.
To provide a broad explanation is the beginning of this work. Below, I shall briefly indicate the characteristics of the meaning of "wondrous penetration" according to the text.

Within this, first there is the exposition by way of the Dharma and next by way of the person; although the scriptural text is extensive, it does not go beyond these two, and thus they are presented for illustration.
"Pointing out" means subtle penetration. The "inner jewel" refers to the essential nature of the temporal [manifestation], which is fundamentally perfect and complete.

The "jewel on the crown" refers to the ultimate perfection of cultivated virtue. There is no duality or distinction between them, for although their hidden and manifest aspects differ, their essence and function are one.
The Way is not otherwise than this; it is not by means of "perfect completeness" that one explains the "mysterious," for only by meeting with this text is it truly harmonized.

Although the treasure within the garment is mentioned here, it does not take up the meaning of establishing karmic affinity (*karmapratyaya*), but rather takes up the fact that the square shape is fundamentally round to manifest the meaning of cultivation and realization (and so forth).
Next, regarding the person, it refers to one who has attained wondrous penetration precisely because of this.
The person who acts as a laborer was originally the son of a wealthy elder; because he did not know this himself, he was pointed out to him.

Although there is a distinction between near and distant relatives, there is no difference in their essential nature. Such cases are precisely what is taught in two places in the Sūtra, both clarifying the same principle:
that when one attains wondrous penetration, both nature and practice are perfected. Therefore, it is called "the secret and wondrous. The following text is likewise for this purpose.
Citing the scriptural evidence, one observes that these [passages] do not seem to accord; they appear to be distinct names for "self" and "other.

First, it clarifies that this is what the Buddha himself has realized—namely, his own sublime mastery (*sva-suvijñāta*). The repeated injunctions, "Stop! Stop! I shall not speak," are intended to lead others to sublime mastery.
Thus, he first suppresses their desire, waiting for their most earnest request before speaking, so as to lead them to sublime mastery. Therefore, it says: "You have already three times..."
How could one not explain this most clearly? It must necessarily be so. The following section concludes the argument:

because of the relationship between self and others according to the meaning of these words, it is necessary to perform this "opening and merging" (*kaikai*) to explain the meaning of the provisional means (*upāya*).
The following is the fifth summary, which clarifies this point. As the Sūtra says: "This opens the gate of provisional means to reveal the mark of reality. Now, regarding this...

First, there was a general explanation regarding the distinctions among the various gates of giving in the past; next, there was a specific clarification of the intent behind those partial gates of giving in the past to explain this present third [section].
This section explains how the partial capacities of the past are all subsumed within the perfect capacity;
this is precisely what is called "expediency" (*upāya*) from the perspective of the wondrous capacity, because it enables both oneself and others to reach the wondrous essence. As it says:
If it were not for this power, who could bring about such a thing? These words originate from two gates;

though all the Buddha-dharmas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are most supreme and vast, none transcend these two characters. Not only is the Sūtra itself wondrously capable [of teaching], but the commentary on its names is also truly wondrously capable.
Next, the "clarification and analysis" (liao jian) explains and establishes the meaning of the three preceding interpretations.
The meaning of these two characters is as lofty and vast as previously described; since their scope involves many points, they require clarification and analysis.

This serves as the basis for the extensive explanation that follows, which is the purpose of this work. However, according to the conventional explanations of the world, both of these characters should [be understood as follows]:...

"From the hand" (*shǒu*) refers to relying on this [term] to pick out and select the characters; that is, to organize, explain, and clarify the preceding meanings so that they are free from obstruction.
Because this term has been used by tradition throughout the past and present, it is employed here as well. Within this, there are also three sections;
although their number is the same as before, their meanings differ in terms of being general or specific. The *Record* (*Jì*) states: "The first is based on the three phrases."

Relying on the first of the three explanations to exclude [the other two], and relying on the second explanation to exclude the three texts, one uses the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) to collectively exclude the three explanations (and so forth).
The *Quan* (Complete) commentary states: "The first section correctly analyzes the questions and answers; what follows below is the subsequent reconciliation of different names.
This intent differs from the preceding [section]. For now, I shall briefly record that the first section relies on the three terms and is attached to the beginning.
The explanation by means of "eliminating the three" (*jiǎn sān*) relies on the three phrases of subject and object (*néng-suǒ*) through the gate of sequential reliance;

the explanation by means of "eliminating the three" relies on the four phrases through the third [gate]. The reason for this is that there are many paths of meaning which cannot follow a single track.

What preceded was based on the particular (*bié*); now, furthermore, it is based on the universal (*tōng*), simultaneously synthesizing various general outlines and specifically providing a detailed analysis precisely for this purpose.

The first section directly reveals what is correct; the second section excludes what is incorrect to reveal what is correct; and the third, having already clarified that [the two] are identical yet distinct, is likewise both exclusion and revelation.

The meaning of "deliberate examination" (liao-jian) is further illustrated by this. Now, regarding the interpretation of the commentary’s text on the three sections of deliberate examination, there are still two distinctions:
the first two distinguish similarities and differences based on the general name, while the last one distinguishes similarities based on their differences.
"Different names for the same thing" refers to *upāya* (expedient means). This term appears frequently throughout this sutra; thus, it is called "universal.
"Different meanings" refers to the various distinctions among its meanings, yet fearing that people might not understand them, they are clarified by being categorized according to their sequence.
Regarding "different names," this name for *upāya* is properly called *sukauśalya* (skillful means); in other sutras, it is sometimes called *sukauśalya*, and at other times called *upāya*.
These are names that differ while their meanings may be either identical or different. To reconcile these previous differing names within the initial meaning:

the first two sections primarily distinguish between identity and difference, while the final section concludes by summarizing and assigning the fault. Regarding the first section: it speaks specifically of the "three sides" (*trikoṇa*) as being square and not applicable to a circular compass;
"substance" (*tattva*) means reality. This refers generally to reality and should not be spoken of specifically, as this was the case in the past.

Because that which is unopened is not the actual authority, it constitutes the substance [of the teaching] externally; this is because, regarding the meaning of practice and teaching, it is as explained above in the "Middle" and "Outer" sections.

This is precisely the convergence of the different names for the three dharmas. Although this appears to be a provisional explanation based on the dharmas employed, their functional significance is contained therein.

we maintain that the names explained in the preceding and succeeding sections of this sutra differ. The essential point is as follows: although the names "self" and "other" were initially employed, since these terms are still too general, a subsequent scripture is cited to clarify and establish the specific distinction.
This refers to the meaning of "opening the provisional to reveal the real," which serves to manifest that the title of this sutra’s chapter is precisely derived from this principle;
thus, both names and both meanings reach their ultimate subtlety. The specific citation of these two [scriptures] is because the primary intent lies herein within this school.
Since this is so, if one does not understand it, what could there be for the subsequent section on the conclusion and praise of the Tathāgata’s skillful means?

This refers to the essential point of the "wondrous person and dharma. Furthermore, the "wondrous" refers to the capacity [of the means]; likewise, the praise of the Tathāgata’s skillful means refers to the perfection of its essence.

"Encompassing all" praises the wondrousness of its function, which is precisely the ability to open and harmonize. The metaphors of space and the ocean illustrate the vastness and depth of its essence.
The "encompassing" (*bao*) and the "receiving" (*na*) metaphorically represent their capacity; the "ocean" and the "streams" collectively metaphorize all dharmas that are opened up and converge.
This is the meaning of the title of this present chapter. How could it be otherwise? This concludes the refutation of various interpretations, which fail to grasp the essential convergence.
The "single branch" and the "single school" metaphorize the gradual differentiation of the flow of form (*rūpa*) among those things that have been opened up. As for what was opened up...
If one attempts to reconcile minute phenomena in order to explain the capacity for the ultimate, what principle of reconciliation could there possibly be?
The *dharmadhātu* is the supreme designation for the essence and function of all phenomena; it is precisely this skillful means (*upāya*).

Since it opens up and unifies all dharma-gates into a single wondrous locus where nothing remains outside, it constitutes the great totality of all phenomena—namely, the three truths and the three... [the three thousand worlds].
Wisdom is the non-localized entity of all dharmas. In the *Tianwang Banruo Jing* (The Sutra of the Wisdom of the Heavenly Kings), the meaning of skillful means (*upāya*) is explained extensively;
it is thus that all such explanations cite a single minute point to illuminate its two essential aspects. One must certainly rely upon the accumulation of study to avoid falling into this [error].
How much more so for those who differ from or are outside [the tradition]; they ought to be especially meticulous and cautious, lest they fall into delusion and error.

therefore, they are explained in detail. Regarding the first [section], there are four parts: first, the initial presentation in contrast to the previous "Perfect" (yuan) school.

Regarding the title, the ancient commentators maintained that this chapter fully elucidates two meanings: it clarifies the provisional (*upāya*) in contrast to the real (*bhūta*), and reveals the real by means of the provisional.

The explanation clarifies that the essence of skillful means (*upāya*) inherently possesses four meanings; it is not manifested through mutual contrast, nor is it merely twofold.
This heading is established because the preceding is explained extensively in relation to the succeeding. The essence of skillful means must necessarily possess these four aspects;

yet, because the meaning remains difficult to grasp, one must turn toward the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna-darśana*) before one can properly reconcile them. Within the context of principle and teaching (*li-jiao*), the "matter-principle" (*shi-li*) should be taken as "principle," for the text itself is clear on this point.

Practice arises from hearing this sutra; therefore, it is wholesome practice, which is to say, sublime practice (*praṇīta-caryā*).

Next, it clarifies that one who can penetrate expedient practice is one who practices the ultimate reality (*bhūta-caryā*) and transcendent, non-referential practice. Next, regarding the phrase "having practiced the Way," this subsumes the preceding text:

it is practicing the Great Nirvana and the Tathāgata’s practice, which is also the Practice of Peaceful Abiding (*sukha-vihāra-caryā*). These various causes and conditions apply universally to the teaching.

Having practiced, one acts in accordance with the teachings; thus, while the words "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) are general, their meaning is specific, clarifying that this refers precisely to the cultivation of the six perfections and myriad practices.
Furthermore, the initial "good practice" collectively enumerates the three types of conduct; the subsequent phrase, "penetrating the provisional as the real," refers to the ultimate;

It is said: "Cloud upon cloud. Furthermore, the first [part] concerns the dissemination; the next two concern the formal exposition; and the last one concerns the introduction. Thus it is said.

Were this text not present, how could this interpretation be made? And were this interpretation not made, how could one fully comprehend this text?
"It is beautiful! It is exquisite! Nothing more can be added.

First, within the section on verifying the principle through the teaching, since the treatise is introduced following the sutra, the text says "Now" (*atha*). First, the citation from the treatise explaining "profound" (*gambhīra*); there are two types of profundity:
first, the profundity of realization (*adhigama-gambhīratā*), and second, the profundity of the gateways (*mukha-gambhīratā*). "Realization" refers to the wisdom of all Buddhas.
The "gate" is precisely its gate of wisdom. The *Treatise* states that there are five ways of realizing the profound; the names cited in the present text are identical [to those].

As for why it says "realizing the profound," none of the commentaries explain this. I maintain that it is called "realization" (*zhèng*) because cultivation merges with the intrinsic nature (*xìng*), and it is called "profound" (*shēnshēn*) because the realization of the nature is perfectly consummate.
Since that which is realized is already profound, the means of realization is necessarily profound; thus, both are "profound. This is the general [explanation].

The meaning is as follows: if one were to further clarify that there are five distinct aspects capable of realization, it is not necessary to state definitively that there are five because their essential natures (*svabhāva*) differ.

Rather, the principle is that True Suchness (*tathatā*) contains immeasurable names and meanings; thus, it is designated by immeasurable varieties such as *dharmatā*, *bhūtalakṣaṇa*, and *paramārtha*.
As for "essential nature," it means that this True Suchness serves as the single reality for all phenomena.

The internal realization within the body that serves as the basis is itself that which is realized; therefore, the support is suchness (*tathatā*), which serves as the basis for both delusion and awakening.
Here, we take the basis of awakening, not the distant basis. "Unsurpassed" applies generally to both *bodhi* (enlightenment) and *nirvāṇa*;

while it was previously described as unsurpassed in contrast to what precedes it, here it refers to the meaning of the most supreme principle. "Essence" (*tattva*) refers to the true reality of all phenomena.

"Nature" (*dhātu*) refers to that which is internally realized, for it is what is realized by correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*); "basis" (*āśraya*) refers to the objective sphere in which correct wisdom abides;

and "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) is a general term because both the means of realization and the object realized therein are ultimate. Therefore, it is called "unsurpassed great enlightenment" (*anuttara-mahābodhi*).
The section above clarifies the profundity of realization, while the section below elucidates the profundity of the gateways of scripture (*āgama*), formerly known as *dharmaparyāya*.
It is also called *Anupama* (Incomparable); the new term is *Āgama*, which means "teaching," "pure teaching," or "transmission.

It refers to that which has been handed down through successive generations from the Buddhas of antiquity until the present day. Its meaning encompasses both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; it does not refer exclusively to the four or five treatises.

Regarding the *Āgamas*, there are eight kinds of profundity: first, the profundity of upholding, reciting, and chanting; second, the profundity of practice; third, the profundity of the fruit of practice.
Fourth, the mind that increases merit; fifth, delightful and wondrous matters; sixth, the unsurpassed; seventh, entry; eighth, that which is not shared with the two vehicles.

These eight are all named "the profoundness of the Āgamas. Below, the text concludes by citing the treatise to provide proof for the present discussion. a brief understanding shall suffice. (Note: The term *āgama* is used here as a technical designation for the specific categories of profoundity within the Abhidharma literature.)

Although this is explained extensively, it does not go beyond the principle and the teaching; that which was previously realized is the principle (*tattva*), while the *āgama* (scriptural transmission) refers to the teaching that explains those realized dharmas.

Because it represents wondrous function, it constitutes the unsurpassed realization. The fifth supporting proof states that "merit belongs to the cause and accomplishment belongs to the fruit.

However, I maintain that when the treatise speaks only of the cause, it implicitly includes the fruit, as it possesses both meanings. Furthermore, the seventh supporting proof states that the teaching and transformation (*vinaya*) applies universally to the three [vehicles].

It omits two points and does not provide full proof, as was already indicated in the previous commentary. If one insists on exhausting every detail of this matter...
Second, there are matters that have not yet been seen, which you should know.

Furthermore, according to the sutras, it is indeed appropriate to discuss this; moreover, the character "fu" (扶) in the general outline should properly be "fu" (符).
If it were written as "fu" (扶), it would carry the meaning of "supporting," which I suspect is an error from later transcription.

Some say that this is intended to mean "approximating the meaning" (*yue-yi hui*), rather than "darkly coinciding" (*an-he wei ming*). According to the old tradition of Vasubandhu, it is said that he composed several hundred treatises.

Regarding his subsequent rank, those of recent times have all claimed that his position corresponds to the stages of *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, while in the Mahāyāna it corresponds to the stage of *pariṇāmanā*.

However, as for the present claim that he was a "Noble One" (*ārya*), it may be that this was not recorded at the time; perhaps the tradition has been lost, and people have merely followed along with such a statement.
Regarding the fifth section on the "Conclusions" (*kṣepa*): the preceding portion has completed the formal explanation of the names and meanings;

from this point forward, the ten pairs are synthesized and harmonized with all phenomena—both horizontal and vertical—to manifest that their essence is entirely wondrous reality. The commentary itself contains three parts: first, the synthesis of the four teachings;

For this reason, the previous explanation was made, and because such functional power exists, the Buddha offered this praise. This skillful means is itself self-cultivation (*svayam-carita*).

Although traditional commentaries have all followed the previous format and cannot be described in detail here, I shall now state my view on this matter.
Regarding the meaning of the distinctions between the gates as clearly explained by Zhongzheng: even if one were to provide other titles, I fear they would deviate from the fundamental tenets;

In the first part, there may also be three sub-sections: first, clarifying that attempting to accommodate others directly through one’s own gate is unfeasible; second, [the next] four clarify... [text fragment ends].

It is taught that by taking the transformation of others as the gateway, there are those who attain and those who do not; later, it clarifies that when the transformation of others is set aside and one takes only one’s own practice as the gateway, all are able to enter.
In the first instance, this refers to the intention to cease transformative activity because the audience lacks the capacity (the "unfit vessel").

As for the realization of the provisional and the real, this universally discusses the nature of cause and effect; because the cultivation of the wondrous reaches its ultimate limit, it is ineffable. One's own provisional [wisdom] is itself the real.
The separate mention of the "perfect cause" refers to the gateway of wisdom. As for the term "expounding," this refers to the initial intention to expound it;

it signifies the Buddha’s intent to preach what is appropriate, rather than implying that he has already spoken what is inappropriate. That which is unsuitable means the capacity and the teaching do not correspond;
this is the meaning of "inexplicability," which implies the cessation of transformative activity. The four subsequent sections below refer to the four [periods] of the past.

Because this is explained according to the gates [of teaching], there are those who gain entry and those who do not. Regarding the initial mention of "single" (*dan*) and "exclusive" (*bian*), the application of the method is universal;

Therefore, this treatise focuses exclusively on transforming others. While the "other" is universal, the "distinct" (*bie*) is particular. Now, because it is not universal at the beginning, it is called "distinct. Thus, it generally refers to the ten kinds within the distinct [teachings]. Or...

The thirty types collectively constitute the gates. Regarding the phrase "this clarifies the benefit of the gate-dharma for those of equal capacity" and so forth: this refers to what is attained according to the present treatise.

"Those of sharp capacity" refers to those of the Perfect Teaching (yuan), who, by means of the distinct [teachings], assemble at the Perfect Gate. "Those of dull capacity" refers to those of the Distinct Teaching (bie), who for the time being rely upon their own respective divisions.
As for the phrase "the substance is not appropriate," it is because the Perfect Gate is not yet commensurate with the Distinct; therefore, it was not explained immediately at that time.

The preceding items each stated "set aside for now," while the current ones all say "it is not permissible to transmit them successively"; these are expressions that conclude the former section and introduce the latter.

There is no place where [the teaching] is not appropriate, and it cannot be fully described;

the beginning is the *Avataṃsaka*, and the end is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Because the skillful means (*upāya*) can cause sentient beings to penetrate the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*), it is so designated.

It serves as a gateway because of this capacity; for this reason, the Buddha praised it. In the past, [the teaching] was sometimes self-directed and sometimes other-directed, yet with respect to the Buddha, it was always his own practice;

Therefore, it must be explained in this way. What is called "being able to know" refers to the method employed. As for "being able to employ," it is as previously stated.
The application of the five periods is one of yielding and compliance; by following and conforming to them, one is able to enter through the gate.

Previously, it was established that what is not compliant cannot serve as a gate, and for this reason, it is now possible to establish the meaning of being a gate. Furthermore, the first [section] concerns the capacity to employ [the teaching], while the second concerns the Buddha’s intention:
his intent is to cause sentient beings to comply with the provisional (upāya) so that they may subsequently enter the wondrous gate. The Buddha is able to know the wondrous through the wondrous.
This is intended to cause beings to attain wondrous knowledge; by being able to accord with and follow [the Way], one attains entry into the wondrous gate.

Furthermore, while the former was the function of the wondrous essence (*tattva*), this is the destination of the wondrous function (*vṛtti*). Although these were not both present in the past, they are both wondrous now.

These two meanings—of essence and function—pervade both the subject and the object; the text merely cites them alternately for convenience. In reality, there are all these various implications, which is why the commentary states: ... [omitted] ... because there are these various meanings. Thus it is annotated.
