This is called "wondrously penetrating the directions," which is the profound secret of the Real. All things reach [this state].
Because the wondrous is ultimate, there is nothing that can surpass it.

First, the concluding summary brings together the initial section on "Distinguishing the True from the False. Second, it brings together the various names. Third, it explains the names by correlating them with the three dharmas.
Fourth, it establishes the application of the chapter title to conclude the beginning and end. As for "things conforming to the beginning and end," this refers to the treatise itself.

From beginning to end (and so forth), these five periods each contain these three meanings; only in this way is the essential purport of this sutra fully exhausted. Furthermore, regarding the previous brief explanation:

the first two [periods] pertain only to the past, while the current one applies to both past and present; the third explanation pertains only to the present sutra, yet it still applies to the preceding four.
Only by being thus can the preceding explanation be fully exhausted. For now, we shall follow the specific terminology: "the perfect cause" refers to...
The capacity for meaning is twofold: first, the capacity to accomplish the fruit; second, the capacity to manifest the essential nature (*dharmatā*).

If it is the capacity to accomplish the fruit, then the various stages that approximate the ultimate reality are collectively termed "cause. If it is the capacity to manifest the essence, then both cause and fruit are termed "cause.
Therefore, the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) takes the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle as its central tenet (*zōng*), and this tenet serves to manifest the essence.

Only by means of this can the essence of the true mark (dharmatā) be manifested; therefore, the *Mysterious Meaning* (*Xuanyi*) of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* takes the eternal cause and fruit as its central theme because it can manifest the essence of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* takes the perfect cause and fruit of the Buddha as its central theme because it can manifest the essence of true nature and liberation (*tathatā-vimukti*).

If one speaks of the cause as that which accomplishes the fruit, it refers exclusively to cultivation (*bhāvanā*); if one speaks of cultivation arising from nature (*xingqi*), it refers to the manifestation of nature.
Thus, since both cause and effect are equally termed "cause," the Great Sūtra states: "The meaning of Buddha-nature is the seed of the Middle Way for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This clarifies that among the five kinds of Buddha-nature, it is not only the Middle Way that serves as the cause;

the other two—the effect and the cause—are also all causes, and therefore they are collectively called "seeds. The reason they are all termed "causes" is that they are the *jñāna-hetu* (the cause of realization).
It is also said that this is capable of clearly manifesting the true cause; therefore, the subsequent text states: "The Buddha-seed arises from conditions.

Thus, the teaching and practice of the One Vehicle are explained as the conditions for manifesting the nature, wherein the condition is itself the cause—meaning it is the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*).

The title of this chapter possesses these two meanings, and the commentary’s explanation is likewise so; yet while it applies to both meanings, its primary intent lies in the "self" [the self-nature].
The meaning of its manifestation is termed the "cause. To explain it in this way is to encompass the meaning exhaustively without exception;

otherwise, one would truly fail to penetrate the intent of both the sutra and the commentary. One should examine the meaning of the sutra and the commentary in detail rather than speaking based on ordinary opinions.
Now, regarding those who enter from the beginning, all [teachings] are explained according to gradual-capacity practitioners. As for sudden-capacity practitioners, they are likewise [included].

Regarding the phrase "mutually dependent" (and so forth), it is said that what is immediate is the true reality (*tattva*). What was previously called "true mystery" is here briefly and directly termed "true reality";
this is precisely the meaning of the character "true" (*zhen*) from before. Because true reality is perfectly complete (*paripūrṇa*), there is no need to further discuss its meaning as "mystery.

It concludes by stating that "names" refer to the practice of self-cultivation (*svayaṃ-carita*) which can manifest the essential nature (*dharmatā*); these are also called "expedient means" (*upāya*). This thus encompasses the four pairs of ten [categories].

The phrases are recorded in their entirety without omission. If one were to restrict oneself to a fixed, definitive cause, then one would only obtain the first four and a half pairs and the latter five and a half pairs, which would have no further utility;
thus, all must be distinguished. How much more so when, whether horizontally or vertically, one takes a single provisional phrase as the essence—this is truly something unheard of.
If it is argued that although it is one, it is essential because it encompasses one-third of the three, then indeed...
Regarding the term "comprehensive" (*she*), it refers to that which was not originally present but is established through the force of its meaning.

Now, what is called here the "Dharma" is, by its very nature (*dharmatā*), primordially and perfectly complete with all things—whether horizontal or vertical, whether the four or the ten, or the subsequent thirty.

Because there is nothing external to it, it is the entirety itself; thus, it is called the "great totality of the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*). It cannot be explained by means of a single branch or a single stream.

The text has reached its conclusion here by refuting partial and limited views to reveal the capacity of the Perfect [Teaching]. Why, then, does it still take up the derivative branches to explain their significance? I beg the later students to rely strictly upon the meaning of the Sūtras and the Commentaries; one should not merely follow human sentiment. Someone might say: "If everything is as you have described—merely expedient means—then what remains of the ultimate reality? To this, I reply: ... [The text continues with the argument that while all teachings are expedient, they lead toward a single truth, which is the ultimate reality. ... Therefore, although the various gates of teaching differ, they all converge upon the same principle.

It is like a great ocean where the waters flow from different rivers yet become of one taste once they reach the sea. Thus, while the provisional teachings are diverse, the ultimate reality is singular and unchanging. This is why the text returns to the derivative branches to clarify how they serve as skillful means to lead beings toward that very reality. It is not that the reality is absent; rather, it is that the provisional teachings are necessary to guide those of varying capacities. One must understand that the purpose of the provisional is precisely to manifest the real. To deny the provisional is to lose the path to the real; to cling to the real while rejecting the provisional is to remain trapped in dogmatism. Only by relying on the Sūtras and the commentaries can one grasp this profound intent. Do not allow personal preferences to distort the true meaning. As it is said: "The Dharma is like a raft; even the teachings themselves must eventually be abandoned. How much more so the non-teachings! Yet, without the raft, one cannot cross the river. Thus, the provisional and the real are mutually dependent. This is the essential point of the Great Vehicle. May all practitioners realize this and not fall into the error of either rejecting the means or clinging to them as ends in themselves. This concludes the explanation. May there be peace.
Since the one is already subsumed within the three, by what further means could one establish what is "real"? If the cause is contrasted with the fruit, then the fruit itself constitutes reality;
how, then, can such a doubt arise? Now, it must be said: how profound this principle is! Cause and fruit mutually constitute the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*);

since the fruit is itself subsumed within the cause, how could there be a separate "fruit-reality" (*phala-tattva*)? What was previously stated—that citing the宗 (proposition) reveals the體 (essence)—is its meaning.
It is sufficient to understand that this meaning is not required; the meaning is as follows: of the ten pairs, the latter five are all for the sake of transforming others.

Why, then, is it said [only] that they are "one's own practice"? Based on the literal meaning of the text, it must indeed be so. This is because when speaking of one's own practice versus transforming others, the entirety of transforming others is [included within] one's own practice.

To distinguish this from what is not comprehensive, it is simply called "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*), clarifying that both gradual and sudden [enlightenment] possess both self and other. What is meant by this?
Although the Great Matter of the appearance in the world manifests various paths, its reality is for the sake of the Buddha-vehicle;

opening the fundamental is for the purpose of convergence—why, then, would one further harbor such delusion? "Complete" means that the secret and wondrous skillful means universally encompass the ten kinds of causes and fruits.

Furthermore, since the ten meanings set forth within this chapter are already complete, why speak only of the perfect cause? This interpretation is resolved by the fact that the text and its meaning are inherently inclusive.
"Be assured that it is exactly as you have said. The present opening, revealing, awakening, and entering constitute the primary intent of this chapter;

therefore, we extract the essentials from the specific and speak of them alone, concluding the meaning of the chapter solely through the Perfect Cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*). Moreover, to realize the Perfect Cause is itself to encompass the remaining nine causes.
The title of the chapter is centered upon this point; henceforth, the various passages will mostly rely upon the Perfect [Teaching]."

Consequently, regarding this discussion on "expedient means" (*upāya*), the current commentary results from a failure to understand the purport of the term "cause" (*hetu*) and an ignorance of the meaning of the name "expedient means";

thus, such forced constructions have been produced. Now, examining these various intentions, it appears that the title of the sutra chapter intends for "expedient means" to be the name for that which stands in opposition to "reality" (*bhūta-tattva*); yet [the commentator] fails to realize that there must necessarily be two distinct entities.
It skillfully causes this to be the ultimate reality, and it is also entirely the skillful means (*upāya*).

Furthermore, one does not know that these are names for cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and nature (*prakṛti*), nor does one know that the entirety of cultivation and nature constitutes their mutual characteristics. These three points were not considered in the Commentary (*ṭīkā*).

Regarding the statement on "cause," it is said that [the term] is restricted solely to the name applied to the fruit; one does not know its two meanings as a cause, as previously explained. The correct intent lies in following its functional application.

Therefore, the resulting failure is as described above. Now, it is said that the title of this chapter precisely clarifies cultivation through the perspective of self-practice (*svayam-caryā*) in contrast to nature (*prakṛti*);
by means of cultivation, it reveals nature. To fully comprehend these two meanings within both the Sūtra and the Commentary leaves nothing remaining.

Nevertheless, although the fourteen phrases, ten pairs, and eight gates are all skillful means (*upāya*), they must not be exceeded or diminished. Furthermore, these two characters [“cultivation” and “nature”] possess two aspects.

Regarding the two aspects of contemplation: first, the identity of the two meanings of absolute reality and absolute power; second, the distinction between the general and the specific. In general discourse, these mutually interpenetrate cultivation and nature;

in specific discourse, one is nature and the other is cultivation. As stated in the Sūtra, "Thus," and as explained in the Commentary, there are also two aspects: first, the four propositions, and second, the ten pairs.
Both of these pertain to cultivation and nature, and both possess general and specific dimensions. Thus, while they are called different in meaning, they are in reality one.
Furthermore, next is the discernment of the Truth of Illumination (*āloka-satya*). Some say this clarifies the function of skillful means (*upāya*) through illumination;

however, here we clarify the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna*) by means of the Truth of Illumination, so that the meaning of skillful means may be further elucidated. This is also to raise the nature (*prakṛti*) to manifest cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and to raise the reason [for cultivation] to manifest the conclusion.
Furthermore, the fifth section previously [discussed] the threefold correct manifestation of the essence of skillful means; that essence is wisdom (*jñāna*).

Since wisdom arises from the truths (*satya*), it is now further clarified through the truths to demonstrate the perfection of wisdom. That is to say, the praise of the two types of wisdom extensively clarifies these two wisdoms by way of their two respective objects;

Having previously reconciled the two kinds of the Two Truths with the two kinds of wisdom, this section further clarifies how the three kinds of the Two Truths fully reconcile the meaning of the sutras.

This [present section] thus cites the mother to manifest the perfection of her offspring, precisely because one contemplates these three kinds of the Two Truths.
This is because one attains the awakening of the three types of knowledge; as this meaning is most essential, it must be clarified.

This is because it is restricted to itself; the reason this is not fixed is that it contains its own meaning, and thus it should be brought forth (as explained at length).
Now, since this principle exists, what was previously omitted has been stated here; the previous intent is thereby made manifest without the need for redundant text.

Next, concerning the various sūtras: this refers to the teachings of the five periods across all sūtras.

This is thus a comprehensive discussion of all things, both horizontal and vertical; it is indeed "faith" (*śraddhā*).

"Teaching" refers to the provisional and the perfect; "flavor" refers to the five similes; "dharma" refers to wisdom and the truths; "person" refers to those for whom the teaching is intended;

The essential point of this assembly is as follows: first, regarding the term "full," that sutra itself refers to it as the "Perfect Sūtra" (*paripūrṇa-sūtra*).

When discussing the "time," it is by means of time that the "flavor" is revealed. Since the meaning of "milk" has already been stated, one should now speak of the "flavor" in order to harmonize with the parable of the five flavors in the Great Sūtra;
thus, the meaning is identical. However, what is called "milk" is the *amṛta* (nectar) in the sudden teaching, while in the gradual teaching, it is designated as [the first stage].

Because it is milk, if a cow eats it, it immediately produces *sarpis* (clarified butter) and eventually *mārdvika-sarpis* (the finest clarified butter). Now, speaking in terms of gradual progression, it is called "milk.
Furthermore, there are two types of milk: that which is first consumed is a metaphor for reaching the heterodox, while that which is later encouraged to be consumed is the True and Constant;

its efficacy is identical in function to *mārdvika-sarpis*. What is said here is explained according to the gradual approach, employing expedient means to adapt to those whose faculties are suited to the gradual teaching.
It is beneficial for the preservation of life, like milk; this is explained extensively in other texts. "One self and one other" refers to the Perfect [Teaching] and the Separate [Teaching].
"Bodhisattvas" means that both are Bodhisattvas. In the first six locations and eight assemblies, there is no mention of the Two Vehicles at all.

Although the second vehicle is listed at the beginning of the ninth assembly, they neither hear nor see it; this is merely intended to distinguish the inferior and manifest the superior. As that sutra states: "Just as..."
To be "deaf as if blind" means not hearing or seeing the supreme person and the supreme Dharma; what is meant here is that there is no benefit for oneself or others.

Regarding the term "birth-body" (*janmakāya*), it is mentioned in contrast to the name "dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*); the text appears in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise), where it is explained briefly as before.

This may refer to those individuals prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) who have not yet realized the true essence of the *dharmatā*; therefore, with respect to these two types of knowledge (*jñāna*), they do not possess them.
The events described in the current scriptural text refer to that time. This has both a general and a specific meaning.

The specific meaning refers to the time when [the Buddha] was formerly in that assembly and had not yet spoken of the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*) and so forth to the bodhisattvas; this concerns the matter of having previously established the causal conditions for wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*).
The general meaning refers generally to the fact that he had not yet spoken of all [teachings], but rather shared in this one superior wisdom (*jñāna*). Thus it is said.
This is precisely the beginning of differentiation; thus, it is distinct. Within the scriptures of the *Pitaka*, this very analogy is used to illustrate that teaching.
The Dharma generally comprises three types, and here we refer to only one of those three: namely, the transformation of others (*parārtha*).

Within the transformation of others, there are three further categories, and this is the most inferior of them. As for the time, it is the second stage, having already become a Lesser Sage (*śrāvaka*); its "flavor" is like the taste [of salt].
Next, it gradually becomes more profound. Regarding the mention of "outside the gate," this refers to both the analogies and the discourse on faith-and-understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*);

since these are universally capable of being identified with the object [of comparison], they are called "people of the two vehicles. If one takes the discourse on faith-and-understanding as a whole, then "standing by the side of the gate" refers to the object;
the subsequent phrase then refers to that which is capable of being identified with the object, namely, the people of the two vehicles, which is stated inclusively to clarify the point of reference.
The meaning of "human" refers only to the two vehicles and does not include bodhisattvas. Next, regarding the term "correspondence" (*dai*):

because it is communicated through the sense of "half," one cannot say that there is exclusively this distinction; thus, "half" and "full" refer simply to the Small and Great Vehicles. Regarding the phrase "clarifying both together":

this means that by possessing the two conditions of the Small and Great Vehicles, both are explained simultaneously, so that the Small Vehicle may secretly achieve the benefits of both the general and the specific. Furthermore...

It may also be said that "curd" (*dadhi*) refers to the *Tripiṭaka* (Āgama) and *Vaipulya* (Prajñāpāramitā) teachings, while "butter" (*navanīta*) refers to the *Vaipulya* (Ekayāna) teaching. Regarding the phrase "believing in the essence":

since one has already realized the Small Vehicle, one is no longer able to harbor doubts regarding the Great Vehicle. This point will be explained in detail in the subsequent text; although this specific passage is missing, the meaning is not absent.

As for the "Three-in-One" Dharma and the persons it is intended for, it encompasses both: it universally reaches those of the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as those of the provisional and the real.

The term "carrying" (*dai*) refers to that which encompasses the teachings of the Two Vehicles; "arising" (*sheng*) refers to what is common [to both], while "convergence" (*jù*) refers to what is specific.

It also means that by means of the Dharma one includes the persons—that is, carrying the Small along with the Great, leading the Small to return to the Great. The passages cited in the present text will be fully explained in sequence below.
Next, regarding this sutra, first we shall provisionally follow the previous example to clarify the five aspects, and finally conclude by returning to the title of the chapter. First:
Regarding "abandoning [the literal] through the mere teaching": the flavor [of the teaching] culminates here, and the instruction culminates in sublime wisdom.

As for the Dharma, it is solely the thirty kinds of self-practice. The term "solely" (唯) excludes anything further, meaning it is absolute. Regarding the phrase "opening [the meaning]," etc.: this is taken from the sense;
as for the text itself, it refers to "opening," "showing," and so forth. This applies to the entire section as a whole; what follows below is the specific [analysis].
This passage combines the "One Man" and the "Wondrous Man. The bestowal of the prediction of Buddhahood corresponds to the aforementioned entrustment of wealth and family estate.
The preceding section clarified the five dharmas; up to this point, they are unified as a single wondrous [teaching]. Section Five concludes.

Regarding the subsequent teaching, the following further analyzes the two functions of "opening" (*ka*) and "abolishing" (*fei*) to demonstrate how the present chapter fulfills its meaning in contrast to the past. The first phrase indicates that it was not taught immediately; it also represents the opening and manifestation.
"Abolishing the provisional meaning" (*yì fèi*) is precisely "opening" (*kāi*); the following phrase is "revealing and manifesting" (*fā xiǎn*). This also establishes the aforementioned meaning.
These two points represent the essentials among the ten functions. "Opening and clarifying" both constitute "abolishing," for once clarified, they are no longer employed.

"The Unsurpassed Way" refers to the meaning of the skillful means of self-cultivation, which encompasses both cause and fruit. The provisional aspect of self-cultivation is the perfect cause (*yuán yīn*).
The meaning is as previously explained. "One's own treatise and others" refers to the former four periods (*catur-yuga*), namely those not mentioned before.

"Self and other" refers to the former contrast between the Perfect [Teaching] and the three [other] teachings. Alternatively, "transforming others" is as stated before, or it may refer to the *pitaka* that encompasses both.
The previous mention of "comprehensive" refers here to the meaning of the former explanations. However, at first glance, this phrase appears as if it were not... [incomplete].

Upon careful investigation, it appears there are two intentions: first, to establish the previously mentioned discarded dharmas; second, to initiate the subsequent detailed clarification of essentials.
Therefore, this has profound significance and is not in vain. Regarding the "subsequent detailed clarification," the *Jì* (Record/Commentary) states:
"In contrast to the previous five types, this refers exclusively to persons" (*etc.*). *Quán* (Complete) states: "This clarifies the number of persons and dharmas. Now, observing these two passages:
The previous section explained "skillful means" (*upāya*) by showing how various skillful means enable others to enter [the path] through one's own correct practice;
this current section explains "skillful means" by way of the recipient who enters through their own practice based on what they have received.

That is to say, it takes up the aforementioned capacity for application and explains that all that is received in this treatise serves the purpose of entering one's own practice for the benefit of others; whereas previously, it discussed only the capacity of the transformer (*pariṇāyaka*).

It is not yet discussed that those to be converted have entered [the path]; rather, it is now discussed from beginning to end how beings enter. Therefore, this is explained by means of the "cause" (so-yi) to manifest the "capacity" (neng).
Thus, at the outset, not hearing and not understanding constitutes the non-attainment of entry into one's own practice.
In the current passage, both the citations and the conclusion concern the benefit of beings entering; therefore, this clarifies the capacity by means of what is manifested. This is the citation.
In the textual evidence, first there is the specific [reference] to the three vehicles, and then the general statement "all" (*sarva*).
This means that because persons of the nine vehicles can all realize the reality (*tattva*), it is called "all"; this refers to a partial discussion of "all. Now, I say:

first, it is said to be "all" with respect to those who have the karmic affinity to receive transformation at this particular assembly; second, it is said to be "all" with respect to the capacity for opening and revealing [the truth].
Nothing exists that does not emerge from the ten realms; now all are opened, and all are caused to enter the Buddha’s wisdom and vision.
Therefore, it is said that "all" means that the former vows have already been fulfilled, as explained in detail below.
This is precisely the meaning of "all," wherein nothing is not penetrated. Why, then, is the term "a small portion" (or "partial") employed? It detracts from the essential core.
The meaning of the subsequent passage, which clarifies this by itself without further elaboration, is roughly as stated above.

Next, regarding the explanation based on the "Original" (hon) and the "Traced" (jaku): while it is certainly the case that the meaning of "expedient means" (upāya) is established in this sutra, the *Shiki* states that this is not yet the intent of the chapter.

This is because within the discussion of the Original and the Traced, both possess expedient means; here, we are merely borrowing the term "expedient means" to clarify the point, as the name is used in a remote sense.

[The preceding section] has already discussed the "Profound Differences" (Yongyi) [in detail]. Now, it is clarified that the title of this sutra, as a skillful means (*upāya*), is the collective name for two gates.

The reason these two gates are able to be opened and revealed is entirely due to this profound efficacy (*xuan-gong*). To explain this title, one must necessarily proceed in two stages: first, a direct and straightforward explanation of the meaning of the name;
second, an analysis based on the distinction between the fundamental (*hon*) and the manifested (*seki*). Only by doing so will its full potential be exhausted.
However, since its meaning was not yet fully exhausted, I first set forth four propositions and extensively elucidated ten pairs;

subsequently, through the eight gates of interpretation, the explanation of the names and meanings of the first seven [sections] was completed. Yet, as the meaning of the "Primordial and Traces" (honji-suijaku) had not been distinguished, I now clarify it by means of this [eighth gate].
Only in this way can the full force and extent of the names and numbers of this sutra be exhausted; therefore, it must be placed last.

Regarding this single interpretation, there are eight minor distinctions from the preceding classification. This [name] is a specific designation whose meaning is comprehensive, as it encompasses the entire sense of the treatise;
it is precisely for this reason that it is so called. If one asks, "In that case, how does this differ from the general title of the scripture?"—the distinction is indeed profound.
Now, I say: the general title is derived from the fruit with which it is associated, whereas this name is derived from the cause; it is based on the grounds upon which the name is established.
That which is "wondrous" arises precisely through the power of skillful means (*upāya*); thus, the "consummated" (*phala*) is the object, and this [means] is the agent.
If one approaches this from the perspective of the meaning of "no spatial direction," then there is nothing external to the object, nor is there anything remaining apart from the agent;

both together constitute the great totality of the *dharmadhātu*. Therefore, this single interpretation represents the ultimate profundity of this chapter; it must not be treated as a mere superficial investigation.
What a pity, what a pity that the understanding of "the eternal" (śāśvata) is so superficial!

One should contemplate this to the utmost; do not merely follow such a trend. The commentary consists of two parts: first, the correct elucidation of the meaning of the "original" (hon) and the "traced" (jaku);

second, a summary of the meaning to clarify the names. In the first part, there are two sections: first, concerning the Buddha; second, concerning Śāriputra, because both teacher and disciple possess both the original and the traced aspects. Now, [the text] begins...

The meaning of "expedient" (*upāya*) applies generally to both persons and dharmas. If one is explaining its name and meaning, it should follow the dharma; if one is discussing its fundamental and manifested aspects (*honji-suijaku*), it should properly be restricted to the person.

Therefore, while the previous explanation of the name and meaning of "expedient" correctly discussed the truths and wisdoms, the present clarification of the fundamental and manifested aspects is made in relation to teacher and disciple.

Nevertheless, they are not separate; both are inherently possessed within non-duality, and it is within this non-duality that duality is discussed. As for... this is a brief explanation. Furthermore, although the origin is one, it also possesses the four phrases, all of which are called the "self-substance" (*zishi*) in the interim.

From this point downward concerns Śāriputra. In other sūtras, he is sometimes said to have originally been a Buddha, or sometimes said to have originally been a bodhisattva;

however, in the subsequent sections of this sūtra, because he "conceals within and manifests without" (inner secrecy and outer manifestation), these instances are cited as examples to illustrate the general principle.

Furthermore, regarding the traces (*śeṣa*), the three [bodies] are first clarified and then concluded by manifesting the four. The initial clarification of the reality of the "all" is also as explained previously, though the text does not explicitly state it.

the subsequent summary of the fourfold set follows the same pattern as before, differing only in that the disciples are the subject. Next, regarding the meaning of the "Chapter on the Return to the Source," there are two parts: first, a detailed explanation of the four meanings by distinguishing between teacher and disciple; second, a general summary.

As for why there are two [meanings] each for the teacher and the disciple: it clarifies that they each descend from their distant fundamental essence (*dharmatā*) to manifest traces (*nirmāṇa*) in order to guide sentient beings;

and it clarifies that by following these traces, one returns to the essence, thereby showing how the function arises from the self-essence so that sentient beings may rely upon the "other-power" (*parāśraya*).

Because it brings together the self-substance, this is designated as the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*upāya-paṭala*) both in terms of function and cultivation; that is, it corresponds to the two meanings previously mentioned regarding "skillfully attaining the directions.

The two meanings concerning Śāriputra are likewise so. However, since both the teacher and the disciples possess their own practice in their original ground (*mūla-bhūmi*), which is entirely expedient means, why is it discussed only in terms of transforming others?
It is because the provisional function of guiding beings brings them to the realization of the Perfect [Truth], thereby connecting the trace with the origin.
Because one's own practice (*svayaṃ-caryā*) is not distinct [from these], it is not explained separately. Why? Because both employ the subsequent "cause of self-teaching" (*sva-śāsana-hetu*).

Since they arise through the application of function, they are first discussed in terms of function. If one does not introduce them into one's own practice, they are merely traces of others and not one's own current practice;

therefore, the subsequent clarification of their convergence constitutes the two gates. Through the means (*upāya*), the two gates serve as the means; that is, the essence of the cause gives rise to function, and the cause gives rise to function through the two gates.

This is because it accords with the essence [of the teaching]; it is precisely based on the meaning of the master and disciple employing [the teaching] for their own causes and for the sake of others that the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (Fangbian-pin) is named.

Regarding the summary at the end: "those who take up" refers to the "agents," while "by means of" refers to the "causes. "The various [beings]" refers to the four types of masters and disciples explained above.
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the "reason for being. It is because this master and disciple established these four types—self-cultivation and transformation of others—that this name was given;

it is explained through a commentary (*vṛtti*), hence it is called the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*upāya-paṭala*). Some say that this phrase universally concludes all the meanings previously explained;
thus, following the previous structural divisions of the chapters, it is commented upon as follows: "That is to say, for the sake of what has been extensively [discussed] above..."

This is because it abbreviates various meanings and so forth. Furthermore, it is said that while on the surface it appears to conclude the proximate [section], the underlying principle is actually quite different;
one must not merely grasp the proximate while losing sight of the remote. A "conclusive summary" (paryanta-samāsa) allows both the proximate and the remote to be attained.

Now, I say that this person is confused about the remote and the proximate—taking the remote for the proximate and the proximate for the remote—and thus incurs this error, failing to reach this very distinction between the proximate and the remote.
How could all these delusions and errors have reached such an extent? Students of later generations should therefore revere this.

Of the eight sections discussed above, the essential points are twofold: the first seven horizontally explain the names and meanings of the *upāya* (expedient means), while the eighth section vertically explains the names and meanings of the *upāya*.
"Horizontal" refers to the revelation within a single lifetime across the ten realms; "vertical" refers to the three periods of time.
From nine lifetimes up to immeasurable lifetimes, within each and every lifetime there are the meanings of the eight gates.

Although these meanings are presented horizontally in relation to one another, they are also vertical. By means of this expedient meaning, how could it be compared with what is taught in the various sutras or explained by the various masters?
If one says that the name is derived from the three [periods] of the past, this is entirely... [incomplete].

Because this is the subject under discussion, the text breaks off and says nothing further. Even if one were to interpret it by summarizing the two types of wisdom (*jñāna*) of the Mahāyāna, although such a summary is mentioned, it is merely a praise based on provisional means (*upāya*).

Furthermore, since the distinction between the square and the circle, or the gradual and the sudden, was not yet clarified in the various sutras of the past, how much less so in this present "opening and uniting" (*kaikai*)?
Not even a single phrase has been established, let alone being able to fully embody the four [teachings]; and even those four have not yet been realized.

How much more so for those who can further master the ten pairs and eight gates; if one has not yet attained penetration even within the *Jiemo* (Trace Gate), how much less could one grasp the long-term merit of the Fundamental [Gate]?
One should contemplate all things through this principle, and the various interpretations of the sutra will become self-evident without the need for prolixity of words.
Thus it was said previously: "To gaze afar with profound insight, vast and expansive, supremely brilliant—how true this is! (etc.). Nevertheless...
The first eight gates discuss two essentials; furthermore, there are three [additional points]: the first six all explain names and meanings, which correspond to the "causes and conditions" (nidāna);

the seventh, having already been treated in relation to various sutras, now treats them in relation to the teachings (śāsana); and the eighth treats them in relation to the meaning of the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku).

Regarding the gate of contemplation, there is one interpretation of this which is most essential and convenient; why is it not clearly explained? Although the meanings are many, they do not go beyond these essentials.

Regarding the four sets of four propositions, they consist merely of the three truths and the three contemplations; this is found everywhere and can be understood by analogy, so I shall not explain it at length.
Furthermore, the meaning of these four contemplations is identical to that of the four contemplations explained later in the "Revelation" (Kai-shi) section.

This clearly demonstrates that the former is precisely the latter, and since it will be clarified by itself later on, it is not mentioned here. However, since the preceding six [contemplations] are intended as the cause...
The conditions (*pratyaya*) shall likewise possess four meanings; although these are not explicitly stated in the text, their significance is inherently present.
Previously they were not discussed, so I shall briefly explain them now. This has already been indicated in brief within the initial listing of the four propositions;

since this current section is more extensive than that, the four meanings can be understood of themselves. Should you still not understand, I shall further clarify them briefly. As for what was previously...
The four intentions have already been clarified previously; these first three sections explain the names and characteristics listed in the preceding headings, expanding upon the "World" section.

Next, they extensively cite sūtras and śāstras to provide evidence for the ten [categories], which is the same as the previous citation of evidence. The four phrases constitute the fourth [section], namely "For Others.

Fifth, the three types of wisdom and the four phrases are established to provide an extensive explanation of the essence of wisdom; by presenting the entire essence, its functions are revealed—all of these are [contained herein].

The single, perfect Dharma is extensively explained as it pervades the four directions; the six knots illuminate the two truths. "Truth" (諦) refers to the principle (*li*) and the objective realm (*jing*).
This explains the preceding contemplation and observation: attaining mastery of the principle brings benefit, which is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

For this reason, one knows that the six [knots] are an extensive explanation of the four preceding meanings. When their essentials are grasped, there is nothing with which they do not accord. How could it be otherwise? This is roughly the case.
It is fitting that one should reflect upon this, as it has not yet been fully detailed.

Regarding these two sections, we shall now briefly demonstrate their respective approaches by following what is proximate. First, to indicate the single text:

"Those who advance and attain" refers to the fact that this sutra contains two meanings; since the interpretations adopted by the Northern and Southern schools in the past have differed, yet neither contradicts the intent of the sutra, both are preserved here.
This is why it is stated thus. As will be explained in detail later, the reason for presenting these two views here is for the sake of the preceding section.
The text contains these two layers; from this point onward, it corresponds to the second section, the "Correct Exposition" (zhengshuo), and is therefore indicated here.

Within this indication, we provisionally follow the "Trace Gate" (jimen); thus it is said "following the near," as the distant [teaching] is not permanently set aside, hence the word "provisionally" (qie).

One must proceed from this because it is the essential core of the sutra, the primary principle of our school, and provides the necessary convenience for interpreting the text. As stated previously...
The *Jieyao* states: "Now, having followed the previous three [sections], I shall briefly distinguish the errors through ten meanings;

this is the first of them. One must follow the previous three sections, for how could it be otherwise than this text? Quan says: "Those who recently followed the 'traces' (the provisional) each established three sections because their reasoning was close and detailed.
If one follows from the latter [the ultimate], it would be close and detailed; yet the previous statement said that following the first three sections is coarse—is this not a contradiction?"
Those who follow the text superficially and lose sight of its essential meaning fail to achieve a comprehensive understanding of both the sutra and the commentary; thus, one must reflect upon this.
Why are these two [sections] not presented directly as the three cycles (*trivartman*), but instead are separately opened up?

This would be inconsistent with the latter two cycles and the Root Chapter (*mūlaparivarta*), and furthermore, it would forfeit the central tenet of the "Exquisite Exposition" (*sūkṣma-deśanā*); therefore, such an approach is untenable.

For those [three], it is necessary to treat these two as such. Furthermore, although this does not immediately constitute three cycles (*trivartman*), it is nonetheless divided into three major sections:

first, the brief opening of the three to reveal the one, which moves fixed attachments and gives rise to doubt; second, the movement of attachment and the arising of doubt, leading to the presentation of the resolution and the request for teaching;
third, the extensive opening of the three to reveal the one, which severs doubt and engenders faith. Although the classification is thus made...
Even if one has not yet grasped the essential point, it is still superior to what preceded; now, regarding the structure of this text, there are generally three parts:
first, the praise of the Buddha’s wisdom; second, the brief opening and manifestation [of the teaching];
third, the extensive opening and manifestation that severs doubts. If categorized according to the persons involved, there may be three sections as follows: [...]

Regarding the three [aspects] previously mentioned, since the first and last belong to the Buddha and the middle one belongs to the assembly, they may be categorized as three from the perspective of the persons involved.
However, if one were to clarify the essential tenets of the sutra itself, it must be categorized as two: namely, the brief and the extensive manifestations.
This, then, integrates the essential meaning of the sutra and unifies its essential passages—whether manifest or fundamental, whether textual or doctrinal.

"To call upon a stone and have it easily change [into something else] is the ultimate limit of this; therefore, we now exclusively follow this path and do not concern ourselves with other methods—this is truly sufficient.
One must deeply grasp this meaning (and so forth)."
The text states: "First, briefly opening up the three to reveal the one"; it then says: "Moving from attachment and giving rise to doubt. Why is this taken as distinct?

Because the initial passage belongs to the Buddha, while this [subsequent] passage belongs to the assembly. Now, if these two names were established, their meanings would both belong to the Buddha. How then could they be opened up for the assembly?

Thus, the former is the essence (*tattva*) and the latter is the intention (*abhiprāya*); the former also possesses functional capacity (*kāritra*), whereas the latter lacks intention, and the latter lacks [functional capacity].

How could the underlying principle be such? This passage must certainly contain both the sense of "completeness" (*jù*) and the sense of "mutuality" (*hù*). The meaning of completeness is readily understood;

however, if one wishes to distinguish the wording and clarify their mutual relationship, the subsequent text should state: "Grasping at motion gives rise to doubt; this belongs to the assembly. Only then can [the text] be harmonized.
Otherwise, even if one were to forcefully provide an interpretation, it would certainly not accord with reason. This must be due to errors in the later transmission of the original text.
It certainly cannot be as [you] say. To briefly open up the three and manifest the one, there are both prose and verse; this text can no longer be reconciled [with your interpretation].

If it were left as it originally was, there would surely have been a profound reason for its transmission, though errors may indeed have occurred.
Since that which lacks a cause cannot be brought about, how could one, in a context of such ultimate importance, merely cite the text while omitting its essential meaning?
Truly, this should not be so; yet, as it was previously stated that both [aspects] were not discussed, I deeply lament this.
Having admired this beyond measure, I shall now attempt to explain it. For the text should properly state: "First, the brief opening and manifestation has two parts: first, praising all Buddhas..."
Regarding the second point, "The two wisdoms subsequently briefly open up three to reveal one," there are further two parts: the prose (*gadya*) and the verse (*śloka*).

Second, this is the individual explanation of those two meanings. First, to exclude what is not [the case], it relies on the person of "wonderful" (*miao*);

second, to correctly manifest what is [the case], it relies on the "wonderful Dharma" (*miaofa*). The Buddha is the person of ultimate, perfect wonder, which stands in contrast to the practitioners of the three teachings.
Because the Dharma attained is not [ultimately] real, it is said that the Buddhas manifest this as their own practice;

in contrast to the aforementioned practice for others, "real" refers here to the provisional [teachings] of the subsequent *Vimalakīrti* and *Saṃdhinirmocana*. Regarding the "three" within the essence, these refer to the three types of knowledge (*sarvajñatā*, etc.), as explained later.

"One mind" refers to the attainment of the three knowledges within a single moment of mind (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*), as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*; the present meaning, however, refers to the Buddha’s pure and wondrous mind.
The middle [section] possesses the three functions of illumination, distinguishing it from the others in their sequential attainment.

This encompasses the meaning of the five pairs and a half from the preceding text exhaustively without omission. Please do not further remove or disregard this; the subsequent explanation of praise refers to its profundity and vastness.

Although these virtues have no external limit, they do not exceed the sublime and the expansive; therefore, they are praised by way of analogy and examples according to the principle. Thus it is said: "As it is in reality..."
Only True Suchness (tathatā) is the ultimate principle of the wondrous reality. Vertically, it exhausts the heights and depths, yet there is no high or low;

horizontally, it penetrates all boundaries, yet there are no boundaries. To further speak of its being "immeasurable and profound" is to collectively manifest the essential subtlety of both the horizontal and vertical dimensions.
Although the sutra speaks of the "profound and immeasurable," here we clarify that a single phrase is simultaneously complete as four phrases; therefore, [it is said again].
Regarding the statement "immeasurable and profound," since these two have been raised, the remaining two can be understood by themselves.

This clarifies that even the simultaneous negation of both [existence and non-existence] is yet "without direction" (amārga); therefore, it is precisely the meaning of "perfectly wondrous" (pariniṣpanna). Next, an analogy is raised to manifest these two meanings; both are analogized as being "profound and vast.
Because it is profound, it is vast; because it is vast, it is profound. There are also four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) here. The Master Miaoyi fully explains this as the first analogy.

Regarding the sequence of "profound" followed by "vast," the details are not yet clear. As for the subsequent examples used to clarify: both types of wisdom possess the qualities of profundity and vastness.

Although these meanings exist within the provisional [teachings], they are not explicitly manifest in the text; therefore, following this explanation, we shall employ these examples to elucidate them, and so forth.

This is the general sense. Next, in explaining the praise of the provisional, there are two parts: first, a brief commentary on the scriptural text, and second, a detailed explanation of the meaning of the gates. Within the first part: [The text continues with the specific commentary.]
First, the meaning of what is praised is explained; next, the text of the praise itself is explained. Regarding the first part:
the initial three characters point back to the "Reality" (shí), while the single character "Gate" (mén) corresponds precisely to the "Expedient Means" (quán).
As for the question "What is this?", it refers to the essence itself, which emerges from [the phrase] "Self-etc. In brief, this is the wondrous Way realized through one's own practice.
Prior to the ultimate perfection, the "subtle capacity" (*miao-neng*) constitutes its substance; because it accords with its descriptive title, it is called the "expedient means" (*fangbian*).

Generally, this is the cause that penetrates to the perfect fruit (*yuan-yin*); specifically, regarding the stages of the true cause, since the preceding [stage] was designated as the position of ultimate fruition (*ji-kuo*), this must necessarily be understood as the meaning of the cause.
One should know that the meanings of the four pairs and a half mentioned previously are all subsumed within the characters of this single gate.
One must not err in the selection and rejection of these objects; each is designated as a "gate" (*mukha*).

Therefore, the text below explains this by means of the sense of "advancing toward" and "penetrating entry. Furthermore, because it manifests the provisional causes in contrast to the ultimate fruits, it says, "from the gates," and so forth.
Within the Path lies the meaning of the direct realization and the perfect fulfillment of the wondrous principle.

Next, the explanation of the section on "Praise" consists first of a direct praise and second of a praise directed toward others. In the initial part, there is first the citation of the text to indicate the topic, followed by the formal explanation of its meaning.

Regarding the two phrases "not deliberating" and "difficult to understand and difficult to enter," these explain the initial stage of wondrous understanding in the Ten Abodes and the subsequent stage of wondrous realization in the Ten Grounds; that is, "understanding" refers to the wondrousness of non-deliberation. It is like this:

The bright mirror is wondrous because it is without fixed direction; its great function is the entry of both self and other. Furthermore, it is the realization of the central essence. "Entry" refers to the function of dual illumination.

Alternatively, the first [phrase] indicates vertical depth, while the second indicates horizontal breadth; these are mentioned alternately. These two phrases are praises of the Dharma according to its own essential nature.
Regarding the phrase "the seven kinds," etc., this distinguishes the person in order to manifest the Dharma. First, the seven directions are raised.
Furthermore, because it is not known and is profound and vast, it cannot be measured. Next, it is explained that only those who possess the four kinds of true persons can know it;
this also demonstrates its profundity and vastness, as will be explained in the subsequent text. This is precisely why this gate is difficult to understand and enter.
If one follows the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra*, there are still five phrases here: namely, "difficult to see," "difficult to... [The text ends abruptly.]
This realization is difficult to know, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter. Other commentaries explain it by correlating it with the preceding proof of the five kinds of profundity;

the sequence is also the same as before, differing only in that this version distinguishes between the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*). However, this [interpretation] merely captures the meaning of the specific passage and does not harmonize with the preceding and following contexts;
therefore, it is not employed here. What I intend now is to provide a horizontal and vertical integration of all textual meanings.

Therefore, I shall directly rely on the subsequent text to explain the record; that the first three constitute the preparatory expedients prior to the stage of reality (*bhūta-artha*) and correspond to the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) also has its own significance, but for now I shall follow the commentary (*śāstra*).

The subsequent section specifically explains the meaning of the "separate" [teaching] by contrasting it with other persons to manifest the Dharma. Within this, first is a brief explanation of the intent behind separately citing two individuals;
second is a detailed exposition throughout the five periods regarding the manner in which the three vehicles do not know [this Dharma]. Regarding the former:
this wondrous gate, according to the verses below, cannot be known by anything except for the Perfect [Teaching]. Having already provided a general explanation above, now...

Furthermore, because the general meaning is presented here to clarify the specific textual passages, it is stated separately. The commentary explains that "those with heavy attachments" refers to those with dull faculties and heavy obstructions.
Below this, the text extensively examines the five periods of the present day to manifest the meaning of their lack of understanding.

First, it addresses the Two Vehicles; subsequently, it reveals the Bodhisattvas. The first section also carries the intent of the *Śraddhāparivarta* (Chapter on Faith and Understanding). This is the first [section].
From the beginning of the first section, after self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*), up until before the *Avataṃsaka*, one should always apply this wondrous gate to it.

"Original" (*yuan*) means the beginning; it refers to applying it at the very moment of the initial inception. This still applies generally to all those without the capacity for enlightenment (*agotra*), etc., which specifically refers to the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*).
That is, from the time after they have regressed from the Great Vehicle, up until the point where they are currently seen engaging in [worldly] activity.

Having had this thought, he departed in haste. As for the deaf and mute, they were born later with differences [as explained at length]. Above, it was shown that there is currently no benefit for oneself or others;
below, it is shown that there is currently no seed for either seeing or hearing. That he still harbors doubts is precisely what occurs at the beginning of the three cycles [of teaching].
Next, regarding the Bodhisattvas, there are again two categories, which are also as clarified previously and subsequently.

This is because [the nature of reality] is profound, vast, and subtle, and those who do not know it remain ignorant. Regarding the "Extensive Explanation" section below: this is the essential method for entering reality through the perfect and wondrous practice of one's own cultivation.

Although the meaning of the essence was briefly indicated previously, the principles concerning the provisional and the real, as well as right and wrong, were not yet clarified; furthermore, in order to refute the errors of the old [schools], this is specifically provided.

Furthermore, regarding the explanation within this section: first, citing the interpretations of others; second, clarifying the principles of inclusion and exclusion; third, the main extensive explanation; and fourth, recounting the commentary’s resolution.
First, recounting the other’s presentation of the method for this gate: it refers to the skillful means of the two vehicles, namely the seven stages of skillful means (*saptavidha-upāya*).

Thus, the causes of the two vehicles constitute this gate, and this gate is also the gate of the two vehicles. Next, within the clarification of inclusion and exclusion, there is first the heading and then [the explanation].

The explanation regarding "giving" and "taking away" is as follows: because that which they understand is both vast and yet possesses two faults—namely, being narrow and shallow—they merely speak of the Two Vehicles.

This refers to their narrowness in terms of their cause and fruit taken collectively; how much more so when considering only their cause? Furthermore, since it is not their own inherent nature, it is shallow.
This initial "giving and taking away" briefly refutes their shallowness; next, the central point is to provide a formal refutation.

First, one refutes their restricted framework; subsequently, one doubly refutes their shallow framework. Regarding the first [refutation], one seizes upon their lack of reality and their shallow capacity.
As the Sūtra says at the beginning: "This gate is the gate through which the Buddha himself entered. How could the fruit of Buddhahood rely upon the gates of the Two Vehicles as its cause?
Since this error is most grave, it is completely refuted. Next, regarding the term "bestowal" (*yu*), there is that which may be opened up for reconciliation.

For this reason, and because it is included among the various gates as the most inferior of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), and is further supplemented by skillful means (upāya), it is called "the shallowest" of the subject and object;
yet since they have not heard of the Buddha-fruit wisdom at all, how could it be considered shallow?
This is the general meaning of the refutation, which is roughly as explained above, and will be explained in detail below. Next, in the main explanation, we shall discuss this comprehensively.
The text consists primarily of four statements: first, entering the Real through the provisional gate; second, entering the provisional through the provisional gate;

third, entering the Real through the real gate; and fourth, entering the provisional through the real gate. Of these, the first two concern the three vehicles (the three teachings), both in their distinct and common aspects, while the latter two concern the causes and the functional application of the fruit in the Perfect Teaching.
In the context of the present passage, it corresponds precisely to the third statement.

Regarding the first meaning of the "meaning of the phrases" (*padārtha*), there is first a specific treatment according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*), followed by a general treatment according to the three teachings, concluding with a summary to clarify the limited and narrow scope of the Guangzhai school’s interpretation.
Within the first section, there is first a heading and then an explanation based on the sutra concerning the Middle Way and the Buddha-wisdom; this refers to the stage from the first bhūmi upward.

Next, there is a general clarification regarding the entry into the Middle Way through the third and fourth [concentrations]. As for the specific entry into the Middle Way, it is as previously described; the remainder follows.

Second, how is it that the meaning of the Middle Way is established such that it is neither existent nor non-existent? It is as stated in the subsequent text: "All dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent;

they are without arising and without cessation; they are without greatness and without smallness," and so forth. This is precisely the meaning of the Middle Way according to its respective category (*pradeśa*). While the names are identical, the entities are distinct;
thus, when speaking in accordance with their characteristics, one may also take the underlying intent to explain them. This refers to their causes according to their respective categories.
That "opening the assembly" all enables entry into the true Middle Way is the meaning of attaining entry into the real by means of the provisional cause.

Regarding what is called "a single contemplation," it refers to entering emptiness through both the essence and the analytical breakdown; it is simply the entry into emptiness by breaking down the conventional.

Because this does not clarify the four [truths] of the Lesser Vehicle, one can only attain the "one. It is said that this is merely the gate of existence—the Gate of Existence (yōmon). The Gate of Existence...
Because there are seven expedient means (*upāya*), it is now said that both emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*astitva*) possess expedient means. How do we know this?
It is because they speak of these seven; furthermore, as they follow the previous "one gate of emptiness" (*eka-śūnyatā-dvāra*), they must correspond to the one gate of emptiness.
In essence, their discussion is narrow and limited, capturing only one aspect—why then insist on having a fixed intention? This is merely a brief summary.
Therefore, the commentary states [as follows]. Next, the cause and effect specific to each of the three teachings can be understood.

Regarding the third phrase, first there is the heading, followed by the reconciliation of the four meanings. As for the "perfect" (yuan) four gates: first, the *Ji* does not provide an explanation, stating in its entirety that "the perfect has four gates, namely:
teaching, wisdom, practice, and principle. These are its gates; it refers to the gate of wisdom. This meaning has not yet been [fully] addressed.

Regarding what was heard [previously]: it is now said that the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) of provisional and real, and so forth, are themselves the four gates, which comprise ten layers of four gates.

Now, if these are considered horizontally, they correspond to the gate of the provisional; if discussed vertically, they correspond to the gate of the cause. Therefore, it says, "The first" (and so forth).

The fourth phrase refers to the wondrous function following the realization of the Path; as in the subsequent text, it is called a "gate" (mukha) because it can facilitate access through skillful means (*upāya*).
This constitutes the function upon the aforementioned fruit (*phala*). If one speaks of the "gate" now, it properly corresponds to the third phrase.
The concluding summary below—stating that those who value the shallow and the limited are thus explained—refers collectively to the preceding four phrases, which are rich and clarify the profound.
"Vast, clear, expansive, and profound" breaks through the shallow and breaks through the narrow; thus, it is a dual refutation of the shallow and the narrow.
"Narrow and cramped" describes a state of being constrained and lacking freedom—a single sense as explained previously.
Examining his interpretation, not even one of the four phrases [of the original] is attained therein; therefore, by calling them "shallow and narrow," he doubly refutes those two meanings. Below...

In this expository treatise, first the commentary is presented, followed by the three stages of opening up and expanding [the text] so that one may understand according to the principles of the treatise.

Since the words of the treatise are general and concise, they must be expanded upon to reveal the various teachings of the present; these are precisely fourfold. Regarding the phrase "according to contemplation" (*guan*), "contemplation" refers to practice (*xing*).

Since the previous four phrases were all based on wisdom (*zhi*), they now correspond to the meaning of contemplative practice (*guanxing*). Thus, the contemplative wisdom of the various teachings is clarified.
This clarifies that among the various teachings and their various gates—namely the four "ones" and sixteen gates—the present sutra corresponds precisely to the four wondrous gates.
Although the *Śāstra* does not contain this specific meaning, it must be so because there is at least this general sense; hence the commentary states [“and so forth”].
In the subsequent section providing paired explanations, first the divergent views are briefly stated, and next the specific meaning of the text is directly analyzed.

First, because after the paired praise, the inquiry and the explanation are clearly distinct; second, because the subsequent text says, "I follow [the Buddhas] such as Sakyamuni," the praise and the inquiry-explanation are likewise self-evident.
Thus, it is clear that this explains all Buddhas and is not merely a praise of Śākyamuni. Next, the main point...
Regarding the separate explanation: according to various commentaries, all treat the initial inquiry as a distinct topical heading (*ko-mu*).

However, since the present intention is neither to raise an objection nor to provide a formal refutation, these inquiries are all omitted here. The meaning of this inquiry is to investigate the reason for both the praise and the two types of wisdom (*jñāna*).
That is to say, it asks what is the reason why these two wisdoms are so profound and vast, and furthermore, what is the reason why the two wisdoms are thus profound.
"What is 'extensive'? This is an inquiry into the reasons for its depth and extensiveness; it now relies upon the second meaning. Below follows the specific explanation.

First, in explaining "reality," the text provides a general indication by citing the passage. Second, there are two texts for the specific explanation which synthesize and reconcile the depth and extensiveness, praising the existence of such depth and extensiveness.
Since the reasons have already been explained, there are again two [sections]. As for those reasons, this is what they are. Next is the explanation.

Within the section on the provisional (*upāya*), the text first presents the passage that collectively demonstrates the inclusion of the "equal" and other qualities, which is indeed due to the preceding passage of praise.

Below this, there is a formal explanation of the text in two parts: first, a direct commentary on the words; second, a reconciliation of the profound and the vast. The subsequent explanation that establishes the preceding [section] is likewise easy to understand.
Although the praise and explanation within the provisional section do not explicitly contain these two specific textual passages, they both encompass these two meanings precisely because...

One may know by analogy with the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*) that [the essence] does not reside in elaborate formalism; thus the commentary (which says "and so forth") has its meaning summarized in brief.
The following double conclusion refers to the fact that for this reason, the two wisdoms (*jñāna*) are thus profoundly deep and vast. Regarding the four phrases of the sūtra text:

the first two conclude the aspect of reality (*satya*), and the latter two conclude the aspect of skillful means (*upāya*). There are two rounds of explanation: the first directly relies on the literal text, and the second...
This is explained in terms of the understanding of oneself and others, because the sūtras contain these meanings. First is the wondrous culmination of self-realization;
second is the universal transformation of others. First is the profound; second is the vast. These are also mentioned alternately. Furthermore, each has two meanings:

first is the profundity of its own essence; second is the vastness of its transformative function. These are likewise mentioned alternately, as can be considered according to the perspective of conventional sentiment.
The term "etc. (*ādi*) serves as a re-explanation of what is difficult to understand by citing what is easy to illustrate the difficult; it provides scriptural evidence for two meanings.
If one deeply contemplates the intent of this passage, the Sūtra cites the past to reveal the present, while the Commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains by means of the present to reveal the past.

Why is this? Because in the past, [the teachings] were provisional and thus difficult to understand; whereas the present reveals that which is according to reality and definitive in meaning, and is therefore easy to know. Thus concludes the Commentary.
To explain this, [the author] takes the present to illuminate the past by citing the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and its distinction between the definitive and the non-definitive.

However, since the verses of that treatise were composed by Maitreya Bodhisattva and the commentary was composed by Vasubandhu, each having written their own works, it is not a direct commentary on this sūtra;
therefore, its meaning remains general. If one intends to clarify the specific intent within this [sūtra], one must further rely upon the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.

The discourse on "with remainder" and "without remainder" precisely accords with this intent. By opening two gates of expedient means and manifesting two aspects of ultimate reality, the final and most profound discussion within these two gates and three sections explains the most authentic matters; thus, the full meaning of clear elucidation is contained herein.
Therefore, all phenomena are entirely one wondrous [reality], and once this is realized, there is no further room for disagreement—this is the point where all conceptualization ceases.

One must wait for the ultimate, definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Next, to further explain by way of self and other, the commentary states that "at times" does not refer to the time of listening or to a subsequent period of private consultation and resolution. It may also directly clarify that it is not exclusively as previously stated;
rather, "at times" refers to when one again provides this particular explanation, because the text still contains this sense. What distinguishes this from the previous [explanation] is as follows:

Previously, it was stated that "self" refers exclusively to the real and "other" refers exclusively to the provisional; thus, both self and other each possess two aspects—the provisional and the real.

If explained in relation to one another, the "provisional" of the self is entirely "real" because it pertains to one's own practice, while the "real" of the other includes both [the real and the provisional] because it pertains to the transformation of others.

Thus, the provisional and real aspects of self and other constitute four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), as clarified previously; however, since only two are present in the current text, [only these two are mentioned].
The reason for the omission of the phrase "and so forth" is simply that it has been abbreviated.

Next, the praise of the World-Honored One’s two types of wisdom is explained; this corresponds to the previous clarification that the path of all Buddhas is identical, and here it clarifies that [the Buddha] is equal to all Buddhas.

Within this, there are four sections: first, a reiterated indication; second, an account of the ancient interpretation; third, a refutation of the errors in that ancient interpretation; and fourth, the establishment of the correct meaning.
Regarding the fourfold correct analysis of the initial meaning, it is briefly as explained above. Next, within the "Old" [commentary], there are three parts:
first, stating its distinct heading; second, presenting its specific characteristics; and third, explaining the intent behind the analysis of these differences.

Regarding the first point, the term "each and each" (*ge ge*) indicates that this is different from the preceding two sections, which were combined for both praise and explanation; thus, because they are treated individually, it is said "each. This is its meaning.
Regarding the distinct characteristics that first appear in this sequence: from the beginning is the praise of the provisional and the explanation of the provisional;

second, from "Śāriputra" onwards is the praise of the real and the explanation of the real; third, from "Śāriputra" onwards is the dual conclusion praising and explaining both the provisional and the real.
In the original text, the character for "provisional" (權) is frequently omitted; this is the state of its variation. Next follows the narration of its explanation.

The intention behind the differences is indicated, explained, and concluded within this section. Regarding the indication: "the former" refers to the various Buddhas, and "the latter" refers to Śākyamuni;
there are three points of difference between these two. Although there are three points, they explain only two types of difference.

These two differences consist of: first, opening versus closing (expansion versus contraction); and second, priority versus posteriority. The characteristics of these two differences have already been described above: the first explains opening versus closing, and the subsequent two explain priority.

The latter three [sections] merely explain the former two; in both the beginning and the middle, one first restates [the subject] and then explains the reasons why it is so, which is why there is this opening and closing.
Regarding the sequence of the next two explanations: the first clarifies the perspective of the "root" (hon) and the "trace" (jaku), while the second clarifies the perspective of "self" and "others";

because of these two intentions, there are these two differences. Finally, as for the summary, the intent is to clarify that although the text opens and closes and proceeds sequentially, [the underlying meaning remains consistent].

The essential nature [of these] emerges reciprocally as eternally perfect and so forth; it cannot be partial. Next, regarding the critique of the refutation: first, one critiques its lack of straightforwardness and its circuitousness;
next, one critiques the contradiction between its words and its actions. If one says it is not so, then one should not provide such a critical interpretation.
As for the sequence of the text, that which is now interpreted follows the sequence of the text. Regarding the ease of understanding the meaning, [it concerns] what precedes and follows.
When principles and precedents correspond, there is no need for convoluted analysis; to provide such a detailed exegesis would be circuitous.

To be circuitous is to lose the sequence of the text, whereby the meaning remains obscure. When it is said that the paths are identical, this refers entirely to the statement regarding the perfect nature of the essence (*tattva*).
If this were not the case, it would mean that all such statements are found within the very passages being explained themselves.

Furthermore, by citing analogous cases, it is shown that since his words and actions are contradictory, he should not act in such a manner; the general meaning is roughly as stated above. What follows is the formal analysis (*kośa*).

It is divided directly into three chapters; the first is the same as before. Since there are no differences regarding the second or third [chapters], it would be redundant to labor over a convoluted explanation.

Regarding the explanation of the first [chapter], the "Reality" (*satya*): first, the heading is presented; then, following "If it were real," the explanation begins. First, the lack of completeness is cited.
It is not established that [the previous] was inferior; since it is now stated that it is "established," one knows that all is complete, and thus it is the reality.
To say "all is established" means that at the stage of the ultimate fruit (*phala-bhūmi*), there is no wisdom or merit whatsoever that is not fully possessed.

This is precisely what was previously praised as the threefold wisdom within the single mind. However, since it is said that this praises the real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) as before, there are some who [hold a different view].
In this context, Master Fa explains that although there is only the person and the dharma being praised, by what means is this praise expressed?
If it were non-existent, from what basis would this name be established? Regarding all such points where [the text] does not explicitly state "what is meant," I shall now provide the explanation.

Although the meaning is not explicitly manifest in the text of the Sūtra and its commentary, it is certainly present in both. That which is present is precisely these words "attaining Buddhahood," which constitute the object of praise. Furthermore, it is precisely these [words].

This is an expression of praise. To achieve Buddhahood is the perfection of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*); since true wisdom is already perfected to the ultimate degree, there are no further virtues to be discussed.

Thus, it is both an expression of praise and the actual accomplishment of true wisdom. The phrase "the vertical depth of all is accomplished" refers to its profundity, while "the horizontal breadth of all is accomplished" refers to its vastness.
The text states, "When one is accomplished, all are accomplished," which clearly explains the meaning of this praise. This has been fully detailed in the preceding sutra and its commentaries.
Since this can be inferred by analogy, all [subsequent points] are omitted. Xiang considers this phrase to refer to the timing for the employment of skillful means (*upāya*).

Now, it is said that this praise of the Real (*bhūta*) is also immediately followed by the subsequent praise of the Wisdom of Skillful Means; therefore, the text includes the words "and so forth" (*yǐlái*) from that point onward.

Next, regarding the praise of skillful means: although this passage designates both the subject (*neng*) and the object (*suǒ*), it contains only the praise itself, and thus the subject is also implied.
This simultaneously encompasses both the object and the subject. Previously, when praising true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), we mentioned only the object while implicitly including the subject;
