Separately, the two retributions based on the primary [retribution] are presented; these two are the principal [factors], as they are the actual analogies from which the inconceivable characteristics of the realm proceed.
Therefore, the text does not explain them further. Next, in the explanation, there are two parts: first, clarifying the four matters; second, clarifying the five paths.

Regarding the first four types, first the scripture is cited to list them, and then each is explained individually. First, the explanation of "sentient beings" is brief and consists of only two [points].
The preceding phrase refers to the fruit, while the following phrase refers to the cause;
because these two matters are beyond the reach of worldly speech and deliberation, although one observes their coming and going, one does not know the reason for their origin.

One merely observes that there is birth and death, yet one cannot fathom how they are brought about. Since this cannot be conceived by thought, who else could explain it? Therefore, it is beyond thought.
This is a brief discussion of the two matters of cause and effect; subsequently, this will be further expanded by means of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*).
Next, in explaining the world, the first three phrases correctly clarify that words and deliberation cannot reach it. In the *Āgama* and below, examples are cited to manifest these [matters].
Within the first three phrases, the first two directly concern present phenomena: the first is horizontal and the second is vertical. The final phrase expresses doubt regarding its cause.

Next, an event is cited to demonstrate that [the Buddha] does not fall short of the Middle Way. The Buddha says it is not madness; he says it is reality (*satya*). What is this reality? It is the matter described below.
Although this primarily clarifies the world, it simultaneously reveals that these types of sentient beings are likewise inconceivable (*acintya*).
The phrase "this is equal" serves as a warning to manifest and establish this inconceivability. The text consists of four parts.
The first sentence provides a general clarification that [these states] are not causes for emerging from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);

the following three sentences specifically clarify that if one lacks the three benefits regarding the Path, one cannot accord with correct principle, cannot penetrate the essence and characteristics of phenomena (*dharmas*), and cannot attain the fruit of liberation.
Not only do these conditions lack such benefits, they conversely lead to harm, namely, causing one to go mad. Among people today, many...
If one does not strive for what is essential but instead pursues that which is inappropriate, how could one not reflect upon this? Such is the general meaning.

Next, regarding the explanation within the section on dragons: as for "contemplating good and evil," if one contemplates good, sweet rain falls in due season, providing sustenance and nourishing all things;
if one contemplates evil, bitter rain falls out of season, violently harming all species. The causes for these outcomes are explained below and may be understood there.
Next, those of great power are likewise of the dragon class; all are brought about by the power of their vows and karma.
Next, the five destinies are summarized to expand upon the matters concerning sentient beings mentioned previously. Furthermore, there are indications, explanations, and conclusions, and so forth;
these are all the natural law of karmic retribution, as well as matters that lie beyond the reach of worldly speech and thought.

The following is the fourth general summary, which uses worldly matters as an analogy to reveal the profound and subtle supramundane principle. "Causes and conditions" refers to the preceding three [sections];

"profound realm" refers to the previous four explanations. Having concluded with these praises of the wondrous principle, it is said that if even coarse matters are thus, how much more so must the refined and subtle principle be believed.
Since these are called "causes and conditions," they likewise possess four aspects; this is not based on a specific technical definition.
Observing it, one finds it is certainly not non-existent. First, the explanation of names and meanings generally encompasses what follows, namely the world (*loka*).

Second, the discernment of characteristics: "characteristic" refers to that which can be aspired to, namely the person (*pudgala*); regarding the causal fruit of the mundane world (*saṃvṛti-loka*) which can be eliminated, this is the counteractive (*pratipakṣa*).
Finally, the conclusion summarizes and reveals the wondrous principle, namely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Thus, the principles and the teachings are both excellent.

It is understood; the reason for explaining it again is precisely this same principle. Previously, it was stated that according to the structure of the text, since both [the title and the body] have already been indicated, there should subsequently follow a citation, an explanation, and a conclusion.
While the previous section provided a direct explanation without the initial and final parts, here it is precisely appropriate to provide the conclusion:
namely, that "this is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. This is because all ten [categories] encompass both the provisional and the ultimate. Although the text is concise...
The essential meaning must necessarily be thus, and it cannot be unknown; furthermore, this is not merely a separate conclusion, for there should also be a general conclusion.

Why? Because the text of the formal praise itself contains both a challenge and a response. Since the two meanings within the response have already been established, there should likewise be a general conclusion.
Although the scripture is concise and lacks explicit transitional phrases, every section explains the significance of its respective conclusion. Therefore, [this general conclusion] must exist.
Knowing that this is merely an abridgment and lacks an extensive version, it must have existed; furthermore, since this meaning is essential to understand, it is briefly clarified here.

Next, in explaining the verses, the first section is divided into two chapters. Regarding the "substantial reality" (*vastu*), it should properly have been placed at the beginning; thus, it is first briefly divided into two parts. First, the brief [explanation].

Regarding the "Revealing" (*kai-gen*), following the sequence of doubt and request: if discussed in detail, it should be stated that first, the brief opening reveals the three as one, which moves fixed attachments and gives rise to doubt;
next, based on those moving attachments and doubts, the doubt is raised and the request is made. The first [section] has two parts: first, praising the Buddhas' wisdom;
second, the actual brief clarification of the revelation. The first [of these] has two parts, namely, the prose and the verse. The prose above is concluded.

The following clarifies the verses. Within these verses, there are two parts; the first consists of four lines which, by their very nature, ought to be thus and should not have anything further added.
Although this is a verse, it is an independent utterance (*udāna*), which is easily understood and not difficult to grasp;
all previous commentators have treated it as such. However, the preceding text was omitted and corrupted, and thus this has been further elaborated here.
This section is overly elaborate and lacks propriety; therefore, it should not be so. This is entirely due to later generations who did not deeply grasp the essential points of actual practice.
To further provide an explanation would only increase the fault; thus, it should not be done.
Those of later learning should certainly pay close attention and avoid following this text blindly. This concludes the first section and second chapter; next, we shall explain the two meanings.
First, the explanation of the former distinction in meaning; next, the explanation of the latter distinction in meaning. First, regarding the difference between the brief and the extensive:

as indicated by the preceding text, the prose (*gadya*) that relies on words is extensive while the verse (*śloka*) that transcends words is brief; conversely, the prose that transcends words is brief while the verse that relies on words is extensive.

The reason for this is to ensure that the meaning remains equivalent—this is the explanation thereof. Through the extensive, the essential points of the brief are revealed; through the brief, the extensive is made manifest.
The meaning clearly indicates that this must indeed be so. To state it exhaustively, there are two senses: first, the explanation of the nature of things (*dharmatā*);
second, its being due to two conditions. It is for these two reasons that it is thus.

Next, regarding the explanation of the differences between "opening" and "closing": this text should properly have been discussed after the two chapters of the subsequent section, yet it is explained here now for the sake of convenience following the preceding exposition.
In all cases, stating the subject first and then explaining it makes it easy to understand;

thus, these verses in scattered form distinguish the differences from the ancients, who simply analyzed the distinctions directly within the prose commentary. Furthermore, when both chapters are referred to as "combined," it means they are spoken of together as a continuous whole.

Because it is not distinct from the prose section, it is said to be "in agreement. As explained previously, this is easily seen in the text. Regarding the beginning, there should be two further parts:
the first verse concerns all Buddhas, and the second verse concerns Śākyamuni; the latter briefly includes both. As for the term "Hero of the World" (*lokanātha*):
"world" refers to time and place, and "hero" means strength. Among all times and places, nothing is more powerful than this.

The Buddha therefore uses this as a sequence for praise; the "three provisional wisdoms" refer to the preceding section. Regarding the "three differences," this clarifies that the text of this single verse praising the two wisdoms of all Buddhas differs from the preceding prose in three respects. Within these, there is both a heading and an explanation. The "Duality and Singularity" section differs from the whole in three ways: first, it is the difference between the dual and single aspects of person and dharma; second, it is the difference between the opening and closing of these two Buddhas;
third, it is the difference in the number of deluded beings. Now, I say that such a categorization certainly has not yet reconciled the text;

I shall now clarify these three as six, where the first three names are: first, the difference between the dual and single aspects of person and dharma; second, the difference between the opening and closing of the two dharmas.
Third, regarding the distinction between the general and the specific in the sequential correspondence: the prose is "double" (referring to both person and dharma), while the verse is "single.
The prose is "expansive," while the verse is "concise. The prose is "specific," while within the verse there is the "general.
As for the characteristics: the Buddha is the person and wisdom is the dharma; since the prose speaks of "all Buddhas" and also speaks of "wisdom," it is thus "double" (person and dharma).
The verse speaks only of "Buddhas and persons," whereas the prose is singular; first it praises wisdom and subsequently praises its gate, thus opening [the meaning].
In the verse, both are praised together as "Buddhas," which combines the prose. It speaks only of the "two vehicles," whereas the verse says "all sentient beings," which is universal.
Next, to clarify the reason for this, one should follow the sequence of the explanatory text to understand it.

Regarding what is being clarified: first, it refers exclusively to real wisdom (*jñāna*); second, it applies to both types of wisdom; third, it refers exclusively to provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

Next, concerning the interpretation of the commentary’s text: although it encompasses the various essential natures of these [wisdoms], the beginning of the text merely provides a general enumeration of their numbers;
next, within the explanation, it first indicates their characteristics and briefly explains the reasons for them; finally, the last one belongs solely to the True [Wisdom].

Regarding the third [verse], only its characteristics are indicated and there is no commentary; it is entirely omitted. To say "it leads people" is an explanation of the meaning of the word "person" (*pudgala*) in the verse.
Here, this is precisely a praise of the Dharma; why then is it directly praising the person? It is explained thus for that reason.
Having already been set forth in detail previously, it is now stated briefly: the person is the Dharma itself, for it is precisely through the person that the Dharma is attained.
This Dharma makes a person a hero of the world. In the subsequent passage, the text directly employs parallelism without explicitly indicating its formal characteristics;

consequently, later commentators have differed and failed to reach a consensus. Why is this? Herein, we are merely discussing the prose of praise (*stuti*), whereas the prose of the commentary and the prose of the conclusion have never failed to be elucidated.
How much less could one immediately leap over to the prose of the conclusion while still engaged in the praise of Śākyamuni?
In all cases, one should reflect upon this; there is no great error or discrepancy. Now, regarding the previous opening:
first "wisdom" was mentioned, followed by its "gate. In the present synthesis, the three subsequent phrases together complete the preceding phrase.

Because two [aspects] are spoken of together as "persons," the preceding phrase says "Hero of the World" (*lokanātha*), while the subsequent phrase simply says "Buddha. Thus, the two types of wisdom and their dharmas are both contained therein.

The person is clear; regarding the "explanation" (*śeṣa*) of the Dharma, the record states that because the timing of its application to sentient beings differs, it is said in full that the two Buddhas' teachings each correspond to different capacities and conditions, and thus the Dharmas are distinct. Since the essence of the two Buddhas is identical, the persons are collectively [the same];

however, as this is too extensive to be described in detail, such errors are indeed profound. Now, I maintain that this is a correct praise not involving an explanation of the conclusion, but rather correctly clarifies the various [points].
Why did the Buddha open [this teaching]? It is the orthodox treatise of Śākyamuni; how could his own practice be said to be merely for the sake of transforming others?

The correct words regarding the Dharma consist of the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real, whose causes and fruits differ and are thus distinct. To manifest this meaning, it was necessary to open [the teaching] previously, which has now been completed.
Now, I shall set forth its essentials to clarify that these two dharmas are both contained within the person; it is to manifest that every person must necessarily possess these two dharmas.
Therefore, it is essential that these be combined; this is indeed their actual reality.
Next, regarding the explanation of the third section on the distinction between the general and the specific, I shall merely provide a brief indication without explaining the underlying reasons.

As for the "general" and "specific," there are two meanings for these terms, which were already individually refuted above; now they are discussed again collectively. This has already been explained extensively previously.

Therefore, it will not be discussed further here. Having already explained the meaning of the praise for true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) through the single word "Buddha" as previously stated, the subsequent verse concerns expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
This refers to the merit obtained through the cultivation of effort within the causes of one's own practice;

thus, it is said that this "merit" shares the same meaning as the previous presentation of the cause to reveal the fruit. As for the phrase "other dharmas" and so forth, transforming others is precisely the application of expedient means.
"Practice" (caryā) refers to merit; "transforming others" (parārtha) refers to the application of skillful means (upāya). These are two meanings of a single entity.

Regarding the phrase "the remainder of true wisdom" (jñāna), this refers to its function at the stage of fruition (phala). There are five phrases above, of which we now briefly cite the first. One should understand that this [first phrase] generally applies to all five, hence the commentary states: "... (etc.)."
Next, regarding the combination of verses for the explanation of the "tying of knots," this also involves a sequential connection that differs from the preceding section.

Specifically, the first verse explains the tying of knots by all Buddhas, and the second verse explains the tying of knots by Śākyamuni. Within the first [verse], the first two lines explain the "tying" and the subsequent two lines explain the "knots";
these are easy to understand from the text. Within the next line, the first two lines explain the "tying" and the final line explains the "knots. Thus it is said:

Regarding "the causes and so forth," this is because the preceding commentary contains two kinds of fulfillments. "Fully knowing and seeing" refers to the two aspects of the provisional and the real, which are termed "fully.
Thus, these are double conclusions; although the words are concise, the meaning is complete. Next, there is another layer of explanation:
previously, the verses were completed according to the sequence of the preceding prose, whereas now they are explained directly based on the verses themselves.

Regarding the textual phrasing, although this principle—that the wondrous Way is boundless yet still possesses such numerical limits—is presented here for the sake of exhausting its full enumeration, there is nothing improper in providing this further explanation.
However, since the text consists of four lines with two layers of interpretation, it is a point very easy to understand;
yet, because people fail to grasp its essential meaning, the addition of further textual elaborations has become excessively prolix, and it is therefore appropriate to omit them.

Next, the prose commentary on the verses of the "Exhaustive Praise" (Juetan) is divided into five parts; the long prose section is further divided into two major divisions: namely, "by means of" (*yīyóu*) and "the actual basis" (*zhèngyīyóu*).
Within the "actual basis," there is the "object" (*yǒngjìng*) and the "correct praise" (*zhèngzhōng*). Within the "correct praise," there are two parts:

the "person" (*rén*) and the "object" (*jìng*). These constitute the five parts of these verses. This is because the scriptural text does not follow the previous sequence and is also incomplete. Furthermore...
The reason for this extended exposition is that it constitutes five parts. It is so because, being perfectly wondrous, it is without fixed direction.
Among these, the first verse directly praises the profoundly deep realm; the next praises the grounds for such supreme admiration; the third verse offers the actual praise;

and the fourth verse explains the reason why those who do not know this within [the teaching] are stopped. Although these specific phrases do not appear in the preceding text, their meaning is certainly present therein.
The term "stopping" (*zhi*) has two meanings: first, to reveal the subtlety of the Dharma; second, to serve as a condition for those with karmic capacity.
Since these conditions—meaning people—are unable to know it, and since it is stated that only a Buddha can know it, this section exists to reveal that others cannot.
Fifth, the general summary verse expresses the meaning of ultimate praise. For these reasons, there are five points that should be deeply contemplated.

Regarding the initial statement that mentions only the "beginning" and "end," there are ten aspects to this realm (*dhātu*). In the present verse, two are mentioned for both the beginning and the end:

the "beginning" refers to nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), while the "end" refers to retribution (*vipāka*). The six intermediate aspects are omitted. Furthermore, because it follows the natural flow of the discourse, nature is placed first.

"Various kinds" refers to the ten realms (*daśadhātu*), and "beginning and end" refers to the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*). The meaning of these textual passages is as clear as looking at one's own palm; yet, some claim that five textual passages constitute [the core].
Regarding the explanation of the meaning of "ten" as "correct": what is the meaning? There are both general and specific meanings. "General" refers to principle (*tattva*);
"specific" refers to substantial reality (*dravya*). Here, it encompasses both. If all ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*) possess [the same nature], why would this not be the general meaning?

If the ten were identical in their sense of a single substance, then it would indeed be the specific meaning. As for "great" and so forth: that text uses the term "great" to refute the Guangzhai school’s view that the latter four [suchnesses] constitute the great.

The preceding five [realms] are the provisional (upāya), while the various [realms] are the manifold; the present intent is that both the Great [Vehicle] and the manifold are common to both the provisional and the real.
One should know that the ten [realms] pervading the ten realms—namely, the ten of the Buddha-realm—are the Great, while the ten of the nine realms are the manifold.
This is so for each and every realm, and this principle is thus fully exhausted.

Next, regarding the verse on the "extension by way of the object" (*viṣaya-vistara*), both the prose commentary and this [verse] are complete with both the capacity (*śakti*) and the object (*viṣaya*). In the preceding prose, the object comes first and the capacity follows;

here, however, the capacity comes first and the object follows. This "object" refers to the actual phenomenon (*vastu*). The subsequent verse primarily offers praise and correctly clarifies that the principle transcends words.

Because the true mark (*dharmatā*) is without marks (*animitta*), it is said to be "without direction" (*an-uddeśa*). That which exists can be demonstrated; since this does not exist, it cannot be demonstrated. The Way (*mārga*) is able to penetrate through.
It is also said that the practice of the Way is signless (*animitta*) and beyond the reach of words; therefore, it was previously stated that one cannot "arrive" at it.
Next, the verse concerning those who do not know refers back to the meaning of the preceding section regarding existence. Following this, the selection of those who are capable contains two meanings.
First, there are those who possess the capacity for faith in the perfectly wondrous; this very capacity for faith is itself identical [to the truth].

Second, there are those who have previously received the teachings of the Shared Doctrine and entered the stage of the ten levels of faith; among them, those who are keen regarding the wondrous Way are precisely the intended recipients of these teachings, for they are not reached by the cessation of words.
Although the single character "faith" (śraddhā) contains both of these meanings, it is intended to suppress one and exalt the other, thereby achieving perfect penetration from beginning to end.

Therefore, it is necessary to mention them alternately. To speak of "the first faith" is in contrast to the subsequent ultimate [faith]; to speak of "the ten faiths" as being the beginning does not mean they are distinct [stages].
This is because, intending to clarify the future transformation, one first mentions the foremost among the sons of Śāriputra from the ten directions, and thus mentions him specifically.

Since it is intended to show generally that none can know [this], one again mentions them collectively. "Hypothetically" (*jia*) means to concede for the sake of argument; "actually" (*zheng*) means to state the reality.
"Even the Pratyekabuddhas, though superior, cannot know the reality"—this refers generally to both types of self-cultivation.

"A small portion" means that these seven stages of expedient methods are considered real for those seven classes of people; however, the Buddha’s true wisdom does not perceive them as such, as they are merely provisional.
Thus, it is said that [others] cannot know even a small portion. Now, this meaning correctly states that although those who rely on expedients may be numerous, in the end...

Regarding the "small portion" of the true wisdom capable of knowing [the Dharma] mentioned previously—which stated that all except Bodhisattvas are unable to know it—this current passage clarifies that the designation [of "all"] is inclusive;
therefore, it is necessary to exclude [those who do not possess such knowledge]. Furthermore, there are two categories: first, based on the sūtras, referring to the one great teaching;

second, according to the present intent, it encompasses both positions. The term "arousing the mind" (bodhicitta) is general in application; thus, it must not be interpreted as referring to only a single type of understanding.

The explanation of "non-retrogression" is likewise so because there is no one who does not interpret it as a single phrase. First, regarding the provisional teaching (*yōkyō*), because it is not definitive, the word "or" is used.
From "three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*" onwards, the meaning of "newly resolved" is explained;

this intent precisely clarifies that, in contrast to the stage of non-retrogression, one still resides in the stage of retrogression, and thus even after such a long period of time, one is still termed "one of newly resolved mind. Next, the actual [explanation]...

Regarding the explanation according to the next two teachings: first, we exclude those who are not yet prepared for the initial stage, because since they have not yet severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), they still abide in these two stages, which correspond to the seven preparatory practices (*saptavidha-prayoga*).
Next, we clarify that they are indeed prepared for the two teachings and point out the name of their stage prior to non-retrogression.
Although they may make offerings to countless [Buddhas], this is merely categorized as merit; because they still regress regarding the Path, they are called "new" [practitioners].
He spoke, saying: "One who brings forth a single-minded recollection of the Wondrous Wisdom" means that such a person concentrates their mind and perfects their wisdom;
this clarifies that even if many people were to share one mind and perfect their wisdom, they still could not know it after a long period of time.

Next, regarding the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), first it clarifies why those in the common stage of non-retrogression do not know [it]: although they abide in non-retrogression, they are only able to...

Because they sever pervasive afflictions and penetrate universal principles, they are unable to know that there exists a distinct and sublime path; by analogy with this intermediate stage, one should understand that according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are four types of non-retrogression:

first, non-retrogression in faith (*śraddhā-avinivartanīya*), which refers to the sixth mind of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), from which point on one no longer retrogresses into false views;

second, non-retrogression in the [bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi-avinivartanīya*), which refers to the seventh mind of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), from which point on one no longer retrogresses into the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

Therefore, there are three types of non-retrogression: first, the non-retrogression of the noble wisdom attained from the first bhūmi onward, because once attained it is forever free from loss or regression;
second, the non-retrogression of practice from the eighth bhūmi onward, because one proceeds spontaneously and the afflictions of marks and functions cannot disturb it.

Based on this, one might argue that there should also be non-retrogression in the stage of faith prior to the bhūmis; yet, why is it said here that non-retrogression pertains only to those who have realized the stages?

The master Quan-yun, following the *Dilun* masters, establishes the ten stages (*bhūmi*) as the stage of non-retrogression in principle, the ten practices (*caryā*) as the stage of non-retrogression in position, and the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*) as the stage of non-retrogression in practice. Because the meanings of this teaching are manifold, its explanations are not uniform.

Now, since the previous explanation of non-retrogression has already described many interpretations, I shall here briefly cite one path; thus it is said. Although this constitutes non-retrogression...
Yet, because they have not truly realized [the truth] and instead received teachings that lack integration, how could they know the perfectly wondrous Way?
Thus, they are unable to understand it clearly. First, the seven [stages] were raised collectively; next, the five were raised individually.

Taken as a whole, this serves to suppress the seven provisional means and exalt the one true reality—the intent of this "striking and exalting" is found herein. One should know that these constitute the first eight passages.
Regarding the statement "only two or three," the first [section] generally excludes seven; the second excludes one; and the third clarifies the three vehicles individually:
among the Śrāvakas there are three branches, while for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas there is only one each. Second, the "three" are actually only "two," namely suppression and encouragement:
suppressing those who have not yet attained faith so that they may believe, and encouraging those who already believe so that they may progress. This is the encouragement.
There are two aspects: the general and the specific.

The following is the fifth section, which provides a general verse summarizing the preceding expressions of supreme praise. The commentary (*śāstra*) consists of four parts: first, citing the text to indicate the heading;

second, providing a general explanation of the text; third, providing a specific explanation of the "inconceivable"; and fourth, synthesizing the previous four explanations. Regarding the first: the preceding...
Having briefly versified the Dharma, I shall next extensively suppress the person; now, to once again exalt that Dharma in order to bring forth that person, I say "furthermore" (*yòu*).
Next, to directly explain the text: however, the essential points of what preceded do not exceed two, namely, wisdom (*jñāna*) and its object (*viṣaya*).
Now, among the six lines of the verse, excluding the first, the remaining five lines correctly versify these two essentials.
The first two lines of the verse correctly praise the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-viṣaya*). The subsequent three lines praise the aforementioned wisdom that knows them.

It should be understood that these four are one substance, namely the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*); one is the four, and the four are the one. Furthermore, even in terms of the four lines, the object is none other than the wisdom itself.
Regarding the four meanings in the commentary text: the first two explain the object, and the latter two explain the meaning of wisdom. Both are included here.
In this prose section, I have merely provided a direct correspondence; however, the state wherein one abides must be the unprecedented Dharma (*apūrva-dharma*).

Because its provisional and ultimate aspects are without fixed direction, it is untainted (*anāsrava*) and inconceivable (*acintya*). Because it is profound and subtle, it is rare and difficult to understand.
One should know that this final term "Dharma" subsumes the four preceding meanings; this truly wondrous realm pervades all.

Because it pervades all places, it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*); because it transcends form and sound, it is called "inconceivable"; because it exhausts principle and fulfills nature, it is called "profoundly deep";

because it transcends the four propositions and leaves behind the hundred negations, it is called "subtle and wondrous"; and because it is that which all Buddhas take as their teacher, it is called the "Dharma.
The next three phrases cite the wondrous person and wondrous wisdom capable of ultimate illumination and understanding. Furthermore, to briefly clarify the meaning of the final two phrases: if...

If the Buddhas were not identical, then sentient beings would likewise not be identical; however, because they are taught so that sentient beings may equally realize and enter [the truth], it is expressed through words.

Furthermore, one should know that this passage can also be interpreted in four, three, two, or one [ways]. Regarding the fourfold interpretation, it is as explained in the text. Regarding the threefold interpretation:
the first phrase is divided into two parts, while the second phrase combines its two parts into one; the final three phrases are then combined together.
Because it is one, it is three; it is also two: namely, object and wisdom, the capable and the incapable, and person and dharma.
These three together belong to the two. It is also one, which means that by summarizing and concluding these points, the essential purport of the discourse on the "ineffable" (jueyan) is clarified.

Next, regarding the separate explanation of the "inconceivable" (*acintya*), among the four [aspects], this single name and meaning is the most essential, whether in terms of its nature (*svabhāva*) or...

Cultivating the contemplation that clarifies the objective realm must necessarily rely on this; once this single principle is attained, the other three can be understood by analogy. The text contains metaphors and their applications. Within the metaphors, there are three points:
first, although it is formless and lacks existence, its true nature (*dharmatā*) is all-pervasive—this is its "perfection" (*pariniṣpanna*).

Second, because it is devoid of all marks, it is called "unborn," which means it has no existence. Yet, it is able to give rise to the nature-virtue of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*). This is truly profound.
Even the subtle capacity to produce all dharmas of cultivated virtue and all qualities of merit possesses four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) both in their literal meaning and as metaphors;

because they transcend the reach of speech and thought, they are called "inconceivable" (*acintya*). Next, the reason for reconciling the four [permutations] is that the words and their meanings mutually clarify and establish one another.

Although the relevant passages have already been cited above, I provide this further explanation now in order to demonstrate that there is no point at which [the teaching] is not encountered or touched upon.
They are all analogous and mutually consistent; however, the definitive conclusion lies in their mutual establishment and manifestation.

This clarifies that what was previously explained is the meaning of this present text, and the meaning of this present text is what was previously explained. Therefore, they first establish and manifest one another.
Within this, there is first a general indication, followed by specific correlations. Regarding the first, it correctly demonstrates that the four preceding meanings arise based on this present text.
This clearly reveals the meaning of this passage. It is precisely the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem). Its form is exceedingly subtle, yet it can rain down celestial jewels.
This text is extremely concise, yet it possesses the four kinds of great meanings mentioned previously; furthermore, it is inconceivable.
The first two characters constitute three fundamental bases, for these three are all the perfection and pervasiveness of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*). They are untainted (*anāsrava*).
This clarifies that all dharmas are nothing other than the wondrous object and wondrous wisdom; outside of these, there is no further dharma.

Now, by explaining this in terms of the ten realms (*daśadhātu*), it is shown that they are subsumed within the three virtues (*triguṇa*); beyond these, there is no further dharma, which is precisely the meaning of being "without outflows" (*anāsrava*).

For this reason, they mutually manifest one another. In the text, first there is the heading, followed by the explanation. The unification of ordinary beings and sages refers to the nature of the ten realms—that is, the principle-body (*dharmatākāya*), the ten [realms].

The essence of the realms (dhātu) must necessarily be the three truths; the objects of the truths must necessarily be the wisdoms. Since the three are two and the two are three, the meaning of "outflow-free" (anāsrava) is thus established.

Therefore, it is elucidated through ten explanations. Next, the inconceivable is specifically identified and explained to clarify the principle that the provisional and the real are neither fixed nor separated, yet can be opened or merged at will.
This serves as the explanation because they are mutually identical, and thus their characteristics are manifested. Next...

In the middle [section], only the headings are given without explanation; therefore, it is said that [the meaning] can be understood. This correctly clarifies that what is profound and subtle is the meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and that the Buddha-dharma is the meaning of what is profound and subtle.

Because they mutually illuminate one another, this is used as an explanation to manifest what preceded it. As for why the former [section] opens [the topic] while this one combines [it], although there are four [aspects], they are but one;

thus, opening and combining are applied freely according to what is appropriate. Furthermore, because the subsequent [section] also only provides the headings, it is said that [the meaning] can be understood.
Knowing that this passage represents the ultimate of the complete cultivation, it is presented to reveal the beginning and middle of the nature;
the preceding sections were explained according to the stages (*bhūmi*) precisely for the purpose of revealing these positions.

Now, since the Buddha has finished his praise of the upholding [of the teaching], he again summarizes it to highlight its essentials. Following the Buddha’s intention here, the previous detailed explanations are now brought into alignment with this meaning.

Now, having concluded [the previous section], I shall once again manifest this here in a further assembly; it is not merely that the Buddha’s intent is earnest and exhaustive regarding the subtle, but my current commentary also exhausts the aforementioned intent of the Buddha.
Thus, from the initial explanation of the title of the chapter up to this point, there have been three or four [sections];
yet, when one summarizes their essentials, they are one. One should know that the two characters of the title, "All Dharmas" (*sarvadharma*), are like these five phrases herein.

If one unifies these four [categories] by means of the One, then it can truly be said that though they fall apart, they return to the same source; though there are a hundred concerns, they accord with a single principle.
When one meets this essential point, what further thought or deliberation is there? If one has not yet reached this state, one must certainly strive to attain it.

One should know that although the "extreme praise" (*jue-tan*) appears to refer to the objects [of cognition], it is in fact praise for wisdom; since its intent lies in cultivation, it is expressed through the metaphor of the "extreme."
The difference lies merely in the praise of the two wisdoms. Now, by explaining the "wondrous object" (*miao-jing*) through four meanings, one explains the "wondrous wisdom" (*miao-zhi*).

Explaining that which is beyond words (*jue-yen*) simultaneously explains that which is expressed by words (*ji-yen*). Explaining the two simultaneously explains the four. Explaining cultivation (*xiu*) simultaneously explains nature (*xing*).
Explaining all Buddhas simultaneously explains all sentient beings. Therefore, all meanings are exhausted within this; believe in this single passage as true.
It is a wondrous jewel; however, the essential point lies in praising its inherent nature (*dharmatā*). This is also called praising the reality, praising the one, and praising the wondrous.
It is like a wondrous jewel which, when about to be given to someone who has never known it, must first be praised to the utmost before being bestowed.
This is likewise: in order to reveal this single locus of the wondrous nature for the sake of all sentient beings and cause them to achieve cultivation, [the Buddha] praises it.
Because of his virtue, he first offers this supreme praise; its essence lies in this: to know only how to praise the Buddha is not yet to know how to praise sentient beings.
Failing to comprehend this meaning, how could one's own existence have anything to do with the countless Buddhas? One should reflect deeply upon this.
The preceding prose and verses constitute the conclusion of the eulogy; what follows is the formal, concise revelation, which is precisely where the aforementioned eulogy resides.
The initial phrase "concise revelation" serves as a topical heading; its purpose is to shake up attachments and give rise to doubt.
The reason this text marks this point as the very core of the essential meaning is that such a concise revelation is intended specifically to provide an awakening stimulus.
At that time, the long-standing tenets of the assembly gave rise to new doubts in the present because they were ancient tenets.

The ancient tenets held that the Three Vehicles were real and did not say that there was another, separate truth. Now it is said that the former three were not true and that the present one is their actual reality;
for this reason, the old is moved and the new is produced. This is a brief response to the extensive discussion of the "three and one," spoken from the perspective of distinct enumerations.

Regarding the distinction between the provisional and the real, the coarse and the subtle, these apply universally to all things; yet for now, we shall follow the specific perspective while ensuring one knows their universal application.
Although the two meanings—universal and specific—have never been different from the outset, people are largely confused about them, so it is fitting to pay deep attention to this.

As for the sequence of "first revealing and later opening," this too is not fixed; however, because we are currently praising the reality (the Real) by virtue of the momentum of the context, we reveal it first. Furthermore, "first" refers to the Buddha.

This also follows the established convention; the pattern of being concise at the beginning and expansive at the end applies to all such texts. Regarding the term "mutually," it is because they all possess the quality of opening and revealing [the truth].
Furthermore, one should know that their characteristics are identical and together constitute a single consistency. The initial passage also contains three meanings, as assigned in the text:
first, the brief correspondence; second, the individual explanation; and third, the two subsequent intentions. When the Sūtra says "after a long time," it refers to the immeasurable.

The meaning is that for over forty years the true reality has not been revealed; it was based on the "Chapter on Resolute Belief" at the time of his impending passing, and based on the "Parable of the Grass" when he was about to die.
It is also now, as you speak, that the most ultimate reality is being presented. What is this true meaning?
It is that all sentient beings fundamentally possess the One Vehicle, the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas. To speak of it in brief, it is as follows:

This praises the two kinds of wisdom of all Buddhas. Regarding the latter two [sections], first is the explanation of the latter [part] which reveals reality, and next is the explanation of the former [part] which exhorts faith;

these two meanings mutually establish one another. First, the heading is cited and indicated; second, its meaning is clarified; third, the latter [section] is raised to provide proof and establish the truth.
This is precisely because what was heard briefly at first was not yet understood, leading to this profound doubt; it is truly the fundamental basis for the brief opening [of the teaching].

Regarding the phrase "The Buddha, as he truly abides," and so forth: in the commentary, this is not explained, and it states in full that "this question-and-answer passage is concise and its meaning is hidden;
I shall now cite and elaborate upon it. The intent of the question is this: although the Buddha exhorted [Śāriputra] to have faith, Śāriputra instead harbored doubt;
was not this exhortation to believe therefore rendered futile? The intent of the answer is this: Śāriputra demonstrated that although he had momentarily given rise to doubt...
One who seeks to believe and awaken through practice does not, because of doubt, give rise to slander; such slander is not what the encouragement of faith is intended to prevent.
What the encouragement of faith prevents lies in those of shallow practice. As for those who, due to doubt, further give rise to slander, they must indeed be encouraged in their faith.

Now, it is said that this [section] is for the purpose of resolving doubts, yet the text appears to be somewhat abbreviated. Although it is brief, the force of its meaning remains present and can be fully articulated—this is the beginning.
The section beginning with "Doubt serves as a defense" is an explanation. First, regarding the doubt: doubt arises from what has been clarified above. To raise this doubt, it is said:
"If the Buddha did not exhort one to have faith, it would be understandable for doubt to arise; but since the Buddha speaks with sincerity and exhorts us to have faith, why does doubt instead arise?

Since one remains in doubt, what need is there to exhort one to have faith? The explanation states: "If he did not exhort one to have faith, then because of that doubt, one might give rise to slander."
Regarding those who fall into suffering: if one first encourages them to have faith, then even if they harbor doubts, they will not slander [the teaching].

This is because the primary purpose of providing a ford to liberation is precisely to prevent the cause of falling into slander. Therefore, it is necessary to encourage faith. In the text, at the beginning there is only doubt without a concluding explanation;
later there is only a conclusion without a cessation [of doubt]. Thus, it appears to be somewhat omitted; I shall now briefly clarify this.
Next, regarding the brief exposition on the provisional (*upāya*), the text is divided into three parts. Generally speaking, according to the literal sequence, there should be four parts:
first, two lines addressing the former assembly of the provisional; second, two lines citing the former provisional transformation; third, two lines formally opening and subverting the provisional;

and fourth, two lines explaining the meaning of this opening and subversion. Alternatively, it may be condensed into two parts: the first is the address to the assembly, and the latter three constitute the formal opening and subversion.
The first [part] is precisely the separation from the two [extremes of] illumination; the second is the liberation from birth and death to realize nirvana.
Since there is already this proclamation, it is a restatement of the former transformation. Because this is a restatement, what follows is the formal opening and refutation.

The characters "I" (我) and "let" (令) run through the subsequent text, while the character "one" (一) subsumes the preceding passage. The word "will" (將) means "desire"; the underlying intention is that [the Buddha] secretly intended [this teaching] for the sake of bodhisattvas. Therefore...

The inclusion [of these] within the assembly addressed by the teaching is profoundly significant and must not be treated with superficiality. Next, regarding the further progression toward the explanation of the Bodhisattva assembly:
one takes the latter two phrases in their entirety as referring to the Bodhisattva assembly. Here, the character "this" (此) belongs to the person;

within this, there is a heading, an inquiry, and an explanation. Within the explanation, there are two parts: first, an explanation according to the meaning, and second, an explanation according to the text. Furthermore...
There are two [aspects]: first, concerning one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), and second, concerning the transformation of others (*parārtha*).

By examining it through these two, it must be so. Next, this is spoken in terms of number; as for "text" (*vyañjana*), since numbers arise from text, it says "below, sentence," where "sentence" is precisely text.
Because the meaning of this text is definitive, one knows it to be thus. The following two texts together constitute the appropriate convergence for the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

If one cannot deviate from the literal meaning and instead denounces [the teaching] as false and deceptive, this precisely constitutes the refutation of the provisional meaning (*pratikṣepa-artha*), while the reconciliation of the meaning (*saṃgraha-artha*) is contained therein.

Within the latter intention, two points are included: first, to cause [beings] to leave suffering; second, to act as a gateway and a skillful means (*upāya*). This is precisely what is meant by "gateway.
Although the preceding passage of praise is extensive, it does not transcend two meanings: praising the real (*satya*) and denouncing the provisional (*neyārtha*). Praising the real is for...

This reveals that the actual practice [of the One Vehicle] is the basis for refuting the provisional, and it serves as the reason for opening up the three [vehicles]. Even when contrasted with what follows at length, it is exactly like this.
Since the sequence is thus established, why was it not stated previously that "first one praises the single reality, and next one opens up the three to reveal the one"?

Instead, it says, "one praises the two wisdoms. However, there is a profound meaning here: it is intended to manifest the essence of what precedes and what follows. Those capable of reflection should consider this.
The essential point has been grasped.
Regarding the subsequent request by [Śāriputra] to ascend [the seat], the preceding section "Opening and Manifesting" already briefly reveals that this is the Buddha;

this is done from the perspective of the assembly, and it also encompasses both the subjective and objective aspects, each containing two meanings. Since the preceding textual analysis already possesses these two, it is said to be "opened and manifested," and thus there is no need for a further separate explanation here.
Although the middle section contains two [aspects], the text is but one; therefore, the text further provides a separate explanation of its underlying cause.

Since it speaks of "ascending and requesting," there must first have been doubt; and since doubt does not arise in isolation, it must have a cause and condition. Thus, it is necessary to clarify three things:

because the false is threefold, grasping and movement immediately destroy the provisional; because the true is one, the arising of doubt is used to manifest the real. "Ascending" (Teng) is a summary point that describes this sudden [realization].
"Manifesting their doubts" means to bring them forth; it signifies reaching the ultimate limit of one's mind in order to seek a definitive resolution.

"Narrating the doubts" refers to the act of raising those doubts and seeking resolution, which is precisely what "bringing forth" entails. When the compilers of the Sūtra (the *jīngjiā*) narrate these events, they describe the state when the person’s doubts were still within their mind and had not yet been voiced;
once the words were spoken, they belonged to the subsequent section on the presentation of doubts. Therefore, what is doubted here is likewise part of the compilers' narrative.
The distinction between the general and the specific regarding these two assemblies mentioned above can be understood. "Expedient means" (*upāya*) is the general term;
the phrase "these two wisdoms" refers to the text of praise for the two wisdoms found in both the preceding prose and verse sections.

This term "expedient means" comprehensively encompasses the meaning of the four lines and ten pairs of eight gates without omission. The title of this chapter is established precisely from this point as its central thesis.
If you insist on taking only the phrase "merely provisional" as the definitive meaning and do not believe in the universal [truth], then please excise this passage;

for one should follow the meaning of this text rather than conforming to common sentiments. The explanation of the reasons for these two doubts is clearly revealed by contrasting the present and the past, as can be understood.

Second, regarding the formal request (*yācanā*): the preceding section concludes the presentation of doubts, while the following section constitutes the actual formal request. The textual explanation has four parts: first, the general heading; second, the classification of the text; third, the explanation of its meaning;

and fourth, the detailed explanation according to the classification. Within the classification, there are two sections, as the current text intends to comprehensively clarify the three types of intent;

thus, it further takes up the previous [sections], each of which also contains three parts. Third, the three instances of cessation belong to the Buddha, and the three requests [belong to the Bodhisattva].

Because the Buddhas of the assembly [act] for these three reasons, they remain silent; because the assembly [acts] for these three reasons, they offer their requests. Since the essential requirements are fully met, there are only three instances of requesting each.
The meaning described within [these passages] follows the profound principles of other commentaries as previously stated, concerning oneself, others, and the sequence, as well as manifesting oneself;

these may be sought within the scriptural text itself, so there is no need for further elaboration here. Next, the intention of the Master [Vasubandhu] contains two aspects, namely: the literal text and...

Furthermore, regarding the remote indication mentioned previously, its full intent was not yet exhausted in the current passage; therefore, I have clarified this intent by adding [this explanation] here, which is why the word "or" (*vā*) is used.
If one were to interpret the text according to the three distinctions as explained in the *Xiàngxià* (向夏), the meaning of the "three" would remain unclarified.
Consequently, I shall briefly elucidate it once more, for this point must be made clear. This merely cryptically indicates that the assembly possesses three [aspects].
The "Root" (Mūla) is intended to clarify its wondrous Dharma through a threefold exposition;

because the enumeration of these expositions is extraordinary, it is a secret indication of their number rather than an immediate revelation of their specific contents. It is erroneous for some to arbitrarily establish the doctrine of three cycles within these three [sections], thereby contradicting the original intent.

Regarding the "presentation" (cénqǐng), there is also a passage in the sūtra where the compiler’s text is abbreviated and does not explicitly state that it is combined with the words of the speaker; therefore, it is called "presentation.

The text concerning the presentation of doubts extends from the beginning up to the phrase "the dharma that is difficult to understand. The text concerning the presentation of requests extends from the phrase "I myself," etc., to the end of the initial section.
This first part clarifies that this is the Buddha’s own practice of skillful means; thus, it is called the "first. Others say that the "first" refers to [the first of the three turnings].
If "actual skillful means" (bhūta-upāya) refers to the provisional (upāya), then how should the text of the following line be interpreted?
"To request" means to entreat the Buddha to definitively eliminate doubts for both oneself and others.
Regarding the six verses, the prose commentary is abbreviated and contains only two; although there are six here, their essential meaning does not differ.

Of the preceding [verses], the first two state the doubts; the subsequent four state the requests for resolution by oneself and others. Thus, the six [verses] are sufficient when combined with the first two.

Regarding the four [verses] concerning oneself and others, one is for removing [doubts] oneself, while the remaining three concern the assembly. If one wishes to correlate these two textual sections, they should also be broadly divided into two:
namely, the first two verses of the preceding section further open into two, and the second [section] opens into four textual units.
Because it is convenient for the followers to understand, it is thus established as the sixfold essence that should be known. Within the first verse, "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is like the sun;
it is also the sun itself. To speak in general terms, it can destroy all darkness and manifest all things;

it destroys the darkness of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*) or manifests the principles of the Three Truths (*tri-satya*). There is nothing in which the Sage does not penetrate, and he greatly illuminates this.

"Ultimate and Honored" refers to the World-Honored One (*Lokanātha*). Among the six meanings, one is "Dharma," which refers to the One Vehicle (*Ekayāna*) consisting of the two aforementioned wisdoms;
its textual meaning is as previously explained. Following this, taking the cause as the fruit constitutes the "Reality. As previously praised, this is termed "Explanation.

Next, within the verse on the provisional (*upāya*), the meaning of reality is also included; this is spoken in terms of the "Great. If discussed according to the theory of cultivation and nature (*śikṣā-prakṛti*), this furthermore—
All is due to the cultivation of virtue; all is expedient means (*upāya*). The two lines within the section on "Suspecting Oneself" concern the meaning of cause and effect.

Alternatively, that which is practiced by oneself and others is the meaning of "transcending function," which belongs to the discourse on transforming others. Regarding the "great number," it has already been explained as before.
As for "possessing the Way," there are two meanings: first, the completeness of the dharmas of the Way, which is perfect and subtle; second, [the meaning of] speech.
I request that you also explain in full the reasons why the preceding section praises the One while rejecting the Three;

herein, both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings contain two meanings which cannot be understood from a single perspective. The text briefly clarifies the intent behind the differences between the Sūtra and the Commentary’s interpretations (the "Note" [云云] refers to what has already been explained above).
In the subsequent section on "Cessation" (*śamatha*), there are two parts: cessation itself and its explanation.
In the subsequent section on "Request," the text consists of both prose and verse, each of which further has two parts: the request and the explanation.

Regarding the verses, the first two lines constitute the request, while the following two lines constitute the explanation. Furthermore, the text on the subsequent "Cessation" also contains both prose and verse, as well as sections of formal *śamatha*.
It can be understood that the explanatory prose for these two locations each consists of a single sentence.

Regarding the third section, the text of the request also contains both prose and verse, each having two parts: the first part requests [the teaching], and the second explains the long prose; this can be understood from the commentary.

Within the verses, the first two lines correspond to the request, while the remainder corresponds to the explanation. As for the term "eldest son," it refers to the one of wisdom among the assembly of śrāvakas.
Because his wisdom is foremost, it was previously stated that the Buddha declared him to be "foremost among me.

Furthermore, because he was the first to whom the Buddha spoke in this assembly, the first to receive a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), and the first to be entrusted with the teaching, he is called "foremost.

The general meaning of the three pauses and three requests has already been explained extensively at the beginning of the previous chapter; since this is merely a summary of those expedient means (*upāya*), it is called "concise" (*saṃkṣipta*).
The provisional is opened to reveal the real. *Sijiki*, Volume Eleven;

*Myōkyō Monku Sijiki*, Volume Twelve (from the section "Extensively Opening and Revealing" through the chapter "Exhausting the Buddhas of the Past," including the general questions and answers regarding the vehicles of humans and devas).
