Commentary, Volume Four. Regarding this passage, there are three sections: first, the division of chapters to indicate the roots; second, the analytical classification by means of topical categories (*arthamukha*); third, the formal explanation according to the text.

The first section has four parts: first, citing the sūtra to establish the chapter; second, listing the chapters to delineate the scope; third, also titled "The Three Below"; fourth... [text continues].

The four citations from the *Zhōuyì míng* (Explanations of Different Names in the Book of Zhou) serve as examples to clarify the present text, which is divided into three parts: first, the sectioning of the scriptural text;

second, the analytical examination by way of thematic categories; and third, the word-by-word commentary. Now, I maintain that this text may be broadly divided into five sections: first, the reiterated indication of its major structural divisions;

second, the general demonstration of the scope and limits of the text; third, the application of these divisions to the text itself; fourth, [the analytical examination]; and fifth, [the word-by-word commentary].

The eight topical gates (*aṣṭārtha-mukha*) provide a critical analysis (*viniścaya*) of the fivefold classification; according to that analysis, they are used to judge and explain [the text]. Regarding the first of these, "reiteration" (*punar-uddeśa*):
this refers to the repeated citation of the sūtra text to extensively clarify the opening of the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle.

It is called "reiteration" because it has already been cited previously at the beginning of the major structural divisions (*mahā-vibhāga*), and is now stated once more. This principle applies throughout the preceding and following sections. Furthermore, "extensive" (*vistara*) is contrasted with "concise" (*saṃkṣepa*).
The names are as explained later; the three categories—general and specific—may be understood by analogy with what precedes. There are seven chapters and a half in total.
This single phrase serves as a general indication of the textual boundaries, encompassing the entirety of the formal exposition (*bhāṣya*) of the Trace Gate (*jìmén*).

Previously, I cited the beginning so that one might know its commencement, but the full extent of the scripture was not yet known; therefore, it is stated here in its entirety. This text clarifies what was previously presented in summary.
The section on "the nature and limits of arising" follows; this is the next distinct topical division (*pṛthak-vibhāga*).
The text is divided into three parts [as indicated by the phrase "the text consists of three"]: this is based on the previous general classification, yet it is further subdivided and examined.

Within this text, as one approaches its conclusion, its essential nature (*tattva*) should properly be treated in six sections: first, indicating the number; second, listing their names; third, clarifying alternative names; fourth, citing examples; fifth... [and so forth].

Regarding the six modes of explanation (*ṣaḍ-vyākhyāna*) presented here, it is only through this method that their full scope is exhausted; otherwise, one would not know the extent of their categories at all.

How could this be called an "explanation of the text"? Following the direct meaning, there are four distinctions. Nevertheless, although there are these four and six [modes], they ultimately consist of only two:
namely, the agent and the object, or person and dharma. First, the enumeration is stated; second, the names are listed; third, the differences [are explained].
Regarding the title "The Four Examples," the first number refers to the general text, while the specific meaning consists of seven and a half items;

furthermore, there are three more to follow. This heading is placed first as an introduction. Below, three names are listed, each containing three meanings. Although each contains three, two are manifest and one is hidden.
"Hidden" refers to the textual location. Although there is this manifestation and concealment, one must not fail to recognize that each necessarily possesses all three meanings.
"Dharma-discourse" (dharmaparyāya) is the primary designation of its name; it refers to those of superior faculties (*agradhika*), who are the intended audience.

It is also called "the reason why" (*hetu*) and "the intention" (*abhiprāya*), which refers to the basis for the initial Dharma-discourse. These two [meanings] are explicit, whereas the textual passages do not mention them because they are implicit and can be understood by oneself.
The following two cases should be known by analogy. As for the term "superior faculties," this name is derived in contrast to the other two [levels of faculties].

The middle and lower [categories] are likewise so. Regarding the explanation of the names and meanings of the dharmas, they shall be revealed in sequence; they should universally apply to all. Why then speak of them separately as "upper"?
The preceding text already clarifies this, so there is no need for such prolixity here. As for the two distinct names for the "lower," each possesses its various meanings;

the examples can be understood from what precedes, so they will not be elaborated upon here. They are also called the "eight lower," which clarifies the alternative names for the dharmas; that is to say, the first three names are also [included therein].
Because they are named as such, these are the intended meanings of the three preceding dharmas;
that is, by manifesting them through alternative names, the meaning of the three preceding dharmas is made easy to understand. However, these two and three names are both mutually relative;

"dharma" is a name used in contrast to "analogy," and "principle" (li) is a designation used in contrast to "phenomenon" (shi). The same applies to the remaining two. Furthermore, principle has both general and specific aspects.
The present passage explains that "understanding" (tō) refers to the comprehension of the principles of past events; thus, it shares the same meaning as "principle" (ri).
This means that because one speaks by directly examining the underlying principle, it is called "Dharma-exposition" (hōsetsu). Here, Dharma is principle, and principle is Dharma.
"Events" (ji) are the analogies, and analogies are events; this is because worldly matters of principle are used as metaphors for the sublime principles of the supramundane Dharma.

"Formative activity" (*saṃskāra*) carries the meaning of proceeding toward, constructing, and assembling; because it is the functional capacity of conditions (*pratyaya*), it is called "formative activity.
Thus, these are three synonymous names for the same thing, which further clarifies the previous three meanings.
This is its specific [definition], while its general name is "pervasive" (*parispharaṇa*). It is so named because it is explained as pervading three times over a single function.
"To explain 'comprehensive' means to reveal and manifest. Next, regarding the examples that manifest [this], those have already been clarified as alternative names.
Here, it is shown that the faculties and dispositions (*indriya-mūla*) are likewise diverse; thus, the preceding "rivers" are established as three.

The *Record* cites the twenty-first chapter of that sutra, the "Chapter on Expedient Means," which contains teachings both extensive and concise. It further states: 'One who studies this abbreviated Prajñā knows all dharmas.'"

Regarding the relationship between the extensive and the concise: it is further stated that those of sharp and medium faculties, whether their minds are concentrated or distracted, all enter this gate;
since this gate is unimpeded, it is said that those of inferior faculties must necessarily enter as well. That the sutra does not explicitly mention them is due to brevity.

Furthermore, it is said that some refer to other sections [of the canon], where the teaching is understood to accommodate the three types of persons, thereby establishing the three faculties; these followers of the Three Vehicles study the Mahāyāna together.

The Master [Daoxuan] takes what is encompassed by these categories as his standard for classification, illustrating that to speak of the *Prajñāpāramitā* alone is "abbreviated," while to fully explain all six *pāramitās* is "extensive.

To begin from form and mind and conclude with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is "extensive"; whereas to simply say "the purity of form" and proceed directly to "the knowledge of all modes" constitutes the "abbreviated" aspect.
Now, although [others] compete to cite that scripture, it is essential that they do not [contradict] its literal meaning and intent.
How can these [passages] be reconciled? This refers to the three roots being explained in three cycles, as summarized in the essential teaching of that aforementioned sutra.
It is said that there is nothing beyond the brief and extensive teachings intended for those of lower, middle, and superior capacities. How, then, can this be reconciled with the present text?
Now, I shall forcefully provide a reconciliation: since there are already the superior and middle [capacities], they necessarily include the lower, as well as the brief and extensive explanations.

I have included [this] within my own summary; however, how can these three cycles of exposition be called "concise"? As for the principle of "the medium being broad," it is truly difficult to comprehend.

Now, I fear that what has been cited does not even reach the essential point, as it has not yet been thoroughly investigated. Even if one were to grasp the actual meaning, it would still not coincide with the intent of this section.
Herein, the primary purpose is to reveal the provisional to manifest the real; the Dharma is subtle and difficult to understand, and the capacities and natures of sentient beings are not uniform.
Because they are equal, there are distinctions of two or three; that sutra is not so—how can it serve as an example? From the beginning, it has never been said that this meaning is direct;
thus, its words have also been harmonized accordingly. To assume arbitrarily that although the text speaks of "examples," the intent lies in "analogy"—for what reason?
That sutra was not yet like this, for it still had three [categories] and spoke of them as three; how much more so in this case, which is already...?

It was not for the sake of explaining that there is this intention here; thus the commentary says (and so forth). If one grasps this intention, the designation "existence" can be understood as consistent;
otherwise, it would merely be a vain proliferation.
Next, the fourth section of critical analysis refers to organizing and clarifying what was previously categorized. Within this, there are four parts, the first of which is general.

This consists of four parts: first, the indication of the meaning; second, the enumeration and sequential listing of their names; third, the explanation according to those names; and fourth, the establishment of the preceding meaning.

Within this, the essential point is to analyze the previously categorized sections by means of ten meanings, and further to analyze and establish those three categories through five successive rounds of question and answer.
Because the significance and scope of these ten meanings are profound and extensive, they are explained sequentially in turn. First, the explanation:
Regarding the enumeration of the headings, one should know that these three cycles of text contain names, power, and number.

First, each of these eleven items possesses two meanings, which constitute ten pairs; the textual meaning fully contains these ten pairs, yet many of the ancients and moderns have errantly lost their perfect intent.

Now, in order to clarify the distinction between the partial and the perfect, this commentary is provided. Second, the "ten" simply clarifies the two aspects of person and dharma for the practitioner.
Third, among the nine types of persons, the first is a śrāvaka, while the remaining eight all pertain to the three vehicles.
Fourth, furthermore, among these persons, the first three correspond to the capacities of the roots of beings addressed by the three cycles of the formal teaching (*samyag-deśanā*) in this treatise;
they all obtain benefit upon hearing the three cycles. Within these benefits, the first is horizontal and shallow, while those below are vertical. Within the first horizontal category: [the first]...
The second [point] concerns the three cycles of realization (*parivarta*), while the first concerns the three cycles of bestowing predictions (*vyākaraṇa*); the remainder is discussed generally.
Furthermore, since the ten pairs constitute fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), there are [various] meanings [to be derived] (and so forth).

Next, although these ten chapters list ten titles, their broad essential meaning consists of only two: namely, the "discrimination" (*pien-chien*) of the two aforementioned essentials—person and dharma.
The first chapter discriminates the dharmas of the preceding three cycles; the subsequent nine chapters discriminate the three types of persons for whom those dharmas were intended.
By grasping this single principle, one may comprehend the essential core of the teaching; otherwise, one will not understand its significance.
The sequence of these ten [points] is self-evident from the text itself and does not require prior explanation.

Within the first chapter, there are three sections: first, the formal explanation; second, the clarification of the general and specific aspects; and third, the illustration of the person through questions and answers regarding the method.

Regarding the first, there are three distinct divisions; within each of these, the text first presents the heading and then proceeds according to it. There are three such textual passages, each of which first establishes the heading and subsequently follows it.

The sūtra text demonstrates their characteristics; within these demonstrations, each instance individually shows that, based on the specific [meaning], the general meaning is present along with the other two.

The first analogy is an illustration of the rare occasion when the teaching of the opening and revealing [of the Buddha-knowledge] occurs. Next, all [the following] are listed as analogies for the causes and conditions for opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*);
within these, the meaning of causes and conditions is demonstrated. Because the initial phrase regarding the cause has two directions, it is further distinguished below.
"Taking up" refers to being startled and entering [the teaching] due to what was induced by past conditions; thus, it carries the meaning of "causes and conditions.

The "Guide" is a direct metaphor for revealing and leading one to the place of treasure; thus, it is an explanatory parable. The above explanation concludes by citing specific instances to illustrate the general principle.

Below, the intention of the general within the specific is clarified. Since the primary focus is on the majority and the principal matter, it specifically mentions the "three cycles" rather than the brief or incidental aspects.

It is said that while the "penetration" (*tong*) applies to both names and meanings, here we follow the names because the meaning is general while the name is specific. Thus, we speak of the "three cycles" (*san-zhou*) based on these three meanings;

"one intent" (*yi-yi*) refers to one among the three, which is the specific within the general. Since the capacity of the sentient beings (*ji*) possesses two meanings, it cannot be definitively categorized as either general or specific.
Below, the Dharma is used as an analogy to clarify the capacity. In the initial part of the question, the preceding person’s Dharma-nature is cited as being originally specific.

Now, the current explanation of the Dharma still applies by analogy to persons; it should be understood in this way. In the response, the first example illustrates what was previously explained generally, while the subsequent example illustrates what was previously explained specifically.
This is not merely a matter of logical inference; there is also textual evidence for it, which one will know for oneself later on. To avoid prolixity, I shall not elaborate further here.
Thus, this first question also clarifies the person; why then speak only of the Dharma? It is because the preceding text and its meaning serve as the precedent for this.

(As stated above). Next, regarding the proponents of existence and non-existence: this refers to those śrāvakas who are to be converted, who maintain that [phenomena] truly and definitively exist or do not exist. Although the text contains both meanings, ancient masters were biased in their adherence;
therefore, I shall now refute and reconcile them to reveal their perfect interpenetration. While this is presented in the context of the śrāvaka vehicle, its meaning applies universally.
Third, regarding the statement that "the initial practice of the three vehicles is discussed separately," there are two parts: first, the introduction; second, the formal explanation.
Within the explanation, there are three sections: first, the presentation of the old [interpretations]; second, the refutation of those two [positions]; third, the correct explanation.

Regarding the first, the presentation of the two schools: the first school first presents its thesis that [emptiness] definitely exists, and subsequently presents its refutation of non-existence to demonstrate that it definitely exists.

There are those who maintain that there is a sequence, which is also twofold: first, describing their thesis that a sequence definitely exists; second, refuting that thesis to establish that it definitely does not exist.

Regarding the establishment of its being indeterminate, within the refutation, first the sutra is cited, then the meaning of that sutra is used to refute existence and clarify non-existence, and third, this sutra is reconciled to clarify the intent behind the mention of "existence.
Furthermore, the *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness) is the initial practice; the refutation therein concerns the outer ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).

This refers to the initial stage of practice; knowing the One Vehicle means not being deluded regarding the Dharma. This citation presents the essential meaning of that sutra. How could it be anything less than this?
The following section correctly refutes the attachment to existence; the two preceding schools each fixed their calculations on either existence or non-existence.
Next follows the refutation of errors, which consists of two parts: first, the statement of the deviation; second, the detailed explanation of the deviation.

"Deviation" refers to contradicting the text, and "error" refers to abandoning the meaning. Both schools should each possess these two faults; however, in this commentary, we shall first clarify how the Guangzhai school contradicts the text.
The text states: "This is based on the illumination of reality. Now, [the Guangzhai school] insists that [emptiness] definitely exists; therefore, it is [in error].

Regarding those who deviate from the sequence of the text and lose the meaning—since the three points being refuted are all matters of meaning, they are cited alternately. Below, taking the underlying intent, [the author] separately critiques Guangzhai and Kaishan;
for them, [the teaching] is exclusively provisional (*upāya*). Guangzhai maintains that the provisional should be employed to manifest the real (*bhūta-artha*), and thus he specifically refutes it.
The initial citation of his position corresponds to the second phrase of the preceding text. As for the phrase "it should also," etc., this takes up [that point].
I shall challenge this meaning to illuminate the principle that the four vehicles are appropriate for the world.

If one grants that there are three baskets (tripiṭaka) based on the doctrine of the three vehicles, then since the three vehicles have those who are to be transformed, there must also be a principal who transforms them; this is called the Buddha of the Three Baskets.

Since those transformed by this teaching possess reality while the transformer is exclusively provisional, it is now appropriate that these two serve as the transformer and the transformed. This point is not analogous to the previous case.
The *Jì* (Commentary) states: "The 'present' in the current text refers to this [position]; it is a provisional concession made to that school in order to rescue its doctrine.
This meaning generally clarifies that while the cause exists, the fruit does not."
Now, from "The present explanation" onwards is the third section, the formal exposition. Within this, there are three parts: first, a brief clarification of the essential meaning;

second, an extensive explanation by citing sutras and treatises; and third, a specific clarification of the great significance. Regarding the first part, it begins by stating that one must not hold biased attachments, followed by an explanation of the reasons for this.

It clarifies that the sutra possesses two meanings; thus, the first phrase [of the previous section] previously refuted the Guangzhai school’s insistence on a fixed [interpretation], as their view deviates from the literal text and its underlying meaning. This is now being demonstrated.
Regarding this, one cannot say that it definitely exists; the second phrase [of the verse] refutes the Kai-shan school’s position that it definitely does not exist.
Thus, while both meanings are present, neither can be definitively adhered to—this is the essential meaning of this sutra.
Below, the sutras and treatises are cited to provide a broad explanation, which consists of four parts; first, the citation of the treatise.

Regarding the sequential explanation of the sutras: first, [the text] examines whether there is or is not [attainment] from the following three assemblies; second, it provides a general conclusion based on the following four points, beginning with the exhortation.
First, citing the treatise to clarify that śrāvakas receive the prediction (vyākaraṇa), it initially clarifies the distinctions among śrāvakas, which are fourfold.

Furthermore, it clarifies whether or not they obtain the prediction; since this text cites them in full, the meaning is explained according to the sequence. The first two [points] are not from the sutra.
That which was addressed by the latter two [sections] is precisely this. Next, regarding the reconciliation of the scriptural text, there are four meanings, yet they are not exhaustive;

therefore, by adding what is clarified in the present sutra to reconcile and explain them, there are five types that fully exhaust the reality. Within these, there is a general heading followed by specific explanations, and within the explanations, there are five distinct parts:
first, the explanation of those with fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*); second, the regression of the great [bodhisattvas]; third, the response and transformation; fourth... [fifth].
Regarding those of the five types of overweening pride who are initially fixed in the Mahāyāna: they are so named from their past state because they take the small fruit as certain;
thus they are called "fixed in nature. Next, in explaining "regression," the causes for taking the small [vehicle], such as weariness and fatigue, are as stated in the text:

"The Buddha-way is long and distant," and so forth. The citations from the sūtras are given under different names; it is not that there are two distinct types based on beginning and end, or sudden and gradual.
Therefore, it is said that they are distinct; because these individuals regress from the Great Vehicle and take up the Lesser Vehicle, they are said to have "regressed from the bodhicitta.
Regarding the Śrāvakas, there are three explanations: the first two concern the real (the "object"), while this one concerns the provisional (the "agent").

Because the provisional and the real respond to one another through the benefit of "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*), they are called "responsive manifestations" (*nirmāṇa-śrāvaka*). Fourth, regarding "arrogance," it is not a mistake to call them "superior"; rather, they are arrogant toward what is superior.

Regarding the "five types of conceit" (*abhimāna*) mentioned above, the Mahayana has both a heading and an explanation. There are those who, having heard little of the sound of the Four Truths, awaken to themselves;
and those who, having heard the sound of the Buddha-way’s great function, benefit others. "Little" refers to hearing that sound, while "great" refers to the sound being heard by them.
These five—the first four do not go beyond the provisional and the real, and generally concern the past—while this fifth one is precisely this sutra.

Regarding the fourth point, "Opening the Assembly": this is so named because it concludes the explanation of the "upper assembly" above and clarifies the two meanings of existence and non-existence below.

According to the intent of this passage, there should be four propositions: first, clarifying that [the teaching] exists from the perspective of the past; second, clarifying that it does not exist from the perspective of the present;

third, clarifying that since the real (the ultimate) possesses both [existence and non-existence], the provisional (the conventional) is identical to the real, and thus likewise possesses both existence and non-existence; and fourth, clarifying that those of the class who harbor overweening pride do not fall into any of the preceding three cases.
Since it is neither existent nor non-existent, there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) that summarize [the teaching] and exhort the practitioner:
even the realization of the fourfold lack of direction (*anupāda*) cannot be grasped, let alone adhering to each one individually; therefore, it is simply "not so.

Below this, the third section further distinguishes between the Mahāyāna and Śrāvaka perspectives regarding existence and non-existence. Because this single principle remains while all else is exhausted, there are three parts within it.

This means that within the fourfold structure of the introduction, the explanation, the conclusion, and the summary: first, the provisional [teaching] is clarified; second, the real [teaching] is clarified; third, the intent of the three sutras correctly clarifies one’s own reality;

and fourth, having clarified one’s own [reality], one is then able to [benefit] others. As for the subsequent conclusion: the previous conclusion exhorted the universal application of both the capacity and the object, whereas the present conclusion specifically discusses the capacity alone.

The above concludes the general discussion on whether the Śrāvakas transformed by the three cycles [of teaching] possess provisional or ultimate [attainments]. Below is the explanation of the two meanings of "thick" and "thin.

As for those who are "deluded," it means they are capable of being confused and disordered; it does not mean they are not fixed [in their nature]. If that were so, the character [for delusion] would properly follow the radical for the mind (*xin*).

Next, regarding "thin" (*bo*), it retains the radical for "broad" (*bo*); it is not the case that following "broad" (*bo*) and then "bondage" (*bo*) constitutes using "broad" as a loan character (*jiezi*). This was previously [stated].
Regarding this person discussed in the treatise, their nature and conduct reveal the origins of the distinctions among the three cycles. Within this, there are three parts:

first, citing the old interpretations to refute them; second, the correct explanation; and third, the initial section which, without yet explaining the delusions of those with superior faculties, subsequently explains the thickness and thinness [of the afflictions] of those with inferior faculties.
In the initial section, one first identifies the causes of their delusions, which will necessarily differ from those of the inferior faculties, and subsequently clarifies those very delusions.

The description of this state of "hesitation" (zhíchú) below clarifies the causes of success and failure. In the initial section, it is precisely because the entry and exit via principle and teaching differ that confusion arises.
In the subsequent section on success and failure, "hesitating over principle and teaching" and "floundering over entry and exit" both describe an appearance of indecision and instability;
for this reason, success and failure result. Below, this is further analyzed in relation to the three [vehicles].

The faculties reveal their degrees of thickness or thinness; those whose delusions regarding the teachings are manifold cling to the oneness of principle, and thus it is not appropriate for them to be manifold.

For this reason, one realizes that the next two [categories] can be understood accordingly. Because these correspond to the thick, the medium, and the thin, they constitute three; it is precisely for this reason that the teaching is presented in three ways.
Next, the refutation of that which is not the Middle Way is divided into three parts: first, a general refutation; second, specific objections; and third, a concluding summary of the refutation.

Regarding the statement "it is not so," the reason it is not so is as follows in the subsequent objections. As for the initial objections that refute [the position], they directly seize upon the essential points of the preceding argument to challenge and dismantle them.

The first sentence is a general censure of the conditions for meditative concentration (*samādhi*); because there is no definitive certainty regarding its meaning, this serves as a comprehensive critique.
If they are further distinct, it means that "small" and "great" are themselves further divided into "small" and "great," thus constituting a subordinate classification of these three.
Within this, each instance first restates what is asserted and then subjects it to refutation. Regarding the first, one should conclude by stating:

"Since it is said that after attaining the fruit, one wanders in contemplation, there should no longer be such delusions. Regarding the middle [category], since they are clearly not mutually inclusive, there should likewise be none.

Regarding this doubt, as for the subsequent difficulty concerning the confusion of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-saṃmoha*), [the text] restates the previous two [points] as being from the past, while this one point corresponds to the present correct assembly.

This is because, since his words do not distinguish [them], this doubt arises without cause, leading to this objection (and so forth). As for the conclusion stating "advancing and retreating" (*jin-tui*):
Yuanxian says that "advancing" refers to great confusion and "retreating" refers to small confusion. However, I say that the previous two [points] refer to the past.
To raise an objection against this is to retreat; to resolve it according to the present context is to advance.
Since neither path has a fundamental tenet and the reliance on provisional teachings lacks a basis, it cannot be employed.

Next, within the formal explanation, there are two parts. First, the preliminary determination of the faculties (*indriya*) and afflictions (*kleśa*), which serves as the basis for what follows; this constitutes the second part of the formal explanation.
Regarding the first of these, the reason for determining these two at the outset is that they constitute the essential core (*siddhānta*) of this section.

The reason the previous explanation failed was precisely because it lacked this essential core. Since these two are mutually dependent, one must first determine the three vehicles (*triyāna*). [This leads to] the attainment of the state of an *ārya*.

Since the fruit does not reside in further discussion of the nature of the faculties (*indriya*)—as both the pervasive delusions and their specific counterparts have already been eliminated—it is necessary to discuss its specific delusions.
If one were to speak directly of the nature of the faculties and the delusions, cause and effect would not be distinguished, nor could the pervasive and the specific be discerned;

this is not the intended meaning here, and therefore it is necessary to first establish the distinctions. In the subsequent formal explanation, there are two parts: first, an explanation based on four propositions and four types of persons; second, [an explanation based on...]

Regarding the explanation of the three faculties (*indriya*) in three grades: first, at the beginning, four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are presented; subsequently, the four types of persons are explained in detail.
The initial statement that "this constitutes four" means that the two aforementioned matters together form the four propositions.
The four names listed below all result from differences caused by past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), which give rise to these three cycles. By means of these four...

Regarding the four types of people corresponding to the three cycles [of teaching]: the first three phrases correspond sequentially to the three cycles, while the latter phrase—referring to those who have already established a karmic connection—is the primary audience for the preceding three.
As for the subsequent re-explanation in the text, it takes those four and condenses them into three;
the *Ji* (Record) states: "In the second explanation, the middle two phrases should be taken as the main text," which is what the current text says.
For those of middling or inferior capacity, some leave out the remaining characters or treat the characters for the inferior faculty as a separate lower verse.
Now, since it was previously stated that the first two [verses] constitute the superior faculty, the third verse should be taken as the middling faculty and the fourth as the inferior faculty.

Furthermore, since it was subsequently stated that the "middle" refers to the intermediate portion, the first verse should be taken as the superior faculty and both the second and third verses as the middling faculty.
Because it is the same as the previous case, the text simply says "those of inferior faculties" and provides a commentary (as indicated by "云云").

Since this principle applies universally, even those who are of the fourth [level] can be considered "suitable vessels," for although they are heavy and dull, they have the karmic affinity to hear [the teaching] three times from beginning to end.

Thus, the subsequent passage states: "If one hears even a single phrase and rejoices in it, all are granted the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; how much more so for those who hear it in its entirety?"

Regarding the sequential explanation according to the three faculties and three grades, the previous discussion addressed the direct path alone, where differences in the thickness of afflictions were considered;

thus, three distinct explanations were given. Here, we further clarify that for those of the three faculties entering the direct path, there are likewise three grades based on the thickness of their delusions.

The preceding analysis was a single, isolated treatment, whereas this current one appears to be a comprehensive exposition. Among these, the first three grades correspond to the "thin" level, while the middle three grades correspond to the "medium" level.

Because the lower three [levels] are extremely thick and the upper is thin, one hears it once; because the middle is middling, one hears it twice; and because the lower is extremely thick, one hears it thrice.
This is also due to differences in awakening and understanding; thus, knowledge and vision are likewise not uniform. Why is this so?

Next, by citing the Small Vehicle as an analogy to reveal the Great, the *Record* states: "All sixteen moments are called untainted (*anāsrava*); yet until the fifteenth moment, one still undergoes [the results of past karma]."
Regarding the names [of the stages], all three grades enter the first dwelling (*ādikṣānti*). Above, this is explained by taking the noble ones (*ārya*) of the Three Vehicles as the basis;

below, it may further be explained by taking ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) as the basis. That is to say, regarding the three delusions that obstruct the principle of the three truths: in the upper grade, one breaks all three upon first hearing;

in the middle grade, one breaks two; and in the lower grade, one breaks one. In the middle grade, one breaks three upon first hearing; in the middle grade, one breaks two; and in the lower grade, one breaks one.
Upon hearing this, one understands that these are all examples of the same essence, such as the principle that gross afflictions are eliminated first;
since this meaning also exists [in other contexts], one should reflect upon it according to this explanation.

The following clarifies "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) and "non-transformation. "Transformation" is a term for change or transition. Above, it was clarified that because the [karmic] thickness and thinness are uneven, there are three cycles of unequal duration.
From here on, it clarifies the distinctions in the benefits obtained by receiving the teachings of these three cycles;

that is, because there are differences between transformation and non-transformation, there is awakening and understanding attained at three distinct locations. This, then, clarifies the benefits of the three cycles.

Because it begins with the gradual, it proceeds gradually; within this, there are also three parts: first, describing the old [interpretation]; second, refuting it; and third, the correct explanation.
Regarding the first of these, three points are clarified, the first of which is awakening, and the second two clarify the meaning of "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*).

This is easily understood. However, this merely clarifies the sense of transformation without further discussion of non-transformation; thus, it does not fully accord with the headings of the treatise. Below, [the correct explanation] follows.
The difficult statement clarifies that [the opponent's position] is incorrect. First, the commentary on "for the sake of benefit" (*li*) and what follows is cited to challenge and censure it.

If one acts for the sake of benefit, then all would equally become superior; yet if all were superior, there would be no middle or inferior. Since there are indeed middles and inferiors, there is no sense of "transformation. Next, an analogy is raised to manifest this point; the example is extremely pertinent.
Within this, there are four logical sequences (*shishu*): first, stating the established position; second, raising the objection; third, providing the refutation; and fourth, concluding the argument.

The text omits its definitive conclusion, yet it can be inferred through reflection. Having heard the testimony of the first fruit (*srotāpatti*), one realizes what was previously non-existent; hearing it again, there is a difference. This case is likewise so (and so forth).

Because this [previous explanation] is not yet appropriate, the following provides the correct interpretation. This section has two parts: first, the correct interpretation; second, the critical examination (*viniścaya*). Within the first part, there are four sections:

first, a general explanation of the four [noble truths]; second, a specific explanation; third, the conclusion; and fourth, the analogy. First, the general explanation of the meaning of "turning" (*parivṛtti*).

Because they are indeterminate, they proceed from conditions; because they are twofold, they serve as the transforming conditions (*pariṇāmanapratyaya*). One should know that since the shallow teaching briefly cites both good and evil, it thereby encompasses all [phenomena], and thus it is "universal" (*sāmānya*).
Below, the text correctly clarifies these three [aspects], and thus they are "particular" (*viśeṣa*). Regarding the points where this differs from the old [interpretations], there are two meanings:
first, the old [view] refers only to the present, whereas this treatise includes past lives; second, the old [view] possesses only the "transforming" [aspect].
If it were neither manifest nor evolving, or if there were only present conditions without a cause, or if there were only evolution, the faults would be the same as those mentioned previously.

Although this differs from the former [position], it accords with the essential meaning of our own tenet. One should categorize the three metaphors within the illustration: the metaphor of the three knives corresponds to the three faculties;

the metaphor of cutting one piece of wood with them all corresponds to the simultaneous severing of afflictions and realization of the principle; and the metaphor of the equal benefit corresponds to the three [faculties] having distinctions of sharpness and dullness.

The following section correlates with the previous analogy, merely clarifying that although they differ, they are ultimately the same. Within the "Discrimination" (Liao Jian) section, there are two rounds of question and answer:

the first clarifies the identity or difference of the initial realization (*prathama-adhigama*), while this section clarifies the difference or identity regarding subsequent entry into realization (*anupraveśa*). The first question asks: "If one has not yet realized as previously [described], does one still possess it in this stage?

The response is: "No. This clarifies that there is no substantial essence of true cultivation; this reveals the meaning of its non-existence. Cultivation proceeds in accordance with principle (*tattva*), yet remains free from conceptual grasping.

"Cultivating that which is not cultivated" refers to the next stage, "cultivation by means of conditions" (*pratyaya-bhāvanā*). This arises because of the preceding [stage]. That which is not yet realized is called "conditioned" (*pratyaya*);

once realized, it is called "real" (*bhūta*). Looking toward what is above, that which has not yet reached the ultimate is further cultivated and advanced; this is also termed "conditioned. "Real" is "suchness" (*tathatā*).

What was previously differentiated, the subsequent is likewise so. [The questioner] did not answer; within each of these meanings, there is nothing that is not clearly elucidated. Among them, there is...
The reason why these two [aspects] can be known as "non-existent" is that they resemble the meanings of horizontal and vertical, respectively;

none of these have been explained, so one may reflect upon them. Next, regarding the explanation of "awakening" and "non-awakening," this is the second point within the benefits of the three turnings.

The previous section clarified the beginning and used "turning" (*parāvṛtti*) as its name; this section clarifies the actual state, and thus uses "awakening" (*bodhi*) as its heading—hence the phrase "awakening and non-awakening."

The Awakened One explains that although the meaning of the three faculties discussed previously applies generally to all three vehicles (*yāna*), for the time being, the text uses the three faculties to provide an interpretation.
From this point downward, the discussion of the meaning of the three faculties is conducted specifically in relation to the three vehicles, whereby the meaning becomes clear and manifest.

Although it concerns the three faculties, the text only clarifies the "favorable prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) for the śrāvaka; thus, it appears to clarify only one [faculty], while the other two remain as yet unmanifest.

Now, based on the principle that those who have not awakened to the clarity [of reality] and those who have not awakened to its exhaustion must all awaken, this is established as the structural outline (*ko-in*). Within this, there are two parts:
first, the general; second, the specific. First, regarding the general: this generally discusses the three vehicles and the three faculties, noting their similarities and differences.

It consists of an initial question and a subsequent explanation. In the question, first the three [faculties] as taught in other sutras are cited, and then, based on those sutras, they are shown to be identical to these three.

These two [terms] are expressions of doubt, meaning: "Is it like this, or is it not like this? However, from the following passage in the Sūtra, there is a subsequent combined explanation of the text consisting of two sentences:
the first is a response to the distinct meanings listed in the Sūtra, and the second is a response to the correct and comprehensive meaning.

Yet, because the distinct [meanings] have not yet been fully understood, it says "for the time being" (*yǐwǎng*). Now, since this mind-attainment cannot follow the distinct [meanings], the [previous] interpretation is incorrect.

This is precisely because the meaning that the three vehicles (triyāna) universally possess the three faculties (indriya) is intended here. From the following section of the present sutra onward, there is a desire to provide a specific explanation;
since it discusses the three vehicles individually, each possessing its own three faculties, it is termed "specific" (betsu).
All of them awaken and understand, and there are none who do not awaken. Within this, one first poses questions based on the sutra, as there are many such doubts, which will now be explained.

Because this [delusion] is destroyed, this question arises; it constitutes the three cycles of realization (*parivarta*). From "Pratyekabuddhas and below" onwards is the second section, which explains the assembly:

first the Pratyekabuddhas, then the Bodhisattvas. Regarding the first [section], there is no need for further elaboration on the meaning; it clarifies the realization of the Śrāvakas, which subsumes the Pratyekabuddhas.
There are three faculties (*indriya*) and three types of realization, which subsume the three faculties and three realizations of the Pratyekabuddhas. Next, he cites the beginning...
The final two passages establish the meaning through scriptural evidence; because the textual meaning is complete, it is certain that [the three faculties] exist. The old commentary states:
