First, while the four points of the preceding general chapter are all discussed in terms of the "transformer" (the Buddha), the chapters on the three times are all explained in terms of the "transformed" (sentient beings). Thus, the text consistently states: "These sentient beings follow the Buddha..."
The "hearing the Dharma" mentioned in the verse below refers precisely to the transformation, practice, and realization [of the teachings].
Furthermore, whereas the preceding principle of "oneness" contained four phrases—opening and so forth—here there are only three, and the "opening" is not explicitly clarified.

This is because it is either a mutual abbreviation or the underlying principle is actually equal. Alternatively, one may interpret this according to the intent of the treatise. For now, we shall follow the general outline of our own school’s tenets.

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent "Extensive Explanation of the Chapter on Śākyamuni": previously, in the first section, two chapters were presented—namely, the extensive explanation of the two brief [chapters] above—which constituted the general and specific fourfold [exposition].

Having already extensively explained the brief opening and manifestation of all Buddhas, what follows here is precisely the extensive explanation of the chapter on Śākyamuni; therefore, it is stated thus.
Within this section there are four parts: first, the presentation of the headings; second, the six meanings with one omitted; third, the classification of these five;

and fourth, the detailed explanation thereof. The first three [parts] are understandable from the context. Next, regarding the explanation of "opening the provisional" (*kaikwan*), the scriptural text has three sections:

first, clarifying the illumination of capacities, beginning with "according to their... and so forth; second, clarifying the bestowing of transformation, which describes the past; these two together are termed "opening the provisional."
Furthermore, the entire literary style should be divided into two main sections: first, clarifying the identity of the Way; second, correctly elucidating the manifestation of transformation.
Within the section on the manifestation of transformation, the five or six categories are further opened up; this is because the text follows a principle of brevity and essentiality.

Thus, the passage concerning the identity of the Way is still situated within the explanation of the opening of provisional means—this should be understood. In the commentary, all three texts are fully explained. First, regarding the "conformity through identity," it begins as follows:

Next, I shall explain the term "I," followed by the explanation of "Thus am I. "I" refers to one's own person. "Thus" correctly clarifies that the methods of transformation and guidance are identical;

it means first there was divergence, and subsequently there was reunion. The reason for this is precisely because their essence (*tattva*) is the same, and therefore their function (*vṛtti*) cannot but be the same;
furthermore, they both emerged from the turbid world. Next is the explanation of "illuminating the provisional capacities," which consists of two phrases and contains three meanings.

The "three" refers to the faculties (*indriya*), desires (*chanda*), and dispositions (*gotra*). Although this passage contains the two terms "desires" and "dispositions," it simultaneously encompasses these three meanings.

Why is this so? The text states "desires," followed by "original disposition" (*mūlagotra*); these two terms, together with the phrase "profound mind" (*gambhīracitta*)—which carries the meaning of "faculties"—thus comprise all three.
Furthermore, the verse states, "Knowing the desires and dispositions of sentient beings," which comprehensively summarizes them to manifest their presence throughout the three periods of time.

There are three aspects. Next, the three meanings are explained: first, because it is practiced from the beginning, it is called the "faculty" (*indriya*); second, because there is present delight, it is "desire" (*chanda*);

third, because it arises when meeting conditions at a later time, it is "nature" (*prakṛti*). Taking these three together as the cause, and the Buddha’s illumination that transforms them as the condition, there is the "response.
Regarding the "expedient means" (*upāya*) explained below, "expedient response" refers to the benefit [of the teaching]. "Opening" means bestowing.
This also generally refers to the provisional teachings (*upāya*) of the four periods in the past. The subsequent explanation clarifies the revelation of the reality (*tattva*);

the phrase "in this manner" generally refers to the provisional dharmas of the three [vehicles] within the four [periods]. While the previous chapters on the Buddhas all stated "this dharma," the present statement "in this manner" clarifies that the provisional is established for the sake of the real;
thus, making such a statement is precisely the revelation of the real. The preceding general chapter merely concerned the capacity for the three [vehicles].

In the "Chapter on the World," the Buddha-vehicle belongs to the subject (the capacity), while the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā) pertains to the object; however, these two phrases here both pertain to the subject and the object alike.

Nevertheless, because the revelation of reality must necessarily possess the fourfold [truth], this is clarified by the term "all. That which is to be known by the knowledge of all modes is precisely the "one" that constitutes the practice;
thus, one should know that "all" applies to both the subject and the object, and that which is to be known is precisely the object of the knowledge of all modes.

This principle is expressed through a single phrase for the sake of brevity and clarity; since these three aspects are mentioned interchangeably, the meaning of "person" (*pudgala*) is self-evident and thus not explicitly stated.

Next, regarding the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), the term "explanation and opening" (*śe-kai*) combines the underlying intent to establish the heading, thereby explaining and clarifying what was previously opened up.
The reason for this is clearly explained in the subsequent text. The phrase "about to raise the equality" (*jǔděng*) refers to further dividing this passage into two sections;
as for the term "meaning" (*yì*), it refers to the great purport regarding the concealment and manifestation of the ancient and the present.

As the text itself explains, at the beginning of that explanation, its meaning is indicated by the words "that which was not yet clear," which means that what was previously obscure is now being elucidated here. Regarding the section beginning with "its dharma" (*qífǎ yǐxià*):

This is the correct elucidation. Within it are two parts: first, an explanation based on the current text regarding how existence is non-existence; second, taking the main body of the text below to clarify how non-existence is existence.

Regarding the first part, there are again two meanings: first, the cause of existence and non-existence; second, the actual cause of existence and non-existence. As for the actual cause of existence and non-existence:
it is precisely because the essential nature of the *dharmadhātu* is pure, tranquil, and uniform like space that its phenomena...
This refers to the state of the essence being pure; it is the profound, singular characteristic, illustrated by the metaphor of space. All natures within the *dharmadhātu* rely upon this purity;
they are signless, free from defilement, profoundly unified, omnipresent, and immovable—like space.

These three meanings are eternally pervasive and unimpeded, and thus serve as metaphors for the aforementioned three meanings. Precisely because of these meanings, there is only one, not two or three. This passage merely clarifies...
Because the prose section (*nirgāthā*) fully clarifies both existence and non-existence, the verse says, "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions," and so forth.

The mention of the "Buddha-lands of the ten directions" is precisely intended to rely upon the universal manifestation of the Dharma-body (*dharmatā*) to clarify the basis for existence and non-existence. Furthermore, one should correctly understand that because there are no five [aggregates], there is existence;
because there are five, there is non-existence; and because there are five, there is non-existence, as clearly explained in the text. That is to say:
"There are no five" (and so forth). The passage beginning with "furthermore, there are none" clarifies their non-existence.

Briefly stated, since there is nothing existing during the three intermediate times, there are simply no things corresponding to the numbers five, three, seven, or nine. The section beginning with "it is only because" clarifies that existence does not occur.

Previously, it was shown that while there is [existence], there is only one and not three; now, based on that very existence, it is clarified that there is both existence and non-existence, yet only one.

That there are three [aspects] also has its reasons. That there is the "correct" [aspect] despite the heavy obstructions of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) is the reason why that which is non-existent appears as existent.
The fact that it cannot actually be proclaimed clarifies that there is no reality. The necessity of employing the following [teachings] clarifies the existence of skillful means (*upāya*).

Because it is the correct elucidation, it is said that "existence" exists; thus, the subsequent citation of evidence and the analysis below serve as examples to manifest this. This is the intent of citing the five turbidities to explain the opening [of the teaching].
This meaning is particularly important and should be contemplated to the utmost.
Next, in the formal explanation of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), it says "singing the number": "five" is the number, which is expressed through speech;
because they are spoken of together, they are called "singing the number. Since it speaks of all Buddhas, how could it refer solely to Śākyamuni? It applies generally to those who preceded him.
Because they are distinct, it was previously stated that they are "mutual. As for "turbidity" (*kaṣāya*), it carries the meaning of being dregs, defilement, darkness, evil, and a lack of clarity;

therefore, other sutras also refer to them as the "five turbidities" (*pañca-kaṣāya*). Next, regarding the listing of the five names: these five things are all equally dark and filthy, causing the wondrous Way not to be manifest.
Below, to clarify their essence and characteristics, the phrase "such as this" (*evam*) is a term referring back to what precedes. That is to say—
This indicates the essential nature (*tattva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of what preceded. The *Record* states: "Regarding 'such as these' being the essential nature and characteristics:

the nature and characteristics of the [five] turbidities (*kaṣāya*) cannot be fully set forth in verse; therefore, it is merely stated briefly as 'such as these. Although the sūtra does not provide them in full, the commentary briefly describes them, referring back to the explanatory text to constitute the essential nature and characteristics together.
The text cited below is this very point: "Greed, stinginess, and so forth" refers to the two turbidities of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-kaṣāya*).

Furthermore, unwholesome speech pertains to both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), whereas only the corruption of life (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) is not explained in the sutra text because the three [corruptions] such as sentient beings necessarily exist within it.
As for the "essence and characteristics" (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), they range from "thus" (*evam*) up to "jealousy" (*īrṣyā*).
The term "thus" is used to introduce the name; first, the names listed above are further indicated as the preceding essence and characteristics.
However, since the sutra treats this concisely, it only mentions the three turbidities such as the *kalpa*; their essential characteristics must still be explained together.
As it says, "the time of the *kalpa*-turbidity" refers to the period when the four turbidities, such as life-span, have gathered; only then is it called the "time of disorder.

Thus, the sutra states that the "time of disorder" is precisely the time of the *kalpa*-turbidity, and "disorder" is itself the characteristic of the turbid and evil state. Next, [it speaks of] sentient beings.
"The gravity of defilements" refers to the period of the *sattva-kaṣāya* (the turbidity of sentient beings); the gravity of defilements is also the very characteristic of turbid evil.
Next, the mention of "avarice, greed, jealousy, and envy" briefly sets forth the essence of the *kleśa-kaṣāya* (the turbidity of afflictions), which is likewise the characteristic of turbid evil.
The Sūtra combines these points concisely to clarify them, while the Commentary (*Śāstra*) strives for ease of understanding by dividing them separately. Thus, [the text] first distinguishes them.
Emerging from its substance to manifest its characteristics, since these characteristics are the characteristics of the substance, both opening and closing are permissible.

The commentary text is divided into four parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; third, the arising; and fourth, the analysis. Regarding the initial passage, which states, "Thus it is" (*evam*), clarifying the substance and characteristics:
this is a brief citation of two characters from the Sūtra; it does not merely refer to these two characters alone.

Regarding the essence and characteristics (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), it is said that up to this point the text has not been able to provide a definitive determination; for now, we shall follow the commentary (*ṭīkā*). Within this section, there are five parts: first, the formal analysis of the essence and characteristics; second, the clarification of their sequence; third, the extensive detailed examination; fourth, the explanation of the four *siddhāntas*; and fifth, various miscellaneous explanations. Regarding the first part, the essence and characteristics, there are two sections: first, the combined heading, and second, the individual explanation. First, as for the [heading]: [The text continues: "The essence and characteristics are briefly explained in ten ways. What are these ten? First, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmadhātu* (the realm of phenomena); second, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena); third, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (the characteristics of phenomena); fourth, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmaviśeṣa* (the distinctions of phenomena); fifth, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmasamgraha* (the compendium of phenomena); sixth, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmaparyāya* (the categories of phenomena); seventh, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmanirukti* (the etymological explanation of phenomena); eighth, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmapravṛtti* (the manifestation of phenomena); ninth, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmavyavasthāna* (the systematic establishment of phenomena); and tenth, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmānupūrvī* (the sequential order of phenomena). These ten encompass all phenomena. Furthermore, regarding the first, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmadhātu*: the *dharmadhātu* is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*) which is the object of the wisdom of the Tathāgata. It is called "essence" because it is the fundamental substance of all phenomena. It is called "characteristic" because it is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena. This is because all phenomena are non-different from the *dharmadhātu*. As the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* says: "The *dharmadhātu* is the essence of all phenomena. As the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya* says: "The *dharmadhātu* is the characteristic of all phenomena. Thus, the *dharmadhātu* is both essence and characteristic. The following nine categories should be understood in the same manner. Second, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmatā*: *dharmatā* refers to the true nature of phenomena, which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It is called "essence" because it is the reality of all phenomena. It is called "characteristic" because it is the mark of the non-arising of all phenomena. This is because all phenomena are ultimately empty and without arising. As the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. As the *Madhyānta-vibhāga* says: "The *dharmatā* is the absence of the imagined nature within the dependent nature. Thus, the *dharmatā* is both essence and characteristic. The following eight categories should be understood in the same manner. Third, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmalakṣaṇa*: *dharmalakṣaṇa* refers to the specific characteristics of phenomena, such as the characteristic of solidity in earth, the characteristic of moisture in water, and so forth. It is called "essence" because it is the particularity of each phenomenon. It is called "characteristic" because it distinguishes one phenomenon from another. This is because all phenomena possess their own unique defining marks. As the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "The characteristic of earth is solidity. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "The *dharmalakṣaṇa* is the basis for the establishment of all phenomena. Thus, the *dharmalakṣaṇa* is both essence and characteristic. The following seven categories should be understood in the same manner. Fourth, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmaviśeṣa*: *dharmaviśeṣa* refers to the distinctions among phenomena, such as the distinction between wholesome and unwholesome, or the distinction between superior and inferior. It is called "essence" because it constitutes the specific quality of each phenomenon. It is called "characteristic" because it differentiates phenomena according to their varying natures. This is because all phenomena have diverse attributes. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The *dharmaviśeṣa* is the differentiation of the various faculties and powers of sentient beings. As the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* says: "The *dharmaviśeṣa* is the cause for establishing the various categories of phenomena. Thus, the *dharmaviśeṣa* is both essence and characteristic. The following six categories should be understood in the same manner. Fifth, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmasaṃgraha*: *dharmasaṃgraha* refers to the inclusion of all phenomena within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). It is called "essence" because it is the comprehensive totality of all phenomena. It is called "characteristic" because it demonstrates how all phenomena are subsumed under these categories. This is because all phenomena are contained within these classifications. As the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* says: "The *dharmasaṃgraha* is the gathering of all phenomena into the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. As the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* says: "The *dharmasaṃgraha* is the means by which all phenomena are gathered. Thus, the *dharmasaṃgraha* is both essence and characteristic. The following five categories should be understood in the same manner. Sixth, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmaparyāya*: *dharmaparyāya* refers to the various names and designations applied to phenomena, such as the names "form," "feeling," and so forth. It is called "essence" because it is the conventional expression of phenomena. It is called "characteristic" because it serves as the signifier for the meaning of phenomena. This is because all phenomena are designated by various names. As the *Mahāvyutpatti* says: "The *dharmaparyāya* is the gate through which the Dharma is taught. As the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* says: "The *dharmaparyāya* is the skillful means for entering the meaning of the Dharma. Thus, the *dharmaparyāya* is both essence and characteristic. The following four categories should be understood in the same manner. Seventh, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmanirukti*: *dharmanirukti* refers to the etymological explanations of phenomena, such as explaining that "form" (*rūpa*) is so called because it is subject to transformation (*rūpaṇa*). It is called "essence" because it reveals the underlying meaning of phenomena. It is called "characteristic" because it clarifies the linguistic definition of phenomena. This is because all phenomena require etymological analysis to understand their true meaning. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The *dharmanirukti* is the explanation of the words and phrases of the Dharma. As the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* says: "The *dharmanirukti* is the basis for the correct understanding of the Dharma. Thus, the *dharmanirukti* is both essence and characteristic. The following three categories should be understood in the same manner. Eighth, the essence and characteristics of the *dharmapravṛtti*: *dharmapravṛtti* refers to the arising and ceasing of phenomena, such as birth, abiding, change, and extinction. It is called "essence" because it is the temporal mode of existence of phenomena. It is called "characteristic" because it demonstrates the process by which phenomena manifest. This is because all phenomena undergo the cycle of arising and passing away. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "The *dharmapravṛtti* is the succession of causes and conditions. As the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* says: "The *dharmapravṛtti* is the
Regarding these two characters, "thus" (*evam*), they serve as a concluding reference to what was previously enumerated;

that is to say, that which possesses a substance and characteristics is called a "named object," and it is said that such an object must necessarily possess formal appearances (*lakṣaṇa*). Although the text here is somewhat abbreviated, the meaning is certainly present.
Therefore, after listing the names, it directly points [to them] by saying "thus," whereby both name and substance-characteristics are included therein. The Commentary follows this principle.
I have thus cited and designated them based on their etymological explanations (*nirukti*).

Next, in the list of explanations, regarding the first [category], the "essence" (*svabhāva*), there should be both a general and a specific essence, as there are two names—general and specific. However, in the text, only the specific one is mentioned.

Regarding the first *kalpa*, it is said to be "without distinction" (*nirviśeṣa*) because, in contrast to the other four which possess distinct essences, this one is the totality of those four; therefore, it is called "without distinction. These are equal.

The term *kalpa* (劫) is translated here as "time" (*kāla*). While it applies generally to long durations, although it may also apply to short ones, sūtras and śāstras frequently refer to *kalpa* as a long period;
therefore, it is rendered here in that sense. Regarding the short duration of a *kṣaṇa*, the treatise states:
"The shortest possible time is one *kṣaṇa*. Thus, a verse in the treatise says: "One hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute the measure of one *tatkṣaṇa*. *Kalpa* [is the term].
Sixty of these [kṣaṇas] constitute one *lava*; thirty of these [lavas] constitute one *muhūrta*; thirty of these [muhūrtas] constitute one day and night;
thirty days and nights constitute one month; twelve months constitute one year. Therefore, the *kṣaṇa* is the ultimate limit of brevity.

According to the sequence of this textual style, one should first translate the names and explain their meanings, as well as distinguish their durations; next, one should correctly identify their essential nature—that is, they have no separate substance, but...
The establishment of the meaning through the four immeasurables and the cited passages is easy to understand; however, the current text appears not to follow a sequential order.

For a detailed explanation, one should consult the two chapters on the "Great" and "Small," which have not yet been reconciled here. Regarding the sequence of the cited text that follows the explanation of the main body, it precisely clarifies that the four [immeasurables] collectively constitute the essence, and it also precisely clarifies the meaning of "turbidity.
Next is the essence and meaning of sentient beings, which shall be explained in the subsequent text; for now, I shall merely state:
That which has no separate substance refers to sentient beings; "sentient beings" have no separate substance other than being established as this designation upon the two dharmas of cause and effect.
The cited passage also explains the meaning of "turbidity" (*kaṣāya*). Because it is a name applied to these dharmas of cause and effect, it is a heavy defilement;
because it is heavy, it is turbidity. Next, the two substances and their meanings follow in sequence.

Within the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the mutual continuity of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) is spontaneously revealed; this is precisely the functional power of the seeds of prior karma, which likewise manifests spontaneously in the subsequent [moments].
Thus it is annotated (*yùn*). This is the sequential explanation, which is a specific interpretation. If explained generally, nothing transcends ignorance (*avidyā*);
thus, ignorance serves as the totality of the turbidities (*kaṣāya*). Next, regarding the explanation of the characteristics: this refers to the manifest forms and states of the five turbidities.

Yexian correctly explains the subsequent conclusion by broadly demonstrating the brief outline; within this, there are five distinct sections. Regarding the first section on the characteristics of the kalpa, it contains a heading, an explanation, and a conclusion.

As for the initial phrase "the four turbidities (*caturkaṣāya*) and so forth," the *Jì* (Commentary) states: "There are three—emptiness, formation, and destruction—but there is no 'turbidity of the kalpa' (*kalpakaṣāya*).

Within the abiding kalpa (*sthāyikalpa*), according to the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, from eighty thousand years down to thirty thousand, there was likewise no turbidity; it was only upon reaching twenty thousand years that turbidity arose."

Because the four *kaṣāyas* (defilements) increase and accumulate at the beginning of the five *kaṣāyas*, a minor eon (*antarakalpa*) is termed "defiled"; this is the general heading. Below, the four *kaṣāyas* are individually examined to reveal the characteristics of the eon-defilement (*kalpakaṣāya*).
Within this, there are the elements, the metaphors, and the application of the metaphors. Due to the accumulation of the four *kaṣāyas*, the three minor calamities arise.

Next, from the passage on "malice" (*vyāpāda*) onwards, it clarifies that the minor calamities arise due to the flourishing of afflictions (*kleśa*). Following that, it clarifies [the arising of the calamities] through the three minor [calamities].
Therefore, as the four turbidities increase, afflictions double in intensity; this is clarified by the section on the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

Following that, the section on the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) clarifies that because the afflictions of the eon are flourishing and blazing, the turbidity of views becomes intensely active. Next, the section beginning with "coarse and debased" clarifies that because of the preceding three, the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) arises.

Regarding the phrase "the years are crushed," it means that because of the four turbidities, the turbidity of life span (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) occurs: as the years accumulate to form a lifespan, the years are crushed and the lifespan is diminished.
Therefore, this is the summary of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). Within the analogies, the water represents the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*):

due to winds and waves, the water becomes turbulent and murky; because of the other four [turbidities], the eon is brought to turbidity. The wind represents the two turbidities of views and afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), while the waves represent the turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).

The fish and dragons represent the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). In the synthesis, the first part provides the formal correspondence, followed by two examples to assist in the understanding.

The first part clarifies that when it is said "time causes them to burn," it means they mutually defile one another. Next, two examples are cited: the burning of the grounds of the desire realm and the burning of the gardens;
these serve as clear illustrations of how time causes turbidity, thereby intensifying the other four turbidities (*kaṣāya*).

This concludes the summary of the characteristics of the *kalpa-kaṣāya*. One should know that the detailed exposition is as explained in the second chapter; herein, all descriptions refer to the most extreme cases.

The meaning of "turbidity" as explained in the treatise is as follows; the four subsequent examples illustrate the characteristics of the afflictions (*kleśa*) by means of metaphors corresponding to each of the five dull fetters (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*).
The characteristic of the mind of greed (*lobha*) is like the ocean receiving all streams; the characteristic of the mind of anger (*dveṣa*) is like a venomous snake (*āśīviṣa*) sucking poison.

The three subsequent examples illustrate how it agitates the world. [Note: *Rēhu* may be written as *rōhu*, but it should correctly be *āśīviṣa*; therefore, the term "poison" appears in the following text.]

The "snake" (*shé*) refers to the *huǐ* or *fù*, venomous serpents that "absorb poison," meaning they indulge excessively in their venom. "Nào" (pronounced *nǎo*, with the alternative reading *hāo*) means to disturb;

its meaning is the same as that of the *wán*. "Jù" (pronounced *xūyáo*) means clamor; it does not fit the context here. It is also pronounced *áo* and glossed as "distressed," but this is also not the intended meaning.

It should correctly be written as *yín* (pronounced *yújīn*). The commentary states: "A mind that cannot fathom virtue and righteousness is called *wán*; a mouth that does not speak [of them] is called *yín*."
Loyalty and trustworthiness constitute wisdom; however, those in this [present] state do not recognize at all the principles of right and wrong regarding both the mundane and supramundane realms.
"Measures" (du) refers to the standards of the Dharma; thus, the *Xiaojing* says, "Advancing and retreating may be measured.

To call it "not obtained" is to fail to enter [the truth]. A doubting mind is like casting a net: when things arise with doubt, how can one speak of the reality of the Way? These five conditions are thus distinct.
This was the characteristic of the *kleśa-kaṣāya* (defilement-turbidity). Next, the characteristic of the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya* (view-turbidity) is clarified:

these are the five sharp-facultied *mithyādṛṣṭis* (false views), which should likewise possess five characteristics. In the text, four are mentioned; the first two correspond to the second and third [of the five], while the latter two correspond to the remaining categories of the five.

To say there is no person when there is one is called *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (personality-view); to say there is a path when there is none is called *mithyādṛṣṭi* (false view). Furthermore, it should also be...

On the contrary, to claim that there is no path is what is called "adherence to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). That which is attained is not supreme is "adherence to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
To be biasedly attached to existence or non-existence is "extreme view" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). The *Ṣoḍaśākārajñāna-śāstra* lists their names at the beginning as follows:

first, self (*ātman*); second, sentient being (*sattva*); third, life-sustainer (*jīva*); fourth, living being (*jantu*); fifth, one who is born (*jāyaka*); sixth, nourisher (*poṣaka*); seventh, the multitude (*pudgala*); eighth, person (*manuja*); ninth, agent (*kāraka*).

Regarding these: the first is the "doer" (the ten *anusayas*), the second is the "ariser" (the eleven), the third is the "one by whom the *anusayas* arise" (the thirteen), the fourth is the "receiver" (the fourteen), the fifth is the "one by whom the *anusayas* are received" (the fifteen), the sixth is the "knower" (the sixteen), and the seventh is the "viewer. The sequential commentary explains:

within the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), there is ignorance and lack of clarity; to falsely conceptualize a self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*)—that which is actually non-existent—is designated as the "self."
This means that because one falsely conceives of a self arising within the aggregates (*skandha*) and other phenomena, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*).

Because one falsely conceives of existence within the aggregates and other phenomena, and falsely conceives of a self capable of receiving the long or short duration of a single lifetime's karmic retribution, they are called "living beings.

Because one falsely conceives of a self within the aggregates and other phenomena whose life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) maintains continuity without interruption, they are called "those who possess life" (*jīvaka*), and so forth, as explained at length in the treatise.

The explanations found in the *Zhonglun* (Madhyamaka-śāstra) and the *Fajie Cidi Chumen* (Introduction to the Stages of the Dharma Realm) cannot be recorded in full here. However, these sixteen [views] are provisionally based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

As for more recent interpretations, their numerical counts vary—increasing or decreasing—and their collective names differ; these are detailed in separate texts, which I have not yet had the opportunity to synthesize.

Because the deluded mind cannot comprehend this, it seizes upon it and establishes it as a "false self"; therefore, it is called the "sovereign master.

Such delusion is extreme; because of these extreme conceptualizations, one creates karma, and thus drifts and wanders through the suffering of the six realms of existence.
Regarding the sequence of retribution, there is again a further analogy to clarify that although one undergoes birth in various places, there is no fixed reality whatsoever;
yet to erroneously cling to it as being so extreme is the characteristic of turbidity.

Next, within the characteristics of life, because karma is indeterminate, the resulting life-span is likewise so; this is the characteristic of turbidity. Below is the summary and extensive demonstration.

The middle intends to clarify that both the Great and Small Vehicles are attained; therefore, it employs the four gates as a correspondence to the four kinds of characteristics.

In the first two sets of four gates, the subject and object are not distinct; because the means of entry may be skillful or clumsy, there is a second [set].
The second pair is likewise so. Thus, those who could not enter via the first two now all gain entry; they do not depend on another.

One should know that the four categories—knowing the faculties (*indriya*), obstructing the faculties, and so forth—are explained in the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as clarifying the meaning of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Since this meaning applies to both the Small and Great Vehicles, it is now being correctly employed here.
That principle is thus: if one thoroughly grasps the meaning of the preceding sections concerning the vehicle, the precepts, and the urgency of "warmth," then everything can be understood.

Next, regarding the fourth [section] of the previous summary of the ancient intent, this section uses the intent of this sutra to examine the meaning of the fourth phrase within the first of the four initial sections, thereby clarifying the supreme [truth].

At first, it was not permitted to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* because this particular class [of beings] constitutes an obstacle to this wondrous vehicle; however, this is not the case for all such individuals.

Therefore, it is said that at first they were not permitted to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Thus, it is said that while the obstacle is great, they immediately obtain the benefit of hearing the "Small" [teachings], and so these do not constitute an obstacle to the Small.
The question asks: "What is the reason for this? In the response, the first part answers regarding the greatness of the obstacle.

Therefore, the following response explains why it does not obstruct the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Regarding the first part of this, there is an interpretation that cites the intent of the Mahāyāna sūtras to provide a proof for the explanation.

Within that explanation, the initial section clarifies the fundamental turbidity; the section beginning with "If one hears... clarifies the dullness of the faculties; and the section beginning with "Hearing [the Dharma] increases the growths" cites the Mahāyāna sūtras to manifest the meaning of increasing obstructions.
"Old" refers to externalists and false teachers; "swift and foolish" (*jùn-chí*) refers to the milk, which is the Dharma; and "fond" refers to the swift [teacher].
"Evil" refers to the heterodox and the orthodox; "not knowing" refers to not knowing the medicine and the disease.

When the disease—consisting of both the general and specific delusions—arises from its root, it originates from the two medicines of the heterodox and the orthodox. "Medicine and tonics" refers to taking the medicine, which means practicing the two methods.
First, one uses impermanence and so forth to break the disease of false attachments to permanence and so forth, thereby providing a remedy.
Furthermore, instructing them to cultivate the permanent and so forth in order to eliminate their afflictions such as the impermanent is "opening.
That they do not understand this at all is "not knowing whether the medicine should be administered"; being thus ignorant, they are bound by obstacles and hindered from the Great [Vehicle].

Next, the citation of scriptural evidence serves to establish the Great [Vehicle]. The passage beginning with "If one hears... next clarifies that there is no obstruction and so forth; this refers to the visiting physician.

This is the reverse of the former [case]: one grows weary of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) and rejoices in the Path and Cessation (*mārga-nirodha*). By destroying such false calculations, one is able to eliminate suffering and its origin and realize the Path and Cessation.
The conclusion states: "For this reason, it does not constitute an obstacle. This citation serves as proof that it is not an obstacle.
Next, regarding the four *siddhāntas*: five are the objects to be remedied (*pratipakṣya*) and four are the remedies (*pratipakṣa*); thus, by relying on the former, the latter is manifested.

The *Record* states that "kalpa" and "life-span" refer merely to the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—thereby classifying them under the *loka-siddhānta*. However, I maintain that both are dharmas of retribution and are equally categorized as non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
While "kalpa" applies to both the primary and secondary, "life-span" is restricted to the primary; thus, while the primary is what is specifically revealed, the secondary is also included within it.
Because there are two times, they constitute the world; the next two both pertain to the person for whom [the teaching] is intended, so that they may achieve wholesome right view.
Next is that which is to be remedied; the sequence of the ultimate meaning can be understood. Generally speaking, each possesses four aspects according to the sense of removing hindrances;
therefore, these are discussed in pairs as four.
Regarding the fifth section below, there is a further detailed analysis through various categories concerning the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*). First, regarding cause and effect:
the two causes refer to afflictions (*kleśa*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*); the remaining three are effects, as they are produced by those causes. Second, regarding the categories of persons and phenomena:
"persons" refers to sentient beings, while "phenomena" refers to the other four [corruptions], as these are all that which sentient beings rely upon and utilize.

Regarding these dharmas: among the four types of dharmas, "dharmas as time" refers to time and kalpas; the remaining four belong to dharmas themselves. When explained in relation to time, birth also belongs to dharmas.
Regarding the two retributions below, this is an exposition based on the three obstacles. The two retributions refer to life and the second, affliction—namely, views and the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Generally speaking, both are termed afflictions. Between afflictions and karma, it is karma that can summon retribution. Therefore, [the text] says... (as per the original context).
It is said that among these, the section on sentient beings below consists of the three gates of provisional designation (*prajñapti*). The first two are understandable;

as for what is said to be "understandable through mutual dependence," this refers to kalpas, afflictions (*kleśa*), and views (*dṛṣṭi*). The commentary states: "Kalpa" refers to long and short durations in mutual dependence; "affliction" refers to opposition and so forth, and thus is mutually dependent;

"view" refers to existence and non-existence and so forth, which are mutually dependent. If one takes this as a general proof, each possesses the three provisional designations regarding both the primary and secondary retributions (*āśraya-vipāka* and *upabhoga-vipāka*).

There is nothing that is not formed through the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*). Now, for the sake of analytical exposition, they are explained separately; therefore, they are addressed individually.
For sentient beings, there is the gateway of the three provisional designations. Regarding the three expositions [of these], the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* records:

"The aggregation of sentient beings receives the name 'sentient being. Life and so forth are all considered to be sentient beings. Furthermore, regarding dharmas, there is also that which is conceptually grasped."

Because "name" (ming) refers to sentient beings in contrast to [the unconditioned], it is said that the name applies to both locations. A detailed explanation is found in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (*Mohe Zhiguan*), specifically in the notes on the section concerning afflictions (*kleśa*) below.
Regarding the gate of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and sages (*ārya*), the notes state: "Afflictions exist among ordinary persons means that all ordinary beings definitely possess them.

However, while insight (*darśana*) necessarily resides only in ordinary persons, afflictions pervade both sages and ordinary persons—as seen in those who are bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) as well as Arhats."

Regarding the three types of "passage" mentioned previously: when the kalpa is in decline, there is a Buddha; when the kalpa is increasing, there are only ordinary beings. Furthermore, during decline there is a Buddha, while during increase it is common to other noble ones (*ārya*).

Moreover, both the periods of increase and decline each have instances where no Buddha appears, because the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ. The term "sentient beings" (*sattva*) applies generally to both ordinary beings and noble ones.

Regarding "life," there are ordinary and noble types; their karmic retribution (*vipāka-jīvita*) differs. As for the brevity or length of life, it is categorized as inferior or superior based on its duration.

Because they are born repeatedly within a single kalpa, there is a distinction between long and short [lifespans]; this is explained in terms of humans and the gods of the desire realm regarding the places where they see the Buddha.

If one discusses the first dhyāna, its lifespan is equal to the kalpa; from the second dhyāna upward, the kalpa is short while the lifespan is long, and so it may be understood by analogy up to the formless realms.
Third, as for the distinction between long and short: because afflictions persist among ordinary beings, [the lifespan] is long.

It is short because it exists in the Noble Ones; it is long because it exists in other ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). It is short because it exists in those of sharp faculties among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*);
it may also be short because it exists in other ordinary persons. It is long because it exists in those of dull faculties among the non-Buddhists;

it may also be long because it is "great," as it remains for a long time to sustain the afflictions (*kleśa*) that moisten rebirth and cause entry into *saṃsāra*. Furthermore, it is seen from the preceding [context].

All that is short is affliction; subsequently, all that is long is [the result]. Now, to distinguish this: those who enter birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) through turbidity are not called "turbid sentient beings.

This is explained according to the kalpas, based on the distinction between whether they are accompanied by or unaccompanied by the gates of life and destiny. These are factors of non-concomitant formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma*); they must be accompanied by the aggregates (*skandha-dharma*) when discussing the duration of time.
All others belong to the category of dharmas themselves and do not necessarily involve such accompaniment, as they are not directly accompanied. Therefore, it is only [in these cases] that...

Regarding the "Dharma-aeon" (*dharmakalpa*), it encompasses both the lower and upper gates of the internal and external. It is called "external" because the great aeon (*mahākalpa*) destroys the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*);

it is called "internal" because the minor aeons (*antarakalpa*) harm sentient beings. Alternatively, during the period when the four turbidities (*caturkaṣāya*) gather, they specifically pervade both the internal and external;

the three minor [aeons] involve the gate of harming or not harming below, while the objects [of the external] are the receptacle world. When the great aeon arises, humans are born above [the earth], according to the differences among the three [types of aeons].

In the third dhyāna stage, there is a minor kalpa (*antarakalpa*). Regarding the five destinies (*gati*) and the three realms (*dhātu*), they should properly be discussed separately; however, because the three and five intersect, they are explained together here.
As previously stated regarding the pervasive [attainment] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the same applies to the pervasive attainment of life (*jīvitendriya*).

Furthermore, it should be said that the other four [pervasive attainments] extend across the three realms and five destinies, while the attainment of life is fully explained as it appears in the *Abhidharmakośa*: the lifespan of the five destinies differs, being fifty years in the human realm.
The [four] modes of birth (*yoni*) and so forth should also be said to apply universally to all four modes of birth, because each mode of birth has its own varying lengths.
As for the *kalpa*, this is easily understood as the common and specific gates. From "eighty thousand" downward, the text explains the aforementioned great and small *kalpas*.

It states that within the *vivartakalpa* (the kalpa of abiding), there are twenty *kalpas* in total; the first of these consists solely of decrease, referring to the period when the lifespan decreases from an immeasurable number of years.
Thus, one complete cycle of increase and decrease consists of eighteen kalpas, beginning from the reduction of the lifespan by one year every hundred years until it reaches ten years.

From that point of ten years, the children’s age doubles that of their fathers, increasing the lifespan until it reaches eighty thousand years. Then, from eighty thousand years, the lifespan again decreases by one year every hundred years until it reaches ten years;
this period is designated as one kalpa. The subsequent kalpa involves only an increase up to eighty thousand years, though this [latter] is not [considered a full cycle].

The duration of twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*) is equal in measure for all [the periods of increase and decrease]; however, in this present text, because it refers specifically to the initial period, it discusses only the decrease.

As for the statement that [the lifespan] decreases from eighty thousand years, its source is not clearly identified; according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the decrease begins from an immeasurable number of years.
Thus, that treatise states: "First, it decreases from an immeasurable [lifespan] until the lifespan is only ten years; then it increases and decreases eighteen times, after which..."
Regarding the increase to eighty thousand years as constituting a *kṣudra-kalpa* (small kalpa): this is based on the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Lokasthiti-sūtra*.

However, the Liang dynasty’s *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* refers to it as a *mahā-kalpa* (great kalpa), while treatises such as the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, and the *Citta-bhūmi-śāstra* refer to it as a *madhya-kalpa* (intermediate kalpa).
Furthermore, there are many types of intermediate kalpas: some consist of twenty cycles of increase and decrease, some forty, and some sixty; all of these are designated as intermediate kalpas.

Regarding the statement that there are eighty cycles [of increase and decrease], since the kalpa of abiding already consists of twenty such cycles of increase and decrease, the remaining three [kalpas] are likewise determined by the same number as the kalpa of abiding;
when these four kalpas are combined, they constitute a great kalpa (mahākalpa), thus totaling eighty [cycles]. (And so forth.)
The preceding twelve sections conclude the miscellaneous analysis of the meaning of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). Below follows a single question-and-answer session;

this is intended to clarify that "Buddha" is a relative designation based on the turbidities. It also serves to manifest and establish the principle that the turbidities possess degrees of lightness and heaviness.
The initial question is self-evident. In the response, an example is cited to illustrate the whole: that which is contrary to principle is called "perverse" (*mithyā*).
Now, it is said that by way of contrast, the principle is established as correct. It is known that those who have attained the first fruit possess correctness and lack error.

The Confucians say: "Ordinary people follow their emotions; when they feel joy or anger, they deviate from principle. Yan Hui, however, followed the Way, so his anger did not exceed proper bounds. This too approaches the meaning of "stopping" (*zhi*) that is close to error. Quan says:

"Based on this, using clarity to reverse turbidity—this refers to the period before the two intermediate cycles of twenty thousand years during the increasing eon (*vivartakalpa*) and the decreasing eon (*saṃvartakalpa*). Since...

The "un-named turbidity" (*anāmaka-kaṣāya*) is entirely included within the five purities. Since the above five gates have already explained the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), one should proceed according to their sequence:
first, the essential nature and characteristics; second, the successive order; third, the combined analysis; and finally, the selection and determination through the four *siddhāntas*.

Because the three [gates] correctly explain the five turbidities, the discussion of what constitutes an obstacle and what does not follows next. Finally, because the five [turbidities] function as both the subject and object of treatment, there are four [sections].

All this is precisely as it should be in sequence; reflect upon it, reflect upon it. Below this, the text that explains and concludes [the section] should be clarified, yet the *Śū* (Commentary) omits this explanation, and the *Jì* (Record) likewise does not state it definitively.
From the passage "From the time of the turbidity of the kalpa" onwards is the explanation of the various Buddhas; from "By means of skillful means" onwards is the conclusion.

It explains only the three turbidities (*kaṣāya*) and does not explain the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) or the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*). This is because sentient beings are already subsumed within the turbidity of lifespan.
Because they maintain life in accordance with those sentient beings, and because these are seen to be subsumed within the afflictions (*kleśa*);

since it is stated that "all unwholesome roots" (*akuśalamūla*) subsume all afflictions, the subsequent passage—"From the accomplishment of all unwholesome roots..."—is precisely the text that explains the conclusion.
Thus, because the disciples to be converted have accomplished the unwholesome roots of the various turbidities, it consequently leads to [the aforementioned result].
To "come and employ expedient means while concealing the truth" is precisely the explanation for the formation of the turbidities;

it is also the conclusion of that meaning, which is why it is called "explaining and concluding. Regarding the phrase "all unwholesome roots," this refers generally to the five turbidities, for it is because these five exist that faults and evils arise extensively.
Now, as for the first dwelling, following the initial explanation of the text, it appears to be similar—that is, it explains the preceding five knots.

The previous five [explanations] may have this intention, yet their meaning is not definitively clarified. As for the subsequent interpretation, from the beginning to the end of the text, it appears as though it has not yet reached the point;
the explanation of the conclusion (*kṣepa*) constitutes a single meaning, which is why the word "also" (*api*) is used.

Now, I say that from "Thus" (*evam*) onwards, it is a comprehensive explanation of the conclusion. The two characters "Thus" (*evam*) contain two meanings: they both refer back to what preceded and initiate what follows.
This means that, Śāriputra, it is because of these five turbidities that the Buddhas employ various skillful means, and so forth.
Since this passage thus contains both the preceding and subsequent meanings, the commentary takes up the aspect of the former meaning and designates it as "essence and characteristics" (*tǐxiàng*).

The following section serves as an explanation of the conclusion, establishing the reasons for the provisional teachings (*huánquán*) bestowed in the past; it also serves to summarize the essential intent of the teaching in this manner.

The preceding and succeeding sections, as well as the explanation and the conclusion, are all inseparable. In the verses of the following text, whenever these names are cited, they are all referred to as "concluding and returning" (*jiegui*) to explain the intended meaning;
this is because the two meanings are identical and thus not fixed. This shall be clarified further below, but for now it remains so.

Furthermore, regarding the word "hence" (*gu*) in the sutra, its usage across ancient and modern, upper and lower texts is not fixed; I maintain that although the meaning may be broadly applicable, [the specific context must be determined].
The same applies to the detailed explanation that follows, which should properly belong to the subsequent section.

Next, regarding the explanation of "distinguishing the true," the entire passage states: "The 'true' refers to those who have already realized the small fruits [of the Śrāvaka path] and are now being earnestly exhorted.

However, I fear this is not the case. The preceding section concluded the doubt regarding the provisional teachings (*upāya*) of the past; the present section concerns distinguishing the false to ensure firm and certain faith.
Regarding "the reality revealed by the Sun," "thorough" (dun) refers to being profound and earnest; it means pressing [the truth] so that one must necessarily believe it.
The two chapters into which this is divided first discuss "true and false," meaning that the non-true is eliminated and the false is revealed.
Each of these two chapter titles inherently contains two meanings. The "two" in the first chapter are precisely the two points previously explained; the Sūtra itself makes this clear.

The first section, "Briefly Distinguishing Those Who Are Not [True Disciples]," consists of three phrases in the sutra text. The first two phrases cite those who are not truly authentic—these are the objects of the exclusion;
the final phrase is the actual exclusion itself. Regarding the first phrase, "the three persons," the first refers to disciples in general, while the latter two refer to specific types.

Now I shall explain this general category; the following two cases are both excluded. First, a brief commentary on the text; second, an extensive analysis according to the meaning. First, clarifying the true disciple.
"Conforming" means hearing and knowing, which implies continuity; since one does not hear [the truth] and so forth, it is therefore not the reality.

The Sūtra says that a Bodhisattva is a person of perfect realization (*pariniṣpanna*). Next, to further explain according to the meaning in contrast to what was previously attained: that which was attained then is not what is attained now.

This means that the provisional (*upāya*) is employed precisely to manifest the real (*tattva*), and is thus considered "not" [the ultimate]. This concludes the two-fold comprehensive explanation for distinguishing and rejecting what is not [the truth].

Below, there is a further separate clarification regarding those whose conduct is not based on the meaning [of the teaching]. Since this knowledge and understanding is rooted in realization, although the character "true" (zhen) does not appear in this passage, its meaning is fully present.
In the subsequent passage, although the realization of the true essence is complete, it is not yet the wondrous reality;

therefore, it is not the ultimate principle. A single disciple who penetrates all three [vehicles] is such a person; since he is not merely a [limited] disciple, he is not a mere person. First, we clarify those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

"Universal" means that they are universal among ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*); "particular" means that each has its own specific cause. Both are explained according to what is most prevalent.

Furthermore, it is precisely these five thousand who are meant, not implying that all are like this. There are seven types of pride as previously explained. These three groups serve to manifest two others.

One who gives rise to overweening pride through the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)—claiming to have attained the four fruits of the path and relying on this to exalt themselves—refuses to advance further.

The World-Honored One, having explained the preceding causes and conditions, spoke these verses:

The fourth dhyāna is not opened for those who are arrogant and rely on their own excellence. As for the *śuklavidarśanā* (pure-vision) practitioner, how much more so would this apply?

It is said that among the types of pride (*māna*), there is "increased pride" (*adhimāna*), and among those with increased pride, there is one called "supreme increased pride" (*abhimāna*). Now, it is explained that "supreme" refers to a superior state;

To claim that one has attained the ultimate when one has only attained a slight realization of the Dharma—such as the four dhyānas—is called 'overweening pride' (*adhimāna*).

Because those who harbor this [pride] have a mind directed toward the superior path, it is indeed pride; however, in this context, it refers specifically to claiming to have attained what one has not yet attained."
Because the path of integrity is profound, those of shallow capacity cannot believe in it. One who does not reflect upon themselves fails to examine their own faults;

This [state] has not yet been attained; thus, by mentioning what exists, that which is absent is revealed. Regarding "precepts and so forth," it refers to the precepts.

To know right from wrong yet remain small within the small refers to the wisdom of the four fruits of the path; this is already the smallness of the four dhyānas.

Later, in the correct commentary on this passage, it is said that there are four propositions regarding the differences between the Sūtras and the Śāstras:
First, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna possess the twelve divisions [of scripture], yet they are complete in the Mahāyāna while being partial in the Hīnayāna.

The reason for clarifying the twelve divisions is that this number represents a perfect totality, and furthermore, because it serves as the remedy for the disease of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) in sentient beings. Because their realization is small and lacks the sense of "filling the place" (*apūra-sthāna*), the teaching on prophecies is excluded. Because it is shallow and there are those capable of questioning, the category of "unasked self-explanations" (*aprśṭavyākaraṇa*) is excluded.
Furthermore, it is said that because a Great Being (mahāsattva) can act as a friend who does not wait to be requested, there is "unasked" [teaching];
