The second section, the detailed analysis of the text, has two parts. Regarding the terms "condition" (pratyaya) and "cause" (hetu): since both refer to the performance of wholesome karma, they are "condition-causes" (pratyaya-hetu).

Because it is stated that one "hears the Dharma," these are "revealing causes" (parijñā-hetu), as they are all capable of bringing about the actual fruit; the condition-cause is thus the seed, and the revealing-seed is likewise so.
The initial mention of the "celestial vehicle" (deva-yāna) includes both a heading and an explanation, which is easy to understand from the text; the scripture does not [further elaborate].
It is said that this refers to the "Celestial Vehicle" (*devayāna*) and does not speak of karmic retribution; rather, one observes their conduct and infers the fruit from the cause.

Thus, it is known that this is the Celestial Vehicle. Regarding the construction of stupas and the various ritual implements offered, these were made of the seven treasures—not because of diligent effort or the exhaustion of resources, but because they were naturally provided here without seeking karmic reward. All of this is worldly.
To practice the causes for the sake of the supreme fruit is the "Celestial Vehicle" (*devayāna*). Regarding the term in the text, it is as previously explained.
As for the *stūpa*, ancient and modern explanations of its name differ; it is called *stūpa*, *thūpa*, or *dauṣpa*.

This is translated as "square mound," and is also said to mean "heaped up" or "great accumulation," as already explained before. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that there are four things by which one attains [merit].
There are four types of Brahma-merit: first, the establishment of a stūpa; second, the harmonious assembly of the noble Sangha; third, the restoration of ruined temples;

and fourth, requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma from the Buddha shortly after his initial enlightenment. Regarding "Brahma-merit," the merit of all sentient beings within the four continents up to the six heavens of the desire realm does not equal that of a single Brahmā heaven.
As for "temples" (miao), this is a term for shrines; the veneration of sacred images in monasteries and stūpas is similar in kind to ancestral shrines.

Regarding the appearance of the divine spirit: "Mudim" (木密) is the auspicious cloud-fragrance sandalwood (*kakkola*); its shape resembles white sandalwood and it has a slight fragrance; I personally saw it in Chang'an.
As for "drawing forth radiance," this proves that the previous offerings constitute the celestial vehicle (*devayāna*); this is also an illustration.
If even something so minute produces such results, how much more so when the cause is far superior?

Next, the explanation of the Human Vehicle (*manuṣya-yāna*) also follows the same structure of heading, commentary, and enumeration as before. Because its cause and fruit are the most inferior, it is called "human.

This refers to being merely general rather than specialized or ultimate, being casual and indifferent rather than urgent or earnest. The two matters within the fruit correspond to the two causes mentioned above.

The final two lines summarize and reveal that [the factors] equally constitute the conditions for the Perfect Cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*) and the Contributory Causes (*pratyaya-hetu*). I do not wish to be overly prolix.
Because the text is thus, it reveals the reality through a single bond.

Next, regarding the four verses that open the celestial vehicle (*devayāna*): they are also "refined and ultimate" (*sūkṣma-prakarṣa*). "Refined and ultimate" means that their essence is superior, and because their number is great;
for these reasons, they are refined and ultimate. Thus, the text says "for the sake of Buddhahood," and since it speaks of "seeking," [it refers to the goal].

To create [images] for the sake of Buddhahood is what constitutes sublime practice; why then do you not all understand that this is called "heavenly dust"? Now I fear it may be a semblance rather than the reality.

Why? It is because one creates images for the purpose of making offerings to the Buddha, yet this act of creating and offering is done with the desire to be born in heaven, rather than seeking Buddhahood through such creation and offering.
As for what is called "tree resin," it refers to wood resin, as will be found in the text below.
This refers to *jiaoxiang* (gum resin incense). Regarding the statement that "the offense of harboring thoughts of gain or loss" means it cannot cause people to give rise to reverence;

because this [attitude] does not arise, one brings about evil results. As for the phrase "in the hall," etc., because one initially conforms to worldly conventions, there are four modes of deportment.
In the secular world—except for the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra—people mostly establish images in standing or sitting postures. Among these, standing and sitting images are most commonly used.

Because [the text] gives rise to wholesome states, the principles elucidated in the sutras are very numerous; however, as these are not the primary intent here, they are briefly annotated (as indicated by "etc.").
Nevertheless, the primary purpose here is to clarify the opening of the provisional (*upāya*). If one were to distinguish these characteristics, there are briefly two meanings:

first, for those whose [provisional teachings] have not yet been opened and unified, it serves as a causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*) because it plants the seeds for the opening and unification; second, if the opening and unification occurs, there will be understanding.

The practitioner’s actions are none other than wondrous deeds, which are themselves wondrous conduct. As for the phrase "and so forth," although these are extremely subtle, they are nonetheless the most excellent meritorious practices performed upon the stupa;
therefore, they can bring about the fruits among human beings. Thus, although the retributions among humans are manifold, there is indeed a profound reason for this.
Regarding the term "concluding the connection," this should collectively refer to the preceding discussion on humans and devas; hence it says, "Thus."

For all such persons, first they accomplish it for themselves, and subsequently they cause others to accomplish it halfway. Once this has been revealed, one immediately achieves the perfect cause that leads toward the fruit;
therefore, it is said that "gradual" refers to the perfect gradual, not to a mere gradual progression.
The preceding section has already explained the latter two phrases. Since [the teaching] itself constitutes the "Four-in-One," it can further transform others, leading them to enter the "Four-in-One.
The former stage consists only of three, while the subsequent stage of transformation consists only of one; these mutually illuminate one another (as indicated by the note "and so forth").

"Transformation" refers to the preaching of the wondrous teaching for the purpose of transforming and delivering beings, and thus belongs to the "One of Teaching. This clarification of the "Four-in-One" has already been fully explained as previously stated.
Next, regarding the various objects (*viṣaya*), these refer to the six objects. In the text, there are mention of form, fragrance, sound, and a respectful and virtuous mind;

this already includes the object of mental phenomena (*dharmaviṣaya*), with only taste and touch being absent. Although the text lacks them, their meaning and intent must be fully present; others call these the "three karmas.
Furthermore, because they are vast and focused, these are considered "heavenly karmas. Regarding the copper cymbals and so forth, the commentary states: "Cháng'ān."
Furthermore, there is no such sound or voice that has been transformed; it is merely recorded according to oral tradition.
Now, as for these minor matters within music, how could Danqiu not have known them and yet make such a statement?

Moreover, according to the biographies, Emperor Yang was ordered four times in succession to enter Chang’an; each time he departed, it was two years prior, and thus there were four such occasions in total.
"How could this matter not have been heard of for eight years? It certainly should not be so; it is mostly due to errors in later transcription.
It should correctly be 'the sound of the *lingbao* (resonant gong) is transformed,' which is mistakenly written as 'exposed basin. This is the *niao* (gong), also called the *zheng* (bronze bell);
it is held in the army to alert the multitude, and it is also struck in musical performances to provide harmony—it is the 'metallic sound' (*jin-yin*) among the eight sounds."

Since these both belong to the sense-object of sound, it is naturally so. Next, regarding the karma of the person, one gradually beholds innumerable Buddhas and thereby attains the manifestation of the Buddha-way.
Next, concerning the karma of the body, the term "heavenly beings" is used because within that karma, the intermediate [state] is formed and extensively established;
thus, it applies to both. The explanation in the text is clear. Next, regarding the phrase "forming a connection," this refers to the benefits accomplished through the preceding karma.
By virtue of these karmic actions, one is able to bring both oneself and others into reality.

This means that having attained one's own reality, one gives rise to function from the essence and returns function to the essence. Because this principle is extremely vast, the commentary states "and so forth" (*yún yún*);

such is the general outline. Next, the karma of speech is also called the karma of verbal action; this karma is also very extensive. If it is focused and extensive, it belongs to the karma of the heavens; if it is distracted, it is otherwise.
Because it is recited once, it is brought about solely by the merit of human action; it likewise enters into reality and should also be briefly annotated (as follows).
Next, the meaning of *namo* is explained. First, the meaning is indicated in its full extent; next, the detailed characteristics of that full extent are elucidated.
*Namo*, *namo*, *nāmo*, *namu*, and *nāmu* all share these various pronunciations; if one were to apply the correct phonetic analysis (*qiezheng*), they are as follows.

Regarding the phrase "Namo" (那慕), it should be stated that within the text, it does not necessarily require the departing tone (*qùshēng*) for the repeated call; it is also permissible to follow the rising tone (*shǎngshēng*). It emerges from within the character *mò* (麼).
If one calls it according to its direct phonetic sound, it is not an accurate transcription. Various ancient and modern commentators have offered different interpretations:

some say "taking refuge" (*guīmìng*), others "reverential homage" (*guījìng*), others "seeking deliverance" (*jiùdù*), others "prostration" (*jìnglǐ*), and others "bowing the head to the ground" (*jīshǒu*); thus, there are many differing views.

Regarding the statement that "the term 'Great' (Mahā) has many meanings," this refers to the fact that when this single word is explained in the sūtras and śāstras, there are many reasons for its interpretation.
As will be explained below, although there are indeed many meanings in the exposition, they do not exceed four types. First is the general explanation of the name;
then, from "Worldly Devadatta" onwards, it clarifies the benefit of generating faith, which corresponds to the *puruṣakāra* (human effort) [of the teaching].

First, the following clarifies that which can extinguish sins and eliminate evil, which corresponds to the *Tāizhì jīng* (Sūtra on Counteracting); the following clarifies that which can attain the Way, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the first [section], the text has three turns: "delivering me" and "warning against fear" pertain to two meanings belonging to sentient beings, while "taking refuge" pertains to one meaning belonging to the Buddha.
Thus, this single phrase possesses these two orientations; as for the explanation that it may be applied, it means:
One may provisionally establish [the term] for sentient beings; within this passage, the meaning of the text is such that it cannot be absent in the subsequent section.
Therefore, it is next translated as "startled fear" (*jīngbù*), following the sense of being startled into entering the burning house as explained later.

There is both a translation and an explanation; within the explanation, there is a thesis, an exposition, and a conclusion. Within the conclusion, there is further an exposition. Although the word "joy" (*xǐ*) does not appear in the subsequent text...

Because this [term] has the meaning of "joy," the ancient commentators have all maintained that one says "Namo" because the mind experiences joy through receiving the encouragement and consolation of the Buddhas.
Some say there is an original text that reads "Xi" (Joy), which I have not yet seen. Next, regarding the phrase "taking refuge in life" (*guiming*):

it means to surrender one's life to the Buddhas of the ten directions and request their deliverance. As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Taking refuge throughout the ten directions. This is what is meant.
Such meanings can all be applied to the realm of sentient beings; it does not mean that one can actually bestow [the Dharma] upon sentient beings, for there would be many errors.
The *Nanshan nico shak* (Exegesis on the *Nanshan Niche*) cites the *Tiwai jing*, stating:
"Nan" means "to take refuge," "wu" means "life," and "fo" means "awakening. This is thus called "taking refuge in the Great Awakened One. Furthermore, regarding "nan":
"Li" (禮) means "great" (大), and "Fo" (佛) means "longevity" (壽); thus, this is called "Great Longevity. These meanings together encompass all sentient beings.
In the second matter, there are three parts:
first, one recites the two characters; later, one attains the supreme fruit. Next, one recites the full three characters.

The celestial images have wheel-shaped heads, and all people return their faith to them; these three points constitute an exhortation to cultivate sincerity. Regarding the first two, their origins are unknown;

they are called "thieves," while the following section is an exhortation to the worthy, namely those who take refuge in the Buddha during the final age. The passage beginning with "In the ten directions" and so forth clearly explains the benefits as a concluding exhortation.
As for the readers of this text, they are not uniform; some say that the honored deities of the ten directions do not act with integrity.

"However, [the phrase] 'only through diligence' below concludes the exhortation; this means that all spirits and deities do not dare to obstruct or conceal [the truth], for it is said that the Buddha's power is the greatest and can subdue and destroy everything.

Alternatively, it is said that the character 'gǎn' (感) should be used, meaning that while the honored deities of the ten directions do not respond, one should instead cause the Buddhas of the ten directions to respond and arise.
The portion beginning with "dāng dàn xià" (當但下) is the concluding exhortation within the text; there is an error in the wording.
Regarding the character "Gǎn" (敢): today it is said that although both of these two interpretations are logically consistent, the latter meaning will likely be superior;
one should examine this further. As for the second interpretation, within the third point, the mention of "Naxian" refers to the name of a bhikṣu.
Because the sutra is named after the person, it is so called. The sutra consists of one fascicle. This bhikṣu had long-standing ties with a minor king and was skilled at posing difficult questions.

In the *Nāgasena Bhikṣu Sūtra*, there are many questions and answers regarding the discussion of principles; all that was asked concerned erroneous attachments, which Nāgasena answered by completely refuting those errors.

What is cited here is but one instance. Although the beauty of all those questions and answers—refuting the false and revealing the correct—is extensive, I fear it would be too cumbersome to describe them all.
Among them, there is one question: "Does the Buddha possess the marks and signs? The King did not answer that he does.

When asked whether the Buddha has parents, he did not answer; when asked whether there is no king, he did not answer; and when asked whether the Buddha was not born but all things arise resembling their parents, Nāgasena replied:
"Does Your Majesty see a lotus flower? You answer, 'I see it. Does it grow from mud? You answer, 'It grows from mud.
But would you say that because the lotus grows from mud, it resembles the mud? "The Buddha is likewise," [Nāgasena said]. The King exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Although this is not the primary intent of the text, it nonetheless serves as an ancillary refutation of heterodox views; therefore, it is a form of therapeutic remedy (*pratipakṣa*).
The four subsequent meanings concern those who attained the fruits of sainthood during the third assembly of that Buddha’s initial teaching;

when they reach the fifth period, they are all brought into the harmonious revelation of the Buddha-way. What follows is a brief clarification of that initial stage, which is likewise provisional (*upāya*).
Because it is the path of reality, it is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The general meaning of "Great" is roughly as explained above.

Next, regarding the "enabling cause" (*vyañjana-hetu*), this refers to the understanding-mind of the five vehicles. The former [the substantial cause] opens up their practice; now, this [enabling cause] opens up their understanding.
Because it opens the distinct understanding-minds of the five vehicles so that they together become the wondrous wisdom of the One Vehicle, it is called the "enabling cause."
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'as in the previous examples,' the Sūtra directly says, 'If there are those who hear this Dharma... It is not known what constitutes 'this Dharma.
Since the intent here is precisely to reveal the ultimate reality by opening up the provisional, 'this Dharma' must refer to the teachings of the five vehicles within the provisional dispensation.

If the Sūtra were to simply say 'hearing this Dharma,' how could one distinguish that it possesses the five fruits? Following the previous examples, it refers only to the single practice of the six perfections."

Furthermore, regarding the distinctions between the three teachings, the practices of devas and humans differ only in their degree of ultimateity or dispersion; this case is likewise understandable as such.

That is to say, one hears of the existence of marks, hears of the non-existence of marks, hears of both the existence and non-existence of marks, and hears of that which is neither the existence nor the non-existence of marks.

This is because the Separate Teaching (biejiao) involves hearing the teaching of the three truths in successive order; thus, it must be presented in this way to serve as a transition from the preceding state of existence.

To say that "non-existence" means it is not existent at all is incorrect. If one hears the precepts with a sincere mind, and even if one hears the precepts with a distracted mind, they are likewise beneficial.
Taking refuge in the precepts serves as the cause for becoming a celestial being or a human; such is this Dharma.

If one fears that this wondrous Dharma might not correspond with the present text, then the meaning of "opening up the provisional to reveal the real" throughout the prose and verse sections of the Five Buddhas chapter would be entirely consistent.
Now, following the sequence of the text, we first reveal the provisional practice to manifest the causal conditions;
now, by revealing the provisional to clarify the consummate, the meaning becomes easy to understand and the text remains free of contradiction. As the Sūtra says:

"Whether during his lifetime or after his passing, how could there be a Buddha present who, having already revealed the wondrous, would wait for further revelation? Even if such a meaning were to exist, it would merely be a general principle and not the specific point intended here.
The mental focus (and so forth) may be considered as being roughly similar to what was stated above.
Next, the questions and answers provide a systematic analysis to resolve doubts and clarify the underlying intent. Regarding the first question:

while in the prose section of the chapter on the five Buddhas all [five] are treated briefly, and in the verse section four Buddhas are likewise treated briefly without individually traversing the five vehicles, it is precisely here [in the case of the past Buddha] that the individual traversal is extensive; this is indeed the established principle.
For this reason, it is revealed here. In the response, first, the efficacy of striking and moving in the two periods of present and future is slight;
therefore, it is treated briefly. Next, the efficacy of realizing and manifesting in the past is established; therefore, it is treated extensively.

Furthermore, by citing examples of the same kind, the "empty words" represent the two periods [of present and future], while the "verified reality" represents the past. Although the text is from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*), it is not the word of the Buddha.
This is indeed the established principle; therefore, he cites scriptural evidence.
Next, regarding the two verses on the future [state]: in the preceding prose section there were only the two [topics] of "opening" and "revealing," which are now being versified as those same two.

Next, regarding the verses on "revealing the reality": although in the preceding text there were only two, their meaning encompasses four; here, they are treated according to their respective divisions.
This is precisely its fourth aspect. Regarding the initial verse on practice (*caryā*), a single phrase is most prominent: "The path first traversed is itself practice.
This means one vows to cause all beings to likewise attain this sublime practice. Furthermore, because there is an inherent principle, this path belongs to practice;

moreover, it specifically refers to that which is capable of practicing. Thus, this name is manifest. Since the teaching states, "Although it is so said," and "Therefore it is said," it is indeed the teaching.

The hundreds of thousands of billions [of teachings] essentially rely on the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); that is, the prose section [states] that all these dharmas are for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle.

First, the initial practice correctly clarifies the teaching; second, the subsequent practice explains and establishes why they must be the One Vehicle, which correctly reveals the principle because there is no duality.
Regarding the "explanation and establishment": previously it was clarified that the principle is non-dual, therefore they are one; now it is clarified that they must necessarily [be so].

Relying on the capacity [of the listener] to manifest [the meaning], the second section of the commentary on the first intent is explained in two parts: first, by way of the teaching (*śāsana*), and second, by way of practice (*caryā*).

Furthermore, within the first part (by way of the teaching), there are two explanations: first, explaining by way of the two dharmas of subject and object; second, explaining by way of the three causes.

Within the first explanation (by way of the teaching), the nature of reality (*tattva*) is first discussed as the reason for providing the teaching. It is said that if one considers the "Worthy One with Two Feet" (*dvipadottama*) in terms of his internal virtues, these are precisely meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Merit and wisdom are the two feet; the Sublime Ultimate is the most honored. If we speak of its external form, it is the Honored One among Gods and Humans.

"To know that phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature" means "to know" is to realize and illuminate. It refers to personally realizing the ultimate and illuminating the essential nature of all phenomena.
"Phenomena are eternal," and so forth, refers to the objects of knowledge. "Phenomena" is the essence; "eternally without intrinsic nature" is the quality.

It is also said that "the virtue between existence and non-existence" is the commentary. The *Sūtra Commentary* states: "The 'true mark' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) indicates the essence, which is the explanation of 'Dharma.
Because it is the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), it is called the 'true mark. 'Permanently abiding' indicates the attribute, which is the explanation of 'constant.

The aforementioned explanation of the possessed attributes is the 'wondrous existence' (*pranītasat*). Why is it named 'constant'? Because it is fundamentally wondrous existence, and because it is the wisdom-life of the inherent attributes (*prakṛtiguṇa*). Below...
To explain the virtue of non-existence is precisely to explain the virtue of the true emptiness of non-nature. What kind of nature is absent? It refers to the two natures:

the nature of essence (*svabhāva*) and the nature of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). "Nature" here refers to the four types of nature; being devoid of these four natures is called "non-nature," which is the emptiness of essence (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

"Even non-existence is non-existent" means that even this capacity for non-existence is non-existent, which is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). If there were such a non-existence, then non-existence would still [be present].

The characteristic of accomplishment (*siddha-lakṣaṇa*) is also empty because this non-existence does not exist; it is the emptiness of characteristics. Because these two natures do not exist, it is called "naturelessness" (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Now, since the subsequent passage speaks of the Middle Way, this refers to the absence of both existence and non-existence, as well as the two kinds of nature.

The commentator states that because there are no two natures—emptiness and existence—it is called "naturelessness. This is indeed correct. One should understand in its entirety that within this essence, there are three aspects: existence, non-existence, and [the Middle].

Regarding the meaning, it is said that "one knows that dharmas are eternally without self-nature. This is roughly the same as the previous meaning of "quiescence," though the commentary (*śāstra*) contains slight differences.

There are two ways of illuminating "absence of self-nature": first, the refutation of self-nature; second, the revelation of the fundamental. Since this is the revelation of the fundamental, it is said to be "eternally without [self-nature].
If it were not explained in this way, how could it be the seed of the Buddhas? That is, the seeds of the three Buddhas. If it were not explained in this manner...
If the commentary (*śāstra*) is difficult to interpret, it is because the commentary does not explain it in this way;

if the sutra text is difficult to understand, it is because the preceding section has already explained the cause, while the following section now correctly explains the conditions—namely, that the wondrous teaching is expounded based on these wondrous seeds.

First, the explanation of "Buddha-seed" refers to the aforementioned essence and virtue. Because this wondrous object can produce wondrous wisdom, it is called the "Buddha-seed. Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

It is said that because it is the seed of unsurpassed bodhi, it is called Buddha-nature. Below, the dependent origination is explained: first, its general principle is discussed; second, the text itself is analyzed.
First, delusion is clarified; next, awakening is clarified. Delusion is raised to manifest awakening. Delusion is precisely non-awakening (*abodha*);
therefore, "sentient beings arise" refers generally to those in the five abodes, collectively clarifying ignorance rather than referring to it specifically. From this...
Because delusion is directed toward the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, the sentient beings of the nine realms arise.

Next, regarding the "Exposition" (the second part), since it teaches both practice and principle as being collectively caused by delusion, it also refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*); because these are easy to understand, they are mentioned briefly as one.
Although the Sūtra mentions only "teaching," its meaning necessarily includes "practice. Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is wondrous wisdom that pervades both the beginning and the end.
The commentary on the sequence is as follows: Therefore, the statement of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) is spoken precisely to manifest this single principle;

because this teaching of the One Vehicle is spoken, it is called the "One Vehicle of Teaching. The above concludes the section on Teaching. Below is the explanation according to Practice, which is the very method for manifesting the principle.

The first phrase refers to the True Cause (dharmadhātu); the second phrase refers to the Conditions and the Aids (pratyaya and upaniṣad); the final phrase concludes that the three natures are originally non-existent.

Therefore, it is called the "True Cause" (*zhengyin*); because it can produce cultivated virtues (*xiude*), it is called "Buddha-nature" (*foxing*). The "Buddha-seed" (*fuzhong*) refers to the True Cause, which is that which is produced;

"conditioned arising" (*yuanqi*) refers to the conditions of the Expedient and the Ultimate (*yuanliao*), which are that which can produce. The Expedient and the Ultimate are precisely the two practices of the Sublime and the Auxiliary (*zhengzhu erxing*).

When the primary seed arises, these three types arise simultaneously; thus it is said that "all" [arise], because within the nature-virtues (*xingde*) all things are fully contained—this is wisdom (*zhi*).
It is the nature of all three kinds of merit, such as the severance of duality; its manifestation as inherent virtue is termed "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).

The reason for providing this further explanation is that while the Sūtra states that "dharmas are eternally without self-nature," it also speaks of the "Buddha-seed"; therefore, this explanation is required.

Thus, the previous explanation stated that the true characteristic is eternally abiding and the non-dual nature of emptiness—this is precisely the original presence of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and it is based on this [that the present explanation is given].
The cultivation that reveals the intrinsic nature (prakṛti) possesses three aspects, because both the cultivated and the intrinsic natures are endowed with the three virtues.

Furthermore, explaining these three by means of this [cultivation] constitutes the meaning elucidated by the One Vehicle; it is taught for this purpose, and thus it is the teaching of the One Vehicle.

This refers to the "object of knowledge" (*jñeya*) and the "seeing-knowledge" (*jñāna*), which is the "subject that knows and sees. To speak of them briefly in combination, it is said: "One knows that phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature. This is for the sake of... [end of fragment].
The reason for teaching the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is to cause [sentient beings] to cultivate and realize their inherent nature; this is the basis for its exposition.
Although it is said that the teaching is one, it also subsumes all meanings. Next, regarding the "Unity of Principle" (*liyi*):

since it is stated that the "abiding locus of phenomena" (*dharmasthiti*) is eternally constant, once this is known, the Unity of Principle reveals that all sentient beings inherently possess this wondrous principle. The first two phrases of the sutra text explicitly clarify this Unity of Principle.

The next two lines provide an explanation that establishes the preceding point; within this explanation of the initial "Middle," there are also two sections: first, an explanation by contrasting the ordinary person with the Buddha;
second, an explanation focusing solely on sentient beings. Furthermore, in the first of these, there are two parts: first, regarding persons; second, regarding phenomena.

In the former, the first two lines equally reveal the single principle (*ekayāna*), yet the first line serves as the cause for what follows—namely, the reason why [the Buddha] is eternally abiding—and thus differs from those who are not eternally abiding because they do not occupy that same stage.

Because their abiding is identical and because they are eternal, one knows that their status (*avasthā*) is identical. "Status" refers to the divisions of stages (*bhūmi*), locations, and the fundamental principle (*tattva*).
The commentary states: "Sentient beings and perfect enlightenment"—this explains what is meant by "dharmas. These dharmas refer to all phenomena;
although they are generally categorized by type, both Buddhas and sentient beings, as well as the mundane and the supramundane, are collectively termed "dharmas. That is to say:
"The ten realms are one suchness, without duality" explains the abiding in the stage of the Dharma (dharmapada). This takes the true suchness of the dharma-nature (dharmatā-tathatā) as the stage;

since all are equally contained within it, this constitutes the stage. Although there are differences between cultivation and non-cultivation, or manifestation and concealment, there is no further distinction in their fundamental portion.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "Sentient beings and Maitreya are both suchness. This cites their equality in nature.

This explains the reason why the characteristics are eternal. The following section clarifies the eternity of characteristics: previously, it was explained that the nature is identical; now, it is explained that the characteristics are identical.

First, it is raised that because the Perfectly Enlightened One abides in the state of the nature of suchness (*tathatā*), the characteristics are eternal; since the nature of sentient beings is identical [to that of the Buddha], the characteristics are likewise eternal.
The conclusion states: "Therefore, this principle is one," because both nature and characteristics are identical. Alternatively, it says: "The world..."
If sentient beings were indeed of a permanent nature, how could there be [change]? If one believes in their nature, how could their characteristics be definitively non-existent?

As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says, "That which is neither born nor extinguished is the meaning of impermanence"—this example makes it clear. This passage precisely clarifies that within the single principle, there is nothing that can be confused by phenomena;
this may be reflected upon. What follows below specifically explains this in terms of worldly sentient beings. Furthermore, the preceding section was a general cultivation.

Regarding "nature," this refers specifically to nature (and so forth). As for the explanation of the "worldly" (*loka*), the previous section concerned people who follow [the path], whereas this concerns actual phenomena (*dharmas*).

That is to say, the actual phenomena of the nine realms are precisely these dharmas; and these dharmas are entirely the direct cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). Because they are the direct cause, they are eternally abiding.
To explain "eternal abiding" means that the dharmas such as the aggregates (*skandha*) are eternally abiding. The reason for this is precisely because they are the direct cause.
Because it is entirely the true cause of Buddha-nature, its essence has already emerged; however, from this point downward, the meaning of "permanence" (nitya) is explained.
Regarding the "six dharmas," these refer to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the self (*ātman*).

Although the three categories (*triskandha*) were previously mentioned, the present mention of six dharmas occurs because the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* speaks thus in order to refute false attachments. Following the words of the Sūtra, it is said that they are neither identical nor separate.

Likewise, citing these six also subsumes the three truths. Although the text mentions them alternately, it should properly state that the true cause (the *dharmadhātu*) is neither identical to nor separate from the five aggregates (*skandhas*), and furthermore, it is neither identical to nor separate from the conditions and the acquired wisdom (*pratyaya* and *labdha-jñāna*). The Record states: "The principle of the six dharmas of the true cause is such that they are not separate; however, because it is merely the principle, they are not identical. The same applies to the conditions and the acquired wisdom in relation to these six. Regarding this: 1. The true cause is not separate from the five aggregates, yet it is not identical to them. 2. The true cause is not separate from the conditions and the acquired wisdom, yet it is not identical to them. 3. The conditions and the acquired wisdom are not separate from the five aggregates, yet they are not identical to them. 4. The conditions and the acquired wisdom are not separate from the true cause, yet they are not identical to it. This is because the true cause is the fundamental substance, while the five aggregates are its phenomenal manifestations; thus, they are neither one nor different. Furthermore, the true cause is the principle, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the practice; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the nature (*prakṛti*), while the five aggregates are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the essence (*tattva*), while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the function (*vṛtti*); thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the reality (*dharmatā*), while the five aggregates are the phenomena (*dharma*); thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), while the five aggregates are the form-body (*rūpakāya*); thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the path of cultivation; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *tathatā*, while the five aggregates are the various modes of existence; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *śūnyatā*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the means of realization; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *anātman*, while the five aggregates are the objects of attachment; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *nirvāṇa*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the process of liberation; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *bodhi*, while the five aggregates are the obstacles to be removed; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *samyaksambodhi*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the stages of progress; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *mahāyāna*, while the five aggregates are the vehicles of the two lesser paths; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *ekayāna*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the provisional teachings; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *anutpāda*, while the five aggregates are the arising of delusion; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *asaṃskṛta*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the conditioned phenomena; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *amala-vijñāna*, while the five aggregates are the defiled consciousnesses; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *svabhāva-śūnyatā*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the *parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *dharmadhātu*, while the five aggregates are the *dharmas*; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *tathāgata-garbha*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the *gotra*; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *buddhatva*, while the five aggregates are the *kleśas*; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *jñānakāya*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the *upāyakauśalya*; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *mārgasatya*, while the five aggregates are the *duḥkhasatya*; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *nirodhasatya*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the *mārgapratipatti*; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *dharmakāya-buddha*, while the five aggregates are the *nirmāṇakāya*; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *sambhogakāya*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the *śrāvakayāna*; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *svābhāvikakāya*, while the five aggregates are the *viparyāsa*; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *dharmatā-kāya*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the *vyavahāra*; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *anāsrava-dhātu*, while the five aggregates are the *sāsrava-dhātu*; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *lokottara*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the *laukika*; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *nirvāṇadhātu*, while the five aggregates are the *saṃsāradhātu*; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *tathāgata-jñāna*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the *bodhisattva-caryā*; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *sarvajñatā*, while the five aggregates are the *avidyā*; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *prajñāpāramitā*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the *upāyapāramitā*; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *dharmadhātu-viśuddhi*, while the five aggregates are the *pañca-skandha-parikalpa*; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *tathatā-ananyathā*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the *pratītyasamutpāda*; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *buddhabhūmi*, while the five aggregates are the *pṛthagjana-bhūmi*; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *arhat-phala*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the *śaikṣa-mārga*; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *pratyekabuddha-yāna*, while the five aggregates are the *kleśa-bandhana*; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *mahāsattva-gotra*, while the conditions and the acquired wisdom are the *caryā-prasthāna*; thus, they are neither one nor different. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the true cause is the *anuttara-samyaksambodhi*, while the five aggregates are the *viparyāsa-citta*; thus, they are neither one nor different. Moreover, the true cause is the *dharmakāya-svabhāva*,
Because those who provide partial explanations do so for the sake of ease of manifestation, they do not deviate from the fundamental principle;

however, by adding "not identical" (*bujaku*) to "neither identical nor different" (*fuzen-furi*), and adding "not separate" (*furi*) to "neither identical nor different," it becomes necessary for each to be complete in order to be called the full exhaustion of principle. This is precisely the analogy of the blind men feeling the elephant found in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Therefore, these six [causes] are also called the "True Cause" (*shōin*), as they equally belong to suffering; they are also called "Conditions and Understanding" (*enryō*), as they encompass both afflictions and karma.

Therefore, within this context, there must be both general and specific pairings. Regarding the specific: among the six [elements], mental activity (*saṃskāra*) and the divine self (*ātman*) are seeds of the *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition);

the remaining numbers and form (*rūpa*) are seeds of the *vijñapti-hetu* (perceiving-condition); and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the seed of the *samyag-hetu* (correct cause). Regarding the general pairing:

as fully detailed in the present text, the six dharmas, their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*), the correct cause, and the perceiving-condition are essentially one and no different; it should be understood that the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are precisely these.

That which is eternally abiding herein is precisely what is explained in the commentary; yet the reason for providing this further explanation is to facilitate the understanding of the text by clarifying the meaning of "eternal abiding.
Since the principle revealed through the meaning is one and the same, it is definitively stated that the remaining numbers and forms are taught as seeds of the *jñāna-hetu* (cause of understanding).

I fear that [other] interpretations might lead to error. Now, I maintain that the two meanings of "neither identical nor separate" are illustrated in the sutra by the analogy of the elephant and the Buddha-nature; if these were distinct, [the analogy would fail].
Taken together, these six constitute the Buddha-nature, just as the blind men each grasped one part of an elephant. It is not identical to the six, because there is no elephant apart from them;

yet it is not separate from them, because the six dharmas grasped by each individual are not themselves the Buddha-nature. It is neither identical to nor separate from the six, for there is no distinct Buddha-nature apart from them.

Since this clarifies that they are neither the whole nor the sum of their parts, it is said to be "neither identical nor separate. Next, [this is explained] in terms of cultivation and nature (*xi-xing*).

Because it is the nature [of all things], it is not separate from cultivation; because it is cultivated, it is not identical [to them]. By discussing them as neither identical nor separate, the three Buddha-natures are precisely revealed.
Thus, the six dharmas collectively encompass the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)—indeed, all phenomena.

Within this totality, there is both the general and the specific; here, we follow the general. One must consult the Great Commentary (*Dàshù*) to reconcile what has not yet been reached. First, the explanation of "the world" (*loka*).

Regarding the statement that [the Buddha] "permanently abides in the world," the reason he permanently abides is precisely because the Buddha is identical to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and these three natures permanently abide in the world.

Since he is identical to their nature, he permanently abides. Because he permanently abides by virtue of his nature, he is identical to the single principle (*ekārtha*). The reason for providing this further explanation is twofold:

first, it facilitates the interpretation of the text to clearly establish the meaning of permanent abiding; second, it clarifies the principle through its significance, thereby demonstrating that they are of one principle. Thus it is said.
Regarding the "explanation and establishment" (*śichéng*): by citing past expedient means (*upāya*), it establishes and explains the present revelation of the ultimate truth (*bhūtatathatā*).

The term "luminously clear" (*lǎngrán*) explains the meaning of the character "knowing" (*zhī*); because it is self-realized and understood, it is called "luminously clear. "For a long time it has been widely propagated" refers only to the prior self-realization, hence "for a long time it has been widely propagated.
This does not concern the original state or the past; rather, this is the section on future Buddhas, which serves as an analogy for the present by pointing forward in anticipation.
It is indeed so that the dispositions of sentient beings are dull by nature and their obstructions are heavy—this refers to the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).

These points are all discussed in terms of the three [vehicles] within the four flavors (*catasraḥ paripācaka-rasāḥ*) of the past, and do not refer to the Perfect [Teaching]. Regarding this, the various commentators of both ancient and modern times have all stated that because one provisionally explains with names and marks within that which is nameless and markless, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Jiaxiang [Jizang] was incorrect in claiming that the two types of "verbal expression" and "divine power" manifest the true principle.

Because it was stated above that this is through verbal expression and through skillful means (*upāya*), one knows that the skillful means of this sutra are manifold. Now, although it is said they are manifold, they are in fact only three kinds;
this is merely to manifest their multiplicity, like drops of water in a vast expanse. The meaning of the annotation (*yù zhù*) [marked as "云云"] is roughly as explained above.

Next, regarding the present [verse], first we shall distinguish it from the preceding prose. As for the "four" mentioned in the previous text, the commentary states that the previous text only mentions three—namely, the supramundane intention, the opening of the provisional, and the manifestation of the real. Since the current text speaks of "four," the previous section must have referred to four as a summary.

Furthermore, there are two differences: first, in the previous section, the opening comes first and the manifestation follows, whereas here, the manifestation comes first and the opening follows; second, [the sequence of the teachings differs].

In the preceding section on revealing the reality, it was stated that there is only teaching and practice; now, in this [section], there is no contradiction in the fact that principle and teaching, or principle and practice, may differ.

Therefore, they are not mentioned separately. Within the first meaning, it is also said that such a Dharma is taught specifically for the purpose of manifesting in the world by preaching the sublime Dharma.

Regarding the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*), if considered in terms of what is taught, it pertains to the teaching (*śāsana*); if considered in terms of cultivation, it pertains to practice (*caryā*). Thus, all three [aspects] are contained therein.

Next, regarding the "opening of the provisional" (*kaikwan*): there was an illumination of capacities and the bestowing of transformation in the past; what was bestowed then is precisely what is opened now.

The following section is the commentary on the verses of the *Gāthā* chapter; this passage is somewhat lengthy, and various commentators each clarify its beginning and end, yet their interpretations differ from one another.
As I am unable to reconcile them all, I shall proceed for the sake of brevity by dividing it into five distinct parts, the first of which again cites the text.

The first section, "Marking the Chapter Headings," explains that while the preceding text lacks subsequent [sections], it provides a brief clarification regarding the presence or absence of the prose (long-king).

Second, from "Ancient" onwards, the third section clarifies the reasons why ancient and modern interpretations belong to this [work]. Fourth, "Ancient and Modern" describes the characteristics of how ancient and modern interpretations belong to it.
Fifth, within the summary verse, the middle and lower sections clarify what is being explained here; within these five [sections], each has its own [subdivisions].
The next three [sections] both possess ancient and modern versions, while the fifth exists only in its modern form, consisting of two parts: the concise and the extensive.

By examining these headings from beginning to end, they are somewhat easy to discern. Regarding the first: within the "Teaching by the Dharma" (Hōsetsu), five Buddhas are generally cited to clarify the revelation and manifestation;
both the prose and verse sections contain these two, wherein in both cases the four Buddhas are presented first, followed by the elucidation of Śākyamuni as mentioned above.
The verses for these four Buddhas having been completed, what follows below is precisely the second section: the verses for Śākyamuni Buddha; therefore, it is marked as such.
Next, regarding the omission of the full [verses]: as previously explained, each of the five Buddhas possesses six meanings.

Although they are equal in terms of their meaning—each having six—their textual expressions remain elliptical, mutually illustrating one another through omission. Within those verses, the verses for Śākyamuni Buddha fully contain all six; this is now being discussed.
The former text was thus lacking one [section] while this one possesses all six.

The reason for this is precisely that the contemporary Lord of Transformation intends to fully elucidate this revelation, as it serves as the foundation for the latter two weeks; these matters will manifest themselves later, so there is no need for further elaboration here.
Next, the explanation of "the reason for" (*yō*) clarifies both the ancient and modern sections regarding the grounds upon which this work is based.
As for what the reasons are, they are first set forth here; therefore, it is necessary to clarify them. Within this, there are two parts:

first, clarifying the reason why the narrator (*shosha*) composed [this], and second, clarifying the reason why the author (*sassha*) composed [it]. The first part consists of five sentences; the first four are a record of what was previously stated.
The latter [section] clearly explains the intent of the *Shuji* (Commentary): by means of the middle and upper two phrases, it indicates the capacity and number of the author;

by means of the lower two phrases, it indicates the difficulties faced by the student. For this reason, the *Shuji* must first be presented here. "Compiled in the Qi" refers to the period prior to this.
"Reaching the text" means reaching the subsequent entry into the main text and the section on the following analogies. "Intermingled" [refers to the integration of these elements].

This refers to the convergence of the Dharma, similes, phrasing, and meaning. Question: Since the prose and verse of the five Buddhas are all termed "Dharma-exposition" (dharmadeśanā) and should equally serve as the basis for the similes, why is it that [the similes] appear only in the verse of Śākyamuni, and why are they categorized and attributed to the text at this specific point?
Answer: There is indeed a profound reason. For what reason? Śākyamuni is the presiding teacher of the current age; he cites the other four [Buddhas] to...
Because they act as auxiliary supports, if one considers them solely from the perspective of the principal [subject], then among the remaining four, there is not one that does not assist.

Therefore, if one were to explain this directly regarding the Buddha Śākyamuni as presented in the prose (long-form), it would be addressed by the questions in the verse; yet to state it again would be prolix and inconvenient.
The Buddha’s intention was likewise such that he treated the prose briefly while providing the verses in full detail. For this reason, both ancient and modern [scholars] have [agreed upon this].
Regarding this, it is categorized as follows (and so forth). As for the explanation below concerning the reason for the author’s composition:
since the intent of the sutra is precisely thus, one cannot help but first categorize it under this heading, nor can one avoid encountering difficulties. First, to correctly clarify that reason:
the upper portion of the verse is for the purpose of enabling those with superior faculties to attain realization; the lower portion is for the sake of those with middling and inferior faculties.
This is because the dharma and the analogy depend upon one another. The final phrase explains the meaning of why it serves as the "basis" (mūla).

Therefore, this is a general clarification that all ancient and modern commentators have consistently followed this precedence; it cannot be said to apply solely to the recent or the old [traditions].
This is roughly the case; I have not yet had the leisure for a detailed exposition.

Next follows the fourth section, which fully describes the characteristics of the historical and contemporary classifications; this consists of two distinct parts: first the ancient, and second the contemporary. Within the first part, there are further two sections:

first, the enumeration and description of the five schools (with the phrase "now, as for... [jin wei yi xia] indicating the transition), and second, the summary refutation that serves as the introduction to the main classification.
Regarding the initial section on the five schools, there are five distinct divisions; however, since all five are equally inadequate, they are all... [text continues].

One should explain that although the refutations are not explicitly stated in the text for the middle section—since the first and last sections suffice as examples—they are omitted here because they will be summarized and refuted later.
Regarding the first school, the names are listed below; however, since their proponents are unknown, there are two distinct ways of describing the refutations.
Within the middle section, there are five analogies, each of which must first have its respective analogical passage identified and then contrasted with the scriptural teaching (*dharma*).
Regarding the text within the verse, one may understand for oneself that it was not yet time to align it with the subsequent passage;

as for why it only employs analogies, those [analogies] ought to have been explained in full, but since the names of the analogies established there do not accord with the intended meaning and were merely conceived from personal inclination, they were cited selectively—thus, the correspondence between the dharma and the analogy is simply inappropriate. Later, the conclusion clarifies that this fault does not apply, and therefore it is employed here.
Next, Master Yao’s commentary consists of two parts: first, a description of his classification of the teachings (*ko-fa*), and second, a description of his analogies (*hui-pi*).

Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the statement of the central tenet; second, the detailed differentiation of the beginning and end of the judgment; and third, the conclusion that returns to the central tenet.

Regarding the initial statement, "four and three," this refers merely to the Three Vehicles. The term "four and three" is used because the four dharmas are set in contrast to what follows. Within the first of these [three sections], looking back...
Regarding other passages, there are still two intended meanings. First, one should interpret them specifically with respect to Śākyamuni while interpreting them generally with respect to all Buddhas.
Second, one should primarily interpret them according to the verses (gāthā), yet do so by following the prose (prose commentary); thus, this differs from the usual practice.
Furthermore, although it clarifies that all Buddhas are identical in manifesting the ultimate truth, the prose serves as the foundation; by citing the foundation, the verses are thereby established.
Since its ultimate meaning can be known, and because that [previous section] did not clarify the five Buddhas and the six meanings, the subsequent "convergence of parables" (hui-pi) is presented;

this is precisely to clarify the mutual interpenetration of the Dharma and the parable. As for the statement that "the third cannot be illustrated," its intended meaning likely refers to the fact that the text is concise within the parable.
Other points may be understood accordingly; that [explanation] represents the ultimate contemplation, which for now cannot yet be fully realized.

Later, he himself elucidated [the meaning], subsequently describing how the two schools are largely identical with minor differences. The first is designated as being based solely on analogy, while the latter five are titled according to the Dharma.
The first corresponds to the current general analogy of the manifold interactions, as clarified in the prose and verse sections of the sutra;

the remaining five may be understood accordingly. Regarding the "Dragon Master" (Longshi), his enumeration is entirely the same as before, though there are slight differences in the meaning of the names within it.
The superiority over the preceding [section] is twofold: first, general superiority, meaning that both the analogy and the dharma it illustrates possess meanings that are easy to comprehend;

second, specific superiority, as in the initial case where, although both are general analogies, the names and meanings are superior to those preceding them. The remaining cases may be understood accordingly.

Since these have not yet been fully detailed and are intended only for those who seek conceptual understanding (*yijie*), they are presented collectively at the end rather than through prolixity of text.

The following is the fifth section, describing the Guangzhai [Temple] commentary, which contains two parts: first, the description of its structural categories; second, the detailed refutation of its errors.
Regarding the first part, there are ten textual passages, each of which contains three points:
(1) citing this verse text; (2) clarifying the meaning elucidated by that text; and (3) showing how it serves as the basis for the subsequent analogies. Among these ten, the first two state:
Regarding the remaining [points] above the verse, they are treated solely in accordance with the current text;

as for those below the verse, the reason is that the verse and the prose commentary both contain these two meanings. One should reflect upon this well. Next, in distinguishing what is incorrect, there are two parts:
first, recounting the critiques of others regarding its four faults; second, following that, providing a general clarification of the six [faults].
Regarding the first four errors in meaning: the *Píngjiā* (the Commentator) merely clarifies the errors in their meaning without explicitly stating the number of those errors;

however, the current text, having already set forth [the views], concludes by stating there are "four errors. All commentators maintain that while the *Píngjiā* only possesses the first two meanings, everything from "Furthermore, ten" (*yòu shí*) onwards belongs to the current text, which analyzes those errors. As for what are called the "four," they are all...

This refers to the four citations concerning priority and posteriority, magnitude and minuteness, existence and non-existence. Now, observing these four errors, they all belong to the critiques of others;

I fear they have not yet opened up the intended meaning of our own school. Since it has already been stated that there are four errors according to the critiques of others, one must then respond to them by saying, "Now we do not have these four.
If that were the case, then the nine and the six, as well as the subsequent three, would again constitute four errors. Hereafter...

The purpose of exhausting these explanations is to clarify and establish the meaning of the preceding nine phrases; they do not constitute a count of four types of faults. To say otherwise is incorrect.
Furthermore, the character "jiǎn" (又) has no source [in the original text]. If that were the case, the first would be a fault of textual meaning, which it is not;

the second would be called a fault of textual meaning and judgment; the third would be a fault of discrepancy between the Dharma and the analogy; and the fourth would be a fault of contradiction between the Great and Small Vehicles.
Regarding this, what is the fault in [the argument] that [the categories] are either redundant or missing?

First, since it was stated that there are "phrases" (*pada*), and subsequently that there are "meanings" (*artha*), is it not the case that the meaning [of the text] implies that, according to the textual passages and their meanings, there should be only nine or six [categories], and not ten?

Therefore, the meaning of the text must not be lost. Since the text presents both [nine and six] as headings, they should both be explained; yet, while only the six are explained, the nine are not. Why is this?

The meaning is easy to perceive because the text itself clarifies it for those who follow; this is why it is said at the outset that "there was a person," meaning that at that time there still existed such a person of penetrating insight.

"Ping" (評) means to level, and it also implies to evaluate or discern; that is, to evaluate the meaning by speaking from a middle standpoint, thereby ensuring that the matters undertaken attain a state of balance and correctness.
Thus, the character "ping" (評) is composed of the radical for speech with the phonetic element "zi" (自).
"Comprehensive and level" is the first [of the ten meanings]. Regarding the "nineteen," this refers to the numerical correspondences of what they signify.
As detailed in various commentaries, the original text contains only a single sentence, yet the explanations often exceed half a sheet of paper.

Among those who have attempted to explain them, many are either able to provide a coherent exposition or are unable to do so at all. Even for those who manage to grasp them, they remain personally distressed in the end, finding no [resolution].
Not only is it of no benefit, it even leads to further harm; this has not been so from the beginning, yet people take it to be so, thereby needlessly exhausting later students.
Since this is the case, I shall not trouble paper and ink with further elaboration here, nor shall I describe why it is so.
The meaning of this text is clear, yet those who awaken to it are few; this is generally because they do not investigate the words and meanings of the sutra, which is why such a situation arises.
If one examines the scriptural text closely, these errors will naturally become apparent; it is precisely for this reason that people of Changhua have offered their critique.

Furthermore, since both [the *daśottara* and the *ekottara*] are presented as headings, one should not explain only one of them. Moreover, since the former contains many items while the latter contains few, one should not explain the fewer while omitting the more.
Finally, the "nineteen" [verses] are entirely intended to manifest their specific meanings and are not to be called mere "phrases"; this is most unacceptable. Thus, there are ten [points].
The statement that "nine" is not trustworthy is now clarified: the original text should have read "there should be nine phrases," yet it contains ten characters;
this is clearly due to an error in later transcription. This principle is sufficiently evident, yet because it has been stagnant and difficult to extract, I shall further illustrate it by analogy.
For instance, in Danqiu’s *Great Sūtra Commentary*, he initially sets forth six phrases, and...
Later, he pointed back to what preceded and said, "The eighteen phrases are precisely because of this. Scholars of that time failed to reflect upon whether this was appropriate;
they sought a definitive reality solely through the words "eighteen," ultimately giving rise to forced interpretations.

Intoxicated by the scriptural text, they were intent only on reconciling the numerical count of the phrases, unaware that there was no underlying principle whatsoever. How could this possibly be of any benefit?
The reduction has already been accounted for; whenever one reaches this point of decline, it cannot cease.
Now, as for these nineteen [stages] arising from those eighteen, the numerical principle is one and the same. Since this is not perceived, that can indeed be so.
The intent of this critique is that if one were to follow the textual divisions according to their respective categories, they should properly be nine grades rather than ten, because of the fifth.
The sixth [section] is, in the sutra, actually a single chapter that is grouped together with the fifth as the "Parable of Seeking the Chariot to Avoid Danger.

It should not be separated into two; rather, by combining these two into one, there are nine [sections]. Even if they were divided into two, although the names would exist, the meaning would ultimately be absent.
Therefore, [the author] further states: "Not grasping the meaning of the text stems entirely from this one word."

To omit all laborious words and value brevity over prolixity, this text consists of nineteen sections; reducing it by one-fifth results in eighteen sections, and further condensing it by two-thirds leaves us with nine.
Can such a reduction be considered comparable [to the original]? This is not merely for my own convenience, but for the benefit of future scholars.
These nine points are thus summarized. Next, regarding the "six meanings," "meaning" refers to principle (*yili*); that is to say, if one were to analyze them...
