the "five paths" (pañca-gati) refer to the five destinies (pañca-gati), which are largely the same with minor differences that shall be explained in due course (*et cetera*). Both the preceding passage and this one clarify six [paths], while later sections mention either five or six;
other sūtras are likewise. Later, we shall reconcile these ourselves: although there is a distinction between "paths" (*gati*) and "destinies" (*gati*), they are also interchangeable.
Now that the cause has already been raised, the cause should be investigated by means of its effect. That which comes from the source is the cause;

since there is an effect, there must necessarily be a cause. Therefore, by citing the effect, one investigates the cause—asking from what causes and conditions it comes to these five places of fruition.
Some say the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) are themselves the cause, but here we maintain that the "original source" is what constitutes the cause. This is explained below as follows:

The text states that these are all cases where the result corresponds to its cause. Below, it next clarifies that the absence of such worldly causes and results for the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) constitutes the causes and results of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) of the supramundane. The "five" refer to the obstacles, while the "three" refer to the remedies;

since both arise through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they can be remedied and extinguished (and so forth). This is also an instance of using the non-existent to reveal the existent. As for the term "five destinies," it refers once again to... [text continues].

The five paths (pañca-gati) pertain only to the subject and object; in the former case, they face the path of causes, which is itself the fruit. Here, facing the destination of the fruit, they should reside within the causes—the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) as fruit.

The six sense-fields (ṣaḍ-āyatana) pervade both the subject and the object: the "able" (subject) refers to the six objects (ṣaḍ-viṣaya), and the "objected-to" (object) refers to the six faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya).

Since these twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana) are already included therein, there is no longer the cycle of birth and death consisting of the three realms (tridhātu) as cause and fruit; this is therefore Nirvana. Next—
Because one immediately aspires to seek Buddhahood, one immediately receives the prediction of the fruit of Buddhahood; this also applies to both the provisional and the ultimate (and so forth).

Below, in explaining the treatise, it is stated differently from before: first, the statement from the treatise is cited, followed by a conclusion clarifying the preceding point. The previous section explained the ten unwholesome acts as the cause for rebirth in hell, whereas here only one is explained;
this is the difference. If one wishes to reconcile this, the previous mention of "ten" was a general enumeration of those within that category.

Each and every one is thus; this further clarifies the meaning of what preceded. It also demonstrates that a single evil act possesses all ten, and by extension, possesses everything—not merely the ten.
Therefore, all are causes. Since it is so for one realm of rebirth (*gati*), it is likewise for the others;
by briefly citing one, the rest may be inferred accordingly.

Next, regarding the explanation by way of karmic fruition (*vipāka*), there are two parts: first, clarifying the function of fruition; second, clarifying the essential function of the stage of fruition.
As for the phrase "furthermore" (*yù yún*), it should be understood as continuing the explanation from the preceding treatise. First, the general heading states:

"Spontaneous" (*zì'ěr*) means that it functions through natural spontaneity rather than being caused by external agency; thus it is called "spontaneous. "Real" (*shí*) refers to what is brought about by the preceding causes; it refers directly to—

Since the present fruit does not mention past causes, it is said to be "spontaneous" (*svataḥ*). Otherwise, it would be equivalent to being causeless, which is not the fundamental tenet of the Buddha.
Next, the following passage explains that there are five distinct types [of beings]. Ghosts do not merely come as they are; they are also capable of various transformations.

Regarding the three matters among humans, there is both a heading and an explanation. It says that among humans there are such types, but this does not mean that all are so. As for the term "liberation," it refers to... [text ends].

"Nirvāṇa" is this name; it refers generally to the *prativedhabhāgīya* (stages conducive to penetration). Specifically, the record states: "The roots of goodness cultivated that do not abide in birth-and-death are called *prativedhabhāgīya*;

attaining correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) is the first fruit (*prathamaphala*). Since this is explained extensively and naturally within the section on the heavens, it is abbreviated here and merely annotated as "[etcetera].

The above concludes the discussion on karmic activity (*karmaprayoga*). Below, the nature and function of the retribution-ground (*vipākabhūmi*) are clarified. Regarding "retribution": [text continues].

Although the stages (bhūmi) are distinct, they mutually possess one another within their own natures; yet because these are all functional capacities within a single essence, they are the functioning of that nature. The text consists of three sections:

first, it clarifies how the lowest stage possesses the four causes and effects of the higher stages; second, it clarifies how the highest stage possesses the four causes and effects of the lower stages;
third, it concludes by using the examples of the upper and lower to show that the intermediate stages are likewise all thus, each possessing the three paths in brief.
Since this cause and effect are clearly stated in the text and it is said that they do not manifest, these seeds must exist fully within the nature (*prakṛti*).
If the Hīnayāna does not speak of seeds, how can this treatise make such a statement? Furthermore, as there are differing views among the various schools, one cannot be absolute;
[these seeds] should pertain to all three realms, yet the fact that it mentions only the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) should simply...
Whether this is an abbreviated or distinct meaning, these two passages were already briefly cited previously in the explanation of the inconceivable.
If even what is clarified by the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is thus, how much more so the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna)? Precisely because of this nature, it can be cultivated and realized;
such a thing is difficult to conceive—how could one not believe in its cultivation? One must contemplate it, one must contemplate it.
Next follows the third section, which explains the names and meanings. While the preceding section dealt only with five types of beings, this present section fully explains all six;
it is precisely here that the term "six realms" from the sūtra text is directly interpreted. First, regarding the hells:

we first translate the name and explain its meaning, second, we distinguish what is not the actual number, third, we distinguish what is correct and incorrect, and fourth, we clarify whether they may or may not be avoided. Within the initial translation and explanation, *niraya* is the new [Sanskrit] term.
Regarding *nāraka*, *naloka*, and *abhi*: the translations and explanations for the first two names differ slightly, as briefly indicated above.
As for *abhi*, this is translated as "uninterrupted" (*wújiàn*); there are five such [types], as explained elsewhere (*etc.*).

Furthermore, although the explanations provided in the text regarding "there being nothing else" (*yì wú yǒu děng*) are extensive, they still require further reconciliation, which has not yet been undertaken. As for the phrase "those who fall early," it refers to the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*).
Because it is the most inferior among [the realms], it is called "falling down"; this explains the meaning of everything from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) downward.
This refers to the form in which one is born there among humans. To say "without release" means abandonment; because it is brought about by one's own karma, no one is able to grant release.
Next, regarding "not a real number," this refers to seeing such things as being produced by one's own karma. Next, it is distinguished...
"Right and wrong" refers here to physical form; at the beginning, they still possess human form, but once they undergo suffering, they no longer belong to the category of human form.
To interpret it thus, [some] say these four characters are entirely devoid of meaning and must be a scribal error.

I, however, maintain that "above" (the preceding part) distinguishes form, while "hearing" (the following part) distinguishes speech; thus, one considers whether the words of such offenders can be understood.
The commentary explains that "intelligible" means that when one has not yet received the retribution for one's offenses, one's speech is correct and intelligible;

however, at the time one is undergoing the suffering of retribution, it can no longer be understood. Thus, we know that this term was somewhat omitted from the heading, which is why it is insufficient.
What, then, is meant by "redundant"? Next, the explanation of the animal realm follows; here, the local vernacular is used to express the Sanskrit name, and the text consists of three parts.

The commentary explains that whenever the term "animal" (*tiryagyoni*) appears in various sūtras and śāstras, its meaning is taken as "that which is raised or kept," similar to the concept of the "six domestic animals" (*ṣaḍ-gava*) in this region;
however, this narrow definition is not exhaustive. As for those who explain it by the term "sideways-born" (*tiryañc*), "sideways" does not carry the sense of "being raised";

thus, the name and the reality do not correspond. This is because the old translations were not perfected; the new translation uses "sideways-born beings" (*tiryañca*), which correctly captures the two senses of "sideways."
Regarding the correspondence of meaning (*artha-yukti*): the character "xing" (行) is pronounced level tone when read in general, but it may also be read with a departing tone;

its meaning can be understood accordingly. In the subsequent section on meaning, there is a heading, an explanation, and a clarification. Within the third meaning, there is likewise a heading, an explanation, and a discernment of their initial and final similarities and differences.
As for the term "noble speech" (*ārya-vāk*), "noble" (*ārya*) means correct; it refers to that which is able to accord with the correct human language. Hereafter follows the cause.
Yet they cannot [do so]. The term *preta* (鬼言闍梨哆者) is the Sanskrit *pīluṭa* (薜茘哆); it is likely that this was originally *bī*, but later students erroneously wrote it as *jā*.
This is translated as "hungry ghost" (*jiegui*). However, the name "ghost" (*gui*) generally encompasses many distinct categories;
as detailed in the *Śrāddhavidhi-sūtra* (施食經), there are more than thirty types [and so forth]. What is now referred to as "grandfather" (*zǔfù*) is an older translation. Next...
The explanation of the meaning begins with the general and proceeds to the specific. First, regarding the term "ancestor" (*zu*) as the beginning: "ancestor" means the start.

When the beginning serves as the progenitor for what follows, the subsequent generations also receive this name by following the origin; this is analogous to the terms for grandfather (*gao*) and great-grandfather (*zeng*) in this land. As for the terminology of this land:

Heaven is called *shen* (spirit), Earth is called *qi* (numinous), and when a person dies they are called *gui* (ghost). *Gui* means "to return"; [the spirit] ascends from the void and the vital breath (*qi*).
They come and then return to their own place; thus, from the character "again" (又) onwards, the text explains the specific [category].

It is called "hungry ghost" (preta) because it distinguishes them from others by means of hunger. For these two reasons, they are named hungry ghosts. Their forms are explained in detail in the *Āhāra-sūtra* (Food Sūtra), which has not yet been fully described here.
Next, the human realm is explained: first, it is translated as "mind" (意). There are three meanings for this, which can be understood from the text. First...
As for Cloud-Born (Sudarśana), he was a Golden Wheel-Turning King who transformed the world through the ten wholesome deeds; thus, all three [of these beings] are described as "wholesome" (*śubha*).

If one follows the conventions of people here in this land, "human" (*manuṣya*) means one who is patient and able to settle themselves in the Way while enduring worldly emotions; hence they are called humans. Next, regarding the explanation of *asura*:
why is this mentioned here when it ought to have come earlier? It may be that the order is intentional, or perhaps this sequence occurs in certain sūtras and śāstras.
This is because either the whole or a portion of them is included within the celestial realm (*deva-gati*).
The new [translation] states that "Asura" is explained in the text through three meanings: they are called "Non-Gods" (*a-deva*) because their physical form and conduct differ from those of the gods.

Among these three meanings, the first is expressed as "non-," the second as "not-," and the last as "without-"; all are the meaning of the syllable *a*, pronounced with a short vowel, just as described above.

The explanation of "Deva" (the term for Heaven/God) has been completed. In the Sanskrit language, it is *deva* (pronounced *ti-va*; the second syllable is pronounced with the *fangke* [approximating *e*] tone), which is translated here as "Heaven.

The explanation provided in the text is somewhat difficult to perceive; according to the underlying meaning and structural logic, one should first provide a dual definition: "Heaven" (*deva*) signifies that which is spontaneous and natural (*svabhāva*), and it is also termed "Supreme" (*jaya*).
The character "also" (*yi*) has been omitted from the text. Below, the term "Victorious in Bliss" (*sukha-jaya*) follows, which explains the preceding point by means of two matters.
"Ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*) refers to the body of bliss, which is the mental body (*cittakāya*). From "all matters" below, it is a summary:
because all various matters of the mental body surpass all other realms, they are called "supreme" (*jaya*). From "always" (*nitya*) below, it next explains "spontaneity" (*svayambhū*):

because it is eternally present and naturally possesses radiant illumination, it is called "natural" (*tianran*). From "from again" (*you*) below—[the character] "yi" (一) is likely a scribal error from later transmission.
The remaining errors should not be employed.

The preceding explanation of the names and meanings of the six realms is now complete. Below follows the fourth section, which explains them according to essential practice: first, a general clarification of the mental activities of the six destinies;
second, a specific clarification of those mental activities; third, a dual conclusion and exhortation to practice; and finally, a dual presentation of the provisional and the real, also known as...

Regarding "person" (*pudgala*) as a phenomenon (*dharma*): since it was previously stated that "name" is a designation, this is a real entity. This real phenomenon consists of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

As for the term "element" (*dhātu*), it refers to the distinct differences between matter and mind, which are the objective bases [of cognition]. Alternatively, it refers to the meaning of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

Below, regarding the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), it clarifies that because the provisional and the real are combined, they may collectively be termed "sentient beings" (*sattva*), which is precisely the mind.
This refers to the convergence of conduct and phenomena (*dharma*). If one further distinguishes the five destinies (*gati*) for sentient beings, there are four propositions:
first, unwholesome mental states as cause result in the three evil destinies; second, wholesome mental conduct as cause results in the human and celestial realms;
the next two propositions state that "superior" refers to the human and celestial realms, while "vile" refers to the remaining destinies.

Now, as for the claim that the two preceding phrases concerning good and evil have already exhausted the six destinies (*ṣadgati*), and that these two phrases are now being stated once more—this is certainly not the case.

Here, "destinies" refers to transcending the three realms; both the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*) and the realm without outflows (*anāsrava*) are considered base from the perspective of the enlightened mind.

This is because the preceding states of good and evil within the realm of outflows are obstructive and not the Path; therefore, they are termed "base. "Base" (*bi*) is also synonymous with "shameful" (*chi*).
To summarize the exhortation: the various realms do not transcend the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the supramundane.

One who thoroughly understands these realms cultivates the wholesome to eliminate the unwholesome, and cultivates the supramundane to eliminate the mundane; this is the full extent of the meaning. It differs from the various other interpretations, as one may reflect upon it.
The following is the fifth section, a summary that clarifies the essential two meanings of what has been explained previously.
The preceding "causes and conditions" refers to the three prior sections. Next, regarding the term "resembling" (*sadr̥śa*): this is used in the sutra as a provisional designation based on the mind;

it differs from ordinary usage because the contemplation is clarified by concluding the preceding matters. Therefore, it is called "resembling. The *Commentary* states: "Within the preceding causes and conditions, the four [aspects] may also be fully present."
The five destinies differ according to the mind; that which is done by people in this world is what breaks through [the mundane], which is the first principle (paramārtha).
Later, it appears as if the observer judges the meaning based on the mind, yet the meaning should actually be observed within the mind.

Now, it is said that the preceding prose section on the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) treats them as the objects to be remedied by the three kinds of truth (*trīṇi-saṃvṛti*), after which the first principle is explained. Since this verse now summarizes the preceding [prose] as four [truths], it is difficult to reconcile.

This is because both the agent and the object are unestablished. Furthermore, among the verses on the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) by the Buddhas mentioned previously, four passages correspond to four meanings.
Moreover, the first three are obstacles and their remedies, which constitute the three *paryāya-satyas*; the fourth is the reality that is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Now, within this passage, the preceding major section contains four meanings; the first provides a general clarification of causes and conditions, while simultaneously citing the supramundane to manifest [the teaching].
Regarding the world, this clarifies the two functions of the world in succession to demonstrate that it is profoundly worthy of faith and aspiration; this constitutes the person.

Next, the distinctions among the six destinies are analyzed to show that conditioned and outflowing phenomena are deeply loathsome; this serves as the antidote. These three are all that which is to be eliminated.
The fourth [function] causes one to observe skillfully: by means of the wholesome, one understands the unwholesome, and through the realization of the superior and the base, one abandons the base.

From the supreme realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the four [meanings] are thus concluded. Previously, there were three sections where all were discussed in terms of both the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*tattva*).
Now, this section briefly explains the four meanings from the perspective of the provisional; yet, if one considers the meaning of the provisional, it also fully encompasses the real.

Why is this? Because at the beginning, the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*), and the causes and conditions for attaining Buddhahood were clarified—namely, the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*).
Next, by means of the two functions, the inconceivable is clarified; this can serve as an analogy to manifest the meaning of the ten realms of the Mahāyāna.
Next, since the names and meanings of the six paths are thus, how much more so are the names and meanings of the remaining four noble ones difficult to conceive.

Since the fourth [section] states that the various realms—whether wholesome or unwholesome, superior or base—are each naturally pervasive throughout the ten realms, therefore, at the very beginning...
Following the "Five and Three," it further clarifies the three vehicles precisely through the meaning of "penetrating manifestation";

thus, the four meanings are explained in combination regarding the provisional and the real across the first three locations. Now, this section relies upon the four provisional penetrations to clarify the four aspects of the real.
Of the first three [locations], the first corresponds to the preceding two wisdoms; the prose section has not yet explained the "inconceivable. The first three belong to the mundane.
The third meaning concludes with the fourth, which summarizes the first meaning. This passage differs from the usual style precisely because it serves as a summary of the preceding three;
this intention is profound and far-reaching, and one should contemplate it well. One must not revert to ordinary views and understandings.
Let this suffice for now, as it has not yet been fully elaborated. Next, the arousal of compassion immediately removes turbidity. It says:

The subject and object of seeing are the cause for the arising of compassion (*karuṇā*). "Impulse" (*kṣuṇa*) has the meaning of striking or stimulating; compassion is that which initiates [the mind], while the "mind and so forth" are that which is initiated.

Although the text fully contains the meanings of the three types of action (*trikarma*) and the various ritual arrangements (*prajñapti*), because it generally applies to the three pairs [of subject and object] mentioned previously, it specifically pertains here to vocal action (*vākkarman*).

Whether [the gates] are opened or closed in the past and present, the beginning and end of a single transformation are all contained therein. This is indicated by taking up the subsequent passage to complete [the argument].
The meaning herein cannot be explained in any other way than this.

Next, regarding the verse on the "expedient means of giving," it takes its name from ancient usage; this is precisely the opening [of the topic], as the narration of the ancient practice of giving is itself the present opening.
One must always maintain this intention and not lose the essential point. Next, the first section is further clarified in three parts:

Although the phrasing consists of two parts, the essential meaning is simply this: the first is the "correct" [teaching], while the subsequent two are the reasons for ceasing the transformation [of beings].

The term "Great" (Mahā) refers precisely to the present "Wondrous" (Miao). The initial [section] corresponds to this Wondrous [teaching], for it is because of this Great Matter that [the Buddha] appeared in the world.

As for the term "appropriate" (ni), it refers to what is stated in the following text: "only then will he be able to provide rescue and relief. The subsequent [sections] rely correctly upon this meaning.
As for the statement that this name is established based on that text, it must be because this [state] is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the same essence;
all Buddhas, being mindful of their original vows, cease [their activity] because there is no such capacity [in sentient beings].

This initial passage concerning "what is appropriate" is explained somewhat extensively in the commentary (*ṭīkā*). Having finished listening to the explanation, I do not yet know what the meaning of this explanation is, whether in the sutra or in the commentary.

The reason we have not yet been able to harmonize [the text] is precisely because it lacks its presiding master. Now, first, I shall rely on the *Śū* (Commentary) to establish the topical divisions (*ko*) and personally harmonize the sutra;
next, I shall harmonize the explanations found within the *Śū*. Regarding the first: the first phrase at the beginning of the sutra corresponds to the time and place of the intended audience;
the next line and phrase correctly clarify the intended audience itself. Within this central section, there are again two parts: the first phrase is general, and the next...
Regarding the classification of the practice, the entry into the sutra is briefly as follows. Next, concerning the text of the commentary: first is the explanation of the time and place;

from "feeling the tree's grace" downward is the explanation of the central section’s general suitability; and from "the past causes and effects" downward is the explanation of the central section’s specific suitability.
Within the initial explanation of the time and place, there are two distinct parts. First is the explanation of the time and events; the explanation follows below.

The commentary on the first word "initial" (*ādi*) clarifies that this "initial" excludes both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), as well as the self-manifestation and the manifestation for others.

Since the ultimate reality is like space and is not subsumed within the three periods of time, how could there be such a "time"? However, in terms of the cultivation and attainment of phenomena, there is indeed time.

Since its nature has no spatial direction, how could its cultivation and attainment have a fixed location? Yet, from the perspective of transforming others, there is indeed time. This is all explained in relation to...
Whether it be during inconceivable time, this is for the sake of transforming those below; it clarifies the present intent.

To speak precisely, since this refers to the very first moment of transforming sentient beings, it is called "the beginning. "To act" (*wei*) means to bestow or to initiate. From the essence, function arises;

this bestowing and acting to transform sentient beings consists of five periods. Since we are now speaking of the first, it is described thus. This is precisely the time when [the Buddha] manifests completion for the sake of sentient beings.

...Furthermore, the subsequent explanation of its location refers to the *bodhimaṇḍa* (place of enlightenment). Within it, there is both a site (*maṇḍa*) and a tree; since both constitute the location, it is so called.

As for the "explanation by way of phenomena" (*vastu-vyākhyāna*), it is termed "phenomena" because it is explained in relation to the dharmas sought, based on the successive stages of meditative practice. "Way" (*mārga*) refers to—

The Buddha’s knowledge and vision—cultivation and purification—is precisely the method by which they are attained; that is to say, it refers to the practice of opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
"Attainment" specifically refers to reaching the ultimate state of opening, showing, awakening, and entering.

Since both rely upon this place as the site where the Way is realized, it is called the "site of the Way" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). As explained extensively in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, I have not been able to provide a full account here.
Regarding "the tree of the Way" (*mārga-vṛkṣa*): this refers to the location where the tree stands; it is the site beneath that tree, and the tree itself belongs to that site.

Furthermore, because of the two capacities [of the place and the tree] mentioned immediately below, these two objects are first explained together. Both are derived from their respective bases of capacity; they are designated as "the Way" (*mārga*) subsequent to the "Correct World" (*samyag-loka*).
To discuss the matter according to its facts, both this location and the tree are as extensive as described in the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions); this has not yet been detailed here.

One should know that being able to fully comprehend this involves the penetration of both provisional and ultimate [truths] regarding time and place. Since this [teaching] is now presented as being appropriate for those of great capacity, it must be the ultimate;
thus, it is the wondrous time and place.

The above concludes the section on time and place. Below is the explanation of the first general summary of the "Correct" [Teaching]. The text contains both the subject and the object, serving as a preface.

Having already explained the two "objects" (*ālambana*) concluded above, we now proceed directly to explain the two "capacities" (*karana*), namely, *vipaśyanā* (contemplation) and *caṅkramaṇa* (walking meditation).
Within this section, first, following the momentum of the preceding text, there is an explanation based on the literal meaning of the phenomena; second, an explanation based on what they symbolize.

Regarding the first of these, there is first a separate explanation of contemplation and walking meditation, followed by a combined clarification of their significance. As for the intent of the [first] passage: since the previous section symbolized the realization of the essence within oneself, it says "sitting here."

It is explained that because [the tree] arises from its essence to function for the benefit of others, it is said that the tree of contemplative practice possesses the grace of providing shelter, while the earth possesses the virtue of providing a stable foundation;
both are supreme conditions for attaining the Way. Therefore, one must maintain mindfulness and reflection. The meaning of "wherein the Way is perfected" is as follows:
once the Way is perfected through these [conditions], one will repay them. "Sai" (賽) means recompense, and "ze" (澤) means bounty.
How can the grace of the Superior be repaid? It is intended to be done by means of the following.

Next, regarding the explanation based on what is manifested (*saṃsūcita*): although it is said that the primary intent of "contemplating the mind" (*guanxin*) lies in manifesting the internal Dharma, the previous section directly explained the two capacities (*neng*) in contrast to the two objects (*su*).
Now, this section provides a general explanation of both capacity and object. Within this, there are three parts; first:
This explains the contemplation of the tree, following the explanation of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), to clarify together the two meanings of the three-week period.

Regarding the first [the tree]: first is the tree, then the contemplation. First, as for the "tree," it refers to this very tree. It is called a "tree" because its flowers and fruits are inexhaustible.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The two members of the past constitute the root; the five members of the present..."
The three present factors are taken as the flower, and the two future factors are taken as the fruit. To have both flower and fruit refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
to have no flower but fruit refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*); and to have neither flower nor fruit refers to those in the state of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

Some say that by logical inference, having little flower and fruit refers to those in training, while having no flower and fruit refers to those with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*); this is the meaning according to the *Pitaka* and the *Āgama*. (From the *Ratnagotravibhāga*).
It is said that when the four matters of conditions, arising, destruction, and existence are all absent, one is then called "seeking conditions.

Here, "conditions" (pratyaya) are the root, "arising" (utpāda) is the substance, "existence" (bhava) is the flower, and "destruction" (vibhava) is the fruit. This refers to the two types of twelvefold dependent origination outside the realms—the distinct and the perfect meanings.
Now, it is said that such a tree pervades the Dharma-realm and extends through the three periods of time; it is not only vast but also exceedingly high. This represents that which is... [the object].

"Contemplating the objects" refers to the profound contemplation (*gambhīra-darśana*) and so forth; this correctly clarifies the nature of contemplation. Because one contemplates by means of the wisdom of wondrous insight (*prajñā-jñāna*), exhausting the principles and exhausting the nature, it is called "profound.

Every single dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is none other than the realm of the three truths (*tri-satya*); the contemplation of these realms should ultimately result in the attainment of *bodhi*.

Furthermore, the twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the contemplation of the three paths (*tri-mārga*); the contemplation of the three paths is itself the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), the three bodies (*tri-kāya*), and *bodhi*.
This great tree—this tree of *sambodhi*—has a substance and virtue that extend horizontally and vertically, pervading all things, and is thus "high and great.
This section below generally clarifies the meaning symbolized by the contemplation of the tree:

principle (*tattva*), teaching (*dharma*), and practice (*caryā*). Next, the *Record* (*Jì*) states: "That is, within the two gates of 'Simile' and 'Faith and Understanding' (*adhimukti*), each has..."

One might propose that there is no fixed occasion for the cessation of transformative activity, and that this principle should likewise apply to these three periods. Now, according to Jiaxiang’s account of the ancients, it is further stated:

"The first seven days, by means of the gate of exhortation (*kuanmen*), one cannot preach the Mahāyāna; the second seven days, by means of the gate of admonition (*jimen*), one cannot preach the Mahāyāna;
on the third seven days, through both admonition and exhortation, one is able to preach it. Is this not indeed the case? For the ancients...
This is because the three names—Establishing, Proposing, and Appropriate—are set forth. Next, regarding the Master [Huiyuan]: first, he generally clarifies the intent;
second, he specifically explains the text; third, he cites scriptural evidence. This means that since the ultimate Great Matter cannot be approached with haste, there are two points:

first, to manifest the locus of the wondrous transformation; second, to admonish and encourage those who have not yet arrived. Thus, there are two instances of the word "to" (zhì), and the sevenfold contemplation correctly represents these three.
The sequence of the cited proofs establishes these three points. Next, below, that which clarifies their incorrectness provides a dual refutation of both schools:

first, it elucidates the correct principle, and then it rebukes their interpretation as being inconsistent with this [principle], stating that it is therefore unacceptable. This rebuke is leveled because they both provide definitive interpretations.
Regarding the characters *lǎn* (覽) and *jiàn* (鑒), both meanings are applicable; however, *jiàn* (鑒) is more elegant. The *Erya* states: "To soak" (*yān*).

Having lingered for a long time, the second part is the formal explanation, which has two sections: first, a general clarification of the intent; second, a detailed analysis of the text. The first section contains both a heading and an explanation.

This is expressed through provisional words to manifest the underlying intent; it does not mean that things are actually so. However, when this sutra is preached, it must be an act of revelation and manifestation.
If, at the beginning, nothing was concealed, what would there be to reveal? This is because it speaks to the fundamental intention of the Buddha’s appearance in the world. Second.
Since the nature of all things has always possessed the ten realms, this very statement made at the outset is itself the revelation; how could there be anything that cannot be so?

This precisely relies on the later [sections] to clarify the meaning of the beginning. Within the subsequent detailed explanation, first it is treated according to the teaching (jiao), and then according to contemplation (guan).

Regarding the former, first there is a direct application of this sutra’s three cycles (san-zhou), followed by a summary of the preceding as the Perfect (yuan), which again gives rise to the latter three [cycles].

Regarding the explanation of the "beginning" and "middle" [of the *Lotus Sūtra*], this refers specifically to the causal-condition (*nidāna*) interpretation of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). First, it clarifies the three cycles of provisional suitability;

next, it indicates that because there were those without the capacity [for the Great Vehicle], the Buddha ceased his transformative activity and bestowed the Lesser [Vehicle]. This serves as the explanation for the completion [of the teaching], which should be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, since this is discussed in terms of the teachings, it should also possess the four meanings of causal conditions (*nidāna*), even though various commentators have not explicitly stated them; yet these four meanings are certainly present, so I shall now briefly state them.
This first section comprehensively clarifies the meaning and purpose; since it encompasses all three [aspects], it corresponds to the "Worldly" (loka) teaching that directly reveals the principle.

It corresponds to the "Ultimate Truth" (paramārtha) teaching by using metaphors to illustrate the principle. It corresponds to the "For Others" (pudgala) teaching by relying on events to lead various disciples.

It corresponds to the "Causal" (nidāna) teaching as it addresses long-standing, excessive indolence. This is the intended meaning of the "remedial" (pratipakṣa) aspect. Alternatively, for those who may find this not to be the usual method, one should contemplate the fivefold stages.

The previous four instances successively concluded by summarizing what preceded and indicating what followed; since this sutra consists of three cycles, it is thus the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), which is the perfect that transcends the partial.

Below, the section "Correctly Classifying According to the Teachings" (*zheng yue jiao*) proceeds as follows: since there are four distinct divisions within the gates of teaching, a provisional classification cannot be universally applied, nor can it be definitively established beforehand;

only then does one explain the three [cycles]. All of these are interpretations based on the text itself, and when one’s own understanding accords with them, they are all elegantly consistent with this [teaching].
"Exquisite indeed! Someone said: "The three manifestations [are explained] in relation to the three meanings; yet you speak of seven repetitions. What do these signify?

Furthermore, seven is one of the essential numbers of that region; as in the holy teachings where it is sometimes said 'one,' 'seven,' 'thirty-seven,' or 'seventy-seven'—all such frequent mentions are spoken in accordance with worldly convention. Thus, they signify the Mahāyāna."
The essentials for entering the Way are the seven categories of the *bodhipākṣika-dharmas* (factors conducive to enlightenment).
Since each of these expositions leads one into these seven categories of the Dharma-gate, they are called "seven days. This signifies that the seven categories of wisdom are named *bodhipakṣa*;

"bodhi" means awakening, and "pakṣa" indicates that these are the branches of the wisdom of awakening. Thus, they are all represented by "days," and furthermore, the "day" symbolizes knowledge and vision.
Because one attains the opening, showing, awakening, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision by means of these seven [aspects], they are manifested in this manner.

Thus, whether interpreted according to the specific or general sense of the text, all converge without contradiction. This meaning has not been discussed by scholars of past or present; my intention here is merely to state it briefly (etc.).
Someone might say: "To employ the Great [Vehicle] as a provisional accommodation when there is no capacity for it, so that the transformation ceases—this is precisely what must be contemplated."

The scriptural text itself is already clear and its meaning easy to understand; why then is a divergent interpretation required? If that were so, this would merely be a general principle (*sāmānya-naya*);
what relevance would it have for the present sutra? Furthermore, if one cannot even yet preach the Dharma, how could one possibly comprehend the three stages (*traya-parivarta*)? Why is this so?

Since one has no choice but to bestow the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), this is merely a general application of the Mahāyāna and thus does not concern this [sutra]. Although you speak of "three meanings," it is not known what these are.

To speak of [the first] three weeks alone may appear to be an exposition of the Dharma; yet, to omit the remaining two weeks and speak of them in isolation is likewise not an exposition of the Dharma, because it does not speak of the Dharma at all.
Since even the first week cannot be considered such, how much less so the latter two? Therefore, this is not the intent of this sutra.
Since it is not its intent, what is the purpose of applying these words here? Thus, it is untenable. Next, regarding the teaching for the practitioner:
This is the essential purport. The "four contemplations" explained therein refer to the contemplative practices (*guanxing*) of the four teachings.

Within each of the first three [teachings], there are the three principles of "provisional suitability," "lack of capacity," and "cessation of transformation. Regarding the fourth, as it lacks these three [principles] found in the preceding ones, it is revealed that it possesses the three [principles].
Next, regarding the "lack of capacity," the text speaks of those with "heavy obstructions"; as the *Sūtra* says, they are "attached to delusion," and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says...
"From ignorance there is feeling, and thus my illness arises"—this refers to the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), which is why it is said that the obstacles are heavy.

Next, regarding those who are incapable of hearing: because their obstacles are heavy and their faculties dull, they cannot believe or accept [the teaching]; thus they are incapable of hearing. Because they lack the capacity (*anabhavyatva*), I do not speak;

for if I were to speak, it would simply trigger their capacity. Since their obstacles are heavy and their faculties are dull, there is nothing that can be triggered; therefore, even though they request it, [I do not speak].

Regarding this, it is now said that this passage is somewhat difficult to discern. Why? Because although it states, "Though they requested to know [the absence], he did not preach the sutra," there is only the mention of the request and no mention of "knowing the absence" or "not preaching.
If one understands this section, one must further proceed to the initial passage on the cessation of transformation;
it is precisely because there was no receptive capacity (*anāśrayatva*) that the transformation ceased. Alternatively, there may be two interpretations.

To suffer harm upon hearing [the Dharma] entirely is simply due to a lack of spiritual capacity (*mūka*); however, it is far more convenient to place such cases within the category of those lacking capacity.
One should reflect further on this. These three points clarify the meaning of "lack of capacity. Next, regarding the cessation of transformation (*nivṛtti-vyāpāra*), there are two types:
first, that which is not merely useless but causes great harm; second, that which, while not beneficial, yet does not cause great harm. This is intended to clarify...

This is the Tathāgata’s great function of skillful means and wondrous capability. Next, the four chapters on the "Correct Bestowal of Expedients" (zhèngshīquán) invert the preceding section to clarify how, because there are those with spiritual capacity, benefits are brought about.
Since the initial text first says "seeking and reflecting" and then says "it should also be so," these two opening phrases constitute the preliminary stage of "provisional suitability.
The subsequent two phrases reflect upon the meaning of "conforming and agreeing. Within this text, at the beginning...

Regarding the explanation of "recollection" (*smṛti*) as "investigation" (*vitarka*), it refers to following in succession. Why does it follow what preceded and then speak of investigation? Because the text should be explained accordingly, it is thus interpreted.
Next, regarding the explanation of recollecting the minds of all Buddhas: why is it that one does not practice giving until after having practiced recollection?

It is because if one has not previously known how to practice the three kinds of giving, one only comes to know them through recollection; therefore, it is explained in this way. It is not that [recollection] is not [necessary].

This is known to be for the purpose of manifesting the Way so that it may be easily believed by all; thus, where the text should read "yǔn" (conformity), it reads "yǐn" (to lead), which is likely a scribal error.
"Yǔn" means to accord with. There are two reasons for the Buddha’s manifestation, namely the two meanings within the section on "Adapting to Suitability.

As for "consoling and exhorting," he accords with the Buddhas above and takes pity on the multitude of sentient beings below; he conceals the ultimate truth and employs provisional means, bending his ways to accommodate them.
"Laoqian" (Laborious Humility) is therefore "consolation. Consolation means peace. Because one exerts oneself for the sake of others, there must be consolation;
"metaphor" means encouragement, clarifying principles to provide mutual exhortation. Both follow worldly convention.
Next, regarding the formal praise: a single line and a single phrase consist entirely of the words of all Buddhas expressing their difficulty [in finding such a person].
The first two phrases are the praise; the following three phrases explain the meaning of the former. "Skillful" (*śubha*) refers to the ultimate limit of skillful capability.

The subsequent phrase praises its utility as being the most supreme among all benefits. The text explains the initial meaning: it is the ultimate limit of being able to conceal while simultaneously being able to bestow. This is the second explanation.

The latter phrase states that "being able to open [the way] through giving" is the most supreme quality of a teacher. Next, I shall explain the following three phrases, first clarifying the meaning of the preceding one.
The initial phrase clarifies that he has personally attained the reality (*tattva*). The subsequent [phrase] infers his ability to benefit others;

this explains the first "excellence" (*ādi-kalyāṇa*), wherein he is able to conceal the reality and employ provisional means. The primary meaning is deferred to the later explanation. The final [phrase] clarifies that he has reached the Buddha-way in common with others.
Next, regarding the paired explanation: the first two lines of the sutra text merely clarify the reason for concealment without concluding with the clarification of the aggregates (*skandha*);

the latter two lines merely conclude with the clarification of bestowal without clarifying its reason. The commentary (*śāstra*) provides both aspects for each, which is the efficacy of this explanation.
It is appropriate that it is called a "paired conclusion," as it concludes by clarifying the concealment of the real and the manifestation of the provisional.
The meaning of this has been clarified by the preceding explanation of the first "Guide," which is now manifest here.

One should understand that, with the exception of the first two lines which are exclusively expressions of praise, all subsequent parts combine both praise and exhortation. Next, regarding the term *choushun* (酬順):

it refers to the praise and exhortation of the Buddhas; because one responds to their praise, it is called "repayment" (*chou*), and because one follows what is exhorted, it is called "compliance" (*shun*). This explains *namo*.
This is intended to show the meaning of reverently following the correct illumination and complying with the exhortations. Xiangyun says: "Namo" means "to take refuge in" and "to save me.

To take refuge in means to surrender one's life to the Buddhas of the ten directions. When the Buddhas encourage and instruct regarding the Three Vehicles, they draw near to the life-intelligence (*prajñā-jīvita*) of sentient beings;
this is precisely drawing near to the life of Śākyamuni. Therefore, Śākyamuni takes his own life and surrenders it to the [Buddhas of the] ten directions.

The Buddhas and all the various Buddhas exhort [beings] to the Three Vehicles; since this is the salvation of sentient beings, it is also the salvation of Śākyamuni, and thus it is said, "It saves me.
Now, if one explains this according to its meaning, what is there that is not acceptable? It is essentially a circuitous path.

Since the ancients have already stated, "Respectfully follow the words and meanings," which is elegant and convenient, we shall now proceed directly from them without the need for convoluted interpretation. This first statement responds to the beginning of the middle section.

The first two lines are a response; the latter two lines are an affirmation. "Noble" (*ārya*) means correct and universal; because one possesses mastery and fearlessness regarding the universal, correct, and perfect path, one is called a "Noble Lion.
This refers to the phrase "Excellent, Śākyamuni! which precedes the *hṛdaya* (the finest essence).

Because he is able to employ skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to ultimately lead beings back to the perfect and wondrous, it is called the "Profound, Pure, and Subtle Voice. This is the response to what preceded.
"The First Teacher’s Praise" (the first line) is followed by "Obediently Following," which means following what was previously attained;
this constitutes the first dharma among those [teachings] below that are exhorted. This initial passage of one line consists of three phrases, but its meaning comprises only two points, namely:
repaying and following. These three phrases and two meanings fully exhaust the essential points of the response to the previous exhortation. Next, it says: "Mindfully following all things."
"Capacity" (*ki*) refers specifically to the preceding passage concerning those who possess limited wisdom and delight in inferior teachings.

Previously, it was clarified that the Buddhas, having personally attained the ultimate Dharma, concealed the truth and established provisional means in order to accord with the capacities of sentient beings. Now, as well, because [the Buddha] accords with that same intention, it is said that "he reflects upon and accords with the capacities of beings.
This interpretation is thoroughly excellent and complete.
This refers to the fact that when those to be transformed have the appropriate capacity (*indriya*), they should be inspired by means of the teaching; thus it is said.

The first two phrases of the sutra clarify the place and time; "this matter" refers to the moment when one’s mindfulness is identical to that of all Buddhas, in accordance with the conditions and capacities of sentient beings, and when thought has reached a definitive resolution.
The next phrase concerns the location, here called the Deer Park; formerly there was a king because of this forest.
Because of the deer, it is also called the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva), the Deer Grove, or the Land of the Rishis (Rishipatana), for there were formerly rishis who dwelt here.
It is also newly called Vārāṇasī, which means "the city surrounded by rivers. However, there are both general and specific designations;

specifically, the Deer Park is but one location within that kingdom. When the scriptural texts refer to the location in its general sense, they speak of it as distinct from the others. This was the case with the ancients.

Regarding the distinct translations of these meanings, one should know that they generally include those not yet fully understood: the sudden [approach] begins with the *bodhimaṇḍa*, while the gradual [approach] begins right here;

it is now the gradual approach that is being discussed. The following line correctly explains the beginning of the teaching: the first phrase clarifies that, in ultimate reality, it is truly ineffable;
the next two phrases clarify that, in terms of conventional phenomena and skillful means, there is indeed teaching. This is also as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*: "Both..."

It cannot be said [that this is explained] by means of causes and conditions; rather, the commentary explains this passage through three turns. The first turn discusses the essential nature (*tattva*) specifically;
the second turn discusses it generally in terms of the provisional and the real; the third turn again discusses it entirely separately in terms of the phenomena and the principle of the provisional.

Regarding the first of these, it first restates what has already been established and then sets forth its essential nature. Having explained it as before, this constitutes the explanation of "the mark of the quiescence of all dharmas."
Furthermore, this principle is not merely a restatement of the preceding meaning to clarify why it is "inexpressible"; it is the direct explanation of why it cannot be proclaimed in words.
It is precisely because it is quiescent, formless, and nameless that it is neither numerical nor expressible—this is the one true, wondrous essence attained through one's own cultivation.
Now, by means of the term "equality" (*samata*), three teachings are formulated in response to the three types of spiritual capacities.
This is spoken as a triad because there are causes and conditions; it refers to both self and others, and is also an explanation based on meaning.
What follows is an explanation based on the text, and furthermore, an explanation based on specific meanings. As for "text," the text says: "Quiescent, quiescent" means non-arising and non-ceasing.
This cannot be proclaimed in words; yet, because there are causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, it is taught through skillful means (*upāya*).

The teaching of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-vyaya*) was established as a "common" (*tong*) doctrine because it is directed toward the three [lower] teachings; this [present teaching], however, is restricted to the initial stage and is therefore called "distinct" (*bie*).

The text states, "For the sake of the five bhikṣus," necessitating this distinct explanation. Furthermore, the subsequent three stages are even more restricted, focusing exclusively on what is permissible or impermissible within the aforementioned context of arising and ceasing.
"Ultimate truth" (*zhēn lǐ*) refers to the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); "not manifesting" means that the four [marks] do not appear.
That which is not spoken cannot be made into speech; this too is the mark of quiescence (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*), meaning it is ineffable.

Thus, the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states: "The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is without sound or letters. The Venerable Kauṇḍinya hearing [the Dharma] and awakening to the Way is precisely this meaning.
Furthermore, because of these causes and conditions, there can be the four [truths] and their exposition. Moreover, the first [point] is established in contrast to the Perfect [Teaching].

The partial explanation next uses the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) to explain the Piṭakas; the third [explanation] specifically concerns the phenomena and principles of the Three Piṭakas, for this meaning truly exists therein.
Regarding the statement "the gate of impermanence," since the four [truths] beginning with impermanence first treat the four types of examples, it is the gate of existence (*bhava-mukha*).
As all texts state that the Four Truths are taught first, why is it said to be "impermanence" and so forth? This is not contradictory, for impermanence...
Regarding these four aspects of suffering, the first four are stated briefly; the remaining three sets of four may be understood by analogy. Thus, each gate contains the Four Noble Truths.
To speak of the "Four Truths" refers to their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), while to speak of the "four aspects" refers to their specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

These two are not separate; the general and the specific can be known together. As for the meaning of the "five bhikṣus," this has already been explained previously in the passage concerning the initial vision [of the truth]. This text is correct.
This should be placed below this text.
Next, the section explaining "receiving and practicing" and so forth concludes the matters concerning the transformer; what follows concerns those who receive transformation and obtain benefit.

Although the benefits obtained are many, they do not exceed these four; therefore, it is said as such. As for the phrase "receiving and practicing," the *Jì* (Record/Commentary) states: "The capacity [of the recipient]."

When one assembles, one receives [the teachings] and, according to what is heard, the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) proceeds; from the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) onward, this is called "practice" (*caryā*).

If one follows the Sarvāstivāda school, although the duration of each stage is brief, it does not prevent one from fully traversing the stages of both the outer and inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) until reaching the first fruit, which is termed "awakening.

If one attains the first fruit, it is called "entry" (*praveśa*). What is said here is from a specific perspective; however, speaking generally, the benefit of the initial transformation may also be understood through hearing.

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is termed "receiving" (*śruta*), while cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is termed "practice" (*caryā*). The first fruit is termed "awakening" (*bodha*), and the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is termed "entry" (*praveśa*).

This is spoken of collectively as the benefit of the initial transformation; thus it should be so. (As stated... The scriptural text says: [The] Commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains in detail. First, regarding the turning of the wheel:

having already briefly explained the virtues of the Bodhisattva who overcomes the aforementioned difficulties, the term "turning" (*vartana*) refers to the Dharma-wheel, which is the principle and the teaching—that which is turned.
"Turning" (vartana) distinguishes it from other wheels; thus it is called "Dharma. It refers back to what was previously explained, and therefore it is a "name.

The meaning of "wheel" (cakra) is manifold; yet, regarding its essential point: it proceeds from here to there, and furthermore, it can skillfully crush one's own ground as well as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and can further reach the Dharma.

As for the meaning of "turning," it transforms both self and others. Skillfully [it deals with] various fetters (*saṃyojana*), or it manifests the principle of emptiness from the perspective of causes.

Regarding the fruits, I shall briefly state their four types; regarding the texts, I shall briefly explain the first one. That which is "one" already encompasses the remaining three meanings, which are easy to understand from the text.
Next, I shall explain *nirvāṇa*, here translated as "quiescent extinction" (*jimiè*) or "perfect quiescence" (*yuánjì*).

This term applies to both the partial and the ultimate, as well as to both existence and non-existence, because its causes have not yet been fully exhausted; thus, it is described in terms of both aspects. As for the word *yin* (sound), it refers to names, and also to the teachings of sound.
This refers to the teaching that is free from the names of birth and death. Next, the term "Arhat" is explained: "by this" means by virtue of the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).
This is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) with remainder, wherein both [aspects] are perfected. By this, it is revealed that the preceding stages are those of training and partial realization;

therefore, because they have reached perfection, they are "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). Below, the Dharma and Sangha are explained, which constitute the Three Jewels; because of this, [the title] is bestowed.

That which is spoken of in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* regarding the Three Jewels is precisely this. For now, these are distinct entities at the initial stage of the gradual teaching, rather than being a single entity.
One should know that the four names—Dharmacakra, Nirvāṇa, Arhat, and the Three Jewels—all first originated at this time.
The previous explanation of the meaning of "turning the wheel of Dharma" should properly be placed here below.

Next, regarding the resolution of doubts: the preceding section described the matters of past initial conversions and the benefits thereby conferred; this section resolves the doubts currently present in the minds of the assembly.

The doubt resides within the hearts of the assembly, while the resolution resides in the Sun of the Buddha. Thus, the hidden doubt is made manifest by the resolution, and the internal doubt is clarified by the external teaching.
As for the cause of this doubt’s arising, it originates from the previous correct teaching and the realization of benefit by its recipients.

Within this [section], there are first the correct explanation and second the exclusion of errors to reveal the correct view. In the first part, there are two doubts: first, regarding the Master, and second, regarding the Disciple.

Regarding the cause for the former, it is the capacity to transform others; regarding the cause for the latter, it is the benefit previously received. This clarifies that both the transformer and the transformed have existed for a vast duration.

However, as for this "vast duration," according to the subsequent text, it refers to the period after the Buddha of Great Pervasion (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū), when he temporarily withdrew from the Great Vehicle and used skillful means to receive others through the Small Vehicle; at that time, it was designated by that name.
Regarding the phrase "from long ago": the initial doubt within the commentary suggests that at first [the Buddha] did not know the capacities [of beings] and thus could not employ transformation;

this is because it was stated previously that he only thought about them before saying they were "equal. In the explanation, he first refutes the view that the two [vehicles] cannot be the primary ones, as it would not accord with the principle of equality;

next, he correctly reveals that [the Buddha] has known [beings] for a long time and has already employed [transformation] for a long time. His long-standing knowledge that they delight in the Lesser Vehicle is his long-standing knowledge of their capacities, which he has already praised and demonstrated.
It is said that Mingjiu was able to transform [others] through his words of praise; "praise" here means exhortation, which carries the sense of the three turnings (trivṛtti) in brief form as two.
The commentary explains this by clarifying that he had long heard and practiced [the teachings]. Below, the manifest person is distinguished:

first, the views of the ancients are recounted, and next, their meaning is clarified—this constitutes the third point revealing the present intention. The "ancient" refers specifically to those who spoke of the distant past.
Furthermore, regarding the localization of the "Later Gate" (Jūmon), it is not permissible for the secret covenant of the Buddha-mind to be slightly revealed;

when explaining this, one must ensure that the assembly does not perceive even a trace of such meaning. As for the subsequent explanation that this is not the case, it is because such a principle simply does not exist, and therefore it is impermissible.

Although the term "long distant" (kyūen) may generally apply, it is sufficient to follow [the interpretation] from the cause, as this has already been frequently stated in the *Shushōkyō* (Sutra on the Primary Teaching).

These are none other than the sixteen princes. In this passage, the subsequent section is used to challenge this profound implication (*xuanzhi*), and the conclusion below clarifies and establishes the present meaning;

thus, it must be so. Jiaxiang says: "The 'Dispelling Doubts' chapter secretly reveals the *Śāyusya* (Life Span) chapter. My view is that regarding "Dispelling," there is a basis for it, whereas regarding "Revealing," there is no sequential order.
To neglect these two meanings and speak of them as a pair is incorrect. The character "profound" (*xuan*) therein should precisely correspond [to the present context].

"Xuánxuán" (懸懸) means "far-reaching"; "xuánshēnmiào" (玄深妙) means "profound, deep, and subtle. Because it points distantly to the original ground (*mūla-bhūmi*), it should be read as "xuán. Next, the verse reveals the reality (*tattva*).

What was previously described as the past transformation [teaching] is precisely the opening of the provisional (*upāya*). Since the provisional has been opened, the true aspect (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) is revealed;
this refers to that very point. Within the commentary (*śūtra-vyākhyāna*), there are two parts: first, regarding the previous four lines of the verse, the text is analyzed and further explained.
Regarding the following section, which uses the analogy of the "four" to explain the initial statement that there are four: first, the preceding text states, "This alone is the one reality;
all else is not true. Here, "one" refers to reality (*satya*). Since reality must necessarily possess four aspects, it is called the "fourfold one. This is the first reason.

Because they are the words of the Buddha’s sons, these people are one in their provisional aspect and three in their real aspect; all are sons of the Buddha. Since the sons are identical, these people are one.

In the preceding passage there were three meanings that included "people" (human beings) when it said "thus," meaning that all are for the sake of attaining equality—that is, for the sake of causing sentient beings [to attain it].
The preceding section merely included them by implication, whereas the present text explicitly praises them; therefore, it is shown as follows:

That the various forms of knowledge constitute a single principle means that, fundamentally, this subject-object capacity exists as one; it is now manifested for this reason, and thus they are a single principle.

Since we specifically take the "only" (but) from the teaching, it is that which the teaching proceeds from. Because it pertains to the capacity, it is "one"; this "one" should be understood as the fruit.

The fruit arises from the cultivation of causes, and the cause is precisely practice. By citing the fruit to clarify the cause, it is shown that this practice is identical to the practice of the Buddha-fruit. Therefore, it is [the same].
Since these are one, the four meanings of revealing reality are thereby fully exhausted.
Next, regarding the explanation by means of the following metaphors: this is primarily intended to serve as the basis for the metaphors so that they may be easily understood later;

therein, first is the general heading, second is the itemized listing, and third is the detailed explanation. First, concerning the "four meanings," they do not refer to True Suchness moving toward subsequent states.

This demonstrates that such an interpretation is made based upon the scripture. Therefore...

Furthermore, there is another separate explanation of the first two passages. First, regarding the explanation of "seeking" (*suo*): first, we harmonize the text; second, we explain the meaning.

This explanation of "fruit" follows the previous heading; the mere mention of "seeking fruit" is the same as what Guangzhai stated.

Therefore, this section further clarifies the meaning by relying on the text. Next, the explanation of the term *sō* (seeking/inquiry) has four parts: first, a general heading; second, a detailed explanation; third, a clarification of the present and the past;

While the ultimate state of the Sage (*ārya*) is entirely devoid of it, and although it may pervade all things, here it refers specifically to this [cultivated seed]. It is called "emotion" because it is contrasted with the aforementioned "subtle," and it is contrasted with... [the preceding].
