Because one takes gain and loss as emotional attachments, they instead become a mechanical impediment; thus, there is a divergence from the profound.

Now, according to the meaning of the following passage, it may also be said that the primordially existing wondrous principle, augmented by the seeds of past habituation, possesses the sense of being moved and inspired;

this is the reason for the "rope" of the mechanism. Hearing the two flavors [of teaching] and rejecting them through a torrential cleansing, while the mind gives rise to base envy, is the reason for the "rope" of emotion.

Now, hearing the praise of the One as real and the disparagement of the Three as false, one’s attachments are stirred and doubt arises; thus, the reason for the three earnest requests is that they seek [the truth] through words.

Therefore, the subsequent mention of the "three names" refers to seeking through the faculty (indriya), which can be understood. Next, the correspondence with the two flavors (rasa) refers to seeking through emotion (bhāva).

The first three requests in this sutra refer to seeking through speech (vāk). Thus, we know that the faculty seeks directly at the root while emotion and speech are comprehensive and not distinct from it.

Reflect upon it, reflect upon it! Next, the distinction between the present and the past can be understood. The reason why these three [aspects] must be established is that after leaving the house, the duration of time is long;
thus, these three meanings are contained therein. Otherwise, the meaning would not be exhaustive. If this were so, there would be no "three searches" within the *Immeasurable Meanings Sūtra*;
yet, although the three times are absent, all three are complete within each single moment. Reflect upon it, reflect upon it! Next, the analysis.
Regarding the meaning of the initial question in the *Jian*: this arises because the previous statement—“seeking the Great and not seeking the Small”—had not yet been fully understood;

thus, he cites the previously quoted text and subsequently raises the objection. In the response, the phrase “it is seen that [he] has departed” means precisely that, having departed, he has been rejected as not being authentic.
This is the very meaning of the text’s statement: “Now we do not know where this principle tends. This is the path.
The term "principle" (*yukti*) is also synonymous with "meaning" (*artha*). This means that once one has already attained the third [point], one must further seek this principle;

thus, it is the search for the subsequent section. The detailed explanation follows, and the meaning of the second phrase of the initial passage is clarified according to the traditional interpretation, while the present proof is evident within the text itself.

The preceding section has concluded the meaning of "seeking the fruit through great capacity. Below is the commentary on the latter half of the verse concerning the removal of hindrances. The Sūtra states: "All Buddhas... This means:

first, they have all equally received and studied [the teachings]; second, by citing the general to reveal the particular, it shows that the path of all Buddhas is identical because it is based upon the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Regarding the initial stage of tasting, practicing, and receiving [the teaching], the specific reference to the "initial taste" concerns the three vehicles (*triyāna*), while the subsequent general reference applies to those below that level.

The two flavors and the three vehicles, etc., are precisely the five expedient means (*upāya*). Because of these, obstacles are removed; because these obstacles are removed, the capacity [of the practitioner] is activated;

and because this capacity is activated, there is the "requesting the Great" (*mahāyāna*). Furthermore, how can it be said that what was previously unsevered is now removed? It was previously said that the capacity is not yet removed;
moreover, speaking from the perspective of the few following the many, the subsequent text shall provide a more extensive explanation. Next, the removal is explained.
Regarding the three lines and one phrase of the *Xi jingwen* (Text on Rejoicing): the first line is a direct transition; next, one line and one phrase contrast the past to manifest the present.
In the commentary (*shu*), the phrase "obstacles removed" (*zhang chu*) points toward the main text. The Buddha’s rejoicing corresponds exactly to the text;

it is simply because the removal [of obstacles] constitutes rejoicing that this is cited to make it clear. Each of these two passages contains two aspects: all who have generated [the mind] remove [obstacles], and at times there is rejoicing. In reality, this is due to what preceded.
Both [commentaries] arrive at this point; the two commentaries are skillful yet concise, each expressing one aspect, hence it is said: "excluding joy.

Although the sutra text first directly clarifies [the meaning], it now contrasts the present with the past to reveal the commentary’s explanation of both aspects, each contrasting the present with the past to manifest the present.

Regarding the first of these, there is first the presentation of the intended meaning, followed by two phrases citing the past. Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, that which cannot be spoken of, and second, the initial section.
Next, there is one "you" (yǒu), which refers to the fact that the great capacity [for enlightenment] has not yet been aroused;

thus, the final phrase clarifies that now is precisely the right time, stating, "Now is precisely its time. The preceding phrase speaks only of the removal of obstacles, while the subsequent phrase speaks only of the arousal of capacity;

this too is a skillful and wondrous artistry. Next, in explaining "joy without fear," it first cites the former presence and absence [of these states], thereby showing that [otherwise] there would be sorrow.

Because it is revealed that [the Dharma] does not exist now, the faculty of joy (*muditīndriya*) is dull; because the obstacles of the five turbidities (*pañcakaṣāya*) are heavy and one’s wisdom is small, there is no great capacity (*mahādhimukti*), and thus there is sorrow rather than joy.
Next, since this is the reverse of the preceding three, joy can be understood accordingly. Furthermore, "fear" (*bhaya*) is itself sorrow;
because there is joy without sorrow, they are explained together below. Due to this dullness and smallness, one clings to what is small and slanders [the Great Vehicle].
Grasping the great as small and grasping [the truth] with slander toward the great constitutes the cause for generating sinful karma, which results in falling into the evil realms (*durgati*).

Because these obscurations are removed, the faculties become sharp; because the faculties are sharp, the resolve becomes great; and because the resolve is great, one does not grasp [the great] as small nor slander it.

Because one does not grasp or slander, there is no cause for sinful karma, and thus no result of the evil realms; therefore, there is fearlessness. One should know that within this, three meanings are presented, the first of which corresponds to the initial point.
The former was not manifest, while the latter is manifest; therefore, the second [pair] contrasts the former’s sorrow to manifest the latter’s joy.
The third [pair] contrasts the former’s existence to manifest the latter’s non-existence. The underlying reasons for each of these have already been explained previously (*etc.*).
The phrase "manifesting reality" (*zhèng xiǎn shí*) below specifically clarifies the ultimate truth. Since this states it is "correctly," the preceding two [phrases] are thereby included.
The first sentence of the sutra refers to the person for whom it is intended; because that person previously sought to cause the Way to flourish, they are now all referred to as "bodhisattvas.
The latter two sentences manifest reality specifically for this person. Although there are two parts in the text, the first excludes what is not [the case], while the second reveals what is.
Regarding the meaning of the phrases, there are three commentaries; for these two phrases, there are three meanings clearly evident in the text.
First, it explains "straightforwardness" (*ṛju*). Since "straightforwardness" is a term contrasted with "deviation," it first cites deviation to explain straightforwardness.
The "five vehicles" are its substance, and "is-ness" (*asti*) is its meaning. This is because the Way is circuitous and thus deviant; it cannot be immediate.

It is not a direct path; rather, its substance is precisely this "is" and "is-not," which constitutes its meaning. Because it is neither [of these two extremes], it is a "partial branch" (*pāṅ-p'iang*).
Being a partial branch, it is not the primary [path]. By means of this "is-not," the perfect path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is revealed as being upright and direct.
Below, "abandoning the provisional" (*shě fāngbiàn*) is explained: "provisional" refers to the aforementioned seven provisional stages that are biased and crooked. Such is their bias and crookedness.
Now, as these are all completely abandoned and no longer discussed, it is called "abandonment. The subsequent explanation speaks only of the Unsurpassed Way (*anuttara-mārga*).

"Upright" (*ṛju*) corresponds to the previous "crooked" (*vakra*); the first refers to the true Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), in contrast to the five or seven provisional methods (*upāya-dharma*).
"Way" (*mārga*) refers to the Unsurpassed Way, in contrast to the previous "having an above" (*sopariṣṭha*). These three names differ, yet in reality they are one.
Furthermore, because these three meanings are summarized and clarified, it is called "Perfectly Equal" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Someone may say: "The Ultimate Way has no fixed direction;
everything is the Way. What is there to abandon? Now I say: If this were so, there would likewise be no cultivation. To directly realize that all things are [the Way] is what is called "cultivation.
This does not mean abandoning the non-true and following the true—this is what is called cultivation. If one realizes...

If one does not understand that all things are neither identical to nor distinct from equanimity (*upekṣā*), yet can practice relinquishment and non-relinquishment while being neither identical to nor distinct from equanimity—nor even non-distinct from it—then how can such a person comprehend this wondrous relinquishment?
Since they cannot attain this, how could they possibly master true cultivation? Indeed, they are not yet fit to discuss the wondrous Path.
Someone may say: "The Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is perfectly complete and encompasses all without exception; what dharma is there that is not included within it?"

To say that one abandons the provisional and retains only the real is not yet a complete teaching. I now maintain that while other sutras may be described in such a way, the intent of this sutra is not so.
After a long period, the Buddhas must necessarily speak the truth; they appear in the world solely for the sake of the One Great Matter.

From the beginning, I established my vow to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself. As it says: [The Buddha said: "I have made a vow from the beginning, desiring to cause all sentient beings to be no different from me."
The vows I made in the past have now been fulfilled, for I have transformed all sentient beings and caused them all to enter the Buddha-way;

thus we know that this alone is the single reality, while all other expedient means were not the Buddha’s original intention. Regarding the Buddha’s transformations, though they are immeasurable, they do not transcend two categories:

those that manifest through the provisional to accord with differences, wherein both the provisional and the real coexist; and those where, through such an accord, both the provisional and the real are simultaneously extinguished.

In the past, when the various scriptures had not yet been reconciled, it was appropriate for them both to coexist; now that this scripture has opened and unified them, they must certainly be set aside.

It is for this reason that I speak of "setting them aside. Someone may say: "Your words here are erroneous and you have failed to perceive this. Why? Because 'setting aside' is not the same as 'opening and unifying,' nor is 'opening and unifying' the same as 'setting aside.
Since you have already spoken of opening and unifying, how can you then speak of setting them aside? Is such a meaning tenable? This indicates a failure to understand.

The essential point is that this delusion arises because the wondrous function of this sutra possesses ten essentials within twenty categories: namely, breaking (*po*), opening (*kai*), abandoning (*fei*), and reconciling (*hui*).

These are further divided into two types each: the relative (*xiangdai*) and the absolute (*juedai*). The previous statement, "All dharmas from the very beginning are eternally quiescent and extinguished," refers to the reconciliation and the absolute.
The current passage’s mention of "abandoning" (*she*) refers to breaking, abandoning, and the relative. Such is the case.

The meaning of "equality" (sameness) is difficult to reconcile with the text’s apparent differences; yet, while the expressed meanings may seem distinct, their underlying essence has never differed. If there is not one, then there is none at all; if there is one, then there are ten.

Since it is thus with the provisional traces (the *jimen*), it is certainly so with the fundamental opening (the *honkai*). If one has not yet understood the traces of a single lifetime, how much less can one know the fundamental reality of the distant past?

If one does not yet understand these two—the fundamental and the trace—how can one know the non-duality (*advaya*)? Such a teaching, being both horizontal and vertical without fixed direction, may truly be called "perfect" (*en*).

Furthermore, regarding the wondrous Way and persons, they do not recognize that [the distinction between] identical and different bodies is resolved through the opening [of the teaching]. Once opened, even within a single wondrous body, there are still four propositions;
how much more so for those two alone? If the wondrous has not yet been opened, whether few or many, all are merely coarse phenomena and traces.
Since it is thus with the gate of the opening, it is likewise with the fundamental gate. Only in this way can it be called perfectly wondrous; yet most people fall into error and delusion.
I have merely recorded this in haste; you do not yet know even one, so how could you know two?
Since you do not yet know one or two, how can you know ten? One must believe that it is improper to speak with such haste.
Next, the practitioner clearly reveals their own substance and receives the benefit [thereof]. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states at length:

"By virtue of the power of faith, one receives [the teaching], which constitutes the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); practice constitutes the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

'Awakening' refers to the initial stage of true realization; 'entry' refers to the profound higher stages. This is explained in general terms. If considered specifically, it may also correspond to the meanings of revealing, showing, awakening, and entering.
Furthermore, one must understand that both the general and specific meanings are required; it cannot be said categorically that they contradict the preceding and following contexts.

For those whose doubts regarding the meaning of "receptive faith" (*śraddhā*) are deep, they should contemplate the title of the "Chapter on Receptive Faith" (*Śraddhā-viniścaya-parivarta*) so as to be free from delusion. The text states: "All subtle doubts have been eliminated. Is this not precisely because of receptive faith?

Thus, all are included within the stage of true faith (*bhūta-śraddhā*). Although there are four aspects in meaning, the text consists of only one line; although the text is one, [the implications are manifold].
The practice of the essentials still consists of two parts: the first half removes doubt, and the second half bestows the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

Furthermore, the first part concerns one’s own realization through practice, while the second concerns enabling others to realize through practice. Regarding the commentary, there are two sections: first, the explanation of the text; second, the analysis and clarification.

Within the first section, there are three parts: first, the removal of doubt; second, the explanation of the prediction; third, the reconciliation of the two. Within the first of these, there are two sub-sections: first, clarifying the doubt; second, explaining its removal.

The three examples clarify that the first two bodhisattvas are those who were previously doubtful; "initially hearing [the teaching] and so forth" refers to the cause of their doubt, while "new doubts arise" refers to the actual generation of doubt.
The characteristics of this doubt are as described later. Now, all such doubts are eliminated in accordance with the two teachings (and so forth).

This is also due to the fact that it has already been extensively explained through the teaching of the Dharma. The meaning of the character *yi* (以) corresponds to this; for *yi* signifies "cause," and all these are causes.
The *Dachuye jing* (Sūtra on the Removal of Doubt) consistently transmits this [teaching] as such; one should know it accordingly.

Next, the following examples clarify that even Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas have doubts that can be removed—how much more so for Śrāvakas who do not doubt their removal [of obstacles]. Below, the text explains the reason why only Śrāvakas are mentioned regarding the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*):
because they lack the purpose of attaining Buddhahood for the benefit of others, and thus lack the causal basis for receiving a prediction, no prediction is granted to them.

Now, as the teachings have been opened up, they are equal to those of a Bodhisattva because the causal conditions exist; thus, he grants them a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), saying: "The practitioner of today has performed the practice.
This is read with the phonetic *yín* (音), referring to the single practice of the present verse-text and its subsequent prediction. This should not be understood in that way.
Many commentators say this is merely a dialectical pronunciation from the region along the Yangtze River, but this is certainly not the case. Formerly, during the Wei dynasty...
In a letter Emperor Wen sent to Yiqi, he wrote: "Since parting from you, several years have already passed. How could this not refer to the great antiquity of the Jiang region?
The sages and worthies of old frequently used such expressions, though I cannot detail them all here. However, the character *xíng* (行) is glossed as "to go" or "to depart";
it means that from now on, one should proceed with the successive accounts of partings. Therefore, the text below says: "Now, when I am about to..."

This is precisely the meaning of bestowing the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of the three types of perfect enlightenment (*trividha-samyak-sambodhi*) in successive order. Furthermore, the practitioner is like a leader;

now, as one is about to bestow the prediction upon them, one first uses these words. This meaning is most convenient, for it refers to the practitioner "turning around" (*khuǎn*), which means turning back to bestow the prediction upon the whole assembly.
This interpretation is close [to the literal sense], yet even this phrasing is not elegant. How could the bestowal of the prediction concern only those below?
Regarding the first section, "Explaining the Two Differences": First, it clarifies that the two intentions are equal; next, it explains the differences in the phrasing of the reconciliation.
This merely involves alternating the wording so that its meaning is fully revealed.

Next, there is a further analysis and clarification to resolve the preceding doubts and eliminate the underlying meanings. First, as for the question: although doubt was previously mentioned, it has not yet been resolved.
Regarding its characteristics, this is asked because they are about to be elucidated. In the response, first the characteristics of the doubt are clarified, and subsequently its removal is explained.
First, it is shown that the teachings previously received by the two individuals constitute what they cling to as being real. The section beginning with "First hearing...
clarifies the cause of their doubt. The phrases "formerly true" and "formerly established," etc., specifically set forth the characteristics of their doubt.

The appearance [of these differences] immediately gives rise to doubt that this is what was previously taught. Furthermore, regarding those of the third rank and below—those Bodhisattvas of Clear Penetration (Prativedha)—who share the same path as their fellow students, they wonder why there is a distinction from what was previously taught. As for the reason for doubting the present teaching, it is the same as the previous case;
it is merely a brief explanation. Since the "One Path" is the ultimate reality (*tattva*), where else could there be another reality? Yet, why is it said that there is a "necessity"?

The statement "prior to the teaching of reality" refers to the fruit of doubt; this refers to the principle of doubt. Having finished explaining above the causes of doubt and the actual doubting itself, what follows below explains its removal.

"Now hearing [the teaching]" and so forth refers to the cause for its removal, namely, the extensive opening and revealing [of the truth]. "Sweeping away" clearly indicates that it is completely removed.
The various doubts are as previously explained, both general and specific. The primary reason is that the former expedient means lacked true reality.

Now, this is precisely the truth; for this reason, it can be said that [doubts] are eliminated and exhausted. As for what is called "distinct," although the teaching is not yet ultimate, it possesses a portion of real meaning.
If one relies on the preceding text, which clarifies the power of faith and distinguishes it from non-retrogression, one would certainly give rise to doubt;

yet upon hearing the extensive exposition of the firm principle, those doubts are likewise eliminated and exhausted. The text says: "The various doubts regarding distinct meanings are also included therein."

This is because it is difficult to explain from the outset; therefore, the specific doubts and difficulties are not separately presented. Since those [difficulties] have already been removed, the easy cases may be understood by analogy, and thus they are omitted.
One should know that this single passage contains two meanings, which collectively refer forward:

the Tathāgata’s foresight and discernment—knowing the intent of the Dharma-exposition, that [the disciples] will certainly attain awakening and entry, and will certainly receive their predictions (vyākaraṇa)—as well as his striking them so that they must awaken and enter. This does not refer to what was stated above.
It should not be so, because one has already attained realization prior to this and because of the bestowal of the prophecy.

Next, regarding the verse praising the Dharma: although it is absent from the prose section of the Buddha’s discourse, its meaning is implicitly present; thus, one takes the text from the chapter on the Buddhas.
Since this is now presented in verse, we know that the meaning must certainly have existed in the prose; therefore, as stated previously, it is said that [the omission] is not definitive.
It has already been clarified that the prose section consists of two parts—the subject (*dharmin*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—and this [verse] is likewise so.
However, upon examining this passage, I fear it is not so; for although the prose is extremely concise and contains both the subject and the example, it lacks the formal application (*upanaya*).

It merely presents two initial items: first, the "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*), and second, the "time" (*kāla*), which are spoken of as a praise. Now, these two names are simply being versified here.

Regarding these two [sections], at the time of the subsequent recitation, one should open them into two parts within the section on praise. While the text does not explicitly list the names, it follows the sequence to provide the explanation;
this has led to much confusion among later readers. One should therefore clearly divide them into two: first, the single verse of the *śloka* which first presents the "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*);
second, the four and a half verses which present the "time" for the sake of praise. Within the subsequent section on praise, one may likewise immediately divide it into two.

The third [point] refers to the text consisting of the dharma, the parable, and their combination, which appears to consist merely of these two. Regarding the explanation of the first meaning, one first correlates it with the main prose (*chángxíng*), as in the passage "as in the three periods," and so forth.
Next, one correctly explains the text itself. First, regarding the correlation with the main prose: this specifically takes the non-discriminative Dharma as being "wondrous.
Below, the essence of the wondrous is set forth; as for the terms "expedient" (*quán*) and "real" (*shí*), the *Jì* states that they refer to what is explained in the *Xuánqiān*.
That interpretation [of the title] as "the inconceivable Dharma of the ten realms and ten suchnesses" refers to the provisional and real teachings (*upāya-tattva*).

Even if one follows that interpretation, it still cannot be reconciled with this [present teaching], which is specific; for it is merely the "trace gate" (*jia-men*) and thus represents the provisional aspect that is entirely identical to the essence.

Therefore, it is called the "Wondrous Dharma. Now, I say that this interpretation further fails to reconcile the Dharma, and moreover, the meaning of "wondrous" has not yet been established. Why? Because...

Up to this point, it was as before, for there had not yet been communication [between the provisional and the real]. Now, it is said that the provisional and the real are non-dual and have no fixed locus.
The previous praise of what follows and the present praise of what precedes both concern the revelation and manifestation of things; these are called the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma).

Their meaning will naturally become clear in the subsequent text, so here it is stated briefly as such. Next, in the formal explanation, there are two sections; the first concerns the opening of the provisional to reveal the real.

The actual [meaning] comprehensively explains all four phrases; next, by synthesizing the provisional to enter the real, it specifically explains the latter two phrases. Regarding the first of these two [explanations], the two Buddhas cite each other to clarify the opening and revealing.
Because they previously employed this as a bestowal, it was a ritual form—a ritual form being a fixed rule, which is to say, a conceptual distinction.
Now, this is the opening; once opened, there is no fixed direction, for how could there be a definitive distinction? Therefore, this is the revealing of the real.

The Sūtra states: "Thus and thus" (*evam evam*). The meaning of "accordant and identical" (*shuntong*) should properly be rendered as "congruent" (*yun*), yet the text consistently uses "induced" (*yin*);
this is likely due to the similarity in sound during transcription. Regarding the second interpretation, it refers to manifesting non-discrimination by means of discrimination;
it is also explained in terms of relativity (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to clarify the absolute (*anupāya*). That which was previously "non-dual yet dual" is likewise non-discriminative.
Furthermore, the discernment that "the two in this present assembly are non-dual" is itself a form of discernment;

that this very discernment is non-discernment is the meaning of the emergence and reabsorption of the *Ananta-artha* (Infinite Meanings). That which is thus is collectively termed the "Sublime Dharma" (*Saddharma*).
Since the manifestation of the Sublime Dharma is identical for both Buddhas, the conclusion is drawn generally, stating: "All Buddhas are likewise."
The following explains the subsequent praise. Although the preceding statement that "the wondrous Dharma" (*saddharma*) itself constitutes praise, it was merely directed toward the object;

now, this is the formal praise that reveals the Dharma to be truly wondrous. Since the Dharma is taught at the appropriate time, the parable is manifested at the appropriate time, and the application (*upanaya*) surpasses what preceded it, all of these constitute praise that establishes the wondrous Dharma.
First, regarding persons, the Buddha is praised as a wondrous person, and the Dharma is praised as a wondrous Dharma.
Because it is attained by humans, this is the most sublime Dharma; that it emerges from such difficulty is truly worthy of admiration.
As explained in detail in the preceding text, one then cites the statement that "this Dharma is difficult to attain" as a response to the person before them; thus, it is called "Dharma.
Regarding the note stating "it is precisely in the difficulty of its exposition," one should clarify in detail the reasons why it is difficult, on account of its subtlety.

The preceding portion, which establishes the subject and provides the textual basis, concerns the Buddha’s praise of this [Dharma]. The following two sections concern the assembly’s objections. Next, as for those who hear the objection:
they find it difficult even in ordinary circumstances, let alone when it comes from the Buddha. "Brahma-voice" refers to the Buddha’s own voice;
it is one of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*dvātriṃśan mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*). According to the *Lakṣaṇānuvyañjana-sūtra*, it is the thirtieth [mark].
Among the two [aspects], the foremost characteristic is that which can universally pervade the Dharma-realm and manifest through transformation as a Buddha;
thus, "Brahman" (梵) signifies pure excellence (*miao*). This function arises from the essence of wondrous purity. Furthermore, "purity" is the virtue of the lotus;
since this is the sound of the "wondrous lotus," it is described as such. Because there is no cause for him to remain seated, it is called "Jixi" (紀廗).

Regarding the difficulty of hearing and receiving [the teaching]: if it is already impossible to hear even for a moment when facing the light, how much more so is it that once one has heard it, one can then hear and receive it from beginning to end?

This is because it is not through mere subtle faith and understanding that such a state is brought to maturity; thus, although it is said that hearing is easy, it is difficult to attain true faith and understanding.

This preceding section uses four points of praise to address the difficulty of the text, which possesses both general and specific meanings, likewise manifesting the excellence of the Dharma as a whole. Let [it be known].
This matter is definitively resolved through faith and understanding (*adhimukti*); as has been explained in detail above, I do not wish to further proliferate the text.

Regarding the subsequent analogy, the first phrase is that which is praised, while the three following phrases praise the object of praise; collectively this refers to the "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*), and individually it refers to its four aspects.

The subsequent three [phrases] concerning the difficulty likewise contain both collective and individual meanings, and the application (*yoga*) is the same. However, since the listeners hear it by means of words, I shall now say:

The term "hearer" (*śrotṛ*) encompasses the latter two of the four [types of persons]. Since the capacity to hear is itself "hearing," the reason for mentioning only the two types of "hearers" is specifically to encourage the assembly to give rise to faith.
Furthermore, those who know nothing at all might think that among these four, only one type can hear the Dharma;

thus, hearing the Dharma would be difficult to achieve, and rejoicing and praising it would be difficult to achieve faith and understanding. If one lacks faith and understanding, how could [one attain the goal]?
Because of the joy of praising, there are two [aspects]. Regarding the quantity of the words of praise, even a single word possesses what merit? It is already equal [to much more].
Furthermore, the comparative evaluation states that it is as difficult to obtain as the *utpala* flower. As for the term "a single word," there is both the general and the specific.
The specific refers to a single character; the general applies to both long and short [syllables]. The specific single character is as stated in the text below: "It is able to follow..."
To praise the virtuous is what this means; taken to its ultimate extent, it refers to what is called "thus" (*evam*). As for "penetrating," the *Li* (Book of Rites) commentary explains it as follows:
a single phrase of speech is termed a "single word. Later, in the *Hai Jin* (Entering the Sea), it says: "The people of Qi presented their request to Lord Sa, seeking a single word.
The four characters "There is a great fish in the sea" constitute a single phrase of speech. This is what is meant by "speech."
It is said that "one word summarizes all": the three characters "thoughts are without depravity" constitute this one word.

Furthermore, because it consists of so few [characters], it is called "one word," just as in the expression "one word can bring about rise or fall. This is not merely a case of a general or specific application;
rather, it is called "one word" simply because it is concise. Now, within this context, it should pertain to both the general and the specific, yet here we speak of "offering."
Those who provide sustenance are as numerous as previously described; this is itself the Dharma-offering, and it is also an offering in accordance with the Dharma.
Among all offerings, it is that which all Buddhas require without exception, for it causes sentient beings to have faith and understanding in this Dharma.
Because hearing and believing in it, and praising it, accords with the minds of the Sages, it constitutes a sublime offering. This is a small portion [of what is to be said].

Regarding the essential mutual explanation of the words and their meanings, they are entirely not expressed through metaphor; for now, I have merely provided this brief account as I have not yet had the leisure to be exhaustive.
Next, the verse stating that [the teaching] is not in vain is likewise an establishment of the aforementioned sublime Dharma; since it is the sublime Dharma, it is devoid of falsehood.
This is truly trustworthy. In the prose section (*gadya*), this chapter naturally exists; its text stands at the very end of the "Chapter on All Buddhas" (*sarvabuddha-parivarta*).
It follows immediately after the preceding meaning, and there must necessarily be a sequential order. There is no reason to divide it into two chapters.

Since these two passages exist in the prose section, their sequence is likewise easy to understand and need not be described in detail. Since he is called the "Dharma King," he is therefore a person. Since he is called... [text ends]... he is therefore... [text ends].
Because the wondrous Dharma is such, this Dharma is wondrous; because the person is such, the person is trustworthy. Because the Dharma is wondrous, the Dharma is trustworthy;

because the person and the King are not two, they cause the whole world to follow a single Dharma-king. Because the Dharma-king is not false, he causes the Dharma-realm to be real. Thus, his words are not false and are trustworthy.

Previously, among the "persons," the person was cited to manifest that the Dharma is not false; here, by citing the "Dharma," the provisional is used to manifest the real, thereby establishing that it is certainly trustworthy.
"Yi" (doubt) means "or.

Next, in explaining the sixth chapter of the verse, first the old interpretation is presented, followed by the correct explanation. Regarding the former, first its general outline is presented, then its specific explanation.

Regarding the former, first the non-accordance with the preceding verse is distinguished, then the reasons for establishing a separate outline are set forth. Initially, it says "does not accord with the verse."

Regarding the observation on the word "only" (*kevalam*): since the text following it does not correspond to what preceded, the phrase "but only" (*kevalam*) serves both to exclude what was not the verse and to manifest what it is;
thus it says "but only," etc. The intention of exhorting faith in the sublime Dharma so that it may be propagated is naturally revealed in the subsequent text.
The passage beginning with "the text below this" is the next section, which describes its specific headings and explains the text. This is the first heading.

The second chapter next explains its two [sections]: the second and third knots and their two meanings. Regarding the first, it merely exhorts one to practice the cause and bestows upon one the constant fruit.
First, the initial passage shall be further divided into four sections; following the sequence as they arise, these four are: exhortation, explanation of the essence, and the conclusion.
In the first section, "the secret essentials of all Buddhas" refers to the wondrous fruit of person and dharma; those who wish to attain this fruit should...
One must cultivate causes; the essential requirement for cultivating causes is that one must widely propagate this wondrous sutra.

The following explanation of the two characters [“cause” and “cultivation”] concerns both person and dharma, as well as the agent and the object. Each of these further possesses two meanings: self and other, and essence and function.

These are easily seen within the text. "Merit" refers to accumulation; it is what is attained through cultivation. The subsequent explanation refers to the fact that, due to the absence of causes, its essentials were kept in secret. This...
The first two intentions merely cite the Dharma with the aim of exhorting its propagation. The subsequent clarification of the "essence" (tǐ) teaches the standard for the essence of its proclamation.
These two intentions, when interpreted according to the text in a general sense, are indeed quite consistent; this has always been so. Next, regarding the double conclusion:
the first concludes the preceding two [intentions], and the second concludes the two within the third [intention]. Although this structural analysis is not...
The essential point is that because [the author] possesses skillful insight regarding the text, he provides a full exposition without refutation;
however, this is not necessarily the correct interpretation. Next, the second section, "The Analysis of Prophecy" (*vyākaraṇa-vibhāga*), is explained, which further contains three meanings.

The phrase "having understood" (*jñātvā*) means "already knowing"; the following two points are easy to understand. Furthermore, the preceding two points are restated as the basis for the prophecy; therefore, this constitutes the general summary.
This concludes the mutual record. Above, the explanation of the two chapters is finished; below, the dual conclusion clarifies the two meanings, which can be understood.
Below, the summary indicates the meaning of the former [tradition]. These three sections constitute the initial explanation; the words are concise and the essentials are urged.

Following the text for analysis, there is indeed some discernment, and a portion of the underlying principle is preserved. Since the interpretation provided by Guanqing contains no errors, it is recorded in full.
It does not refute [the preceding], but rather directly refutes its errors and clarifies the correct meaning; therefore, it concludes with those words.

Below, the text provides a formal commentary on the passage, where several points of difference can be discerned. This section contains three parts: first, the presentation of the chapter title; second, the critique of the old interpretation; and third, the formal analysis.

Regarding the first point, "distinguishing and exhorting" (*jianquan*): "distinguishing" refers to distinguishing the false assembly, while "earnestly exhorting" refers to urging the true assembly to necessarily believe in the ultimate reality.
It is because of the Dharma; the phrase "fortunately there is" precisely accords with the verse (*gāthā*). This is because the prose (*prose commentary*) corresponds to the text of the verse;

the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) and the circulation [of the teaching] are proximate, whereas those situated further back are remote. As for "proximate" and "remote," the remote is primary and the proximate is secondary; why is this so?
It is said that they mutually exclude one another, their phrasing being explicit and their meaning equal. It is said that "evil persons" refers to those who lack faith.
Those who follow the correct principle, because they lack the seeds of compliant faith in the One Vehicle, do not believe or accept it.

Because they do not accept it, it is difficult for them to understand its meaning. Since [the Dharma] responds to conditions and brings about penetration, there is the encounter with it; this possesses three meanings.

Having already completed the detailed explanation as set forth above, the following section emphasizes and strikes [the reader] so that they must necessarily believe it. If one does not believe, etc., [it leads to] the drawing forth [of karmic consequences].

The preceding passage is the "waiting for" (伺) that earnestly exhorts [the listener]. "Trusting in the provisional" (信權) means having deep faith that the previously taught Three Vehicles were skillful means.

"That which is taught today is definitively true" (今日所說決定是真) means that these words are substantial and real. To say that "the Buddhas are the teachers of the world" means they are the teachers who appear in the world for the great task of benefiting beings;
this is "trusting in the real" (信實). That which accords with what is appropriate through skillful means is "trusting in the provisional" (信權).
Because one clearly understands and resolves [the truth] within these two divisions, there is no doubt or confusion.

This is precisely the Perfect and Wondrous Path of Enlightenment (*bodhi-mārga*), which, by spontaneously reaching the ultimate limit, brings about self-awakening and the awakening of others; hence it is said that "one knows for oneself that one shall become a Buddha.

Although the preceding sections have provided brief, extensive, general, and specific explanations through many passages, they all collectively constitute a verse-commentary on the Exalted One’s prose exposition of "opening the provisional to reveal the real" (*vivṛta-guhyaka*). The above summarizes the five [aspects].
The ten verses on the Buddha’s long-term practice contain six distinct meanings, all of which extensively reveal and clarify the first primary meaning:
the revelation of the True Dharma. How could this be far removed? It is precisely the mind itself.

To realize that one's own mind is without fixed direction in its provisional and ultimate aspects—that the mind-dharmadhātu is entirely wondrous—is profound and far-reaching; thus, the sixth point concerns the wondrousness of the stages and dharmas.

This concludes the thirteenth fascicle of the *Private Notes on the Words and Phrases of the Wondrous Sutra*. Fascicle Fourteen of the *Private Notes on the Words and Phrases of the Wondrous Sutra*: [The Parable Chapter]. It is understood that this has been grasped through the intended meaning; there is no need to wait for prolixity of words.
*Private Notes on the Words and Phrases of the Wondrous Sutra*, Fascicle Thirteen. *Private Notes on the Words and Phrases of the Wondrous Sutra*, Fascicle Fourteen (The Parable Chapter).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhìyún of Shígǔ.
The various origins of the titles for the chapters have already been distinguished above; here, they are designated solely according to their metaphors.
If one speaks of the "Great" as being beyond metaphor, this is a provisional, distinct meaning, which has also been explained previously; here, it refers to the primary [meaning].

Regarding the general principle, Yong says: "In this present chapter, both the provisional and the real are employed as the title. Why? Because since the 'Teaching of the Dharma' was completed, both the provisional and the real were clarified;
therefore, two analogies are used for the Dharma. In the past, it was necessary to speak of the three carts at the Deer Park;

in the present, it is necessary to speak of the equal bestowal of the one great vehicle. Thus, both the provisional and the real are named 'Parable. Now, I say that this person has slept for a long time."
If one finds it difficult to awaken even from a dream, how could it reach such a state? Yet you still speak thus; if this is so for those with long-standing habits, how much more so for beginners?

Previously, you spoke of "briefly and extensively opening the three to reveal the one," where the "extensive" refers precisely to opening the three and revealing the one within the three weeks of teaching.

You also spoke of "the beginning and the end mutually riding upon each other. How is it that you have now abandoned this very principle of opening and revealing, instead employing both [the provisional and the real] simultaneously as the essence?
Now, as for using the methods of previous teachings to explain the meaning of other sutras, how does that relate to the intent of this sutra?

How can three chapters all be named "Complete Faith" (*zhōuxìn*)? One knows from this that this person has not yet realized the meaning of the "Three Rounds" (*sānzhōu*). The commentary text makes this self-evident;
why then is it said that later students should be startled by this? One should know that although the title of the chapter refers to the parable, the text is but one part.

This still belongs to the first section; it will be explained and recorded later. Regarding the commentary on this text, there are no separate topical headings; now, in explaining the text of this chapter, there are three parts:
first, the explanation of the title; second, the determination of its location; and third, the word-by-word analysis of the sutra text. This is not the case here.

I say that the explanation of this consists of two parts: first, the title, and second, the main text. Within the explanation of the title, the *Ji* (Record/Commentary) states that there is both a general and a specific [explanation]. Entirely so.

It is said that there is both the specific and the general; within the specific, there are four parts: first, the heading; second, the analogy (the section beginning with "The following explains..."); third, the extensive explanation of the preceding (the section beginning with "...the intention of what follows");

and fourth, the conclusion (the section beginning with "Therefore, it is said..."). Now, regarding the first part, the general, there are three components: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion. The heading refers to the word "General" (*zong*).
It is said that the two characters of this text each explain the two characters below, while together they manifest the whole; yet here the translation uses the term "General."
Regarding the statement that [the preceding section] is "general" (總) because it encompasses the four distinct explanations that follow, I maintain that all commentators share this view;

they simply designate it "general" because it directly clarifies the four subsequent distinct explanations. However, this [present work] is even more capable of providing detailed analysis to establish the argument.
Although it is indeed thorough, it does not proceed by direct exposition. As for why I cannot yet believe or accept [this]: [it is because... (The remainder of the passage follows).
Within this single section, there is no consistent structural pattern from beginning to end; it is not only logically untenable, but also contradicts the textual phrasing.

Therefore, I am unable to accept it. Now, I maintain that it is sufficient to simply explain the general and specific [aspects] based on the initial causal conditions themselves, rather than establishing these names and meanings by way of a fourfold interpretation. However, upon first hearing of these four accumulations, one must certainly...
To admonish oneself against doubt: if one now summarizes the structural patterns from top to bottom, then there will be no confusion.

Why is this? First, regarding the general and specific within the four types of explanation in the *Śāstra*: the single explanation of "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) constitutes the general, while the remaining three explanations constitute the specific;
the reason for this is clarified above. Second, regarding the general and specific within the very first explanation of "causes and conditions," it itself further possesses [subdivisions].
The fourth [point] refers to discussing the general and the specific by means of both names and meanings: explaining the name as the general and explaining the meaning as the specific.
"Name" is that which reveals the "meaning," which consists of the four *siddhāntas*. Thus, in this passage, the two characters constitute the general and the four meanings constitute the specific.

Second, there is the discussion of the general and the specific by means of meaning alone; that is, taking the *loka-saṃvṛti* (worldly convention) as the general and the other three as the specific, as in the following:
The third [type of title] is that which is exclusively specific and lacks a general [meaning], explaining directly according to four distinct meanings;

for example, the explanations of the titles of the remaining chapters are like this. The fourth [type of title] is that which is exclusively general and lacks the specific, such as the subsequent explanation of the title of the "Dharmadatta" chapter, which contains the four meanings in a general sense but lacks the specific names of those four. This is the third [type].

Within the general and specific explanations of the names and meanings of the initial [chapter], there are furthermore three further modes: either first explaining generally and subsequently explaining specifically—as is the case with this "Parable Chapter" (Upamā-parivarta);

or first explaining specifically and subsequently explaining generally—as in the explanation of the "Dharma-Teacher Chapter" (Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta), where one first explains the numbers four, five, six, and so forth, and only then explains the two characters for "Dharma-Teacher"; or where both the beginning and end are general while the middle is specific.

This is as seen in the "Chapter on the Bestowal of Prophecies" (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*). While the beginning and end both discuss the two characters "bestowal of prophecy" (*vyākaraṇa*), the middle section distinguishes various specific meanings;
